An optimization that combines adjacent operations into fewer kernels so intermediate values stay on chip and memory traffic or launch overhead falls.

optical circuit switching (OCS)

A physical networking architecture that redirects optical signals directly between fiber ports using micro-electromechanical mirror (MEMS) arrays without intermediate optical-electrical-optical conversions.

orchestration

The coordination of fleet resources and workloads, including scheduling, placement, scaling, sequencing, recovery, and resource allocation across distributed infrastructure.

out-of-distribution (OOD) detection

The algorithmic task of identifying whether a given input sample originates from a different data distribution than the dataset on which the model was trained.

over-selection

A federated client scheduling strategy where the coordinator selects more clients than required for a training round and aggregates the first responding cohort to mitigate stragglers.

oversubscription

A topology design in which aggregate downstream capacity exceeds upstream capacity, reducing switch cost while creating a shared bandwidth bottleneck under simultaneous traffic.

oxide breakdown

The failure of an oxide layer in transistors due to excessive electric field stress, causing permanent hardware faults.

title: Glossary
text:
packet spraying

A dynamic multipath routing technique that disperses individual packets belonging to the same transport flow across multiple equal-cost network paths simultaneously, maximizing bisection bandwidth utilization.

PagedAttention

An attention computation algorithm and dynamic memory manager inspired by operating system virtual memory paging that partitions key-value cache tensors into non-contiguous physical page blocks linked via page tables.

PAM4

Pulse Amplitude Modulation 4-Level, a multilevel signaling scheme that encodes two bits per baud across four distinct electrical voltage levels, doubling channel throughput over traditional NRZ encoding.

parallel file system (PFS)

A distributed file system (such as Lustre or GPFS) that decouples metadata operations from striped data blocks across multiple storage nodes to aggregate high concurrent bandwidth.

parameter

A learnable variable in a machine learning model, such as weights and biases in neural networks, that are adjusted during training to optimize performance.

parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)

Adaptation methods that update only a small subset of parameters or added modules while keeping most pretrained weights frozen.

partition skew

An uneven distribution of records or keys that leaves one distributed-pipeline partition with disproportionate work and makes it determine stage completion time.

permanent faults

Hardware defects that persist irreversibly until repair or component replacement, consistently affecting system behavior.

personalization layers

Model components, typically the final classification layers, that are adapted locally to user-specific data while keeping shared backbone layers frozen.

PFC deadlock

A permanent buffer starvation condition in a multi-hop lossless Ethernet network where cyclical priority flow control PAUSE-frame dependencies among switch queues halt packet forwarding indefinitely.

PFC storm

A cascading congestion phenomenon in lossless fabrics where buffer saturation at a single slow-draining endpoint causes priority flow control PAUSE frames to propagate upstream across multiple tiers, freezing unrelated victim flows.

physical attack

Direct manipulation or tampering with computing hardware to compromise the security and integrity of machine learning systems, bypassing traditional software defenses.

pipeline bubble

Idle accelerator time in pipeline parallelism while stages wait for the pipeline to fill or drain. For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) balanced stages and \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches, the bubble fraction is \((\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree-1+\MicrobatchCount)\).

pipeline parallelism

A distributed training strategy that partitions layers into sequential stages and uses microbatches to overlap work across devices.

placement group

A scheduler abstraction that enforces spatial or topological co-location constraints across multiple workers, minimizing cross-switch communication latency in distributed model training.

pluggable optics

Modular, field-replaceable optical transceiver units (such as QSFP and OSFP form factors) mounted to switch and NIC faceplates that interface SerDes electrical traces with optical fibers.

point-in-time correctness

The requirement in feature computation that training datasets reflect the exact feature values available at the precise historical timestamp of the prediction event, preventing data leakage.

point-in-time join

A join that retrieves feature values valid for a historical prediction and available at that prediction time, preventing future or late-arriving information from leaking into training.

post-hoc explanations

Explanation methods applied after model training that treat the model as a black box and infer reasoning patterns from input-output behavior.

power delivery network (PDN)

The physical electrical distribution hierarchy, spanning rack-scale busbars, board power planes, voltage regulator modules, and package decoupling capacitors, that supplies stable sub-volt, kilo-ampere current to low-voltage silicon gates.

power usage effectiveness (PUE)

The ratio of total data-center facility energy to the energy delivered to IT equipment. A value of 1.0 would mean no energy spent on cooling, power conversion, or other facility overhead.

predictive parity

A fairness criterion requiring that the positive predictive value of a classifier is equal across different protected demographic subgroups.

preemption cascade

A systemic failure mode where preempting one job causes cascading resource evictions across dependent or lower-priority jobs, incurring compounding checkpointing and cold-start overheads.

preemption tax

The cumulative unproductive overhead incurred by preempting and restarting a distributed training job, comprising time spent checkpointing, reloading weights, reconstructing communication groups, and recomputing lost iterations.

prefetch buffer

A host DRAM queue that stages and holds pre-decoded, augmented training batches ahead of accelerator execution to absorb storage access jitter and tail latency spikes.

prefill-decode disaggregation

A distributed serving architecture that physically decouples prompt prefill processing onto compute-dense GPU nodes from token decoding onto memory-bandwidth-optimized GPU nodes, transferring intermediate KV cache activations across network fabrics.

prefill phase

The initial LLM inference phase that processes the prompt and populates the KV cache, often dominated by compute.

prefix caching

A KV cache optimization that detects and retains precomputed attention activations for shared prompt prefixes (such as system instructions or few-shot exemplars), bypassing redundant prefill computation across sessions.

principle of least privilege

A security concept where users are given the minimum access levels necessary to complete their job functions, reducing security risks.

priority flow control (PFC)

An IEEE 802.1Qbb link-layer flow-control standard for lossless Ethernet that pauses upstream senders via PAUSE frames on a designated traffic class before switch ingress buffers saturate.

privacy budget

The differential-privacy parameters governing the permitted change in output distributions on neighboring inputs. The parameter \(\PrivacyBudget\) controls a multiplicative bound of \(e^{\PrivacyBudget}\), \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) allows additive slack, and privacy accounting tracks how guarantees compose across releases.

privacy-preserving techniques

Methods intended to protect privacy at specified boundaries, including differential privacy and cryptographic protocols. Federated learning and local processing reduce raw-data movement but do not alone guarantee that updates or outputs reveal no private information.

privacy-utility trade-off

The fundamental tension between preserving individual privacy and maintaining the utility of data for machine learning, requiring careful balance through techniques like differential privacy.

program goodput

In the ML Productivity Goodput decomposition, the efficiency of execution during productive work, such as the fraction of peak throughput a training program achieves while it runs.

projected gradient descent (PGD)

An iterative gradient-based adversarial attack that repeatedly perturbs an input and projects it back into an allowed norm ball.

prompt engineering

The practice of designing and optimizing text prompts to effectively communicate with large language models and achieve desired outputs from AI systems.

prompt injection

An attack against large language models where untrusted input content overrides system instructions and directs the model to perform unauthorized actions.

pruning

A model compression technique that removes unnecessary connections or neurons from neural networks to reduce model size and computational requirements without significantly impacting performance.

title: Glossary
text:
quantization

The process of reducing the precision of model weights and activations from floating-point to lower-bit representations to decrease memory usage and accelerate computation on edge devices.

quantization-aware training (QAT)

Training that simulates low-precision arithmetic so a model remains accurate after deployment with quantized weights or activations.

quota governance

The organizational policies and control mechanisms (such as guaranteed vs. burst allocations, review cycles, and utilization-based reclamation) that regulate multi-tenant capacity reservation.

title: Glossary
text:
rail-optimized routing

A communication mapping that aligns corresponding model shards with the same local GPU and network rail across nodes. It can distribute traffic across available NICs, but shared links, placement, and competing traffic still determine contention.

rail-optimized topology

A cluster network topology tailored for multi-accelerator servers where identical GPU ranks across nodes are connected to separate, dedicated leaf-switch fabrics, minimizing switch traversals for data-parallel collectives.

randomized smoothing

A certified-defense method that classifies noisy versions of an input to obtain probabilistic robustness guarantees.

RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE)

A protocol that carries remote direct memory access semantics over Ethernet, relying on carefully managed low-loss or lossless behavior.

recursive halving-doubling

A collective reduction algorithm that pairs ranks at exponentially increasing distances across \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds, achieving both logarithmic latency and bandwidth optimality for power-of-two participant counts.

red teaming

A structured adversarial testing exercise where security and safety experts deliberately probe ML systems, interfaces, and serving pipelines for safety vulnerabilities, security flaws, and compliance failures.

ReduceScatter

A collective communication operation that reduces inputs across ranks and scatters distinct shards of the reduced result back to ranks.

regularization

Methods used in machine learning to prevent overfitting by adding penalty terms to the loss function, constraining model complexity.

reliability collapse

The exponential decline, \(\ComponentAvailability^\RequiredComponentCount\), in the probability that all \(\RequiredComponentCount\) required components of a tightly coupled job are available, even when each component’s availability \(\ComponentAvailability\) is high.

reliability gap

The difference between component reliability and the much lower probability that every component required by a large, tightly coupled job remains available. The gap widens as fleet size and job duration increase.

remote direct memory access (RDMA)

A networking mechanism that lets one machine read or write another machine’s memory without kernel-mediated copies on the data path.

renewable energy

Energy collected from renewable resources that are naturally replenished, including solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, and biomass sources.

resource-constrained environments

Deployment contexts with limited computational power, network bandwidth, or power availability, typically requiring specialized system design and optimization techniques.

responsible AI

The practice of developing and deploying AI systems in ways that are ethical, fair, transparent, and beneficial to society while minimizing potential harms and biases.

reward hacking

The phenomenon where AI systems exploit unintended aspects of reward functions to maximize scores while violating the intended objectives.

ridge point

The operational arithmetic intensity on a roofline model where the memory bandwidth ceiling meets the peak computational ceiling, delineating the boundary between memory-bound and compute-bound operational regimes.

ring AllReduce

A bandwidth-optimal collective communication algorithm that organizes participants into a logical ring, executing sequential ReduceScatter and AllGather neighbor transfers so each node communicates a constant volume of data independent of rank count.

RLHF

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback - a training method that uses human preferences to guide model behavior, enabling AI systems to better align with human values and intentions.

robust AI

The ability of artificial intelligence systems to maintain performance and reliability despite internal errors, external perturbations, and environmental changes.

robustness

A model’s ability to maintain stable and consistent performance under input variations, environmental changes, or adversarial conditions.

robustness margin

The minimum distance or perturbation magnitude required to alter a model’s prediction on a given input sample under defined perturbation norms.

robustness metrics

Quantitative measures for evaluating model stability under various perturbations, including adversarial accuracy, certified robustness bounds, and performance under distribution shift.

roofline model

A performance model that compares arithmetic intensity with peak compute and memory bandwidth to identify compute-bound and bandwidth-bound regimes.

runtime goodput

In the ML Productivity Goodput decomposition, the fraction of allocated time that yields retained training progress after runtime overheads such as checkpointing, failure recovery, and lost work.

title: Glossary
text:
scale moment

A critical threshold where an ML workload outgrows the memory capacity, arithmetic throughput, or reliability envelope of a single node, necessitating distributed execution and exposing systems to the network wall, energy wall, and reliability collapse.

scaling efficiency

The ratio of actual distributed training throughput to ideal linear speedup (\(\ScalingEfficiency = \SingleDeviceRunTime / (\DeviceCount\cdot \MultiDeviceRunTime)\)), quantifying capacity loss from communication, synchronization barriers, and idle pipeline bubbles.

scaling laws

Empirical power-law relationships between model loss and training compute, parameter count, or dataset size, of the form \(\ScalingLawLoss(\ScaledResource) = \ScaleCoefficient{}\ScaledResource^{-\ScalingExponent} + \IrreducibleLoss\), valid within the regime in which they were fitted. They explain why each further gain in model quality requires multiplicatively more resources.

scheduling goodput

In the ML Productivity Goodput decomposition, the fraction of time a workload has all of the resources it requires available together.

scope 1 emissions

Direct greenhouse gas emissions from sources that are owned or controlled by an organization, such as on-site diesel backup generators and company facilities.

scope 2 emissions

Indirect greenhouse gas emissions associated with the generation of purchased electricity, steam, heating, or cooling consumed by an organization.

scope 3 emissions

All other indirect greenhouse gas emissions that occur throughout an organization’s upstream and downstream value chain, including hardware manufacturing and supply chain logistics.

secure aggregation

A cryptographic protocol that lets a coordinator recover an aggregate of participating clients’ updates without seeing individual unmasked updates, under stated participation and collusion assumptions. It does not by itself bound information revealed by the aggregate or final model.

secure boot

A hardware-backed startup process that cryptographically verifies firmware and software before execution.

secure computation

Cryptographic protocols that enable multiple parties to jointly compute functions over private inputs without revealing those inputs to each other.

secure multi-party computation

A cryptographic method that allows multiple parties to jointly compute a function over their private inputs without revealing those inputs to each other.

self-supervised learning

A machine learning paradigm where models learn representations from unlabeled data by predicting parts of the input from other parts, reducing dependence on manually labeled datasets.

sequence parallelism

A distributed technique that shards activations along the token sequence dimension across tensor-parallel ranks during non-GEMM operations (LayerNorm, Dropout) using ReduceScatter and AllGather without increasing total communication volume.

service level objective (SLO)

A measurable target for service behavior such as latency, freshness, availability, or model quality.

shadow deployment

A deployment mechanism where production traffic is duplicated and routed to a candidate model alongside the active production model to validate performance and latency without affecting user experience.

SHAP

SHapley Additive exPlanations, a feature-attribution framework based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory.

sharded checkpointing

A checkpointing approach where each worker saves only its assigned model, gradient, or optimizer shard.

sharded data parallelism

A distributed training strategy (exemplified by ZeRO and FSDP) that partitions model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across data-parallel ranks, reconstructing full layers on demand via collective communication.

side-channel attack

An attack that exploits information leaked through the physical implementation of computing systems, such as power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, or timing variations.

silent data corruption (SDC)

A hardware error in compute units, memory, or data paths that changes a stored or computed value without raising any detectable error, so the corrupted result propagates silently into training or inference.

single instruction, multiple threads (SIMT)

A parallel execution model where multiple independent threads execute the same instruction stream in lockstep across vector execution units, hiding high memory latency through hardware warp scheduling over large thread pools.

small file problem

A data-loading bottleneck where accessing millions of individual sample files exhausts storage metadata server request capacity long before physical data transfer bandwidth saturates.

software fault

Unintended behavior in software systems resulting from defects, bugs, or design oversights that can impair performance or compromise security.

sparse training

A training approach that maintains sparsity in neural network weights throughout the training process, reducing computational requirements and memory usage.

sparse updates

A training strategy that selectively updates only a subset of model parameters based on their importance or contribution to performance, reducing computational and memory overhead.

specification gaming

When AI systems find unexpected ways to achieve high rewards that technically satisfy the objective function but violate the intended purpose.

speculative decoding

An inference acceleration mechanism where a compact, lightweight draft model speculatively generates multiple candidate tokens in parallel that are subsequently verified in a single forward pass by the large target model.

speculative execution

A performance optimization in processors that executes instructions before confirming they are needed, which can inadvertently expose sensitive data through microarchitectural side channels.

split learning

A distributed learning paradigm and model partitioning technique where a neural network is divided between an edge client and a central server, with intermediate activations and gradients exchanged at a cut layer.

stale synchronous parallel (SSP)

A synchronization model that lets faster workers advance a bounded number of steps ahead of the slowest worker.

straggler

A correct but slow worker that delays synchronous progress for the rest of a distributed job.

straggler amplification

The slowdown of a synchronous job to the pace of its slowest required participant. Because the probability that at least one of \(\DeviceCount\) workers is delayed, \(1-(1-\WorkerDelayProbability)^\DeviceCount\), approaches 1 as \(\DeviceCount\) grows, a delay that is rare for any one worker becomes nearly certain on every step at fleet scale.

strong scaling

Adding processors to a fixed problem to finish it sooner. Its speedup is bounded by Amdahl’s Law.

stuck-at fault

A permanent hardware fault where a signal line becomes fixed at a logical 0 or 1 regardless of input, causing incorrect computations.

supply chain attack

An attack that compromises hardware or software components during the manufacturing, distribution, or integration process, potentially affecting multiple downstream systems.

sustainable AI

The practice of developing and deploying artificial intelligence systems that minimize environmental impact while maintaining effectiveness and accessibility.

switch radix

The number of ports on a network switch, which constrains endpoint fan-out, topology depth, and the number of switching tiers needed at a given cluster scale.

symbol rate

The number of signaling symbols transmitted per second on a link; multilevel modulation carries multiple bits per symbol without increasing this physical transition rate proportionally.

synchronous tight coupling

A distributed execution dependency where all participating nodes must complete local computation and synchronize states at global barriers before any worker can proceed, coupling cluster progress to the slowest device.

synthetic data generation

The creation of artificial datasets that approximate the statistical properties of real data while reducing privacy risks and avoiding direct exposure of sensitive information.

systolic array

A specialized grid of tightly coupled processing elements that rhythmically computes and streams matrix data directly between neighbor cells without writing intermediate partial sums back to register files or memory.

title: Glossary
text:
tail latency

High-percentile request latency, such as p99, that captures rare slow responses affecting distributed service reliability.

targeted attack

A type of data poisoning attack that aims to cause misclassification of specific inputs or classes while leaving the model’s general performance largely intact.

tensor core

A specialized accelerator execution unit designed to perform mixed-precision fused matrix multiply-accumulate operations (\(\MatrixMultiplyDestination= \GemmLeftOperand\cdot \GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\)) on matrix tiles as a single hardware instruction.

tensor parallelism

An intra-layer model parallelism technique that shards individual weight matrices and operations (such as column- and row-parallel linear layers in multi-head attention and MLPs) across accelerators connected via high-bandwidth interconnects.

thermal design power (TDP)

The vendor-specified maximum sustained rate of heat energy in watts that a cooling subsystem must dissipate under maximum expected operating workloads to maintain silicon below its critical junction temperature.

thermal stress

Hardware degradation caused by repeated cycling through high and low temperatures, leading to material fatigue and potential failures.

threat modeling

A structured security analysis that identifies assets, adversary capabilities, attack paths, and defensive priorities for a system.

tiered storage

A hierarchical data placement architecture spanning hot local NVMe, warm parallel file systems, cold object storage, and deep archive tiers to optimize throughput against capacity economics.

time per output token (TPOT)

The average wall-clock time required to generate each subsequent token during autoregressive decoding, governed primarily by accelerator memory bandwidth.

time to first token (TTFT)

The latency elapsed between submitting an inference request and receiving its initial generated token, reflecting the duration of the compute-bound prefill phase and serving as a primary interactive responsiveness metric.

time-travel query

A database or feature store capability that reconstructs the exact state of feature data as it existed at any historical point in time.

TinyML

Machine learning architectures, runtimes, and optimization techniques engineered to execute inference and ultra-lightweight adaptation on microcontrollers operating under milliwatt power and sub-megabyte memory limits.

topology-aware scheduling

Placement that accounts for GPU and interconnect locality such as NVLink domains, racks, rails, or switch hierarchy.

TorchDynamo

A Python frame evaluation hook that intercepts CPython bytecode to dynamically extract computation graphs into FX intermediate representation while installing validation guards.

TorchInductor

The default deep learning compiler backend for torch.compile that lowers captured computation graphs into optimized Triton GPU kernels or C++ CPU loops.

total cost of ownership (TCO)

A comprehensive financial assessment of the complete direct and indirect costs associated with designing, deploying, and maintaining machine learning infrastructure throughout its operational lifecycle.

TPU

Tensor Processing Unit, a specialized AI accelerator chip developed by Google specifically designed for machine learning workloads, particularly neural network computations.

trackable resource (TRES)

A fine-grained accounting and scheduling abstraction (standardized in Slurm) that treats individual accelerators, licenses, memory, and interconnect rails as distinct consumable scheduling units.

training

The process of teaching a machine learning model to make predictions by showing it examples and adjusting its parameters based on performance feedback.

training-serving skew

A discrepancy in performance between training and production environments caused by differences in data processing pipelines, feature definitions, or serving runtime environments.

transfer learning

A machine learning technique that uses knowledge from a pretrained model on one task to improve learning on a related task, enabling efficient adaptation with limited data.

transformer

A neural network architecture that uses self-attention mechanisms to process sequential data, forming the foundation for many modern language models.

transient faults

Temporary hardware faults that do not persist or cause permanent damage but can lead to incorrect computations if not handled properly.

transient voltage droop

A rapid drop in core supply voltage caused by the product of parasitic loop inductance and high current slew rates (\(\FiniteChange \SupplyVoltage= \ParasiticLoopInductance\frac{d\AcceleratorSupplyCurrent}{d\TimeInstant}\)) when thousands of execution cores abruptly transition between idle barriers and dense computation.

transparency

Openness about how AI systems are built, trained, validated, and deployed, including disclosure of data sources, design assumptions, and limitations.

tree AllReduce

A latency-oriented collective algorithm that reduces data up a spanning tree to a root before broadcasting results down, achieving \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) round-trip latency at the expense of higher link bandwidth consumption on large payloads.

triple modular redundancy (TMR)

A fault-tolerance technique that runs three replicas of a computation and uses majority voting to mask one independent faulty result; it does not guarantee correctness under multiple or common-mode faults.

Triton

A domain-specific language and compiler for tiled neural network programming that abstracts thread scheduling and memory coalescing while exposing block-level memory hierarchy management.

two-phase commit (2PC)

A coordination protocol with prepare and commit phases that ensures participants commit atomically or abort.

title: Glossary
text:
uncoordinated checkpointing

A checkpointing scheme where distributed nodes record local state independently without cross-node synchronization, risking domino-effect rollbacks during recovery.

title: Glossary
text:
value alignment

The principle that AI systems should pursue goals consistent with human intent and ethical norms, addressing the challenge of encoding human values in machine objectives.

value-sensitive design

A methodology for incorporating human values into technology design through systematic stakeholder engagement and ethical consideration of system impacts.

Volcano

A cloud-native batch scheduling system for Kubernetes designed for distributed ML and big-data workloads, providing gang scheduling, fair-share queuing, and resource reservation primitives.

title: Glossary
text:
wafer-scale engine (WSE)

An accelerator architecture that integrates compute, memory, and communication across most or all of a silicon wafer to reduce the bandwidth and latency costs of crossing separate package boundaries.

wake-word detection

An always-on keyword spotting workload executed on low-power edge processors that detects specific acoustic trigger phrases with minimal latency and sub-milliwatt power draw.

warehouse-scale computer (WSC)

A building-scale computing system operated as one coherent machine, with the network fabric and storage hierarchy treated as system-level resources.

watchdog timer

A hardware component that monitors system execution and triggers recovery actions if the system becomes unresponsive or stuck.

water usage effectiveness (WUE)

The liters of water a data center consumes per kilowatt-hour of IT energy, determined largely by its cooling and heat-rejection design.

watermark

A streaming-system estimate that event time has advanced far enough to close a window, subject to an explicit policy for arrivals that appear later.

weak scaling

Growing the problem in proportion to the number of processors so that work per processor stays roughly constant. Gustafson’s Law describes its speedup.

WebDataset

A high-throughput sequential data loading format that packages dataset samples inside standard POSIX tar archives, enabling direct linear streaming over object storage without per-file filesystem overhead.

weight freezing

A technique that fixes most model parameters during training while allowing only specific layers or components to be updated, reducing computational requirements for on-device adaptation.

white-box attack

An adversarial attack where the attacker has complete knowledge of the model’s architecture, parameters, training data, and internal workings, enabling highly effective attack strategies.

title: Glossary
text:
Young-Daly formula

The first-order optimal checkpoint interval \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \CheckpointWriteTime \, \SystemMtbf}\), which balances checkpoint write time against expected rework after failures. It is accurate when writes are short compared with the system MTBF.

title: Glossary
text:
ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer)

A memory-optimization paradigm that progressively eliminates redundant state across data-parallel workers by partitioning optimizer states (ZeRO-1), gradients (ZeRO-2), and model parameters (ZeRO-3).

zero-bubble pipeline parallelism

An advanced pipeline scheduling strategy that decouples backward passes into activation gradient computation (B) and deferred weight gradient computation (W), using the W kernels to fill startup, turnaround, and drain bubbles.

zero-day vulnerability

A previously unknown security flaw in software or hardware that can be exploited by attackers before developers have had a chance to create and distribute a patch.

title: Inference Foundations
text:
Serving a model at scale is governed by the mathematics of waiting lines and the physics of the key-value cache. This appendix develops the analytical serving models that the book’s inference and operations chapters draw on, establishing how queuing dynamics and attention-cache memory arithmetic combine into a single serving constraint under strict latency service-level objectives (SLOs). In C\(^3\) terms, inference turns compute capacity, communication with memory and clients, and coordination across queues into one serving constraint.


This appendix is a quantitative reference for serving systems. Use the queuing surrogate to screen batch sizes and estimate mean delay under its stated assumptions, then validate tail latency with measurements or simulation; use the key-value cache arithmetic to size memory or determine when the cache, rather than compute, caps throughput.

When a serving tier misses its latency target under load: Use the queuing model in section 1.1.1 to separate waiting, batch-formation, and service time.
When choosing a batch size: Use the worked example in section 1.1.1.4 and the decision framework in section 1.1.1.5.
When memory, not compute, caps concurrency: Use the KV-cache sizing in section 1.1.2.




Serving performance analysis has two coupled layers. The queue determines how requests wait, batch, and shed under stochastic arrivals; the key-value cache determines how much live state the accelerator can hold while meeting the latency budget. The subsections that follow derive the queuing model first, then connect that model to memory-capacity limits in the worked serving examples.


The batching efficiency curve provides intuition about throughput-latency trade-offs, but production systems require rigorous analysis to determine optimal batch sizes under stochastic arrival patterns. Queuing theory provides the mathematical framework to derive these optimal operating points and to understand why certain batch sizes outperform others under specific conditions.


The M/G/c/K notation names four characteristics that a production GPU-serving model may need to represent:

M (Markov arrivals): Requests arrive according to a Poisson process with rate \(\ArrivalRate\). This models the memoryless property of user requests, where arrival of one request does not predict the timing of the next.
G (General service distribution): Service times follow a general distribution, not restricted to exponential. GPU inference times depend on batch size and exhibit deterministic components (compute) mixed with stochastic variation (memory contention, kernel scheduling).
c (Number of servers): The system has \(\QueueServerCount\) parallel GPU workers, each capable of serving requests independently.
K (System capacity): At most \(\QueueSystemCapacity\) requests may be present, including those in service. Requests arriving to a full system are rejected (load shedding).

The notation comes from the same systems-performance lineage that sized telephone networks before it was applied to GPU clusters.

Systems Perspective 1.1: Queuing theory and performanceQueuing theory, developed by Agner Krarup Erlang in 1909 for telephone network analysis, remains foundational to systems performance engineering (Erlang 1909). The same mathematical framework that sized telephone exchanges now informs GPU cluster capacity. Standard systems texts develop the component queuing models and approximations on which this notation builds (Jain 1991; Kleinrock 1975).



Kleinrock, L. 1975. Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory. Wiley-Interscience.

Jain, R. 1991. The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis: Techniques for Experimental Design, Measurement, Simulation, and Modeling. John Wiley & Sons.

Erlang, Agner Krarup. 1909. “The Theory of Probabilities and Telephone Conversations.” Nyt Tidsskrift for Matematik B 20: 33–39.
For a batched inference system with batch size \(\BatchSize\), service time becomes a function of batch size. Let \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) denote the time to process a batch of \(\BatchSize\) requests. From the physics of batching (Batching Strategies at Scale), equation 1 models this as:
\[\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = \BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \MarginalRequestServiceTime\cdot \BatchSize \tag{1}\]
where \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) represents fixed service overhead (kernel launch, weight loading from high-bandwidth memory (HBM)) and \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) represents marginal per-request computation time. This linear model captures the first-order behavior observed in production systems, though actual service times may exhibit slight sublinearity due to memory bandwidth saturation at large batch sizes.
The Effective Service Rate for batched processing is:
\[\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)} = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \MarginalRequestServiceTime\cdot \BatchSize}\]
The effective rate increases with batch size, approaching the asymptotic limit \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) as \(\BatchSize\to \infty\).



The total response time \(\RequestResponseTime\) for a request consists of three components:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime] = \mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime] + \mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay] + \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime] \]
where:

\(\mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime]\) is the expected waiting time in queue before joining a batch
\(\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay]\) is the expected per-request batch-accumulation delay before dispatch
\(\mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime]\) is the expected inference time once the batch executes

For dynamic batching with maximum wait time \(\BatchingWindow\) and maximum batch size \(\MaxBatchSize\), the first request triggers the batching window. Let \(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\ArrivalRate{}\BatchingWindow)\) count subsequent arrivals during that window and let \(\BatchFillArrivalCount=\MaxBatchSize-1\). For \(\MaxBatchSize>1\), the realized batch size is \(\BatchSize=\min(\MaxBatchSize,1+\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount)\), including the trigger request, so:
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchSize] = \sum_{n=0}^{\BatchFillArrivalCount-1}(\RealizedArrivalCount+1)\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount) + \MaxBatchSize\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount\geq \BatchFillArrivalCount)\]
Let \(\SubsequentArrivalTime_k\) be the Erlang-distributed time of the \(\BatchFillArrivalCount\)th subsequent arrival. A full batch closes when \(\SubsequentArrivalTime_k \leq \BatchingWindow\), while a timeout batch closes at \(\BatchingWindow\) with \(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount<\BatchFillArrivalCount\). The mean per-request accumulation delay within each realized batch is:
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay \mid \text{full}] = \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[\SubsequentArrivalTime_k \mid \SubsequentArrivalTime_k \leq \BatchingWindow]\]
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay \mid \TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount,\ \text{timeout}] = \frac{\BatchingWindow}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\RealizedArrivalCount+1}\right), \qquad 0 \leq \RealizedArrivalCount< \BatchFillArrivalCount\]
Weighting each batch outcome by its realized request count gives the mean delay of a randomly selected request:
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay] = \frac{\MaxBatchSize\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount\geq \BatchFillArrivalCount)\mathbb{E}[\SubsequentArrivalTime_k/2 \mid \SubsequentArrivalTime_k\leq \BatchingWindow] + \sum_{n=0}^{\BatchFillArrivalCount-1}(\RealizedArrivalCount+1)\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount)\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay \mid \TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount,\ \text{timeout}]}{\mathbb{E}[\BatchSize]}\]
When batches reliably fill before timeout, this expression approaches \(\mathbb{E}[\SubsequentArrivalTime_k]/2=(\MaxBatchSize-1)/(2\ArrivalRate)\). For \(\MaxBatchSize=1\), the batch contains only its trigger request and accumulation delay is zero.



The optimal batch size \(\BatchSize\) minimizes expected response time subject to throughput requirements:
\[\BatchSize= \operatorname{arg\,min}_{\BatchSize} \mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime(\BatchSize)] \quad \text{subject to} \quad \EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) > \ArrivalRate\]
The constraint ensures system stability (service rate exceeds arrival rate).
For a high-traffic regime in which batches of size \(\BatchSize\) reliably fill before timeout, substituting the response time components gives:
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime(\BatchSize)] = \mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime(\BatchSize)] + \frac{\BatchSize-1}{2\ArrivalRate} + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\]
For a tractable waiting-time estimate, use an M/G/1 surrogate that treats batches as Poisson “super-requests.” If the request arrival rate is \(\ArrivalRate\) and the average batch size is \(\BatchSize\), this surrogate uses batch arrival rate \(\BatchArrivalRate=\ArrivalRate/\BatchSize\). This is not the exact process produced by grouping Poisson request arrivals, because fixed-size grouping yields Erlang inter-batch times; finite \(\QueueSystemCapacity\) or \(\QueueServerCount>1\) requires a bulk-service model or simulation. Within the explicit surrogate, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula gives:
\[\mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime] = \frac{\BatchArrivalRate\cdot \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime^2]}{2(1 - \ServingUtilization)}\]
where \(\ServingUtilization = \BatchArrivalRate\cdot \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime] = \ArrivalRate \cdot \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime]/\BatchSize\) is the server utilization. The second moment \(\mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime^2]\) captures service time variability.
For the linear service time model with deterministic service in this surrogate:
\[\mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime(\BatchSize)] = \frac{\ArrivalRate \cdot \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)^2}{2\BatchSize(1 - \ArrivalRate \cdot \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)/\BatchSize)}\]
For production sizing, teams often first enforce a utilization headroom target rather than solving the full latency minimization problem. With \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)=\BatchFixedOverheadTime+\MarginalRequestServiceTime \BatchSize\), the constraint \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)/\BatchSize\leq \TargetServingUtilization\) yields the target-utilization batch bound (equation 2):
\[\TargetUtilizationBatchSize(\TargetServingUtilization) = \frac{\ArrivalRate \BatchFixedOverheadTime}{\TargetServingUtilization- \ArrivalRate \MarginalRequestServiceTime} \tag{2}\]
where \(\TargetServingUtilization\) is the target utilization (typically 0.7–0.8 for production systems to maintain latency headroom) and \(\TargetServingUtilization> \ArrivalRate \MarginalRequestServiceTime\).

Systems Perspective 1.2: Target-utilization batch sizingThe target-utilization batch bound (equation 2) reveals a fundamental insight: minimum utilization-feasible batch size grows with fixed overhead and arrival rate. This means:

Higher traffic \((\ArrivalRate)\): Required batch size increases.
Higher fixed overhead \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime)\): Required batch size increases to amortize overhead.
Higher target utilization \((\TargetServingUtilization)\): Required batch size decreases, but with less latency headroom.

This utilization-constrained sizing explains why large language models (LLMs) (high \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) from weight loading) benefit from larger batches than vision models (low \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\)), even at the same arrival rate.





Consider a hypothetical prefill-stage sizing exercise for a GPT-3 class model (175B parameters). The following assumed service-time coefficients illustrate the queuing calculation; they are not a measured GPT-3 benchmark:

Arrival rate: \(\ArrivalRate =\) 100 requests/second
Hardware: 8\(\times\) A100 GPUs (one DGX A100 node) with tensor parallelism
Fixed prefill-stage service overhead: \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime=\) 50 ms
Marginal prefill-stage service time: \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime=\) 0.5 ms per request
Target utilization: \(\TargetServingUtilization=\) 0.75

For the prefill phase (processing input prompt), service time follows equation 1:
\[\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = 50 + 0.5 \cdot \BatchSize \text{ ms}\]
Applying equation 2 to compute the minimum batch size that meets the 75 percent target utilization (leaving 25 percent headroom):
\[\TargetUtilizationBatchSize \approx \frac{100 \times 0.05}{0.75 - 100 \times 0.0005} = \frac{5}{0.70} \approx 7.14\]
Rounding up gives \(\BatchSize=\) 8 as the smallest batch size that meets the target utilization headroom. Evaluating the surrogate response-time expression under the full-batch assumption then shows how larger batches reduce utilization but add batch-accumulation delay:

Four operational regimes emerge across these batch sizes:

Unstable regime (batch sizes 1 to 5): Utilization exceeds 100 percent, so the system cannot keep up with arrivals and queues grow without bound. The stability boundary of equation 3, \(\MinimumStableBatchSize\approx\) 5.3, falls inside this range.
Utilization-target threshold (batch size 8): At 67.5 percent utilization, the system meets the 75 percent target, but queuing delay still contributes substantially to latency (56.1 ms). Latency knee (batch sizes 8 to 16): Mean latency is lowest in this range, with the model’s minimum near \(\BatchSize=\) 10. This matches the response-time decomposition: roughly 6 requests are in service and roughly 9 are waiting or accumulating into batches on average.

Production systems must select batch size to meet Service Level Objectives (SLOs), typically specified as latency percentiles (for example, p99 latency < 200 ms). The following framework systematizes this decision:


Measure \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) and \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) empirically by profiling inference at batch sizes 1, 8, and 32. Fit the linear model \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = \BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \MarginalRequestServiceTime \BatchSize\).



Find minimum batch size \(\MinimumStableBatchSize\) such that \(\EffectiveServiceRate(\MinimumStableBatchSize) > \ArrivalRate\):
\[\MinimumStableBatchSize= \frac{\BatchFixedOverheadTime\ArrivalRate}{1 - \MarginalRequestServiceTime\ArrivalRate} \tag{3}\]
Choose an integer batch size strictly above this boundary, assuming \(\ArrivalRate{}\MarginalRequestServiceTime<1\). Equality leaves no stability margin; if the denominator is nonpositive, batching alone cannot sustain the arrival rate.



Under the same Poisson-super-request surrogate and full-batch assumption, for each candidate \(\BatchSize\in \{\MinimumStableBatchSize, 2\MinimumStableBatchSize, ..., \MaxBatchSize\}\), compute:
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime(\BatchSize)] = \frac{\ArrivalRate \cdot \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)^2}{2\BatchSize(1 - \ArrivalRate \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)/\BatchSize)} + \frac{\BatchSize-1}{2\ArrivalRate} + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\]



If measured response times are approximately Gaussian, their p99 can be estimated as:
\[\TailRequestLatency \approx \mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime] + 2.33 \cdot \ResponseTimeStandardDeviation\]
where \(\ResponseTimeStandardDeviation\) is the standard deviation of response time. This Gaussian rule is not a general heavy-traffic approximation because queuing response times are commonly skewed. For exponential response times, p99 is \(-\ln(0.01)\mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime] \approx 4.6 \cdot \mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime]\); use measured percentiles for production sizing.



When the objective is maximum throughput under the increasing service-rate model, choose the largest stable, memory-feasible integer batch size whose p99 latency meets the SLO:
\[\BatchSize= \max\{\BatchSize: \TailRequestLatency(\BatchSize) \leq \text{SLO}\}\]
Operating rules for batch size selection (table 2) balance stability, latency SLOs, and cost efficiency:

These rules generate candidate configurations; load tests must verify their latency, capacity, and cost under the actual request distribution.




Figure 2 charts the competing pressures of batch execution by plotting normalized throughput against batch service time across batch sizes \(\BatchSize\in [1, 128]\) on a logarithmic scale. While throughput climbs with diminishing returns as fixed overheads are amortized, batch service time expands steadily, defining the envelope where latency budgets constrain throughput gains.














Figure 2: Batch Size Trade-Off Curves: Dimensionless schematic with batch service time t(B) = 1 + 0.15(B − 1) and throughput B/t(B), each normalized to its batch-1 value. Larger batches amortize fixed work but take longer to complete. These hypothetical curves are not a benchmark, exclude queuing and batch-formation delay, and establish neither a memory-capacity boundary nor an optimal batch size.



The trade-off curve demonstrates several key insights:

Pareto Frontier: An operating point is Pareto efficient when no other candidate provides at least as much throughput and no more latency, with a strict improvement in at least one objective. The frontier is the set of these nondominated points.
Knee of the Curve: A knee marks diminishing throughput gains relative to increasing service time; it does not by itself select the best operating point.
SLO-Constrained Optimum: The best feasible batch size depends on the optimization objective and measured end-to-end latency, including queuing and batch formation. An SLO boundary can constrain that choice without guaranteeing an intersection or a unique optimum.
Diminishing Returns: In the schematic, fixed work becomes a smaller fraction of each batch, so successive batch-size increases yield smaller throughput gains.

The queuing-theoretic framework provides the mathematical foundation for the batching strategies introduced in Batching Strategies at Scale. Where intuition might suggest “larger batches are better for throughput,” stability constraints, latency targets, and diminishing returns create a well-defined optimal operating region that varies by model type and deployment requirements.




Memory management evolution from preallocation to paging defines the KV cache and the paged allocation that manages it, and Transformer Arithmetic gives its per-token size. This section expands the sizing math behind that definition: why the cache reduces per-token compute, why its memory grows with sequence length and batch size, and why unmanaged allocation can fragment HBM (Kwon et al. 2023).

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
For a standard attention implementation at fixed model width, autoregressive generation without caching requires \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) computation per token because each transformer layer recomputes the full prefix, including attention among its tokens. The KV cache stores previously computed key and value vectors, allowing each new token to attend to the prefix in \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) computation. For serving at scale, this compute saving creates a critical memory-management challenge since KV cache memory can exceed model weights for long contexts.
The cache size grows with context as calculated by equation 4:
\[\KvCacheMemory = 2 \times \LayerCount \times \HiddenDimension\times \SequenceLength\times \BatchSize\times \ElementStorageSize \tag{4}\]
For standard multihead attention, where the aggregate KV width equals the hidden width, \(\LayerCount\) is the number of layers, \(\HiddenDimension\) is the hidden dimension, \(\SequenceLength\) is sequence length, \(\BatchSize\) is batch size, \(\ElementStorageSize\) is storage size per element in bytes, and the factor of 2 accounts for both keys and values. Grouped-query or multiquery attention instead uses the aggregate KV-head width in place of \(\HiddenDimension\).
For the 175B GPT-3 model (\(\LayerCount =\) 96, \(\HiddenDimension=\) 12,288, FP16 \(\ElementStorageSize =\) 2 bytes) at its training context length \(\SequenceLength=\) 2,048, each request requires:
\[ M_{\text{KV/req}} = 2 \times 96 \times 12288 \times 2048 \times 2 \text{ B} \approx 9.66 \text{ GB/request} \]
Across 8\(\times\) A100 80-GB GPUs (687.2 GB total HBM), storing model weights in FP16 consumes 350 GB, leaving 337.2 GB for activation and KV cache memory. Dividing that residual capacity by the per-request cache gives a capacity-only upper bound of 34 concurrent requests. This bound assumes balanced sharding and reserves no memory for activations, workspaces, runtime state, or allocator losses; an implementable batch must be smaller. Device nameplate capacities are converted to decimal GB before subtracting the decimal model footprint.




Serving performance is bounded by queues and by memory. As utilization \(\ServingUtilization\) approaches 1, queue depth and latency grow without bound, so production systems retain headroom suited to their workload and SLO. Larger batches raise throughput but add batch-accumulation delay, which produces a latency knee rather than monotonic improvement; the best batch size depends on whether the objective is minimum mean latency, maximum SLO-compliant throughput, or cost. Little’s Law, \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\), gives a one-line consistency check on any serving measurement. The KV cache grows with sequence length, batch size, and KV-head width and can exceed the model weights (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)); paging reduces fragmentation and reservation losses without removing the underlying footprint.

title: Inference Foundations
text:
This appendix is a quantitative reference for serving systems. Use the queuing surrogate to screen batch sizes and estimate mean delay under its stated assumptions, then validate tail latency with measurements or simulation; use the key-value cache arithmetic to size memory or determine when the cache, rather than compute, caps throughput.

When a serving tier misses its latency target under load: Use the queuing model in section 1.1.1 to separate waiting, batch-formation, and service time.
When choosing a batch size: Use the worked example in section 1.1.1.4 and the decision framework in section 1.1.1.5.
When memory, not compute, caps concurrency: Use the KV-cache sizing in section 1.1.2.

title: Inference Foundations
text:
Serving performance analysis has two coupled layers. The queue determines how requests wait, batch, and shed under stochastic arrivals; the key-value cache determines how much live state the accelerator can hold while meeting the latency budget. The subsections that follow derive the queuing model first, then connect that model to memory-capacity limits in the worked serving examples.


The batching efficiency curve provides intuition about throughput-latency trade-offs, but production systems require rigorous analysis to determine optimal batch sizes under stochastic arrival patterns. Queuing theory provides the mathematical framework to derive these optimal operating points and to understand why certain batch sizes outperform others under specific conditions.


The M/G/c/K notation names four characteristics that a production GPU-serving model may need to represent:

M (Markov arrivals): Requests arrive according to a Poisson process with rate \(\ArrivalRate\). This models the memoryless property of user requests, where arrival of one request does not predict the timing of the next.
G (General service distribution): Service times follow a general distribution, not restricted to exponential. GPU inference times depend on batch size and exhibit deterministic components (compute) mixed with stochastic variation (memory contention, kernel scheduling).
c (Number of servers): The system has \(\QueueServerCount\) parallel GPU workers, each capable of serving requests independently.
K (System capacity): At most \(\QueueSystemCapacity\) requests may be present, including those in service. Requests arriving to a full system are rejected (load shedding).

The notation comes from the same systems-performance lineage that sized telephone networks before it was applied to GPU clusters.

Systems Perspective 1.1: Queuing theory and performanceQueuing theory, developed by Agner Krarup Erlang in 1909 for telephone network analysis, remains foundational to systems performance engineering (Erlang 1909). The same mathematical framework that sized telephone exchanges now informs GPU cluster capacity. Standard systems texts develop the component queuing models and approximations on which this notation builds (Jain 1991; Kleinrock 1975).



Kleinrock, L. 1975. Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory. Wiley-Interscience.

Jain, R. 1991. The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis: Techniques for Experimental Design, Measurement, Simulation, and Modeling. John Wiley & Sons.

Erlang, Agner Krarup. 1909. “The Theory of Probabilities and Telephone Conversations.” Nyt Tidsskrift for Matematik B 20: 33–39.
For a batched inference system with batch size \(\BatchSize\), service time becomes a function of batch size. Let \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) denote the time to process a batch of \(\BatchSize\) requests. From the physics of batching (Batching Strategies at Scale), equation 1 models this as:
\[\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = \BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \MarginalRequestServiceTime\cdot \BatchSize \tag{1}\]
where \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) represents fixed service overhead (kernel launch, weight loading from high-bandwidth memory (HBM)) and \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) represents marginal per-request computation time. This linear model captures the first-order behavior observed in production systems, though actual service times may exhibit slight sublinearity due to memory bandwidth saturation at large batch sizes.
The Effective Service Rate for batched processing is:
\[\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)} = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \MarginalRequestServiceTime\cdot \BatchSize}\]
The effective rate increases with batch size, approaching the asymptotic limit \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) as \(\BatchSize\to \infty\).



The total response time \(\RequestResponseTime\) for a request consists of three components:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime] = \mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime] + \mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay] + \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime] \]
where:

\(\mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime]\) is the expected waiting time in queue before joining a batch
\(\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay]\) is the expected per-request batch-accumulation delay before dispatch
\(\mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime]\) is the expected inference time once the batch executes

For dynamic batching with maximum wait time \(\BatchingWindow\) and maximum batch size \(\MaxBatchSize\), the first request triggers the batching window. Let \(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\ArrivalRate{}\BatchingWindow)\) count subsequent arrivals during that window and let \(\BatchFillArrivalCount=\MaxBatchSize-1\). For \(\MaxBatchSize>1\), the realized batch size is \(\BatchSize=\min(\MaxBatchSize,1+\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount)\), including the trigger request, so:
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchSize] = \sum_{n=0}^{\BatchFillArrivalCount-1}(\RealizedArrivalCount+1)\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount) + \MaxBatchSize\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount\geq \BatchFillArrivalCount)\]
Let \(\SubsequentArrivalTime_k\) be the Erlang-distributed time of the \(\BatchFillArrivalCount\)th subsequent arrival. A full batch closes when \(\SubsequentArrivalTime_k \leq \BatchingWindow\), while a timeout batch closes at \(\BatchingWindow\) with \(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount<\BatchFillArrivalCount\). The mean per-request accumulation delay within each realized batch is:
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay \mid \text{full}] = \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[\SubsequentArrivalTime_k \mid \SubsequentArrivalTime_k \leq \BatchingWindow]\]
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay \mid \TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount,\ \text{timeout}] = \frac{\BatchingWindow}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\RealizedArrivalCount+1}\right), \qquad 0 \leq \RealizedArrivalCount< \BatchFillArrivalCount\]
Weighting each batch outcome by its realized request count gives the mean delay of a randomly selected request:
\[\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay] = \frac{\MaxBatchSize\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount\geq \BatchFillArrivalCount)\mathbb{E}[\SubsequentArrivalTime_k/2 \mid \SubsequentArrivalTime_k\leq \BatchingWindow] + \sum_{n=0}^{\BatchFillArrivalCount-1}(\RealizedArrivalCount+1)\Pr(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount)\mathbb{E}[\BatchFormationDelay \mid \TriggeredWindowArrivalCount=\RealizedArrivalCount,\ \text{timeout}]}{\mathbb{E}[\BatchSize]}\]
When batches reliably fill before timeout, this expression approaches \(\mathbb{E}[\SubsequentArrivalTime_k]/2=(\MaxBatchSize-1)/(2\ArrivalRate)\). For \(\MaxBatchSize=1\), the batch contains only its trigger request and accumulation delay is zero.



The optimal batch size \(\BatchSize\) minimizes expected response time subject to throughput requirements:
\[\BatchSize= \operatorname{arg\,min}_{\BatchSize} \mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime(\BatchSize)] \quad \text{subject to} \quad \EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) > \ArrivalRate\]
The constraint ensures system stability (service rate exceeds arrival rate).
For a high-traffic regime in which batches of size \(\BatchSize\) reliably fill before timeout, substituting the response time components gives:
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestResponseTime(\BatchSize)] = \mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime(\BatchSize)] + \frac{\BatchSize-1}{2\ArrivalRate} + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\]
For a tractable waiting-time estimate, use an M/G/1 surrogate that treats batches as Poisson “super-requests.” If the request arrival rate is \(\ArrivalRate\) and the average batch size is \(\BatchSize\), this surrogate uses batch arrival rate \(\BatchArrivalRate=\ArrivalRate/\BatchSize\). This is not the exact process produced by grouping Poisson request arrivals, because fixed-size grouping yields Erlang inter-batch times; finite \(\QueueSystemCapacity\) or \(\QueueServerCount>1\) requires a bulk-service model or simulation. Within the explicit surrogate, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula gives:
\[\mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime] = \frac{\BatchArrivalRate\cdot \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime^2]}{2(1 - \ServingUtilization)}\]
where \(\ServingUtilization = \BatchArrivalRate\cdot \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime] = \ArrivalRate \cdot \mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime]/\BatchSize\) is the server utilization. The second moment \(\mathbb{E}[\BatchServiceTime^2]\) captures service time variability.
For the linear service time model with deterministic service in this surrogate:
\[\mathbb{E}[\QueueWaitTime(\BatchSize)] = \frac{\ArrivalRate \cdot \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)^2}{2\BatchSize(1 - \ArrivalRate \cdot \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)/\BatchSize)}\]
For production sizing, teams often first enforce a utilization headroom target rather than solving the full latency minimization problem. With \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)=\BatchFixedOverheadTime+\MarginalRequestServiceTime \BatchSize\), the constraint \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)/\BatchSize\leq \TargetServingUtilization\) yields the target-utilization batch bound (equation 2):
\[\TargetUtilizationBatchSize(\TargetServingUtilization) = \frac{\ArrivalRate \BatchFixedOverheadTime}{\TargetServingUtilization- \ArrivalRate \MarginalRequestServiceTime} \tag{2}\]
where \(\TargetServingUtilization\) is the target utilization (typically 0.7–0.8 for production systems to maintain latency headroom) and \(\TargetServingUtilization> \ArrivalRate \MarginalRequestServiceTime\).

Systems Perspective 1.2: Target-utilization batch sizingThe target-utilization batch bound (equation 2) reveals a fundamental insight: minimum utilization-feasible batch size grows with fixed overhead and arrival rate. This means:

Higher traffic \((\ArrivalRate)\): Required batch size increases.
Higher fixed overhead \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime)\): Required batch size increases to amortize overhead.
Higher target utilization \((\TargetServingUtilization)\): Required batch size decreases, but with less latency headroom.

This utilization-constrained sizing explains why large language models (LLMs) (high \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) from weight loading) benefit from larger batches than vision models (low \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\)), even at the same arrival rate.





Consider a hypothetical prefill-stage sizing exercise for a GPT-3 class model (175B parameters). The following assumed service-time coefficients illustrate the queuing calculation; they are not a measured GPT-3 benchmark:

Arrival rate: \(\ArrivalRate =\) 100 requests/second
Hardware: 8\(\times\) A100 GPUs (one DGX A100 node) with tensor parallelism
Fixed prefill-stage service overhead: \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime=\) 50 ms
Marginal prefill-stage service time: \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime=\) 0.5 ms per request
Target utilization: \(\TargetServingUtilization=\) 0.75

For the prefill phase (processing input prompt), service time follows equation 1:
\[\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = 50 + 0.5 \cdot \BatchSize \text{ ms}\]
Applying equation 2 to compute the minimum batch size that meets the 75 percent target utilization (leaving 25 percent headroom):
\[\TargetUtilizationBatchSize \approx \frac{100 \times 0.05}{0.75 - 100 \times 0.0005} = \frac{5}{0.70} \approx 7.14\]
Rounding up gives \(\BatchSize=\) 8 as the smallest batch size that meets the target utilization headroom. Evaluating the surrogate response-time expression under the full-batch assumption then shows how larger batches reduce utilization but add batch-accumulation delay:

Latency exceeds target


\(\ServingUtilization < 0.5\)
Consider reducing replicas to save cost
System is overprovisioned


\(\ServingUtilization > 0.85\)
Add replicas for headroom
Approaching instability






These rules generate candidate configurations; load tests must verify their latency, capacity, and cost under the actual request distribution.




Figure 2 charts the competing pressures of batch execution by plotting normalized throughput against batch service time across batch sizes \(\BatchSize\in [1, 128]\) on a logarithmic scale. While throughput climbs with diminishing returns as fixed overheads are amortized, batch service time expands steadily, defining the envelope where latency budgets constrain throughput gains.














Figure 2: Batch Size Trade-Off Curves: Dimensionless schematic with batch service time t(B) = 1 + 0.15(B − 1) and throughput B/t(B), each normalized to its batch-1 value. Larger batches amortize fixed work but take longer to complete. These hypothetical curves are not a benchmark, exclude queuing and batch-formation delay, and establish neither a memory-capacity boundary nor an optimal batch size.



The trade-off curve demonstrates several key insights:

Pareto Frontier: An operating point is Pareto efficient when no other candidate provides at least as much throughput and no more latency, with a strict improvement in at least one objective. The frontier is the set of these nondominated points.
Knee of the Curve: A knee marks diminishing throughput gains relative to increasing service time; it does not by itself select the best operating point.
SLO-Constrained Optimum: The best feasible batch size depends on the optimization objective and measured end-to-end latency, including queuing and batch formation. An SLO boundary can constrain that choice without guaranteeing an intersection or a unique optimum.
Diminishing Returns: In the schematic, fixed work becomes a smaller fraction of each batch, so successive batch-size increases yield smaller throughput gains.

The queuing-theoretic framework provides the mathematical foundation for the batching strategies introduced in Batching Strategies at Scale. Where intuition might suggest “larger batches are better for throughput,” stability constraints, latency targets, and diminishing returns create a well-defined optimal operating region that varies by model type and deployment requirements.




Memory management evolution from preallocation to paging defines the KV cache and the paged allocation that manages it, and Transformer Arithmetic gives its per-token size. This section expands the sizing math behind that definition: why the cache reduces per-token compute, why its memory grows with sequence length and batch size, and why unmanaged allocation can fragment HBM (Kwon et al. 2023).

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
For a standard attention implementation at fixed model width, autoregressive generation without caching requires \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) computation per token because each transformer layer recomputes the full prefix, including attention among its tokens. The KV cache stores previously computed key and value vectors, allowing each new token to attend to the prefix in \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) computation. For serving at scale, this compute saving creates a critical memory-management challenge since KV cache memory can exceed model weights for long contexts.
The cache size grows with context as calculated by equation 4:
\[\KvCacheMemory = 2 \times \LayerCount \times \HiddenDimension\times \SequenceLength\times \BatchSize\times \ElementStorageSize \tag{4}\]
For standard multihead attention, where the aggregate KV width equals the hidden width, \(\LayerCount\) is the number of layers, \(\HiddenDimension\) is the hidden dimension, \(\SequenceLength\) is sequence length, \(\BatchSize\) is batch size, \(\ElementStorageSize\) is storage size per element in bytes, and the factor of 2 accounts for both keys and values. Grouped-query or multiquery attention instead uses the aggregate KV-head width in place of \(\HiddenDimension\).
For the 175B GPT-3 model (\(\LayerCount =\) 96, \(\HiddenDimension=\) 12,288, FP16 \(\ElementStorageSize =\) 2 bytes) at its training context length \(\SequenceLength=\) 2,048, each request requires:
\[ M_{\text{KV/req}} = 2 \times 96 \times 12288 \times 2048 \times 2 \text{ B} \approx 9.66 \text{ GB/request} \]
Across 8\(\times\) A100 80-GB GPUs (687.2 GB total HBM), storing model weights in FP16 consumes 350 GB, leaving 337.2 GB for activation and KV cache memory. Dividing that residual capacity by the per-request cache gives a capacity-only upper bound of 34 concurrent requests. This bound assumes balanced sharding and reserves no memory for activations, workspaces, runtime state, or allocator losses; an implementable batch must be smaller. Device nameplate capacities are converted to decimal GB before subtracting the decimal model footprint.

title: Inference Foundations
text: Serving performance is bounded by queues and by memory. As utilization \(\ServingUtilization\) approaches 1, queue depth and latency grow without bound, so production systems retain headroom suited to their workload and SLO. Larger batches raise throughput but add batch-accumulation delay, which produces a latency knee rather than monotonic improvement; the best batch size depends on whether the objective is minimum mean latency, maximum SLO-compliant throughput, or cost. Little’s Law, \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\), gives a one-line consistency check on any serving measurement. The KV cache grows with sequence length, batch size, and KV-head width and can exceed the model weights (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)); paging reduces fragmentation and reservation losses without removing the underlying footprint.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Distributed training spends a substantial fraction of execution time synchronizing gradients, redistributing activations, and routing tokens across network fabrics. Rather than cluttering chapter text with step-by-step proofs, this appendix provides the quantitative communication cost models used throughout the book: point-to-point formulations (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) and LogGP), collective execution bounds (AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll), pipeline bubble math, and gradient compression thresholds.


This appendix is designed as a reference when translating a distributed training symptom (“AllReduce is slow,” “pipeline bubbles are killing throughput,” “should we compress gradients?”) into a quantitative diagnosis.
Conventions used here follow the book-wide notation: \(\MessageStartupLatency\) denotes per-message startup latency, \(\LinkBandwidth\) denotes link bandwidth in bytes per second, \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) denotes point-to-point message size, \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\) denotes the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) crossover point, \(\DeviceCount\) denotes the number of participating GPUs, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) denotes collective payload size in bytes.

When AllReduce is slow: Use section 1.2 to compute the expected time and compare ring vs. tree costs.
When choosing ring vs. tree: Use section 1.3 and the crossover analysis to match algorithm to message size.
When pipeline bubbles dominate: Use section 1.4 to compute bubble fraction and determine the required microbatch count.
When gradient compression is proposed: Use section 1.5 to run the break-even calculation before committing engineering effort.





Systems Perspective 1.1: Why this mattersEstimating how long a gradient synchronization will take across 256 GPUs must happen before committing to a cluster topology. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model is the “roofline for networks”: it gives a first-order prediction of transfer time from just two hardware parameters and the message size.


Every point-to-point transfer on a network follows the same fundamental pattern: the sender pays a fixed startup cost to initiate the message, then transmits the payload at a rate determined by the link’s bandwidth. This two-parameter model captures the essential physics of network communication.
The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (equation 1) predicts the time to transfer a point-to-point message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes:
\[ \PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth}  \tag{1}\]
where:

\(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the Startup Latency (seconds), the fixed cost of initiating a message, including software overhead, network interface card (NIC) processing, and routing setup
\(\LinkBandwidth\) is the Link Bandwidth (bytes/s), the sustained data rate after startup
\(\PointToPointMessageSize\) is the Message Size (bytes)

The model decomposes every transfer into exactly two costs: a per-message tax (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) paid regardless of size, and a per-byte tax (\(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\)) that scales linearly with the payload. This decomposition drives all the algorithm selection decisions in section 1.3.

The \(\LinkBandwidth\) column uses one-way or per-direction bandwidth, so the H100 NVLink entry is half of the 900 GB/s bidirectional aggregate specification. The InfiniBand NDR \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the per-message base latency of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model, which is smaller than the fabric’s end-to-end one-way latency; the other rows are end-to-end startup latencies, so compare NDR with them only loosely. NVLink and PCIe operate within a node; InfiniBand and RoCE operate between nodes. TCP latency is dominated by kernel software stack overhead.
