The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model reveals two distinct operating regimes. For small messages, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) dominates, and the link spends most of its time starting transfers rather than sustaining them. For large messages, the bandwidth term \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) dominates, and the startup cost becomes negligible.
The Crossover Message Size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), defined by equation 2, is the point where both terms contribute equally:
\[ \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth \tag{2}\]
Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is Latency-Dominated: sending more small messages wastes time on repeated startups. Above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is Bandwidth-Dominated: payload transfer dominates; reducing bytes or increasing effective bandwidth can lower its cost.

Napkin Math 1.1: Worked example: Crossover on InfiniBand NDRSetup: InfiniBand NDR has \(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s.
Question: At what message size does the bandwidth term equal the latency term?
Math:
\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth=\) 1.5 μs \(\times\) 50 GB/s \(=\) 75 KB
Analysis: Messages smaller than 75 KB are latency-dominated on IB NDR. Gradient tensors from a single layer of a large model are typically 10–100 MB, well above this threshold. Control messages, heartbeats, and barrier synchronizations, however, are well below it.
Systems insight: This is why NCCL and Gloo batch small gradient tensors into larger “buckets” before launching AllReduce. Sending each tensor individually would pay the 1.5 μs startup cost hundreds of times per iteration instead of a handful.





The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model assumes a message is a single, atomic transfer. In practice, networks pipeline messages: a sender can inject a new packet before the previous one has been fully received. The LogGP Model (Alexandrov et al. 1995) extends LogP with a long-message gap parameter:

Alexandrov, Albert D., Mihai F. Ionescu, Klaus E. Schauser, and Chris J. Scheiman. 1995. “LogGP: Incorporating Long Messages into the LogP Model—One Step Closer Towards a Realistic Model for Parallel Computation.” Proceedings of the Seventh Annual ACM Symposium on Parallel Algorithms and Architectures - SPAA ’95 30: 95–105. https://doi.org/10.1145/215399.215427.

\(\MessageInjectionGap\) (gap): The minimum interval between consecutive message injections at the sender. This models the NIC’s injection rate limit.
\(\SenderOverhead\), \(\ReceiverOverhead\) (overhead): The CPU time consumed by the processor to initiate or complete a message, during which it cannot do useful compute.

For a long message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes, LogGP models transfer time as approximately: \[\LoggpLongMessageTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx \SenderOverhead + \LogpNetworkLatency + (\PointToPointMessageSize- 1)\LongMessageGapPerByte+ \ReceiverOverhead\]
where \(\LogpNetworkLatency\) is the network latency, \(\SenderOverhead\) and \(\ReceiverOverhead\) are sender and receiver overheads, \(\LongMessageGapPerByte\) is the gap per byte for long messages, and \(\MessageInjectionGap\) controls the minimum interval between consecutive message injections. Informal alpha-beta-style approximations can be useful for ML profiling, but the standard LogGP model keeps these gap parameters distinct from a simple bandwidth term.
In most ML training scenarios, the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model is sufficient because gradient tensors are large enough that pipelining effects are secondary to raw bandwidth. The LogGP model becomes important when analyzing the overhead of many small control messages or when modeling the interaction between communication and computation overlap, situations that arise in fine-grained pipeline parallelism and asynchronous gradient updates.
The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model describes point-to-point transfers. Collective operations, in which all GPUs participate, compose multiple point-to-point transfers, and their cost formulas derive directly from the model above.





Systems Perspective 1.2: Why this mattersEvery distributed training step ends with a collective synchronization. The cost of that collective, rather than the cost of the matrix multiplies, often determines whether scaling from 8 GPUs to 256 is feasible. Understanding the exact complexity of each collective reveals which parallelism strategy (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) will dominate wall time at a given scale.


Collective operations move data between all \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs simultaneously. Each collective has a characteristic bandwidth term (how much data flows) and latency term (how many sequential message steps are required). The formulas below use the Bandwidth-Optimal Ring Algorithm unless otherwise noted; section 1.3 discusses when other algorithms are preferable.


AllReduce is the workhorse of data-parallel training: every GPU starts with a local gradient tensor of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and ends with the globally reduced (summed) result. The ring algorithm decomposes AllReduce into a ReduceScatter phase followed by an AllGather phase. Ring AllReduce time is given by equation 3:
\[ \RingAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \cdot \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2(\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{3}\]
The factor \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) approaches 2 as \(\DeviceCount\) grows. Each rank sends that factor times \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and receives the same amount. With full-duplex links, sending and receiving overlap; \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the effective bandwidth in one direction, so sent-plus-received bytes must not be divided by that one-direction rate. The latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\), which makes the ring algorithm expensive in latency for large GPU counts.
Tree AllReduce trades that linear latency growth for logarithmic depth. Equation 4 charges both the bandwidth and the latency term once per tree level, \(2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\) times in total:
\[ \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{4}\]
This unsegmented tree algorithm trades bandwidth efficiency for latency efficiency: the latency term grows as \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) instead of \(\DeviceCount\), but the bandwidth term sends the full message \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) at each tree level instead of \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) chunks.

Napkin Math 1.2: Worked example: Ring vs. tree AllReduceSetup: 256 H100 GPUs connected via InfiniBand NDR (\(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs, \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s). The gradient tensor is 1 GB (a 500M-parameter model in FP16).
Question: How long does AllReduce take with ring vs. tree?
Ring AllReduce:
\(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 40.6 ms
Tree AllReduce:
\(\TreeAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 320 ms
Analysis: For this 1 GB message, ring AllReduce takes 40.6 ms, and tree takes 320 ms. The ring is significantly faster because it distributes the bandwidth load across all links. The tree’s logarithmic latency advantage is negligible compared to its bandwidth penalty for large messages.
Systems insight: For the large gradient tensors typical of data-parallel training, ring (or ring-based) algorithms dominate. This unsegmented tree model favors small messages. Production tree variants can pipeline or partition messages and must be evaluated with their own cost models.





AllGather is the complement of ReduceScatter: each GPU starts with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard and ends with the complete \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor. It is the core communication primitive in fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) for reconstructing parameters before each forward pass, and in tensor parallelism for reassembling split activations.
Ring AllGather execution time (equation 5) requires half the transfer volume of AllReduce:
\[ \AllGatherCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{5}\]
For this comparison, the full gathered tensor has the same byte size as each rank’s AllReduce input payload. In this model, AllGather takes half the communication time of AllReduce for that matched tensor size and link parameters: it uses one ring pass instead of two. Local reduction work and implementation overheads can change the measured ratio.



ReduceScatter is the dual of AllGather: each GPU starts with a full \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor and ends with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard that contains the globally reduced values for that shard. It is the gradient synchronization primitive in FSDP and ZeRO, replacing the full AllReduce with a cheaper operation when each GPU only needs its own parameter shard’s gradient.
Ring ReduceScatter execution time (equation 6) provides the gradient sharding primitive:
\[ \ReduceScatterCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{6}\]
The symmetry is not a coincidence: ring AllReduce decomposes into one ReduceScatter followed by one AllGather, and the costs add up exactly to equation 3.



AllToAll is the most general collective: each GPU sends a distinct \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized chunk to every other GPU, and receives a distinct chunk from each. It is the routing primitive for mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, where tokens must be dispatched to the correct expert and the results gathered back.
Pairwise-exchange AllToAll execution time (equation 7) trades personalized data chunks across peers:
\[ \AllToAllCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{7}\]
Although the formula matches AllGather and ReduceScatter in form, the communication pattern is fundamentally different: AllToAll is a personalized exchange (each GPU sends different data to each peer), which makes it harder to overlap with computation and more sensitive to network congestion.



Broadcast sends a single \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte tensor from one root GPU to all \(\DeviceCount- 1\) others. It is used for distributing initial model weights, updated learning rates, and configuration changes during training.
Tree Broadcast execution time (equation 8) scales logarithmically with the participating GPU count:
\[ \BroadcastCompletionTime= \log_2 \DeviceCount\left(\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\right)  \tag{8}\]
Broadcast is inherently asymmetric (one sender, many receivers), which makes a tree topology natural. In an unsegmented tree broadcast, the full \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte payload is forwarded at each tree level, so both the latency and bandwidth terms appear along the \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\)-level critical path. Segmented or scatter-allgather broadcast variants can reduce the bandwidth term, but they require a different algorithm-specific model.



With the individual formulas in place, table 2 provides a compact reference for comparing the cost structure of each collective operation.

Two patterns emerge from this table. First, the ring and pairwise-exchange models contain the \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) factor, which approaches 1 for large \(\DeviceCount\). Per-rank communication therefore approaches a constant multiple of the relevant size: about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) for ring AllReduce, about \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) for ring AllGather or ReduceScatter, and about \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) for pairwise AllToAll. Aggregate traffic still scales with the number of ranks. Second, the latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\) for ring algorithms but logarithmically for tree algorithms, creating the algorithm selection trade-off analyzed next.





Systems Perspective 1.3: Why this mattersNCCL automatically selects a collective algorithm based on message size and GPU topology, but understanding why it chooses ring for large messages and tree for small ones helps diagnose when the auto-selection is suboptimal and how to structure communication to stay in the efficient regime.




The ring algorithm minimizes bandwidth usage but pays a latency cost that grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\). The tree algorithm minimizes latency but wastes bandwidth because it sends the full message at each level. Recursive halving-doubling splits the difference: it uses halving (like a tree) for the reduce phase and doubling for the gather phase, achieving near-optimal bandwidth with \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) latency steps.
The decision boundary between ring and tree depends on both message size and participant count. For the power-of-two case modeled by equation 3 and equation 4, equating the two times gives the crossover in equation 9:
\[ \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount) = \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize \times \frac{(\DeviceCount-1)-\log_2 \DeviceCount}{\log_2 \DeviceCount-(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount}, \qquad \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize=\MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth \tag{9}\]

\(\CollectivePayloadSize> \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (large gradients): The ring has the lower modeled cost because its smaller bandwidth coefficient outweighs its additional startup steps.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize< \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (barriers, scalars): The tree has the lower modeled cost because its logarithmic startup term outweighs its additional bandwidth cost.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize\approx \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (medium tensors): The two modeled costs are similar, so benchmark them alongside recursive halving-doubling on the target topology.

Modern clusters have a two-level topology: GPUs within a node are connected by NVLink (450 GB/s), while nodes are connected by InfiniBand (50 GB/s). Hierarchical AllReduce exploits this asymmetry in three phases:

Intra-node reduce (NVLink): Each node reduces its 8 local GPUs to a single result using NVLink’s 450 GB/s bandwidth. This is fast because NVLink’s per-direction rate is 9× that of an InfiniBand NDR port.
Inter-node AllReduce (InfiniBand): The per-node results are all-reduced across nodes. Only one representative per 8 local GPUs participates, so the inter-node ring has one-eighth as many participants as a flat GPU-level ring.
Intra-node broadcast (NVLink): Each node broadcasts the global result to its 8 local GPUs.

The hierarchical approach reduces the inter-node ring size from all GPUs to one representative per 8 local GPUs, cutting the latency-step term by about 8\(\times\) while keeping local aggregation on fast intra-node links. The inter-node representative still exchanges the full reduced tensor; the gain is not a universal reduction of payload bytes by the number of local GPUs. NCCL selects among topology-aware algorithms such as Ring, Tree, CollNet variants, NVLS/NVLSTree, and PAT based on the collective, message size, topology, architecture, and version; hierarchical communication is common on multi-node systems but is not a universal default.
Understanding the cost structure of collectives enables reasoning about data-parallel overhead. Pipeline parallelism introduces a different kind of overhead: idle time caused by the sequential dependency between pipeline stages.





Systems Perspective 1.4: Why this mattersPipeline parallelism splits a model across multiple GPUs so that each GPU holds only a fraction of the layers. The trade-off is Bubble Time: idle cycles where GPUs wait for activations or gradients from upstream or downstream stages. Quantifying the bubble fraction reveals whether pipeline parallelism is worth the complexity at a given scale.




In a pipeline with \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) stages and \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches, equation 10 defines the Bubble Fraction as the proportion of total GPU-time spent idle:
\[ \PipelineBubbleFraction = \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount}  \tag{10}\]
For balanced stages with negligible transfer overhead, this formula applies to both GPipe (where all forward passes complete before any backward pass begins) and 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward interleaving). The 1F1B schedule has the same asymptotic bubble fraction but uses less peak memory because it retires microbatches earlier.
The bubble fraction depends on the ratio of stages to microbatches. Adding more microbatches (for a fixed number of stages) amortizes the pipeline fill and drain across more useful work.
Rule of thumb: Keeping bubble overhead at or below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\); strictly below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount> 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\). The practical rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) is a convenient conservative target.
Pipeline depth and microbatch count (table 4) govern the effective bubble fraction.

As the table demonstrates, scaling to deeper pipelines requires proportionally more microbatches to maintain high accelerator utilization. When activation memory bounds limit the microbatch count, systems must adopt alternative scheduling strategies to mitigate bubble overhead.



Interleaved scheduling (used in Megatron-LM) assigns \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages to each physical GPU instead of one. Each GPU processes \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) nonconsecutive chunks of the model, which means the pipeline has \(\PipelineParallelDegree \times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages but the bubble overhead uses the original \(\PipelineParallelDegree\), as equation 11 shows:
\[ \InterleavedPipelineBubbleFraction= \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount\times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice}  \tag{11}\]
The microbatch term in the denominator is multiplied by \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) compared to equation 10, so the bubble reduction approaches \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) when \(\MicrobatchCount\) dominates \(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1\). For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) = 8, \(\MicrobatchCount\) = 16, and \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) = 4, the bubble fraction drops from 30.4 percent to 9.9 percent, a 3.1× reduction that comes at the cost of more frequent, smaller communication between stages.
Interleaved scheduling highlights a recurring theme in distributed ML: communication granularity is a tunable knob. Smaller, more frequent transfers improve overlap and reduce idle time, but increase the aggregate latency overhead. The same trade-off governs gradient compression.





Systems Perspective 1.5: Why this mattersGradient compression promises to reduce communication volume by 10–1000\(\times\), making AllReduce nearly free. Compression, however, has overhead (encoding and decoding time), and it only helps if that overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves. A quick break-even analysis prevents wasted effort on compression schemes that will not actually speed up training.




Gradient compression replaces the original \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte gradient with a compressed representation of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio\), where \(\CompressionRatio\) is the compression ratio. Equation 12 expresses the total time with compression:
\[ \CompressedCommunicationTime = \CodecEncodeTime + \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right) + \CodecDecodeTime  \tag{12}\]
Compression is beneficial when \(\CompressedCommunicationTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\). Rearranging this inequality yields the break-even condition in equation 13:
\[ \CodecEncodeTime + \CodecDecodeTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) - \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right)  \tag{13}\]
In the bandwidth-dominated regime (\(\CollectivePayloadSize\gg \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\)), the communication time scales linearly with message size, and the right-hand side simplifies to approximately \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) \times (1 - 1/\CompressionRatio)\). For high compression ratios (\(\CompressionRatio \gg 1\)), this approaches \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\), so compression is worthwhile as long as the codec overhead is less than the uncompressed communication time.

Napkin Math 1.3: Worked example: Is compression worth it?Setup: Ring AllReduce of a 1 GB gradient across 256 H100 GPUs on InfiniBand NDR, taking 40.6 ms uncompressed. Assume a collective-compatible compressed representation achieves 64× compression with 2 ms total encode + decode overhead.
Question: Does compression reduce the total AllReduce time?
Math:

Uncompressed AllReduce: 40.6 ms
Compressed communication: 1.4 ms
Total with compression: 3.4 ms
Speedup: 12×

Result: Compression shortens communication time by 12×. The 2 ms codec overhead is a small fraction of the 40.6 ms uncompressed baseline.
Systems insight: Compression saves communication time under the assumed payload ratio, codec cost, and unchanged collective structure. Independent top-k selections do not generally preserve that structure: sparse indices, differing supports, and merge operations must also be modeled. Lossy compression can require more iterations to reach the same accuracy, negating a per-iteration gain.


Break-even codec overhead limits (table 5) scale with compression ratio and uncompressed AllReduce time. Higher compression ratios tolerate larger codec overheads, up to the bandwidth-dependent portion of the uncompressed collective.



Table 5: Compression Break-Even Thresholds: Maximum tolerable codec overhead (encode + decode) for compression to reduce total time, computed as the actual collective-time difference \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)-\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio)\). The shared startup latency cancels, so even at high compression ratios it is not part of the codec budget.

Ultimately, these break-even limits show that gradient compression delivers the highest net benefit on lower-bandwidth interconnects where transfer times dominate. On high-speed fabrics, the tolerable codec overhead budget is tightly constrained, requiring lightweight quantization or sparsification algorithms.




The communication models in this appendix rest on two hardware parameters, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and the bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\) of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)), and on two workload parameters, the payload (\(\PointToPointMessageSize\) or \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)) and, for collectives, the participant count \(\DeviceCount\). The crossover size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\) separates latency-dominated from bandwidth-dominated transfers. Ring collectives carry a \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) bandwidth factor and a latency term linear in \(\DeviceCount\), while tree algorithms trade bandwidth for logarithmic latency, so message size relative to the crossover \(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) selects the algorithm. Pipeline parallelism adds the bubble fraction \(\PipelineBubbleFraction = (\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree-1+\MicrobatchCount)\), which the rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) keeps below 20 percent, and gradient compression pays only when codec overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves and convergence is unaffected. Measuring \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) for a cluster therefore yields a first-order prediction of its communication overhead.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
This appendix is designed as a reference when translating a distributed training symptom (“AllReduce is slow,” “pipeline bubbles are killing throughput,” “should we compress gradients?”) into a quantitative diagnosis.
Conventions used here follow the book-wide notation: \(\MessageStartupLatency\) denotes per-message startup latency, \(\LinkBandwidth\) denotes link bandwidth in bytes per second, \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) denotes point-to-point message size, \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\) denotes the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) crossover point, \(\DeviceCount\) denotes the number of participating GPUs, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) denotes collective payload size in bytes.

When AllReduce is slow: Use section 1.2 to compute the expected time and compare ring vs. tree costs.
When choosing ring vs. tree: Use section 1.3 and the crossover analysis to match algorithm to message size.
When pipeline bubbles dominate: Use section 1.4 to compute bubble fraction and determine the required microbatch count.
When gradient compression is proposed: Use section 1.5 to run the break-even calculation before committing engineering effort.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.1: Why this mattersEstimating how long a gradient synchronization will take across 256 GPUs must happen before committing to a cluster topology. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model is the “roofline for networks”: it gives a first-order prediction of transfer time from just two hardware parameters and the message size.


Every point-to-point transfer on a network follows the same fundamental pattern: the sender pays a fixed startup cost to initiate the message, then transmits the payload at a rate determined by the link’s bandwidth. This two-parameter model captures the essential physics of network communication.
The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (equation 1) predicts the time to transfer a point-to-point message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes:
\[ \PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth}  \tag{1}\]
where:

\(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the Startup Latency (seconds), the fixed cost of initiating a message, including software overhead, network interface card (NIC) processing, and routing setup
\(\LinkBandwidth\) is the Link Bandwidth (bytes/s), the sustained data rate after startup
\(\PointToPointMessageSize\) is the Message Size (bytes)

The model decomposes every transfer into exactly two costs: a per-message tax (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) paid regardless of size, and a per-byte tax (\(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\)) that scales linearly with the payload. This decomposition drives all the algorithm selection decisions in section 1.3.
Parameterizing physical interconnects (table 1) provides the baseline \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) values for hardware commonly found in ML clusters:



Table 1: \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) Parameters by Interconnect: Startup latency and sustained bandwidth for interconnects used in ML clusters. The \(\LinkBandwidth\) column uses one-way or per-direction bandwidth, so the H100 NVLink entry is half of the 900 GB/s bidirectional aggregate specification. The InfiniBand NDR \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the per-message base latency of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model, which is smaller than the fabric’s end-to-end one-way latency; the other rows are end-to-end startup latencies, so compare NDR with them only loosely. NVLink and PCIe operate within a node; InfiniBand and RoCE operate between nodes. TCP latency is dominated by kernel software stack overhead.

The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model reveals two distinct operating regimes. For small messages, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) dominates, and the link spends most of its time starting transfers rather than sustaining them. For large messages, the bandwidth term \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) dominates, and the startup cost becomes negligible.
The Crossover Message Size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), defined by equation 2, is the point where both terms contribute equally:
\[ \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth \tag{2}\]
Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is Latency-Dominated: sending more small messages wastes time on repeated startups. Above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is Bandwidth-Dominated: payload transfer dominates; reducing bytes or increasing effective bandwidth can lower its cost.

Napkin Math 1.1: Worked example: Crossover on InfiniBand NDRSetup: InfiniBand NDR has \(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s.
Question: At what message size does the bandwidth term equal the latency term?
Math:
\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth=\) 1.5 μs \(\times\) 50 GB/s \(=\) 75 KB
Analysis: Messages smaller than 75 KB are latency-dominated on IB NDR. Gradient tensors from a single layer of a large model are typically 10–100 MB, well above this threshold. Control messages, heartbeats, and barrier synchronizations, however, are well below it.
Systems insight: This is why NCCL and Gloo batch small gradient tensors into larger “buckets” before launching AllReduce. Sending each tensor individually would pay the 1.5 μs startup cost hundreds of times per iteration instead of a handful.





The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model assumes a message is a single, atomic transfer. In practice, networks pipeline messages: a sender can inject a new packet before the previous one has been fully received. The LogGP Model (Alexandrov et al. 1995) extends LogP with a long-message gap parameter:

Alexandrov, Albert D., Mihai F. Ionescu, Klaus E. Schauser, and Chris J. Scheiman. 1995. “LogGP: Incorporating Long Messages into the LogP Model—One Step Closer Towards a Realistic Model for Parallel Computation.” Proceedings of the Seventh Annual ACM Symposium on Parallel Algorithms and Architectures - SPAA ’95 30: 95–105. https://doi.org/10.1145/215399.215427.

\(\MessageInjectionGap\) (gap): The minimum interval between consecutive message injections at the sender. This models the NIC’s injection rate limit.
\(\SenderOverhead\), \(\ReceiverOverhead\) (overhead): The CPU time consumed by the processor to initiate or complete a message, during which it cannot do useful compute.

For a long message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes, LogGP models transfer time as approximately: \[\LoggpLongMessageTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx \SenderOverhead + \LogpNetworkLatency + (\PointToPointMessageSize- 1)\LongMessageGapPerByte+ \ReceiverOverhead\]
where \(\LogpNetworkLatency\) is the network latency, \(\SenderOverhead\) and \(\ReceiverOverhead\) are sender and receiver overheads, \(\LongMessageGapPerByte\) is the gap per byte for long messages, and \(\MessageInjectionGap\) controls the minimum interval between consecutive message injections. Informal alpha-beta-style approximations can be useful for ML profiling, but the standard LogGP model keeps these gap parameters distinct from a simple bandwidth term.
In most ML training scenarios, the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model is sufficient because gradient tensors are large enough that pipelining effects are secondary to raw bandwidth. The LogGP model becomes important when analyzing the overhead of many small control messages or when modeling the interaction between communication and computation overlap, situations that arise in fine-grained pipeline parallelism and asynchronous gradient updates.
The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model describes point-to-point transfers. Collective operations, in which all GPUs participate, compose multiple point-to-point transfers, and their cost formulas derive directly from the model above.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.2: Why this mattersEvery distributed training step ends with a collective synchronization. The cost of that collective, rather than the cost of the matrix multiplies, often determines whether scaling from 8 GPUs to 256 is feasible. Understanding the exact complexity of each collective reveals which parallelism strategy (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) will dominate wall time at a given scale.


Collective operations move data between all \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs simultaneously. Each collective has a characteristic bandwidth term (how much data flows) and latency term (how many sequential message steps are required). The formulas below use the Bandwidth-Optimal Ring Algorithm unless otherwise noted; section 1.3 discusses when other algorithms are preferable.


AllReduce is the workhorse of data-parallel training: every GPU starts with a local gradient tensor of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and ends with the globally reduced (summed) result. The ring algorithm decomposes AllReduce into a ReduceScatter phase followed by an AllGather phase. Ring AllReduce time is given by equation 3:
\[ \RingAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \cdot \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2(\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{3}\]
The factor \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) approaches 2 as \(\DeviceCount\) grows. Each rank sends that factor times \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and receives the same amount. With full-duplex links, sending and receiving overlap; \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the effective bandwidth in one direction, so sent-plus-received bytes must not be divided by that one-direction rate. The latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\), which makes the ring algorithm expensive in latency for large GPU counts.
Tree AllReduce trades that linear latency growth for logarithmic depth. Equation 4 charges both the bandwidth and the latency term once per tree level, \(2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\) times in total:
\[ \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{4}\]
This unsegmented tree algorithm trades bandwidth efficiency for latency efficiency: the latency term grows as \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) instead of \(\DeviceCount\), but the bandwidth term sends the full message \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) at each tree level instead of \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) chunks.

Napkin Math 1.2: Worked example: Ring vs. tree AllReduceSetup: 256 H100 GPUs connected via InfiniBand NDR (\(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs, \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s). The gradient tensor is 1 GB (a 500M-parameter model in FP16).
Question: How long does AllReduce take with ring vs. tree?
Ring AllReduce:
\(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 40.6 ms
Tree AllReduce:
\(\TreeAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 320 ms
Analysis: For this 1 GB message, ring AllReduce takes 40.6 ms, and tree takes 320 ms. The ring is significantly faster because it distributes the bandwidth load across all links. The tree’s logarithmic latency advantage is negligible compared to its bandwidth penalty for large messages.
Systems insight: For the large gradient tensors typical of data-parallel training, ring (or ring-based) algorithms dominate. This unsegmented tree model favors small messages. Production tree variants can pipeline or partition messages and must be evaluated with their own cost models.





AllGather is the complement of ReduceScatter: each GPU starts with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard and ends with the complete \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor. It is the core communication primitive in fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) for reconstructing parameters before each forward pass, and in tensor parallelism for reassembling split activations.
Ring AllGather execution time (equation 5) requires half the transfer volume of AllReduce:
\[ \AllGatherCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{5}\]
For this comparison, the full gathered tensor has the same byte size as each rank’s AllReduce input payload. In this model, AllGather takes half the communication time of AllReduce for that matched tensor size and link parameters: it uses one ring pass instead of two. Local reduction work and implementation overheads can change the measured ratio.



ReduceScatter is the dual of AllGather: each GPU starts with a full \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor and ends with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard that contains the globally reduced values for that shard. It is the gradient synchronization primitive in FSDP and ZeRO, replacing the full AllReduce with a cheaper operation when each GPU only needs its own parameter shard’s gradient.
Ring ReduceScatter execution time (equation 6) provides the gradient sharding primitive:
\[ \ReduceScatterCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{6}\]
The symmetry is not a coincidence: ring AllReduce decomposes into one ReduceScatter followed by one AllGather, and the costs add up exactly to equation 3.



AllToAll is the most general collective: each GPU sends a distinct \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized chunk to every other GPU, and receives a distinct chunk from each. It is the routing primitive for mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, where tokens must be dispatched to the correct expert and the results gathered back.
Pairwise-exchange AllToAll execution time (equation 7) trades personalized data chunks across peers:
\[ \AllToAllCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{7}\]
Although the formula matches AllGather and ReduceScatter in form, the communication pattern is fundamentally different: AllToAll is a personalized exchange (each GPU sends different data to each peer), which makes it harder to overlap with computation and more sensitive to network congestion.



Broadcast sends a single \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte tensor from one root GPU to all \(\DeviceCount- 1\) others. It is used for distributing initial model weights, updated learning rates, and configuration changes during training.
Tree Broadcast execution time (equation 8) scales logarithmically with the participating GPU count:
\[ \BroadcastCompletionTime= \log_2 \DeviceCount\left(\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\right)  \tag{8}\]
Broadcast is inherently asymmetric (one sender, many receivers), which makes a tree topology natural. In an unsegmented tree broadcast, the full \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte payload is forwarded at each tree level, so both the latency and bandwidth terms appear along the \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\)-level critical path. Segmented or scatter-allgather broadcast variants can reduce the bandwidth term, but they require a different algorithm-specific model.



With the individual formulas in place, table 2 provides a compact reference for comparing the cost structure of each collective operation.

The bandwidth term determines cost for large messages (gradients, parameters); the latency term determines cost for small messages (scalars, barriers). \(\DeviceCount\) = GPU count, \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) = per-rank input payload in bytes, and \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) = full tensor size in bytes for AllGather and ReduceScatter.

Two patterns emerge from this table. First, the ring and pairwise-exchange models contain the \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) factor, which approaches 1 for large \(\DeviceCount\). Per-rank communication therefore approaches a constant multiple of the relevant size: about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) for ring AllReduce, about \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) for ring AllGather or ReduceScatter, and about \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) for pairwise AllToAll. Aggregate traffic still scales with the number of ranks. Second, the latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\) for ring algorithms but logarithmically for tree algorithms, creating the algorithm selection trade-off analyzed next.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.3: Why this mattersNCCL automatically selects a collective algorithm based on message size and GPU topology, but understanding why it chooses ring for large messages and tree for small ones helps diagnose when the auto-selection is suboptimal and how to structure communication to stay in the efficient regime.




The ring algorithm minimizes bandwidth usage but pays a latency cost that grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\). The tree algorithm minimizes latency but wastes bandwidth because it sends the full message at each level. Recursive halving-doubling splits the difference: it uses halving (like a tree) for the reduce phase and doubling for the gather phase, achieving near-optimal bandwidth with \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) latency steps.
The decision boundary between ring and tree depends on both message size and participant count. For the power-of-two case modeled by equation 3 and equation 4, equating the two times gives the crossover in equation 9:
\[ \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount) = \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize \times \frac{(\DeviceCount-1)-\log_2 \DeviceCount}{\log_2 \DeviceCount-(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount}, \qquad \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize=\MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth \tag{9}\]

\(\CollectivePayloadSize> \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (large gradients): The ring has the lower modeled cost because its smaller bandwidth coefficient outweighs its additional startup steps.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize< \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (barriers, scalars): The tree has the lower modeled cost because its logarithmic startup term outweighs its additional bandwidth cost.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize\approx \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (medium tensors): The two modeled costs are similar, so benchmark them alongside recursive halving-doubling on the target topology.

Table 3 provides guidance for choosing the right algorithm.

Modern clusters have a two-level topology: GPUs within a node are connected by NVLink (450 GB/s), while nodes are connected by InfiniBand (50 GB/s). Hierarchical AllReduce exploits this asymmetry in three phases:

Intra-node reduce (NVLink): Each node reduces its 8 local GPUs to a single result using NVLink’s 450 GB/s bandwidth. This is fast because NVLink’s per-direction rate is 9× that of an InfiniBand NDR port.
Inter-node AllReduce (InfiniBand): The per-node results are all-reduced across nodes. Only one representative per 8 local GPUs participates, so the inter-node ring has one-eighth as many participants as a flat GPU-level ring.
Intra-node broadcast (NVLink): Each node broadcasts the global result to its 8 local GPUs.

The hierarchical approach reduces the inter-node ring size from all GPUs to one representative per 8 local GPUs, cutting the latency-step term by about 8\(\times\) while keeping local aggregation on fast intra-node links. The inter-node representative still exchanges the full reduced tensor; the gain is not a universal reduction of payload bytes by the number of local GPUs. NCCL selects among topology-aware algorithms such as Ring, Tree, CollNet variants, NVLS/NVLSTree, and PAT based on the collective, message size, topology, architecture, and version; hierarchical communication is common on multi-node systems but is not a universal default.
Understanding the cost structure of collectives enables reasoning about data-parallel overhead. Pipeline parallelism introduces a different kind of overhead: idle time caused by the sequential dependency between pipeline stages.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.4: Why this mattersPipeline parallelism splits a model across multiple GPUs so that each GPU holds only a fraction of the layers. The trade-off is Bubble Time: idle cycles where GPUs wait for activations or gradients from upstream or downstream stages. Quantifying the bubble fraction reveals whether pipeline parallelism is worth the complexity at a given scale.




In a pipeline with \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) stages and \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches, equation 10 defines the Bubble Fraction as the proportion of total GPU-time spent idle:
\[ \PipelineBubbleFraction = \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount}  \tag{10}\]
For balanced stages with negligible transfer overhead, this formula applies to both GPipe (where all forward passes complete before any backward pass begins) and 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward interleaving). The 1F1B schedule has the same asymptotic bubble fraction but uses less peak memory because it retires microbatches earlier.
The bubble fraction depends on the ratio of stages to microbatches. Adding more microbatches (for a fixed number of stages) amortizes the pipeline fill and drain across more useful work.
Rule of thumb: Keeping bubble overhead at or below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\); strictly below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount> 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\). The practical rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) is a convenient conservative target.
Pipeline depth and microbatch count (table 4) govern the effective bubble fraction.



Table 4: Pipeline Bubble Fraction: Percentage of GPU-time lost to pipeline bubbles for various stage counts and microbatch counts. The conservative choice \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) keeps the modeled fraction below 20 percent.

As the table demonstrates, scaling to deeper pipelines requires proportionally more microbatches to maintain high accelerator utilization. When activation memory bounds limit the microbatch count, systems must adopt alternative scheduling strategies to mitigate bubble overhead.



Interleaved scheduling (used in Megatron-LM) assigns \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages to each physical GPU instead of one. Each GPU processes \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) nonconsecutive chunks of the model, which means the pipeline has \(\PipelineParallelDegree \times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages but the bubble overhead uses the original \(\PipelineParallelDegree\), as equation 11 shows:
\[ \InterleavedPipelineBubbleFraction= \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount\times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice}  \tag{11}\]
The microbatch term in the denominator is multiplied by \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) compared to equation 10, so the bubble reduction approaches \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) when \(\MicrobatchCount\) dominates \(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1\). For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) = 8, \(\MicrobatchCount\) = 16, and \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) = 4, the bubble fraction drops from 30.4 percent to 9.9 percent, a 3.1× reduction that comes at the cost of more frequent, smaller communication between stages.
Interleaved scheduling highlights a recurring theme in distributed ML: communication granularity is a tunable knob. Smaller, more frequent transfers improve overlap and reduce idle time, but increase the aggregate latency overhead. The same trade-off governs gradient compression.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.5: Why this mattersGradient compression promises to reduce communication volume by 10–1000\(\times\), making AllReduce nearly free. Compression, however, has overhead (encoding and decoding time), and it only helps if that overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves. A quick break-even analysis prevents wasted effort on compression schemes that will not actually speed up training.




Gradient compression replaces the original \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte gradient with a compressed representation of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio\), where \(\CompressionRatio\) is the compression ratio. Equation 12 expresses the total time with compression:
\[ \CompressedCommunicationTime = \CodecEncodeTime + \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right) + \CodecDecodeTime  \tag{12}\]
Compression is beneficial when \(\CompressedCommunicationTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\). Rearranging this inequality yields the break-even condition in equation 13:
\[ \CodecEncodeTime + \CodecDecodeTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) - \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right)  \tag{13}\]
In the bandwidth-dominated regime (\(\CollectivePayloadSize\gg \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\)), the communication time scales linearly with message size, and the right-hand side simplifies to approximately \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) \times (1 - 1/\CompressionRatio)\). For high compression ratios (\(\CompressionRatio \gg 1\)), this approaches \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\), so compression is worthwhile as long as the codec overhead is less than the uncompressed communication time.

Napkin Math 1.3: Worked example: Is compression worth it?Setup: Ring AllReduce of a 1 GB gradient across 256 H100 GPUs on InfiniBand NDR, taking 40.6 ms uncompressed. Assume a collective-compatible compressed representation achieves 64× compression with 2 ms total encode + decode overhead.
Question: Does compression reduce the total AllReduce time?
Math:

Uncompressed AllReduce: 40.6 ms
Compressed communication: 1.4 ms
Total with compression: 3.4 ms
Speedup: 12×

Result: Compression shortens communication time by 12×. The 2 ms codec overhead is a small fraction of the 40.6 ms uncompressed baseline.
Systems insight: Compression saves communication time under the assumed payload ratio, codec cost, and unchanged collective structure. Independent top-k selections do not generally preserve that structure: sparse indices, differing supports, and merge operations must also be modeled. Lossy compression can require more iterations to reach the same accuracy, negating a per-iteration gain.


Break-even codec overhead limits (table 5) scale with compression ratio and uncompressed AllReduce time. Higher compression ratios tolerate larger codec overheads, up to the bandwidth-dependent portion of the uncompressed collective.



Table 5: Compression Break-Even Thresholds: Maximum tolerable codec overhead (encode + decode) for compression to reduce total time, computed as the actual collective-time difference \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)-\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio)\). The shared startup latency cancels, so even at high compression ratios it is not part of the codec budget.

title: Communication Foundations
text: The communication models in this appendix rest on two hardware parameters, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and the bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\) of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)), and on two workload parameters, the payload (\(\PointToPointMessageSize\) or \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)) and, for collectives, the participant count \(\DeviceCount\). The crossover size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\) separates latency-dominated from bandwidth-dominated transfers. Ring collectives carry a \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) bandwidth factor and a latency term linear in \(\DeviceCount\), while tree algorithms trade bandwidth for logarithmic latency, so message size relative to the crossover \(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) selects the algorithm. Pipeline parallelism adds the bubble fraction \(\PipelineBubbleFraction = (\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree-1+\MicrobatchCount)\), which the rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) keeps below 20 percent, and gradient compression pays only when codec overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves and convergence is unaffected. Measuring \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) for a cluster therefore yields a first-order prediction of its communication overhead.

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
How to Use This Appendix
This appendix is designed as a reference. Start with the diagnostic summary table, form a hypothesis about which C\(^3\) axis dominates, and then pick the tool that can confirm (or falsify) that hypothesis.
When training throughput is low, check model FLOPs utilization (MFU), communication fraction, and goodput ratio, then map each to its compute, communication, or coordination axis. When scaling efficiency drops below expectations, use the Fleet Law decomposition to identify which term grew. When cost is exploding, use the C\(^3\) scorecard to ensure that effort targets the dominant term, not a nonbottleneck.
The C\(^3\) Taxonomy is the diagnostic framework for fleet-scale ML systems engineering. Where the single-machine D·A·M framework (The D·A·M Taxonomy) diagnoses bottlenecks within a single node (data starvation, algorithmic overhead, or hardware saturation), the C\(^3\) taxonomy diagnoses bottlenecks across the distributed fleet. Most fleet-scale performance problems can be diagnosed by identifying the dominant axis: Compute (are the accelerators doing useful math?), Communication (is the network moving data fast enough?), or Coordination (is the system spending too much time on synchronization, failure recovery, and scheduling?). Many production bottlenecks sit at intersections between these axes.

text:
From D·A·M to C\(^3\)
The C\(^3\) taxonomy does not replace D·A·M; it extends it. When a workload moves from one machine to a fleet, each D·A·M axis acquires new failure modes that the single-machine framework cannot capture. Table 1 shows how the transition works.

The most important row in table 1 is the last one. On a single machine, the overhead term (\(\Latency\)) in the iron law is typically small, consisting of kernel launch latency, Python dispatch, and synchronization barriers. At fleet scale, coordination becomes an axis in its own right: checkpoint writes, failure detection and recovery, pipeline bubble overhead, scheduler preemptions, and maintenance windows collectively consume a significant fraction of wall time. Coordination is the axis that single-machine diagnosis lacks, and much of this book is devoted to it.

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
The Fleet Law
Under ideal partitioning of fixed work, the same classification can be written as a time budget for each distributed step. The Fleet Law, introduced in The Fleet Law, decomposes every distributed training step into the distributed-step time budget:
\[ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \]
This equation is the fleet-scale counterpart of the iron law. Where the iron law decomposes single-machine execution into data movement, compute, and overhead, the Fleet Law decomposes distributed execution into local arithmetic, network data transfer, and synchronization logic. The diagnostic strategy is identical: measure each term, identify which dominates, and direct engineering effort at the dominant term.

Component decomposition
Each Fleet Law term maps to specific measurable activities:

\(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\): Forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer step, all local arithmetic after distribution across \(\DeviceCount\) devices. Governed by MFU and per-GPU kernel efficiency. Improvements come from better kernels, mixed precision, and operator fusion.
\(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\): AllReduce of gradients, AllGather of parameters (in FSDP/ZeRO), activation transfers in tensor/pipeline parallelism. Governed by network bandwidth and collective algorithm choice. Improvements come from gradient compression, hierarchical collectives, and compute-communication overlap.
\(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\): Synchronization barriers, checkpoint writes, failure detection and recovery, pipeline bubble idle time, scheduler preemptions, and maintenance windows. Governed by cluster reliability and orchestration software. Improvements come from asynchronous checkpointing, elastic training, and faster failure detection.
\(\OverlappedTime\): Communication or coordination time hidden behind useful arithmetic. Governed by scheduling and implementation overlap.

Operational events may be amortized into the step budget or accounted for separately in operational goodput. The same checkpoint or recovery delay must not appear in both. The compute-time fraction follows:
\[ \UsefulComputeFraction = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount}{\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)} \]
When \(\UsefulComputeFraction\) drops below 0.5, the fleet spends more time on communication and coordination than on useful arithmetic. This compute-time fraction is not total fleet efficiency; useful fleet efficiency also depends on MFU, scaling efficiency, and goodput. The C\(^3\) taxonomy identifies which noncompute term is responsible.

In production, bottlenecks rarely present as a single isolated axis; they arise at the pairwise and central boundaries where two or more of these dimensions compound. Diagnosing compound bottlenecks requires mapping observed symptoms back to the governing intersection before selecting an engineering intervention.

Compute \(\cap\) communication
This intersection governs whether the system can hide communication behind computation. The communication-to-compute ratio (\(\CommunicationComputeRatio= \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)/(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\)) is the key diagnostic metric (The communication-computation ratio). When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio< 1\), computation takes longer than communication and there is enough arithmetic duration to hide the transfer in principle; dependencies and resource contention determine whether that overlap is achievable. When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio> 1\), GPUs complete their local work before the network delivers the next round of operands, and the system becomes communication-bound.
In a GPU trace, this bottleneck appears as exposed communication intervals where tensor cores sit idle awaiting collective completion (such as ncclKernel_AllReduce or ncclKernel_AllGather). Engineering at this intersection focuses on overlap and compression: launching AllReduce during the backward pass before all gradients are finalized, pipelining activation transfers in 1F1B schedules, increasing microbatch sizes or gradient accumulation steps to dilute communication frequency, and applying wire quantization to reduce payload bytes, while accounting for metadata, codec time, and numerical error (Distributed Training, Collective Communication).


Compute \(\cap\) coordination
This intersection captures the idle compute caused by orchestration and resilience mechanisms. While compute engines should ideally remain saturated with arithmetic, coordination overhead repeatedly forces hardware into idle states.
Three distinct mechanisms govern this intersection:

Pipeline bubbles: In pipeline parallelism (PP), stages idle during pipeline fill (warmup) and drain (cooldown). For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) pipeline stages and \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches, the bubble fraction \(\PipelineBubbleFraction = (\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount)\) (Bubble fraction) is accelerator time lost to idling; more microbatches or interleaved schedules shrink it.
Checkpoint stalls: Synchronous checkpoint writes that block the training loop to serialize terabytes of weights and optimizer states convert expensive compute time into storage wait time. Asynchronous checkpointing mitigates this by snapshotting host-pinned or local Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) memory in milliseconds, delegating remote persistence to background I/O threads.
Recovery rollback: When a node fails in an \(\DeviceCount\)-device cluster, training halts and rolls back to the last valid checkpoint, squandering the arithmetic executed since that snapshot. Minimizing the failure blast radius through fast health heartbeats and dynamic node replacement bounds this compute loss (Fault Tolerance, Fleet Orchestration).



Communication \(\cap\) coordination
This intersection captures the synchronization cost embedded in network communication. A collective operation (AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter) moves data over physical wires (\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\)) while creating dependencies among its participating ranks (\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)). It need not impose a separate cluster-wide barrier, but a delayed contribution can prevent dependent outputs from becoming ready.
The governing failure mode is straggler amplification. If a single GPU or link experiences packet drops, thermal throttling, or ECC retry delays, every other GPU in the collective waits, transforming a localized degradation into a cluster-wide halt. At fleet scale (\(\DeviceCount\ge 10{,}000\)), tail latency dominates the barrier time: the probability of at least one node straggling approaches unity (\(1 - (1 - \NodeStragglerProbability)^\DeviceCount\to 1\)).
Engineering at this intersection focuses on decoupling synchronization from raw communication: using hierarchical collectives that isolate high-bandwidth intra-node NVLink domains from inter-node InfiniBand fabrics, adopting bounded-staleness asynchronous training to absorb transient tail latency, and enforcing topology-aware gang scheduling to align collective communication rings with physical spine-leaf switch rails (Collective Communication, Fault Tolerance).


Fleet-scale ML systems engineering
At the center (\(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\cap \FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\cap \FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)), all three constraints converge simultaneously. This is the discipline of Fleet-Scale ML Systems Engineering. Systems engineers at this center do not optimize a single accelerator or a single network switch; they manage the trade-offs of the distributed machine as an integrated whole.
The central engineering challenges encompass:

4D parallelism co-design: Balancing Data Parallelism (DP), Tensor Parallelism (TP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), and Expert Parallelism (EP) so that memory consumption fits within accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM) (\(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\)), high-frequency communications map to intra-node NVLink and low-frequency communications map to inter-node fabrics (\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\)), and pipeline bubbles and barrier dependencies are minimized (\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)).
Memory sharding vs. communication volume: Frameworks like PyTorch FSDP2 and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 eliminate memory redundancy (\(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\)) by partitioning model states across workers, but pay a strict tax in repeated AllGather communication (\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\)) and state coordination metadata (\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)).
Holistic goodput optimization: Google’s ML Productivity Goodput metric decomposes fleet productivity into program goodput (\(\ProgramGoodput\)), runtime goodput (\(\RuntimeGoodput\)), and scheduling goodput (\(\SchedulingGoodput\)). These factors cut across the C\(^3\) axes rather than mapping one to one onto them. Communication overlap improves program goodput, while checkpointing and recovery, which are Coordination costs, determine runtime goodput (The Fleet Law).

Just as single-node execution transforms the additive iron law into a maximum bounded by dependencies (D·A·M coordination from sum to max), overlap at fleet scale transforms the Fleet Law (equation 1.3) by maximizing \(\OverlappedTime\). Storage as the persistent substrate
A common diagnostic question is why Storage does not appear as a fourth explicit coordinate in the C\(^3\) taxonomy or as an independent \(\Glyph{T_{\text{storage}}}\) term in the Fleet Law.
The physical data center is procured around Compute, Network, and Storage (Data Storage). At runtime, however, storage devices execute no model arithmetic. Storage overhead therefore manifests dynamically through the three C\(^3\) dimensions:

In Compute (\(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\)): High-throughput local NVMe drives function as the tier-3 extension of the accelerator memory hierarchy (below SRAM and HBM), serving parameter offloading (ZeRO-Offload) and activation spilling.
In Communication (\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\)): Remote dataset streaming from parallel file systems (Lustre, GPFS) or object stores (S3, Ceph) shares cluster network bandwidth and network interface card (NIC) capacity with collective communication traffic.
In Coordination (\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)): Durable distributed storage provides the persistent state anchor required for checkpoint serialization, node failover, and job rescheduling.

When storage latency stalls a training run, profilers identify the symptom not as raw disk latency, but either as a network communication bottleneck (\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\), dataset starvation) or as a blocking coordination barrier (\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\), synchronous checkpoint flush). Storage is the persistent substrate supporting all three dimensions, rather than a separate term in the step execution budget.

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
C\(^3\) Case Studies
Theoretical constraints manifest as confusing symptoms in production. These scenarios illustrate how to apply the C\(^3\) taxonomy to fleet-scale performance problems. Each case isolates one dominant axis before showing which optimization levers follow from that diagnosis.

Case 1 on the underutilized compute fleet

Symptom
An engineering team provisions 4,096 H100 GPUs for a large language model training run. The training loop runs without errors, but the PyTorch Profiler shows MFU of only 15 percent. The network profiler shows communication accounts for less than 10 percent of step time. The cluster is running but barely working.


Diagnosis
The Compute axis is the leading hypothesis to investigate. With 15 percent MFU, 85 percent of the fleet’s peak capacity is not credited to useful model FLOPs. Low exposed communication makes local execution a useful starting point; kernel traces and host-side waits must distinguish inefficient arithmetic from data starvation or unobserved coordination gaps.


The fix
If traces confirm inefficient local execution, target the compute axis across 4,096 accelerators:

Mixed precision: Ensure BF16/FP8 Tensor Cores are engaged. A common culprit is FP32 fallback in normalization layers or loss computation.
Operator fusion: Use torch.compile or similar just-in-time (JIT) compilation to fuse element-wise operations and reduce kernel launch overhead.
Batch size tuning: If per-GPU batch size is too small, the matrix multiplications have insufficient arithmetic intensity to saturate the Tensor Cores.

Raising MFU from 15 percent to 50 percent on the same hardware delivers 50 percent/15 percent = 3.3× more useful work, the equivalent of tripling the fleet without buying a single GPU.



Case 2 on the communication wall

Symptom
A 512-GPU data-parallel training run achieves 45 percent illustrative compute-phase efficiency during compute kernels on each GPU, which is good per-device kernel efficiency. Wall-clock MFU over the full step (including AllReduce) is only 20.2 percent because AllReduce consumes 55 percent of every training step. Scaling from 64 GPUs to 512 GPUs yields only 4× speedup instead of the expected 8×, or 50 percent scaling efficiency.


Diagnosis
The Communication axis dominates. Each GPU has healthy compute-phase efficiency, but more than half the step time is spent synchronizing gradients across the network. The system is Communication-Bound: adding more GPUs can worsen the exposed communication fraction. Under fixed-work scaling, local computation shrinks while the collective retains startup and transfer costs.


The fix
Target the communication axis without touching the per-GPU computation:

Compute-communication overlap: Launch AllReduce during the backward pass rather than waiting until it completes. Modern frameworks (FSDP, DeepSpeed) support this natively.
Gradient compression: Apply Top-k sparsification or quantization to reduce the bytes crossing the network by 10–100\(\times\).
Hierarchical collectives: Use intra-node NVLink for the first reduction stage, then inter-node InfiniBand only for cross-node aggregation, reducing inter-node participants relative to a flat rank-level algorithm. Actual traffic savings depend on the collective layout, NIC allocation, and topology.

If communication were eliminated entirely, throughput would increase by 2.2× (Amdahl’s Law applied to the 45 percent compute fraction). Realistically, reducing communication from 55 percent to 20 percent of step time would recover most of the lost scaling.



Case 3 on the coordination tax

Symptom
A 10,000-GPU training run shows 40 percent compute-phase model FLOPs utilization per device, measured only while kernels execute, and communication accounts for only 15 percent of step time. Both figures look healthy. This case uses a broad Goodput Ratio that includes both pipeline and operational losses relative to an ideal step rate; it is not the separate operational factor in the multiplicative capacity model. Its value is only 60 percent. The remaining 40 percent of wall time is consumed by checkpoint writes, failure recovery restarts, pipeline bubble idle time, scheduler preemptions (17 percent of wall time), and maintenance windows.


Diagnosis
The Coordination axis dominates. Per-GPU computation and inter-node communication are both efficient, but nonproductive overhead consumes 40 percent of wall time. Scheduler preemptions take 17 percent, failure recovery 10 percent (at 10,000 GPUs, GPU failures occur about every 5 hours), pipeline bubbles 5 percent, checkpoint writes 3 percent, and maintenance windows 5 percent. Faster arithmetic alone does not recover this lost time. Checkpoint bandwidth, recovery mechanisms, and scheduling must be evaluated against the specific overhead they can reduce.


The fix
Target the coordination axis:

Asynchronous checkpointing: Overlap checkpoint writes with the next training step, reducing visible checkpoint overhead from 3 percent to near zero.
Elastic training: When a node fails, shrink the job and continue rather than halting all 10,000 GPUs for recovery. This converts the 10 percent failure recovery cost into a smaller throughput reduction.
Pipeline schedule optimization: Switch from GPipe to an interleaved 1F1B schedule to reduce bubble fraction, or increase microbatch count per pipeline flush.
Faster failure detection: Reduce heartbeat timeout from 30 seconds to 5 seconds with hardware-level health monitoring, cutting the idle time between failure occurrence and recovery initiation.

title: Rules of Thumb
section: Scaling Laws Through the C\(^3\) Lens
text:
Scaling Laws Through the C\(^3\) Lens
Scaling laws are usually written in algorithmic FLOPs, but a training fleet delivers only the useful FLOPs that survive utilization, communication, and coordination losses. Scaling-law targets translate directly into C\(^3\) terms: the hidden perfect-systems assumption abstracts away losses, while effective FLOP/s defines the usable throughput connecting model-quality forecasts to real cluster capacity.

The ideal-system assumption in scaling laws
Scaling laws (Kaplan, Chinchilla, and their successors) predict model quality as a function of algorithmic training compute. They usually abstract away systems efficiency: wall-clock time, accelerator peak FLOP/s, compute-phase efficiency, communication overhead, and scheduler losses enter later when teams provision hardware to deliver the target compute budget. In C\(^3\) terms, scaling-law FLOPs must be converted into raw fleet capacity after compute-phase, distributed-step, and operational-goodput losses.
The gap between scaling-law predictions and observed training outcomes is, in large part, a C\(^3\) gap. A team that budgets \(10^{24}\) peak hardware FLOPs of capacity will deliver fewer useful model FLOPs after three multiplicative losses: per-GPU compute-phase efficiency, inter-node scaling efficiency (\(\ScalingEfficiency\)), and operational goodput.


The effective FLOP/s concept
A fleet’s Effective FLOP/s is the usable throughput after compounding three disjoint C\(^3\) efficiency factors:
\[\EffectiveFleetThroughput = (\DeviceCount\PeakRate) \times \underbrace{\ModelFlopsUtilization}_{\text{Compute}} \times \underbrace{\ScalingEfficiency}_{\text{Distributed step}} \times \underbrace{\GoodputRatio}_{\text{Operational goodput}}\]
MFU, the single-device baseline, measures useful model arithmetic against peak throughput only while local computation is active. This compute-phase factor is not the step-averaged fleet MFU of table 9, whose \(\DistributedStepTime\) denominator already includes the in-step losses that \(\ScalingEfficiency\) counts, so the product does not count them twice. Scaling efficiency captures communication and other distributed-step losses, including pipeline bubbles. Operational goodput captures time outside those measured steps, including checkpointing, failure recovery, scheduler preemptions, and maintenance. These disjoint measurement windows prevent the same loss from being counted twice.
A concrete estimate makes the multiplicative loss visible at fleet scale.

Systems Perspective 1.1: The C³ tax on a 100,000-GPU clusterConsider a 100,000-GPU H100 cluster with 98,900 PFLOP/s of peak aggregate throughput. After the three disjoint C\(^3\) efficiency factors:
\[\text{Effective} = 98,900 PFLOP/s \times 0.50 \times 0.56 \times 0.65 \approx 17999.8 PFLOP/s\]
The fleet delivers 18.2 percent of its peak capacity as useful training work. The C\(^3\) Tax, the ratio of peak to effective compute, is 5.5×, so achieving a given effective compute budget requires 5.5× the raw hardware. The compute phase retains a 50 percent efficiency factor. The distributed step retains a 56 percent scaling factor, using the modeled 8,192-GPU tier as an illustrative proxy that includes pipeline losses. Operations retain a 65 percent goodput factor after checkpoints, failures, scheduler preemptions, and maintenance.
These losses reflect the physics of fleet-scale computation rather than a failure of engineering. The C\(^3\) taxonomy quantifies where the losses occur so that optimization effort targets the dominant term.

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
Summary
The C\(^3\) taxonomy provides a systematic framework for diagnosing fleet-scale bottlenecks. Each axis maps to a distinct physical constraint: arithmetic throughput and MFU bound compute; network bandwidth and collective algorithm efficiency bound communication; and synchronization overhead, failure recovery, and operational losses bound coordination. The Fleet Law quantifies these constraints, enabling systematic diagnosis. Use the C\(^3\) traffic light for quick triage, the bottleneck diagnostic table to choose the right lever, and the C\(^3\) scorecard to grade fleet health.

Key Takeaways: Where to look first at fleet scale

Every fleet-scale bottleneck has a dominant C\(^3\) axis: Compute, Communication, or Coordination, with many real bottlenecks spanning intersections. Identify the dominant axis before optimizing.
Measure the C\(^3\) scorecard: Compare MFU, scaling efficiency, and goodput with workload-specific baselines. The displayed thresholds screen for problems; traces must confirm the cause before selecting an optimization.
The C\(^3\) tax is multiplicative: Peak FLOP/s \(\times\) compute-phase efficiency \(\times\) scaling efficiency \(\times\) operational goodput = effective FLOP/s. The illustrative 100,000-GPU case retains ~18.2 percent of peak.
Coordination is the new axis: Single-node overhead remains relevant, while distribution adds cross-machine dependencies. The coordination case attributes 40 percent of its modeled budget to checkpoints, failures, pipeline bubbles, scheduling, and maintenance.
Optimizing the wrong C\(^3\) axis yields limited improvement: Faster GPUs cannot fix a communication-bound fleet by themselves; faster networks help coordination only where transfer time, such as checkpoint I/O, contributes to that overhead.
