The four metrics measure different quantities by construction. The disparate impact ratio of 0.57 means the lower-approval group receives approvals at only that fraction of the higher-approval group’s rate, below the illustrative 0.8 screening threshold. The additive 0.30 gap, the 0.29 opportunity gap, and the 0.32 average absolute odds gap each quantify a distinct dimension of the same disparity. No single number is sufficient, which is why the impossibility results in this section force an explicit choice about which metric a deployment will prioritize.


Stated for both groups at once, a model satisfies score calibration with respect to a sensitive attribute if, among individuals assigned score \(\ModelScore\) by the model, the fraction with positive outcomes equals that score within each group (Kleinberg et al. 2017): \[
\Pr(\TrueOutcome= 1 \mid \ModelScore(\ModelInput) = \ModelScore, \ProtectedGroupMembership = \FirstComparedGroupLabel) = \ModelScore= \Pr(\TrueOutcome= 1 \mid \ModelScore(\ModelInput) = \ModelScore, \ProtectedGroupMembership = \SecondComparedGroupLabel), \quad \forall \ModelScore\]
The condition applies at score levels supported within each group. Matching the groups’ outcome frequencies is insufficient if those frequencies differ from the score itself. For hard binary predictions, a distinct condition is equal positive predictive value (PPV) (precision) among predicted positives. Groupwise score calibration does not by itself guarantee equal PPV after thresholding, because the selected groups can have different score distributions: \[
\text{PPV}(\FirstComparedGroupLabel) = \frac{\Pr(\TrueOutcome=1, \BinaryClassifier(\ModelInput)=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\FirstComparedGroupLabel)}{\Pr(\BinaryClassifier(\ModelInput)=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\FirstComparedGroupLabel)} = \text{PPV}(\SecondComparedGroupLabel)
\]
Evaluating this condition on the loan-approval example yields the respective predictive values: \[\begin{align*}
\text{PPV}(a) &= \frac{40}{70} = 0.571 \\
\text{PPV}(b) &= \frac{30}{40} = 0.750
\end{align*}\]
The positive predictive value gap is \(0.750 - 0.571 = 0.179\). Group B’s predicted positives are actually positive 75 percent of the time, while Group A’s are only 57 percent accurate. This violates predictive parity for hard decisions and reveals that the model is less reliable when predicting approval for Group A. Demonstrating score calibration itself would require comparing observed outcome frequencies with predicted probabilities within each group, using score bins with sufficient support.
Calibration is critical for high-stakes decisions where individuals rely on predicted probabilities. A miscalibrated model systematically over- or underpredicts risk for specific groups, leading to misallocated resources and eroded trust.



In practice, fairness metrics can be changed by adjusting classification thresholds per group. In the equations below, a larger score favors a positive decision, as with predicted repayment probability. Given a scoring function \(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput)\), define group-specific thresholds \(\FirstGroupClassificationThreshold\) and \(\SecondGroupClassificationThreshold\) such that \(\FirstGroupThresholdClassifier(\ModelInput) = \mathbb{1}[\DecisionScore(\ModelInput) \geq \FirstGroupClassificationThreshold]\) for group \(\FirstComparedGroupLabel\) and similarly for group \(\SecondComparedGroupLabel\).
To achieve demographic parity, solve: \[
\Pr(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput) \geq \FirstGroupClassificationThreshold\mid \ProtectedGroupMembership = \FirstComparedGroupLabel) = \Pr(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput) \geq \SecondGroupClassificationThreshold\mid \ProtectedGroupMembership = \SecondComparedGroupLabel)
\]
To achieve equal opportunity, solve: \[
\Pr(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput) \geq \FirstGroupClassificationThreshold\mid \ProtectedGroupMembership = \FirstComparedGroupLabel, \TrueOutcome= 1) = \Pr(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput) \geq \SecondGroupClassificationThreshold\mid \ProtectedGroupMembership = \SecondComparedGroupLabel, \TrueOutcome= 1)
\]
For equalized odds, both true positive and false positive rate constraints must hold simultaneously. A single deterministic threshold per group need not satisfy both. Postprocessing can instead randomize between threshold rules within each group to attain a shared pair of rates (Hardt et al. 2016). The resulting criterion constrains group-level probabilities, so validation must evaluate the randomized policy rather than only its component thresholds.

Hardt, Moritz, Eric Price, and Nathan Srebro. 2016. “Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 29: 3315–23.
Threshold adjustment still requires evaluating the other criteria. When base rates differ (that is, \(\Pr(\TrueOutcome=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\FirstComparedGroupLabel) \neq \Pr(\TrueOutcome=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\SecondComparedGroupLabel)\)), calibration and error-rate constraints can conflict under the conditions discussed earlier. The effect of a particular threshold policy must be measured on the joint score and label distribution; a base-rate difference alone does not determine its accuracy cost.



Lifting Group B’s approval rate to parity costs 4 points of accuracy.
The accuracy cost of a threshold policy becomes concrete on a separate credit model, distinct from the running loan example. Its score is a predicted default probability, so a lower score favors approval and each cutoff admits applicants below it. The scenario enforces demographic parity, the first threshold equation above, and prices the accuracy that enforcement costs.

Napkin Math 16.3: The fairness taxProblem: Consider a credit model with 85 percent accuracy. Group A (majority) has a 20 percent default rate. Group B (minority) has a 40 percent default rate due to systemic factors. If demographic parity (equal approval rates) is enforced, what happens to accuracy?
Math:
This scenario holds Group A’s approval rate fixed and raises Group B’s rate to match it; demographic parity alone does not require that particular choice. The accuracy values are assumed held-out validation results, where the additional Group B approvals carry higher default risk.

Unconstrained: Model approves everyone with predicted default prob < 30 percent.

Group A approval: 80 percent.
Group B approval: 60 percent.
Total Accuracy: 85 percent.

Constrained (parity): Holding Group A’s rate fixed, approve Group B at 80 percent rate.

New threshold for Group B: Approve default prob < 50 percent.
The revised cutoff admits Group B applicants with higher predicted default risk than the original policy allowed.
New Total Accuracy: 81 percent.


Systems insight: This parity policy cost 4 percentage points of accuracy (about a 4.7 percent relative accuracy drop in this credit-scoring scenario). The drop is the scenario’s fairness tax, not a universal cost of fairness. Accuracy still measures prediction against the specified default labels; whether those labels capture the legitimate lending objective is a separate question. Engineers must report the predictive trade-off while making the target and policy assumptions explicit.


The 4 percentage points cost belongs to one parity policy on one prediction target. A different criterion moves the thresholds for a different reason, and the next scenario, which returns to the repayment-score convention, targets equal opportunity by comparing the score distributions among qualified applicants. Differential thresholds require access to sensitive attributes at inference time and raise concerns about explicit group-based treatment, which may itself be considered unfair or illegal in certain jurisdictions. The required thresholds depend on those distributions and the chosen criterion; a lower threshold for the minority group is not a universal fairness rule.

Napkin Math 16.4: Threshold for equal opportunityProblem: Calculate group-specific thresholds required to equalize true positive rates (equal opportunity) across Group A and Group B in a credit scoring model.
Variables: Let the score \(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput)\) be an unbounded decision score, not a calibrated probability, and write Group A as \(\ProtectedGroupMembership=\FirstComparedGroupLabel\) and Group B as \(\ProtectedGroupMembership=\SecondComparedGroupLabel\). Assume \(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput)\mid(\TrueOutcome=1,\ProtectedGroupMembership=\FirstComparedGroupLabel)\sim\GaussianDistribution(0.72,0.15^2)\) and \(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput)\mid(\TrueOutcome=1,\ProtectedGroupMembership=\SecondComparedGroupLabel)\sim\GaussianDistribution(0.65,0.16^2)\). These are hypothetical positive-class distributions; no negative-class distribution or prevalence is specified.
Math:

Single threshold: At \(\FirstGroupClassificationThreshold=\SecondGroupClassificationThreshold=0.60\), \(\text{TPR}_\FirstComparedGroupLabel=1-\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution(-0.8)\approx0.788\) and \(\text{TPR}_\SecondComparedGroupLabel=1-\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution(-0.3125)\approx0.623\), where \(\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.
Equalizing thresholds: Preserve Group A’s threshold and match its standardized cutoff, \((\SecondGroupClassificationThreshold-0.65)/0.16=-0.8\). Thus \(\SecondGroupClassificationThreshold=0.522\) yields the same true positive rate.
Unspecified costs: Lowering Group B’s threshold cannot decrease its false positive rate, but its magnitude requires \(\DecisionScore(\ModelInput)\mid(\TrueOutcome=0,\ProtectedGroupMembership=\SecondComparedGroupLabel)\). Precision also requires Group B’s prevalence. Neither quantity follows from the positive-class distributions alone.

Systems insight: Equal opportunity determines a threshold only relative to the stated score distributions and target rate. Before deployment, evaluate the resulting false positives, precision, and review workload on representative data. Threshold policies change decisions, not the underlying score calibration.


Figure 3 presents a separate illustrative loan scenario, with applicants partitioned into Subgroup A (higher score distribution, blue band) and Subgroup B (lower score distribution, amber band). The summary panels contrast two operating regimes: applying a single global threshold (\(\ClassificationThreshold = 0.75\)) approves qualified applicants in Subgroup B at only 25 percent TPR compared to 75 percent for Subgroup A, a threefold opportunity disparity. Conversely, shifting to group-adapted thresholds (\(\FirstGroupClassificationThreshold= 0.75\) for Subgroup A and \(\SecondGroupClassificationThreshold= 0.45\) for Subgroup B) equalizes true positive rates at 75 percent. That policy requires the authorized decision component to access the relevant group attribute and log the governing threshold. Neither the attribute lookup nor the policy decision must run on the client, but the system must preserve evidence explaining why identical scores receive different decisions.














Figure 3: Threshold-Dependent Fairness: Varying classification thresholds across subgroups allows equal true positive rates but introduces complexity in model serving and necessitates access to sensitive attributes at inference time. Achieving fairness requires careful consideration of subgroup-specific performance, as a single threshold may disproportionately impact certain groups, highlighting the tension between accuracy and equitable outcomes in machine learning systems.






Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests help assess whether sampling variation plausibly explains an observed disparity under a stated sampling model. For demographic parity, the null hypothesis \(\StatisticalHypothesis_0: \Pr(\BinaryClassifier(\ModelInput)=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\FirstComparedGroupLabel) = \Pr(\BinaryClassifier(\ModelInput)=1 \mid \ProtectedGroupMembership=\SecondComparedGroupLabel)\) can be tested using a two-proportion z-test when observations are independent and expected approval and rejection counts in both groups support the normal approximation. Repeated decisions for the same person or correlated observations require an uncertainty estimate that accounts for that dependence. Under the independent-sample assumptions, the test statistic is: \[
\ProportionTestStatistic= \frac{\FirstGroupSampleApprovalRate- \SecondGroupSampleApprovalRate}{\sqrt{\PooledSampleApprovalRate(1-\PooledSampleApprovalRate)\left(\frac{1}{\FirstGroupSampleSize} + \frac{1}{\SecondGroupSampleSize}\right)}}
\]
where \(\FirstGroupSampleApprovalRate\) and \(\SecondGroupSampleApprovalRate\) are the sample approval rates, \(\PooledSampleApprovalRate= \frac{\FirstGroupSampleSize\FirstGroupSampleApprovalRate+ \SecondGroupSampleSize\SecondGroupSampleApprovalRate}{\FirstGroupSampleSize+ \SecondGroupSampleSize}\) is the pooled proportion, and \(\FirstGroupSampleSize\), \(\SecondGroupSampleSize\) are sample sizes.
For the loan example with \(\FirstGroupSampleSize= \SecondGroupSampleSize= 100\), \(\FirstGroupSampleApprovalRate= 0.70\), \(\SecondGroupSampleApprovalRate= 0.40\): \[\begin{align*}
\hat{p} &= \frac{100(0.70) + 100(0.40)}{200} = 0.55 \\
z &= \frac{0.70 - 0.40}{\sqrt{0.55(0.45)(0.02)}} = \frac{0.30}{0.0704} = 4.26
\end{align*}\]
With \(\ProportionTestStatistic = 4.26\) (far exceeding critical value \(\ConfidenceCriticalQuantile = 1.96\)), the test rejects \(\StatisticalHypothesis_0\) and concludes the demographic parity violation is statistically significant at \(\ObservedSignificanceLevel < 0.001\). Similar tests can be constructed for equal opportunity and equalized odds by restricting to subpopulations where \(\TrueOutcome=1\) or \(\TrueOutcome=0\) respectively. Statistical significance does not establish the severity or acceptability of a disparity. Even a small rate difference can affect many people at fleet scale; the decision depends on the consequences and approved criteria as well as magnitude. Conversely, large disparities in small samples may not reach statistical significance but still warrant investigation or intervention.
The running loan example establishes how to measure a disparity and its sampling uncertainty. Applying that framework still requires identifying whether a positive decision grants a benefit or imposes a burden, checking the criteria a headline metric misses, and choosing the requirement that fits the deployment.

Example 16.1: Choosing a fairness metricScenario: A hiring recommendation engine must select its primary fairness constraint before production launch across heterogeneous applicant pools. The accountable reviewers prioritize equal access for qualified applicants and have independently validated qualification labels for both selected and rejected applicants.
Diagnosis: Demographic parity forces equal selection rates regardless of candidate qualification, while calibration requires predicted probabilities to match outcome frequencies within each group. Equal opportunity specifically mandates equal true positive rates among qualified applicants (\(\text{TPR}_\FirstComparedGroupLabel = \text{TPR}_\SecondComparedGroupLabel\)), directly matching the goal of equal opportunity for qualified talent.
Systems lesson: Metric selection is a governance decision that sets the operational objective of the serving pipeline. System designers must align the mathematical constraint with the domain’s legal and ethical requirements before training or thresholding.


The chosen fairness definition determines which error trade-off the system is allowed to make, so the choice precedes optimization against that criterion. These calculations, and the choice behind them, point to the chapter’s central thesis. A model can satisfy a specified fairness criterion, but responsibility depends on the system that uses it. Data collection, labels, modeling choices, evaluation procedures, and decision thresholds all affect the resulting outcomes. Postprocessing can repair a selected rate disparity without resolving an invalid target or an unsupported deployment. Privacy, explainability, robustness, and accountability likewise require evidence about the relevant pipeline, beyond properties of the weights. A fairness policy is therefore realized through coordinated data collection, evaluation, threshold policy, and monitoring across the lifecycle (table 3), and group-specific thresholds are one possible intervention within that policy, not a universal requirement.
The system boundary extends past the model’s decisions to the infrastructure that runs them, because who can reach the safeguards and who bears their environmental costs are distributional effects of the same system (section 16.3.1.1). Collecting the evidence creates a further constraint, because demographic attributes useful for auditing may also increase privacy exposure. Governance must justify both the fairness claim and the data practices used to support it.





Fairness also presents a deployment problem, and its binding constraint is data visibility. A cloud platform with authorized access to demographic labels and outcomes can compute group-level metrics, run fairness-aware training, and audit post-hoc. A federated9 or on-device deployment, the regime of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet), needs an explicit evidence path, such as aggregate client statistics or a separately governed audit sample. Without sufficient evidence, the corresponding metric is unmeasurable; local execution alone does not make the audit impossible. The fairness row of table 4 shows how this limit varies by tier, and two of its consequences recur across deployments.
9 Federated Learning and Fairness: Google’s public Gboard trial illustrated training across devices without centralizing raw examples. Model updates alone do not necessarily reveal the demographic labels and outcomes needed for a fairness audit. The deployment therefore needs an authorized evidence path, which may use aggregate statistics or a separate audit sample, with communication cost, privacy protection, and statistical uncertainty evaluated for that design.
Dwork, Cynthia, Moritz Hardt, Toniann Pitassi, Omer Reingold, and Richard Zemel. 2012. “Fairness Through Awareness.” Proceedings of the 3rd Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science Conference, 214–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/2090236.2090255.
The first consequence concerns decision policy. Equal aggregate accuracy across groups does not establish equal opportunity under a uniform threshold, as the illustrative gap in figure 3 demonstrates. A deployment must select and evaluate a policy against its approved criterion; group-specific thresholds are one possible intervention, not a requirement imposed by edge execution. The second consequence sharpens the personalization conflict raised in section 16.4.1. Local adaptation aims to improve a user’s utility, whereas individual fairness requires similar individuals to receive similar decisions under a task-relevant similarity metric (Dwork et al. 2012). Personalization does not establish that requirement, and adaptation on sparse or unrepresentative observations can reinforce existing gaps. When the relevant evidence stays local, fleet operators need an authorized way to assess the resulting disparities. Section 16.9.5.1 analyzes the feedback mechanism and its intervention points; the deployment consequence is that a fleet which cannot centralize outcomes must budget an explicit evidence path for detecting it.
That evidence path creates a further responsible AI tension. Keeping sensitive data local reduces centralized exposure, while fleet-level audits still need adequate group statistics. Privacy architecture (section 16.6.2) determines which records or aggregates may cross the boundary and under what protections.



Suppose a nationally deployed credit model begins rejecting applicants from a specific ZIP code at twice its previous rate. Monitoring can expose that change before a periodic audit, but the rate alone does not establish its cause. An investigator must check population changes, data quality, and decision policy against the approved fairness criteria. Bias detection turns formal definitions into operational telemetry, using slice-based analysis to identify subpopulations whose outcomes warrant examination.


The criteria of section 16.5.1 define what a disparity is and how to test one. Computing them continuously on a production system that serves thousands of predictions per second is where the engineering cost appears, and that cost has computational, data, and organizational parts that decide which metrics a system can afford to monitor.
Measurement overhead arises because computing group-specific metrics requires maintaining separate statistics for each protected group. For \(\MonitoredGroupCount\) groups and \(\MonitoredFairnessMetricCount\) metrics, this requires \(\mathcal{O}(\MonitoredGroupCount \MonitoredFairnessMetricCount)\) additional counters and \(\mathcal{O}(\MonitoredGroupCount \MonitoredFairnessMetricCount)\) statistical tests per evaluation cycle. Streaming counters can update cheaply per prediction, with statistical tests scheduled at a separate evaluation interval. Profiling the number of groups, windows, and tests determines whether sampling or asynchronous aggregation is needed; request rate alone does not establish that choice.
Data requirements depend on the metric. Error-rate criteria need outcome labels (\(\TrueOutcome\)) as well as sensitive attributes \((\ProtectedGroupMembership)\) for a sample that supports the intended population claim; demographic parity needs group membership and decisions but not outcomes. In federated or privacy-preserving settings, collecting the required evidence may conflict with privacy goals. Encrypted aggregation or differentially private group statistics can limit exposure, with their assumptions and estimation error included in the audit.
Sensitive-attribute availability requires an explicit governance and engineering decision. A system may use authorized direct collection, restricted audit records, encrypted or differentially private group statistics, or an offline sample. If it uses inferred attributes, the audit must evaluate inference errors rather than treat the inferred groups as known. Each choice changes the available evidence and the privacy risk created by monitoring. When the evidence cannot support a metric, the system must report that limitation instead of interpreting missing measurements as fair behavior.
Threshold selection demands domain expertise and stakeholder input to establish acceptable disparity thresholds. The four-fifths rule is a screening convention from U.S. employment selection, not a universal legal test for lending or fraud detection and not a determination of unlawful discrimination. Context-specific harm assessments, statistical uncertainty, and applicable legal requirements should inform thresholds. Document threshold rationale to support audits and regulatory compliance.
Temporal stability requires monitoring fairness metrics over time to detect degradation due to distribution shift, feedback loops, or model updates. Automated alerting (for example, “alert if \(|\text{SPD}| > 0.15\) for 7 consecutive days”) defines when an owner receives a signal. The persistence window can reduce sensitivity to brief fluctuations but also delays response, so its acceptability depends on the harm and exposure during that interval. Section 16.9.3 develops the monitoring and response path.
Offline and CI-stage audits are the first place these metrics run, and open-source toolkits such as Fairlearn package the per-group bookkeeping (Bird et al. 2020).

Bird, Sarah, Miro Dudı́k, Richard Edgar, Brandon Horn, Roman Lutz, Vanessa Milan, Mehrnoosh Sameki, Hanna Wallach, and Kathleen Walker. 2020. “Fairlearn: A Toolkit for Assessing and Improving Fairness in AI.” Microsoft Technical Report MSR-TR-2020-32.
Listing 1 runs that bookkeeping as an offline or CI-stage audit. Applied to the running loan example, its per-group table would report approval rates of 0.70 for Group A and 0.40 for Group B, the disparate impact ratio of 0.57 that falls below the 0.8 screening threshold in table 6. That comparison is an audit signal, not a lending-law verdict. The architecture must supply aligned decisions and group membership through an authorized audit path. Metrics that require outcome labels must use the relevant observed outcomes rather than substitute past decisions; an offline audit does not require exposing group attributes throughout runtime serving.



Listing 1: Bias Detection with Fairlearn: Illustrative audit excerpt for evaluating a loan-approval model across demographic groups. The excerpt assumes aligned arrays of observed outcomes, predictions, and demographic labels.


import numpy as np
from fairlearn.metrics import MetricFrame, selection_rate
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score

def false_positive_rate(y_true, y_pred):
    y_true, y_pred = np.asarray(y_true), np.asarray(y_pred)
    negatives = y_true == 0
    if not negatives.any():
        return float("nan")  # No observed negatives: rate is unmeasurable.
    return ((y_pred == 1) & negatives).sum() / negatives.sum()

# Loan approval model evaluation across demographic groups
mf = MetricFrame(
    metrics={
        "approval_rate": selection_rate,
        "accuracy": accuracy_score,
        "precision": precision_score,
        "false_positive_rate": false_positive_rate,
    },
    y_true=loan_repaid_actual,  # observed repayment outcome, not past approval
    y_pred=loan_approvals_predicted,
    sensitive_features=applicant_demographics["ethnicity"],
)

# NaN means a group lacks negative examples, not that its FPR is zero.
# Display performance disparities across groups
print("Loan Approval Performance by Group:")
print(mf.by_group)
# Hypothetical output on the running loan example:
# approval_rate 0.70 for group A, 0.40 for group B



Practical implementation is often shaped by limitations in data access and system instrumentation. In many real-world environments, especially in mobile, federated, or embedded systems, sensitive attributes such as gender, age, or race may not be available at inference time, making it difficult to track or audit model performance across demographic groups. Data collection and labeling strategies are essential for fairness assessment throughout the model lifecycle. Without attributes at inference time, group-specific thresholds may be infeasible, but restricted offline audits can still guide data changes, retraining, or a revised policy that does not require an attribute lookup on each request. Even when data is available, continuous retraining pipelines that incorporate user feedback can reinforce existing disparities unless explicitly monitored for fairness degradation. For example, an on-device recommendation model that adapts to user behavior may amplify prior biases if it lacks the infrastructure to detect demographic imbalances in user interactions or outputs.
Fairness interventions may be applied at different points in the pipeline, but each comes with system-level implications. Preprocessing methods change the training distribution through sampling, reweighting, or augmentation. Their data requirements depend on the method; group-targeted reweighting needs group information, while feature augmentation also needs access to the affected examples. Versioning and lineage must preserve which transformation produced the training data. In-processing approaches instead embed fairness constraints directly into optimization. They require support for the chosen loss or constrained solver and may add training work or validation requirements.


↩︎ Feature versioning and the lineage records that trace each training input are established in Feature versioning and lineage.
At the serving layer, postprocessing methods apply an approved decision rule to model outputs. Group-specific thresholds require the component choosing the threshold to obtain authorized group information; other policy rules may use different inputs. The dual-threshold policy diagrammed in figure 3 (\(\FirstGroupClassificationThreshold= 0.75\), \(\SecondGroupClassificationThreshold= 0.45\)) therefore needs a controlled attribute lookup and a record of the applied policy, but not propagation of the attribute through every routing and inference component. Access controls should limit that exposure. Validation must evaluate the resulting decisions, operational stability, and applicable restrictions on attribute use.
Multicalibration10 extends the calibration requirement to a specified family of computationally identifiable subgroups, which can overlap (Hébert-Johnson et al. 2018). Its implementation must support the chosen subgroup family, calibration-error estimation, and model corrections; the required resources depend on that scope and the available data. This work can occur in backend training infrastructure even when the resulting model runs on a constrained endpoint. A training-time result does not establish calibration after deployment conditions change. If telemetry cannot support renewed subgroup audits, the operator must record that evidence limitation and restrict the approved operating envelope accordingly.
10 Multicalibration: Developed by Hébert-Johnson et al. (2018), this technique seeks calibrated predictions across many computationally identifiable, intersecting subgroups, addressing the failure mode where global calibration masks severe miscalibration for minority intersections. The systems cost comes from repeated subgroup auditing and model updates rather than from a fixed multiplier. Multicalibration is one important scalable approach for diverse platforms where single-axis fairness audits miss compounded disparities, but it is not the only possible fairness strategy.
Hébert-Johnson, U., M. P. Kim, O. Reingold, and G. N. Rothblum. 2018. “Multicalibration: Calibration for the (Computationally-Identifiable) Masses.” In Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2018, Stockholmsmässan, Stockholm, Sweden, July 10-15, 2018, edited by Jennifer G. Dy and Andreas Krause, vol. 80. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. PMLR.
Mitigation also decays after launch. A fairness-aware model may degrade if retraining pipelines omit fairness checks, if logging cannot track subgroup outcomes, or if user feedback introduces biases absent from the training distribution, so retraining protocols need subgroup-labeled validation data under data-governance review. Deciding which disparity to remediate, and at what cost to other objectives, remains a stakeholder decision (section 16.9.5.3). The architecture’s job is to make each disparity visible, in time, to the owner who must make that decision.




Implementing responsible AI principles in production systems requires architectural patterns that integrate fairness monitoring, explainability, and privacy controls directly into the model serving infrastructure. Figure 4 partitions this production infrastructure into two decoupled tiers: a synchronous request path that enforces access control, data minimization, and low-latency inference, staged alongside an asynchronous governance tier that ingests bounded execution evidence and delayed labels to drive fairness auditing, post-hoc explanations, and owner-governed release gates.






Figure 4: Production Responsible AI Architecture: The request path performs access controls, minimization, and inference. Bounded evidence collection feeds asynchronous fairness monitoring and explanation services. Delayed outcomes support label-dependent metrics; a governed update path returns approved changes to serving.



The request path applies access controls and data minimization before inference and records only the evidence needed for the approved monitoring policy. Group-level fairness analysis and expensive explanations can run asynchronously; synchronous checks must fit the serving service-level objective (SLO). Delayed labels enter the analysis path when outcomes become available, and a named owner approves model or policy changes.
Real-time fairness monitoring updates prediction-only metrics such as demographic parity as decisions arrive, maintaining rolling statistics across protected groups. Label-dependent metrics such as equalized odds and equality of opportunity update when delayed outcomes or audited labels arrive. Groups whose labeled windows are too small must remain visible as having insufficient evidence, with a defined collection or escalation policy. The system flags supported disparities that exceed configured thresholds and separately reports gaps in coverage. Storage and compute requirements depend on the number of groups, decision segments, and retention windows.
The explanation engine generates evidence for the audience and decision under review. Its budget depends on the method and model; exact model-specific attribution may be feasible where exhaustive subset evaluation is not. Approximation, caching, selective generation, and asynchronous execution offer different cost and delivery-time trade-offs. Listing 2 illustrates the monitoring part of this architecture, collecting predictions and computing rolling group metrics with threshold alerts. It omits delayed outcome ingestion, the full equalized-odds calculation, and explanation generation, so it is a partial implementation rather than a complete governance service.



Listing 2: Production Fairness Monitoring: Simplified monitoring pseudocode for processing predictions and computing rolling fairness metrics. Delayed outcome ingestion is omitted.


import numpy as np


class RealTimeFairnessMonitor:
    # alert_threshold mirrors the |SPD| > 0.15 rule; persistence check omitted.
    def __init__(self, window_size=1000, alert_threshold=0.15, min_group=30):
        self.min_group = min_group  # Illustrative policy; set from precision needs.
        self.window_size = window_size
        self.alert_threshold = alert_threshold
        self.window = []

    async def process_prediction(self, prediction, demographics,
                                 actual_label=None):
        # Slide a fixed window over the stream, then re-check fairness.
        self.window.append((prediction, demographics, actual_label))
        self.window = self.window[-self.window_size :]
        metrics = self._compute_metrics()
        if (metrics["demographic_parity"] is not None
            and metrics["demographic_parity"] > self.alert_threshold) or (
            metrics["equalized_odds"] is not None
            and metrics["equalized_odds"] > self.alert_threshold
        ):
            await self._trigger_bias_alert(metrics)
        return metrics

    def _compute_metrics(self):
        # Bucket predictions and labels by protected group.
        by_group = {}
        for pred, demo, label in self.window:
            bucket = by_group.setdefault(
                demo.get("ethnicity", "unknown"), {"preds": [], "labels": []}
            )
            bucket["preds"].append(pred)
            if label is not None:
                bucket["labels"].append((pred, label))

        rates = [np.mean(d["preds"]) for g, d in by_group.items()
                 if g != "unknown" and len(d["preds"]) >= self.min_group]
        parity = max(rates) - min(rates) if len(rates) > 1 else None
        return {
            "demographic_parity": parity,
            # Requires sufficiently labeled outcomes per group; omitted here.
            "equalized_odds": self._equalized_odds_gap(by_group),
            "groups": {g: len(d["preds"]) for g, d in by_group.items()},
            "eligible_groups": len(rates),  # Compare with required group coverage.
        }

    def _equalized_odds_gap(self, by_group): ...
    async def _trigger_bias_alert(self, metrics): ...  # page and audit



This simplified pattern separates metric availability from metric values: an unavailable comparison is not a zero disparity. A production monitor must also enforce required group coverage, sample-size policies, and freshness before interpreting a result. The overhead ranges summarized in table 5 explain why fairness monitoring, privacy transformations, and explanation generation need explicit capacity budgets. Request metadata collection may be synchronous, while metric aggregation, delayed-label analysis, and explanation generation can run asynchronously under their own freshness requirements. These overheads must be balanced against reliability and compliance requirements when designing production systems.

Checkpoint 16.1: Operationalizing bias detection
The bias-detection and monitoring sections turned static fairness definitions into live telemetry: slice-based detection with Fairlearn, CI-stage audits, production monitoring of demographic parity and equalized odds, the evidence paths that federated and on-device deployments require, and the distinction between observing a disparity and remediating it.
Detecting the disparity

Serving-path detection: identify the request metadata needed to detect a rising rejection rate for one ZIP code, and explain how asynchronous aggregation can detect that change within an agreed monitoring delay.
Metric selection: explain why the running loan example’s approval rates of 70 percent for Group A and 40 percent for Group B do not select a fairness criterion. State the harm priority, label validity, and outcome evidence needed to choose one; then justify a criterion if reviewers prioritize avoiding denial to applicants who would repay.

From signal to action

Detection vs. remediation: explain why a fairness alert with no remediation owner is evidence without action, and name what the system must add to close that loop.
Constrained deployments: reason about why slice-based detection may be infeasible in a federated deployment where demographic labels cannot be centralized, and infer the implication for safeguard selection.




Self-Check: Question

A loan approval model evaluates two demographic groups (Group A and Group B). Group A has a baseline approval rate of \(70\%\) (\(\text{PPV} = 57.1\%\)), while Group B has a baseline approval rate of \(40\%\) (\(\text{PPV} = 75.0\%\)). If the engineering team lowers the decision threshold for Group B to enforce demographic parity (\(70\%\) approval for both groups), what is the immediate system-level consequence?

Group B’s positive predictive value increases while overall model accuracy remains completely unchanged
Lowering the threshold admits additional applicants with lower predicted repayment scores; the effects on approval precision and overall accuracy must be evaluated rather than inferred from approval rates alone.
The model automatically satisfies equalized odds without any change to false positive rates
The underlying true default base rates of both populations become mathematically equalized

For risk scores, the chapter’s score-balance impossibility result combines calibration within each group with equal mean scores across groups among positive outcomes and, separately, among negative outcomes. Which cases escape the stated incompatibility?

Whenever the training dataset contains more than \(10^6\) balanced records across all demographic slices
Whenever the model is trained with \(L_2\) regularization and post-hoc isotonic calibration
Whenever demographic parity is explicitly enforced via multi-task adversarial training
Only in degenerate or trivial cases, such as perfect prediction (zero error) or identical base rates across groups

Explain how single-axis fairness audits can enable ‘fairness gerrymandering’ and describe the evaluation strategy required to detect it.
True or False: In a two-proportion hypothesis test for demographic parity disparities, achieving a statistically significant result (\(p < 0.001\), \(z > 1.96\)) automatically implies that the disparity is large enough to warrant immediate algorithmic intervention in production.
Which statement correctly differentiates Preprocessing, In-processing, and Postprocessing fairness interventions with respect to ML system infrastructure requirements?

Preprocessing modifies serving thresholds at inference, In-processing requires anonymizing logs, and Postprocessing alters training labels in feature stores
All three methods require identical runtime compute overhead on the live model serving path
Preprocessing is only applicable to TinyML devices, while In-processing and Postprocessing can only run in cloud clusters
Preprocessing changes training data and needs lineage; in-processing changes training optimization; group-specific threshold postprocessing requires authorized group information at the component applying the decision rule.

A streaming loan-approval service records authorized group attributes and decisions immediately, but repayment outcomes arrive months later. Why can demographic-parity statistics update earlier than equalized-odds statistics?

Demographic Parity depends only on model predictions and input demographics available at inference time, whereas Equalized Odds requires true outcome labels that arrive with substantial real-world latency
Demographic Parity requires calculating matrix inverses that execute faster on GPU tensor cores
Equalized Odds is a convex optimization problem that cannot be evaluated on streaming CPU worker nodes
Demographic Parity violates privacy regulations if processed asynchronously in background databases

True or False: Applying distinct group-specific postprocessing thresholds to incoming requests can be performed without access to protected demographic attributes at inference time.
A scalable fairness guarantee that ensures model predictions remain calibrated across a rich, combinatorial collection of computationally identifiable, overlapping demographic subgroups is known as ____.
A responsible AI service must return predictions within a tight SLO, while repayment labels arrive later and explanations are needed for appeals. Which work belongs on the request path, and which work can run asynchronously?

title: 16 Responsible AI
text:
Every fairness audit and monitor in the preceding section consumed demographic evidence, and that evidence is itself sensitive data. The threat models and privacy mechanisms of Security & Privacy provide the technical controls; governance defines the evidence, ownership, and lifecycle interfaces that production systems require when inheriting them. A deletion workflow must identify which records and derived artifacts fall within an applicable obligation, such as an erasure requirement under the GDPR (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016). Removing a database row may leave replicas, backups, or trained models to address. Where removal of training influence is required, lineage, retraining, validation, deployment, and audit become part of the same workflow.
11 Machine Unlearning: Removing training-data influence requires a stated removal criterion; Cao and Yang (2015) develops an approach based on updating stored summaries. Full retraining on retained data provides a reference, with cost determined by the retained dataset and training procedure. The sharded sizing scenario in section 16.6.3.1 illustrates a smaller retraining surface under explicit cost assumptions, rather than a measured saving for every model. Where removal is required, the workflow must budget validation and redeployment as well as computation within the applicable response deadline.
Cao, Yinzhi, and Junfeng Yang. 2015. “Towards Making Systems Forget with Machine Unlearning.” 2015 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 463–80. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2015.35.
Governing these risks coordinates two classes of control that are easy to conflate. Privacy mechanisms bound specified information exposures, while machine unlearning11 targets the influence a record retains in trained weights under a stated removal criterion. A privacy guarantee does not by itself remove a record from the training history, so the assurance case must distinguish these obligations and supply evidence for each. Robustness and generative-system controls receive the same evidence-and-ownership treatment in section 16.8.


A fairness audit may need the same demographic field that a data-minimization policy would otherwise exclude. Privacy mechanisms constrain exposure and leakage; governance determines whether collecting the field is justified, who may use it, and how long the audit needs it. This decision connects privacy to fairness (section 16.5.1) and to transparency (section 16.7.1). Group-based monitoring needs evidence about group membership, but the audit design determines whether operators receive individual fields, restricted audit records, or aggregate statistics. Explainability methods can also reveal information about training examples, while detailed disclosure can conflict with individual privacy. Responsible AI systems must justify the evidence collected and limit its exposure while retaining enough information to evaluate the chosen requirements.


↩︎ Federated learning, encrypted computation, and synthetic data, each bounding who can observe raw records, are established in Privacy-preserving data techniques.
Machine learning systems often rely on extensive collections of personal data to support model training and allow personalized functionality. This reliance introduces significant responsibilities related to user privacy, data protection, and ethical data stewardship. The quality and governance of this data directly impacts the ability to implement responsible AI principles. Responsible AI design treats privacy not as an ancillary feature, but as a core constraint that must inform decisions across the entire system lifecycle.
One of the core challenges in supporting privacy is the inherent tension between data utility and individual protection. Rich, high-resolution datasets can enhance model accuracy and adaptability but also heighten the risk of exposing sensitive information, particularly when datasets are aggregated or linked with external sources. For example, large language models trained on broad text corpora have been shown to memorize12 specific strings that can later be retrieved through model queries or adversarial prompting (Carlini et al. 2021).
12 Model Memorization: Carlini et al. (2021) demonstrated that GPT-2 could reproduce verbatim training strings, including contact information, through carefully crafted prompts. The systems implication is narrower but still serious: models that expose generative outputs to user-facing queries can create a privacy attack surface where the serving layer itself becomes a data exfiltration vector, requiring output filtering, rate limiting, and data-minimization controls as defense-in-depth measures.
Carlini, N., F. Tramer, E. Wallace, M. Jagielski, A. Herbert-Voss, K. Lee, A. Roberts, et al. 2021. “Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models.” 30th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 21), 2633–50.
Privacy risks also depend on how records are linked over time and across sources. A wearable device’s heart-rate or location record can already be sensitive; combining physiological and behavioral signals can reveal additional details about a user’s health, routines, or relationships. Limited visibility or control over processing, retention, and transmission makes it harder for users to understand or contest these uses.
Addressing these challenges requires understanding privacy as a system principle that entails robust data governance. This includes defining what data is collected, under what conditions, and with what degree of consent and transparency. Foundational data engineering practices, including data validation, schema management, versioning, and lineage tracking, provide the technical infrastructure for implementing these governance requirements. Responsible governance requires attention to labeling practices, access controls, logging infrastructure, and compliance with jurisdictional requirements. These mechanisms serve to constrain how data flows through a system and to document accountability for its use.
Figure 5 diagrams the defensive boundaries partitioning a federated training pipeline into three distinct protection tiers. Client-side data locality confines raw records and gradient clipping to edge devices, an intermediate secure aggregation protocol blinds individual updates under bounded collusion and dropout assumptions, and a trusted curator executes central differential privacy by injecting calibrated noise and tracking privacy-budget depletion with a privacy accountant before publishing the released model across the untrusted network perimeter. Here the curator is trusted to protect the aggregate and add noise correctly; protecting against that curator requires a different mechanism, such as distributed noise generation with its own assumptions. The privacy unit, clipping rule, dropout and collusion assumptions, and composition across rounds define the guarantee (Bonawitz et al. 2017; Dwork and Roth 2014).

Bonawitz, Keith, Vladimir Ivanov, Ben Kreuter, Antonio Marcedone, H. Brendan McMahan, Sarvar Patel, Daniel Ramage, Aaron Segal, and Karn Seth. 2017. “Practical Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning.” Proceedings of the 2017 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, 1175–91. https://doi.org/10.1145/3133956.3133982.

Dwork, Cynthia, and Aaron Roth. 2014. “The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy.” Foundations and Trends® in Theoretical Computer Science, Foundations and trends in theoretical computer science, vol. 9 (3-4): 211–487. https://doi.org/10.1561/0400000042.






Figure 5: Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training: Clients retain raw records and contribute clipped updates through secure aggregation. In this central differential privacy design, a trusted curator receives the aggregate, adds calibrated noise, and accounts for repeated releases before publishing a model. Secure aggregation protects individual updates under its protocol assumptions; differential privacy bounds the released model relative to the specified privacy unit. Neither implies a universal ordering of privacy strength.



Weak data governance can obscure both quality defects and privacy exposures, but they require different evidence. COMPAS, a proprietary recidivism-risk score used in the U.S. criminal justice system, illustrates the first kind. Limited access to model internals and training provenance constrained investigation and remediation, although external outcome audits still exposed disparities. In clinical applications, missing values or demographic skew can compromise predictive performance; neither alone establishes a privacy violation. Privacy assessment must also examine identifiability, access, and disclosure. Documentation should make these distinct risks traceable to the data practices that create them.
Privacy is not solely the concern of isolated algorithms or data processors; it must be addressed as a structural property of the system. Decisions about consent collection, data retention, model design, and auditability all contribute to the privacy posture of a machine learning pipeline. This requires anticipating risks during inference and continuous operation as well as during training. Threats such as membership inference, which infers from a deployed model’s outputs whether a record was in its training set, underscore the importance of embedding privacy safeguards into both model architecture and interface behavior.


↩︎ Membership inference and where it sits among likelihood-and-impact threat priorities are established in Threat prioritization framework.
13 CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act): CCPA grants California residents rights over covered personal information, including a deletion right subject to statutory exceptions (California Legislature 2023). For ML serving infrastructure, deletion requests create an architectural constraint that must be planned from the data pipeline forward, because raw-record deletion does not automatically remove a record’s influence from trained model parameters.
California Legislature. 2023. California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018. California Legislative Information.

Personal Information Protection Commission, Japan. 2023. Act on the Protection of Personal Information. Personal Information Protection Commission, Japan.
Legal frameworks make privacy an enforceable design concern. The GDPR, the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA),13 and Japan’s Act on the Protection of Personal Information establish different obligations and individual rights within their respective scopes (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016; California Legislature 2023; Personal Information Protection Commission, Japan 2023). An implementation must identify which rules govern its collection, use, retention, and removal of data rather than treating consent or deletion as a uniform requirement across jurisdictions. That applicability decision belongs in the system’s documented data-governance requirements.
Privacy is the second instance of the system-level thesis established for fairness in section 16.5.1: it is a commitment that spans consent collection, retention policy, model design, serving, and auditability, not a property of any single stage. It requires coordination across technical and organizational domains to ensure that data usage aligns with user expectations, legal mandates, and societal norms. Rather than viewing privacy as a constraint to be balanced against functionality, responsible system design integrates privacy from the outset by informing architecture, shaping interfaces, and constraining how models are built, updated, and deployed.
Privacy mechanisms limit specified data exposures under their threat models; they do not establish that a system’s decisions are safe. A model may satisfy its privacy requirements while still failing catastrophically on unexpected inputs, a complementary concern about how systems fail that section 16.8 takes up. Within privacy itself, the next decision is where the protected boundary sits in each deployment architecture.



Privacy inherits the same centralization trade-off that the privacy row of table 4 summarizes by tier. Aggregating data in the cloud enables high-capacity modeling and monitoring but concentrates exposure to breaches and surveillance, so it must be paired with strong encryption, access control, and auditability. Keeping data local on mobile, federated, or TinyML clients reduces that central exposure but changes the evidence available to fleet operators. Privacy controls must cover local storage, outputs, telemetry, and update channels; an endpoint with no update path needs controls that remain valid for its approved service life.
The constraint the table cannot show is that privacy claims must name their boundary. Differentially private training bounds training-data leakage through the released model; ordinary inference on fixed weights remains within that post-processing guarantee. It does not protect new private inputs copied into service logs or unrelated private-data accesses. Interface design, retention rules, rate limiting, and access control address those separate exposures. Opaque data collection can also violate user expectations, making consent surfaces and clear disclosure part of the privacy architecture.
An architecture decides where the privacy boundary sits; the model decides how much crosses it. A service can keep raw records behind every access control and still release training data through the weights it serves, which is where algorithmic privacy preservation begins.



Privacy constraints extend across data collection, model behavior, and user interaction. They are shaped by the architectural properties of the system and its deployment context alongside ethical and legal obligations. Technical methods for privacy preservation aim to prevent data leakage, limit memorization, and uphold user rights such as consent, opt-out, and data deletion, particularly in systems that learn from personalized or sensitive information.
Large language models have been shown to memorize and expose individual training strings, including names, locations, or excerpts of private communication (Carlini et al. 2021). This memorization presents risks for privacy-sensitive text-generating systems, such as assistants trained or adapted on user logs, where training data may encode protected or regulated content. For example, a voice or chat assistant that adapts to user speech or messages may inadvertently retain specific phrases, which could later be extracted through carefully designed prompts or queries.
The memorization risk extends beyond language models. Figure 6 pairs an original training-set photograph with a diffusion model’s near-identical reconstruction under the study’s extraction protocol (Carlini et al. 2023). The left panel shows the training image and the right panel shows the generated output, with closely matching pose, clothing, necklace, and background, but visible differences in detail. Recognizable identity alone would not establish memorization; the comparison must concern the specific training instance rather than merely the same subject. The example motivates evaluating training-data exposure without treating every similar-looking output as evidence of extraction.






Figure 6: Diffusion Model Memorization: Image diffusion models can reproduce training samples (Carlini et al. 2023), revealing a risk of unintended memorization beyond language models and highlighting a general vulnerability in contemporary neural architectures. This memorization poses privacy concerns when training on sensitive datasets.


Carlini, Nicholas, Jamie Hayes, Milad Nasr, Matthew Jagielski, Vikash Sehwag, Florian Tramèr, Borja Balle, Daphne Ippolito, and Eric Wallace. 2023. “Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models.” 32nd USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 23), 5253–70.


Membership inference remains a governance concern after training because even an attacker limited to model queries may infer whether a record participated in training. Other threat models give the attacker access to parameters or additional information, so the audit must specify the access it assumes. In high-stakes applications such as healthcare or legal prediction, training-set membership itself can disclose sensitive information about an individual.
For differential privacy, governance consumes the mechanism and accounting established in Differential Privacy. A differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) deployment must retain the clipping, noise, sampling, and composition configuration that supports its reported bound (Abadi et al. 2016). Reviewers then evaluate that bound alongside utility, subgroup performance, and the private-data accesses outside training. Naming the method is insufficient evidence for approving the complete service.

Abadi, M., A. Chu, I. Goodfellow, H. B. McMahan, I. Mironov, K. Talwar, and L. Zhang. 2016. “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy.” Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, CCS ’16, 308–18. https://doi.org/10.1145/2976749.2978318.
Differential privacy introduces system-level trade-offs on the path where private data is accessed. Training noise can reduce utility, and attempts to recover it through additional data or optimization steps must be evaluated with the resulting privacy accounting and compute cost. If training occurs centrally, those costs do not automatically become extra work for an edge device performing ordinary inference on the released model. Local training or local randomization places different demands on the device. Data minimization, retention limits, and access controls remain separate requirements; feature obfuscation alone provides no differential privacy guarantee.

Systems Perspective 16.2: The price of privacyTraining a large language model on sensitive messages with DP-SGD reduces training-data extraction risk, but the protection is priced in compute and accuracy.
The privacy parameter \(\PrivacyBudget\) bounds privacy loss; smaller values provide a stronger bound when the neighboring relation and \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) are fixed. The accountant derivation in Differential Privacy shows what moves \(\PrivacyBudget\). Adding more noise relative to the clipping norm, sampling a smaller fraction of the data per step, or taking fewer steps each lowers it, and each also tends to cost accuracy or require more training to recover. A reproducible DP-SGD result must therefore record the dataset size, batch sampling scheme and rate, number of optimization steps, clipping norm, noise multiplier, neighboring relation, \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\), and privacy accountant. Those records, not the \(\PrivacyBudget\) value alone, are what a governance review retains. The three configurations below are planning assumptions whose \(\PrivacyBudget\) values an external accountant would have to confirm, as the CIFAR-10 accountant inputs of DP-SGD accountant inputs for image classification illustrate. Read them for the direction of each trade. The stronger configuration doubles the noise multiplier of the weaker one but also trains for more epochs, and more steps by themselves raise \(\PrivacyBudget\); only the accountant can confirm that the extra noise more than offsets the extra steps.
Illustrative stronger-privacy configuration (assumed accountant result \(\PrivacyBudget=\) 1): The scenario assumes per-example gradients are clipped to norm \(\GradientClippingNorm= 1.0\), 40 percent of updates are affected by clipping, and the noise multiplier is \(\PrivacyNoiseMultiplier= 1.0\). It further assumes 3× more epochs, a training-cost increase from a GPT-3-scale baseline of $4.6M to approximately $13.8M, and an accuracy drop of 6 percent.
Illustrative weaker-privacy configuration (assumed accountant result \(\PrivacyBudget=\) 8): The scenario assumes a noise multiplier of \(\PrivacyNoiseMultiplier= 0.5\), training overhead of 30 percent, and an accuracy drop of 1 percent.
Illustrative weakest configuration (assumed accountant result \(\PrivacyBudget=\) 10): The scenario assumes less noise and less than 1 percent accuracy loss, with a weaker formal privacy bound than the other two configurations under otherwise comparable accounting assumptions.
These scenarios compare formal privacy bounds, utility, and training cost; none of those quantities alone establishes user trust. Once a fixed model has been trained with differential privacy, ordinary inference is post-processing and does not consume additional training-data privacy budget. Additional privacy loss must be accounted for when a postdeployment mechanism makes new accesses to private data or releases additional differentially private statistics. The key engineering decision is to document and account for every private-data access and communicate the resulting trade-offs to users and regulators.


Released datasets need a boundary of their own. For example, \(\Glyph{k}\)-anonymity14 groups records in a specified release so that each quasi-identifier combination occurs at least \(\AnonymitySetSize\) times. Transforming one request without defining that reference dataset does not establish this condition. Differential privacy likewise requires a defined release mechanism, neighboring relation, and privacy accountant; noise injection alone does not establish a guarantee.
14 k-Anonymity: A property of a released dataset (Sweeney 2002) requiring every combination of designated quasi-identifiers to occur in at least \(\AnonymitySetSize\) records. Generalization can achieve this property at the cost of information loss. It does not bound inference from homogeneous sensitive attributes or auxiliary knowledge and is not a per-request privacy guarantee.
Sweeney, Latanya. 2002. “K-ANONYMITY: A MODEL for PROTECTING PRIVACY.” International Journal of Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-Based Systems 10 (05): 557–70. https://doi.org/10.1142/s0218488502001648.
Privacy enforcement also depends on infrastructure beyond the model itself. Data collection interfaces must support informed consent and transparency. Logging systems must avoid retaining sensitive inputs unless strictly necessary, and must support access controls, expiration policies, and auditability. Model serving infrastructure must be designed to prevent overexposure of outputs that could leak internal model behavior or allow reconstruction of private data. These system-level mechanisms require close coordination between ML engineering, platform security, and organizational governance.
Privacy must be enforced throughout the machine learning lifecycle. Retraining pipelines must respect the approved deletion and data-use policies. Monitoring should collect only the identifying information justified by its purpose, with access and retention controls appropriate to that information. Privacy-aware telemetry collection and protected per-user audit trails can support investigation and remedy without making sensitive records broadly available in logs or dashboards.
The privacy assurance case therefore spans the whole pipeline. The formal privacy accountant covers the private-data accesses in its stated mechanism; interface controls, retention policies, and access records support separate claims about the surrounding service. Keeping these claims distinct makes gaps visible when a model, telemetry path, or data source changes.
Privacy preservation techniques create complex sociotechnical tensions that extend well beyond technical implementation. Differential privacy mechanisms may reduce model accuracy in ways that disproportionately affect underrepresented groups, creating conflicts between privacy and fairness objectives. These challenges require ongoing stakeholder engagement as detailed in section 16.9.5.3, where organizations must navigate competing values around data control, personalization, and regulatory compliance. These privacy challenges become even more complex when considering the dynamic nature of user rights and data governance.


Deleting a raw record does not remove its influence from learned parameters. When the approved deletion policy also requires addressing retained model state, machine unlearning supplies a technical response. The requirement and the evidence of removal must be specified separately; retained influence alone does not establish that every deployment violates a deletion obligation.
Privacy preservation does not end at training time. In many real-world systems, users may have rights to revoke consent or request deletion of their data, even after a model has been trained and deployed (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016; California Legislature 2023). When the approved response requires removing training influence, the architecture must support the chosen method and its verification. An endpoint without sufficient data, training state, or compute may need a replacement model trained elsewhere; a device with the required resources may perform the work locally. Placement follows those requirements rather than the deployment label alone.
Full retraining requires access to the permitted remaining training data and a defined training procedure. Figure 7 contrasts three update strategies. Retraining from scratch on the retained data, the training set with the forget set \(\ForgetDataset\) removed, supplies a reference for exact removal relative to that procedure. Gradient ascent on the forget set increases its loss through updates of the form \(\ModelParameters + \LearningRate \nabla \LossFunction\), but increased loss alone does not demonstrate removal. Sharded, isolated, sliced, and aggregated (SISA) training partitions data into isolated shards \(\SisaTrainingShard_1, \SisaTrainingShard_2, \SisaTrainingShard_3\) and aggregates their predictions. A deletion affects the constituent model trained on its shard; saved states before the affected slice can reduce the retraining work.







Figure 7: Model Update Strategies: Three approaches to removing a data point’s influence. Full retraining gives exact unlearning at the highest cost; gradient ascent provides an approximate update by maximizing loss on the forget set; and SISA training partitions data into shards so only the affected shard is retrained. The accompanying cost model quantifies the full-retraining and SISA cases.



Full retraining is a useful reference, but its feasibility depends on access to the permitted remaining data, the training procedure, and sufficient compute within the response deadline. A retention policy may remove data that retraining would need; a large training run may exceed the available budget. An alternative unlearning method must state its own data and state requirements rather than assume that avoiding full retraining also eliminates those dependencies.
Machine unlearning seeks to remove specified training influence without repeating the entire training run. Cao and Yang (2015) proposed converting suitable learning algorithms into a summation form, allowing a deletion to update the affected summaries and recompute the model. SISA instead localizes retraining to affected shards (Bourtoule et al. 2021). It still needs the retained data and training state required by that procedure. The removal claim must specify its reference and verification method; a loss increase on deleted examples is different evidence from retraining without them. Method selection therefore depends on retained state, model quality, operational cost, and the removal guarantee the deployment must support.

Bourtoule, Lucas, Varun Chandrasekaran, Christopher A. Choquette-Choo, Hengrui Jia, Adelin Travers, Baiwu Zhang, David Lie, and Nicolas Papernot. 2021. “Machine Unlearning.” 2021 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 141–59. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp40001.2021.00019.


For one isolated erasure, SISA cuts retraining cost about 100 times; a daily batch that touches most shards erodes the saving.


Napkin Math 16.6: The cost of forgettingA user requests erasure of personal data under GDPR Article 17 (“Right to Erasure”). This scenario assumes that the approved response includes removing its influence from a model trained on 1 TB of data; that model-removal requirement is a scenario premise, not a conclusion derived from invoking the article.
Baseline (full retraining): In this sizing scenario, a 175B-parameter model at GPT-3 scale retrains on 1,024 NVIDIA A100 (80 GB SXM4) GPUs (dense FP16 \(\PeakRate =\) 312 TFLOP/s per accelerator at an assumed model FLOPs utilization (MFU) of about 32 percent) for approximately 36 days at a cost of roughly $4.6M.
Engineering fix: SISA training partitions data into \(\SisaShardCount=\) 100 independent shards, training 100 sub-models. For one datum confined to one shard, the example retrains that shard (1 percent of data). Assuming cost and elapsed time scale linearly with the data fraction at the same resource allocation gives $46,000 and approximately 8.6 hours. This simplified estimate omits slicing, checkpoint storage, validation, and deployment overhead; it is not a measured GPT-scale SISA result.
Trade-off: The scenario assumes an accuracy drop of 3–7 percent; the cost calculation does not establish that quality result. Serving must evaluate and aggregate 100 sub-models, with latency depending on parallelism and aggregation. Batch removal cost depends on how many of the 100 shards are touched. If the 1,000 requests/day arrive independently and uniformly across shards, a daily batch is likely to touch nearly all of them, eroding the sharding-only saving. Concentrated requests, batching policy, and saved slice states change the work. The operating comparison must therefore include the request distribution and response deadline, rather than the shard count alone.


The motivation for machine unlearning is reinforced by regulatory frameworks. Deletion or erasure rights under laws such as GDPR, CCPA, and similar statutes in other jurisdictions can create pressure to account for personal data used in training (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016; California Legislature 2023). Machine unlearning is a technical strategy for reducing or removing a deleted record’s influence where model state itself may retain personal data, but the legal requirements are context-dependent and not a universal statutory command to retrain every model. High-profile incidents in which generative models have reproduced personal content or copyrighted data highlight the practical urgency of integrating deletion-aware mechanisms into responsible system design.
From a systems perspective, machine unlearning introduces nontrivial architectural and operational requirements. Systems must be able to track data lineage, including which datapoints contributed to a given model version. This often requires structured metadata capture and training pipeline instrumentation. Additionally, systems must support user-facing deletion workflows, including authentication, submission, and feedback on deletion status. Verification may require maintaining versioned model registries, along with mechanisms for testing the stated removal guarantee against its reference training procedure. These operations must span data storage, training orchestration, model deployment, and auditing infrastructure, and they must be robust to failure or rollback.
Resource-constrained deployments amplify these challenges further. A TinyML device may lack the compute needed for retraining while still accepting a replacement model trained elsewhere. Unlearning then requires fleet inventory, authenticated updates, and evidence that affected versions have been replaced or retired. If no update path exists, operators must plan for physical servicing or withdrawal; initial data minimization reduces exposure but does not erase influence already present in deployed weights. Even in cloud-based systems, unlearning must coordinate model replicas, snapshots, and logs.
The need to remove training influence should be assessed during architecture and policy design, when teams can still plan the required lineage, retained state, and update paths. Retrofitting those capabilities after deployment may require reconstructing provenance or rebuilding training infrastructure. The assurance case should specify which removal obligations apply, how the chosen method will be evaluated, and how approved replacement models reach deployed instances.
Machine unlearning represents a shift in privacy thinking, from protecting what data is collected to controlling how long that data continues to affect system behavior. This lifecycle-oriented perspective introduces new challenges for model design, infrastructure planning, and regulatory compliance, while also providing a foundation for more user-controllable, transparent, and adaptable machine learning systems.

Self-Check: Question

An engineering team implements Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, and Aggregated (SISA) training with \(K = 100\) independent shards to support GDPR Article 17 (‘Right to Erasure’) for a 175B-parameter model. Under what operational workload does this sharded unlearning strategy lose its computational cost advantage over full model retraining?

When the model is quantized from FP16 to INT8 for edge deployment
When the daily volume of data erasure requests is high enough that requests touch essentially all \(K\) shards in every retraining batch
When the primary storage system transitions from NVMe SSDs to distributed object storage
When the training pipeline uses Adam optimizer instead of stochastic gradient descent

In Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), what are the two core operations applied to gradients before weight updates, and what are their primary systems impacts?

Gradient quantization to 4 bits and dropout pruning, reducing GPU memory by \(50\%\)
Gradient checkpointing and layer freezing, eliminating backpropagation overhead
Per-example gradient clipping to a maximum norm \(C\) and calibrated Gaussian noise addition, whose privacy bound requires sampling and composition accounting and whose compute and utility costs depend on the configuration
Spectral normalization of weight matrices and label smoothing, which eliminate adversarial vulnerability with zero compute overhead

Why can deleting a user’s record from a primary database leave an incomplete ML deletion workflow, and what evidence must a machine-unlearning procedure provide?
True or False: Once a neural network has been trained with DP-SGD under a privacy budget \(\epsilon = 1.0\), executing standard user inference queries in production consumes additional training-data privacy budget.
A privacy attack in which an adversary queries a deployed model’s prediction API to determine whether a specific target individual’s record was included in the training dataset is called a ____ attack.
