title: 16 Responsible AI
text:
A rejected loan applicant, a clinician questioning a risk score, and an auditor reconstructing a contested decision each need a different account of the same model output, on a different deadline. Serving them requires disclosure about the system as a whole, explanation methods whose cost and fidelity fit the deployment, and an appeal path through which the affected person can act on what is disclosed.


Machine learning systems are frequently criticized for their lack of interpretability. In many cases, models operate as opaque “black boxes,” producing outputs that are difficult for users, developers, and regulators to understand or scrutinize. This opacity presents a significant barrier to trust, particularly in high-stakes domains such as criminal justice, healthcare, and finance, where accountability and the right to recourse are important. For example, ProPublica’s evaluation of COMPAS, the recidivism-risk score whose provenance limits arose in section 16.6.1, found racial disparities in false positive and false negative rates.15 The proprietary nature of the system, combined with limited access to interpretability tools, hindered efforts to investigate or address the issue.
15 COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions): ProPublica’s 2016 analysis found Black defendants were falsely flagged as future criminals at nearly twice the rate of white defendants (45 percent vs. 23 percent false positive rate). The proprietary, black-box nature of the system limited full inspection of model internals and training data, making the source of the observed error-rate disparity harder to investigate. Error-rate parity and predictive parity are distinct criteria, so the evaluation must name the criterion rather than treating one rate as a complete fairness verdict.The COMPAS case separates the two properties defined among the core principles. What investigators lacked was transparency, meaning disclosure of data sources, training procedures, evaluation protocols, and known limitations. Explanations of individual scores would have been a different kind of evidence, about particular decisions rather than the system. An attribution describes how a method assigns influence under its assumptions rather than supplying a causal account, a normative justification, or a path to recourse. Section 16.7.3 develops the methods, their costs, and their limits; the principle established here is that both properties are obligations the architecture must provision.
The importance of explainability and transparency extends beyond technical considerations to legal requirements. In many jurisdictions, these principles are legal obligations rather than optional guidance. Under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects trigger Article 22 safeguards and related transparency duties, including meaningful information about the logic involved under access and notice provisions, subject to statutory exceptions (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016; European Data Protection Board 2018).16 Similar regulatory pressures in other domains reinforce the need to treat explainability and transparency as core architectural requirements.
16 GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) Article 22: Article 22 gives data subjects protections against decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects, with exceptions for contract necessity, authorization by law, or explicit consent plus safeguards (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016). Related notice and access provisions, including Article 15, require meaningful information about the logic involved for qualifying automated decision-making, and EDPB guidance treats those duties as part of a broader profiling and automated-decision governance regime (European Data Protection Board 2018). For ML systems, this creates an architectural constraint: high-stakes automated-decision systems need explanation, recourse, and governance infrastructure rather than opaque serving-only APIs.
European Parliament, and Council of the European Union. 2016. Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016. Official Journal of the European Union.

European Data Protection Board. 2018. Guidelines on Automated Individual Decision-Making and Profiling for the Purposes of Regulation 2016/679.
Implementing these principles requires anticipating the needs of different stakeholders, whose competing values and priorities are examined comprehensively in section 16.9.5.3. Designing for explainability and transparency therefore necessitates decisions about how and where to surface relevant information across the system lifecycle.
Transparency and explainability also support system reliability over time. As models are retrained or updated, mechanisms for interpretability and traceability allow detection of unexpected behavior, enable root cause analysis, and support governance. Embedded into the structure and operation of a system, these mechanisms provide the foundation for trust, oversight, and alignment with institutional and societal expectations.
While transparency and explainability enable stakeholders to understand system behavior, they do not guarantee that this behavior is equitable. A model can be fully transparent about how it makes decisions while still systematically disadvantaging certain groups. This distinction is why the fairness criteria of section 16.5.1 remain a separate test even for a fully transparent model.



Computational capacity, latency budget, interface design, and data access constrain both the explanation method and where it runs. A cloud worker can execute expensive SHAP or LIME attribution;17 a constrained endpoint may use a cheaper gradient-based saliency map18 if its runtime supports gradients. Devices unable to generate explanations locally may preserve bounded decision records for later analysis by a backend or during servicing, the per-tier split that the explainability row of table 4 records.
17 LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations): Introduced by Ribeiro et al. (2016), LIME explains individual predictions by perturbing the input, querying the black-box model many times, and fitting a weighted linear surrogate to approximate local behavior. The systems trade-off is that explanation latency scales with the number of perturbation samples and model-call cost, so production deployments often use sampling budgets, caching, asynchronous explanation workers, or model-specific methods when the architecture permits.
Ribeiro, Marco Tulio, Sameer Singh, and Carlos Guestrin. 2016. “Why Should I Trust You?: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier.” Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 1135–44. https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939778.
18 Saliency Maps: Gradient-based explanation that highlights which input regions most influenced a prediction by computing a backward pass, the same infrastructure used for training. Saliency methods are often cheaper than perturbation-heavy or subset-enumeration methods, making them attractive for edge and mobile deployments when the model supports gradients. The trade-off is that raw gradients can be noisy and may highlight input artifacts rather than meaningful features, so smoothing or repeated-gradient variants trade additional compute for more stable visualizations.Audience and timing further constrain explanation design. An end user may need a concise summary (“elevated heart rate during sleep”), while a developer or auditor may need attribution maps, concept activations, or decision traces. The required evidence depends on what each person must understand or do. A drone or industrial controller must keep explanation work within its control deadline or move that work off the critical path. Financial and clinical workflows likewise need a specified delivery deadline, which may allow analysis after the automated decision but before review or appeal. Planning for the audience and deadline, within the deployment’s resource limits, makes interpretability a design constraint.



A loan officer using a traditional rules-based system can identify the rule that produced a rejection: “The debt-to-income ratio exceeds 40 percent.” A neural network, however, produces a score through many interacting operations for which no single rule supplies the decision rationale. Explainability and interpretability provide bounded evidence about model behavior, such as feature influence, sensitivity, representative examples, or counterfactual changes. That evidence can support investigation and communication, but it becomes a justification only when the institution connects it to a valid decision policy, and it becomes recourse only when the user can take a feasible action that the system will honor.
Explanation evidence plays a role in system validation, error analysis, incident investigation, user communication, and some compliance workflows. In high-stakes domains such as healthcare, financial services, and autonomous decision systems, explanation methods can generate hypotheses about spurious correlations that engineers must test independently. For instance, a saliency or sensitivity analysis might indicate that a diagnostic model responds to image artifacts rather than medical features; controlled evaluation must then determine whether that dependence is causal and operationally significant. For qualifying automated decisions under GDPR-style access and notice provisions, systems may need to provide meaningful information about the logic involved, reinforcing the need for systematic support for explanation, documentation, and contestability.
Two scopes of explanation place different demands on the system. Local explanations characterize influences or sensitivities around an individual prediction, so their cost depends on which decisions are explained and whether results can be reused. Global explanations characterize broader model behavior, using model structure, representative inputs, or aggregated decision evidence. They may be computed offline or updated as new evidence arrives. Scope describes what the explanation covers; the method and delivery requirement determine where and when it runs.
Explainability methods can be broadly categorized based on when they operate and how they relate to model structure. Post-hoc methods are applied after training, but they are not necessarily black-box methods. Model-agnostic approaches such as LIME (Ribeiro et al. 2016) and KernelSHAP can operate through model queries, whereas input gradients, integrated gradients19 (Sundararajan et al. 2017), and gradient-weighted class activation mapping (GradCAM)20 (Selvaraju et al. 2017) require differentiable-model access to gradients or internal activations. Other SHAP implementations (Lundberg and Lee 2017) may exploit model structure.
19 Integrated Gradients: An attribution method that integrates gradients along the straight path from a baseline input to the actual input. Sensitivity requires a nonzero attribution when a single changed feature accounts for a changed prediction; implementation invariance requires identical attributions for functionally equivalent models (Sundararajan et al. 2017). The authors argued that most earlier attribution methods violate at least one of these axioms. These properties concern the exact method, while numerical integration introduces an approximation whose accuracy depends on the sampling of the path. The deployment must therefore budget repeated gradient evaluations and check approximation error rather than treating a fixed step count as sufficient for every model and input.
Sundararajan, Mukund, Ankur Taly, and Qiqi Yan. 2017. “Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 70: 3319–28.
20 GradCAM (Gradient-Weighted Class Activation Mapping): Selvaraju et al. (2017) generalized Class Activation Mapping to any convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture by using gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce spatial importance maps. Because it reuses gradient computation, GradCAM can be far cheaper than perturbation-heavy explanation methods, but whether it fits real-time medical imaging or autonomous-vehicle pipelines depends on the model, hardware, batch size, and explanation-frequency budget.
Selvaraju, R. R., M. Cogswell, A. Das, R. Vedantam, D. Parikh, and D. Batra. 2017. “Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization.” 2017 IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), 618–26. https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv.2017.74.
21 Shapley Values: From cooperative game theory, Shapley values fairly distribute a payoff among players based on marginal contributions across all possible orderings. In ML explainability, features are “players” and the prediction is the “payoff.” The mathematical guarantees (efficiency, symmetry, null player) make SHAP a widely used attribution framework with clear axiomatic appeal, but exact subset enumeration grows as \(2^{\AttributionFeatureCount}\) for \(\AttributionFeatureCount\) features, which is why production systems often rely on model-specific algorithms, sampling approximations, caching, or asynchronous explanation paths (Lundberg and Lee 2017).
Lundberg, Scott M., and Su-In Lee. 2017. “A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30: 4765–74.
Post-hoc approaches are widely used in image and tabular domains, where explanations can be rendered as saliency maps or feature rankings. To illustrate how SHAP attribution works in practice, consider a trained random forest model predicting loan approval (\(\text{approve}=1\), \(\text{deny}=0\)) based on three features: income, debt_ratio, and credit_score. For a specific applicant who was denied, with income of $45,000, debt ratio of 0.55 (55 percent of income goes to debt), and credit score of 620, the model outputs \(\Pr(\text{approve}) = 0.08\), that is, denial with probability 0.92. SHAP values, based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory,21 measure each feature’s contribution to moving the approval probability from a baseline (the expected prediction over a declared background distribution, here \(\Pr(\text{approve}) = 0.50\)) to this individual prediction.
The contribution of a feature depends on which other features are already known, so adding income first and adding it last can shift the prediction by different amounts. SHAP resolves that ambiguity by averaging a feature’s marginal contribution over every order in which the features could be added, under a specified value function. In this illustrative decomposition the averaged contributions are \(-0.05\) for income, \(-0.25\) for debt_ratio, and \(-0.12\) for credit_score.
Shapley values are additive, so the contributions sum from the baseline to the prediction: \(0.50 - 0.05 - 0.25 - 0.12 = 0.08 = \Pr(\text{approve})\), which is \(\Pr(\text{deny}) = 0.92\). Under this attribution setup, debt ratio has the largest assigned contribution to the output, followed by credit score and income. This ranking is a hypothesis about model sensitivity under the chosen background distribution, not evidence that debt ratio caused the decision or that lowering it below 40 percent would flip the output. A recourse claim requires a separately validated counterfactual that respects feature dependencies, immutable attributes, feasible user actions, and the decision policy that will apply when the user returns.



Exact subset enumeration grows exponentially; model-specific algorithms can avoid it.
The computational cost depends on the attribution algorithm. Enumerating all subsets would evaluate \(2^3=8\) coalitions in this example and \(2^{20}\approx1\) million for twenty features. A random forest need not use enumeration: TreeSHAP exploits tree structure to compute exact attributions under its supported value-function assumptions. KernelSHAP estimates contributions from sampled coalitions, while DeepSHAP propagates approximations through network components. Explanation capacity must therefore be budgeted for the chosen method rather than inferred from feature count alone.
Another post-hoc approach involves counterfactual explanations,22 which estimate how a model output changes under specified input modifications. These are relevant for decision-facing applications such as credit or hiring systems, but a mathematical output flip is not automatically recourse. A useful counterfactual must distinguish mutable from immutable features, preserve domain constraints and feature dependencies, identify an action within the user’s control, and remain valid under the institution’s future decision policy (Wachter et al. 2017). Counterfactual generation and validation therefore require domain models, policy versioning, and operational commitments in addition to constrained optimization.
22 Counterfactual Explanations: Formalized for ML by Wachter et al. (2017), counterfactuals answer how a modeled output would differ under a specified input change rather than establishing why a decision occurred. A counterfactual supports recourse only when the change is feasible, within the person’s control, consistent with domain constraints, and honored by the operative decision policy. Generating candidates requires constrained optimization; validating recourse additionally requires policy ownership, stability testing, and monitoring for changes that invalidate the promised action.
Wachter, Sandra, Brent Mittelstadt, and Chris Russell. 2017. “Counterfactual Explanations Without Opening the Black Box: Automated Decisions and the GDPR.” SSRN Electronic Journal 31: 841. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3063289.

Kim, B., M. Wattenberg, J. Gilmer, C. Cai, J. Wexler, F. Viegas, and R. Sayres. 2018. “Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV).” Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 80: 2668–77.
A third class of techniques relies on concept-based explanations, which attempt to align learned model features with human-interpretable concepts. For example, testing with concept activation vectors (TCAV) represents user-defined concepts as vectors in activation space and tests how sensitive a model’s predictions are to those concepts in its internal representation (Kim et al. 2018). These methods are especially useful in domains where subject matter experts expect explanations in familiar semantic terms. However, they require training data with concept annotations or auxiliary models for concept detection, which introduces additional infrastructure dependencies.
Post-hoc methods answer method-specific questions about model behavior. Even an exact attribution under a chosen value function does not recover a causal rationale or justify the decision policy. Approximate methods add estimation or surrogate error to those interpretive limits. Evaluation must therefore establish both what the method computes and whether that evidence serves the intended debugging, communication, or review task.
Inherently interpretable models expose a decision structure that the intended audience can inspect. Small decision trees, short rule lists, and sparse linear models with meaningful features can support this goal; a very large tree or high-dimensional linear model may not. Nearest-neighbor comparisons likewise require an understandable similarity metric and representative examples. Interpretability therefore depends on structure, features, and audience, not merely the model-family label. In high-stakes applications, model selection should evaluate whether a sufficiently accurate, inspectable model meets the task before assuming that post-hoc explanations are necessary (Rudin 2019).

Rudin, C. 2019. “Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead.” Nature Machine Intelligence 1 (5): 206–15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-019-0048-x.
Figure 8 arranges six model families along an interpretability continuum, grouping them into models that are interpretable by design (sparse linear models via coefficients, small decision trees via split paths), hybrid architectures (prototype and concept models via exemplars), and models requiring post-hoc explanation (tree ensembles via TreeSHAP, deep networks via gradients and SHAP, and foundation models via probing). While this ordering provides a structural heuristic across model families, dimensionality and scale can shift boundaries: a million-node decision tree or dense linear regression can prove just as opaque as a deep neural network. This distinction is central to choosing an appropriate model for a given application, particularly in settings where regulatory scrutiny or stakeholder trust is essential.







Figure 8: Model Interpretability Spectrum: A heuristic ordering by model family. Small linear models and shallow decision trees can offer transparent reasoning, while neural networks typically require post-hoc explanation techniques; size, feature meaning, and audience can move any model along the spectrum. This distinction guides model selection based on application needs, prioritizing transparency in regulated domains or when stakeholder trust is important. The label under each family names the handle an explanation typically uses.



Hybrid approaches aim to combine the representational capacity of deep models with the transparency of interpretable components. Concept bottleneck models (Koh et al. 2020), for example, first predict intermediate, interpretable variables and then use a simple classifier to produce the final prediction. ProtoPNet models (Chen et al. 2019) classify examples by comparing them to learned prototypes, offering visual analogies for users to understand predictions. These hybrid methods are attractive in domains that demand partial transparency, but they introduce new system design considerations, such as the need to store and index learned prototypes and surface them at inference time.

Koh, Pang Wei, Thao Nguyen, Yew Siang Tang, Stephen Mussmann, Emma Pierson, Been Kim, and Percy Liang. 2020. “Concept Bottleneck Models.” Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2020, 13-18 July 2020, Virtual Event, Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 119: 5338–48.

Chen, Chaofan, Oscar Li, Daniel Tao, Alina Barnett, Cynthia Rudin, and Jonathan Su. 2019. “This Looks Like That: Deep Learning for Interpretable Image Recognition.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2019, NeurIPS 2019, December 8-14, 2019, Vancouver, BC, Canada, edited by Hanna M. Wallach, Hugo Larochelle, Alina Beygelzimer, Florence d’Alché-Buc, Emily B. Fox, and Roman Garnett. Curran Associates.

Olah, C., N. Cammarata, L. Schubert, G. Goh, M. Petrov, and S. Carter. 2020. “Zoom in: An Introduction to Circuits.” Distill 5 (3): e00024–001. https://doi.org/10.23915/distill.00024.001.

Geiger, Atticus, Hanson Lu, Thomas Icard, and Christopher Potts. 2021. “Causal Abstractions of Neural Networks.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2021, NeurIPS 2021, December 6-14, 2021, Virtual, edited by Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Alina Beygelzimer, Yann N. Dauphin, Percy Liang, and Jennifer Wortman Vaughan. Curran Associates.
Work such as Olah et al. (2020) and Geiger et al. (2021) applies mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer the internal operations of neural networks. This line of work, inspired by program analysis and neuroscience, attempts to map neurons, layers, or activation patterns to specific computational functions. Claims about such mechanisms require instrumentation and tests that support the proposed interpretation. These research methods can contribute evidence about internal computation, but do not establish a complete audit of every deployed model.
From a systems perspective, explainability introduces a number of architectural dependencies. Explanations must be generated, stored, surfaced, and evaluated within system constraints. The required infrastructure may include explanation APIs, memory for storing attribution maps, visualization libraries, and logging mechanisms that capture intermediate model behavior. Models must often be instrumented with hooks or configured to support repeated evaluations, particularly for explanation methods that require sampling, perturbation, or backpropagation.
These requirements interact directly with deployment constraints and impose performance costs that must be factored into system design. SHAP and LIME can require repeated model evaluations, perturbation sampling, surrogate fitting, or subset enumeration, while counterfactual methods require constrained optimization (Lundberg and Lee 2017; Ribeiro et al. 2016; Wachter et al. 2017). In production deployments, these costs translate into concrete architecture choices: explanations may need asynchronous workers, sampled explanation rates, caching, or separate models chosen partly for interpretability.
Gradient-based attribution can require fewer model evaluations than perturbation-heavy methods, but the deployment must support gradient computation and its memory requirements. A training framework’s capabilities do not imply that a constrained inference runtime exposes the same operations. Lower computational cost also does not establish explanation quality. Teams must evaluate fidelity and stability for the intended use, including any precomputed summaries or surrogate rules chosen to meet the delivery budget.
Storage requirements also scale significantly with explanation needs. Storing SHAP values for tabular data requires approximately 4–8 bytes per feature per prediction, so monthly storage is 30 million predictions times the feature count times 4–8 bytes for a system logging 1 million predictions daily. Gradient attribution maps for images can require 1–10 MB per explanation depending on resolution; logging every image explanation at the same 1 million-per-day rate would require roughly 30–300 TB per month unless explanations are sampled, compressed, or retained for a shorter window. These volumes necessitate careful data lifecycle management and retention policies.
Explainability spans the full machine learning lifecycle. During development, interpretability tools are used for dataset auditing, concept validation, and early debugging. At inference time, they support accountability, decision verification, and user communication. Postdeployment, explanations may be logged, surfaced in audits, or queried during error investigations. System design must support each of these phases, ensuring that explanation tools are integrated into training frameworks, model serving infrastructure, and user-facing applications.
Compression and optimization techniques also affect explainability. Pruning, quantization, and architectural simplifications often used in TinyML or mobile settings can distort internal representations or disable gradient flow, degrading the reliability of attribution-based explanations. In such cases, interpretability must be validated postoptimization to ensure that it remains meaningful and trustworthy. If explanation quality is important, these transformations must be treated as part of the design constraint space.
Explainability requires budgeted evidence collection and delivery across the lifecycle. The audience, question, and response deadline determine whether that work belongs in training, the serving path, an asynchronous worker, or an audit process. Designing these paths together allows an institution to preserve decision evidence and deliver an appropriate explanation when someone must act on it.
The sociotechnical challenges of explainability center on the gap between technical explanations and human understanding. While algorithms can generate feature attributions and gradient maps, stakeholders often need explanations that align with their mental models, domain expertise, and decision-making processes. A radiologist reviewing an AI-generated diagnosis needs explanations that reference medical concepts and visual patterns, not abstract neural network activations. This translation challenge requires ongoing collaboration between technical teams and domain experts to develop explanation formats that are both technically accurate and practically meaningful. Explanations can shape human decision-making in unexpected ways, creating new responsibilities for how explanatory information is presented and interpreted. That gap between a technically valid explanation and a usable one is the first instance of a broader problem. Every control in this chapter operates inside human workflows and institutions that no model-level method governs.



Explanations serve accountability only when stakeholders can understand and challenge system decisions. Transparency allows users, developers, auditors, and regulators to understand how a system functions, assess its limitations, and identify sources of harm. Transparency alone, however, is not sufficient. In high-stakes domains, individuals and institutions must be able to challenge, correct, or reverse system behavior when necessary, rather than merely inspect it. This capacity for contestability, which refers to the ability to interrogate and contest a system’s decisions, is an important feature of accountability.
Transparency in machine learning systems typically focuses on disclosure: revealing how models are trained, what data they rely on, what assumptions are embedded in their design, and what known limitations affect their use. Documentation tools such as model cards and datasheets for datasets support this goal by formalizing system metadata in a structured, reproducible format. These resources can improve governance, support compliance, and inform user expectations. However, transparency as disclosure does not guarantee meaningful control. Even when technical details are available, users may lack institutional support, interface tools, or procedural access to contest a decision that adversely affects them.
To move from transparency to contestability, machine learning systems must integrate mechanisms for explanation, recourse, and feedback. Explanation provides understandable reasons for system outputs, tailored to the operational context and needs of the person receiving them. Recourse identifies feasible changes through which individuals could receive a different outcome under the stated decision policy. A proposed change needs to be actionable for that person; a counterfactual prediction alone does not guarantee an outcome after the model or policy changes. Feedback enables users and domain experts to dispute outcomes, report errors, or signal concerns, routing those signals into oversight processes and model updates.
These mechanisms can be missing from the user-facing workflow even when internal documentation exists. A mobile loan application might display a rejection without explaining how to submit additional information or reach an appeal reviewer. An external appeal process can still exist, but users need a discoverable route to it and access to the evidence relevant to their case. Similarly, a clinical model may produce a risk score without giving the physician enough context to question its use for a particular patient. If subgroup errors are neither observable nor contestable, the resulting harm becomes harder to diagnose and correct.
From a systems perspective, enabling contestability requires coordination across technical and institutional components. Models must expose sufficient information to support explanation. Interfaces must surface this information in a usable and timely way. Organizational processes must be in place to review feedback, respond to appeals, and update system behavior. Logging and auditing infrastructure must track user interventions and override decisions alongside model outputs. Human overrides and decision abstention can support this process only when qualified reviewers have capacity, evidence, and authority to resolve the deferred cases within the required deadline.
Implementing contestability imposes concrete infrastructure costs that scale with system throughput and complexity. Storing the necessary metadata to reconstruct a decision (input features, model version, and decision thresholds) requires persistent storage whose footprint depends on feature dimensionality, explanation payloads, and retention windows. Generating on-demand explanations using Shapley values or counterfactuals can add enough latency that contested decisions often need asynchronous processing queues to preserve serving service level agreements (SLAs). Meeting record-keeping and automatic-logging obligations for high-risk systems under frameworks such as the EU AI Act requires storage, provenance, retention controls, and oversight capacity to be budgeted as part of the inference fleet rather than as a separate policy artifact (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024).

War Story 16.1: Apple Card: A systems reconstruction of contested decisions (2019)Context: In 2019, Apple and Goldman Sachs faced intense public scrutiny after a customer reported a credit limit 20\(\times\) that offered to his wife despite joint tax filings. Other customers raised similar concerns about unequal terms (New York State Department of Financial Services 2021).
Evidence boundary: The public record documents complaints, the investigation, the regulator’s finding, and changes to appeal policy. It does not disclose the underwriting pipeline’s latency target or internal explanation architecture. The systems account below is therefore an explicit reconstruction, not a report of Apple or Goldman Sachs implementation details.
Reconstructed mechanism: A low-latency underwriting service that returns only a limit and generic adverse-action reason leaves support staff unable to inspect the decision snapshot, distinguish data errors from policy effects, or route a contested outcome to a reviewer. The missing interface is broader than feature attribution: it includes versioned input provenance, policy and model versions, reasons appropriate to the decision process, appeal state, and authority to correct an error.
Observed impact: The New York Department of Financial Services found no violation of fair-lending law in its investigation, but the complaints still exposed a trust and contestability failure: customers and frontline staff lacked a satisfactory account of how apparently inconsistent outcomes could be reviewed (New York State Department of Financial Services 2021).
Systems lesson: High-stakes decision systems need a contestability interface, not merely an attribution API. A defensible architecture preserves the decision-time evidence needed for audit, generates appropriate reasons without claiming that attribution is causation, routes appeals to an authorized human, records remediation, and tests the full workflow under its latency and retention constraints.



New York State Department of Financial Services. 2021. Report on Apple Card Investigation. New York State Department of Financial Services.
The Apple Card reconstruction names the pieces such a system lacks. One architectural pattern that supplies them is a contestability stack, analogous to distributed tracing in microservices, that coordinates four coupled stages across the operational pipeline. Decision provenance preserves a verifiable link from each output back to its governing policy, model version, and input snapshot, protected by authenticated logs or cryptographic integrity checks. Explanation generation budgets explanation methods tailored for appeals, audits, and routine communication, offloading compute-intensive methods to asynchronous workers while keeping lightweight techniques on the request path. When decisions are challenged, appeal routing directs contested cases to qualified human reviewers equipped with domain context. Closing the loop, outcome tracking records whether the appeal upheld or overturned the machine decision, feeding empirical discrepancies back into evaluation and retraining. Missing decision-time records can prevent investigators from reconstructing a contested decision, even if aggregate debugging remains possible; the required records follow the investigation and remedy contract.



Provenance anchors every appeal; tracked outcomes loop back into retraining.
The stack need not run where the decision runs. An edge or TinyML endpoint can hand its decision records to a backend review process at the next synchronization or servicing visit, which lengthens the appeal’s evidence path without removing the obligation to offer one. In every tier, transparency supports accountability only when users and institutions can use the disclosed information to question and correct automated decisions.

Self-Check: Question

Because cooperative game theory axioms prohibit computing feature contributions on tabular data
Because exact SHAP requires accessing the client’s raw hardware registers during inference

In the chapter’s explicitly hypothetical systems reconstruction of the Apple Card controversy, which architectural omission would prevent customer support from explaining or contesting credit decisions?

Explain the two fundamental axioms satisfied by Integrated Gradients—Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance—and why they make Integrated Gradients superior to vanilla input gradients.
Why do local and global explanations place different demands on explanation infrastructure?

Local explanations characterize an individual prediction; global explanations characterize broader model behavior using model structure, representative inputs, or aggregated evidence. Their methods and delivery deadlines determine execution and capacity needs.

title: 16 Responsible AI
text:
A model that withstands every tested perturbation can still cause harm when the operating environment leaves its validated envelope or when its objective rewards the wrong behavior. Safety governance therefore spans robustness claims bounded by a threat model, control surfaces for generative systems whose outputs cannot be enumerated in advance, and the alignment of the objective itself as systems act with greater autonomy.


Safety and robustness connect technical failure behavior to its consequences for people. Evidence that a model tolerates specified hardware faults, adversarial attacks, or distribution shifts supports a bounded robustness claim. It does not establish that every deployment is safe or that the objective serves users’ interests. A model may tolerate the tested bit flips and perturbations yet fail under untested conditions, or reliably optimize an objective misaligned with user welfare.


↩︎ The three robustness pillars, environmental shifts, input-level attacks, and system-level faults such as bit flips, are established in The three pillars of robust AI.
The governance task is to connect robustness evidence to the consequences of failure. An evaluation may bound errors under a specified input variation without establishing that the surrounding workflow is safe. The assurance case must therefore name the operating conditions, affected population, fallback action, and owner who can restrict deployment when those conditions no longer hold.
Ensuring safety and robustness in practice requires a declared operating envelope, evaluation within that envelope, and fallback behavior for unsupported or unknown conditions. This requires managing input variability while addressing how models respond to unexpected correlations, rare events, and deliberate attempts to induce failure. Automated-driving failures show why the envelope must cover more than the model, because they can combine perception, prediction, safety-driver, and organizational-control problems rather than reduce to a single model error; section 16.8.5 examines one such crash.
One illustrative failure mode is the adversarial input, a perturbation that looks benign to people yet changes the model’s prediction. Such vulnerabilities appear across image, audio, text, and structured data, so a robustness claim must name the perturbations it covers. These behaviors highlight that robustness is an operational property of how systems interact with real-world complexity, not a property evaluated solely during training.


↩︎ Adversarial perturbations and the attacks that construct them are established in Adversarial attacks.
A related challenge is distribution shift, the mismatch between training data and the conditions encountered in deployment. Whether due to seasonality, demographic changes, sensor degradation, or environmental variability, such shifts can degrade model reliability even in the absence of adversarial manipulation. Addressing distribution shift challenges requires systematic approaches to detecting and adapting to changing conditions.
Responsible machine learning design treats robustness as a systemic requirement. Addressing it requires more than improving individual model performance. It involves designing systems that anticipate uncertainty, surface their limitations, and support fallback behavior when predictive confidence is low. This includes practices such as setting confidence thresholds, supporting abstention from decision-making, and integrating human oversight into operational workflows. These mechanisms are important for building systems that degrade gracefully rather than failing silently or unpredictably.
These individual-model considerations extend to broader system requirements. Safety and robustness also impose requirements at the architectural and organizational level. Decisions about how models are monitored, how failures are detected, and how updates are governed all influence whether a system can respond effectively to changing conditions. Responsible design demands that robustness be treated not as a property of isolated models but as a constraint that shapes the overall behavior of machine learning systems. The same system-level perspective determines which safety controls each deployment tier can run.


The latency budget constrains which safety checks can run before an action. A cloud service may combine uncertainty estimators, distributional-change detectors, adversarial input filtering, and API rate limiting. A control loop with a millisecond budget needs bounded local checks and fallback actions that meet its deadline, with heavier analysis deferred to fleet services, the division the safety row of table 4 records by tier. Even a disconnected TinyML endpoint can execute input-range checks or watchdog logic; the absence of a remote update channel instead limits how operators change those controls after deployment.
Fallback is itself a latency-budget problem. A delivery robot that abstains23 when pedestrian-detection confidence is low still needs a validated response before the physical safety deadline. A bounded local maneuver may place it in a safe state while a human reviewer resolves the case on a longer timescale. The response and review paths therefore need separate deadlines and capacity budgets. Whether the system can fail visibly, controllably, and safely depends on sensing, confidence estimation, fallback routing, and recovery. Those choices also define who can observe harm, who can intervene, and who remains accountable for the outcome.
23 Abstention: The practice of refusing predictions when confidence falls below a threshold. Abstention can reduce high-risk errors, but only by shifting some cases to fallback infrastructure such as human reviewers, rule-based defaults, or escalation queues. A driving system must select a validated fallback, such as a minimal-risk maneuver; handing control to a driver is viable only if a driver is present, ready, and has sufficient response time. Medical AI may route ambiguous cases to specialist review, subject to its own queue-capacity and response-time budget.



Robust AI owns the attack models, robustness evaluations, adversarial training, certification, corruption testing, drift detection, and abstention mechanisms. Governance consumes those mechanisms through an evidence interface. The responsible-AI question is not which attack or defense to implement, but whether the robustness claim has a bounded operating envelope, evidence appropriate to the threat model, an accountable owner, and a rule that invalidates approval.
A robustness claim should specify the protected task and population, attacker knowledge and capabilities, perturbation or corruption set, evaluation distribution, model and preprocessing versions, quality and latency constraints, fallback behavior, and known exclusions. Empirical attack results show observed failures under a test protocol; they do not establish robustness against adaptive or untested attacks. A certificate proves a property only for its stated norm, radius, confidence, and model configuration; it does not establish safety for the end-to-end workflow. Governance records those boundaries so a narrow result cannot be promoted into a general safety assertion.
The evidence bundle must also connect model behavior to system action. It identifies who owns the robustness claim, which team can stop serving, how abstentions and low-confidence cases are routed, which telemetry detects departure from the approved envelope, and how an incident reaches affected users and downstream operators. A fallback must meet the relevant safety deadline. A monitoring signal becomes an operational safeguard only when it reaches an authorized response path, whether that response is local containment, restricted use, or a validated rollback.
Approval expires when the threat model, model, preprocessing, sensor, data distribution, tool access, deployment environment, or fallback path changes materially. The invalidation rule should state which change triggers a full red-team evaluation, which permits a narrower regression suite, and which requires restricted operation while evidence is rebuilt. This ownership-and-invalidation contract is the governance contribution: it turns those robustness mechanisms into a reviewable claim that remains bounded over time.



Generative AI does not replace core fairness, privacy, and explainability concerns; it changes the control surface. Instead of only auditing labels or feature attributions, operators of large language models (LLMs) such as Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) must govern prompts, retrieved context, reward models, and open-ended outputs. Fairness remains concerned with how quality, refusals, errors, representation, and access are distributed across people and groups, but open-ended outputs make those quantities harder to define and sample. Alignment introduces a separate problem, which is keeping stochastic outputs and actions consistent with intended objectives and policies across a combinatorial range of prompts. The two questions differ in kind. Fairness asks how benefits, errors, and burdens are distributed among affected people; alignment asks whether an optimizing system pursues the objective its designers and legitimate stakeholders intended. An aligned system can implement an unfair objective faithfully, and a statistically fair classifier can still optimize the wrong social goal, so production systems need both fairness evaluation and behavioral alignment rather than relabeling one as the other. Figure 9 diagrams this multi-stage alignment pipeline across two coupled lanes: an upper execution path that advances the policy from pretraining through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to proximal policy optimization (PPO), and a lower supervision path where human preference comparisons train a reward model \(\RewardModel(\ModelInput, \GeneratedResponse)\). The reward signal drives PPO updates, while the frozen SFT checkpoint supplies a reference for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence penalty. The penalty discourages departure from that reference; it does not impose a hard bound on every response or establish policy compliance.







Figure 9: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline: The top lane carries the policy from a pretrained model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and proximal policy optimization (PPO) to the aligned policy. The bottom lane turns human judgment into an objective: raters compare sampled SFT outputs, and those comparisons train a reward model whose score drives PPO. The SFT model also serves as the KL reference that limits how far PPO moves the policy, so every human preference reaches the weights only through the learned reward model.



A common instruction-tuning pipeline in large language models circa 2022–2024 uses reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)24 as a sociotechnical bridge between human preferences and model weights. Training a reward model on human comparisons produces a scalar scoring function for sampled responses, and collecting those judgments carries a direct cost. In this scenario, 50,000 to 500,000 pairwise comparisons at $0.50 to $5 per label put the labeling budget between $25,000 and $2.5M, a hundredfold spread set by how many judgments the organization buys and how expert its raters must be. Proximal policy optimization (PPO) then updates the policy using those rewards and a penalty for divergence from the supervised baseline. This process can create an alignment tax, a regression in some capability metrics when optimization shifts toward preference or safety objectives; its direction and magnitude depend on the model, data, objectives, and evaluation suite rather than following a universal percentage. The reliance on human raters also introduces a representativeness gap. If the labeling budget buys judgments from only a narrow demographic slice, the resulting model may encode that pool’s preferences while performing differently for other populations. Constitutional AI offers an alternative engineering path, using explicit principles to guide AI feedback on outputs (Bai et al. 2022), which changes rather than eliminates the questions of whose values are represented and how they are governed.
24 RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): Christiano et al. (2017) demonstrated deep reinforcement learning from human preferences by training agents from non-expert comparisons between trajectory segments. In the LLM setting, Ouyang et al. (2022) operationalized a related pipeline for InstructGPT: supervised fine-tuning from demonstrations, reward-model training from ranked model outputs, and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning against the learned reward model. The systems cost is an additional human-feedback data pipeline, reward-model training and evaluation, and governance over rater instructions; the representativeness of the rater pool and labeling policy shapes whose preferences the model internalizes.
Christiano, P. F., J. Leike, T. B. Brown, M. Martic, S. Legg, and D. Amodei. 2017. “Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems 2017, December 4-9, 2017, Long Beach, CA, USA, edited by Isabelle Guyon, Ulrike von Luxburg, Samy Bengio, Hanna M. Wallach, Rob Fergus, S. V. N. Vishwanathan, and Roman Garnett. Curran Associates.

Ouyang, L., J. Wu, X. Jiang, D. Almeida, C. L. Wainwright, P. Mishkin, C. Zhang, et al. 2022. “Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 27730–44. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2011.

Bai, Yuntao et al. 2022. Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback.

↩︎ The four-model coordination that a PPO-style RLHF step imposes on distributed training is established in The multi-model coordination problem.

In retrieval-augmented generation architectures, responsibility extends beyond the core model. An LLM may pass alignment evaluations yet generate harmful responses when retrieval supplies context outside those evaluations. A retrieval index that disproportionately surfaces biased historical documents can influence the resulting answers despite safety training. Context filtering is one possible control, alongside source selection, retrieval evaluation, and output checks. Its effectiveness must be tested on the intended use; a toxicity filter does not establish that retrieved material or generated answers are unbiased.
In many LLM serving stacks, the system prompt operates as an early configuration control alongside retrieval filtering, policy classifiers, telemetry, and rollout gates. These instructions (for example, “You are a helpful assistant. Do not provide medical advice.”) express intended behavior; they do not independently enforce authorization or prevent every prohibited output. When one model serves many products, each with its own system prompt, managing the prompts becomes a distributed configuration-management problem akin to weight distribution. An unversioned prompt change can alter behavior across many interactions, so prompt version control, alignment regression testing, and gradual rollouts belong in the release process.
Together, system prompts and RLHF alignments act as important, yet fragile, technical guardrails. Jailbreaks and other edge cases can violate the policy learned during training; the reward model is not necessarily a runtime filter. Safety therefore requires evaluating the deployed control system as well as its training objective. Each of these guardrails, like the privacy and robustness controls before it, is credible only with evidence that it still holds in the system that actually runs.



When a system acts faster than anyone can review its individual decisions, the governing question changes. It is no longer only whether the outputs are fair, private, or explainable, but whether the objective the system optimizes still serves the people it acts on, and what bounds its actions before review. Human launch authority remains necessary, but continuous human intervention may be unavailable. AI safety examines how systems can optimize objectives misaligned with human intentions, operate in unpredictable environments, or pursue goals through methods their designers never anticipated, and which controls can bound those actions.
The controls of the preceding sections retain their roles, but none governs autonomous action by itself. Bias detection (section 16.5.1.6) yields metrics rather than a remediation policy. A perception system that under-detects pedestrians with mobility aids needs an operating envelope that connects the metric to bounded runtime responses and to fleet-level investigation or suspension. Explanation (section 16.7.3) needs an audience and an action path; SHAP attributions from an autonomous trading system cannot influence a decision if no control consumes them before thousands of trades execute. Differential privacy (section 16.6.3) bounds leakage about a protected unit without determining whether the objective serves that person’s welfare, so a recommender can satisfy a local differential privacy guarantee while optimizing an engagement metric that rewards harmful content. Each method needs a defined connection to the runtime controls and human authority that can respond to its findings.
AI safety work frames the resulting risks as accidents from wrong objectives, reward hacking, scalable supervision, safe exploration, and distributional shift (Amodei et al. 2016), while alignment work emphasizes keeping a system’s pursued objectives consistent with human intentions over time (Russell 2021). A central challenge is that capable ML models often optimize proxy metrics, such as loss functions, reward functions, or engagement signals, that do not fully capture human values.
25 CTR (Click-Through Rate) and Engagement Optimization: Click-through rate, watch time, and related engagement measures are convenient proxies for user satisfaction. YouTube’s published recommender architecture discusses ranking videos by expected watch time (Covington et al. 2016), while later audits studied recommendation paths through politically extreme content (Ribeiro et al. 2020). The systems lesson is that proxy metric selection is an architectural decision with system-wide behavioral consequences, not merely a hyperparameter choice.
Covington, Paul, Jay Adams, and Emre Sargin. 2016. “Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations.” Proceedings of the 10th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems, 191–98. https://doi.org/10.1145/2959100.2959190.

Ribeiro, M. H., R. Ottoni, R. West, V. A. F. Almeida, and Jr. Meira Wagner. 2020. “Auditing Radicalization Pathways on YouTube.” Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 131–41. https://doi.org/10.1145/3351095.3372879.
26 Reward Hacking: When an AI system maximizes its reward function through unintended means that violate designer intent. A hypothetical cleaning robot rewarded for collected dirt might create messes it can clean up, illustrating how a proxy can reward behavior contrary to the intended task. Specification gaming is an overlapping term; the gap may lie in the stated objective or in its implementation, so neither term is restricted to software bugs. For production ML systems, reward hacking manifests subtly: recommendation models that maximize engagement by promoting addictive content, or chatbots that maximize helpfulness ratings by being sycophantic rather than accurate. The failure mode scales with model capability.Recommendation systems illustrate why a measurable engagement proxy such as clicks or watch time25 needs evaluation against broader user welfare. A published production architecture optimizes expected watch time (Covington et al. 2016), while a separate audit examines recommendation paths through politically extreme content (Ribeiro et al. 2020). Those observations motivate investigating proxy misalignment; together they do not prove that a particular reward objective caused an individual user’s beliefs or behavior. Specification gaming and reward hacking26 describe the risk that optimizing a measured objective defeats its intended purpose (Amodei et al. 2016). Figure 10 illustrates a possible feedback mechanism in which engagement rewards content that undermines long-term user value and the resulting interactions become new training data. Establishing that mechanism in a deployment requires evidence about both the policy’s effects and the welfare criterion it is meant to serve.







Figure 10: Reward Hacking Loop: Maximizing measurable rewards, like clicks, can incentivize unintended model behaviors that undermine the intended goal of user satisfaction. In the illustrated possible feedback loop, the recommender serves content and the resulting clicks enter later training data. If optimizing clicks rewards behavior that undermines long-term user value, retraining can reinforce the mismatch. Establishing this mechanism requires evidence about the deployed policy and the user-value criterion; targeting a proxy does not by itself prove that it has ceased to provide useful information.



Norbert Wiener wrote, “if we use, to achieve our purposes, a mechanical agency with whose operation we cannot interfere effectively… we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we desire” (Wiener 1960).

Wiener, N. 1960. “Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation: As Machines Learn They May Develop Unforeseen Strategies at Rates That Baffle Their Programmers.” Science 131 (3410): 1355–58. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.131.3410.1355.
Wiener’s warning becomes a systems requirement when optimization runs beyond continuous human intervention. Value alignment asks whether the objective embedded in the model, reward function, and deployment policy continues to represent the human purpose the system was meant to serve. As Russell (2021) argues in Human-Compatible Artificial Intelligence, much AI research presumes that the objectives to be optimized are known and fixed, focusing instead on the effectiveness of optimization rather than the design of objectives themselves.
In deployment, the hard part is specifying an objective that remains valid as systems interact with dynamic environments, multiple stakeholders, and feedback loops. Static objective functions and reward signals cannot encode all of those conditions. Value-Sensitive Design (Friedman 1996) supplies a formal process for eliciting stakeholder values and incorporating them into system design, but the systems obligation is broader: objective design, oversight, and postdeployment monitoring must be treated as coupled controls.

Friedman, B. 1996. “Value-Sensitive Design.” Interactions 3 (6): 16–23. https://doi.org/10.1145/242485.242493.
Without that coupling, intelligent systems may pursue narrow performance objectives (for example, accuracy, engagement, or throughput) while producing socially undesirable outcomes. Achieving robust alignment under such conditions remains an open and important area of research in ML systems. The resulting failure modes are familiar in systems that optimize complex objectives. In reinforcement learning, for example, models often learn to exploit unintended aspects of the reward function, the reward hacking pattern of figure 10.
Such failures arise when variables not explicitly included in the objective are manipulated in ways that maximize reward while violating human intent. RLHF, whose pipeline and costs appear in section 16.8.3, attempts to narrow that gap by learning a reward model from human preferences. Policy optimization still uses a scalar reward, so its success depends on how faithfully that learned signal represents the intended behavior (Christiano et al. 2017; Ouyang et al. 2022).

Ngo, Richard, Lawrence Chan, and Sören Mindermann. 2022. “The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective.” ArXiv Preprint abs/2209.00626.
Human-feedback training can improve behavior on its evaluations while leaving deeper governance risks unresolved. In their analysis of learned-reward optimization, Ngo et al. (2022) examine possible failure modes beyond RLHF, including exploitation of human evaluation blind spots, misaligned goals outside the training distribution, and behavior that undermines oversight. These are risks to investigate under specified assumptions, not evidence that every deployed model exhibits them. An assurance case must distinguish a proposed failure mechanism from an observed capability and from a demonstrated deployment failure.
These concerns are not limited to speculative scenarios. In their foundational taxonomy of concrete AI safety problems, Amodei et al. (2016) outline five practical systems challenges: avoiding negative side effects during policy execution, mitigating reward hacking, ensuring scalable oversight when ground-truth evaluation is costly, designing safe exploration strategies that prevent catastrophic damage, and achieving robustness to distributional shift. For fleet operators, the five challenges map in order onto five control-plane requirements: constraining side effects, instrumenting reward-hack monitors, budgeting scalable review capacity, bounding exploration envelopes, and stress-testing distribution shift prior to rollout. Each requirement becomes more acute as systems are scaled up, deployed across diverse settings, and integrated with real-time feedback or continual learning.

Amodei, D., C. Olah, J. Steinhardt, P. Christiano, J. Schulman, and D. Mané. 2016. “Concrete Problems in AI Safety.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1606.06565, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1606.06565.



Value alignment concerns the objective; autonomy concerns the operating envelope within which a system pursues that objective without a human reviewing each action. The consequences of autonomous systems operating with limited real-time human oversight are especially visible in autonomous driving. In October 2023, the California Department of Motor Vehicles suspended Cruise’s deployment and driverless testing permits over safety concerns; testing with a safety driver was outside that suspension (CNBC 2023). The 2018 Uber fatality in Tempe, Arizona shows how such a failure spans the whole system rather than one model. The National Transportation Safety Board found that the vehicle, in autonomous mode, failed to classify a pedestrian pushing a bicycle as a pedestrian requiring avoidance, and that perception, prediction, the safety driver’s role, and organizational safety controls all contributed (National Transportation Safety Board 2019). For governance, the lesson is that detecting an object did not establish that the system would act safely on the detection, and no single component owner could have certified the outcome alone.

CNBC. 2023. California DMV Suspends Cruise’s Self-Driving Car Permits. CNBC news article.

National Transportation Safety Board. 2019. Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, Tempe, Arizona, March 18, 2018. HAR-19/03. National Transportation Safety Board.

↩︎ The Uber crash timeline, from unstable classification through suppressed action to the late operator alert, is established in Edge device vulnerabilities.

Reuters. 2023. Human-Machine Teams Driven by AI Are about to Reshape Warfare. Reuters news article.

Centre for International Governance Innovation. 2023. Who Is Responsible When Autonomous Systems Fail? CIGI policy article.

While autonomous driving systems are often the focal point of public concern, similar risks arise in other domains. Reports from recent conflicts have documented increasing use of remotely piloted and autonomous military systems (Reuters 2023), raising safety and operational concerns alongside difficult questions about ethical oversight, rules of engagement, and responsibility. These debates concern how accountability applies across developers, deployers, and operators (Centre for International Governance Innovation 2023); they do not justify treating every autonomous-system failure as an absence of applicable responsibility. The engineering task is to preserve the evidence and authority needed to investigate the specific failure.
At its core, this challenge concerns the authority delegated to an automated system. Productivity and throughput gains do not establish that a system can act safely outside its validated operating envelope. Runtime controls must detect relevant boundary violations and invoke a fallback whose assumptions and response time fit the hazard. Human intervention is an available safeguard only when the operator can recognize the condition and act before harm occurs; faster hazards require an appropriate local response.
Specifying that operating envelope is difficult in dynamic environments because the model may omit conditions that matter for safe action. Two classical representation problems help explain this difficulty (McCarthy 1981). The frame problem concerns representing what changes and what remains unchanged after an action without listing every unaffected fact. The qualification problem concerns the potentially unlisted preconditions needed for an action to have its intended effect. These motivate explicit operating assumptions and fallback behavior, rather than constituting a universal proof that safe action is impossible. In practice, such limitations manifest as brittle autonomy: systems that appear competent under nominal conditions but fail silently or dangerously when faced with ambiguity or distributional shift.

McCarthy, J. 1981. “Epistemological Problems of Artificial Intelligence.” In Readings in Artificial Intelligence. Elsevier. https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-934613-03-3.50035-0.

Shalev-Shwartz, Shai, Shaked Shammah, and Amnon Shashua. 2017. “On a Formal Model of Safe and Scalable Self-Driving Cars.” ArXiv Preprint abs/1708.06374.
To address this, researchers have proposed formal safety frameworks such as Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS) (Shalev-Shwartz et al. 2017), which decompose abstract safety goals into mathematically defined constraints on system behavior, such as minimum distances, braking profiles, and right-of-way conditions. These formulations allow safety properties to be verified under specific assumptions and scenarios. However, such approaches remain vulnerable to the same limitations they aim to solve: they are only as good as the assumptions encoded into them and often require extensive domain modeling that may not generalize well to unanticipated edge cases.
For an ML systems team, the practical artifact is a safety case rather than a statement of trust. Table 8 shows the pattern: name the operating envelope, the evidence that the model has been tested inside that envelope, and the controls that halt or roll back the fleet when the evidence no longer holds.



Table 8: Autonomous System Safety Case: Trustworthy autonomy is operationalized as an auditable safety case: a validated operating envelope, coverage evidence, runtime guardrails, and fleet-level rollback controls. The same pattern applies beyond vehicles to drones, robots, trading systems, and other ML systems that act faster than continuous human review permits.










Safety-case element
Systems evidence
Operational gate




Operating envelope
Operational design domain, sensor assumptions, weather, geography, speed, and autonomy level
Block deployment outside validated envelope


Scenario coverage
Rare-event corpus, simulation coverage, replay logs, disengagements, and near-miss telemetry
Require coverage thresholds before canary expansion


Runtime guardrails
RSS-style distance rules, confidence thresholds, fallback maneuvers, and human override latency
Trigger safe stop, human takeover, or constrained mode when guardrails trip


Fleet control
Canary rollout, centralized safety dashboard, violation budget, and circuit-breaker rollback path
Halt rollout or revert model when fleet-level safety metrics exceed threshold






Human-centered system design complements formal safety constraints by examining how people exercise judgment and control within the validated system. Applied to human control, Value-Sensitive Design explicitly considers factors such as capability, complexity, misrepresentation, and the fluidity of user control. The METUX model (Motivation, Engagement, and Thriving in the User Experience) extends this thinking to six spheres of technology experience, namely adoption, interface, tasks, behavior, life, and society, each of which can support or undermine human flourishing (Peters et al. 2018). Both draw on self-determination theory’s account of autonomy as the ability to act in accordance with one’s own values and goals, rather than as control in a technical sense (Ryan and Deci 2000). In an ML system those requirements become concrete artifacts, namely interface affordances, user controls, feedback channels, escalation paths, and audit evidence. A recommender that optimizes engagement, for instance, can shape user preferences in ways the user cannot see. Evaluating it across the outer spheres of behavior, life, and society exposes effects that a short-term engagement metric never measures, so preserving autonomy requires controls and evidence beyond that metric.

Peters, D., R. A. Calvo, and R. M. Ryan. 2018. “Designing for Motivation, Engagement and Wellbeing in Digital Experience.” Frontiers in Psychology 9: 797. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00797.

Ryan, R. M., and E. L. Deci. 2000. “Self-Determination Theory and the Facilitation of Intrinsic Motivation, Social Development, and Well-Being.” American Psychologist 55 (1): 68–78. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066x.55.1.68.



The technical safety challenges examined in section 16.8.4 become fleet-level design constraints once autonomous systems interact with workers, users, regulators, and billions of requests. The broader implication is that safety cannot be reduced to a model metric; it depends on the operating environment that determines how automation changes work, how users calibrate trust, how policy varies by region, and how rare failures accumulate at scale.
Automation changes work organization in ways that influence safety design decisions. The MIT Work of the Future task force (Work of the Future 2020) argues that technological change and labor-market institutions jointly determine whether automation improves job quality or concentrates harms. For ML systems, the safety implication is that removing human roles can also remove contextual judgment and system-level debugging that remain difficult to encode in models. Metrics focused solely on throughput may inadvertently penalize human-in-the-loop designs that preserve oversight capability.

Work of the Future, MIT Task Force on the. 2020. The Work of the Future: Building Better Jobs in an Age of Intelligent Machines. Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Center, Pew Research. 2023. What Americans Know about AI, Cybersecurity and Big Tech.

Schäfer, Mike S. 2023. “The Notorious GPT: Science Communication in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.” Journal of Science Communication 22 (02): Y02. https://doi.org/10.22323/2.22020402.
Public knowledge about AI is uneven (Center 2023), and science-communication failures can amplify misunderstandings about how AI systems work (Schäfer 2023). That matters for deployment safety: when users lack understanding of model uncertainty, data bias, or decision boundaries, they may trust system outputs in contexts where human judgment should intervene. From a systems engineering perspective, public comprehension is part of the deployment context: the safety properties of a human-AI system depend on whether users can appropriately calibrate their trust and recognize situations requiring human override, not on technical mechanisms alone.
The engineering requirements for safety are shaped by regulatory frameworks that classify uses and assign obligations, rather than reducing AI risk to one verifiable metric. The EU AI Act (2024) uses a risk-based structure that includes prohibited practices, high-risk systems, transparency duties for some systems, and minimal or no-risk uses; high-risk deployments face conformity, documentation, and logging obligations (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024). United States federal policy has changed repeatedly since 2023. The safety reporting thresholds of Executive Order 14110 were revoked in January 2025, and later orders redirected agency emphasis toward AI innovation, cybersecurity, and critical-infrastructure defense (Executive Office of the President 2023, 2025a, 2025b, 2026). China’s Interim Measures for Generative AI (2023) subject some public-facing services to security assessment and algorithm-filing requirements rather than a universal pre-release assessment (Cyberspace Administration of China et al. 2023). For a global ML fleet, applicable obligations depend on the service, affected population, organizational role, and jurisdiction, not server location alone. The control plane must bind approved safety and retention policies to those deployment conditions, preserve their versions, and propagate changes to the components that enforce them.

Executive Office of the President. 2023. Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Order 14110, 88 FR 75191.

Executive Office of the President. 2025a. Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions. Executive Order 14148, 90 FR 8237.

Executive Office of the President. 2025b. Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. Executive Order 14179.

Executive Office of the President. 2026. Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security. Executive Order 14409, 91 FR 34565.

Cyberspace Administration of China, National Development and Reform Commission, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Science and Technology, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, Ministry of Public Security, and National Radio and Television Administration. 2023. Interim Measures for Administration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services. State Council Gazette.


At fleet scale, rare failures become expected incidents.

Safety must also be engineered as a fleet-level property rather than a model-level attribute alone. A single model with 99.9 percent safety compliance seems robust in isolation, but when deployed across 10,000 inference nodes serving billions of requests per day, a sustained 0.1 percent per-request failure probability implies millions of expected safety failures daily. The realized count can differ, and correlated failures can concentrate harm across the fleet. Mitigating this requires distributed safety patterns borrowed from reliability engineering: circuit breakers that automatically halt serving when aggregate safety metrics degrade below a threshold, canary deployments that bound exposure while collecting release evidence, with sample size and allowed risk chosen for the failure modes being tested, and centralized telemetry dashboards that aggregate per-node safety violations into a global view. The operational infrastructure must treat safety violations as critical system alerts, invoking a validated containment or fallback policy. A rollback is appropriate only if the previous version and transition are safe; active physical control may require a minimal-risk maneuver instead. Exposure is the multiplier that makes this concrete. Figure 11 illustrates cumulative mileage rising from 0.3 million miles in 2012 to 80 million in 2024. Because exposure grows by that ratio over twelve years, at any constant per-mile failure rate the expected cumulative incident count grows by the same factor even though no individual vehicle became less safe. That figure is an expectation, not an inevitable realized outcome, and it is cumulative; an operator sizing weekly incident-response capacity needs weekly mileage instead.


↩︎ The circuit-breaker states and backpressure contract that isolate a failing serving path are established in Circuit breakers and backpressure.














Figure 11: Autonomous Deployment Scaling: Cumulative autonomous miles by year for a hypothetical public-road fleet, rising from 0.3 million in 2012 to 80 million in 2024. The values are illustrative, chosen to show the shape of exposure growth; they are not reported or audited figures for any operator. Multiplying exposure by an applicable per-mile failure probability gives expected incidents over the same period. Cumulative mileage supports a cumulative expectation; weekly estimates require weekly mileage.



The core AI safety principle holds: technical excellence alone is insufficient. Safe systems require attention to the human and organizational context in which they operate, including the economic incentives that shape design decisions and the understanding that end users bring to their interactions with autonomous systems.
