Label smoothing, because target probabilities were regularized during training.
Hardware bit corruption, because inference activations deviated from ground truth.

A monitoring service evaluates an input feature over 1,000,000 requests, reporting a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test \(p\)-value of \(10^{-5}\) (\(p < 0.001\)), but the calculated Population Stability Index (PSI) is 0.04 and model precision is unaffected. Explain why the team should continue monitoring rather than triggering an immediate retraining job.
A fraud detection team uses service-calibrated drift alerts. Which scenario most strongly warrants urgent investigation and containment, with retraining considered after the cause and candidate update are validated?

A non-predictive logging metadata feature exhibits \(\text{PSI} = 0.28\) while all predictive features show \(\text{PSI} < 0.05\).
A primary feature shows \(\text{PSI} = 0.06\) and \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}} = 0.03\), with downstream precision and recall holding steady.
A two-sample KS test on a continuous feature yields \(p = 0.01\) over \(10^6\) samples, but \(\text{PSI} = 0.08\) and accuracy is unchanged.
A critical predictive feature crosses \(\text{PSI} = 0.29\) accompanied by a confirmed 7 percent drop in production precision.

Order these stages of a drift investigation that considers a validated model update, while treating urgent containment as a separate response when needed: (1) Compute drift metrics against versioned reference distributions, (2) Compare the signal with available predictive and business outcomes, (3) Ingest and log production features and outcomes, (4) Validate a candidate response and apply it only if the evidence and release gate support it, (5) Investigate pipeline faults, environmental changes, and temporary events.
True or False: If PSI, KL divergence, and two-sample KS tests on every input feature remain within green thresholds for six months, the engineering team can guarantee that no concept drift has occurred without checking ground-truth labels.

See Answers →

title: 14 Robust AI
text:
Consider an attacker who modifies an image of a benign skin lesion to induce a malignant prediction while preserving its apparent clinical content. Whether that attack succeeds depends on the classifier, the allowed modifications, and the evaluation conditions. The high-dimensional decision boundaries learned by deep neural networks possess counterintuitive blind spots that malicious actors can deliberately exploit. The practical question is what the attacker can see or control: gradients, queries, physical sensors, or training data. Adversarial attacks expose these blind spots.



Definition 14.3: Adversarial attack
Adversarial attack is a deliberate manipulation of a model’s input, interaction, or environment designed to violate a specified behavioral objective. The manipulation may be norm-bounded and visually subtle, but it can also be semantic, physical, query-based, or conspicuous.

Significance: Adversarial evaluation asks whether an attacker can choose inputs or transformations that drive the model outside its intended behavioral envelope. High-dimensional, norm-bounded image perturbations are one important case, but patches, rotations, printed objects, malicious text, and repeated black-box queries expose different system boundaries.
Distinction: Unlike random corruption sampled independently of the target, an adversarial manipulation is selected to cause failure. It need not use gradients: attackers may use surrogate models, decision-only queries, search, semantic edits, or control over the physical sensing environment.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that adversarial vulnerability is a “bug” to be patched. In reality, it is a structural vulnerability of many standard neural networks trained by empirical risk minimization; robust defense typically requires fundamental changes to the objective function (for example, adversarial training).



Adversarial attack categories encode access and cost. A white-box attacker can use gradients directly, a black-box attacker uses surrogate transfer or queries to the target, and a physical attacker must survive cameras, lighting, and distance. Figure 9 demonstrates this vulnerability on an image-classification network: adding an imperceptible perturbation that follows the sign of the loss gradient (\(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget = 0.007\)), the fast gradient sign method defined below, flips GoogLeNet’s prediction from panda (57.7 percent confidence) to gibbon (99.3 percent confidence), leaving the classifier paradoxically more confident in the erroneous label than the ground truth.






Figure 9: Imperceptible Misclassification in GoogLeNet: Adding a perturbation of \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget = 0.007\) in the sign direction of the loss gradient changes GoogLeNet’s prediction from panda (57.7 percent confidence) to gibbon (99.3 percent confidence), although the two images look identical to a person. The attack does not merely flip the label; it leaves the model more confident in the wrong answer than it was in the right one. Source: (Goodfellow et al. 2015).



A visually small change need not produce a small change in a classifier’s score.9 Adversarial perturbations exploit how input changes accumulate in the model’s decision function. Even a linear function can be sensitive to many small, aligned changes across input dimensions; nonlinearity alone does not explain the vulnerability. The relevant constraint is whether the allowed perturbation can move the input across the learned decision boundary.
9 Human vs. Machine Perception: First highlighted by Szegedy et al. (2013), neural networks learn statistical correlations in pixel space rather than the semantic invariances human vision enforces. Agreement on clean examples does not establish agreement under every small image change. Evaluation must therefore specify which transformations should preserve the label and test whether the model preserves that behavior; gradient-based training alone neither explains every attack nor guarantees the required invariance.
Szegedy, Christian, Wojciech Zaremba, Ilya Sutskever, Joan Bruna, Dumitru Erhan, Ian Goodfellow, and Rob Fergus. 2013. “Intriguing Properties of Neural Networks.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1312.6199.


The useful axis is not the attack name by itself but the attacker’s access. Each mechanism reveals a different cost that the defense must raise: gradient access, optimization time, surrogate-model construction, or physical control over the sensor environment.
The most direct case is white-box gradient access. Neural networks compute gradients to learn how parameter changes reduce loss; an attacker with access to gradients can run that logic against the input instead. For an image classifier that correctly identifies a panda, the gradient with respect to the input image gives a local, first-order estimate of how pixel changes affect the loss. The fast gradient sign method (FGSM)10 turns that idea into a single-step attack by choosing each feature’s perturbation sign to maximize that first-order increase within a coordinate-wise budget.
10 Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM): Proposed by Goodfellow et al. (2015) at ICLR, FGSM generates adversarial examples in a single gradient step, making it practical to use during training. This dual role is its lasting systems significance: the same attack that exposed neural network fragility became a simple adversarial-training primitive, where FGSM-generated perturbations augment clean batches with examples chosen to increase loss.
Goodfellow, I. J., J. Shlens, and C. Szegedy. 2015. “Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
The underlying mathematical formulation captures this intuitive process:
\[
\AdversarialExample= \ModelInput+ \AdversarialPerturbationBudget \cdot \text{sign}\big(\nabla_\ModelInput\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)\big)
\]
In this formulation, \(\ModelInput\) denotes the original input, \(\AdversarialExample\) is the generated adversarial example, and \(\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)\) represents the prediction loss evaluated at model parameters \(\ModelParameters\) and true label \(\ExampleLabel\). The gradient term \(\nabla_\ModelInput\LossFunction\) describes local loss sensitivity, \(\text{sign}(\cdot)\) extracts each component’s sign to maximize the linearized loss within the coordinate-wise budget, and the scalar \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\) bounds the maximum allowable perturbation magnitude under the \(\ell_\infty\) norm. This single step need not maximize the nonlinear loss or cause misclassification. Image implementations also clip the perturbed input to its valid pixel range. The subscript distinguishes this adversarial radius from other uses of \(\Glyph{\epsilon}\) in the book, such as the differential-privacy budget.
Figure 10 geometricizes this single-step perturbation within the \(\ell_\infty\) budget \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\): moving along the sign vector of \(\nabla_\ModelInput\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)\) propels input \(\ModelInput\) to a corner of the bounding cube, producing \(\AdversarialExample\) and crossing the decision boundary into the adjacent class region in this illustration. A different boundary or gradient need not produce a successful attack within the same budget.






Figure 10: Gradient-Based Attack Geometry: Around a correctly classified input \(\ModelInput\), the dashed square marks every perturbation allowed by the \(\ell_\infty\) budget \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\). FGSM moves each coordinate by the full budget in the sign direction of the loss gradient \(\nabla_\ModelInput \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)\), which lands \(\AdversarialExample\) on a corner of that square, the allowed point that maximizes the first-order increase in loss. A step no larger than \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\) in any coordinate therefore carries the input across the decision boundary. The class labels are illustrative.



FGSM is cheap because it takes one step. The projected gradient descent (PGD) attack (Madry et al. 2018) spends more compute for a stronger attack: it repeatedly applies gradient updates and projects each step back into the allowed norm ball around the original input. That iterative refinement makes PGD a standard white-box robustness benchmark. The Jacobian-based saliency map attack (JSMA) (N. Papernot et al. 2016) uses the Jacobian to identify the most influential input features and perturb a smaller set of dimensions toward a target class. These methods are most effective in white-box settings,11 where the attacker knows the model architecture and gradients.

Papernot, N., P. McDaniel, S. Jha, M. Fredrikson, Z. Berkay Celik, and A. Swami. 2016. “The Limitations of Deep Learning in Adversarial Settings.” 2016 IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P), 372–87. https://doi.org/10.1109/eurosp.2016.36.
11 White-Box Attack: Adversarial attack with complete model knowledge (architecture, weights, gradients); methods like PGD and Carlini-Wagner (C&W) are strong because they optimize directly against the model rather than probing it from the outside. Though less realistic than black-box scenarios for many deployed systems, white-box analysis establishes a demanding benchmark within a specified norm, perturbation budget, and attack procedure. Passing PGD is evidence for that threat model, not a universal guarantee against every weaker-looking attack.12 Carlini and Wagner (C&W) Attack: Proposed in 2016 (IEEE S&P 2017), C&W formulates adversarial example generation as a constrained optimization problem that searches for a small perturbation causing misclassification without guaranteeing a global minimum. Its significance is methodological: C&W broke defensive distillation (an early defense that masked gradients to blunt weaker attacks) and other evaluated defenses, establishing the principle that robustness claims must be evaluated against optimization-based attacks, not merely gradient-sign heuristics.When the attacker cares less about speed and more about stealth, the attack becomes an optimization problem. The Carlini and Wagner (C&W) attack12 (Carlini and Wagner 2017) searches for a small perturbation that causes misclassification under a chosen distance measure. Minimizing that distance encourages similarity, but does not certify human perceptual equivalence or a globally minimal perturbation. Instead of merely following the sign of a gradient, C&W optimizes a custom objective that trades perturbation size against confidence in the wrong answer.
C&W perturbations can be visually subtle, but human imperceptibility alone does not establish whether a detector will identify them. The attack can search under different norm constraints, such as \(\ell_2\) or \(\ell_\infty\). The elastic net attack to DNNs (EAD) adds elastic net regularization, combining \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) penalties to generate sparse, localized perturbations. DeepFool (Moosavi-Dezfooli et al. 2015) takes a geometric route to the same goal: it linearizes the classifier around the input, steps to the nearest boundary of that linear approximation, and repeats until the label flips, giving a fast estimate of the smallest perturbation that suffices. These optimization-based methods are more computationally intensive than gradient-sign attacks, but they give the attacker finer control over the adversarial example’s geometry.

Moosavi-Dezfooli, Seyed-Mohsen, Alhussein Fawzi, and Pascal Frossard. 2015. “DeepFool: A Simple and Accurate Method to Fool Deep Neural Networks.” 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2016: 2574–82. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2016.282.
Black-box attackers lose direct gradient access but keep two routes. Transfer attacks rely on transferability, the tendency of an adversarial example to fool models other than the one it was crafted on. The attacker crafts examples offline on a surrogate model and submits them to the target, typically through its public API, without seeing its weights or gradients. Query-based attacks probe the target itself. A decision-based, or boundary, attack needs only the returned label. It starts from an input the model already misclassifies and walks along the decision boundary toward the original input, querying at each step to stay on the wrong side. Its cost is the number of queries, which is why query budgets and rate limits belong to the defense.


↩︎ Transferability and the black-box threat model are established in Adversarial attacks.

Tramèr, Florian, Alexey Kurakin, Nicolas Papernot, Ian Goodfellow, Dan Boneh, and Patrick McDaniel. 2017. “Ensemble Adversarial Training: Attacks and Defenses.” International Conference on Learning Representations abs/1705.07204.
Transfer success depends on model similarity, training-data overlap, and regularization, and attackers can improve it with input diversity, such as random resizing or cropping, and with momentum during optimization. Closing that route costs the defender training work. Ensemble adversarial training trains against perturbations generated on several models to improve transfer robustness, but the extra attack generation and model diversity make it a deliberate training-budget decision rather than a free mitigation (Tramèr et al. 2017).



An example crafted on a surrogate fools similar models more often than dissimilar ones.
Physical-world attackers face an additional constraint: the perturbation must survive sensors, distance, lighting, viewing angle, and ordinary deployment variation. Adversarial patches are printed patterns placed on objects so that cameras and detectors misread the scene. Modified road signs, clothing patches, and 3D-printed objects move the attack from the digital input tensor into the physical environment. That makes the robustness question operational rather than merely mathematical: a defense that works on a saved image may fail once the attack passes through a camera lens, compression, motion blur, and changing illumination. These threats matter most for AI systems deployed in physical spaces, such as autonomous vehicles, drones, and surveillance systems, where a model error becomes a safety, security, and accountability problem in the world.

Example 14.1: The stop sign attackScenario: The road-sign sticker attack, already familiar as a security threat, places black and white stickers on a stop sign so that a vision model reads it as a speed limit sign (Eykholt et al. 2018). The robustness question is what its two reported success rates say about how an evaluation must be run.
Diagnosis: The attack succeeded on every tested laboratory image but on 84.8 percent of frames in the moving-vehicle field test. Each number is evidence only for its own capture conditions, and the gap between them does not isolate any one factor, such as distance, viewing angle, lighting, or motion.
Systems lesson: A physical attack must be evaluated through the full sensor loop, not on saved benchmark images. The evaluation should optimize the attack over the expected range of transformations (expectation over transformation) and then test it with real captures, and any claimed mitigation, such as spatio-temporal validation or sensor fusion, must be tested against attacks on the complete perception stack.



Eykholt, K., I. Evtimov, E. Fernandes, B. Li, A. Rahmati, C. Xiao, A. Prakash, T. Kohno, and D. Song. 2018. “Robust Physical-World Attacks on Deep Learning Visual Classification.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 1707.08945: 1625–34. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00175.

↩︎ The road-sign sticker attack is established as a security threat in Adversarial traffic sign attack case study.

Physical perturbations also need not be subtle to matter. The perturbations in figure 11 range from a poster covering the whole sign to graffiti-style markings and sticker patches that pass for ordinary vandalism. The associated study evaluates whether these physical modifications induce misclassification through the camera pipeline without digital access to the captured input (Eykholt et al. 2017).






Figure 11: Physically Realizable Road-Sign Perturbations: Physically realizable modifications can cause machine learning models to make incorrect predictions. The three panels show perturbations from the original study, from a subtle full-sign poster to conspicuous graffiti-style camouflage and black-and-white sticker patches that look like ordinary vandalism yet trigger misclassification (Eykholt et al. 2017).


Eykholt, Kevin, Ivan Evtimov, Earlence Fernandes, Bo Li, Amir Rahmati, Chaowei Xiao, Atul Prakash, Tadayoshi Kohno, and Dawn Song. 2017. “Robust Physical-World Attacks on Deep Learning Models.” ArXiv Preprint abs/1707.08945 (July).


The attacker’s access determines the evaluation a defense must survive. Table 7 distinguishes gradient access, optimization, surrogate transfer, and physical sensor manipulation so that a result under one attack mechanism does not become a claim about all of them.



Table 7: Adversarial Attack Categories: Attack mechanisms determine defense selection: gradient and optimization attacks require robustness against explicit decision-boundary crossing, transfer attacks test black-box exposure, and physical attacks require evaluation through the deployed sensor loop.










Category
Method
Mechanism




Gradient
FGSM
Perturbs inputs along the loss gradient



PGD
Iterative multi-step FGSM refinement



JSMA
Targets the most influential features


Optimization
C&W
Minimizes perturbation size subject to misclassification



DeepFool
Estimates a small boundary-crossing perturbation by local linearization



EAD
Elastic net regularization for sparse perturbations


Transfer
Transferability
Adversarial examples transfer across models (black-box)


Physical
Patches
Printed patches fool detectors in the real world



3D Objects
Sculpted objects deceive sensors in deployment






Medical-imaging attacks can cause misdiagnosis (Tsai et al. 2023), while fraud and trading models face analogous manipulation risks. The common vulnerability is reliance on features that remain predictive on clean data but fail under crafted perturbations (Goodfellow et al. 2015; Madry et al. 2018). Defense shifts the resource cost: adversarial training adds training work (Bai et al. 2021), while runtime detection such as feature squeezing adds inference evaluations (Xu et al. 2018). The choice among these spending points motivates the defenses in section 14.6.

Tsai, Min-Jen, Ping-Yi Lin, and Ming-En Lee. 2023. “Adversarial Attacks on Medical Image Classification.” Cancers 15 (17): 4228. https://doi.org/10.3390/cancers15174228.




The attacks so far perturb a fixed model at inference time. Poisoning instead changes the data from which the model learns. Systems that accept user contributions must distinguish evidence for learning from instructions that merely request a response. Microsoft’s Tay incident illustrates the broader danger of adversarial interaction: the company reported a coordinated attack that defeated its filtering and stress testing within a day of launch (Lee 2016). The public account does not detail the mechanism, but the robustness lesson does not depend on it. Once live interaction can shape a model’s later behavior, every user is a potential contributor of training evidence, and coordinated users can supply it on purpose. For systems that do learn from user feedback, the engineering question is therefore which contributions may enter training and how their influence can be audited.

Lee, Peter. 2016. Learning from Tay’s Introduction. The Official Microsoft Blog.

↩︎ Data poisoning, the corruption of training data or updates so that the learned model misbehaves later, and its sequence of admission, training, and exploitation are established in Data poisoning.

Automated collection, web scraping, and crowdsourced annotation make poisoning a pipeline-integrity problem: the system must identify compromised contributions before the learner incorporates them.
A classic early formulation in ML security is the attack by Biggio et al. (2012) on support-vector machines. More recent poisoning work broadens the target to web-scale and generative-model data pipelines (see also Shan et al. 2023). The dirty-label attack sampled in figure 12 corrupts training data by pairing cat images with misleading ‘dog’ captions, attempting to induce fraudulent associations during multimodal pretraining. The consequences are especially severe in high-stakes domains like healthcare, where even small disruptions to training data can lead to dangerous misdiagnoses (Marulli et al. 2022).

Biggio, Battista, Blaine Nelson, and Pavel Laskov. 2012. “Poisoning Attacks Against Support Vector Machines.” Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2012, Edinburgh, Scotland, UK, June 26 - July 1, 2012.

Marulli, Fiammetta, Stefano Marrone, and Laura Verde. 2022. “Sensitivity of Machine Learning Approaches to Fake and Untrusted Data in Healthcare Domain.” Journal of Sensor and Actuator Networks 11 (2): 21. https://doi.org/10.3390/jsan11020021.






Figure 12: Dirty-Label Data Poisoning: Mismatched image-text pairs represent a dirty-label poisoning attack where cat images are paired with misleading ‘dog’ captions in training data. Incorporating these corrupted pairs can cause models to learn incorrect multimodal associations.



Because admitting a poisoned record does not by itself guarantee that training will learn the attacker’s behavior, the evidence that matters is behavioral, and it differs by attacker objective. Poisoning attacks divide by that objective into the four classes of the security threat model. An availability attack degrades the model’s accuracy across the board, a targeted attack makes chosen inputs receive a chosen wrong output, a backdoor attack teaches the model to switch to the attacker’s output whenever a trigger appears, and a subpopulation attack degrades one cohort while leaving the rest intact. The robustness question is which evidence exposes each class and what that evidence costs (Oprea et al. 2022). Successful availability attacks can lower aggregate validation accuracy, giving broad evaluation a signal to investigate. Targeted and subpopulation attacks can leave that aggregate nearly intact, making evaluation on the named targets and cohorts particularly important. Backdoors can also preserve clean-data accuracy while responding to a trigger the evaluator has never seen. In the BadNets construction, a small pixel pattern is stamped onto some training images that are relabeled to the target class, so the network learns that the pattern alone decides the output while clean images classify normally (Gu et al. 2017); possible detection strategies include trigger search, canary inputs, and activation-space inspection when poisoned and clean representations separate (Tran et al. 2018).

Oprea, Alina, Anoop Singhal, and Apostol Vassilev. 2022. “Poisoning Attacks Against Machine Learning: Can Machine Learning Be Trustworthy?” Computer 55 (11): 94–99. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2022.3190787.

Gu, Tianyu, Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, and Siddharth Garg. 2017. “BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1708.06733.

Lighthouse 14.1: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): Fake profile injectionArchetype B (DLRM at Scale) is especially exposed to fake profile injection. Because recommendation systems often use online learning to adapt to user trends in real time, an adversary can create a network of “sybil” accounts, fake identities controlled by the same attacker, that interact with specific items to artificially boost their popularity or associate them with high-value demographics. This poisoning bypasses traditional firewalls because the malicious interactions look like legitimate user behavior, motivating checks on contributor identity, interaction patterns, and learned representations. Spectral-signature defenses (developed in section 14.7.1.1) search activation patterns for suspicious separation, but their effectiveness depends on whether the poisoned and clean contributions separate in that representation.


Poisoned records can resemble legitimate data, so clean aggregate validation accuracy alone cannot establish that a training corpus is trustworthy. Detectability depends on the attacker’s objective and on which records, representations, and behavioral slices the evaluator inspects. Attacks may originate from internal actors with privileged pipeline access or from external adversaries who exploit weak points in data collection, particularly in crowdsourced environments or open data pipelines that lack integrity checks and lineage tracking.

Example 14.2: Targeted poisoning classificationScenario: An attacker modifies the labels of a small subset of training data so that one deployed classifier consistently maps a particular protected class or object pattern to the wrong output.
Diagnosis: This is a targeted attack. The attacker is not trying to degrade overall model performance; they are inducing a specific error while preserving enough general accuracy that aggregate validation metrics may still look healthy.
Systems lesson: Defending against targeted poisoning requires slice-level evaluation, provenance checks, and canary examples for high-risk classes. Aggregate accuracy alone is a weak detector because the attack is designed to hide inside otherwise normal performance.


Distributed and federated training adds a contributor axis to the same threat. A malicious client need not insert a visible record into a central corpus; it can submit a model update chosen to move the aggregate, implant a backdoor, or exploit sybil identities to gain disproportionate weight. Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) makes this concrete: the server aggregates updates from a large population of smartphone-class clients whose raw data it never sees. Contributor-level checks can screen updates before aggregation, while held-out behavioral tests can reveal harmful effects in the resulting global model. The evaluation must vary the number and coordination of malicious contributors, their data heterogeneity, participation schedule, and knowledge of the aggregation rule. Global clean accuracy is again insufficient: the gate needs attack success on the trigger or target subpopulation, contributor-level anomaly recall, and the clean-utility cost of robust aggregation. Krum, coordinate-wise median, and trimmed mean tolerate bounded Byzantine behavior only under their stated assumptions (Blanchard et al. 2017; Yin et al. 2018); high dimensionality and non-i.i.d. client updates can make honest contributors look anomalous. These rules also change the collective. A mean can be computed by an AllReduce that sums partial results, but a median, trimmed mean, or Krum selection needs the individual updates, and a direct gather-based implementation raises per-worker traffic by about a factor of \(\DataParallelDegree/2\) relative to ring AllReduce, where \(\DataParallelDegree\) here counts the contributing replicas rather than accelerators. That cost lands on \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) in the Fleet Law unless it overlaps with computation. Provenance, participation limits, robust aggregation, and held-out canaries must therefore work together rather than treating one distance rule as a poisoning proof.

Blanchard, Peva, El Mahdi El Mhamdi, Rachid Guerraoui, and Julien Stainer. 2017. “Machine Learning with Adversaries: Byzantine Tolerant Gradient Descent.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 119–29.

Yin, Dong, Yudong Chen, Kannan Ramchandran, and Peter Bartlett. 2018. “Byzantine-Robust Distributed Learning: Towards Optimal Statistical Rates.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 5650–59.

↩︎ The traffic cost of gather-based robust aggregation relative to ring AllReduce is established in Gradient synchronization integrity.



The four categories above describe an attacker’s objective; the attack mechanism depends on the attacker’s access to the system and knowledge of the data pipeline. As diagrammed in figure 13, all of them share a common shape: a poisoned record enters the training pipeline alongside clean data and attempts to alter the resulting model’s behavior. The most direct mechanism is label modification, where an attacker selects a subset of training samples and alters their labels, flipping \(\ExampleLabel= 1\) to \(\ExampleLabel= 0\) or reassigning categories in multi-class settings. Even small-scale label corruption can shift decision boundaries significantly.






Figure 13: Data Poisoning Impact: A nominal pipeline (top) and a poisoned pipeline (bottom) pass through the same four stages. In the illustrated successful attack, a poisoned record admitted at ingestion contaminates the training corpus, pulls the optimizer’s gradients toward the attacker’s trigger, and yields a backdoored model whose clean accuracy can remain intact, so aggregate validation alone can miss it.



After label modification, the attacker can keep the label intact and corrupt the features instead, the strategy known as clean-label poisoning. Because every label is correct, label audits cannot flag these records. Imperceptible image perturbations, subtle shifts in structured fields, and fixed trigger patterns all aim for the same outcome: the training example still appears legitimate, but it bends the learned decision boundary toward a future failure. Generative methods and data-synthesis tools raise the same risk at larger scale because they can create natural-looking examples whose only purpose is to distort what the model learns.
Whether those examples become poisoning depends on the data boundary. Web scraping, social media feeds, crowdsourced annotation, and untrusted user submissions all allow poisoned records to enter upstream and pass through weak cleaning checks in a “trusted” form. Physical systems add a second path: a sticker on a road sign is an inference-time adversarial attack when the car sees it, but harvesting that image into a training corpus creates a potential poisoning path only if the contribution serves an attack on the learner. Correctly labeled examples of such inputs can instead help train resistance to them. Online learning systems tighten the feedback loop further, allowing an attacker to introduce small increments of malicious data until model behavior drifts without a single obvious anomaly. As diagrammed in figure 14, collaborative settings widen the boundary again: when many clients each contribute model updates to a central aggregator, a single malicious participant can poison the shared global model that aggregation produces.






Figure 14: Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation: In a collaborative learning setting, multiple clients each train on local data and contribute model updates to a central server that aggregates them into a shared global model. A single malicious participant can inject poisoned updates that the server folds into the aggregated model, so the corruption spreads to every client without any one obvious anomaly. This attack surface differs from adversarial examples because it targets the model during training rather than at inference.



Insiders such as annotators or data vendors can exploit knowledge of the model and training procedure to make these attacks harder to detect. Clean benchmark performance therefore does not establish training-data integrity.



Data poisoning is not always malicious. Researchers have begun exploring it as a defensive tool, particularly for protecting creative work from unauthorized use by generative AI models.
Nightshade, developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, aims to deter unauthorized training by poisoning images that a scraper may collect (Shan et al. 2023). It does not block scraping itself. Its perturbations preserve the apparent image content while changing how a model learns from it; the reported experiments show targeted concept corruption when the modified images enter the tested training pipelines.

Shan, S., W. Ding, J. Passananti, S. Wu, H. Zheng, and B. Y. Zhao. 2023. “Nightshade: Prompt-Specific Poisoning Attacks on Text-to-Image Generative Models.” 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP) abs/2310.13828: 807–25. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp54263.2024.00207.
The dose-response matrix in figure 15 charts this progressive corruption across four poison doses (0 to 300 samples) and eight prompt concepts: as the dose increases, Stable Diffusion XL outputs morph away from source concepts (generating cows for “car” or cats for “dog”) under the tested training conditions. These outputs demonstrate changed behavior without, by themselves, identifying the internal representation that caused it. The experiment demonstrates concept poisoning: poisoned samples distort a model’s semantic associations.






Figure 15: Concept Poisoning Dose-Response: Stable Diffusion XL outputs across four poison doses (clean, 50, 100, 300 samples) and eight source prompts (dog, car, handbag, hat, fantasy art, cubism, cartoon, concept art). As the dose grows, outputs morph from the intended source concept toward the attacker’s destination concept, demonstrating Nightshade-style concept poisoning of a pretrained model.



The Nightshade experiments also report effects on concepts related to the poisoned target. This spillover extends the observed attack beyond the exact target prompt, but its reach depends on the model, poison construction, and training procedure. The same technique used to protect artistic content could also be repurposed to sabotage legitimate training pipelines, highlighting the dual-use dilemma13 at the heart of machine learning security.
13 Dual-Use Dilemma: The structural tension that defensive ML capabilities (adversarial training, data poisoning tools, red-teaming frameworks) are simultaneously offensive capabilities. This creates an arms race where defensive research publications become attack playbooks. For ML systems engineering, the consequence is architectural: robustness mechanisms must assume attacker knowledge of the defense, ruling out security-through-obscurity and motivating formal guarantees where feasible and adaptive empirical evaluation within the remaining threat model.The mechanics of these input-level attacks, from adversarial perturbations and data poisoning to their interaction with natural distribution shifts (section 14.4), define the threat surface. The next question is how to engineer the algorithmic defenses required to protect production models against them.

Self-Check: Question

Why can a small gradient-directed perturbation change a high-dimensional classifier’s score more than independently sampled, zero-mean noise of comparable coordinate scale?

Random noise changes model parameters directly, whereas gradient perturbations only affect input metadata.
Gradient-directed perturbations require visible, large-scale pixel alterations that physically overwhelm convolutional filters.
The perturbation aligns coordinate changes with local loss sensitivity, while independent zero-mean changes can cancel in the first-order sum.
Random noise affects only training data, whereas adversarial noise can only exist during inference.

An attacker lacking access to a commercial vision API’s internal weights or gradients trains a local ResNet surrogate, crafts PGD adversarial images against that surrogate, and successfully fools the target API on 50 percent of queries. Which property of adversarial examples enables this black-box attack?

Differential privacy, which guarantees perturbation bounds across diverse neural architectures.
Transferability, where adversarial examples crafted to exploit decision boundaries of one model frequently deceive different models trained on similar tasks.
Quantization noise, which forces all deployed models into identical weight matrices.
Batch normalization collapse, which disables activation functions across distributed API servers.

Compare availability poisoning with backdoor poisoning, and explain why an evaluation that checks only aggregate clean accuracy can miss a successful backdoor.
Which scenario represents a physical-world adversarial attack rather than a digital evasion attack or an environmental covariate shift?

An attacker submits a JSON payload containing an \(\ell_\infty\)-perturbed pixel array directly to a cloud inference API endpoint.
A sudden heavy snowfall changes ambient lighting and road surface reflections, reducing camera detection accuracy by 15 percent.
An engineer accidentally inverts the normalization constants in a client-side image preprocessing script.
An attacker places small, calibrated black-and-white stickers on a roadside stop sign that cause a vehicle camera to classify it as a speed limit sign across varying distances, angles, and lighting.

True or False: If an adversary poisons 0.1 percent of a training dataset with a backdoor trigger, collecting and adding 10\(\times\) more clean training data will reliably eliminate the backdoor behavior through clean-data dilution.
The foundational single-step adversarial attack method that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the input and perturbs features by \(\epsilon \cdot \text{sign}(\nabla_x \mathcal{L})\) is called the ____.

See Answers →

title: 14 Robust AI
text:
The classifier that called a panda a gibbon in figure 9 was not broken by random noise; a perturbation budget of 0.007 per pixel, spent along the gradient sign, was enough. Defending a deployed perception model against that attacker requires a threat model that names the attacker’s access and a budget for testing and mitigation. The resulting robustness claim must state what the system pays in clean accuracy, training compute, inference latency, or operational coverage.


The adversarial-defense workflow has four ordered layers:

Define the threat model: Specify the perturbation budget, attacker knowledge, and whether the attack occurs at inference time or during training.
Choose the robustness budget: Decide whether to spend the budget in training, certification, input detection, or serving-time guardrails.
Measure the trade-off: Evaluate both sides of the defense, because improving worst-case behavior can reduce clean accuracy, raise inference latency, or multiply training cost.
Keep evaluation adversarial: Test the defense against attacks stronger than the ones used to design it.

The order matters because an uncalibrated threat model makes the budget and evaluation loop meaningless.
For model-facing perturbation threats, the most direct training-time defense is adversarial training, which incorporates adversarial examples into the training process itself. The mechanism reuses the attacks of the previous section as a data generator. Each training step augments the batch with perturbed copies of its own inputs, so the model is trained on the high-loss points an attacker would choose. Listing 1 implements this pattern using FGSM to generate perturbations and mix clean and adversarial examples in each batch.



Listing 1: Adversarial Training Pseudocode: Framework-neutral adversarial training using FGSM-style perturbations during training, mixing clean and perturbed data to improve robustness against gradient-based attacks.


function adversarial_training_step(model, clean_batch, labels, epsilon):
    logits = model(clean_batch)
    clean_loss = loss(logits, labels)

    input_gradient = gradient(clean_loss, clean_batch)
    perturbation = epsilon * sign(input_gradient)
    adversarial_batch = stop_gradient(
        clip(clean_batch + perturbation, valid_input_range))

    mixed_batch = concatenate(clean_batch, adversarial_batch)
    mixed_labels = concatenate(labels, labels)

    return loss(model(mixed_batch), mixed_labels)



In listing 1, the sign step bounds each coordinate’s change by the perturbation budget, while clipping keeps the perturbed input inside the valid input range (for example, \([0,1]\) for normalized pixels). Concatenation doubles the effective batch size. The stop-gradient operation treats generated adversarial inputs as fixed during the outer weight update, rather than differentiating through attack construction. The caller differentiates the returned loss with respect to the model parameters and performs the optimizer update. The perturbation budget \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\) (the epsilon argument) bounds the allowed input change, while the attack algorithm determines how effectively it searches that set; computation reuse can reduce its training overhead (Shafahi et al. 2019).
Adversarial example generation increases training time because each training step requires additional forward and backward passes through the model (Madry et al. 2018; Bai et al. 2021). Memory overhead depends on whether the implementation stores clean and adversarial examples together, recomputes perturbations, or reuses gradient information. Iterative attacks like PGD add multiple optimization steps, so the implementation must budget that gradient work; optimized variants reduce overhead by reusing computations rather than treating every attack step as a separate full training pass (Shafahi et al. 2019).
A robustness recipe that increases model capacity also adds memory and training cost. The perturbation budget and training recipe require matched clean and adversarial validation, and the perspective below shows why that matching decides what the robustness tax actually is.

Systems Perspective 14.1: Pricing the robustness tax correctlySuppose a standard ResNet-50 records 76 percent Top-1 accuracy on clean ImageNet, while an adversarially trained model records about 50 percent under a specified \(\ell_\infty\) attack at \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget=4/255\), the budget conventionally used for ImageNet. Subtracting these values yields 26 percentage points, but that gap compares different models under different evaluation conditions. It is not the clean-accuracy cost of robustness.
The clean-accuracy tax must compare standard and robust models on the same clean test set. The robustness benefit must compare those models under the same attack, perturbation budget, and attack strength. The four cells are the standard model on clean data, the standard model under attack, the robust model on clean data, and the robust model under attack. The tax is the first minus the third, the benefit is the fourth minus the second, and the quoted pair supplies only the first and the fourth. Reporting all four cells prevents an apparent trade-off from mixing a model effect with an evaluation-condition effect.
Systems insight: Robustness can reduce clean accuracy and increase compute, but each tax needs a like-for-like baseline. A deployment gate should report clean accuracy, empirical robust accuracy, attack specification, and evaluation cost separately.


The robustness compute penalty (principle \(\ref{pri-robustness-compute-penalty}\)) quantifies this cost: PGD-style adversarial robustness can demand several times more compute per epoch than standard optimization because each batch runs inner attack steps. In Fleet Law terms (equation 1.3) the multiplier lands on \(\IronLawComputeTime\). At a fixed worker count it adds local work, but the elapsed-time penalty depends on reuse and on which term limits the step. Adding workers changes communication and synchronization costs with \(\DeviceCount\) and may not recover the original duration. Notebook 14.2 makes the multiplier concrete.

Napkin Math 14.2: The cost of defenseProblem: A team is training a robust classifier for an autonomous vehicle. Instead of the single FGSM step in listing 1, it uses adversarial training with a seven-step PGD attack (PGD-7) that searches for a high-loss perturbation inside a specified norm ball for every training batch, and, following the standard PGD adversarial-training recipe (Madry et al. 2018), it trains on the adversarial batch alone rather than on the listing’s doubled clean-plus-adversarial batch. How much does this extra attack-generation work slow down the training run?
Math: In this example, generating the adversarial input uses \(\AttackStepsPgd\) additional gradient steps per training sample, each a forward and backward pass with respect to the input, before the one weight-update pass on the adversarial batch. The estimate treats each attack step as equal in cost to the standard training pass, with no reuse; it is a work model rather than a measured wall-clock slowdown. By the same accounting, the FGSM listing spends one attack pass plus an update pass over a batch twice the original size, about three standard passes in all, so PGD-7 trades a further factor of more than two in training work for a stronger inner attack.

Forward/backward passes: 1 (Standard) + 7 (Attack Generation) = 8 total passes.
Training slowdown: 8× under the equal-cost-pass assumption.
Utility evidence: The added work must be justified by measured robust accuracy under the specified attack. Generalization to other attacks requires separate evaluation. Pricing any clean-accuracy cost requires the like-for-like comparison in perspective 14.1, not a subtraction of robust accuracy from another model’s clean accuracy.

Systems insight: In this PGD-7 work model, the team budgets 8× the baseline compute before measuring the robustness benefit or actual elapsed-time penalty. In a machine learning fleet, robustness is not a setting that can be switched on; it is a budget the team spends, and the budget must be justified by the failure consequence of the component being hardened.


For lower-risk components, external guardrails such as input filtering and output verification can cost less than training intrinsic robustness into the weights, provided adaptive evaluation (section 14.6.1.4) supports acceptable residual risk against an attacker who knows the guardrail. Passing a finite set of attacks does not prove that no bypass exists. Safety-critical paths more often justify the training and certification budget.

Example 14.3: Defense selection by threat modelScenario: Production teams must select defenses across three distinct system settings: an image classifier facing evasion attacks, a recommendation system facing training data poisoning, and a fraud detector facing natural distribution shift.
Diagnosis: An inference-time input filter alone cannot meet all three needs. It adds work on the image classifier’s serving path, but does not establish the integrity of recommendation training data or track changes in the fraud detector’s deployment population.
Systems lesson: Defense selection must be tailored to the threat model. Adversarial training targets the specified evasion threat, source controls, sanitization, and robust training objectives (section 14.7) limit some poisoning mechanisms, and drift monitoring identifies shifts for investigation. Each choice needs evaluation against its own failure conditions; detection alone does not restore valid predictions.




Adversarial training provides empirical resistance that must be tested against the deployment threat model. It can generalize beyond the examples generated during training, but attack evaluation alone does not prove invariance throughout an allowed perturbation set. Certified robustness offers a mathematical guarantee: for a given input \(\ModelInput\) and radius \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\), no perturbation \(\|\AdversarialPerturbation\|_\PerturbationNormOrder< \AdversarialPerturbationBudget\) exists that changes the model’s prediction. This certifies local prediction stability, not that the unchanged prediction is correct. The certified radius is a provable lower bound on the input-perturbation part of the robustness margin that compression and other efficiency changes must preserve. The guarantee formalizes the intuition, met in the pipeline overview, that a robust model limits how quickly its outputs can change as its inputs change. The model’s Lipschitz constant14 bounds that rate, so a prediction cannot change within any radius over which the largest possible score change stays below its top-class margin. A widely used technique for scaling this idea to high-dimensional inputs like ImageNet is randomized smoothing. Instead of classifying \(\ModelInput\) directly, it classifies the smoothed function \(\SmoothedClassifier(\ModelInput)\), defined as the most probable class predicted by the base classifier \(\ModelPredictor\) under Gaussian noise: \(\SmoothedClassifier(\ModelInput) = \operatorname{arg\,max}_\ClassIndex \Pr(\ModelPredictor(\ModelInput+\RandomizedSmoothingNoise) = \ClassIndex)\) where \(\RandomizedSmoothingNoise \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix)\).
14 Lipschitz Continuity: A mathematical property that bounds how much a function’s output changes relative to its input change (\(\lVert \ModelPredictor(\ModelInput) - \ModelPredictor(\AlternateModelInput) \rVert \le \LipschitzConstant\lVert \ModelInput- \AlternateModelInput\rVert\)). A small Lipschitz constant \((\LipschitzConstant)\) limits score movement, but it does not by itself prevent a label flip. A robustness certificate additionally requires the top-class score margin over the runner-up to exceed the worst-case score change within the perturbation radius; reducing \(\LipschitzConstant\) can enlarge that certified radius, though enforcing a low constant can trade away clean-data accuracy and add training cost.
Cohen, Jeremy, Elan Rosenfeld, and Zico Kolter. 2019. “Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 97: 1310–20.
Cohen et al. (2019) proved a tight multiclass bound for the certified radius \(\CertifiedRadius\) using a lower bound on the top-class probability \(\SmoothedTopClassProbability\) and an upper bound on the runner-up probability \(\SmoothedRunnerUpProbability\): \(\CertifiedRadius= \frac{\SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation}{2}\left(\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}(\SmoothedTopClassProbability) - \StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}(\SmoothedRunnerUpProbability)\right)\), where \(\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}\) is the inverse standard normal CDF. In the binary special case, where \(\SmoothedRunnerUpProbability= 1 - \SmoothedTopClassProbability\), this reduces to \(\CertifiedRadius= \SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}(\SmoothedTopClassProbability)\). This Gaussian-smoothing bound certifies a Euclidean (\(\ell_2\)) perturbation radius, measured in the same units as the input to which the noise is added; it does not automatically certify the other norms used in attack benchmarks. If a binary decision has top-class probability \(\SmoothedTopClassProbability\) = 0.999 under noise \(\SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation\) = 0.5, the simplified radius is approximately 1.5 in those input units. For an image scaled to \([0,1]\), that radius bounds the Euclidean length of the whole perturbation vector. It is not directly comparable to the per-coordinate \(\ell_\infty\) budget of the robustness-tax comparison, because an \(\ell_\infty\) perturbation of size \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\) spread over \(\InputCoordinateCount\) pixels can have Euclidean length up to \(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\sqrt{\InputCoordinateCount}\), so a per-pixel budget that looks tiny can correspond to a long Euclidean vector on a high-dimensional image.
The multiclass case rarely estimates the runner-up probability separately. Because the class probabilities sum to one, no competing class can exceed \(1 - \SmoothedTopClassProbability\), so a lower bound on \(\SmoothedTopClassProbability\) alone also bounds every competitor. Estimating that lower bound from samples turns certification into a statistical estimation problem and adds a confidence level to the certificate; an observed class frequency alone is not a certified probability bound. Certification also carries accuracy and compute trade-offs. On ImageNet, the same work reports nontrivial certified accuracy for randomized smoothing, including certification at radius 0.5, but certification requires sampling many noise vectors per inference to estimate class probabilities with sufficient confidence. The increase in inference latency makes the sample budget a deployment constraint. Two designs keep certification outside the tight serving budget. Asynchronous auditing certifies a sampled fraction of served requests offline, so the fleet learns how often its answers were certifiable without delaying any of them. A selective safety interlock certifies only the requests routed to a safety-critical action, such as a braking decision, and lets the remaining traffic take the uncertified path.
Certified defenses cover one part of the adversarial workflow. Production systems still need detection paths for suspicious inputs, mitigation strategies that change training or serving behavior, and evaluation procedures that verify which threat models remain covered.



Detecting adversarial examples before they reach the model forms the first line of defense only when the signal reaches a serving decision: reject, transform, route, or audit. A population-level signal asks whether a window of current inputs still resembles the reference population. The two-sample tests of section 14.4.2.3 serve here unchanged. A KS test, or the Anderson-Darling test, a variant that weights differences in the distribution tails more heavily, can flag a traffic window whose inputs no longer resemble the reference. Such an alert does not identify an individual request as adversarial; per-request rejection requires an additional decision rule. These tests also inherit the drift monitors’ blind spot, since an adversarial perturbation can preserve each feature’s marginal distribution while corrupting the joint structure that joint-distribution or embedding-space comparisons would expose.
An attack that preserves marginal distributions can evade that signal, motivating a complementary comparison under input transformations. Feature squeezing15 (Xu et al. 2018) reduces input-space complexity through color bit-depth reduction or spatial smoothing, then compares the model’s prediction before and after the transformation. A large prediction change flags sensitivity to the transformation. It does not by itself establish malicious intent or identify which image detail caused the change; legitimate inputs can also trigger the detector.
15 Feature Squeezing: Defense proposed by Xu et al. (2018) that reduces input precision (for example, 256 to 16 color levels) or applies spatial smoothing (median filtering) to disrupt some fine-grained perturbations. Such transformations can also alter useful clean-input features and do not cover every attack mechanism. In their evaluation, feature squeezing eliminated many adversarial examples while maintaining high clean accuracy; adaptive attacks require validation before treating the defense as production-ready.
Xu, Weilin, David Evans, and Yanjun Qi. 2018. “Feature Squeezing: Detecting Adversarial Examples in Deep Neural Networks.” Proceedings 2018 Network and Distributed System Security Symposium 26. https://doi.org/10.14722/ndss.2018.23198.

Lakshminarayanan, Balaji, Alexander Pritzel, and Charles Blundell. 2017. “Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation Using Deep Ensembles.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30.
Another signal asks whether the model is uncertain about its own answer. An uncertainty estimate can route an input for rejection, human review, or a more robust model. Bayesian neural networks estimate uncertainty by placing a probability distribution over each weight and averaging predictions over sampled weights, so disagreement among those samples signals uncertainty, while ensemble methods compare predictions from independently trained models and use disagreement as the warning signal (Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017). Their detection value depends on whether uncertainty distinguishes harmful inputs from legitimate ones under the chosen attack. Repeated predictions add inference work, so deployments must evaluate both missed attacks and serving cost rather than assume that a more expensive estimator detects more.
Dropout, the training-time regularizer that randomly deactivates neurons (Hinton et al. 2012), offers a cheaper approximation to that weight sampling. It can be repurposed for uncertainty estimation through Monte Carlo dropout16 at inference time, where multiple forward passes with different dropout masks approximate the uncertainty distribution. Monte Carlo dropout is itself an approximate Bayesian method. Its uncertainty estimates must be validated on the deployment population rather than ranked by the original purpose of dropout. Hybrid approaches that combine dropout with lightweight ensemble methods or Bayesian approximations balance computational efficiency with estimation quality, making uncertainty-based detection more practical for production deployment.

Hinton, G. E., N. Srivastava, A. Krizhevsky, I. Sutskever, and R. R. Salakhutdinov. 2012. “Improving Neural Networks by Preventing Co-Adaptation of Feature Detectors.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1207.0580.
16 Monte Carlo dropout: Proposed by Gal and Ghahramani (2016), MC dropout reinterprets dropout as approximate Bayesian inference by keeping dropout active across repeated stochastic forward passes. The variance across predictions provides an uncertainty estimate with no architectural changes. Each additional sample adds inference work, so deployments must select the sample count against their latency and uncertainty budgets.
Gal, Yarin, and Zoubin Ghahramani. 2016. “Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning.” Proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 48: 1050–59.



Adversarial training, certification, and detection do not exhaust the options. The remaining strategies move the spending point rather than eliminating the cost. Defensive distillation (Nicolas Papernot et al. 2016) teaches a student model from the teacher’s soft labels, but its apparent adversarial protection proved vulnerable to attacks that bypassed the resulting gradient masking (Carlini and Wagner 2017). It illustrates why making an attack optimizer fail is not evidence that nearby adversarial inputs are absent. Input preprocessing spends the defense budget at serving time: image denoising, JPEG compression, random resizing, padding, and random transformations try to erase perturbations before the model sees them. Ensembles spend it through redundancy, combining models with different architectures, training data, or preprocessing paths so that a perturbation that fools one member is less likely to fool all of them.

Papernot, Nicolas, Patrick McDaniel, Xi Wu, Somesh Jha, and Ananthram Swami. 2016. “Distillation as a Defense to Adversarial Perturbations Against Deep Neural Networks.” 2016 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 582–97. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2016.41.

Carlini, Nicholas, and David Wagner. 2017. “Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks.” 2017 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 39–57. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2017.49.



Evaluating adversarial defenses closes the budget loop: the system must measure which attacks the defense actually covers and what performance it sacrifices under controlled attack conditions. Robustness metrics quantify resilience through accuracy on adversarial examples, the distortion required to fool the model, and performance over attack budgets. Standardized benchmarks such as MNIST-C (Mu and Gilmer 2019), CIFAR-10-C, and ImageNet-C (Hendrycks and Dietterich 2019) measure common corruptions rather than malicious worst-case behavior, so their results occupy a different cell of table 1.

Mu, Norman, and Justin Gilmer. 2019. MNIST-C: A Robustness Benchmark for Computer Vision.

Hendrycks, Dan, and Thomas Dietterich. 2019. “Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1903.12261.
Empirical attack evaluation must be adaptive to the defense. The evaluator should know the preprocessing, detector, randomness, ensemble, and rejection rule; optimize through differentiable components; use expectation over transformation for randomness; test transfer and query-based attacks when gradients are unavailable; and include the complete pipeline rather than a saved model alone. Multiple random restarts and attack budgets can strengthen evidence within that threat model, but a passed PGD test proves neither that PGD found the inner maximum nor that semantic, physical, or differently normed attacks are covered. Only a certificate establishes a guarantee, and only for its stated input, norm, radius, and assumptions.




The defenses above were built for classifiers, and generative models need the same discipline in a new form. An aligned language model of the Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) class can pass its safety evaluations and still comply with a harmful request once an automatically optimized suffix is appended to the prompt, and suffixes optimized against open models transfer to other models (Zou et al. 2023). That suffix is an adversarial example in token space, found by gradient-guided search over discrete tokens rather than continuous pixels. Generative models also fail without any attacker. Their output is open-ended text rather than a label, so the robustness question changes from whether a label flips under perturbation to whether the generated content preserves factuality, policy constraints, and task intent across prompt variations. A fluent answer can be factually baseless while latency and uptime stay healthy, which makes hallucination the generative form of silent failure.

Zou, Andy, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini, Milad Nasr, J. Zico Kolter, and Matt Fredrikson. 2023. Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models.
The evaluation discipline of table 1 carries over with three adjustments. First, correctness needs a named reference. A hallucination rate is meaningful only against a stated evidence source, such as the retrieved context, a verified knowledge base, or an expert-labeled answer set, and it counts the generated claims that this reference does not support. The measured rate also depends on the model, the retrieval context, the prompt design, and the sampling temperature, so a reported rate holds only for its prompt set and decoding settings and cannot be carried to another domain without re-measurement. Second, the perturbation budget becomes a family of prompt variations. Paraphrases, reordered context, and inserted distractors play the role that the \(\ell_\infty\) ball plays for an image classifier, and robustness is reported for each family. Third, the slices are domains and user populations, because an aggregate rate can hide a domain in which the model invents answers, just as the Google Photos failure hid inside aggregate image accuracy.
Detecting a hallucination on an individual request is the per-request competence problem of section 14.4.4 with an open-ended output. Token entropy and log-probability can expose instability in a generation, but neither is a factuality score. A model can assign high probability to a false statement learned from its data, or low probability to a correct but rare statement. Production routing must therefore calibrate these signals against task-specific errors and combine them with evidence checks, retrieval support, or external verification.
The self-consistency technique samples multiple reasoning paths or answers for the same query. Disagreement supplies an instability signal that can route the request for review; agreement supplies weaker evidence because correlated samples can repeat the same misconception or unsupported claim. Sequence-level entropy has the same limitation: it can serve as a calibrated routing feature for a named task, but it does not transform uncertainty into truthfulness. The signal also has a price. Each additional sample repeats the decode phase for that request, so drawing \(\SelfConsistencySampleCount\) samples multiplies its decode work roughly \(\SelfConsistencySampleCount\)-fold; only the prompt’s prefill can be shared, when the serving system reuses the prompt’s cached key-value state. Like the noise samples of randomized smoothing, this cost lands on the compute term of every request it covers, and the same remedy applies. The expensive signal should be spent on the requests whose cheap signals already indicate uncertainty rather than on all traffic. The operational contract must measure error conditional on the routing score and provision the refusal, retrieval, tool, or human path that receives flagged generations.


↩︎ Reuse of a shared prompt’s cached key-value state across requests is established in Prefix caching.
In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architectures, robustness depends heavily on the quality of the retrieved context. Retrieval noise, the injection of irrelevant or conflicting documents into the prompt, can distract the model, causing it to ignore its internal parametric knowledge and propagate errors from the context. Robust RAG deployments can use re-ranking models and context verifiers to filter out noise before it reaches the generation step. Their evaluation must separate retrieval failure from generation failure. Measuring answer support separately for requests whose retrieved context contains the answer and for requests whose context does not shows whether errors come from the retriever or from a model that ignores or overrides good evidence. The retrieval corpus is also an input an attacker may be able to write to, so a planted document can corrupt retrieval evidence or carry prompt injection, and the ingress controls of section 14.7 apply to it. It becomes a training-poisoning path if the pipeline later admits it into learning.
Language interfaces also carry the input-level attacker into text. Prompt injection, a failure of the boundary between control and data, embeds instructions in user content or retrieved documents so that the model overrides its system prompt. The payload can arrive through a legitimate input channel, so permission to submit content does not make that content trustworthy. External access controls still constrain which data or tools the surrounding system exposes. From the robustness side, evaluation asks whether the content induces behavior outside the intended output contract, and it is measured the way adversarial robustness is measured: as an attack success rate over an injection suite matched to the threat model, run by an evaluator who knows the system prompt and filters. Keeping those details secret is not a defense, because optimized suffixes transfer across models.


↩︎ Prompt injection as a failure of the boundary between control and data is established in LLM-specific attack vectors.
A common deployment pattern adds output guardrails, lightweight classifiers that scan generated text for policy violations or toxicity before the response returns to the user. A guardrail threshold trades the same two quantities as a selective-prediction threshold. Each false positive refuses or escalates a legitimate response, so the false-positive rate multiplied by the legitimate-request rate estimates false refusals or escalations; each false negative is residual risk that reaches the user. Total diverted load also includes correctly flagged harmful responses. The arrival rate at each refusal, retrieval, or human path is the incoming request rate multiplied by the fraction routed to that path under the policy, counting both true and false flags. Choosing the threshold from a curve measured on representative traffic, rather than from the classifier’s default, allows the team to compare that load with the path’s capacity. The guardrail also adds a model inference to every response, so its latency counts against the serving deadline. Finally, a guardrail is itself a model with its own decision boundary, so it carries the same obligation as any other defense and must pass the adaptive evaluation above against an attacker who knows it is there.
Adversarial training, certified defenses, and generative guardrails address attacks on model inputs at inference time within bounded threat models. They do not establish that the model was trained on trustworthy data. If an adversary compromises the data pipeline long before the model is compiled, inference-time behavioral tests may reveal a backdoor, but cannot by themselves establish the integrity of the training pipeline. The data poisoning attacks described earlier demand their own class of defenses.

Checkpoint 14.3: Choosing and budgeting an adversarial defense
An adversarial defense is a budgeted response to a specific threat model. Stronger guarantees commonly change clean accuracy, compute, latency, or coverage, but the direction and magnitude depend on the workload, model, defense, and evaluation boundary.
Matching defense to threat

Worst-case evaluation: explain why passing a white-box PGD test provides empirical evidence only for the evaluated model, norm, budget, restarts, and attack implementation rather than a general worst-case guarantee.
Threat-model fit: match the defense emphasis to an API-facing classifier and a safety-critical road-sign detector, and explain why adversarial training alone does not transfer between them.

Reasoning about the budget

Certified vs. empirical: explain when randomized smoothing’s sampling cost favors asynchronous auditing or a selective serving path rather than assuming that every certified deployment has the same latency constraint.
Defense budget: compare input detection with intrinsic model robustness for a low-risk component using measured clean accuracy, robust accuracy, compute, latency, and coverage rather than assuming a fixed clean-accuracy tax.




Self-Check: Question

How does multi-step adversarial training (such as PGD-7) improve a neural network’s robustness against evasion attacks during inference?

It approximately searches for high-loss perturbations within the threat set and trains the model to reduce loss on those perturbed inputs.
It encrypts the model’s weight matrices so attackers cannot estimate loss gradients via backward passes.
It removes all non-linear activation functions from the architecture, ensuring the decision boundary is strictly linear.
It replaces model weights with random distributions at inference time without requiring any changes during training.

In the chapter’s equal-cost-pass PGD-7 work model, one update pass and seven attack-generation passes cost eight standard passes per batch. Standard-model clean accuracy is 76 percent, and robust-model accuracy under the specified attack is 50 percent. Explain what these quantities establish and what further measurements are needed to isolate a clean-accuracy tax and elapsed-time penalty.
Which statement correctly distinguishes certified robustness (such as randomized smoothing) from empirical robustness (such as PGD adversarial training)?

Empirical robustness provides mathematical guarantees across all possible norm balls, whereas certified robustness is validated only against specific attacks.
Certified defenses require zero additional compute at inference time, making them ideal for high-throughput microservices.
A valid certificate bounds prediction stability within its stated set and assumptions; empirical attack tests supply evidence for tested cases, while randomized smoothing adds sampling cost on the inputs certified.

Order the four stages of the chapter’s adversarial defense workflow: (1) Choose the robustness budget across training-time, inference-time, and guardrail layers, (2) Define the threat model by specifying perturbation bounds (\(\epsilon\)), norm constraints, and attacker access, (3) Keep evaluation adversarial by testing defenses against adaptive and stronger optimization attacks, (4) Measure the trade-off between clean accuracy, training compute, and serving latency.
A real-time image moderation service with a strict 50 ms p99 latency SLA cannot afford randomized smoothing, which requires thousands of forward passes. Design an adversarial defense portfolio that fits this latency budget and explain the trade-offs involved.
