Figure 4 breaks down the memory row. Panel (a) starts with 40 MB of FP32 weights for a 10M-parameter model and adds 40 MB of gradients, 80 MB of Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) state for its two moment arrays, and 200 MB of assumed activation state to reach 360 MB, a \(9\times\) amplification over the weights. The same accounting spans the table’s range. Weights, gradients, and Adam’s two moments alone are four weight-sized arrays, the 4\(\times\) floor reached when saved activations are negligible, and activations between five and eight times the weight bytes carry the total from 9\(\times\) to 12\(\times\). Panel (b) holds the 9\(\times\) proportions fixed across model scales from 1M to 100M parameters, so its constant ratio is an assumption rather than a finding. What it shows is the absolute cost of that ratio. The gap between weights and training stack grows from tens of megabytes at 1M parameters to gigabytes at 100M, so a model whose weights fit comfortably can still have a training stack that does not. Actual peak memory depends on optimizer choice, batch size, activation checkpointing, and how many layers are updated, and the 4–12\(\times\) range describes these configurations rather than predicting any particular device.


↪ The bytes per parameter that weights, gradients, and optimizer state occupy in mixed-precision Adam training are developed in Numeric Precision and Training Memory.














Figure 4: The training memory amplifier: (a) On a linear axis, the training stack for a 10M-parameter FP32 model shows what fills memory: gradients match the weights, Adam state doubles them, and activations dominate. (b) On a log axis, inference and training totals keep the same ratio from 1M to 100M parameters. The configuration is illustrative (activations assumed at 5\(\times\) the weights), producing a representative 9\(\times\) amplification.





Memory consumption changes over an update as tensors are allocated and released. The peak depends on when weights, saved activations, gradients, optimizer state, and temporary workspace coexist; it need not occur at the same operation in every implementation. For the 10M-parameter model of figure 4, 40 MB of FP32 weights belong to a 360 MB training working set, of which 200 MB is saved activations. Set against a smartphone’s 8 GB of installed RAM, that working set looks small, but installed RAM is not the budget. A background task receives only the allowance the operating system grants after itself and the foreground applications, 200 MB–300 MB in the keyboard profile of section 11.2, and 360 MB exceeds even the top of that range. Activation checkpointing (also called gradient checkpointing) discards selected intermediate activations and recomputes them during the backward pass (Chen et al. 2016), the same trade that cuts activation memory in data-center training. It trades extra computation for lower activation storage, so its value depends on both the peak it removes and the additional time and energy the device can afford.

Chen, Tianqi, Bing Xu, Chiyuan Zhang, and Carlos Guestrin. 2016. “Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1604.06174.

↩︎ Activation checkpointing, which recomputes selected activations in the backward pass to cut activation memory at the cost of extra FLOPs, is established in Compute-phase forward and backward passes.

That allowance, not installed RAM, is the ceiling for a working-memory budget that every adaptation strategy in this chapter must meet (figure 5). The runtime stages frozen weights from nonvolatile flash into volatile working memory and reserves headroom below the physical device ceiling \(\DeviceMemoryCapacity\) for runtime and application state. Within the working-memory envelope \(\AdaptationPeakMemory\), four quantities contribute: let \(\ResidentWeightMemory\) be the backbone weights that must reside in working memory, \(\TrainableStateMemory\) the trainable parameters plus their gradients and optimizer state, \(\ActivationMemory(\TimeInstant)\) the saved activation state, and \(\OperatorWorkspaceMemory(\TimeInstant)\) operator workspace. With all terms counted in bytes and disjoint, the required working memory is
\[
\AdaptationPeakMemory= \ResidentWeightMemory+ \TrainableStateMemory+ \max_t\left[\ActivationMemory(\TimeInstant) + \OperatorWorkspaceMemory(\TimeInstant)\right].
\tag{1}\]
Admission then requires \(\AdaptationPeakMemory+ \ReservedDeviceMemory\le \DeviceMemoryCapacity\), where \(\ReservedDeviceMemory\) holds the runtime, the operating system, and the foreground application; for a background task, \(\DeviceMemoryCapacity- \ReservedDeviceMemory\) is the allowance just described. Weights stored in nonvolatile memory still consume deployment storage, and any staging buffers belong in \(\OperatorWorkspaceMemory(\TimeInstant)\). The maximum must follow the actual execution schedule because activation and workspace peaks need not coincide. Each term is a separate lever, and the adaptation strategies of section 11.8 differ in which term they shrink. Freezing weights removes their gradients and optimizer state from \(\TrainableStateMemory\), but it does not make the frozen base or every backward dependency disappear.






Figure 5: Adaptation memory budget: Working memory must hold the resident weights \(\ResidentWeightMemory\), the trainable state \(\TrainableStateMemory\), and the peak of live activations plus workspace; together these form \(\AdaptationPeakMemory\), which must fit under the device limit once the runtime and foreground application are reserved. Frozen weights kept in nonvolatile flash count toward storage, not working memory, until they are staged, and staging buffers belong to the workspace term. Segment heights are schematic, not to scale.



An inference optimization therefore needs a second feasibility check before it is used for adaptation. Reducing stored weights may leave activations or optimizer state as the dominant cost. Selecting which parameters to train changes that accounting, linking the memory analysis to the adaptation choices that follow.

Checkpoint 11.1: On-device training constraints
Verify understanding of how training amplifies edge constraints:

Training memory blowup: Explain where the 4\(\times\) floor of the chapter’s 4\(\times\) to 12\(\times\) training-memory range comes from, and which term pushes a configuration toward the upper end.
Timing of the peak: Explain why peak training memory depends on when weights, saved activations, gradients, optimizer state, and workspace coexist, rather than on the sum of every tensor the update ever touches.
Backward-pass OOM: Explain why a 10M parameter model can still trigger out-of-memory errors during the backward pass on a smartphone with 8 GB of RAM.
Checkpointing energy: Evaluate the claim that activation checkpointing reduces the total energy consumed by on-device training.







The structure and size of the machine learning model directly determine whether on-device training is possible. Cloud-deployed models can span billions of parameters and rely on multi-gigabyte memory budgets; models intended for on-device learning must conform to tight constraints on memory, storage, and computational complexity. Training tightens each of them by the factors of table 2.
The scale of these constraints becomes concrete across the device spectrum. MobileNetV2, commonly used in mobile vision tasks, requires approximately 14 MB of storage in its standard configuration. While feasible for smartphones with gigabytes of available RAM, this far exceeds the 256 KB of SRAM and 1 MB of flash storage on microcontrollers such as the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense.5 On such severely constrained platforms, even a single convolutional layer may exceed available RAM during training due to intermediate feature maps and gradient storage.
5 Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense: With 256 KB SRAM, roughly 65,536× smaller than a flagship smartphone’s 16 GB, a single \(224{\times}224{\times}3\) RGB image occupies ~151 KB and consumes roughly 60 percent of available memory; activation and gradient storage add several more live tensors, and optimizer state can push the training footprint far beyond the inference footprint. A convolutional neural network (CNN) layer can therefore exceed SRAM during backpropagation even when its weights fit. Quantization can reduce this footprint, but feasibility also depends on input size, saved activations, and which parameters are updated.Training adds state whose size cannot be inferred from layer count alone. Backpropagation retains or recomputes intermediate activations, with storage determined by tensor shapes, precision, batch size, and the update schedule. The arithmetic grows quickly. A 10-layer convolutional model processing \(64{\times}64\) images saves feature maps of \(64{\times}64\) values per channel when its layers keep the input resolution, so at FP32 every channel of every retained map costs 16,384 bytes, about 16 KB. Ten layers of even a few channels each therefore outgrow the 256 KB of microcontroller SRAM before a single gradient or optimizer value is stored. The relevant comparison is that peak against the memory available to learning after runtime and application reserves, which is why the techniques later in this chapter attack saved activations as well as trainable parameters.
Model complexity also affects runtime energy consumption and thermal limits. In smartwatches or battery-powered wearables, sustained training can deplete the energy allowance or trigger thermal throttling even when its tensors fit in memory. Arithmetic precision alone does not determine feasibility; the update duration and measured power determine its energy cost. Benchmarks such as MLPerf Tiny provide small quantized inference targets for constrained devices (Banbury et al. 2021). On-device adaptation techniques address the additional training cost by freezing most parameters, reducing activation storage, or selecting sparse update sets (Cai et al. 2020; Kwon et al. 2024).

Banbury, Colby, Vijay Janapa Reddi, Peter Torelli, Jeremy Holleman, Nat Jeffries, Csaba Kiraly, Pietro Montino, et al. 2021. “MLPerf Tiny Benchmark.” arXiv Preprint.
Battery and thermal constraints also determine when learning can run. The illustrative smartphone profile uses a sustained processing envelope of 2–3 W and brief bursts of 5–10 W. An update that fits during an idle interval may exceed the available headroom when foreground work starts. Charging supplies energy, but the runtime must still monitor heat and contention, reducing the update duty cycle or suspending learning when limits are approached. An overnight idle-and-charging policy provides one candidate window; measured device conditions determine whether that window remains usable.
These constraints make adaptation feasibility part of architecture selection. When the base model exceeds device capacity, partitioning, quantization, offloading, or a smaller architecture can change the deployment footprint, each with its own execution cost. Lightweight architectures such as MobileNets, SqueezeNet (Iandola et al. 2016), and EfficientNet (Tan and Le 2019) address resource-constrained inference through mechanisms such as depthwise separable convolutions,6 bottleneck/fire modules, and compound model scaling. Fitting the forward path is the starting point; quantization support and selective-update costs must then be established for the training path.

Iandola, Forrest N., Song Han, Matthew W. Moskewicz, Khalid Ashraf, William J. Dally, and Kurt Keutzer. 2016. “SqueezeNet: AlexNet-Level Accuracy with 50x Fewer Parameters and <0.5MB Model Size.” ArXiv Preprint abs/1602.07360.

Tan, Mingxing, and Quoc V Le. 2019. “EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 6105–14.
6 Depthwise Separable Convolutions: Decomposes a standard convolution into a per-channel depthwise filter followed by a \(1{\times}1\) pointwise combination. For a \(3{\times}3\) convolution with 512 input/output channels, this reduces parameters from 2.36 M to about 267 K, an 8.8\(\times\) reduction in weight storage and arithmetic, though not in activation storage. The intermediate depthwise output can add saved state, so training-memory savings depend on tensor shapes and whether the implementation fuses, retains, or recomputes that intermediate.
Howard, A. G., M. Zhu, B. Chen, D. Kalenichenko, W. Wang, T. Weyand, M. Andreetto, and H. Adam. 2017. “MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications.” CoRR abs/1704.04861.

Sandler, Mark, Andrew Howard, Menglong Zhu, Andrey Zhmoginov, and Liang-Chieh Chen. 2018. “MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 4510–20. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00474.
Modularity is a key design property. MobileNets (Howard et al. 2017) and MobileNetV2 (Sandler et al. 2018) can be configured with different width multipliers and resolution settings to balance performance and resource usage. A complete MobileNetV2 with width multiplier \(\MobilenetWidthMultiplier=1.0\) has approximately 3.5M parameters (14 MB in FP32). With \(\MobilenetWidthMultiplier=0.5\), the complete 1000-class model has approximately 2.0M parameters (7.9 MB), while a feature-extractor-only deployment with a small task-specific head can be as small as 0.69M parameters (2.8 MB), fitting within a 4 MB model budget.



Model architecture determines the memory and computational baseline for on-device learning, but data availability and quality introduce equally fundamental limitations that shape every aspect of the learning process. Data available to on-device ML systems differs dramatically from the large, curated datasets used in cloud-based training. At the edge, data is locally collected, temporally sparse, and often unstructured or unlabeled. The resulting challenges in volume, quality, and statistical distribution directly affect the reliability and generalizability of on-device learning.
Useful training data can remain scarce even when sensors produce many readings. A smart fitness tracker may record an entire exercise session while receiving only one activity label. Sampling frequency, windowing, and temporal correlation determine how those readings become examples, and a whole session of correlated readings can still amount to a single labeled observation. The learning policy must therefore budget for usable supervision as well as stored bytes.
On-device data is also frequently non-i.i.d. (Zhao et al. 2018). A voice assistant deployed across households encounters variation in accents, languages, speaking styles, and command patterns. Smartphone keyboards observe individual typing patterns, autocorrect preferences, and multilingual usage. Centralized systems also encounter such variation, but a federated coordinator cannot freely shuffle raw examples across clients. Local updates therefore reflect different data distributions, complicating the balance between shared generalization and personalization.
Label scarcity compounds the distribution problem. Most edge-collected data is unlabeled by default, requiring systems to learn from weak or implicit supervision signals. A smartphone camera may capture thousands of images throughout the day, but only a few are associated with meaningful user actions (tagging, favoriting, or sharing) that could serve as implicit labels. In many applications, including anomaly detection in sensor data and gesture recognition adaptation, explicit labels may be entirely unavailable, making traditional supervised learning infeasible without alternative methods for weak supervision or unsupervised adaptation.
Data quality introduces further challenges. Environmental sensors or automotive ECUs can experience calibration changes, interference, or mechanical wear that corrupt or shift input signals. An adaptation loop may learn from those changes as if they represented useful new behavior. Local input checks and validated outcome signals must distinguish sensor faults from changes the model should learn, especially when raw observations are unavailable for central inspection.
Privacy and security requirements can further restrict which examples may be retained or shared. Keeping health data, personal communications, or behavioral traces on the device narrows raw-data exposure, but local storage and transmitted updates remain sensitive. The learning design must specify access, retention, and permitted disclosures alongside the data needed for adaptation and validation.



The edge hardware landscape provides the computational substrate for machine learning, spanning from microcontrollers like STM32F4 and ESP32 at the most constrained end, to mobile-class processors with dedicated AI accelerators (Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon, Google Tensor) in the middle, and high-capability edge devices at the upper end. While these devices offer varying levels of inference capabilities (computational throughput, memory bandwidth, and energy efficiency when executing pretrained models), training workloads exhibit fundamentally different computational characteristics that reshape hardware utilization patterns.
The update path adds work that an inference rating does not measure. Backpropagation reads saved or recomputed activations, produces gradients, and updates parameters and optimizer state. These operations add memory traffic, with the amount determined by the trainable subset and execution schedule. Each device class that follows therefore gets the update-path test from the start of the chapter, applied to its own memory, operators, and power, rather than a verdict read from its inference rating.
At the most constrained end, devices such as the STM32F47 or ESP32-S3 microcontrollers offer only a few hundred kilobytes of SRAM and limited compute and power budgets (Warden and Situnayake 2020). Although these families include single-precision floating-point support, practical ML deployments commonly rely on quantized or fixed-point kernels for efficiency. Libraries like CMSIS-NN (Lai et al. 2018) provide optimized neural network kernels for Arm Cortex-M processors, achieving 4.6\(\times\) runtime improvement through fixed-point arithmetic and single instruction, multiple data optimizations. These severe limitations preclude conventional deep learning libraries and require models designed for quantized arithmetic and minimal runtime memory allocation. Quantization-aware training8 can prepare models for efficient quantized inference. Executing local updates requires a separately supported training path, potentially with selective updates, quantized gradients, or a compact floating-point working set.
7 STM32F4 Microcontroller: With 192 KB SRAM, a 168 MHz clock speed, and a single-precision floating-point unit, the main constraint is not the absence of floating point but the tiny memory and energy envelope. A dense layer with 1,000 input features and 10 hidden units requires approximately 40 KB for weights and biases in FP32, consuming about 20 percent of total SRAM before accounting for activations or gradients. Local updates must therefore fit around the device’s primary workload and power budget, and INT8 or fixed-point kernels remain preferable when accuracy allows.
Warden, Pete, and Daniel Situnayake. 2020. TinyML: Machine Learning with TensorFlow Lite on Arduino and Ultra-Low-Power Microcontrollers. O’Reilly Media.

Lai, Liangzhen, Naveen Suda, and Vikas Chandra. 2018. “CMSIS-NN: Efficient Neural Network Kernels for Arm Cortex-M CPUs.” ArXiv Preprint abs/1801.06601.
8 Quantization-Aware Training (QAT): Simulates quantization during training to adapt the model to low-precision inference (Jacob et al. 2018; Krishnamoorthi 2018). Fake-quantization operations commonly retain floating-point training tensors, so QAT does not itself imply integer backward kernels or a smaller training-state budget. On-device adaptation must separately establish supported update arithmetic, state storage, and measured energy costs.
Jacob, Benoit, Skirmantas Kligys, Bo Chen, Menglong Zhu, Matthew Tang, Andrew Howard, Hartwig Adam, and Dmitry Kalenichenko. 2018. “Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference.” 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2704–13. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2018.00286.

Krishnamoorthi, Raghuraman. 2018. “Quantizing Deep Convolutional Networks for Efficient Inference: A Whitepaper.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1806.08342 abs/1806.08342.
9 SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent): Plain SGD stores parameters and gradients, while Adam additionally retains two moment arrays. At the same precision and with all arrays resident, that is four parameter-sized arrays instead of two, before activations and workspace. Momentum, master weights, gradient accumulation, and offloading change this accounting. Optimizer choice also affects convergence, so lower state cost must be evaluated against the updates needed to reach the quality target.Microcontroller memory rules out training configurations whose live tensors exceed SRAM, rather than every convolutional model. Feasibility depends on tensor shapes, update scope, numerical representation, and the compiled execution schedule. Plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) reduces optimizer state compared with methods that retain additional moment arrays.9 Non-neural adaptation, such as \(\ClusterCount\)-means clustering, offers a different way to update local centroids for sensor analysis. The method and its arithmetic must still fit the available memory and produce a validated improvement; neither a simple optimizer nor integer execution establishes that result alone.
Moving up the computational hierarchy, mobile-class hardware represents improvement but still operates under severe constraints. Platforms including the Qualcomm Snapdragon, Apple Neural Engine,10 and the Google Tensor system-on-chip (SoC) provide significantly more compute power than microcontrollers, often featuring dedicated AI accelerators and optimized support for 8-bit or mixed-precision matrix operations. These accelerators offer dedicated matrix multiplication units, on-chip memory hierarchies, and power management features specifically designed for neural network inference, with varying support for local training workloads. While these platforms can support more sophisticated training routines, including full backpropagation over compact models, they still fall far short of the computational throughput and memory bandwidth available in centralized data centers. For instance, training a lightweight transformer on a smartphone is technically feasible but must be tightly bounded in both time and energy consumption to avoid degrading the user experience, highlighting the persistent tension between learning capabilities and practical deployment constraints.
10 Apple Neural Engine: Apple’s dedicated neural accelerator, first shipped in the A11 Bionic in 2017; its rating growth through the A18 Pro is tracked in figure 1. Which of an update’s operators actually reach it, rather than falling back to the CPU or GPU, is the runtime question worked through in section 11.7.5.3.Published benchmark results from MLPerf Tiny and vendor data illustrate the range of edge inference costs in figure 6. The plotted tiers span roughly 100\(\times\) in energy per inference. Dedicated neural processors such as the Syntiant Core 2 and STM32N6 NPU occupy the sub-millijoule MCU and application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) band (30 to 444 \(\Glyph{\mu}\)J per inference across keyword spotting, visual wake words, and small-image classification, with keyword spotting finishing in under 5 ms), Google Coral appears near 4.8 mJ, and the Jetson AGX Orin appears near 15 mJ for ResNet-50. The roughly 100\(\times\) gap mixes different workloads with different hardware, so it is not a matched-task efficiency comparison. Energy per inference does not determine battery lifetime on its own, because inference frequency, sleep power, sensing, radio use, and usable battery capacity also enter that budget. For a learning device the figure sets the scale against which an update must be judged. One evaluation costs microjoules to millijoules, while each second of training inside the 2–3 W sustained envelope spends joules, more than a thousand keyword-spotting evaluations at the plotted 30 to 160 \(\Glyph{\mu}\)J. An update can therefore be a substantial energy cost, but its share of the device budget depends on how often training and inference run. Both paths need measurement over the same operating period.














Figure 6: The edge inference landscape: Published inference latency and energy measurements from MLPerf Tiny and official benchmarks reveal three distinct hardware tiers separated by approximately 100\(\times\) in energy per inference; because the tiers run different workloads (keyword spotting and small-image tasks versus ResNet-50), the gap mixes hardware efficiency with workload size. Dedicated neural processors (Syntiant, STM32N6) achieve keyword spotting in under 5 ms at 30–160 microjoules, while edge GPUs (Jetson Orin) deliver sub-millisecond latency at 15 mJ.



These computational limitations become especially acute in real-time or battery-operated systems. The foreground latency budgets established in section 11.3 constrain the interference local training may introduce; they do not require training to finish within an inference deadline. The harder constraint is that adaptation cannot have the device to itself. In a smartphone-based speech recognizer, on-device adaptation must seamlessly coexist with primary inference workloads without interfering with response latency or system responsiveness. Similarly, in wearable medical monitors, training must occur opportunistically during carefully managed windows (typically during periods of low activity or charging) to preserve battery life and avoid thermal management issues.
Beyond raw computational capacity, the architectural implications of these hardware constraints extend into fundamental system design choices. Training operations exhibit fundamentally different memory access patterns than inference workloads: gradient computation, activation storage, and optimizer updates add memory traffic whose magnitude depends on which parameters train and which intermediate states are retained. These transfers can create bottlenecks that pure computational metrics do not capture. Hardware designs can address these challenges with specialized support, but a particular device must expose that support through its training runtime. Mixed-precision datapaths may execute different formats in forward and backward kernels when those kernels exist. Sparse-update savings require an execution path that can actually skip the selected work; zero gradients alone do not establish reduced hardware cost (section 11.8.3). Near-memory compute architectures11 reduce data movement costs by performing gradient updates directly adjacent to weight storage, addressing the memory bandwidth bottleneck. However, many edge accelerators remain fundamentally optimized for inference workloads, creating hardware-software co-design opportunities for on-device training accelerators designed to handle the unique demands of local adaptation.
11 Near-Memory Computing: Places processing elements adjacent to or within memory arrays, reducing the data movement that often dominates arithmetic energy in conventional architectures (Horowitz 2014). Near-memory accelerator designs such as TensorDIMM illustrate how moving tensor operations closer to memory can improve throughput and energy behavior for memory-bound deep learning workloads (Kwon and Rhu 2018). For edge training, where gradient computation generates write-heavy access patterns that overwhelm cache hierarchies, this architectural shift could make some forms of on-device backpropagation more practical.
Horowitz, Mark. 2014. “1.1 Computing’s Energy Problem (and What We Can Do about It).” 2014 IEEE International Solid-State Circuits Conference Digest of Technical Papers (ISSCC), 10–14. https://doi.org/10.1109/isscc.2014.6757323.

Kwon, Youngeun, and Minsoo Rhu. 2018. “TensorDIMM: A Practical Near-Memory Processing Architecture for Embeddings and Tensor Operations in Deep Learning.” Proceedings of the 52nd Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture, 740–53. https://doi.org/10.1145/3352460.3358284.


Rising NPU ratings tempt designers to read device capability from TOPS, but every byte a local update moves crosses the same memory interface as inference traffic, and an update moves far more bytes than an inference. Counting them for the 10M-parameter model of figure 4, under the simplest assumption that each tensor crosses DRAM once per use with no cache reuse, shows how far. The forward pass reads the weights and writes the saved activations, and the backward pass rereads the activations and weights and writes the gradients. An Adam step then reads the weights, gradients, and both moments and writes the weights and moments back. One update step moves about 800 MB, 20× the weight bytes a single inference reads, and at the 51 GB/s peak bandwidth of an A17 Pro that traffic alone needs about 16 ms per step before any arithmetic is counted. Mobile language-model decode, the case already met as the autoregressive bottleneck (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)), shows the same ceiling at its starkest, since decode pressure falls on memory and interconnect rather than peak arithmetic throughput (Ma and Patterson 2026). The interface itself is narrow by data-center standards. Data-center HBM3 on an H100 provides 3,350 GB/s of peak unidirectional DRAM memory bandwidth, while flagship mobile systems sit near 51 GB/s (A17 Pro, LPDDR5) to 77 GB/s (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, LPDDR5X), a gap of roughly 44–65×.

Ma, Xiaoyu, and David Patterson. 2026. Challenges and Research Directions for Large Language Model Inference Hardware. No. 5. Vol. 59. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2026.3652916.

↩︎ The memory wall, the widening gap between arithmetic throughput and the memory bandwidth that feeds it, is established in The Memory Wall.


Datacenter high-bandwidth memory (HBM) outruns flagship mobile memory bandwidth by about 44 times.


A bandwidth gap of this size gives a corresponding gap in a bandwidth-only time ceiling only when both devices stream the same bytes and sustain the same fraction of their peak bandwidth; precision, batching, cache reuse, and runtime overhead all move the measured ratio. Low-precision weights attack that ceiling when weight traffic is what binds. Storing FP32 weights at 4 bits, for example, reduces weight bytes by 8\(\times\) and reduces that component of traffic by the same factor if the runtime consumes the compressed representation efficiently. It does not increase physical bandwidth or remove cache-state traffic and decoding overhead, and the precision choice must satisfy both quality and measured latency requirements. For an on-device update the relief is smaller still. In the count above, the three weight reads are only about 15 percent of the step’s traffic, and a quantized base leaves the saved activations, gradients, and optimizer state that make up the rest untouched.

Systems Perspective 11.2: Why bandwidth, not TOPS, is the binding constraintIn small-batch decoding, weights too large to remain in cache must repeatedly travel from memory to the compute units. The data term \((\DataVolume / \Bandwidth)\) of the single-machine iron law (The Single-Machine Iron Law) dominates only when that transfer takes longer than the required computation. Cache capacity alone cannot decide it, because weight reuse, batch size, and sustained throughput also matter. Weight quantization shrinks the weight component of \(\DataVolume\) without proportionally reducing the mathematical operation count. For a decoding workload measured to be memory bound, sustained bandwidth and bytes transferred per token are therefore more useful than peak TOPS for evaluating accelerator options. Local adaptation needs the same comparison applied to its own forward, backward, and optimizer traffic, counted per update step rather than per token, where the count above puts it at about 800 MB.






Beyond the individual constraints of models, data, and computation, on-device learning systems must navigate the underlying physics of mobile computing: power dissipation, thermal limits, and energy budgets. These physical constraints are fundamental design drivers that determine the entire feasible space of on-device learning algorithms.


Energy and thermal management represent the most challenging aspects of on-device learning system design, as they directly impact user experience and device longevity. Mobile devices operate under strict power budgets that fundamentally determine feasible model complexity and training schedules.

Napkin Math 11.1: Battery drain: The cost of edge learningProblem: A team is designing a background fine-tuning job for a personalized voice assistant on a smartphone. Run unconstrained, the training job draws 4.5 W, above the 2–3 W sustained envelope given earlier, and takes 30 minutes to complete. If the phone has a 15 Wh battery, how much of the user’s battery will this “invisible” update consume?
Math:

Total energy: 4.5 W \(\times\) 0.5 h = 2.25 Wh.
Battery impact: 2.25 Wh/15 Wh = 15 percent.

Systems insight: Consuming 15 percent of a user’s battery for one background task makes update frequency a deployment decision. That energy cannot be translated into a fixed amount of screen-on time without specifying the foreground workload. A policy of opportunistic scheduling admits learning when device conditions permit it; a federated policy might require charging, Wi-Fi, and thermal headroom. Charging supplies energy but does not remove heat or foreground contention, so those constraints still need separate checks.


This battery calculation is the local edge-learning version of a broader energy constraint: training must satisfy the user’s energy budget in addition to the model’s accuracy target. A production design therefore has to account for energy at scheduling time, compare local computation against communication cost, and defer learning when the user’s device cannot absorb the update.
That decision can be expressed as a background-work admission condition. Let \(\AdaptationWindowEnergy\) be the predicted energy for one adaptation window, \(\AdaptationEnergyAllowance\) the energy the policy permits before the next charging opportunity, \(\DevicePower\) the current sustained power, \(\AdaptationPowerIncrement\) the adaptation increment, and \(\ThermalPowerLimit\) the thermally sustainable limit. Let \(\ForegroundLatency\) be measured foreground latency, \(\AdaptationLatencyIncrease\) the worst-case latency increase under concurrent adaptation, and \(\CompletionDeadline\) the foreground deadline. The runtime admits an update only if
\[
\AdaptationWindowEnergy\le \AdaptationEnergyAllowance\quad \land \quad
\DevicePower+ \AdaptationPowerIncrement\le \ThermalPowerLimit\quad \land \quad
\ForegroundLatency+ \AdaptationLatencyIncrease\le \CompletionDeadline.
\tag{2}\]
Charging can enlarge the energy allowance, but it does not waive the thermal or foreground-latency tests. The quantities must come from device- and workload-specific profiling, and the runtime must revoke admission when the measured envelope changes. Shorter update windows, a lower duty cycle, or a smaller trainable parameter set can make a rejected update feasible; allowing background learning to consume the foreground deadline cannot.
The same test also decides who teaches a shared model. Passing it correlates with hardware class, charging habits, and connectivity, so devices that are old, rarely charged, or thermally tight contribute few updates, and the population a federated model learns from is the admitted population rather than the deployed one (principle \(\ref{pri-participation-selects-population}\)). The admission policy that protects each device is therefore also a sampling policy, and section 11.11.1 measures the skew it creates.






Device memory spans more than four orders of magnitude, phone to microcontroller.

Han, Song, Jeff Pool, John Tran, and William J. Dally. 2015. “Learning Both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NeurIPS 2015), 1135–43.

Hinton, Geoffrey, Oriol Vinyals, and Jeff Dean. 2015. “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network.” arXiv Preprint.
Capacity is the question equation 1 already answers. The update fits only if its peak working set stays inside the allowance left after the runtime and foreground reserve. Across device classes, installed memory spans more than four orders of magnitude, from about 16 GB on flagship phones through 64 MB–1 GB on IoT embedded systems to 256 KB–2 MB of microcontroller SRAM, and in every class learning sees only a share of the installed total. Quantization, pruning, and distillation can each shrink the resident and trainable terms of that working set (Jacob et al. 2018; Han et al. 2015; Hinton et al. 2015), but their gains are workload-specific and do not combine automatically, so they must be validated together against the same budget. Once the working set fits, capacity says nothing about the second question, which is how much traffic the update drives through the hierarchy and how much of that traffic the caches can absorb.
Cache locality affects execution time after the working set fits in device memory. Representative mobile hierarchies span L1 caches of 32–64 KB, L2 caches of 1–8 MB, and system memory of 4–16 GB, with access-latency differences of 10–100\(\times\) across levels; the exact capacities and costs are device-specific. The entire training batch need not fit in cache. Operator tiling and memory layout aim to reuse active tensor blocks before eviction, while batch size controls activation storage and available parallelism. Gradient accumulation can limit the microbatch working set, but it also retains accumulation state and adds accesses, so its effect on traffic must be measured.
Training adds gradient and optimizer traffic to the tensor reads and writes already required by inference. When these transfers saturate memory bandwidth, additional arithmetic capacity cannot shorten the update. The activation checkpointing introduced with peak memory usage shows why capacity and traffic must be counted separately. Recomputing activations lowers the peak footprint while adding forward work and its memory reads, so capacity can improve as traffic and energy rise. Mixed-precision training changes bytes per stored tensor, but numerical stability and supported backward kernels determine whether the smaller representation is useful. Capacity, traffic, and update time therefore need separate measurements.



Accelerator choice depends on the training primitives that the device’s software stack exposes. Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon DSP, and Google Tensor devices have different compiler and runtime contracts, so the same update can follow different paths on each. A useful execution plan identifies where feature extraction, head or adapter training, and optimizer updates run. A dedicated engine may accelerate the frozen forward path while another processor handles learning, but transfers and duplicate representations then enter the cost. The supported operators and data movement must be established for the actual device and runtime version.
A local update may therefore execute on a CPU or GPU even when inference uses the dedicated neural accelerator. On a real device, the update-path test from the start of the chapter becomes a short procedure.

List the update’s operators in execution order: the forward pass, each backward operator that the trainable subset requires, and the optimizer step.
For each operator, record the processor the runtime actually places it on, noting every fallback from the neural engine to the CPU or GPU.
At each change of processor, add the transfer and any duplicate tensor representation to the update’s memory and traffic accounting.
Measure time, peak memory, and energy for the complete traced path while a representative foreground workload runs.
Feed those measurements into equation 2 and equation 1, which decide whether the update may run.

The hardware mechanisms described under section 11.7.4 can reduce those costs, but sparse-update support or near-memory compute is not a prerequisite for training. What matters is whether the available runtime can execute the required operators within the device envelope. Architecture selection therefore shapes update precision, parameter selection, communication, and thermal policy together.




The constraint analysis yields three linked design decisions. The training amplification of table 2 motivates measuring the update footprint against equation 2 and choosing which parameters to adapt. Information scarcity, including limited local datasets, non-IID distributions, restrictions on data sharing, and minimal supervision, motivates data efficiency methods that reuse available evidence. When shared learning is useful, device heterogeneity and intermittent availability motivate federated coordination with explicit validation and privacy controls. Each pillar addresses a different constraint within the same deployment budget.
Table 3 reveals how this on-device learning constraint-solution mapping creates a systematic engineering framework: Model Adaptation addresses memory and compute limits through selective parameter updates, Data Efficiency maximizes learning from scarce private samples, and Federated Coordination enables privacy-preserving collaboration. Rather than viewing these as independent techniques, robust systems orchestrate all three approaches to create coherent adaptive systems that operate effectively within edge constraints.



Table 3: Constraint-Solution Mapping: The three fundamental constraint categories in on-device learning each drive corresponding solution approaches through direct necessity.










Constraint Category
Key Challenges
Solution Approach




Resource Amplification
• Training workloads (4–12\(\times\) memory)• Memory limitations• Power constraints
Model Adaptation• Parameter-efficient updates• Selective layer fine-tuning• Low-rank adaptations


Information Scarcity
• Limited local datasets• Non-IID distributions• Privacy restrictions
Data Efficiency• Few-shot and streaming adaptation• Experience replay• Compressed representations


Coordination Challenges
• Device heterogeneity• Intermittent connectivity• Distributed validation complexity• Scalability requirements
Federated Coordination• Federated averaging and asynchronous aggregation• Secure aggregation and differential privacy• Client selection and straggler handling






Each solution pillar addresses a different decision. Model adaptation determines what the device can update, and data efficiency determines what it can learn from the available examples. Federated coordination becomes relevant when compatible updates can benefit a shared model. Local-only adaptation can use the first two pillars without federation; a federated deployment must make all three work within the same device budgets.

Self-Check: Question

A mobile engineering team observes that fine-tuning a 10M parameter vision model on a smartphone with 8 GB of RAM causes the background training process to be killed by the operating system’s out-of-memory (OOM) killer during backpropagation. Why does training memory demand spike so severely compared to inference for the exact same model?

The base model weights dynamically expand by \(100\times\) during the forward pass due to weight unpacking.
Floating-point units on mobile SoCs automatically convert all INT8 weights to FP64 double precision during training.
Training adds gradients, optimizer state, and saved backward activations to the weights; the simultaneous peak can exceed the app’s budget even when inference fits.
The mobile operating system creates a separate virtual machine sandbox for every individual neuron in the neural network.

A quantized 7B-parameter language model achieves 12 tokens/sec on a mobile SoC advertised at 45 peak TOPS. Profiling shows that low-batch decode saturates available DRAM bandwidth while arithmetic units wait. Which hardware resource is the binding constraint?

Insufficient CPU integer arithmetic capacity for calculating cross-entropy loss.
Thermal throttling of the wireless 5G modem during token generation.
Flash storage read latency when loading the token tokenizer vocabulary.
Mobile LPDDR5X memory bandwidth (\(64\text{–}100\text{ GB/s}\)), which is roughly \(34\times\) lower than data-center HBM3, causing the memory streaming term \((D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW})\) to dominate execution time per token.

A proposed background personalization task on a smartphone draws \(4.5\text{ W}\) of sustained SoC power and requires 30 minutes to complete. Calculate the total energy consumed (in \(\text{Wh}\)) and the percentage drain on an idealized \(15\text{ Wh}\) smartphone battery. Explain why this result mandates opportunistic scheduling.
True or False: Gradient checkpointing reduces the total electrical energy consumed by an on-device training workload because it reduces peak SRAM/DRAM memory allocation.
Consider the end-to-end memory lifecycle of a single gradient update during on-device backpropagation for a convolutional layer. Order the following operational stages from first to last in execution sequence:


Discard intermediate activations and compute parameter updates in optimizer state
Forward pass computes and caches layer activations
Fetch batch inputs into SRAM buffer
Loss evaluation and backward pass calculates layer gradients using cached activations
