title: 11 Edge Intelligence
text:
The 10M-parameter model of figure 4 is an inference candidate for a smartwatch with 500 MB of total system memory, because its FP32 weights occupy 40 MB. Training every parameter would need the full 360 MB stack, most of the watch’s memory before its operating system and foreground application take their share. The weight footprint alone does not establish inference fit; activation buffers, runtime workspace, and foreground reserve must also fit. Full-model training leaves much less room for that remaining state. Freezing parameters removes their gradients and optimizer state but not the storage or execution cost of the frozen network, so the system trains only a compact, strategically placed parameter set and, where it can, also shrinks the activations that the backward pass must keep. Resource-efficient model adaptation then determines both the local work a device can complete and the shared update format the fleet can aggregate.
The engineering choice balances adaptation expressivity against resource consumption. Full fine-tuning exposes all parameters to learning and can fit sufficiently small models; retaining a fixed model can be adequate when local context already supplies the needed personalization. Between these choices, selective updates offer smaller training state. The device resource envelope determines which candidates fit: a wearable-class device with 1 MB RAM has a different budget from a smartphone with 8 GB. The local variation then determines how much trainable capacity is useful. Bias updates may capture calibration changes, while shifts requiring new features need a richer update space. Runtime support, inference cost, shared-update compatibility, and rollback determine whether the candidate can enter the deployed system.
The selection of adaptation techniques follows this matching logic, from weight freezing (section 11.8.1) to structured and sparse updates (section 11.8.3). Their order of presentation is not a universal ranking of cost or expressivity; placement, update size, and runtime support determine those properties. Building on the resource accounting in section 11.7, the target is the smallest update space that captures the local variation: preserve what works globally, adapt what matters locally. That target is reachable only under the transfer premise of section 11.4, that the frozen representations already carry most of what the local task needs. Weight freezing restricts training to selected existing parameters, such as bias terms or final layers. Structured updates add low-rank or residual components to a frozen base. Sparse updates select existing parameters according to their adaptation value and measured cost. Each choice must preserve enough useful capacity while fitting the device’s update budget.


The most direct approach to on-device learning is to freeze the majority of a model’s parameters and adapt only a minimal subset. Bias-only adaptation holds all weights fixed and updates only the bias terms (scalar offsets applied after linear or convolutional layers). The constraint reduces trainable parameters by 100–1000\(\times\), removes the weight gradients and their optimizer state from \(\TrainableStateMemory\), and helps mitigate overfitting when training data is sparse or noisy.
Consider a standard neural network layer: \[
\LayerOutputVector= \WeightMatrix\LayerInputVector+ \BiasVector\] where \(\WeightMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\WeightMatrixRowCount\times \WeightMatrixColumnCount}\) is the weight matrix, \(\BiasVector\in \mathbb{R}^\WeightMatrixRowCount\) is the bias vector, and \(\LayerInputVector\in \mathbb{R}^\WeightMatrixColumnCount\) is the input. In full training, gradients are computed and applied to both \(\WeightMatrix\) and \(\BiasVector\). In bias-only adaptation, the system freezes the weight tensor (\(\FiniteChange\WeightMatrix= \ZeroMatrix\)) and computes gradients exclusively for the bias: \[
\WeightMatrix\leftarrow \WeightMatrix, \quad \BiasVector\leftarrow \BiasVector- \LearningRate\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \BiasVector}
\]
This reduces the number of stored gradients and optimizer states, enabling training to proceed under memory-constrained conditions. The smaller trainable state helps only if the device also supports the arithmetic and activation schedule required by the update. Listing 1 makes the constraint explicit: all convolutional and fully connected weights remain frozen, while only bias terms adapt to local data.



Listing 1: Bias-Only Adaptation: Freezes model parameters except for biases to reduce memory usage and allow on-device learning.


# Freeze all parameters
for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    param.requires_grad = False

# Enable gradients for bias parameters only
for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    if "bias" in name:
        param.requires_grad = True



This pattern restricts optimizer updates to bias terms. What it saves, and what it does not, follows from the two derivatives of the layer above. The weight gradient \(\partial \LossFunction/\partial \WeightMatrix= (\partial \LossFunction/\partial \LayerOutputVector)\,\LayerInputVector^T\) needs the layer’s saved input \(\LayerInputVector\), whereas the bias gradient \(\partial \LossFunction/\partial \BiasVector= \partial \LossFunction/\partial \LayerOutputVector\) needs only the gradient arriving from above. A frozen linear layer therefore no longer has to keep its input for its own sake. Reaching a bias in an earlier layer, however, still sends the gradient back through every later layer, and each nonlinearity or normalization on that path needs its own saved state (a ReLU needs at least the mask of which inputs were positive). Freezing parameters thus shrinks \(\TrainableStateMemory\) without eliminating backward computation or all saved activation state. This is valuable when adapting pretrained models to user-specific or device-local data where the core representations remain relevant but require calibration.
Tiny Transfer Learning (TinyTL) (Cai et al. 2020) targets the activation term of equation 1 as well as trainable state. It builds on the derivative argument above. Frozen linear layers drop their saved inputs, so what remains is the backward state of nonlinearities and normalization. TinyTL combines bias adaptation with activation and normalization choices that reduce that state; optional lite residual modules restore some adaptation capacity at an additional memory cost.
Figure 7 diagrams the structural contrast between full fine-tuning (Panel A) and TinyTL (Panel B). Whereas standard fine-tuning computes gradients for every intermediate layer weight, TinyTL freezes the convolutional backbone (gray blocks) and confines parameter updates to lightweight residual side-paths and bias vectors \(\BiasVector\) (blue blocks). Crucially, the dashed backward-pass arrow spans the full network depth in both architectures: TinyTL’s memory reduction stems not from truncating the backward pass, but from avoiding the storage of intermediate feature maps needed to compute weight gradients.






Figure 7: TinyTL adaptation paths: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every weight and retains the state needed for their gradients. (B) TinyTL freezes the backbone weights (gray) and trains only each block’s bias vector (\(\BiasVector\)), small lite residual modules beside the blocks, and the classifier (blue). The backward pass still traverses every frozen block to reach those biases, so the saving comes from what must stay live for it, not from a shorter backward path; the activation and normalization choices determine that state.



The memory reduction is useful only when the frozen backbone remains expressive enough for the downstream task. The bias terms allow for minor but meaningful shifts in model behavior, particularly for personalization tasks. When domain shift is more significant, TinyTL can optionally incorporate small residual adapters to improve expressivity, all while preserving the system’s tight memory and energy profile.
TinyTL demonstrates that reducing saved activation state can matter more than reducing the number of trainable parameters alone (Cai et al. 2020). On its image-classification transfer benchmarks, TinyTL reports training-memory savings of up to 6.5× relative to fine-tuning the full network with little accuracy loss, so the adaptation working set can shrink to roughly 15 percent of the full fine-tuning footprint. The lite residual modules that recover adaptation capacity add only about 3.8 percent memory overhead in that study. Those savings depend on the selected feature extractor, input resolution, batch size, normalization, and residual-module configuration, and a saving measured on those benchmarks says nothing about whether an arbitrary frozen backbone fits into microcontroller SRAM.

Cai, Han, Chuang Gan, Ligeng Zhu, and Song Han. 2020. “TinyTL: Reduce Activations, Not Trainable Parameters for Efficient on-Device Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 11285–97.



When bias-only updates cannot capture the local change, the system can add trainable capacity while retaining a frozen backbone. Residual adaptation modules (Houlsby et al. 2019) and low-rank parameterizations (Hu et al. 2021) implement this choice in different ways. They restrict learning to added components, but their training cost includes the backward path through the surrounding network. The comparison with bias-only or full fine-tuning therefore requires both a quality target and a peak-memory measurement.

Houlsby, Neil, Andrei Giurgiu, Stanislaw Jastrzebski, Bruna Morrone, Quentin de Laroussilhe, Andrea Gesmundo, Mohammad Attariyan, and Sylvain Gelly. 2019. “Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP.” Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 97: 2790–99.


A common implementation involves inserting residual adapters, which are small residual bottleneck layers, between existing layers in a pretrained model. Consider a hidden representation \(\HiddenActivation\) passed between layers. A residual adapter introduces a transformation: \[
\AdaptedHiddenActivation= \HiddenActivation+ \ResidualAdapterFunction(\HiddenActivation)
\] where \(\ResidualAdapterFunction(\cdot)\) is a trainable function, typically composed of two linear layers with a nonlinearity: \[
\ResidualAdapterFunction(\HiddenActivation) = \WeightMatrix_2 \, \AdapterActivationFunction(\WeightMatrix_1 \HiddenActivation)
\] with \(\WeightMatrix_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{\AdapterRank\times \HiddenDimension}\) and \(\WeightMatrix_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{\HiddenDimension\times \AdapterRank}\), where \(\AdapterRank\ll \HiddenDimension\). This bottleneck design ensures that only a small number of parameters are introduced per layer.
The adapters act as learnable perturbations on top of a frozen backbone. Because they are small and sparsely applied, their weights add little storage, although their saved activations and optimizer state still count against the training budget, and they let the model shift its predictions in response to new inputs.
Listing 2 implements this residual bottleneck. Its down-projection plays the role of \(\WeightMatrix_1\), mapping width \(\HiddenDimension\) to the bottleneck width \(\AdapterRank\), a ReLU supplies \(\AdapterActivationFunction\), and its up-projection plays the role of \(\WeightMatrix_2\), restoring width \(\HiddenDimension\) before the input is added back. Such modules can be implemented efficiently on edge devices, particularly when the two projection matrices are small and fixed-point representations are supported.



Listing 2: Residual Bottleneck Adapter: The code implements a compact adapter module with down-projection and up-projection layers, reducing trainable parameter count while enabling efficient model adaptation on edge devices.


import torch.nn as nn


class Adapter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, bottleneck_dim):
        super().__init__()
        # Project from full dimension to bottleneck (e.g., 768 -> 16)
        self.down = nn.Linear(
            dim, bottleneck_dim
        )  # W1: learns compression
        # Project back to original dimension (e.g., 16 -> 768)
        self.up = nn.Linear(
            bottleneck_dim, dim
        )  # W2: learns expansion
        self.activation = nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        # Residual connection: original + nonlinear bottleneck
        # Only adapter params trained; base model frozen
        return x + self.up(self.activation(self.down(x)))



This adapter adds a small residual transformation to a frozen layer. When inserted into a larger model, only the adapter parameters are trained.



Another efficient strategy is to constrain weight updates themselves to a low-rank structure. Rather than updating a full matrix \(\WeightMatrix\), the update is approximated as: \[
\FiniteChange\WeightMatrix\approx \LowRankLeftFactor\LowRankRightFactor^T
\] where \(\LowRankLeftFactor\in \mathbb{R}^{\WeightMatrixRowCount\times \AdapterRank}\) and \(\LowRankRightFactor\in \mathbb{R}^{\WeightMatrixColumnCount\times \AdapterRank}\), with \(\AdapterRank\ll \min(\WeightMatrixRowCount,\WeightMatrixColumnCount)\). This reduces the number of trainable parameters from \(\WeightMatrixRowCount \WeightMatrixColumnCount\) to \(\AdapterRank(\WeightMatrixRowCount+ \WeightMatrixColumnCount)\). The LoRA paper and figure 8 name the same two factors \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix= \LowRankLeftFactor\) (the up-projection) and \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix= \LowRankRightFactor^T\) (the down-projection), so \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix= \LowRankLeftFactor\LowRankRightFactor^T\) throughout this section.
The mathematical intuition behind this decomposition connects to fundamental linear algebra principles: any matrix can be expressed as a sum of rank-one matrices through singular value decomposition. Constraining updates to low rank (typically \(\AdapterRank= 4\) to \(16\)) captures a restricted set of variation modes while reducing parameters. For a typical transformer layer with dimensions \(768{\times}768\), full fine-tuning requires updating 589,824 parameters. With rank-4 decomposition, only \(768{\times}4{\times}2 =\) 6,144 parameters are updated, a 99 percent reduction. Whether this retains most of the adaptation quality depends on the task, rank, and base model; low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reports that low-rank adapters can match or approach full fine-tuning on several transformer adaptation benchmarks (Hu et al. 2021).
During adaptation, the new weight matrix is computed as: \[
\AdaptedWeightMatrix= \FrozenWeightMatrix+ \LowRankLeftFactor\LowRankRightFactor^T
\]
This formulation is commonly used in LoRA,12 originally developed for transformer models (Hu et al. 2021) but broadly applicable across architectures. From a systems engineering perspective, LoRA makes the trainable adapter the artifact that can be stored, transmitted, scheduled, and rolled back separately from the frozen base model.
12 LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): Hu et al. (2021) learn rank-\(\AdapterRank\) decomposition matrices \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\) and \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\) instead of updating full weight matrices, reporting a 10,000\(\times\) reduction in trainable parameters for their GPT-3 comparison. That reduction does not apply to the full model footprint: a model with 7B parameters has about a 14 GB FP16 weight footprint before gradients, optimizer state, and activations. Even at rank 16, adapter storage depends on the dimensions and number of adapted matrices, and deployment must still accommodate the frozen base model.
Hu, Edward J., Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, and Weizhu Chen. 2021. “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2106.09685.
Figure 8 traces the parallel dataflow of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA): input \(\LayerInputVector\in \mathbb{R}^\HiddenDimension\) passes through a frozen base matrix \(\WeightMatrix_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{\HiddenDimension\times \HiddenDimension}\) and a trainable path with down-projection \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\AdapterRank\times \HiddenDimension}\) and up-projection \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\in \mathbb{R}^{\HiddenDimension\times \AdapterRank}\). Their outputs sum to \(\HiddenActivation= \WeightMatrix_0 \LayerInputVector+ \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\LayerInputVector\), with the update restricted to rank \(\AdapterRank\ll \HiddenDimension\). The base weights need no parameter gradients or optimizer state, although backward computation may still traverse the base path. Folding the product into the base weights (\(\WeightMatrix_0 + \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\)) removes separate adapter arithmetic for that merged model. Numerical compatibility, any requantization, and the cost of retaining merged copies determine whether this is the appropriate serving representation.






Figure 8: LoRA architecture: The input \(\LayerInputVector\) passes through the frozen base matrix \(\WeightMatrix_0\) and, in parallel, through a trainable low-rank path: down-projection \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\) (\(\AdapterRank \times \HiddenDimension\)) and up-projection \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\) (\(\HiddenDimension \times \AdapterRank\)), which play the roles of \(\LowRankRightFactor^T\) and \(\LowRankLeftFactor\) in the low-rank update above. Only \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\) and \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\) carry gradients and optimizer state. For serving, the product \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\) can be folded into \(\WeightMatrix_0\), removing the separate adapter operations when the merged representation is supported. End-to-end latency still needs measurement.



Consider a mobile deployment where a language model with 7B parameters has a 14 GB FP16 weight footprint, before accounting for the additional gradients, optimizer states, and activations required by full fine-tuning. That footprint exceeds smartphones with about 8 GB total memory unless the base model is quantized, partitioned, or offloaded. Choosing LoRA rank 16 restricts the update space, and this chapter’s fleet examples budget a reference adapter update of 50 MB. That figure is a communication payload, not a training-memory estimate. The device must also fit the base model, gradients, optimizer state, and live activations under its execution plan.
The smaller payload also matters under intermittent connectivity. Transferring the full FP16 model in this example requires 14 GB, while the reference adapter update is 50 MB. Transfer time depends on encoded bytes, effective link throughput, and interruptions. An adapter-only transfer provides the saving only when the receiving device already holds a compatible base model; base-version changes must be included in the communication budget.
The residual bottleneck and LoRA mechanisms both support device-tiered configurations, but they are distinct. LoRA modifies a weight matrix through a linear low-rank update; the residual bottleneck of section 11.8.2.1 includes a nonlinear activation and remains a separate module at inference. The letter \(\Glyph{r}\) plays the same role in both, as the bottleneck width of a residual adapter and the rank of a LoRA update, and in both it sets the trainable cost, so a deployment can size \(\AdapterRank\) to the memory each device class leaves for learning. Which mechanism each class receives in the first place is decided by the device-tier framework of section 11.8.2.4.

Example 11.1: On-device keyboard learningScenario: Consider a mobile keyboard that trains its next-word predictor locally and contributes updates to a shared model through federated averaging (McMahan et al. 2017).
Diagnosis: In the illustrative profile of section 11.2, one local update needs 50 MB–100 MB of working memory against a background allowance of 200 MB–300 MB, so at the selected operating point the update alone claims 25 percent of the allowance before the keyboard’s own state is counted, and the resident weights in \(\AdaptationPeakMemory\) claim more. Exceeding the allowance risks process eviction mid-update. Energy is the second constraint. An unconstrained job like the one in notebook 11.1 would take 15 percent of the battery, more than a policy that protects the user’s charge is likely to grant as \(\AdaptationEnergyAllowance\) in equation 2 while the phone runs on battery. The pipeline therefore admits training only when the device is idle, charging, and on Wi-Fi, and it quantizes update vectors to shrink the transmitted payload \(\DataVolume\).
Systems lesson: A federated keyboard must satisfy all three terms of equation 2 (energy \(\AdaptationWindowEnergy\le \AdaptationEnergyAllowance\), sustained power under \(\ThermalPowerLimit\), and typing latency under its deadline), fit \(\AdaptationPeakMemory\) within its memory allowance, respect uplink bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\), and meet its declared privacy guarantees together. Differential privacy adds a specific release guarantee and its associated costs; it is not implied by keeping raw text local.





Adapters support multiple personalized contexts with one frozen backbone. For an input width \(\HiddenDimension\), a residual bottleneck of width \(\AdapterRank\) uses \(2d\AdapterRank\) matrix parameters, plus \(\AdapterRank+\HiddenDimension\) biases when both projections include them. A deployment with several adapters must sum this count over their insertion sites; rank or bottleneck width alone does not determine the total. Stored bytes then equal parameter count times bytes per stored value. With \(\HiddenDimension= 768\) and \(\AdapterRank= 16\), one adapter holds 25,360 parameters, about 50.7 KB in FP16; one adapter after each of 12 blocks totals 304,320 parameters, roughly 0.6 MB. During training, gradients, optimizer state, and saved activations add to that storage footprint. A device can swap context-specific modules while sharing the much larger base model, provided it can hold the base and active adaptation state together.
This adapter switching pattern lets a smartphone select context-specific behavior without replacing the entire backbone. When the user enters a low-light environment, the system can load a compatible adapter into the vision pipeline; selecting an existing adapter does not itself require learning. The modularity extends naturally to federated learning: transmitting only the adapted parameters can reduce upload traffic relative to a full-model update, with savings determined by the total adapter count and encoding. Residual-adapter studies show that small trainable modules can adapt a shared visual backbone across multiple visual domains (Rebuffi et al. 2017), making them a useful design point between personalization quality and system resources. Freezing the backbone preserves its parameters, while adapters provide a bounded place for user- or context-specific updates. The resulting model can still suffer catastrophic forgetting, the loss of previously learned behavior after new updates (defined in section 11.9.2).

Rebuffi, Sylvestre-Alvise, Hakan Bilen, and Andrea Vedaldi. 2017. “Learning Multiple Visual Domains with Residual Adapters.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30.

Napkin Math 11.2: The hidden cost of personalizationProblem: A team is deploying a 10M parameter vision model to a smartphone with support for 10 different “User Contexts” (Home, Office, Car, etc.). If a full fine-tuned model requires 40 MB, how much storage does using residual adapters save instead?

Math:

Full fine-tuning: 10 contexts \(\times\) 40 MB = 400 MB.
Adapter approach: (1 \(\times\) 40 MB backbone) + (10 \(\times\) 200 KB adapters) \(\approx\) 42 MB.
Storage savings: 400 MB/42 MB \(\approx\) 9.5× total device storage reduction.
Per-context efficiency: 40 MB/0.2 MB = 200×.

Systems insight: Multiple personalized models create a storage cost even when only one runs at a time. Storing 10 copies of a 40 MB model consumes 400 MB. In this example, sharing the frozen backbone and storing separate adapters reduces the marginal storage cost of a new context by 200×. This comparison establishes storage savings; the device must still accommodate the active model, adaptation state, and context-switching cost.




Each new context costs an adapter, not a full model copy.
In smartphone camera pipelines, environmental lighting, user preferences, and lens distortion vary between users. Residual modules can adapt a frozen shared model to these differences while leaving its base weights unchanged; the combined model’s behavior still requires validation. In voice-based systems, adapters similarly provide a way to test personalized speech recognition without retraining the full acoustic model. Keeping the base and adapter versions compatible also supports rollback or switching between user-specific versions when adaptation degrades performance.



Selecting an adaptation strategy requires accounting for both resource cost and expressivity. Bias-only updates retain a small trainable state but may lack the capacity to handle structural domain shifts. Full fine-tuning exposes every parameter to adaptation and adds corresponding gradient and optimizer state. LoRA and residual adapters offer intermediate choices whose cost depends on rank or width, insertion sites, and numerical representation. The same budget, equation 1, governs each of these strategies. Because peak working memory \(\AdaptationPeakMemory\) must jointly contain resident weights, trainable state \(\TrainableStateMemory\), and the peak of live activations under the device ceiling \(\DeviceMemoryCapacity\), each strategy shrinks a different term: bias-only and adapter methods shrink \(\TrainableStateMemory\), TinyTL-style choices also shrink the activation term, and training only the final classifier, whose backward pass stops at the head, removes most of that term. Parameter storage alone therefore cannot determine whether background adaptation fits.
LoRA and residual adapters impose different deployment costs. For a fixed adapter and compatible numerical representation, LoRA’s linear update can be merged into the backbone before inference \((\MergedWeightMatrix= \FrozenWeightMatrix+ \LowRankLeftFactor\LowRankRightFactor^T)\), avoiding separate adapter arithmetic in the forward path. A quantized base may require requantization and renewed quality validation after merging. Keeping a separate merged backbone for every context also sacrifices the storage benefit of sharing one base. Residual adapters remain distinct modules (\(\LayerOutputVector= \FrozenBackboneFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \text{Adapter}(\LayerInputVector)\)); their latency cost depends on shape, placement, and runtime, while switching contexts requires only the corresponding adapter state.
The runtime must support the selected adapter’s forward operators and its training path. These can use a dynamic graph or a statically compiled update schedule; dynamic graph construction is not itself a requirement. For an inference engine such as Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) Runtime Mobile, a runtime that executes an adapter’s forward path may still lack its backward operators, optimizer, or state management. The deployment must verify both paths, including any transfers between the processor that runs inference and the processor that performs updates.
For this multi-context personalization workload, where one device switches among several adapters, system architects can use a device-tier framework to organize candidate mechanisms. On flagship phones (Tier 1) with dedicated Neural Engines and 8 GB of RAM or more, residual adapters provide a strong balance of modularity and speed, because switching contexts swaps only adapter state. On mid-range devices (Tier 2) with 1 GB up to that ceiling, LoRA may fit when a fixed adapter can be merged into a compatible base representation before inference, trading switching flexibility for zero added inference arithmetic. For ultra-constrained IoT endpoints (Tier 3) with less than 1 GB RAM, bias-only updates may be the only practical option. Budget phones show that the tier follows the memory available to learning rather than installed RAM. Their 4 GB places them in Tier 2, yet only 1 GB–2 GB remains for ML work after the operating system, and a background adaptation task may be granted less, so a deployment can reasonably hold them to the Tier 3 mechanism. The assignments follow from the workload as much as from the hardware. A workload that keeps one adaptation per user, rather than many switchable contexts, loses the reason to keep adapters separate and can favor merged LoRA even on flagship devices. The runtime must still verify the base-model footprint and admit training within the measured device envelope.

Checkpoint 11.2: Edge personalization
Verify understanding of efficient on-device adaptation:

Adapter switching: Explain why Adapter Switching is more storage-efficient than maintaining separate full-model copies for different user contexts.
Adapter size: Derive the parameter count of a residual adapter from its input width and bottleneck width, then identify the additional inputs needed to compare its storage with a full model.
Residual vs. LoRA: For a multi-context workload, identify the deployment tier (Tier 1, 2, or 3) where residual adapters are preferred over LoRA and justify the choice, then explain why a workload with one adaptation per user changes the answer.
Adapter bandwidth: Evaluate the claim that transmitting adapter weights in federated learning consumes more bandwidth than transmitting the entire model.







Sparse updates adapt selected existing parameters rather than adding modules. Their expressivity relative to adapters depends on the selected locations and parameter budget. A task-adaptive policy selects those locations using evidence about the current task or user. The resulting update space can target changes that a fixed subset misses, but selection itself consumes resources and does not guarantee that the complete training path fits the device.
The useful savings depend on what the runtime can omit. Unselected parameters need no gradient or optimizer state, but their operations may still lie on the backward path to selected parameters. A policy must therefore compare the measured update cost with its adaptation benefit; the fraction of trainable parameters alone does not predict the reduction in compute.
The key insight is that layers do not contribute equally to local performance gains. If the system can identify the minimal subset with the highest adaptation value, it can spend scarce training capacity where it changes the model’s behavior most.


Let a neural network be defined by parameters \(\ModelParameters= \{\ModelParameters_1, \ModelParameters_2, \ldots, \ModelParameters_{\LayerCount}\}\) across \(\LayerCount\) layers. In standard fine-tuning, gradients are computed and updates are performed on all parameters: \[
\ModelParameters_i \leftarrow \ModelParameters_i - \LearningRate\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ModelParameters_i}, \quad \text{for } \LayerSelectionIndex= 1, \ldots, \LayerCount
\]
In task-adaptive sparse updates, the system selects a small subset \(\SelectedLayerSet\subset \{1, \ldots, \LayerCount\}\) such that only parameters in \(\SelectedLayerSet\) are updated: \[
\ModelParameters_i \leftarrow
\begin{cases}
\ModelParameters_i - \LearningRate\frac{\partial \LossFunction}{\partial \ModelParameters_i}, & \text{if } \LayerSelectionIndex\in \SelectedLayerSet\\
\ModelParameters_i, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
The challenge lies in selecting the optimal subset \(\SelectedLayerSet\) given memory and compute constraints. A principled strategy is contribution analysis, an empirical method that estimates how much each layer contributes to downstream performance improvement. For example, one can measure the marginal gain from updating each layer independently:

Freeze the entire model.
Unfreeze one candidate layer.
Finetune briefly and evaluate improvement in validation accuracy.
Rank layers by performance gain per unit cost (e.g., per KB of trainable memory).

This layer-wise profiling yields a candidate ranking from which \(\SelectedLayerSet\) can be constructed subject to a memory budget. Gains measured one layer at a time need not add when layers train together, and shared backward dependencies change the combined cost. The selected set therefore needs a joint quality and resource check, with the profiling cost included in the adaptation budget.
Figure 9 places that ranking inside a complete selective fine-tuning pipeline. Stage 1 meta-trains the network in the cloud, which means training its initial weights so that a few later updates on new data adapt it well (the idea behind model-agnostic meta-learning, taken up in section 11.11.3). Stage 2 ranks layers or channel groups by adaptation benefit per unit of device cost and lets the device budget set the cut, and Stage 3 updates only the units above the cut on local data. Freezing the units below the cut removes their gradient and optimizer state, but the backward pass still runs through any frozen layer that lies between the loss and a selected one, so the selected set must be costed under the complete execution schedule.






Figure 9: Selective on-device fine-tuning: (1) The full network is meta-trained in the cloud on generic data. (2) Each layer or channel group is ranked by its expected adaptation benefit per unit of device cost, and the device’s data, compute, and memory budget sets the cut. (3) On the device, only units above the cut are updated on local data while the rest stay frozen. Scores and cut position are schematic.



A concrete example is TinyTrain, a method designed to allow rapid adaptation on-device (Kwon et al. 2024). TinyTrain combines offline preparation with a task-adaptive sparse-update method that dynamically selects layers or channels to update using user data, memory limits, and compute limits. At runtime, the system updates only the selected subset rather than treating the whole network as trainable.
In implementation, selective layer updating turns the ranking into requires_grad decisions or equivalent graph masks. Listing 3 extends this pattern to profiling-driven layer selection, demonstrating how hardware profiling determines which layers to update based on contribution scores and memory constraints.



Listing 3: Selective Layer Updating: This technique allows fine-tuning specific layers of a pretrained model while keeping others frozen, optimizing computational resources for targeted improvements.


# Selective layer update based on contribution analysis
# Layers selected via profiling: conv2 and fc have highest
# accuracy-per-KB impact for this task

for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    if "conv2" in name or "fc" in name:
        param.requires_grad = True  # Train high-impact layers
    else:
        param.requires_grad = False  # Freeze low-impact layers

# Parameter fraction follows layer shapes; adaptation quality requires evaluation
# Memory savings: gradient storage only for selected layers



TinyTrain makes the runtime motivation concrete. Consider a scenario where a user wears an augmented reality headset that performs real-time object recognition. As lighting and environments shift, the system must adapt to maintain accuracy, but training must occur during brief idle periods or while charging. TinyTrain addresses this constraint through task-adaptive sparse updates: the deployment process selects a small update set that fits the device’s memory and compute budget. The approach keeps adaptation fast, energy-efficient, and memory-aware when the target task and device profile match the method’s assumptions.
Task-adaptive sparse updates still introduce system-level trade-offs. Contribution analysis has a nontrivial computational cost even when it occurs during pretraining or initial profiling, so the deployment pipeline must budget for it. Stability also requires attention: if too few parameters are selected for updating, the model may underfit the target distribution, so teams need validation thresholds for the selected subset before deployment. The selection policy must also account for hardware-specific execution costs because some parameters show high contribution scores but prove expensive to update on certain architectures. Despite these trade-offs, task-adaptive sparse updates provide a practical mechanism to scale adaptation across deployment contexts from microcontrollers to mobile devices (Kwon et al. 2024).

Kwon, Y. D., R. Li, S. I. Venieris, J. Chauhan, and N. D. Lane. 2024. “TinyTrain: Resource-Aware Task-Adaptive Sparse Training of DNNs at the Data-Scarce Edge.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML).



The design target is the smallest update space that captures the local change. Full fine-tuning pays every term of equation 1; bias-only updates and head-only training fit minor calibration or new output categories; LoRA and residual adapters add bounded capacity beside a frozen backbone; task-adaptive sparse updates spend profiling effort to select valuable existing parameters. A larger update space is justified only if the measured quality gain fits the device’s training budget. Table 4 collects these adaptation strategy trade-offs, keyed to the budget term each one shrinks, so the choice can be checked against expressivity, runtime support, and selection cost.



Table 4: Adaptation Strategy Trade-Offs: Six approaches to model adaptation compared by trainable parameters, the term of the peak-memory budget (equation 1) they shrink, expressivity, suitability, and system requirements. Methods that shrink only the trainable state \(\TrainableStateMemory\) still keep the activations their backward pass needs, while head-only training also removes most of the activation term by stopping the backward pass at the classifier.

Once an adaptation mechanism fits the device’s memory and execution budget, it must still learn from the available examples. Reducing trainable state does not create labels or ensure that a user’s recent observations represent future use. The next constraint is therefore statistical: extracting reliable learning signal from sparse local data while retaining useful prior behavior.

Self-Check: Question

Why does Tiny Transfer Learning (TinyTL) freeze convolutional backbone weights and adapt biases with optional lite residual modules?

Freezing removes backbone weight-gradient and optimizer state; suitable activation and normalization choices also reduce saved backward state.
Microcontroller hardware units physically short-circuit if matrix multiplications are performed in reverse during backpropagation.
Bias parameters have mathematical properties that prevent all forms of numerical underflow in 8-bit fixed-point arithmetic.
Training bias parameters modifies the underlying kernel weights directly through implicit singular value decomposition.

A mobile vision engineer chooses between Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Residual Bottleneck Adapters for on-device camera personalization. The system requires zero additional inference latency during real-time 60 FPS video capture, while another use case requires hot-swapping between 10 user contexts without reloading the base model. How do LoRA and Residual Adapters compare across these requirements?

Residual Adapters introduce zero inference latency because they replace the backbone, while LoRA requires recomputing matrix inverses on every video frame.
LoRA updates can be merged into compatible base weights to remove the adapter execution path, while residual adapters retain separate computation and support modular context switching.
LoRA updates require storing 10 full copies of the 7B base model in SRAM, whereas Residual Adapters operate without trainable parameters.
Both methods require identical memory footprints and add exactly 50 ms of inference latency per layer.

A smart camera supports 10 personalization contexts. Its base model has 10M parameters (\(40\text{ MB}\) in FP32), and assume each complete adapter checkpoint occupies \(200\text{ KB}\). Compare storage for 10 full fine-tuned models with one shared base plus 10 adapters. Explain the architectural advantage.
In structured parameter adaptation, a technique that approximates a full weight matrix update \(\Delta W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) as the product of two low-rank matrices \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}\) and \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}\) (where \(r \ll \min(m, n)\)) is known as ____ (or Low-Rank Adaptation).

title: 11 Edge Intelligence
text:
A user corrects smartphone keyboard autocorrect perhaps three times a day. The system cannot require 10,000 labeled sentences to train a local language model. Data efficiency at the edge means learning aggressively from a sparse, noisy, and uncurated trickle of implicit user feedback, maximizing the signal extracted from each interaction.
The systems trade-off is data collection cost against adaptation quality. Every retained example costs user friction, energy, storage, and privacy exposure. A voice assistant adapting to speech samples weighs model improvement against battery drain and user comfort with always-on recording, and a keyboard chooses between logging shallow keystroke statistics and keeping full typing sessions. Unlike a central pipeline, the device cannot reach into a larger dataset when its own evidence runs short, and an application that needs a decision before enough evidence accumulates may be better served by a validated fixed model than by immediate learning. Whatever the device does learn must also stay compatible with the adaptation mechanism of section 11.8 and with any federated protocol that later consumes it.
The strategy choice depends on which scarcity binds first, and practical systems usually combine several. Few-shot learning fits cases where a few labeled or weakly labeled examples must drive personalization. Streaming updates fit settings where useful data arrives incrementally and cannot be batched in advance. Experience replay spends memory to stabilize continual updates by reusing scarce examples. Data compression reduces the storage cost of those histories so replay and lightweight training remain feasible within edge memory budgets. Data scarcity thus becomes an allocation problem, in which the device spends labels, memory, compute, and privacy budget where they produce the most reliable local signal.


In conventional machine learning workflows, effective training typically requires large labeled datasets, carefully curated and preprocessed to ensure sufficient diversity and balance. On-device learning, by contrast, must often proceed from only a handful of local examples, collected passively through user interaction or ambient sensing, and rarely labeled in a supervised fashion. These constraints motivate two complementary adaptation strategies: few-shot learning, in which models generalize from a small, static set of examples, and streaming adaptation, where incremental observations support updates scheduled within device budgets.
Few-shot adaptation uses limited labeled or weakly labeled evidence for a new task or user condition (Wang et al. 2020). Bias-only updates, adapter modules, and prototype-based classification restrict what must be learned, but each still needs validation against overfitting. Let \(\FewShotSupportSet= \{(\ModelInput_i, \ExampleLabel_i)\}_{i=1}^{\SupportSetSize}\) denote the local support set; here \(\SupportSetSize\) counts all examples in the set, rather than examples per class. A candidate policy might permit few gradient steps (\(\FewShotStepCount\ll 100\)) and a small trainable subset (\(|\UpdatedParameterSubset| \ll |\ModelParameters|\)). These are illustrative restrictions, not universal feasibility conditions. The actual step and parameter budgets follow from measured device cost and the quality target, including retained performance on earlier tasks.

Wang, Y., Q. Yao, J. T. Kwok, and L. M. Ni. 2020. “Generalizing from a Few Examples: A Survey on Few-Shot Learning.” ACM Computing Surveys 53 (3): 1–34. https://doi.org/10.1145/3386252.

Warden, Pete. 2018. “Speech Commands: A Dataset for Limited-Vocabulary Speech Recognition.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1804.03209, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1804.03209.
Keyword spotting (KWS) systems are a common target for data-efficient on-device adaptation; Speech Commands provides a dataset for training and evaluating limited-vocabulary KWS models (Warden 2018). A detector must distinguish its target phrase from background speech while meeting latency and false-activation requirements. One design uses a pretrained acoustic encoder, such as a small convolutional or recurrent network, to map audio into embeddings for a lightweight classifier. A shared encoder supplies reusable features, while local examples can support a custom wake word or an underrepresented accent. Whether those examples justify local training depends on their coverage, transfer restrictions, and the improvement over the shared detector.
Few-shot adaptation can train an output classifier or another small parameter subset from utterances collected directly on the device. A user might provide 5–10 recordings of a custom wake word while the acoustic encoder remains frozen. Those positive examples define what to recognize, but the false-activation rate on other speech and background noise is a separate measurement, and the personalized detector should not be accepted until it has been made.
Head-only adaptation is cheap in a way the peak-memory budget of equation 1 makes precise. Because the backward pass stops at the classifier, the encoder’s saved activations leave the activation term, and the encoder outputs for the support set can be computed once and reused across update steps. What remains is running the encoder forward, holding the support examples or their features, and evaluating the adapted classifier. Those costs, not the size of the head, decide whether the update fits a particular phone or microcontroller.
Beyond static few-shot learning, many on-device scenarios benefit from streaming adaptation, where models must learn incrementally as new data arrives (Hayes et al. 2020). Streaming adaptation generalizes this idea to continuous, asynchronous settings where data arrives incrementally over time. Let \(\{\ModelInput_t\}_{t=1}^{\infty}\) represent the observations selected from the stream for admitted updates. In streaming settings, observations arrive continuously, but the runtime admits training only when memory, energy, and foreground-latency budgets permit. The following rule describes one admitted update; it does not require a gradient step on every arrival. The index \(\OptimizerStepIndex\) counts these update steps. The computable loss may come from implicit feedback, pseudo-labels, self-supervised objectives, reconstruction error, or a task-specific proxy rather than explicit human labels. The model update can be written generically as: \[
\ModelParameters_{t+1} = \ModelParameters_t - \LearningRate_t \nabla \LossFunction(\ModelInput_t; \ModelParameters_t)
\] where \(\LearningRate_t\) is the learning rate at time \(\OptimizerStepIndex\). This form of adaptation is sensitive to noise and drift in the input distribution, and thus often incorporates mechanisms such as learning rate decay, meta-learned initialization, or update gating to improve stability.
Aside from KWS, practical examples of these strategies abound. In wearable health devices, a model that classifies physical activities may begin with a generic classifier and adapt to user-specific motion patterns using only a few labeled activity segments. In smart assistants, user voice profiles are fine-tuned over time using ongoing speech input, even when explicit supervision is unavailable. Local corrections, repetitions, or downstream task completion can provide implicit signals, but only after the system defines which event counts as feedback and tests its validity. A user may accept a suggestion because it is convenient rather than correct, abandon a task for reasons unrelated to the model, or correct an error that the model itself induced. Production adaptation should therefore separate observed events from inferred labels, retain a nonadapting control cohort, measure delayed outcomes when available, and gate learning when the proxy-to-outcome relationship drifts.
Few-shot and streaming adaptation form the foundation for more advanced memory and replay strategies that address the stability challenges of continuous on-device learning.




Definition 11.3: Catastrophic forgetting
Catastrophic forgetting is the phenomenon in which a neural network trained sequentially on new tasks or data distributions rapidly loses performance on previously learned tasks, because gradient updates that optimize the new objective overwrite weight configurations that supported the old ones.


Significance: Without explicit mitigation, fine-tuning a deployed classifier on a new domain can sharply reduce prior-task accuracy, even when the new domain is closely related to the old one (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017). This is the central failure mode of on-device and federated learning: every device that adapts locally to its user’s recent data risks erasing the general capabilities the centralized training run paid for, and the loss is invisible until inference encounters out-of-recent-context inputs.
Distinction: Unlike overfitting (a generalization failure on a single fixed task) and distribution shift (a deployment-time mismatch between training and inference data), forgetting is a training-time phenomenon caused by the sequential structure of the update stream itself; updates for new data can interfere with earlier solutions even when a representation capable of supporting both tasks exists.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a small experience-replay buffer is sufficient protection. A small buffer can hold aggregate accuracy on a held-out set while rare classes, which it samples too seldom, continue to degrade. Forgetting must therefore be measured per class or per cohort, and the remedies range from capacity-proportional or prioritized buffers to weight-regularization methods such as elastic weight consolidation, which store no examples (section 11.12.2).





Learning a new task can erode accuracy on an earlier one.

Mnih, Volodymyr, Koray Kavukcuoglu, David Silver, Andrei A. Rusu, Joel Veness, Marc G. Bellemare, Alex Graves, et al. 2015. “Human-Level Control Through Deep Reinforcement Learning.” Nature 518 (7540): 529–33. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14236.
Experience replay addresses forgetting by retaining examples from earlier learning episodes and reusing them during later updates. Replay also appears in reinforcement learning (Mnih et al. 2015); here its role is to keep earlier local observations represented as new data arrives. It is one stability mechanism with an explicit storage cost. Section 11.12.2 returns to the problem with parameter-importance penalties, bounded update footprints, and rollback.
Unlike server-side replay strategies that rely on large datasets and extensive compute, on-device replay must operate with extremely limited capacity, often with tens or hundreds of samples, and must avoid interfering with user experience (Rolnick et al. 2019). Buffers may store only compressed features or distilled summaries, and updates must occur opportunistically (e.g., during idle cycles or charging). These system-level constraints reshape how replay is implemented and evaluated in the context of embedded ML.

Rolnick, David, Arun Ahuja, Jonathan Schwarz, Timothy Lillicrap, and Greg Wayne. 2019. “Experience Replay for Continual Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS).
Let \(\ReplayBuffer\) represent a memory buffer that retains a fixed-size subset of training examples. At time step \(\OptimizerStepIndex\), the model receives a new data point \((\ModelInput_t, \ExampleLabel_t)\) and appends it to \(\ReplayBuffer\). A replay-based update then samples a batch \(\{(\ModelInput_i, \ExampleLabel_i)\}_{i=1}^{\BatchSize}\) of size \(\BatchSize\) from \(\ReplayBuffer\) and applies a gradient step: \[
\ModelParameters_{t+1} = \ModelParameters_t - \LearningRate\nabla_\ModelParameters\left[ \frac{1}{\BatchSize} \sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \LossFunction(\ModelInput_i, \ExampleLabel_i; \ModelParameters_t) \right]
\] This is the streaming update of section 11.9.1 with one change of data source, from the newest observation to a batch drawn from \(\ReplayBuffer\). The systems cost lies in what that change requires, namely buffer storage that competes with model state and forward and backward work on old examples in every admitted window. Over time, this replay mechanism allows the model to reinforce prior knowledge while incorporating new information.
A practical on-device implementation might use a ring buffer to store a small set of compressed feature vectors rather than full input examples. Listing 4 implements this minimal replay buffer design, demonstrating how a circular storage mechanism enables efficient memory management while balancing historical knowledge retention with new information incorporation.



Listing 4: Replay Buffer: Implements a circular storage mechanism for efficient memory management in constrained environments. This approach allows models to efficiently retain and sample from recent data points, balancing the need to use historical information while incorporating new insights.


import random


# Ring buffer for experience replay on memory-constrained devices
# Stores compressed features (not raw inputs) to minimize footprint
class ReplayBuffer:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity  # Fixed size, e.g., 1000 examples
        self.buffer = []
        self.index = 0  # Circular write pointer

    def store(self, feature_vec, label):
        if len(self.buffer) < self.capacity:
            self.buffer.append((feature_vec, label))  # Fill phase
        else:
            self.buffer[self.index] = (
                feature_vec,
                label,
            )  # Overwrite oldest
        self.index = (self.index + 1) % self.capacity  # Wrap around

    def sample(self, k):
        # Uniform sampling within the retained buffer; older examples are absent
        return random.sample(self.buffer, min(k, len(self.buffer)))



This implementation maintains a fixed-capacity cyclic buffer, storing compressed representations (e.g., last-layer embeddings) and associated labels. Uniform sampling here covers only the retained recent window; it does not remove the history bias introduced by overwriting old examples. Reservoir sampling is an alternative when the goal is to represent the full stream, though any finite buffer still requires coverage checks.
In TinyML applications, experience replay has been applied to problems such as gesture recognition, where devices must continuously improve predictions while observing a small number of events per day. Instead of training directly on the streaming data, the device stores representative feature vectors from recent gestures and uses them to finetune classification boundaries periodically. Similarly, in on-device keyword spotting, replaying past utterances can improve wake-word detection accuracy without the need to transmit audio data off-device.
Experience replay spends storage and additional update work to preserve earlier behavior. Raw inputs can exceed storage or retention budgets, especially in vision and audio applications. Cached feature vectors reduce that footprint, but an update starting from those vectors trains the downstream model without reconstructing the original encoder computation. If the encoder changes, old features may no longer match its current representation; the system must retain a compatible encoder, refresh the features from retained inputs, or expire incompatible entries. Persistent replay also consumes flash write cycles. Buffer contents, representation versions, and replay frequency therefore belong in the same resource and retention policy.



In many on-device learning scenarios, the raw training data may be too large, noisy, or redundant to store and process effectively. This motivates the use of compressed data representations, where the original inputs are transformed into lower-dimensional embeddings or compact encodings that preserve salient information while minimizing memory and compute costs.
Compressed representations serve two complementary goals: they reduce the footprint of stored data, allowing devices to maintain longer histories or replay buffers under tight memory budgets (Hayes et al. 2020), and they simplify the learning task by projecting raw inputs into more structured feature spaces, often learned via pretraining or meta-learning, in which efficient adaptation is possible with minimal supervision.

Hayes, T. L., K. Kafle, R. Shrestha, M. Acharya, and C. Kanan. 2020. “REMIND Your Neural Network to Prevent Catastrophic Forgetting.” In Computer Vision – ECCV 2020. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-58598-3_28.
One common approach is to encode data points using a pretrained feature extractor and discard the original high-dimensional input. For example, an image \(\ModelInput_i\) might be passed through a CNN to produce an embedding vector \(\StoredEmbedding_i = \FrozenFeatureEncoder(\ModelInput_i)\), where \(\FrozenFeatureEncoder(\cdot)\) is a fixed feature encoder. This embedding captures visual structure (e.g., shape, texture, or spatial layout) in a compact representation, usually ranging from 64 to 512 dimensions, suitable for lightweight downstream adaptation.
Mathematically, training can proceed over compressed samples \((\StoredEmbedding_i, \ExampleLabel_i)\) using a lightweight decoder or projection head. Let \(\ModelParameters\) represent the trainable parameters of this decoder model, which is typically a small neural network that maps from compressed representations to output predictions. As each example is presented, the model parameters are updated using gradient descent: \[
\ModelParameters_{t+1} = \ModelParameters_t - \LearningRate\nabla_\ModelParameters\LossFunction\big(\PredictionHeadFunction(\StoredEmbedding_i; \ModelParameters), \ExampleLabel_i\big)
\] The rule is the same gradient step once more, now applied to stored embeddings \(\StoredEmbedding_i\) and a small head whose prediction is \(\PredictionHeadFunction(\StoredEmbedding_i; \ModelParameters)\), rather than to raw inputs. Only the head’s parameters \(\ModelParameters\) change, so this is the head-only case of equation 1, and the encoder runs once per example when the embedding is stored rather than on every update. This bounds the trainable portion of the model, but feasibility still depends on the head’s activations and optimizer state alongside the replay buffer and runtime reserves.
When replay storage rather than model compute binds, a device can go further and learn a dictionary of recurring sensor-trace patterns, storing each example as a few nonzero coefficients over that dictionary instead of as raw samples. A dataset of traces \(\SensorTraceMatrix\) then factorizes as \(\SensorTraceMatrix\approx \SensorPatternDictionary\DictionaryCoefficientMatrix\), where the columns of \(\SensorPatternDictionary\) are the basis patterns and the block-sparse coefficient matrix \(\DictionaryCoefficientMatrix\) records which patterns are active in each example. The saving is real only if the dictionary plus all stored coefficients is smaller than the raw replay examples, and updating the dictionary changes the representation of every stored example, so reconstruction quality and compatibility become part of the replay policy.
Compressed representations can reduce how long raw inputs remain stored, but an embedding is not anonymized merely because it is lower dimensional. It may preserve identity, attributes, or enough structure for inversion, and it must receive the same access-control, retention, and deletion analysis as the source data unless a separate privacy mechanism establishes a stronger guarantee. Compression can also act as an implicit regularizer, smoothing learning and mitigating overfitting when only a few training examples are available.
In keyword spotting, raw audio can first be transformed into mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs),13 a compact, lossy representation derived from the speech power spectrum. Storing these vectors instead of waveforms reduces the replay payload. The complete adaptation budget must still include feature extraction, model state, and the working memory needed for updates.
13 MFCCs (Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients): For a 320-sample audio window (20 ms at 16 kHz), 16-bit samples occupy 640 bytes, while 12–13 coefficients stored at 32 bits each occupy approximately 50 bytes. The roughly 13\(\times\) reduction compares one waveform window with one feature vector; overlapping windows, additional features, and metadata change the storage ratio for a complete recording. Replay capacity depends on that complete representation, and keyword detection quality must be evaluated separately from byte savings.


The choice of data-efficiency mechanism depends on what is scarce. Few-shot adaptation uses a small informative support set, replay spends memory and compute to preserve prior behavior, and compressed representations extend the history that fits on-device. Their limits remain different: weak pretrained features can defeat few-shot adaptation, a replay buffer can omit rare cases, and compression can discard task-relevant information. Table 5 summarizes these on-device learning trade-offs; combinations must fit the same memory, energy, and privacy budget.



Table 5: On-Device Learning Trade-Offs: Technique choice depends on the binding edge constraint: few-shot adaptation minimizes labeled-data needs, replay improves stability under drift at the cost of memory, and compressed representations extend retention when raw data is too large or too sensitive to keep.











Technique
Data Requirements
Memory/Compute Overhead
Use Case Fit




Few-Shot Adaptation
Small labeled set (\(\SupportSetSize\) examples)
Low
Personalization, quick on-device finetuning


Experience Replay
Streaming data
Moderate (buffer & update)
Non-stationary data, stability under drift


Compressed Representations
Unlabeled or encoded data
Low to Moderate
Memory-limited devices; privacy-sensitive contexts






In practice, these methods are not mutually exclusive. Many real-world systems combine them to achieve robust, efficient adaptation. For example, a keyword spotting system may use compressed audio features (e.g., MFCCs), finetune a few parameters from a small support set, and maintain a replay buffer of past embeddings for continual refinement.
Efficient adaptation and data strategies establish how a single device can learn from its user. Sharing those gains requires another decision: whether local updates contain information useful to a common model and can be combined within communication and privacy constraints. Federated learning supplies that coordination protocol. Personal state can remain local when sharing would not improve the population objective, and privacy controls must separately limit what transmitted updates disclose.

Self-Check: Question

A developer of a keyword spotting (KWS) system for smart home appliances wants users to configure custom wake words using 5 to 10 spoken samples. Why is few-shot adaptation of a classification head on top of a frozen acoustic encoder preferred over end-to-end retraining?

End-to-end retraining of acoustic encoders produces audio waveforms that violate device speaker impedance limits.
Spoken custom wake words cannot be processed by neural networks unless the entire encoder architecture is expanded by \(10\times\).
Updating only the head restricts trainable state and preserves frozen encoder representations, reducing adaptation cost and overfitting risk relative to full retraining.
The Fourier transform algorithm only converges when supervised labels exceed 100,000 samples.

An edge health tracker adapts a continuous activity classifier to a user’s walking gait over several weeks. When the user starts cycling, the device adapts its model, but suddenly misclassifies normal walking as cycling. What core failure mode has occurred, and why did it happen?

Overfitting on a single static batch caused by excessive L2 regularization.
Numerical floating-point overflow in the hardware accelerometer sensor buffer.
Model inversion attack where cycling data erased the operating system kernel.
Catastrophic forgetting, where sequential gradient updates on new data distributions overwrite the weight configurations responsible for preserving performance on previously learned tasks.

In on-device continuous learning, why do production experience-replay implementations store compressed feature embeddings (e.g., penultimate-layer activations or MFCCs) in a circular ring buffer rather than saving raw sensor observations (such as raw images or audio waveforms)?
True or False: In on-device experience replay, maintaining a small buffer of 100 uniformly sampled past examples guarantees that the adapted model will not suffer from catastrophic forgetting across rare or long-tail edge cases.
In continuous edge adaptation, the fundamental trade-off between retaining previously acquired knowledge and acquiring new patterns from dynamic local data is known as the stability-____ trade-off.
