The dimensions in table 1 interact in nonobvious ways. Increasing batch size can improve throughput and cost efficiency while degrading latency. Reducing precision can lower memory demand and improve throughput but may degrade quality. Speculative decoding can improve latency but may increase per-token cost. The performance engineer’s task is to navigate these trade-offs guided by the application’s specific requirements.
An interactive chatbot might target time-to-first-token under 200 ms and inter-token latency under 50 ms, accepting a higher per-token cost to meet those illustrative limits. An offline document-summarization pipeline may instead prioritize completed work per dollar, subject to a deadline and a quality threshold. A quality-sensitive application can impose a stricter acceptance criterion while retaining its own latency constraints. These requirements select different feasible operating points; performance engineering must make the trade-off explicit before choosing an optimization.
For the recurring 70B deployment, a latency-oriented configuration might use small batches and speculative decoding to reduce the time a request waits for tokens. A throughput-oriented configuration might use larger batches and INT4 weights to amortize weight reads and free memory for concurrent requests. The larger batch raises aggregate throughput while lengthening each request’s token intervals, and reduced precision is usable only if the model still meets its quality criterion. Once batching has been analyzed, section 9.5.1 prices both operating points in time and cost per token.



The efficiency frontier fixes the objective; memory bandwidth sets the first bound on reaching it. The wall itself is a hardware fact the replica inherits. Batch-one decode streams the active weights from HBM for about one multiply-accumulate per weight read, and on an NVIDIA H100 989 TFLOP/s of dense FP16 Tensor Core compute faces only 3.35 TB/s of peak HBM bandwidth. Performance engineering adds the kernel’s view of that wall. Batching, sparse activation, and on-chip reuse all change the traffic, so the diagnostic question is how far a given kernel sits from the bandwidth bound and which of those levers can move it. The answer depends on the constraint each level of the memory hierarchy places on a kernel’s schedule (table 2).

Two consequences follow for kernel design. Register pressure becomes a first-class constraint in custom kernels, whether written in CUDA or in a tile-level language such as Triton (section 9.10.5), because tile size sets both arithmetic intensity and register demand. Data placement becomes the optimization target whenever HBM traffic limits execution: operator fusion removes intermediate round trips when a legal schedule can keep the values in registers or shared memory, tiling organizes reuse within limited SRAM (which is why on-chip reuse matters so much for attention), and precision engineering shrinks each trip’s payload by representing values in FP8 or INT4 instead of FP16. Graph compilers apply supported versions of these transformations automatically. Each intervention must still be checked against launch overhead, dependencies, and on-chip resource limits, which can stop a low-intensity kernel before it saturates HBM bandwidth.


The memory wall becomes a diagnostic instrument once each kernel is placed on the roofline model1 (Williams et al. 2009). A kernel with arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) attains at most \(\min(\PeakRate, \ArithmeticIntensity\times \Bandwidth)\), and the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) separates the memory-bound side of this ideal envelope from its compute-bound side. The tighter ceiling bounds performance; a measurement below that ceiling still requires investigation of latency, dependencies, and implementation limits.

Definition 9.1: Measured arithmetic intensity
Measured arithmetic intensity is the ratio of the floating-point operations a kernel actually executes to the bytes observed crossing a named memory boundary, such as HBM, during that execution (FLOP per byte).

Significance: It places a profiled kernel on the same roofline as the bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\)) and compute (\(\PeakRate\)) ceilings, so its distance below the algorithmic estimate exposes traffic that the algorithm did not require.
Distinction: Unlike algorithmic intensity, which counts the data movement an idealized algorithm requires under a stated memory model, measured intensity includes tiling, cache behavior, fusion, padding, and redundant transfers.
Common pitfall: Arithmetic intensity is not a fixed property of a model. Batch size can change algorithmic reuse, while fusion and tiling primarily change measured HBM intensity by keeping intermediates on chip. A roofline point is interpretable only when its FLOP convention and memory boundary match the ceilings on the same plot.



The H100’s FP16 ridge, established in Roofline model, is the reference point for every placement that follows:
\[I_{\text{ridge}}^{\text{H100, FP16}} = \frac{989\text{ TFLOP/s}}{3.35\text{ TB/s}} \approx 295\text{ FLOP/byte}\]
Below that intensity, the HBM bandwidth bound is tighter than the H100’s FP16 compute bound. FP8 doubles the Tensor Core rate to 1979 TFLOP/s while bandwidth stays at 3.35 TB/s, so the ridge rises to about 590.7 FLOP/byte. If all counted operand traffic halves while the operation count stays fixed, arithmetic intensity doubles as well, preserving the kernel’s position relative to the ridge. In that ideal comparison, lower precision raises the bandwidth-limited ceiling by moving more values per second. Actual gains depend on which tensors change precision and on conversion, scaling, and kernel costs.
The ridge also moves across hardware generations, because peak arithmetic has outgrown HBM bandwidth for the physical reasons The Memory Wall develops. For diagnosis, the ridge column of table 3 matters more than the growth trend, because a kernel’s regime can change with the hardware even when its intensity does not.

At 200 FLOP/byte, an operation lies on the compute side of the V100 and A100 envelopes but on the bandwidth side for the H100 and B200, whose ridges sit roughly 2× above the V100’s 139 FLOP/byte. The following operations span three orders of magnitude in estimated arithmetic intensity. Their roofline positions identify candidate limits; the traffic assumptions explain what must be checked against a real implementation.
Large general matrix multiply (GEMM) operations expose substantial opportunities for data reuse. A square matrix multiplication of dimension \(4096{\times}4096\) in FP16 performs approximately 137.4 billion FLOPs. Counting one read of each input matrix and one write of the output gives roughly 100.7 MB of traffic and an arithmetic intensity of approximately 1365.3 FLOP/byte. This idealized intensity sits above the H100’s ridge point. Reaching the compute ceiling still requires a kernel whose tiling, instruction mix, and parallelism exploit that reuse; tile reloads can increase measured HBM traffic.
Element-wise operations expose much less reuse. For a Gaussian error linear unit (GELU) activation applied to a \(4096{\times}4096\) tensor, the illustrative accounting assumes 5 operations per element and one load and store, yielding an arithmetic intensity of approximately 1.2 FLOP/byte. The operation count depends on the activation approximation and is not an instruction count for a specific kernel. The low intensity makes HBM traffic a candidate limit, while launch cost, nonlinear-function execution, and memory-access efficiency determine how closely the kernel approaches that bound.
Autoregressive large language model (LLM) decoding at batch size one is the kernel-level form of the whole-step decode placement in Roofline model. One dense matrix-vector product against a weight matrix of hidden dimension 4096 gives approximately 1 FLOP/byte, and a decode step streams many such matrices before cache reads, communication, and dispatch add time. The estimate covers the weight-streaming component, not every operation in a decode step. Recommendation serving in the style of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) has a different low-intensity component: embedding lookups gather rows from large tables and perform little arithmetic on them. Memory-access latency, bandwidth, and any remote communication then matter more than Tensor Core peak throughput for that component.


↩︎ Archetype B’s sharded embedding tables and their lookup-dominated serving path are established in Archetype B (DLRM at Scale).
Attention’s intensity depends on phase, implementation, and the traffic boundary. Counting the full score matrix, each head performs \(4\SequenceLength^2 \AttentionHeadDimension\) FLOPs for its two matrix products. For the Llama 2 70B head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension =\) 128 and a sequence of \(\SequenceLength=\) 2,048 tokens, the unfused accounting writes and rereads the \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score and probability matrices in FP16, \(4\SequenceLength^2\) two-byte transfers beside the four \(\SequenceLength{\times}\AttentionHeadDimension\) operand tensors. Dividing \(4\SequenceLength^2\AttentionHeadDimension\) FLOPs by \(2(4\SequenceLength^2 + 4\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension)\) bytes gives about 60 FLOP/byte, and the quadratic traffic caps the ratio near \(\AttentionHeadDimension/2\) however long the sequence grows. An ideal tiled accounting retains scores on chip and counts one read each of \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\), and one output write, four \(\SequenceLength{\times}\AttentionHeadDimension\) tensors of 2-byte values. The ratio is \(4\SequenceLength^2\AttentionHeadDimension / (4 \times 2\SequenceLength\AttentionHeadDimension) = \SequenceLength/2\), about 1,024 FLOP/byte. Finite SRAM and the tile schedule can require additional reads, so this value is an upper bound on intensity under that accounting rather than a prediction for every tiled kernel. For decode, counting one full KV-cache read per query head gives approximately 1 FLOP/byte. Grouped-query attention (GQA), which Llama 2 70B uses, lets 8 query heads share each cached key and value head, so one read of the cache can serve the whole group. If the implementation realizes that reuse, the corresponding estimate rises to about 8 FLOP/byte, still below the ridge.
Under these traffic assumptions, only batched GEMM and tiled prefill attention expose enough reuse to approach the compute-bound regime; every other example has a bandwidth ceiling below peak arithmetic throughput (table 4). That placement identifies where reducing bytes may help; profiling determines whether memory traffic is the exposed cost.

The workload comparison explains why peak FLOP/s alone cannot predict small-batch decode performance. When weight streaming dominates, memory bandwidth limits token generation, while memory capacity constrains the requests that can be batched. Larger batches can reuse weights across requests and move the workload toward the compute ceiling; the serving regime determines how far that shift remains useful.




The weight-streaming estimate from workload placement is the source of the chapter’s opening figure. Decoding LLM requests one at a time performs about one operation per byte of weights streamed, which leaves nearly all of an H100’s FP16 compute idle during each decode step. Batching requests amortizes those reads across many tokens, but combining prompt processing and token generation without accounting for their different costs can increase latency. The serving regime, meaning how a system manages the batch dimension and divides prompt processing from token generation, shapes both weight reuse and interference between requests. These two features establish the workload conditions under which subsequent optimization techniques must be evaluated.


For memory-bound LLM serving, batch size is often the first performance lever to test, and also one of the most constrained. Increasing the batch size raises arithmetic intensity where requests reuse the same weights. For the weight-dominated portion of an LLM decode step, the following estimate is approximately linear in batch size:
\[
\DecodeArithmeticIntensity(\BatchSize) = \frac{2\Parameters \BatchSize}{\Parameters\ElementStorageSize + \BatchSize \HiddenDimension\, \ElementStorageSize}
\tag{2}\]
Here, \(\Parameters\) is parameter count, \(\BatchSize\) is batch size, \(\HiddenDimension\) is hidden width, and \(\ElementStorageSize\) is bytes per element, assuming weights and activations share one precision. The numerator counts the whole model’s arithmetic, while the activation term counts only one matrix’s input vectors; even summed over every weight matrix, the activations stay far smaller than the \(\Parameters\ElementStorageSize\) weight bytes at the batch sizes considered here, so the shortcut does not change the estimate. This simplified weight-reuse estimate excludes KV-cache traffic and inter-device communication; it describes why batching helps before those other costs become binding. At batch size 1, the denominator is dominated by the weight term \((\Parameters\ElementStorageSize)\), and \(\DecodeArithmeticIntensity\approx 2/\ElementStorageSize \approx 1\) FLOP/byte for FP16. At batch size 256, the weight term still dominates, but the same weight bytes are amortized across more requests, so \(\DecodeArithmeticIntensity\approx 2 \times 256/\ElementStorageSize \approx 256\) FLOP/byte, approaching the compute-bound regime.



Larger batches raise arithmetic intensity toward the ridge.
Batching moves weight-dominated execution toward the compute ceiling until cache traffic and memory capacity stop it. End-to-end serving reference values put model FLOPs utilization (MFU) at about 5 percent at batch size 1, against an illustrative large-batch value of about 40 percent. Both include prefill work, which is why the batch-one value sits above the pure decode bound that notebook 9.1 computes later in this section. With hardware, price, and useful work per token held fixed, that utilization ratio is a 8× reduction in cost per token, which is the economic reason serving systems are designed around batch size. A deployed service still has to measure its own prompt/decode mix, completed throughput, and latency together before planning capacity on that ratio.
The same economics can be priced on the recurring deployment, for the latency-oriented and throughput-oriented operating points of section 9.3, once the KV cache that the weight-reuse estimate omitted is added back. Take the FP16 weights of the 70B model, sharded across eight GPUs, and let every request hold a full 4,096-token KV cache. At batch one, each GPU streams about 17.7 GB per decode step, so a step takes at least 5.3 ms and the replica emits at most 190 tokens/s. At a batch of 32 requests, each GPU streams 22.9 GB, giving a step-time lower bound of 6.8 ms and an aggregate output upper bound of 4,690 tokens/s. At $2.50 per GPU-hour, the corresponding cost lower bounds per million output tokens are $29 and $1.19. Their ratio is roughly 25×, while the step-time bounds differ by only 1.3×. The batched point buys a large cost reduction for a smaller latency penalty, and that asymmetry is the shape of the frontier trade-off.
This bandwidth-only cost ratio is larger than the 8× of the end-to-end MFU anchors above, mainly because the two comparisons count different work. Both bandwidth bounds count decode alone and assume every step streams at peak bandwidth with no launch, communication, or queueing delay, whereas the anchors’ batch-one value already includes compute-dense prefill, which raises its utilization and so narrows the ratio. Realized ratios come from completed throughput and per-request latency recorded together at a stated offered load. One accounting rule matters when converting those measurements to cost: a tensor-parallel replica produces one shared output stream per request, so its aggregate token rate must not be counted once for every participating GPU.
Memory limits that reuse: active requests need KV cache for prompt and generated tokens, alongside model weights and runtime state. On the recurring deployment, 140 GB of FP16 weights exceed one H100’s memory; sharding across the node leaves a 17.5 GB weight shard per GPU. Remaining capacity must cover cache, workspace, and runtime overhead. INT4 reduces the weight payload to a quarter of its FP16 size before metadata, and section 9.9.3 later prices how that saving and a compressed cache change batch capacity.
A serving scheduler can add new requests as others finish, provided demand and available memory permit admission. Local performance engineering supplies the capacity and execution-time measurements that make those decisions feasible. Weight quantization reduces shared model storage, while cache compression and allocation efficiency reduce the capacity needed for active requests. Continuous batching for large language model (LLM) inference develops the scheduler; the local point here is that memory savings can expand its feasible batch range without guaranteeing that the largest batch meets latency targets.
PagedAttention (Kwon et al. 2023) reduces allocation waste by storing KV cache in fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, rather than reserving contiguous space for the longest sequence each request might reach. Reserving 4,096 tokens for requests that average 500 leaves much of that reserved capacity unused. Block allocation lets other requests use capacity that would otherwise remain reserved, although partially filled blocks and runtime headroom still consume memory. The benefit is a larger feasible active-request set when allocation waste is the limiting factor.

PagedAttention and KV cache quantization address complementary sources of memory pressure. PagedAttention reduces memory waste from fragmentation, while quantization reduces memory usage from precision. Their joint batch-size gain depends on the model-weight footprint, request-length distribution, and scheduler headroom, so the two savings do not simply multiply.



Modern LLM serving systems decompose each request into two distinct phases with fundamentally different performance characteristics. The distinction between these phases drives system architecture and optimization strategy.
The prefill phase processes the entire input prompt in parallel. If the prompt contains \(\SequenceLength\) tokens, the prefill phase executes a single forward pass over all \(\SequenceLength\) tokens simultaneously. The GEMM operations have shape \([\SequenceLength,\HiddenDimension]{\times}[\HiddenDimension,\HiddenDimension]\), making the batch dimension equal to \(\SequenceLength\). For a prompt of 1024 tokens, this is arithmetically intensive: the arithmetic intensity is approximately \(2 \times 1024/2 = 1024\) FLOP/byte for FP16 weights, well into the compute-bound regime. This weight-reuse estimate places the example GEMM above the FP16 ridge point; it omits activation and output traffic. Short prompts, kernel shapes, and other operators can produce different limits, so prefill as a whole still requires profiling.
The decode phase generates output tokens one at a time, autoregressively. Each step has a batch dimension of 1 for a single request or the number of requests scheduled together for batched serving. The weight-streaming analysis in section 9.4.2 explains why dense batch-one decode often has a bandwidth limit, while cache traffic, launches, and communication can add further exposed costs.
The prefill-decode decomposition connects serving design to the two operational regimes mapped in figure 2. Long-prompt prefill GEMMs can have enough arithmetic intensity to place their roofline bound on the compute ceiling, while weight-dominated, low-batch decode usually has a bandwidth ceiling; prompt length, batch size, and kernel implementation determine how closely execution approaches each bound. A real serving system must handle both phases, often simultaneously across different active requests, so their competition for accelerator resources also matters.
Disaggregated serving addresses this interference by running prefill and decode on separate hardware pools. The roofline placement tells each pool what to buy. The prefill pool wants arithmetic throughput for its compute-bound GEMMs, while the decode pool wants memory bandwidth and capacity for weight streaming and KV cache, which also makes it the natural home for aggressive weight quantization. Each pool can then choose its own batch size and parallelism strategy for its latency target. The KV cache computed during prefill is transferred to a decode server, which handles the subsequent autoregressive generation. Separation therefore introduces a communication cost as it removes competition between the phases. Its benefit depends on whether the reduced interference and independent tuning outweigh cache-transfer time and waiting for capacity in either pool.


↪ Disaggregated prefill and decode pools, joined by a KV-cache transfer on the critical path, are developed in Prefill-decode disaggregation.
The performance characteristics of each phase guide the choice of optimization. FlashAttention reduces attention’s memory traffic mainly during prefill, because only prefill forms the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score matrix that a tiled kernel avoids writing to HBM; a decode step has a single query row and no quadratic intermediate. Decode attention benefits from a different fused kernel, one that reads each cached key and value once and computes scores, softmax, and the weighted sum in a single pass rather than in separate kernels with their own launches and intermediate writes. Either kernel’s effect on total latency still depends on how much of the forward pass attention consumes. Speculative decoding targets the decode phase. KV cache quantization reduces decode storage and read traffic, while its encoding cost begins when prefill creates the cache. Precision engineering can help both phases through different mechanisms. Supported FP8 kernels offer a higher compute ceiling for compute-bound prefill, while FP8 or INT4 weights reduce the bytes streamed during weight-dominated decode. The resulting speedup depends on format support, conversion overhead, and the costs left unchanged by the precision reduction; the model must also retain the required output quality.
For the recurring 70B replica, the decode phase’s distance below the ridge can be priced in two steps: its arithmetic intensity, then the token rate that HBM bandwidth alone permits.

Napkin Math 9.1: The Roofline diagnosticProblem: A 70B parameter LLM is deployed on 8\(\times\) H100 GPUs with tensor parallelism. At batch size 1, each GPU holds approximately 8.75B parameters in FP16 (17.5 GB of weights). Each decode step reads its weight shard to produce one token. What is the achieved arithmetic intensity, and what is the theoretical maximum token generation rate?
Math:
Step 1: Arithmetic intensity. Each decode step per GPU: FLOPs \(=\) \(2 \times 8.75 \times 10^{9}\) \(=\) 17.5B FLOPs. Bytes loaded \(=\) \(8.75 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \text{ bytes}\) \(=\) 17.5 GB.
\(\ArithmeticIntensity = \frac{1.75 \times 10^{10} \text{ FLOP}}{1.75 \times 10^{10} \text{ bytes}} = 1 \text{ FLOP/byte}\)
At 1 FLOP/byte, the operation sits far below the H100 ridge point of ~295 FLOP/byte: deeply memory-bound.
Step 2: Token rate. Since the operation is memory-bound, performance is limited by bandwidth, not compute:
\(\WeightStreamingDecodeTime = \frac{17.5\,\text{GB}}{3.35\,\text{TB/s}} \approx 5.2\,\text{ms per token}\)
Because all eight shards stream their weights in parallel and together emit one token per step, the bandwidth-only ceiling is approximately 191.4 tokens/s for the whole replica, not per GPU. In practice, overheads from KV cache reads and NVLink synchronization reduce this substantially below the ideal bandwidth-only limit.
Systems insight: At batch size 1, the bandwidth-only calculation reaches about 0.3 percent of the H100’s FP16 peak FLOP/s, leaving idle the more than 99 percent of compute that opened the chapter. This is the decode-only bound; the end-to-end batch-one anchor of about 5 percent MFU sits higher because it also counts compute-dense prefill. Larger batches amortize weight reads across requests, quantization reduces the weight payload, and speculative decoding seeks multiple accepted tokens per target-model pass. Each changes the weight-streaming budget, with additional costs to evaluate before claiming a speedup.


The decode calculation identifies weight streaming as a limit, while the prefill analysis exposes a different opportunity in attention intermediates. These are distinct sources of HBM traffic, and which one dominates depends on the deployed service’s prompt and output lengths. Profiling must locate the exposed cost and establish a reproducible baseline before an optimization can be selected.

Self-Check: Question

In modern Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems, why do the prompt prefill phase and the token decode phase exhibit fundamentally different performance bottlenecks on GPU hardware?

Prefill generates tokens sequentially one by one, making it memory-bound by weight reads, whereas decode processes all prompt tokens in parallel, making it compute-bound by Tensor Cores

Suppose the recurring 70B replica misses its inter-token latency objective. Before any kernel is rewritten, the engineer needs to know which interval of the decode step is exposed: weight streaming, attention, element-wise work, collectives, or host dispatch. A kernel made several times faster changes nothing if the interval it shortens was small or already hidden behind other work. System profiling answers that question by showing where execution waits and which intervals an intervention could shorten. The candidate remedies mapped across the branches of figure 1 are hypotheses: fusion removes intermediate transfers, graph replay reduces repeated host submission, and precision reduction moves fewer bytes. Their detailed mechanisms follow the measurement method; selecting one first requires evidence that its target cost is exposed.

Systems Perspective 9.1: The physics of profiling (the Heisenberg effect)Instrumentation adds work to a distributed ML system. Gathering high-resolution telemetry, such as tracking every CUDA kernel launch or memory allocation, consumes host cycles and memory and can introduce additional transfers or synchronization. In heavily optimized serving pipelines, profiling can induce the very latency spikes the engineer is trying to diagnose. This observer effect favors low-overhead telemetry for continuous monitoring and short, targeted traces for diagnosis. Detailed tracing in production requires a bounded collection window and an overhead budget; isolated runs are useful when they reproduce the relevant workload and contention.
The cost must be measured for the selected workload and collection settings. The PyTorch profiler and Nsight Systems can both perturb execution, and neither has a fixed overhead independent of the events collected; richer options, such as recording tensor shapes or allocation history, perturb more. An engineer should record the enabled options, compare instrumented and uninstrumented runs, and use traces to explain execution structure while measuring production latency with instrumentation overhead controlled.




Profiling levels are useful only if they guide the drill-down from symptom to intervention. ML system profiling partitions observability across four tiers, trading observational breadth for diagnostic detail. Figure 3 structures this descent from top-level application symptoms down to hardware root causes, tracing how diagnostic scope narrows from fleet-wide metrics over hours to streaming multiprocessor counters over microseconds.






Figure 3: The profiling hierarchy: Diagnosis descends from the application symptom to the hardware root cause. Each rung names the evidence that level exposes and a representative tool; the navy label under each tool gives the scope and time scale one sample covers, and each highlighted window expands into the trace below it. Each lower level trades breadth for the detail needed to isolate a root cause.



The drill-down starts at the application level, where end-to-end metrics such as tokens per second, time-to-first-token, p99 latency, and GPU utilization reveal whether the user-facing system meets its target. Framework profiling then associates time with model operations and exposes scheduling, data-transfer, and collective-communication dependencies. Kernel profiling narrows the diagnosis to execution intervals, launch gaps, and overlap opportunities. Hardware counters complete the chain: tools such as NVIDIA Nsight Compute report achieved memory bandwidth, occupancy, and instruction mix for a selected kernel. Distributed scope cuts across these levels. Application metrics describe the fleet outcome, while synchronized traces across ranks identify imbalance before an engineer drills into one rank’s kernels.
For example, an application trace may reveal missed token-latency targets; framework traces across ranks may then expose a lagging collective. Kernel timelines distinguish late arrival from slow communication, and hardware counters test whether the preceding computation suffered from memory stalls or register pressure. Tensor Core use is also a measurement question: matrix alignment can affect kernel efficiency, but a misaligned shape does not universally force a fallback to scalar CUDA Core instructions. Library version, datatype, hardware, and kernel selection determine the executed path. Inspecting the instruction mix is more reliable than inferring that path from tensor dimensions alone.



Metrics are not interchangeable; each answers a different bottleneck question (table 5). Model bandwidth utilization (MBU), achieved memory bandwidth divided by peak bandwidth, is the decode counterpart of MFU. Together they diagnose useful hardware work, TTFT and ITL diagnose serving latency, and throughput exposes capacity under batching. Reading the wrong one hides the bottleneck: a decode path at a few percent MFU can be running its memory system near saturation.

The metric choice in table 5 reflects the fundamental bottleneck shift between training and inference. MFU is usually the right training-efficiency lens, while MBU is often the right inference-efficiency lens when decode is limited by HBM traffic. The roofline model from section 9.4.1 becomes a diagnostic tool when combined with profiling data. Diagnosis follows three steps:

Measure the achieved FLOP/s and memory bandwidth for a kernel using Nsight Compute.
Compute measured arithmetic intensity from executed FLOPs and observed bytes at the same memory boundary used for the bandwidth ceiling (FLOP/byte). Compare it with the algorithmic estimate to expose extra traffic.
Plot the measured performance against the roofline ceiling.

The plotted position then sorts the kernel into one of three cases, provided the ceilings match its datatype and operations. A kernel far below both ceilings has an execution problem rather than a resource limit, because dependencies, instruction mix, memory-access latency, or too little parallel work keep it from either peak. A kernel near its bandwidth ceiling gains little from faster arithmetic; only moving fewer bytes, through fusion or lower precision, moves it. A kernel near its compute ceiling can be helped only by doing less arithmetic or by a faster supported execution format or device. The roofline narrows the search, while the trace and counters establish which cost an intervention can actually remove.
Consider an illustrative profiling result: a LayerNorm kernel on an H100 reports 5 TFLOP/s of achieved compute and 2.8 TB/s of achieved memory bandwidth. Its arithmetic intensity is 5 TFLOP/s / 2.8 TB/s \(\approx\) 1.8 FLOP/byte. The H100’s ridge point is approximately 295 FLOP/byte at FP16. Since 1.8 FLOP/byte is far below 295 FLOP/byte, the roofline places the kernel’s bound on the bandwidth slope. Its achieved 2.8 TB/s (83.6 percent of the H100’s 3.35 TB/s peak bandwidth) shows that the kernel is already close to the bound the roofline assigns it. Faster arithmetic cannot help, and even a perfect memory schedule could recover only the small gap between that utilization and peak bandwidth. The material gains come from moving fewer bytes: fusion can eliminate an intermediate HBM round-trip, and a supported lower-precision representation can reduce bytes per element, provided either change preserves the required numerical behavior.



The PyTorch Profiler is most useful when application metrics show a slowdown but the responsible layer is still unknown. Its role is to narrow a global symptom to a layer, kernel family, or synchronization point before a heavier tool is used. It wraps an iteration loop to capture detailed traces with minimal code modification. Here the loop is the replica’s decode loop, one forward pass per step over the active batch; a training loop is profiled with the same schedule:
import torch
from torch.profiler import (
    profile,
    schedule,
    tensorboard_trace_handler,
)

# Profile 2 warmup steps + 3 active steps
with profile(
    activities=[
        torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CPU,
        torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CUDA,
    ],
    schedule=schedule(wait=1, warmup=2, active=3, repeat=1),
    on_trace_ready=tensorboard_trace_handler("./profiler_logs"),
    record_shapes=True,
    profile_memory=True,
    with_stack=True,
) as prof:
    for step in range(6):  # 1 wait + 2 warmup + 3 active
        with torch.inference_mode():
            # One decode step: a forward pass over the active
            # batch that reads and extends each request's KV cache
            next_tokens = decode_step(model, active_batch, kv_cache)
        prof.step()
The schedule parameter defines a warmup period during which the profiler collects events but discards the results, reducing the influence of profiler startup on the retained trace. Application warmup is a separate requirement: just-in-time (JIT) compilation, memory allocation, and CUDA context initialization must settle before a steady-state measurement. A fixed number of profiler warmup steps does not guarantee that this has happened. Check iteration times and compilation activity before choosing the measurement window; include startup costs separately when they matter to the deployment.

NVIDIA Nsight Systems narrows a profiler’s layer-level finding to the CPU, GPU, and communication timeline. A short trace of training or inference iterations reveals whether host submission leaves launch gaps, whether communication serializes execution, and which kernels warrant deeper inspection:

    --output=llm_profile \
    --force-overwrite=true \
    python3 inference_server.py --num-steps=5
The --trace flags control which activities are recorded. The cuda flag captures kernel launches and memory operations. The nvtx flag captures NVIDIA Tools Extension (NVTX) ranges emitted by application instrumentation or an enabled framework profiling context; it does not itself add module annotations. The cublas and cudnn flags capture library-level operations, which helps identify whether a GEMM is using cuBLAS or a custom kernel. The command is useful because these rows expose whether the bottleneck is launch overhead, communication serialization, or kernel implementation.
The resulting .nsys-rep file is opened in the Nsight Systems graphical user interface, which presents a multi-row timeline. Four rows carry the most diagnostic weight.
The CUDA HW row shows the actual kernel execution on the GPU. Each colored bar represents a kernel, with width proportional to execution time. A gap without kernel activity is a reason to inspect the surrounding transfers, host work, dependencies, and request arrivals. It represents a recoverable delay only if useful work could have run during that interval. For a saturated inference pipeline, unexplained gaps can expose an optimization opportunity; under light load, waiting for the next request may be expected.
The CUDA API row shows CPU-side CUDA API calls (kernel launches, memory allocations, synchronization). A long API interval may reflect launch overhead, a blocking synchronization, allocation, or waiting on device work. Identify the API and correlate its interval with GPU activity before diagnosing a CPU launch bottleneck. Graph replay helps when repeated host submission creates exposed launch gaps.
The NCCL row (for distributed workloads) shows collective communication operations. Comparing the NCCL row with compute-kernel intervals reveals whether communication overlaps with useful computation. Concurrent bars establish overlap in time, but not a net speedup: communication can contend with compute for device resources. Compare end-to-end duration with the baseline to establish whether concurrency actually removed exposed time.
The NVTX row shows the ranges emitted by the selected instrumentation. Explicit module-level annotations can associate intervals with names such as Linear, LayerNorm, or Attention. This connects low-level kernel names, cryptic strings that encode the target architecture, data types, and tile shape (an sm90_xmma_gemm_... prefix marks a Hopper GEMM, for example), to the model-level operations that produced them.

A full decode trace shows how several of these smaller bottlenecks can combine into the dominant loss. The example uses a 7B model on one GPU rather than the recurring 70B replica, so that no collective enters the trace and every interval belongs to a single device.

Example 9.1: The profiler detectiveScenario: A 7B parameter LLM running autoregressive generation on an H100 GPU at batch size 1 achieves 84 tokens/s, falling below the 239 tokens/s memory-bandwidth decode ceiling.
Diagnosis: Nsight Compute shows the primary FP16 GEMM operates efficiently (2.8 TB/s bandwidth), but Nsight Systems reveals that 58 percent of step time is spent in unfused LayerNorm/GELU kernels, sampling, and CPU launch gaps across 120 launches per layer. Some of this interval performs required model work; the trace must distinguish that work from avoidable launches and intermediate transfers.
Systems lesson: Systematic profiling reveals bottlenecks where intuition fails. Optimizing GEMM kernels yields diminishing returns when accumulated launch overhead and unfused element-wise operations consume over half the step duration; kernel fusion via torch.compile or Triton is a candidate for reducing the exposed launches and transfers. The end-to-end measurement must establish how much time it saves, since fusion does not eliminate all non-GEMM work or guarantee attainment of the decode roofline.





Effective performance engineering follows an iterative cycle: profile, diagnose, optimize, verify. Engineers frequently neglect the verification step. After applying an optimization, reprofiling confirms whether the intervention relieved the active limiter or merely exposed a secondary bottleneck—the classic waterbed dilemma of computer systems.
A common trap is optimizing based on microbenchmarks rather than end-to-end traces. A kernel that achieves a 2\(\times\) speedup in isolation may yield only a 5 percent gain in end-to-end throughput if its interval was not on the critical path, or if data dependencies serialize execution. Rigorous evaluation demands measuring impact at the application boundary (tokens per second, step time, tail latency percentiles) alongside kernel-level metrics. The same measurement discipline governs rollout risk, because a change that looks local can consume a global resource once it reaches production traffic. In ML serving, the analogous risk is an input shape the tests never exercised, such as an unusually long prompt whose prefill occupies a replica’s compute and cache far longer than the typical request. A well-documented case of an execution cost that escaped this verification step and became a fleet-wide failure comes from outside ML.

War Story 9.1: The regex that saturated the edge (2019)Context: Cloudflare’s web application firewall evaluates rules on HTTP/HTTPS traffic across its global edge (Cloudflare 2019).
Mechanism: A rule deployed on July 2, 2019 caused excessive regular-expression backtracking and drove the CPUs serving HTTP/HTTPS traffic to nearly 100 percent utilization across the network. A previously removed CPU-use protection, missing performance tests, and a global rollout allowed the local computational cost to become a fleet-wide failure.
Impact: The resulting 27-minute outage disrupted proxying, content delivery, and firewall service. Traffic through the network dropped by about 82 percent, and users received 502 errors.
Fix: Disabling the firewall globally restored traffic; the offending change was then removed and the firewall re-enabled after testing. The postmortem reported restoring CPU-use protection and plans for performance tests, staged rule deployment, and a regular-expression engine with runtime guarantees.
Systems lesson: Correct outputs do not establish acceptable execution cost. For ML serving, the analogous discipline is to test expensive input shapes, bound admitted work, and stage performance-sensitive changes so a regression can be detected before it reaches the fleet.

Profiling turns optimization from guesswork into a discipline guided by quantitative evidence. A trace from one device, however, cannot show how a fleet behaves.

When scaling from 8 GPUs to 1,024 GPUs, new sources of overhead emerge that are invisible in local traces. Fleet measurements determine whether optimizing a local kernel is warranted in the first place. A profiler can explain why one kernel stalls; it cannot by itself say whether thousands of accelerators are converting power, memory bandwidth, and network time into useful model progress. Several examples in this section are training jobs rather than serving replicas, for a deliberate reason: every synchronous training step waits for all ranks, so fleet-level loss shows up there directly and at the largest scale. The same accounting applies to the collectives inside the recurring tensor-parallel serving replica, only across eight devices instead of thousands.
Collecting detailed traces from every GPU makes the measurement itself a scaling concern. At a fixed event rate and collection configuration, trace volume grows with the number of GPUs. If a 5-second Nsight Systems trace for one GPU occupies 500 MB, the same window across 1,024 GPUs would produce about 512 GB. This illustrative volume motivates selecting the ranks and intervals needed to answer a diagnostic question rather than collecting every event continuously.
Production systems address this through hierarchical profiling. At the top level, application metrics such as MFU, throughput, and step time detect degradation, while per-rank timing and device telemetry help locate it. Their collection frequency must keep monitoring overhead within budget. Targeted profiling then captures a short window from ranks selected to test a hypothesis, including different pipeline stages or data-parallel groups when relevant. Comparing a suspected straggler with an otherwise similar rank is often more informative than tracing an arbitrary representative GPU.
Another approach is statistical profiling, where a sampling policy selects a small fraction of kernels for detailed timing. Aggregating samples across training steps can estimate the kernel-time distribution with less collection overhead than full tracing. The estimate depends on adequate coverage of ranks and execution phases; rare stalls can remain absent even from a large sample. The approach is analogous to the sampling profilers (like Linux perf) used in traditional systems engineering, adapted for the GPU context.
Intermittent stragglers challenge both short traces and sampled profiles: an accelerator typically runs at expected speed but periodically falls behind due to thermal throttling, hardware degradation, transient network congestion, or host runtime pauses such as memory reclamation and garbage collection. In synchronous execution, a step finishes only when its slowest rank does, so a rank running 10 percent slow during an episode can delay every rank in its communication group by up to that same 10 percent; the fleet-level throughput loss is that synchronization penalty weighted by episode frequency. Continuous per-rank execution timers reveal these tail latency outliers and trigger targeted tracing. Correlating slow intervals with accelerator hardware telemetry, network packet counters, and host runtime event logs then distinguishes the root straggler from the peer ranks that merely idle at collective barriers waiting for it.
Fleet measurement also needs a reproducible measurement contract, one that covers both the local execution boundary and the global efficiency metrics that capture computation, communication, and hardware variability. Without a shared contract, two measurements cannot support an optimization claim. Benchmark suites formalize this principle by fixing workload, quality, and measurement rules before comparing systems (Mattson et al. 2020; Reddi et al. 2019). The contract, whose fields table 9 pairs with the failure each one prevents, fixes the workload envelope, including model, input and output length distributions, batch or concurrency, data distribution, and quality criterion; records hardware topology, accelerator clocks and power limits, software versions, precision, and compiler settings; and states the timing and synchronization boundaries. Cold-start compilation and cache-filling trials must remain separate from warmed steady-state trials. Each reported point needs repeated trials with a dispersion statistic, an output-equivalence or quality check, and latency percentiles at a named offered load. Without those controls, a speedup can come from different work, different machine state, asynchronous timing, or a shifted quality or service-level objective (SLO) rather than from the proposed optimization.

Hardware utilization reports how often GPUs are busy, but it does not distinguish model arithmetic from recomputation or time spent waiting within communication operations. Fleet measurement therefore needs the useful-work metric that table 5 already listed, MFU, which counts only the “useful” FLOPs the model architecture requires. What matters at fleet scale is how that metric aggregates across devices and what it hides. Its comparisons across software stacks and parallelization strategies hold only when the workload, FLOP-counting convention, and hardware peak definition stay fixed.

Definition 9.2: MFU
MFU is the fraction of the hardware’s theoretical peak throughput (\(\PeakRate\)) consumed by FLOPs that directly advance model training or inference, excluding overhead from recomputation, padding, and synchronization.

Significance: At fleet scale, MFU aggregates across all nodes. Communication overhead, load imbalance, and pipeline bubbles tend to lower it relative to a comparable local run, although changes in batch size or memory feasibility can alter that comparison. A one-percentage-point MFU increase across 10,000 identical GPUs adds useful throughput equivalent to 100 GPUs at peak. Realized cost savings depend on whether the recovered capacity displaces hardware or shortens paid runtime.
Distinction: Unlike hardware utilization (which reports how often the accelerator is “busy”), MFU relates the model’s reference FLOP rate to hardware peak. It excludes recomputation and padding from useful work even when they support a feasible or faster implementation; quality and convergence require separate checks.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that high GPU utilization implies high efficiency. A system can show 90 percent hardware utilization while achieving 30 percent MFU when busy intervals include communication or arithmetic that runs far below peak. MFU exposes the gap but does not explain its cause; traces and other metrics must guide the optimization decision.





↩︎ Model FLOPs utilization is established as the compute-axis efficiency measure in Node compute substrate (\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1).


Fleet MFU falls below the single-node baseline.

With MFU defined as useful work rather than raw busyness, the loss between a single node and the fleet becomes a number, here for the recurring 70B model in training.

Napkin Math 9.2: The scaling taxProblem: A 70B parameter model achieves a local node baseline of 65 percent MFU on a single 8-GPU node. When training scales to 128 GPUs, the step time increases to 245 ms, dropping fleet performance to 48 percent MFU. The single-node baseline assumes optimizer state offloaded to host memory, since full training state for a 70B model exceeds one node’s HBM. What relative MFU loss appears at fleet scale under these constructed assumptions?
Math: Both MFU figures come from the same ratio, the useful FLOPs a step performs divided by the FLOPs the cluster could execute at peak in that step’s wall time:
\[\ModelFlopsUtilization = \frac{\UsefulModelFlops}{\DeviceCount\times \PeakRate \times \DistributedStepTime}\]
For the fleet case, a step performs 14.9 PFLOP of useful work, while 128 GPUs \(\times\) 989 TFLOP/s per GPU \(\times\) 245 ms of wall time could execute 31 PFLOP at peak; the quotient 14.9 PFLOP ÷ 31 PFLOP \(\approx\) 48 percent. The same substitution on the single node yields 65 percent, and the scaling tax is \(1 - \text{Fleet MFU}/\text{Local MFU}\), giving 26.2 percent.
Systems insight: The 26.2 percent scaling tax measures the relative efficiency change under these assumptions. It does not isolate network cost: workload shape, parallelism, offload, kernel efficiency, and synchronization can all change the ratio. A scaling regression therefore requires a matched measurement contract and trace evidence before attributing the loss to the network.





Local resource costs can become exposed delays at scale. A small increase in memory demand may cross an allocation threshold, while a longer host pause on one rank can hold up a synchronized step across the fleet. Communication changes can separately increase network contention. These mechanisms require different evidence, so a local memory regression alone does not diagnose a network-buffer problem. Table 10 organizes the tests that connect local changes to distributed behavior before a full-fleet rollout.

Systems Perspective 9.3: Benchmark vs. reality: The hero run taxBenchmark results, including MLPerf submissions, describe performance under a specified workload and measurement protocol. A carefully tuned result is a useful reference, but its operating conditions may differ from those of a production service. Capacity planning requires comparing those conditions with the intended deployment rather than treating the reported throughput as an unconditional capacity guarantee.
Production capacity must account for costs that the reference measurement does not already include. Metrics collection, logging, checkpointing, and health monitoring can consume resources; contention and hardware variability can add further delays. Their combined effect must be measured without counting costs already present in the benchmark a second time. As a planning scenario, if useful throughput is 10–20 percent below the rate that implied 30 days of training, the same work takes approximately 33.3–37.5 days. This is a sensitivity calculation, not a universal production penalty.


The measurement contract makes optimization results comparable across the node and fleet boundaries. A trace dominated by intermediate transfers or repeated host launches motivates fusion and replay; dominant weight traffic motivates precision reduction. The following mechanisms each change one part of that measured budget, and their value must be checked against the same workload, quality criterion, and service objective.

Consider the simple sequence of operations \(\FusionOutputTensor= \text{LayerNorm}(\text{GELU}(\FusionInputTensor\WeightMatrix+ \BiasVector))\). Separate kernels write and reread intermediate tensors through global memory, creating traffic that can dominate the element-wise and normalization work. Operator fusion combines compatible operations so that intermediate values remain in registers or shared memory. The opportunity is to remove transfers and launches; whether the entire sequence fits profitably into one kernel depends on its reduction dependencies and on-chip resource requirements.

Systems Perspective 9.4: Analogy: The short-order cookImagine a kitchen where one chef chops vegetables, puts them in the fridge (HBM), then another chef takes them out to boil them, puts them back in the fridge, and a third chef takes them out to plate them. This is unfused execution: the bottleneck is not the cooking but the constant walking to the fridge.
Operator fusion assigns the recipe to a single chef who keeps the ingredients on their cutting board (SRAM/Registers) and performs all three steps consecutively without ever returning to the fridge until the final dish is ready.




Each GPU kernel launch involves overhead: the CPU must prepare launch parameters, dispatch to the GPU command queue, and the GPU must schedule thread blocks across its streaming multiprocessors (SMs). For a small element-wise operation on an accelerator such as an H100, this overhead runs to several microseconds per launch, a time during which a memory-bound kernel might have already completed its useful work. When a transformer layer comprises dozens of small operations (add, multiply, normalize, activate), the cumulative launch overhead becomes significant. The exposed share depends on how the framework dispatches. In eager execution a Python loop and the framework dispatcher submit each kernel in turn, but not every launch traverses the Python global interpreter lock (GIL), the lock that serializes Python bytecode execution; asynchronous runtime threads, compiled regions, and native extensions can submit work outside that path.
Each unfused kernel also materializes an output in global memory. For the sequence \(\FusionOutputTensor= \text{LayerNorm}(\text{GELU}(\FusionInputTensor\WeightMatrix+ \BiasVector))\), a simplified traffic model assumes these reads and writes reach HBM; cache reuse can reduce the actual off-chip traffic. The GEMM kernel reads \(\FusionInputTensor\) and \(\WeightMatrix\) from HBM, computes \(\FusionInputTensor\WeightMatrix+ \BiasVector\), and writes the intermediate result \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_1\) back to memory. The GELU kernel then reads \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_1\), evaluates \(\text{GELU}(\FusionIntermediateTensor_1)\), and writes a second intermediate tensor \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_2\). Finally, the LayerNorm kernel reads \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_2\), applies normalization, and writes the final output \(\FusionOutputTensor\).
Intermediate tensors \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_1\) and \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_2\) each occupy the same memory as the output \(\FusionOutputTensor\). For the Llama 2 70B shape (hidden dimension 8192) at a batch of 2048 tokens in FP16, each intermediate tensor is 33.6 MB. The unfused execution materializes 67.1 MB of intermediate tensors, corresponding to 134.2 MB of HBM traffic if each write and reread reaches that boundary. A fused kernel can avoid these transfers by keeping the needed tiles of \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_1\) and \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_2\) in registers or shared memory within the SM. Figure 4 illustrates this idealized contrast; it does not require the complete intermediate tensors to fit on chip at once.






Figure 4: Operator fusion before and after: The diagram counts activation transfers. Separate kernels write and reread the intermediates \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_1\) and \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_2\) (red), while the fused kernel passes them between stages on chip, leaving only the read of \(\FusionInputTensor\) and the write of \(\FusionOutputTensor\). Weight reads and small parameter vectors are not drawn. Transfer counts alone do not determine total byte savings when tensors differ in size.



By retaining intermediates within registers and shared memory, the fused pipeline in figure 4 eliminates four one-way transfers between the SM and HBM (the red write and read passes for \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_1\) and \(\FusionIntermediateTensor_2\)). Including one read each of \(\FusionInputTensor\) and \(\WeightMatrix\) and one write of \(\FusionOutputTensor\), the stated dimensions yield a 1.7× byte reduction, ignoring the small bias and normalization vectors. Cache reuse, tile reloads, and workspace can change actual traffic.
Launch overhead creates a second opportunity. Suppose an eager transformer decoder layer issues 30 separate kernels at 5–10 μs per launch. The host then spends 150–300 μs on dispatch. The same layer’s bandwidth-only GPU time in the batch-one 70B example is about 65 μs, making exposed submission time a plausible limiter. Host dispatch can overlap GPU execution, so these totals alone do not establish the length or placement of launch gaps. A launch-bound trace must show that submission leaves useful device work waiting. Fusion reduces the number of launches, while graph replay (section 9.8.3) reduces repeated submission overhead for the kernels that remain.
Fusion nevertheless has a resource ceiling. A larger fused kernel keeps more live values in registers and often reserves more shared memory per thread block. Either demand can reduce the number of resident warps, lowering occupancy and the latency-hiding capacity of the SM; excessive register demand can also spill values into local memory backed by the cache hierarchy or HBM. Fusion is profitable only when the avoided launches and HBM intermediates outweigh this loss of occupancy, spill traffic, and any duplicated computation. Kernel evaluation must therefore compare measured HBM bytes, register and shared-memory use, achieved occupancy, spill transactions, and end-to-end time rather than treating fewer launches as sufficient evidence.



Fusion is profitable when the HBM traffic it removes is worth the kernel complexity it introduces. The three common categories differ by that trade-off: how much data movement they eliminate, how much synchronization they require, and how often a compiler can apply them automatically.
Element-wise fusion sits at the low-complexity end: consecutive element-wise operations (add, multiply, activation functions) combine into a single kernel. For pure operations with compatible iteration spaces, fusion can preserve the same per-element dependencies. Aliasing, side effects, multiple consumers, and numerical requirements can constrain legality or profitability. Deep learning frameworks commonly perform element-wise fusion automatically for supported patterns.
When the sequence includes a reduction, the fusion decision becomes more constrained. Reduction fusion combines an element-wise operation with a subsequent reduction (such as summing elements for a loss function, or computing mean and variance for layer normalization). Threads can use warp-level shuffle instructions or shared memory to combine partial results within a block. Reductions that span blocks may need additional synchronization or an intermediate buffer. When the reduction and its producer fit a compatible schedule, fusion can avoid writing and rereading the prenormalization tensor; that saving depends on the reduction shape and kernel design.
Operator-specific fusion uses custom kernels designed for a particular sequence of operations, such as fused attention or fused GEMM-bias-activation. The kernel architect must reason about data flow, shared memory allocation, and thread scheduling simultaneously. This specialization can remove an intermediate representation that dominates memory demand: FlashAttention, for example, avoids materializing the quadratic attention workspace and keeps the online softmax state linear in sequence length.
To estimate the opportunity, consider each category applied to a transformer layer with hidden dimension 8192, a batch of 2048 tokens, and FP16 values. Fusing a bias-GELU-dropout chain can eliminate two intermediate tensors of 33.6 MB each, avoiding 134.2 MB of traffic per layer under the same HBM accounting assumptions. Across 80 layers, the modeled saving is about 10.7 GB per forward pass. Reduction fusion targets prenormalization tensors and intermediate statistics when their dependencies permit it. Operator-specific attention fusion removes the quadratic score and probability matrices, making it especially valuable when those matrices dominate memory demand. These savings cannot simply be added when candidate fusions eliminate overlapping intermediates. The resulting end-to-end speedup must be measured because remaining traffic and kernel resource use can change the bottleneck.



An orthogonal technique for reducing the overhead term in the iron law is CUDA graphs.2 While operator fusion combines multiple operations into fewer kernels, CUDA Graphs amortize repeated CPU submission of a stable kernel sequence.
2 CUDA graphs: Graph capture records a sequence of GPU work and its dependencies for later replay (NVIDIA Corporation 2026). Replay requires a capture-compatible operation graph and valid referenced storage; it does not require numerically identical results. Dynamic control flow, shapes, or allocations can instead require graph variants, graph updates, or uncaptured regions. Repetitive decode shapes are often easier to capture than heterogeneous prefill shapes.
NVIDIA Corporation. 2026. CUDA Graphs: CUDA Programming Guide.
In standard PyTorch execution, each kernel launch requires the CPU to push a command to the GPU’s command queue, and section 9.8.1 put that cost at 150–300 μs per decoder layer. For the 80-layer 70B example, host-side kernel submission alone totals roughly 12–24 ms per forward pass, and whatever part of it the GPU cannot hide behind running kernels lands on the critical path. That total is several times the 5.2 ms bandwidth-bound decode step computed in notebook 9.1, which is why eager decode, submitted one kernel at a time, can be launch-bound before it is bandwidth-bound.
CUDA Graphs address this by recording a sequence of GPU operations (kernel launches and memory copies) into a replayable graph. The recording happens once during a warmup phase. On subsequent iterations, one replay request submits the recorded graph and avoids rebuilding the launch sequence operation by operation. Replay still incurs host, driver, graph-launch, synchronization, and device scheduling costs, so the saved fraction must be measured for the captured region.
The benefit can be substantial when short kernels leave visible CPU launch gaps, but it shrinks when long kernels or data movement already dominate wall time. The relevant comparison is the end-to-end captured region before and after replay, including warmup and any uncaptured work, rather than the number of launches alone.
The constraint is structural rather than numerical. A graph executable replays captured nodes and dependencies against referenced storage, while supported graph updates can change a bounded set of node parameters (NVIDIA Corporation 2026). Variable sequence shapes, changing batches, conditional expert routes, and allocation patterns may therefore require multiple graph variants or leave dynamic regions in ordinary stream execution. Decode often presents more reusable operation shapes than prefill, but that advantage depends on the runtime’s bucketing and capture strategy.
Operator fusion and CUDA Graphs attack different sources of exposed time: fusion removes kernels and intermediate traffic, while graph replay reduces repeated host submission for the kernels that remain. When a trace attributes a material fraction of end-to-end time to CPU launch gaps and the workload admits stable capture, replay becomes a candidate intervention; profiling after capture must confirm that the gap moved rather than assuming all noncompute overhead disappeared.



Standard self-attention computes \(\text{Softmax}(\AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T / \sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension})\AttentionValuesMatrix\), where \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) are matrices of shape \([\text{sequence length}{\times}\text{head dimension}]\). The naive implementation materializes the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention matrix \(\UnscaledAttentionScoreMatrix= \AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T\) in HBM, where \(\SequenceLength\) is the sequence length. For \(\SequenceLength= 8192\) and FP16 precision, this matrix alone consumes \(8192 \times 8192 \times 2 \approx 134\) MB per attention head, so the quadratic score tensors run to several gigabytes per layer. The simplified HBM-traffic accounting compares HBM-visible bytes for a 64-head Llama-style layer under explicit traffic assumptions.
FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) reformulates attention using tiling. Instead of materializing the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) attention matrix, it processes \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) in small blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM. The algorithm loads tiles of \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\), computes partial attention scores, and maintains running statistics (online softmax) to produce the exact result without ever storing the full attention matrix in HBM.


In this scenario, tiling cuts HBM traffic about 65\(\times\).

The reduction in HBM traffic can be dramatic. For a sequence length of 8192, 64 heads, and head dimension 128 in FP16, the simplified naive estimate writes and reads the score and probability matrices and moves \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\), and output once, totaling approximately 34.9 GB for the full layer, or 545.3 MB per head. The idealized FlashAttention lower bound counts one read of \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) and one output write, totaling approximately 536.9 MB for the full layer, or 8.4 MB per head. The resulting 65× ratio is a scenario comparison, not a claim about allocated memory or realized kernel traffic; actual traffic depends on tile reloads and the implementation schedule.
The key insight behind FlashAttention is the online softmax trick, which processes scores incrementally in a single pass and so makes tiling possible for an operation that appears to require global information. Standard softmax computes \(\text{softmax}(\SoftmaxRowScore_i) = e^{\SoftmaxRowScore_i} / \sum_j e^{\SoftmaxRowScore_j}\), but for numerical stability it first subtracts the global maximum: \(\text{softmax}(\SoftmaxRowScore_i) = e^{\SoftmaxRowScore_i - \SoftmaxRowMaximum} / \sum_j e^{\SoftmaxRowScore_j - \SoftmaxRowMaximum}\) where \(\SoftmaxRowMaximum= \max_j \SoftmaxRowScore_j\). Finding this global maximum seems to require seeing all scores first, which would force materializing the full \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) matrix.
The online algorithm avoids this by maintaining running statistics that are updated incrementally as each tile is processed. When processing tile \(\ProcessedKeyTileIndex\), the algorithm executes four steps:

Computes a local block of scores \({\OnlineSoftmaxScoreBlock}_t = \OnlineSoftmaxQueryBlock {\OnlineSoftmaxKeyTile}_t^T\).
Updates the running maximum: \(\NewSoftmaxRunningMaximum= \max(\OldSoftmaxRunningMaximum, \max({\OnlineSoftmaxScoreBlock}_t))\).
Rescales the previous running sum and output: multiply by \(e^{\OldSoftmaxRunningMaximum- \NewSoftmaxRunningMaximum}\) to correct for the updated maximum.
Computes the local softmax contribution using \(\NewSoftmaxRunningMaximum\) and accumulates into the running output.

After processing all tiles, divide the accumulated weighted numerator by the running softmax denominator. This normalization yields the same mathematical attention result as the standard algorithm, up to floating-point roundoff. The rescaling step (step 3) is the critical innovation: it allows the algorithm to “fix up” previous partial results when a new tile reveals a larger maximum value. The algorithm is exact in the mathematical sense, but floating-point execution order can still change the last few bits relative to an unfused implementation.
The cost of tiling includes additional rescaling, reductions, and scheduling work. Avoiding HBM traffic can outweigh those costs when transfers are exposed on the critical path, but a memory-bound baseline does not make extra arithmetic free. Scalar throughput, reduction dependencies, register pressure, and occupancy can become the new limits. The kernel must therefore be evaluated on its measured traffic and complete execution time.
FlashAttention achieves this traffic reduction by staging matrix blocks across the memory hierarchy, as mapped in figure 5: instead of materializing the quadratic \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score matrix in off-chip HBM, the kernel streams \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), and \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) tiles into on-chip storage and evaluates softmax statistics online. Consider illustrative \(128{\times}128\) tiles. The input payload includes a block of \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\) (\(128 \times 128 \times 2 \approx\) 32.8 KB), a block of \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\) (\(128 \times 128 \times 2 \approx\) 32.8 KB), and a block of \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\) (32.8 KB), totaling approximately 98.3 KB. This input payload is smaller than the H100’s 228 KB of shared memory per SM, but it is not the complete kernel working set: accumulators, softmax state, and buffering also consume registers or shared memory. The tile score \(\AttentionScoreTile= \AttentionQueryMatrix_i \AttentionKeyMatrix_j^T\) is computed and consumed on chip; it is never materialized as a full HBM tensor. The illustrative schedule iterates over \(8192/128 =\) 64 column tiles for each of 64 row tiles, reloading tiles as required. The quadratic \(\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength\) score and probability matrices are never materialized: the persistent per-head tensors are \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), \(\AttentionKeyMatrix\), \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\), \(\AttentionHeadOutput\), and \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) softmax statistics.







Figure 5: FlashAttention memory hierarchy tiling: Block-by-block scheduling of Q, K, and V matrices loaded into on-chip shared memory (SRAM). Attention scores are computed and rescaled online without materializing the quadratic \(\SequenceLength \times \SequenceLength\) intermediate matrix in off-chip HBM, keeping persistent attention workspace linear in sequence length for fixed head dimension. HBM traffic still depends on SRAM capacity and tile reloads.



FlashAttention-2 (Dao 2023) further optimizes the algorithm for GPU architectures with many streaming multiprocessors by restructuring the parallelism pattern. The original FlashAttention parallelizes over batch and head dimensions, meaning each thread block handles one (batch, head) pair and iterates over the full sequence. FlashAttention-2 additionally parallelizes over the sequence dimension of the query matrix, distributing work across thread blocks more efficiently and achieving better occupancy. It also reduces the number of non-GEMM FLOPs by restructuring the rescaling operations and exploiting the asymmetry between the Q loop (outer) and K/V loop (inner).

Dao, Tri. 2023. “FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.08691.
Newer FlashAttention-family kernels target Hopper-era hardware features such as FP8 Tensor Cores and the Tensor Memory Accelerator, a hardware path for asynchronous bulk tensor movement between HBM and shared memory. The systems principle is the same as the original algorithm: as the hardware exposes faster movement and lower-precision execution paths, the attention schedule must be rewritten to use those paths without materializing the quadratic workspace.
The original breakthrough made memory movement part of the algorithmic cost model. Attention still requires matrix multiplication, but reducing its arithmetic alone does not address the cost of materializing and rereading large intermediate tensors. FlashAttention instead trades a small amount of extra arithmetic, the online rescaling and backward-pass recomputation, for the elimination of quadratic HBM-resident state.

Example 9.2: The FlashAttention breakthroughScenario: Standard Transformer attention materializes a full \(\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength\) attention score matrix in high-latency GPU HBM, creating a quadratic memory and bandwidth bottleneck as sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) grows (Dao et al. 2022).
Diagnosis: Materializing attention intermediates creates memory traffic that an arithmetic-only analysis misses. FlashAttention restructures attention via block-by-block tiling and online softmax, holding intermediate state on chip to compute attention without writing the \(\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength\) matrix to global memory.
Systems lesson: FlashAttention demonstrates I/O-aware algorithm design: eliminating quadratic HBM intermediates can improve runtime even when backward execution recomputes values. The commonly quoted 2–4\(\times\) wall-clock speedup is not a general prediction for long-context workloads; measured gains depend on sequence length, hardware, the baseline kernel, and whether the timing covers attention alone or the complete model.



Dao, T., D. Y. Fu, S. Ermon, A. Rudra, and C. Ré. 2022. “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 16344–59. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1189.
The 65× ratio measures traffic, the bytes moved through HBM. Eliminating the quadratic intermediate also frees capacity, the bytes that must be resident at once, and that second quantity grows differently with sequence length. Standard attention’s workspace rises as \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) while FlashAttention’s rises as \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\), so the gap widens with every doubling of context (figure 6); the much larger ratios on that plot are capacity ratios and should not be read as traffic or speed. The freed capacity matters for serving because prefill and decode often share a replica. While a long prompt is being prefilled, its score workspace occupies HBM alongside the KV cache of every request already decoding, so removing that workspace leaves room for the scheduler to admit more concurrent requests.

The green gap is memory freed for KV cache, activations, or larger batches, and it widens with every doubling of context. Its ratios compare resident workspace (capacity), not the HBM traffic ratio quoted in the text.



FlashAttention reduces the memory wall within a single GPU by tiling across the SRAM-HBM boundary. For sequence lengths that exceed the memory capacity of a single GPU, the same tiling principle extends across multiple GPUs via Ring Attention (Liu et al. 2023). Distributing the sequence blocks across a ring of accelerators and overlapping communication with computation enables Ring Attention to handle context windows that would be impractical on single-GPU configurations.
