The scheduler cannot treat the cluster as a static resource pool where resources, once allocated, remain available until voluntarily released. It must anticipate loss of allocated resources during execution and provide replacement capacity or rescheduling paths. The response depends on the fault and the validity of the surviving state. A transient disruption may permit recovery in place if the execution state remains usable; a persistent hardware failure requires replacement resources. Even a short disruption can force checkpoint recovery if the framework cannot safely continue (Tiwari et al. 2015).
When a node heartbeat is missed, the scheduler faces three recovery policies with different delay and capacity costs. It can wait to see whether the heartbeat resumes, though this delays recovery if the machine has permanently crashed. It can instead begin recovery promptly on replacement resources, provided stale execution is fenced before conflicting work resumes. An intermediate approach marks the node as suspect and prepositions replacement capacity while checking its status; this reduces launch delay if replacement becomes necessary, but holds capacity that could otherwise serve pending work. Whichever policy it picks, a timeout is evidence rather than proof of failure, so reuse of the node’s GPUs still waits on fencing. Historical failure and recovery measurements set how long to wait and how much replacement capacity to hold. The recovery-time decomposition of fault tolerance (equation 7.10) shows where scheduler policy intervenes most effectively. Of its detection, restart, load, and warmup terms, the scheduler owns most of \(\JobRestartTime\), the time to allocate replacement resources and launch processes, and that is the term its spare-capacity policy shortens. Waiting longer on a missed heartbeat lengthens \(\FailureDetectionTime\) in exchange for avoiding a needless restart, so the wait is worth extending only while a transient fault remains more likely than a permanent one.

These requirements connect the scheduler directly to checkpoint and recovery infrastructure. Scheduling decisions about spare capacity, preemption policies, and elastic training support determine how quickly the system recovers from statistically expected failures. A scheduler that reserves spare capacity or supports elastic recovery can restore throughput much faster than one that requires every failed job to wait for a full fresh allocation and reload. The reserve fraction follows from the measured failure rate and recovery time of the fleet’s own workloads.

Scheduling policies balance four objectives: throughput, fairness, latency, and cost efficiency. Throughput benefits from allocations that sustain useful work and amortize launch, interruption, and data-movement overhead; a large allocation helps only while the job scales effectively. Maintaining fairness demands an equitable distribution of resources across competing tenants to prevent a single dominant project from monopolizing the fleet; dominant resource fairness (Ghodsi et al. 2011) formalizes this balance by equalizing each tenant’s largest normalized share across GPUs, CPU, and memory. Reducing queue latency helps short, interactive jobs complete promptly, but aggressive preemption can repeatedly interrupt long-running training. Pursuing cost efficiency introduces different costs for different policies: spot capacity risks interruption, off-peak scheduling delays admission, and dense packing can increase interference. Each policy must be evaluated against useful work completed and the delays it imposes.
Fairness requires an outcome metric rather than an input quota rule alone. For job \(\JobIndex\), slowdown \(\JobSlowdown_j=(\JobQueueWaitTime_j+\IsolatedJobRunTime_j)/\IsolatedJobRunTime_j\) compares its queueing-plus-running time with its isolated runtime \(\IsolatedJobRunTime_j\), assuming the running time is unchanged by sharing; a one-hour job that waits nine hours has \(\JobSlowdown_j=10\), even if its team eventually receives its nominal GPU share. When contention or resizing changes execution time, the numerator must instead use the observed queueing-plus-running duration while the denominator retains the isolated baseline. A scheduler should report the distribution of slowdown by user and job class, together with the age of the oldest pending feasible job. Dominant-share parity detects unequal resource allocation, slowdown exposes unequal delay, and the maximum feasible wait exposes starvation risk. These metrics separate a policy that is fair in allocated GPU-hours from one that is fair in the time users wait to obtain useful results.
The trade-off diamond in figure 1 illustrates these operational tensions among throughput, latency, fairness, and cost efficiency. Favoring a large unbroken allocation can delay short experiments, while repeatedly admitting short jobs can prevent a large gang from assembling. These conflicts depend on the workload and available capacity; improving one objective does not necessarily worsen every other objective. Resource-share fairness and completion-delay fairness therefore need separate measurements.

Consider a 64-GPU fine-tuning run of the same 175B-parameter model, a far smaller allocation than its 1,024-GPU pretraining run. If it sustains high utilization for days, an uninterrupted allocation amortizes launch overhead across a long execution. Admitting it may nevertheless require draining 64 suitably placed GPUs, delaying smaller experiments. Conversely, repeatedly filling available gaps with short jobs can prevent the large job from assembling its required group. Preemption or resizing can recover flexibility only if the job supports the transition and its cost is acceptable. The policy must therefore compare useful throughput with completion delay for both job classes. In scheduler terminology, those choices often appear as quality-of-service classes: job-priority tiers that decide which objective wins when throughput, latency, fairness, and cost collide.

Napkin Math 8.1: The queuing theory of GPU clustersTo isolate the effect of runtime variability, consider an M/G/1 queue with first-come-first-served service. Kendall notation names the queue by its arrival process, service-time distribution, and server count: M for memoryless (Poisson) arrivals, G for a general service-time distribution, and 1 for a single server. Treating a fleet as one server means modeling its aggregate capacity as a single resource that works through one job at a time, with each job’s service time equal to its GPU-hours divided by the fleet’s GPU count. That mapping ignores gang packing and parallel admission, so it isolates the variability effect rather than predicting a real fleet’s wait. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process \((\ArrivalRate)\), and independent service times follow a general distribution \((\Glyph{G})\) with mean \(1/\ServiceRate\) and finite standard deviation \(\ServiceTimeStandardDeviation\). When offered load is below service capacity, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula gives the steady-state expected waiting time in the queue \((\QueueWaitTime)\):
\[ \frac{\QueueWaitTime}{1/\ServiceRate} = \frac{\ServingUtilization}{1-\ServingUtilization} \cdot \frac{1+\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient^2}{2} \]
Here, \(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate/\ServiceRate\) represents offered load relative to the model’s service capacity, \(1/\ServiceRate\) is the average job duration, and \(\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient= \ServiceTimeStandardDeviation\ServiceRate\) is the coefficient of variation of job duration. The right-hand side is therefore the waiting time expressed as a multiple of the average job duration; a fleet’s measured GPU-busy percentage is not automatically this model’s load.
An exponential service-time distribution provides a reference case, yielding \(\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient\approx 1\). A mixed ML queue can have much greater variability when short debugging jobs measured in minutes share capacity with training runs measured in weeks. The representative \(\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient=3\) calculation in this callout captures that variability without claiming a universal fleet constant. The impact on wait times is multiplicative. For the scheduling argument here, the single-server multiplier is sufficient; Queuing theory for batched inference develops an explicit single-server surrogate for batched serving and explains why multi-server, finite-buffer M/G/c/K systems require additional modeling.
At 80 percent utilization \((\ServingUtilization = 0.8)\): with an exponential workload \((\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient= 1)\), \(\QueueWaitTime=\) 4 \(\times\) the average job duration. With an illustrative high-variability workload \((\ServiceTimeVariationCoefficient= 3)\), \(\QueueWaitTime=\) 20 \(\times\) the average job duration. In this M/G/1 model, service-time variability multiplies waiting time at the same offered load. The example does not prescribe a universal GPU-utilization threshold or model gang placement directly. It explains why capacity planning needs the service-time distribution and queue-delay objective as well as average load.





A scheduling objective can only choose among allocations that a job can actually run. Fairness must be computed across every resource a tenant consumes, a request must fit every dimension of the node that receives it, a rigid group must arrive whole, and the resources each job holds must not block one another. Each of these constraints narrows the feasible set before any objective selects within it.

For tenant \(\TenantIndex\), define its dominant share as \(\DominantShare_i=\max_\ResourceTypeIndex(\TenantResourceAllocation/\FleetResourceCapacity)\), where \(\TenantResourceAllocation\) is its allocation of resource \(\ResourceTypeIndex\) and \(\FleetResourceCapacity\) is fleet capacity for that resource. The calculation equalizes \(\DominantShare_i\), not every resource share. One A replica raises A’s dominant share by \(1/8\); one B worker raises B’s by \(2/8\). Progressive filling therefore grants roughly two A replicas for each B worker until both dominant shares reach \(0.50\). This is a fair policy target, but it is not yet a feasible placement. If B’s two workers form one four-GPU gang, the four GPUs must become available atomically; if tensor parallelism requires one NVLink domain, four free GPUs scattered across nodes do not satisfy the allocation; and if the job requires 80 GB HBM accelerators, four incompatible GPUs do not count at all. A production scheduler therefore applies capability, gang, and topology constraints to the feasible set, then uses DRF to choose fairly among allocations that can actually run. The order is not a convenience. Feasibility comes before fairness (principle \(\ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}\)) because a fair share of accelerators on which the job cannot run delivers no progress to the tenant who holds it. When no equal-share placement exists, the scheduler should report the constraint causing the deviation rather than silently presenting an infeasible entitlement as service delivered.

Lighthouse 8.1: Lighthouse archetypes: Placement changes fairnessThe same resource share has different meaning across the three lighthouse workloads introduced in Three systems archetypes:

Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) needs a rigid, topology-compatible gang. Fractional allocations below its minimum parallel configuration deliver no progress, so fairness must include maximum feasible wait for a contiguous placement rather than GPU-hours alone.
Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) couples accelerator memory to sparse-routing bandwidth. A nominal GPU allocation is infeasible when embedding shards or network capacity cannot follow it, so network and memory must enter the dominant share and placement must protect the serving-latency envelope.
Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) schedules participation rather than data-center GPUs. Eligibility filters for power, connectivity, and device capability can systematically exclude parts of the population, so fairness must be audited through participation and outcome rates across device and user groups, not equal device counts in a round.

The common rule is to define the feasible bundle first and assess fairness over useful progress second. Treating every accelerator or client as interchangeable would conceal the constraint that makes each archetype difficult.





Bin packing4 captures a basic placement problem: fitting jobs of varying sizes into fixed-capacity nodes. This problem is NP-hard in its general form, meaning no known algorithm finds optimal solutions in polynomial time. Practical heuristics such as first-fit decreasing and best-fit decreasing offer tractable choices, but their performance depends on job sizes and placement constraints. How much usable capacity a heuristic recovers in a heterogeneous ML fleet has to be measured against that fleet’s job mix, because the classical guarantees cover only one-dimensional packing.
4 Bin Packing: First-fit decreasing has a classical asymptotic \(11/9\) approximation ratio for one-dimensional bin packing, with an additive constant in the finite-instance bound. That result does not guarantee the same ratio for ML placement with several resource dimensions, topology constraints, and indivisible gangs. A scheduler must evaluate its heuristic against feasible placements and the stranded capacity it leaves.Consider a 64-node cluster with 8 GPUs per node, totaling 512 GPUs. If every job requires 6 GPUs within one node, only one such job fits per node, leaving 2 GPUs unused and reducing effective capacity for this workload to 75 percent. The remaining 2 GPUs per node cannot be combined across nodes into another feasible six-GPU allocation, although smaller compatible jobs could use them. With a mix of 1-GPU, 3-GPU, and 7-GPU jobs, fragmentation depends on the placement and the pending requests; total free capacity can exceed a waiting job’s demand while no individual node has enough space. Figure 2 maps this stranded capacity across an 8×8 allocation grid: although 19 slots (30 percent of cluster capacity, dashed white cells) sit idle across nodes 0 through 7, active allocations (J1 through J15) leave every node partially occupied, blocking a pending 8-GPU job that requires an entire unfragmented node.
ML placement is a multi-dimensional packing problem. Jobs require GPUs together with CPU cores for data preprocessing, host memory for data loading and augmentation pipelines, local SSD storage for dataset caching, and network bandwidth for gradient synchronization. A job requesting 4 GPUs, 32 CPU cores, and 256 GB of RAM may not fit on a node that has 4 free GPUs but only 16 free CPU cores because other jobs have consumed the host CPU for preprocessing. The scheduler must simultaneously satisfy all resource dimensions, and the job fits only if every dimension has sufficient capacity on the selected node. A bottleneck in any one dimension can therefore strand capacity in the others.
Locality constraints further restrict placement beyond simple resource availability. A training job may require tensor-parallel groups to remain within NVLink-connected nodes when its communication budget cannot tolerate the lower per-endpoint bandwidth of the external fabric (450 GB/s per direction intra-node vs. 50 GB/s per port inter-node). On this topology, where NVLink does not connect the nodes, a job requesting “4 GPUs with NVLink connectivity” cannot use 2 GPUs from node A and 2 from node B, even if all 4 GPUs are individually available and the total capacity is sufficient. These topology constraints turn resource counts into a placement problem where which specific resources are available matters as much as how many. A capacity-feasible packing must also pass the job’s locality constraints.
Schedulers address fragmentation through several complementary strategies, each targeting a different aspect of the problem. The first, backfill, lets smaller jobs run in the gaps while a large job waits for contiguous resources; section 8.5.3 develops it together with the reservation it must protect and the runtime estimates it depends on.
Periodic defragmentation migrates or preempts low-priority jobs to consolidate free resources into contiguous blocks, analogous to memory compaction in operating systems. The scheduler identifies nodes where partial allocations leave stranded resources, preempts the jobs occupying those resources, and re-schedules them on nodes where they can be packed more efficiently. The cost includes state transfer and restart, plus replay of work not captured by a valid checkpoint. A graceful checkpoint can preserve recent progress, but still takes time and storage bandwidth. The scheduler must weigh these costs against the benefit of starting large jobs sooner. Low-demand periods reduce the number of competing jobs affected by the move.
A third strategy, over-subscription, admits more demand than a capacity dimension can sustain simultaneously, but only where the resource is divisible and the scheduler can bound interference. Average activity of a GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs), its compute units, does not create fractional whole GPUs. A job that reserves device memory, requires an exclusive CUDA context, or belongs to a rigid gang still occupies its assigned device while kernels are idle. Statistical multiplexing can be safe for explicitly shareable CPU, network, storage, or partitioned GPU capacity when tenants have measured, weakly correlated peaks and enforceable limits. It is unsafe to convert 70 percent average GPU utilization into a 1.4\(\times\) device overcommit ratio. Whole-device capacity should instead be recovered through preemption, elastic resizing, or an isolation mechanism such as Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) hardware partitioning or NVIDIA’s Multi-Process Service (MPS), which lets several processes’ kernels share one device, provided the scheduler models each mechanism’s memory, compute, and fault-sharing contract explicitly. Both reappear with the serving workloads they suit best in section 8.11.1.

Partial allocation of rigid multi-GPU jobs creates a distributed scheduling failure mode in which two jobs each hold half the resources they need and block each other indefinitely while every allocated GPU sits idle. In the left panel of figure 3, jobs J1 and J2 each hold 4 of the 8 GPUs they require, and the whole pool stalls. Atomic gang scheduling (right panel) instead grants J1 all 8 GPUs as one allocation while J2 waits without holding any, which prevents this allocation deadlock.






Figure 3: The distributed deadlock (hold and wait): In a non-gang scheduler (left), job J1 acquires half the cluster and waits for the rest, while job J2 acquires the other half and waits for J1 to release its GPUs. Neither can proceed, and 100 percent of the cluster sits idle. Gang scheduling (right) solves this by mandating atomic allocation: a job is either granted its entire \(\DeviceCount\)-GPU requirement simultaneously or it waits in the queue without holding any resources.




Definition 8.1: Gang scheduling
Gang scheduling is the ML cluster scheduling policy that atomically allocates the resources required by a job’s minimum viable execution group, so a rigid group either receives its complete allocation or waits without retaining a partial one.

Significance: A rigid synchronous job configured for 1,024 GPUs but holding only 512 GPUs completes zero training steps, not half as many: each collective stalls until every rank in its communication group arrives, so the held GPUs consume power and capital at zero useful output. Without atomic allocation, two such jobs can each acquire half the cluster and deadlock, both at zero progress while consuming the full cluster’s operating cost.
Distinction: Unlike a malleable service or parallel job that can make progress across a resource range, rigid synchronous training has step-function utility: the minimum viable gang or nothing. The distinction is a property of the execution graph, not of whether the workload is labeled ML, cloud, or HPC.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that priorities or quotas alone solve this. Atomicity must extend to every co-scheduled resource the job needs to make progress (accelerators, high-bandwidth interconnect domains, network capacity for collectives); enforcing it at GPU granularity alone recreates the deadlock one resource layer down.



The partial-allocation pattern is a hold-and-wait deadlock5 in which two jobs each hold half the cluster and neither can proceed. Its price is the whole allocation for as long as the cycle persists. At the scale of the chapter’s reference workload, two 1,024-GPU gangs that have each acquired 900 GPUs from a pool too small to complete either one burn about $1,800 per hour apiece. The limiting case is two jobs that each request the entire cluster, the example OpenAI used to motivate group admission (war story 8.1). On the 10,000-GPU cluster, a deadlock that strands every device wastes $20,000 per hour at the chapter’s rate while producing no progress for either job. Measured against the stake computed at the start of the chapter, raising utilization from 50 percent to 80 percent recovers about $144,000 per day in equivalent capacity value, so about 7 hours of such a deadlock erase a full day of that gain. Gang scheduling does not create the gain, but it protects it. For a rigid job \(\RigidGangJob\) requiring \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs, the scheduler must grant all \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs atomically or leave the job queued without a partial allocation. This removes hold-and-wait for the resources covered by that allocation; it does not prevent later deadlocks in application code or auxiliary resources. Implementing atomic admission efficiently remains a central challenge in cluster scheduling algorithm design.
5 Hold-and-wait: One of the four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait), all of which must hold for deadlock to occur (Coffman et al. 1971). Gang scheduling removes hold-and-wait through atomic allocation, which is why it prevents this deadlock by construction; the price is reduced packing flexibility.

Lifka, David A. 1995. “The ANL/IBM SP Scheduling System.” In Job Scheduling Strategies for Parallel Processing, edited by Dror G. Feitelson and Larry Rudolph, vol. 949. Lecture Notes in Computer Science. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-60153-8_35.
Naive gang scheduling is wasteful in predictable ways. Atomic allocation means the waiting job holds nothing, yet a large gang will never assemble if every freed GPU goes to a smaller job. The scheduler therefore places a reservation for the job at the head of the queue, draining capacity toward it by declining to start new work on GPUs that the gang will need. If the cluster has 900 free GPUs and that job requests 1,024, the reservation keeps the 900 GPUs idle until 124 more become available, potentially wasting thousands of GPU-hours. Backfill scheduling addresses this by identifying jobs in the queue that can fit within the 900 available GPUs without delaying the large job’s expected start time, an idea popularized in the ANL/IBM SP scheduling system (Lifka 1995). A 128-GPU job with an estimated runtime of 2 hours is a backfill candidate if the 124 additional GPUs needed by the large job will remain unavailable for at least 2 hours. Protecting the reservation requires an enforced runtime bound or a preemption contract that releases the backfill allocation in time, including any checkpoint and cleanup delay. The estimate identifies an opportunity; the release contract makes the reservation enforceable.
The accuracy of runtime estimates determines backfill effectiveness, and this creates a game-theoretic challenge. If users overestimate runtimes, fewer jobs appear to fit a backfill window. If they underestimate, the scheduler may need to preempt a backfilled job to honor the reservation, paying recovery costs and losing unsaved progress. A policy that kills jobs at their declared limit encourages conservative estimates. Tiresias (Gu et al. 2019), discussed in section 8.10.1, avoids duration estimates when setting priority by using observed resource consumption. That choice addresses ordering under uncertainty, while reservation protection still needs an enforced runtime bound or release contract that says when a backfilled job will give its capacity back.
Gang scheduling removes the hold-and-wait deadlock, but another waiting pattern remains. Priority inversion can still strand reserved GPUs behind jobs that cannot finish their own exit path.



Priority inversion is a wait-for chain, not a root-failure tree.



Gang scheduling eliminates the hold-and-wait condition for the atomically allocated bundle, but it does not immunize the cluster against all forms of resource contention. Later requests for auxiliary resources can still create a cycle of dependencies. Priority rules can also prevent a resource holder from making progress without creating a cycle. Distinguishing these cases matters because breaking a deadlock and providing a starved job with enough resources to exit require different interventions.
Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority job waits on a low-priority resource holder whose progress other work delays. Consider the 64-GPU fine-tuning run of the 175B-parameter model, submitted at high priority. The scheduler has reserved 60 available GPUs, but the remaining 4 are held by a low-priority data processing job. Normally, the scheduler would preempt the low-priority job to satisfy the high-priority request. However, if a stream of medium-priority development jobs saturates the cluster’s CPU or network bandwidth, starving the low-priority job of the resources it needs to checkpoint and exit, the low-priority job stalls. Its graceful release path cannot complete. The high-priority job waits for the low-priority job, which is effectively blocked by the medium-priority jobs. The 60-GPU idle block persists until the exit path receives resources or an enforced termination policy reclaims the remaining GPUs, potentially losing uncheckpointed work.



Priority inversion: the high-priority job waits on a low-priority holder that medium-priority work starves.

Definition 8.2: Priority inversion
Priority inversion is an ML cluster scheduling pathology in which a high-priority task is forced to wait for a lower-priority task to release a shared resource.

Significance: It ties the progress of a high-priority job, and the accelerators reserved for it, to the progress of the lowest-priority job in the wait-for chain. In ML clusters, this typically occurs when a low-priority job holding GPUs is starved of auxiliary resources (for example, bandwidth for checkpointing), preventing it from finishing and releasing the accelerators needed by high-priority workloads.
Distinction: Unlike standard queuing (where tasks wait their turn), priority inversion involves an active blockage: the high-priority task is ready to run but is transitively dependent on a task that the scheduler does not prioritize.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that strict priority levels solve this. Raising the waiting job’s priority does not supply the CPU or bandwidth that its lower-priority resource holder needs to exit; the preemption policy must protect that release path.



Prevention and detection address different parts of this problem. Atomic allocation prevents hold-and-wait for the resources included in the gang, while reserving checkpoint bandwidth allows a preempted job to complete its exit path. Timeouts instead bound how long the system waits before investigating or reclaiming an allocation; they do not prevent deadlock states from arising. Monitoring can trigger recovery when progress stops, but safe reclamation still requires enforcing the new ownership decision.
Detection, unlike exact placement search, is computationally cheap. Before feasibility filtering, a cluster with 10,000 GPUs and 500 pending jobs can have more than \(10^{15}\) candidate allocations, which puts exhaustive allocation search out of reach. Detection instead works on a wait-for graph, a directed graph with one vertex per job and an edge from job A to job B whenever A waits for a resource that B holds. A cycle identifies a potential deadlock. It establishes deadlock when every edge is an unavoidable blocking dependency and no alternative resource allocation can let a member proceed. Finding a cycle in an already constructed graph takes time linear in its vertices and edges. The difficulty lies in construction. Resource state changes continuously across a distributed control plane, so the scheduler rarely holds a complete, current graph, and a cycle detected on stale state may already have resolved while a real one goes unseen.
Large-scale schedulers therefore supplement wait-for detection with mechanisms that preserve liveness under incomplete state. A lease-based resource gives every allocation a time-to-live; expiry authorizes reclamation only when the resource manager enforces revocation and cleanup before reuse. Progress monitoring checks advancement through signals such as completed-step counters, using GPU utilization and heartbeats as supporting observations rather than proof of useful work. When the scheduler must preempt a lower-priority job, holistic preemption reserves the CPU, network, and storage bandwidth needed for that job to checkpoint and exit cleanly; otherwise, the victim can be too starved to release the accelerators. False failure suspicions can cost useful work, but must not bypass the ownership checks required for safe recovery.



The homogeneous case uses a bulk synchronous parallel workload with \(\DeviceCount\) workers executing the same compute graph, but atomic allocation does not require identical workers. Some training workflows contain several roles with different resource profiles. In preference-training pipelines such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), for example, one component may update the policy while another scores outputs or supplies reference behavior. The scheduler still sees one job, but the gang contains trainers, evaluators, and inference-style workers that need different GPU counts, memory footprints, and lifetimes.

Systems Perspective 8.1: Routing over synchronyHeterogeneous gang scheduling extends atomic allocation to the roles that must coexist for a workflow to progress. A viable group might pair high-HBM nodes for memory-bound generation with compute-oriented nodes for policy updates. The orchestration problem then shifts from packing a homogeneous ring toward routing data: rather than reducing gradients among identical workers, the job streams rollouts from generation workers to the workers that compute policy updates, so placement must also support the data exchanged between those roles. Rollout and training stages may exchange work in batches or through a buffered pipeline; their measured production and consumption rates determine where queues grow or accelerators wait. The scheduler needs a minimum viable resource bundle and a supported scaling policy for each role, rather than an assumption that all workers are interchangeable or perfectly balanced.


Homogeneous and heterogeneous jobs share an allocation requirement: the scheduler must assemble a viable group before expecting progress. Backfill can use capacity while that group waits, provided runtime estimates or preemption contracts protect the reservation. Enforcing these policies requires a control plane that represents ownership and reconciles allocations after failures.




A pending gang and a queue of small backfill jobs need both a policy for sharing capacity and a control plane that can enforce it. The policies just developed apply across platforms; the orchestration paradigm determines how the platform represents allocations and recovers when observed state diverges from them. Slurm, shaped by HPC batch systems, favors explicit resource requests and predictable allocation. Kubernetes, shaped by cloud-native service management, favors declared desired state and continuous reconciliation. The choice is therefore not Slurm vs. Kubernetes as products; it is which control model best matches the workload mix, failure behavior, and operational culture of the fleet.
The control-plane architectures in figure 4 contrast two control models. Slurm follows an imperative batch model: the user states the resources a job needs, and the central slurmctld dispatches that allocation through per-node slurmd daemons. Kubernetes follows a declarative model: the user states what should be running, and controllers reconcile observed state toward that declaration through the API server and node agents. Both platforms accept explicit resource requirements and track execution state, so the useful distinction is which lifecycle the platform manages directly: an allocated batch job or a collection of workloads maintained by controllers. That distinction shapes how ML workloads are admitted, monitored, and recovered from failure, and distributed training still needs framework-level coordination under either model.






Figure 4: Architectural paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes: Slurm (left) uses an imperative batch model where users submit explicit resource requests to a centralized controller (slurmctld) providing deterministic atomic allocation. Kubernetes (right) uses a declarative service model where controllers continuously reconcile observed cluster state in etcd against desired state specifications.





The Slurm Workload Manager6 originated at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory as a scalable, fault-tolerant resource manager for Linux clusters (Yoo et al. 2003). Its batch-oriented design fits the distinctive requirements of scientific computing: long-running jobs, expensive shared hardware, and users who can specify resource needs in advance. In ML infrastructure, the same model maps to GPU training through partitions for heterogeneous accelerator pools and predictable allocations for long-running distributed jobs.
6 Slurm Workload Manager: Originally “SLURM,” an acronym for Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management, the project dropped the acronym capitalization in 2012. Developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory beginning in 2002, Slurm’s centralized controller (slurmctld) maintains a single authoritative view of resource allocations. At very large scale, operators may partition fleets or federate schedulers to keep scheduling latency, policy isolation, and failure domains manageable.
Yoo, A. B., M. A. Jette, and M. Grondona. 2003. “SLURM: Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management.” In Job Scheduling Strategies for Parallel Processing. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/10968987_3.
Slurm’s batch submission model makes resource requirements explicit. Users submit job scripts, and the scheduler allocates resources within eligible partitions according to policy and availability. A submission of sbatch --gres=gpu:8 --nodes=4 requests 8 GPUs on each of 4 nodes, a 32-GPU allocation. The request supplies a capacity contract, but useful execution still depends on the selected hardware and the application’s launch configuration. Overstating requirements strands resources; understating them can cause memory failures or poor performance.
Slurm’s architecture consists of a central controller daemon (slurmctld) that maintains the global view of cluster state and makes scheduling decisions, and per-node daemons (slurmd) that manage local resources and execute jobs. This centralized architecture provides the authoritative allocation model discussed in section 8.2: the controller is the source of truth for resource assignments, reducing the risk of conflicting allocations. The cost is a potential single point of failure (addressed through active-passive failover) and a scheduling-throughput limit. As fleets grow, organizations may partition the cluster or federate schedulers to bound scheduling latency and failure impact.

Within a partition, a request specifies both the number of GPUs a job needs and the allocation shape: how those GPUs are distributed across nodes. In Slurm, --gres=gpu:N or --gpus-per-node=N requests a per-node count, while --gpus=N requests a job-wide total. Whether the scheduler may split a node between jobs is a separate consumable-resource policy (Slurm’s select/cons_tres plugin), and a node-exclusive policy strands the unused devices in the six-on-eight example of section 8.5.2. Shape decides communication. In an eight-GPU-per-node pool, a 16-GPU request that also fixes eight GPUs per node (--gpus-per-node=8) yields two fully populated nodes, whose NVLink domains follow from the node hardware rather than the count. A request for 16 GPUs with no per-node constraint gives the scheduler more freedom, so it can start sooner on partially occupied nodes, but it may spread the group across several of them. Whether that flexibility is useful depends on the parallelism configuration and its communication budget. Tensor-parallel groups with frequent exchanges may justify compact placement, while data-parallel groups with well-overlapped communication may tolerate a wider allocation.
The fair-share scheduling mechanism uses past consumption to influence future priority under contention. An illustrative heuristic combines base priority, the user’s target fair share (\(\TargetFairShare\)), recent actual consumption (\(\RecentUsageShare\)), and a small stabilizing constant (\(\FairShareStabilizingConstant\)); it illustrates the feedback without reproducing Slurm’s multifactor priority calculation:
\[\text{Priority}_{\text{effective}} = \text{Priority}_{\text{base}} \times \frac{\TargetFairShare}{\RecentUsageShare+ \FairShareStabilizingConstant} \tag{1}\]
With base priority and target share fixed, equation 1 lowers priority as recent consumption increases. Doubling consumption approximately halves this illustrative priority when the stabilizing constant is negligible. Actual admission also depends on other priority factors and feasible resources; low recent usage does not guarantee an immediate start.
The time decay of usage history determines how quickly the system “forgives” past heavy usage. A half-life of one week means that a researcher’s heavy usage from two weeks ago contributes only 25 percent to their current usage calculation. Short half-lives make the policy more responsive to recent changes but can encourage alternating bursts of usage. Long half-lives retain the effect of a completed large project when its researchers return with smaller jobs. The useful decay window depends on the fleet’s job durations and the period over which the organization intends to balance access.
Preemption policies enable high-priority jobs to reclaim resources from running workloads, and for ML training the reclaim must leave time to save state. Slurm expresses that time as a grace period. It signals the selected job (SIGTERM), waits the configured GraceTime, and only then kills it (SIGKILL); under PreemptMode=REQUEUE it can also requeue an eligible job to run again later. Neither the signal nor the requeue saves model state. The application must handle the signal, publish a valid checkpoint within the grace period, and restore it on restart. If termination precedes completion of that save, recovery uses the last valid checkpoint and replays subsequent work.


↩︎ Checkpointing for progress preservation, including the checkpoint interval and coordination patterns, is established in Checkpointing and Progress Preservation.
Preemption improves access for high-priority work but can reduce overall useful throughput. Forced termination loses progress after the last valid checkpoint and adds restart and reload time. A graceful preemption can save that progress, but still incurs checkpoint and transition overhead. If checkpoint intervals are long (for example, hourly) and forced preemptions are frequent, replay can dominate the cost. A cooldown policy can limit repeated interruption, at the expense of delaying later high-priority requests.
Slurm’s strengths for ML training include explicit batch allocations, configurable fair-share policies, and integration with MPI-based distributed training frameworks. A mixed training-serving fleet also needs a service lifecycle that maintains ready replicas as demand and failures change. Inside a batch scheduler, adding or removing an inference replica means submitting or canceling a job, a far heavier operation than a controller adjusting a replica count, and a failed replica stays down until something resubmits it. Operators must integrate replica health, replacement, and demand-driven scaling with the batch scheduler, or assign those responsibilities to a service orchestration platform.



Once Slurm owns batch training, the remaining question is how much ML semantics the batch system can see. Standard partitions and fair-share policies schedule ordinary jobs; large-scale deep learning needs configuration that exposes sweep structure, asymmetric pipeline resources, hardware health at job boundaries, and the economic weight of different accelerator types.
A hyperparameter sweep is the opposite of a gang. Job arrays submit many trials as one record (for example, --array=0-99), and each trial reads its index from the SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID environment variable to select its configuration. Slurm schedules the elements independently, so individual trials become ideal backfill candidates that fill small gaps in capacity, while the array keeps submission and management overhead low without making the trials one indivisible gang.
Heterogeneous jobs carry the heterogeneous gang of section 8.5.5 into a batch allocation. One job can contain components with distinct resource requests, admitted together. The 64-GPU fine-tuning run of the 175B model, for example, could request 8 GPU nodes for training and 2 CPU-only nodes for on-the-fly tokenization as a single allocation, then launch training on the GPU component and data workers on the CPU component (srun --het-group=0 and --het-group=1). This separation helps only if the data workers and transfer path sustain the training stage’s consumption rate; a heterogeneous allocation exposes that choice but does not itself balance the pipeline.
Prolog and epilog scripts turn job boundaries into admission health checks. A prolog runs on each allocated node before launch and can check reported topology (nvidia-smi topo -m), ECC counters, and InfiniBand link status. A node that fails is drained and the job requeued elsewhere, preventing launch on hardware that failed those checks. An epilog can remove job-owned orphan processes and shared-memory segments (/dev/shm) and record final utilization. These checks reduce exposure to known faults; they do not establish delivered bandwidth or exclude all silent corruption. For the 64-GPU fine-tuning run, testing peer-to-peer throughput across the intended eight-GPU groups would provide evidence beyond the reported topology alone.
Finally, trackable resources (TRES) let accounting distinguish resource classes rather than count only CPU time. Configured billing weights can charge different amounts for different accelerators and feed that weighted usage into fair-share policy. The weights express an administrative valuation; they track economic cost only to the extent that the chosen values reflect it. Resource accounting and physical capacity enforcement remain separate responsibilities.
These extensions make Slurm more ML-aware while preserving its batch-scheduler model. Kubernetes starts from a different contract: users declare the desired state of services and jobs, and controllers continuously reconcile the cluster toward that state.



Kubernetes is a common platform for ML infrastructure, particularly for organizations requiring unified management of training and serving workloads (Burns et al. 2016; Cloud Native Computing Foundation 2024). Its declarative model expresses a workload’s desired state and uses control loops to reconcile observations with that state. The unit it places is the pod, one or more containers that share a node and a network identity, and its default scheduler places pods one at a time. The name collides with the hardware pod of The Pod, the many racks joined under one fabric. A Kubernetes pod is a software unit that never spans more than one node, so a 64-pod training job is 64 container groups placed onto nodes, all of which can sit inside one hardware pod. Controllers above the scheduler give groups of pods a purpose: a Deployment keeps a set number of identical replica pods running, while a Job runs pods until they complete, retrying failures under a stated policy. The workload controller therefore determines what completion, replacement, or continued availability means.

Failure handling reveals the importance of the workload contract. Slurm can detect node failures and requeue eligible jobs when configured to do so. Kubernetes controllers maintain workload-specific goals, such as a Deployment’s replica count or a Job’s completion and retry policy. A replacement pod still has to be placed, become ready, and rejoin the distributed training run before progress resumes. Training operators can coordinate worker creation, while the framework remains responsible for valid state and group recovery. Both platforms therefore require an explicit agreement between allocation, process lifecycle, and application recovery.
Kubernetes’ control loop architecture uses the controller pattern:7 controllers observe and update API objects through the API server, which persists cluster state in etcd, a replicated key-value store. Those objects contain desired state and reported observations, not instantaneous physical truth. The pattern repeats at every level: the Deployment controller reconciles the number of pod replicas, the scheduler binds pending pods to nodes, the kubelet (the agent on each node) keeps its assigned containers running, and the node controller marks nodes that stop reporting. Each component acts independently and communicates only through API objects, which makes the system resilient to the failure of any single controller. The price of that independence is that their interactions require clear ownership and retry behavior, particularly when a failed node’s last reported state no longer describes its execution.
7 Controller Pattern (Reconciliation Loop): A “level-triggered” design reconciles the current desired and observed states rather than depending on every intermediate event. A restarted controller can resume from durable state if its actions tolerate retries and its observations expose unfinished work. Multiple controllers still need distinct responsibilities so that one controller’s correction does not repeatedly undo another’s.Kubernetes needs an explicit resource representation before it can place GPU workloads. In the device-plugin model, device plugins expose accelerators as schedulable extended resources. The NVIDIA device plugin registers GPUs with the kubelet, enabling pod specifications that request GPU resources declaratively through the standard Kubernetes resource model. When the device plugin exposes exclusive whole GPUs, a small model serving occasional requests can reserve a device while using only a fraction of its compute and memory capacity. Whole-device allocation suits workloads that need the capacity or isolation, but can strand resources for smaller workloads. The resource unit exposed by the plugin therefore matters: sharing or partitioning changes what the scheduler can allocate and what isolation each allocation receives.
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)8 technology addresses this inefficiency by partitioning A100 (80 GB) and H100 (80 GB) GPUs into hardware-isolated instances. Unlike software-based GPU sharing, such as time-slicing that context-switches several processes over one whole device, MIG dedicates memory, cache, and compute resources to each instance, reducing interference through those partitioned resources and limiting the noisy neighbor9 effect. The A100 MIG profiles in table 3 show the scheduling consequence: a single physical A100 becomes several fixed-size resources that the device plugin can expose as independently schedulable accelerators.
8 Multi-Instance GPU (MIG): Introduced with the A100 (2020), MIG partitions a single GPU into up to 7 hardware-isolated instances with dedicated memory controllers, L2 cache slices, and compute units (NVIDIA Corporation 2020). The isolation is enforced at the hardware level, not by time-slicing, reducing noisy-neighbor interference relative to software-only sharing. Changing the partition layout requires stopping affected GPU workloads; the scheduler must include that disruption when adapting profiles to a changing workload mix.

9 Noisy Neighbor: In GPU clusters, interference arises when one job’s bursty network traffic or memory bus utilization slows down a co-located job on the same node. In synchronous training, a delayed flow can extend collective completion when it lies on the communication critical path, propagating one tenant’s interference across a worker group.

Kubernetes’ default scheduler places pods independently, so it does not supply the group admission that section 8.5.3 requires. Under that default, a 64-pod training job receives 64 separate placement decisions, with no guarantee that all will succeed. If the cluster has resources for 60 pods but not 64, those 60 can occupy capacity while the remaining 4 wait. The platform must therefore configure a group-level admission and placement contract for a rigid job. PodGroup-style abstractions give that contract a unit matching the job’s minimum viable execution group rather than an individual pod.
The mechanism that closes this gap is group admission. A PodGroup declares a group’s minimum runnable membership. The scheduler tentatively reserves a placement for each member as it finds one but binds none of them to nodes until the minimum membership is placed, and it releases every reservation if the attempt fails or times out. Admission and placement thereby become two decisions, with the group admitted only when placement has succeeded for enough of it. The Volcano10 batch scheduler and the Coscheduling scheduler plugin both implement this pattern. Group admission does not make physical launches simultaneous; nodes can still fail or start at different times, so the framework must establish the communication group before training proceeds.
10 Volcano: Volcano provides a scheduler with batch and gang-scheduling mechanisms. Pods select it through their scheduler name, so it can coexist with Kubernetes’ default scheduler. The operational contract must account for interactions between schedulers sharing the same nodes; installing Volcano does not automatically transfer every workload’s scheduling to it.
War Story 8.1: OpenAI's gang-scheduling example (2021)Context: OpenAI scaled Kubernetes clusters to 7,500 nodes for workloads including GPT-3, CLIP, and DALL-E. Its account explains that MPI-coordinated optimizer groups needed all members scheduled before training could progress (Sigler 2021).
Mechanism: The account illustrates the risk with two experiments each requesting the entire cluster. Incremental pod placement could allocate half the capacity to each, leaving neither with a complete group.
Impact: In that example, both jobs hold capacity without making progress. It demonstrates the deadlock mechanism rather than documenting a particular pair of stalled production runs.
Fix: OpenAI reports adopting the coscheduling plugin to add group-aware admission to the Kubernetes scheduler.
Systems lesson: Distributed ML scheduling must encode the job’s execution semantics. For MPI-style training, “some pods scheduled” is not partial progress; it is wasted allocation. Production schedulers need gang scheduling, quota controls, and workload-aware policies rather than generic pod placement alone.


Priority classes control scheduling precedence and preemption eligibility. A fleet might give inference higher priority than training to help protect serving service-level objectives (SLOs), but priority cannot replace ready capacity during a demand spike. With preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority, a pending pod can displace lower-priority pods when their removal makes placement feasible. With preemptionPolicy: Never, it retains queue precedence without initiating preemption and remains subject to higher-priority preemption. Termination, cleanup, and replacement startup take time. Training applications also need a checkpoint-aware shutdown path that fits the allowed grace period; assigning priorities does not create that path. The policy must balance serving readiness against repeated interruption of training.
Kueue11 makes admission a separate control decision. It manages when workloads may consume quota, while a compatible scheduler binds their pods to nodes. The admission policy and placement policy must agree on resource types, group requirements, and topology. Separating these responsibilities lets each layer run its own policy, at the price of keeping the two consistent.
11 Kueue: Kueue separates workload admission from pod placement. Its all-or-nothing mechanisms include waiting for admitted pods to become ready and requeuing workloads that exceed the configured timeout. Aggregate quota admission alone does not prove that a gang fits the physical topology; the guarantee depends on the configured readiness, topology, and placement mechanisms.Kueue represents each team or project as a queue with a configured quota (a ClusterQueue) and groups queues into cohorts whose members may lend one another unused quota and reclaim it according to preemption policy. A research queue might borrow production capacity off peak, but returning quota is only part of restoring service capacity. Borrowed work must release its resources, and the production workload must obtain a feasible placement and become ready. The reclaim policy must account for that delay rather than treating a quota transfer as instantaneous recovery.



Group admission handles one constraint that microservice orchestration leaves implicit and distributed training cannot. Four more remain. Workers must launch knowing their peers, collective traffic must avoid network layers built for request traffic, checkpoint writes need bandwidth rather than only storage capacity, and progress must be observable below the container. Operators and plugins add each constraint to the platform; the mechanism matters more than the product that happens to implement it.
Peer discovery is the job of the training operator ecosystem, which extends Kubernetes with job-specific resource types (custom resource definitions). In the Kubeflow Training Operator, a PyTorchJob declares the number of workers, the container image, and resource requirements; the operator creates the pods and injects the rendezvous address (MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT), the group size, and each worker’s rank (WORLD_SIZE and RANK), which the framework uses to form its communication group. If a worker pod fails, the operator can detect the deviation and create a replacement pod to restore the desired replica count, but training-state recovery still depends on the framework’s checkpoint and rendezvous logic.
Collective traffic is the second constraint. The pod overlay network that the Container Network Interface (CNI) configures, designed for microservice requests, routes packets through software switching on the host CPU, which adds latency and caps bandwidth when it sits on the critical gradient-synchronization path. For bandwidth-sensitive training, host networking (hostNetwork: true) places pods in the host’s network namespace, bypassing the ordinary pod overlay path. It does not itself allocate remote direct memory access (RDMA) devices or grant permission to use them; device exposure, resource requests, drivers, and access controls require separate configuration. Operators such as NVIDIA’s Network Operator automate that exposure through RDMA device plugins and GPUDirect RDMA configuration, letting containerized workloads approach bare-metal interconnect performance once the rest of the stack is configured.
Checkpoint bandwidth is the third constraint, because storage integration must account for the checkpoint storm of definition \(\ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}\), in which many workers write large amounts of state together. Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) request capacity on a configured storage system but do not reserve checkpoint throughput. A 1,024-GPU training job writing the 2.45 TB resumable checkpoint of the 175B model needs a measured write budget shared with other workloads. Backend bandwidth controls, client throttling, or staggered writes can limit interference; the platform must verify which controls the storage implementation enforces.
Visibility into progress is the fourth. The observability stack for training clusters combines general-purpose cluster monitoring with specialized hardware telemetry. Prometheus and Grafana provide the collection and visualization layer, while the Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) exporter exposes granular GPU metrics: utilization, memory bandwidth, temperature, and ECC errors. These observations locate symptoms; correlating them with step progress, input waits, and communication traces distinguishes useful computation from stalls. Identifying which dependency limits a training job takes that correlation, not a utilization dashboard.
The 1,024-GPU pretraining run for our 175B model illustrates how these responsibilities fit together. One possible deployment defines a PyTorchJob with 128 worker pods, each requesting 8 GPUs. Host networking removes the pod overlay from the gradient path, and the Network Operator exposes each node’s InfiniBand adapters to the workers through RDMA device plugins. A PVC backed by Lustre provides access to the 6 TB tokenized training corpus and a checkpoint path whose sustained bandwidth must be validated. DCGM metrics stream to Prometheus, supporting alerts on uncorrectable ECC errors and deviations from workload-specific communication baselines.



Selecting a control plane requires matching its allocation and recovery contract to the workload mix. Rigid training groups need reliable atomic placement and checkpoint-aware interruption; serving replicas need readiness checks and continuous recovery. Existing operational expertise and the cost of running a second control plane also shape the choice. A fleet dedicated to long, homogeneous training runs that use bare-metal collectives, operated by a team fluent in batch scheduling, gains most from Slurm’s authoritative allocation and mature fair-share. A fleet that mixes training with always-on serving, and already runs cloud-native deployment and observability tooling, gains more from Kubernetes with a gang-admission layer added for its rigid jobs. The comparison that follows separates those requirements before the hybrid designs show how to divide ownership between systems.
The Slurm vs. Kubernetes trade-off organizes around the dimensions most relevant to ML workloads (table 4).

The gang-scheduling row of the table compresses a naming collision that is easy to miss. This chapter uses gang scheduling for atomic allocation of a whole execution group, which is the requirement distributed training imposes. Slurm reserves the name for the older, Ousterhout-style meaning of the term, in which co-scheduled jobs share nodes by time-slicing in synchronized rounds. Slurm provides atomic multi-node allocation under its ordinary job model, so the requirement is met even though Slurm’s “gang scheduling” option means something else.
The choice of scheduling paradigm also reflects organizational trajectory. Teams starting with HPC-focused training infrastructure may begin with Slurm and add Kubernetes for serving. Teams starting from cloud-native application infrastructure may begin with Kubernetes and add HPC-oriented extensions (Volcano, Kueue) for training. Either path can reach a functional hybrid architecture, but the starting point determines which capabilities are strongest and which require the most investment to develop.



While the choice between Slurm and Kubernetes often appears binary, engineering organizations can deploy hybrid architectures that use the strengths of both systems. The relevant boundary again follows workload semantics rather than labels. Rigid, topology-sensitive jobs fit a batch scheduler’s atomic allocation contract, while malleable services fit a reconciliation loop that adjusts replica count continuously. Some training jobs are elastic, and some serving replicas are rigid multi-accelerator gangs, so neither “training” nor “serving” selects a control plane by itself.
The Kubernetes-over-Slurm pattern wraps the HPC scheduler within a cloud-native control plane. Kubernetes manages the lifecycle of training jobs through custom operators while delegating batch admission and placement to Slurm. The central engineering problem is ownership: exactly one control plane must authorize each placement, while the outer controller reconciles lifecycle state without issuing a conflicting allocation. The arrangement combines a declarative management surface with Slurm’s batch and topology policies, but it also creates a cross-control-plane failure boundary that operators must fence explicitly.
The Slurm-alongside-Kubernetes pattern takes a coarser-grained approach, maintaining separate clusters for training and serving that draw from a shared pool of physical nodes. A meta-scheduler or capacity broker acts as an arbitrator, dynamically reassigning nodes between the Slurm partition and the Kubernetes cluster based on demand signals. During intensive training campaigns, nodes are drained from Kubernetes and joined to Slurm; during product launches or traffic spikes, the flow reverses. The primary challenge is the mode-switching cost: draining a node, changing its ownership and configuration, and admitting it to the other control plane takes much longer than an ordinary placement decision. This latency limits sharing to planned capacity shifts rather than second-by-second inference bursts.
A shared application runtime such as Ray provides task and actor abstractions for both training and serving. Ray’s placement groups, unlike the cloud network-locality abstraction of the same name, reserve bundles of logical resources for work that must run together, and serving replicas can also require multi-device groups. Inside a shared runtime the workloads keep their different state, latency, and recovery requirements, so the platform must still coordinate Ray’s logical allocations with the underlying resource manager and validate the isolation and recovery behavior needed by each workload.
Threading these patterns together, consider the lifecycle of our 175B parameter model. A hybrid platform can allocate the training gang through Slurm and later place serving replicas through Kubernetes. The orchestration boundary concerns resource ownership: the training job releases its allocation, and the serving control plane admits replicas against its own capacity and readiness requirements. Deciding whether the trained artifact is ready for production requires validation and release policy beyond the scheduler; CI/CD for ML at Scale develops those validation gates and rollout policies.
A hybrid platform is useful when its separate allocation contracts justify the additional ownership and recovery boundary. The cost to measure is the coordination between control planes, including node draining and reassignment, rather than a presumed performance advantage from either product name.

Systems Perspective 8.2: The convergence of HPC and cloudHPC and cloud-native platforms increasingly address overlapping fleet requirements. Kubernetes has acquired queues, priorities, and gang admission through Volcano and Kueue, while Slurm has added a REST interface and container support. Batch admission, service reconciliation, and resource sharing can coexist in one deployment, and each guarantee of the separate systems survives the combination only where one layer clearly owns it. The durable design question is which layer owns each allocation and recovery decision, and how the other layers observe and respect that ownership.


The overlap in capabilities makes the paradigm choice a workload-specific design decision. Teams must establish the allocation and recovery guarantees they need before layering physical placement constraints on top of them.

A scattered allocation can place frequent collective traffic on shared cross-rack paths, exposing latency or bandwidth limits that a more compact allocation avoids. The penalty is set by how much of the job’s traffic crosses those paths and how much capacity the fabric provisions there, not by the rack count itself. The earlier feasibility rules already required compatible topology; topology-aware scheduling makes that requirement explicit in the placement objective, accounting for communication paths as well as raw compute.


Modern GPU clusters exhibit a multi-level communication hierarchy, with different bandwidth and latency budgets across placement domains. This hierarchy is not an implementation detail that the scheduler can ignore; it is a physical constraint that affects training throughput for communication-intensive workloads. Understanding the hierarchy is essential for making placement decisions that translate allocated resources into useful work.
Within a single node, GPUs communicate via NVLink, providing 600 GB/s aggregate bidirectional bandwidth (300 GB/s per direction) per GPU on A100 systems and 900 GB/s (450 GB/s per direction) on H100 systems. This high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnect enables efficient tensor parallelism, where matrix operations are split across GPUs that must exchange intermediate results (activations and gradients) at every transformer layer. Whether these exchanges overlap computation depends on the tensor sizes and execution schedule; high local bandwidth improves the budget but does not guarantee near-ideal scaling.
Between nodes within the same rack or leaf switch domain, communication traverses an external fabric such as InfiniBand or RoCE. An NDR InfiniBand link provides 400 Gb/s, roughly 50 GB/s per direction. Compared per direction, the H100’s NVLink rate is 9× the rate of one such port, the same NVLink-to-InfiniBand cliff as in Bandwidth hierarchy. Delivered job bandwidth also depends on how many ports each node has and how traffic spreads across them. Bucketed data-parallel gradient synchronization can overlap the remaining backward computation, reducing its exposed cost. Frequent tensor-parallel exchanges may be more sensitive to placement even when each exchange is smaller.
Between racks connected through spine switches, communication crosses additional switch hops, introducing both higher latency and potentially reduced effective bandwidth due to network congestion. Fat-tree topologies provide full bisection bandwidth in theory, while concurrent flows, routing inefficiencies, and switch buffer limitations can reduce delivered cross-rack bandwidth. Cross-rack communication also adds tail latency variability: while median latency may be only slightly higher, p99 latency can spike during congestion events, creating straggler effects in synchronous training where the slowest communicator determines the pace for all workers.


↩︎ Bisection bandwidth and fat-tree network topologies are established in Fat-tree (Clos) networks.
A 64-GPU job within one rack can avoid cross-rack paths that a spread allocation must use. It outperforms the spread allocation only when those paths add exposed latency or bandwidth contention; a non-blocking, uncongested spine need not reduce sustained throughput. The performance difference stems directly from the hierarchical communication analysis in Hierarchical AllReduce: a flat ring AllReduce runs at the speed of the slowest link in the ring, and cross-rack hops introduce both higher latency and increased contention risk. For synchronous training, every iteration waits for the slowest worker to complete its AllReduce, so even occasional cross-rack congestion inflates the Fleet Law’s communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) (equation 1.3) on every step it touches.
The scheduler must therefore model the cluster as a hierarchical graph with discrete bandwidth boundaries (figure 5). In the illustrated H100 fleet, per-direction bandwidth steps down from 450 GB/s across the NVSwitch inside a node to 50 GB/s per port under a leaf switch, and to roughly 12.5–25 GB/s per endpoint when balanced traffic saturates an oversubscribed spine. A node boundary can introduce a large bandwidth reduction, but a non-blocking rack or pod boundary need not reduce per-endpoint bandwidth. Oversubscription adds a separate constraint when traffic saturates shared uplinks. Topology-aware placement minimizes the communication cost of the job’s actual traffic pattern rather than applying a fixed penalty to every boundary.






Figure 5: Physical topology hierarchy and bandwidth cliffs: Hardware boundaries dictate communication performance across three distinct domains. The example compares a 450 GB/s per-direction NVLink endpoint budget with a 50 GB/s per-direction external port. Under balanced load saturating a 2:1 to 4:1 oversubscribed spine, the external per-endpoint share falls to approximately 12.5–25 GB/s. A non-blocking spine need not impose this reduction. The bar in each domain’s header draws its bandwidth on one shared linear scale.



For a 4-GPU collective group, the routing paths make that cost concrete (figure 6). In the illustrated contended fabric, scattering ranks across Rack A and Rack B forces a 3-hop leaf-spine-leaf path with about 12.5 GB/s of effective bandwidth per endpoint, a share of contended uplinks rather than a physical link rate. Consolidating all four ranks (G0–G3) under Rack A’s leaf switch avoids those shared uplinks and provides about 50 GB/s per GPU under the example’s load assumptions.

The illustrated 4× bandwidth difference between the 1-hop leaf path and the 3-hop spine route (figure 6) stretches the transfer component by the same factor when transfer time is bandwidth-dominated. Crossing a spine does not impose that ratio independently of load and topology. Whether communication exceeds computation also depends on the model and overlap schedule, and repeated exchanges can amplify the exposed cost. Topology-aware placement algorithms assign jobs to nodes that reduce this cost, turning resource packing into graph optimization over the physical topology. A simple locality cost, defined in equation 2, penalizes allocations spanning multiple topology domains:
\[ \text{Cost}_{\text{locality}} = \sum_{i < j} \LocalityPenaltyFunction(\GpuTopologicalDistance(\AssignedJobGpu_i, \AssignedJobGpu_j))  \tag{2}\]
where \(\AssignedJobGpu_i\) and \(\AssignedJobGpu_j\) are GPUs assigned to the job, \(\GpuTopologicalDistance(\AssignedJobGpu_i, \AssignedJobGpu_j)\) is their topological distance (0 for same node, 1 for same rack, 2 for different racks), and \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(\cdot)\) is a weighting function that increases with distance. The scheduler minimizes this score when selecting an allocation from the set of feasible placements. An illustrative heuristic assigns the following locality penalties: \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(0) = 0\) (same node, NVLink, no penalty), \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(1) = 1\) (same rack, one switch hop), \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(2) = 10\) (different racks, multiple switch hops). These dimensionless weights are policy assumptions, not measured latency or bandwidth ratios. A deployment should calibrate them to its traffic and topology; an unweighted pairwise score also cannot distinguish heavily communicating rank pairs from pairs that rarely exchange data.
More sophisticated algorithms distinguish the communication requirements of different parallelism strategies. Frequent tensor-parallel activation exchanges favor a high-bandwidth, low-latency domain that meets the measured communication budget; that domain need not coincide with one server. Pipeline parallelism exchanges activations across stage boundaries rather than between every layer, but its tolerance for link delay depends on microbatch size and the pipeline schedule. Data-parallel gradient synchronization can overlap computation, making wider placement feasible when the exposed communication remains within budget. These patterns guide placement without establishing a universal ranking for every model or fabric.
Algorithm 1 combines the all-or-nothing gang constraint of section 8.5.3, the locality cost of equation 2, and an illustrative parallelism-to-topology mapping. Its enumeration expresses the decision conceptually: construct feasible rank mappings, score their allocations, and choose the lowest illustrative locality score, leaving the job queued when none fits. This surrogate does not guarantee minimum communication time or completion time. A fleet-scale implementation must restrict that search using heuristics rather than enumerate every allocation.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Topology-aware placement}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require job requesting $N$ accelerators with tensor-, pipeline-, and data-parallel groups; cluster topology with illustrative per-level locality weights $w(\cdot)$
\Ensure an all-or-nothing feasible placement with the lowest illustrative locality score, or the job stays queued
\State enumerate candidate slots: sets of $N$ free accelerators that satisfy every resource dimension \Comment{gang: all or nothing}
\State retain only slots that admit a rank mapping satisfying the job's tensor-, pipeline-, and data-parallel communication constraints
\If{no feasible slot exists}
    \State leave the job queued without holding any accelerators \Comment{prevents hold-and-wait deadlock}
    \State \Return no placement
\EndIf
\For{each feasible slot}
    \State use a feasible rank mapping: tensor-parallel ranks within an NVLink domain, pipeline stages within a rack, data-parallel replicas across racks where permitted
    \State score the slot by $\text{Cost}_{\text{locality}} = \sum_{i < j} w(d(g_i, g_j))$
\EndFor
\State \Return the feasible slot of least $\text{Cost}_{\text{locality}}$ \Comment{minimum score among enumerated feasible placements; atomic allocation}
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

Applied to a whole job, the same reasoning ranks placement strategies. The latencies in this comparison are illustrative, not derived. They are constructed to stay above the ring-AllReduce bandwidth bound for the payload, and they show the order in which placement removes delay rather than values a reader could recompute from topology names. For a 0.5 GB gradient synchronization on 64 GPUs, random placement spans multiple racks and spine switches and takes an assumed 120 ms. Each successive strategy removes a source of delay that the previous one leaves. Confining the group to a single rack removes spine hops and reduces latency to 85 ms. Rail-optimized alignment maps ranks so that every member of each collective group sits at the same local GPU index and therefore on the same network rail (developed in section 8.7.3). Traffic that previously hopped between rails through the spine now stays within one rail’s switches, which cuts latency to 40 ms. Topology-optimal placement additionally avoids leaf ports that other jobs are using and reaches 25 ms, a 4.8× reduction (figure 7, where each bar also carries its algorithm throughput). This ratio compares whole collectives under four assumed placements, so it need not match the link-bandwidth ratio of the two-rack paths above.
