A hierarchical placement algorithm applies these constraints from the most restrictive communication domain outward. In the illustrated fleet, it places each tensor-parallel group within an NVLink-connected node, then places consecutive pipeline stages under the same leaf switch. It distributes data-parallel replicas across racks only when the resulting collective fits the external bandwidth budget. This alignment reduces costly boundary crossings, but placement alone cannot reserve the fabric’s full bisection bandwidth against other jobs.
The computational cost of topology-aware placement is nontrivial. Evaluating all possible placements for a 256-GPU job across a 10,000-GPU cluster is combinatorially intractable. Production schedulers use heuristic approaches: greedy algorithms that build placements bottom-up (first fill NVLink domains, then fill racks, then spread across racks), tree-search algorithms with pruning that explore the most promising placements first, or scoring-based approaches that evaluate a sample of feasible placements and select the best. Long jobs can amortize a more expensive search, but frequent submissions, short jobs, and recovery bursts also consume scheduler capacity. The useful comparison is end-to-end completion time, including placement delay, rather than execution throughput alone.

Napkin Math 8.2: Placement impact on 3D-parallel trainingScenario: Consider a 256-GPU training job using 3D parallelism: 8-way tensor parallel, 4-way pipeline parallel, 8-way data parallel.
Good placement (topology-aware):

Tensor parallel groups: 32 groups of 8 GPUs, each confined to one 8-GPU node (NVLink: 450 GB/s per direction)
Pipeline stages: 4 consecutive nodes within the same rack (1 switch hop, InfiniBand: 50 GB/s per direction)
Data parallel replicas: 8 racks (3 switch hops through leaf-spine-leaf paths)

Bad placement (topology-unaware):

Tensor parallel groups split across 2 nodes (InfiniBand instead of NVLink)
Pipeline stages scattered across racks (3 switch hops instead of 1)
Data parallel replicas randomly distributed

Math: The tensor parallel communication alone illustrates the impact. With NVLink delivering 450 GB/s per direction, a 1 GB activation transfer takes approximately 2.2 ms. Over InfiniBand at 50 GB/s, the same transfer takes approximately 20 ms, a 9× slowdown.
Systems insight: This calculation prices only the tensor-parallel component of the bad placement. Splitting a tensor-parallel group across nodes makes each activation exchange 9× slower, and the group performs such exchanges at every transformer layer of every step, so the penalty multiplies with model depth rather than appearing once. How much of it reaches step time depends on how much of the exchange was hidden behind computation, and it is why hierarchical placement gives tensor-parallel groups the fastest tier first. The scattered pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas add their own penalties on top, and the scheduler must profile the complete job before assigning a throughput benefit to the placement.





In rail-optimized topologies, corresponding GPU positions across nodes connect through parallel network “rails.” The design supplies separate paths that a suitable rank mapping can use concurrently. Balanced bandwidth depends on distributing traffic across those paths rather than concentrating it on a subset. Keeping a collective group on one rail avoids cross-rail transfers for that group, while the placement of other groups determines how much rail capacity it must share.


↩︎ Rail-optimized fabric architectures and rail-to-rail traffic isolation are established in Rail-optimized topology.
Rail-aware scheduling assigns corresponding model shards across data-parallel replicas to GPUs attached to the same rail. In the eight-GPU-per-node example, local GPU index \(\LocalRankIndex\) connects to rail \(\LocalRankIndex\). Every replica’s copy of shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) therefore stays at that local index on its selected node; the data-parallel replica rank varies across nodes, not across local GPU indices. The resulting collective can remain within the rail fabric. This removes cross-rail transfers for that group, but other groups or tenants can still contend for the same rail’s links, so full dedicated bandwidth requires an explicit capacity and sharing contract.
Rail alignment therefore acts at two levels, and they belong to different components. Within a node it is a rank-mapping decision. The launcher or framework must give every member of a data-parallel group the same local GPU index on its node, which is what removes the cross-rail hops in the placement comparison above; a mapping that puts shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) at index \(\LocalRankIndex\) on one node and at another index elsewhere sends that group’s traffic between rails. Across nodes it constrains the scheduler only when allocations are smaller than a node. When each replica’s pipeline stage occupies a complete node and every node wires local GPU \(\LocalRankIndex\) to rail \(\LocalRankIndex\), any free node already offers every rail, so rail alignment does not narrow which racks the scheduler can choose. With partial-node allocations, a job can receive different local indices on different nodes, and the scheduler must then choose GPU positions as well as nodes so that each group’s members share a rail. Those positions can conflict with the tensor-parallel budget and the paths between pipeline stages when only particular GPU positions remain free, so the packing cost follows the allocation granularity and the available topology rather than an inherent conflict among the three parallelism dimensions.
Resolving these conflicts means matching each 3D parallelism dimension to the interconnect tier its traffic can tolerate (figure 8). Per-layer tensor-parallel activation exchanges stay on intra-node NVLink at 450 GB/s, pipeline stage boundaries cross intra-rack leaf switches at 50 GB/s, and the once-per-step data-parallel gradient synchronization spans the oversubscribed spine at roughly 12.5–25 GB/s. Even a single-node allocation can have meaningful topology constraints when GPUs occupy different interconnect, PCIe, or non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domains. Packing efficiency should therefore be optimized only among placements that satisfy the job’s local and external communication contract.






Figure 8: Hierarchical placement for 3D parallelism: This placement example maps distributed training dimensions to physical interconnect layers. Tensor parallelism (TP), which exchanges activations at every layer, stays inside a node on NVLink (450 GB/s); pipeline parallelism (PP) maps across adjacent nodes under one leaf switch (50 GB/s); and data parallelism (DP), which exchanges gradients only once per step, spans racks through the oversubscribed spine. Bandwidths are per direction, as in figure 5.






Static configuration files like Slurm’s topology.conf or Kubernetes node labels provide a baseline map of the cluster. Runtime topology discovery supplements that map with information exposed by the operating system and device libraries. NCCL uses system topology information, including the PCIe hierarchy and network devices exposed through paths such as /sys/class/infiniband, to identify communication paths and network interface card (NIC) proximity. The discovered graph describes reported connectivity; health checks and traffic measurements must establish whether those paths deliver the expected performance.
Cluster topology is an operating state, not a fixed schematic. Hardware failures, maintenance windows, and thermal throttling change the paths and effective capacity available to the scheduler. A spine switch failure in a redundant Clos network can leave connectivity intact while removing capacity. The effect on our 175B parameter model’s data-parallel AllReduce depends on rerouting, concurrent traffic, and how much bandwidth the job was using. If the failure increases exposed communication time, the scheduler must compare continuing at reduced throughput with the cost of moving to a healthier allocation.
A checkpoint-and-restart migration spends time saving state, releasing the old allocation, obtaining a new one, and restoring execution. Its value depends on measured transition cost and remaining work. If migration takes 10 minutes and restores throughput after a sustained 20 percent penalty, it pays back in less than an hour of subsequent training. That comparison assumes a healthy destination is available and the gain persists. A practical policy also accounts for queue delay and requires evidence that placement causes the slowdown, such as rising collective time on the affected path, before it moves the job.

Example 8.1: The limping switchScenario: A multi-node foundation model training job exhibits a 30 percent throughput drop while static topology maps show full bandwidth and GPU hardware health checks report green.
Diagnosis: A single leaf switch transceiver experienced high CRC error rates and packet retransmissions. Binary up/down probes passed, but reduced effective bandwidth on the affected path delayed AllReduce completion and therefore the training group.
Systems lesson: Binary health checks are insufficient for distributed training fabrics. Schedulers require performance-aware topology monitoring that tracks retransmissions and collective bandwidth, dynamically quarantining degraded network links.



War Story 8.2: Performance-aware health checks (2021)Context: OpenAI’s account of scaling Kubernetes describes automated health checks that remove misbehaving nodes from the schedulable pool (Sigler 2021).
Mechanism: Passive checks monitor reachability, disks, and GPU errors, but error codes do not expose every hardware or driver problem. Active GPU tests exercise the device before admitting ordinary workloads and periodically during its lifetime.
Fix: Nodes enter with a preflight taint, a node marking that repels ordinary pods, which blocks normal scheduling until the tests pass. Failed passive checks cordon a node; more serious failures can trigger eviction requests.
Systems lesson: Reachability alone is not a sufficient admission test. A scheduler needs health evidence that reflects the resources its jobs depend on, together with a policy for removing suspect nodes from placement.



Sigler, Eric. 2021. Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 Nodes. OpenAI Blog.
12 Taints and Tolerations: Node taints can block scheduling of pods without matching tolerations. A toleration permits consideration of a node but neither requires placement there nor reserves it exclusively for training. Dedicated GPU pools also need controlled toleration assignment and placement constraints; removing existing workloads requires an eviction or drain policy appropriate to the taint’s effect.The general scheduling idea is quarantine: when runtime evidence says a node, rack, or link is degraded, the scheduler should stop placing sensitive work there even if the nominal resource count still looks available. Kubernetes implements this pattern through taints and tolerations,12 while Slurm clusters commonly use drain states, node features, or partition rules. The complementary problem is how jobs adapt when available resources change dynamically. Rather than treating resource allocation as fixed for a job’s lifetime, elastic training allows logical jobs to grow, shrink, and recover. Whether worker processes restart depends on the framework; TorchElastic restarts its worker group when membership changes.

When cluster demand fluctuates, rigid allocation creates two categories of waste. During off-peak hours, a job running on 256 GPUs cannot absorb idle resources to speed up training. During peak demand, the same job cannot release excess resources to accommodate higher-priority work without being fully preempted. The scheduler’s only options are “let it keep all its resources” or “kill it entirely,” with nothing in between.
Elastic scheduling expands this binary choice. The recovery mechanics of elastic training show how a distributed job can adjust its worker count, adapt its batch policy, and reconstruct its communication group after a failure. From the scheduler’s perspective, the same capability solves a resource-allocation problem under fluctuating demand. A training job might start with 128 GPUs, scale up to 256 when resources become available, and scale back to 192 when higher-priority work arrives, provided each allocation supports a viable worker group. Resizing may pause training and restart workers from saved state. The scheduler therefore chooses among supported allocation sizes, each with a transition cost, rather than assuming uninterrupted progress at any resource level.


↩︎ Batch-size and learning-rate adjustment and communication-group contraction during elastic recovery are established in Recovery adaptation mechanisms.


Elastic scheduling requires a well-defined contract between the scheduler and the training framework. For planned resizing, the scheduler and framework coordinate resource release through defined signals and an agreed adaptation window. Unexpected failures can bypass that window, so the framework must also recover from valid saved state. Its recovery path reconstructs communication groups and either preserves the global batch or applies a validated batch-size and learning-rate policy. The worker-membership lifecycle therefore behaves as a state machine centered on active training (figure 9). Idle GPUs trigger scale-up, preemptions trigger scale-down, and host timeouts or ECC errors divert ranks to worker replacement; each path returns to active training once the communication group is rebuilt or a spare node joins.






Figure 9: Elastic training worker lifecycle and state machine: The state machine governing dynamic worker membership. Active training loops on step completion and leaves that state along three paths: idle GPUs trigger scale up, a preemption for higher-priority work triggers scale down, and a host timeout or ECC error triggers worker replacement. Each path rebuilds the communication group and returns to active training (dashed arrows), and a spot reclamation deadline can force a shrinking job straight into replacement. Worker processes may restart during resizing, so recovery requires the application to restore valid training state.



From the scheduler’s perspective, this contract is defined by three governing parameters: the elastic range, the transition cost, and the scaling efficiency curve. The elastic range, \([\ElasticMinimumWorkerCount, \ElasticMaximumWorkerCount]\), specifies lower and upper worker bounds; the job’s parallelism layout determines the valid allocation increments within them. The transition cost includes any checkpoint, restart, state redistribution, and rendezvous required by the runtime. Measuring the full interruption determines how frequently the scheduler can trigger reallocations before transition overhead wipes out any throughput advantage. Finally, the scaling efficiency curve quantifies the marginal throughput gained from each added worker, indicating whether assigning idle GPUs to this job yields more aggregate progress than holding them for an assembling gang-scheduled workload. Together, these parameters provide the scheduler with the quantitative bounds needed to resize jobs dynamically without treating elasticity as free capacity.
The scheduler must also account for the effect of worker count on global batch size (\(\GlobalBatchSize = \PerWorkerBatchSize\times \DeviceCount\)), where the per-worker batch counts examples contributing to one optimizer update, including gradient accumulation. Holding the global batch constant requires each remaining worker to process more examples after a shrink. Larger microbatches consume more memory; additional accumulation steps extend the update time. Preserving the batch removes one source of optimization change but does not guarantee identical convergence. Allowing the global batch to change instead requires validating the learning-rate policy and resulting model quality, so throughput alone cannot determine the best allocation.
Frameworks like TorchElastic expose the worker-membership range in their launch configuration, as listing 2 illustrates.



Listing 2: TorchElastic Launch Configuration: The --nnodes=4:16 range configures the elastic worker group to admit 4 to 16 nodes, or 32 to 128 workers. A separate cluster scheduler or operator must acquire, launch, and release nodes within that range.


# Launch elastic training with min 32 to max 128 workers
torchrun \
  --nnodes=4:16 \
  --nproc_per_node=8 \
  --rdzv_backend=c10d \
  --rdzv_endpoint=head-node:29500 \
  --max_restarts=3 \
  train.py



The --nnodes=4:16 specification configures TorchElastic’s rendezvous and worker-membership range as 4 to 16 nodes (32 to 128 workers with 8 processes per node). It does not acquire or resize cluster resources. A separate cluster scheduler or operator must place the nodes and start or stop elastic agents as capacity changes.

Systems Perspective 8.3: Elastic vs. rigid schedulingConsider a congested cluster where a 128-GPU job waits 8 hours for a full gang allocation. This first comparison assumes throughput scales linearly with worker count, equivalent learning progress per processed example, and negligible resize overhead; the later scaling decision relaxes the throughput and transition assumptions.
Rigid scheduling: Wait 8 hours, then train for 24 hours at full throughput. Total wall-clock: 32 hours.
Elastic scheduling (min 32, max 128):

Start immediately with 32 GPUs (throughput = 25 percent of full)
At hour 2, when 64 GPUs free, scale to 64 (throughput = 50 percent)
At hour 8, when the full gang frees and the rigid job would also start, scale to 128 (throughput = 100 percent)

Work completed during the 8-hour queue wait, in hours of full-scale training:

Hours 0 to 2: 25 percent throughput \(\times\) 2 hours = 0.5
Hours 2 to 8: 50 percent throughput \(\times\) 6 hours = 3
Total: 3.5 hours of equivalent full-scale work

The elastic job completes in approximately 28.5 hours (8 hours of partial-scale training plus 20.5 hours at full scale), saving 3.5 hours compared to rigid scheduling. This improvement of about 11 percent comes entirely from using resources productively during what would otherwise be idle queue time.


The scheduler cannot treat every worker count as a valid elastic configuration. Model parallelism constrains the allocation increment when the resize policy keeps tensor and pipeline layouts fixed and adds or removes whole data-parallel replicas. For a 175B-parameter job that relies on 8-way tensor parallelism within each node and 8 pipeline stages across nodes, this policy operates at the granularity of a whole model replica of 64 GPUs. The pipeline depth of 8 is the smallest power of two at which each GPU’s share of the mixed-precision Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) training state fits in its HBM when that state is not sharded across replicas. The feasible layout of Distributed Training instead uses a shallower pipeline and shards optimizer state across the data-parallel group with ZeRO (Memory-efficient data parallelism with ZeRO and FSDP). Keeping each replica’s state self-contained costs memory, but it lets the scheduler add or remove a replica without redistributing every other replica’s optimizer shards. The job can scale between 128 nodes (1,024 GPUs) and 32 nodes (256 GPUs) one replica at a time, changing the data-parallel degree. Removing a single GPU from a tensor-parallel group would instead require a new sharding layout and redistribution of training state. Changing the pipeline degree would also require repartitioning stages and rebuilding the pipeline schedule. A runtime that supports these transitions can expose them to the scheduler, but their feasibility and measured costs belong in the resize contract rather than following automatically from data-parallel elasticity.
The transition cost also constrains the scheduler’s resize frequency. Each scaling event can interrupt useful work while the framework reconstructs its communication group and restores or redistributes state. The duration must be measured for the chosen runtime and checkpoint path. The scheduler must amortize this cost over the subsequent run duration, so small resize increments are only worthwhile if the job will run at the new scale for significantly longer than the transition window; section 8.8.3 shows the thrashing that results when a policy ignores this amortization.



The scheduler uses the declared \([\ElasticMinimumWorkerCount, \ElasticMaximumWorkerCount]\) range to choose when a job starts and how its allocation changes. Starting at the minimum can reduce queue delay; expanding into newly idle capacity can increase progress; shrinking can release borrowed capacity without terminating the logical job. Which of these wins depends on the job’s scaling curve and transition cost, and the policies below compare the choices by the work completed over the same time window.
Each action must respect the framework contract. The most consequential of the three is graceful preemption: when higher-priority work arrives, the scheduler first shrinks an elastic job toward \(\ElasticMinimumWorkerCount\), reclaiming whole replicas at the next resize boundary, and resorts to checkpoint-and-preempt only when the final viable group itself must yield. Quota borrowing across teams, developed in section 8.12, depends on this primitive whenever an owner reclaims capacity it lent. Scaling curves and transition costs determine whether the extra progress repays the disruption. Because batch changes can affect convergence, the test of a resize is time to target model quality, not throughput.



Adding resources to a running job does not always accelerate time-to-convergence. Communication and synchronization overhead limit throughput gains, requiring the scheduler to enforce elastic scaling policies based on empirical efficiency curves rather than resource availability alone. A job’s scaling efficiency \(\ScalingEfficiency(\ScalingCurveWorkerCount)\) compares observed throughput at \(\ScalingCurveWorkerCount\) workers with the throughput predicted by ideal linear scaling from a reference allocation. With fixed global work per step, it typically passes through three regimes: a near-linear regime where per-worker computation dwarfs every fixed per-step cost, a sublinear regime where pipeline fill and drain and the unhidden part of gradient synchronization become a visible share of each step, and a saturation regime where those fixed costs rival the shrinking computation itself. Assigning available GPUs to a saturated job can yield less useful progress than serving queued work. The lower allocation bound answers a different question. Below its minimum viable scale, a job may lack the memory or complete parallel groups needed to execute at all. A policy can impose a higher minimum to meet a deadline, even when a smaller allocation remains computationally efficient.



Throughput falls away from ideal linear scaling and saturates.
The 175B reference job shows these regimes with the chapter’s own numbers. Modeled at a fixed global batch with the step-time decomposition of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3), its scaling efficiency falls from 87 percent at 256 GPUs to 83 percent at 1,024 GPUs and 69 percent at 4,096 GPUs (figure 10, panel a). Efficiency falls, yet quadrupling from 1,024 to 4,096 GPUs still raises throughput 3.3×, so a lower efficiency is a declining marginal return rather than a slowdown. Panel (b) locates the loss. Tensor-parallel communication shrinks along with each worker’s computation, so its share of the step never rises above 11 percent. The decline comes instead from pipeline fill and drain and unhidden gradient synchronization, which take roughly fixed time per step while each worker’s share of the batch shrinks. The pipeline bubble grows fastest of the three, for a reason the bubble fraction \((\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\MicrobatchCount+\PipelineParallelDegree-1)\) of Pipeline parallelism makes explicit. With the global batch fixed, each added replica takes a share of the sequences, so the microbatch count \(\MicrobatchCount\) per replica falls while the stage count stays at 8, and the idle fraction rises. The shaded window from 256 to 1,024 GPUs is therefore a policy choice, not an interval derived from these efficiencies alone. A minimum allocation could follow from a completion deadline or the job’s declared resource contract. It does not follow from insufficient per-worker computation at smaller scale, since with fixed global work fewer workers generally perform more work each. The upper limit likewise requires comparing additional useful progress with resize cost and the value of serving queued jobs. A real scheduler must obtain those inputs from profiling and the workload’s quality target.














Figure 10: Modeled scaling efficiency and elastic operating range: (a) Scaling efficiency (\(\ScalingEfficiency\)) of the 175B reference job from 64 to 4,096 GPUs, computed with 8-way tensor parallelism within each DGX H100 node, 8 pipeline stages, HDR InfiniBand, and a fixed global batch of 1,536 sequences. The shaded window is an assumed admission policy; efficiency alone establishes neither its minimum nor its maximum. (b) Share of each step lost to tensor-parallel communication, pipeline bubble, and exposed gradient synchronization. Lower efficiency does not imply that adding workers reduces throughput.



This logic extends to the temporal dimension, where the scheduler must weigh the immediate progress of a smaller allocation against waiting for a larger one. If a 512-GPU job can start immediately with 128 GPUs or wait for the full request, the better choice depends on the integration of throughput over time. The resize overhead (the cost of stopping, checkpointing, and restarting when the runtime requires them) must be amortized over the subsequent run duration. A policy of “opportunistic scaling” that resizes a job every time a single node becomes free can lose its throughput advantage to repeated interruptions, completing less useful work than a stable allocation.

Napkin Math 8.3: The elastic scaling decisionThe comparison of elastic and rigid scheduling above assumed linear scaling and free resizing; this decision drops both assumptions. Consider a training job with a target batch size that requires 512 GPUs for the highest throughput among the configurations considered. Three scheduling strategies are evaluated over a window of 24 hours.
Given: Throughput at 128 GPUs is 1 epoch/hour (baseline). Throughput at 256 GPUs is 1.8 epochs/hour (90 percent scaling efficiency relative to that baseline). Throughput at 512 GPUs is 3.2 epochs/hour (80 percent scaling efficiency). Re-scaling cost is 10 minutes (0.17 hours) to checkpoint, re-shard, and restart.
Strategy 1 (immediate start, no scaling): The job starts immediately with 128 GPUs and runs for the full 24 hours. Total work: \(24 \times 1.0 = 24\) epochs.
Strategy 2 (wait for the full allocation): The job waits in the queue for 4 hours until 512 GPUs become available, then runs for 20 hours. Total work: \(20 \times 3.2 = 64\) epochs.
Strategy 3 (elastic step-up): The job starts immediately with 128 GPUs. After 4 hours, the capacity that lets Strategy 2 start frees up, but the elastic policy caps growth at 256 GPUs so that the remaining GPUs stay available to queued jobs. The job pauses, scales up, and resumes. Phase 1: \(4 \times 1.0 = 4\) epochs. Phase 2: \((24 - 4 - 0.17) \times 1.8 \approx 35.7\) epochs. Total work: 4 + 35.7 = 39.7 epochs.
The elastic strategy completes nearly 1.7× the epoch-equivalent work of the immediate small-scale run, but still trails the full allocation by about 38 percent. That comparison counts this job’s epochs, not the GPU-hours spent on them. Strategy 2 holds twice as many GPUs as Strategy 3 for most of the window and runs them at 80 percent scaling efficiency against Strategy 3’s 90 percent, so the elastic job does more work per GPU-hour, and the GPUs it leaves free serve queued jobs. Which strategy wins therefore depends on whether the fleet values this job’s completion time or the total work completed across all jobs. That gap shrinks when queue waits grow or peak capacity stays scarce; re-scaling overhead is only 10 minutes, so the step-up strategy keeps its lead over the immediate small-scale run unless slow checkpoint transfer or compilation stretches that tax beyond about 9 hours.


Placement and elasticity determine which allocations are feasible and how much useful progress they produce across competing jobs. Fleet economics adds the price of those choices. Every placement, preemption, and reservation consumes capacity that could serve another workload, so the scheduler must compare both useful progress and opportunity cost.

An idle accelerator in an enterprise fleet incurs operational costs every hour whether computing or blocked in a queue, turning placement and preemption decisions into direct financial trade-offs. The orchestrator translates this utilization-to-dollars relationship from section 8.1 into an online scheduling signal, balancing resource prices, reservation commitments, interruption risk, checkpoint cost, and job deadlines to decide whether to admit, delay, preempt, or resize work. Capital planning, portfolio return, cost attribution, and lifecycle total cost of ownership are larger, slower decisions developed in Fleet Economics and Utilization; the scheduler consumes their outcomes as prices and constraints.
At a fixed utilization, idle capacity grows linearly with fleet size, so the dollar cost of a scheduling inefficiency grows with every procurement (figure 11). At 10,000 GPUs operating at 50 percent utilization, annual waste reaches $87.6M under the chapter’s $2/GPU-hour accounting scenario. Published measurements show that such underutilization occurs in production. Microsoft’s Philly cluster study (Jeon et al. 2019) measured mean GPU utilization of approximately 52 percent. The 30 to 70 percent shaded band in the figure is an illustrative operating range for the cost model, not a universal empirical claim about all production clusters. Moving from 50 percent to 80 percent utilization on a 10,000-GPU cluster recovers over $52M annually in equivalent capacity value under this pricing scenario. That value equals the opening’s annual waste at 30 percent idle for a simple reason. Both scenarios concern 30 percent of the same 10,000 GPUs at the same rate, so both price 3,000 GPU-equivalents of capacity, once as waste and once as recovery. Cash savings require avoiding billed usage or a planned purchase.

The idle-capacity figure establishes the economic target; the remaining cost controls explain how the scheduler moves toward it. Interruptible capacity lowers the price of tolerant work, reservation and quota policy decide which jobs deserve scarce guaranteed capacity, and accountability mechanisms make idle GPUs visible to the teams that create demand.


Cloud providers sell spare capacity through spot instances13 (AWS) or preemptible VMs (GCP), retaining the right to reclaim it. This chapter uses a 60 to 90 percent discount band for its pricing comparison; actual discounts depend on the resource and market. The reference interruption windows range from up to 30 seconds for GCP preemptible shutdown to 2 minutes for AWS stop or termination notices, with best-effort delivery rather than a guaranteed recovery interval. At the scenario rates of $0.70/GPU-hour instead of $2/GPU-hour, the worked comparison below shows how savings can exceed half the on-demand cost after accounting for its assumed interruption overhead.
13 Spot Instances: The scenario’s 60 to 90 percent discount purchases reclaimable capacity, not a guaranteed interval for saving state. AWS’s best-effort stop or termination notice targets 2 minutes, while GCP preemptible shutdown allows up to 30 seconds; AWS hibernation begins immediately. If a job’s measured checkpoint time exceeds the reference 30-second window, a notice-triggered save cannot be its only recovery path.The viability of spot instances for ML training depends on two factors that determine whether the discount translates into actual savings: the cost of each interruption (checkpoint overhead plus restart time plus lost work since the last checkpoint) and the frequency of interruption (which varies by instance type, region, time of day, and overall cloud demand). Equation 3 gives the effective cost of spot training:
\[ \EffectiveSpotTrainingCost= \SpotHourlyPrice\times \frac{\BilledAllocationTime}{\RetainedProductiveTime}  \tag{3}\]
where \(\BilledAllocationTime\) is billed allocation time, including checkpointing, recovery, and work later discarded after an interruption, and \(\RetainedProductiveTime\) is the equivalent training time represented by retained progress. The ratio assumes a fixed allocation size and price, with unchanged useful throughput while training; variable allocations require summing the cost of each allocation interval. Waiting for replacement capacity extends completion time but contributes to billed time only while resources remain allocated. When checkpointing and interruption losses consume a small fraction of billed time, effective cost stays near the spot price. Frequent interruptions, expensive recovery, or substantial replay can instead erase the discount.
Spot savings and fault tolerance infrastructure are coupled. Fault tolerance mechanisms (frequent asynchronous checkpointing, fast checkpoint loading, elastic recovery) make spot capacity usable by lowering the cost of each interruption. Elastic training can resume a logical job with fewer workers after reclamation, provided the remaining allocation is viable, although the framework may still restart worker processes and restore checkpointed state, so elasticity reduces recovery cost rather than eliminating it. The same infrastructure therefore earns a double return. It protects against hardware losses, and it enables the deliberate use of interruptible capacity. Both benefits require measurement. The scheduler combines observed interruption rates, recovery costs, and retained training progress with resource prices to estimate whether spot savings repay the additional recovery infrastructure. The same evidence supports valuing protection against hardware failures; neither benefit follows from the discount or checkpoint mechanism alone.



Spot capacity pays off only when an interruption rarely removes the whole job at once, so schedulers that use it diversify where capacity comes from instead of simply retrying on failure. Availability zone diversification reduces the probability of simultaneous fleet-wide reclamation. Cloud providers typically manage spot pools independently per availability zone (AZ). If a training job requires 1,024 GPUs, allocating them as a single block in one zone exposes the job to a complete stop if that specific zone’s spot pool is reclaimed. Diversifying independent jobs or restart destinations across zones reduces exposure to one exhausted pool. Splitting a single synchronous gang across zones also changes its communication paths, so the scheduler must include cross-zone bandwidth, latency, and transfer costs before accepting that placement. The scheduler still must model correlation carefully: independent per-instance interruptions make large simultaneous losses unlikely, but pool-level or AZ-level reclamations can remove hundreds of GPUs at once and must be treated as elastic-shrink or failover events rather than ordinary isolated failures.
Instance type diversification expands the set of capacity pools a job can use, though availability across those pools can remain correlated. A job that requests only one instance type cannot use spare capacity in another pool. Accepting alternatives therefore requires a compatibility list that includes memory capacity, runtime support, communication paths, and measured throughput. An instance with more memory can still be an unsuitable substitute if its runtime support, communication paths, or throughput differ. The scheduler compares each feasible alternative’s price and recovery cost per unit of retained progress; mixing devices within a synchronous gang also requires accounting for unequal worker speeds.
Spot capacity signals can guide placement but do not necessarily predict interruption frequency. For example, the AWS Spot Placement Score estimates the current likelihood that a capacity request will succeed in a region or availability zone; it explicitly does not predict interruption risk. A scheduler can use this signal to choose where to request capacity, but estimating interruptions per day requires separate historical measurements for the instance type and region. If the resulting workload-specific recovery model shows that interruption overhead erases the discount, the scheduler should migrate the job to on-demand capacity or a different region.
Checkpoint frequency optimization for spot instances extends the reliability logic. The Young-Daly formula developed in The Young-Daly checkpoint interval models losses from unpredicted interruptions, whether caused by hardware failure or reclamation without a usable warning. Provider notices offer an additional opportunity to save state, using the reference windows of 2 minutes on AWS and up to 30 seconds on GCP preemptible VMs. A two-tier checkpointing approach combines periodic checkpoints, with an interval chosen for the workload’s interruption model, and a best-effort checkpoint triggered by a notice. The notice-triggered checkpoint reduces lost work only if it becomes durable before reclamation. Otherwise, the job restores its last durable state, whether produced by a periodic, asynchronous, or incremental checkpoint, and replays subsequent work.
The same need for contingency planning becomes acute when spot interruptions are correlated rather than isolated.

Systems Perspective 8.4: Correlated spot riskContext: Spot capacity is cheap because it is reclaimable. That risk is not independent across instances: cloud regions, instance types, product launches, and deadline cycles can create correlated demand.
Failure mode: A fleet that concentrates all interruptible training in one region and one instance type can lose a large fraction of workers at once, even if each individual worker appears restartable.
Consequence: Checkpointing handles isolated interruptions; it does not solve fleet-wide preemption when every retry targets the same exhausted pool.
Systems insight: A robust scheduler diversifies compatible restart destinations, monitors interruption risk, and plans an on-demand fallback when spot capacity cannot meet the job’s deadline or cost target. That fallback still depends on available capacity and the time needed to restore state.

The scheduler must match each workload’s deadline and recovery contract to the capacity tier: reserved capacity can support the steady serving load or a training job’s base allocation, while spot can support elastic replicas or independent experiments that tolerate reclamation. Systems Perspective 8.5: Spot vs. on-demand trainingConsider training a 70B parameter model, a smaller workload than the chapter’s 175B reference, on 512 GPUs for 14 days. The scenario fixes the event budget at 196 interruptions over the run and treats each as graceful, so no progress is replayed.
On-Demand: 512 GPUs \(\times\) 336 hours \(\times\) $2/GPU-hour = $344,064
Spot (65 percent discount, 5 percent checkpoint overhead, 14 interruptions per day of useful training with 30 minutes restart):

Base cost: 512 GPUs \(\times\) 336 hours \(\times\) $0.70/GPU-hour = $120,422
Checkpoint overhead: \(5\%\) \(\times\) 336 hours = 16.8 hours
Restart overhead: 196 interruptions \(\times\) 0.5 hours = 98 hours
Total time: 336 hours + 16.8 hours + 98 hours = 450.8 hours
Total cost: 512 GPUs \(\times\) 450.8 hours \(\times\) $0.70/GPU-hour = $161,567

Savings: $182,497 (53.0 percent), at the cost of approximately 34.2 percent longer wall-clock time.
The economics are compelling when fault tolerance infrastructure is already in place. Without checkpointing, a single interruption forces restart from scratch, potentially wasting days of compute and negating all savings.





Cost-aware scheduling adds financial efficiency to the completion-time, utilization, and fairness objectives already introduced. The orchestrator evaluates three recurring classes of trade-offs: waiting versus running immediately, preempting existing tasks versus paying more for on-demand capacity, and falling back versus shrinking elastically. For example, it might compare an immediate launch on reserved A100 GPUs with waiting two hours for spot H100 instances. If workload profiling and the price model predict twice the throughput at half the execution cost, the remaining question is whether those gains repay the delay and interruption risk. When capacity becomes constrained, the scheduler must balance preempting a low-priority hyperparameter sweep on reserved capacity against routing a high-priority training run to more expensive on-demand instances. When a provider reclaims spot instances, the policy compares replacing them with on-demand nodes against shrinking elastically. These choices require the costs of waiting, recovery, and displaced work as well as the price of the new allocation.
These decisions require the scheduler to model both the time-value of computation (the organizational cost of a 2-hour delay in researcher productivity, product launch schedules, or competitive position) and the financial cost of different resource allocations. Delaying a production model retrain by 2 hours might violate a service level agreement (SLA), while the same delay to an exploratory experiment can postpone a research decision or block dependent work. A workload class’s delay tolerance is therefore a policy input grounded in its dependencies and deadlines, not an assumption that exploratory work has no time cost.
Production systems can define cost policies per workload class that encode these trade-offs as configuration rather than requiring per-decision human judgment. One policy places steady inference demand on reserved capacity and maintains ready replicas to meet its latency target; the reservation alone does not guarantee application availability or latency. Large training runs can combine a reserved minimum viable allocation with interruptible elastic expansion, requesting on-demand replacements when a deadline justifies the cost and capacity is available. Exploratory workloads with flexible deadlines can use spot capacity while accepting interruptions and variable completion times. These assignments express the organization’s priorities rather than a universal mapping from workload type to purchasing tier.
The scheduler does not implement the organization’s financial accounting system. It consumes the resulting price and policy signals: the marginal price of each capacity tier, the reservation a project may claim, the interruption risk it may accept, and the deadline it must meet. Showback, chargeback, and attribution belong to that accounting system; the scheduler uses their outputs only to rank feasible scheduling actions.

Total cost of ownership (TCO) determines the price signals exposed to the scheduler, but it is not itself a scheduling mechanism. The orchestrator needs only the resulting per-resource opportunity costs and policy constraints, including whether capacity is owned, reserved, on demand, or interruptible.

A short experiment waiting behind a long training run can suffer even when every running job has an efficient placement. Improving that outcome requires a policy for deciding which job receives the next available resources. Custom ML schedulers use different signals to make that decision: consumed service can prioritize jobs without runtime estimates, iteration boundaries can make preemption cheaper, normalized finish time can expose unfair delay, and measured goodput can guide joint resource and batch-size changes. Only the last of these requires a model of learning progress; the others improve completion time, utilization, or fairness without predicting convergence.


Tiresias (Gu et al. 2019) addresses the fundamental problem identified in section 8.5.3: ML job durations are unpredictable, and scheduling policies that rely on exact duration estimates can make poor decisions when those estimates are unavailable or unreliable. Rather than fighting this information asymmetry, Tiresias eliminates the requirement for duration estimates entirely. It uses a two-dimensional attained service14 scheduler that makes priority decisions based on what a job has already consumed, not what it claims it will consume. Jobs accumulate “service” based on GPU-time consumed, with priority decreasing as service increases. The two dimensions are time (how long the job has been running) and resources (how many GPUs the job uses), capturing both elapsed duration and resource intensity.
14 Attained Service Scheduling: A discipline that uses consumed service to set priority when remaining work is unknown. Unlike shortest remaining processing time (SRPT), it cannot distinguish a newly arrived long job from a short one before either receives service. Its benefit depends on the workload distribution; protection against starvation remains necessary when new jobs repeatedly displace older ones.A discretized version groups jobs into service bins (illustratively, less than 1 GPU-hour, 1 to 10 GPU-hours, 10 to 100 GPU-hours, greater than 100 GPU-hours), giving lower-service bins higher priority. When job durations are heavy-tailed, a job that has consumed little service is likely to be short, so favoring low-service jobs approximates shortest-remaining-processing-time ordering without any runtime estimate. New jobs can receive service before long-running jobs, but their eventual duration remains unknown, and a high-priority gang still needs a feasible allocation. Tiresias also promotes jobs that have waited too long, trading some average-completion-time benefit for protection against starvation. The priority rule therefore replaces runtime prediction with an observable signal and an explicit waiting-time policy; it does not guarantee that every short job starts promptly.
The Tiresias evaluation reports lower average job completion time (JCT) on its testbed and trace-driven workloads (Gu et al. 2019). The result depends on job arrivals, sizes, and the comparison policy. Prioritizing low-service jobs can delay long-running jobs, so average completion time must be evaluated alongside starvation prevention and the delay experienced by each job class.

Gu, J., M. Chowdhury, K. G. Shin, Y. Zhu, M. Jeon, J. Qian, H. H. Liu, and C. Guo. 2019. “Tiresias: A GPU Cluster Manager for Distributed Deep Learning.” Proceedings of the 16th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI ’19), 485–500.



Gandiva (Xiao et al. 2018) exploits repetitive training iterations to profile jobs and share GPUs. Its central mechanism is time-slicing at iteration boundaries. To give a GPU to another job, Gandiva suspends the running job at the end of a minibatch, copies its live GPU memory to host memory, and resumes another job on the device; switching back reverses the copy. Several jobs can therefore take turns on one GPU, and the same suspend-and-resume path lets Gandiva migrate a job to better-placed devices or pack compatible jobs onto one GPU when their combined memory fits. The boundary is the cheap place to switch because temporary activations have been released, so far less state must move than in the middle of a step. Weights, optimizer state, and runtime allocations remain, so each switch still costs a transfer proportional to that persistent state, and a job whose persistent state nearly fills the device cannot share it. The scheduler must measure memory demand, interference, and transition cost before admitting additional jobs.

Xiao, Wencong, Romil Bhardwaj, Ramachandran Ramjee, Muthian Sivathanu, Nipun Kwatra, Zhenhua Han, Prabal Patel, et al. 2018. “Gandiva: Introspective Cluster Scheduling for Deep Learning.” 13th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 18), 595–610.
Gandiva also implements grow-shrink elasticity, applying the allocation mechanism of section 8.8 to jobs that explicitly permit resizing. It expands eligible jobs into idle capacity and shrinks them when demand returns, using profiles to estimate which jobs benefit. The published implementation limits growth to one server and waits through an idle period before expanding. Its contribution is the connection between measured job behavior and resource control, rather than a claim that arbitrary training jobs can resize cheaply.



Equal GPU-time shares can produce unequal completion delays when workloads respond differently to placement. Themis (Mahajan et al. 2020) measures fairness in normalized finish time. Each application, which can contain related training jobs, compares its completion time in the shared cluster with its completion time on an isolated \(1/\ContendingApplicationCount\) share of the cluster, where \(\ContendingApplicationCount\) is the number of applications contending for it. The ratio has the same form as the slowdown \(\JobSlowdown_j\) defined with the scheduling objectives, except in its denominator. Themis divides by the completion time on a fair share of the cluster rather than by the isolated runtime on the job’s own allocation, so a ratio of one means the application finished no later than its fair share would have allowed.

Mahajan, Kshiteej, Arjun Balasubramanian, Arjun Singhvi, Shivaram Venkataraman, Aditya Akella, Amar Phanishayee, and Shuchi Chawla. 2020. “Themis: Fair and Efficient GPU Cluster Scheduling.” 17th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 20), 289–304.
Themis targets the worst finish-time fairness ratio across applications. Its auction rounds offer available resources to applications farthest from fair completion, while allowing placement efficiency to influence the allocation within a round. With two applications whose current estimates are 1.2 and 2.0, the second is projected to finish twice as late as its fair share would allow, so it is offered the next round’s GPUs first. The first application’s ratio rises while it waits, and once it overtakes the second it moves to the front of later rounds. The signal is relative completion delay, not proximity to completion or GPU-hours already consumed.
Applications bid by reporting estimated finish-time fairness for candidate GPU subsets. These bids expose placement preferences rather than monetary willingness to pay. The auction trades short-term allocation efficiency against the long-term fairness objective, making the quality of completion-time and placement estimates part of the scheduler’s operating assumptions.



Pollux (Qiao et al. 2021) extends resource adaptation to include training hyperparameters. Gandiva already changes allocations; Pollux jointly considers allocation, batch size, and learning-rate scaling because a larger batch can use more devices efficiently while changing the amount of work needed to converge. The preferred configuration can therefore change with both cluster demand and the stage of training.
Pollux uses goodput to connect system throughput, measured in training examples per second, with statistical efficiency, which measures progress per example relative to a reference batch size. This is a third use of the word. The run-level goodput of The Fleet Law discounts work lost to failures and restarts, and Google’s ML Productivity Goodput multiplies program, runtime, and scheduling factors; Pollux’s version instead discounts each example by the optimization progress it contributes at the current batch size. Statistical efficiency falls as the batch grows past the critical batch size of Critical batch size and diminishing returns, which is why more GPUs at a larger batch can raise throughput while lowering goodput. It estimates how allocation and batch changes affect both quantities, then uses those estimates to guide resource sharing across jobs. Additional GPUs are valuable only when their throughput gain survives the corresponding change in statistical efficiency and the cost of changing the allocation.
The Pollux evaluation reports average job completion times 37 to 50 percent lower than the state-of-the-art deep learning schedulers it was compared against, which do not make the same combined adjustment of resources and batch size (Qiao et al. 2021). The number belongs to that testbed and trace. Its durable lesson is the coupling: an allocation can increase samples per second while reducing progress per sample. The scheduler must estimate both effects and validate completion time at the same target quality, rather than transferring a reported improvement to a different workload.

Qiao, Aurick, Sang Keun Choe, Suhas Jayaram Subramanya, Willie Neiswanger, Qirong Ho, Hao Zhang, Gregory R. Ganger, and Eric P. Xing. 2021. “Pollux: Co-Adaptive Cluster Scheduling for Goodput-Optimized Deep Learning.” 15th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 21), 1–18.

The table separates policies by what the platform must observe and control. Attained-service scheduling can work from accounting records, while iteration-aware sharing needs reliable timing profiles. Adaptive goodput policies require the training loop to accept allocation and batch-size changes. Additional control creates additional failure modes: inaccurate profiles can increase interference, and inaccurate learning-progress models can choose allocations that fail to improve convergence.
For our 175B parameter model, the practical distinction is whether the runtime supports those interventions at an acceptable transition cost. A policy that only changes queue priority needs less training-loop integration than one that resizes the execution group. The production discussion that follows evaluates that integration against the fleet’s topology and recovery requirements.
The common lesson is to match the policy signal to the scheduling objective. Attained service addresses runtime uncertainty, iteration boundaries expose cheaper opportunities to interrupt work, normalized finish time measures unequal delay, and goodput couples resource allocation to learning progress. Only the goodput-based policy models convergence, and only the iteration-aware one lowers the cost of interrupting work. A platform should test the chosen policy against queue delay, starvation risk, and measured recovery cost before adopting it.
The challenge for production systems is incorporating these insights while maintaining the operational reliability, policy flexibility, and organizational governance that production environments require. Production platforms usually adopt scheduler ideas selectively because reliability, governance, heterogeneous hardware, and user policy constrain pure research designs.



A research scheduler’s evaluation establishes results for a particular workload, hardware configuration, and set of runtime controls. A production fleet must test whether its own conditions preserve those results. A cluster containing V100s alongside A100s and H100s, with both InfiniBand and Ethernet paths, can give the same allocation count different performance across placements. Jobs can also crash, hang, or exceed declared memory needs. Deploying a policy therefore requires integrating its decisions with admission, failure recovery, and the existing orchestrator, then measuring its benefit under the fleet’s actual workload.
Consider applying adaptive allocation to our 175B-parameter model training run. The runtime must first expose viable resize configurations and their costs. A checkpoint-and-restart path can require persisting and restoring large optimizer state, while other state-transfer mechanisms impose different costs. Repeated resizing can consume the expected throughput gain before the job benefits from its new allocation. The policy should therefore compare predicted additional progress over the expected allocation duration with the measured transition tax, retaining a stable placement when resizing does not repay that tax. The decision follows the workload and cluster demand, not a universal training phase.
The production decision is whether a specialized policy improves marginal allocation enough to justify its operational burden, judged by the measures this chapter has already built: queue delay and slowdown, useful GPU-hours, preemption tax, and placement efficiency. Group admission settles whether a gang can start at all; the research schedulers answer the next question, which feasible group to admit, and each imposes different requirements on the runtime. Selecting a policy therefore means matching its objective and assumptions to the fleet rather than choosing a single scheduler as universally best.

When an e-commerce platform launches a major sale, requests can arrive faster than its serving replicas can process them. A training job may tolerate waiting in the admission queue; a serving request misses its deadline while additional capacity is still starting. To the fleet orchestrator, serving is therefore a claim on accelerators that must be honored quickly and that competes with training gangs for the same devices.
The orchestrator’s unit is the serving replica, a ready execution group with a loaded model that may occupy one accelerator, a device partition, or a multi-accelerator gang. A 175B-parameter model may make an eight-GPU tensor-parallel group the schedulable replica, and Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) imposes the same constraint through its embedding tables: a replica whose tables are sharded across several accelerators can serve only when every shard is placed. Each replica has a measured request-processing capacity at a specified workload mix and latency target, and that measured capacity is the quantity the orchestrator uses to size and place replicas. It decides how many such groups exist, where they reside, how they are protected from interference, and which lower-priority allocations yield when serving demand grows. Language models add a memory dimension to the claim. Each in-progress response retains per-token attention state, the key-value (KV) cache, whose footprint grows with context length and concurrency even though the weights stay fixed, so a replica can exhaust its memory before it exhausts its compute.
How many replicas to run at each moment is a control problem with its own signals and delays. Accelerator utilization alone does not identify the capacity needed to meet a request-latency target, and loading large models can delay a new replica’s readiness. The controller must combine demand signals with measured startup time and ready reserve capacity; Autoscaling and Capacity Control develops that control loop. For the orchestrator, the immediate consequence is that reclaiming a device from training does not instantly make it available for serving. Three fleet-level questions follow, namely how serving workloads share devices without unacceptable interference, when sharing pays for itself, and where the boundary between training and serving pools should sit.


When multiple inference workloads share physical hardware, noisy-neighbor contention arises whenever one workload’s resource consumption degrades another’s execution speed. On GPUs, shared execution units can limit concurrent kernels, while saturated HBM interfaces constrain memory-bound work. Contending working sets can evict lines from the shared L2 cache, and simultaneous host-to-device transfers can compete for PCIe bandwidth. Aggregate power and temperature limits can also reduce operating clocks. These mechanisms connect the placement decision to the request’s critical path. A placement that fits every model in memory can still miss its service-level objective if sharing extends execution or queueing enough to exhaust the latency budget.
MIG sits at the strong resource-isolation end of this design space. Table 3 already showed the fixed profiles; the operational implication is that hardware partitioning reduces cross-workload interference but turns partition choice into a placement constraint. MIG is available on supported MIG-capable NVIDIA data-center GPUs, profiles may require draining affected workloads before reconfiguration, and fixed partition sizes may not match workload requirements. The memory-fit and sharing examples use the displayed device and profile capacities as conservative decimal-GB admission budgets, rather than as conversions of their modeled byte capacities. A workload that needs 15 GB of GPU memory leaves 5 GB of a 20 GB MIG instance budget unused or exceeds a 10 GB instance budget.
Software sharing offers different controls over execution, memory, and fault isolation; these do not form a single performance-versus-security scale. At the simplest level, CUDA time-slicing allows multiple processes to share a GPU by context-switching the compute resources. While flexible, it offers weak performance isolation because contexts compete for the entire device over time. NVIDIA’s Multi-Process Service (MPS)15 allows kernels and memory copies from different processes to overlap, reducing context-switch overhead and improving utilization when one process cannot fill the device (NVIDIA 2026). In the shared-resource MPS configuration considered here, Volta and newer clients have distinct GPU virtual address spaces but compete for execution and memory-system resources. Additional partitioning controls depend on the hardware, software version, and selected mode, and those configured limits, not address-space separation, determine how much performance and fault isolation MPS provides.
15 CUDA MPS (Multi-Process Service): NVIDIA’s runtime supports concurrent CUDA clients, with distinct virtual address spaces on Volta and newer GPUs. Its isolation contract depends on configured resource limits and partitioning support; the shared-resource mode used in this example does not reserve an independent hardware slice for each client. A deployment must also account for its fault domain, since address-space separation alone does not contain every GPU fault (NVIDIA 2026).
NVIDIA. 2026. NVIDIA CUDA Multi-Process Service.
GPU memory accounting must still prevent one model from consuming capacity reserved for another. A distinct virtual address space blocks direct addressing of another client’s allocations, but it does not create a fixed memory-capacity partition. Without enforceable per-client limits, a memory leak or unexpectedly large batch can exhaust shared device memory and disrupt colocated workloads. MPS therefore fits mutually trusting workloads whose aggregate memory footprint and interference have been measured; MIG or full-device assignment fits stronger trust and predictability requirements.
At the CPU level, core pinning restricts inference processes to selected cores, reducing migrations that lose cache locality. For latency-sensitive workloads, isolcpus kernel parameters and taskset affinity can reduce scheduling interference, but affinity alone does not remove interrupts or other kernel activity. Combined with NUMA-aware16 placement, CPU affinity can reduce interference and avoid unnecessary remote-memory traffic. The tail-latency benefit depends on the host topology and request path. For a request path limited by host-memory access, cache eviction, remote NUMA access, and address-translation misses can increase tail latency. CPU placement addresses those costs only when they lie on the critical path.
16 NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access): Host-memory latency and bandwidth depend on which socket owns the memory and where the accelerator’s PCIe connection terminates. CPU, memory, and device placement should therefore be evaluated together; a remote allocation can add inter-socket traffic, but its end-to-end inference penalty must be measured for the workload.The GPU mechanisms form a spectrum from flexible software sharing (time-slicing and MPS) through hardware partitioning (MIG) to exclusive assignment, and each point gives up packing efficiency for isolation (table 7). For serving, the choice turns on interference and memory accounting; when colocated workloads belong to different teams, it also becomes a trust-boundary decision, which section 8.12.5 takes up with the rest of multi-tenant security.

The decision to co-locate multiple models on a single GPU trades potential capacity savings against interference. Choosing exclusive access avoids competition from another device tenant but can leave capacity unused when one workload cannot fill the device. Production evidence suggests such stranded capacity is common. On NERSC’s Perlmutter supercomputer, Li et al. (2023) found that 50 percent of jobs used less than 25 percent of their allocated GPU memory. Moving to aggressive sharing (via MPS or time-slicing) can admit more work, provided contention does not erase the gain or violate latency objectives. Exclusive device assignment still depends on the surrounding host, driver, identity, network, and storage controls for tenant security. The scheduler must therefore evaluate memory fit and measured service capacity together.

Sharing packs two tenants, cutting the unused memory budget from 67.5 percent to 35 percent.

Using the same conservative admission budget, consider an A100 GPU with a 80 GB memory budget serving a 7B parameter model. The model weights in FP16 consume approximately 14 GB. With the scenario’s assumed KV cache and activation overhead, the total runtime footprint is roughly 26 GB. Exclusive access leaves 54 GB (67.5 percent) of the memory budget unused at this load. That budget is reclaimable only to the extent that it exceeds required runtime and burst headroom. A MIG partition (for example, a 3g.40gb profile) leaves roughly 35 percent of the assigned partition budget unused; the remaining device capacity is subject to valid partition combinations. Packing two such models onto the same 80 GB device through MPS consumes 52 GB, leaving 35 percent of the device memory budget unused under the same footprint assumption. Reducing the device count also requires enough compute and bandwidth headroom to preserve throughput and latency under concurrent demand; fitting the models in memory is only the first admission condition.
This density introduces interference. When two workloads share execution and memory resources through MPS, their demands can overlap on SMs and memory bandwidth. A compute-bound model paired with a memory-bound model is a candidate for complementary placement because, in isolation, each saturates a different resource, but the bottleneck labels describe isolated behavior, not a guarantee of compatibility. Both workloads still use multiple resources, and concurrent demand can change the limiting resource. The scheduler must measure the pair’s throughput and tail latency across its expected load range before treating memory density as usable capacity.
For a heterogeneous fleet, this logic dictates a bifurcated strategy. Our 175B parameter model requires about 350 GB just for FP16 weights; with the 80 GB per-device admission budget that means at least 5 GPUs before KV cache, activation buffers, runtime workspace, and tensor-parallel granularity are included. In practice, an 8-GPU tensor-parallel replica is the cleaner scheduling unit and is a candidate for exclusive access. Conversely, the dozens of 1B to 7B parameter support models, such as toxicity classifiers, query embedding encoders, and auxiliary generation models, are prime candidates for sharing. Packing these smaller models onto shared “utility nodes” liberates high-performance clusters for the heavy lifting of foundation model inference.

Separate training and serving pools simplify capacity ownership but can leave useful work queued beside idle devices. Consider a serving pool reserved for peak traffic while a training pool remains backlogged. This static partitioning protects serving capacity from training demand, but unused serving resources cannot help the training queue. Dynamic sharing allows that borrowing only when the orchestrator can return ready serving capacity before it is needed. The mode-switching cost determines how much capacity can safely move between the pools.
Repurposing a GPU from training to serving can require saving training state, releasing the old allocation, launching the inference runtime, loading weights, and warming the replica. The orchestrator must measure the complete path to readiness, including any overlap between these operations. If that path takes minutes, reclaiming training capacity cannot cover a burst that exhausts the serving reserve in seconds. Forecasts can schedule transfers ahead of predictable demand, while already-ready headroom covers shorter bursts; the required reserve depends on forecast error and measured reclaim time.
Consider a daily traffic pattern with low demand at 3 AM, growth at 8 AM, a peak at 2 PM, and a decline at 10 PM. A forecast with a 30-minute lead allows the orchestrator to begin reclaiming training allocations at 7:30 AM, provided measured replica startup fits within that lead time. As traffic falls, it drains surplus replicas before returning their devices to training. Pricing that policy against a static split needs three quantities: what serving reserves, what it uses on average, and how much of the difference training can absorb without eroding the surge buffer. The example below assumes its surge buffer suffices; a production policy must size the buffer against its own burst distribution and forecast errors.

Napkin Math 8.5: The diurnal GPU shiftConsider a fleet of 1,024 GPUs managed under two regimes:
Scenario A (static partitioning): The serving pool reserves 400 GPUs. That reservation is the forecast peak of 283 GPUs plus a 117-GPU surge buffer that absorbs forecast error and bursts shorter than a replica’s startup time, but average usage is only 150 GPUs (37.5 percent utilization). The training pool takes the rest of the fleet after the serving reservation and 6 GPUs held back as maintenance headroom, which leaves 618 GPUs, and its backlog keeps them at 100 percent utilization. Result: 150 GPUs + 618 GPUs = 768 active GPUs. Fleet utilization: 75 percent. The maintenance headroom stays unallocated in both scenarios.
Scenario B (dynamic sharing): Serving holds forecast demand (average 150 GPUs) plus the same 117-GPU surge buffer. Training reclaims the rest of the serving reservation, which is the unused 250 GPUs on average minus the buffer and averages 133 GPUs over the course of the day (the medium-blue band in figure 13). Because each role switch costs minutes, the orchestrator moves this capacity on the forecast rather than chasing individual traffic spikes. Result: serving (150 GPUs) + training (618 GPUs + 133 GPUs) = 901 active GPUs (the second training term is reclaimed serving capacity). Fleet utilization: 88 percent.
Dynamic sharing recovers 133 GPUs of effective capacity. At $2/GPU-hour, this creates approximately $2.3M per year in value without purchasing a single additional accelerator.

Safe sharing requires both a measured interference budget and an enforceable right to reclaim capacity. Isolation mechanisms address the first requirement; they do not decide which team owns a device or when a borrower must release it. That second requirement is an allocation contract across teams, and it applies to every pool the orchestrator manages, serving and training alike.
