When the computer vision team hoards 500 GPUs for a week while the natural language processing team sits blocked trying to push a critical bug fix to production, shared clusters devolve into a tragedy of the commons. Teams with the most aggressive job submission rates, the largest jobs, or the most persistent resubmission scripts consume disproportionate resources, while teams with more modest or intermittent needs find the cluster perpetually occupied. The result is organizational friction and underinvestment in slower-moving but potentially higher-value projects whose teams cannot compete for capacity on submission volume alone. A static serving reservation faces the same pressure from the other direction, since a training team that sees idle serving devices will want them.
Multi-tenancy and quotas turn organizational priorities into rules for resource allocation, borrowing, and reclamation that the scheduler can enforce. A quota defines an entitlement or a limit. Whether that entitlement becomes prompt, productive access depends on three further mechanisms developed below: borrowing that lends idle guarantees to other teams, reclamation and preemption that return them within a bounded time, and accounting that separates capacity a team holds from capacity it uses well.


GPU quota allocation typically operates at the namespace or project level, defining how much of the cluster each team is entitled to use. The simplest approach allocates fixed GPU counts per team: Team A gets 500 GPUs, Team B gets 300 GPUs, Team C gets 200 GPUs. This approach is easy to understand and implement but leads to systematic underutilization when teams have variable workloads. If Team A’s 500-GPU allocation sits 50 percent idle during a quiet period while Team B’s queue overflows with urgent work, the cluster wastes 250 GPUs of capacity that rigid quotas forbid Team B from using. The alternative, allocating less quota to each team, creates a different problem: teams are blocked from running legitimate work during peak periods even when the cluster has overall spare capacity.
Hierarchical quotas, which Slurm expresses through its account hierarchy and fair-share accounting (equation 1) and Kueue through ClusterQueues grouped into borrowing cohorts, separate a team’s guaranteed share from its maximum permitted allocation. In equation 4, \(\TeamQuotaCap\) denotes that maximum cap, not the guarantee; \(\DepartmentQuotaLimit\) is the department’s total capacity limit, and \(\SiblingTeamAllocation\) is each sibling team’s current allocation. Assuming those allocations remain within the department limit, the equation gives an admission ceiling before any reclamation:
\[ \EffectiveAdmissionCeiling= \min\left(\TeamQuotaCap,\ \DepartmentQuotaLimit- \sum_{\text{other teams}} \SiblingTeamAllocation\right)  \tag{4}\]
The ceiling caps what a team may hold; it encodes neither fair-share weights nor guarantees. When demand exceeds capacity, the scheduler still applies its fairness policy, the dominant-resource calculation of section 8.5.1, to the feasible gangs that fit under each ceiling. Unused guaranteed capacity can be lent within the hierarchy: if Team A uses only 60 percent of its 500-GPU allocation, the remaining 200 GPUs become available to other teams within the same department.



Lending turns unused guarantees into burst capacity. Suppose a small team holds a guarantee of 64 GPUs but needs 256 for a weekend-long training run while a sibling team’s guaranteed share sits idle. The small team may borrow idle whole devices up to its maximum quota. Those devices remain part of physical cluster capacity rather than becoming virtual capacity, and they carry lower preemption priority than owned resources. When the sibling team submits work that needs its guarantee, the scheduler reclaims the borrowed devices by preempting or shrinking the borrower’s opportunistic jobs.
Borrowing is what allows a multi-tenant cluster to reach high utilization. Without it, organizations face a painful choice between reserving enough quota to handle each team’s peak demand, which leaves capacity idle when peaks do not coincide, and allocating less, which blocks teams during peak periods even when reclaimable capacity exists elsewhere. Borrowing provides a reclaimable entitlement subject to the platform’s response-time objective, safety headroom, and current physical capacity. A team entitled to 500 GPUs can reclaim borrowed devices according to that contract, but the scheduler must not promise an immediate 500-GPU allocation when failures, nonpreemptible reservations, or recovery headroom reduce reclaimable capacity.
Burst capacity therefore expands aspirational maxima and fair-share weights, not simultaneous guarantees. The sum of guarantees that the platform promises to honor concurrently must fit reclaimable physical capacity after nonpreemptible reservations and safety headroom. Teams may advertise higher maximums or weights because borrowed jobs yield when guaranteed demand returns, but those values are not guarantees. Fractional sharing is a separate mechanism that requires an explicit MIG, MPS, or time-slicing contract.
Reclamation couples quota policy to the checkpoint infrastructure. The admission controller separates guaranteed jobs, which run on the team’s owned quota and face preemption only from higher-priority work, from opportunistic jobs, which run on borrowed capacity, yield first, and must checkpoint often enough that reclamation wastes little work. Elastic jobs soften reclamation further through the graceful preemption of section 8.8.2, shrinking one replica at a time toward their minimum viable allocation rather than terminating.
One policy for quota borrowing uses four tiers. Production serving (Priority 0) holds capacity protected from routine preemption. Production training (Priority 1) yields only under a defined serving-failover policy. Interactive and debug sessions (Priority 2) receive short execution limits to preserve iteration speed without indefinite resource occupation. Batch and research tasks (Priority 3) use surplus capacity and yield under their reclamation contract. These numbers label this example’s tiers; they are not Kubernetes priority values, where larger integers indicate higher priority. The hierarchy establishes precedence, but deadline protection still requires feasible capacity and bounded reclamation time, while lower-priority work needs an explicit starvation policy.
As the over-subscription discussion in section 8.5.2 showed, a partly idle device is still a whole allocated device, so the safe burst limit follows from reclaimability rather than average SM utilization. The scheduler must measure how quickly borrowed jobs can checkpoint, shrink, or terminate; reserve the I/O and network bandwidth required for that transition; and bound the amount of opportunistic capacity that can be reclaimed within the guarantee’s response-time objective.






Each eviction can evict again, so one admission reaches \(\PreemptionFanoutCount + \PreemptionFanoutCount^2\) jobs.
When a high-priority job enters a saturated cluster, the scheduler must decide which running workloads to terminate to free up resources. This decision is rarely isolated. In tightly packed clusters, evicting a medium-priority job to accommodate a high-priority request often triggers a preemption cascade, where the evicted job immediately attempts to reschedule itself by displacing lower-priority workloads. The disruption multiplies with each level. If the urgent job displaces \(\PreemptionFanoutCount\) medium-priority jobs and each of those, on rescheduling, displaces \(\PreemptionFanoutCount\) lower-priority jobs, one admission interrupts \(\PreemptionFanoutCount+ \PreemptionFanoutCount^2\) jobs after two levels, every one of which pays the preemption tax quantified below and adds a checkpoint reload to the storage system at the same moment. Two dampening controls cap that growth. A rule that evicted jobs requeue without preempting anyone themselves stops the chain at the first level, so one admission costs at most \(\PreemptionFanoutCount\) interruptions. A preemption budget limits how often any single job, or what fraction of capacity, may be displaced in a time window, which protects the jobs at the bottom of the priority order that every chain would otherwise reach.
The engineering cost of preemption extends beyond scheduling latency. The preemption tax depends on the exit path. A successful graceful checkpoint adds saving and restart overhead while preserving completed progress; a forced stop can instead discard work since the last durable checkpoint. Consider such a victim, a forced interruption of the 64-GPU fine-tuning run for our 175B parameter model. The scenario assumes lost work equivalent to 15 minutes of execution, followed by 20 minutes to reload optimizer state and 10 minutes of warmup as data pipelines refill and just-in-time (JIT) compilation and runtime initialization complete. The calculation prices replay and restart across the same allocation; it does not also charge for a successful final save.
Reconstructing the distributed data pipeline also belongs in the preemption contract. The checkpoint must preserve the sampling and loader state needed to resume the intended data order, alongside model and optimizer state. If the restart path omits that state, it can repeat or skip samples and lose exact replay of the training trajectory. A different shuffle order does not by itself prove statistical corruption, but the recovery policy must specify which changes are acceptable. The scheduler should therefore measure restoration and pipeline warmup as part of recovery cost, rather than assume that reloading model weights alone makes the job productive.
The resulting 45-minute tax combines discarded execution with reload and warmup time; it is not a measurement of continuous kernel activity after eviction. Spread over the run, it belongs to the Fleet Law’s coordination term \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) (equation 1.3), which counts scheduling decisions and failure recovery alongside barrier waits, so frequent preemption lengthens the average step exactly as frequent failure does. At $2/GPU-hour, the scenario values each event at $96 in allocation time. A low-priority run sits at the bottom of every cascade, so without a budget it can be struck many times a day. At the scenario’s 12 forced preemptions per day, it loses 9 hours of equivalent allocation time, or 576 GPU-hours for this 64-GPU run. A per-job budget bounds that loss directly. When a budget binds, the scheduler must consider waiting, another placement, or a defined emergency exception. The trade-off is reduced recovery churn against delayed admission, measured under the workload’s deadlines.



The 64 GPUs that sat idle for a weekend because a researcher forgot to cancel a reservation represent invisible waste in a multi-tenant cloud fleet. In a dedicated cluster, such waste is at least visible: the lights are on, but the fans are quiet. In a shared environment, the cost is hidden and compounds across thousands of jobs. Effective governance requires moving beyond simple “allocation” metrics to a tiered accounting model that distinguishes between what was requested, what was used, and what was useful.
Three tiers of measurement expose this gap between requested hardware and actual progress. Allocated capacity counts resources reserved for a job. Compute utilization measures hardware activity under a stated counter definition, which can include communication kernels or work later replayed. Productive utilization requires a workload-level measure of retained training progress or serving work that meets its objective, normalized to a declared reference rate. For example, a team allocated 500 GPUs might average 350 active-device equivalents (70 percent activity) while delivering 280 device-equivalents of useful work at the reference rate (56 percent of its allocation). These are time-averaged equivalents, not necessarily distinct sets of active and productive devices. The gap motivates profiling; it does not identify its cause or imply that necessary communication and recovery can all be eliminated.



Allocated, active, and productive capacity in GPU equivalents, each tier counting less than the one above.
Attribution in a shared fleet presents a control problem. Every admitted job needs an owner, project, workload class, and preemption contract so the scheduler can apply quota and recovery policy consistently. Kubernetes labels and Slurm accounts carry this scheduling identity.
This data feeds the utilization dashboard, the cluster operator’s primary instrument for fleet health. This view must synthesize per-team utilization against quotas, queue depth by priority class, and the fragmentation index, a measure of free GPUs that cannot be allocated due to topology constraints. It must also track preemption rates, spot interruptions, checkpoint traffic, and the recovery overhead they induce. These measurements let the scheduler distinguish idle capacity it can reclaim from allocated capacity whose apparent idleness reflects communication, I/O, or a rigid gang dependency.
Automated anomaly detection turns these metrics into investigation triggers. A sudden spike in a team’s consumption to 3\(\times\) its historical norm might reflect a runaway submission script or an intentional experiment. A growing queue can indicate insufficient capacity, but it can also reflect quota limits, fragmented placements, or a stalled dependency. A sudden power drop can accompany a shared storage stall, though job completions and changes in workload mix can produce a similar signal. Operators must correlate these alerts with admission decisions and job progress before changing capacity or policy.

Systems Perspective 8.6: The three utilization metricsEach tier narrows the investigation. Low allocated utilization calls for checking demand, quotas, device health, and placement feasibility. Low compute utilization on allocated devices calls for tracing input supply, communication waits, and runtime execution. Low productive utilization despite busy kernels calls for comparing retained progress with replay, synchronization, and other overhead. The metric selects the next evidence to collect; it does not by itself select the remedy.





Multi-tenancy requires both fair resource allocation and security isolation to prevent teams from interfering with or observing each other’s workloads. The stakes are real: ML models represent significant intellectual property, training data may contain sensitive information subject to privacy regulations, and the models themselves may encode proprietary business logic. Without proper isolation, a compromised or misconfigured workload in one team’s namespace could access another team’s model weights, training data, or inference traffic.
In Kubernetes environments, namespace separation provides an administrative boundary that must be reinforced by host, device, network, and storage controls. Role-based access control can restrict a team’s Kubernetes API operations, including job submission and access to pod logs, within its namespaces. Model artifacts in external storage require their own authorization policies, and cluster-wide scheduling controls require appropriately scoped permissions. Each boundary needs its own enforcement beyond namespace ownership.
Network policies restrict permitted traffic when the installed network plugin enforces them. A policy can allow communication among an admitted gang while denying unwanted cross-namespace connections, but it must cover the paths the workload actually uses. Ring AllReduce exchanges chunks along ring neighbors, while other collective algorithms use different peer patterns. Host networking and additional device interfaces require verification of the applicable enforcement boundary. Connection filtering does not encrypt gradient traffic; confidentiality on permitted paths requires separate controls. Egress restrictions can reduce exfiltration opportunities, subject to the same enforcement and coverage checks.
Across teams, the isolation spectrum of table 7 becomes a trust-boundary choice, because colocated workloads now belong to owners with different exposure to one another. Security in multi-tenant environments extends beyond simple resource fairness. Side-channel attacks on shared GPUs are a documented vulnerability; by monitoring contention on shared caches or memory controllers, a malicious tenant can infer the architecture or even data properties of a co-resident model. In sensitive environments, MIG or dedicated devices can strengthen device-resource isolation, but neither creates a complete external-tenant security boundary by itself. A multi-tenant platform combines device partitioning with VM or container isolation, IOMMU configuration, driver and runtime hardening, authentication and authorization, and network and storage controls. Single-organization workloads with a narrower trust boundary can use MPS or time-slicing when weaker fault and performance isolation is acceptable.



Schedulers manage immediate resource assignments, while quota governance determines the entitlements and limits those assignments must honor. Periodic quota review cycles compare observed use, forecast demand, and the cost of meeting each team’s capacity promise. A team using only 40 percent of a 128-GPU guarantee does not necessarily block other teams if unused devices can be borrowed. The governance question is whether the guarantee remains justified and whether its reclamation contract lets the fleet use spare capacity productively between demand peaks.
The central tension in quota management is the hoarding problem. Teams can retain idle reservations to avoid queuing again when work becomes ready. For example, a workflow that pauses policy training while awaiting human annotations can leave its reserved accelerators unused. A training run delayed by unfinished tokenization can create the same pattern. These examples concern dependencies in particular workflows, not an unavoidable idle phase of all training. Utilization-based reclamation can release idle physical allocations to borrowers, provided the platform preserves any promised return time. Revising the team’s longer-term guarantee instead requires comparing expected demand with observed use. Clear return contracts reduce the incentive to hold idle devices without making low activity alone grounds for breaking a capacity promise.
Quota accounting should remain close to the scheduling decision. GPU-hours charged against a reservation, borrowed share, or preemption class make the opportunity cost of hoarding visible and let the control plane reclaim idle guarantees.
A concrete quota scenario shows how quickly idle reservations become expensive.

Example 8.2: Quota hoardingScenario: A research team reserves a static block of 500 GPUs for an upcoming model refresh.
Diagnosis: Upstream data delays postpone training, but the team retains the reservation to ensure future availability. The GPUs sit idle for 3 weeks, accumulating $504,000 in capital waste while other teams’ queues back up.
Systems lesson: An idle reservation should trigger a review of lending eligibility and future demand. The orchestrator can admit opportunistic borrowers under a bounded reclamation contract without changing the owner’s guarantee. Reducing that guarantee is a separate governance decision; lending owned capacity does not turn it into cloud spot capacity.


The “use it or lose it” reclamation policy addresses the most visible symptom of quota hoarding, but it raises a second-order question: when idle capacity is lent to another team, the system must distinguish borrowed capacity (preemptible on short notice) from guaranteed reservations (protected by SLOs). Defining borrowing, preemption, and guaranteed tiers as first-class policy primitives is the core multi-tenancy design decision.

Checkpoint 8.4: Multi-tenancy design decisions
Consider a 2,000-GPU cluster shared between a research team (60 percent allocation) and a production team (40 percent allocation):

Idle reclamation: decide whether the production team can borrow the research team’s allocation while half of it sits idle, and describe the preemption behavior when the research team submits a large job.

Even with isolation, quotas, and dynamic sharing in place, the cluster can still fall victim to systemic bottlenecks that defy simple monitoring. When utilization drops inexplicably despite full queues, operators must move from dashboards to systematic utilization debugging.

Self-Check: Question

A cluster monitoring dashboard reports \(85\%\) GPU utilization, yet researchers complain of slow progress and low experiment output. What distinction between fleet utilization metrics explains this apparent contradiction?

Allocated utilization (GPUs reserved by containers) may be high (\(85\%\)) while compute utilization (SM active time) is low (\(20\%\)) due to data loader stalls, or productive utilization (goodput advancing converged training steps) is near zero due to unhandled AllReduce synchronization deadlocks.
Hardware sensors on GPUs report utilization in hexadecimal rather than decimal percentages.
Grafana dashboards invert metric percentages when cluster temperature exceeds 25 degrees Celsius.
GPU utilization metrics only count CPU core cycles, concealing whether the GPU is plugged into power.

What is a ‘preemption cascade’ in a multi-tenant GPU cluster, and how can orchestrators mitigate its destructive impact on cluster throughput?

A preemption cascade occurs when a single GPU catches fire and burns adjacent GPUs in the same server rack; it is mitigated by Halon fire suppression systems.
A preemption cascade occurs when Slurm automatically deletes user source code repositories upon job completion; it is mitigated by Git branch protection.

High-level metrics can hide the gap between reserved capacity and useful progress. A dashboard reporting 85 percent allocation says how much capacity is assigned, not how effectively jobs use it. Debugging requires comparing that allocation with hardware activity and workload progress, then correlating telemetry with execution timelines to test the suspected bottleneck.
A zombie job retains an allocation after its useful execution has stopped. In a distributed run training a 175B parameter model, a rank failure can leave a 128-GPU group idle if worker cleanup or failure propagation does not complete. The surviving ranks may block inside a collective that will never finish, or a process left behind by a driver-level fault may resist reaping by the container runtime, so the devices stay allocated until a timeout or node-level remediation clears them. Persistent memory allocation combined with low SM activity is an investigation signal, not proof of a driver fault; valid input or communication waits can look similar. The operator must compare runtime health, step progress, and the workload’s timeout contract, then verify that old workers have stopped before releasing or reassigning their devices.
The data starvation pattern manifests as a high-frequency sawtooth wave in GPU utilization, where the device oscillates between 100 percent load (forward/backward pass) and 0 percent load (waiting for the next batch). While the average utilization might appear acceptable at 60 to 70 percent, the GPU is effectively idling for a third of its life. This occurs when the CPU-bound data pipeline cannot sustain the throughput required by the GPU, a common scenario in computer vision where JPEG decoding and augmentation saturate host CPUs. The data stall ratio of equation 4.4 quantifies the loss as the fraction of each step spent waiting for input, and a timeline that aligns the idle intervals with input waits supports the diagnosis; utilization variance alone does not identify the cause. The remedy depends on whether decoding, storage, or transfer limits the input path.
A communication bottleneck can leave ranks waiting for collectives, though communication kernels can also keep SM activity high. Per-rank gradient traffic depends on gradient precision, sharding, and the parallelism layout, so the ratio of step time to compute-only time (forward plus backward passes in isolation) is a quicker first bound on exposed overhead. If total iteration time exceeds 1.5\(\times\) compute-only time, non-compute overhead exceeds 0.5\(\times\) compute time, which is material but not dominant. Setting \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) and \(\OverlappedTime\) to zero in the Fleet Law (equation 1.3) leaves \(\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount+ \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), under which communication exceeds per-device computation only when the ratio is greater than 2\(\times\). Real steps also contain synchronization waits and input stalls, so profiling must separate communication from those before the ratio is read as a communication diagnosis. Placement can reduce exposed communication when it improves the relevant paths. Gradient accumulation can reduce synchronization frequency only when the runtime defers gradient exchange across accumulation steps.
Memory fragmentation can prevent admission even when aggregate free memory appears sufficient. An allocator requiring a large contiguous KV-cache region may fail to place a new sequence when free space is split across smaller regions. The diagnosis therefore depends on the allocator’s requirements, rather than merely the percentage of HBM occupied. Comparing live token demand with reserved cache capacity helps expose unusable space. Paged cache allocation reduces the need for contiguous sequence storage. For the fleet scheduler, the allocator matters through its result, the number of concurrent requests a replica can hold, because that measured capacity sets how many replicas the serving envelope needs. Any throughput gain depends on request lengths, batching, and the allocator baseline.

The debugging example illustrates a broader principle that applies to every system across the fleet stack: scheduling systems are only as effective as the policies they implement, and policies must evolve alongside infrastructure. When infrastructure changes (new hardware generations are added, network topologies are upgraded, workload mixes shift from training-dominant to serving-dominant), the policies encoded in scheduler configuration, job templates, and organizational practices must be re-evaluated and updated. The most expensive scheduling bug is often not a software defect but a policy that was correct for the old infrastructure and was never updated for the new one.
This principle connects scheduling mechanics to fleet governance. Technical policies (GPU type matching, gang scheduling timeouts, preemption grace periods) interact with organizational policies (team quotas, priority hierarchies, cost allocation) and human behavior (job template reuse, resource request habits, queue submission patterns). Effective fleet orchestration requires attending to all three layers simultaneously.

Those policy-infrastructure mismatches recur as a small set of misconceptions that can make an apparently healthy scheduler waste expensive fleet capacity. It is tempting to look at a cluster running at 98 percent utilization and declare victory, only to discover that researchers have stopped submitting jobs entirely because wait times have stretched into weeks. Each misconception below follows the same pattern, in which optimizing one visible metric degrades the outcome the fleet exists to deliver.

Fallacy: More sophisticated scheduling algorithms always improve utilization.
Engineers facing low utilization often reach for more advanced schedulers, assuming the algorithm is the bottleneck. As the debugging example in section 8.13 demonstrates, the root cause is frequently policy misconfiguration, not algorithmic limitation. A simple FIFO scheduler with correct policies (capability-based matching, backfill with timeouts, appropriate gang scheduling constraints) often outperforms a sophisticated scheduler with incorrect policies. Before upgrading the scheduler, audit the policies: confirm that users are not requesting resources they do not need, that heterogeneous resources are properly exposed, and that gang-scheduling timeouts are configured.


Pitfall: Treating all GPU-hours as equal when measuring utilization.
An unlabeled “GPU utilization” percentage can conflate allocation with activity or useful work. For example, 80 percent of fleet capacity might be allocated while 15 percent of the fleet waits in incomplete groups and another 5 percent waits for input, leaving at most 60 percent executing useful training in that snapshot. Such a breakdown comes from scheduler and runtime evidence, which an activity counter cannot supply. The allocated, compute, and productive tiers of section 8.12.4 keep these measurements distinct, with productive capacity tied to a stated workload objective and reference rate.


Fallacy: Gang scheduling is always necessary for distributed training.
Gang scheduling prevents partial-allocation deadlock for a rigid synchronous group, but the required group need not equal the job’s maximum requested size. Asynchronous workers may progress independently, while elastic training can begin with its minimum viable gang and resize at supported boundaries. Independent hyperparameter trials can also run separately. The scheduler gains flexibility by admitting the actual unit of progress, while preserving atomic allocation wherever synchronous dependencies require it. Changes to worker count or synchronization policy still require convergence validation.


Pitfall: Setting static quotas based on peak demand.
Organizations commonly set team quotas to handle worst-case demand, reasoning that teams need guaranteed access during crunch periods. If Team A’s peak demand is 500 GPUs and Team B’s is 300 GPUs, the cluster needs 800 GPUs with static quotas. In practice, peaks rarely coincide. A 600-GPU cluster can accommodate either peak when the other team’s simultaneous demand leaves enough capacity, but it cannot guarantee both peaks concurrently. Hierarchical fair-share with borrowing uses that statistical opportunity only when the declared guarantees fit physical capacity and borrowed work can yield within the reclamation contract. In this example, sizing static quotas to the sum of the peaks provisions 200 GPUs, a quarter of the 800-GPU cluster, as guarantees that sit unused whenever the peaks do not coincide.


Fallacy: Spot instances are always cheaper for training.
Actual savings depend on the billed overhead each interruption adds, not on the scenario’s 60 to 90 percent discount band. Consider 15-minute checkpoint overhead and 30-minute restart overhead, totaling 45 minutes of billed nonproductive time per event. If each event follows 2 hours of retained training progress, the nominal 65 percent discount becomes about 52 percent savings under the fixed-allocation model. This illustration assumes a successful save and no replay; a real interruption budget must also include discarded progress when the save cannot finish. The scheduler must separately account for unbilled capacity waits when evaluating deadlines. Sufficient billed overhead can erase the discount, regardless of the advertised rate.


Pitfall: Ignoring topology when scheduling distributed training.
Schedulers that ignore connectivity can place communication-intensive groups across paths with less available bandwidth or more contention. On a fleet with NVLink confined to each node, spreading a tensor-parallel group across nodes moves its traffic onto the inter-node fabric; other hardware can expose larger NVLink domains. Crossing a spine switch does not itself prove congestion, so the placement decision must compare effective path capacity and competing traffic. A measured throughput penalty accumulates over a long run and may exceed the delay of waiting for a more suitable allocation. The scheduler must weigh that gain against queue delay and fragmentation.


Pitfall: Using elastic training to avoid gang-scheduling decisions.
Elastic training complements gang scheduling by moving between viable execution groups. With a fixed 8-way tensor-parallel layout, each group still requires eight workers; changing the number of data-parallel replicas does not relax that requirement. A runtime that changes the tensor or pipeline layout must also redistribute state and establish a new viable group. The scheduler must honor the supported resize granularity, atomic admission requirements, and placement budget for each configuration. Elasticity adds feasible choices; it does not make an incomplete group productive or an arbitrary placement efficient.


Fallacy: The scheduler needs no workload-specific validation.
Scheduler configuration needs revalidation as workloads evolve. A preemption grace period that suffices for one model may be too short for another to save state, while placement weights suited to an earlier topology can strand capacity after an expansion. The constructed debugging example in section 8.13 raises utilization from 60 percent to 84 percent through policy changes without new hardware. That result illustrates the value of checking capability matching, gang admission, and recovery contracts; it is not a promised gain from tuning defaults. The operator must compare queue delay, retained progress, and service objectives before and after a policy change.


Pitfall: Treating high utilization as proof of cluster health.
A high allocated-GPU percentage does not establish that the cluster has enough headroom to admit new work promptly. The exponential-service case of notebook 8.1, an M/M/1 queue, shows the pressure near saturation, since mean queue wait divided by mean service time is \(\ServingUtilization/(1-\ServingUtilization)\), where \(\ServingUtilization\) is offered service load relative to service capacity. This model assumes Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, and a single server; it does not turn a GPU-busy percentage into a prediction for a gang-scheduled fleet. Real headroom targets depend on arrival bursts, job sizes, placement constraints, and the queue-delay or serving-latency objective. The operator must measure those outcomes instead of applying a universal utilization threshold.

Recognizing these fallacies prevents platform teams from chasing false optimizations that look good on dashboards but degrade developer velocity. The core orchestration principles that successfully navigate these trade-offs share a common thread: they treat scheduling as an engineering discipline, not an administrative function.

Fleet orchestration transforms raw data center capacity into productive ML infrastructure by governing how silicon, bandwidth, and state interact across time and space. Orchestration spends Coordination, the third axis of C³, so that Compute and Communication capacity turn into useful progress. In Fleet Law terms (equation 1.3), placement sets the communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) of every step, and preemption and recovery, amortized over the run, enter the coordination term \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\). Queue wait and gang admission are coordination costs too, but they delay the first step rather than lengthening any step, so they appear in end-to-end completion time rather than in the per-step law. Multi-tenancy and quota policy decide how much of that time allocated compute spends doing useful work. Hardware capability sets the feasible choices; the scheduler turns those choices into useful allocations by preserving ownership, coordinating recovery, and matching placement to workload demand.
Feasibility is the first filter. Gang size, topology locality, multi-dimensional fit, and accelerator compatibility decide which allocations a job can actually run, and only then can a fairness policy choose among them (principle \(\ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}\)). Quota borrowing extends the same reasoning across teams, since a guarantee is worth what the platform can reclaim within its response-time objective rather than the number printed on the quota.
Placement changes the physical paths available to a workload. Aligning model parallelism with the network hierarchy reduces exposed communication when placement is the binding constraint, but it cannot create fabric capacity that is not there. Elastic resizing and spot capacity widen the set of feasible choices by trading worker continuity for flexibility and price, and ML-aware schedulers sharpen the choice among them with workload signals such as attained service, iteration boundaries, finish-time ratios, and goodput. Every one of these levers pays a transition or integration cost that must be measured against the progress it buys.
At serving time, the fleet scheduler preserves a capacity envelope of indivisible replicas with SLO headroom and moves the training-serving boundary on measured demand, leaving request-level routing and batching to the serving system. When that envelope, the quotas around it, or the placements inside it go wrong, the symptom is usually a full queue beside idle accelerators, and the cause is more often a policy written for an earlier fleet than a defect in the scheduling algorithm.

Key Takeaways: Scheduling is systems engineering

Distributed scheduling is fundamentally hard: Cluster scheduling must coordinate allocation ownership across machines despite partial failures, network partitions, and stale observations. Control planes balance prompt recovery against the risk of authorizing a replacement while an old worker still runs.
Gang scheduling prevents deadlock but reduces flexibility: Gang scheduling gives rigid execution groups atomic resource allocation to prevent hold-and-wait deadlocks, while backfilling and elastic resizing recover flexibility within the job’s minimum viable gang and transition constraints.
Fairness is measured over feasible bundles: DRF equalizes each tenant’s dominant normalized share across GPUs, CPU, memory, and network, but only among bundles that already pass gang, topology, and compatibility constraints (principle \(\ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}\)). Slowdown and maximum feasible wait test whether the resulting policy avoids delay and starvation, and a quota guarantee holds only as far as lent capacity can be reclaimed in time.
Topology determines performance: Where GPUs are placed within the cluster hierarchy changes the communication paths available to a job. Locality can reduce exposed communication, but waiting for a compact placement also costs time; compare end-to-end completion rather than iteration throughput alone.
Scheduling signals must match the objective: Workload characteristics support different improvements: attained service addresses runtime uncertainty, iteration boundaries reduce interruption cost, finish-time ratios expose unfair delay, and goodput guides adaptive allocation. Each policy requires validation against the fleet’s workload mix and recovery costs.
Useful utilization creates economic capacity: Reducing avoidable idle time can deliver more useful work from an existing fleet. Distinguish allocated, active, and productive capacity before valuing an improvement, and preserve the headroom required for recovery and latency targets.
Policies must evolve with infrastructure: Scheduling algorithms are only as effective as the policies they implement. When infrastructure changes (heterogeneous hardware additions, topology upgrades, workload mix shifts), policies must be re-evaluated and updated.



The same placement decision makes the displacement of overhead (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)) concrete. Co-locating a tensor-parallel gang keeps its collectives on NVLink and shrinks the exposed communication of every step, but the scheduler pays for that locality in coordination time while it waits for a feasible contiguous allocation. The bottleneck moves from collective bandwidth to queue delay or fragmentation rather than disappearing, so the right placement is the one that minimizes end-to-end completion time, not iteration time alone.

What’s Next: From orchestration to optimizationThe orchestrator counts serving capacity in replicas, and a replica that holds a full node of accelerators is allocated whether or not those accelerators do useful work. During autoregressive decode at small batch sizes, every new token streams the model’s weights from memory again, so a fully allocated replica can leave most of its arithmetic units waiting on data. Communication stalls, input delays, and long chains of short host-launched kernels consume an allocation the same way. Performance engineering locates which of these limits binds on the request’s critical path and tests whether a fix survives at the replica and fleet boundaries. The per-replica capacity it measures is the number this chapter’s serving envelope divides demand by, so every gain inside a replica changes how many replicas the fleet must hold.

For an exponential distribution (\(C_s = 1\)), the variance term is \(\frac{1+1^2}{2} = 1\), yielding \(W_q = 4 \times (1/\mu)\). For an ML cluster with heavy-tailed durations (\(C_s = 3\)), the variance term is \(\frac{1+3^2}{2} = 5\), yielding \(W_q = 4 \times 5 = 20 \times (1/\mu)\), which represents a \(5\times\) increase in expected wait time. Describe how priority inversion occurs when a high-priority distributed training job requires accelerators held by a low-priority job, and explain why simply setting higher priority levels does not resolve the blockage.
Answer: Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority job is blocked waiting for accelerators held by a low-priority job that cannot complete its exit path because intermediate-priority jobs are saturating auxiliary resources (such as host CPU, storage I/O, or network bandwidth needed to write a checkpoint). Simply increasing priority levels fails because the blockage is transitive: the high-priority job depends on the low-priority job exiting, which in turn depends on the low-priority job receiving sufficient auxiliary bandwidth (holistic preemption) to finish checkpointing and release the accelerators.

In a 1,024-GPU cluster receiving two 1,024-GPU synchronous training jobs, what condition causes a hold-and-wait deadlock under a non-gang scheduler, and how does gang scheduling eliminate it?

Non-gang schedulers allocate partial subsets (e.g., 512 GPUs to each job) where neither job can progress through synchronous AllReduce collectives, whereas gang scheduling enforces atomic all-or-nothing allocation so unallocated jobs hold zero resources.
Non-gang schedulers force jobs to time-slice GPU compute cycles, causing NCCL timeouts during AllReduce, whereas gang scheduling disables CUDA preemption entirely.
Non-gang schedulers assign GPUs across multiple racks, creating switch contention, whereas gang scheduling restricts all 1,024 GPUs to a single physical server chassis.
Non-gang schedulers allow lower-priority jobs to preempt higher-priority jobs, whereas gang scheduling locks node allocations until all jobs in the queue complete.

Answer: The correct answer is A. In synchronous distributed training, the marginal utility of a partial allocation is zero because every worker must participate in every AllReduce collective. If a non-gang scheduler grants 512 GPUs to Job 1 and 512 GPUs to Job 2, both jobs stall waiting for the remaining GPUs, burning idle power at 0% useful progress. Gang scheduling eliminates the Coffman hold-and-wait condition by mandating atomic all-or-nothing allocation: a job is either granted its full requirement or holds nothing in the queue. The time-slicing distractor confuses multi-tasking with resource allocation. The single-chassis distractor states a physical impossibility for 1,024 GPUs. The lock-queue distractor misrepresents priority preemption.
Learning Objective: Analyze how gang scheduling prevents distributed deadlocks in synchronous multi-node training.
How does heterogeneous gang scheduling differ from traditional homogeneous gang scheduling in the context of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) workflows?
Answer: Traditional gang scheduling allocates identical worker nodes executing symmetric bulk-synchronous parallel graphs. In contrast, heterogeneous gang scheduling atomically co-allocates asymmetric roles within a single logical job—such as memory-optimized nodes with high HBM for inference rollout generation alongside compute-dense nodes for policy gradient updates—requiring viable resource bundles and sufficient data-transfer capacity across roles. Measured production and consumption rates reveal imbalance; continuous or perfectly balanced routing is not guaranteed.

True or False: A hypothetical per-device annual hardware-fault probability of 0.001 is sufficient to conclude that all-cause interruptions will remain rare during multi-week jobs on a 10,000-GPU fleet.
Answer: False. That hypothetical probability covers only the stated device-fault event. Job interruptions also depend on worker count, runtime faults, links, hosts, and shared power or storage domains. A fleet interruption model must include those causes and their dependencies; a device-level annual figure does not establish a measured all-cause job failure rate.

When multi-GPU jobs leave unallocated accelerators spread across nodes that cannot be combined to satisfy pending multi-GPU requests due to intra-node interconnect requirements, the cluster suffers from ____.
Answer: fragmentation (or resource fragmentation). In ML scheduling, fragmentation refers to stranded, non-contiguous capacity across nodes that individually satisfy no pending job, despite the aggregate free GPU count being theoretically sufficient.

True or False: Under Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF), if Team A’s workload requires \(4\text{ GPUs}\) and \(8\text{ CPU cores}\) per worker while Team B’s workload requires \(1\text{ GPU}\) and \(64\text{ CPU cores}\) per worker on a cluster with \(100\text{ GPUs}\) and \(1000\text{ CPU cores}\), DRF equalizes each team’s share of their dominant resource (GPUs for Team A, CPUs for Team B).
Answer: True. Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) multi-resource allocation identifies each tenant’s dominant resource (the resource type for which the tenant requests the largest fraction of total cluster capacity) and equalizes the dominant shares across all active tenants, ensuring multi-resource equity without allowing single-resource monopolies.
Learning Objective: Apply Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) principles to multi-resource ML allocations.
Team A in Department X submits a new 16-GPU job. Which entitlement, feasibility, fairness, and ownership checks must its scheduler enforce before granting the allocation, and why is checking free GPU count alone insufficient?
Answer: Check department and team caps, distinguish guaranteed from borrowed capacity, and establish any required reclamation contract. Candidate bundles must satisfy accelerator capability, every requested resource dimension, gang membership, and topology before fairness chooses among runnable alternatives. Commit the allocation against current authoritative state, enforce its ownership at the resources, and update accounting. Free GPU count alone does not prove a viable group, timely return of borrowed capacity, or absence of conflicting ownership; implementations can interleave checks while preserving these dependencies.
Learning Objective: Explain how hierarchical entitlements and feasible resource bundles constrain fair admission in a multi-tenant fleet.

Self-Check: Answer

An administrator observes that average GPU compute utilization across a 1,000-GPU cluster is only \(55\%\), yet users experience multi-day queue wait times for 64-GPU jobs. Which diagnostic finding points to the primary root cause?

The cluster’s Ethernet cables are physically too long, causing optical signals to decay into radio waves.
Severe resource fragmentation and strict gang scheduling constraints prevent 64-GPU contiguous blocks from forming, while short jobs hold scattered GPUs across nodes without filling them.
The NVIDIA driver automatically caps utilization at 55% when GPU fans are running on low speed.
Python code running in user containers automatically halts execution whenever cluster utilization drops below 60%.

Answer: The correct answer is B. In multi-tenant GPU clusters, moderate average utilization (e.g., 55%) frequently coexists with long queue times due to fragmentation and gang scheduling requirements: uncoordinated, non-gang small jobs occupy 1-2 GPUs per node across many nodes, leaving hundreds of GPUs idle in aggregate but preventing any single 64-GPU contiguous gang allocation from assembling. Cable length, fan speed capping, and Python auto-halting are fictional distractors.
Learning Objective: Analyze the root causes of high queue wait times coexisting with moderate average cluster utilization.
During a multi-GPU training job, GPU SM utilization oscillates between 10 percent and 95 percent, host CPUs are busy, and disk wait is high. What hypothesis should the operator test next before choosing a remedy?

The GPU hardware is defective; the operator should replace the GPUs with CPU-only nodes.
The PyTorch model has too many layers; the model architecture must be pruned to 1 layer.
The input pipeline may be limiting progress; align GPU idle intervals with batch-readiness waits, then measure whether decoding, storage, or transfer is the limiting stage.
The cluster InfiniBand switch is operating in half-duplex mode; the administrator must power cycle the spine switch.

Answer: The correct answer is C. These signals suggest an input-pipeline investigation but do not establish its cause. Confirm that GPU idle intervals coincide with waits for the next batch, then separate storage, decoding or augmentation, and host-to-device transfer costs. Choose and measure a remedy for the limiting stage; adding workers to an already saturated host or moving transforms to a busy GPU need not help. The other choices assign unsupported hardware or model diagnoses.
Learning Objective: Use aligned runtime and host telemetry to test an input-pipeline bottleneck hypothesis before selecting a remedy.
What is a ‘zombie allocation’ (or ghost job) in a GPU cluster, and how can automated health monitors detect and remediate it?
Answer: A zombie allocation remains assigned after useful execution has stopped, for example when failure propagation leaves ranks blocked or orphaned processes retain device state. Low SM activity or retained memory alone cannot establish that diagnosis because legitimate input and communication waits can look similar. Correlate scheduler state with step progress, runtime health, process evidence, and the timeout contract; then enforce termination or node remediation and confirm old execution has stopped before releasing or reassigning the devices.
Learning Objective: Formulate a diagnostic procedure to identify and clean up zombie GPU allocations.
True or False: In a ring AllReduce across 32 nodes, if 31 nodes show \(95\%\) GPU utilization and 1 node shows \(10\%\) utilization, the node with \(10\%\) utilization is the only healthy node while the 31 nodes are encountering network hardware faults.
Answer: False. Utilization alone cannot identify which node is healthy: high activity may be useful compute or waiting inside communication kernels, and low activity may reflect input starvation or another dependency. Correlate per-rank compute and collective timelines, link health, and input waits to identify the rank or path delaying the group before assigning a hardware diagnosis.
Learning Objective: Evaluate telemetry signals to pinpoint straggler nodes in multi-node AllReduce rings.
When diagnosing training performance bottlenecks, operators inspect the ____ throughput (measured in GB/s) to ensure that batches transferred from host memory to accelerator HBM are not constrained by host bus contention.
Answer: PCIe (or PCIe bandwidth, PCIe throughput, PCIe transfer). PCIe transfer bandwidth (Host-to-Device / H2D) is a key diagnostic metric for detecting unpinned memory copies and bus saturation during data loading.
Learning Objective: Identify the hardware metric used to diagnose host-to-device data transfer bottlenecks.

Self-Check: Answer

Why is targeting near \(100\%\) GPU cluster utilization an operational anti-pattern for an interactive AI research and development organization?

GPU hardware components melt if utilization exceeds \(90\%\) for more than 5 consecutive minutes.
Modern deep learning frameworks automatically downgrade model accuracy when cluster utilization exceeds \(85\%\).
Operating above \(95\%\) utilization causes cloud providers to double their hourly billing rates without warning.
Near saturation, queueing delays can rise sharply and delay experimental feedback; allocation utilization alone does not establish a safe headroom target for the fleet.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Simple queue models contain a \(1/(1-\rho)\) delay term as offered load approaches service capacity. This explains why headroom matters, but allocated-GPU utilization is not that model’s load parameter. Actual targets depend on arrivals, job sizes, gang placement, and delay objectives; no universal 80–85 percent threshold predicts multi-day waits.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why operating a research GPU cluster at near 100% utilization is counterproductive to organizational velocity.
Explain the fallacy that ‘more sophisticated scheduling algorithms always improve utilization,’ and describe what operators should audit before replacing their cluster scheduler.
Answer: Low cluster utilization and long wait times are more frequently caused by policy misconfigurations than algorithmic limitations. Before replacing or upgrading a scheduler, operators should audit: (1) Resource request inflation (users requesting 8 GPUs when 1 is needed); (2) Unconfigured gang scheduling timeouts; (3) Mismatched hardware partitions (e.g., jobs requiring A100s when A10s suffice); and (4) Stale fair-share decay parameters that fail to balance contention.
Learning Objective: Explain why policy misconfigurations rather than scheduling algorithm limitations are often the root cause of poor cluster efficiency.
True or False: Gang scheduling is strictly mandatory for every distributed ML workload, including asynchronous parameter-server training, hyperparameter sweeps, and elastic fine-tuning jobs.
Answer: False. The required atomic group follows the execution dependencies, not the workload label or maximum request. Independent trials or asynchronous workers may progress separately, while elastic synchronous jobs still require their minimum viable tensor-, pipeline-, or collective groups and supported resize boundaries. Elasticity permits changing between complete feasible configurations; it does not make an incomplete synchronous group productive. Changes to synchronization or worker count still require quality validation.
Learning Objective: Evaluate when gang scheduling constraints can be relaxed in distributed machine learning workloads.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Which statement best synthesizes the central architectural challenge of fleet orchestration for machine learning?

Orchestration is purely a software compilation task that translates PyTorch code into C++ CUDA binaries without considering cluster hardware.
Orchestration requires balancing physical hardware constraints (NVLink topology, failure rates, power limits) against organizational policies (fairness, priorities, cost) across diverse, long-running, and failure-prone distributed workloads.
Orchestration has been completely solved by standard web application load balancers like NGINX, which handle GPU AllReduce synchronization transparently.
Orchestration only matters for single-GPU laptops and has no relevance to multi-thousand GPU datacenters.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Fleet orchestration operates at the intersection of physical infrastructure (GPU heterogeneity, NVLink topologies, power boundaries, component failure rates) and organizational objectives (fair-share equity, priority preemption, budget optimization, latency vs. throughput). It translates multi-dimensional, distributed resource demands into physical allocations while ensuring high goodput and fault resilience. Software compilation, NGINX load balancing, and laptop-only claims misrepresent the role of orchestration.
Learning Objective: Synthesize the primary architectural trade-offs across the fleet orchestration stack.
How is the historical boundary between HPC batch scheduling (Slurm) and cloud-native service orchestration (Kubernetes) evolving to meet the demands of modern ML lifecycles?
Answer: The boundary is converging: Kubernetes is integrating HPC capabilities (gang scheduling via Volcano/Kueue, topology-aware placement, RDMA bypass, and fair-share queues) to support large-scale distributed training, while HPC environments are incorporating containerization, declarative APIs, and dynamic service management. Organizations increasingly deploy hybrid architectures where outer Kubernetes control planes manage end-to-end pipelines and serving, orchestrating high-performance batch training clusters beneath.
Learning Objective: Explain how the convergence of cloud-native and HPC orchestration paradigms addresses modern AI training and serving needs.
True or False: In large-scale ML cluster management, maximizing raw GPU allocated utilization (the percentage of GPUs assigned to active containers) guarantees optimal economic value and research productivity.
Answer: False. Allocation measures reservation, whereas hardware activity can include communication, replay, or work that fails the quality target. Productive utilization ties retained training progress or SLO-meeting serving work to a declared reference rate. Economic value additionally depends on price, completion delay, fairness, and recovery or serving headroom; maximizing one unlabeled utilization or goodput metric does not establish the best fleet policy.
Learning Objective: Explain why fleet efficiency requires workload progress, declared measurement boundaries, and service objectives beyond raw allocation.

title: 8 Fleet Orchestration
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can jobs wait while expensive accelerators sit idle?
A thousand idle accelerators still incur ownership or reservation costs while queued experiments make no progress. More hardware does not resolve that waste when available resources cannot form the groups that pending jobs need. Free devices may be scattered across machines with unsuitable connections, or several jobs may each hold resources while waiting for the rest. On one machine, improving execution usually begins with the work already running. Across a shared fleet, useful progress also depends on which work can start, how long it waits, and what other work its allocation displaces. A short experiment needs a timely result, a long training run needs continuity, and a serving workload needs capacity before requests miss their deadlines. Favoring any one claim without considering the others can leave the fleet busy while delaying the results it exists to produce. Interrupting a job can free capacity, but preserving its state and restoring progress consume time and bandwidth. Waiting for a better placement can accelerate execution while extending completion time. Fair access therefore cannot be judged from device counts alone, and high utilization cannot establish that capacity is being used well. The engineering challenge is to honor these competing claims under changing demand and uncertain resource availability, while keeping the allocation process itself reliable. In C³ terms, orchestration pays coordination overhead to turn compute and communication capacity into useful progress while preserving fairness and latency headroom.

Learning Objectives

Analyze scheduling objectives, fragmentation, and deadlock risks for distributed training jobs under shared fleet constraints
Compare HPC, cloud-native, and hybrid orchestration paradigms for batch training and self-healing serving workloads
Apply gang, bin-packing, and topology-aware placement policies across NVLink domains and switch hierarchies
Design elastic training and preemption policies that trade throughput, recovery overhead, and spot-instance savings
Evaluate ML-specific schedulers by their workload signals, fairness objectives, and required integration with the training runtime
Design serving capacity, isolation, and multi-tenant quota policies that balance serving headroom, team guarantees, and borrowed capacity against training demand
Diagnose utilization losses from quota hoarding, noisy neighbors, fragmentation, topology mismatch, and data starvation

title: 8 Fleet Orchestration
text:
Consider two research teams sharing a 1,000-GPU cluster: Team A submits a 512-GPU job that will run for a month, while Team B submits hundreds of 8-GPU experiments that each run for an hour. If the scheduler continually admits whichever jobs fit, Team B’s small experiments can indefinitely block Team A’s large training run. The scheduling problem is the challenge of navigating this multi-dimensional conflict between throughput, fairness, and cluster utilization.
Partitioning computation (Distributed Training), synchronizing it efficiently (Collective Communication), and recovering from hardware failures (Fault Tolerance) solve the single-job scaling problem, but each of those mechanisms assumed that the job already held its accelerators. Fault tolerance assumed more than that. Its recovery paths drew on a spare pool deep enough to replace a drained node and on spot capacity whose loss the job could absorb, and neither exists unless something outside the job grants it, holds it in reserve, or takes it back. That something is orchestration, the policy that decides which jobs run, where they run, when one is preempted for another, and how competing demands share the fleet. A useful allocation must first be feasible, then worth granting under the fleet’s fairness, latency, and cost objectives. That ordering motivates the progression from admission and packing constraints to control-plane designs, topology-aware placement, elastic and cost-aware policies, schedulers built around ML workload signals, and finally the serving and multi-tenant contracts under which many owners share one fleet. Training and serving draw on the same fleet, so the capacity envelope this chapter allocates is the one both depend on; how a serving system spends its share, request by request, is the subject of Inference at Scale.
In the Fleet Stack (shown in the margin), orchestration occupies the Reliability & Control row of the distribution band, but the infrastructure band beneath it constrains its decisions. The scheduler must account for GPU heterogeneity, NVLink topology, rack power limits, and network bisection bandwidth. When scheduling goes wrong, debugging can require examining all four bands to identify whether the root cause lies in infrastructure (hardware constraints), distribution (algorithm limitations), serving (workload mismatch), or governance (policy misconfiguration). Orchestration connects physical infrastructure to distributed algorithms, translating resource requests into placements that respect both hardware topology and organizational policy.
The same conflict grows with the fleet. Consider a research organization operating a 10,000-GPU cluster. A single pretraining run of a GPT-3-class 175B-parameter model (Brown et al. 2020), the running instance of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) throughout this book, can hold a 1,024-GPU allocation for weeks. Because the scaling laws of AI Scaling Laws reward larger models trained on more tokens, each new generation of such runs asks for a larger gang held for longer, so the scheduler’s hardest requests keep growing. Suppose enough jobs of that class are queued that together they ask for more GPUs than the cluster holds, alongside thousands of smaller experiments and inference workloads all competing for the same resources. The system must decide which jobs run, when they run, and where they run. A first-come-first-served policy without backfilling or preemption can let large jobs occupy the cluster for weeks, delaying smaller experiments that researchers need to iterate quickly. A fair-share policy that divides capacity without respecting each job’s minimum resource bundle can leave many partial allocations and no runnable large job. The scheduler must navigate a multi-dimensional trade-off space where every decision affects throughput, fairness, cost, and researcher productivity simultaneously.

Brown, Tom B., Benjamin Mann, Nick Ryder, Melanie Subbiah, Jared Kaplan, Prafulla Dhariwal, Arvind Neelakantan, et al. 2020. “Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33: 1877–901. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2005.14165.

↩︎ Archetype A and its 175B-parameter running instance are established in Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3).

The economic stakes make these decisions consequential at every scale. A continuously provisioned 10,000-GPU cluster, valued at the chapter’s cloud-equivalent rate of $2/GPU-hour, represents $480,000 per day in capacity, whether the GPUs are computing useful work or sitting idle while jobs wait in a queue. If scheduling inefficiencies leave 30 percent of GPUs idle, that translates to $144,000 per day in unused capacity value, or about $52.6M annually. Holding useful work per active GPU-hour constant, improving utilization from 50 percent to 80 percent adds 3,000 fully utilized GPU-equivalents of productive capacity without purchasing additional hardware. That count measures the gain in useful work. Procurement planning asks a different question, namely how much hardware the gain replaces, and for that comparison the answer is 6,000 raw GPUs, because new GPUs run under the same scheduling policy would also reach only 50 percent utilization. Recovered capacity becomes cash savings only when it avoids purchases or billed resource time. Scheduling can therefore increase the useful work delivered by an existing investment, even when the fleet’s immediate expenditure remains unchanged.
Workload semantics, rather than an ML-versus-high-performance computing (HPC) boundary, determine scheduling flexibility. Rigid synchronous jobs in both domains require a fixed set of co-scheduled ranks, whereas malleable jobs can make progress across a declared range of resource counts. Gang scheduling1 represents the critical allocation constraint for a rigid training group: a job configured to require 1,024 GPUs cannot complete its distributed iterations with only half of them. Each collective requires participation from all ranks in its communication group, which may be a subset of the job. Ring and tree AllReduce schedules make this constraint physical: allocating a group of \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs but launching only \(\DeviceCount-1\) leaves the collective unable to complete. Partial allocation can create deadlock when rigid jobs retain their incomplete allocations while waiting for resources held by one another. Malleable data-parallel training can instead vary its replica count at explicit reconfiguration boundaries, but tensor- and pipeline-parallel groups usually retain a rigid base allocation. The scheduler must therefore model each job’s minimum viable gang and permitted resize points rather than infer rigidity from the workload’s field.
1 Gang Scheduling: Formalized by Ousterhout (1982) for parallel systems, where the “Ousterhout matrix” co-schedules related threads across processors in synchronized time slices. In a rigid ML training group, incomplete allocation prevents collective completion, so held resources can remain idle until the missing ranks launch. Without atomic allocation, under the chapter’s cloud-equivalent $2/GPU-hour scenario, a 1,024-GPU job that has already acquired 900 GPUs while waiting for 124 more burns approximately $1,800/hour. Gang scheduling prevents the job from holding that partial allocation.
Ousterhout, John K. 1982. “Scheduling Techniques for Concurrent Systems.” Proceedings of the 3rd International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems (ICDCS), 22–30.

↩︎ Ring and tree AllReduce schedules, each of which completes only after every rank’s contribution has been reduced, are established in AllReduce Algorithms and Topologies.
2 Placement Group: A cloud-native abstraction that requests instances be placed within a high-bandwidth, low-latency network domain. For the ML Fleet, placement groups reduce placement scatter and may expose higher network limits than unconstrained placement. They do not guarantee workload-level bisection bandwidth: topology oversubscription, concurrent traffic, routing, and the collective pattern still determine delivered AllReduce bandwidth.
If gang scheduling determines which resources must be available together, topology awareness via placement groups2 determines how efficiently they can communicate. Tensor-parallel groups benefit from placement within a high-bandwidth NVLink domain; a placement across slower links must still meet the job’s communication budget. Two allocations of the same size can therefore deliver very different useful throughput.
GPU heterogeneity is the third dimension. Many clusters contain mixtures of A100 and H100 accelerators with different compute throughput and interconnect bandwidth. Their training-throughput ratio depends on the workload, numerical precision, and communication path, so the scheduler needs measured performance and the applicable allocation cost. Memory capacity adds a hard admission test once pools differ in it. The common A100 and H100 variants both carry 80 GB of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), but smaller-memory variants of the same accelerator and older generations often share the fleet, and a job whose working set fits only the larger devices cannot run on the rest at any priority. The debugging example in section 8.13 returns to exactly such a mixed fleet. The scheduler must match workloads to appropriate hardware based on actual requirements, not user preferences, while maintaining high utilization across heterogeneous pools. When users request specific GPU types out of habit rather than necessity, the mismatch between requested and required resources can leave entire hardware pools idle while queues overflow on preferred hardware.
Job duration unpredictability compounds these challenges further. A training run may converge early and complete in days rather than weeks. Hardware failures may abort jobs unexpectedly, returning resources at unpredictable times. Hyperparameter searches may reveal early that certain configurations will not succeed, leading to voluntary termination. Fixed-step jobs with stable iteration times permit better release-time estimates than jobs whose stopping conditions or execution rates vary. Both ML and scientific computing contain these cases. The scheduler must distinguish an estimated completion time from an enforced runtime limit when deciding whether another job can safely use a temporary gap in capacity.
The interaction between these challenges creates combinatorial complexity. A scheduler must simultaneously handle gang scheduling constraints (atomic allocation), heterogeneous resources (capability matching), topology requirements (NVLink locality for tensor parallelism), priority and fairness policies (organizational equity), preemption decisions (which running jobs to interrupt), and cost optimization (spot vs. on-demand placement). Each dimension constrains the others: a topology-optimal placement may violate fairness policies, a cost-optimal spot placement may violate reliability requirements, and a fairness-driven allocation may fragment resources in ways that prevent gang scheduling.
These constraints define the central problem of orchestration: the scheduler is not merely packing jobs onto GPUs, but maintaining a consistent, economically useful view of a failing, heterogeneous fleet. The first step is to see why cluster scheduling is fundamentally harder than single-machine process scheduling. At fleet scale, placement stops being only an optimization challenge and becomes a distributed systems problem of keeping state coherent across thousands of machines.

Self-Check: Question

Based on the Pollaczek-Khinchine queue model \(\frac{W_q}{1/\mu} = \frac{\rho}{1-\rho} \cdot \frac{1+C_s^2}{2}\), under this illustrative single-server approximation, how does a queue with heavy-tailed job durations (\(C_s = 3\)) operating at \(\rho = 0.8\) utilization compare in expected waiting time (\(W_q\)) to a queue with the same mean service time and exponential durations (\(C_s = 1\)) at the same utilization?

The ML cluster experiences a \(2\times\) increase in expected wait time (\(8\times\) vs. \(4\times\) the average job duration).
The ML cluster experiences a \(5\times\) increase in expected wait time (\(20\times\) vs. \(4\times\) the average job duration).
The ML cluster experiences a \(9\times\) increase in expected wait time (\(36\times\) vs. \(4\times\) the average job duration).

Describe how priority inversion occurs when a high-priority distributed training job requires accelerators held by a low-priority job, and explain why simply setting higher priority levels does not resolve the blockage.
In a 1,024-GPU cluster receiving two 1,024-GPU synchronous training jobs, what condition causes a hold-and-wait deadlock under a non-gang scheduler, and how does gang scheduling eliminate it?

Non-gang schedulers allocate partial subsets (e.g., 512 GPUs to each job) where neither job can progress through synchronous AllReduce collectives, whereas gang scheduling enforces atomic all-or-nothing allocation so unallocated jobs hold zero resources.
Non-gang schedulers force jobs to time-slice GPU compute cycles, causing NCCL timeouts during AllReduce, whereas gang scheduling disables CUDA preemption entirely.
Non-gang schedulers assign GPUs across multiple racks, creating switch contention, whereas gang scheduling restricts all 1,024 GPUs to a single physical server chassis.
Non-gang schedulers allow lower-priority jobs to preempt higher-priority jobs, whereas gang scheduling locks node allocations until all jobs in the queue complete.

How does heterogeneous gang scheduling differ from traditional homogeneous gang scheduling in the context of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) workflows?
True or False: A hypothetical per-device annual hardware-fault probability of 0.001 is sufficient to conclude that all-cause interruptions will remain rare during multi-week jobs on a 10,000-GPU fleet.
When multi-GPU jobs leave unallocated accelerators spread across nodes that cannot be combined to satisfy pending multi-GPU requests due to intra-node interconnect requirements, the cluster suffers from ____.
