Choosing among those interventions requires pricing each exchange, and pricing requires a model of network performance.



Predicting transfer duration across a cluster requires separating two physical variables: the time required to initiate a message and the rate at which data moves once in transit. Across a data center fabric, these two terms govern communication latency and throughput differently depending on message size, network topology, and software overhead.


The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) prices a transfer over a single link (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)), separating a fixed startup tax (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) from a per-byte transit fee (\(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\)) (Hockney 1994). A collective pays that price at every step of its schedule, so the two terms, multiplied by the schedule’s round count and traffic factor, determine algorithm selection across the fleet.

Hockney, Roger W. 1994. “The Communication Challenge for MPP: Intel Paragon and Meiko CS-2.” Parallel Computing 20 (3): 389–98. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0167-8191(06)80021-9.

For collectives, the parameters must describe the effective path. Latency (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) is the startup cost paid at every step of a schedule, so it includes recurring software overhead, PCIe traversal, and network switching time; one-time communicator initialization is a separate setup cost. Bandwidth (\(\LinkBandwidth\)) is the sustained per-direction transfer rate. The critical message size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\), where the two terms are equal, carries over unchanged, but a collective changes what must be compared with it. Each step of a schedule transfers a chunk rather than the whole tensor, and a ring over \(\DeviceCount\) ranks moves \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes per step. A bucket of tens of megabytes split across a thousand ranks therefore yields chunks of tens of kilobytes, below the inter-node crossovers in table 3, even though the bucket itself is far above them. Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), a step is latency-bound; above it, bandwidth-bound.
The crossover explains two recurring optimizations. For InfiniBand NDR at \(\MessageStartupLatency\approx\) 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth\approx\) 50 GB/s, the knee sits at \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize \approx\) 75 KB, the value The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model computed for a single transfer. A 4 KB routing message is far below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so the startup tax dominates. If 100 ready messages have compatible destinations and can share one transfer, fusing them into a 400 KB message reduces the modeled cost from approximately \(100\MessageStartupLatency=\) 150 μs to \(\MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\approx\) 9.5 μs, roughly a 16× improvement before packing costs. More generally, \(\SplitMessageCount\) serialized messages of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\SplitMessageCount\) can cost up to \(\SplitMessageCount\times\) as much as one message of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) when \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\SplitMessageCount\ll \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\). Fusion is the first optimization, and it motivates framework gradient buckets and destination-aware token coalescing.
Compression is the second, and the crossover tells where it pays. A 140 GB gradient tensor sits far above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so shrinking its bytes shrinks the dominant \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) term directly, provided encoding and aggregation costs are counted. Even keeping only the largest 1 percent of values (Top-k sparsification, developed in section 6.9) leaves 1.4 GB of values before their indices are added, still far above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so the saving remains a byte saving. Compressing a 4 KB routing message, by contrast, offers little, because its unchanged \(\MessageStartupLatency\) term already dominates.
Across the typical data center interconnects tabulated in table 3, the critical-size column carries the load-bearing pattern: intra-node NVLink stays latency-bound up to several hundred kilobytes, whereas the inter-node fabrics cross over below roughly 100 KB. A message between those crossover sizes can therefore be latency-bound inside a node but bandwidth-bound once it travels between nodes.

The opening of this section claimed that a bucket far above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\) can still be carried in chunks below it, because a ring divides the bucket among its \(\DeviceCount\) ranks. Pricing one bucket at two group sizes tests that claim and shows what it costs.

Napkin Math 6.1: The critical message sizeProblem: A data-parallel job reduces a 25 MB gradient bucket with Ring AllReduce over InfiniBand NDR, with \(\MessageStartupLatency=\) 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth=\) 50 GB/s. The bucket is hundreds of times larger than the single-transfer knee. Does each step of the ring run in the bandwidth-bound regime on 64 GPUs, and on the 1,024-GPU reference cluster?
Math:

Knee: \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth=\) \(1.5 \times 10^{-6}\) s \(\times\) \(5 \times 10^{10}\) B/s \(=\) 75 KB.
Chunk per step: A ring sends \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) per step, 390.6 KB on 64 ranks (above the knee) but only 24.4 KB on 1,024 ranks (below it).
Ring time \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\left(\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\DeviceCount\LinkBandwidth}\right)\): about 1.2 ms on 64 ranks, of which the byte term is 1.0 ms; about 4.1 ms on 1,024 ranks, where the byte term is still only 1.0 ms.

Systems insight: The regime belongs to the chunk, not to the tensor. The byte term barely moves as the group grows, but at 1,024 ranks each step carries a chunk below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so startup dominates and the same bucket takes several times longer. Large language model (LLM) gradients are bandwidth-bound as tensors, yet a flat ring over a large group can still carry them in latency-bound steps. The levers then shift to larger buckets, fewer rounds, and hierarchy, which is why the algorithms of section 6.6 compete on round count as well as bytes.





Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\) the latency term \(\MessageStartupLatency\) dominates; above it, the byte term \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) does.
For collectives, the two regimes map onto different levers. In the latency-bound regime \((\PointToPointMessageSize< \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize)\), where MoE routing tokens, scalar reductions, and the small chunks of a large-group schedule sit, the levers are fusion, fewer schedule rounds, fewer hops, and a leaner software stack. In the bandwidth-bound regime \((\PointToPointMessageSize\gg \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize)\), where LLM gradients and optimizer states sit, they are compression, a byte-efficient algorithm, and link aggregation across multiple network interface cards (NICs). Classifying each exchange, and each chunk within it, into one regime is the diagnostic skill the rest of the chapter applies.

The α-β model estimates transfer duration without specifying how much independent computation can proceed during that transfer. Adding the entire estimate to compute time therefore overstates step time when overlap is possible. The LogP model (Culler et al. 1993) separates network transit from processor involvement with four parameters:

Culler, David, Richard Karp, David Patterson, Abhijit Sahay, Klaus Erik Schauser, Eunice Santos, Ramesh Subramonian, and Thorsten von Eicken. 1993. “LogP: Towards a Realistic Model of Parallel Computation.” ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28 (7): 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1145/173284.155333.

\(\LogpNetworkLatency\) (latency): The time for a message to traverse the network (similar to \(\MessageStartupLatency\)).
\(\SymmetricMessageOverhead\) (overhead): The processor time spent initiating or completing a transfer. During this work, the same execution resource cannot compute, making \(\SymmetricMessageOverhead\) the nonoverlappable cost. In a distributed training context, dispatch, device-kernel launch, memory registration, and runtime progress can all contribute. The value is an effective parameter of a particular software and hardware path, so it must be measured with the same collective, process group, and topology used by the workload.
\(\MessageInjectionGap\) (gap): The minimum spacing between consecutive sends or consecutive receives at a processor. It limits endpoint message rate but does not describe every source of link contention in a routed fabric.
\(\DeviceCount\) (rank count): The number of ranks in the communication group. The original model names this processor count with its final letter, P; this chapter writes it \(\DeviceCount\) to match its other collective cost formulas.

LogP distinguishes network latency (\(\LogpNetworkLatency\), which can be hidden) from processor overhead (\(\SymmetricMessageOverhead\), which cannot). Independent computation can overlap the network transit interval, while initiation and completion overhead remain exposed on the execution resource that performs them. A small overlap calculation makes this distinction concrete:

Napkin Math 6.2: Hiding communication behind computationProblem: A training pipeline attempts to overlap gradient AllReduce with the next layer’s backward pass. The backward pass takes 500 μs. Represent the complete transfer by a toy budget with network time 100 μs, processor overhead \(\SymmetricMessageOverhead=\) 50 μs to initiate, and \(\SymmetricMessageOverhead=\) 50 μs to receive. Assume both overhead intervals occupy the same execution resource as backward computation, with independent network progress and no contention. Can the communication be hidden under these assumptions?
Math:

Overlappable portion: Network latency \(\LogpNetworkLatency\) = 100 μs (data in flight while GPU computes).
Non-overlappable portion: \(2\SymmetricMessageOverhead\) = 100 μs (GPU busy initiating/receiving).
Compute available: 500 μs.
Hidden: All 100 μs of \(\LogpNetworkLatency\) can overlap with compute.
Exposed: The 100 μs of \(2\SymmetricMessageOverhead\) overhead cannot overlap.

Result: Effective time is 100 μs + max(500 μs, 100 μs) = 600 μs. The network latency is hidden, but the processor overhead remains exposed. Applied to every layer of a backward pass, the same split determines which gradient transfers a training step can hide (section 6.10.1).
Systems insight: The α-β model captures the total communication time. The LogP model reveals how much of it can be hidden. When designing pipelined training, optimize for low \(\SymmetricMessageOverhead\) (kernel bypass, GPUDirect) rather than high \(\LinkBandwidth\) alone.


The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model estimates transfer duration from latency and bandwidth measurements. LogP adds the processor/network distinction needed to estimate exposed delay in pipelined execution. Choosing a communication schedule therefore requires both a transfer budget and the independent computation available to overlap it.
When messages are large and pipelined across the network, the LogGP model (Alexandrov et al. 1995) extends LogP with a gap-per-byte parameter \(\LongMessageGapPerByte\), modeling the streaming cost of long messages. These models describe multiprocessor communication with endpoint rate and capacity limits; they are not restricted to one flow on one link. Their compact parameters do not explicitly represent every shared path, oversubscribed cut, or routing hotspot. For congestion-sensitive workloads, particularly AllToAll for MoE, measurements on the target placement must test whether the model captures the active bottleneck.

Self-Check: Question

A single-transfer model uses effective startup cost \(\alpha=1.5\,\mu\text{s}\) and per-direction bandwidth \(\beta=50\text{ GB/s}\). Which conclusion follows for a 4 KB transfer, and what must be added before classifying a complete gradient AllReduce?

The single-transfer knee is 75 KB, so startup dominates the 4 KB transfer. A complete AllReduce additionally requires the schedule’s round count and chunk size, then calibration for its placement.
The 4 KB transfer is bandwidth-bound because adding ranks makes every individual transfer saturate its port.
The 75 KB knee is a maximum buffer size, so larger messages cannot be sent over this link.
The critical message size defines the maximum possible buffer size that can be transferred in a single CUDA stream without host CPU intervention.

Sending a gradient tensor to a peer does not specify which workers must contribute or where the final result belongs. Collective operations supply that group-level contract, using a vocabulary standardized by MPI and inherited by modern ML communication libraries (Message Passing Interface Forum 2015). The four contracts sketched at the start of the chapter differ in what each rank holds afterward (figure 4). AllReduce leaves an identical sum (\(\Glyph{\Sigma}\)) on every rank, AllGather leaves every rank with the concatenation of all shards, ReduceScatter sums across ranks but leaves each rank one reduced shard (\(\Glyph{\Sigma}_i\)), and AllToAll performs a distributed matrix transpose, routing each rank’s \(\DestinationRankIndex\)-th chunk to rank \(\DestinationRankIndex\). Two further primitives complete the set and serve as building blocks for these four: Broadcast, in which rank 0 sends its data to all ranks, and Reduce, in which all ranks aggregate into rank 0.

↪ The bandwidth and latency cost terms of AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll, and Broadcast, under ring, tree, and pairwise-exchange algorithms, are developed in Collective Operation Complexity.


Definition 6.2: Collective operation
Collective operation is a distributed communication pattern in which every rank in a process group invokes a matching operation to aggregate, broadcast, or redistribute data. The operation’s contract specifies the output at each rank; it does not require simultaneous entry and does not, by itself, impose a general-purpose barrier before or after the call (Message Passing Interface Forum 2015).

Significance: Because the contract names only each rank’s result, the schedule that carries it decides how communication demand spreads as the group grows. A schedule that funnels every contribution through one endpoint makes the communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3) grow with \(\DeviceCount\), while a balanced schedule keeps each rank’s bytes nearly constant; section 6.6.1 quantifies the gap.
Distinction: Unlike point-to-point communication, a collective defines one operation over a process group. Ranks may enter at different times, and some algorithms allow one rank to complete before another has entered; correctness depends on matching the operation sequence and argument contract across ranks, not on barrier semantics.
Common pitfall: Treating a non-blocking collective as complete when its initiation call returns. The returned request or stream event represents work in flight. A dependent consumer must wait for completion, and a late rank can extend that dependency even though the collective is not a barrier.

(1) AllReduce: all aggregate and all receive the result. (2) AllGather: all send to all and concatenate. (3) ReduceScatter: all aggregate and results are distributed in shards. The primitive choice is the first scaling decision because it fixes which ranks must coordinate and which result each must obtain. The algorithm and placement then determine the traffic and its limiting resource. Different model architectures require different operations, and choosing a broader operation than the workload needs can create unnecessary bottlenecks.

AllReduce decomposes into ReduceScatter followed by AllGather. The decomposition is operational as well as mathematical, since Ring AllReduce’s first phase is a ReduceScatter and its second phase is an AllGather. ReduceScatter performs arithmetic, so it does not invert AllGather despite reversing the direction of shard expansion. Full ZeRO-style sharding and PyTorch FSDP7 use related partitioning strategies: AllGather parameter shards before a module needs them and ReduceScatter gradients after backward so each rank retains only its shard for the optimizer step (Rajbhandari et al. 2020). Sharding parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across workers reduces persistent model-state memory roughly by \(\DeviceCount\times\), while temporary full-parameter buffers and prefetching determine peak memory.
The same AllGather/ReduceScatter pair also appears in sequence parallelism, where an AllGather reconstructs the activation view needed for a local operation and a later ReduceScatter redistributes the result along the sequence dimension. A primitive’s semantics stay fixed even when the tensor dimension being sharded changes, so every schedule developed for the pair applies to both uses.
Beyond defining data-movement dependencies, collective operations carry explicit interface and numerical contracts. At the interface level, every rank in a process group must issue collectives in a compatible sequence; mismatched operation orders can deadlock or pair unrelated buffers. Operations also enforce shape and type contracts. AllReduce requires matching element counts and datatypes across all ranks, whereas variable-size exchanges require explicit per-destination counts and displacements. These invariants form the contract between the parallel decomposition and the communication runtime: the model decides which tensor slices each rank owns, and the collective contract guarantees that those slices can be recombined deterministically.
Reduction order introduces a second, numerical contract. Floating-point addition is not associative, so ring, tree, and switch-assisted reductions may accumulate the same values in different orders and produce different low-order bits (Goldberg 1991). A correct AllReduce therefore guarantees the specified reduction over all contributions, not bitwise identity across algorithms, rank counts, or hardware. Reproducibility-sensitive workloads must fix the algorithm and process-group configuration or use a reproducible accumulation scheme; ordinary training should treat small order-dependent differences as numerical behavior while still checking for larger rank disagreement.

The contrast between AllToAll and AllReduce highlights a fundamental difference in how collective operations scale with cluster size.

Systems Perspective 6.1: AllToAll vs. AllReduce: Why scale differsRing AllReduce can pipeline a uniform payload through neighbor exchanges. AllToAll presents a different scaling problem because every rank has destination-specific traffic, but the logical peer count alone does not determine its cost.
An AllToAll over \(\DeviceCount\) ranks creates \(\DeviceCount(\DeviceCount-1)\) logical source-destination transfers, yet each rank’s aggregate payload can remain fixed under weak scaling. Its lower bound is governed by the largest of four terms: source injection time, destination reception time, traffic crossing the fabric bisection, and per-message startup or scheduling overhead. Oversubscription and routing determine how much physical capacity those flows share. Message granularity determines how often they pay \(\MessageStartupLatency\). Routing skew determines whether one destination or link becomes the critical path. A full-bisection network carrying balanced, coarse-grained traffic can therefore scale well despite the quadratic logical connection count, whereas an oversubscribed fabric or skewed expert assignment can stall at much smaller \(\DeviceCount\).

Expert parallelism and large-scale recommendation systems can reach a communication wall earlier than standard data parallelism when their traffic exhausts injection, reception, or bisection capacity, or when routing and destination skew create hotspots. The primitive determines the traffic matrix; the physical fabric and routing distribution determine the scaling ceiling.




Logical pairs grow quadratically while per-rank payload can stay flat.
To make the AllToAll pattern concrete, consider a mixture-of-experts model with 64 experts distributed across 8 GPUs (8 experts per GPU). During each forward pass, a gating network assigns each input token to one or more experts. The tokens assigned to experts on remote GPUs must be physically moved to those GPUs before computation can proceed, and the results must be moved back afterward.

Napkin Math 6.3: AllToAll for MoE token routingProblem: An MoE model processes a batch of 4096 tokens across 8 GPUs (512 tokens per GPU). Each token is a 2048-dimensional hidden state in BF16 (4.096 KB per token). The gating network assigns each token to exactly 1 of 64 experts (8 experts per GPU). Assuming uniform routing (each expert receives 64 tokens), how much data does each GPU send and receive?
Math:
Each GPU holds 512 tokens that need to reach 64 different experts across 8 GPUs. With uniform routing, each GPU sends 64 tokens to each of the other 7 GPUs (keeping 64 tokens local).

Data per GPU-to-GPU transfer: 64 tokens \(\times\) 4.096 KB/token = 262.144 KB
Total data sent per GPU: 7 \(\times\) 262.144 KB = 1.84 MB
Total data received per GPU: 1.84 MB (symmetric)

Latency Analysis (InfiniBand NDR, \(\MessageStartupLatency=\) 1.5 μs, \(\LinkBandwidth=\) 50 GB/s):
Each of the 7 transfers is a 262.144 KB message. From the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model: \(\TransferTimeForPayload\) = 1.5 μs + 5 μs = 6.5 μs per transfer.
If serialized: 7 \(\times\) 6.5 μs = 45.5 μs. If all 7 transfers are issued concurrently, they still share the GPU’s 50 GB/s injection port. The aggregate injection lower bound is therefore \(\MessageStartupLatency+ \text{total bytes sent}/\LinkBandwidth=\) 38.2 μs, before contention and additional collective overhead. Full duplex permits simultaneous sending and receiving; it does not provide one full-bandwidth outgoing port per peer.
Systems insight: The injection result is only a lower bound. If the topology’s usable bisection bandwidth is \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and \(\CutCrossingDataVolume\) bytes must cross its minimum cut, the exchange also obeys \(\AllToAllExchangeTime\geq \CutCrossingDataVolume/\BisectionBandwidth\). Oversubscription reduces \(\BisectionBandwidth\), fine-grained peer messages add startup cost, and expert skew raises the maximum receive volume above the uniform estimate. The forward pass runs the AllToAll twice per layer, once for token dispatch and once for result collection; training also communicates gradients during backward.


With the six contracts defined, every row of the travel manifest in table 1 names a primitive whose output and traffic pattern are precise. The sharded data-parallel row repays closer study, because sharding changes how often those primitives run rather than which ones run.



Fully sharded data parallelism, developed in Distributed Training as a memory technique (Rajbhandari et al. 2020), keeps data parallelism’s mathematics but changes how its communication is invoked. A fully sharded rank holds only \(1/\DeviceCount\) of the parameters, so it calls AllGather before each layer’s forward pass to reconstruct that layer and ReduceScatter after the backward pass to leave each rank the gradients for its own shard, then frees the temporary full parameters.
Distributed Training counted the consequence, a displacement of overhead from memory to communication frequency. With one communication group per layer, a model with \(\LayerCount\) layers issues \(2\LayerCount\) collective calls per step where unbucketed data parallelism issues one AllReduce, or about \(3\LayerCount\) when parameters are resharded after forward and gathered again for backward. The byte volume changes far less. When parameters and gradients travel at the same width and the group is large, each rank sends roughly the AllReduce’s \(2\CollectiveTensorSize\), or about \(3\CollectiveTensorSize\) (\(1.5\times\)) with resharding, where \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) is the model-sized payload without optimizer state; different parameter and reduction datatypes shift that ratio. The call count carries its own price, because every call pays a startup cost. An effective startup cost \(\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) contributes approximately \(2\LayerCount\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) per step before overlap, or \(3\LayerCount\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) with resharding, so FSDP is more sensitive to \(\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) than an unbucketed data-parallel reduction even though its bytes barely change. The counts describe one grouping policy, since FSDP units need not coincide with layers and bucketed data parallelism also splits its reduction to enable overlap. FSDP implementations mitigate the startup cost through prefetching and communication-stream pipelining, but the relevant \(\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) must come from a matched collective benchmark rather than a wire-latency specification.

Selecting the right collective algorithm at each invocation requires distinguishing transfer cost from dependency exposure. An FSDP AllGather is latency-sensitive in the scheduling sense, because a layer cannot compute until its full parameters arrive. Its transfer can nevertheless be bandwidth-bound when the parameter tensor is large. Prefetching can hide part of that gather, while a ReduceScatter can overlap with the remaining backward computation. Neither dependency alone selects Ring or Tree; message size, group size, topology, and the available overlap window jointly determine the useful schedule.
The primitives specify what must be communicated, and sharding shows how often a training step invokes them. The remaining question is how to execute them efficiently on real networks. The most performance-critical primitive, AllReduce, admits multiple algorithmic implementations whose latency and bandwidth characteristics differ sharply. For the 70B gradient across 1,000 ranks, a simple tree that forwards the whole tensor at every level (the schedule section 6.6.4 examines) pays about \(2\log_2 1000 \approx 20\) full-message transfers against the ring’s two, a tenfold difference in byte time, so this choice can decide whether gradient synchronization can be hidden at all.

A correct AllReduce must give each of 1,000 GPUs the reduced sum of all 1,000 gradient contributions, subject to the floating-point reduction contract, and the algorithm that delivers it sets the cluster’s scaling ceiling. The naive answer, in which every GPU sends to one central server whose single network link must carry every worker’s gradient, fails first, which makes it the right place to start.


Consider a naive implementation using a Parameter Server (Star topology), with a dedicated server in addition to the workers. All \(\DeviceCount\) workers send their gradients to that server; it sums them and sends the result back. The server must receive \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and send \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes, so its bandwidth budget grows as \(\CommunicationTime \propto \DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize/ \LinkBandwidth\). At 1,000 GPUs, concentrating those transfers at one server creates a scaling bottleneck even if the arithmetic is fast.
This naive approach captures the pressure that early distributed ML frameworks had to manage: parameter-server systems receive, aggregate, and redistribute model updates through a server tier, while practical implementations shard the parameter space to spread that load (Dean et al. 2012; Li et al. 2014). Sharding reduces the per-server traffic from \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize\) to \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize/\ParameterServerCount\) (where \(\ParameterServerCount\) is the number of servers), but the server tier still grows as workers and model state grow, and it introduces additional complexity in parameter partitioning and consistency management.

The bottleneck comes from concentration, not from total traffic. Every AllReduce algorithm moves more total data as workers are added, because every worker’s contribution must be combined and every worker must receive the result. A star, however, routes all of that traffic through one endpoint, so the server’s time grows as \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\), while a ring spreads the same work so that each rank sends about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) and its time stays near \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\) however large \(\DeviceCount\) becomes. The ratio of the two is about \(\DeviceCount/2\), so at 1,024 workers the server’s byte time is roughly 500\(\times\) the ring’s, before startup, arithmetic, or contention are counted. Bandwidth optimality makes that comparison precise by measuring an algorithm’s required byte movement against a lower bound under a stated communication model, which the next derivation supplies for AllReduce.

War Story 6.1: When the parameter server became the bottleneck (2017)Context: In 2017, Alexander Sergeev and Mike Del Balso’s team at Uber open-sourced Horovod as part of Uber’s Michelangelo ML platform, where TensorFlow training jobs needed to scale across many GPUs without forcing every model author to rewrite large portions of training code (Sergeev and Balso 2018).
Mechanism: TensorFlow’s stock distributed training relied on a parameter-server pattern that concentrated gradient traffic through a central tier. As worker count \(\DeviceCount\) grew, the central server link saturated, degrading scaling efficiency.
Impact: Scaling training beyond a single node resulted in severe throughput bottlenecks and required complex, model-specific parameter partitioning.
Fix: Uber adopted Baidu’s ring-allreduce algorithm (Gibiansky 2017), wrapping bandwidth-optimal collective reduction behind a lightweight API that replaced parameter servers with ring communication.
Systems lesson: A collective algorithm is also a developer interface. Scaling improves when the communication primitive is both bandwidth efficient and easy enough that teams actually use it correctly.





Every specific algorithm can be measured against a lower bound for point-to-point AllReduce with an associative, commutative reduction and no in-network reduction or compression. Reducing one independent data item across \(\DeviceCount\) ranks and distributing its result requires at least \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\) item transfers in aggregate (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009). The count has two halves. Combining \(\DeviceCount\) contributions that start on \(\DeviceCount\) different ranks takes at least \(\DeviceCount-1\) transfers, because each transfer combines at most two partial sums and so reduces the number of separate partial sums by at most one. Delivering the finished value to the other \(\DeviceCount-1\) ranks then takes at least one transfer each. For an \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte tensor, the minimum aggregate sent volume is therefore \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes. At least one rank must send the average share, \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes; a balanced algorithm assigns that share to every rank.
Take \(\LinkBandwidth\) as each rank’s available send bandwidth, with equal receive bandwidth that can operate simultaneously. Dividing the required sent volume by \(\LinkBandwidth\) gives the full-duplex bandwidth lower bound:
\[\AllReduceMinimumBandwidthTime= \frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\]
As \(\DeviceCount\) grows large, the bandwidth lower bound approaches \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\), independent of \(\DeviceCount\). Ring AllReduce matches the required byte volume under this model; startup and local reduction still add time (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009; Thakur et al. 2005). On a 64-GPU cluster synchronizing the chapter’s 1 GB reference buffer over 50 GB/s links, the ring’s byte term is about 39.4 ms. The simple full-message tree, which forwards the whole tensor once per level on the way up and once per level on the way down (the schedule section 6.6.4 develops), pays \(2\log_2 64 = 12\) full-message transfers, about 240 ms. The byte-term difference of roughly 200 ms per step would accumulate to about 5.6 hours over a 100,000-step run if fully exposed. Actual wall-clock savings also depend on startup, placement, and overlap.



Ring AllReduce8 arranges nodes in a logical ring (\(0 \to 1 \to \dots \to \DeviceCount-1 \to 0\)). Each node sends to its successor while receiving from its predecessor. The chunk schedule distributes the required byte volume evenly across ranks, achieving the bandwidth lower bound in the ideal endpoint model (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009).
8 Bandwidth-Optimal: Under the point-to-point model above, Ring AllReduce sends \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes per rank and receives the same amount. With simultaneous full-duplex transfers at bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\) in each direction, its bandwidth time is \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/(\DeviceCount\LinkBandwidth)\). Adding send and receive bytes would double-count elapsed time.The algorithm splits the vector of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) into \(\DeviceCount\) chunks and then alternates communication and local reduction in two phases, a ReduceScatter phase (often called scatter-reduce) followed by an AllGather phase. Algorithm 1 states the mechanics before the figure and trace make the same dataflow concrete.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Ring AllReduce}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require $N$ ranks in a logical ring; each rank $i$ starts with tensor $\mathbf{g}_i$ of $M$ bytes, split into $N$ chunks
\Ensure every rank holds $\mathbf{g} = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \mathbf{g}_i$
\State assign the ring order $0\to 1\to\dots\to N{-}1\to 0$
\For{$N-1$ ReduceScatter steps}
    \State each rank sends one chunk (or partial sum) right, receives one from the left, and adds it into the matching local sum
\EndFor
\State each rank now owns one fully reduced chunk of $\mathbf{g}$
\For{$N-1$ AllGather steps}
    \State each rank forwards a reduced chunk around the ring and stores the chunks it receives
\EndFor
\State \Return the complete reduced tensor $\mathbf{g}$, held on every rank
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(N\)

Across the \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\) send/receive rounds each rank moves \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes per round, for \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes sent and the same received. The bandwidth term therefore reaches the information-theoretic lower bound, while the latency term grows as \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency\). Checkpoint 6.2: Ring AllReduce mechanics
Verify your understanding of bandwidth-optimal reduction:

The performance follows directly from the two-phase schedule in example 6.1. Each node sends and receives \(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\DeviceCount}\) bytes in each of the \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\) steps. \[
\RingAllReduceCompletionTime = \underbrace{2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency}_{\text{Latency Term}} + \underbrace{2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount} \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}}_{\text{Bandwidth Term}}
\]
The bandwidth term approaches \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\) as \(\DeviceCount\to \infty\), reaching the full-duplex lower bound: each rank sends nearly \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes across the two phases and receives the same amount concurrently. In contrast, the latency term scales linearly with \(\DeviceCount\). Across 10,000 nodes, 20,000 sequential hops accumulate substantial latency, which explains why Ring AllReduce becomes uncompetitive for small payloads.

Napkin Math 6.4: AllReduce cost for a 70B modelProblem: Consider a communication-only baseline for a 70B parameter model across 64 GPUs connected by InfiniBand NDR (50 GB/s per port). The bandwidth term barely depends on rank count, so this smaller group reproduces the bandwidth-only estimate from the opening definition while keeping the latency term visible. Each rank contributes a complete logical gradient buffer communicated in BF16 (2 bytes per parameter). This calculation isolates collective cost without establishing that the training state fits on each GPU. How long does one AllReduce take?
Step 1: Size the gradient payload. Each rank in this baseline contributes the complete logical gradient tensor of \(7 \times 10^{10} \times 2\ \text{bytes}\) \(=\) 140 GB. A hybrid layout that partitions the model would instead reduce corresponding gradient shards within smaller groups and requires its own calculation.
Step 2: Apply the Ring AllReduce bandwidth formula. \[\RingAllReduceBandwidthTime= 2 \cdot \frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\]
Substituting: \(\RingAllReduceBandwidthTime\) = 1.96875 \(\times\) 140 GB / 50 GB/s \(\approx\) 5,512.5 ms.
Step 3: Add the latency term. \[\RingAllReduceStartupTime= 2(\DeviceCount-1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency\]
Substituting: \(\RingAllReduceStartupTime=\) 126 \(\times\) 1.5 μs = 0.2 ms.
Step 4: Total communication time. Total: \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 5,512.5 ms + 0.2 ms \(\approx\) 5,512.7 ms.
Systems insight: The modeled full-buffer AllReduce takes over five seconds under the stated link and rank assumptions, and almost all of it is the bandwidth term. Its effect on step time depends on how much remains exposed relative to useful computation. When it is fully exposed, halving it saves about 2.8 s per step; across a 100,000-step campaign on these 64 GPUs, that is roughly 4,900 GPU-hours of reserved accelerator time. Large-scale training systems can launch reductions for output-side gradients while input-side layers are still computing. Partitioned training also changes each rank’s payload and participating group, so this complete-gradient budget must be recomputed for the actual layout.





Ring AllReduce’s byte efficiency comes with many startup rounds. As the group grows, the \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency\) term can exceed the byte-transfer term for a fixed payload; the crossover depends on the measured path parameters. Tree AllReduce reduces the number of dependent rounds. In the simple reduce phase, pairs combine contributions and forward partial sums toward a root, taking \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) steps for a balanced power-of-two group. The broadcast phase distributes the result in another \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) steps. This shorter dependency chain motivates the comparison before bandwidth costs are counted.



Ring latency grows with N; tree stays logarithmic.
The simple full-message tree loses parallel activity as contributions converge. A ring activates all \(\DeviceCount\) logical edges in each round. In a pairwise tree reduction, the first round has \(\DeviceCount/2\) senders and \(\DeviceCount/2\) receivers; receiving is useful work, not idleness. The next round has \(\DeviceCount/4\) senders and \(\DeviceCount/4\) receivers, and the final reduction exchange involves two ranks while the remaining \((\DeviceCount-2)\) have completed their upstream contribution. Sending the full message through successive levels adds byte-transfer time along the dependency path. This is a limitation of the illustrated schedule, not every tree-based implementation or every physical link mapping.
The resulting time complexity depends on the specific tree variant. A simple reduce-then-broadcast tree has logarithmic latency but nonuniform traffic and root/interior bottlenecks. Recursive doubling, in which partners at doubling distances exchange the entire tensor in each of \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds, has the same logarithmic round count and incurs \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) full-message bandwidth per rank. The following simplified model captures the latency advantage and the potential bandwidth penalty of tree-like collectives: \[ \TreeLikeAllReduceTime\approx \underbrace{2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency}_{\text{Latency}} + \underbrace{2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}}_{\text{Bandwidth penalty in full-message exchange variants}} \]
The latency term is logarithmic (\(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\)): for 1024 nodes, Ring needs 2046 steps while Tree needs only 20, and that 100\(\times\) reduction in steps makes Tree attractive for small, frequent collectives across large process groups, such as scalar reductions, control messages, or small-batch activation reductions. The bandwidth term carries the penalty, because tree-like algorithms can underutilize links or concentrate traffic on interior links, and recursive-doubling-style full-message exchanges add a \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) bandwidth factor; these penalties make naive tree variants a poor choice for data parallelism’s large gradient AllReduce, where bandwidth efficiency determines whether the network is saturated or partially idle.
For large-scale data parallelism, this bandwidth penalty decides the comparison whenever the implementation repeatedly exchanges full messages or creates root/interior bottlenecks. In the 64-GPU example of section 6.6.2, the simple tree already pays about 6.1× the ring’s byte time. For a 70B-parameter model’s 140 GB gradient AllReduce across 1,000 GPUs, a bandwidth-inefficient tree-like variant can erase the latency advantage that motivated it. Optimized double-tree algorithms exist precisely to keep logarithmic latency without imposing that naive bandwidth penalty.
Small activation reductions provide a useful case for fewer startup rounds. For an eight-GPU group communicating a 1 MB tensor, the simple model reduces Ring’s \(2(8-1)\MessageStartupLatency= 14\MessageStartupLatency\) to Tree’s \(2\log_2(8)\MessageStartupLatency= 6\MessageStartupLatency\), but Tree’s byte term remains about \(3.4\times\) Ring’s. Whether the saved startups outweigh those extra byte transfers depends on the measured latency and bandwidth. Tensor-parallel collectives also have a scheduling constraint independent of this comparison: a layer that needs the reduced activation must wait for it. A critical-path dependency does not by itself imply a latency-dominated transfer or select a tree algorithm.



The simple full-message Tree reduces startup rounds but repeats more byte-transfer work than Ring. Recursive halving-doubling, sometimes called the Butterfly algorithm, combines logarithmic rounds with the optimal byte volume under the flat-network model. It pairs ranks exactly as recursive doubling does, but where recursive doubling exchanges the whole tensor in every round, halving-doubling halves the exchanged region in each ReduceScatter round and doubles it in each AllGather round, and that difference removes the \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) byte penalty. For a power-of-two group, it uses \(2\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds: \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) ReduceScatter rounds followed by \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) AllGather rounds. A partner-bit index \(\PartnerBitIndex\) selects the XOR pairing with mask \(2^\PartnerBitIndex\). The ReduceScatter trace below visits those bits in increasing order as messages shrink; the matching AllGather reverses that order as the assembled result grows.
In the ReduceScatter phase (first \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds), GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 2^\PartnerBitIndex\) (XOR of indices). The partners retain complementary halves of the current tensor region and send the other half. Each adds the received contribution to the matching half it retained. After \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds, each GPU owns \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes of the fully reduced result. AllGather traverses the partner bits in reverse, exchanging completed regions and doubling the data held at each rank until every rank has the full result.
The performance of Recursive Halving-Doubling is: \[ \ButterflyAllReduceTime= 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency+ 2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \]
This achieves the best of both worlds: logarithmic latency (\(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\), like Tree) and bandwidth-optimal data movement (\(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\cdot \CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\), like Ring). The catch is that it requires nonneighbor communication (GPU \(\RankIndex\) must communicate with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 2^\PartnerBitIndex\), which may be physically distant), and it requires \(\DeviceCount\) to be a power of two. For clusters where \(\DeviceCount\) is not a power of two, additional complexity is needed to handle the irregular cases.
Recursive halving-doubling is used in MPI-style collective implementations and is useful as a theoretical point in the latency-bandwidth trade-off (Thakur et al. 2005). NVIDIA’s GPU collective backend, the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL), offers implementation families that include ring, tree-derived, hierarchical, NVLink/NVSwitch-aware, and pattern-aware choices, with exact names and availability changing by version and topology (Jeaugey 2017; NVIDIA 2026). Whatever a particular release calls them, practical communication libraries select algorithms through a topology-aware cost model because nonlocal communication patterns can create contention on shared network links that erodes theoretical advantages.

Thakur, Rajeev, Rolf Rabenseifner, and William Gropp. 2005. “Optimization of Collective Communication Operations in MPICH.” The International Journal of High Performance Computing Applications 19 (1): 49–66. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094342005051521.
The partner distance is where topology enters. Consider the ReduceScatter phase for 8 GPUs placed four per node on two nodes, GPUs 0–3 on the first and GPUs 4–7 on the second, which proceeds in \(\log_2(8) = 3\) rounds. In round \(\PartnerBitIndex=0\), each GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 1\), pairing neighbors: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7). They exchange half their data and reduce. In round \(\PartnerBitIndex=1\), the distance doubles: GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 2\), creating pairs (0,2), (1,3), (4,6), (5,7). In round \(\PartnerBitIndex=2\), the distance doubles again: GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 4\), creating pairs (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7).
Physical placement determines the cost of these logical pairings. Rounds \(\PartnerBitIndex=0\) and \(\PartnerBitIndex=1\) pair GPUs within a node, but in round \(\PartnerBitIndex=2\) every GPU on the first node exchanges with one on the second, so that round crosses the node boundary. On eight-GPU nodes the same crossing would appear one round later, at \(\PartnerBitIndex=3\) in a 16-rank group. In a separate 1,024-rank example, the final ReduceScatter round pairs GPU \(\RankIndex\) with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 512\). If the two rank halves occupy different racks, those exchanges share the inter-rack fabric. The algorithm’s logarithmic rounds and optimal byte volume therefore do not establish its runtime advantage; placement, shared paths, and the changing chunk size in each round must enter the comparison.



NCCL can use a double binary tree for many message sizes and topologies, which addresses the bandwidth inefficiency of a standard binary tree while allowing topology-aware tree placement (Jeaugey 2017; NVIDIA 2026). The idea is to construct two independent binary trees with complementary interior-node roles, then run both trees simultaneously, each carrying half the data.
The complementary-tree construction balances endpoint work by making ranks that act as interior nodes in one tree act as leaves in the other. With eight ranks, build the first tree by labeling the nodes of a binary tree in the order of an in-order traversal (left subtree, then node, then right subtree). In a balanced seven-node tree labeled from 0, in-order traversal puts the leaves at the even ranks 0, 2, 4, and 6 and the interior nodes at 1, 3, and 5; in one simple construction the eighth rank, 7, joins as one more interior node above that tree. The odd ranks 1, 3, 5, and 7 thus form the first tree’s interior and the even ranks are its leaves; the second tree shifts every rank by one position, so the even ranks become its interior and the odd ranks its leaves. Each tree carries half the tensor, \(\CollectivePayloadSize/2\), and the two halves never meet.
Two further steps bring the byte term down from the simple tree’s \(2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\) to about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\). First, each tree pipelines its half in small chunks, so while one chunk moves up from the leaves, the next is already leaving them and every level works at once; tree depth then adds startup rounds and a short pipeline fill, not repeated full-message transfers. Second, count what one rank sends during the reduce phase. As an interior node of one tree it combines the inputs of its (at most two) children and forwards one \(\CollectivePayloadSize/2\) stream to its parent, and as a leaf of the other tree it sends its own \(\CollectivePayloadSize/2\) contribution, so it sends about \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) in total. The broadcast phase mirrors that traffic, for about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) per rank across both phases, the same per-rank volume as the ring. This logical balance does not guarantee that every physical link stays busy or that both trees avoid shared fabric bottlenecks; rank placement and routing still matter.
The combined performance is approximately: \[ \DoubleTreeAllReduceTime\approx 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{2\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \]
The ideal bandwidth term approaches \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\) while the startup-round count remains logarithmic. This combination makes Double Binary Tree a useful candidate across message sizes that penalize either the ring’s many rounds or the simple tree’s repeated full-message transfers. Complementary endpoint roles do not ensure disjoint physical paths, so topology-aware tree construction seeks a good placement, and measurements must establish the achieved rate under contention.

The intersection near 1 MB in figure 6 marks where the modeled Ring and simple Tree have equal total cost. It is an algorithm crossover, distinct from the startup-versus-transfer crossover for one message. Setting \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime = \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime\) and solving for payload \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) identifies the point where Ring’s lower byte cost compensates for its additional startup rounds:
\[ \RingAllReduceCompletionTime = 2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency+ 2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \] \[ \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime = 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency+ 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \]
For large \(\DeviceCount\), \((\DeviceCount-1) \approx \DeviceCount\) and \(\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount} \approx 1\), so the ring pays a latency term proportional to \(\DeviceCount\) while moving each byte close to the bandwidth limit:
\[ \RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx 2\DeviceCount\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{2\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}, \quad \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime \approx 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \]
The tree has the opposite shape: logarithmic startup cost, but each message byte moves through more stages. Setting the estimates equal isolates the message size where the cheaper latency path stops compensating for the extra bandwidth work:
\[ 2\DeviceCount\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{2\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} = 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \] \[ \frac{2\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} - \frac{2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} = 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency- 2\DeviceCount\MessageStartupLatency\] \[ \frac{2\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}(1 - \log_2 \DeviceCount) = 2\MessageStartupLatency(\log_2 \DeviceCount- \DeviceCount) \]
Since \(\DeviceCount\gg \log_2 \DeviceCount\) for large clusters, \((\log_2 \DeviceCount- \DeviceCount) \approx -\DeviceCount\) and \((1 - \log_2 \DeviceCount) \approx -\log_2 \DeviceCount\), yielding:
\[ \frac{2\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}(-\log_2 \DeviceCount) \approx 2\MessageStartupLatency(-\DeviceCount) \] \[ \boxed{\RingTreeCrossoverPayload \approx \frac{\DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth}{\log_2 \DeviceCount}} \]
The log-aware crossover formula is the large-\(\DeviceCount\) approximation to the exact crossover \(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) derived in Ring vs. tree vs. recursive halving-doubling. Within this two-algorithm model, Ring wins above the crossover because its byte savings exceed its extra startup cost; the simple Tree wins below it because the startup saving is larger. Optimized trees and topology-dependent rates require separate comparisons.
On the reference cluster, with the chapter’s effective NDR \(\MessageStartupLatency=\) 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth=\) 50 GB/s across all 1,024 GPUs, the estimate gives \(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload \approx\) \(\frac{1{,}024 \times 1.5\ \MicroUnitPrefix\text{s} \times 50\ \text{GB/s}}{\log_2 1{,}024} = \frac{1{,}024 \times 1.5\ \MicroUnitPrefix\text{s} \times 50\ \text{GB/s}}{10}\) \(\approx\) 7.7 MB. A gradient bucket of tens of megabytes or the full model gradient therefore sits on the ring side of the crossover, while a reduction of a few hundred kilobytes sits on the tree side. The two other configurations in this section depart from that anchor in stated ways. Figure 6 uses a smaller 256-GPU group on a slower 200 Gbps fabric with \(\MessageStartupLatency= 1\ \MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\), which moves the curves’ intersection down to about 1 MB, and notebook 6.5 uses a 64-GPU group on a still slower, higher-latency fabric, where a 1 MB buffer lands almost exactly on the crossover.
In practice, NCCL’s algorithm selection is more nuanced than a simple two-way split. The Double Binary Tree algorithm offers logarithmic latency with near-optimal bandwidth, making it competitive with both Ring and Tree across a broad range of message sizes. NCCL also considers the number of channels (parallel communication streams), the network topology, and whether inter-node or intra-node links are being used. The effective selection logic resembles a multi-way decision tree indexed by (message size, GPU count, topology type) rather than a single crossover point.
Nevertheless, the crossover formula remains the essential mental model for understanding why libraries make the choices they do. When a library selects an unexpected algorithm, the crossover analysis provides the reasoning framework to evaluate whether the choice is correct or whether manual override is warranted.
Training frameworks decide which payloads reach that analysis. PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) groups gradient tensors into buckets (section 6.10.2), while FSDP groups parameter gathers and gradient reductions according to its sharding units. A bucket size alone does not locate a crossover, because rank count, effective startup cost, and available bandwidth also enter the comparison, so NCCL’s algorithm selection must be evaluated for the actual invocation and topology rather than inferred from a nominal bucket-size range. A single 1 MB buffer on a slower fabric shows how close to the crossover a real bucket can sit.

The crossover analysis makes algorithm selection a comparison under specified conditions. Communication libraries such as NCCL use tuning logic that accounts for message size, rank count, topology, and protocol. The simple model can identify a candidate worth benchmarking, but an apparent disagreement with the library is not proof that its choice is wrong. Compare measured collective duration and exposed training-step time before retaining an override.

The AllReduce cost models in section 6.6 assume a flat network with uniform endpoint bandwidth. A multi-node GPU cluster instead has distinct local and cross-node communication paths. The DGX H100 nodes of the reference cluster show the gap at its starkest, with each GPU’s NVLink capacity roughly nine times its one InfiniBand port, the bandwidth hierarchy that Bandwidth hierarchy established.
Hierarchical communication is the response to that inequality. Intra-node links are abundant and fast, inter-node links are scarce and expensive, and the algorithm must shrink payloads before they cross the scarce tier whenever possible. This is why the same AllReduce can be implemented as a local ReduceScatter, a cross-node reduction, and a local AllGather rather than as one flat exchange across every rank.


On a DGX H100 node, each GPU’s local NVLink capacity is 450 GB/s per direction, while its inter-node port provides 50 GB/s over InfiniBand. These are endpoint capacity budgets, not a promise of uniform achieved rate to every peer. Intra-node connectivity and simultaneous traffic still matter. A flat ring whose ordering repeatedly crosses node boundaries can leave local NVLink capacity unused while loading scarce inter-node links. Hierarchical AllReduce explicitly partitions the global operation into three stages that align communication volume with the fabric tiers (figure 7).







Figure 7: Hierarchical AllReduce: Three-phase decomposition that exploits the intra-node/inter-node bandwidth gap. Phase 2 runs an AllReduce across corresponding GPUs using InfiniBand. Phase 3 completes intra-node distribution over NVLink (the AllGather that returns each GPU to the full result). The schematic shows two representative ranks per node; the same decomposition applies to \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\) ranks.



By decoupling local aggregation from global synchronization, figure 7 stages the dataflow so that slower inter-node InfiniBand links carry traffic only during Phase 2 (Shard AllReduce). Write \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\) for the GPUs per node and \(\ClusterNodeCount\) for the number of nodes. In this middle phase, each corresponding-rank group reduces an \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\AcceleratorsPerNode\)-byte shard across \(\ClusterNodeCount\) nodes. A ring in that group sends \(2(\ClusterNodeCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/(\ClusterNodeCount\AcceleratorsPerNode)\) bytes per participating GPU and receives the same amount. Summing across the node’s \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\) GPUs gives \(2(\ClusterNodeCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\ClusterNodeCount\) bytes sent per node. Smaller per-port payloads improve elapsed time when the node has independent ports and sufficient fabric capacity; sharding does not create bandwidth on a shared uplink.
The three phases form a single causal pipeline. First, an intra-node ReduceScatter over NVLink performs a local reduction among the \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\) GPUs in each node, leaving each GPU with a \(1/\AcceleratorsPerNode\) shard of partially reduced data while consuming only abundant intra-node bandwidth. Next, each corresponding-rank group applies an inter-node AllReduce over InfiniBand to its \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\AcceleratorsPerNode\)-byte input shard, where the chosen collective algorithm dictates the bytes transmitted across the network fabric. Finally, an intra-node AllGather over NVLink redistributes the globally reduced shards within each node, completing the collective without consuming additional inter-node bandwidth.

Systems insight: Hierarchical AllReduce achieves a 4.8× speedup by reducing the inter-node payload from 1 GB to 125 MB per GPU before the Ring traffic multiplier. The flat ring used one port’s worth of fabric bandwidth because a single ring runs at its slowest edge; the hierarchical schedule uses all eight ports at once. That is also its precondition, since a node whose GPUs shared one uplink would carry the eight shard streams one after another and lose most of the speedup. This is why NVIDIA’s NCCL and similar libraries often select hierarchical algorithms on multi-node clusters when the topology supports them.


The speedup carries over to model-sized payloads, because every phase is linear in bytes. Applied to the chapter’s 140 GB 70B gradient across 128 ranks, the same three phases cut a flat ring’s 5,556.6 ms to about 1,200.7 ms, provided each GPU has its own port for the concurrent shard exchanges.
The volume’s running instance makes the same comparison on the cluster it was defined for. Archetype A’s 175B-parameter model produces a 350 GB BF16 gradient, and the reference cluster holds 1,024 GPUs as 128 nodes of 8. A single flat ring over every GPU would spend about 14.0 s per full-gradient reduction. The hierarchical schedule sends one-eighth of the gradient through each GPU’s port in a shard ring that spans every node and completes in about 3.1 s, a 4.5× improvement, of which the cross-node phase still accounts for about 1.7 s. Seconds per step remain a large exposed cost even after hierarchy, which is why the production layout for this instance shards the model so that each data-parallel group reduces a fraction of this payload, and why the overlap and compression techniques later in the chapter still matter at this scale.
These three phases also generalize to additional fabric tiers. For example, 4 racks of 4 nodes with 8 GPUs per node contain 128 GPUs. A rack-local ReduceScatter over 32 GPUs can leave each GPU with one thirty-second of the original payload for the cross-rack phase. The total elapsed time still includes both local phases, the cross-rack collective’s traffic factor, startup, and contention. A cross-rack oversubscription ratio alone cannot determine a speedup over a flat ring.



Hierarchy fits a fabric whose tiers differ in speed. A torus, the direct-connect topology of Google’s Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) pods, has uniform links instead, and its collectives reduce along one dimension at a time. TPU v4 pods support a 3D torus topology, unlike the 2D torus used by TPU v2 and v3. In the regular 3D torus model, each chip links directly to six neighbors \((\pm \Glyph{X}, \pm \Glyph{Y}, \pm \Glyph{Z})\) with equal per-link bandwidth. For collectives, the torus invites dimension-ordered reduction, which decomposes the AllReduce into sequential Ring AllReduces along axis-aligned torus rings. For a pod with \(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount{\times}\TorusSecondAxisChipCount{\times}\TorusThirdAxisChipCount\) chips, ranks first execute independent X-dimension rings for each fixed \((\Glyph{Y},\Glyph{Z})\) coordinate, producing partial sums along each X line. A second phase runs Y-dimension rings to combine those partials across the \(\Glyph{X} \times \Glyph{Y}\) plane, and a third executes Z-dimension rings across fixed \((\Glyph{X},\Glyph{Y})\) coordinates to complete the global reduction.

The byte term does not shrink with the rings. Because every axis processes the full \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte tensor, the bandwidth time is \(2\CollectivePayloadSize[(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1)/\TorusFirstAxisChipCount+ (\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1)/\TorusSecondAxisChipCount+ (\TorusThirdAxisChipCount-1)/\TorusThirdAxisChipCount]/\LinkBandwidth\) for equal per-axis bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), while the startup term is \(2[(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1)+(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1)+(\TorusThirdAxisChipCount-1)]\MessageStartupLatency\). Shorter rings reduce startup cost, but these sequential full-message AllReduces do not retain the bandwidth cost of one global ring. A bandwidth-efficient multidimensional implementation instead partitions the work with dimension-wise ReduceScatter followed by reverse-order AllGather. The X-dimension ReduceScatter sends \(\CollectivePayloadSize(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1)/\TorusFirstAxisChipCount\) bytes per rank and leaves each rank an \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\TorusFirstAxisChipCount\) shard; the Y-dimension ReduceScatter then operates only on that shard and sends \((\CollectivePayloadSize/\TorusFirstAxisChipCount)(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1)/\TorusSecondAxisChipCount\), and the Z dimension continues the pattern. The three terms telescope to \(\CollectivePayloadSize(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) for \(\DeviceCount= \TorusFirstAxisChipCount \TorusSecondAxisChipCount \TorusThirdAxisChipCount\), and the mirrored AllGather doubles that to \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\), the ring’s optimal byte term, while keeping the short rings’ startup count. The torus thus teaches the same lesson as hierarchy, which is to shrink the payload before each successive stage rather than send the full tensor through every one.
Dimension-ordered reduction follows direct neighbor links and separates axis traffic in time; it does not change the network diameter or eliminate contention with other workloads. The torus topology also provides natural fault tolerance through alternate routing paths. If one link in the X-dimension fails, traffic can detour through the Y or Z dimensions (at the cost of increased latency). The compiler and collective runtime must choose a schedule for the actual topology, message size, and available links.



Hierarchical and dimension-ordered schedules redistribute work across links, but their software reduction stages still require endpoint GPUs to receive and combine contributions. NVIDIA’s Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol (SHARP)9 moves that intermediate aggregation into the network. Instead of routing each partial sum through a GPU for arithmetic, an aggregation-capable InfiniBand switch combines contributions as packets pass through it.
9 SHARP (Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol): In-network computing on Quantum InfiniBand switches that performs reduction operations (such as sum, min, and max) as packets traverse an aggregation tree (Graham et al. 2020). The same work reports substantially higher reduction bandwidth than host-based algorithms and describes switch-resource limits on outstanding aggregation groups and trees, which can create contention when many collectives compete for the same in-network resources.

Figure 9 contrasts upstream dataflow in a centralized endpoint reduction against in-switch aggregation. In the endpoint tree of panel (a), intermediate switches merely forward raw packets, forcing all four full gradient tensors (\(\LocalGradient_0\) through \(\LocalGradient_3\)) across the upper links into a single Reducer GPU that executes every addition. In panel (b), SHARP offloads arithmetic to aggregation-capable switch application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs): each intermediate switch computes partial sums (\(\LocalGradient_0+\LocalGradient_1\) and \(\LocalGradient_2+\LocalGradient_3\)) in-flight, leaving only the combined shards for the root switch to finalize. Moving reduction into the network fabric halves the upper link traffic and relieves accelerator endpoints from coordinating arithmetic steps.

(b) Aggregation-capable switches add their inputs, so each upper link carries one partial sum and the root switch finishes the reduction; the result then travels back down the same tree. A software reduction tree also aggregates along its path, but performs arithmetic at endpoints rather than switches. The diagram compares where arithmetic happens, not measured speedup.



SHARP changes both terms of the cost model. On the startup side, it shortens the dependency chain. In a software-based tree reduction, each level waits for an intermediate GPU to receive, reduce, and forward its inputs; with SHARP the switch performs that step in the packet path, so no GPU execution stage or extra endpoint round trip sits between levels. On the byte side, each upper-tier link carries one partial sum rather than every contribution beneath it (figure 9), and in the idealized aggregation tree each GPU sends its contribution up once and receives the result once, where a ring rank sends nearly \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\). Endpoint memory traffic falls for the same reason. Switch processing and contention for aggregation resources add costs of their own, so moving arithmetic into the network changes the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) terms rather than eliminating them.
Which benefit matters follows the regimes of section 6.4. For small and medium messages, where startup rounds dominate, the shorter dependency chain is the main gain, although for very small messages fixed switch-processing overhead can limit it. For large messages the startup saving becomes proportionally small, and what remains is the byte saving at the endpoints and on the upper tier, which shortens the collective only when those links are the binding resource. Graham et al. (2020) report multi-fold reduction-bandwidth improvements and smaller application-level gains for PyTorch workloads when SHARP Streaming-Aggregation is enabled on HDR/Quantum InfiniBand switches.
Strong scaling campaigns (training a fixed model across more accelerators without proportionally growing batch size) expose the importance of this distinction between collective speed and step time. As the per-accelerator batch shrinks, each gradient tensor stays large (proportional to model size) but the backward pass per accelerator shortens, exposing more of the communication budget. The limiting term can still be bandwidth; strong scaling alone does not establish that startup latency dominates. In-switch aggregation helps when its reduction in endpoint work or fabric traffic shortens the exposed critical path.
SHARP does impose constraints. The switch must support the specific reduction operation and the datatype the job reduces, such as FP16 or BF16 gradients, and supported datatypes differ across switch generations. The number of concurrent aggregation trees is limited by switch resources. Large clusters with many simultaneous training jobs may therefore exhaust aggregation capacity. The HDR/Quantum implementation examined here uses InfiniBand; its measured gains cannot be transferred to an Ethernet deployment without an equivalent, supported aggregation path.



Hierarchy and in-network aggregation change where bytes move and where sums are computed. Their benefit still depends on mapping the logical communication pattern onto physical links. A Ring AllReduce among 64 GPUs creates a logical ring, but the paths carrying its hops can either distribute traffic or concentrate it on shared links. Two runs of the same training job on the same hardware can therefore differ substantially in communication throughput because of rank placement and routing.
Communication libraries like NCCL perform topology detection at initialization and use graph search to choose paths through the hardware topology available to them (NVIDIA 2026). For each pair of ranks, the library must determine whether the peer sits behind a local NVLink switch or 100 meters away across an InfiniBand fabric, because that mapping decides which physical links each logical hop occupies. Local GPU, NVLink, PCIe, and NIC connectivity informs those choices, but local discovery does not reveal every remote switch, route, or competing flow. Fabric configuration and placement information must complement the library’s view when diagnosing cross-node contention.
The topology detection process begins with hardware enumeration. NCCL queries the PCIe bus to discover GPU placement, NVLink connectivity between GPUs, and NIC-to-PCIe-switch affinity. From this information, it constructs an internal graph where nodes represent GPUs and edges represent physical links with annotated bandwidth and latency. A graph search algorithm then finds communication paths that maximize aggregate bandwidth while minimizing the number of cross-domain hops (transitions between NVLink, PCIe, and InfiniBand domains). This topology-aware path selection is what allows NCCL to approach theoretical peak bandwidth on well-configured systems, while topology-unaware implementations can leave a large fraction of bandwidth unused.


In the eight-GPU DGX layout considered here, each GPU has a dedicated inter-node NIC, and the fabric connects matching NIC positions to rail switches. Rail-optimized routing fits the corresponding-shard phase of hierarchical AllReduce: GPU 0 on Node A exchanges its shard with GPU 0 on Nodes B and C, GPU 1 exchanges with peer GPU 1s, and so on. The eight rails can carry these groups concurrently (table 9), subject to their physical capacity and competing traffic. Other collectives may require cross-rail paths.

If all eight shard streams converge on one remote NIC, that endpoint faces 8\(\times\) the balanced receive demand. In the equal-shard layout, matching each shard group to its intended rail distributes one-eighth of the payload to each NIC. This removes that particular concentration; achieving the predicted rate still requires sufficient switch, uplink, and bisection capacity for concurrent traffic.
Rail-optimized routing and hierarchical AllReduce reinforce each other. In the hierarchical decomposition described in section 6.7.1, Step 2 (inter-node AllReduce) naturally aligns with rail topology. GPU \(\LocalRankIndex\) on each node communicates only with GPU \(\LocalRankIndex\) on other nodes, which is precisely the rail pattern. This alignment is not coincidental; NVIDIA designed the DGX hardware with rail-optimized communication in mind, and NCCL’s hierarchical algorithms can exploit this structure when the topology is detected and ranks are mapped correctly. When the logical communication pattern matches the physical topology, each NIC carries its intended share of traffic and the cluster can approach its theoretical peak bisection bandwidth.
Misalignment between logical and physical topology is a common source of performance degradation that is difficult to diagnose without careful profiling. If process ranks are assigned arbitrarily (for example, by the job scheduler without topology awareness), the hierarchical AllReduce may route cross-node traffic through the wrong NICs or across rails, creating hotspots. In the worst case, all eight shard exchanges of a node converge on one NIC, cutting that node’s usable injection bandwidth to one-eighth of the rail-aligned value. Large deployments use topology-aware rank assignment (configured through device ordering such as CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, NIC binding, and the scheduler’s GPU placement policies) to ensure alignment.
Hierarchical execution and topology-aware routing connect the cost model to a physical placement. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) terms estimate the service required by each scheduled exchange; hierarchy redistributes work across fabric tiers, and rail alignment can balance corresponding-shard traffic across independent ports. None removes shared-capacity limits. Measured collective duration must confirm that the intended placement shortens the dependency path before the design is accepted.
