title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
A network provisioned for many independent requests can encounter a different load when a training job releases gradient exchanges together. Statistical multiplexing relies on traffic peaks not all coinciding; synchronized workers can instead compete for the same paths at the same time. Web services also have dependency chains and tail-latency requirements, but a bulk-synchronous training job makes the participating workers’ shared completion boundary explicit.
The ML networking inversion in table 1 concerns this change in traffic dependencies. Synchronous collective phases can generate correlated bursts and long-lived flows whose completion gates the next computation. Fabric validation must therefore measure collective completion under the expected load; average per-flow throughput alone does not establish that the job can meet its step-time budget.



Table 1: ML networking inverts traditional data-center assumptions: The comparison contrasts independent-request traffic with synchronized collective phases. Correlated demand and shared completion boundaries change the fabric’s capacity and latency requirements.










Workload pattern
Traditional data-center assumption
ML reality




Traffic pattern
Independent requests can arrive asynchronously
Collective phases can release correlated bursts


Flow type
Many short transfers can share available paths
Large collective transfers can create persistent “elephant” flows


Performance metric
Per-request completion and throughput
Collective completion and exposed step time


Loss tolerance
Recovery delays affected requests
Recovery can delay dependent workers at a barrier


Congestion
Statistical multiplexing relies on noncoincident peaks
Shared paths and fan-in can concentrate synchronized traffic






The bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)1 model, the lockstep at step barriers already met at the scale of one node (The Node), makes the dependency in table 1 explicit. In the synchronous training example, all 1,024 GPUs must complete the required gradient exchange before the next step can proceed. A 100 ms transfer delay adds 100 ms to that step only if it extends the critical path by the full interval; other computation or communication may hide part of it. At a barrier that waits for the last required result, tail latency, the slow end of the completion-time distribution (commonly reported as its 99th percentile, p99), decides when the step ends. Tail latency is not an outlier; it is the bottleneck.
1 BSP (bulk synchronous parallel): Proposed by Valiant (1990) as a bridging model between parallel hardware and software. Synchronous data-parallel training follows the same barrier structure (Goyal et al. 2017; Li et al. 2020).
Valiant, Leslie G. 1990. “A Bridging Model for Parallel Computation.” Communications of the ACM 33 (8): 103–11. https://doi.org/10.1145/79173.79181.

Goyal, Priya, Piotr Dollár, Ross Girshick, Pieter Noordhuis, Lukasz Wesolowski, Aapo Kyrola, Andrew Tulloch, Yangqing Jia, and Kaiming He. 2017. “Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1706.02677 abs/1706.02677.

Li, Shen, Yanli Zhao, Rohan Varma, Omkar Salpekar, Pieter Noordhuis, Teng Li, Adam Paszke, et al. 2020. “PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 13 (12): 3005–18. https://doi.org/10.14778/3415478.3415530.

Definition 3.1: Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)
Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) is a parallel execution model in which every worker completes a local computation phase, exchanges the data required by the next phase, and then waits at a global barrier before any worker begins the next phase, which makes the slowest participant the pacing constraint for the entire cluster.

Significance: The slowest required computation or communication determines when a superstep can complete. Faster workers wait at the barrier, so a localized delay can consume idle accelerator time across the entire participating group.
Distinction: BSP organizes execution into synchronized supersteps; it does not itself prescribe a learning algorithm or an all-to-all exchange. Synchronous data-parallel updates match a single-device reference only under compatible global batches, update rules, and numerical assumptions.
Common pitfall: Removing barriers does not by itself establish faster time-to-quality. Asynchronous training trades waiting against stale updates, and the convergence and wall-clock comparison depends on the workload and update schedule.



The flow inversion compounds this problem. Traditional networks are designed for fairness among millions of “mice flows,”2 yet ML training is dominated by a few “elephant flows” corresponding to the gradient AllReduce. The full 175B model has 350 GB of gradient state at the assumed precision, but a sharded job distributes that state across workers. Each collective operates on its participating group and local payload; its algorithm determines how much each worker sends. Standard flow control and routing mechanisms like equal-cost multi-path (ECMP), which hash each flow onto one of several equal-cost paths, are poorly suited to this traffic pattern. A static hash cannot subdivide one elephant flow across all available links, and it can inadvertently map multiple elephant flows to the same link, creating massive congestion while other links sit idle.
2 Elephant and mice flows: The model-wide gradient size is not the size of one network flow. A collective can split each worker’s local gradient shard across channels and transport connections; the resulting long-lived flows can still collide under ECMP when their static hashes select the same path.The loss inversion completes the picture. TCP was designed to recover across an unreliable network, and an occasional retransmission delays only the request it belongs to. In a synchronous collective, a lost packet delays the transfer that every waiting worker needs, and some NICs that implement remote direct memory access (RDMA), called RDMA NICs or RNICs, recover by resending everything after the missing packet rather than only the lost region (Go-Back-N-style recovery). ML fabrics therefore aim to make loss rare and recovery bounded, either by preventing buffer overflow at the link layer or by building transports that recover quickly from it. Level 2 (section 3.4.3) develops both approaches.
Correlated demand also makes oversubscription, provisioning less uplink capacity at a switch tier than the downlink capacity it serves (written as a downlink:uplink ratio such as 2:1), a workload decision. A fabric with spare capacity under independent requests can become saturated when a collective releases traffic across the same cut. Designing for that traffic requires tracing the constraint from the wire through transport, topology, and congestion control to the job’s synchronization boundary.


Each of these inversions traces back to a specific physical or protocol constraint, and the five levels of figure 1 locate where each one is paid:

Level 1: wire and link (section 3.3). Signal integrity (PAM4, SerDes) and the speed of light in fiber impose hard constraints on latency and cluster geometry.
Level 2: transport (section 3.4). InfiniBand and RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) provide RDMA primitives; the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model quantifies the latency-vs.-bandwidth trade-off for different message sizes.
Level 3: switch and topology (section 3.5). Fat-trees, rail-optimized designs, and dragonflies achieve the \(\BisectionBandwidth\) needed for global collectives through different structural trade-offs.
Level 4: fabric behavior (section 3.6). Link-level flow control and end-to-end congestion control determine whether theoretical bandwidth translates to realized throughput; adaptive routing and incast behavior determine whether that throughput survives real collective traffic (Alizadeh et al. 2010; Zhu et al. 2015; Li et al. 2019; Gangidi et al. 2024).
Level 5: cluster design (section 3.7). Production supercomputers like the NVIDIA SuperPOD and Meta Grand Teton integrate these layers into a unified gradient bus (NVIDIA 2023; Meta Engineering 2024).


Alizadeh, Mohammad, Albert Greenberg, David A. Maltz, Jitendra Padhye, Parveen Patel, Balaji Prabhakar, Sudipta Sengupta, and Murari Sridharan. 2010. “Data Center TCP (DCTCP).” Proceedings of the ACM SIGCOMM 2010 Conference, 63–74. https://doi.org/10.1145/1851182.1851192.
The levels are not an inventory of networking topics; they are the causal chain that turns synchronous ML traffic into infrastructure requirements. Large gradient messages first stress the wire and transport, then force topology choices that preserve bisection bandwidth, then expose congestion behavior that ordinary enterprise networks can hide, and finally determine whether the whole cluster behaves like one training machine.
The traffic pattern determines which fabric metric matters. A global reduction stresses bisection bandwidth and the slowest path; a point-to-point pipeline transfer sits on the critical path, so its full transfer time and hop count matter; an expert exchange stresses path diversity and egress balance; and checkpoint or tenant traffic stresses isolation from the synchronization path. Table 2 provides the compact mapping that the remaining levels develop.



Table 2: Traffic patterns determine fabric metrics: Workload semantics translate into different physical bottlenecks, so no single link-rate benchmark predicts training performance. The table is a map of what follows; the mechanisms in its right two columns (transport offload, adaptive routing, virtual lanes, and the rest) are developed at Levels 2 through 5.

Mapping workload semantics to physical constraints shows why ML fabric design must proceed from the physical layer up. Before higher-level topologies or routing protocols can organize traffic, the physical layer must reliably deliver bits between endpoints without excessive signal attenuation or prohibitive power consumption. Level 1 begins where all fabric architecture originates: at the physical wire.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
At 400 Gb/s and beyond, the physics of signal transmission imposes hard limits on cable length, power consumption, and error rates. Signal attenuation in copper and chromatic dispersion in fiber dictate how far an accelerator can sit from its switches before communication fails. Every higher-level protocol and topology is ultimately constrained by what the physical wire can carry; these limits shape the geometry of the entire cluster. To meet throughput demands without raising the signaling rate into worse attenuation, link designs must carry more bits in each transmitted symbol.


Achieving 400 Gb/s and higher line rates requires balancing signaling speed against channel loss and detection errors. The symbol rate counts transmitted symbols per second; consecutive symbols need not produce a voltage transition. Raising the symbol rate raises the frequencies the channel must carry, and copper loses more signal at higher frequencies. Carrying more bits in each symbol, by using more than two signal levels, raises the bit rate without that penalty, and PAM4 is the scheme high-speed links use to do it.

Definition 3.2: PAM4 signaling
PAM4 signaling is a modulation scheme that represents two bits per symbol with four signal levels, doubling the raw bit rate relative to binary signaling at the same symbol rate.

Significance: PAM4 increases the raw \(\Bandwidth\) available at a given symbol rate. The reduced separation between levels makes error-control design part of that gain. High-speed Ethernet uses forward error correction (FEC), including Reed-Solomon RS(544,514), with processing latency that depends on the physical-layer (PHY) design and implementation (Anslow 2016; Yin et al. 2022). FEC contributes to the fixed path budget modeled by the \(\MessageStartupLatency\) term in section 3.4.4; it is one component alongside propagation, switching, and endpoint processing.
Distinction: At equal symbol rate and voltage swing, NRZ (Non-Return-to-Zero) binary signaling carries one bit per symbol with greater separation between levels. PAM4 carries two bits per symbol with smaller level spacing; the link must compensate through its signal-quality and error-correction design.
Common pitfall: Doubling bits per symbol does not guarantee twice the usable payload throughput or a fixed latency penalty. Coding overhead, channel quality, and the chosen PHY implementation determine delivered performance. FEC processing contributes to the startup budget, which matters most when messages are small or a collective pays startup repeatedly.




Yin, Shuang, Xiang Zhou, and Cedric Lam. 2022. FEC Requirements for 800GbE/1.6TbE Optics: An Operator’s Perspective. IEEE 802.3df Task Force.
The price is noise margin. With four levels packed into the same voltage swing, the gap between adjacent levels in PAM4 shrinks to one third of the NRZ gap (figure 5), making the link highly susceptible to noise. Consequently, high-speed links operate near the physical limits of reliable detection and require forward error correction (FEC) at the physical layer, commonly using Reed-Solomon RS(544,514)-family codes in high-speed Ethernet designs (Anslow 2016; Ethernet Alliance 2025). FEC processing is an implementation-dependent latency term; IEEE 802.3df operator material treats roughly 100 ns of host-side FEC with the RS(544,514) code (called KP4 in the standard) and hundreds of nanoseconds of end-to-end module latency as meaningful at AI/HPC fabric timescales (Yin et al. 2022). Because each switch on a path decodes and re-encodes the signal, the FEC cost accumulates with the number of switches a packet traverses. This chapter counts a path’s length as its hop count, distinguishing inter-switch links from switch traversals when the two differ. A packet that traverses three switches, the leaf-spine-leaf route of a two-tier fabric, incurs a scenario budget of 300 ns–600 ns of one-way FEC latency, or 600 ns–1200 ns for a round trip. Against the 350 GB gradient of the 175B job, a few hundred nanoseconds are negligible, because bulk transfers are governed by bandwidth. The cost lands instead on small, latency-bound messages, such as the control handoffs that coordinate pipeline stages, and on collectives whose many sequential steps each pay it. This “physics tax” sets a floor on the fabric’s fixed startup latency, formalized in section 3.4.4 as the \(\MessageStartupLatency\) term, that no software optimization can remove.






Figure 5: From NRZ to PAM4 signaling: Both panels send six symbols in the same time over the same total voltage swing. NRZ (left) uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol, 6 bits in all; PAM4 (right) uses four levels and carries two bits per symbol, 12 bits in all, doubling the data rate without raising the symbol rate. The cost is noise margin: adjacent PAM4 levels sit one third as far apart (arrows), so high-speed links need forward error correction (FEC), which adds to the fabric’s fixed \(\MessageStartupLatency\) latency.



This signaling shift highlights a key architectural rule: doubling line rate without doubling the symbol rate trades signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for bandwidth, requiring forward error correction to operate near the channel limit.



The choice of physical medium determines how far a link can reach before latency, power, and cost reshape the cluster geometry. Table 3 compares the recurring cable and optics options by the attributes that decide where each one belongs.

The high-speed copper and optical paths considered here both include FEC3, so choosing optics does not by itself remove error-correction overhead. The ranges in table 3 describe representative placements rather than fixed boundaries between media. Optical interconnects can extend the layout beyond a passive copper channel’s budget, while pluggable optics also permit separate replacement of modules and fiber. Reach, delivered latency, power, and serviceability jointly determine the choice.
3 FEC (forward error correction): At 400G and 800G speeds, signal integrity is fragile enough that Ethernet PHY designs rely on FEC to reconstruct corrupted bits (Anslow 2016; Ethernet Alliance 2025). The exact latency depends on the PHY and module architecture; for ML fabric modeling, treating FEC as a per-hop latency budget is the conservative point, because a multi-hop path accumulates that budget before software can hide it.
Anslow, Pete. 2016. RS(544,514) FEC Performance Including Precoding. IEEE P802.3cd Task Force.

Ethernet Alliance. 2025. 2025 Ethernet Roadmap. Ethernet Alliance roadmap.

Systems Perspective 3.2: The cost of distanceIn an ML fleet, distance is money. Assuming two spine-layer optical links per accelerator, a cluster of 10,000 GPUs requires ~20,000 optical links at the spine layer alone. At $500 per complete link, that represents $10 million in cabling. For power, count one selected spine-side pluggable module per link at 20 W per module, giving 400 kW for those endpoints alone. Each optical link also has a module at its opposite end; this subtotal excludes those modules, switch electronics, and cooling, so it is not the full fabric power budget. The cost dictates cluster geometry: architects pack accelerators as densely as possible (70–100 kW per rack) to maximize cheap copper and minimize expensive optics.





Every port depends on a serializer/deserializer (SerDes) circuit that converts parallel data from the switch application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) into a serial stream. Its power cost accumulates across the provisioned ports. For the 1,024 GPUs reference cluster, assume a full-\(\BisectionBandwidth\) fabric with roughly 3,000 high-speed links across its host and switch tiers. Count one selected switch-side port per link in this power subtotal. Each counted 400 Gb/s port is assigned 25 W, more than the 20 W pluggable-module figure in the cost-of-distance estimate because it also counts the switch-side SerDes that drives the module. The model totals 75 kW, equivalent to 10.5 percent of the accelerators’ combined thermal design power. This comparison isolates the assumed power of the selected switch-side ports, excluding the opposite endpoints and the rest of the switch chassis; it does not establish total fabric power or the fraction of measured cluster energy consumed by networking.
The link budget allocates the signal loss a path can tolerate while meeting its error target. Losses are counted in decibels (dB), a logarithmic power ratio in which every 10 dB is a further tenfold attenuation (3 dB is roughly a halving), so the losses of cables and connectors in series simply add. In this simplified accounting, a lane has a 30 dB allowance. A 3-meter DAC cable contributing 18 dB of loss and connectors contributing 2 dB leave 10 dB of margin. Higher signaling frequencies increase copper loss, so preserving reach can require more signal conditioning, a different cable, or optics. Aggregate port speed alone does not determine cable reach; lane rate, channel construction, and active components matter. The design must meet both the signal-quality target and the power budget before the transport layer can rely on the link.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
Large-scale training requires sustained, synchronized bulk transfers. A single AllReduce across 1,024 GPUs forwards every worker’s contribution through many links in lockstep. This pattern favors RDMA transport offload, reliable completion, and bounded loss-recovery time. A physically lossless fabric is one way to make that performance predictable, but it is not the only design.



Definition 3.3: Remote direct memory access (RDMA)
Remote direct memory access (RDMA) is a networking technology that offloads transport processing to network interface hardware, allowing access to registered remote memory without per-transfer kernel processing of the payload.

Significance: RDMA can reduce end-to-end message latency from tens of microseconds for a kernel TCP path to low-single-digit microseconds on a tuned fabric, shrinking the fixed startup cost that every message adds to the Fleet Law’s communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\).
Distinction: Unlike a conventional kernel TCP path, RDMA offloads transport processing to NIC hardware and permits user-space access to registered memory. The resulting CPU-core and memory-bandwidth savings depend on the host, NIC, I/O path, message size, and software configuration rather than on link rate alone.
Common pitfall: RDMA is an access and offload model, not one loss-recovery algorithm. Reliable InfiniBand and RoCE transports detect loss and retransmit (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000). Some RNIC generations use the Go-Back-N-style recovery noted with the loss inversion, which makes a drop expensive (section 3.4.3 quantifies the cost), while other designs support stronger selective recovery or tolerate lossy Ethernet without the link-layer pause mechanism (priority flow control) that many RoCE deployments rely on (Mittal et al. 2018). The requirement is reliable completion with a recovery tail that the synchronized workload can tolerate, not a physically lossless Ethernet fabric in every implementation.



A conventional kernel TCP path charges the host for every byte it moves. Interrupt processing, protocol work, and payload copies consume CPU cycles and memory bandwidth that the training process also needs for data loading and preprocessing, and the charge grows with aggregate I/O as many streams or NICs drive a host at 400 Gb/s link rates. Modern TCP stacks reduce the charge with segmentation offload, receive-side scaling, zero-copy interfaces, and careful non-uniform memory access (NUMA) placement, so a single stream need not exhaust a server’s memory bandwidth. They do not remove it, and the contention becomes harder to provision predictably as nodes add NICs.
RDMA bypasses the kernel data path. Offloading transport logic to the NIC allows applications to read and write registered remote memory without per-message kernel intervention. For ML, GPUDirect RDMA,4 the path that dense nodes pair with one NIC per GPU (Dense node designs), extends this principle to accelerator memory (NVIDIA 2026a). In the sending-node data paths diagrammed in figure 6, GPUDirect RDMA routes an \(\PointToPointMessageSize\)-byte payload (what one participant sends, not the model-wide gradient state) along the solid green peer-to-peer path through the PCIe switch straight to the RDMA NIC, bypassing host memory entirely. Without this direct memory access (DMA) bypass, the dashed gray staging path must first copy \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and subsequently read \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes out to the NIC, generating roughly \(2\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes of redundant host-memory bus traffic. The network still transfers the payload, and the PCIe path may comprise multiple DMA transactions; the optimization removes staging copies rather than collapsing the transfer into one transaction.
4 GPUDirect RDMA: Introduced by NVIDIA for Kepler-class GPUs and CUDA 5.0, GPUDirect RDMA enables a direct PCIe path between GPU memory and third-party peer devices such as network interfaces (NVIDIA 2026a). Before GPUDirect, every gradient transfer had to stage through host memory, consuming CPU memory bandwidth that competes with data loading. Eliminating this bounce path is one reason overlapping communication with backward-pass computation is feasible at scale.
NVIDIA. 2026a. GPUDirect RDMA.






Figure 6: GPUDirect RDMA data path: Without GPUDirect (dashed), a sending node first writes the \(\PointToPointMessageSize\)-byte payload from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and the NIC then reads it back out, about \(2\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes of host-memory traffic per payload. With GPUDirect RDMA (solid), the NIC reads GPU memory directly over the PCIe peer-to-peer path, so the host-memory bounce disappears.






GPU clusters commonly choose between two RDMA transport stacks, and the decision is a reliability-versus-operations trade-off. Both stacks must keep switch buffers from overflowing under synchronized bursts, and they do so in different places. InfiniBand uses credit-based flow control. Each receiver advertises its free buffer space to the sender at the other end of the link in units called credits, and the sender transmits only into space that has been advertised. A buffer therefore cannot overflow; congestion appears as senders waiting for credits rather than as dropped packets. Ethernet was designed to drop packets when buffers fill, so RoCE deployments that want the same behavior add two mechanisms. Priority flow control (PFC) lets a filling switch port send a PAUSE frame that stops its upstream neighbor for one traffic class, and explicit congestion notification (ECN) marks packets that pass through a filling queue so that their senders slow down before a pause is needed. Table 4 compares where each stack places the burden of losslessness and congestion control, and section 3.6.1 develops PFC’s failure modes.



Table 4: RDMA transport stack trade-offs: InfiniBand and RoCE expose RDMA semantics through different operational contracts, one built around native losslessness and the other around Ethernet compatibility.











Stack
Fabric behavior
Operational burden
Typical fit




InfiniBand (IB)
Purpose-built HPC switched fabric (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000) with credit-based flow control, so losslessness is native at the link layer
a central subnet manager computes routes, and virtual lanes (VLs), separate buffer and credit pools on one link, isolate traffic
Dedicated training clusters where predictable tail latency outweighs Ethernet ecosystem flexibility


RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet)
RoCEv2 carries RDMA semantics by encapsulating InfiniBand transport headers in UDP/IP packets
PFC-based deployments suppress loss with PFC, ECN, and routing policy (Guo et al. 2016; Gangidi et al. 2024); PFC-free designs instead place more burden on end-to-end congestion control and loss recovery (Mittal et al. 2018)
Multi-vendor Ethernet fleets that can absorb more congestion-control tuning






The InfiniBand5 row reflects a protocol heritage that favors hardware-managed losslessness over Ethernet compatibility.
5 InfiniBand: Formed in 1999 from the merger of two competing server I/O standards (Future I/O and NGIO), InfiniBand was originally designed to replace PCI as a general-purpose system interconnect. Its pivot to HPC networking preserved the credit-based, hardware-managed flow control that server I/O demanded, and this heritage is precisely why InfiniBand provides native losslessness without the PFC fragility that plagues Ethernet-based RDMA fabrics.This architectural choice is visible at the protocol boundary. Figure 7 partitions the protocol stack across user-space, kernel, and hardware bands, contrasting traditional socket overhead against direct verbs hardware offload. While the conventional copied TCP/IP path illustrated on the left uses two software copies across kernel buffer boundaries and software protocol execution, the RDMA stack (right) traces a single amber bypass arrow straight from the collective communication library (such as the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, or NCCL) and the user-space verbs API to the RDMA NIC, keeping the operating system entirely off the active data path.






Figure 7: Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks: Read each stack top to bottom through the user-space, kernel, and hardware bands. In the illustrated copied TCP/IP socket path (left), a send enters the kernel through a system call, the payload is copied into kernel socket buffers and again toward the NIC’s transmit ring, and the CPU runs the transport protocol in software. With RDMA verbs over InfiniBand or RoCEv2 (right), the collective library posts work requests from user space, the kernel stays off the data path, and the RDMA NIC runs the reliable transport in hardware, reading GPU memory directly through GPUDirect instead of staging a host copy.






By routing the user-space verbs API directly to hardware as diagrammed in figure 7, the architecture decouples collective library calls from the operating system, leaving the transport hardware and fabric to arbitrate reliable delivery and packet loss. Reliable connected transports in both InfiniBand and RoCE detect loss and retransmit (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000); credits and PFC exist to make that retransmission rare (Guo et al. 2016; Gangidi et al. 2024). Losslessness is therefore a deployment contract rather than a property of RDMA as a family. Designs that operate over lossy Ethernet without PFC shift more responsibility to endpoint congestion control, packet reordering, and selective recovery (Mittal et al. 2018).
Recovery granularity therefore matters. On an RNIC with Go-Back-N-style recovery and no out-of-order retention, a lost packet invalidates every packet that arrives after it, and the sender must retransmit from the missing sequence point. The penalty is everything the sender transmitted between the lost packet and the moment it learned of the loss, so it equals link rate times detection delay. If the receiver’s negative acknowledgment reaches the sender after one 5 μs round trip, a sender at 50 GB/s has meanwhile sent 250 KB, all of which it must send again; a drop 900 MB into a 1 GB transfer wastes that window, not the 900 MB already delivered. When detection instead waits for a retransmission timeout, the delay, and with it the resent window, grows with that timeout. An RNIC with selective recovery retransmits only the missing packets, so the same physical loss produces a shorter tail (Mittal et al. 2018). Because the window is line rate times detection delay, resending it takes about as long as detecting the loss did, so a faster link resends more bytes per drop without shortening the stall. Either way the stall spans many packet wire times, and a synchronous collective exposes the slowest recovery to every waiting worker. Fabric designers can reduce that tail by suppressing drops with PFC, by using a loss-tolerant transport with bounded endpoint recovery, or by combining congestion control and admission policy so queues rarely overflow. Each choice moves state and failure modes between switches and endpoints.



Protocol choice determines how the fabric provides reliable completion and bounds loss-recovery time; performance modeling then asks how fast it can carry a given message. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)) decomposes message transfer time as \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\), where \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) is the message size in bytes, \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the fixed startup latency, and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the sustained bandwidth in bytes per unit time (Hockney 1994). The physical topology influences both parameters through path length and available capacity. A collective built from many sequential rounds of messages pays \(\MessageStartupLatency\) once per round, so its startup cost can grow with the number of participants even when the underlying fabric provides short physical paths.

Hockney, Roger W. 1994. “The Communication Challenge for MPP: Intel Paragon and Meiko CS-2.” Parallel Computing 20 (3): 389–98. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0167-8191(06)80021-9.

↪ The same decomposition, multiplied by each schedule’s round count and traffic factor, is developed for collective algorithms in The alpha-beta cost model for network transfers.

The model reveals two regimes that lead to different engineering responses. For messages with \(\PointToPointMessageSize< \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\), startup cost \(\MessageStartupLatency\) exceeds the transmission cost; sufficiently small control messages lie deep in this latency-bound region. For messages with \(\PointToPointMessageSize> \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\), the \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) term is larger; sufficiently large gradient transfers lie deep in the bandwidth-bound region. Near the crossover, both terms matter. A collective’s regime also depends on how its algorithm divides the payload into messages and schedules them across rounds.


↪ The crossover message size that separates the latency-dominated and bandwidth-dominated regimes, with a worked InfiniBand NDR example, is developed in Latency-dominated vs. bandwidth-dominated regimes.
For the modeled NDR InfiniBand path with \(\MessageStartupLatency=\) 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth=\) 50 GB/s, the crossover point \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\approx\) 75 KB. Measured startup latency and delivered bandwidth vary with the NIC, switch path, software stack, and contention, so these parameters describe a scenario rather than a protocol constant. Far below the crossover, more bandwidth removes only a small part of transfer time; far above it, lower startup latency removes only a small part. Shorter paths can lower \(\MessageStartupLatency\), while additional delivered path bandwidth raises \(\LinkBandwidth\); their value depends on the message sizes the workload actually exchanges.

Napkin Math 3.1: The alpha-beta crossoverProblem: A fabric designer is comparing a modeled InfiniBand NDR path (1.5 μs, 50 GB/s) against a modeled RoCE path over slower Ethernet (5 μs, 12.5 GB/s). The comparison deliberately bundles a higher-latency stack with a slower link, so a third path, RoCE on a 400 Gb/s link, separates the two effects. For a 4 KB control message and a 350 MB gradient shard, which part of \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)=\MessageStartupLatency+\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) dominates, and why does the first path help for different reasons in each regime?
Math: Apply \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) for a 4 KB control message and a 350 MB gradient shard.

Small message (4 KB):

InfiniBand: \(1.5\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s} + 4\,\text{KB}/50\,\text{GB/s} = 1.5 + 0.08 = \mathbf{1.58}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)
RoCE (100G): \(5.0\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s} + 4\,\text{KB}/12.5\,\text{GB/s} = 5.0 + 0.32 = \mathbf{5.32}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)
Result: Under these assumed path parameters, the NDR path is 3.4× faster because its modeled \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is lower.

Large message (350 MB):

InfiniBand: \(\PointToPointTransferTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth=\) 7.0 ms
RoCE (100G): \(\PointToPointTransferTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth=\) 28.01 ms
Result: Under these assumed path parameters, the NDR path is 4× faster because its modeled \(\LinkBandwidth\) is higher. That factor is the ratio of the two line rates, so it measures the faster link rather than the transport.

Same line rate (RoCE at 400 Gb/s, RoCE \(\MessageStartupLatency\)):

Small message: 5.08 μs, still 3.2× the NDR time, because \(\MessageStartupLatency\) alone separates the stacks.
Large message: 7.0 ms, essentially the NDR time, because at equal \(\LinkBandwidth\) nothing but a few microseconds of \(\MessageStartupLatency\) separates them.


Systems insight: This scenario places the crossover \((\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth)\) near 75 KB. Because gradients are megabytes to gigabytes, their transfers are usually bandwidth dominated, whereas pipeline coordination can remain latency dominated. A higher line rate produces little benefit for a message whose startup term dominates; transport processing, topology, and hop count then govern the improvement.


In the 175B training job, a 4 KB control message, such as the notification that tells a pipeline stage its next microbatch is ready, costs \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx\) 1.58 μs, with bandwidth contributing only 5.1 percent of the total. Faster links therefore offer little benefit for this handoff. A 350 MB gradient shard, roughly the share of the 350 GB gradient that each of the 1,024 GPUs owns when a reduction partitions it across the whole cluster, costs \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx\) 7.0 ms; doubling bandwidth to 100 GB/s would approximately halve its transfer time.
Across the full range of message sizes, each path traces a flat latency-dominated plateau that bends into a linear bandwidth-dominated regime (figure 8). On the modeled NDR path, the knee at 75 KB marks where transmission time overtakes the 1.5 μs startup latency; the 100 Gb/s RoCE path sits on a higher floor of 5 μs and bends near 62.5 KB. The exact positions reflect the assumed \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) scenario parameters rather than invariant protocol constants. On both paths, startup latency governs sub-kilobyte control handoffs, whereas multi-megabyte gradient shards sit well inside the bandwidth-bound regime.














Figure 8: The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) crossover: Modeled transfer time as a function of message size for an NDR InfiniBand path and a 100 Gb/s RoCE baseline using the scenario parameters in the text. Small messages are latency dominated (flat region), while large messages are bandwidth dominated (linear region); on the InfiniBand path the dotted asymptotes show the knee sitting where the two terms are equal. Measured crossover points vary with the end-to-end path.




Checkpoint 3.1: Protocol selection
Consider the 175B job on the 1,024-GPU reference cluster. Its gradient exchanges move messages of hundreds of megabytes, while its pipeline stages coordinate through frequent control messages of a few kilobytes.

Protocol fit: use the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) crossover to recommend a transport stack, and justify the choice for both the large gradient messages and the small control messages.
RoCE requirements: compare the infrastructure required by PFC-based and PFC-free RoCE designs with InfiniBand’s credit-based fabric.
Line rate vs. startup cost: explain why moving the control messages from a 100 Gb/s path to a 400 Gb/s path with the same \(\MessageStartupLatency\) would barely change their transfer time.



Beyond classifying individual transfers, the same model identifies when communication overtakes computation. That question sharpens as models grow, because the scaling laws that push training toward more parameters (AI Scaling Laws) enlarge, in direct proportion, the gradient that every data-parallel step must reduce. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) analysis in this section focused on the transfer time of individual messages across a single link, treating the network as a point-to-point channel. In a data-parallel training loop, however, the relevant question is whether the collective AllReduce across the full cluster finishes before the next compute step is ready to begin. When the gradient vector grows large enough, the aggregate transfer time for a ring AllReduce exceeds the per-step computation time, and the network becomes the pacing constraint for the entire training job.
A ring arranges participants in a logical cycle, with each forwarding chunks to its next neighbor. Its ReduceScatter phase combines contributions and leaves a different reduced chunk at each participant; its AllGather phase distributes those chunks so every participant has the complete result. This logical ring is a communication schedule over the fabric, not a requirement that the physical switches form a ring.

Napkin Math 3.2: AllReduce cost as gradients growProblem: How does the communication share of a training step change as the gradient grows from GPT-2 scale to 70 billion parameters on a 1024-GPU H100 cluster that reduces the full gradient with a ring AllReduce?
Setup: This is a separate scenario from the running 175B job. Its two models step toward the running example, one at GPT-2 scale and one approaching the running example’s size. It holds each GPU’s work per step fixed, sized so that the compute phase takes 101 ms at 50 percent accelerator utilization, and assumes an NDR path modeled by \(\MessageStartupLatency = 1.5 \;\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) and \(\LinkBandwidth = 50 \;\text{GB/s}\). For a GPT-2-scale model, each worker contributes 6 GB of gradients. The notebook reduces in FP32, as some recipes do for numerical safety, so its payloads are twice the 16-bit figure used elsewhere in this chapter.
Here \(\DeviceCount\) is the number of participating workers, or ranks, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) is the gradient payload contributed by each rank.
Math: Applying the ring cost \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx \frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount}\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency\) gives \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx 242.8 \text{ ms}\). The modeled communication fraction is:
\[ \text{Comm. fraction} = 70.6 \% \]
Each phase takes \(\DeviceCount-1\) rounds and transfers a total of \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) of that payload per rank. The expression therefore counts both the bytes transmitted and the startup cost paid across the two phases. This estimate assumes a uniform path bandwidth and no overlap with computation; it tests whether the fabric can keep pace without requiring the full scheduling derivation developed in Ring AllReduce.
Systems insight: Increasing the payload to the 70 billion case (280 GB) raises the modeled ring time to:
\[ T_{\text{ring}} \approx 11192.1 \text{ ms} \]
Holding the compute phase fixed isolates the effect of payload size; a real 70B step would also compute longer per sample, so its true communication fraction depends on the per-GPU batch. The running example’s 350 GB FP16 gradient is larger still than this 280 GB payload, so a full-gradient ring for the 175B job would sit beyond the right end of this comparison. A ring time of this size shows why such models are not trained with pure data parallelism over this fabric. The conclusion is conditional rather than a universal model-size threshold: parallelism, gradient precision, bucketing, overlap, topology, and delivered bandwidth all move the boundary.


The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model quantifies the speed of a single link, but the 175B-parameter model requires 1,024 GPUs to work in concert. Scaling these transport primitives from a pair of nodes to a warehouse-scale supercomputer demands a network topology: a specific pattern of connections that maximizes \(\BisectionBandwidth\) while minimizing the hop count and cabling cost for global collective operations.

Self-Check: Question

How does GPUDirect RDMA optimize the end-to-end data path during a multi-node AllReduce gradient exchange compared to traditional host-staged network transfers?

It allows the network interface card (NIC) to read and write GPU High Bandwidth Memory directly over the PCIe bus without staging data through host CPU system RAM
It compresses floating-point tensors in GPU L2 cache before writing them directly to the optical switch buffer
It enables the GPU to execute TCP/IP checksum offloading in CUDA streaming multiprocessors
It re-routes inter-node gradient traffic over host SATA storage buses to bypass network switch congestion

An engineer observes that upgrading network links from \(200\text{ Gb/s}\) (HDR) to \(400\text{ Gb/s}\) (NDR) reduces the transfer time of a \(10\text{ KB}\) pipeline control message by only about \(11\%\), whereas the same upgrade halves the transfer time of a \(350\text{ MB}\) gradient tensor. How does the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) performance model explain this discrepancy?

Switch routing tables drop small packets more frequently than large packets due to flowlet timeouts
High-bandwidth optical transceivers disable forward error correction for messages larger than \(1\text{ MB}\)
PCIe bus arbitration introduces dynamic power throttling on transfers smaller than \(64\text{ KB}\)
The \(10\text{ KB}\) message falls below the crossover point (\(n^* = \alpha\beta \approx 75\text{ KB}\)), where fixed startup latency \(\alpha\) dominates, while the \(350\text{ MB}\) message is in the bandwidth-dominated regime (\(n \gg n^*\))

Given an InfiniBand fabric with startup latency \(\alpha = 1.5\,\mu\text{s}\) and bandwidth \(\beta = 50\text{ GB/s}\), calculate the crossover message size \(n^*\). Explain what architectural changes can reduce transfer time for messages below \(n^*\).
On an RNIC that discards out-of-order arrivals rather than retaining them, ______ recovery retransmits from the missing sequence point after packet loss.
