title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
A cluster can have thousands of fast links at the edge and still starve its AllReduce operations if the cross-sectional capacity at the narrowest point in the switching hierarchy is insufficient. The physical arrangement of switches determines whether that cross-section throttles collective communication or sustains full line-rate exchange across all participating workers. Two properties govern this capability: bisection bandwidth \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and whether the fabric is non-blocking, a constraint captured by the bisection bandwidth theorem (principle \(\ref{pri-bisection-bandwidth}\)).
Bisection bandwidth quantifies this worst-case throughput ceiling that the topology imposes on global collectives.

Definition 3.4: Bisection bandwidth
Bisection bandwidth is a network topology metric defined as the minimum aggregate link capacity crossing any partition that divides the cluster into two equal halves, representing the worst-case throughput ceiling for traffic that must cross that partition, including global collectives.

Significance: Bisection bandwidth \(\BisectionBandwidth\) directly sets the cluster-scale bandwidth ceiling for global synchronization. A 1,024-GPU fat-tree with 400 Gb/s links at 1:1 subscription provides \(\text{BW}_{\text{bisect}} = 512 \times 50\,\text{GB/s} = 25.6\,\text{TB/s}\) per direction; a 4:1 oversubscribed spine reduces this to 6.4 TB/s, increasing the transfer-time lower bound for a fixed cut-crossing payload by 4×. Actual AllReduce slowdown depends on rank placement, the collective schedule, and which links are saturated.
Distinction: Unlike aggregate bandwidth (the sum of all edge link speeds, which can be high even in a poorly connected topology), \(\BisectionBandwidth\) measures global connectivity. A star topology with 1,000 edge links all meeting at one central switch has high aggregate bandwidth but \(\BisectionBandwidth\) limited by that switch’s backplane capacity.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that adding more leaf switches always increases \(\BisectionBandwidth\). In a three-tier fat-tree, oversubscribing the spine layer (giving each spine switch fewer uplinks to the core than downlinks to its leaves) reduces \(\BisectionBandwidth\) below the edge-link total regardless of how many leaf switches are present.



ML training includes global collectives and AllToAll phases that can drive traffic across topology partitions, making full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) a useful capacity target. A smaller cut becomes a bottleneck when the workload’s crossing traffic exceeds what it can deliver within the communication budget. Rank placement and the collective schedule determine that traffic.
Bisection bandwidth measures cut capacity; a non-blocking fabric provides paths that can sustain simultaneous input-output pairings at line rate with suitable routing. Full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and balanced uplink capacity support that goal, but routing must also spread traffic across the available paths. In the oversubscribed designs considered here, reducing a cut’s capacity reduces its effective \(\BisectionBandwidth\), increasing the transfer-time bound for a fixed payload that saturates it. A collective that keeps most traffic within each half need not experience the same slowdown.


↪ A slower cut lengthens the training step only when the extra transfer time cannot hide behind computation. The communication-to-compute diagnostic that tests this is developed in Compute \cap communication.

Definition 3.5: Non-blocking fabric
Non-blocking fabric is a network with sufficient internal path capacity to support any permutation of input-output port pairs simultaneously at full line rate under a suitable routing assignment.

Significance: In ML fleets, a non-blocking fabric can support full-rate permutation traffic with suitable routing, preserving the available \(\BisectionBandwidth\) term for global collectives. A 2:1 oversubscribed spine halves the effective \(\BisectionBandwidth\), doubling the communication time when that cut is the saturated bottleneck and dropping scaling efficiency \(\ScalingEfficiency\) accordingly. In a scenario workload assumed to spend 30 percent of each step communicating, doubling that share while the computation share stays fixed lengthens each step, and the longer step costs roughly 23.1 percent of total cluster throughput. Two ratios recur in this section. This definition uses 2:1, a common data-center compromise; the bisection definition above and notebook 3.3 use 4:1, a cost-optimized spine, and the notebook writes out the throughput formula behind both results.
Distinction: The guarantee concerns a permutation, in which each input and output belongs to one pairing. It does not promise full line rate from every sender to every receiver at once, nor does it make an arbitrary routing assignment free of contention.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that non-blocking means zero congestion. Endpoint congestion (incast) can still occur if multiple senders simultaneously target the same receiver port, regardless of how much internal fabric capacity is available.



Fat-trees build on Clos-style non-blocking network principles to supply full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) (Clos 1953), rail-optimized networks trade some global routing flexibility for lower cabling cost, and dragonfly topologies reduce optical link counts while introducing workload-placement constraints (Kim et al. 2008). This fundamental balance between guaranteed bisection bandwidth and economic scalability drives every topology decision in large-scale ML clusters, as the topology comparisons in section 3.5.2, section 3.5.3, and section 3.5.4 illustrate.


The top-of-rack (ToR) switch aggregates traffic and creates a shared failure domain, a set of resources affected by the same outage. Consider a rack containing four nodes with eight GPUs each. If all 32 accelerators depend on one ToR with no alternate path, losing that switch disconnects them from the rest of the job. Recovery then depends on available paths, surviving state, and the job’s recovery policy. Individual links and nodes remain smaller failure domains, while rack power can create a broader shared outage. This one-switch-per-rack wiring is the simpler baseline used here to teach radix and failure domains; the reference cluster itself wires each GPU to a rail switch, a layout developed in section 3.5.3 that reshapes the failure domain, because losing one rail switch cuts one GPU in each of many nodes rather than every GPU in one rack.
The switch radix, its number of ports, determines how many endpoints and uplinks it can connect. In the reference allocation, a 64-port switch assigns 32 ports to servers, one for each of 32 GPUs, and 32 ports to the spine. With equal port rates, the 1:1 ratio avoids oversubscription at that boundary; delivered throughput still depends on forwarding and the paths beyond it. The 1,024 GPUs-GPU cluster requires approximately 32 such endpoint groups. Physical rack count also depends on node density and the cabling layout.
The same boundary shapes state placement. To survive a rack-wide outage, a job needs recoverable state outside that rack and a way to resume on available capacity. Topology-aware scheduling must therefore consider both fast communication paths and the failures that several nearby resources share.


↪ Nested failure domains, and why redundant state must span them to survive a correlated rack or ToR outage, are developed in Correlated failures.



The ToR provides non-blocking bandwidth within a single rack, but connecting the reference cluster’s 32 endpoint groups into a cluster that preserves full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) across every possible communication pair requires a topology that scales cross-sectional capacity with cluster size. The fat-tree (also called a Clos network) achieves this by adding parallel spine switches at each tier, so the aggregate uplink capacity always matches the total edge bandwidth feeding into it. In this vocabulary, leaf switches attach servers or racks, spine switches connect leaves within a pod, and core switches connect multiple pods when a third tier is needed; other sources call the leaf and spine tiers edge and aggregation. A pod here is a switching domain, the group of leaves that one set of spines joins, which can be narrower than the multi-rack pod of The Pod, where the fat-tree and the torus were introduced as the two dominant ways to wire one. A multi-rack pod in that sense can contain several fat-tree pods.

Definition 3.6: Fat-tree
Fat-tree is a hierarchical ML cluster network topology in which the number of parallel paths (and therefore aggregate cross-sectional capacity) increases at each switch tier toward the spine, providing full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and multiple equal-cost routes between any two nodes (Al-Fares et al. 2008).

Significance: A \(\SwitchRadix\)-ary fat-tree built from radix-\(\SwitchRadix\) switches supports \(\SwitchRadix^2/2\) hosts in a standalone two-tier configuration and \(\SwitchRadix^3/4\) hosts in a three-tier configuration with full \(\BisectionBandwidth\). With 64-port switches, a standalone two-tier fabric supports 2,048 GPUs and a three-tier fabric supports 65,536 hosts. This is a capacity bound for suitable routing and admissible traffic; it does not eliminate endpoint contention or guarantee that a particular AllReduce implementation reaches line rate.
Distinction: Unlike a standard tree (where bandwidth at the root is a single bottleneck shared by all leaves), a fat-tree replaces each root with multiple spine switches whose combined uplink capacity matches the total edge bandwidth, eliminating the bottleneck.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that fat-trees guarantee zero network cost. They require \(\mathcal{O}(\TopologyEndpointCount\log \TopologyEndpointCount)\) switches and dense cabling, so a non-blocking three-tier fat-tree at the 4,000-GPU scale needs hundreds of switches and more than ten thousand links before a single accelerator is purchased.




Al-Fares, Mohammad, Alexander Loukissas, and Amin Vahdat. 2008. “A Scalable, Commodity Data Center Network Architecture.” ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 38 (4): 63–74. https://doi.org/10.1145/1402946.1402967.
Figure 9 diagrams this non-blocking topology for a three-tier radix-4 fabric (\(\SwitchRadix=4\)), with four core switches interconnecting four dashed pod modules. Leaf and spine switches split their ports between the tiers below and above; core switches use all their ports to connect pods. Each tier boundary therefore carries 16 links. The highlighted route traverses five switches and is one of \((\SwitchRadix/2)^2 = 4\) equal-cost routes from a GPU in Pod 1 to Pod 4. Parallel paths supply the capacity, while routing must distribute traffic across them to use it.






Figure 9: Non-blocking fat-tree topology: A three-tier fat-tree built from radix-4 switches (\(\SwitchRadix=4\)) connects \(\SwitchRadix^3/4 = 16\) GPUs through four pods. Leaf and spine switches split their ports equally between the tiers below and above; core switches use all their ports to connect pods. Each tier boundary carries 16 links, supporting full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) with suitable routing. The highlighted leaf-spine-core-spine-leaf route between pod 1 and pod 4 is one of \((\SwitchRadix/2)^2 = 4\) equal-cost paths (the other three are drawn lighter), and exploiting those alternatives without excessive reordering requires compatible switch and endpoint mechanisms.



The fat-tree6 is a common default for ML clusters because a non-blocking design can provide full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) across arbitrary partitions. This capacity benefits global AllReduce even though implementations such as rings and trees do not require simultaneous all-to-all communication. The number of hosts that the guarantee can cover depends on switch radix and tier count.
6 Fat-tree (Clos network): The underlying multi-stage switching theory was invented by Clos (1953) at Bell Labs to minimize the number of electromechanical crosspoints in telephone exchanges. Leiserson (1985) at MIT generalized the concept as the “fat-tree,” where the tree is “fat” because link bandwidth increases toward the root, proving it could emulate any network of equal hardware volume. The same cost-minimization logic that drove 1950s telephony now drives ML cluster design: minimize switch count while guaranteeing non-blocking connectivity for global AllReduce.
Clos, C. 1953. “A Study of Non-Blocking Switching Networks.” Bell System Technical Journal 32 (2): 406–24. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1953.tb01433.x.

Leiserson, Charles E. 1985. “Fat-Trees: Universal Networks for Hardware-Efficient Supercomputing.” IEEE Transactions on Computers C-34 (10): 892–901. https://doi.org/10.1109/tc.1985.6312192.
7 Switch radix: High-end switches (for example, NVIDIA Quantum-2) can feature a radix of 64 ports, each at 400 Gb/s. This density allows a standalone two-tier fat-tree to support up to 2,048 GPUs; a path between distinct leaves traverses leaf, spine, and destination leaf, or three switches. As model scale pushes toward 100,000 GPUs, increasing switch radix (to 128 or 256), grouping accelerators into larger local domains, or accepting topology constraints are the main ways to avoid adding more tiers and the resulting latency/cost explosion.A fat-tree built from switches with radix7 \(\SwitchRadix\) supports \(\FatTreeHostCount= \SwitchRadix^{3}/4\) hosts at three tiers. A standalone two-tier non-blocking fabric can instead use \(\SwitchRadix\) leaves, each with \(\SwitchRadix/2\) host ports and \(\SwitchRadix/2\) uplinks, connected to \(\SwitchRadix/2\) spines. Each spine uses all \(\SwitchRadix\) ports to reach the leaves, providing \(\SwitchRadix^{2}/2 =\) 2,048 host ports for radix-64 switches. One pod of the three-tier design has only \(\SwitchRadix/2\) leaves and therefore \((\SwitchRadix/2)^2 =\) 1,024 host ports; its spine switches reserve ports for the core. These are different port allocations and switch counts, not two ways of counting the same fabric. The 1,024-GPU reference cluster fits within a standalone two-tier design. The distinction matters as soon as a cluster outgrows it. A 4,096-GPU deployment cannot join two fully populated standalone 2,048-host fabrics at their spines, because every spine port is already occupied by a leaf connection. It is instead built as four 1,024-host pods of the three-tier design, joined through a core tier.
A concrete bisection estimate shows how quickly oversubscription turns into synchronization delay.

Napkin Math 3.3: Bisection bandwidth: The cost of oversubscriptionProblem: A cluster designer is choosing between a “non-blocking” (1:1) fat-tree and a “cost-optimized” (4:1) spine for a $300M cluster of 1024 GPUs. This is a separate economics scenario rather than the running 175B job: each GPU contributes a 5 GB gradient payload, and the workload is assumed to spend \(\CommunicationTimeFraction=\) 30 percent of each step communicating. That share is a scenario input. It is larger than the 13 percent of the illustrative schedule in figure 4 and far smaller than the exposed share in the introduction’s communication-tax estimate (The energy-scale invariant), which assumes pure data parallelism with no overlap; none of the three is a measured share of the reference job. How much slower will the AllReduce be on the cheaper network, and what does that cost?
Math: Bisection bandwidth (\(\BisectionBandwidth\)) is the minimum pipe diameter between halves of the cluster. Assume a unidirectional ring whose ranks alternate between the two halves of the cluster. Every ring edge then crosses the cut, with \(\AcceleratorCount/2\) senders in each direction. Assume balanced routing, no competing traffic, and negligible startup latency. ReduceScatter plus AllGather contributes a traffic factor \(2(\AcceleratorCount-1)/\AcceleratorCount\) = 1.998 per GPU; multiplying by \(\AcceleratorCount/2\) gives the bytes crossing the cut in each direction. A ring that groups ranks within each half would have fewer crossing edges and a different cut-load bound.

Non-blocking (1:1): \(\BisectionBandwidth =\) 512 \(\times\) 50 GB/s \(=\) 25,600 GB/s per direction.

Time: 5,115 GB / 25,600 GB/s \(\approx\) 0.200 s.

Oversubscribed (4:1): \(\BisectionBandwidth =\) 25,600 GB/s divided by 4 = 6,400 GB/s per direction.

Time: 5,115 GB / 6,400 GB/s \(\approx\) 0.799 s.

Throughput: If the communication share stretches by the slowdown factor \(\CommunicationSlowdownFactor\) while computation stays fixed, then \(\text{relative throughput} = \frac{1}{(1-\CommunicationTimeFraction) + \CommunicationTimeFraction\,\CommunicationSlowdownFactor} = \frac{1}{0.70 + 0.30 \times 4} = \frac{1}{1.90} \approx 0.53\), a loss of about 47.4 percent of cluster throughput.
Cost: That loss times the $300M capital cost is about $142.1M.

Systems insight: For this cut-saturating placement, saving money on core switches creates a 4× bottleneck for global synchronization, and on a $300M cluster that bottleneck idles about $142.1M of compute. The same formula gives the 23.1 percent loss of the 2:1 spine in the non-blocking definition. This is an equivalent-capacity cost under the stated workload assumptions, not a direct equipment loss. Oversubscription must be evaluated against the collective traffic actually crossing the constrained cut.


This oversubscription calculation turns the topology definition into a design rule: the subscription ratio at each tier determines whether a fat-tree can sustain global collectives.
Scaling beyond the 2,048-host two-tier limit requires a three-tier architecture with core switches, enabling the fabric to reach 65,536 hosts, but the added scale carries both cost and latency. A non-blocking \(\SwitchRadix=64\) three-tier tree requires roughly \(5\SwitchRadix^2/4 \approx\) 5,120 switches across the core, spine, and leaf layers; at $10,000 to $50,000 per switch, the switching layer alone represents $51M to $256M. Typical hop counts also rise, from two inter-switch links and three switch traversals for intra-pod traffic (leaf-spine-leaf) to four inter-switch links and five switch traversals for inter-pod traffic (leaf-spine-core-spine-leaf), adding serialization delay and switch processing time to the \(\MessageStartupLatency\) latency term across thousands of synchronization steps. Rail-optimized topologies respond to both pressures by matching the physical cabling pattern to the collective communication pattern.

Checkpoint 3.2: Fat-tree topologies
These questions check whether hierarchical switch-fabric trade-offs are clear:

Radix and scale: compute the maximum number of GPUs a radix-64 two-tier fat-tree can connect without core switches.
Non-blocking ratio: explain why a non-blocking fabric requires a 1:1 subscription ratio at every tier of the network.
Tier vs. latency: determine how \(\MessageStartupLatency\) (startup latency) changes when moving from a two-tier to a three-tier fat-tree.
Aggregate vs. bisection: distinguish aggregate bandwidth from \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and identify the metric that matters for AllReduce.






Rail-optimized topology begins from the communication pattern rather than from a generic switch hierarchy. Dense accelerator nodes partition GPUs by local slot position into independent horizontal rails, as diagrammed in figure 10. In this physical cabling scheme, high-bandwidth internal NVSwitch planes bind GPUs 0 through 3 within each node, while external network ports route by slot position: GPU 0 in every node connects strictly to the Rail 0 switch, GPU 1 connects to Rail 1, and so on across the cluster.


↩︎ Assigning each GPU in a node to its own rail switch, rather than one shared top-of-rack switch, is established in Rack design considerations.






Figure 10: Rail-optimized physical wiring: In dense accelerator nodes such as the DGX H100, each GPU’s network port is cabled by local slot position: GPU 0 in every node connects to the rail 0 switch, GPU 1 to the rail 1 switch, and so on. Three nodes and four of each node’s eight GPUs are drawn, with the rail 0 cables emphasized; further nodes attach to the same rail switches. Tensor-parallel traffic stays on each node’s NVSwitch, same-rank data-parallel traffic stays on its own rail, and a spine layer (not drawn) bridges the rails for cross-rank traffic.



The wiring pattern connects corresponding GPUs across nodes (GPU 0 to GPU 0, GPU 1 to GPU 1) through dedicated rail switches rather than a shared ToR switch. This matters because data parallelism creates a deterministic and highly stratified communication pattern that standard topologies fail to exploit. When tensor-parallel groups stay inside each node, each replica assigns the corresponding model shard to the same local GPU rank. The slot number here is a local rank within a node; workers in the full distributed job also have distinct global ranks. GPU 0 on one node therefore synchronizes that shard’s gradients with GPU 0 on other nodes, but rarely with GPU 1 during this data-parallel exchange. A rail-optimized topology physically hardwires this logic by isolating these same-rank communication paths into dedicated networks. Instead of connecting all 8 GPUs in a node to a single ToR switch, the network connects all GPU 0s across the entire cluster to a dedicated “Rail 0” switch fabric, all GPU 1s to “Rail 1,” and so on. A simple hop-count estimate shows the payoff.

Napkin Math 3.4: The rail-optimized dividendProblem: A team is synchronizing per-rank data-parallel gradients across 128 nodes. In a standard fat-tree, each message between same-rank GPUs traverses its source leaf switch, a spine switch, and the destination leaf switch (3 switch traversals). In a rail-optimized network built from rail switches with at least one port per node, all corresponding GPUs sit on the same rail switch (one traversal). On the reference cluster that requires rail switches with more ports than the radix-64 switch used so far, so the estimate describes a higher-radix design. How much latency dividend does the rail design earn when a rail fits on one switch?
Math: This estimate counts only the switch-traversal contribution to communication latency (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)), using the same assumed delay for each traversal.

Standard latency: 3 traversals \(\times\) 0.6 μs = 1.8 μs.
Rail-optimized: 1 traversal \(\times\) 0.6 μs = 0.6 μs.
Result: 3× lower latency.

Systems insight: For synchronous data-parallel AllReduce, this 3× reduction applies to the modeled switch-latency contribution, not to total collective time. Its effect on scaling efficiency (\(\ScalingEfficiency\)) depends on payload size, delivered bandwidth, compute time, and overlap. The single-switch rail in this example avoids the spine traversal for same-rank traffic. The dividend is conditional. On the reference cluster’s radix-64 switches each rail outgrows one switch and regains the extra traversals, so what rails reliably buy there is isolation, developed below.


The hop saving is only part of the case for rails. Large language model fleets adopt the pattern because it matches how their parallelism plan divides traffic.

Lighthouse 3.1: Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): The rail-optimized fleetArchetype A’s use of 3D parallelism generates two distinct traffic patterns that pull in opposite directions: (1) massive, bandwidth-hungry gradient averaging for data parallelism, and (2) high-frequency, latency-sensitive activation exchanges for tensor parallelism. Keeping tensor parallelism inside each node’s NVLink domain leaves data-parallel gradient traffic on the fabric, and rails give each same-rank data-parallel group its own switch network. A rail can provide a single switch hop between nodes when its endpoint count fits the available switch ports. Larger rails require additional switching stages, so rail alignment alone does not guarantee single-hop communication. Either way, the lesson for Archetype A is that how the fabric is wired to the parallelism plan matters as much as how many accelerators it connects.


For the cluster of 1,024 GPUs spanning 128 nodes, this creates 8 parallel networks of 128 GPUs each, requiring at least one switch port per endpoint in each rail. A single-switch realization therefore needs a radix at least as large as the rail endpoint count; the earlier radix-64 switch cannot realize this rail alone, which is why notebook 3.4 assumed higher-radix rail switches. Built from radix-64 switches instead, each rail becomes a small two-tier fabric that preserves rank alignment but adds hops. For the bandwidth-hungry gradient exchanges of data parallelism, the larger benefit is isolation. Each rail carries only its own rank’s traffic, so the eight rail networks operate concurrently without competing for shared spine capacity. When a rail fits on one switch, the shorter path also trims the startup cost a ring pays on every round. However, this architecture introduces a sharp trade-off: traffic that must reach GPUs of different ranks (such as expert routing in mixture of experts (MoE), or pipeline-stage handoffs that do not align with the rail wiring) requires bridging across rails. Large clusters therefore often employ a hybrid approach, using rail-optimized leaves for same-rank data-parallel traffic while bridging the rails with a full fat-tree spine to support cross-rank communication patterns.

Checkpoint 3.3: Rail-optimized networks
These questions check whether workload-specific network-design trade-offs are clear:

Rail beneficiary: identify the dimension of 3D parallelism (tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, or data parallelism) that benefits most from a rail-optimized design.
Switch hops: explain when a rail-optimized network reduces the number of switch hops for gradient exchanges compared to a standard fat-tree, and what it still provides when a rail needs more ports than one switch offers.
Traffic isolation: explain the traffic isolation benefit of placing all GPU 0s on one rail and all GPU 1s on another.
Core switch need: classify the claim as true or false: a rail-optimized network eliminates the need for high-bandwidth core switches connecting different rails.






A dragonfly8 topology organizes high-radix routers (the dragonfly literature’s name for switches) into fully connected groups joined by global optical links. Each group has \(\DragonflyGroupRouterCount\) routers, and each router has \(\DragonflyTerminalPortCount\) terminal ports and \(\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\) global channels. The ratio of \(\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\) to \(\DragonflyTerminalPortCount\) sets how much global bandwidth each group receives relative to the traffic its terminals can inject, so global bandwidth is a design parameter rather than a fixed percentage of aggregate injection bandwidth. The balanced configuration analyzed by Kim et al. (2008), \(\DragonflyGroupRouterCount=2\DragonflyTerminalPortCount=2\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\), is one setting of that knob. Because the routers in a group are fully connected and the groups are joined by global links, a minimal route between two groups takes at most one local hop to the router holding the right global link, one global hop, and one local hop in the destination group, so no minimal path exceeds three router-to-router hops regardless of system size. Short paths come cheaply, but performance for jobs spanning groups depends on the chosen \(\DragonflyTerminalPortCount/\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\) ratio, routing, and traffic matrix, because every inter-group transfer shares the provisioned global links.
8 Dragonfly topology: Introduced by Kim et al. (2008) at ISCA 2008, the dragonfly uses high-radix routers grouped into fully connected “super-nodes.” For systems with at least 16,000 terminals, the architecture achieves a 52 percent network-cost reduction relative to a folded Clos (the fat-tree of section 3.5.2) of equivalent bandwidth, though global optical link oversubscription can create AllToAll bottlenecks during MoE token routing.
Kim, J., W. J. Dally, S. Scott, and D. Abts. 2008. “Technology-Driven, Highly-Scalable Dragonfly Topology.” 2008 International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 77–88. https://doi.org/10.1109/isca.2008.19.
A torus topology connects each node directly to its neighbors in a multidimensional grid, most commonly a 3D torus where every node links to its six adjacent peers (up/down, left/right, front/back). The design offers full local bandwidth with minimal switching hardware, because every neighbor is a single hop away. However, global communication requires traversing the diameter of the mesh (\(\mathcal{O}(\TopologyEndpointCount^{1/3})\) hops), making latency scale poorly with cluster size. Google adopted this architecture for its Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) pods because the collectives that dominate its training workloads can be scheduled as rings along each torus dimension, a nearest-neighbor pattern that maps naturally onto the physical grid. The limitation becomes apparent with MoE, which relies on AllToAll communication patterns. On a torus, these random permutations can congest the limited \(\BisectionBandwidth\) of the mesh and degrade performance relative to a non-blocking switch fabric.
The trade-off becomes concrete for the 4,096-endpoint deployment that the three-tier fat-tree reached with four pods. Arranged as a \(16 \times 16 \times 16\) torus with wraparound links, the same endpoints need no external switching stages, but only 512 links cross the bisection, against 2,048 in the non-blocking fat-tree. With 50 GB/s per link and direction, the torus offers 25.6 TB/s across the cut against the fat-tree’s 102.4 TB/s, a 4× gap, and its worst-case path crosses 24 neighbor hops against the fat-tree’s five switch traversals. Because a cubic torus’s cut grows only as \(\TopologyEndpointCount^{2/3}\) while its endpoint count grows as \(\TopologyEndpointCount\), that capacity gap widens at fixed link rate. Whether the gap matters depends on the traffic. A ring AllReduce scheduled along each torus dimension moves data only between neighbors and combines contributions before forwarding them, so it leans little on the narrow cut. An MoE AllToAll or an embedding exchange instead sends a large share of its traffic between distant endpoints and drives it straight into the cut, with the exact pressure set by placement and message sizes. The collective schedule and traffic matrix determine whether the torus’s lower cross-sectional capacity limits completion time.
At the scale of the 1,024-GPU reference cluster, the four families range in cut capacity from 25.6 TB/s in the non-blocking fat-tree down to 6.4 TB/s in a 3D torus, while an assumed interconnect cost runs from $1.5/Gb/s for the switchless torus to $4/Gb/s for the tapered dragonfly (figure 11). The cheapest capacity is also the least capacity, which is the trade every topology decision prices. The dragonfly’s assumed cost per Gb/s is the highest here because its savings come from replacing long optical runs and switch tiers at large scale, which Kim et al. (2008) reports for systems of at least 16,000 terminals; at 1,024 GPUs it has few such runs to replace. Radix, endpoint count, link speed, routing mechanisms, and equipment pricing all shift these trade-offs; the topology family alone dictates neither raw cross-sectional capacity nor operational capital cost.














Figure 11: An illustrative bandwidth-cost scenario for ML network topologies: \(\BisectionBandwidth\) (TB/s, horizontal axis) against assumed cost per Gb/s (vertical axis) for four topology configurations on a 1,024-GPU cluster: fat-tree (25.6 TB/s, $3/Gb/s), dragonfly with tapered global links (19.2 TB/s, $4), rail-optimized with a 2:1 bridging spine (12.8 TB/s, $2), and a 3D torus (6.4 TB/s, $1.5). The bandwidths follow from the stated structures at one link rate; the costs are scenario inputs that illustrate the comparison method rather than universal properties of each topology family.



The topology examples above considered one traffic pattern at a time. In practice, clusters serve multiple workloads with different communication patterns, and topology selection must balance their competing demands.

Checkpoint 3.4: Topology selection for your workload
The choice of network topology dictates the upper bound of training efficiency. Warm up by matching each single-workload pattern to its ideal topology, then design a fabric that must serve several at once.
Single-workload picks

AllReduce bandwidth: select the topology that maximizes \(\BisectionBandwidth\) for a standard data-parallel job dominated by AllReduce.
MoE traffic: select the topology that best sustains a mixture-of-experts model’s AllToAll-dominant, bursty communication, in which any rank may send to any other.
Neighbor locality: select the topology that best fits a ring AllReduce scheduled along each dimension of the machine, where every transfer goes to a physical neighbor.

Designing for a mixed cluster
You are designing the network for a new ML cluster that will run two primary workloads: (1) training a 175B-parameter language model using 3D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism), and (2) serving a mixture-of-experts model that relies heavily on AllToAll communication to route tokens to the correct experts.

Training topology: select the topology (fat-tree, rail-optimized, or hybrid) that best matches tensor parallelism within groups of 8 GPUs and data parallelism across all nodes, then justify the choice.
MoE topology: revise the topology choice for unpredictable AllToAll traffic where any GPU may need to communicate with any other GPU.
Oversubscription risk: identify which workload suffers more under 2:1 spine-layer oversubscription and propose a scheduling strategy to mitigate the impact.



Topology provides the structural capacity for the cluster of 1,024 GPUs to communicate, but structure alone does not guarantee performance. When the 1,024 GPUs synchronize contributions to the model’s 350 GB gradient state, that theoretical capacity collides with the reality of fabric behavior: congestion control and routing dynamics determine whether this traffic flows smoothly or gridlocks under the strict synchronization of the BSP model.

Self-Check: Question

A cluster designer builds a three-tier non-blocking fat-tree network using radix-64 switches (\(k = 64\)). What is the maximum number of hosts this fabric can support at 1:1 bisection bandwidth subscription, and how many total switches are required across all tiers?

\(2{,}048\) hosts and \(128\) switches
\(16{,}384\) hosts and \(1{,}024\) switches
\(65{,}536\) hosts and \(5{,}120\) switches
\(262{,}144\) hosts and \(20{,}480\) switches

Why does a rail-optimized network topology significantly reduce synchronization latency for 3D-parallel training jobs compared to a standard uniform fat-tree?

It replaces optical fiber cables with liquid-cooled copper buses across all rows
It physically connects all GPUs of the same local rank (e.g., all GPU 0s) across server nodes to dedicated rail switches, allowing same-rail transfers within a leaf group to use a single switch hop
It eliminates the need for intra-node NVLink by routing all tensor-parallel traffic through Top-of-Rack switches
It dynamically routes all AllReduce packets through the GPU display engine to bypass PCIe contention

A cluster operator considers saving capital expenditure by building a \(4:1\) oversubscribed spine in a 1,024-GPU training cluster. Explain the quantitative and economic impact of this design on a 100 GB per GPU AllReduce collective during distributed training.
Why did Google adopt a 3D torus topology for its TPU Pods, and what communication workload exposes the primary structural limitation of this topology?

The 3D torus minimizes cabling cost and external switch hardware by leveraging direct neighbor-to-neighbor links that suit structured transformer collectives, but suffers high hop count (\(\mathcal{O}(N^{1/3})\)) and bisection congestion under irregular AllToAll traffic from Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models
The 3D torus provides full non-blocking bisection bandwidth for random permutation traffic, but fails when running ring AllReduce due to cyclic buffer dependencies
The 3D torus eliminates Forward Error Correction requirements, but cannot support FP16 numerical precision
The 3D torus reduces power consumption by disabling physical link SerDes, but restricts cluster scale to 32 nodes

True or False: In a data center network, aggregate bandwidth (the sum of all endpoint link rates) and bisection bandwidth (\(\text{BW}_{\text{bisect}}\)) are identical metrics.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
A collective can finish late even when the topology provides full \(\BisectionBandwidth\). Levels 1 through 3 determine how long a transfer takes on an unloaded path; fabric behavior determines how much longer it takes once the job’s own synchronized traffic loads that path. Competing flows can concentrate on one output path, and the BSP barrier introduced in section 3.2 exposes any delay that extends the last required transfer. The relevant paths are those used by the participating workers; a congested link elsewhere in the fleet need not affect the job. In the Fleet Law (equation 1.3), measured transfer durations contribute to \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), while residual waiting at synchronization contributes to \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\), the point where the communication axis of C³ hands its cost to the coordination axis. A timeline must assign each interval consistently so the same congestion delay is not counted twice.
The p99 tail latency introduced with the BSP barrier helps expose delays that an average hides, but a particular barrier waits for its last required participant, not for a percentile. Evaluating a fabric therefore requires both transfer-time distributions and the collective completion times they produce under load.


The BSP weakest-link property means that even a single dropped packet can trigger a retransmission timeout that stalls the global barrier for milliseconds, a delay that can rival the entire communication phase of a training step. PFC-based RoCEv2 fabrics prevent the drop in the first place by running PFC, the pause mechanism introduced with the RDMA stacks (section 3.4.2), in lossless mode, so that upstream senders stop before any buffer saturates (Guo et al. 2016; Gangidi et al. 2024).

Definition 3.7: Priority flow control
Priority flow control (PFC) is a link-layer mechanism used by RoCEv2 ML cluster fabrics to prevent switch buffer overflow by sending PAUSE frames to an upstream sender when a port’s queue depth crosses a configured threshold, throttling injection on a per-priority basis without dropping packets.

Significance: In PFC-based RoCEv2 deployments, PFC is the foundation for a lossless Ethernet service. A PFC PAUSE frame must reach the upstream sender before the buffer overflows, so each pause threshold must leave headroom for the data still in flight during roughly one link round trip.
Distinction: Unlike standard IEEE 802.3 flow control, which pauses all traffic classes on a link, PFC operates per priority class, allowing latency-sensitive control messages to continue flowing while only pausing the congested gradient data queue.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that PFC solves congestion. It transforms packet loss into congestion spreading. PFC itself places no bound on how far PAUSE frames propagate, so a single faulty transceiver can pause traffic far from its own link unless a watchdog intervenes.



The danger of PFC lies in its cascading nature. When a switch port’s buffer fills, it sends a PAUSE frame upstream, which can move congestion into the upstream switch and trigger another PAUSE frame. A slow receiver, routing hot spot, or true fan-in burst can therefore pause links unrelated to the original queue. This behavior, known as congestion spreading, is the primary operational risk of PFC-based lossless Ethernet, and the flows it stalls without ever touching the congested queue are called victim flows. Fan-in is one trigger, but it is not intrinsic to every collective. A bandwidth-optimal ring exchanges data point to point, although multiple ring flows can still collide at a shared egress or an oversubscribed cut and create a hot spot without a single aggregation receiver (section 3.6.5).



One congested port’s PAUSE frames can freeze unrelated flows.



While priority flow control provides the illusion of a lossless physical layer, relying on link-layer backpressure introduces structural failure modes that do not exist in loss-tolerant packet-switched networks. When switch queues cannot drop packets to relieve congestion, pressure propagates backward through the network graph, creating two distinct hyperscale failure modes: buffer-dependency deadlocks and PFC storms.

Definition 3.8: Cyclic buffer dependency deadlock
Cyclic buffer dependency deadlock is a permanent distributed lockup in a lossless network, whether its backpressure uses PFC PAUSE frames or InfiniBand credits, where a set of switch port queues form a closed dependency cycle, each holding packets destined for the next queue while simultaneously paused by backpressure from that same queue.

Significance: A single such deadlock permanently halts traffic across all participating ports and upstream links, requiring manual intervention or watchdog timeouts that discard packets to recover. InfiniBand fabrics prevent it through deadlock-free routing and virtual-lane assignment; this section develops the PFC case.
Distinction: Unlike a PFC storm (which is a transient cascade of backpressure triggered by a slow-draining endpoint), a buffer-dependency deadlock is a static, self-sustaining topological cycle that cannot resolve itself even after traffic injection stops.
Common pitfall: Assuming multi-stage Clos (fat-tree) fabrics are inherently immune to deadlocks. Dynamic multipath routing, link failures, and address resolution flooding can introduce cyclic forwarding dependencies across switch tiers.





In a lossless network, a switch cannot forward a packet to downstream buffer \(\PacketBuffer_j\) if \(\PacketBuffer_j\) is full; instead, it holds the packet in upstream buffer \(\PacketBuffer_i\) and awaits credit or pause clearance. A directed buffer dependency graph \(\BufferDependencyGraph= (\BufferDependencyVertexSet, \BufferDependencyEdgeSet)\) formalizes this relationship, where each vertex \(\PacketBuffer_k \in \BufferDependencyVertexSet\) represents a packet buffer or virtual lane queue at a switch port, and a directed edge \((\PacketBuffer_i, \PacketBuffer_j) \in \BufferDependencyEdgeSet\) indicates that a packet currently occupying buffer \(\PacketBuffer_i\) requires buffer \(\PacketBuffer_j\) along its routing path to make forward progress.
A directed cycle in the buffer dependency graph is a necessary condition for a cyclic buffer dependency deadlock (definition 3.8), but a cycle alone does not establish that progress has stopped. The cyclic dependency in equation 1 becomes a deadlock when the occupied buffers cannot drain and every participant waits for its successor:
\[\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \dots \to \PacketBuffer_k \to \PacketBuffer_1 \tag{1}\]
When each buffer in the cycle fills beyond its configured pause threshold, each port asserts a PFC PAUSE frame to its predecessor. Because no buffer can advance a packet into a paused successor, no buffer can drain, and no port can de-assert its PAUSE signal. The entire cycle freezes permanently. Figure 12 models this mutual protocol interlock across a four-switch ring whose queues (\(\PacketBuffer_1\) through \(\PacketBuffer_4\)) are completely full. Tracing the ring reveals an intractable counter-rotational deadlock: while solid gray arrows trace packet forwarding dependencies advancing clockwise (\(\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \PacketBuffer_3 \to \PacketBuffer_4 \to \PacketBuffer_1\)), dashed red PAUSE frames propagate counterclockwise. Each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while waiting for its downstream successor to drain, permanently freezing all four queues until an external watchdog intervenes to drop frames.






Figure 12: A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency: Four switch queues form the cycle of equation 1. Follow the solid arrows clockwise: each full buffer holds packets that need space in the next. The dashed PAUSE frames run counterclockwise, so each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while awaiting space in its downstream successor, and no queue can drain until a watchdog drops packets.



Routing changes and flooding can create the dependencies needed for deadlock. During link failure or Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) convergence, inconsistent forwarding tables can create transient loops. A lossy IP network eventually discards a looping packet when its time-to-live expires; a lossless class has no such release, so looping traffic can fill the buffers along the loop and hold them. If traffic occupies a cycle of mutually blocked queues, backpressure can prevent progress until recovery breaks the dependency. Multicast or broadcast replication can also fill queues whose dependencies intersect, while cross-connects and asymmetric failover paths can introduce cycles absent from the intended hierarchical route. None of these conditions alone proves a deadlock; the occupied buffers and pause states must form the closed waiting cycle described by the model.
Microsoft’s production RoCE deployment encountered the flooding trigger directly (war story 3.1).

War Story 3.1: Microsoft's PFC deadlock (2016)Context: A team led by Chuanxiong Guo at Microsoft Research deployed RoCEv2 across Microsoft’s data centers, a fleet operating at the scale of tens of thousands of servers, to support latency-sensitive services. Their design provided a lossless fabric with PFC, and the team developed a Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP)-based PFC mechanism to extend the deployment beyond virtual local area network (VLAN) boundaries (Guo et al. 2016).
Mechanism: PFC interacted with Ethernet flooding to create a cyclic buffer dependency. A dead server with an incomplete mapping between an IP address and a media-access-control address caused upstream switches to flood lossless packets to every port; PFC PAUSE frames then propagated upstream in response to the flooded traffic, forming a closed loop of paused buffers.
Impact: Lossless traffic through the switches in the cycle stopped entirely and stayed stopped, because no buffer in the dependency loop could drain without outside intervention.
Fix: Microsoft blocked broadcast and multicast traffic from entering lossless traffic classes, and dropped lossless packets when the corresponding Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) entry was incomplete rather than falling back to flooding.
Systems lesson: PFC backpressure is a structural vulnerability of lossless Ethernet at hyperscale. RoCE fabrics require packet-class discipline, PFC pause telemetry, and hardware-level safeguards because a mechanism designed to avoid packet loss can itself become the failure mode. ML training fabrics built on RoCE inherit this risk directly. A single incomplete ARP entry can freeze the lossless class that carries a multi-thousand-GPU training run’s gradients, with the cluster appearing healthy while no gradient flows between workers.



Guo, Chuanxiong, Haitao Wu, Zhong Deng, Gaurav Soni, Jianxi Ye, Jitendra Padhye, and Marina Lipshteyn. 2016. “RDMA over Commodity Ethernet at Scale.” Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGCOMM Conference, 202–15. https://doi.org/10.1145/2934872.2934908.



In contrast to a static topological cycle, a PFC storm is a dynamic, runaway amplification phenomenon. A single “slow drainer” (an accelerator stalled by memory bus saturation, operating system preemption, or a degraded transceiver with elevated bit error rates) fails to consume packets at wire speed.
The attached ToR switch queue fills and sends a PAUSE frame to the sender. Because multi-port switches aggregate traffic from many sources across shared packet buffers, the paused queue blocks buffer allocation for unrelated packets (head-of-line blocking). The spine switches feeding that ToR then fill their buffers and pause the other leaf switches that send through them. Each additional tier widens the set of paused links until traffic between node pairs that never communicated with the stalled worker also stops. These victim flows turn one slow endpoint into a job-wide barrier delay, because every data-parallel worker whose path crosses a paused spine port now arrives late at the barrier.
Because a degraded transceiver is one such slow drainer, a component-exposure calculation shows how often a cluster should expect at least one. It does not by itself estimate the probability of a PFC storm.

Napkin Math 3.5: Probability of at least one transceiver degradationProblem: A 4096-GPU RoCE cluster, larger than the reference cluster, is in operation. If the probability that a given transceiver begins degrading on a given day is 0.001 percent, what is the chance that at least one transceiver degrades on a given day?
Math: Assume independent transceiver-degradation events with the same per-device probability.

Total exposure: 4096 \(\times\) 3 link tiers = 12,288 links, or 24,576 transceivers.
Probability of zero transceiver degradations: \(\Pr(\text{no degradation}) = (1 - 0.00001)^{24,576} \approx 0.782\).
Probability of at least one degradation: \(\Pr(\text{at least one degradation}) = 1 - 0.782 = \mathbf{0.218}\) (about 21.8 percent).

Systems insight: Under these assumptions, a large RoCE cluster has a 21.8 percent daily chance of at least one degraded transceiver. This result motivates hardware telemetry and automated remediation, but estimating fabric-wide freeze risk additionally requires the conditional probability that a degradation triggers and propagates a PFC storm.





Switches can use PFC watchdog timers to detect prolonged pause states and trigger recovery without a full reboot. The configured threshold \(\PfcWatchdogTimeout\) must fit the deployment’s pause and recovery budgets; a range such as \(50\text{--}200\text{ ms}\) is a configuration example, not a universal requirement. Exceeding it indicates stalled progress, not proof of a cyclic deadlock. Depending on the implementation, mitigation can disable pause handling or discard affected traffic so blocked queues can drain. The transport must then recover any lost data, with the completion penalty determined by retransmission behavior, outstanding traffic, and the collective’s dependencies. On an RNIC with Go-Back-N-style recovery (section 3.4.3), each discarded packet also costs the in-flight window behind it, so breaking a pause converts a stalled queue into a retransmission tail that the waiting collective absorbs.
This systemic brittleness is driving hyperscale operators toward next-generation architectures such as the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) (Ultra Ethernet Consortium 2025), detailed in section 3.10.1, and loss-tolerant RDMA designs (Mittal et al. 2018). Designs that combine packet spraying with congestion control and selective retransmission can operate without link-layer PFC. Removing PFC removes its pause-based deadlocks and storms, but endpoint recovery must still bound the completion-time penalty of congestion and loss.

Mittal, Radhika, Alexander Shpiner, Aurojit Panda, Eitan Zahavi, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Sylvia Ratnasamy, and Scott Shenker. 2018. “Revisiting Network Support for RDMA.” Proceedings of the 2018 Conference of the ACM Special Interest Group on Data Communication, 313–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3230543.3230557.




End-to-end congestion control adjusts injection rates before queues reach their pause or overflow thresholds. For a BSP workload with a completion-time target, this is a latency requirement rather than an optional throughput optimization. Delaying a required transfer can extend the synchronization boundary, so the controller must balance delivered throughput against queueing and recovery tails.
The first widely deployed solution, DCQCN,9 operates as a reactive feedback loop using ECN (Zhu et al. 2015). When a switch’s queue depth exceeds a configured threshold, it marks the ECN bit in the packet header. The receiver echoes this mark back to the sender via a congestion notification packet (CNP), prompting the sender to reduce its injection rate using a multiplicative-decrease algorithm. DCQCN is widely supported, but production AI collectives expose a tuning problem: ECN thresholds and NIC firmware behavior can trade off PFC avoidance, throughput, visibility, and tail latency rather than offering one stable optimum (Gangidi et al. 2024).
9 DCQCN (Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification): Introduced by Zhu et al. (2015) (Microsoft and Mellanox) at SIGCOMM 2015 for large-scale RDMA fabrics, its binary ECN/CNP feedback loop is simpler to deploy than telemetry-rich schemes. However, it creates a delicate tuning surface for training collectives: Meta’s 2024 RoCE deployment showed that aggressive ECN marking reduces PFC pauses but degrades collective completion time (Gangidi et al. 2024).
Zhu, Y., H. Eran, D. Firestone, C. Guo, M. Lipshteyn, Y. Liron, J. Padhye, S. Raindel, M. H. Yahia, and M. Zhang. 2015. “Congestion Control for Large-Scale RDMA Deployments.” ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 45 (4): 523–36. https://doi.org/10.1145/2829988.2787484.

Gangidi, Adi, Rui Miao, Sandeep Hebbani, Gaya Nagarajan, Omar Baldonado, Lixin Gao, Hany Morsy Goes, et al. 2024. “RDMA over Ethernet for Distributed AI Training at Meta Scale.” Proceedings of the ACM SIGCOMM 2024 Conference, 56–69. https://doi.org/10.1145/3651890.3672233.
10 HPCC (High Precision Congestion Control): Introduced by Li et al. (2019) (Alibaba) at SIGCOMM 2019, HPCC replaces binary ECN with per-packet in-network telemetry (INT), giving senders path-load measurements for adjusting injection rates while accounting for feedback delay and changing demand. The systems trade-off is hardware dependency: it requires programmable switch ASICs capable of appending INT metadata at line rate.
Li, Yuliang, Rui Miao, Hongqiang Harry Liu, Yan Zhuang, Fei Feng, Lingbo Tang, Zheng Cao, et al. 2019. “HPCC: High Precision Congestion Control.” Proceedings of the ACM Special Interest Group on Data Communication (SIGCOMM), 44–58. https://doi.org/10.1145/3341302.3342085.
HPCC10 uses in-network telemetry (INT) to give the sender more information about path load (Li et al. 2019). Switch measurements of queue occupancy and transmitted traffic let the controller estimate an appropriate injection rate rather than react only to a binary congestion mark. That information still arrives after a feedback delay, so the controller must account for changing load and avoid overreaction. The evaluated design reduces queue buildup and tail latency, but requires switch telemetry support and compatible endpoint processing. DCQCN needs less detailed switch feedback, trading that simpler deployment requirement against a different tuning problem.



Static routing protocols like ECMP11 distribute traffic by hashing flow headers to fixed paths. This approach works well for many small flows but can create persistent collisions among the small number of elephant flows typical of ML training. Consider a scenario with 4 equal-cost paths and 8 large gradient flows. An even distribution would place 2 flows on each link. Static hashing can instead place 4 flows on one link while another sits idle. In a synchronized training step, the overloaded link then determines completion time and can halve useful bandwidth in this scenario.
11 ECMP (equal-cost multi-path): ECMP selects a path by hashing on the 5-tuple (source/destination IP, source/destination port, protocol), which means the same flow always takes the same path. This determinism is a feature for packet ordering but a liability for ML. Because a single AllReduce ring produces a small number of persistent flows, hash collisions are not transient statistical events but permanent hot spots that persist for the entire training run.12 Packet spraying: Unlike standard Ethernet (which hashes flows to single paths to avoid reordering), packet spraying sends individual packets of a single flow across multiple paths. This can improve \(\BisectionBandwidth\) for AllReduce elephant flows when the transport can tolerate or repair reordering. The Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) specification design explicitly includes multi-path packet spraying and flexible ordering to reduce the ECMP collision problem for AI/HPC traffic (Ultra Ethernet Consortium 2025).
Ultra Ethernet Consortium. 2025. Ultra Ethernet Specification V1.0. Ultra Ethernet Consortium.
Adaptive routing mitigates this problem by allowing switches to select among eligible output paths using congestion information rather than only a static hash. The implementation is protocol- and device-dependent. Packet-level spraying12 can send packets of one connection over different paths, so the receiver may observe reordering. Compatible endpoint support must accept out-of-order placement or restore the transport’s required ordering; the presence of InfiniBand alone does not guarantee arbitrary spraying across every path.
Ethernet fabrics can also employ flowlet switching, changing a flow’s path between bursts separated by a gap large enough to preserve packet order across the candidate paths. Its usefulness depends on the available gaps and path delays. MoE expert exchanges illustrate the demand for path diversity. A dense exchange among 64 expert-parallel ranks contains at most \(64(64-1)=4{,}032\) directed remote rank pairs after excluding self-transfers; active traffic depends on expert placement and token-routing sparsity. Static-hash collisions can concentrate that traffic, while adaptive routing can improve use of the provisioned \(\BisectionBandwidth\). Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) can create similar exchanges when batches of embedding requests and results move among table shards. The batch and shard placement determine the traffic matrix, rather than every individual lookup requiring a global exchange.



Congestion control and adaptive routing manage flows that traverse the interior of the fabric. A different failure mode occurs at the edge, where the traffic pattern itself overwhelms a single port regardless of how much capacity the fabric interior provides.

Definition 3.9: Incast
Incast is a many-to-one ML cluster traffic pattern in which a large number of senders simultaneously transmit data to a single receiver port, concentrating line-rate traffic from multiple sources into a single switch queue and potentially overflowing the buffer if the burst outlasts available buffering and control response, even when the rest of the fabric is uncongested.

Significance: Flat aggregation, synchronized storage reads, or other fan-in phases can direct many senders toward one receiver. The deliberately worst-case scenario here assumes a RoCE fabric whose ports all run at 400 Gb/s. In it, 256 senders each transmit at 50 GB/s toward one switch egress, producing 12.8 TB/s of offered load against a 400 Gb/s port. A 32 MB buffer then overflows in about 2.5 μs under the stated assumptions, after which the switch either drops packets or, in a PFC deployment, pauses its upstream neighbors. The example is a stress bound, not the traffic matrix of a ring AllReduce.
Distinction: Unlike general congestion (which occurs on shared internal links when aggregate traffic exceeds link capacity), incast is an endpoint bottleneck: it occurs even if every internal spine and leaf link is completely uncongested, because the bottleneck is the single destination port, not the fabric interior.
Common pitfall: Incast is not necessarily rare or unpredictable. Training jobs create it on a schedule, whenever many GPUs read dataset shards from or write checkpoints to the same storage node, and in the aggregation step of a tree or hierarchical reduction, where several ranks send partial sums to one parent. A gradient ring is different; its point-to-point flows can still collide at a shared egress, but that is a hot spot rather than many-to-one incast. The severity depends on the collective algorithm, topology, routing, and oversubscription, so it must be measured and mitigated rather than treated as an edge case.



Figure 13 contrasts 12.8 TB/s of offered traffic from 256 senders with a 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) egress. Each sender injects at 50 GB/s in this worst-case scenario. The buffer fills over a finite interval; control feedback can reduce arrivals, drops can discard excess traffic, or backpressure can move the queueing upstream. Whether that pressure spreads depends on shared queues and the paths carrying the traffic. Let the aggregate arrival rate to one egress be \(\ArrivalRate\), the egress service rate be \(\EgressServiceRate\), and the instantaneous queue occupancy be \(\EgressQueueOccupancy(\TimeInstant)\). While a burst persists and \(\ArrivalRate > \EgressServiceRate\), the queue grows at the net rate
\[
\EgressQueueOccupancy(\TimeInstant) = \min\!\left(\EgressBufferCapacity,\; \EgressQueueOccupancy(0) + (\ArrivalRate-\EgressServiceRate)\TimeInstant\right),
\]
where \(\EgressBufferCapacity\) is the finite buffer capacity. The ratio \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate/\EgressServiceRate\) distinguishes a drainable workload from sustained overload: for \(\ServingUtilization<1\), idle intervals can drain the queue; as long-run \(\ServingUtilization\) approaches one, less slack remains to absorb bursts; and for \(\ServingUtilization>1\), occupancy must reach a control threshold or the buffer limit if the overload persists. This is a packet queue, distinct from the request queues of an inference server. Serialization and propagation set the unloaded path latency, whereas queued bytes add approximately \(\EgressQueueOccupancy/\EgressServiceRate\) of waiting time.


⇄ Contrast: Request queues, whose arrival and service rates set serving latency rather than switch buffer occupancy, are developed in Queuing theory for batched inference.
In the deliberately worst-case incast above, \(\ServingUtilization\) is 256×, so the 32 MB buffer fills in about 2.5 μs. Once full, that buffer represents 640 μs of egress waiting time. By contrast, the bandwidth-delay product for the 400 Gb/s egress and an illustrative 5 μs feedback round trip is only 250 KB: it measures data in flight on the path, not the buffering needed to absorb an arbitrary fan-in burst. ECN must mark early enough for feedback to arrive before exhaustion; PFC can prevent a drop, but its backpressure can spread congestion. A larger buffer extends the reaction window at the cost of a larger tail-latency bound.






Figure 13: A true incast burst: This deliberately worst-case fan-in scenario sends 256 sources at 50 GB/s toward one 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) egress with a 32 MB buffer. The 12.8 TB/s offered load oversubscribes the destination egress by 256×. Flat aggregation or synchronized reads can create this pattern; bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce does not, because each rank exchanges point-to-point chunks.



Synchronized ML traffic is susceptible to both true fan-in and shared-egress hot spots. When a layer finishes backward computation, many ranks can inject traffic at once, and flat or hierarchical aggregation phases can create true fan-in. Production clusters mitigate both cases along three complementary dimensions:

Time. Layer-staggering triggers each gradient bucket’s AllReduce as soon as backpropagation produces it. Final-layer gradients reduce while earlier layers are still computing, so communication is spread across the backward pass instead of released as one synchronized burst. The same staggering is communication-computation overlap, so it also hides transfer time behind the backward computation that remains.
Space. Collective algorithm selection bounds fan-in at individual switch ports. Hierarchical and rail-local reductions aggregate gradients in stages so that no single port must absorb all senders at once, and topology-aware placement keeps concurrent ring flows off oversubscribed ports.
Priority. Quality of service (QoS) classification tags gradient traffic with the highest service class to reduce interference from background storage or management traffic; shared links, buffers, and arbitration still constrain isolation.

These mitigations spread the burst in time, space, and priority, but they do not eliminate congestion or tail latency. The question becomes how to build end-to-end clusters that perform despite these realities.


↪ How far layer-staggered overlap hides gradient traffic, and how much communication it still leaves exposed, is developed in Communication-Computation Overlap.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
The final level of the stack is cluster design, where wires, transport, topology, and congestion control combine into a coherent system. The goal of cluster design is to provide an end-to-end gradient bus that makes thousands of distributed GPUs feel like a single machine. At this level, the abstraction layers collapse into concrete engineering decisions: which cables to buy, how to wire the racks, which protocol to deploy, and how to validate that the resulting fabric delivers the bandwidth the training job expects. Two representative large-scale architectures, one built on InfiniBand and one on Ethernet, illuminate the trade-offs that define ML infrastructure (NVIDIA 2023; Meta Engineering 2024; Gangidi et al. 2024).


In a well-designed cluster, the network fabric acts as a scheduler-aware extension of the system bus, not a passive pipe. The ~9× per-direction cliff between NVLink and one external port, measured at the start of this chapter, is the gap the cluster must hide. Communication-computation overlap, which the Fleet Law credits as \(\OverlappedTime\), is the first mechanism for hiding it. Because gradients for the final layers are computed first, the system can launch their AllReduce while the GPUs continue computing gradients for earlier layers. If the backward pass requires 500 ms of computation and the AllReduce takes 300 ms, ideal overlap could hide the communication cost behind computation, reducing the exposed overhead to \(\max(0, 300 - 500) = 0\). In practice, dependency chains and resource contention limit overlap, leaving a last-mile problem: gradients computed near the end of backpropagation have little subsequent computation behind which to hide their transfer time.
Placement is the second mechanism, because it decides which communication crosses each boundary. The placement from the opening of this chapter, tensor parallelism inside the NVLink domain with pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas spanning nodes, becomes a wiring rule at cluster scale, because each fabric tier must be provisioned for the traffic placed on it. The links between nodes must meet the pipeline’s activation-transfer budget, which physical adjacency alone does not guarantee. The full fabric carries the data-parallel exchanges, which gradient accumulation makes less frequent and overlap partly hides. Production designs therefore differ mainly in how they provision that outermost tier, as the two that follow show.



The NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD architecture connects DGX H100 nodes using an NDR InfiniBand network, serving as a concrete implementation of the gradient bus concept (NVIDIA 2023). Each node acts as a dense compute island, with eight H100 GPUs connected via NVSwitch to provide 900 GB/s of internal bandwidth. Externally, each GPU pairs with a ConnectX-7 NIC delivering 400 Gb/s of injection bandwidth. Across a standard scalable unit of 32 nodes (256 GPUs), this yields an aggregate injection bandwidth of 12.8 TB/s (256 \(\times\) 50 GB/s), the rate the scalable unit can offer the fabric when every GPU transmits at once.

NVIDIA. 2023. NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD: Next Generation Scalable Infrastructure for AI Leadership. RA-11333-001 V11. NVIDIA.
This architecture explicitly instantiates the five-level network model. At Level 1, it standardizes on 400 Gb/s NDR links, with media chosen by reach between each node and its leaf and between leaf and spine. At Level 2, it relies on InfiniBand’s native credit-based flow control to guarantee a lossless medium without the fragility of Ethernet PFC. Level 3 implements a rail-optimized fat-tree. GPU rails are aligned across a scalable unit so same-rail traffic stays close and cross-rail traffic traverses the spine layer; the rack-level ToR allocation used earlier to illustrate switch radix is the simpler alternative this wiring replaces. At Level 4, hardware-based adaptive routing can select among spine paths to improve bisection behavior for cross-rank communication. At Level 5, the design is modular: multiple SuperPOD scalable units connect through additional switching to form larger clusters (NVIDIA 2023). For the 175B-parameter model, the physical infrastructure would consist of four SuperPOD scalable units wired together, allowing 1,024 GPUs to function as a single synchronous instrument.



Meta disclosed two Grand Teton-based 24,576-H100 clusters: one using RoCE over an Arista/OCP Ethernet fabric and one using NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand, both with 400 Gb/s endpoints. Meta used both for Llama 3 training and reported ongoing Llama 3 training on the RoCE cluster (Meta Engineering 2024). The primary motivation for Ethernet is operational scale and supply chain resilience: by using Ethernet, Meta can source switches from multiple vendors and use the same optical infrastructure and management tooling shared by their front-end serving fleet, avoiding the operational silo of a dedicated InfiniBand island.

Meta Engineering. 2024. Building Meta’s GenAI Infrastructure. Engineering at Meta Blog.
Meta’s RoCE study shows how Level 4 choices affect the complete fabric. It describes PFC watchdogs for long-duration pause events, iterative routing designs beyond plain ECMP, future-oriented flowlet switching experiments, and a 400G deployment in which DCQCN tuning proved difficult enough that Meta proceeded without DCQCN while relying on PFC plus higher-layer collective controls (Gangidi et al. 2024). The lesson is to validate the combination of endpoint behavior, routing, and flow control under the intended collective traffic. Large-transfer throughput alone does not establish small-message latency or recovery tails, and those results cannot be inferred from the Ethernet or InfiniBand label.

Systems Perspective 3.3: InfiniBand vs. RoCE: The industry verdictThe InfiniBand and RoCE deployments demonstrate different ways to meet a workload’s communication contract. Their equipment, routing, recovery mechanisms, and operational requirements must be compared as complete configurations. InfiniBand’s native credit-based flow control can simplify lossless configuration and tighten small-message tails, while RoCE inherits Ethernet’s multi-vendor switching and shared operational tooling at the cost of tuning buffering, PFC, ECN, and routing policy. For training runs, frequent small exchanges can expose startup latency even when a full step lasts seconds. For inference serving, the importance of fabric latency depends on model partitioning, request shape, and service-level objectives (SLOs). In both cases, delivered performance and operating cost decide the trade-off.


These case studies close the five-level stack by showing how the physical wire, transport protocol, topology, and congestion controls become one production fabric. The remaining operational problem is not how to build a single fast cluster, but how to share that expensive substrate across teams and workloads without sacrificing the predictable performance that training demands.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
Sharing a cluster can recover capacity that a single workload leaves unused. In the scenario of a $300 million system with 30 percent unused capacity, the idle fraction corresponds to $90 million of the equipment budget. Network virtualization must make sharing compatible with bandwidth allocations, latency targets, and access isolation. These requirements interact because tenants still share physical links and buffers. A proposed policy might reserve 80 percent of the cluster’s \(\BisectionBandwidth\) for training and allocate the remaining 20 percent to inference and preprocessing. Enforcing that policy requires admission control and compatible scheduling along the relevant paths; a virtual NIC or separate traffic class alone does not guarantee the end-to-end share.


Cloud providers expose NIC resources to virtualized GPU instances through single-root I/O virtualization (SR-IOV), a standard that allows a physical NIC to present multiple virtual functions (VFs). Each VF exposes its own hardware queues, doorbell registers, and DMA mappings, which software can assign to a workload. A directly assigned VF can remove host software mediation from the active DMA path, while drivers and virtualization software still configure access and manage the device. Performance depends on the NIC, I/O placement, and competing traffic. Because VFs share physical resources, placement logic must reserve NIC capacity and QoS policy alongside GPUs rather than treat the network as an unbounded pool.
However, hardware-level isolation still needs explicit bandwidth policy. SR-IOV exposes multiple VFs that share the NIC’s physical resources; administrators can add per-VF or per-group QoS policies to cap or guarantee bandwidth, such as assigning eight VFs 50 Gb/s each on a 400 Gb/s NIC. For the 175B-parameter model training on a multi-tenant cluster, that configured partitioning can prevent a neighboring tenant from stealing bandwidth, but it also enforces a hard ceiling on peak throughput. The training job must be architected to operate within this slice, as no amount of software optimization can burst beyond the configured VF limit.



Consider a worst-case contention scenario on a shared cluster: the 175B model is midway through a gradient AllReduce when a neighboring job initiates a massive checkpoint save. Without strict isolation, a bursty 100 GB write, which occupies a 400 Gb/s port for 2 s at full line rate, can claim a large share of the shared spine links for that interval and stretch every AllReduce whose traffic crosses them. To prevent this noisy-neighbor effect, high-performance fabrics rely on quality of service (QoS) mechanisms that enforce fairness at the packet level.
InfiniBand virtual lanes (VLs) separate credit and buffer state within a physical link; the architecture allows up to 16 lanes per link, one of them reserved for subnet management (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000). Ethernet/RoCE uses traffic class mappings and queue policies, whose supported counts and behavior depend on the device. In InfiniBand, exhausted credits for a storage lane need not block a gradient lane that has credits available, but both still share link bandwidth and arbitration. On Ethernet, enhanced transmission selection allocates service among traffic classes. Devices may also partition buffer and forwarding resources into network slices. These mechanisms reduce interference when classification, resource allocation, and scheduling agree across the path; shared priorities or buffers can still couple tenants.
Virtualization solves the sharing problem but makes performance diagnosis harder. When a training job slows down on a multi-tenant cluster, the cause could be a physical link degradation, a noisy neighbor exceeding its bandwidth allocation, or a misconfigured QoS policy. Systematic monitoring is essential to distinguish these cases.
