title: Preface
text:
This book is for anyone who understands machine learning on a single machine and now faces the challenge of making it work at scale. The problems of scale are not the problems of a single node, only bigger. They are qualitatively different: networks partition, hardware fails as a statistical certainty, and the societal impact of every design decision is amplified by millions of users.
The assumed foundation is what an introductory ML systems course or equivalent experience supplies, namely local training and inference, accelerator execution, memory hierarchy, and basic performance reasoning. No particular prior textbook is required. The advanced scope here is the transition from that single node to a coordinated fleet. For readers who want a refresher, The D·A·M Taxonomy restates the single-machine foundation this book builds on, including the iron law, arithmetic intensity and the roofline, the accelerator memory hierarchy, the memory cost of mixed-precision training, and transformer arithmetic. The remaining appendices collect the diagnostic tables, the communication, reliability, and serving models, and the reference numbers the chapters use.
The scope ranges from designing the physical substrate of an AI data center, to scaling training beyond the limits of a single accelerator, to reasoning about what happens when a production fleet serves a global user base. Throughout, the focus is on the physics of distribution, the invariants that govern every fleet-scale ML system regardless of the framework, the model, or the era.

title: Preface
text:
In 2012, training AlexNet took five to six days on two GPUs (Krizhevsky et al. 2012). By 2023, public GPT-4-class estimates placed frontier training at roughly 25,000 GPUs running for about three months (Patel and Wong 2023); OpenAI did not disclose the actual hardware configuration (OpenAI et al. 2023). This is not the same engineering problem at a larger scale. It is a categorically different engineering problem.

Krizhevsky, Alex, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. 2012. “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 25.

Patel, Dylan, and Gerald Wong. 2023. GPT-4 Architecture, Infrastructure, Training Dataset, Costs, Vision, MoE. SemiAnalysis Blog.

OpenAI, Josh Achiam, Steven Adler, Sandhini Agarwal, Lama Ahmad, Ilge Akkaya, Florencia Leoni Aleman, et al. 2023. “GPT-4 Technical Report.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2303.08774, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2303.08774.
On a single machine, performance is governed by the memory wall, the gap between processor speed and memory bandwidth. In a distributed cluster, a new wall emerges: the bisection bandwidth wall, where the minimum network bandwidth that bisects the cluster can cap throughput for traffic that must cross that cut. Data no longer moves through local hierarchies alone; it traverses optical fabrics governed by the speed of light between racks and across continents. Hardware failures, rare enough on a single machine to be treated as exceptions, become routine statistical events at fleet scale. Long training runs must plan for interruptions rather than rely on every component remaining available until completion.
These are not operational annoyances. They are physical constraints, as fundamental and as permanent as the memory wall, Amdahl’s Law, or the energy cost of data movement. They require their own engineering discipline, with its own invariants:

The Universal Scaling Law: Within empirically validated regimes, model loss falls as a power law in training compute, data, or parameters, so each further improvement demands multiplicatively more resources. This is the pressure that moves machine learning from single machines onto fleets.
The Bisection Bandwidth Theorem: For communication patterns that must cross the minimum bisection, throughput is bounded by that bisection bandwidth.
The Fleet Law: Under fixed-work scaling, reduced per-node computation competes with communication and coordination costs, so adding workers does not guarantee proportional speedup.
The Young-Daly Checkpoint Law: The optimal checkpoint interval balances the cost of writing state against the expected cost of lost work due to failure.
The Serving Cost Dominance Law: For high-traffic production models, cumulative inference operational expenditure can exceed the one-time training cost, making serving efficiency a lifecycle optimization target.
The Fairness Impossibility Law: With unequal group base rates and imperfect prediction, risk scores cannot satisfy groupwise calibration and equal mean scores across groups within both outcome classes simultaneously. Thresholded error-rate parity and demographic parity are distinct requirements with their own trade-offs.

If single-machine ML systems engineering asks “what can one machine build?”, then fleet-scale ML systems engineering asks “what can a thousand machines build together, and at what cost to reliability, efficiency, and society?”
That final clause is what sets fleet-scale engineering apart. A single machine affects its user; a fleet affects everyone its outputs touch, across millions of decisions per second. At that scale, reliability, efficiency, and fairness stop being features and become engineering constraints as binding as bandwidth or power. A system that scales but cannot be trusted has not been engineered. It has only been enlarged.
This book provides that foundation. It follows the Hennessy and Patterson pedagogical model, extending the quantitative, principles-first approach to the distributed scale (Hennessy and Patterson 2011; Hennessy and Patterson 2019, 2017). Just as their work taught a generation to reason about processor performance from first principles, this book teaches the reader to reason about fleet performance, replacing intuition about distributed systems with measurement, and ad hoc scaling with engineering.

Hennessy, J. L., and D. A. Patterson. 2011. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. Morgan Kaufmann.

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2019. “A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture.” Communications of the ACM 62 (2): 48–60. https://doi.org/10.1145/3282307.

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2017. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. 6th ed. Morgan Kaufmann.
The architectural priorities and operational failure modes explored in these chapters did not originate in an academic vacuum. They were gathered directly from practitioners in industry, through technical exchanges at conferences, engineering meetups, and conversations with colleagues who generously made the time to explain what breaks when scaling models across thousands of accelerators and what practicing systems engineers must understand.
The assumed single-node foundations supply the bricks: tensors, kernels, memory hierarchies, and optimization loops. A fleet is not built from more bricks. It is an orchestra. A single musician can produce music of remarkable beauty, but an orchestra is not simply many musicians playing at once. It requires a conductor, a score, precise synchronization, and the ability to recover gracefully when a player drops out. The acoustics of the concert hall shape the sound in ways that no individual instrument can control. The principles that govern orchestral performance (coordination, communication latency, fault tolerance, and the physics of the performance space) are categorically different from those that govern a solo performer. ML fleets work the same way. A training cluster, a serving fleet, and an edge deployment are vastly different systems, but beneath them sit the same building blocks: parallelism strategies, collective communication primitives, checkpoint protocols, scheduling algorithms, and the trade-offs between throughput, latency, fault tolerance, and cost.

title: Preface
text:
This book focuses on the Machine Learning Fleet: coordinated machines that jointly train, serve, or maintain ML models. Warehouse-scale training clusters are one form; geographically distributed serving replicas and heterogeneous edge devices are others. Across these forms, communication and coordination couple local execution to fleet behavior, while reliability, resource budgets, and governance constrain the design.
The content is organized into four parts:

Part I: The Fleet builds the physical substrate of the AI data center from the ground up: the silicon and cooling of compute infrastructure, the network fabrics that connect thousands of accelerators, and the scalable data storage that feeds training pipelines.
Part II: Distributed ML establishes the logic of distribution beyond a single machine: the parallelism strategies (data, tensor, and pipeline) for training models too large for single devices, the collective communication primitives that synchronize gradients, the fault tolerance mechanisms that ensure reliability when failure is routine, and the orchestration systems that manage the fleet.
Part III: Deployment at Scale takes the trained model from the cluster to the world: performance engineering that connects runtime efficiency to fleet capacity, inference serving at massive scale, edge intelligence across heterogeneous and federated devices, and the operational lifecycle required to manage production fleets.
Part IV: The Responsible Fleet confronts the forces that determine whether the fleet serves its users or harms them: security and privacy, robust system design, environmental sustainability, and responsible engineering as constraints as fundamental as power density or bisection bandwidth.

These four parts trace a path through the Fleet Stack, a layered abstraction that organizes an ML system at distributed scale, from the physical facility up to its governance. The stack has eight rows grouped into four bands, and each band is one part of the book. The Infrastructure band (Part I) holds Facility & Accelerators and Fabric & Storage, the physical substrate. The Distribution band (Part II) holds Distributed Execution and Reliability & Control, which manage parallel work, communication, scheduling, and recovery. The Serving band (Part III) holds Runtime & Serving and Operations, which take models to users and manage the production lifecycle. The Governance band (Part IV) holds Assurance (security, privacy, and robustness) and Governance & Sustainability, which together turn trust, risk, policy, and environmental cost into engineering constraints. Each row provides an abstraction to the row above and consumes the row below. Engineering decisions in the Infrastructure band constrain what is possible in the bands above it, while governance requirements constrain choices throughout the stack. Privacy, acceptable risk, and environmental budgets enter the design from the beginning; Part IV develops their enforcement mechanisms after the infrastructure and operational dependencies are available.
Where the Fleet Stack locates responsibility, a second framework diagnoses cost. The C³ taxonomy divides the wall-clock time of distributed execution into Compute, Communication, and Coordination, and the Fleet Law turns that division into an equation for distributed step time. Every chapter applies this lens to its own layer of the stack. Three recurring workloads, the archetypes, keep the analysis concrete: a large dense language model (Archetype A), a recommendation model with very large embedding tables (Archetype B), and a model trained by federated learning across phone-class devices (Archetype C). Each stresses a different part of the fleet, and the chapters return to whichever one exposes their central constraint.
Throughout the book, a margin figure highlights which rows of the stack each chapter addresses, providing a navigation cue at every chapter opening:
The full stack above shows each row with its scope, grouped into the four parts of the book. The Roman numerals (I–IV) mark those parts; the row intensity marks emphasis. The stack uses one accent color throughout so that shade, not hue, carries the chapter-focus signal.
In the margin figures throughout the book, the intensity of each row reflects how strongly the chapter engages it. Brighter (higher intensity) marks the chapter’s primary focus; dimmer (lower intensity) marks contextual relevance as constraints propagate upward. Consider three chapters that illustrate how the emphasis shifts:
In Compute Infrastructure, the bottom row dominates because the chapter is about silicon, power, cooling, and physical deployment. In Distributed Training, Distributed Execution is brightest while Reliability & Control remains visibly relevant because large training runs depend on scheduling and recovery. In Responsible AI, Governance & Sustainability is primary while Assurance stays strong because accountability depends on measurable trust and risk controls. The same stack tells three different stories, and in each one a decision made in one row ripples through the rows above and below it.
Small visual notes sit in the margins wherever a relationship is fastest to grasp by eye. They are reading aids, not figures to cite later. At fleet scale, this visual grammar makes bandwidth gaps, failure blast radius, checkpoint ratios, and edge-energy trade-offs visible without interrupting the argument. When a miniature uses a log scale, it says so inside the image.
















Alongside these visual miniatures, the margins carry unnumbered marginal navigation pointers that trace architectural dependencies across the fleet without interrupting the reading flow of the prose:

↩︎ Backward pointer: Directs the reader back to the earlier chapter where a physical limit, hardware contract, or analytical model was established.
↪ Forward pointer: Directs the reader ahead to the later chapter, or to the appendix, where the current idea is developed, measured, or enforced.
⇄ Contrast: Marks a place where two chapters treat the same problem differently, so the comparison is visible at a glance.

A pointer only orients. When a sentence depends on another chapter, the reference stays in the text.
Each part builds on the previous one, so sequential reading is recommended. The reading paths below offer alternatives for readers with specific goals.

title: Scaling Machine Learning Systems
text:
Modern machine learning operates at scales that fundamentally change engineering requirements—models too large for single GPUs, services spanning continents, deployments carrying societal responsibilities. This book addresses AI engineering at scale. The treatment follows the lifecycle of a massive-scale system: defining the distributed architecture, building the physical infrastructure fleet, ensuring operational reliability, deploying to global users, and hardening the system for safety and responsibility.
  

  
    
      
    
    Scaling Machine Learning Systems
    Publisher: The MIT Press (2027)
    
      📖 Download PDF
      ·
      📱 Download EPUB
    
  


What You Will Learn

The four parts extend ML systems foundations into production-scale systems by following the Fleet Stack from bottom to top:

  Part I: The Fleet—Build the physical computer. Architect the datacenter infrastructure, high-bandwidth network fabrics, and scalable data storage that form the foundation of every distributed ML deployment.
  Part II: Distributed ML—Master the algorithms of scale. Learn how to coordinate computation across thousands of devices using parallelism strategies, collective communication primitives, fault tolerance mechanisms, and fleet orchestration.
  Part III: Deployment at Scale—Serve the world. Navigate the shift from training to inference, optimize performance across the serving stack, push intelligence to the edge, and manage the operational lifecycle of production fleets.
  Part IV: The Responsible Fleet—Harden and govern the system. Address security, robustness, environmental sustainability, and responsible engineering in large-scale operations.


Prerequisites

This book assumes:

  Foundational or equivalent background in single-machine ML systems
  Programming proficiency in Python with familiarity in NumPy
  Mathematics foundations in linear algebra, calculus, and probability
  Familiarity with distributed systems concepts (networking, parallelism) is helpful for advanced topics


Learn by Doing

Within the broader AI engineering curriculum, this volume is the scale and governance spine. Pair the chapters with Co-Labs for fleet-scale trade-off exercises, MLSys·im for first-principles infrastructure modeling, and StaffML for physics-grounded systems design practice. Instructors can adopt the full scale sequence through The AI Engineering Blueprint.

title: Author’s Note
text:
Author’s Note

When a new model is announced, the world looks at the model. It almost never looks at the fleet.
Behind many frontier models, however, stand thousands of accelerators held in lockstep across a network where one slow link can stall the whole run, cooled by systems that move megawatts of heat, kept alive by protocols that treat failure not as an exception but as a scheduled event. None of this fits in the announcement. The model gets the paper. The fleet gets a footnote, if that.
This book is an argument that the fleet deserves more than a footnote. We have built vast distributed systems before, but none quite like this one, because none of the others had to be right about two things at once. The telephone network had to stay available; it never had to converge. The internet had to deliver the packet; it never had to preserve the gradient inside it. A fleet has to do both. It must move data the way any distributed system does, and it must keep the mathematics of learning intact while it moves. A node that drops out does not only cost capacity; it can break the synchronization a training step depends on and force a rollback that wastes work since the most recent checkpoint. That double obligation, computational and statistical, sustained at the scale of a small campus, is the engineering this book makes visible.
The obligation does not end when training does. A model that cannot be trained is an idea, not a system. A model that cannot be served is a research result, not a product. A model that cannot be governed is a liability, not an asset. At every stage, from the first allocated node to the last served request, the fleet decides what is possible and what remains imagined.
The problem under every chapter is easy to state and hard to solve: what it takes to build not one machine learning system but a thousand, make them work as one, and run them responsibly. I believe that is a defining engineering problem of this generation, and that the people who take it on, the ones who rarely get the headline, deserve a book that treats it as one.
— Vijay Janapa Reddi
Cambridge, Massachusetts
2026

title: Acknowledgments
text:
Earlier teaching on TinyML grew out of the realization that the constraints governing milliwatt devices are the same constraints governing data-center accelerators. This book grew out of a different realization, one that came from working on ML Fleet Efficiency as a visiting researcher at Google. Peter Mattson, who had been a collaborator on MLPerf, made that opportunity possible. What I encountered there changed how I think about ML systems: the engineering required to coordinate thousands of accelerators into a single coherent system is a discipline unto itself, and that discipline had no textbook.
That work introduced me to the ML Productivity Goodput (MPG) metric, fleet-level heterogeneity at a scale I had not seen before, and the daily reality of failure as a statistical certainty rather than an exception. The gap between what practitioners knew and what was written down was enormous. The researchers who built these systems published individual results, but the connective tissue between those results, the principles that made them cohere into a discipline, existed only in the heads of the people doing the work. This book is an attempt to document that connective tissue.



I learned most of what I know about fleet-scale systems from the ML Fleet Efficiency team at Google: Arissa Wongpanich, Tayo Oguntebi, Jose Baiocchi Paredes, Yu Emma Wang, Phitchaya Mangpo Phothilimthana, Ritwika Mitra, and Zongwei Zhou. Naveen Kumar led that effort, and the way he thought about fleet-level optimization shaped how I think about it still. Robert Hundt pushed my understanding of performance engineering at scale. Together, Naveen and Robert showed me what fleet-level efficiency looks like from the inside. David Kanter continued the MLPerf collaboration, and our discussions on benchmarking distributed systems sharpened the quantitative methodology that runs through every chapter. Greg Diamos provided invaluable perspective on scaling laws and their origins at Baidu, where some of the earliest work on large-scale distributed training took shape.
The researchers whose papers fill the bibliography of this book deserve particular acknowledgment. Practitioners and researchers who built the systems, measured the failures, and published what they learned discovered the principles taught here, rather than inventing them for this textbook. This book synthesizes their work into a coherent narrative. The debt is to them.



The Harvard Data Science Initiative, Harvard Extension School, and the National Science Foundation supported this work; the Edge AI Foundation and ICTP supported educational outreach and scholarships; and our industry partners provided infrastructure and tooling that enabled practical experimentation.
At MIT Press, Susan Hartman believed in this project from the beginning and guided it from an open-source experiment to a published textbook. Her editorial judgment and support made this book real. I am equally grateful to MIT Press for agreeing to keep this book available as open access. A textbook about a discipline shaped by the open-source community should be accessible to everyone in it.
An open-source community shaped this book in ways that no single author could. Dozens of contributors caught errors, improved explanations, filed issues, and submitted pull requests. The book improved because people who owed it nothing chose to make it better. I am grateful to every one of them.
For the complete and most up-to-date list of all contributors, please visit the GitHub contributors page. For those interested in contributing, please consult our contribution guidelines.
Every GitHub star is a signal that someone cares about this material, is learning from it, and believes the work matters. The online community of learners, with their questions, their curiosity, and their willingness to engage with an unfinished textbook, kept this project moving when the scope felt overwhelming.
Finally, I thank my wife and my children. I wrote this book in the hours that belonged to them: weekends that disappeared into revisions, evenings that stretched past midnight, mornings when I was present but not quite there. They never complained. They asked how the writing was going, brought me coffee, and gave me the space to finish. Whatever merit this book has, their patience and their support made it possible.

title: Notation
text:
Machine learning at scale sits at the convergence of three disciplines: machine learning, distributed systems, and high-performance data center networking. Training and serving modern foundation models requires orchestrating workloads across thousands of accelerators interconnected by high-speed networks. Each contributing field developed its mathematical conventions independently, creating severe symbol collisions when their concepts appear in the same system equation.
To a machine learning researcher, \(\Glyph{B}\) denotes batch size, while to a network engineer, \(\Glyph{B}\) denotes bandwidth. In distributed systems, \(\Glyph{N}\) represents the count of worker accelerators, whereas in statistics, \(\Glyph{N}\) denotes sample count. In high-performance computing, \(\Glyph{P}\) is commonly used for processor count, but in deep learning, \(\Glyph{P}\) is universally reserved for model parameter count. Similarly, in this book’s communication models, \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) denotes per-message network latency and \(\Glyph{\beta}\) denotes link bandwidth, whereas in statistical learning, \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) represents a power-law scaling exponent and \(\Glyph{\beta}\) represents optimizer momentum.
This book establishes a rigorous, unified mathematical notation tailored specifically to distributed machine learning systems. The conventions defined below eliminate ambiguity across scaling laws, collective communication algorithms, parallel execution schedules, and cluster reliability models.


Performance modeling in distributed machine learning follows a natural two-tier hierarchy: the single-device execution foundation, and its fleet-wide composition.


Every distributed training step or inference pass is fundamentally composed of local execution on individual accelerators. For serialized execution phases on a single accelerator, the iron law of ML Systems decomposes execution time into memory access, arithmetic computation, and latency overhead:
\[\Time = \underbrace{\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}}_{\text{Memory Time}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}}_{\text{Compute Time}} + \underbrace{\Latency}_{\text{Latency Overhead}}\]
Each symbol was chosen deliberately to preserve machine learning conventions while maintaining architectural precision:










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\Time\)
Execution Time
seconds
Total serialized execution time in the iron-law performance decomposition.


\(\Bandwidth\)
Bandwidth
bytes/s
Avoids collision with \(\BatchSize\) (Batch Size). Systems literature often uses \(\Glyph{B}\) for bandwidth, while ML literature often uses \(\Glyph{B}\) for batch size. The notation preserves the ML convention.


\(\DataVolume\)
Data Volume
bytes
Avoids collision with \(\DatasetSize\) (Dataset Size). In scaling laws, \(\Glyph{D}\) means training tokens. Here we need bytes moved through memory. The subscript disambiguates.


\(\EfficiencyHw\)
Efficiency
—
Hardware utilization \((0 \le \EfficiencyHw \le 1)\). Avoids collision with learning rate \((\LearningRate)\).


\(\Latency\)
Latency
seconds
Avoids collision with \(\Glyph{L}\) (Loss). Fixed overhead time (kernel launch, network RTT). The subscript distinguishes from the loss function.


\(\Operations\)
Operations
FLOPs
Total floating-point operations. Clean in equations (vs. “\(\text{Ops}\)”).


\(\PeakRate\)
Peak Rate
FLOP/s
Avoids collision with \(\Parameters\) (Parameters). Roofline presentations often use \(\Glyph{P}\) for performance, while ML literature commonly uses \(\Glyph{P}\) for parameter count. The notation preserves the ML convention.


\(\AsymptoticTightBound\)
Asymptotic Tight Bound
Operator
Asymptotic tight bound: grows at the same rate as its argument, up to constant factors.


\(\BatchDataVolume\)
Batch Data Volume
bytes
Bytes of input data one batch carries to the accelerator.


\(\ClockFrequency\)
Clock Frequency
hertz
Rate at which a processor’s clock ticks, setting how many switching cycles occur per second.


\(\FiniteChange\)
Finite Change
Operator
Finite change in the quantity it prefixes, between two states, configurations or points in time.


\(\MicroUnitPrefix\)
Micro Unit Prefix
Operator
SI unit prefix micro, one millionth, written before a unit such as seconds.


\(\NumericBitWidth\)
Numeric Bit Width
Integer
Number of bits used to represent one numeric value, such as an arithmetic operand or a quantized weight or activation.


\(\PipelinedExecutionTime\)
Pipelined Execution Time
seconds
Execution time of a workload whose data movement and computation overlap, set by the slower of the two plus fixed latency.


\(\SequentialExecutionTime\)
Sequential Execution Time
seconds
Execution time when data movement, computation and fixed overhead run one after another with no overlap, the sum of the iron-law terms.


\(\StepIoTime\)
Step Io Time
seconds
Time the input pipeline needs to read, decompress, decode and stage the data for one training step.


\(\StorageBandwidth\)
Storage Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which the storage system delivers bytes to the input pipeline.


\(\TrainingStepTime\)
Training Step Time
seconds
Wall-clock time of one training step, bounded below by the slower of compute and input I/O.


\(\UnitAliasMultiplier\)
Unit Alias Multiplier
Dimensionless
Number of base units in one unit alias, the conversion multiplier of a unit-conventions table row.






Without careful notation, statements about distributed systems become ambiguous:

“Reducing \(\Glyph{D}\) improves performance.”

In distributed machine learning, this could mean reducing the dataset size (fewer training samples), shrinking the data-parallel degree \(\DataParallelDegree\), or reducing the data volume \(\DataVolume\) moved across the memory bus through quantization. With our notation, we distinguish them precisely:

“Reducing \(\DataVolume\) through FP8 quantization cuts memory traffic across the interconnect while \(\DatasetSize\) (training tokens) and \(\DataParallelDegree\) remain unchanged.”




The root symbol names the fundamental physical quantity, while an upright subscript specifies the precise domain or measurement point:

\(\Glyph{\text{BW}_{\text{memory}}}\), \(\NetworkBandwidth\), \(\Glyph{\text{BW}_{\text{interconnect}}}\): bandwidth across distinct tiers of the distributed memory and fabric hierarchy.
\(\DataVolume\), \(\PeakRate\), \(\Latency\), \(\EfficiencyHw\): single-node iron-law terms, held clear of shared ML symbols.
\(\EnergyPerByteMoved\), \(\EnergyPerOperation\), \(\TotalEnergy\): energy budget components across distributed compute nodes.

The subscript therefore carries part of the claim. Memory and network bandwidth differ by orders of magnitude, so a figure is reproducible only when the subscript says where it was measured.




When scaling a model across a fleet of \(\DeviceCount= \AcceleratorCount\) accelerators, single-device compute time is distributed across workers, while communication and synchronization overheads are introduced. Under partitioned execution of fixed work, the governing equation is the Fleet Law (the distributed step time law, equation 1.3):
\[\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\DeviceCount, \AcceleratorCount\)
Number of Devices
Integer
Accelerator count in a distributed job, the core’s \(\AcceleratorCount\) (\(\DeviceCount= \AcceleratorCount\)); also the rank count of a collective. (Not parameters, use \(\Parameters\).)


\(\AcceleratorsPerNode\), \(\ClusterNodeCount\)
Accelerators per Node, Node Count
Integer
Hierarchical collectives split the fleet as \(\DeviceCount= \AcceleratorsPerNode \ClusterNodeCount\). (Bare \(\Glyph{G}\) is the LogGP gap per byte.)


\(\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)\)
Distributed Step Time
seconds
Wall-clock time for one training step at scale \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\IronLawComputeTime\)
Single-Device Compute Time
seconds
The core’s compute term for one training step (forward + backward pass) on one device.


\(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\)
Communication Time
seconds
Time for collective operations (AllReduce, AllGather); depends on payload, topology, and \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\OverlappedTime\)
Overlapped Time
seconds
Communication hidden behind computation. Reduces effective overhead.


\(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\)
Synchronization Time
seconds
Total nonoverlapped synchronization or coordination cost per step at scale \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\CommunicationComputeRatio\)
Communication-Computation Ratio
Dimensionless
\(\CommunicationComputeRatio= \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)/(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\). Values near or above 1 indicate communication-bound scaling.


\(\CommunicationIntensity\)
Communication Intensity
bytes/FLOP
Network bytes moved per local FLOP, \(\CommunicationIntensity = \CollectivePayloadSize/\Operations\); the fleet analogue of arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\).


\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\)
Communication Axis
Set
Communication axis of the C³ taxonomy, data movement across the network fabric, viewed as the set of techniques it covers so that axis intersections name zones of the taxonomy.


\(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\)
Compute Axis
Set
Compute axis of the C³ taxonomy, local arithmetic and memory within a node, viewed as the set of techniques it covers so that axis intersections name zones of the taxonomy.


\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)
Coordination Axis
Set
Coordination axis of the C³ taxonomy, synchronization, failure recovery and scheduling across the fleet, viewed as the set of techniques it covers so that axis intersections name zones of the taxonomy.


\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension\)
Operational Dimension
Record
One of the three operational dimensions of the C-cubed taxonomy, indexed 1 to 3 as compute, communication and coordination.







Scaling laws anchor the book’s account of why machine learning moved onto fleets. The single-resource power law and the dense-transformer compute rule are:
\[\LossFunction(\ScaledResource) = \ScaleCoefficient \ScaledResource^{-\ScalingExponent} + \IrreducibleLoss, \qquad \TrainingCompute \approx 6\Parameters \DatasetSize\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\ScaledResource\)
Scaled Resource
varies
Training compute, parameter count \(\Parameters\), or training tokens \(\DatasetSize\), depending on the fitted law.


\(\ScalingExponent\)
Scaling Exponent
Dimensionless
Fitted power-law exponent; valid only within the regime in which it was measured. (Not network latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\).)


\(\ScaleCoefficient\)
Scale Coefficient
loss units
Task-dependent fitted constant.


\(\IrreducibleLoss\)
Irreducible Loss
loss units
Loss floor that added resources do not remove within the fitted regime.


\(\TrainingCompute\)
Training Compute
FLOPs
About \(6\Parameters \DatasetSize\) for a dense transformer: \(2\Parameters\) per token forward and \(4\Parameters\) backward.


\(\BaseBatchSize\)
Base Batch Size
Integer
Reference batch size at which the base learning rate was tuned.


\(\BaseLearningRate\)
Base Learning Rate
Dimensionless
Learning rate tuned at the reference batch size before linear scaling.


\(\EpochCount\)
Epoch Count
Integer
Number of full passes a training run makes over its dataset.


\(\ScaledBatchSize\)
Scaled Batch Size
Integer
Batch size a training recipe is scaled to under the linear scaling rule.


\(\ScaledLearningRate\)
Scaled Learning Rate
Dimensionless
Learning rate used at a new batch size under the linear scaling rule.


\(\ScalingLawLoss\)
Scaling Law Loss
Function
Loss a trained model reaches as a function of the resource scaled, such as parameters, training tokens or compute, in an empirical power-law scaling law.







At data center scale, energy and power delivery are primary system constraints. For \(\DeviceCount\) devices that each move the same \(\DataVolume\) bytes and execute the same \(\Operations\) FLOPs over a workload interval, effective per-byte data-movement costs and per-operation compute costs give the following fleet energy model. Here the work and traffic terms are per-device quantities, so multiplying by \(\DeviceCount\) sums the device contributions:
\[\TotalEnergy \approx \DeviceCount\times \left( \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved + \Operations \times \EnergyPerOperation \right)\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\EnergyPerByteMoved\)
Energy per Byte Moved
joules/byte
Effective movement cost; total energy also depends on bytes moved and operations executed.


\(\EnergyPerOperation\)
Energy per Operation
joules/FLOP
Energy cost of a single arithmetic operation.


\(\TotalEnergy\)
Total Energy
joules
Total energy consumed by an ML workload, decomposed into data-movement and compute terms.


\(\AcceleratorSupplyCurrent\)
Accelerator Supply Current
amperes
Electrical current an accelerator draws from its power supply.


\(\ActiveInferencePower\)
Active Inference Power
watts
Average power an accelerator draws while actively running inference.


\(\AveragePower\)
Average Power
watts
Power drawn averaged over a stated period.


\(\CloudOffloadEnergy\)
Cloud Offload Energy
joules
Energy a device spends transmitting an input to the cloud for remote inference.


\(\CoolantHeatLoad\)
Coolant Heat Load
watts
Heat per unit time that a liquid cooling loop must carry away from a rack, the load that sets its coolant mass flow.


\(\CoolantMassFlowRate\)
Coolant Mass Flow Rate
kg/s
Mass of coolant, liquid or air, passing through a cooling loop per second.


\(\CoolantTemperature\)
Coolant Temperature
kelvin
Temperature of the liquid or air coolant in a cooling loop, whose finite change is its rise from inlet to outlet.


\(\DevicePower\)
Device Power
watts
Electrical power one device draws.


\(\DynamicPower\)
Dynamic Power
watts
Power a chip draws switching its transistors, proportional to switched capacitance, supply voltage squared and clock frequency.


\(\ElectricalResistance\)
Electrical Resistance
ohms
Electrical resistance of a circuit or winding.


\(\FacilityHeatRemovalCapacity\)
Facility Heat Removal Capacity
watts
Largest rate at which an installed facility and cooling configuration can remove heat.


\(\FacilityPower\)
Facility Power
watts
Total electrical power a data center facility draws from the grid, its IT load plus cooling, power conversion, lighting and other overhead.


\(\GeneralPurposeEnergyProductivity\)
General Purpose Energy Productivity
FLOP/J
Useful floating-point operations general-purpose silicon delivers per joule on a given workload.


\(\InferenceDutyCycle\)
Inference Duty Cycle
Dimensionless
Fraction of time an accelerator actively runs inference rather than waiting in standby.


\(\InformationTechnologyHeatLoad\)
IT Heat Load
watts
Rate at which a facility’s information technology equipment (servers, accelerators, network gear) produces heat.


\(\InformationTechnologyPower\)
IT Power
watts
Electrical power delivered to a data center’s IT equipment: servers, accelerators, storage and networking.


\(\LeakageCurrent\)
Leakage Current
amperes
Current that leaks through a chip’s transistors when they are not switching.


\(\LeakagePower\)
Leakage Power
watts
Static power a chip dissipates through leakage current regardless of switching.


\(\LocalInferenceEnergy\)
Local Inference Energy
joules
Energy a device spends running one inference on its own hardware.


\(\NetworkEnergy\)
Network Energy
joules
Energy the network fabric, its switches, links and adapters, consumes over a stated interval.


\(\ParasiticLoopInductance\)
Parasitic Loop Inductance
henries
Unintended inductance of the current loop that feeds an accelerator’s core rail, which turns current slew into voltage droop.


\(\SpecializedEnergyProductivity\)
Specialized Energy Productivity
FLOP/J
Useful floating-point operations specialized, domain-specific silicon delivers per joule on a workload suited to its design.


\(\SpecificHeatCapacity\)
Specific Heat Capacity
J/(kg K)
Heat needed to raise one kilogram of a coolant by one kelvin at constant pressure.


\(\StandbyPower\)
Standby Power
watts
Power a device draws in standby, when it is not running inference.


\(\SupplyVoltage\)
Supply Voltage
volts
Supply voltage that powers a digital circuit, the quantity dynamic voltage and frequency scaling lowers.


\(\SwitchedCapacitance\)
Switched Capacitance
farads
Capacitance of the wires and gates a circuit charges when it switches.


\(\SwitchingActivityFactor\)
Switching Activity Factor
Dimensionless
Average fraction of a chip’s gate capacitance that switches each clock cycle.


\(\TotalChipPower\)
Total Chip Power
watts
Total power a chip dissipates, the sum of dynamic switching power and static leakage power.








Collective communications (AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll) transfer payloads across network fabrics structured as rings, trees, or fat-tree fabrics.


Network communication time decomposes into fixed message startup latency and bandwidth-dependent transfer:
\[\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\]
The model keeps its literature’s letters as aliases of core concepts: \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the per-message \(\Latency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is a link’s \(\Bandwidth\), written in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form. Inside \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) formulas, write \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) and \(\Glyph{\beta}\); elsewhere, write \(\Latency\) and a subscripted \(\Bandwidth\).










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\)
Point-to-Point Transfer Time
seconds
Wall-clock time to transmit one message of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) across one link.


\(\PointToPointMessageSize\)
Point-to-Point Message Size
bytes
Size of one message in \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\).


\(\MessageStartupLatency\)
Per-Message Latency
seconds
The core’s \(\Latency\) for one message, in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form: the fixed startup cost. (Not significance level or Rényi order, which carry subscripts.)


\(\LinkBandwidth\)
Link Bandwidth
bytes/s
The core’s \(\Bandwidth\) for one link (\(\SingleLinkBandwidth\)), in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form: effective throughput per link.


\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\)
Crossover Point
bytes
\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize= \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\). Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\): latency-bound. Above: bandwidth-bound.


\(\CollectivePayloadSize\)
Collective Payload Size
bytes
Per-rank gradient, model-state, activation, or compressed payload that a collective moves. Not a memory footprint (those are \(\TotalMemoryFootprint\), \(\WeightMemory\), and so on) and not the core’s GEMM dimension \(\GemmRowDimension\), which appears only in GEMM shape statements.


\(\CollectiveTensorSize\)

At cluster scale, hardware component failures are standard operating conditions rather than rare anomalies.


Assuming independent components with exponential failure distributions, system reliability across \(\RequiredComponentCount\) components is:
\[\SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\]
The aggregate exponent uses the system-level rate \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\), where \(\ComponentFailureRate\) is the per-component failure rate under the independent, identical-component assumption. The exponent \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant\) is dimensionless, so the elapsed time \(\TimeInstant\) must use the same time unit as \(\ComponentFailureRate\) (hours, when \(\ComponentFailureRate\) comes from the FIT-derived rates below).
The optimal checkpoint interval balances I/O overhead against recomputation rework:
\[\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}\]
The formula uses the system-wide mean time between failures (the failure interval for the whole job), not a component lifetime; substituting the per-component value would overestimate \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) by \(\sqrt{\RequiredComponentCount}\). For dimensional consistency, \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) and \(\SystemMtbf\) must be in the same time unit. Industry-standard \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\) is reported in hours; to combine it with seconds-scale write times, multiply the hour value by 3600. The result \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) then carries the time unit chosen for the inputs.
