J/(kg K)
Heat needed to raise one kilogram of a coolant by one kelvin at constant pressure.


\(\StandbyPower\)
Standby Power
watts
Power a device draws in standby, when it is not running inference.


\(\SupplyVoltage\)
Supply Voltage
volts
Supply voltage that powers a digital circuit, the quantity dynamic voltage and frequency scaling lowers.


\(\SwitchedCapacitance\)
Switched Capacitance
farads
Capacitance of the wires and gates a circuit charges when it switches.


\(\SwitchingActivityFactor\)
Switching Activity Factor
Dimensionless
Average fraction of a chip’s gate capacitance that switches each clock cycle.


\(\TotalChipPower\)
Total Chip Power
watts
Total power a chip dissipates, the sum of dynamic switching power and static leakage power.

title: Notation
text:
Collective communications (AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll) transfer payloads across network fabrics structured as rings, trees, or fat-tree fabrics.


Network communication time decomposes into fixed message startup latency and bandwidth-dependent transfer:
\[\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\]
The model keeps its literature’s letters as aliases of core concepts: \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the per-message \(\Latency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is a link’s \(\Bandwidth\), written in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form. Inside \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) formulas, write \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) and \(\Glyph{\beta}\); elsewhere, write \(\Latency\) and a subscripted \(\Bandwidth\).










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\)
Point-to-Point Transfer Time
seconds
Wall-clock time to transmit one message of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) across one link.


\(\PointToPointMessageSize\)
Point-to-Point Message Size
bytes
Size of one message in \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\).


\(\MessageStartupLatency\)
Per-Message Latency
seconds
The core’s \(\Latency\) for one message, in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form: the fixed startup cost. (Not significance level or Rényi order, which carry subscripts.)


\(\LinkBandwidth\)
Link Bandwidth
bytes/s
The core’s \(\Bandwidth\) for one link (\(\SingleLinkBandwidth\)), in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form: effective throughput per link.


\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\)
Crossover Point
bytes
\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize= \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\). Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\): latency-bound. Above: bandwidth-bound.


\(\CollectivePayloadSize\)
Collective Payload Size
bytes
Per-rank gradient, model-state, activation, or compressed payload that a collective moves. Not a memory footprint (those are \(\TotalMemoryFootprint\), \(\WeightMemory\), and so on) and not the core’s GEMM dimension \(\GemmRowDimension\), which appears only in GEMM shape statements.


\(\CollectiveTensorSize\)
Collective Tensor Size
bytes
Full tensor acted on by Broadcast, Reduce, or AllReduce, reconstructed by AllGather, or partitioned by ReduceScatter. An equally sharded AllGather starts with \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes per rank; AllToAll uses the per-rank payload \(\CollectivePayloadSize\).


\(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime\), \(\TreeAllReduceCompletionTime\)
Collective Completion Time
seconds
AllReduce time under the ring or tree algorithm in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form, for example \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime = 2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency+ 2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\). \(\AllReduceCompletionTime\) names an AllReduce whose algorithm the text leaves open.


\(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload\)
Ring-Tree Crossover Payload
bytes
Payload at which \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime = \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime\); approximately \(\DeviceCount\MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth/\log_2 \DeviceCount\) for large \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\AllReduceCompletionTime\)
AllReduce Completion Time
seconds
Time to complete one AllReduce collective over a group of devices, whatever algorithm implements it.


\(\AllToAllCompletionTime\)
AllToAll Completion Time
seconds
Time to complete one AllToAll collective, in which every device exchanges a distinct share of its payload with every other device.


\(\BisectionBandwidth\)
Bisection Bandwidth
bytes/s
Total bandwidth across the narrowest cut that divides a network’s nodes into two equal halves.


\(\LocalRankIndex\)
Local Rank Index
Integer
Position of an accelerator within its node, its local rank, which in a rail-optimized fabric also names the rail it attaches to.


\(\NetworkBandwidth\)
Network Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which a network path delivers bytes between machines.


\(\NetworkTrafficVolume\)
Network Traffic Volume
bytes
Bytes one worker moves across the network over a stated interval, such as one training step.


\(\RankCountBinaryExponent\)
Rank Count Binary Exponent
Dimensionless
Integer exponent for which the rank count equals two raised to it, the condition algorithms such as butterfly AllReduce require.


\(\RankIndex\)
Rank Index
Integer
Position of one rank, a device or worker, within a collective communication group, counted from zero.


\(\SingleLinkBandwidth\)
Single Link Bandwidth
bytes/s
Bandwidth of one network link in one direction, written in the core bandwidth notation outside alpha-beta formulas.


\(\SwitchRadix\)
Switch Radix
Integer
Number of ports on one network switch, its radix.


\(\TopologyEndpointCount\)
Topology Endpoint Count
Integer
Number of endpoints, accelerators or hosts, that one network topology connects, the size variable of its scaling laws.







LogGP refines the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model by separating network transit latency, processor initiation overhead, and long-message injection gaps. The book uses descriptive subscripts for the highest-collision terms; the bare letters \(\Glyph{g}\) and \(\Glyph{G}\) keep their LogGP meanings inside this model only.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\LoggpLongMessageTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\)
LogGP Long-Message Time
seconds
Transfer time for an \(\PointToPointMessageSize\)-byte long message. Reuses \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) from the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model.


\(\LogpNetworkLatency\)
LogP/LogGP Network Latency
seconds
Network transit time of one message, the part of the core’s \(\Latency\) that excludes processor overhead, so \(\MessageStartupLatency\approx \SenderOverhead + \LogpNetworkLatency + \ReceiverOverhead\). The subscript avoids bare \(\Glyph{L}\) collisions.


\(\SenderOverhead\)
Sender Overhead
seconds
Processor/NIC overhead to initiate a message.


\(\ReceiverOverhead\)
Receiver Overhead
seconds
Processor/NIC overhead to complete a message. Symmetric LogP writes \(\SymmetricMessageOverhead= \SenderOverhead = \ReceiverOverhead\), so one message costs \(2\SymmetricMessageOverhead\).


\(\MessageInjectionGap\)
Message Injection Gap
seconds
Minimum interval between consecutive message injections. (Gradients are bold, \(\Glyph{\mathbf{g}}\).)


\(\LongMessageGapPerByte\)
Long-Message Gap per Byte
seconds/byte
Per-byte long-message gap; distinct from \(\LinkBandwidth\) link bandwidth. (Accelerators per node are \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\).)


\(\SymmetricMessageOverhead\)
Symmetric Message Overhead
seconds
Processor time spent initiating or completing one message in the symmetric LogP model, where sender and receiver overheads are equal, during which the processor cannot compute.







Compression models compare codec overhead against the communication time saved by reducing payload size:










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\TransferTimeForPayload\)
Transfer Time for Payload
seconds
Communication time for an \(\Glyph{x}\)-byte payload: \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\Glyph{x})\) for one link, or the relevant collective time.


\(\CompressedCommunicationTime\)
Compressed Communication Time
seconds
Total time after encode, transfer of \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio\), and decode.


\(\CodecEncodeTime\)
Codec Encode Time
seconds
Local compression overhead before transfer.


\(\CodecDecodeTime\)
Codec Decode Time
seconds
Local decompression overhead after transfer.


\(\QuantizationBlockSize\)
Quantization Block Size
Integer
Number of tensor elements in one block of block-wise quantization, all sharing one scale.


\(\QuantizationScale\)
Quantization Scale
Varies
Real-valued step between adjacent integer levels of a uniform quantizer.


\(\RetainedGradientElementCount\)
Retained Gradient Element Count
Integer
Number of largest-magnitude gradient elements top-k sparsification keeps and transmits.

title: Notation
text:
Scaling large foundation models requires combining multiple parallelism strategies across device dimensions.


3D parallelism partitions the training workload across three orthogonal dimensions:
\[\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\DataParallelDegree\)
Data-Parallel Degree
Integer
Number of model replicas. (Bare \(\Glyph{d}\) stays the core’s hidden dimension.)


\(\PipelineParallelDegree\)
Pipeline-Parallel Degree
Integer
Number of physical pipeline stages in model-depth partitioning.


\(\TensorParallelDegree\)
Tensor-Parallel Degree
Integer
Degree of intra-layer partitioning (model width). (Bare \(\Glyph{t}\) stays time or a step index.)


\(\MicrobatchCount\)
Microbatch Count
Integer
Number of microbatches used to fill and drain the pipeline.


\(\PipelineBubbleFraction\)
Pipeline Bubble Fraction
Dimensionless
Fraction of pipeline GPU-time spent idle, \(\PipelineBubbleFraction = (\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree-1+\MicrobatchCount)\); avoids bare \(\Glyph{b}\).


\(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\)
Virtual Pipeline Stages per Device
Integer
Number of interleaved virtual chunks assigned to each physical pipeline stage. (The attention value matrix is bold, \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\).)


\(\GradientStaleness\)
Gradient Staleness
steps
Number of parameter updates between the parameters a gradient was computed on and the parameters it updates; \(\GradientStaleness = 0\) is synchronous training.


\(\AccumulationStepCount\)
Accumulation Step Count
Integer
Number of micro-batches whose gradients are accumulated before one optimizer update.


\(\ClientIndex\)
Client Index
Integer
Position of one client among the clients of a federated round or secure aggregation.


\(\ExpertCapacityFactor\)
Expert Capacity Factor
Dimensionless
Multiplier on an expert’s uniform share of token assignments that sets how many assignments it may accept per step.


\(\ExpertCount\)
Expert Count
Integer
Number of expert subnetworks in one mixture-of-experts layer.


\(\FederatedRoundCount\)
Federated Round Count
Integer
Number of communication rounds a federated training run performs, or needs to reach a quality target.


\(\GlobalBatchSize\)
Global Batch Size
Integer
Number of examples one synchronous optimizer update averages over across all data-parallel workers.


\(\LocalGradient\)
Local Gradient
Vector
Gradient vector one data-parallel worker computes from its local batch in one step, its contribution to the gradient collective.


\(\MicrobatchSize\)
Microbatch Size
Integer
Number of examples in one micro-batch, the unit run through a single forward and backward pass.


\(\ParticipatingClientCount\)
Participating Client Count
Integer
Number of clients whose updates one federated round aggregates.


\(\RoutedExpertCount\)
Routed Expert Count
Integer
Number of experts a mixture-of-experts router sends each token to.


\(\RouterGateProbability\)
Router Gate Probability
Dimensionless
Probability a mixture-of-experts router assigns to the expert it selects for a token.







Scaling efficiency measures realized speedup relative to ideal linear scaling:
\[\ScalingEfficiency = \frac{\SingleDeviceRunTime}{\DeviceCount\times \MultiDeviceRunTime}\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\ScalingEfficiency\)
Scaling Efficiency
Dimensionless
Ratio of measured speedup to ideal linear speedup. \(1.0\) is the ideal linear baseline, not a hard upper bound.


\(\SingleDeviceRunTime\)
Single-Device Time
seconds
Baseline wall-clock time for the same productive work on one device.


\(\MultiDeviceRunTime\)
N-Device Time
seconds
Wall-clock time for the same productive work on \(\DeviceCount\) devices; excludes operational downtime counted by \(\GoodputRatio\).


\(\SerialFraction\)
Serial Fraction
Dimensionless
Share of a fixed workload’s single-device execution time that does not shrink when the work is spread across devices, the serial term of Amdahl’s law.

title: Notation
text:
At cluster scale, hardware component failures are standard operating conditions rather than rare anomalies.


Assuming independent components with exponential failure distributions, system reliability across \(\RequiredComponentCount\) components is:
\[\SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\]
The aggregate exponent uses the system-level rate \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\), where \(\ComponentFailureRate\) is the per-component failure rate under the independent, identical-component assumption. The exponent \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant\) is dimensionless, so the elapsed time \(\TimeInstant\) must use the same time unit as \(\ComponentFailureRate\) (hours, when \(\ComponentFailureRate\) comes from the FIT-derived rates below).
The optimal checkpoint interval balances I/O overhead against recomputation rework:
\[\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}\]
The formula uses the system-wide mean time between failures (the failure interval for the whole job), not a component lifetime; substituting the per-component value would overestimate \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) by \(\sqrt{\RequiredComponentCount}\). For dimensional consistency, \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) and \(\SystemMtbf\) must be in the same time unit. Industry-standard \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\) is reported in hours; to combine it with seconds-scale write times, multiply the hour value by 3600. The result \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) then carries the time unit chosen for the inputs.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\SystemReliability(\TimeInstant)\)
Reliability Function
Probability
Probability of no failure across the whole system before time \(\TimeInstant\). One component has \(\ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\).


\(\ComponentFailureRate\)
Per-Component Failure Rate
failures/hour
Per-component failure rate, written \(\Glyph{\lambda_{\text{fail}}}\) wherever another rate shares the passage; the system-wide rate is \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\) under independent, identical components. The industry-standard reporting unit is FIT (failures per \(10^9\) device-hours): \(\Glyph{\lambda_{\text{hour}}}= \text{FIT} \times 10^{-9}\). (Other rates carry subscripts, such as the core’s arrival rate \(\ArrivalRate\).)


\(\ComponentAvailability\)
Component Availability
Probability
Probability that one component is up at a given instant. A job that needs all \(\RequiredComponentCount\) components at once has availability \((\ComponentAvailability)^{\RequiredComponentCount}\) under independent, identical components.


\(\RequiredComponentCount\)
Required Component Count
Integer
Components (accelerators, hosts, NICs, switches) the job needs up at the same time. Not \(\DeviceCount\), which counts accelerators only.


\(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\)
Mean Time Between Failures
hours
Average time between consecutive failures of a repairable, composed system. \(\SystemMtbf = 1/(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate) = \ComponentMttf / \RequiredComponentCount\).


\(\SystemMtbf\)
System MTBF
hours
Mean time between failures that interrupt the whole job, equal to the per-component \(\MeanTimeToFailure\) divided by \(\RequiredComponentCount\) under independent, identical components. It is the input to the Young-Daly interval. Same time unit as \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) when combined with it.


\(\MeanTimeToFailure\)
Mean Time To Failure
hours
Per-component lifetime constant derived from FIT rates, \(\ComponentMttf = 1/\ComponentFailureRate\). Distinct from system-level \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\) when repair/replacement cycles are modeled.


\(\MeanTimeToRepair\)
Mean Time To Repair
hours
Average recovery time after a failure.


\(\CheckpointInterval\)
Checkpoint Interval
seconds
Useful compute time between consecutive checkpoints.


\(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\)
Optimal Checkpoint Interval
seconds
The \(\CheckpointInterval\) that minimizes total wasted time; Young-Daly formula.


\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)
Checkpoint Write Time
seconds
Time to persist model state to storage.


\(\CheckpointLoadTime\)
Checkpoint Load Time
seconds
Time to read the latest checkpoint state from storage back into accelerator memory during recovery.


\(\ComponentMttf\)
Component Mean Time to Failure
hours
Mean time to failure of one component, the reciprocal of its constant failure rate.


\(\ComponentReliability\)
Component Reliability
Dimensionless
Probability that one component of a system runs without failure up to a given time, its survival function.


\(\ErasureDataFragmentCount\)
Erasure Data Fragment Count
Integer
Number of data fragments an erasure code splits an object into, any that many of the stored fragments recovering the original.


\(\ErasureParityFragmentCount\)
Erasure Parity Fragment Count
Integer
Number of parity fragments an erasure code adds to the data fragments of an object.


\(\FailureDetectionTime\)
Failure Detection Time
seconds
Time from a hardware or process fault until the system classifies it as a failure.


\(\FailureRecoveryTime\)
Failure Recovery Time
seconds
Time from a failure until useful training work resumes: detection, restart, checkpoint load and warmup.


\(\GpuMttf\)
GPU Mean Time to Failure
hours
Mean time to failure of one GPU, its average operating time before it fails.


\(\JobAvailability\)
Job Availability
Dimensionless
Probability that every component a job needs is up at the same instant.


\(\JobRestartTime\)
Job Restart Time
seconds
Time for the scheduler to allocate resources and launch replacement processes after a failure.


\(\LostWorkReplayTime\)
Lost Work Replay Time
seconds
Time to recompute the training steps lost since the last checkpoint after a restart.


\(\RedundantReplicaCount\)
Redundant Replica Count
Integer
Number of independent replicas of a service in a redundancy availability calculation, any one of which can serve the load.


\(\RedundantServiceAvailability\)
Redundant Service Availability
Dimensionless
Probability that at least one of a service’s independent replicas is up at a randomly chosen instant.


\(\ReplicaAvailability\)
Replica Availability
Dimensionless
Probability that one serving replica is up at a randomly chosen instant.


\(\SeriesPsuCount\)
Series Power Supply Count
Integer
Number of power supply units in one node whose failure alone stops the node.


\(\SteadyStateAvailability\)
Steady State Availability
Dimensionless
Probability that a component, replica or repairable system is up at a randomly chosen instant, its long-run fraction of up time.







Fleet capacity metrics compound model arithmetic efficiency, scaling efficiency, and operational goodput:










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\UsefulComputeFraction\)
Useful Compute-Time Fraction
Dimensionless
\((\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)/\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)\). Measures how much step time is useful local arithmetic after distribution.


\(\OperationalOverheadFraction\)
Operational Overhead Fraction
Dimensionless
Fraction of allocated wall time lost outside the productive steps measured by \(\MultiDeviceRunTime\), such as checkpoint pauses, failure recovery, scheduler preemption, or maintenance.


\(\GoodputRatio\)
Goodput Ratio
Dimensionless
Fraction of allocated wall time remaining after the out-of-step losses in \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\); often \(\GoodputRatio = 1 - \OperationalOverheadFraction\).


\(\EffectiveFleetThroughput\)
Effective Fleet Throughput
FLOP/s
\(\EffectiveFleetThroughput = (\DeviceCount\PeakRate) \times \ModelFlopsUtilization \times \ScalingEfficiency \times \GoodputRatio\), where \(\ModelFlopsUtilization\) is the single-device baseline, \(\ScalingEfficiency\) captures all in-step scaling loss, and \(\GoodputRatio\) captures only out-of-step operational loss excluded from \(\MultiDeviceRunTime\).


\(\UsefulModelFlops\)
Useful Model FLOPs
FLOPs
Model FLOPs that advance training, excluding recomputation and padding; \(\ModelFlopsUtilization = \UsefulModelFlops/(\DeviceCount\PeakRate \DistributedStepTime)\) measures fleet MFU and already includes in-step scaling loss. The throughput factorization uses single-device baseline MFU instead.


\(\ProgramGoodput\), \(\RuntimeGoodput\), \(\SchedulingGoodput\)
ML Productivity Goodput Factors
Dimensionless
Program, runtime, and scheduling goodput, with \(\text{MPG} = \SchedulingGoodput \times \RuntimeGoodput \times \ProgramGoodput\). A complementary lifecycle decomposition, not a factorization of \(\EffectiveFleetThroughput\).


\(\FleetEnergyProductivity\)
Fleet Energy Productivity
FLOP/J
Useful computation per unit energy, \(\UsefulModelFlops\) divided by the energy drawn inside the stated boundary.


\(\TrainingCost\), \(\InferenceCost\)
Dollar Cost
dollars
The subscript names the cost component. Carbon quantities use \(\text{CO}_{2,\dots}\), never \(\Glyph{C}\).


\(\AllocatedWallTime\)
Allocated Wall Time
seconds
Total wall-clock time for which a training job holds its allocated resources, productive or not.


\(\JobDuration\)
Job Duration
seconds
Wall-clock time one job or run spends executing, from start to finish.


\(\UsefulTrainingTime\)
Useful Training Time
seconds
Wall-clock time a training job spends on committed, productive steps that contribute to the final model.

title: Notation
text:
Managing distributed memory requires partitioning weights, activations, optimizer states, and KV-cache tensors across nodes and tiers.


Reusable performance and serving quantities follow the same collision-avoidance rule as the iron law. Rates use \(\Glyph{R}\) or descriptive Greek symbols; request counts use \(\RequestConcurrency\) rather than overloading \(\Glyph{N}\); queue utilization uses a subscripted \(\Glyph{\rho}\) so bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\) remains available for other ratio models.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\ActivationMemory\)
Activation Memory
bytes
Retained activations for the backward pass or serving intermediates.


\(\ArrivalRate\)
Arrival Rate
requests/s
Request arrival rate. The subscript keeps bare \(\Glyph{\lambda}\) free for fitted sensitivities.


\(\AttainableComputeRate\)
Attainable Compute Rate
FLOP/s
Roofline bound: \(\AttainableComputeRate \leq \min(\PeakRate, \ArithmeticIntensity\times \Bandwidth)\). Uses \(\Glyph{R}\), not \(\Glyph{T}\), because this quantity is a rate.


\(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\)
Batch Service Time
seconds
Time to serve a batch of size \(\BatchSize\).


\(\CompressionRatio\)
Compression Ratio
Dimensionless
Uncompressed size divided by compressed size. A compressed payload has \(1/\CompressionRatio\) of the uncompressed size; the subscript avoids bare \(\Glyph{C}\) collisions.


\(\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize)\)
Effective Service Rate
requests/s
Batched service rate, typically \(\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \BatchSize/\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\). The unbatched service rate is \(\ServiceRate= \EffectiveServiceRate(1)\).


\(\ElementStorageSize\)
Element Storage Size
bytes/element
Bytes per stored tensor element.


\(\GradientMemory\)
Gradient Memory
bytes
Memory occupied by stored gradients.


\(\ModelFlopsUtilization\)
Model FLOPs Utilization
Dimensionless
Useful model FLOP/s divided by available peak FLOP/s. Text acronym avoids overloading \(\Glyph{\eta}\).


\(\OptimizerStateMemory\)
Optimizer-State Memory
bytes
Momentum, variance, master weights, and related optimizer buffers.


\(\ReplicaCount\)
Replica Count
Integer
Serving replicas among which a router chooses (for example, probing two of \(\ReplicaCount\) and sending to the less loaded). Distinct from \(\DeviceCount\), the devices in one job.


\(\RequestConcurrency\)
Request Concurrency
requests
Average in-flight requests in a stable serving system (\(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem\) via Little’s Law). Avoids overloading \(\Glyph{N}\), which counts devices, elements, or samples elsewhere.


\(\RequestTimeInSystem\)
Request Time in System
seconds
End-to-end queueing/serving latency for Little’s Law. Distinct from \(\Latency\), the fixed-latency term in the iron law.


\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)
Arithmetic Intensity
FLOP/byte
Workload FLOPs per byte moved. The roofline model uses \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) as the independent variable.


\(\RooflineRidgePoint\)
Roofline Ridge Point
FLOP/byte
\(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate/\Bandwidth\). Prefer this explicit form over starred shorthand so the meaning remains clear in prose.


\(\ServingUtilization\)
Serving Utilization
Dimensionless
Queue/server utilization. The subscript keeps bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\) free for other ratio models.


\(\TotalMemoryFootprint\)
Total Memory Footprint
bytes
Sum of explicit memory components; avoids bare \(\Glyph{M}\) ambiguity; the core’s quantity.


\(\WeightMemory\)
Weight Memory
bytes
Memory occupied by model weights (\(\Parameters\times \text{bytes-per-parameter}\)); the core’s quantity.


\(\SustainedMemoryBandwidth\)
Sustained Memory Bandwidth
bytes/s
Empirically achievable memory bandwidth under target access patterns.


\(\AcceleratorDataConsumptionRate\)
Accelerator Data Consumption Rate
bytes/s
Rate at which one accelerator consumes training input data while computing at full speed.


\(\BatchArrivalRate\)
Batch Arrival Rate
batches/s
Rate at which batches arrive at a server when each batch is treated as one super-request, the request arrival rate divided by the batch size.


\(\BatchFillArrivalCount\)
Batch Fill Arrival Count
Integer
Number of arrivals after a batch’s triggering request needed to fill the batch, one less than the maximum batch size.


\(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\)
Batch Fixed Overhead Time
seconds
Part of a batch’s service time paid once per batch whatever its size, such as weight loading and kernel launch.


\(\BatchFormationDelay\)
Batch Formation Delay
seconds
Time a request waits for its batch to fill before the batch is dispatched.


\(\BatchIndex\)
Batch Index
Integer
Position of one batch in the sequence of batches a data loader or runtime delivers.


\(\BatchingWindow\)
Batching Window
seconds
Length of the batching window, the longest a dynamic batcher holds requests before dispatching a batch.


\(\DailyQueryVolume\)
Daily Query Volume
queries/day
Number of queries, requests or transactions a deployed model serves per day.


\(\DecodeArithmeticIntensity\)
Decode Arithmetic Intensity
FLOP/byte
Arithmetic intensity of the weight-dominated part of an LLM decode step, operations per byte of weights and activations moved, as a function of batch size.


\(\DeviceMemoryCapacity\)
Device Memory Capacity
bytes
Total memory a device provides for a model’s weights and activations.


\(\DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability\)
Draft Token Acceptance Probability
Dimensionless
Probability that the target model accepts one drafted token in speculative decoding, taken as independent across draft positions.


\(\EndToEndRequestLatency\)
End-to-End Request Latency
seconds
Time from a request leaving the client to its response returning, summed over every stage on the request path.


\(\ErrorBudgetConsumption\)
Error Budget Consumption
Dimensionless
Share of one reliability target’s error budget a service has used: the fraction of eligible observations that violate the target divided by the violating fraction the target allows.


\(\InferenceLatency\)
Inference Latency
seconds
Time the model takes to compute a request’s output.


\(\LatencySlo\)
Latency Service-Level Objective
seconds
Latency target a serving system’s service-level objective sets for a request.


\(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\)
Marginal Request Service Time
seconds
Additional batch service time that one more request in the batch adds.


\(\MaxBatchSize\)
Max Batch Size
Integer
Largest batch a dynamic batcher forms, the size at which it dispatches without waiting for the window to close.


\(\MinimumStableBatchSize\)
Minimum Stable Batch Size
Integer
Batch size at which a batched server’s effective service rate equals the arrival rate, the boundary that stable batch sizes must exceed.


\(\NetworkLatency\)
Network Latency
seconds
Time a request and its response spend crossing the network, including propagation, routing and protocol handling.


\(\PrefetchBufferCount\)
Prefetch Buffer Count
Integer
Number of buffers holding batches loaded ahead of use.


\(\QueueServerCount\)
Queue Server Count
Integer
Number of identical servers in a multi-server queue with random arrivals and service.


\(\QueueSystemCapacity\)
Queue System Capacity
Integer
Largest number of requests a queueing system can hold at once, waiting plus in service, beyond which arrivals are rejected.


\(\QueueWaitTime\)
Queue Wait Time
seconds
Mean time a request waits in a queue before its service begins, excluding service time.


\(\QueueingLatency\)
Queueing Latency
seconds
Time a request waits in queues before it is served.


\(\RealizedArrivalCount\)
Realized Arrival Count
Integer
One possible value of the number of requests that arrive after the trigger in a batching window, used as a summation variable.


\(\ReliabilityTargetIndex\)
Reliability Target Index
Integer
Position of one reliability target, such as availability, latency, freshness, or model quality, among the targets an evaluation contract budgets.


\(\RequestResponseTime\)
Request Response Time
seconds
Time one request spends in a serving system, the random variable whose distribution gives tail latency.


\(\ResponseTimeStandardDeviation\)
Response Time Standard Deviation
seconds
Standard deviation of the time a request spends in a serving system.


\(\ServiceRate\)
Service Rate
items/s
Rate at which one server, such as a worker, consumer, or model endpoint, completes items or calls.


\(\SpeculativeDraftLength\)
Speculative Draft Length
Integer
Number of tokens a draft model proposes for the target model to verify in one speculative-decoding round.


\(\SubsequentArrivalTime\)
Subsequent Arrival Time
seconds
Time from the request that opened a batching window until a later arrival, indexed by arrival order.


\(\TailRequestLatency\)
Tail Request Latency (99th Percentile)
seconds
99th-percentile time a request spends in a serving system.


\(\TargetServingUtilization\)
Target Serving Utilization
Dimensionless
Serving utilization a system is sized not to exceed, chosen below one to keep latency headroom.


\(\TargetUtilizationBatchSize\)
Target Utilization Batch Size
Integer
Smallest batch size whose serving utilization stays at or below the target utilization, under the linear batch service model.


\(\TriggeredWindowArrivalCount\)
Triggered Window Arrival Count
Integer
Number of requests that arrive after the request that opened a batching window and before the window closes.







At scale, serving is bounded by the memory its key-value cache occupies, and the data behind training is bounded by what it costs to keep. These symbols size both.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\KvCacheMemory\)
KV-Cache Memory
bytes
Total key-value cache footprint for autoregressive serving, \(\KvCacheMemory = \BatchSize\cdot \SequenceLength\cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\).


\(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\)
KV-Cache Bytes per Token
bytes/token
\(\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \LayerCount\KvHeadCount \AttentionHeadDimension \ElementStorageSize\) (keys and values across all layers).


\(\DataStorageCost\)
Data Storage Cost
dollars
Cost of keeping a training dataset in storage over its retention period.


\(\EntityCount\)
Entity Count
Integer
Number of entities, such as users or items, a recommendation table or feature store holds rows for.


\(\StorageRetentionTime\)
Storage Retention Time
months
Length of time a dataset is kept in storage.


\(\StoredDataVolume\)
Stored Data Volume
bytes
Bytes a retained dataset occupies in storage.


\(\TotalDataCost\)
Total Data Cost
dollars
Total cost of a training dataset over its lifecycle: acquisition, labeling, storage and processing.

title: Notation
text:
Distributed algorithms partition neural architectures defined by standard deep learning conventions (Goodfellow et al. 2016):

Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, and Aaron Courville. 2016. Deep Learning. MIT Press.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\HiddenDimension\)
Hidden Dimension
Integer
Size of the hidden state vector. (Parallelism degrees carry subscripts, such as \(\DataParallelDegree\).)


\(\AttentionHeadDimension\)
Attention Head Dimension
Integer
Per-head hidden dimension in attention layers.


\(\LayerInputWidth\)
Layer Input Width
Integer
Number of input features in a layer.


\(\LayerOutputWidth\)
Layer Output Width
Integer
Number of output features in a layer.


\(\ModelParameters\)
Model Parameters
Vector
Trainable model weight and bias parameter vector \(\ModelParameters\).


\(\Policy\)
Policy
Function
Target neural network policy \(\pi_\ModelParameters(\Glyph{a}\mid \Glyph{s})\).


\(\SequenceLength\)
Sequence Length
Integer
Input context or sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) in tokens.


\(\ell\)
Layer Index
Integer
Index for a layer. Use instead of bare \(\Glyph{L}\) when indexing layers, since \(\Glyph{L}\) collides with loss and latency. A numeric subscript marks a norm instead (\(\ell_1\), \(\ell_2\)).


\(\LossFunction\)
Loss Function
Scalar
The objective function minimized during training.


\(\AttentionHeadCount, \KvHeadCount\)
Number of Attention Heads
Integer
Number of attention heads in a multi-head attention layer, and key-value heads \(\KvHeadCount\) (in GQA/MQA).


\(\LayerCount\)
Number of Layers
Integer
Total number of layers in a network.


\(\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)\)
Distribution
Probability mass/density
Use lowercase \(\Glyph{p}(\cdot)\) for generic distributions to avoid collision with \(\Parameters\) (parameter count).


\(\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel\mid \ModelInput)\)
Conditional Distribution
Conditional probability/density
Use this form for generic label relationships.


\(\Pr(\cdot)\)
Event Probability
Probability
Probability of an event \(\Glyph{E}\), as in \(\Pr(\text{batch}=0)\); use \(\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)\) and \(\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel\mid \ModelInput)\) for distributions.


\(\AdamFirstMoment\)
Adam First Moment
Varies
Per-parameter exponential moving average of gradients that Adam keeps, its first moment.


\(\AdamSecondMoment\)
Adam Second Moment
Varies
Per-parameter exponential moving average of squared gradients that Adam keeps, its second moment.


\(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix\)
Adapter Down Projection Matrix
Matrix
First low-rank adapter matrix, which projects a layer’s input down to the adapter rank, the LoRA down-projection.


\(\AdapterRank\)
Adapter Rank
Integer
Rank of a low-rank adapter update, equivalently the bottleneck width of a residual adapter, which sets its trainable parameter count.


\(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\)
Adapter Up Projection Matrix
Matrix
Second low-rank adapter matrix, which projects the rank-sized intermediate up to the layer’s output width, the LoRA up-projection.


\(\AttentionKeyMatrix\)
Attention Key Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of key vectors, one row per token, in an attention layer.


\(\AttentionQueryMatrix\)
Attention Query Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of query vectors, one row per token, in an attention layer.


\(\AttentionScoreEntry\)
Attention Score Entry
Dimensionless
Attention score of query i against key j, one entry of the score matrix.


\(\AttentionScoreMatrix\)
Attention Score Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of attention scores, the scaled dot products of every query with every key before the softmax.


\(\AttentionScoreTile\)
Attention Score Tile
Matrix
Block of attention scores between query tile i and key tile j, computed on chip in tiled attention.


\(\AttentionValuesMatrix\)
Attention Values Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of value vectors, one row per token, that attention weights combine into the output.


\(\BiasVector\)
Bias Vector
Vector
Vector of learned biases one layer adds to its weighted sums, one per neuron or output channel.


\(\ClassCount\)
Class Count
Integer
Number of classes a classifier distinguishes, or vocabulary entries it scores, the length of its softmax output.


\(\ClassIndex\)
Class Index
Integer
Index of an output class.


\(\EncoderLatentRepresentation\)
Encoder Latent Representation
Vector
Intermediate representation a shared encoder computes from an input, consumed by the heads that sit on top of it.


\(\ExampleIndex\)
Example Index
Integer
Index of an example within a batch.


\(\FactoredIntermediateActivation\)
Factored Intermediate Activation
Vector
Intermediate activation vector produced by the first factor of a low-rank layer and consumed by the second.


\(\FusionInputTensor\)
Fusion Input Tensor
Matrix
Input tensor of a chain of elementwise operators that kernel fusion combines.


\(\FusionOutputTensor\)
Fusion Output Tensor
Matrix
Output tensor of a chain of elementwise operators that kernel fusion combines.


\(\GaussianDistribution\)
Gaussian Distribution
Distribution
Gaussian (normal) distribution with the mean and covariance given as its arguments.


\(\GemmLeftOperand\)
GEMM Left Operand
Matrix
Left input matrix of a general matrix multiply, whose rows match the output and whose columns match the right operand’s rows.


\(\GemmOutputMatrix\)
GEMM Output Matrix
Matrix
Output matrix of a general matrix multiply, with the left operand’s row count and the right operand’s column count, which the operation updates in place.


\(\GemmRightOperand\)
GEMM Right Operand
Matrix
Right input matrix of a general matrix multiply, whose rows match the left operand’s columns.


\(\GemmRowDimension\)
GEMM Row Dimension
Integer
Number of rows of the left operand and of the output in a matrix multiply.


\(\HiddenActivation\)
Hidden Activation
Vector
Activation vector a hidden layer outputs and passes to the next layer.


\(\HiddenUnitOutput\)
Hidden Unit Output
Dimensionless
Output of one hidden unit of a small network.


\(\IdentityMatrix\)
Identity Matrix
Matrix
Square matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.


\(\KeyVector\)
Key Vector
Vector
Key vector of one token, one row of the key matrix.


\(\KvTileIndex\)
Key-Value Tile Index
Integer
Index of one key-value tile in tiled attention.


\(\LabelCategoryIndex\)
Label Category Index
Integer
Position of one label category among a classifier’s output classes.


\(\LayerIndex\)
Layer Index
Integer
Position of one layer within a network, counted from the input.


\(\LayerInputMatrix\)
Layer Input Matrix
Matrix
Input to a layer in matrix form, one row per example or token, or a single-channel image.


\(\LayerInputVector\)
Layer Input Vector
Vector
Vector of activations one layer receives as input.


\(\LayerOutputMatrix\)
Layer Output Matrix
Matrix
Output matrix of a layer’s matrix multiplication of the input matrix by the weight matrix, one row per example.


\(\LayerOutputVector\)
Layer Output Vector
Vector
Vector of activations one layer produces.


\(\LossGradient\)
Gradient
Varies
Gradient of the training loss with respect to one model parameter, as an optimizer update uses it.


\(\LossHessian\)
Loss Hessian
Matrix
Matrix of second derivatives of the loss with respect to every pair of model parameters.


\(\LowRankLeftFactor\)
Low Rank Left Factor
Matrix
Tall factor of a low-rank weight factorization, with one row per weight-matrix row and one column per retained rank.


\(\LowRankRightFactor\)
Low Rank Right Factor
Matrix
Second factor of a low-rank weight factorization, with one row per weight-matrix column and one column per retained rank.


\(\MatrixMultiplyDestination\)
Multiply-Accumulate Destination
Matrix
Destination matrix of a matrix multiply-accumulate instruction, which receives the product plus the accumulator input.


\(\MatrixRowIndex\)
Matrix Row Index
Integer
Position of a row within a matrix.


\(\ModelPredictor\)
Model Predictor
Function
Trained model viewed as a function that maps an input to its prediction.


\(\ModelScore\)
Model Score
Dimensionless
Score a classifier assigns to one individual, read as the predicted probability of the positive outcome.


\(\ModelWeight\)
Model Weight
Dimensionless
Value of one learnable weight of a model, such as the weight on one input of a neuron.


\(\NetworkOutput\)
Network Output
Dimensionless
Scalar output of a neuron or of a small network.


\(\OptimalModelParameters\)
Optimal Model Parameters
Vector
Model parameters that minimize the training loss for a given architecture.


\(\OptimizerStepIndex\)
Optimizer Step Index
Integer
Position of one optimizer update in the sequence of training steps.


\(\PredictedClassProbability\)
Predicted Class Probability
Dimensionless
Probability a classifier assigns to one label category for a given input.


\(\PredictedOutput\)
Predicted Output
Vector
Model output for one example, such as its vector of class probabilities.


\(\QueryComponent\)
Query Component
Dimensionless
One component of one token’s query vector.


\(\QueryVector\)
Query Vector
Vector
Query vector of one token, one row of the query matrix.


\(\RawPipelineInput\)
Raw Pipeline Input
Record
Raw input record before feature transformation, as received by the training or serving pipeline.


\(\ServingTransformFunction\)
Serving Transform
Function
Transformation the serving pipeline applies to a raw input to produce model features.


\(\SoftmaxRowMaximum\)
Softmax Row Maximum
Dimensionless
Largest score in a softmax row or block, subtracted before exponentiation to prevent overflow.


\(\SquareGemmDimension\)
Square GEMM Dimension
Integer
Side length of the square matrices in a matrix multiply, the shared row, column and inner dimension.


\(\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution\)
Standard Normal Cumulative Distribution
Function
Cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution.


\(\TopClassCount\)
Top Class Count
Integer
Number of highest-scoring classes a top-k prediction returns or checks for the correct label.


\(\TrainingTransformFunction\)
Training Transform
Function
Transformation the training pipeline applies to a raw input to produce model features.


\(\WeightMatrix\)
Weight Matrix
Matrix
Matrix of learned weights one layer multiplies its input by, or the kernel tensor of a convolution layer.


\(\WeightMatrixColumnCount\)
Weight Matrix Column Count
Integer
Number of columns of a layer’s weight matrix.


\(\WeightMatrixRowCount\)
Weight Matrix Row Count
Integer
Number of rows of a layer’s weight matrix.


\(\WeightPenaltyStrength\)
Weight Penalty Strength
Dimensionless
Coefficient that scales an absolute-value or squared penalty on weight magnitude added to the training loss, equivalent to weight decay under plain gradient descent.


\(\ZeroVector\)
Zero Vector
Vector
Vector whose entries are all zero, such as the mean of zero-centered Gaussian noise.




Latin matrices and vectors are set in bold (\(\Glyph{\mathbf{W}}\), \(\Glyph{\mathbf{x}}\)); scalars, dimensions, indices, and individual matrix entries stay italic (\(\Glyph{N}\), \(\Glyph{d}\), \(\Glyph{i}\), \(\Glyph{W}_{ij}\)). The generic parameter symbol \(\Glyph{\theta}\) is the conventional exception and stays italic. Matrix operands in general matrix multiply (GEMM) are bold (\(\GemmOutputMatrix= \Glyph{\alpha}\GemmLeftOperand\GemmRightOperand+ \Glyph{\beta}\GemmOutputMatrix\)), distinct from the scalar batch size \(\BatchSize\). GEMM dimensions are \(\GemmRowDimension\), \(\Glyph{N}\), and \(\Glyph{K}\). Asymptotic complexity is written \(\mathcal{O}(\cdot)\), distinct from total operations \(\Operations\).

title: Notation
text:
Federated systems, distributed coordination, and cluster operations rely on standardized metrics:


Part IV uses the standard symbols of differential privacy and adversarial robustness, and the operations and robustness chapters use those of hypothesis testing. The same Greek letters appear in several of these fields, so every use other than the one named below carries a subscript.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)
Differential Privacy Budget
Dimensionless
\(\PrivacyBudget\) bounds the privacy loss from adding or removing one protected record; \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) is the allowed failure probability.


\(\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\)
Adversarial Perturbation Budget
input units
Radius of the allowed input perturbation under a stated norm. (Not the privacy budget \(\PrivacyBudget\).)


\(\AttackStepsPgd\)
Attack Steps
Integer
Inner iterations of a projected gradient descent (PGD) attack; adversarial training costs about \(\AttackStepsPgd+1\) passes per batch.


\(\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel\), \(\HypothesisTestFalseNegativeRate\)
Type I and Type II Error Rates
Probability
Significance level and miss rate of a hypothesis test; statistical power is \(1-\HypothesisTestFalseNegativeRate\).


\(\mathbb{E}[\cdot]\)
Expectation
—
Expected value. Blackboard bold keeps it distinct from an event \(\Glyph{E}\) and the energy terms such as \(\TotalEnergy\).


\(\AdversarialExample\)
Adversarial Example
Record
Adversarial example, an input an attacker forms by adding a bounded perturbation to a clean input so the model mispredicts.


\(\AdversarialPerturbation\)
Adversarial Perturbation
Vector
Perturbation an adversary adds to an input to change a model’s prediction.


\(\AnonymitySetSize\)
Anonymity Set Size
Integer
Smallest number of records that share every quasi-identifier value in an anonymized release.


\(\AttributionFeatureCount\)
Attribution Feature Count
Integer
Number of input features a feature-attribution method assigns contributions to.


\(\ClassificationThreshold\)
Classification Threshold
Dimensionless
Score threshold above which a classifier outputs the positive class.


\(\ConfidenceCriticalQuantile\)
Confidence Critical Quantile
Dimensionless
Positive standard-Normal critical value for a two-sided test at the chosen confidence level.


\(\ConformalMiscoverageRate\)
Conformal Miscoverage Rate
Dimensionless
Allowed probability that the conformal prediction set misses the true referent.


\(\ConformalPredictionSet\)
Conformal Prediction Set
Set
Calibrated set of referent candidates that cannot be excluded at the miscoverage rate.


\(\CurrentBinProportion\)
Current Bin Proportion
Dimensionless
Proportion of current production observations falling in one bin of the population stability index.


\(\CurrentDistribution\)
Current Distribution
Distribution
Data distribution a deployed model sees in service at time t.


\(\DriftTestSampleSize\)
Drift Test Sample Size
Integer
Number of observations in one of the two samples a two-sample drift test compares.


\(\EnvironmentResponseFunction\)
Environment Response Function
Function
Response of the environment to a deployed model, mapping the current data distribution and the model’s decisions to the next data distribution.


\(\FairnessGapTolerance\)
Fairness Gap Tolerance
Dimensionless
Largest allowed gap between protected groups in the fairness metric a release gate or monitor enforces.


\(\FeatureRecordTime\)
Feature Record Time
seconds
Time at which a feature record became available, which a point-in-time join requires to be no later than the observation timestamp.


\(\FirstComparedGroupLabel\)
First Compared Group Label
Record
First of two group labels compared in a group-fairness condition, one value of the protected group attribute.


\(\JensenShannonDivergence\)
Jensen Shannon Divergence
Function
Jensen-Shannon divergence between two probability distributions, a symmetric bounded measure of how far they differ.


\(\JensenShannonMixtureDistribution\)
Jensen Shannon Mixture Distribution
Distribution
Equal-weight average of the current and training distributions, the reference against which Jensen-Shannon divergence measures each.


\(\KlDivergence\)
KL Divergence
Function
Kullback-Leibler divergence, the expected extra code length from encoding one distribution with a code built for another.


\(\KolmogorovSmirnovStatistic\)
Kolmogorov Smirnov Statistic
Dimensionless
Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, the largest absolute difference between two empirical cumulative distribution functions.


\(\McnemarTestStatistic\)
McNemar Test Statistic
Dimensionless
McNemar test statistic, the squared difference of the two discordant counts divided by their sum.


\(\MechanismOutputSet\)
Mechanism Output Set
Set
Set of possible outputs of a randomized mechanism over which a differential privacy bound must hold.


\(\MinimumDetectableEffect\)
Minimum Detectable Effect
Dimensionless
Smallest absolute difference in the outcome metric that an A/B test is designed to detect.


\(\MonitoredFeatureLevel\)
Monitored Feature Level
Varies
One value of a monitored feature, the argument at which its distribution or empirical cumulative distribution function is evaluated.


\(\MutualInformation\)
Mutual Information
Function
Mutual information between two random variables, how much observing one reduces uncertainty about the other.


\(\NeighboringDataset\)
Neighboring Dataset
Record

title: Notation
text:
Standardized measurement units, numerical representation formats, and collision-avoidance conventions ensure clarity across distributed systems analysis.



Physical units: This book uses SI (metric) units throughout, including meters, kilograms, seconds, watts, and °C, consistent with standard engineering and scientific practice. Where source data was originally reported in imperial units, the book converts to SI and notes the original values parenthetically. A space always separates the number from the unit (for example, 100 ms, 2 TB/s).
Data and memory: This book uses decimal SI prefixes only: KB = \(10^3\) bytes, MB = \(10^6\), GB = \(10^9\), TB = \(10^{12}\). Binary-prefixed units do not appear in prose; model sizes, activation footprints, throughputs, and transfer volumes are reported in decimal units (for example, 2 TB/s, 102 MB). Hardware memory capacities retain the vendor’s nameplate figure and label. A modeled capacity of \(80 \times 2^{30}\) bytes follows the registered device assumption, not a guarantee implied by an 80 GB label. Where a worked example subtracts a computed footprint from a device capacity, the registered capacity in bytes and the footprint are both converted to decimal; System Assumptions states this exception in full.
Compute: The notation distinguishes operation counts from rates. Total work uses FLOPs (for example, GFLOPs, TFLOPs), while throughput uses FLOP/s with decimal prefixes (for example, GFLOP/s, TFLOP/s).

1 TFLOP = \(10^{12}\) FLOPs
1 TFLOP/s = \(10^{12}\) FLOPs per second
Arithmetic intensity conventionally uses FLOP/byte as a unit ratio (floating-point operations per byte moved).

Network throughput: Reported in bytes/s (GB/s, TB/s) or bits/s (Gbps) depending on convention. InfiniBand and Ethernet specifications use Gbps; application-level throughput uses GB/s. The text states the convention on first use.
Power: Power carries a subscript (\(\AveragePower\), \(\DevicePower\), \(\Glyph{P_{\text{cluster}}}\), \(\InformationTechnologyPower\)); bare \(\Glyph{P}\) remains parameter count.
Latency percentiles: Written p50, p95, and p99 in upright type, inside math as well as in prose.
Currency: Dollar amounts use the dollar sign ($); unless otherwise noted, dollar-denominated costs are U.S. dollars (USD).
Precision:

FP64: Double precision (8 bytes)
FP32: Single precision (4 bytes)
TF32: TensorFloat-32 (19-bit Tensor Core compute mode; inputs and storage remain FP32)
FP16: Half precision (2 bytes, standard range)
BF16: Brain float (2 bytes, wide dynamic range)
FP8: Quarter precision (1 byte, E4M3 or E5M2 format)
FP4: 4-bit floating-point format
INT8: 8-bit integer (1 byte)
INT4: 4-bit integer; lower integer precisions follow the same uppercase INTn pattern (for example, INT3, INT2)

As a general principle, ML conventions take precedence for single letters, while systems concepts get subscripts or multi-letter symbols. This reflects the primary audience (ML practitioners learning systems) and preserves compatibility with the ML literature.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why are single-machine engineering principles insufficient for machine learning at fleet scale?
Machine learning at scale has a physics of its own. On one node, performance is often governed by the memory wall: data must reach the accelerator fast enough to keep the math busy. Scaling laws explain why one node stops being enough, because model quality improves predictably but sublinearly with compute, data, and parameters, so each further gain demands a larger fleet. In a distributed cluster, the memory problem stretches across machines. Data must move through network links between racks, and the slowest shared crossing can limit the entire job. Hardware failures also change character. A failure that stops one local training run can stall a whole distributed job when thousands of workers must advance together. This discontinuity explains why mastery of single-machine ML is no longer sufficient. A faster device may finish its local work sooner yet spend the saved time waiting for other machines. Adding devices can increase capacity while creating more shared work to coordinate and more components to recover. Serving introduces another consequence: spare capacity is useful only if requests can reach it within their deadlines. The engineering decision must therefore account for the behavior of the whole fleet. That wider boundary also amplifies societal impact because these systems may serve billions of users. Bias in any model can cause harm, but bias in a widely reused foundation model can propagate across many downstream systems. In C³ terms, the discipline this book builds is the physics of distribution, in which compute, communication, and coordination turn algorithmic choices into questions of physical topology, fault tolerance, security, and governance.

Learning Objectives

Explain how empirical scaling laws drive fleet growth and where breakdown conditions bound compute-optimal allocation
Diagnose fleet-scale distribution risks using reliability gaps, consistency-availability trade-offs, communication intensity, and routine failure rates
Explain how Compute, Communication, and Coordination extend the Data-Algorithm-Machine lens for production fleets
Apply the Fleet Law to separate a training budget’s useful compute from its communication and coordination overhead
Explain how the fleet stack connects infrastructure decisions to deployment and governance constraints






Machine learning on a single accelerator is governed by local memory hierarchy and arithmetic intensity: the physics of silicon. The boundary of single-machine systems appears when that local machine is no longer the system. As models move from research prototypes to global services, the binding constraints move outward into racks, networks, power delivery, and recovery machinery. That change is not a smooth extrapolation; it is the scale moment.
A synchronous distributed training step gives this change a concrete form. Each worker computes part of the update, exchanges model information with other workers, and waits until the required participants can advance together. These activities give the book its C\(^3\) lens: Compute is local execution, Communication moves data between workers, and Coordination keeps their progress and state consistent, including after failures. The Fleet Law expresses the corresponding time budget. Dividing a fixed workload across more devices can shorten local computation, but the step also pays for communication and coordination, less whatever work can overlap. Faster accelerators help only when the remaining costs allow the saved compute time to shorten the whole step.
This book assumes familiarity with single-machine training, inference, and accelerator memory. Readers who want to refresh that foundation should begin with The D·A·M Taxonomy, which restates it in reference form: the Data · Algorithm · Machine (D·A·M) lens that organizes single-machine diagnosis, the iron law, the roofline and its arithmetic-intensity boundary, the accelerator memory hierarchy, the memory cost of training state per parameter, and the arithmetic of transformer layers. The book’s aim is to develop engineering judgment across infrastructure, distributed execution, deployment, and governance, so that a local improvement can be evaluated against the behavior of the whole fleet. This chapter builds that judgment in the order a fleet engineer meets the problem. It first traces how far training compute and cluster size have grown and what changes when a job leaves one machine. It then turns to the empirical scaling laws that keep driving that growth, the physical, logical, and societal constraints that distribution imposes, and the C\(^3\) taxonomy and Fleet Law that diagnose where a distributed step loses time. It closes with the fleet stack, an eight-row layered map of the fleet that locates each cost in the architecture, and three recurring workloads that test how the dominant cost changes. Parallelism, communication, and recovery techniques appear here only by name. The task in this chapter is to identify the constraint each one must address, and later chapters develop the mechanisms.
The scale moment is the physical and operational transformation that occurs when models encounter three recurring walls: memory, network, and energy. They describe resource limits that the C\(^3\) lens helps diagnose. On one accelerator the memory wall often binds; after distributing a communication-intensive workload across thousands of nodes, the network wall can replace local memory as the primary performance bottleneck. Its hard limits include bisection bandwidth,1 the aggregate bandwidth across the narrowest cut that splits the fleet, and speed-of-light latency. Serving billions of users can then encounter the energy wall, making thermodynamic efficiency a first-order engineering requirement. Crossing those walls also opens a reliability gap, making hardware failure a routine event rather than a rare exception.
1 Bisection bandwidth (from graph theory): The minimum aggregate bandwidth of all links that, if cut, would partition the network into two equal-sized sets of nodes. In distributed ML, this “worst-case” cut bounds any collective whose traffic must cross it, such as a gradient exchange among all workers, and adding workers on either side does not raise that bound.Between 2012 and the mid-2020s, public and third-party estimates place training compute growth from roughly \(10^{18}\) FLOPs for AlexNet to approaching \(10^{25}\) FLOPs for leading large models, seven to eight orders of magnitude. The difference is qualitative, not merely quantitative. A workload that once fit on two GPUs now spans tens of thousands of accelerators. Recent capability leaps have repeatedly come from applying computation at previously impractical scales, and the empirical scaling laws examined in section 1.3 explain why organizations keep paying for each further order of magnitude.
This growth unfolded across a sequence of landmark models. AlexNet trained on two GTX 580 GPUs for approximately 5–6 days (Krizhevsky et al. 2012). BERT required 64 Tensor Processing Unit (TPU)2 chips for 4 days, roughly 6,144 chip hours (Devlin et al. 2019).

Krizhevsky, Alex, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. 2012. “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 25.
2 Tensor processing unit (TPU): Google’s custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) for machine learning, whose matrix units are systolic arrays, grids of multiply-accumulate cells that pass data between neighboring cells (Jouppi et al. 2017). At fleet scale, the inter-chip network matters as much as the array: TPU v4 joins its chips with an optically reconfigurable interconnect, so the topology of the network, not only the speed of each chip, determines how well many accelerators cooperate (Jouppi et al. 2023).
Jouppi, Norman P., Cliff Young, Nishant Patil, David Patterson, Gaurav Agrawal, Raminder Bajwa, Sarah Bates, et al. 2017. “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit.” Proceedings of the 44th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, ISCA ’17, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1145/3079856.3080246.

Jouppi, Norm, George Kurian, Sheng Li, Peter Ma, Rahul Nagarajan, Lifeng Nai, Nishant Patil, et al. 2023. “TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589350.

Devlin, Jacob, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, and Kristina Toutanova. 2019. “BERT: Pre-Training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding.” Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, 4171–86. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/n19-1423.

Chowdhery, Aakanksha, Sharan Narang, Jacob Devlin, Maarten Bosma, Gaurav Mishra, Adam Roberts, Paul Barham, et al. 2022. “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2204.02311.
GPT-3 consumed an estimated 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs during training (Brown et al. 2020). A single A100, a generation newer than the V100 GPUs that trained it, would need about 32 years to perform that work even at its full 312 TFLOP/s peak, which is the plainest answer to why one node is no longer enough. A later carbon accounting instead pairs the budget with 10,000 V100 GPUs sustaining about 24.6 TFLOP/s each (roughly 20 percent of the V100’s peak arithmetic rate) for roughly 15 days of training (Patterson et al. 2021). The gap between that delivered rate and the datasheet peak raises a question this book keeps returning to, namely how much of each accelerator a fleet actually puts to use. PaLM trained on 6,144 TPU v4 chips for roughly 60 days, consuming approximately \(10^{24}\) FLOPs (Chowdhery et al. 2022). OpenAI’s GPT-4 report did not disclose model size, training hardware, or training compute, so the GPT-4-class scenario in this section should be read as illustrative rather than a published configuration (OpenAI et al. 2023). These examples sit within the rapid training-compute growth trend documented by earlier compute-trend studies (Amodei and Hernandez 2018; Sevilla et al. 2022). Collected in table 1, they show training budgets moving from single-machine experiments into distributed systems where hardware count, wall-clock time, and operational coordination are part of the model design.

Plotted run by run from AlexNet to Llama 3 405B, the climb is steady on a logarithmic scale, and it separates early single-node vision models from multi-node transformer training (figure 1).














Figure 1: Training compute trends (2012–2024): The exponential growth of training compute for landmark ML models. The training compute (measured in FLOPs) has grown by roughly seven to eight orders of magnitude, highlighting the shift from single-node experimentation to massive-scale distributed fleets.



The language-model points pull away from the vision points because compute demands escalated sharply as transformer architectures replaced convolutional pipelines. Raw arithmetic volume is only one dimension of scale, however. The number of accelerators allocated to a single run has roughly doubled every year over the same period (figure 2), a rate that quickly outpaced what any single node could host.














Figure 2: The cluster size explosion: Number of accelerators used to train landmark models, 2012–2024. Verified counts from published papers are shown as filled circles; the GPT-3 estimate (hollow marker) reflects approximate cluster size from Microsoft infrastructure announcements rather than a precise published count. The dashed trend line indicates approximately 2\(\times\) annual growth in cluster size, a rate that outpaces Moore’s Law and motivates the infrastructure challenges developed throughout the book.



Across the four-order-of-magnitude climb charted in figure 2, accelerator counts rise from two GPUs for AlexNet to 16,384 H100 GPUs for Llama 3 along an annual doubling trajectory (\(\sim 2\times\) per year). The one estimated point is GPT-3’s, placed at the size of the Microsoft supercomputer built for OpenAI in 2020, more than 10,000 GPUs (Langston 2020). This empirical trajectory is the foundation of the scale moment, because leading models have required far larger accelerator fleets than earlier deep-learning landmarks. The curve alone, however, does not explain which constraint breaks first. Large language-model training, recommendation serving, and federated mobile learning all encounter fleet scale, but each stresses a different part of the system.

Langston, Jennifer. 2020. Microsoft Announces New Supercomputer, Lays Out Vision for Future AI Work. Microsoft Source.

Lighthouse 1.1: Lighthouse archetypes at scale
Lighthouse archetypes are the canonical workloads that keep the scale moment concrete throughout this book. At this point, their role is to show that “more machines” is not one engineering problem: the dominant constraint depends on what must cross the fleet boundary. The full roster with the C\(^3\) taxonomy mapping and binding-constraint analysis appears at section 1.6.1.

Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Very large language models move from memory bounds on one device to multi-node model parallelism, which splits one model across devices, either within each layer (tensor parallelism) or by assigning consecutive groups of layers to different devices as pipeline stages (pipeline parallelism), so communication can become the bottleneck for communication-intensive partitions.
Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): Deep learning recommendation model (DLRM) workloads move from fitting embedding tables in local memory to embedding sharding across hundreds of nodes, so coordinating sparse feature routing, shard placement, and request scheduling can become the bottleneck.
Archetype C (Federated MobileNet): Mobile inference and on-device adaptation move from one smartphone-class device to federated learning across millions of devices, so local work must respect per-device compute and power budgets, while communication and participation can limit the federated round.



These archetypes turn the growth curve into an engineering question. The same increase in accelerator count can produce a network wall, a sparse-routing coordination bottleneck, or a per-device compute ceiling. The fleet stack, the layered map of the fleet developed at the end of this chapter, locates those constraints in the architecture, while C\(^3\) identifies the execution cost they impose. That diversity of constraint regimes, which federated learning extends beyond the data center, has made systems engineering central to ML at scale. A sophisticated algorithm that cannot scale often provides less practical value than a simpler algorithm deployed efficiently across scalable infrastructure.


↪ Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism, and the traffic each places on the fabric, are developed in Distributed Training.

↪ Federated rounds across millions of devices, where dropouts, stragglers, and per-device budgets bind, are developed in Federated Learning Systems at Scale.

Moving from one machine to many changes the governing physics of the system, not merely its device count. A single node is bound locally by the memory wall between its accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and it has no peers to wait for. A fleet executes across a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places and recovers the job, which exposes the workload to the network wall, to stragglers, and to routine node failures (figure 3).






Figure 3: The scale discontinuity: On a single machine (left), the usual binding constraint is the memory wall between the accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and there are no peers to wait for. In a fleet (right), nodes exchange state over a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places the job and recovers it, so the three C\(^3\) roles appear as separate components. The fabric can become the binding network wall, and failed and slow nodes become routine events that hold back the whole job.



At fleet scale, the binding constraint may shift from local silicon to the network fabric, while resilience joins optimization as a primary concern. The unit of compute is no longer a single server but a machine learning fleet, an interconnected distributed system designed to act as a coherent engine.

Definition 1.1: Machine learning fleet
Machine learning fleet is a distributed collection of compute devices, storage, and networks managed together to train or serve machine learning models.

Significance: In tightly coupled synchronous training, the total time \(\Time\) can be governed by the slowest worker (straggler). Sustaining that workload requires balancing bisection bandwidth (\(\BisectionBandwidth\)) against aggregate compute capacity (\(\PeakRate\)). Serving fleets and heterogeneous edge fleets impose different communication and coordination requirements.
Distinction: The fleet is the unit of engineering, but its workers need not all advance together. Synchronous tight coupling makes a training job depend on a shared step barrier; serving replicas can process separate requests, and federated devices can participate intermittently. The workload determines the required coupling and recovery behavior.
Common pitfall: Treating an ML fleet as “just more servers” overlooks shared network, placement, and recovery constraints. A tightly coupled data-center fleet behaves as one machine, the warehouse-scale computer of section 1.2.2; an edge fleet extends the engineering boundary to devices outside that managed facility.



For a tightly coupled job, the network wall of the scale moment is set by the fleet’s bisection bandwidth, which limits how fast data can cross the network midpoint; adding workers does not raise it. That bound is the bisection bandwidth wall, and at fleet scale it often determines model throughput more than compute does.
At the scale of thousands of GPUs, failure modes appear that a single GPU never exhibits. A network partition can leave a synchronous job hung at a collective (an operation, such as a gradient exchange, that every worker must join) until a timeout aborts it, and in loosely synchronized designs it can let groups of workers drift apart. Stragglers (workers that process data slower than peers due to hardware variation or thermal throttling) can bottleneck entire training runs. Even infrequent component failures accumulate across a large fleet, so long training jobs must expect interruptions.3 Systems must preserve recoverable state frequently enough to bound the work lost at each interruption.
3 Hardware failure rates at scale: Notebook 1.1 uses an assumed per-GPU mean time between failures and independent failures to illustrate how interruption frequency grows with fleet size. Production job interruptions include software, networking, and maintenance as well as accelerator faults. Meta’s Llama 3 report provides an observed example of this broader interruption category (Dubey et al. 2024); it does not establish a universal annual GPU failure rate.
Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.


A 25,000-GPU job fails 25,000 times as often as one GPU.

Patel, Dylan, and Gerald Wong. 2023. GPT-4 Architecture, Infrastructure, Training Dataset, Costs, Vision, MoE. SemiAnalysis Blog.

OpenAI, Josh Achiam, Steven Adler, Sandhini Agarwal, Lama Ahmad, Ilge Akkaya, Florencia Leoni Aleman, et al. 2023. “GPT-4 Technical Report.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2303.08774, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2303.08774.

The interruption cadence follows from simple arithmetic. Consider a GPT-4-class training scenario using a hypothetical A100-class cluster of 25,000 GPUs running for 100 days. These values follow a third-party estimate (Patel and Wong 2023) rather than an OpenAI disclosure (OpenAI et al. 2023). In a cluster of this size, the probability of at least one failure over an interval \(\TimeInstant\) becomes a binding constraint. With independent, exponentially distributed failures and system mean time between failures (MTBF) \(\SystemMtbf\), that probability is \(\Pr(\text{failure before } \TimeInstant) = 1 - e^{-\TimeInstant/\SystemMtbf}\). The worked example in notebook 1.1 establishes the arithmetic for one cluster, and that arithmetic, the MTBF cascade, predicts the interruption cadence for any fleet size.


↪ The MTBF cascade, which sums component failure rates into node and cluster MTBF for multi-thousand-GPU fleets, is developed in The MTBF cascade.

Napkin Math 1.1: Scale and reliabilityProblem: A training run for a GPT-4-class model uses 25,000 GPUs. If each individual GPU has an MTBF of 50,000 hours (the modeling assumption used in this example, not a measured fleet-wide failure rate), how often will the training job be interrupted by hardware failure?
Math:

System MTBF: The system MTBF is the component MTBF divided by the number of independent GPUs. With this scenario’s values, 50,000 hours divided by 25,000 GPUs is about 2 hours.
Daily failure rate: 24 hours divided by 2 hours is about 12 failures per day.
Failures over the run: 100 days at about 12 failures per day is about 1,200 interruptions before the run completes.
Uninterrupted stretches: with \(\Pr(\text{no failure in } \TimeInstant) = e^{-\TimeInstant/\SystemMtbf}\), a stretch of 1 hour completes without failure with probability of about 61 percent, and a stretch of 4 hours only about 14 percent of the time.

Systems insight: In this regime, component failures recur throughout a long run, and a job that saved its state only every few hours would usually be interrupted before reaching the next save. Manual restart does not scale; the system must be architected for fault tolerance from the outset. Hardware can no longer be treated as an infallible abstraction, so automated state preservation and recovery become operational requirements.


Meta’s published Llama 3 training run illustrates the operational consequence in a real large-scale system, where interruptions have several causes.

War Story 1.1: The training run that failed every few hours (2024)Context: Meta reports training Llama 3 405B on 16,384 H100 GPUs during a 54-day snapshot of pretraining (Dubey et al. 2024).
Mechanism: The cluster experienced 419 unexpected interruptions during that snapshot. GPU faults and memory errors were major contributors; the report also records software, network, and host issues. These job interruptions are not equivalent to permanent GPU failures.
Impact: Meta nevertheless reported more than 90 percent effective training time, measured as useful training time divided by elapsed time. Significant manual intervention was required only three times.
Fix: Meta reduced job startup and checkpointing time and developed automated diagnosis and recovery tools. Communication traces helped locate stalled collectives and slow workers before restarting useful work.
Systems lesson: The scale moment turns reliability from a hardware specification into a distributed-systems design requirement. A fleet-scale model is trained by the recovery machinery as much as by the optimizer.


4 InfiniBand: A data-center interconnect whose defining feature for ML is remote direct memory access (RDMA), which bypasses the OS kernel to move data directly between application memory on different machines at microsecond-scale latency. HDR InfiniBand provides about 25 GB/s line-rate bandwidth per link and NDR about 50 GB/s; that per-link bandwidth, relative to the computation each worker performs between exchanges, decides whether large-model training is compute-bound or communication-bound. RDMA-capable Ethernet (RoCE) now offers comparable line rates.

Organizations answered these challenges with purpose-built fleets whose defining component is the network as much as the accelerator. Meta’s Research SuperCluster, announced in 2022, was designed to reach 16,000 NVIDIA A100 GPUs connected by 200 Gb/s InfiniBand4 links (AI 2022), and Google’s TPU v4 pods join 4,096 chips delivering 1.1 EFLOP/s of aggregate peak compute (Zu et al. 2024). Later Azure AI data center announcements describe training fabrics of tens of thousands of GPUs (Microsoft 2025). Each accelerator’s share of that aggregate compute must exchange its results through links of a few hundred gigabits per second.
The scale moment establishes why exponential growth in compute demand forces some ML systems beyond any single machine, making the network fabric a potential bottleneck and component failure routine over long runs. The next question is how to organize the engineering response. Established distributed-systems techniques remain essential, but global barriers and large shared model state change their costs and determine which recovery and consistency mechanisms apply. Tracing how the layers of one machine map onto a fleet, starting with how sharply the links between servers fall below the bandwidth inside one, makes those dependencies explicit.
