Inside one H100 server, NVLink moves tensors between accelerators at 450 GB/s in each direction per accelerator. Once a training job spans racks, the same tensors leave through an InfiniBand NDR port at 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) in each direction, a bandwidth step down of roughly 9× for an accelerator served by one such port. That step illustrates a general pattern. The layered structure of an ML system persists across scale, while the physics at each layer changes. The fleet stack names the fleet’s layers by grouping them into four bands, Infrastructure at the bottom, then Distribution, Serving, and Governance at the top, with two rows in each (figure 14). At the bottom, the hardware substrate of one node becomes the Infrastructure band, an RDMA fabric spanning racks, and the binding constraint can shift from the memory wall to the bisection bandwidth wall as network congestion and message-passing latency consume a growing share of step time. One layer up, system software (a single CUDA runtime managing PCIe direct memory access (DMA)) becomes the Distribution band, which holds the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and RDMA libraries that coordinate thousands of processes across the fabric, together with the schedulers that place distributed jobs and the recovery machinery that restarts them. Efficient data movement inside each node remains a prerequisite, because a fleet of underutilized nodes only multiplies the waste.
The upper bands add responsibilities rather than replace the familiar software layers. The ML framework (PyTorch or JAX executing a training loop on one node) remains part of model execution. The Serving band adds request handling and deployment pipelines that manage rolling releases across the fleet. Applications also remain, while the Governance band sets security, robustness, sustainability, and responsible AI requirements for their operation. Section 1.6 returns to the full stack and the eight rows within it as the map that organizes the rest of this book. The stack identifies where a design decision belongs; C\(^3\) identifies how that decision affects execution time.
A map of layers does not by itself explain why the same decision behaves differently once it spans a fleet. Three changes separate a fleet from a larger server: synchronous coupling turns independent tasks into a shared step, the facility itself becomes the computer, and communication can dominate the step. A fourth change, routine failure, was quantified at the scale moment; its availability model returns with the other constraints of scale in section 1.4.1. Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), the large-language-model workload of the book’s canonical roster (section 1.6.1), runs on a reference cluster of NVIDIA H100 accelerators and makes each change concrete where a chapter needs it.


Many distributed systems isolate work into tasks or requests so that one failure need not stop unrelated work. MapReduce (Dean and Ghemawat 2004) partitions an input into tasks and can re-execute failed or slow work, Apache Spark (Zaharia et al. 2016) processes data-parallel tasks with explicit shuffle boundaries, and a web microservice handles requests whose failures can be isolated. Search engines and banking databases use other forms of replication, partitioning, and coordination; they are not uniformly independent or asynchronous. The useful contrast is therefore between failure domains and coupling patterns, not between “traditional” and ML systems.

Large synchronous training jobs operate under synchronous tight coupling. Parameter-server architectures (Li et al. 2014) and collective runtimes manage distributed state, but synchronous optimization updates a large shared model state across thousands of accelerators every few hundred milliseconds rather than completing independent one-shot tasks. At each synchronization point, progress can depend on the slowest participating worker, so a persistent 10 percent slowdown on one worker can approach a 10 percent step-time penalty when that worker lies on the critical path. Communication-heavy partitions can also become bisection-bandwidth bound because large gradient or activation tensors cross the network every step. These properties do not invalidate established recovery techniques; they increase recovery cost and restrict which replication, re-execution, and consistency strategies preserve useful training progress.
The two execution pathways differ at the point of failure (figure 4). In MapReduce, a failed map task is retried on its own while its peers complete. In synchronous data-parallel training, where every worker holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of each batch, every worker must contribute its gradient to an AllReduce, a collective operation that combines the gradients of all workers and returns the result to each of them, before the shared parameter update can occur. A slow map task can delay downstream reduction and job completion, but other map tasks finish without waiting; in synchronous training, by contrast, healthy workers sit idle whenever a straggler delays the collective.






Figure 4: Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps: Map tasks (left) deliver their outputs independently, so a failed task is re-run on its own while the others finish; its missing output delays only the reducers that need it. In synchronous data-parallel training (right), the AllReduce needs every worker’s gradient before the shared update can proceed, so a slow worker on the critical path holds the whole step and the healthy workers wait. How much the step stretches depends on overlap and the other costs of the step.



The collective barrier dependency diagrammed in figure 4 explains why MapReduce-style localized task re-execution cannot be transferred directly to tightly coupled training: when all workers advance a single shared parameter step, recovery must restore mutually consistent model, optimizer, and input state across every participating node before coordinated execution can resume.

A tightly coupled data-center fleet demands the warehouse-scale computer (WSC)5 perspective. A machine-centric view treats the data center as a building that houses many computers; the warehouse-scale view treats the data center itself as the computer. In this paradigm, single-node abstractions map directly onto distributed infrastructure: the network fabric functions as the system bus, distributed storage serves as the local disk, and the fleet orchestrator acts as the operating system.
5 Warehouse-scale computer (WSC): Barroso and Hölzle, later with Clidaras, framed the data center itself as the computer. For ML fleets, power delivery, cooling topology, optical network layout, and bisection bandwidth become first-order constraints; a 100 MW facility can limit training throughput more than any single accelerator’s TFLOP/s.For this data-center regime, the engineering boundary extends from local execution to the shared power, network, and recovery systems that sustain the entire facility. The warehouse-scale computer is a common paradigm for large models, while alternative architectures like wafer-scale engines, single processors built from an entire silicon wafer rather than one reticle-sized die, attempt to collapse this entire hierarchy back into a single piece of silicon, trading the modularity of a distributed cluster for the extreme bandwidth of on-chip communication. Both designs answer the same constraint, the cost of moving data between chips, from opposite directions.



Distributing these workloads beyond one machine can make communication the dominant cost, the network wall of the scale moment. On one GPU, a dense training workload may spend most of its time performing matrix multiplications and incur no inter-node communication. Distribution introduces communication whose share depends on the model, partitioning strategy, collective algorithm, topology, precision, and overlap with computation.



Ring AllReduce moves about twice the gradient per step; 16-bit gradients halve it.
At large scale, communication can dominate communication-intensive partitions. Distributed data-parallel training synchronizes gradients across workers after each batch. For a model with 175B parameters, FP32 gradients occupy about 700 GB before any collective algorithm is applied. Ring AllReduce arranges the AllReduce exchange among neighbors in a logical ring; with \(\DeviceCount\) workers, each worker sends roughly \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) times the gradient tensor size and receives the same amount across the reduction and distribution phases (Ring AllReduce derives this factor). For large \(\DeviceCount\) the factor approaches two, so each worker moves about twice the FP32 gradient per step, and half that when mixed-precision training exchanges 16-bit gradients. Network traffic therefore depends on precision, worker count, collective implementation, and partitioning. On slower interconnects or partitions with little computation per communicated byte, it can consume a large fraction of each iteration rather than a negligible one; notebook 1.2 later converts the 16-bit volume into seconds of exposed transfer per step.

This exposed transfer cost explains why distributed training systems optimize communication so aggressively, and their many mechanisms answer one problem. Distributing work also distributes state that must move or be kept consistent. Horovod, for example, runs Ring AllReduce and fuses many small gradient tensors into fewer large transfers, so that the fixed cost of starting each exchange is paid fewer times (Sergeev and Balso 2018). Splitting each layer across devices, as Megatron-LM does with tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al. 2019), and sharding optimizer state across workers, as ZeRO does (Rajbhandari et al. 2020), trade per-device memory for different traffic patterns; Distributed Training develops both. The design decision at this stage is which cost prevents progress; selecting a particular mechanism requires the workload and fabric models developed later.
Routine failure, the other consequence of distribution, was already quantified at the scale moment. Under that example’s assumptions the job meets a hardware failure every few hours, so checkpointing, replacement capacity, and automated recovery must keep each interruption short; section 1.4.1 develops the availability model behind that cadence. Communication and recovery costs describe how a fleet executes work. Neither explains what drives the relentless growth in fleet size, or how much work a model should receive. Both answers lie in empirical relationships between model quality and resource investment, relationships that have made warehouse-scale infrastructure an economic necessity rather than an engineering luxury.

The seven to eight orders of magnitude of training compute traced at the scale moment, from AlexNet to GPT-4-class estimates near \(10^{25}\) FLOPs, were not an accident of ambition. Each order-of-magnitude increase in compute demanded a corresponding expansion of the machine learning fleet, and organizations paid for those expansions because the return on them had become predictable. Predictable is not the same as free. Measured learning curves estimate the quality a training budget buys, while device throughput, execution efficiency, and the completion deadline determine how much fleet capacity that budget requires.
Rich Sutton’s “bitter lesson” articulated the underlying principle: performance in machine learning is primarily driven by applying general methods at massive scale rather than encoding human knowledge into algorithms (Sutton 2019). Scaling laws formalize this observation quantitatively: model loss improves sublinearly as a power-law function of compute, dataset size, and parameters, \(\ScalingLawLoss(\ScaledResource) \propto \ScaledResource^{-\ScalingExponent}\) for a resource \(\ScaledResource\) (stated in full, with its irreducible floor, in theorem 1.1) (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022). Each equal-sized loss improvement therefore requires disproportionately more resources, a systems consequence this book later names as the universal scaling law. Each scaling dimension (parameters, data, and compute) interacts with infrastructure constraints differently, making multi-dimensional efficiency optimization essential at production scale.

Sutton, Richard S. 2019. “The Bitter Lesson.” Incompleteideas.net 43.


The growth trajectory establishes demand for larger fleets; empirical scaling laws guide how that demand should be allocated. At the budgets traced at the scale moment, estimating the return on additional resources is an engineering necessity rather than a research curiosity. Over the longer history of AI, the fitted growth rate of training compute itself changed around 2010, from about 1.4\(\times\) per year, close to Moore’s Law, to about 4\(\times\) per year in the deep learning era (Sevilla et al. 2022) (figure 5). A fourfold annual rise is two doublings a year, while accelerators per run doubled about once a year over the period traced at the scale moment. Training compute is the product of accelerator count, per-accelerator throughput, and run duration, so faster accelerators and longer runs supply the other doubling. A demand curve that steep makes misallocation expensive, which is why the model-loss measurements that follow matter.

Because each equal loss improvement costs disproportionately more, allocation grows more consequential as budgets grow. The question is how to divide a budget between the size of the model and the training data it consumes.



Empirical studies of large language models (LLMs) show that, for a fixed computational budget and within the studied scaling regime, balancing model size and dataset size (measured in tokens6) can minimize training loss.
6 Tokens: Subword units produced by algorithms like byte-pair encoding, which iteratively merges the most frequent character pairs in a corpus. Token vocabulary size creates a direct systems trade-off: larger vocabularies can reduce sequence length for some languages and domains, but they expand the embedding table roughly in proportion to vocabulary size. GPT-3 used a 50,257-token vocabulary; moving to 100K+ tokens in newer models therefore trades tokenization efficiency against additional embedding memory.7 FLOPs vs. FLOP/s: A critical distinction: FLOPs denotes total computational work (operations performed), while FLOP/s denotes hardware throughput (operations per second); confusing the two leads to incorrect cost estimates. GPT-3 required 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs of work; an A100 delivers 312 TFLOP/s of throughput. Dividing work by peak throughput gives ideal wall-clock time, the roughly 32 years on one A100 computed at the scale moment. Actual time is approximately \(\text{work}/(\EfficiencyHw \PeakRate)\), where the hardware utilization \(\EfficiencyHw\) is the achieved fraction of peak throughput, so utilization below one multiplies ideal time by \(1/\EfficiencyHw\).Figure 6 decomposes this compute-optimal allocation across three empirical views. In the left panel, U-shaped IsoFLOP contours plot training loss against parameter counts for fixed compute budgets, with each curve’s valley minimum identifying the optimal model capacity for that FLOP ceiling. The center and right panels track how optimal parameters and training tokens scale along coordinated power-law trajectories as compute expands, confirming that compute-optimal training requires advancing model size and token volume in tandem. The highlighted projection markers extrapolate these fits to larger budgets, for example 63B parameters trained on 1.4T tokens for a total of a little over \(5 \times 10^{23}\) FLOPs,7 illustrating how compute-optimal frontiers guide resource allocation before cluster execution begins.

The center and right panels quantify how optimal parameter counts and token requirements scale predictably as compute increases, demonstrating the need to scale model size and data together to use large training budgets efficiently.



Kaplan et al. (2020) demonstrated that transformer-based language-model loss follows predictable power-law relationships with model parameters, dataset size (measured in tokens), and total computational budget. The result was not a license to increase every dimension blindly; it showed that model quality depends on coordinated allocation across those resources, a point later sharpened by Chinchilla’s compute-optimal scaling analysis (Hoffmann et al. 2022).
Two further results appear in Kaplan’s measurements across parameter scales from \(10^3\) to \(10^9\) (figure 7). Larger models are more sample-efficient, reaching a target loss with substantially fewer training tokens. Compute-efficient training therefore stops far short of full convergence, because an early-stopped larger model attains the target loss with less total compute than a smaller model trained to its plateau.






Figure 7: Scaling laws and compute optimality: Larger models consistently achieve better performance with increased training data and compute, but diminishing returns necessitate careful resource allocation during training. Optimal model size and training duration depend on the available compute budget, as evidenced by the convergence of loss curves at different parameter scales and training token counts.



Within the studied regime, the Chinchilla result indicates that model size and training tokens should scale approximately proportionally for compute-optimal training, with a ratio on the order of 20 training tokens per parameter (Hoffmann et al. 2022). The projection marker of figure 6, 1.4T tokens for 63B parameters, sits at that ratio. This corrected earlier guidance that favored making models larger while training them on comparatively fewer tokens. The objective is loss at a fixed training-compute budget. A deployment that serves the model repeatedly must also account for inference cost; its preferred allocation need not minimize training compute alone.

The power-law proportionality stated with the bitter lesson has a full form that includes an irreducible floor. That form explains why the same fleet can enter different operational regimes, and the following analysis takes three cuts through them, each with its own fleet consequence: how compute and data are allocated (which resource to buy next), where diminishing returns set in with dataset size (when storage and data pipelines matter more than accelerators), and when in the model’s lifecycle computation is spent (which part of the fleet, training or serving, carries the load).

Theorem 1.1: Power-law scaling formulationScaling laws are expressed formally as power-law relationships. The general formulation is:
\[
\ScalingLawLoss(\ScaledResource) = \ScaleCoefficient \ScaledResource^{-\ScalingExponent} + \IrreducibleLoss
\]
where loss \(\ScalingLawLoss\) decreases as resource quantity \(\ScaledResource\) increases, following a power-law decay with rate \(\ScalingExponent\), plus a baseline constant \(\IrreducibleLoss\), the irreducible loss (a constant of the fit, not one of the C\(^3\) labels). Here, \(\ScalingLawLoss(\ScaledResource)\) represents the loss achieved with a resource quantity such as parameters, tokens, or compute; \(\ScaleCoefficient\) and \(\IrreducibleLoss\) are task-dependent constants; and \(\ScalingExponent\) is the scaling exponent that characterizes the rate of performance improvement. A larger value of \(\ScalingExponent\) signifies more efficient performance improvements with respect to scaling.


For a fleet, the exponent is the price list. Halving the reducible term \(\ScaleCoefficient \ScaledResource^{-\ScalingExponent}\) requires multiplying the resource \(\ScaledResource\) by \(2^{1/\ScalingExponent}\), so the smaller the exponent, the larger the multiple of accelerators, tokens, or training time that each further step in quality demands.
These power-law predictions find empirical validation in the family of learning curves plotted in figure 8: across six model scales spanning from 393.2K to 708M parameters, test loss descends predictably as dataset size grows from \(10^7\) toward \(3\times 10^{10}\) tokens, with smaller architectures flattening into parameter-capacity plateaus while larger models sustain power-law error reduction.


Applying scaling laws in practice is a scarcity diagnosis: the useful question is which resource prevents balanced growth first. Compute budget, data availability, and model size create three regimes with different optimal responses.
In a compute-limited regime, compute scarcity restricts scaling potential despite abundant training data; measured learning curves guide the allocation between model size and training tokens within that budget. In a data-limited regime, computational resources exceed what the available dataset can support, meaning that increasing model size is useful only if validation measurements show that the available data can support additional capacity. Between these extremes lies the optimal regime, where compute and data grow in balance following compute-optimal scaling laws, as DeepMind demonstrated with Chinchilla by outperforming much larger models through proportional scaling of model size and training data (Hoffmann et al. 2022). Recognizing which regime governs a given project prevents common inefficiencies: over-parameterized models with insufficient training data, or under-parameterized models that waste available compute. For the fleet, the diagnosis decides where the next investment goes. A compute-limited project needs accelerator-hours, while a data-limited one gains more from the storage and data pipelines of Data Storage than from additional accelerators.














Figure 8: Loss vs. dataset size across model scales: Test loss curves show how models of different sizes (393.2K to 708M parameters) benefit from increased training data. Larger models achieve lower loss, but all curves exhibit diminishing returns at high token counts.



The second cut follows the return on additional data as a dataset grows, which decides when buying data stops paying. The third follows lifecycle stage, because additional compute can be spent on the foundation run, on adapting the model afterward, or on each request in deployment.
Figure 9 partitions dataset scaling into three distinct empirical regimes on log-log coordinates. In the initial Small Data Region, generalization error lingers near the upper Best Guess Error ceiling; as data volume expands into the central Power-Law Region, error drops sharply along a constant slope where data investment yields predictable returns; finally, in the Irreducible Error Region, the curve flattens asymptotically against the Bayes noise floor where further dataset expansion provides negligible gain. The systems consequence is that finite high-quality data, not compute, becomes the binding constraint once a model enters the saturation regime, which is why data efficiency complements brute-force scaling. An observed plateau does not by itself establish that the irreducible floor has been reached, however. Limited coverage, insufficient model capacity, and incomplete optimization can also flatten a learning curve, so the engineering task is to rule out these remediable limits before purchasing more data or compute.

Figure 10 distinguishes three points in the lifecycle where additional computation can change model behavior. Pretraining scaling (orange curve) increases the resource investment in the foundation run. Posttraining scaling (blue curve) adapts an existing model through fine-tuning or preference optimization. Test-time scaling (green curve, “long thinking”) spends additional computation on a particular request through intermediate generation, search, or sampling, trading serving latency and throughput for a possible quality gain. Each phase stresses a different part of the fleet. Pretraining is one long, failure-sensitive foundation run whose scaling-law gains must be realized in wall-clock time; posttraining replaces that single massive job with many smaller, coordination-heavy runs; test-time scaling moves computation into the serving path, where it competes with latency targets. The schematic curves do not establish a universal efficiency ranking among these choices, so the full treatments belong with their workloads; test-time compute at serving is treated in The logic wall and test-time compute scaling. A resource plan must compare measured task improvements and costs before choosing where to spend the next increment of compute.

As models expand, training and deployment costs grow disproportionately, creating tension between performance gains and system efficiency. A resource plan must also identify where its empirical fit ceases to apply, because scaling laws are fitted within the regimes in which they were measured and need not hold beyond them. Most breakdowns at those boundaries share one root cause, growth in one dimension that outpaces the others. Hoffmann et al. (2022) show that many large language models were undertrained because model size grew faster than training-token budgets, and that compute-optimal training requires scaling parameters and tokens together. Hardware ceilings belong to the same family, because memory bandwidth, interconnect capacity, and I/O throughput cap how far a larger model can be distributed at all. Each imbalance requires different evidence. Training measurements can reveal an unsuitable optimization schedule; held-out evaluation can distinguish improved generalization from memorization; and execution traces can reveal whether bandwidth or I/O prevents the fleet from completing the planned work. A lower benchmark loss also does not establish robustness to adversarial or out-of-distribution inputs. Checkpoint 1.2: Applying scaling laws
These questions check whether scaling laws are being used as resource-allocation tools:

Scaling laws reveal the walls; efficiency engineering builds the paths around them. Data saturation, infrastructure bottlenecks, and diminishing returns set hard limits on what brute-force scaling can achieve. The same constraints, however, point toward solutions along three interconnected dimensions. Algorithmic efficiency relies on techniques such as sparsity and distillation to extract more capability per FLOP. Data efficiency uses curriculum learning and active selection to extract more information per training example. Systems efficiency uses communication hiding and pipeline overlap to extract more utilization per accelerator. Each dimension addresses a different breakdown condition from table 2, so identifying the limiting resource determines whether efficiency work should target the algorithm, the data, or the execution system. Systems efficiency is the subject of Distributed Training and Collective Communication, algorithmic levers such as reduced precision and sparse mixture-of-experts execution appear in Performance Engineering, and data efficiency under device budgets returns in Data Efficiency.
Scaling laws and efficiency techniques determine how much computation large models require and how well the fleet uses it. They do not, however, address the physical and logical constraints that the fleet itself imposes. Hardware fails, bandwidth saturates, distributed systems face fundamental impossibility results, and societal impact at scale demands governance. These constraints cannot be optimized away; they must be engineered around.

Scaling laws set how much work the fleet must perform; the three walls of the scale moment describe where performing it binds. The constraints behind those walls are broader. The machine learning fleet operates under three categories of irreducible constraint: physical (the memory, network, and energy walls themselves, plus the reliability gap that opens as fleet size grows), logical (distributed systems face impossibility results like the CAP theorem), and societal (scale amplifies the impact of every technical decision). For an initial C\(^3\) diagnosis, the distinctions matter because a slow step may reflect a communication limit or coordination loss, while an otherwise fast design may exceed its energy or governance budget. The formal time decomposition follows after these examples establish what it must account for.


High individual-component availability does not guarantee high availability for a tightly coupled fleet. This distinction opens the reliability gap: high component reliability in isolation does not ensure that every component required by an unreplicated job will be available simultaneously. Notebook 1.1 measured the gap as a rate, how often the job is interrupted; availability measures it as a probability, how likely it is that every required component is up at a given instant. Both views rest on the same independence assumption and degrade the same way as the job grows. For a 25,000-GPU job that can make progress only while every GPU is available, equation 1 multiplies the component availabilities under an independence assumption to give the probability that all required components are available at the same instant (\(\JobAvailability\)):
\[ \JobAvailability= (\ComponentAvailability)^\RequiredComponentCount \tag{1}\]
Here, \(\RequiredComponentCount\) is the number of independent components that the job requires simultaneously, and \(\ComponentAvailability\) is the availability of one component. The engineering implication is the exponent: every added required component lowers the probability that the full set is available, so reliability engineering becomes a scaling problem rather than a cleanup task.
For a single component, 99.99 percent availability corresponds to 52.56 minutes of unavailability per 365-day year. This is a time fraction, not a count of failures.
If each node has an illustrative 99.9 percent availability and an unreplicated job requires every node, the probability that all 1,000 required nodes are available simultaneously is only 36.8 percent. Scale that job to 10,000 required nodes, and this probability drops to 0.0045 percent. Adding a nine to every node only postpones the collapse, because the exponent \(\RequiredComponentCount\) eventually overwhelms any per-node availability below one (figure 11).














Figure 11: The reliability collapse: The simultaneous availability of every node required by an unreplicated job, shown as a function of job size for two per-node availability levels under an independence assumption. At 99.9 percent per-node availability (blue), all-node availability is only 36.8 percent for a 1,000-node job and approaches zero for a 10,000-node job. Even 99.99 percent per-node availability (green) yields 36.8 percent at 10,000-node scale.



The collapse zone isolated in figure 11 makes the architectural consequence clear: because simultaneous all-node availability drops precipitously toward zero as job size expands into the thousands, an unreplicated synchronous workload cannot rely on unbroken component uptime. Failure Probability at Scale replaces this single per-node availability figure with the full failure-probability model, from component failure rates to the chance that a job fails before it finishes. The engineering lesson is that failure is the common case. At scale, resilience replaces prevention as the governing objective: the system trades absolute uptime for recovery speed, checkpoint quality, and automated repair.


↪ The shift from keeping every component running to a fleet that recovers automatically when components fail is developed in Fault Tolerance.



If arithmetic intensity governs where a single accelerator stalls, communication intensity (CI) governs where a fleet stalls. On a single accelerator, the roofline model determines whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound. At fleet scale, this analysis elevates to the network.
Equation 2 defines communication intensity as the ratio of data moved across the network to the operations performed locally. The numerator counts bytes and the denominator counts operations for the same worker and interval, such as one training step; the ratio therefore has units of bytes per operation. A comparison must also state whether it counts sent bytes, received bytes, or both:
\[\CommunicationIntensity = \frac{\NetworkTrafficVolume}{\Operations} \tag{2}\]
where \(\NetworkTrafficVolume\) is the number of bytes the worker moves across the network and \(\Operations\) is the number of operations it performs locally in the same interval.



Past the fabric balance point, step time grows with communication intensity.
Low communication intensity describes compute-heavy workloads whose accelerators spend most of their time doing math, so scaling is comparatively easy. High communication intensity describes workloads whose network demand approaches the available fabric balance; in that regime, bisection bandwidth can bind and adding more accelerators can slow training rather than speed it up. The boundary is configuration-specific because it depends on both local compute throughput and effective network bandwidth.
Communication and scaling optimizations, from gradient sparsification (sending fewer gradient bytes) to 3D parallelism (partitioning data, tensor, and pipeline dimensions across different fabric tiers), change how much data moves and where it moves. Overlapping a transfer with independent computation can instead reduce exposed waiting time without changing bytes per operation. The ratio describes workload demand; the fabric and execution schedule determine how much of that demand delays progress.

Scale forces distribution: no single machine provides the compute required for the largest models, and no centralized system can collect every data source that global user bases generate. Coordinating computation across physically separated machines connected by finite-bandwidth networks, however, creates constraints that no engineering can eliminate.
The first stressor appears inside data centers, where synchronous training must choose how much consistency to preserve under partitions and failures. The second appears at the edge, where the devices themselves are unreliable, power-limited, and policy-constrained.


The CAP theorem10 establishes that an asynchronous distributed system subject to a network partition cannot guarantee both atomic consistency and availability. Partition tolerance describes the network condition under which that trade-off applies, not a third interchangeable property that a system can simply discard.
10 CAP (Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance) Theorem (Brewer’s Theorem): Brewer formulated the conjecture (Brewer 2000), and Gilbert and Lynch proved that an asynchronous system cannot guarantee both atomic consistency and availability when the network may partition (Gilbert and Lynch 2002). Synchronous and asynchronous training provide a useful analogy for this trade-off, but gradient freshness is not the atomic consistency property in the theorem.
Brewer, Eric A. 2000. “Towards Robust Distributed Systems (Abstract).” Proceedings of the Nineteenth Annual ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing, 7. https://doi.org/10.1145/343477.343502.

Gilbert, Seth, and Nancy Lynch. 2002. “Brewer’s Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services.” ACM SIGACT News 33 (2): 51–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/564585.564601.
Training is not a replicated database, and gradient freshness is not the theorem’s atomic consistency, yet training faces the same forced choice when a worker becomes unreachable, whether to wait for it or proceed without it. Synchronous training favors a shared current model state but can halt when a required worker becomes unreachable. Asynchronous training can continue through stragglers or unavailable workers but may use stale model versions. Federated learning similarly accepts temporarily divergent local models so that intermittent edge devices can participate without continuous connectivity.



The coordination challenges discussed so far assume data-center distribution, where machines run in managed facilities. At the network edge, these challenges intensify along every dimension.
Billions of smartphones and IoT devices operate in uncontrolled environments with unreliable connectivity and limited power. Privacy, consent, or policy constraints may prevent raw data from leaving the device, making federated learning a natural architecture (McMahan et al. 2017). Intermittent connectivity requires a participation policy, which may select currently available devices for a round or admit delayed updates under stated rules. Keeping raw data local does not by itself protect information exposed through model updates. Device budgets and the threat model determine whether additional compression, privacy mechanisms, or local execution are appropriate.

McMahan, Brendan, Eider Moore, Daniel Ramage, Seth Hampson, and Blaise Agüera y Arcas. 2017. “Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data.” International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 54: 1273–82.




Scale and distribution amplify impact beyond engineering. When a system serves billions of users, a technical bug becomes a societal risk. This amplification increases the reach of governance failures; smaller deployments still require controls appropriate to their uses and potential harms. Governance functions as the control plane of the machine learning fleet, not as a set of external rules.
That control plane first has to defend the fleet. ML systems face unique security threats that intensify at production scale. Model extraction attacks steal proprietary intellectual property through API queries. Data poisoning manipulates training data to alter learned behavior; one objective is a backdoor that activates on a chosen input. At fleet scale, these threats become economically attractive targets for sophisticated attackers. Defending the fleet requires systematic approaches: access controls, differential privacy (calibrated noise that bounds how much any single training record can influence what the model reveals), and continuous behavioral monitoring that go far beyond traditional perimeter security.


↪ Defenses against data poisoning, model extraction, and gradient inversion across distributed fabrics are developed in Security & Privacy.
The same control plane must make the fleet auditable. Systems operating at scale attract regulatory attention. Regimes such as the EU AI Act and local privacy laws make auditability, the ability to reconstruct after the fact which data, code, and decisions produced a model’s behavior, an architectural requirement for many deployments. Auditing whether a model trained on 10,000 GPUs ingested prohibited data requires end-to-end data lineage tracking, supported by controls that capture ingestion and subsequent transformations. A lineage record cannot establish the absence of inputs that were never recorded. Generating a human-interpretable explanation for a recommendation served within a tail-latency budget of tens of milliseconds demands techniques designed into the serving architecture. Meeting these requirements calls for technical capabilities (audit trails, bias testing, and consent management) built into the infrastructure from day one.
Beyond legal compliance, the machine learning fleet carries ethical obligations. Recommendation algorithms shape public discourse; hiring algorithms affect livelihoods. These systems rarely fail loudly; harm accumulates silently through bias and polarization, without a crash log. Responsible AI turns fairness, transparency, and accountability requirements into operational invariants with defined evidence, owners, and responses. A violation may require withholding a release, routing affected decisions to review, or suspending an unsafe operation; the response must contain the relevant harm. Together, these physical, logical, and societal constraints define the operating envelope of the fleet. Turning them into actionable systems decisions requires a diagnostic taxonomy that can isolate whether execution time is lost to local arithmetic, wire transit, or orchestration overhead.

An idle accelerator does not identify its own bottleneck. It may be waiting for local operands, a gradient transfer, or a failed peer. The C\(^3\) lens introduced at the scale moment separates these explanations and gives the preceding examples a common diagnostic language. On a single machine, diagnosing performance follows the Data · Algorithm · Machine (D·A·M) taxonomy. In that framework, Data governs what information the model learns from; the Algorithm defines the mathematical operations to execute; and the Machine supplies the silicon and memory hierarchy executing those operations.


↪ The D·A·M taxonomy as a complete single-node framework, with its diagnostic summary, roofline bound, and scorecard, is developed in The D·A·M Taxonomy.
When workloads stretch across thousands of interconnected nodes, the execution bottleneck shifts. Data-center hardware is procured and cabled around three physical pillars: Compute, Network, and Storage. At runtime, however, distributed execution spends wall-clock time in three distinct operational dimensions: Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)), Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)), and Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)). Together, they form the C\(^3\) taxonomy.
Storage is not absent from this runtime model; rather, storage serves as the persistent physical substrate spanning all three dimensions. It acts as an extension of the node memory hierarchy in Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)), a high-throughput streaming pipeline across Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)), and the durable checkpointing engine required for fault-tolerant Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)).
Each dimension leaves different evidence. Suppose a training job’s step time grows by half after its cluster doubles. If time inside each node’s kernels grew while their model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the fraction of peak arithmetic throughput spent on the model’s own operations, fell and memory-bandwidth counters saturated, local execution is responsible; if link utilization and collective timing rose, transfers are; if barrier waiting and recovery records grew, coordination is. The three diagnoses call for different interventions, and optimizing the wrong mechanism leaves the end-to-end bottleneck in place.
As in single-machine systems, the governing limit is the binding constraint: the bottleneck whose relaxation yields an end-to-end reduction in training time or serving latency. The C\(^3\) taxonomy is therefore an operational diagnostic loop: identify the binding axis, apply the appropriate systems intervention, and remeasure, because relaxing one limit frequently shifts the bottleneck to another.

Definition 1.2: The C³ taxonomy
C\(^3\) taxonomy is a diagnostic framework that classifies distributed machine learning execution time and system bottlenecks along three operational dimensions: Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\), the math), Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\), the wire), and Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\), the logic). The goal is to identify which dimension binds fleet-scale performance.

Significance: The diagnostic power is concrete even before inspecting complex distributed traces. If accelerators are computing at low MFU because tensor cores starve for local operands or un-fused kernels, the binding axis is Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)). If accelerators sit idle waiting for AllReduce gradient transfers or activation tensors across the network fabric, the binding axis is Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)). If progress halts due to straggler-induced barrier waiting, node recovery rollbacks, or gang scheduling preemptions, the binding axis is Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)).
Distinction: Unlike data center procurement categories (Compute, Network, Storage), which classify physical hardware assets, the C\(^3\) taxonomy classifies runtime execution cost. Storage does not execute model arithmetic; rather, it serves as the persistent physical substrate across all three dimensions (local NVMe in \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\), remote dataset streaming in \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\), and durable checkpointing in \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)).
Common pitfall: Treating the three dimensions as independent variables. Upgrading to faster accelerators (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)) often converts a compute-bound job into a communication-bound job (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)). Sharding model states to eliminate memory redundancy (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)) increases collective communication volume (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)) and state coordination complexity (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)). The dimensions move together.



The three dimensions specify what to measure before selecting an intervention. Their descriptions below locate familiar local costs alongside the new costs of distribution.




Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\), the math) captures execution within the server node, including arithmetic units, memory, and local Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) storage.
The memory wall binds this axis when operands cannot reach arithmetic units fast enough. Improving MFU then requires reducing local data movement, for example through operator fusion, rather than merely increasing peak arithmetic throughput.


↪ The memory wall, from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth to the roofline model that locates it for one accelerator, is developed in The Memory Wall.



Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\), the wire) captures data movement between worker devices, both within and across nodes. It includes scale-up fabrics inside a server and scale-out networks between servers.
This traffic includes gradients, activations, and dataset shards. Finite bisection bandwidth can expose a communication tax (\(\CommunicationTime\)) that leaves accelerators waiting for remote data. Reducing bytes transferred or overlapping transfers with useful work can reduce that tax.



Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\), the logic) captures the orchestration software (schedulers, synchronization protocols, and state-management mechanisms) that binds thousands of separate, failing machines into a coherent distributed computer.
Thread synchronization and kernel launches already impose local coordination costs; distribution adds network and failure boundaries. Schedulers, barriers, and checkpointing must manage reliability collapse (equation 1) and straggler amplification, where a synchronous job waits for its slowest required participant. The objective is goodput, the rate of useful training progress after wasted and repeated work are accounted for. Overlap where dependencies permit and bounded recovery rollback improve that rate.



One straggler holds every synchronous peer.




The single-machine D·A·M taxonomy and the fleet-scale C\(^3\) taxonomy operate in tandem. D·A·M describes the workload: the nouns of the system (the training data, the executed algorithm, the hardware substrate). The C\(^3\) taxonomy describes the execution tax: the verbs of the fleet (computing the math, communicating the results, coordinating the state). The C\(^3\) taxonomy projects that workload onto a distributed fleet.
Stretching an algorithm across nodes creates communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)), such as the activation and gradient exchanges that tensor and pipeline parallelism add between partitions of one model. Stretching data across nodes also moves shards and gradients over the fabric (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)), as when AllReduce synchronizes data-parallel replicas, and it requires coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) through distributed samplers, gradient-aggregation barriers, and non-blocking checkpointing. Finally, managing hardware faults across a warehouse-scale machine requires orchestration and dynamic node recovery (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)). Fleet-scale ML systems engineering requires solving the cross-products of D·A·M and C\(^3\) rather than addressing each dimension in isolation.



The dimensions interact at their pairwise intersections, where an intervention along one axis alters costs across another. At the intersection of compute and communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)), overlapping transfers with arithmetic can hide network latency, but only while independent computation remains available. Between compute and coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)), checkpointing preserves progress against failure to maximize fleet goodput, yet it consumes execution resources; its frequency and placement trade present overhead against future recovery loss. Across communication and coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)), collective synchronization depends jointly on transfer completion and participant readiness, so faster physical links alone cannot eliminate straggler waiting.
At the center (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)), all three constraints converge simultaneously. Partitioning a model determines both which device computes each operation and what information must cross the network; recovering a failed partition requires restoring the corresponding shared state. These dependencies explain why parallelism, state sharding, and serving policies must be designed together.
Each dimension contributes one term to the distributed step time, and each pairwise overlap names an interface where the dimensions trade costs: hiding latency, preserving goodput, and synchronizing collectives (figure 12).






Figure 12: The C\(^3\) Intersection Landscape: Each circle is one operational dimension (Compute, \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\), the node substrate; Communication, \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\), the network backbone; Coordination, \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\), the orchestration layer), labeled with the Fleet Law term it contributes to step time. Each pairwise lens names the interaction between two dimensions: hiding network latency behind computation, maximizing fleet goodput against failure, and synchronizing collectives. At the center, where all three meet, is fleet ML systems engineering. C^3 Intersection Reference lists the techniques and chapters for each region.



The diagram organizes competing explanations for the same observed delay. A diagnosis may begin with one dimension or with a coupled mechanism, such as checkpoint traffic delaying a collective. The evidence determines which interaction to investigate; the diagram does not prescribe an order in which the dimensions must be optimized.
Surrounding these three operational dimensions are the non-negotiable operating invariants developed across Part IV: the thermodynamic energy and cooling limits that constrain data centers, the adversarial security and differential privacy guarantees required of distributed pipelines, the robustness against silent corruption and distribution shift, and the systemic governance, auditing, and safety invariants essential when operating at societal scale. Every chapter ahead uses the C\(^3\) figure the same way, diagnosing which intersection binds before intervening.



The C\(^3\) intersection landscape defines where distributed execution spends time and where trade-offs bite. The Fleet Law turns that diagnostic map into a first estimate of distributed step time. Its terms are a simplified accounting model, so a prediction must state how work is divided and which costs overlap. On a single machine, execution time is governed by the iron law of performance, \(\Time= \DataVolume/\Bandwidth + \Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw) + \Latency\), decomposing into data movement, computation, and overhead. At fleet scale, that single-machine view no longer suffices. Equation 3 establishes the Fleet Law, which decomposes the idealized distributed training step into the terms of the C\(^3\) engine:
\[ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime  \tag{3}\]
The arithmetic idealization used below assumes that local memory can supply operands fast enough to sustain the modeled compute rate. A measured local-execution reference can instead include local memory stalls and dispatch costs in the Compute term, provided those costs divide with the work as assumed. The interpretation of the compute-time fraction follows that convention, measuring local execution time for the measured reference and useful math for the arithmetic idealization. Each term in the Fleet Law maps directly onto a region of the C\(^3\) landscape in figure 12:

\(\frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount}\) is the Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)) term, assuming ideally divisible local arithmetic for a fixed workload distributed across \(\DeviceCount\) devices.
\(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) is the Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)) term, capturing the wire transit time moving gradients, activations, and parameter shards across the network fabric.
\(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) is the Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) term, capturing time consumed by barrier semantics, straggler waiting, cluster scheduling decisions, and failure recovery.
\(\OverlappedTime\) is the Co-Design (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\), \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\), \(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2 \cap \OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) term, representing communication or coordination hidden behind useful compute via techniques such as interleaving forward and backward work across pipeline stages, running transfers on separate execution streams, and writing checkpoints asynchronously.

Doubling the device count shows why the subtraction matters. The local compute term falls to \(\IronLawComputeTime/(2\DeviceCount)\), but communication and barrier synchronization persist, and the shorter compute window leaves less room to hide transfers, so \(\OverlappedTime\) shrinks as well. The step on \(2\DeviceCount\) devices therefore takes well over half as long as the step on \(\DeviceCount\) (figure 13).






Figure 13: Anatomy of a Fleet Law step: Each row is one training step for the same workload, with local computation on the upper lane and communication and synchronization on the lower lane. Read the step length from the bracket, not from any single bar: overlap (gray band) removes only the transfer time that runs beneath compute, so doubling the devices halves \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) yet leaves \(\DistributedStepTime(2\DeviceCount)\) well past the ideal half-length step (dashed line), by the hatched span. Bar lengths are illustrative, not measured.



Weak scaling, load imbalance, memory-capacity changes, and algorithmic changes require modifying these terms rather than treating \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) as invariant. Measurements must also separate transfer from coordination time: a barrier interval that includes an unfinished transfer cannot be charged in full to both terms. Subtract only overlap supported by the execution timeline. Equation 4 rewrites this decomposition as the compute-time fraction. It measures useful arithmetic under the arithmetic idealization and local execution under the measured-reference convention:
\[ \UsefulComputeFraction = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount}{\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)}  \tag{4}\]
This decomposition is a diagnostic instrument. When \(\UsefulComputeFraction\) drops below 0.5, more than half the step lies outside the modeled Compute term; under the arithmetic idealization, that means outside useful local arithmetic. The C\(^3\) taxonomy identifies where the time goes: if \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) dominates, upgrade interconnects or overlap communication with computation; if \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) dominates, consider asynchronous methods or reduce barrier frequency; if \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) dominates, the modeled local execution sets the step time. The displacement of overhead is a diagnostic heuristic: reducing one overhead can relocate cost among the three dimensions. Asynchronous training removes some coordination barriers but introduces gradient staleness, in which workers apply updates computed from an older copy of the model; pipeline parallelism can reduce some communication exposure but adds bubble time, the intervals in which pipeline stages sit idle waiting for work.
The compute-time fraction describes one configuration. A production team also needs a scalar that says whether extra devices are shortening the training step or merely increasing coordination overhead. The scaling efficiency (\(\ScalingEfficiency\)) of the fleet is the ratio of ideal parallel step time to actual step time: \[ \ScalingEfficiency = \frac{\SingleDeviceRunTime}{\DeviceCount\times \MultiDeviceRunTime} \] where \(\SingleDeviceRunTime\) is the single-device time for the same work and \(\MultiDeviceRunTime = \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)\) is the step time on \(\DeviceCount\) devices.

Systems Perspective 1.1: Amdahl's distributed pitfallThe Fleet Law applies Amdahl’s reasoning (Amdahl 1967) to a strong-scaling experiment: a fixed amount of useful work is divided across more devices while communication and coordination terms are measured for that configuration. A common shortcut reads a measured 20 percent network share as a 5\(\times\) speedup ceiling, but Amdahl’s bound applies only if that 20 percent of the original workload remains irreducibly serial as compute is accelerated. A network share measured at one device count is not automatically invariant; changing the partition, topology, collective algorithm, or overlap can change both its absolute time and its fraction of the step. The Fleet Law therefore diagnoses the scaling limit of a stated workload and configuration rather than asserting a universal network fraction.



Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.
Several efficiency measures have now appeared, and each answers a different question. Percent of peak, and its model-specific form MFU, compares achieved arithmetic throughput with peak throughput over a stated measurement interval; GPT-3’s roughly 20 percent and Megatron-LM’s 52 percent are measures of this kind. GPT-3’s estimate averages over the training run, so it includes idle time within that interval; a measurement restricted to active kernels uses a different denominator. The compute-time fraction asks how much of one step belongs to the modeled local-execution term, and scaling efficiency asks how close \(\DeviceCount\) devices come to an \(\DeviceCount\)-fold speedup over one. Goodput widens the window from one step to the whole run by discounting work lost to failures and repeated after restarts; Meta’s report of more than 90 percent effective training time for Llama 3 is a measure of this last kind. A fleet can score well on one measure and poorly on another, so a claim about fleet efficiency must name the measure and measurement interval it uses.
Google’s ML Productivity Goodput provides a complementary view of fleet efficiency (Wongpanich et al. 2025). Despite the shared name, ML Productivity Goodput is a normalized productivity measure composed of three multiplicative factors, rather than the useful-progress rate defined with the Coordination dimension. Program goodput (\(\ProgramGoodput\)) measures execution efficiency during productive work; runtime goodput (\(\RuntimeGoodput\)) measures productive progress retained from allocated resources after runtime overhead and lost work; and scheduling goodput (\(\SchedulingGoodput\)) measures whether a workload has its required resources available together. These factors cut across C\(^3\) rather than extending the Fleet Law. Communication overlap can improve program goodput, while checkpointing and recovery affect runtime goodput but belong to Coordination in the Fleet Law. Productivity factors locate losses across the execution lifecycle; C\(^3\) identifies the mechanisms responsible for them.

Wongpanich, A., T. Oguntebi, J. Baiocchi Paredes, Y. E. Wang, P. M. Phothilimthana, R. Mitra, Z. Zhou, N. Kumar, and V. J. Reddi. 2025. Machine Learning Fleet Efficiency: Analyzing and Optimizing Large-Scale Google TPU Systems with ML Productivity Goodput.
The Fleet Law, the compute-time fraction, and scaling efficiency together describe the time side of fleet efficiency. They separate modeled local execution from exposed communication and synchronization costs and compare the resulting step time with the single-device baseline. Fleet efficiency also has an energy side, because every exposed transfer and every idle accelerator still draws power.



While the Fleet Law accounts for time, the energy-scale invariant requires a consistent energy-accounting boundary when comparing fleet designs. What the invariant holds fixed is the accounting boundary, not any particular efficiency value. Equation 5 defines fleet energy productivity (\(\FleetEnergyProductivity\)), measured in FLOP/J, within a simplified operational boundary:
\[ \FleetEnergyProductivity = \frac{\UsefulModelFlops}{\DeviceEnergy+ \CoolingEnergy+ \NetworkEnergy}  \tag{5}\]
where \(\UsefulModelFlops\) is useful work in FLOPs. The three energy terms cover compute devices, attributable cooling, and the network fabric, without counting the same consumption twice. Host, storage, and other facility loads must be added explicitly for a complete operational estimate; embodied impacts lie outside this boundary. Comparisons must use the same boundary and useful-work definition. The resulting Pareto frontier balances minimizing \(\DistributedStepTime\) with maximizing \(\FleetEnergyProductivity\).

Napkin Math 1.2: The communication and energy taxProblem: What compute-time fraction and endpoint network-energy cost result in an illustrative GPT-3 synchronization scenario using 100 Gb/s Ethernet versus 200 Gb/s InfiniBand? Assume 1.2 seconds of local computation per worker per iteration, with no communication overlap. This chosen input defines the scenario; it is not a measured GPT-3 training-step time.
Physics: To synchronize 175B parameters (FP16), a Ring AllReduce with many workers transmits approximately 700 GB of data per participating accelerator endpoint per iteration, using the large-worker-count approximation of twice the FP16 gradient size. This is the 16-bit case of the ring traffic described in section 1.2.3, so it is half the ring traffic of FP32 gradients and numerically equal to the FP32 gradient size quoted there.
Analysis: The Fleet Law exposes the communication tax across interconnect choices. Over 200 Gb/s InfiniBand, an optimistic line-rate transfer of that volume takes about 28 seconds, against 1.2 seconds of computation, which yields a compute-time fraction of only 4.1 percent, meaning accelerators compute for 4.1 seconds out of every 100 seconds while the remainder is exposed communication time. Across 100 Gb/s Ethernet, the transfer stretches to about 56 seconds and the compute-time fraction falls further to 2.1 percent, leaving the devices productive for roughly 2.1 seconds out of every 100 seconds.
Energy: The energy wall is the thermodynamic cost of the same synchronization. Charging each transmitted bit once at the InfiniBand fabric energy cost, each endpoint’s gradient synchronization consumes approximately 196 J across the network fabric (at 35 pJ/bit). In a training run of 1,000,000 steps, the endpoint network movement alone accounts for about 196 MJ of energy before multiplying by the number of participating accelerators.
Systems insight: Advertised line rate gives an optimistic transfer estimate that excludes latency, software overhead, and contention. Conversely, omitting overlap exposes all communication, so the summed step time is not a lower bound for an implementation that hides transfers. The compute-time fraction changes with local workload, partitioning, and overlap; the small fraction here diagnoses the chosen scenario, not every large fleet.

Three architectural maps organize this book: the fleet stack locates system responsibility, C\(^3\) and the Fleet Law diagnose execution cost, and the lighthouse archetypes test those costs across representative production workloads. The fleet stack arranges the fleet into eight rows grouped into four ascending bands (figure 14). Capabilities fixed in the lower rows, from facility cooling and RDMA fabrics up through distributed execution, constrain the serving runtimes and governance mechanisms above them.






Figure 14: The Fleet Stack: The organizing framework for this book, eight rows grouped into four bands, one band per part. Each band is labeled with its part number and a short functional name for that part, and each row lists what it holds beside the icon that marks it in the chapter margin stacks; the Reliability & Control row, for example, is where orchestration, scheduling, and recovery live. Capabilities decided in a lower band constrain the choices available in the bands above it. The same stack, shaded to show each chapter’s focus, appears beside the Purpose of every chapter.



The four bands correspond to the book’s four parts: the physical substrate, distribution, deployment, and the responsible fleet. The chapter map at section 1.7 follows that dependency order.
Six engineering practices guide decisions at every band of the stack: instrument first, reserve headroom for recovery and tail latency, expect bottlenecks to migrate, treat failure as steady state, compound small efficiency gains across the fleet, and co-design hardware with algorithms. For example, faster accelerators can expose a network bottleneck; instrumentation identifies that migration, and hardware co-design aligns the fabric with the workload. The practices describe how a fleet engineer works. The principles of distributed ML systems describe what the physics of the fleet makes true, whatever the practice. Each part of this book establishes its share of those principles; Six Principles of Distributed ML Systems gathers them into six, one or two for each part, and pairs each with the practice it demands.


Abstract frameworks become concrete through specific workloads. Three lighthouse archetypes at scale recur where they illuminate a chapter’s central constraint; no chapter must force all three into its argument. Together they sample distinct C\(^3\) regimes by stressing communication, coordination, or compute in different ways.


GPT-4 and Llama-3 are autoregressive transformer architectures that generate text one token at a time. At single-accelerator scale, autoregressive language models are memory-bandwidth probes; at the scale of hundreds of billions of parameters, and in some proprietary systems potentially more, training demands ExaFLOP/s of sustained compute distributed across thousands to tens of thousands of accelerators, while serving requires memory bandwidth sufficient to load billions of weights for every generated token. The fleet challenge is partitioning very large models across accelerator fleets using 3D parallelism (data, tensor, and pipeline) without exposing enough gradient or activation traffic to make the network the binding bottleneck. Archetype A therefore probes the communication dimension of C\(^3\), although its actual dominant term depends on the model, partition, topology, and degree of overlap.
Where a chapter needs a concrete instance, Archetype A is a 175B-parameter dense transformer of the GPT-3 class, chosen because its configuration is published while GPT-4’s is not, trained with mixed precision and the Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) optimizer. Its training state occupies 16 bytes per parameter (BF16 weights and gradients, FP32 master weights, and two FP32 Adam moments), or 2.8 TB; a resumable checkpoint omits the gradients and needs 14 bytes per parameter, or 2.45 TB. The reference cluster is 1,024 H100 GPUs, arranged as 128 nodes of 8 accelerators each. A chapter that studies a larger cluster or a different model says explicitly how it varies this reference.



DLRM is the deep learning recommendation model that Meta published as a reference architecture for personalized content ranking. Unlike LLMs, which are dominated by dense matrix multiplications, recommendation models derive their capacity from massive embedding tables, sparse lookup structures that map billions of user and item features into dense vectors. A single production DLRM-style model may hold 10 TB or more of embedding-table parameters, far exceeding any single accelerator’s memory. The fleet challenge is sharding these embedding tables across hundreds of nodes while processing on the order of 10 million queries per second (QPS) with <100 ms tail latency, all while coordinating all-to-all exchanges between embedding shards and dense layers. There are \(\mathcal{O}(\DeviceCount^2)\) potential communicating pairs, but byte volume and contention depend on the request batch, partitioning, and network topology. In the C\(^3\) taxonomy, Archetype B stresses coordination: sparse feature routing, shard placement, request scheduling, and embedding-update consistency determine whether the all-to-all traffic can be served within tail-latency limits.



MobileNet is a family of efficient convolutional neural networks designed for on-device inference under tight power and memory budgets. In a federated learning setting, MobileNet instances train locally on millions of heterogeneous smartphone-class devices, whose power budgets span roughly 2 W to 10 W (a few watts sustained, with brief bursts toward 10 W), while raw training data remains on the device. Microcontroller-class sensors that run on hundreds of kilobytes of memory and milliwatts of power lie at an extreme below this archetype. The constraint regime is qualitatively different from the data-center archetypes: power budgets are measured in watts rather than megawatts, and privacy or policy constraints can prohibit centralized data aggregation. In the C\(^3\) taxonomy, Archetype C probes the per-device compute envelope: local execution must fit within the device’s power, memory, and thermal limits. That local constraint does not determine the bottleneck of a federated round. Uploading updates can expose communication limits, while selecting available participants and waiting for their results can expose coordination limits. The fleet challenge is coordinating model updates across millions of such compute-constrained, unreliable devices using federated averaging, which periodically averages device updates at a coordinator. Data distributions that are not independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) and intermittent participation affect the resulting learning process; convergence claims must state the assumptions under which they hold.
Read the three archetypes as constraint probes, not as a catalog of model families. The LLM case asks whether dense synchronization can keep thousands of accelerators useful, the DLRM case asks whether sparse feature routing can meet tail-latency budgets, and the federated MobileNet case asks whether local device constraints can be coordinated into a statistically coherent update. This textbook organizes around the fleet stack, progressing from the physical substrate through the logic of distribution to societal governance. The chapter sequence is a dependency map rather than a topic inventory. Silicon, cooling, and network limits constrain training partitioning; partitioned algorithms create fault-tolerance and orchestration obligations; and those mechanisms support production operation. Requirements also flow in the other direction: security, governance, and service targets constrain which lower-layer designs are acceptable. Part I builds the physical cluster substrate, Part II coordinates distributed execution and fault recovery, Part III optimizes deployment and inference at scale, and Part IV enforces governance, security, and sustainability invariants (figure 15).






Figure 15: The chapter roadmap: The chapters in reading order, top to bottom. The introduction frames the book; the four parts then climb the fleet stack of figure 14 from physical infrastructure through distribution and deployment to governance, as the small stack beside each part shows by lighting that part’s band; the conclusion gathers the principles of all four parts.



The infrastructure arc begins with the impediment no algorithm can ignore: no single server has enough memory, power, cooling, or I/O to train the largest models. Compute Infrastructure therefore starts with high-density silicon and facility physics, Network Fabrics turns isolated machines into a cluster-scale gradient bus, and Data Storage completes the substrate by keeping accelerators fed without letting storage become the hidden bottleneck.
The distribution arc begins once the physical fleet exists and the coordination tax becomes unavoidable. Splitting math across machines creates two new problems: replicas must exchange state fast enough to behave like one optimizer, and failures become routine rather than exceptional. Distributed Training develops partitioning strategies for models with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, Collective Communication explains the communication primitives that bind independent nodes into a coherent computer, Fault Tolerance treats recovery speed as more important than individual-node uptime, and Fleet Orchestration manages the multi-tenant cluster where those jobs must be placed, isolated, and rescheduled.
The deployment arc shifts from training a model to serving it economically. Once a model reaches production, the binding question is no longer only time-to-train; it is whether latency, utilization, and lifetime serving cost stay inside the operating envelope. Performance Engineering measures which execution term limits a replica before applying fusion, precision, and compilation, Inference at Scale turns that measured envelope into admission, batching, and routing policy for millions of users, Edge Intelligence moves learning onto phone-class devices whose memory, battery, and thermal budgets decide what adaptation they can afford, and ML Operations at Scale develops the shared controls (registries, release gates, monitoring, and cost ledgers) that govern hundreds of models as one fleet.
The governance arc treats responsibility as an engineering layer rather than an afterword. At global scale, technical bugs become societal hazards: adversaries can poison data or extract weights, open-world inputs can break brittle models, energy use becomes a fleet constraint, and governance failures can turn technical capability into social harm. Security & Privacy, Robust AI, Sustainable AI, and Responsible AI develop those obligations as system properties that must be designed, measured, and operated.

The following fallacies and pitfalls capture architectural mistakes that waste development resources, miss performance targets, or deploy systems critically mismatched to their operating constraints. Each represents a pattern observed repeatedly in the transition from single-machine ML to the machine learning fleet.

Fallacy: Faster accelerators always shorten the training step.
An accelerator upgrade that changes only arithmetic throughput shrinks the \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) term of the Fleet Law while leaving the other costs unchanged. In the no-overlap scenario of notebook 1.2, local computation takes 1.2 seconds per iteration while the exposed Ring AllReduce over 200 Gb/s InfiniBand takes about 28 seconds. Accelerators 2× faster shorten that step by only 2.1 percent. The scenario is deliberately communication-heavy, but the direction of the effect is general: relieving the Compute axis tends to expose Communication or Coordination as the binding cost, the displacement of overhead described with the Fleet Law. A real upgrade may also change memory capacity, transfer rates, or available overlap. An accelerator purchase must therefore be judged against the fleet’s measured step decomposition, not against the datasheet ratio.


Pitfall: Assuming that reliable components make a reliable job.
A per-GPU MTBF of 50,000 hours describes a part that rarely fails. A synchronous job, however, needs all of its parts at once. Notebook 1.1 shows that a job spanning 25,000 GPUs has an MTBF of about 2 hours, or roughly 12 interruptions per day. Component reliability characterizes one part; the reliability gap (section 1.4.1) characterizes the job, whose availability decays exponentially with the number of parts it requires simultaneously. Recovery practices that suit a single machine, such as manual restart and infrequent checkpoints, fail at fleet scale even though no individual part has become less reliable.


Fallacy: Edge deployment efficiency requirements are simply scaled-down versions of cloud requirements.
This “Cloud-Lite” fallacy treats edge systems as resource-constrained cloud systems. Edge devices face qualitatively different constraints. For example, an autonomous vehicle traveling at 120 km/h covers 3.33 m during every 100 ms of processing delay, adding that distance to its reaction distance. While cloud deployments scale to kilowatts, a phone-class device of the kind Archetype C models sustains only a few watts. A cloud-optimized model with 95 percent accuracy and 50 ms latency might be unusable on an edge device where thermal throttling increases latency to 200 ms and drains the battery in under an hour.


Pitfall: Treating a compute budget as a wall-clock performance prediction.
This pitfall, sometimes called the linear scaling fallacy, confuses useful computational work with the time required to execute it. The empirical loss relation \(\ScalingLawLoss(\ScaledResource) = \ScaleCoefficient \ScaledResource^{-\ScalingExponent} + \IrreducibleLoss\) estimates model quality within a validated regime; the Fleet Law separately estimates the time needed to perform that work. A team distributing a fixed training workload might predict a 3× improvement but achieve only 1.8× if coordination and communication overhead consumes 40 percent of the scaled step time. This shortfall does not by itself invalidate a loss scaling law. It shows why a resource plan needs both a model-quality estimate and a measured execution-cost estimate.
