Fleet planning now separates two questions that single-machine practice could merge. Scaling laws answer how much model size, data, and useful computation a quality target requires; the Fleet Law answers how long a fleet takes to execute that work. Single-machine diagnostic skills remain necessary at that scale, but the engineering boundary expands, because a fleet can lose useful progress to network transfers, inconsistent shared state, or failed participants even when its local kernels are efficient. C\(^3\) distinguishes compute, communication, and coordination costs, while the fleet stack locates the decisions that shape them. With these tools, a resource plan can be traced through to execution behavior, subject to the reliability, energy, and governance constraints of the mission.

Key Takeaways: Scale makes a new machine

More devices change the engineering boundary: Distributing work introduces shared network and failure dependencies. Local performance remains necessary, but fleet decisions must also account for synchronization, recovery, power delivery, and governance across that wider boundary.
Communication can consume the speedup: Dividing fixed work across accelerators shortens ideal local compute time while exposing communication and coordination costs. A 175B-parameter model can move hundreds of gigabytes of gradients per step, so scaling gains depend on the workload, fabric, and overlap.
Failure becomes steady state: In the modeled 25,000-GPU job, independent component failures interrupt tightly coupled training every few hours despite long per-GPU lifetimes. Checkpointing, recovery, and observability must therefore be designed into normal operation.
Scaling laws set the demand; the Fleet Law sets the price: Within a validated regime, loss falls as a power law in compute, data, and parameters, so each equal quality gain needs disproportionately more resources, and compute-optimal plans grow parameters and tokens together. Those laws say how much work is worth buying; the Fleet Law says how long the fleet takes to deliver it. Task-level evaluation, not loss alone, establishes whether the predicted gain justifies the resources, and training-compute optimality alone does not establish the lowest lifetime serving cost.
C\(^3\) extends local intuition: The Data, Algorithm, Machine lens describes the workload and substrate; Compute, Communication, and Coordination expose the costs of fleet execution. The Fleet Law connects useful local work to transfer, synchronization, and overlap costs as device count changes.
Impact needs a control plane: Foundation-scale systems amplify security, privacy, fairness, and policy failures across large user populations. Governance is not an appendix to infrastructure; it is the mechanism that decides what the fleet is permitted to optimize and deploy.



The premise of this book is that scale can move the binding constraint outside the node. A local speedup is therefore evidence about one component, not yet evidence that the fleet makes more useful progress. Engineering judgment requires tracing that change through communication, coordination, and the mission’s operating constraints before accepting it as an improvement.

What’s Next: From requirements to siliconThe scaling laws set how much work a frontier model demands, the walls of the scale moment mark where that demand meets physical limits, and the Fleet Law prices each distributed step. Those requirements say what the fleet must sustain, not what hardware can sustain it. Compute Infrastructure turns to that hardware. It begins where the scaling laws leave a growing model, too large for one accelerator’s memory, and climbs from the accelerator through the node and rack to the pod, asking at each scale which physical resource runs out first: memory bandwidth, power and cooling, communication bandwidth, or failure exposure. Those limits form the Facility and Accelerators row at the base of the fleet stack, the substrate on which every later chapter builds.

Synchronous ML training maintains shared state (model weights) updated synchronously across all ranks via an AllReduce barrier every step. Re-executing an iteration on a spare node while other workers continue would violate synchronization invariants, causing model weights to diverge or forcing all workers to stall until the replacement finishes the collective exchange.

In the Fleet Law (\(T_{\text{step}} = T_{\text{compute}}/N + T_{\text{comm}} + T_{\text{sync}} - T_{\text{overlap}}\)), communication (\(T_{\text{comm}} = 1.0\text{ s}\)) represents 50% of the total 2.0 s step time, while \(f_{\text{compute}} = 0.40\) identifies the modeled compute share, not measured accelerator idle time. Investigating fabric limits or feasible overlap with backward-pass compute (\(T_{\text{overlap}}\)) targets the largest measured term; an upgrade still requires evidence that available bandwidth is the limit. Buying faster GPUs would only cut the 0.8 s compute term (e.g. to 0.4 s), reducing total step time to 1.6 s while lowering \(f_{\text{compute}}\) to \(0.4 / 1.6 = 0.25\). The smaller compute fraction does not mean the faster configuration makes less progress. Increasing node count \(N\) typically increases \(T_{\text{comm}}\) and \(T_{\text{sync}}\) rather than reducing them, and asynchronous updates do not eliminate network data transfer.
Learning Objective: Apply the Fleet Law diagnostically to select system optimizations targeting the dominant step-time component.
Order the following steps in the execution of a simplified, non-overlapped synchronous data-parallel training step with an explicit pre-collective barrier from first to last: (1) Execute forward pass matrix math locally, (2) Apply updated weights using optimizer step, (3) Synchronize gradients across all workers via AllReduce, (4) Execute backward pass and compute local parameter gradients, (5) Wait at barrier for all ranks to complete local computation.
Answer: The correct order is: (1) Execute forward pass matrix math locally, (4) Execute backward pass and compute local parameter gradients, (5) Wait at barrier for all ranks to complete local computation, (3) Synchronize gradients across all workers via AllReduce, (2) Apply updated weights using optimizer step. The step begins with local forward arithmetic, followed by backward gradient computation; workers then reach the synchronization barrier where gradients are communicated across all nodes via AllReduce; once collective reduction finishes, each worker updates its local model weights with the optimizer step. Reversing forward and backward passes or attempting to apply weight updates before AllReduce gradient synchronization violates optimization logic.
Learning Objective: Order the operational phases of a synchronous distributed training step from forward execution to optimizer weight update.
Under the Fleet Law decomposition (\(T_{\text{step}}(N) = T_{\text{compute}}/N + T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}}\)), a team training a 175B model on 1,024 GPUs uses a hypothetical single-device compute baseline \(T_{\text{compute}} = 1{,}024\text{ s}\), raw network communication time \(T_{\text{comm}} = 0.8\text{ s}\), barrier synchronization time \(T_{\text{sync}} = 0.2\text{ s}\), and an actual measured step time of \(T_{\text{step}} = 1.6\text{ s}\). What is the value of \(T_{\text{overlap}}\), and what does it signify?

\(T_{\text{overlap}} = 0.4\text{ s}\); it represents the communication time successfully hidden behind concurrent backward-pass compute.
\(T_{\text{overlap}} = 1.0\text{ s}\); it represents the total exposed network stall time.
\(T_{\text{overlap}} = 0.2\text{ s}\); it represents the time spent recovering from straggler delays.
\(T_{\text{overlap}} = 0\text{ s}\); because communication and computation cannot execute concurrently on GPU architectures.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Substituting into the Fleet Law: \(T_{\text{step}} = (T_{\text{compute}} / N) + T_{\text{comm}} + T_{\text{sync}} - T_{\text{overlap}} \implies 1.6\text{ s} = (1{,}024 / 1{,}024) + 0.8 + 0.2 - T_{\text{overlap}} \implies 1.6 = 1.0 + 1.0 - T_{\text{overlap}} \implies 1.6 = 2.0 - T_{\text{overlap}} \implies T_{\text{overlap}} = 0.4\text{ s}\). This term quantifies the 0.4 seconds of gradient communication that ran concurrently with local tensor arithmetic, reducing total exposed step overhead. Conflating overlap with total communication time, confusing it with straggler recovery time, or claiming overlap is impossible on modern GPUs contradicts basic asynchronous CUDA stream execution.
Learning Objective: Calculate communication overlap (\(T_{\text{overlap}}\)) using the Fleet Law and explain its physical significance in distributed step efficiency.
True or False: According to the principle of Displacement of Overhead, switching from synchronous training to asynchronous parameter updates eliminates coordination overhead from the system entirely.
Answer: False. Displacement of overhead is a diagnostic heuristic, not a conservation law. Asynchronous updates can reduce barrier waiting but introduce stale gradients and may require more optimization steps. The net benefit must be measured as useful progress to a target quality; eliminating one wait does not establish that all coordination costs disappear.
Learning Objective: Apply the principle of Displacement of Overhead to explain why relaxing synchronization barriers relocates rather than eliminates system overhead.

An infrastructure team argues that the four bands of the fleet stack (Infrastructure, Distribution, Serving, Governance) can be optimized in complete isolation by independent teams without cross-layer coordination. Why does the chapter reject this architectural view?

The Fleet Stack is a strict constraint-propagation hierarchy where lower layers physically constrain upper layers: facility power and network fabric bisection bandwidth constrain feasible distribution strategies, which constrain serving tail-latency SLOs, which in turn determine whether runtime governance invariants can be enforced.
The Fleet Stack requires all four layers to be compiled into a single monolithic C++ binary that executes directly on GPU bare metal.
The Fleet Stack only applies to single-GPU workstations and breaks down whenever multiple nodes are connected.
The Fleet Stack is an administrative corporate organization chart rather than a technical systems model.

Answer: The correct answer is A. The Fleet Stack is defined as a layered constraint-propagation framework: decisions at the bottom constrain possibilities at the top. Physical infrastructure limits (e.g. 200 Gb/s link limits and facility power budgets) bound which distribution strategies (tensor vs pipeline parallelism) are viable; distribution choices bound serving latency and throughput envelopes; and serving architectures determine how data lineage, access control, and auditability invariants are maintained at runtime. Proposing monolithic binary compilation misrepresents software architecture, claiming it applies only to single nodes contradicts the fleet-scale definition, and viewing it as an administrative org chart misses its technical engineering purpose.
Learning Objective: Analyze how the Fleet Stack acts as a constraint-propagation hierarchy where lower-layer physical decisions bound upper-layer operational capabilities.
During capacity planning for a frontier model, an engineering leadership team doubles the target model parameter count from 100B to 200B while keeping the target calendar training window fixed. Explain how this model-side change cascades into concrete requirements on the training data and on the fleet’s infrastructure.
Answer: If the plan retains the approximate Chinchilla allocation, doubling parameters from 100B to 200B doubles the token target from roughly 2T to 4T. Parameter and optimizer memory also double at fixed precision. Since \(C \approx 6ND\), useful training FLOPs quadruple. Finishing in the same time therefore requires four times the effective aggregate compute throughput, which may require more than four times the devices if utilization falls. Data delivery, placement, and communication must be checked separately; no fixed network multiplier follows from parameter count alone.
Learning Objective: Trace how a change in model size cascades into data and infrastructure requirements under a fixed calendar window.
Which of the following correctly pairs each of the textbook’s three Lighthouse Archetypes with its representative C\(^3\) diagnostic regime and primary fleet challenge?

Archetype A: Coordination (edge battery); Archetype B: Compute (matrix math); Archetype C: Communication (InfiniBand).
Archetype A: Compute (single-thread CPU clock); Archetype B: Communication (local PCIe); Archetype C: Coordination (disk I/O).
Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Communication (dense gradient/activation synchronization across thousands of GPUs); Archetype B (DLRM): Coordination (sharding 10 TB+ embedding tables with \(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) all-to-all routing under <100 ms tail latency); Archetype C (Federated MobileNet): Compute (watt-scale power and memory limits on local edge devices).
All three archetypes share the identical dominant constraint: local GPU HBM capacity.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The archetypes probe communication for dense distributed LLM workloads, coordination for sparse DLRM routing and placement, and compute for MobileNet’s per-device envelope. These are representative regimes rather than permanent bottleneck assignments: partitioning and overlap can change the binding cost, and communication or participation can dominate a federated round. The other choices misidentify these diagnostic roles.
Learning Objective: Classify the three Lighthouse Archetypes by their dominant C\(^3\) constraint and fleet-scale systems challenge.
Order the four bands of the fleet stack from bottom (physical foundation) to top (mission context): (1) Governance, (2) Infrastructure, (3) Distribution, (4) Serving.
Answer: The correct order is: (2) Infrastructure, (3) Distribution, (4) Serving, (1) Governance. Each band contains two rows: Facility and Accelerators plus Fabric and Storage; Distributed Execution plus Reliability & Control; Runtime and Serving plus Operations; Assurance plus Governance and Sustainability. Job orchestration, cluster scheduling, and recovery belong to Reliability & Control within Distribution. Serving handles inference requests and deployment operations. Physical capabilities constrain the choices above them, while service and governance requirements constrain acceptable lower-layer designs.
Learning Objective: Order the four bands of the fleet stack and locate their eight rows, including scheduling and recovery within Distribution.
True or False: Observability across a 10,000-accelerator training fleet can be achieved simply by running single-node GPU profilers on every machine and aggregating their individual kernel execution logs.
Answer: False. Aggregated local kernel logs do not by themselves explain inter-node collective delays, barrier waiting, stragglers, or shared-fabric congestion. Fleet observability requires correlated measurements across those boundaries, with clock alignment accurate enough for the events being compared. The required timing precision depends on the diagnosis; it is not universally sub-microsecond.
Learning Objective: Explain why single-node profiling tools fail to capture emergent distributed bottlenecks across large accelerator fleets.

How are the four Parts of this textbook sequenced, and what architectural principle dictates this ordering from Part I to Part IV?

Part I: The Responsible Fleet -> Part II: Deployment at Scale -> Part III: Distributed ML -> Part IV: The Fleet; starting with high-level societal policies and deriving physical silicon top-down.
Part I: Deployment at Scale -> Part II: The Fleet -> Part III: Distributed ML -> Part IV: The Responsible Fleet; prioritizing user-facing inference before hardware infrastructure.
Part I: Distributed ML -> Part II: The Fleet -> Part III: The Responsible Fleet -> Part IV: Deployment at Scale; grouping software training algorithms before facility physics.
Part I: The Fleet -> Part II: Distributed ML -> Part III: Deployment at Scale -> Part IV: The Responsible Fleet; following the Fleet Stack bottom-up from physical silicon and network fabrics to distribution logic, operational serving, and societal governance.

Answer: The correct answer is D. The textbook progresses bottom-up along the Fleet Stack constraint-propagation hierarchy: Part I (The Fleet) establishes the physical silicon, network fabric, and storage foundation; Part II (Distributed ML) develops the multi-node parallelism, collective communication, and fault-tolerance mechanisms; Part III (Deployment at Scale) tackles operational inference serving, compilation, and edge economics; and Part IV (The Responsible Fleet) addresses security, robustness, environmental sustainability, and ethical governance. Top-down ordering would require analyzing governance policies before understanding the distributed systems being governed, and placing Deployment before Infrastructure breaks physical dependency ordering.
Learning Objective: Order the four Parts of the textbook according to the bottom-up constraint-propagation hierarchy of the Fleet Stack.
Order the four Parts of the book according to their governing Scale Impediment as presented in the textbook’s roadmap, from the physical substrate to the societal control plane: (1) Operational Economics (Deployment at Scale), (2) Physical Limits (The Fleet), (3) Societal Impact (The Responsible Fleet), (4) Coordination Tax (Distributed ML).
Answer: The correct order is: (2) Physical Limits (The Fleet), (4) Coordination Tax (Distributed ML), (1) Operational Economics (Deployment at Scale), (3) Societal Impact (The Responsible Fleet). Part I tackles Physical Limits (accelerator memory, power delivery, and cooling ceilings); Part II tackles the Coordination Tax (communication bottlenecks, barrier synchronization, and routine hardware failures across nodes); Part III tackles Operational Economics (inference latency SLOs, serving throughput, and edge power constraints); and Part IV tackles Societal Impact (data privacy, adversarial robustness, carbon footprint, and algorithmic fairness). Swapping Physical Limits and Coordination Tax or placing Societal Impact at the bottom breaks the textbook’s structural dependency arc.
Learning Objective: Order the governing Scale Impediments across the four Parts of the textbook.
The textbook structures its curriculum bottom-up (silicon -> distribution -> serving -> governance) rather than top-down (governance -> serving -> distribution -> silicon). Explain why this ordering is a pedagogical necessity of the Fleet Stack, using a concrete example of an upper-layer concept that cannot be understood without its underlying layer.
Answer: The ordering establishes the mechanisms needed to reason about later design decisions. For example, deciding whether distributed inference can meet a latency target requires understanding local execution costs and inter-node communication. Likewise, tracing which training data contributed to a model requires understanding distributed data pipelines and checkpoint lineage. The stack makes these dependencies explicit while allowing mission requirements to constrain the lower layers in return.
Learning Objective: Justify the textbook’s bottom-up pedagogical progression using cross-layer technical dependencies.

A fixed-work training step takes 1.2 s of local computation and 28 s of exposed communication, with no overlap or additional synchronization cost. An accelerator upgrade halves only local compute time. What happens to step time, and what does this imply for the purchase decision?

Step time falls from 29.2 s to 28.6 s, about a 2.1% reduction; the upgrade leaves the dominant communication cost unchanged.
Step time falls from 29.2 s to 14.6 s because doubling accelerator throughput halves every distributed cost.
Step time remains exactly 29.2 s because communication-bound steps cannot benefit from any compute improvement.
Step time falls to 0.6 s because faster accelerators eliminate the need to exchange gradients.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Without overlap, the original step is 1.2 + 28 = 29.2 s; after the upgrade it is 0.6 + 28 = 28.6 s. The 0.6 s saving is about 2.1% of the original step. Faster arithmetic helps, but its datasheet improvement does not propagate to the unchanged transfer term. The purchase decision needs the measured fleet decomposition and any additional changes to memory, links, or overlap.
Learning Objective: Calculate the end-to-end effect of a compute-only upgrade and explain why a local throughput gain need not justify a fleet purchase.
True or False: For the same fixed work with no overlap, configuration A takes 1.0 s of compute, 0.8 s of communication, and 0.2 s of coordination per step, while configuration B takes 0.5 s, 0.8 s, and 0.3 s respectively. Since B has a shorter step, it must reach the same target model quality sooner even if its update semantics change.
Answer: False. The supplied execution budgets give 2.0 s per step for A and 1.6 s for B, a 20% reduction for that fixed-work comparison. Reaching a quality target also depends on how many useful updates are required and how much progress survives interruptions. If update semantics change, compare measured learning curves and recovery costs under the same target and evaluation protocol. A shorter step alone does not establish shorter time to quality.
Learning Objective: Separate fixed-work execution speed from evidence that a changed training configuration reaches a quality target sooner.
The ‘Cloud-Lite’ Fallacy treats edge ML systems as simply smaller, resource-constrained versions of cloud servers. Using the chapter’s autonomous vehicle example (a car traveling at 120 km/h with a 100 ms inference delay), explain why edge deployment constraints differ qualitatively rather than merely quantitatively from cloud data centers.
Answer: At 120 km/h, a vehicle moves about 3.33 meters in 100 ms, so processing delay contributes directly to reaction distance. Edge deployment must therefore satisfy the application’s physical deadline as well as device-specific power, thermal, and connectivity limits. Dedicated cloud cooling and elastic capacity cannot simply be assumed on the device. These are workload-specific constraints, not a universal battery lifetime or throttling multiplier for all edge hardware.
Learning Objective: Analyze how physical safety, latency-distance physics, and strict thermal limits create qualitative differences between edge and cloud ML systems.

An engineer summarizes the book by stating: ‘Single-machine engineering taught us to optimize one GPU; fleet-scale engineering is simply applying those exact same single-node kernel optimizations across thousands of GPUs in parallel.’ Which critique best captures why this summary is flawed?

The summary is flawed because single-GPU kernel optimization stops mattering entirely once models are distributed.
The summary is flawed because distributed ML relies entirely on CPU clusters where GPU optimizations do not apply.
The summary is flawed because fleet scale introduces qualitatively new binding constraints (network bisection bandwidth, shared failure dependencies, CAP consistency trade-offs, and governance obligations) that cannot be solved by local kernel optimization alone.
The summary is flawed because distributed training eliminates all communication overhead through automatic hardware compression.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The book establishes that scaling from one machine to a fleet is a qualitative discontinuity: an ML fleet is not merely ‘more servers,’ but a warehouse-scale computer governed by communication dominance, bisection bandwidth limits, routine interruptions in large tightly coupled jobs, and governance requirements. While single-node efficiency remains necessary, it is insufficient when the binding constraints sit in the network fabric, coordination logic, and fault-recovery systems. Claiming kernel optimization stops mattering is too extreme, asserting that fleets use only CPUs is factually false, and claiming distributed training has zero communication contradicts the physics of data movement.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the qualitative discontinuity between single-node optimization and fleet-scale systems engineering.
Why does making one training kernel faster not establish that the fleet makes more useful progress? Give a concrete cross-node constraint that could limit the benefit.
Answer: A local speedup changes only one part of the fleet’s execution cost. If gradient exchange or waiting for a slow worker sets the step time, faster arithmetic may simply increase idle time. For example, shortening a kernel does little for a step dominated by exposed AllReduce transfers; reducing or overlapping those transfers may help instead. Remeasure end-to-end progress while preserving the required quality and operating constraints.
Learning Objective: Explain why a local speedup must be evaluated against communication, coordination, and mission constraints before accepting it as a fleet improvement.
True or False: In a large-scale foundation model fleet, governance requirements such as data lineage tracking, differential privacy, and multi-tenant access control can be treated as post-deployment administrative audits that operate independently of training data pipelines and cluster orchestration.
Answer: False. Governance requirements must be implemented in the running ML system: data pipelines retain lineage and consent records, privacy mechanisms modify data or update processing, and serving infrastructure enforces access controls and monitors abuse. These controls support evidence and risk management; lineage or monitoring alone does not prove that all prohibited data or extraction attacks have been excluded.
Learning Objective: Justify why governance functions as an active runtime control plane rather than an ex-post administrative audit.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why are single-machine engineering principles insufficient for machine learning at fleet scale?
Machine learning at scale has a physics of its own. On one node, performance is often governed by the memory wall: data must reach the accelerator fast enough to keep the math busy. Scaling laws explain why one node stops being enough, because model quality improves predictably but sublinearly with compute, data, and parameters, so each further gain demands a larger fleet. In a distributed cluster, the memory problem stretches across machines. Data must move through network links between racks, and the slowest shared crossing can limit the entire job. Hardware failures also change character. A failure that stops one local training run can stall a whole distributed job when thousands of workers must advance together. This discontinuity explains why mastery of single-machine ML is no longer sufficient. A faster device may finish its local work sooner yet spend the saved time waiting for other machines. Adding devices can increase capacity while creating more shared work to coordinate and more components to recover. Serving introduces another consequence: spare capacity is useful only if requests can reach it within their deadlines. The engineering decision must therefore account for the behavior of the whole fleet. That wider boundary also amplifies societal impact because these systems may serve billions of users. Bias in any model can cause harm, but bias in a widely reused foundation model can propagate across many downstream systems. In C³ terms, the discipline this book builds is the physics of distribution, in which compute, communication, and coordination turn algorithmic choices into questions of physical topology, fault tolerance, security, and governance.

Learning Objectives

Explain how empirical scaling laws drive fleet growth and where breakdown conditions bound compute-optimal allocation
Diagnose fleet-scale distribution risks using reliability gaps, consistency-availability trade-offs, communication intensity, and routine failure rates
Explain how Compute, Communication, and Coordination extend the Data-Algorithm-Machine lens for production fleets
Apply the Fleet Law to separate a training budget’s useful compute from its communication and coordination overhead
Explain how the fleet stack connects infrastructure decisions to deployment and governance constraints

title: 1 Introduction
text:
Machine learning on a single accelerator is governed by local memory hierarchy and arithmetic intensity: the physics of silicon. The boundary of single-machine systems appears when that local machine is no longer the system. As models move from research prototypes to global services, the binding constraints move outward into racks, networks, power delivery, and recovery machinery. That change is not a smooth extrapolation; it is the scale moment.
A synchronous distributed training step gives this change a concrete form. Each worker computes part of the update, exchanges model information with other workers, and waits until the required participants can advance together. These activities give the book its C\(^3\) lens: Compute is local execution, Communication moves data between workers, and Coordination keeps their progress and state consistent, including after failures. The Fleet Law expresses the corresponding time budget. Dividing a fixed workload across more devices can shorten local computation, but the step also pays for communication and coordination, less whatever work can overlap. Faster accelerators help only when the remaining costs allow the saved compute time to shorten the whole step.
This book assumes familiarity with single-machine training, inference, and accelerator memory. Readers who want to refresh that foundation should begin with The D·A·M Taxonomy, which restates it in reference form: the Data · Algorithm · Machine (D·A·M) lens that organizes single-machine diagnosis, the iron law, the roofline and its arithmetic-intensity boundary, the accelerator memory hierarchy, the memory cost of training state per parameter, and the arithmetic of transformer layers. The book’s aim is to develop engineering judgment across infrastructure, distributed execution, deployment, and governance, so that a local improvement can be evaluated against the behavior of the whole fleet. This chapter builds that judgment in the order a fleet engineer meets the problem. It first traces how far training compute and cluster size have grown and what changes when a job leaves one machine. It then turns to the empirical scaling laws that keep driving that growth, the physical, logical, and societal constraints that distribution imposes, and the C\(^3\) taxonomy and Fleet Law that diagnose where a distributed step loses time. It closes with the fleet stack, an eight-row layered map of the fleet that locates each cost in the architecture, and three recurring workloads that test how the dominant cost changes. Parallelism, communication, and recovery techniques appear here only by name. The task in this chapter is to identify the constraint each one must address, and later chapters develop the mechanisms.
The scale moment is the physical and operational transformation that occurs when models encounter three recurring walls: memory, network, and energy. They describe resource limits that the C\(^3\) lens helps diagnose. On one accelerator the memory wall often binds; after distributing a communication-intensive workload across thousands of nodes, the network wall can replace local memory as the primary performance bottleneck. Its hard limits include bisection bandwidth,1 the aggregate bandwidth across the narrowest cut that splits the fleet, and speed-of-light latency. Serving billions of users can then encounter the energy wall, making thermodynamic efficiency a first-order engineering requirement. Crossing those walls also opens a reliability gap, making hardware failure a routine event rather than a rare exception.
1 Bisection bandwidth (from graph theory): The minimum aggregate bandwidth of all links that, if cut, would partition the network into two equal-sized sets of nodes. In distributed ML, this “worst-case” cut bounds any collective whose traffic must cross it, such as a gradient exchange among all workers, and adding workers on either side does not raise that bound.Between 2012 and the mid-2020s, public and third-party estimates place training compute growth from roughly \(10^{18}\) FLOPs for AlexNet to approaching \(10^{25}\) FLOPs for leading large models, seven to eight orders of magnitude. The difference is qualitative, not merely quantitative. A workload that once fit on two GPUs now spans tens of thousands of accelerators. Recent capability leaps have repeatedly come from applying computation at previously impractical scales, and the empirical scaling laws examined in section 1.3 explain why organizations keep paying for each further order of magnitude.
This growth unfolded across a sequence of landmark models. AlexNet trained on two GTX 580 GPUs for approximately 5–6 days (Krizhevsky et al. 2012). BERT required 64 Tensor Processing Unit (TPU)2 chips for 4 days, roughly 6,144 chip hours (Devlin et al. 2019).

Krizhevsky, Alex, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. 2012. “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 25.
2 Tensor processing unit (TPU): Google’s custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) for machine learning, whose matrix units are systolic arrays, grids of multiply-accumulate cells that pass data between neighboring cells (Jouppi et al. 2017). At fleet scale, the inter-chip network matters as much as the array: TPU v4 joins its chips with an optically reconfigurable interconnect, so the topology of the network, not only the speed of each chip, determines how well many accelerators cooperate (Jouppi et al. 2023).
Jouppi, Norman P., Cliff Young, Nishant Patil, David Patterson, Gaurav Agrawal, Raminder Bajwa, Sarah Bates, et al. 2017. “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit.” Proceedings of the 44th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, ISCA ’17, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1145/3079856.3080246.

Jouppi, Norm, George Kurian, Sheng Li, Peter Ma, Rahul Nagarajan, Lifeng Nai, Nishant Patil, et al. 2023. “TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589350.

Devlin, Jacob, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, and Kristina Toutanova. 2019. “BERT: Pre-Training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding.” Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, 4171–86. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/n19-1423.

Chowdhery, Aakanksha, Sharan Narang, Jacob Devlin, Maarten Bosma, Gaurav Mishra, Adam Roberts, Paul Barham, et al. 2022. “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2204.02311.
GPT-3 consumed an estimated 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs during training (Brown et al. 2020). A single A100, a generation newer than the V100 GPUs that trained it, would need about 32 years to perform that work even at its full 312 TFLOP/s peak, which is the plainest answer to why one node is no longer enough. A later carbon accounting instead pairs the budget with 10,000 V100 GPUs sustaining about 24.6 TFLOP/s each (roughly 20 percent of the V100’s peak arithmetic rate) for roughly 15 days of training (Patterson et al. 2021). The gap between that delivered rate and the datasheet peak raises a question this book keeps returning to, namely how much of each accelerator a fleet actually puts to use. PaLM trained on 6,144 TPU v4 chips for roughly 60 days, consuming approximately \(10^{24}\) FLOPs (Chowdhery et al. 2022). OpenAI’s GPT-4 report did not disclose model size, training hardware, or training compute, so the GPT-4-class scenario in this section should be read as illustrative rather than a published configuration (OpenAI et al. 2023). These examples sit within the rapid training-compute growth trend documented by earlier compute-trend studies (Amodei and Hernandez 2018; Sevilla et al. 2022). Collected in table 1, they show training budgets moving from single-machine experiments into distributed systems where hardware count, wall-clock time, and operational coordination are part of the model design.

Plotted run by run from AlexNet to Llama 3 405B, the climb is steady on a logarithmic scale, and it separates early single-node vision models from multi-node transformer training (figure 1).














Figure 1: Training compute trends (2012–2024): The exponential growth of training compute for landmark ML models. The training compute (measured in FLOPs) has grown by roughly seven to eight orders of magnitude, highlighting the shift from single-node experimentation to massive-scale distributed fleets.



The language-model points pull away from the vision points because compute demands escalated sharply as transformer architectures replaced convolutional pipelines. Raw arithmetic volume is only one dimension of scale, however. The number of accelerators allocated to a single run has roughly doubled every year over the same period (figure 2), a rate that quickly outpaced what any single node could host.














Figure 2: The cluster size explosion: Number of accelerators used to train landmark models, 2012–2024. Verified counts from published papers are shown as filled circles; the GPT-3 estimate (hollow marker) reflects approximate cluster size from Microsoft infrastructure announcements rather than a precise published count. The dashed trend line indicates approximately 2\(\times\) annual growth in cluster size, a rate that outpaces Moore’s Law and motivates the infrastructure challenges developed throughout the book.



Across the four-order-of-magnitude climb charted in figure 2, accelerator counts rise from two GPUs for AlexNet to 16,384 H100 GPUs for Llama 3 along an annual doubling trajectory (\(\sim 2\times\) per year). The one estimated point is GPT-3’s, placed at the size of the Microsoft supercomputer built for OpenAI in 2020, more than 10,000 GPUs (Langston 2020). This empirical trajectory is the foundation of the scale moment, because leading models have required far larger accelerator fleets than earlier deep-learning landmarks. The curve alone, however, does not explain which constraint breaks first. Large language-model training, recommendation serving, and federated mobile learning all encounter fleet scale, but each stresses a different part of the system.

Langston, Jennifer. 2020. Microsoft Announces New Supercomputer, Lays Out Vision for Future AI Work. Microsoft Source.

Lighthouse 1.1: Lighthouse archetypes at scale
Lighthouse archetypes are the canonical workloads that keep the scale moment concrete throughout this book. At this point, their role is to show that “more machines” is not one engineering problem: the dominant constraint depends on what must cross the fleet boundary. The full roster with the C\(^3\) taxonomy mapping and binding-constraint analysis appears at section 1.6.1.

Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Very large language models move from memory bounds on one device to multi-node model parallelism, which splits one model across devices, either within each layer (tensor parallelism) or by assigning consecutive groups of layers to different devices as pipeline stages (pipeline parallelism), so communication can become the bottleneck for communication-intensive partitions.
Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): Deep learning recommendation model (DLRM) workloads move from fitting embedding tables in local memory to embedding sharding across hundreds of nodes, so coordinating sparse feature routing, shard placement, and request scheduling can become the bottleneck.
Archetype C (Federated MobileNet): Mobile inference and on-device adaptation move from one smartphone-class device to federated learning across millions of devices, so local work must respect per-device compute and power budgets, while communication and participation can limit the federated round.



These archetypes turn the growth curve into an engineering question. The same increase in accelerator count can produce a network wall, a sparse-routing coordination bottleneck, or a per-device compute ceiling. The fleet stack, the layered map of the fleet developed at the end of this chapter, locates those constraints in the architecture, while C\(^3\) identifies the execution cost they impose. That diversity of constraint regimes, which federated learning extends beyond the data center, has made systems engineering central to ML at scale. A sophisticated algorithm that cannot scale often provides less practical value than a simpler algorithm deployed efficiently across scalable infrastructure.


↪ Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism, and the traffic each places on the fabric, are developed in Distributed Training.

↪ Federated rounds across millions of devices, where dropouts, stragglers, and per-device budgets bind, are developed in Federated Learning Systems at Scale.

Moving from one machine to many changes the governing physics of the system, not merely its device count. A single node is bound locally by the memory wall between its accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and it has no peers to wait for. A fleet executes across a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places and recovers the job, which exposes the workload to the network wall, to stragglers, and to routine node failures (figure 3).






Figure 3: The scale discontinuity: On a single machine (left), the usual binding constraint is the memory wall between the accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and there are no peers to wait for. In a fleet (right), nodes exchange state over a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places the job and recovers it, so the three C\(^3\) roles appear as separate components. The fabric can become the binding network wall, and failed and slow nodes become routine events that hold back the whole job.



At fleet scale, the binding constraint may shift from local silicon to the network fabric, while resilience joins optimization as a primary concern. The unit of compute is no longer a single server but a machine learning fleet, an interconnected distributed system designed to act as a coherent engine.

Definition 1.1: Machine learning fleet
Machine learning fleet is a distributed collection of compute devices, storage, and networks managed together to train or serve machine learning models.

Significance: In tightly coupled synchronous training, the total time \(\Time\) can be governed by the slowest worker (straggler). Sustaining that workload requires balancing bisection bandwidth (\(\BisectionBandwidth\)) against aggregate compute capacity (\(\PeakRate\)). Serving fleets and heterogeneous edge fleets impose different communication and coordination requirements.
Distinction: The fleet is the unit of engineering, but its workers need not all advance together. Synchronous tight coupling makes a training job depend on a shared step barrier; serving replicas can process separate requests, and federated devices can participate intermittently. The workload determines the required coupling and recovery behavior.
Common pitfall: Treating an ML fleet as “just more servers” overlooks shared network, placement, and recovery constraints. A tightly coupled data-center fleet behaves as one machine, the warehouse-scale computer of section 1.2.2; an edge fleet extends the engineering boundary to devices outside that managed facility.



For a tightly coupled job, the network wall of the scale moment is set by the fleet’s bisection bandwidth, which limits how fast data can cross the network midpoint; adding workers does not raise it. That bound is the bisection bandwidth wall, and at fleet scale it often determines model throughput more than compute does.
At the scale of thousands of GPUs, failure modes appear that a single GPU never exhibits. A network partition can leave a synchronous job hung at a collective (an operation, such as a gradient exchange, that every worker must join) until a timeout aborts it, and in loosely synchronized designs it can let groups of workers drift apart. Stragglers (workers that process data slower than peers due to hardware variation or thermal throttling) can bottleneck entire training runs. Even infrequent component failures accumulate across a large fleet, so long training jobs must expect interruptions.3 Systems must preserve recoverable state frequently enough to bound the work lost at each interruption.
3 Hardware failure rates at scale: Notebook 1.1 uses an assumed per-GPU mean time between failures and independent failures to illustrate how interruption frequency grows with fleet size. Production job interruptions include software, networking, and maintenance as well as accelerator faults. Meta’s Llama 3 report provides an observed example of this broader interruption category (Dubey et al. 2024); it does not establish a universal annual GPU failure rate.
Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.


A 25,000-GPU job fails 25,000 times as often as one GPU.

Patel, Dylan, and Gerald Wong. 2023. GPT-4 Architecture, Infrastructure, Training Dataset, Costs, Vision, MoE. SemiAnalysis Blog.

OpenAI, Josh Achiam, Steven Adler, Sandhini Agarwal, Lama Ahmad, Ilge Akkaya, Florencia Leoni Aleman, et al. 2023. “GPT-4 Technical Report.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2303.08774, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2303.08774.

The interruption cadence follows from simple arithmetic. Consider a GPT-4-class training scenario using a hypothetical A100-class cluster of 25,000 GPUs running for 100 days. These values follow a third-party estimate (Patel and Wong 2023) rather than an OpenAI disclosure (OpenAI et al. 2023). In a cluster of this size, the probability of at least one failure over an interval \(\TimeInstant\) becomes a binding constraint. With independent, exponentially distributed failures and system mean time between failures (MTBF) \(\SystemMtbf\), that probability is \(\Pr(\text{failure before } \TimeInstant) = 1 - e^{-\TimeInstant/\SystemMtbf}\). The worked example in notebook 1.1 establishes the arithmetic for one cluster, and that arithmetic, the MTBF cascade, predicts the interruption cadence for any fleet size.


↪ The MTBF cascade, which sums component failure rates into node and cluster MTBF for multi-thousand-GPU fleets, is developed in The MTBF cascade.

Napkin Math 1.1: Scale and reliabilityProblem: A training run for a GPT-4-class model uses 25,000 GPUs. If each individual GPU has an MTBF of 50,000 hours (the modeling assumption used in this example, not a measured fleet-wide failure rate), how often will the training job be interrupted by hardware failure?
Math:

System MTBF: The system MTBF is the component MTBF divided by the number of independent GPUs. With this scenario’s values, 50,000 hours divided by 25,000 GPUs is about 2 hours.
Daily failure rate: 24 hours divided by 2 hours is about 12 failures per day.
Failures over the run: 100 days at about 12 failures per day is about 1,200 interruptions before the run completes.
Uninterrupted stretches: with \(\Pr(\text{no failure in } \TimeInstant) = e^{-\TimeInstant/\SystemMtbf}\), a stretch of 1 hour completes without failure with probability of about 61 percent, and a stretch of 4 hours only about 14 percent of the time.

Systems insight: In this regime, component failures recur throughout a long run, and a job that saved its state only every few hours would usually be interrupted before reaching the next save. Manual restart does not scale; the system must be architected for fault tolerance from the outset. Hardware can no longer be treated as an infallible abstraction, so automated state preservation and recovery become operational requirements.


Meta’s published Llama 3 training run illustrates the operational consequence in a real large-scale system, where interruptions have several causes.

War Story 1.1: The training run that failed every few hours (2024)Context: Meta reports training Llama 3 405B on 16,384 H100 GPUs during a 54-day snapshot of pretraining (Dubey et al. 2024).
Mechanism: The cluster experienced 419 unexpected interruptions during that snapshot. GPU faults and memory errors were major contributors; the report also records software, network, and host issues. These job interruptions are not equivalent to permanent GPU failures.
Impact: Meta nevertheless reported more than 90 percent effective training time, measured as useful training time divided by elapsed time. Significant manual intervention was required only three times.
Fix: Meta reduced job startup and checkpointing time and developed automated diagnosis and recovery tools. Communication traces helped locate stalled collectives and slow workers before restarting useful work.
Systems lesson: The scale moment turns reliability from a hardware specification into a distributed-systems design requirement. A fleet-scale model is trained by the recovery machinery as much as by the optimizer.


4 InfiniBand: A data-center interconnect whose defining feature for ML is remote direct memory access (RDMA), which bypasses the OS kernel to move data directly between application memory on different machines at microsecond-scale latency. HDR InfiniBand provides about 25 GB/s line-rate bandwidth per link and NDR about 50 GB/s; that per-link bandwidth, relative to the computation each worker performs between exchanges, decides whether large-model training is compute-bound or communication-bound. RDMA-capable Ethernet (RoCE) now offers comparable line rates.
AI, Meta. 2022. Building the Most Powerful AI Supercomputer: Meta’s AI Research SuperCluster. Meta AI Blog.

Zu, Y., A. Ghaffarkhah, H.-V. Dang, B. Towles, S. Hand, S. Huda, A. Bello, et al. 2024. “Resiliency at Scale: Managing Google’s TPUv4 Machine Learning Supercomputer.” 21st USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 24), 761–74.

Microsoft. 2025. Inside the World’s Most Powerful AI Datacenter. The Official Microsoft Blog.
Organizations answered these challenges with purpose-built fleets whose defining component is the network as much as the accelerator. Meta’s Research SuperCluster, announced in 2022, was designed to reach 16,000 NVIDIA A100 GPUs connected by 200 Gb/s InfiniBand4 links (AI 2022), and Google’s TPU v4 pods join 4,096 chips delivering 1.1 EFLOP/s of aggregate peak compute (Zu et al. 2024). Later Azure AI data center announcements describe training fabrics of tens of thousands of GPUs (Microsoft 2025). Each accelerator’s share of that aggregate compute must exchange its results through links of a few hundred gigabits per second.
The scale moment establishes why exponential growth in compute demand forces some ML systems beyond any single machine, making the network fabric a potential bottleneck and component failure routine over long runs. The next question is how to organize the engineering response. Established distributed-systems techniques remain essential, but global barriers and large shared model state change their costs and determine which recovery and consistency mechanisms apply. Tracing how the layers of one machine map onto a fleet, starting with how sharply the links between servers fall below the bandwidth inside one, makes those dependencies explicit.

Self-Check: Question

A team scales a well-tuned training run from 8 accelerators to 25,000. Per-device arithmetic throughput stays constant, yet end-to-end wall-clock time per step roughly doubles, and the job now experiences hardware-induced interruptions every few hours. Applying the Scale Moment analysis, which explanation is most consistent with the evidence?

The arithmetic units on each accelerator are the bottleneck, so the team should enable lower precision to double local matrix throughput.
Distribution has exposed additional fleet costs and routine component failures; communication, straggler waiting, and recovery are candidate causes of the longer steps, requiring correlated measurements.
The kernel compiler is failing to fuse operations at fleet scale, increasing redundant high-bandwidth memory traffic on each device.
The input data loader has become single-threaded, starving all 25,000 GPUs uniformly.

Meta reported 419 unexpected interruptions during a 54-day snapshot of Llama 3 training on 16,384 H100 GPUs, averaging one interruption about every three hours. Explain why this cadence motivates automated recovery rather than manual restart after every interruption.
True or False: If individual data center accelerators achieve a 99.9% annual uptime reliability, a synchronous training job requiring 10,000 such accelerators simultaneously will experience hardware failures only a few times per year.
A frontier model training run utilizes 25,000 independent GPUs, where each GPU has a modeled mean time between failures (MTBF) of 50,000 hours. Under an exponential independent failure model, what is the expected system MTBF, and approximately how many job interruptions will occur per 24-hour day?

System MTBF is 2.0 hours, resulting in approximately 12 interruptions per day.
System MTBF is 50 hours, resulting in approximately 0.48 interruptions per day.
System MTBF is 50,000 hours, resulting in approximately 0.00048 interruptions per day.
System MTBF is 24 hours, resulting in exactly 1 interruption per day.

Order the following landmark training milestones by the number of accelerators utilized during training, from smallest to largest: (1) PaLM (6,144 TPUs), (2) AlexNet (2 GPUs), (3) Llama 3 (16,384 GPUs), (4) BERT-Large (64 TPUs), (5) Megatron-LM (512 GPUs).

title: 1 Introduction
text:
Inside one H100 server, NVLink moves tensors between accelerators at 450 GB/s in each direction per accelerator. Once a training job spans racks, the same tensors leave through an InfiniBand NDR port at 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) in each direction, a bandwidth step down of roughly 9× for an accelerator served by one such port. That step illustrates a general pattern. The layered structure of an ML system persists across scale, while the physics at each layer changes. The fleet stack names the fleet’s layers by grouping them into four bands, Infrastructure at the bottom, then Distribution, Serving, and Governance at the top, with two rows in each (figure 14). At the bottom, the hardware substrate of one node becomes the Infrastructure band, an RDMA fabric spanning racks, and the binding constraint can shift from the memory wall to the bisection bandwidth wall as network congestion and message-passing latency consume a growing share of step time. One layer up, system software (a single CUDA runtime managing PCIe direct memory access (DMA)) becomes the Distribution band, which holds the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and RDMA libraries that coordinate thousands of processes across the fabric, together with the schedulers that place distributed jobs and the recovery machinery that restarts them. Efficient data movement inside each node remains a prerequisite, because a fleet of underutilized nodes only multiplies the waste.
The upper bands add responsibilities rather than replace the familiar software layers. The ML framework (PyTorch or JAX executing a training loop on one node) remains part of model execution. The Serving band adds request handling and deployment pipelines that manage rolling releases across the fleet. Applications also remain, while the Governance band sets security, robustness, sustainability, and responsible AI requirements for their operation. Section 1.6 returns to the full stack and the eight rows within it as the map that organizes the rest of this book. The stack identifies where a design decision belongs; C\(^3\) identifies how that decision affects execution time.
A map of layers does not by itself explain why the same decision behaves differently once it spans a fleet. Three changes separate a fleet from a larger server: synchronous coupling turns independent tasks into a shared step, the facility itself becomes the computer, and communication can dominate the step. A fourth change, routine failure, was quantified at the scale moment; its availability model returns with the other constraints of scale in section 1.4.1. Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), the large-language-model workload of the book’s canonical roster (section 1.6.1), runs on a reference cluster of NVIDIA H100 accelerators and makes each change concrete where a chapter needs it.


Many distributed systems isolate work into tasks or requests so that one failure need not stop unrelated work. MapReduce (Dean and Ghemawat 2004) partitions an input into tasks and can re-execute failed or slow work, Apache Spark (Zaharia et al. 2016) processes data-parallel tasks with explicit shuffle boundaries, and a web microservice handles requests whose failures can be isolated. Search engines and banking databases use other forms of replication, partitioning, and coordination; they are not uniformly independent or asynchronous. The useful contrast is therefore between failure domains and coupling patterns, not between “traditional” and ML systems.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Sanjay Ghemawat. 2004. “MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters.” Proceedings of the 6th Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI), 137–50.

Zaharia, M., R. S. Xin, P. Wendell, T. Das, M. Armbrust, A. Dave, X. Meng, et al. 2016. “Apache Spark: A Unified Engine for Big Data Processing.” Communications of the ACM 59 (11): 56–65. https://doi.org/10.1145/2934664.

Li, M., D. G. Andersen, J. W. Park, A. J. Smola, A. Ahmed, V. Josifovski, J. Long, E. J. Shekita, and B.-Y. Su. 2014. “Scaling Distributed Machine Learning with the Parameter Server.” Proceedings of the 2014 International Conference on Big Data Science and Computing, 583–98. https://doi.org/10.1145/2640087.2644155.
Large synchronous training jobs operate under synchronous tight coupling. Parameter-server architectures (Li et al. 2014) and collective runtimes manage distributed state, but synchronous optimization updates a large shared model state across thousands of accelerators every few hundred milliseconds rather than completing independent one-shot tasks. At each synchronization point, progress can depend on the slowest participating worker, so a persistent 10 percent slowdown on one worker can approach a 10 percent step-time penalty when that worker lies on the critical path. Communication-heavy partitions can also become bisection-bandwidth bound because large gradient or activation tensors cross the network every step. These properties do not invalidate established recovery techniques; they increase recovery cost and restrict which replication, re-execution, and consistency strategies preserve useful training progress.
The two execution pathways differ at the point of failure (figure 4). In MapReduce, a failed map task is retried on its own while its peers complete. In synchronous data-parallel training, where every worker holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of each batch, every worker must contribute its gradient to an AllReduce, a collective operation that combines the gradients of all workers and returns the result to each of them, before the shared parameter update can occur. A slow map task can delay downstream reduction and job completion, but other map tasks finish without waiting; in synchronous training, by contrast, healthy workers sit idle whenever a straggler delays the collective.






Figure 4: Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps: Map tasks (left) deliver their outputs independently, so a failed task is re-run on its own while the others finish; its missing output delays only the reducers that need it. In synchronous data-parallel training (right), the AllReduce needs every worker’s gradient before the shared update can proceed, so a slow worker on the critical path holds the whole step and the healthy workers wait. How much the step stretches depends on overlap and the other costs of the step.



The collective barrier dependency diagrammed in figure 4 explains why MapReduce-style localized task re-execution cannot be transferred directly to tightly coupled training: when all workers advance a single shared parameter step, recovery must restore mutually consistent model, optimizer, and input state across every participating node before coordinated execution can resume.

Checkpoint 1.1: The fleet mindset
These questions check whether the fleet mindset is clear:

Straggler impact: compare how a slow map task can delay job completion with how a persistent straggler can delay repeated synchronous training steps.
Bisection bottleneck: explain when frequent cross-rack tensor exchanges would make synchronous training more bandwidth-sensitive than a service handling mostly independent requests.
Tight coupling: explain synchronous tight coupling and connect it to the need for all participating contributions before a shared training update completes.
Linear speedup myth: using the barrier argument above, explain why doubling the GPUs in a synchronous training job need not halve its step time.






A tightly coupled data-center fleet demands the warehouse-scale computer (WSC)5 perspective. A machine-centric view treats the data center as a building that houses many computers; the warehouse-scale view treats the data center itself as the computer. In this paradigm, single-node abstractions map directly onto distributed infrastructure: the network fabric functions as the system bus, distributed storage serves as the local disk, and the fleet orchestrator acts as the operating system.
5 Warehouse-scale computer (WSC): Barroso and Hölzle, later with Clidaras, framed the data center itself as the computer. For ML fleets, power delivery, cooling topology, optical network layout, and bisection bandwidth become first-order constraints; a 100 MW facility can limit training throughput more than any single accelerator’s TFLOP/s.For this data-center regime, the engineering boundary extends from local execution to the shared power, network, and recovery systems that sustain the entire facility. The warehouse-scale computer is a common paradigm for large models, while alternative architectures like wafer-scale engines, single processors built from an entire silicon wafer rather than one reticle-sized die, attempt to collapse this entire hierarchy back into a single piece of silicon, trading the modularity of a distributed cluster for the extreme bandwidth of on-chip communication. Both designs answer the same constraint, the cost of moving data between chips, from opposite directions.



Distributing these workloads beyond one machine can make communication the dominant cost, the network wall of the scale moment. On one GPU, a dense training workload may spend most of its time performing matrix multiplications and incur no inter-node communication. Distribution introduces communication whose share depends on the model, partitioning strategy, collective algorithm, topology, precision, and overlap with computation.



Ring AllReduce moves about twice the gradient per step; 16-bit gradients halve it.
At large scale, communication can dominate communication-intensive partitions. Distributed data-parallel training synchronizes gradients across workers after each batch. For a model with 175B parameters, FP32 gradients occupy about 700 GB before any collective algorithm is applied. Ring AllReduce arranges the AllReduce exchange among neighbors in a logical ring; with \(\DeviceCount\) workers, each worker sends roughly \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) times the gradient tensor size and receives the same amount across the reduction and distribution phases (Ring AllReduce derives this factor). For large \(\DeviceCount\) the factor approaches two, so each worker moves about twice the FP32 gradient per step, and half that when mixed-precision training exchanges 16-bit gradients. Network traffic therefore depends on precision, worker count, collective implementation, and partitioning. On slower interconnects or partitions with little computation per communicated byte, it can consume a large fraction of each iteration rather than a negligible one; notebook 1.2 later converts the 16-bit volume into seconds of exposed transfer per step.


↪ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) communication model, with the per-interconnect latency and bandwidth parameters that turn a link’s specifications into a predicted transfer cost, is developed in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth Communication Model.

Sergeev, Alexander, and Mike Del Balso. 2018. “Horovod: Fast and Easy Distributed Deep Learning in TensorFlow.” CoRR abs/1802.05799.

Shoeybi, Mohammad, Mostofa Patwary, Raul Puri, Patrick LeGresley, Jared Casper, and Bryan Catanzaro. 2019. “Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1909.08053.

Rajbhandari, Samyam, Jeff Rasley, Olatunji Ruwase, and Yuxiong He. 2020. “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models.” SC20: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1109/sc41405.2020.00024.
This exposed transfer cost explains why distributed training systems optimize communication so aggressively, and their many mechanisms answer one problem. Distributing work also distributes state that must move or be kept consistent. Horovod, for example, runs Ring AllReduce and fuses many small gradient tensors into fewer large transfers, so that the fixed cost of starting each exchange is paid fewer times (Sergeev and Balso 2018). Splitting each layer across devices, as Megatron-LM does with tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al. 2019), and sharding optimizer state across workers, as ZeRO does (Rajbhandari et al. 2020), trade per-device memory for different traffic patterns; Distributed Training develops both. The design decision at this stage is which cost prevents progress; selecting a particular mechanism requires the workload and fabric models developed later.
Routine failure, the other consequence of distribution, was already quantified at the scale moment. Under that example’s assumptions the job meets a hardware failure every few hours, so checkpointing, replacement capacity, and automated recovery must keep each interruption short; section 1.4.1 develops the availability model behind that cadence. Communication and recovery costs describe how a fleet executes work. Neither explains what drives the relentless growth in fleet size, or how much work a model should receive. Both answers lie in empirical relationships between model quality and resource investment, relationships that have made warehouse-scale infrastructure an economic necessity rather than an engineering luxury.

Self-Check: Question

Which responsibility assignment matches the fleet stack described in this section, while retaining ML frameworks and applications as parts of the system?

Infrastructure handles request admission; Distribution sets fairness policy; Serving supplies network links; Governance runs gradient collectives.
Infrastructure places training jobs; Distribution cools accelerators; Serving defines privacy requirements; Governance answers inference requests.
Infrastructure supplies accelerators and fabrics; Distribution handles collectives, job placement, and recovery; Serving handles requests and deployment; Governance sets security and responsible-operation requirements.
Infrastructure supplies accelerators and fabrics; Distribution handles collectives; Serving owns training-job scheduling and recovery; Governance replaces applications.

Contrast the impact of a 10% performance slowdown (straggler) on a single worker node in a 1,000-worker MapReduce job versus a 1,000-accelerator synchronous ML training job. Explain why the two architectures respond so differently.
True or False: Because MapReduce and synchronous distributed ML both distribute data across thousands of nodes, an ML training cluster can adopt MapReduce’s straggler-mitigation technique of simply re-executing lagging tasks in parallel on spare nodes without pausing other workers.
Under the Warehouse-Scale Computer (WSC) perspective required for the ML fleet, the datacenter is treated as the computer: the orchestrator acts as the operating system, distributed storage acts as the local disk, and the network fabric acts as the ____.
When scaling an autoregressive model from a single GPU to a 10,000-accelerator cluster, an engineer observes that the local CUDA arithmetic kernels execute without modification. Why does distributed execution nonetheless introduce failure modes that never occur on a single machine?

Distributed coupling introduces network partitions that cause state divergence, stragglers that stall global synchronization barriers, and collective communication deadlocks.
