Packaging removes the per-file cost within one node, but no node-local format gives every node the same view of the data. That requirement belongs to the next tier.



Beyond the single node, the workload requires a shared namespace where all workers can access the same datasets and where durable checkpoints are globally visible. This is the role of the parallel file system.

Definition 4.1: Parallel file system
Parallel file system (PFS) is a distributed storage architecture for ML training clusters that stripes data across many storage servers to provide aggregate throughput exceeding the capacity of any single device.

Significance: A PFS aggregates storage I/O bandwidth \((\StorageBandwidth)\) across object storage servers (OSS). Twenty OSS nodes delivering 10 GB/s each offer 200 GB/s aggregate. When the client and network sustain that full rate, a 10 GB striped shard loads in about 50 ms rather than the 1 second a single 10 GB/s server would need. The rate that enters the data-movement term \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\) of the single-machine iron law recalled in The Fleet Law is the bandwidth that reaches the actual consumer, not the aggregate rating.
Distinction: Unlike network-attached storage, where every I/O request routes through a single server, a PFS client receives stripe location metadata from a dedicated metadata server (MDS) and then reads data directly from multiple OSS nodes in parallel: the MDS and OSS paths are architecturally separated, so data bandwidth scales with OSS count while metadata operations scale with MDS count.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a PFS has unlimited throughput if enough OSS nodes are added. In reality, a Lustre MDS handles roughly 100,000–300,000 metadata operations per second; a one-time burst of 10,000 opens does not by itself establish sustained saturation. The MDS becomes a throughput bottleneck when the aggregate metadata-operation arrival rate exceeds its service rate, regardless of spare bandwidth at the OSS nodes.



Figure 2 traces how a Lustre-style parallel file system decouples metadata lookups from bulk data movement, separating two concerns that traditional file systems handle together (Schwan 2003). Metadata servers (MDS) manage the namespace (persisting file layouts and attributes on metadata targets, or MDTs): file creation, directory listings, permission checks, and lock management. Object storage servers (OSS)6 manage the actual data blocks, each serving a stripe of every large file. When a client opens a 10 GB training shard, the MDS tells the client which OSS nodes hold which stripes, and the client reads from all of them in parallel. A Lustre7 deployment with 100 OSS nodes, each providing 10 GB/s, delivers an aggregate 1 TB/s.

Schwan, P. 2003. “Lustre: Building a File System for 1,000-Node Clusters.” Proceedings of the 2003 Linux Symposium, 380–86.
6 OSS (Object Storage Server): In parallel file system terminology, “object” means a chunk of striped file data managed by an object storage target, a usage that predates cloud object storage (S3, GCS) by over a decade. Confusing the two is a common source of miscommunication: when a Lustre administrator says “add more OSS nodes,” they mean adding data-serving capacity to the parallel file system, not provisioning cloud buckets.7 Lustre: A portmanteau of “Linux” and “cluster,” developed at Carnegie Mellon University and first deployed in production in 2003. Lustre is common in HPC and ML infrastructure because its architecture scales aggregate bandwidth linearly with the number of OSS nodes, the same property that makes it a natural choice for training clusters where a single job may demand hundreds of GB/s of sustained read throughput.






Figure 2: Parallel file system architecture: A client makes one metadata request (MDS \(\to\) MDT) to learn a file’s stripe map, then reads the stripes directly from the object storage servers (OSS \(\to\) OST) in parallel. Each OST holds every Nth stripe of the file in round-robin order, so consecutive stripes (dark) sit on different servers and one client reads them at once. The shared data path lets every client draw on every OSS, so aggregate bandwidth grows with the number of servers while metadata traffic stays on a separate path.



This abstract architecture has concrete implications for performance tuning. When a training job creates a new dataset directory on Lustre, the administrator configures the stripe count (the number of object storage targets, or OSTs, a file is spread across) and stripe size (the chunk size written to each OST) for that directory (Lustre Wiki 2017). For large sequential-read training shards, administrators may choose wider striping and multi-megabyte stripe sizes so a single file can draw bandwidth from multiple OSS nodes; Lustre’s striping guide treats wide striping as useful for very large files or files accessed by many clients, while smaller files often use fewer stripes to reduce overhead (Lustre Wiki 2019). A 4 GB data shard striped across 100 OSTs with 4 MB stripes places roughly 10 stripes on each OST. When a data loader reads large contiguous ranges, the Lustre client can issue parallel read requests to the OSS nodes holding those stripes, aggregating their bandwidth. The client also maintains its own read-ahead buffer, prefetching the next several stripes while the application processes the current ones. This file-system-level read-ahead is distinct from the data loader’s application-level prefetch buffer; the two layers of prefetching compound to provide deep latency hiding, making the physical distance to the OSS nodes nearly transparent to the training process.

Lustre Wiki. 2017. lfs setstripe: Set Striping Pattern of a File. Lustre Wiki manual page.

Lustre Wiki. 2019. Configuring Lustre File Striping. Lustre Wiki.
8 GPFS (General Parallel File System): Developed by IBM Research starting in 1998, now marketed as IBM Spectrum Scale. Unlike Lustre’s dedicated metadata-server/object-server organization, GPFS is a shared-disk parallel file system that can stripe data and metadata and uses token-based locking to coordinate concurrent client access. For ML checkpoint writes, this distributed coordination model can reduce reliance on a single dedicated metadata path, but it also makes lock behavior part of the performance envelope.The separation between metadata and data paths is what enables the aggregate bandwidth that ML workloads demand. In GPFS8 (IBM Spectrum Scale), the architecture takes a different approach: it stripes data and metadata across shared disks and coordinates concurrent access through token-based distributed locking (Schmuck and Haskin 2002). The result is not a simple MDS/OSS split; it is a shared-disk design whose metadata and data placement can be distributed while the lock protocol preserves consistency across clients. The trade-off is greater complexity in lock management, which must scale to thousands of nodes.
The data path scales with the number of object storage servers, but every file still begins with a request to the metadata service, and that service has a finite operation rate. That finite rate is the source of the small file problem. The per-open cost that section 4.3.5 charged to one node’s CPU now lands on a metadata service shared by the whole fleet. Each open() system call requires a metadata lookup, lock acquisition, and attribute fetch. When a dataset of millions of 10 KB images is stored as individual files and 10,000 workers, a fleet several times the running cluster, each open a new file every few samples, the aggregate open rate exceeds the few hundred thousand operations per second an MDS typically serves. The MDS becomes the serialization point, and delivery collapses to its operation rate long before the data links saturate.

Definition 4.2: Small file problem
Small file problem is an ML data-loading pathology in which per-file operations overwhelm a storage system’s metadata service.

Significance: open, stat, and close requests from 10,000 workers can serialize at the metadata service, idle the cluster, and reduce effective I/O bandwidth \((\StorageBandwidth)\).
Distinction: This is a metadata request-rate and latency \((\Latency)\) problem, not a bulk bit-rate problem.
Common pitfall: Faster SSDs do not fix this format problem. Packing samples into sequential containers such as TFRecord or Parquet amortizes metadata operations across many samples.



At production scale, the metadata bottleneck can collapse an otherwise high-bandwidth file system.

Example 4.1: The metadata meltdownScenario: A large-scale training cluster migrates from a preprocessed sequential dataset to 200 million raw image files stored individually on a parallel file system provisioned for 500 GB/s aggregate bandwidth.
Diagnosis: The file system delivers less than 1 percent of rated throughput. Millions of per-second stat() and open() calls overwhelm the metadata servers, choking data loaders despite abundant network and storage bandwidth.
Systems lesson: Metadata contention limits delivery when operation demand exceeds metadata service capacity. Bundling 200 million raw images into 50,000 large tar shards (for example, WebDataset) reduces the file count by 4,000\(\times\) and amortizes per-file operations across samples. Packaging alone does not prevent startup contention if loaders still enumerate files with per-file stat() calls; distributing a precomputed dataset manifest removes those repeated lookups from the hot path. Measure metadata operation rate alongside byte bandwidth to determine which service limits delivery.


Striping and aggregation solve different problems. Striping distributes large files across data servers; aggregation, the shard packaging of section 4.3.5, reduces the number of files the MDS must track. Realized bandwidth depends on the reader. A read contained within one stripe uses one server, while enough concurrent reads spanning stripes can use several servers. Wider striping helps only when the read sizes and concurrency exploit those paths; small files usually need fewer stripes.
Parallel file systems provide a shared namespace and lock management that support coordinated checkpoints (Schmuck and Haskin 2002). Recovery requires every reader of a committed checkpoint to observe the same completed state. The file system supplies storage primitives, but the training system must coordinate the shards into one restorable generation. A completed write to one file does not establish that all other checkpoint files are complete.

Schmuck, Frank, and Roger Haskin. 2002. “GPFS: A Shared-Disk File System for Large Computing Clusters.” Proceedings of the USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies (FAST ’02), 231–44.
The consistency model has subtleties that matter for ML workloads. For training data reads, immutable shards remove conflicts with concurrent writers once the dataset version has been published. Readers must still agree on which completed version belongs to the run. Checkpoints require more. File-system locks can coordinate individual writes, but they do not by themselves make a checkpoint that spans many files atomic, so a multi-file generation needs an application-level publication protocol, developed in section 4.6.
The performance of a parallel file system depends on the balance of load across OSS nodes as well as their number. If a shard uses 10 of 100 equally provisioned OSS nodes, those servers offer at most 10 percent of the system’s aggregate server bandwidth. Realized delivery can be lower because of client limits, request size, or insufficient concurrency. Conversely, when many concurrent readers draw on shards striped across all 100 servers, demand spreads over every server and realized bandwidth can approach the system’s rating, provided the clients and network keep pace. Placement and access scheduling therefore matter alongside the number of storage servers.
At the scale of thousands of nodes, tail latency (Dean and Barroso 2013a) can dominate exposed input wait. If a training step requires data from 100 storage servers and each independently has a 1 percent chance of being slow, the probability that all 100 respond quickly is \(0.99^{100} = 0.366\), meaning over 63 percent of these request sets contain at least one slow response. Shared congestion can correlate delays, changing that probability. A slow response delays the step only when prefetching fails to hide it and the required input lies on the step’s critical path. When it does, the delay is not confined to one worker, because synchronous data-parallel training waits for every worker at the next collective, so one late fetch stretches the whole fleet’s step.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013a. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80. https://doi.org/10.1145/2408776.2408794.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013b. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80.
Systems can mitigate tail latency through hedged requests: after a chosen delay, the client issues a redundant read to another replica and uses the first valid response. The trigger delay trades faster tail completion against extra work (Dean and Barroso 2013b). An independence model can multiply the probabilities of two slow replicas, but shared congestion and the later start of the hedge invalidate a simple squared-probability latency guarantee. Issuing a hedge at the median response time would duplicate roughly half of requests before accounting for cancellation; that load can worsen the congestion the scheme aims to avoid. A hedge therefore pays off only when its trigger sits in the measured tail and the duplicate traffic it adds stays within the spare service capacity.
The effectiveness of hedged requests depends on the replicated data layout. If both replicas reside on OSS nodes that share the same network switch, a switch failure makes both copies simultaneously unavailable. Effective hedging requires failure-domain-aware placement: replicas should reside in different racks, connected through different top-of-rack switches, so that the failure of any single component affects at most one replica.
In production clusters, the parallel file system is a shared utility, simultaneously servicing dozens of concurrent training jobs with different I/O patterns. At any given moment, a large language model job might be streaming sequentially through text shards, a computer vision job might be reading random image shards, and a checkpoint storm from a third job could be saturating write bandwidth. This concurrency gives rise to the noisy neighbor problem, where one job’s I/O pattern severely degrades performance for all other jobs. A checkpoint save that consumes a disproportionate share of the PFS’s internal network bandwidth causes read latency for other jobs to spike, potentially stalling their training pipelines. PFS administrators mitigate this through I/O scheduling policies (quality-of-service tiers, bandwidth quotas per job), but these policies add administrative complexity and can reduce peak single-job throughput.
A related challenge is namespace isolation. Different teams and workloads require different storage configurations. A team training on millions of 100 KB images first needs to aggregate samples to reduce metadata operations; increasing stripe count does not remove per-file metadata work. A team working with large video shards can use wider striping when read sizes and concurrency exploit the additional data paths. Misconfigured striping for one team’s workload can create hotspots that degrade performance for the entire shared file system. The impact of sharing is easy to quantify: a PFS with 1 TB/s aggregate bandwidth, shared across 10 concurrent training jobs, provides only 100 GB/s per job on average. If one job’s checkpoint storm consumes 400 GB/s for 10 seconds, the remaining nine jobs share 600 GB/s, a 33 percent reduction that can trigger data stalls in their accelerator pipelines.

Checkpoint 4.2: Parallel file system design
Consider a training cluster with 512 nodes, each running 8 GPUs. The training job requires 400 GB/s of aggregate read bandwidth.

OSS count: calculate the number of OSS nodes required when each Lustre OSS delivers 10 GB/s.
Metadata cost: calculate the time required to open 200 million 116 KB image files sequentially when each open() call takes 50 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\)s on the MDS, then state the practical implication.
Shard count: calculate the number of metadata operations needed to read the full dataset when images are bundled into 4 GB tar files.



Parallel file systems solve the shared-namespace problem for active training clusters, but their cost per byte is too high for the organization’s complete data holdings. The petabytes of raw training data, historical checkpoints, and preprocessed datasets that an ML organization accumulates over years require a tier optimized for capacity and durability rather than bandwidth.



At the scale of petabytes, object storage provides the durable, cost-effective foundation of the hierarchy. Services like Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage organize data in object namespaces where objects are retrieved by keys rather than by POSIX directory paths (Amazon Web Services 2026c; Google Cloud 2026). Unlike file systems, which organize data in hierarchical directories with metadata-rich operations (rename, link, permission inheritance), object storage treats each object as an opaque blob identified by a unique key. The simpler interface changes the namespace operations exposed to clients; the service still manages metadata for placement, versions, access control, and integrity as capacity grows.

In storage systems, Reed-Solomon-style codes and later local-reconstruction variants trade storage overhead against repair bandwidth and degraded-read cost (Plank 1997; Huang et al. 2012). Local-reconstruction codes, for example, read fewer surviving fragments to rebuild a lost one, cutting repair traffic at the price of a little extra capacity.

Services such as Amazon S3 publish an “eleven nines”9 annual durability target (99.999999999 percent). Erasure coding,10 replication, placement, and repair contribute to storage protection, but a coding scheme alone does not establish a service’s durability target. Selecting a source-of-truth tier for training data and checkpoint archives requires checking the chosen service’s failure model alongside versioning, lifecycle policy, access control, and recovery testing.
Three different guarantees govern whether that source of truth is usable. Durability asks whether acknowledged data survives failures; availability asks whether the storage service responds when a client needs it; and consistency asks which version a read is allowed to observe when writes overlap or replicas disagree. Replication can improve durability and availability without by itself guaranteeing that a reader sees the newest committed checkpoint. A recovery design must therefore state all three properties instead of treating a durability percentage as a complete reliability contract.

Definition 4.3: Erasure coding
Erasure coding protects stored data by adding redundant fragments, with the Reed-Solomon scheme considered here encoding \(\ErasureDataFragmentCount\) data and \(\ErasureParityFragmentCount\) parity blocks so that any \(\ErasureDataFragmentCount\) remaining fragments recover the original.

Significance: Coding can protect against fragment loss with less capacity overhead than full replication. A 4+2 Reed-Solomon code stores four data fragments and two parity fragments, tolerating two unavailable fragments at 1.5\(\times\) storage overhead instead of the 3\(\times\) overhead of triple replication. Actual durability also depends on failure correlation, placement, detection, and repair.
Distinction: Unlike replication (which stores complete copies), erasure coding uses mathematical encoding (for example, Reed-Solomon) to distribute redundant information across different failure domains (disks, racks, or sites).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that erasure coding is “free durability.” In reality, it is a latency-compute trade-off: reconstructing data after a failure requires additional CPU cycles and increases the p99 latency of the storage read.



Erasure coding lets the service recover data without requiring the training application to manage fragments. In the form considered here, the service retains the original \(\ErasureDataFragmentCount\) data fragments alongside parity, so healthy reads can use the data fragments directly. When a required fragment is unavailable, reconstruction uses surviving data and parity fragments. The object interface hides that recovery procedure, but additional I/O, network traffic, and decoding can remain visible as longer read latency. Protection against data loss does not imply unchanged service time during a failure.
The cost advantage of object storage is significant: at a representative $0.02/GB/month, its recurring capacity rate is 5× lower than the local-NVMe rate assumed here, and section 4.7 converts that ratio into annual costs for a 100 TB dataset. Comparing it with HBM acquisition cost additionally requires a hardware lifetime and utilization assumption. This cost advantage makes object storage a common home for the organization’s training data lake, where raw data, preprocessed datasets, and archived model artifacts can reside durably.
Request latency also matters. Design estimates use 50 to 100 ms for an object GET as a representative planning range rather than a universal service guarantee. Much of that delay is the price of the indirection that provides durability. The service looks up the object’s location in a distributed metadata index, determines which fragments to read, fetches them from potentially different storage nodes, and reconstructs data when a fragment is unavailable, all on top of the client network path and queueing. Large transfers amortize per-request overhead across more bytes, while small transfers can spend most of their elapsed time on that overhead. Request size and concurrency therefore enter the delivery budget alongside aggregate bandwidth.
The remedy is the shard packaging of section 4.3.5, applied here to request latency rather than metadata operations. Formats like WebDataset (Aizman et al. 2019) or Mosaic Streaming (Databricks 2026) bundle samples into multi-gigabyte shards that transform high-latency random access into high-bandwidth sequential streaming. Rather than issuing billions of small GET requests, the data loader issues hundreds of large reads in parallel, each fetching an entire shard that contains thousands of samples. With sufficient parallelism and colocated network capacity, object storage can sustain high aggregate throughput, enough to feed large training clusters for some workloads. The streaming pattern works by assigning each data loader worker a subset of shards and having it read them sequentially. Within each shard, samples are stored contiguously, so the worker decodes them in order and shuffles them in a local buffer. This approach achieves pseudo-random access across the dataset while maintaining sequential I/O at the storage level.

Databricks. 2026. Mosaic Streaming: Main Concepts. Databricks Mosaic AI Training Documentation.
The architecture of a streaming data loader for object storage differs from a local-storage loader in important ways. A local-storage loader can use memory-mapped I/O to treat the dataset as a virtual memory region, relying on the operating system’s page fault mechanism to load data on demand. This approach is elegant but incompatible with object storage, which does not support the POSIX file system interface that memory mapping requires. Instead, an object-storage loader must explicitly manage HTTP connections, issue ranged GET requests for specific byte ranges within shards, handle retries on transient failures, and manage a local buffer pool for decoded samples. Libraries like WebDataset and Mosaic Streaming encapsulate this complexity, presenting a simple iterator interface to the training loop while managing the HTTP transport and buffering internally.
Applying this streaming architecture to the running example makes the design concrete as an alternative to the staged path the chapter adopts. Instead of copying shards to local NVMe at job start, the cluster would read them from the object store throughout the run. The tokenized training set is stored in an S3-like object store as roughly 2,000 shards of 3 GB each. The streaming architecture assigns each of the 256 compute nodes a unique subset of roughly 8 shards. Within each node, 8 data loader worker processes issue concurrent HTTP Range requests to fetch 256 MB chunks from their assigned shards. Across the cluster, this results in 2,048 concurrent requests, allowing aggregate throughput in the 50–100 GB/s range when the object store and network path are provisioned for it, far exceeding the roughly 167.8 MB/s required by the generic text job in the text-versus-image comparison. The running example’s average input demand is lower still. At these provisioned service rates, the network between the compute virtual private cloud (VPC) and the object-storage endpoint can limit maximum streaming throughput without making input delivery the running job’s bottleneck. Organizations that co-locate compute and storage in the same cloud availability zone can reduce cross-network latency, directly reducing the required prefetch buffer depth and improving overall pipeline efficiency.
That request parallelism is what object storage rewards. Each of the 2,048 GET requests is independent and can be served by a different storage node within the cloud provider’s infrastructure, and the count grows with the fleet. With each request fetching a 256 MB chunk of a shard, the aggregate throughput depends on the cloud provider’s network capacity, internal bandwidth, and request-rate quotas. The practical limit is often the network bandwidth between the compute cluster and the object storage service, not the storage service’s internal media bandwidth.
Many object storage services provide strong read-after-write consistency, which means that a subsequent read of an acknowledged object sees the completed write. Amazon S3 announced strong read-after-write consistency for object writes and overwrites, together with strongly consistent listing, in December 2020 (Amazon Web Services 2020). The relevant contract is the documented behavior of the chosen backend, not a blanket assumption about object storage. Per-object consistency still does not make a checkpoint spanning many objects atomic, so the publication protocol of section 4.6 applies here as it does on a file system.

Amazon Web Services. 2020. Amazon S3 Update – Strong Read-After-Write Consistency. AWS News Blog.

Amazon Web Services. 2026a. Checking Object Integrity in Amazon S3. Amazon S3 User Guide.
The immense scale of ML datasets makes them vulnerable to silent data corruption: subtle bit flips in the storage medium or during network transfer that can introduce training artifacts nearly impossible to diagnose. Object storage services provide per-object checksums that verify integrity on upload, copy, or download; Amazon S3, for example, documents checksum options including CRC-family and cryptographic hashes (Amazon Web Services 2026a). Parallel file systems often rely on underlying RAID or erasure coding for physical integrity but may not provide end-to-end checksums visible to the application. A well-engineered large-scale ML pipeline computes and stores a checksum for each data shard during preprocessing and verifies it when the shard is first loaded by a training worker. The verification overhead is negligible compared to the cost of training on corrupted data. For model checkpoints, integrity verification is even more critical: a single bit flip in a weight or optimizer state can corrupt the model, causing training to diverge silently after recovery. Frameworks and checkpoint libraries can include integrity verification, but the pipeline should not assume it without testing the checkpoint format.
Training datasets can contain sensitive information, including personal data, proprietary text, and licensed images. Storage design must carry the organization’s access and retention policies through every copy. Object services expose identity policies and encryption options; parallel file systems provide POSIX permissions and access-control lists. Audit coverage and enforcement depend on the configured platform, not the tier’s name. Versioned manifests should identify derived shards and retained copies so that access reviews, retention decisions, and deletion workflows can locate the relevant artifacts; a deletion request, for example, must reach every immutable preprocessed shard derived from the deleted record. Storage controls protect stored bytes; evaluating what a trained model retains requires additional model-level analysis.
The transition from Tier 4 to Tier 5 is driven primarily by economics. Data that is accessed rarely should move to archive storage when retrieval latency and governance requirements allow it, because archive capacity is cheaper still.



The final tier provides long-term preservation for compliance and auditability. Archive services (such as S3 Glacier) are designed for data that is rarely accessed: training logs from previous years, superseded model checkpoints, audit trails for regulatory compliance. At a representative $0.004/GB/month, archive storage is 5× cheaper than the $0.02/GB/month object-storage assumption used in section 4.3.7. The trade-off is retrieval latency measured in minutes to hours, making this tier unsuitable for operational access.
The primary value of archive storage is organizational memory. When a model trained two years ago produces unexpected behavior in production, the ability to recover the exact training data, hyperparameters, and intermediate checkpoints for forensic analysis depends on archive storage. Organizations that aggressively purge old data to save costs discover, often at the worst possible moment, that they cannot reproduce or explain the behavior of deployed models.
Automated lifecycle policies govern the transition of data between tiers based on access recency. As one illustration of how such automation is expressed, a time-based rule for ML infrastructure might move checkpoints as follows: the most recent three checkpoints remain on the parallel file system for fast recovery; checkpoints older than 72 hours are transitioned to object storage; checkpoints older than 90 days are transitioned to archive storage; and checkpoints older than two years are deleted unless flagged for regulatory retention. S3 Lifecycle rules provide the same general transition/archive/delete mechanism for object lifetimes (Amazon Web Services 2026b). The running example’s checkpoint retention in section 4.6 adopts a count-based variant of the same idea, where the transition rule keys on checkpoint count rather than age. Without automation, teams either hoard data on expensive tiers (wasting budget) or delete data too aggressively (losing reproducibility). The lifecycle policy encodes the organization’s cost-recovery trade-off in a declarative rule that requires no manual intervention.

Amazon Web Services. 2026b. Managing the Lifecycle of Objects. Amazon S3 User Guide.
For the 175B model training run, the archive tier holds the complete training lineage: the raw 3 TB compressed source corpus, the 6 TB serialized shard set, all preprocessing scripts, the final checkpoint, and a sampled subset of intermediate checkpoints. Capacity must include every retained full checkpoint as well as both corpus representations; table 5 computes that total for the declared retention policy. A round dataset-only allowance would underprovision the archive. The asymmetry between archive cost and compute cost makes retention inexpensive relative to the run it documents; failures to archive usually reflect missing lifecycle ownership, unclear retention policy, or retrieval-process neglect rather than raw capacity cost.
Archive storage services offer multiple retrieval speed tiers, each with different pricing. In an S3 Glacier-style service, standard retrieval may complete within hours at moderate cost, expedited retrieval may complete within minutes at a higher cost, and bulk retrieval may trade still more latency for the lowest retrieval price (Amazon Web Services 2026d). The choice of retrieval tier depends on the urgency of the use case. Forensic analysis of a production incident warrants faster retrieval; annual compliance audits can use slower bulk retrieval. Designing the lifecycle policy requires understanding the storage cost, the expected retrieval frequency, and the urgency for each class of data.

Amazon Web Services. 2026d. Understanding Archive Retrieval Options. Amazon S3 User Guide.
Training data provenance links a deployed model to the data versions and preprocessing that produced it. The organization’s governance policy determines which records to retain and for how long; the storage design must make those records identifiable and retrievable throughout that period. Archive is a candidate when its retrieval delay meets that requirement. Records needed during frequent investigations may justify a warmer tier even when archival capacity is cheaper.
The six tiers now have their roles, capacities, and prices, but a role does not say how fast bytes must climb the hierarchy. That rate is set by the accelerators consuming them, and it is the next quantity to derive.

Every training job eventually raises the concrete sizing question of how much storage bandwidth the pipeline must deliver before accelerators stall. The required rate depends on the training configuration, and miscalculating in either direction is expensive. Under-provisioning storage bandwidth starves accelerators. Over-provisioning wastes budget on storage capacity that sits partially idle. The data pipeline throughput equation in equation 2 quantifies the bandwidth the pipeline must sustain for a target training rate:
\[\RequiredInputBandwidth = \InputConsumerAcceleratorCount \times \TargetComputeTimeFraction\times \frac{\BatchDataVolume}{\IronLawComputeTime} \tag{2}\]
where \(\InputConsumerAcceleratorCount\) counts accelerators consuming distinct local input batches, \(\TargetComputeTimeFraction\) is the target fraction of wall-clock time spent computing (typically 0.8 to 0.95), \(\BatchDataVolume\) is one local batch in bytes, and \(\IronLawComputeTime\) is its uninterrupted compute time. This utilization is an active-time fraction, not model FLOPs utilization. If iteration time already includes stalls, multiplying by utilization again would count the slowdown twice. Eliminating sustained input stalls requires supplying batches at the full compute rate; the target fraction sizes a lower accepted training rate. Devices that cooperate on one batch do not each require an independent storage read, so their shared input must be counted once at the tier being sized. The text-versus-image comparison of notebook 4.2 already applied this equation with \(\TargetComputeTimeFraction= 1\); the equation makes the target fraction explicit, and the service chain below adds the requirement that every stage, rather than the accelerator-facing endpoint alone, meet the resulting rate.
The demand equation sizes the accelerator-facing endpoint, but bytes must traverse the complete service chain. Let \(\InputStageServiceRate_{\InputPipelineStageIndex}\) denote the measured service rate of stage \(\InputPipelineStageIndex\), including object-store reads, network transfer, decoding and augmentation, host-memory copies, and host-to-device transfer. Express all rates in the same output-equivalent bytes per second, using each stage’s expansion or compression ratio; raw compressed-read bandwidth cannot be compared directly with decoded-tensor bandwidth. With bounded buffers and no sustained backlog, the pipeline can deliver at most
\[\InputPipelineServiceRate= \min_{\InputPipelineStageIndex} \InputStageServiceRate_{\InputPipelineStageIndex}, \qquad \InputPipelineServiceRate\geq \RequiredInputBandwidth. \tag{3}\]
Capacity at one tier cannot compensate for a slower downstream stage. Compression may raise the storage-read rate while lowering the decode rate; additional loader workers may raise decoding throughput while saturating the host-memory or PCIe stage. The end-to-end inequality in equation 3 therefore turns the chapter’s hierarchy into a testable contract: measure every stage under representative concurrency, then provision or overlap the stage whose service rate is the minimum.
The throughput equation in equation 2 exposes four levers on storage demand, and none of them is free. Reducing the accelerator count (\(\InputConsumerAcceleratorCount\)) lowers aggregate input demand by reducing the number of distinct consumers, but it lowers training throughput with it. Lowering target utilization (\(\TargetComputeTimeFraction\)) relaxes the delivery rate by accepting idle accelerators. Decreasing the per-batch data volume (\(\BatchDataVolume\)) through a more compact representation of the same samples helps only while decoding keeps pace; shrinking the batch itself changes the training configuration and its statistical efficiency. Increasing compute time (\(\IronLawComputeTime\)) gives storage longer to deliver each batch, but every iteration takes proportionally longer, which is also why a faster accelerator can expose an input bottleneck the slower one hid. The equation therefore sizes the pipeline for a chosen training configuration; deliberately slowing useful computation does not improve delivery.
As a separate image-training example, consider 256 GPUs training with ImageNet-scale images, 200 ms iterations, and 80 percent target utilization. This configuration requires 30.3 GB/s of aggregate storage throughput. The bandwidth must be sustained continuously for the duration of training, which may last days or weeks. If sustained delivery falls below 30.3 GB/s, the input path cannot support that target rate once its buffers drain. For the chapter’s 175B language-model running example, tokenized text has a much lower per-batch bandwidth demand, but the total data volume and checkpoint traffic over the run are much larger, shifting the bottleneck from peak training-data bandwidth to sustained throughput and checkpoint movement over weeks.
The consequences of falling short are captured by the data stall ratio, defined in equation 4 as the fraction of each training step where the accelerator waits for data:
\[\text{Data Stall \%} = \frac{\TrainingStepTime- \IronLawComputeTime}{\TrainingStepTime} \times 100 \tag{4}\]
Equation 4 describes one worker’s input path with communication excluded, so its \(\TrainingStepTime\) is compute plus exposed input wait. The Fleet Law of The Fleet Law carries no input-wait term, so it implicitly treats the next batch as already resident; whatever input wait the loader fails to hide adds to the distributed step on top of \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) and \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\), as compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)) capacity that sits idle while storage catches up. In a real distributed job, the gap \(\TrainingStepTime- \IronLawComputeTime\) also contains exposed communication and synchronization, so the ratio implicates storage only when that gap is measured as time spent waiting on the input queue, separately from collectives and barriers. Without overlap, step time adds compute and I/O time. Pipelining reduces step time to the longer of the two durations and stall time to the positive difference between I/O and compute.

Napkin Math 4.5: The data stall ratioProblem: A GPU processes a batch in 200 ms, but storage takes 250 ms to deliver the next batch. What fraction of each training step is the accelerator idle, and how much does pipelining I/O with compute reduce that stall?
Without pipelining (sequential I/O then compute):
\[T_{\text{step}} = T_{\text{IO}} + T_{\text{compute}} = 250 + 200 = 450 \text{ ms}\] \[\text{Stall \%} = \frac{250}{450} = 55.6\%\]
With pipelining (I/O overlapped with compute):
\[T_{\text{step}} = \max(200, 250) = 250 \text{ ms}\] \[\text{Stall \%} = \frac{250 - 200}{250} = {20\%}\]
Systems insight: Even with pipelining, the accelerator is idle 20 percent of the time. To eliminate the stall entirely, the next batch must arrive within the 200 ms compute window, either by increasing effective storage bandwidth or by adding parallel I/O streams. Deeper prefetch buffers cannot help here, because the delivery time exceeds the compute window on every step rather than merely in the tail.


The data stall ratio measures time lost waiting for inputs relative to the chosen iteration window. Acceptable stall time depends on the fleet’s cost and throughput objectives; a threshold is a policy choice, not a universal storage-health boundary. Instrument batch-ready times and accelerator execution in the same trace to distinguish input starvation from synchronization, CPU preprocessing, and other idle intervals. General profiling tools can expose these events, but an idle accelerator alone does not identify storage as the cause.

A storage pipeline that met its budget at launch can drift out of it as datasets grow, jobs contend, and drives age, so it requires continuous monitoring to keep silent bottlenecks from eroding training efficiency. Key metrics to track in real time include per-tier bandwidth utilization (NVMe, network, object storage), prefetch buffer depth (how many batches are queued and ready), the data stall ratio per GPU, the parallel file system’s metadata operation rate, and NVMe drive health indicators (wear level, temperature, error counts). Alert thresholds should trigger before stalls become visible in training loss curves. An undetected 5 percent increase in data stall ratio across the 1,024-GPU reference cluster (half the running cluster) for just one week wastes about $17,203 in idle compute (1,024 GPUs \(\times\) $2/GPU-hour \(\times\) 168 hours \(\times\) 5 percent), making comprehensive storage monitoring a first-order economic concern rather than an operational nicety.
Diagnose a storage stall at three levels. The application timeline identifies when the accelerator waits; per-worker rates and queue depth identify the pipeline stage that falls behind; device and shared-server counters show which resource limits that stage. Correlating those observations distinguishes a byte-bandwidth shortage from metadata contention or insufficient decoding capacity.
A small development dataset may hide the contention and accumulated state of a production run. A pipeline stress test should therefore use representative data volume and concurrency and run long enough to expose queue depletion, resource leaks, and memory pressure before the loader is coupled to an expensive training job.
Different ML workloads have dramatically different bandwidth profiles, even when using the same cluster. Image classification with ResNet-50 on ImageNet produces a high bandwidth demand because each batch contains hundreds of large images (116 KB each on average) and iteration times are short (100 to 200 ms). Language model pretraining produces a lower per-batch bandwidth demand because tokenized text is compact (each token is a 4-byte integer, so a packed sequence of 4,096 tokens occupies only 16 KB), but the total data volume over the training run is enormous (trillions of tokens). Recommendation model training, the Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) workload, produces a mixed bandwidth demand: embedding lookups require high-IOPS random access to the embedding table, while the dense layers consume standard sequential training data. Each workload’s bandwidth profile determines which storage tier is the bottleneck and where optimization effort should focus. Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) falls outside this shared-storage analysis, because its raw training data stays on the devices that produce it; there is no central corpus to stage, and its storage constraints become per-device capacity and upload limits.

The pipeline equation also reveals a scaling challenge that worsens with cluster size. As \(\InputConsumerAcceleratorCount\) increases, the required bandwidth \(\RequiredInputBandwidth\) increases linearly, but the storage system’s aggregate bandwidth does not automatically scale to match. Adding more compute nodes to a cluster that shares a parallel file system increases the demand on a fixed storage resource. Eventually, the storage system saturates and every additional GPU beyond the saturation point contributes zero additional training throughput while increasing cost. This saturation point is the practical upper limit on cluster scaling for a given storage configuration, and identifying it quantitatively requires applying equation 2 to the specific storage system’s measured bandwidth.

Pipelined loading (b) reads and prepares batch \(\BatchIndex+1\) while the GPU trains on batch \(\BatchIndex\), so four batches finish in about the time sequential loading needs for two (dashed line). The shaded column marks one instant with three batches in flight. The overlap hides storage latency only while delivery keeps pace with compute and the prefetch buffer is deep enough to absorb variance.



While the dual timelines in figure 4 demonstrate how pipelining converts a sequential bottleneck into overlapped execution, continuous saturation hinges on maintaining a prefetch buffer deep enough to absorb variance in I/O latency. Stage durations need not be deterministic if ready batches cover the delays. Storage systems exhibit I/O jitter: variation in read latency caused by contention and background work. NVMe drives experience occasional latency spikes during internal garbage collection (when the controller reorganizes NAND flash blocks) or wear-leveling operations. Parallel file systems exhibit latency spikes when multiple training jobs contend for the same OSS nodes, when the MDS processes a burst of metadata operations, or when background scrubbing detects and repairs bit errors. Object storage likewise exposes delays from shared-service contention and maintenance.
A single slow I/O creates a “bubble” when it exhausts the pipeline’s ready work. If the CPU is preparing batch \(\BatchIndex+1\) with no additional batches ready, a delayed read can leave batch \(\BatchIndex+1\) unavailable when the GPU finishes batch \(\BatchIndex\). The GPU then idles until the batch is ready. A longer queue tolerates a longer interruption, and delivery faster than consumption can refill it afterward. Rather than preparing just one batch ahead, the CPU maintains a queue of \(\PrefetchBufferCount\) preloaded batches.
A buffer sized to the measured p99 I/O delay needs enough ready batches to cover that delay without draining:
\[\MinimumPrefetchBufferCount= \left\lceil \frac{\TailStepIoTime}{\IronLawComputeTime} \right\rceil \tag{5}\]
The prefetch depth equation in equation 5 estimates how many ready batches cover the selected latency window. Outstanding reads contribute to replenishing that buffer but do not count as ready batches until they complete. The equation assumes that the long-run data supply rate is at least as high as the accelerator’s consumption rate; prefetching absorbs latency variance, not a sustained bandwidth deficit. When average throughput is sufficient but p99 latency exceeds compute time, deeper prefetching absorbs delays within the provisioned window; rarer or correlated delays can still cause stalls. When sustained delivery is lower than demand, identify the limiting stage before choosing more storage bandwidth, additional decoding capacity, a different representation, or local staging. The equation uses the p99 delay rather than the mean because a buffer sized for the mean drains whenever a slow read arrives, and the tail-latency arithmetic of section 4.3.6 shows that when a step depends on many servers, some read is slow on most steps. Even the p99 window leaves rarer events and correlated interruptions to test.
If object-storage reads take 500 ms at the 99th percentile and compute takes 200 ms, then \(\MinimumPrefetchBufferCount= 3\) batches; provisioning five ready batches adds a margin. In practice, data loaders like PyTorch’s DataLoader use prefetch_factor and num_workers parameters to control work ahead of consumption. Setting prefetch_factor=2 with 4 workers permits eight prefetched batches across workers, but some may still be loading or undergoing preprocessing. The configured count is therefore not a guarantee of eight ready batches; the quantity that protects the accelerator is completed-queue occupancy and its refill rate, measured against the delay window on whichever tier serves the reads.



A 500 ms p99 read spans 2.5 steps of 200 ms, so three ready batches must cover it.
To illustrate the memory cost of prefetch buffer depth, return to the image job of notebook 4.2. Each GPU processes its batch in roughly 200 ms, and once its 256 images are decoded into \(224{\times}224{\times}3\)-byte tensors, the collated batch occupies about 40 MB per GPU. Reading from local NVMe, the p99 I/O latency for that batch is approximately 50 ms. Under the p99-window model, the minimum ready-buffer depth is \(\lceil 50/200 \rceil = 1\) batch, and this example provisions a depth of 2. Reading from a parallel file system, the p99 I/O latency rises to roughly 200 ms due to network jitter and contention, requiring a minimum depth of \(\lceil 200/200 \rceil = 1\), with an illustrative provisioned depth of 3. Reading from object storage, the p99 latency can exceed 500 ms, requiring a depth of at least 3, with an illustrative provisioned depth of 5 or more. These numbers translate directly into host DRAM consumption: at 40 MB per batch, a depth-5 prefetch buffer per GPU consumes 200 MB, and 8 GPUs per node consume 1.6 GB. At 40 MB per batch with a depth of 1, the same node needs only 320 MB. Measured delivery delays, batch size, and the chosen protection window determine this memory budget. Queue occupancy and refill rate must still be tested under correlated delays.
The representation decides whether that depth is cheap. Text barely registers, because a per-GPU batch of a few packed 4,096-token sequences occupies tens of kilobytes, so even a deep text queue is negligible. Decoded images are where depth costs memory. The 256-image batch above is roughly 39 MB before rounding, and a buffer of 8 such batches consumes about 310 MB per GPU, modest against a node’s 512 GB of DRAM even after multiplying by the GPUs on the node. Higher-resolution images and video raise the per-batch size by an order of magnitude or more, at which point the prefetch buffer competes with embedding tables and other DRAM consumers.
The interaction between prefetching and the storage hierarchy creates a layered defense against stalls. The first layer is the prefetch buffer in host DRAM, absorbing I/O variance from NVMe reads. The second layer is the local NVMe warm cache, absorbing network variance from shared storage, whether a parallel file system or an object store. The third layer is the parallel file system read-ahead cache, absorbing variance from disk seeks across the OSS cluster. Each layer adds latency tolerance at the cost of memory or storage capacity. The system designer must check each active path against the interruption window it is intended to absorb and verify that sustained delivery replenishes the consumed batches. The running example’s shards come from object storage, whose 500 ms p99 against a 200 ms step would call for 3 ready batches if every read went to that tier. Once the shards are staged on local NVMe, every training read is a local hit, and the prefetch buffer needs to absorb only the 50 ms local p99, which a single ready batch covers.

A single CPU core cannot keep a high-throughput accelerator fed, even when the storage hardware is fast enough, because of the CPU work required between the storage read and the GPU transfer. Consider the throughput required for image training: decoding a 116 KB JPEG image into a \(224{\times}224{\times}3\) raw tensor requires entropy decoding of Huffman-coded coefficients, inverse discrete cosine transform, chroma upsampling, and pixel-format conversion. This process takes roughly 1 to 5 ms per image on a server CPU core. After decoding, augmentation adds further CPU work: a random crop requires computing crop coordinates and copying the sub-region; horizontal flip requires copying with reversed column order; color jitter requires per-pixel multiplication and addition. Each augmentation adds 0.5 to 2 ms per image.
The image job of notebook 4.2 feeds each GPU 256 images every 200 ms step, more than 1,000 images per second. At 1,000 images per second per GPU and 8 GPUs per node, a single core would need to decode and augment 8,000 images per second, a throughput 10\(\times\) to 40\(\times\) beyond what a single core can sustain. The solution is multi-worker data loading, where \(\DataLoaderWorkerCount\) worker processes each read from storage, decode, augment, and enqueue batches independently. The effective I/O throughput scales approximately linearly with \(\DataLoaderWorkerCount\) until one of three bottlenecks is reached: the storage device’s bandwidth saturates, the PCIe bus between host and device saturates, or the workers exhaust host CPU cycles.
In PyTorch’s DataLoader, each worker is a separate process with its own file descriptors and memory space. The num_workers parameter controls \(\DataLoaderWorkerCount\). Setting \(\DataLoaderWorkerCount\) too low leaves the GPU starved; setting \(\DataLoaderWorkerCount\) too high wastes CPU resources on context switching and contention. A good heuristic is to start with \(\DataLoaderWorkerCount= 4 \times \AcceleratorsPerNode\), where \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\) is the number of GPUs per node, and profile the data stall ratio, adjusting until it meets the fleet’s chosen target. For a node with 8 GPUs, this yields 32 workers, which on a system with 64 CPU cores leaves 32 cores for the PyTorch runtime, GPU-to-GPU communication threads, and operating system overhead. The division of CPU resources between data loading and training orchestration is itself a capacity planning exercise.
The interaction between multi-worker loading and the storage hierarchy matters. When reading from local NVMe, workers can issue concurrent reads to the same RAID array, using NVMe’s deep command queues to expose device parallelism until shared drive or controller capacity saturates. When reading from a parallel file system, workers distribute their reads across different OSS nodes, naturally aggregating bandwidth. When reading from object storage, workers issue concurrent GET requests, each to a different shard, achieving parallelism at the HTTP level.
A subtle pitfall in multi-worker loading is shuffle quality vs. I/O efficiency. Perfect shuffling requires that each batch contain samples drawn uniformly from the entire dataset, which implies random access across all shards. Random access, however, defeats the sequential I/O patterns that storage systems optimize for. The practical compromise is shard-level shuffling combined with within-shard shuffling: the loader shuffles the list of shards at epoch start, assigns contiguous groups of shards to each worker, and then shuffles samples within each shard’s local buffer. This approach usually provides enough randomness for convergence while maintaining sequential I/O at the storage level. Its adequacy depends on how the shards were built. A corpus whose shards are internally homogeneous, such as one source or one class per shard, needs finer shards or a larger shuffle buffer, so the layout should be validated against the loss curve of a fully shuffled baseline on a subset before the run commits to it.
The shuffle buffer size creates a memory-randomness trade-off. A larger buffer provides better randomness (because samples are drawn from a larger pool) but consumes more host DRAM. For the running example with text data, a shuffle buffer of 10,000 sequences at 2,048 tokens each, with each token represented as a 4-byte integer, consumes roughly 82 MB. This is negligible relative to the 512 GB of host DRAM. For image data, where each decoded image occupies 151 KB, a shuffle buffer of 10,000 images consumes 1.5 GB, still manageable but a nontrivial fraction of the prefetch budget. The data loader designer must balance shuffle buffer size against prefetch depth, since both compete for the same host DRAM capacity.
The data loading pipeline, from storage read through decode, augmentation, and transfer to accelerator, is the complete fuel delivery system for the training engine, and when any stage becomes the bottleneck the accelerator starves. Local reads can reduce network and shared-storage wait, which makes shard placement across nodes the next decision when that path limits delivery.



In a distributed training cluster, the placement of data shards across the storage hierarchy determines pipeline performance. Each training worker needs efficient access to its assigned portion of the dataset. The core trade-off is between the flexibility of shared storage and the raw speed of local storage. Local NVMe avoids shared-network and service contention, but its advantage depends on the local drive configuration and the bandwidth allocated to the same client by remote storage. Compare measured client rates rather than assuming a fixed local-to-remote ratio.
The simplest strategy is static placement. At the beginning of a training job, the orchestrator assigns a fixed subset of data shards to each node. The node stages this data by copying its shards from shared storage (the object store in the running example, a parallel file system in many on-premises clusters) to local NVMe drives. Reads remain local while the assigned shards fit and the sampling policy uses that assignment. A changed dataset or assignment requires restaging, so the placement policy must preserve the intended sample distribution as well as local throughput.
The alternative is dynamic placement, where nodes fetch shards from shared storage as needed and can retain them locally for reuse. This supports datasets larger than aggregate local NVMe capacity and sampling policies that change the active subset over time. Cache misses consume shared-storage bandwidth and expose remote latency unless prefetching hides it; cache hits retain the benefit of local reads.
The cache view of equation 1 puts a number on that trade. Take the multi-modal job of section 4.3.4, whose 35 TB corpus overflows a node’s 30.7 TB of local NVMe. If the job samples uniformly and the cache holds that fraction of the corpus, about 88 percent of reads hit the 28 GB/s local stripe and the remaining 12 percent fall through to the node’s 4 GB/s share of the parallel file system. Taking the time to deliver one byte as the service time, the mean delivered rate is about 16 GB/s, only 58 percent of the all-local rate. A miss rate near one in eight costs about two-fifths of the bandwidth because each missed byte takes 7× as long as a hit, and that mean is the optimistic case; misses that cluster in time drain the prefetch buffer faster than the average suggests.
A more advanced approach is locality-aware scheduling. The scheduler keeps track of which data shards are cached on which nodes’ local NVMe drives. When it starts a new job or replaces a failed node, it prefers a node that already has the required data cached, rather than treating all nodes as interchangeable. This uses the principle of data gravity,11 co-locating compute with data to minimize transfer times. Scheduling avoids a staging copy only when an available node holds the required, validated shard versions. The next requirement is therefore to identify the cached contents precisely enough to reuse them safely.
11 Data gravity: A metaphor treating large datasets as massive objects that attract compute. The gravitational analogy is apt: moving a 100 TB dataset out of one cloud provider to another costs roughly $9,000 in egress fees and takes hours, while launching compute next to the data is near-instantaneous. In ML fleet design, data gravity means the storage location of the training dataset often dictates the physical placement of the entire training cluster.For the 6 TB serialized dataset distributed across 256 nodes, each node is responsible for approximately 23.4 GB of data. If a node fails, its replacement must restage that shard subset from shared storage. Drawn at the uncontended 4 GB/s per-node share of the chapter’s parallel file system, the copy takes about 5.9 seconds. At an effective 400 MB/s per-node rate, which recovery contention can impose and which is also the order of the per-node share of the 50–100 GB/s object-store streaming path described in section 4.3.7, the same copy stretches to about 58.6 seconds. If the orchestrator can instead schedule the replacement workload on an idle node that already has the data cached from a previous run, staging time is zero and training resumes as soon as the replacement joins. The saving is modest per event but recurs. At a per-GPU mean time between failures of 50,000 hours, the 256-node cluster sees about 1 node failure per day, and each contended restage idles the whole synchronous job for the copy time above. Larger fleets fail proportionally more often, although each node’s share of the corpus shrinks as the node count grows.



Knowing where data lives is only half the problem; at scale the storage infrastructure must also record which version of the data each run uses and how it flows through the pipeline. Versioning turns the storage hierarchy into a reproducibility system: the fleet must record both the exact bytes read and the preprocessing code, shuffle seed, schema, and integrity checks that produced those bytes before the run began.

Lighthouse 4.1: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): Feature store latencyWhile Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) deals with static, versioned datasets of trillions of tokens, Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) deals with dynamic, high-velocity feature streams. For a recommendation system, the “ground truth” changes every second as users click and interact. This forces a move from simple file-based storage to a feature store architecture that must solve the point-in-time correctness problem: ensuring that the features retrieved for training exactly match what the model would have seen at the moment of inference, without “leaking” future information.


That same reproducibility requirement becomes harder when the inputs are live features rather than immutable text shards. Feature store architectures address point-in-time correctness12 by maintaining an immutable feature ledger or a “time-travel” query engine, significantly increasing storage complexity.
12 Point-in-Time Correctness: In recommendation systems, features (for example, user click history) must be retrieved exactly as they existed at the moment of the historical interaction. Retrieving current features for a past event, a form of temporal leakage, inflates training accuracy but causes the model to fail in production. At petabyte scale, the ledger that prevents it must retain every feature version a training query might request.13 Hash Cost (SHA-256): Verifying the integrity of a 100 TB dataset using SHA-256 consumes approximately 55.6 CPU-core hours at a per-core hashing rate of 500 MB/s. The work parallelizes across shards, but it still competes with decoding for host cores and must read every byte, so the validation step is best pipelined with ingestion rather than run as a separate pass before the fleet starts.At fleet scale, even an immutable collection of files produces a distributed stream of consumed samples whose versions and order must be recorded. Foundation-model runs can last weeks or months; in the 30-day running example, the dataset version and sampling policy must remain identifiable throughout the run. Samples and shuffle order can change across epochs, but the pipeline must record enough state to reconstruct the sequence consumed. Otherwise, an engineer cannot distinguish between a model regression and a silent change in the input distribution. Dataset versioning provides the necessary “Git for data” capability by snapshotting the cryptographic hashes13 of every data shard, the exact preprocessing code used for tokenization, and the random seeds governing the global shuffle. This level of rigor is essential for audit trails and for debugging the subtle “loss spikes” that characterize large-scale training, where engineers must be able to replay the exact batch that caused a divergence to determine if the cause was a corrupted data sample or a numerical instability in the optimizer.
At petabyte scale, the data pipeline has to make every transformation reproducible. Raw documents are cleaned, tokenized, packed into training examples, and sharded across storage tiers. Each stage writes an immutable artifact, and each artifact records the input version, code version, schema, and statistical checks it satisfied. Once those dependencies are explicit, the pipeline forms a directed acyclic graph: later artifacts depend on earlier artifacts, and no stage is allowed to rewrite its own history. When a training job starts, the cluster manager verifies that each worker’s local NVMe shards match the data snapshot declared for the run. Treating the data pipeline as a graph of versioned artifacts rather than a simple file transfer makes silent data drift detectable and attributable to a specific stage, code version, or input snapshot. Immutability also pays a storage dividend. Because an artifact never changes once written, a manifest can name it by content identifier, and many experiments can reference the same unchanged shards without copying entire datasets.


Versioned artifacts identify what a pipeline produced; execution semantics determine whether failures can change that result. Consider the tokenization stage that built the running example’s shards, in which many workers each read raw documents and write packed token shards. When a worker crashes halfway through a shard, its replacement must decide which documents to process again. The storage system’s part in that decision is the commit boundary, the point at which a stage’s output becomes durable and visible downstream, the same contract that section 4.6 later applies to checkpoint generations. That shared contract is why a storage chapter owns these semantics, because whether a replay loses or duplicates data is decided by what the store has committed. The restarted worker compares its input position with the last committed output and replays everything after it, so the work at risk is whatever accumulated past the last commit. Two service-rate effects govern how much accumulates. Records are assigned to workers by a partition key, such as a document’s source or a user identifier, and partition skew arises when one key owns disproportionate work and holds its stage open while the rest of the fleet idles. Backpressure propagates a slow downstream stage’s limit upstream by slowing admission or bounding in-flight data, a control response to overload rather than another name for slow processing.
Failures near that boundary raise a correctness question, and three guarantees answer it differently. At-most-once processing never replays uncertain work, so a document that was read but whose output was never confirmed is lost. At-least-once processing replays everything after the last confirmed commit, so a document whose output was written but not yet confirmed is written twice. An effectively exactly-once outcome combines replayable inputs with idempotent writes, writes that leave the same result however many times they repeat, or with transactional output keyed by a stable event or transaction identifier (Akidau et al. 2015). Reliable message delivery between workers cannot provide this guarantee on its own, because the duplicate arises from the worker’s own replay.

Example 4.2: The acknowledgment gapFailure trace: A feature-pipeline worker writes the output row for click event e42, then crashes before it records that the write succeeded. Its replacement cannot tell whether e42 was committed. Skipping the event risks losing it. Replaying it with an append writes the feature row a second time, so that click counts twice in every training set built from the table. Writing the row under the stable key (feature_version, e42) turns the replay into an overwrite of the same row, so the uncertain event can be reprocessed safely.
Systems lesson: Exactly-once belongs at the output commit boundary, whose record must bind the input position, transformation version, stable identifier, and commit state.


Streaming adds a time boundary to the contract. Event time records when an event occurred; processing time records when a worker handled it. A pipeline that aggregates clicks per hour must decide when an hour is finished, even though events can arrive late. A watermark is its running estimate that every event up to some event time has arrived, which lets it close that window and emit the result; a late-data policy determines whether later arrivals update, retract, quarantine, or drop the result (Akidau et al. 2015). Watermarks therefore trade freshness against completeness rather than prove that no older event remains.

Akidau, Tyler, Robert Bradshaw, Craig Chambers, Slava Chernyak, Rafael J. Fernández-Moctezuma, Reuven Lax, Sam McVeety, et al. 2015. “The Dataflow Model: A Practical Approach to Balancing Correctness, Latency, and Cost in Massive-Scale, Unbounded, Out-of-Order Data Processing.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 8 (12): 1792–803. https://doi.org/10.14778/2824032.2824076.
Each of these mechanisms buys one property at the cost of another. Buffering absorbs finite bursts or temporary slowdowns but increases recovery state and freshness lag; sustained overload still requires backpressure or more service capacity. Aggressive watermarks reduce delay but exclude more late data, while retries help only when writes are safe to repeat. These choices change the stored result, because a feature table closed under an aggressive watermark holds different rows from one closed under a lenient watermark. A reproducible training snapshot must therefore record source and code versions alongside partitioning, replay policy, stable identifiers, watermark state, and late-data decisions. That record is what lets a later feature backfill, a replay of history under new code, rejoin features at the correct points in time without mixing old and new histories.

The pipeline equation, the prefetch queue, the loader workers, and the versioned artifacts together determine which bytes reach host memory and when. On the conventional path, however, every one of those bytes is also copied by the CPU through host DRAM before the accelerator’s DMA can start, and at high request rates that copy competes with decoding for the same cores. No amount of orchestration removes that copy; only a direct data path between storage and accelerator does.

The storage hierarchy can provide enough aggregate bandwidth and still leave GPUs waiting when the CPU copies data for thousands of small transfers. In the traditional path, every shard read bounces through host DRAM before reaching GPU HBM; GPUDirect Storage (GDS) removes that host-memory bounce copy for local or RDMA-attached NVMe, which pays off when the copy itself limits throughput. The CPU still submits and coordinates I/O through the software stack. Understanding the traditional path first makes the GDS optimization clear.
The traditional data path for loading training data follows three hops: storage \(\to\) host DRAM \(\to\) GPU HBM. Data is first read from NVMe into a kernel buffer in host DRAM (via a DMA transfer initiated by the NVMe controller), then copied to a user-space buffer (the data loader’s tensor, via a memcpy that the CPU executes), and finally transferred to GPU memory via the PCIe bus (using a cudaMemcpy or cudaMemcpyAsync call that programs the GPU’s DMA engine). Each hop adds latency and consumes CPU resources. The CPU must orchestrate every transfer, manage buffer allocation, and handle interrupts from both the storage device and the GPU. For a single transfer, this overhead is negligible. When eight GPUs each demand thousands of small transfers per second, however, the aggregate CPU load for data movement alone can saturate multiple cores, leaving insufficient CPU capacity for the data augmentation that is also essential to the pipeline.14
14 GDS (GPUDirect Storage): Part of NVIDIA’s GPUDirect family, which also includes GPUDirect RDMA (network adapters writing directly to GPU memory) and GPUDirect Peer-to-Peer (inter-GPU memory access); GDS extends this data-copy-bypass approach to NVMe storage via the cuFile API. With RDMA and GDS, payload data can traverse the path remote storage \(\to\) network \(\to\) GPU memory without a CPU-mediated bounce copy. The CPU still issues and coordinates cuFile operations, but it spends less time copying payloads and can devote more capacity to augmentation and pipeline orchestration.
Definition 4.4: GPUDirect Storage
GPUDirect storage (GDS) is a technology that enables a direct DMA path between NVMe storage devices and GPU memory, bypassing the system-DRAM bounce buffer and CPU payload copies while retaining CPU submission and control.

Significance: It eliminates the “bounce buffer” through system memory. In the small-transfer model detailed in notebook 4.6, the assumed active CPU service per request falls by 75 percent. That model estimates CPU capacity savings, not an end-to-end latency guarantee. Whether the storage link saturates depends on the remaining bottlenecks.
Distinction: Unlike traditional I/O, where payload data is staged through host buffers and copied between them, GDS provides direct memory access between the storage controller and the accelerator. CPU-issued cuFile calls and kernel storage drivers remain in the control path.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that GDS makes all storage “faster.” The direct path depends on supported storage and interconnect configurations; it does not eliminate media latency, network latency, or queueing.



The software layers in the traditional I/O path contribute control overhead as well as payload-copy work. A buffered read traverses the runtime, file system, and device driver, then makes the completed bytes available to the application. Direct I/O and pinned buffers can avoid some copies even without GDS, so the correct baseline is the actual data path rather than a fixed number of copies for every read. The GDS design guide distinguishes the payload path from the CPU control work that remains.
GDS changes the payload path without eliminating the software control path. The cuFile API registers a GPU memory region for direct DMA. Subsequent reads transfer payload data from NVMe to GPU memory without an intermediate system-memory bounce buffer, while cuFile, the virtual file system, kernel storage drivers, and nvidia-fs remain involved in submission and coordination. The CPU issues the I/O and checks for completion but avoids the payload-copy work of the traditional path.
The benefit from GDS matters when host payload movement is a limiting stage after other pipeline work is accounted for. Figure 5 diagrams these hardware interfaces, contrasting the two-hop DMA and intermediate host-DRAM bounce buffers of the conventional path against the single direct DMA transfer of GDS. While the direct path eliminates the CPU payload-copy stage, the dashed control link emphasizes that the host CPU still orchestrates transfer submission and completion.







Figure 5: Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage path: Both panels draw the same node: CPU and host DRAM above a PCIe switch, NVMe and GPU below it. Green routes are DMA transfers of payload bytes. In the buffered path (a), payload climbs into host DRAM and comes back down, and the CPU copies every payload from the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer before the accelerator’s DMA can start. In the GDS path (b), NVMe transfers directly into GPU memory, and the dashed CPU link shows the submission and completion work that remains.



GDS benefits depend on the bottleneck, request sizes, alignment, concurrency, and storage topology. Removing host bounce buffers can improve throughput when those copies limit the path; it does not imply that the smallest transfers benefit most. Small I/O may remain submission- or latency-limited and require concurrency to approach the available bandwidth. NVIDIA’s GDS benchmarking guide therefore evaluates I/O size and per-device behavior as well as throughput. The benefit appears only in an end-to-end comparison of the pipeline with and without the direct path, and the clearest case is the one where host CPU time per request is the limiting stage.
