Self-Check: Answer

A team selects RAID 5 for a disposable local training-data cache whose immutable source is durably stored elsewhere. The fleet can tolerate restaging after drive failure. Why might RAID 0 be a better throughput-and-capacity trade-off under this failure contract?

RAID 5 cannot be formatted with modern Linux filesystems such as ext4 or XFS.
RAID 5 disables hardware DMA transfers, preventing the GPU from accessing host DRAM.
The cache can be reconstructed from its durable source, so RAID 0 can aggregate drives without parity overhead when restaging disruption is acceptable.
RAID 5 increases drive endurance wear by \(10\times\) compared to single-drive configurations.

Answer: The correct answer is C. A disposable cache need not own durability when its source remains available. RAID 0 removes parity overhead but increases exposure to cache loss and restaging. RAID 5 can still be justified by availability requirements; checkpoints awaiting durable replication are not disposable. Filesystem support and DMA are not disabled by RAID 5, and the stated endurance multiplier is unsupported.
Learning Objective: Evaluate RAID parity and striping trade-offs for disposable ML caches under explicit durability and availability requirements
A training team upgrades its cluster from A100 to H100 GPUs, expecting a \(3\times\) end-to-end training speedup. However, wall-clock epoch time barely improves, and GPU utilization drops from \(85\%\) to \(35\%\). Traces show shorter uninterrupted compute time, unchanged measured input-delivery rate, and increased time waiting for ready input batches, while communication and checkpoint pauses remain unchanged. Diagnose the measured bottleneck and explain why faster compute exposed it.
Answer: The traces establish an input-delivery limit: compute finishes sooner, but the unchanged pipeline does not supply ready batches at the new consumption rate. More of the iteration is therefore exposed input wait. Prefetching can hide delays within its queue window but cannot overcome a sustained delivery-rate deficit. The utilization and epoch-time figures alone would not identify this cause; the supplied timing measurements distinguish it from communication or checkpoint pauses. Profile individual read, decode, and transfer stages before selecting a remedy.
Learning Objective: Analyze training throughput regressions following accelerator compute upgrades using the I/O wall framework
A team replaces a lighter codec with a denser codec on local-NVMe training shards. On this corpus, illustrative measurements give the lighter codec a 3:1 ratio and 1.5 GB/s decoded output per core, versus 4:1 and 0.5 GB/s for the denser codec. Before the change, worker profiles show decoding and augmentation saturating the host CPU and the ready-batch queue repeatedly draining. Afterward, decompression consumes more CPU time, the queue drains more often, and training step time increases although stored bytes decrease. What caused this measured regression?

Compressed shards cannot be read by NVMe controllers because flash drives require raw uncompressed binary blocks.
The pipeline was already CPU-bound on data decoding and augmentation, so adding heavy decompression work saturated the host CPU, starving the GPU of assembled batches.
The denser codec introduces non-deterministic bit flips that cause stochastic gradient descent to diverge.
The parallel file system rejects compressed shards larger than 1 GB due to POSIX file locking constraints.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The supplied worker profiles and ready-batch queues establish a host-processing limit before the change; additional decompression work further reduces completed-batch delivery. The denser codec saves stored bytes but requires more CPU work for the same decoded output under these corpus-specific measurements. These illustrative rates are not fixed properties of named compression levels. Compare output-equivalent stage rates and input wait when choosing a representation.
Learning Objective: Analyze the CPU-versus-I/O trade-offs of data compression and identify when decompression overhead degrades pipeline throughput
True or False: Sizing a data loader’s prefetch buffer depth based on average storage read latency ensures that training runs will not experience data stalls during multi-week training jobs on shared object storage.
Answer: False. Average latency does not bound tail stalls. A starting buffer budget is \(Q_{\text{prefetch}} = \lceil T_{\text{I/O,p99}} / T_{\text{compute}} \rceil\) plus margin, but longer or correlated delays can still drain it; sustained delivery bandwidth must also keep pace with consumption.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why prefetch queues sized to average latency fail to prevent accelerator stalls under tail-latency variance
A team creates full \(10\text{ TB}\) copies of a pretraining dataset for every snapshot version, creating 20 versions over six months (\(200\text{ TB}\) total storage). Explain how content-addressable storage or delta encoding optimizes this workflow when successive versions differ by only \(5\%\).
Answer: The first version requires \(10\text{ TB}\). Nineteen subsequent versions with \(5\%\) new content each add \(0.5\text{ TB}\), for \(19.5\text{ TB}\) total before metadata and replication, saving \(180.5\text{ TB}\) against 20 full copies. Content-addressable storage references unchanged blocks rather than copying them; the reduction assumes changes remain localized at the stored block or shard granularity.
Learning Objective: Compare naive full-copy dataset versioning against delta-encoded content-addressable snapshotting in terms of storage efficiency

Self-Check: Answer

A 2,048-GPU training cluster reports \(40\%\) GPU hardware utilization. Telemetry reveals: (1) GPUs spend \(45\%\) of iteration time waiting for data tensors, (2) Storage data disks on the parallel file system report less than \(5\%\) bandwidth utilization, (3) Data loader host CPU cores report \(100\%\) utilization, and (4) The dataset is stored as 50 million individual JPEG files. A worker CPU profile attributes most active CPU time to JPEG decoding, the MDS shows a sustained queue at its operation-rate limit, and the completed-batch queue repeatedly drains. Which remediation targets the two measured limiting stages?

The parallel file system network fabric is saturated; upgrade InfiniBand links between compute nodes and storage servers.
GPU HBM capacity is exhausted; apply aggressive 4-bit activation quantization to free GPU memory.
NVMe drive endurance limits have triggered write throttling; replace compute node local SSDs.
The workload is suffering from both metadata server saturation (individual small files) and CPU-bound decoding; repackage the dataset into large WebDataset tar shards and evaluate GPU JPEG decoding against its compute and HBM budget.

Answer: The correct answer is D. The MDS queue at its operation-rate limit confirms metadata contention, and the worker profile confirms decoding consumes the host CPU budget; the drained completed-batch queue connects these limits to input starvation. Sequential shards reduce per-file metadata demand, and GPU decoding is a candidate when the supported decoder, available compute, and HBM budget permit it. Compare completed-batch throughput and input wait after each change. High host CPU activity and idle data disks alone would not prove both causes.
Learning Objective: Evaluate composite storage and host-CPU data loading bottlenecks from multi-tier cluster telemetry and prescribe architectural remediations
Synthesize how the ML storage hierarchy (spanning HBM, DRAM, NVMe, PFS, Object Storage, and Archive) co-designs bandwidth physics with capacity economics to prevent accelerator starvation.
Answer: The hierarchy places small, frequently accessed working sets near compute and larger datasets and checkpoint histories on cheaper tiers. HBM serves internal tensor traffic; DRAM supports preprocessing and buffers, NVMe stages inputs and snapshots, and shared durable tiers retain authoritative artifacts. Workload input bytes and compute time size delivery, while measured service rates, tail latency, and cache misses determine buffering. Prefetching hides bounded delays but cannot overcome a sustained rate deficit, and durability claims depend on the chosen service contract.
Learning Objective: Explain how the ML storage hierarchy balances bandwidth physics and capacity economics to sustain high accelerator utilization
Generation g is durably committed and retained. Training resumes after locally staging all shards of g+1, but a node fails before durable publication of g+1 and its required shard is lost. Which generation may restore, and what evidence is required before g+1 could become a restore candidate?
Answer: Restore the retained committed generation g after verifying its manifest and shards. Resuming training after local staging does not publish g+1; the lost required shard prevents that generation from satisfying the restore contract. Before g+1 becomes a candidate, every expected same-step shard must be durably persisted and verified against the generation manifest, which is published last using the backend’s atomic publication primitive.
Learning Objective: Apply the distinction between local staging and durable checkpoint publication to a failure trace

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why does storage become the invisible bottleneck that prevents accelerators from reaching their potential?
A training job can leave expensive accelerators idle even when its models fit in memory and its network has ample capacity. The next batch must arrive before computation needs it, and a saved checkpoint must remain usable when a worker fails. Storage becomes an invisible bottleneck because accelerator benchmarks often begin with data already in place, excluding the work needed to deliver inputs and preserve results. A pipeline that keeps one machine busy can fail when many workers compete for the same data source. A burst of checkpoint writes from one job can delay input reads for others, turning a local pause into lost progress across the fleet. Adding compute increases demand without necessarily increasing the shared system’s ability to serve it. The consequences depend on the workload: compact training inputs may be easy to deliver even when saving model state dominates storage traffic, while larger samples can make continuous input delivery the limiting factor. Bringing data closer to the accelerator reduces some delays but adds staging traffic, capacity cost, and responsibility for preserving complete versions. A faster local save also provides little protection if the only copy disappears with the failed machine. Storage decisions therefore determine both how quickly the fleet advances and how much of that progress survives disruption. In C³ terms, storage design coordinates data movement and durable state so that available compute produces recoverable progress.

Learning Objectives

Compare storage demands of full-corpus training, checkpoint writes, and model serving across local and shared tiers
Calculate input bandwidth and mean cache service time from workload demand and tier behavior
Design prefetching, sharding, locality, and direct-storage paths that reduce fleet-scale accelerator starvation
Specify storage commit and replay contracts that preserve correctness when distributed pipeline stages fail
Select checkpoint staging and replication strategies that balance pause time, recovery risk, and storage cost
Evaluate staging and tiering choices by total delivery cost, including transfer fees and idle accelerators
Assess retrieval indexes and synthetic-data pipelines as storage workloads with distinct latency, consistency, and governance constraints

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
The dense accelerator nodes of Compute Infrastructure pack eight GPUs delivering petaFLOP/s of aggregate compute, and the InfiniBand fabrics of Network Fabrics connect thousands of such nodes at hundreds of gigabits per second. Within the multi-tier fleet stack diagrammed in The Fleet Stack, data storage completes that physical foundation, staging training data, model weights, optimizer state, and intermediate checkpoints at the right distance from the accelerator. An engine without fuel is expensive sculpture. The engineering question is how to deliver that fuel fast enough that the accelerators of a training cluster never starve. This chapter poses that question on 256 eight-GPU nodes, 2,048 accelerators in all, deliberately twice the 1,024-GPU (128-node) reference cluster used elsewhere in this book, because the larger fleet makes the pressure on shared storage easier to see. Every worked number for the 175B job uses this running cluster; a side scenario with a different workload or fleet size names its own scale where it appears.



Storage is the physical substrate spanning Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)), Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)), and Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)).
Consider the running example for the storage analysis, an instance of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3). A 175-billion parameter language model trains on 1.5 trillion tokens of text: roughly 3 TB in compressed source form, or 6 TB once represented as 4-byte token IDs. That token budget is set upstream of storage. Under the compute-optimal scaling results of AI Scaling Laws, the training-token count grows in proportion to parameter count, so each step up the model-size curve enlarges both the corpus the fleet must hold and the bytes each epoch must read. This corpus already sits below the compute-optimal allocation for a 175B-parameter model, so a compute-optimal run would raise both figures further. The run makes a single pass (one epoch) over this corpus, reading every selected token once in an order determined by the shuffle seed. No small “hot” subset dominates access. Meanwhile, each accelerator processes its local batch in roughly 200 ms, then waits for the next. If storage cannot deliver data within that 200 ms window, the accelerator sits idle, and the organization pays for silicon that produces heat instead of gradients.
The problem is deceptive because storage technology has improved substantially. Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) drives achieve 7 GB/s of sequential throughput, a figure that would have seemed out of reach a decade ago. An H100 moves data internally through high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at 3.35 TB/s, roughly 479× the sequential bandwidth of a single NVMe drive. This ratio contrasts two tiers; it is not the rate at which storage must supply training inputs, because HBM bandwidth also carries repeated weight, activation, and tensor traffic during computation. The storage feed requirement is instead determined by the input-batch bytes each accelerator needs per iteration. Dividing those bytes by the compute window gives one worker’s required delivery rate; summing across workers gives the fleet demand. That rate must be evaluated at each tier using the representation stored there, since compressed inputs and decoded tensors occupy different numbers of bytes. A hierarchy becomes useful when the durable source cannot meet that rate or its latency varies enough to interrupt computation. Faster tiers stage upcoming batches while the durable tier supplies capacity and preserves the source data.
The storage problem joins physics with economics. Physics favors the memory closest to the accelerator, which offers the highest bandwidth in the smallest capacity; economics favors shared storage, which pools far more capacity at lower cost per byte behind additional interfaces and service queues. Device technology, interconnects, and contention then determine the rate a particular consumer actually receives. The engineering task is to place and move data so that the accelerator receives each batch before it is needed. The resulting design problem is quantitative. It asks how fast each tier must be, how deep the pipeline must run, and which bytes are worth keeping close to the accelerator. Improving arithmetic throughput alone does not improve input delivery or checkpoint persistence. Those paths require their own bandwidth and latency budgets.



Over the run, checkpoint writes exceed one epoch of training-data reads by more than 1,000 times.
The canonical training-data footprint for this example is roughly 9 TB across the hierarchy, combining the example’s compressed corpus and tokenized shards. Additional shuffled or packed variants can raise the staging footprint, but the per-epoch training read over 4-byte token IDs is 6 TB. This chapter adopts one resumable mixed-precision Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) checkpoint contract: FP16 model weights, FP32 master weights, and two FP32 Adam moments, for 14 bytes per parameter. This is the 16-byte training state of Node memory partitioning without its 2-byte FP16 gradients, which are recomputed after restore, while scheduler, random-number-generator, and data-loader metadata are negligible at this scale. The resulting checkpoint is 2,450 GB every 10 minutes.
Over a 30-day training run on the 256-node cluster, the storage system must deliver 6 TB of tokenized training data in the run’s single epoch, absorb 10.6 PB of checkpoint writes, and stage model weights for evaluation runs. The sections that follow use this same contract for every checkpoint size, duration, retention total, and lifetime-write calculation.
Those numbers force the storage path. ML access patterns first invert the assumptions behind conventional storage systems; that inversion forces a hierarchy from HBM to cold archive; the hierarchy then requires a pipeline equation that sizes delivery, direct data paths that remove host copies, a checkpoint protocol for the dominant write traffic, and economics that decide which bytes belong at each tier. Serving-time model loading, retrieval indexes, and synthetic-data provenance are variations on the same fuel-line problem, and devices that move the boundaries between tiers close the chapter. In each workload, the storage system must place the right representation at the right distance before the accelerator asks for it.

Self-Check: Question

An H100 accelerator consumes data from its HBM at roughly \(3.35\text{ TB/s}\), while a single local NVMe drive delivers sequential reads at roughly \(7\text{ GB/s}\). A team is designing the storage infrastructure for a 1,000-accelerator training fleet. Which conclusion follows directly from this bandwidth ratio?

The gap is easily bridged by standard NVMe RAID arrays because sequential read throughput scales without bound across drives.
The roughly \(480\times\) device-bandwidth gap motivates tiered staging, but required input bandwidth must be calculated from batch bytes and compute time rather than equated with HBM traffic.
The bandwidth gap is negligible because large-scale training is entirely compute-bound and rarely exercises HBM bandwidth.
The bandwidth gap disappears when high-speed InfiniBand fabrics deliver data directly into HBM from remote storage endpoints without local staging.

A 175B-parameter model trains for 30 days on 256 nodes, writing resumable mixed-precision Adam checkpoints of roughly \(2.45\text{ TB}\) (\(350\text{ GB}\) FP16 weights, \(700\text{ GB}\) FP32 master weights, and \(1.4\text{ TB}\) of Adam moments) every 10 minutes. Explain why ML storage design is fundamentally a joint physics-and-economics optimization problem.
True or False: A cluster benchmark demonstrating that compute hardware achieves advertised peak TFLOP/s and network fabric achieves advertised bisection bandwidth is sufficient evidence that end-to-end training throughput will scale linearly with accelerator count.
An accelerator upgrade reduces compute time per batch while the input representation and storage delivery time remain fixed. What is the primary systems consequence for training cluster design?

Training pipelines automatically increase data compression ratios to prevent accelerator starvation without requiring architectural adjustments.
Storage hierarchies can eliminate intermediate DRAM and NVMe caching tiers because modern network fabrics directly absorb the difference.
Checkpoint intervals must be decreased proportionally to the compute growth to keep local NVMe buffers from overflowing.
The compute window available to deliver each batch shrinks, so input I/O can become the bottleneck unless the measured delivery path keeps pace.

In large-scale distributed training, when hundreds of nodes simultaneously pause computation to write gigabytes of model weights and optimizer states to persistent storage, the resulting synchronized burst of write traffic is called a ____.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
A database administrator moving to an ML infrastructure team would find that full-corpus pretraining workloads invert many familiar storage design principles. The 175B running example makes the inversion concrete. Its training pass reads every selected token once, in shuffled order, and a run that makes several passes reshuffles the same corpus for each one. Under this scenario, no small “hot” subset dominates access. Fine-tuning, curriculum learning, hard-example mining, recommendation features, and retrieval do create skewed working sets, so the inversion is a workload property rather than a universal property of ML.
Transactional databases emphasize small random accesses and strong consistency. A database server might issue thousands of 4 KB reads per second to serve user queries. Storage designs for this workload combine caching algorithms that exploit repeated access, write-ahead logs that support recovery, and redundant array of independent disks (RAID)1 configurations that trade capacity and performance for fault tolerance. The caching layers assume that recently accessed data will soon be accessed again. A full-corpus training scan breaks that assumption and changes the access pattern, while retaining the need to protect durable state.
1 RAID (redundant array of independent disks): A Berkeley taxonomy of drive-combining strategies that trade redundancy, capacity, and I/O performance (Patterson et al. 1988). RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy and can suit a disposable cache backed by a durable source. A drive failure then requires restaging; redundancy may still be worthwhile when that recovery cost or the required availability justifies it. Unreplicated checkpoints and sole dataset copies require a different durability contract.
Patterson, David A., Garth Gibson, and Randy H. Katz. 1988. “A Case for Redundant Arrays of Inexpensive Disks (RAID).” Proceedings of the 1988 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 109–16. https://doi.org/10.1145/50202.50214.
Full-corpus pretraining inverts these assumptions when samples are packaged into sequential shards, allowing the pipeline to stream through datasets that span hundreds of terabytes. Individual accesses are large (megabytes rather than kilobytes) because models consume batches of images or text sequences. Immutable, versioned training shards avoid read-write conflicts during a run; checkpoint publication and live feature updates still require explicit consistency guarantees. Image and video workloads can demand hundreds of gigabytes per second for days or weeks; compact tokenized text can require much less input bandwidth even when checkpoint writes dominate total traffic. The mismatch between what storage was optimized for and what ML actually needs creates the I/O wall (principle \(\ref{pri-io-wall}\)): when storage throughput cannot deliver training data as fast as accelerators consume it, GPUs idle regardless of their computational power. For bandwidth-heavy image and video inputs, that wall arrives when accelerator count grows faster than provisioned storage throughput, making the data pipeline, not the model, the limiting factor.


↪ How storage stalls surface as communication or coordination bottlenecks in the C\(^3\) taxonomy is developed in Storage as the persistent substrate.
A simple shard-assignment calculation shows how this bottleneck can emerge even when aggregate storage capacity looks ample.

Napkin Math 4.1: The thundering herd: Shard contentionProblem: A dataset is split into 1000 shards on a shared file system. If 32 workers each pick a shard at random to start their next epoch, what is the probability that at least two GPUs “collide” on the same shard, creating a potential read hotspot? A shard collision does not imply a server collision unless the placement maps each shard to a distinct server.
Math: This is a variant of the “Birthday Problem” in probability.

Probability of No Collision: \(\approx e^{-\ShardReaderCount^2/(2\DatasetShardCount)} = e^{-32^2/2{,}000} \approx 0.60\).
Probability of Contention: \(1 - 0.60 = 40\%\).

Systems insight: With 32 workers and 1,000 shards, the 40.1 percent collision probability identifies a potential storage-shard hotspot. Whether that collision delays workers depends on shard placement, caching, and available service capacity. Coordinating shard assignments can reduce this source of tail latency when assignments spread demand across independently serving devices while preserving the intended sampling policy.


Shard collisions are one runtime symptom of the I/O wall. Even without contention, a fixed input service time can become the limiting stage when compute becomes faster.

Systems Perspective 4.1: The moving I/O bottleneckHold the batch representation and storage path fixed while improving compute throughput. The batch now finishes sooner, leaving less time to deliver the next one. Prefetching can overlap delivery with execution, but it cannot overcome a sustained service-rate deficit. This compute-to-storage imbalance does not imply that every larger model is input bound: a model that performs more computation on the same batch can instead give storage more time. The design must follow workload service times, not advertised peak-throughput trends.


A normalized example isolates the effect. Suppose input delivery takes one quarter of the original compute time and overlaps perfectly with computation, so each batch takes the longer of the two service times. Doubling compute speed halves batch time, and quadrupling it halves batch time again, at which point compute and delivery take equal time. Beyond that point the pipeline is delivery bound. A sixteenfold faster accelerator still raises batch throughput only fourfold, and the remaining compute sits idle behind the input path. That plateau is an I/O wall for this workload and allocation. Faster storage, a more compact representation, or additional independent input paths can move it; deeper prefetching alone cannot.
The first inversion is access pattern. Where database workloads exhibit random access patterns that benefit from seek-time optimization, full-corpus pretraining performs massive sequential scans. An epoch in the running example reads each selected sample once, in the order produced by shard and buffer shuffling. This pattern resembles video streaming more than database queries. Storage systems optimized for random IOPS2 waste capabilities on this workload, while systems optimized for sequential throughput excel. The distinction is quantitatively dramatic: a Gen4/Gen5 NVMe drive delivers roughly 7–14 GB/s for sequential reads, while small 4 KB random reads can fall near 0.5 GB/s, an order-of-magnitude to 30\(\times\) penalty for the wrong access pattern. The penalty is even more severe on hard drives, where mechanical seek times impose a 100\(\times\) throughput reduction for random access compared to sequential.
2 IOPS (Input/Output Operations Per Second): The metric that dominated storage procurement for decades because database workloads issue millions of small random reads. ML training inverts this priority: a pipeline streaming 256 MB shards sequentially needs sustained GB/s throughput, not per-operation speed. Provisioning storage by IOPS rating for an ML workload over-spends on random-access capability the pipeline never exercises.The shuffling that ML training requires adds a complication rooted in the requirements of stochastic gradient descent. Stochastic gradient descent requires that each mini-batch be drawn approximately uniformly from the training distribution; presenting samples in a correlated order (all samples from the same document, all images from the same class) biases the gradient estimates and slows or destabilizes convergence. True global shuffling would satisfy this requirement perfectly, but it requires random access across the entire dataset, destroying the sequential access pattern that storage hardware demands. Even for a multi-terabyte corpus, random per-sample seeks are I/O-prohibitive: a dataset of 1 trillion 4-byte tokens (about 4 TB) stored as individual elements on NVMe, accessed at random, would take hundreds to thousands of hours to read at the drive’s random-read IOPS rate rather than about ten minutes of sequential streaming. The practical solution is therefore a compromise: shuffle the order of large data shards, then shuffle samples within each shard’s local buffer. This preserves sequential I/O, but adequate mixing depends on shard composition, buffer size, and the intended sampling policy. Larger shards do not add diversity when their samples remain homogeneous or the buffer sees only a small correlated window. Finer shards or larger mixing buffers can improve mixing; compare the loss curve with a fully shuffled baseline on a subset before committing the run.
The second inversion is working set size. Traditional applications exhibit temporal locality: a web server repeatedly accesses popular pages, and a cache holding the top 10 percent of content serves 90 percent of requests. In the chapter’s full-corpus pretraining scenario, the 6 TB serialized corpus has no “popular” token range; each selected token is consumed once per epoch. A cache of any practical size holds only a small fraction of the corpus, and most samples are effectively “cold” when accessed. This access pattern makes traditional recency caching much less effective. A least recently used (LRU)3 cache can approach a 0 percent hit rate for a cyclic scan larger than the cache. With independently reshuffled epochs, cross-epoch hits are low but nonzero and depend on the cache fraction and sample order.
3 LRU (Least Recently Used): LRU is effective when recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon; a cyclic full-dataset scan larger than the cache can evict each sample before its next access and drive the hit rate toward zero. Independent reshuffling changes the boundary behavior because some samples retained from the end of one epoch may be reused before eviction in the next, so the hit rate depends on the cache-to-dataset ratio and ordering rather than being universally zero. Teams should measure this reuse before allocating DRAM that could otherwise serve as prefetch buffers.Other training policies create different locality. Multi-task or curriculum learning, hard-example mining, and filtered sampling access some subsets more frequently during particular phases. This temporary working set lets the NVMe tier exploit locality. Large-scale pretraining jobs that repeatedly scan a fixed corpus remain the scenario for the hierarchy derived here; systems serving another sampling policy should measure its reuse distribution before adopting the same cache design.
The third inversion is write pattern. Transactional systems generate continuous streams of small writes, each immediately durable. ML systems generate occasional massive writes when saving checkpoints. A 175B parameter model checkpoint, including optimizer state, occupies roughly 2,450 GB. Saving it every 10 minutes generates concentrated bursts that saturate bandwidth for seconds, followed by long idle periods. These synchronized bursts, called checkpoint storms and defined formally in definition 4.5, must be absorbed by the shared file system without disrupting ongoing training reads. The bursty write pattern is particularly challenging because all nodes in the cluster write their checkpoint shards simultaneously. If 256 nodes each write 10 GB, the parallel file system receives 2.4 TB of writes in a single burst, which blocks training if the job writes synchronously to that tier. Local staging and asynchronous replication can shorten this pause, as section 4.6 develops. When checkpoint and gradient traffic share one fabric, traffic isolation also keeps the burst from delaying the job’s collectives.


↩︎ Traffic isolation and quality-of-service mechanisms are established in Traffic isolation and quality of service.
The fourth inversion is subtler. The read/write ratio shifts dramatically by lifecycle phase. During the intervals between checkpoints, the input pipeline reads continuously. Across a complete run, however, the read/write ratio depends on input size, epoch count, checkpoint size, and save frequency. The running language-model example produces far more checkpoint bytes than training-input bytes despite spending most of its time between saves. During data preprocessing, both reads and writes are heavy, and the access pattern more closely resembles a MapReduce job than a training loop: tokenization, deduplication, and shuffling scan the raw corpus once (large sequential reads), write intermediate artifacts (large sequential writes), and then scan those artifacts again for the next stage. A 3 TB compressed text corpus typically expands to 6 TB of tokenized shards before the first training epoch begins, loading each storage tier differently from the read-only training phase that follows. No single storage configuration optimizes for all phases, which is why ML systems require a multi-tier hierarchy rather than a single storage technology.
A fifth inversion emerges when comparing training and inference workloads. Training reads datasets sequentially and writes checkpoints in bursts. Weight-resident inference, by contrast, performs one large model read at startup and then serves requests from HBM. Its storage challenge is cold-start latency: the time required to load a model when scaling up or recovering from failure. The binding constraint flips from sustained dataset throughput to a bulk read whose duration depends on which tier supplies the weights. Retrieval, state offload, and models larger than aggregate HBM create additional serving-time I/O, so this weight-resident case is a baseline rather than a universal inference pattern. Section 4.8 derives the load times and connects that baseline to the retrieval workload that follows.
When scaling from a single user to thousands of concurrent inference requests, the storage challenge shifts from a single-stream throughput problem to a massive fan-out distribution problem. A serving cluster with 100 replicas of our 175B parameter model holds 35 TB of FP16 model weights across the cluster. When a new model version is deployed (a model rollout), all 100 replicas must be updated, triggering a 35 TB data distribution event that must complete within minutes to minimize serving disruption. This is analogous to the checkpoint storm in training but in reverse. Instead of many nodes writing to a central location simultaneously, many nodes are reading the same data simultaneously. The storage system must sustain this burst read bandwidth for model distribution while continuing to serve inference requests from the existing model version without degradation.



Table 1: ML Workloads Invert Traditional Storage Assumptions: The five inversions of full-corpus training and serving. Where databases optimize for random IOPS with cacheable working sets, ML training streams sequentially through datasets that exceed all cache levels and writes state in bursts, its read/write balance shifts by lifecycle phase, and serving replaces dataset streaming with bulk model loads.










Workload Pattern
Traditional Assumption
ML Reality




Access pattern
Random access
Sequential streaming


Working set
Fits in cache, with strong temporal locality
Exceeds all cache levels; low locality in full-corpus scans


Write pattern
Continuous small writes
Bursty large writes


Read/write ratio
Balanced
Phase-dependent (read-only to write-dominated)


Training vs. inference
One access pattern for all phases
Corpus streaming in training; bulk model loads and fan-out in serving






Table 1 collects the five inversions, and together they reduce to one procurement rule, which is to optimize for streaming reads and bursty writes rather than database-style random IOPS. An organization provisioning storage for ML based on database-era heuristics will over-invest in random IOPS for sequential training shards, under-invest in the sustained bandwidth those shards require, and fail to account for the bursty write patterns that checkpointing creates.

Checkpoint 4.1: Storage workload analysis
Consider the storage subsystem for a new ML training cluster with 512 GPUs. The primary workload will train large language models on a 10 TB text dataset.

Database heuristics: use the five storage workload inversions to name at least three database optimization strategies that would be counterproductive for this workload.
Epoch reads: calculate the total data volume read when each training epoch reads the full 10 TB dataset once and the cluster trains for 100 epochs, then compare it to a typical database workload.
Checkpoint bandwidth: calculate the minimum write bandwidth required when the model saves a 500 GB checkpoint every 15 minutes and each save must complete within 30 seconds.
Write duty cycle: calculate the percentage of time the storage system spends in “write mode” vs. “read mode” under bursty checkpoints every 15 minutes.



Which storage tier can keep accelerators fed depends on workload demand, not on a model’s parameter count. The required rate is the aggregate input bytes consumed during a delivery window divided by that window, and demand above a tier’s allocated service rate cannot be sustained by prefetching alone. A larger model need not require a higher input rate, because representation, batch size, parallelism, and compute time jointly determine it; section 4.4 turns that dependence into a sizing equation. Adding clients can raise the aggregate service a shared tier provides, while contention lowers the share available to any one job.
The practical consequence for the running example is stark. The 1.5 trillion tokens of training data produce roughly 6 TB of sequential token-ID reads per epoch, even though the compressed source corpus is only 3 TB. Stored as one file per sample, the corpus would spend its storage service on file opens rather than payload bytes, a metadata request rate rather than a byte rate that section 4.3.6 develops as the small file problem. Preprocessing it into large sequential shards (Aizman et al. 2019) amortizes the fixed cost of open, seek, and close across many tokens, reducing metadata demand without changing the required payload rate; section 4.3.5 compares the shard formats that make this packaging work. Where those shards should live, and how close to the accelerator, is the question the storage hierarchy answers.

Self-Check: Question

A storage procurement team is sizing storage hardware for a cluster dedicated to pretraining foundation models on a \(200\text{ TB}\) immutable text corpus. Which purchasing decision represents the most severe misallocation of budget based on ML workload characteristics?

Paying a premium for enterprise SSDs optimized for high \(4\text{ KB}\) random-read IOPS while under-provisioning sustained sequential read bandwidth (GB/s).
Aggregating raw text samples into \(256\text{ MB}\) to \(4\text{ GB}\) contiguous binary shards prior to training to amortize file-system metadata operations.
Provisioning local NVMe drives on compute nodes to serve as a warm read cache for multi-epoch training passes.
Sizing the parallel file system write tier to absorb synchronized multi-terabyte checkpoint write bursts from hundreds of nodes.

True or False: An in-memory LRU cache sized to \(300\text{ GB}\) placed in front of a \(3\text{ TB}\) uniformly shuffled pretraining dataset will achieve roughly a \(90\%\) hit rate after the first epoch warms the cache because all samples are reused across epochs.
Explain why ML data loaders implement shard-level shuffling combined with within-shard buffer mixing rather than true global per-sample random shuffling across petabyte-scale training corpora.
When an inference platform deploys a new version of a 175B-parameter model (\(350\text{ GB}\) FP16 weights) across 100 serving replicas, how does the storage access profile contrast with a training checkpoint save?

It generates continuous small random writes to update parameter journals on each replica node.
It streams an incremental delta of only modified parameters over hours to minimize bandwidth utilization.
It creates a synchronized fan-out read burst of roughly \(35\text{ TB}\) (\(100 \times 350\text{ GB}\)) that must complete within the deployment latency budget while serving traffic continues.
It requires sustained multi-gigabyte-per-second sequential write bandwidth to central durable object storage.

Order the sequence of performance degradation steps that occurs when a training cluster attempts to load a dataset stored as 200 million individual small JPEG files from a parallel file system: (1) Storage data disks and network links sit largely idle despite abundant rated bandwidth, (2) Thousands of concurrent workers execute open(), stat(), and close() system calls for every 10 KB sample, (3) The training loop stalls and GPU utilization collapses while waiting for batch collation, (4) Dedicated metadata servers (MDS) become saturated by hundreds of thousands of lock acquisitions and attribute lookups per second, (5) Data loader worker threads block on serialized file descriptor operations.

See Answers →

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
A system architect must organize storage to serve workloads that simultaneously demand terabytes-per-second bandwidth for computation, petabyte-scale capacity for datasets, and durable checkpoints. No single technology satisfies all three requirements. HBM supplies high local bandwidth at limited capacity; object storage pools durable capacity, but delivery depends on its service and client paths. A multi-tier hierarchy combines these resources rather than requiring one technology to meet every demand. Each tier offers a different balance of bandwidth, latency, capacity, and cost. The hierarchy extends the familiar processor memory hierarchy across nodes. The new fleet-level decision is how local staging reduces demand on shared storage while preserving a durable, consistently versioned source. Table 2 compares the resources at their stated device, node, and service scopes.



Table 2: Extended Memory Hierarchy for ML Systems: HBM bandwidth is per accelerator, host DRAM and local NVMe are per node, and parallel-file-system and object-storage figures are aggregate service rates. These different scopes are not directly comparable tier ratios; divide shared bandwidth among active clients and account for each client path before sizing prefetching and caching. Memory costs are acquisition dollars per GB, while storage costs are recurring dollars per GB-month; comparing them requires an explicit amortization period and utilization assumption.

A central property of table 2 is that HBM’s advantage over host DRAM is bandwidth, not latency. Random-access latency for both technologies sits in the ~80–150 ns range; HBM achieves its bandwidth lead (10–20\(\times\)) through thousands of parallel traces on a silicon interposer and 3D stacking, not faster cells. The latency cliff between adjacent tiers only opens up at NVMe and below, where the physical distance from the accelerator grows from millimeters to meters.
The storage hierarchy model (principle \(\ref{pri-storage-hierarchy}\)) governs storage tiering and pipeline design. The local tiers exchange bandwidth for capacity, while shared tiers aggregate many devices and expose a different client path. The per-client bandwidth depends on allocation and contention rather than a fixed factor between tiers. Data format choices, caching strategies, prefetch buffer sizing, and tiering policies all exist to manage the movement of data upward through the hierarchy so that the accelerator never starves.
The rest of the chapter numbers the six tiers by distance from the accelerator, from Tier 0 (HBM) through Tier 1 (host DRAM), Tier 2 (local NVMe), Tier 3 (parallel file system), and Tier 4 (object storage) to Tier 5 (archive). Distance alone hides an important distinction, because each tier’s bandwidth figure describes a different scope: per accelerator, per node, or a shared service divided among its clients (figure 1).







Figure 1: ML storage hierarchy: The six tiers of table 2 stacked by distance from the accelerator, with band width showing schematically how capacity grows toward the base; the table carries the numbers. The left brackets give the scope of each tier’s bandwidth figure, and each glyph shows what shares it: one accelerator, the accelerators of one node, or many nodes drawing on one aggregate shared service. The right column gives the physical path each byte travels to reach the accelerator. Blue memory tiers are bought per GB; green storage tiers are rented or provisioned per GB-month; the gray archive tier is offline media.



The physical tiers diagrammed in figure 1 govern the trade-off among access distance, capacity, and cost. Shared services can aggregate more bandwidth than an individual local device, so the ordering is not a monotonic ranking of aggregate throughput. This trade-off is not arbitrary; it reflects the physics of data proximity. HBM sits on the same silicon interposer as the accelerator, connected by thousands of parallel traces measured in millimeters. Host DRAM connects to the CPU memory controller; transfers from host memory to the accelerator traverse the host-device interconnect. NVMe reaches across a circuit board via a PCIe connector. The parallel file system traverses meters of cable and network switches. Object storage may span kilometers of fiber between data centers. Distance, protocol overhead, and contention can increase access latency, while media technology and provisioning determine capacity cost. Distance is therefore a guide rather than a measurement; only the complete client path establishes all three properties for a given consumer.
The engineering challenge is to deliver each batch to HBM before the accelerator needs it. Return to the running example: the durable corpus lives in object storage (Tier 4) as a 3 TB compressed source copy plus 6 TB of tokenized training shards, but the accelerator needs each batch in HBM (Tier 0) within 200 ms. The chapter’s reference design fixes one path between them. At job start, each node copies its share of the tokenized shards from object storage to its local NVMe (Tier 2); the single training epoch then reads from that local copy, prepares batches in host DRAM, and transfers them to HBM, while the parallel file system (Tier 3) holds checkpoints rather than training inputs. Streaming the shards directly from object storage, or serving them from a parallel file system, are the alternatives the chapter weighs against this design, and the hierarchy describes placement choices, not a requirement that every byte visit every level.


The bandwidth ratios between adjacent tiers reveal the severity of each transition in the hierarchy only when the scope of each rate is explicit, because a per-accelerator, per-node, or shared-service figure describes a different resource, as bracketed in figure 1. For one accelerator’s HBM compared with the whole host’s DRAM, the illustrative ratio is roughly 16.8× (3.35 TB/s vs. ~200 GB/s). A node-level comparison must account for all eight accelerators sharing that host-memory bandwidth. Between host DRAM and NVMe, the ratio is roughly 7.1× (200 GB/s vs. ~28 GB/s from a 4-drive RAID-0). Between NVMe and a parallel file system, the ratio depends on the per-node allocation: if a 1 TB/s aggregate parallel file system (PFS) serves 256 nodes, each node receives roughly 4 GB/s, a 7× reduction from the local RAID-0 stripe. Object-storage throughput likewise depends on the client path and allocation; there is no fixed ratio to a parallel file system.



Per-client bandwidth falls roughly 7 to 17\(\times\) at each step from HBM to a node’s share of the parallel file system.
As section 4.1 established, a cliff is not a feed requirement; the feed rate remains input-batch bytes divided by iteration time, summed over distinct consumers. What the cliffs decide is where buffering must sit. Along the chosen path, host DRAM can buffer prepared batches and NVMe can cache shards from shared storage. Each buffer must cover the delay of the tier below it while that tier sustains the consumption rate; durable repositories need not act as intermediate buffers.
The same hierarchy can be analyzed as a cache rather than as six isolated devices. If a request hits the hot tier with probability \(\HotTierHitProbability\), taking \(\HotTierServiceTime\), and otherwise falls through to a colder tier, taking total end-to-end miss-path time \(\MissPathServiceTime\) (including the failed hot-tier lookup), its mean service time is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\TieredRequestServiceTime] = \HotTierHitProbability \HotTierServiceTime+ (1-\HotTierHitProbability)\MissPathServiceTime.
\tag{1}\]
For fixed-size records served serially, the corresponding effective bandwidth is the record size divided by \(\mathbb{E}[\TieredRequestServiceTime]\). The arithmetic makes small miss rates consequential: with a 95 percent hit rate and a cold-tier access 100\(\times\) slower than a hot-tier access, \(\mathbb{E}[\TieredRequestServiceTime]=5.95\HotTierServiceTime\), so the effective request rate is only about one-sixth of the all-hot rate. Concurrent requests and prefetching can overlap service, so this mean is a sizing baseline rather than a fleet-throughput or latency guarantee. Correlated misses or a heavy-tailed cold tier can drain the prefetch buffer even when the average satisfies the pipeline budget, so production designs must check a tail percentile and miss bursts as well as \(\mathbb{E}[\TieredRequestServiceTime]\).
The batch-volume arithmetic also explains why increasing cluster size creates storage pressure. Aggregate demand is each consumer’s batch bytes divided by its compute window, summed over consumers, so at a fixed per-node rate it grows linearly with node count. The per-node rate itself spans orders of magnitude across data modalities, as text and image training on the running cluster show.



Image training demands 1,800× the storage bandwidth of text.

Napkin Math 4.2: Text vs. image bandwidthProblem: How much aggregate storage bandwidth does a 2,048-GPU cluster require for text training vs. image training?
Setup: Compare two declared batch representations at the same compute window and number of independent input consumers. The result depends on batch volume and rate, not modality alone. Both jobs are generic ones sized to the running cluster, not the 175B running job. Each GPU consumes one per-GPU batch every step, a pace that fits a model far smaller than 175B parameters.
For text training, the demand is surprisingly low. With a per-GPU batch of one packed sequence of 4,096 tokens and a 200 ms step time, the aggregate bandwidth is:
\[2{,}048 \text{ GPUs} \times 4{,}096 \text{ tokens/GPU} \times 4 \text{ bytes/token} \div 0.2\text{s} \approx {167.8 MB/s}\]
This is easily served by a single network-attached storage node.
For image training, the picture changes dramatically. Using a common batch size of 256 per GPU (ImageNet at \(224{\times}224\), roughly 116 KB/image), the aggregate bandwidth explodes:
\[2{,}048 \text{ GPUs} \times 256 \text{ images/GPU} \times 115.7 \text{ KB/image} \div 0.2\text{s} \approx {303.2 GB/s}\]
Systems insight: Under the stated batch representations and compute times, image training requires 1,800× higher input bandwidth than text training. The text example is volume-heavy but bandwidth-light. One network-attached storage server can carry its input feed, so its storage design is shaped by total corpus volume and, as later sections show, by checkpoint traffic. The image example is bandwidth-heavy, with a feed that exceeds any single storage server and calls for the aggregate bandwidth of many servers or of local caches. Whether either demand becomes an actual bottleneck still depends on the measured delivery rate of the path that serves it.


The 175B running job sits lower still. Its 6 TB epoch spread over the 30-day window averages about 2.3 MB/s for the whole cluster, corpus bytes divided by run length, roughly 70× below the notebook’s generic text job. Each token of a 175B model carries so much computation that the corpus trickles in, which is why the running example’s storage design is shaped by checkpoint traffic rather than by its input feed.
The image result is a floor for visual data rather than a ceiling. At about 303.2 GB/s across 256 nodes, the image job already consumes nearly a third of a 1 TB/s parallel file system built from 100 data-serving nodes (the architecture section 4.3.6 develops). Higher-resolution images and video clips, at megabytes per sample rather than the roughly 116 KB of a compressed ImageNet image, raise the per-node demand by an order of magnitude or more, and a fleet several times larger multiplies it again. Demand at that scale exceeds what a shared file system of this size can serve, so the architecture must rely on local NVMe caching to take repeated reads off shared storage.
The bandwidth cliff between tiers also has implications for the data format at each level. Computation consumes float16 tensors, packed token IDs, or other supported representations, while NVMe and object storage can retain compressed records. Compression reduces bytes stored and transferred but adds decoding work. The chosen format must let CPU or GPU decoding keep pace with consumption; maximum compression can reduce end-to-end throughput when decoding becomes the limiting stage. A host-decoded path stages the resulting tensors in DRAM, while a GPU-decoded path moves the transformation and its resource demand to the accelerator.
The format challenge intensifies for multi-modal training, which combines text, images, audio, and video in a single model. Serialized sizes span orders of magnitude, from 4 bytes per text token to roughly 116 KB per compressed image to megabytes per short video clip, depending on representation, compression, resolution, and duration, and each modality requires its own decoding and augmentation work. A multi-modal training job must manage these parallel streams and provision for their combined service demand. For a corpus containing 3 TB of text, 50 TB of images, and 200 TB of video, video dominates retained capacity. Its bandwidth contribution also depends on how frequently training samples it and how many bytes each sampled batch reads. Corpus size alone determines neither the delivery rate nor the modality’s contribution to model quality.
The descent starts where computation actually consumes bytes: HBM, the tier fast enough to keep accelerator arithmetic fed but far too scarce to hold the full training corpus.



The scarcest resource in the system sits closest to the arithmetic. On the H100 used here, HBM holds the active weights and activations served to the accelerator, while caches and on-chip buffers reuse portions of that state. Its stacked packaging supplies 3.35 TB/s of aggregate bandwidth, the top of the cliffs just measured. That bandwidth is what makes large-scale deep learning feasible, because a matrix multiplication involving billions of parameters reads those parameters from memory on every forward and backward pass. What HBM lacks is room.


↩︎ High-bandwidth memory packaging, the 3D stacking and through-silicon vias behind this bandwidth, is established in HBM and the memory wall.
For placing the unpartitioned running model, the immediate constraint is capacity. Once state fits, HBM bandwidth can still limit execution. An H100 provides 80 GB of HBM, enough to hold a 40-billion parameter model in FP16 (2 bytes per parameter), but nowhere near enough for the 175B parameter running example. The training budget for the 175B model shows how far short one device falls. The model weights in FP16 consume 350 GB. FP16 gradients require another 350 GB. The Adam optimizer maintains two additional states (momentum and variance) in FP32, consuming \(175 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times 2 = 1{,}400\text{ GB}\). Activations for a single batch, depending on sequence length and batch size, can consume another 100 to 400 GB. The node-memory subtotal of Node memory partitioning stops at weights, Adam moments, and gradients; the mixed-precision contract this chapter checkpoints also retains 700 GB of FP32 master weights, which is why the total here is larger. Weights, gradients, master weights, and Adam moments therefore occupy 2.80 TB before activations and communication buffers. This capacity pressure is precisely why the partitioning in table 3 is mandatory. From the storage hierarchy perspective, HBM is the destination that every lower tier exists to serve. The data pipeline’s purpose is to ensure that the 80 GB of HBM always contains the data the accelerator needs next, not the data it needed a second ago.
Because HBM capacity is so limited relative to both model size and dataset size, the accelerator processes data in batches. Each batch occupies a fraction of HBM for the duration of one forward-backward pass, then is discarded to make room for the next. The rate at which batches must be supplied sets the bandwidth requirement for all lower tiers.
That batch lifecycle sits inside a much larger resident footprint, and the footprint creates a “spill” dynamic down the hierarchy. When state does not fit in one HBM pool, the system has only two basic choices: split it across accelerators, or keep some of it outside HBM and fetch it when needed. The FP16 weights alone, 350 GB, need at least five 80 GB H100 accelerators, and Adam’s FP32 moments add another 1.4 TB. Splitting this footprint across the cluster makes the run possible, but every shard becomes a separate piece of state that lower tiers must stage, save, and restore in step with the others. HBM scarcity is what forces the rest of the hierarchy to exist.
The razor-thin margin is a defining feature of large model training. Table 3 shows the HBM memory budget that each 80 GB H100 carries while the fleet trains the 175B parameter model. The table treats partitioning as a storage layout, and the chapter keeps this one layout throughout. Tensor parallelism splits the model weights eight ways inside each node, so every node holds one complete copy of the weights spread across its GPUs. Optimizer, master-weight, and gradient state are additionally sharded across the 256 nodes, so each GPU holds only its slice of that state rather than a full replica. Sharding optimizer and gradient state across data-parallel replicas while each replica keeps its weights is the second stage of the Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO), a training technique in its own right; its third stage also partitions the weights. Here only the resulting per-GPU slices matter, because they set the storage pressure HBM sees.


↪ Sharded data parallelism (ZeRO and FSDP), which partitions optimizer, gradient, and weight state across workers, is developed in Memory-efficient data parallelism with ZeRO and FSDP.



Table 3: HBM Memory Budget for 175B-Parameter Training: Per-GPU allocation when splitting a 175B model eight ways inside the node and sharding optimizer and gradient state across 256 nodes. The optimizer, master-weight, and gradient rows are per-GPU shards after both levels of partitioning. The resulting budget occupies most of a 80 GB HBM device, leaving limited buffer for the incoming data pipeline. Any delay in fetching the next batch from host memory risks starving the accelerator.









Component
Size per GPU




Model Weights (FP16, 8-way shard)
43.75 GB


Optimizer State (node-sharded)
0.7 GB

0.34 GB
