Even with aggressive partitioning, the total memory footprint reaches 56.9–68.9 GB in decimal gigabytes, about 66.3–80.3 percent of the HBM pool. The percentage is lower than the gigabyte figures suggest because the device’s nominal 80 GB is a binary capacity, \(80 \times 2^{30}\) bytes, slightly more than 80 decimal gigabytes. The remaining headroom shrinks further once fragmentation and framework workspaces are included, and that headroom is all the incoming data pipeline has to work with.
An input batch and its activations occupy HBM for one training step, while model weights and optimizer state persist across steps. Prefetching the next batch therefore competes with the live training footprint for scarce capacity; a deeper input queue is useful only if the memory budget can accommodate it.
From the data pipeline’s perspective, Tier 0 is not a storage tier to be managed but a constraint to be satisfied. The pipeline’s purpose is to ensure that the batch the accelerator needs next is already resident in HBM before the current batch’s computation completes. If it arrives late, the accelerator stalls. If it arrives early, it consumes HBM that could hold activations. The tension between “just in time” and “just too late” defines the pipeline’s buffer management strategy, quantified in section 4.4.



One level below HBM, host DRAM serves as the staging area for the data pipeline. Every byte of training data that reaches the accelerator passes through host DRAM first (unless GPUDirect Storage bypasses it, as described in section 4.5). A typical training node contains 512 GB to 2 TB of system memory shared across the host CPU and its peripherals. While the bandwidth between host DRAM and the accelerator is limited to what PCIe Gen 5 (about 64 GB/s per direction, 128 GB/s bidirectional) can provide, host DRAM plays three roles in the ML storage hierarchy: it is the prefetch buffer, a home for embedding tables too large for HBM, and the augmentation workspace. Only CPU-accelerator superchips with a coherent NVLink-class host link raise that path toward the 900 GB/s that NVLink provides between accelerators. The data loader occupies two of these roles at once, because its augmentation stage and the prefetch buffer it fills both live in host DRAM.
The data loader pipeline that runs in host DRAM follows four ordered stages:

Read: I/O threads read compressed data from NVMe or network storage into read buffers.
Decode: Decode threads decompress the data, such as JPEG decoding for images or decompression for text.
Augment: Augmentation threads apply transformations, including random cropping, flipping, and normalization for images or tokenization and sequence packing for text.
Collate: The collation stage assembles individual samples into batches and places them in pinned memory for efficient direct memory access (DMA) transfer to the accelerator.

That final placement matters because pinned, or page-locked, memory (exposed in PyTorch as pin_memory=True on the DataLoader) prevents the operating system from paging out the buffer before the DMA transfer completes, providing a stable host buffer for the subsequent host-to-accelerator DMA transfer. Pinning the collated batch does not make an ordinary file read a direct NVMe-to-batch transfer; storage reading and CPU preprocessing still follow their configured paths. Each stage runs concurrently, forming a pipeline that overlaps I/O, CPU computation, and data transfer. The efficiency of this pipeline determines whether host DRAM can keep up with the accelerator’s appetite.
Host DRAM’s most critical function is serving as a prefetch buffer. The CPU data loader reads data from lower tiers (NVMe or network storage), decodes compressed formats (JPEG, gzip), applies augmentations (random crops, flips, color jitter), and assembles tensors in host DRAM. When the accelerator finishes processing batch \(\BatchIndex\), batch \(\BatchIndex+1\) should already be assembled in host memory, ready for transfer to HBM. The depth of this prefetch buffer determines how much I/O variance the pipeline can absorb without stalling.
Recommendation workloads, the regime of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale), place a different demand on host DRAM: hosting embedding tables that can exceed 100 GB, far too large for HBM. These tables reside in host DRAM and are accessed through lookups that fetch only the rows needed for the current batch. The bandwidth between host DRAM and HBM becomes the critical bottleneck for these workloads, and some systems go further, pooling embedding tables in the DRAM of dedicated CPU servers and returning only the requested rows over remote direct memory access (RDMA).
Host DRAM also provides the augmentation workspace that the CPU pipeline requires. Data augmentation operations (resizing images, tokenizing text, applying noise) execute on the CPU and require temporary memory for intermediate results. A training pipeline that applies five augmentations to a 256-image batch at 116 KB per image needs tens of megabytes of working space for each augmentation stage. Although modest per-batch, this memory accumulates when multiple data loader workers run in parallel.
Some augmentation pipelines have moved from CPU to GPU execution, using libraries like NVIDIA Data Loading Library (DALI) to perform image decoding and augmentation on the accelerator itself. This approach eliminates the CPU augmentation bottleneck and reduces the host DRAM bandwidth demand, because compressed data (smaller) is transferred to the GPU instead of decoded data (larger). The trade-off is that augmentation on the GPU consumes HBM capacity and compute cycles that would otherwise be available for training. For compute-bound workloads (where the GPU is already saturated with matrix multiplications), GPU-based augmentation is counterproductive. For I/O-bound workloads (where the GPU waits for data), it can improve overall throughput by shifting work from the bottleneck (CPU) to the resource with spare capacity (GPU).
The three roles interact in subtle ways. The prefetch buffer and the augmentation workspace compete for the same physical DRAM, and embedding tables consume capacity that could otherwise serve as deeper prefetch queues. A node with 512 GB of DRAM hosting a 200 GB embedding table has only 312 GB remaining for prefetching and augmentation. If the data loader uses 8 workers, each maintaining a decode buffer of 1 GB, the effective prefetch capacity drops further. System architects must balance these competing demands by profiling the actual memory consumption of each pipeline stage and provisioning DRAM accordingly.
The physical layout of DRAM has performance implications that are invisible in single-socket benchmarks but critical at production scale. Multi-socket servers exhibit non-uniform memory access (NUMA) topology where each CPU socket has “local” DRAM that it can access at full bandwidth and “remote” DRAM attached to the other socket at roughly half bandwidth. In a dual-socket DGX node with eight GPUs split four per socket, a data loader thread running on socket 0 that allocates its prefetch buffer in socket 1’s DRAM pays a roughly 2\(\times\) bandwidth penalty on every buffer access. The fix is NUMA-aware allocation: pin each data loader worker to the same CPU socket (the same NUMA domain) as the GPUs it serves, and use numactl or libnuma to ensure memory allocation stays local. Proper NUMA pinning can improve data loading throughput by 30–50 percent on dual-socket systems, a gain that is invisible in development environments but essential when every percentage point of utilization translates to thousands of dollars per day.
Host DRAM sits below the first cliff of section 4.3.1, and the host-to-GPU interconnect adds a separate cliff, with effective transfer bandwidth depending on whether the node uses PCIe or NVLink. In the conventional path that stages payloads through host memory, a depleted DRAM prefetch buffer leaves the accelerator waiting for lower tiers. The direct path of section 4.5 removes that staging copy when the data layout and devices support it. In the running example, the 256-node cluster requires each node’s host DRAM to sustain a continuous flow of decoded, augmented batches ready for PCIe transfer. If the NVMe-to-DRAM read pipeline falls behind by even a few hundred milliseconds, the prefetch buffer drains and the accelerator idles until the next batch arrives.



When the working set exceeds host DRAM, the system falls to Tier 2: the local NVMe drives attached directly to the compute node. NVMe4 provides a high-performance protocol designed specifically for solid-state drives, achieving 7 GB/s of sequential throughput per drive. With four drives in a RAID-0 configuration, a single node can sustain roughly 28 GB/s of sequential reads before overhead, sufficient to stream the 6 TB serialized dataset from local disk in about 3.6 minutes under ideal sequential conditions.
4 NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express): A storage protocol designed for SSDs, connecting directly to the CPU via PCIe lanes. NVMe replaced Advanced Host Controller Interface (AHCI)’s single queue of 32 commands with 64K queues of 64K commands each, a 130-million-fold increase in maximum outstanding I/O. This deep queue parallelism is what allows a multi-worker ML data loader to saturate the drive’s bandwidth; under AHCI, the single 32-command queue caps the outstanding requests that many loader workers can expose, regardless of flash speed.In ML training, local NVMe acts as a warm cache, storing data shards fetched from distributed storage. Workers can reread resident shards across epochs without fetching them over the network again. The savings depend on reuse, cache capacity, and whether remote reads cross a charged transfer boundary (section 4.7). Staging pays an initial transfer cost and provisions local capacity in exchange for avoiding later remote reads; it does not eliminate storage cost or read latency.
The warm cache pattern requires careful capacity planning. A training node with four 7.68 TB NVMe drives provides approximately 30.7 TB of local storage. For the running example, the 6 TB serialized dataset fits comfortably on a single node’s local storage, with room for checkpoint staging and temporary augmentation buffers. A multi-modal training job combining 20 TB of images, 10 TB of text, and 5 TB of audio totals 35 TB, exceeding local capacity by about 4.3 TB and forcing the pipeline to stream from the parallel file system for at least part of the dataset. The design trade-off is between provisioning more local NVMe (which increases node cost) and accepting network-dependent reads (which risks latency spikes).
NVMe’s internal parallelism is key to its throughput advantage over traditional storage. A data loader with 32 workers, each issuing asynchronous reads, can keep the NVMe controller’s internal pipeline saturated because the protocol’s deep queues admit far more outstanding commands than AHCI’s single 32-command queue. This queue architecture, together with PCIe lanes that far exceed the roughly 550 MB/s ceiling of a 6 Gb/s SATA link, explains why NVMe delivers 10\(\times\) to 50\(\times\) the throughput of SATA SSDs with identical NAND flash, even though the storage medium is the same.
The I/O wall takes a deceptive form at this tier. The HBM-to-NVMe ratio of section 4.3.1 does not set demand, so the question here is whether the stripe meets the input-batch rate, not whether it approaches HBM. Pipelining overlaps that delivery with compute (section 4.4), while GPUDirect Storage (section 4.5) can remove host payload copies when those copies limit throughput. The wall is easy to miss because NVMe performance is excellent by historical standards. A storage engineer accustomed to HDD-era throughput of 150 MB/s might view 28 GB/s from a local RAID-0 stripe as superabundant. Whether 28 GB/s suffices depends on the batch representation and consumption rate. Compact text may fit within this budget, while image or video inputs may require more bandwidth; overlap hides transfer time only when sustained supply keeps pace with demand.
Local NVMe also supports local checkpoint staging. Writing a consistent snapshot locally and replicating it to shared storage in the background can shorten \(\CheckpointWriteTime\), the time training pauses to save a checkpoint, when the shared write would otherwise be slower. Resuming after a local save accepts a period during which a node failure can destroy the new shard. The storage design must therefore specify both the exposed pause and the later durability boundary, while retaining a previous recoverable generation. Section 4.6 develops this trade-off and its timing model.
The same local NVMe tier also pays for itself by recovering utilization lost to remote-read latency.

Napkin Math 4.3: Return on investment of local NVMe cachingProblem: A vision-model training pipeline, a separate workload from the 175B language model, runs each step in 800 ms on the 1,024-GPU reference cluster. It reads from a shared parallel file system, and even with prefetching, congestion bursts on that shared service drain the loader’s buffer and leave an average of 150 ms of exposed I/O wait per step. Assume that serving the same shards from local NVMe leaves only 10 ms of exposed wait per step, the residue of local tail latency that the prefetch queue does not cover. How much does adding local NVMe SSDs to each node improve GPU utilization?
Math: GPU utilization here means the fraction of step time spent in computation, an active-time fraction rather than model FLOPs utilization.

Remote Only: 800 ms / (800 ms + 150 ms) \(\approx\) 84.2 percent.
Local Cache: Prefetching from local NVMe removes the congestion bursts of the shared service, leaving the assumed local residue.

New Util: 800 ms / (800 ms + 10 ms) \(\approx\) 98.8 percent.


Systems insight: Local storage can act as a GPU utilization multiplier. In this scenario, adding a $500 NVMe drive to a node whose accelerators each cost $30,000 recovers 14.6 percent of the GPU’s capacity that was previously wasted on I/O wait. Across the 1,024-GPU cluster, that utilization gain is equivalent to adding 149 GPUs worth of useful work without buying that many more accelerators. The gain is exactly the exposed remote wait that local reads remove, so it is large only when shared-storage congestion leaves a wait of this size; where it does, local NVMe is not auxiliary but the physical buffer that decouples expensive compute from unpredictable shared storage.


A practical concern at this tier is SSD endurance. NAND flash memory can sustain a limited number of write-erase cycles before the cells degrade. Enterprise NVMe drives are rated for 1 to 3 drive writes per day (DWPD) over a 5-year lifespan. For a 7.68 TB drive at 1 DWPD, this means the drive can absorb 7.68 TB of writes per day, or roughly 14 PB total over its lifetime. ML training workloads are predominantly read-heavy (the dataset is written once and read many times), which is favorable for SSD endurance. However, checkpoint writes can be intensive: if each node saves its roughly 10 GB share of the running example’s checkpoint every 10 minutes, that is about 1.4 TB per day of checkpoint writes spread across the node’s drives, well within a four-drive node’s 1 DWPD budget. The risk emerges when local NVMe is used as a staging buffer for both checkpoint writes and dataset caching: the combined write volume from initial dataset staging plus repeated checkpoint saves must remain within the drive’s endurance rating.



Local NVMe can stream 28 GB/s per node, but packaging determines how much of that bandwidth reaches the loader. The same multi-terabyte dataset stored in different formats can yield I/O throughput that differs by over 100\(\times\) on identical hardware, because each format charges a different access cost: per-file metadata, unnecessary feature reads, or sequential shard traversal. A directory containing one JPEG per sample pays a separate file open and metadata lookup for every image. At roughly 10 to 50 microseconds per open in the kernel’s file-system layer, a node reading 8,000 images per second spends 80 to 400 ms of CPU time per second on opens alone, before it decodes a single byte. On a shared file system the same operations also queue at a metadata service, the fleet-scale form of this cost that section 4.3.6 develops as the small file problem. A standard ImageNet training pipeline makes the cost of the wrong format visible.

Napkin Math 4.4: The ImageNet bottleneck analysisProblem: A ResNet-50 training job on ImageNet (1.28M, ~116 KB average) targets 1000 images/s. Can individual JPEG files on an HDD sustain that rate, or does the job need NVMe?
Math:

Raw Bandwidth: 1000 images/s \(\times\) 116 KB = 116 MB/s.
HDD reality: A 7200 RPM hard disk drive (HDD) delivers 100 IOPS at random reads. Sustaining 1000 images/s requires 10× more IOPS than the disk provides.
Result: When every image is a separate random read, shuffling individual files on an HDD will starve the GPU, capping utilization at about 10 percent before decode, seek, and file-system overheads.

Systems insight: Two fixes work, and they remove different limits. NVMe answers a random read in roughly 100 μs rather than the milliseconds of a mechanical seek, so even one outstanding request covers the 1000 images/s that the HDD’s 100 IOPS cannot. Alternatively, converting the dataset to a sequential format (TFRecord/WebDataset) removes the random reads altogether and turns the HDD problem into a bandwidth one, in which the job needs 116 MB/s, within the roughly 150 MB/s that one HDD streams sequentially.


The first format choice is the record layout. Row-oriented formats, such as CSV or JSON lines, store successive records together and are easy to inspect and debug. They can stream many records from one file, although parsing text and reading unused fields consume CPU cycles and bandwidth.
A second choice solves a different storage problem. Columnar formats like Apache Parquet and Apache Arrow avoid unnecessary reads when tabular features can be selected before transfer. They organize data by column rather than by row, which allows for excellent compression as data within a column is typically of the same type and has lower entropy. Column pruning lets the reader fetch only required features. Predicate pushdown applies filters at the storage reader and can skip groups of records using their metadata, further reducing unnecessary I/O. These formats are well-suited for tabular ML tasks and feature engineering but are less natural for unstructured data like images or audio, which are treated as atomic blobs.
A third choice addresses the training access pattern directly. Sequential streaming formats reduce per-sample metadata to the cost of opening a shard. TFRecord, Mosaic’s StreamingDataset format (Databricks 2026), and WebDataset5 group many samples into large, contiguous binary files called shards. WebDataset uses standard tar archives, in which each sample keeps its image, label, and metadata entries while the loader streams the archive in order. A data loader opens a single shard and streams its contents sequentially, amortizing the open over thousands of samples. The tar-based formats have the added advantage of being valid targets for HTTP byte-range requests, making them ideal for streaming data directly from object storage without downloading the entire file first.
5 WebDataset: A data format that repurposes standard POSIX tar archives for ML training. The design insight is that tar’s sequential header-then-data layout, invented in 1979 for tape backup, maps perfectly onto the streaming access pattern that ML data loaders need. Because tar archives are valid HTTP byte-range targets, a data loader can stream training samples directly from object storage without staging them on a parallel file system or local NVMe first.A key trade-off within streaming formats is the presence of an index. TFRecord readers often rely on a separate index file that records each sample’s byte offset within a shard, while HDF5 embeds its index in the file itself. This enables efficient random access within a shard but introduces a metadata dependency: the index must be read and held in memory. WebDataset is indexless, because each record in the tar archive contains its own header specifying its size, allowing for purely sequential streaming without any external metadata. The trade-off is that indexless formats cannot efficiently seek to an arbitrary sample within a shard, a capability that matters for curriculum learning or active learning workloads that require nonsequential data access.
Compression integration also varies across formats, and it trades storage bytes against CPU decoding work. Parquet integrates compression at the column level, exploiting type homogeneity for high ratios. WebDataset and TFRecord typically leave compression to the individual sample: a WebDataset of images stores already-compressed JPEG files, while a text dataset might apply zstd compression per shard, and the host CPU pays for that decompression. Consider two illustrative codecs on the same corpus: a lighter codec compresses 3:1 and produces 1.5 GB/s of decoded output per CPU core, while a denser codec compresses 4:1 and produces 0.5 GB/s per core. These are scenario assumptions, not fixed properties of named codec levels. At the 28 GB/s local NVMe rate, their potential decoded output rates are 84 GB/s and 112 GB/s, respectively, provided decoding keeps pace. Sustaining those different output rates requires 56 versus 224 cores, so the denser codec needs 4× as many. Running each codec at the drives’ full output is the worst case, an upper bound on decode work; a node needs only enough cores to decode its own share of demand. The generic text job of notebook 4.2 asks the entire cluster for about 167.8 MB/s, which a single core of either codec covers, so these core counts bind only for image and video feeds whose decoded demand per node approaches the drives’ rate. With fewer cores than that demand requires, decoding limits delivery before storage saturates, so compression is chosen from the measured corpus, decoder, and available CPU budget rather than from the compression ratio alone.
For the running example, the 1.5 trillion token dataset is stored as roughly 2,000 shards of 3 GB each in a custom binary format. Each shard contains a small header (token count, vocabulary size, byte order) followed by a contiguous array of 4-byte token IDs. The number of open() calls per epoch is therefore the number of shards, not the number of tokens (trillions), an approximately 750,000,000× reduction in metadata operations that makes streaming from both local NVMe and remote storage feasible at training scale. When staged on POSIX storage such as local NVMe or a parallel file system, the data loader memory-maps the shard and indexes directly into the token array by position, achieving near-peak read bandwidth with zero per-sample metadata overhead. When the same shards are read directly from object storage, the loader uses HTTP ranged GET streaming and an explicit local buffer rather than memory mapping. Packaging removes the per-file cost within one node, but no node-local format gives every node the same view of the data. That requirement belongs to the next tier.



Beyond the single node, the workload requires a shared namespace where all workers can access the same datasets and where durable checkpoints are globally visible. This is the role of the parallel file system.

Definition 4.1: Parallel file system
Parallel file system (PFS) is a distributed storage architecture for ML training clusters that stripes data across many storage servers to provide aggregate throughput exceeding the capacity of any single device.

Significance: A PFS aggregates storage I/O bandwidth \((\StorageBandwidth)\) across object storage servers (OSS). Twenty OSS nodes delivering 10 GB/s each offer 200 GB/s aggregate. When the client and network sustain that full rate, a 10 GB striped shard loads in about 50 ms rather than the 1 second a single 10 GB/s server would need. The rate that enters the data-movement term \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\) of the single-machine iron law recalled in The Fleet Law is the bandwidth that reaches the actual consumer, not the aggregate rating.
Distinction: Unlike network-attached storage, where every I/O request routes through a single server, a PFS client receives stripe location metadata from a dedicated metadata server (MDS) and then reads data directly from multiple OSS nodes in parallel: the MDS and OSS paths are architecturally separated, so data bandwidth scales with OSS count while metadata operations scale with MDS count.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a PFS has unlimited throughput if enough OSS nodes are added. In reality, a Lustre MDS handles roughly 100,000–300,000 metadata operations per second; a one-time burst of 10,000 opens does not by itself establish sustained saturation. The MDS becomes a throughput bottleneck when the aggregate metadata-operation arrival rate exceeds its service rate, regardless of spare bandwidth at the OSS nodes.



Figure 2 traces how a Lustre-style parallel file system decouples metadata lookups from bulk data movement, separating two concerns that traditional file systems handle together (Schwan 2003). Metadata servers (MDS) manage the namespace (persisting file layouts and attributes on metadata targets, or MDTs): file creation, directory listings, permission checks, and lock management. Object storage servers (OSS)6 manage the actual data blocks, each serving a stripe of every large file. When a client opens a 10 GB training shard, the MDS tells the client which OSS nodes hold which stripes, and the client reads from all of them in parallel. A Lustre7 deployment with 100 OSS nodes, each providing 10 GB/s, delivers an aggregate 1 TB/s.

Schwan, P. 2003. “Lustre: Building a File System for 1,000-Node Clusters.” Proceedings of the 2003 Linux Symposium, 380–86.
6 OSS (Object Storage Server): In parallel file system terminology, “object” means a chunk of striped file data managed by an object storage target, a usage that predates cloud object storage (S3, GCS) by over a decade. Confusing the two is a common source of miscommunication: when a Lustre administrator says “add more OSS nodes,” they mean adding data-serving capacity to the parallel file system, not provisioning cloud buckets.7 Lustre: A portmanteau of “Linux” and “cluster,” developed at Carnegie Mellon University and first deployed in production in 2003. Lustre is common in HPC and ML infrastructure because its architecture scales aggregate bandwidth linearly with the number of OSS nodes, the same property that makes it a natural choice for training clusters where a single job may demand hundreds of GB/s of sustained read throughput.






Figure 2: Parallel file system architecture: A client makes one metadata request (MDS \(\to\) MDT) to learn a file’s stripe map, then reads the stripes directly from the object storage servers (OSS \(\to\) OST) in parallel. Each OST holds every Nth stripe of the file in round-robin order, so consecutive stripes (dark) sit on different servers and one client reads them at once. The shared data path lets every client draw on every OSS, so aggregate bandwidth grows with the number of servers while metadata traffic stays on a separate path.



This abstract architecture has concrete implications for performance tuning. When a training job creates a new dataset directory on Lustre, the administrator configures the stripe count (the number of object storage targets, or OSTs, a file is spread across) and stripe size (the chunk size written to each OST) for that directory (Lustre Wiki 2017). For large sequential-read training shards, administrators may choose wider striping and multi-megabyte stripe sizes so a single file can draw bandwidth from multiple OSS nodes; Lustre’s striping guide treats wide striping as useful for very large files or files accessed by many clients, while smaller files often use fewer stripes to reduce overhead (Lustre Wiki 2019). A 4 GB data shard striped across 100 OSTs with 4 MB stripes places roughly 10 stripes on each OST. When a data loader reads large contiguous ranges, the Lustre client can issue parallel read requests to the OSS nodes holding those stripes, aggregating their bandwidth. The client also maintains its own read-ahead buffer, prefetching the next several stripes while the application processes the current ones. This file-system-level read-ahead is distinct from the data loader’s application-level prefetch buffer; the two layers of prefetching compound to provide deep latency hiding, making the physical distance to the OSS nodes nearly transparent to the training process.

Lustre Wiki. 2019. Configuring Lustre File Striping. Lustre Wiki.
8 GPFS (General Parallel File System): Developed by IBM Research starting in 1998, now marketed as IBM Spectrum Scale. Unlike Lustre’s dedicated metadata-server/object-server organization, GPFS is a shared-disk parallel file system that can stripe data and metadata and uses token-based locking to coordinate concurrent client access. For ML checkpoint writes, this distributed coordination model can reduce reliance on a single dedicated metadata path, but it also makes lock behavior part of the performance envelope.The separation between metadata and data paths is what enables the aggregate bandwidth that ML workloads demand. In GPFS8 (IBM Spectrum Scale), the architecture takes a different approach: it stripes data and metadata across shared disks and coordinates concurrent access through token-based distributed locking (Schmuck and Haskin 2002). The result is not a simple MDS/OSS split; it is a shared-disk design whose metadata and data placement can be distributed while the lock protocol preserves consistency across clients. The trade-off is greater complexity in lock management, which must scale to thousands of nodes.
The data path scales with the number of object storage servers, but every file still begins with a request to the metadata service, and that service has a finite operation rate. That finite rate is the source of the small file problem. The per-open cost that section 4.3.5 charged to one node’s CPU now lands on a metadata service shared by the whole fleet. Each open() system call requires a metadata lookup, lock acquisition, and attribute fetch. When a dataset of millions of 10 KB images is stored as individual files and 10,000 workers, a fleet several times the running cluster, each open a new file every few samples, the aggregate open rate exceeds the few hundred thousand operations per second an MDS typically serves. The MDS becomes the serialization point, and delivery collapses to its operation rate long before the data links saturate.

Definition 4.2: Small file problem
Small file problem is an ML data-loading pathology in which per-file operations overwhelm a storage system’s metadata service.

Significance: open, stat, and close requests from 10,000 workers can serialize at the metadata service, idle the cluster, and reduce effective I/O bandwidth \((\StorageBandwidth)\).
Distinction: This is a metadata request-rate and latency \((\Latency)\) problem, not a bulk bit-rate problem.
Common pitfall: Faster SSDs do not fix this format problem. Packing samples into sequential containers such as TFRecord or Parquet amortizes metadata operations across many samples.



At production scale, the metadata bottleneck can collapse an otherwise high-bandwidth file system.

Example 4.1: The metadata meltdownScenario: A large-scale training cluster migrates from a preprocessed sequential dataset to 200 million raw image files stored individually on a parallel file system provisioned for 500 GB/s aggregate bandwidth.
Diagnosis: The file system delivers less than 1 percent of rated throughput. Millions of per-second stat() and open() calls overwhelm the metadata servers, choking data loaders despite abundant network and storage bandwidth.
Systems lesson: Metadata contention limits delivery when operation demand exceeds metadata service capacity. Bundling 200 million raw images into 50,000 large tar shards (for example, WebDataset) reduces the file count by 4,000\(\times\) and amortizes per-file operations across samples. Packaging alone does not prevent startup contention if loaders still enumerate files with per-file stat() calls; distributing a precomputed dataset manifest removes those repeated lookups from the hot path. Measure metadata operation rate alongside byte bandwidth to determine which service limits delivery.


Striping and aggregation solve different problems. Striping distributes large files across data servers; aggregation, the shard packaging of section 4.3.5, reduces the number of files the MDS must track. Realized bandwidth depends on the reader. A read contained within one stripe uses one server, while enough concurrent reads spanning stripes can use several servers. Wider striping helps only when the read sizes and concurrency exploit those paths; small files usually need fewer stripes.
Parallel file systems provide a shared namespace and lock management that support coordinated checkpoints (Schmuck and Haskin 2002). Recovery requires every reader of a committed checkpoint to observe the same completed state. The file system supplies storage primitives, but the training system must coordinate the shards into one restorable generation. A completed write to one file does not establish that all other checkpoint files are complete.

Schmuck, Frank, and Roger Haskin. 2002. “GPFS: A Shared-Disk File System for Large Computing Clusters.” Proceedings of the USENIX Conference on File and Storage Technologies (FAST ’02), 231–44.
The consistency model has subtleties that matter for ML workloads. For training data reads, immutable shards remove conflicts with concurrent writers once the dataset version has been published. Readers must still agree on which completed version belongs to the run. Checkpoints require more. File-system locks can coordinate individual writes, but they do not by themselves make a checkpoint that spans many files atomic, so a multi-file generation needs an application-level publication protocol, developed in section 4.6.
The performance of a parallel file system depends on the balance of load across OSS nodes as well as their number. If a shard uses 10 of 100 equally provisioned OSS nodes, those servers offer at most 10 percent of the system’s aggregate server bandwidth. Realized delivery can be lower because of client limits, request size, or insufficient concurrency. Conversely, when many concurrent readers draw on shards striped across all 100 servers, demand spreads over every server and realized bandwidth can approach the system’s rating, provided the clients and network keep pace. Placement and access scheduling therefore matter alongside the number of storage servers.
At the scale of thousands of nodes, tail latency (Dean and Barroso 2013a) can dominate exposed input wait. If a training step requires data from 100 storage servers and each independently has a 1 percent chance of being slow, the probability that all 100 respond quickly is \(0.99^{100} = 0.366\), meaning over 63 percent of these request sets contain at least one slow response. Shared congestion can correlate delays, changing that probability. A slow response delays the step only when prefetching fails to hide it and the required input lies on the step’s critical path. When it does, the delay is not confined to one worker, because synchronous data-parallel training waits for every worker at the next collective, so one late fetch stretches the whole fleet’s step.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013a. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80. https://doi.org/10.1145/2408776.2408794.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013b. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80.
Systems can mitigate tail latency through hedged requests: after a chosen delay, the client issues a redundant read to another replica and uses the first valid response. The trigger delay trades faster tail completion against extra work (Dean and Barroso 2013b). An independence model can multiply the probabilities of two slow replicas, but shared congestion and the later start of the hedge invalidate a simple squared-probability latency guarantee. Issuing a hedge at the median response time would duplicate roughly half of requests before accounting for cancellation; that load can worsen the congestion the scheme aims to avoid. A hedge therefore pays off only when its trigger sits in the measured tail and the duplicate traffic it adds stays within the spare service capacity.
The effectiveness of hedged requests depends on the replicated data layout. If both replicas reside on OSS nodes that share the same network switch, a switch failure makes both copies simultaneously unavailable. Effective hedging requires failure-domain-aware placement: replicas should reside in different racks, connected through different top-of-rack switches, so that the failure of any single component affects at most one replica.
In production clusters, the parallel file system is a shared utility, simultaneously servicing dozens of concurrent training jobs with different I/O patterns. At any given moment, a large language model job might be streaming sequentially through text shards, a computer vision job might be reading random image shards, and a checkpoint storm from a third job could be saturating write bandwidth. This concurrency gives rise to the noisy neighbor problem, where one job’s I/O pattern severely degrades performance for all other jobs. A checkpoint save that consumes a disproportionate share of the PFS’s internal network bandwidth causes read latency for other jobs to spike, potentially stalling their training pipelines. PFS administrators mitigate this through I/O scheduling policies (quality-of-service tiers, bandwidth quotas per job), but these policies add administrative complexity and can reduce peak single-job throughput.
A related challenge is namespace isolation. Different teams and workloads require different storage configurations. A team training on millions of 100 KB images first needs to aggregate samples to reduce metadata operations; increasing stripe count does not remove per-file metadata work. A team working with large video shards can use wider striping when read sizes and concurrency exploit the additional data paths. Misconfigured striping for one team’s workload can create hotspots that degrade performance for the entire shared file system. The impact of sharing is easy to quantify: a PFS with 1 TB/s aggregate bandwidth, shared across 10 concurrent training jobs, provides only 100 GB/s per job on average. If one job’s checkpoint storm consumes 400 GB/s for 10 seconds, the remaining nine jobs share 600 GB/s, a 33 percent reduction that can trigger data stalls in their accelerator pipelines.

Checkpoint 4.2: Parallel file system design
Consider a training cluster with 512 nodes, each running 8 GPUs. The training job requires 400 GB/s of aggregate read bandwidth.

OSS count: calculate the number of OSS nodes required when each Lustre OSS delivers 10 GB/s.
Metadata cost: calculate the time required to open 200 million 116 KB image files sequentially when each open() call takes 50 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\)s on the MDS, then state the practical implication.
Shard count: calculate the number of metadata operations needed to read the full dataset when images are bundled into 4 GB tar files.



Parallel file systems solve the shared-namespace problem for active training clusters, but their cost per byte is too high for the organization’s complete data holdings. The petabytes of raw training data, historical checkpoints, and preprocessed datasets that an ML organization accumulates over years require a tier optimized for capacity and durability rather than bandwidth.



At the scale of petabytes, object storage provides the durable, cost-effective foundation of the hierarchy. Services like Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage organize data in object namespaces where objects are retrieved by keys rather than by POSIX directory paths (Amazon Web Services 2026c; Google Cloud 2026). Unlike file systems, which organize data in hierarchical directories with metadata-rich operations (rename, link, permission inheritance), object storage treats each object as an opaque blob identified by a unique key. The simpler interface changes the namespace operations exposed to clients; the service still manages metadata for placement, versions, access control, and integrity as capacity grows.
