title: 4 Data Storage
text:
The storage hierarchy can provide enough aggregate bandwidth and still leave GPUs waiting when the CPU copies data for thousands of small transfers. In the traditional path, every shard read bounces through host DRAM before reaching GPU HBM; GPUDirect Storage (GDS) removes that host-memory bounce copy for local or RDMA-attached NVMe, which pays off when the copy itself limits throughput. The CPU still submits and coordinates I/O through the software stack. Understanding the traditional path first makes the GDS optimization clear.
The traditional data path for loading training data follows three hops: storage \(\to\) host DRAM \(\to\) GPU HBM. Data is first read from NVMe into a kernel buffer in host DRAM (via a DMA transfer initiated by the NVMe controller), then copied to a user-space buffer (the data loader’s tensor, via a memcpy that the CPU executes), and finally transferred to GPU memory via the PCIe bus (using a cudaMemcpy or cudaMemcpyAsync call that programs the GPU’s DMA engine). Each hop adds latency and consumes CPU resources. The CPU must orchestrate every transfer, manage buffer allocation, and handle interrupts from both the storage device and the GPU. For a single transfer, this overhead is negligible. When eight GPUs each demand thousands of small transfers per second, however, the aggregate CPU load for data movement alone can saturate multiple cores, leaving insufficient CPU capacity for the data augmentation that is also essential to the pipeline.14
14 GDS (GPUDirect Storage): Part of NVIDIA’s GPUDirect family, which also includes GPUDirect RDMA (network adapters writing directly to GPU memory) and GPUDirect Peer-to-Peer (inter-GPU memory access); GDS extends this data-copy-bypass approach to NVMe storage via the cuFile API. With RDMA and GDS, payload data can traverse the path remote storage \(\to\) network \(\to\) GPU memory without a CPU-mediated bounce copy. The CPU still issues and coordinates cuFile operations, but it spends less time copying payloads and can devote more capacity to augmentation and pipeline orchestration.
Definition 4.4: GPUDirect Storage
GPUDirect storage (GDS) is a technology that enables a direct DMA path between NVMe storage devices and GPU memory, bypassing the system-DRAM bounce buffer and CPU payload copies while retaining CPU submission and control.

Significance: It eliminates the “bounce buffer” through system memory. In the small-transfer model detailed in notebook 4.6, the assumed active CPU service per request falls by 75 percent. That model estimates CPU capacity savings, not an end-to-end latency guarantee. Whether the storage link saturates depends on the remaining bottlenecks.
Distinction: Unlike traditional I/O, where payload data is staged through host buffers and copied between them, GDS provides direct memory access between the storage controller and the accelerator. CPU-issued cuFile calls and kernel storage drivers remain in the control path.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that GDS makes all storage “faster.” The direct path depends on supported storage and interconnect configurations; it does not eliminate media latency, network latency, or queueing.



The software layers in the traditional I/O path contribute control overhead as well as payload-copy work. A buffered read traverses the runtime, file system, and device driver, then makes the completed bytes available to the application. Direct I/O and pinned buffers can avoid some copies even without GDS, so the correct baseline is the actual data path rather than a fixed number of copies for every read. The GDS design guide distinguishes the payload path from the CPU control work that remains.
GDS changes the payload path without eliminating the software control path. The cuFile API registers a GPU memory region for direct DMA. Subsequent reads transfer payload data from NVMe to GPU memory without an intermediate system-memory bounce buffer, while cuFile, the virtual file system, kernel storage drivers, and nvidia-fs remain involved in submission and coordination. The CPU issues the I/O and checks for completion but avoids the payload-copy work of the traditional path.
The benefit from GDS matters when host payload movement is a limiting stage after other pipeline work is accounted for. Figure 5 diagrams these hardware interfaces, contrasting the two-hop DMA and intermediate host-DRAM bounce buffers of the conventional path against the single direct DMA transfer of GDS. While the direct path eliminates the CPU payload-copy stage, the dashed control link emphasizes that the host CPU still orchestrates transfer submission and completion.







Figure 5: Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage path: Both panels draw the same node: CPU and host DRAM above a PCIe switch, NVMe and GPU below it. Green routes are DMA transfers of payload bytes. In the buffered path (a), payload climbs into host DRAM and comes back down, and the CPU copies every payload from the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer before the accelerator’s DMA can start. In the GDS path (b), NVMe transfers directly into GPU memory, and the dashed CPU link shows the submission and completion work that remains.



GDS benefits depend on the bottleneck, request sizes, alignment, concurrency, and storage topology. Removing host bounce buffers can improve throughput when those copies limit the path; it does not imply that the smallest transfers benefit most. Small I/O may remain submission- or latency-limited and require concurrency to approach the available bandwidth. NVIDIA’s GDS benchmarking guide therefore evaluates I/O size and per-device behavior as well as throughput. The benefit appears only in an end-to-end comparison of the pipeline with and without the direct path, and the clearest case is the one where host CPU time per request is the limiting stage.

Napkin Math 4.6: The CPU bypass dividendProblem: A training node with 8 GPUs loads 116 KB images at 8,000 images/s per GPU (64,000 images/s total). That rate is deliberately aggressive, several times the per-GPU image rate of notebook 4.2, to isolate the case in which per-request CPU work is the limiting stage. Assume active CPU service of 120 μs per request on the buffered path and 30 μs on the direct path. These illustrative service times exclude time blocked on I/O; compare the implied CPU load rather than treating elapsed transfer latency as CPU time.
Traditional path: In the assumed buffered implementation, each image requires a DMA from NVMe to DRAM, a host copy from kernel to user space, and a PCIe transfer to GPU. At 64,000 images/s with 120 μs of CPU time per image, the CPU spends 7.68 seconds of CPU time per wall-clock second, consuming roughly 8 cores worth of processing just for data movement.
GDS path: Each image is transferred directly via DMA from NVMe to GPU. At 30 μs of CPU time per image (for initiating the DMA), the CPU spends 1.92 seconds of CPU time per wall-clock second, freeing roughly 6 cores for data augmentation.
Systems insight: Under the assumed CPU-service costs, bypassing payload copies releases processing capacity for preprocessing. The calculation does not predict end-to-end transfer latency, nor prove that preprocessing or storage throughput can sustain this request rate.


GDS has practical limitations. Not all NVMe controllers support peer-to-peer PCIe transfers. The data must be in a format that the GPU can consume directly, which means it must already be decoded or GPU-decodable (raw pixel values, token IDs, or formats handled by GPU decoders, not arbitrary compressed JPEG or gzip streams). In practice, many pipelines use a hybrid approach: CPU-side decoding for compressed formats followed by a normal pinned-memory GPU transfer, while GDS is reserved for direct reads of GPU-consumable data from supported local or remote storage.
The architectural evolution from CPU-mediated copies to direct storage access reflects a broader trend of removing CPU payload copies from the critical data path wherever possible. RDMA allows network payloads to move without CPU copying, while GDS provides the same bypass for storage payloads. Together, RDMA and GDS let data flow from remote storage (such as NVMe over Fabrics, or NVMe-oF), through the network fabric, and into GPU memory without a host-memory bounce copy. The CPU still submits and coordinates the operation, while more of its capacity remains available for data augmentation, pipeline orchestration, and error handling.


↩︎ RDMA and kernel-bypass network paths are established in RDMA and GPUDirect.
The GDS design principle also extends to checkpoint writes. A host-staged path transfers checkpoint bytes from GPU HBM through host DRAM to NVMe. A supported direct path can bypass that host staging for a 2,450 GB checkpoint. Removing the copy reduces \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) only when that movement contributes to the exposed pause; snapshot consistency, serialization, storage service, and durable publication remain separate requirements.


Combining GDS with the multi-tier hierarchy, the complete data path connects the tiers for the running example. At the beginning of the training job, the 6 TB serialized shard set, derived from the 3 TB compressed source corpus, is staged from object storage into the cluster’s local NVMe caches, with each node receiving its assigned shard subset during setup. The data loader workers read tokenized shards from NVMe, assemble packed sequences in pinned host DRAM, and transfer those batches to the accelerator. With GDS enabled, token IDs that are already in a GPU-consumable layout can be loaded directly into GPU memory without CPU payload copying; compressed formats still require CPU or GPU decompression before use.
During steady-state training on the host-staged path, CPU data loader workers read from local NVMe and fill a prefetch queue in host DRAM. The GPU receives batches from this queue via PCIe DMA; the supported GDS alternative bypasses that host payload staging. The compute phase (forward pass, backward pass, optimizer step) consumes the batch and updates model state in HBM. Every 10 minutes, the training framework captures a consistent checkpoint, writes it to local NVMe through the chosen path, and copies it to the parallel file system in the background. The checkpoint protocol must still establish when all required shards are safe to publish for recovery.
At the end of the training job, the final model checkpoint is promoted from the parallel file system to object storage for long-term retention. The local NVMe copies are deleted during job cleanup. If the model is deployed for inference, it is loaded from object storage into the serving cluster’s HBM, completing the lifecycle of data movement through the hierarchy.
The total number of data copies in this lifecycle is instructive. Each training sample traverses: object storage \(\to\) NVMe (staging), NVMe \(\to\) host DRAM (read), host DRAM \(\to\) GPU HBM (transfer). Each checkpoint traverses: GPU HBM \(\to\) NVMe (local save), NVMe \(\to\) parallel file system (async copy), parallel file system \(\to\) object storage (long-term retention). Every copy consumes bandwidth and contributes latency. The engineering goal is to minimize copies on the critical path (the training loop) and tolerate additional copies on noncritical paths (staging and archival). Figure 6 maps these dual lifecycles across the tiers, visually distinguishing synchronous critical-path copies (solid arrows) from asynchronous background transfers (dashed arrows). For training inputs moving rightward, the active loop waits only on local promotion into HBM (or the optional GDS bypass); for checkpoints flowing leftward, the exposed pause is confined to the local NVMe save while parallel-file-system replication and archival retention proceed off the critical path.






Figure 6: The complete data path: Columns are storage tiers, ordered from the durable object store (left) to accelerator memory (right). Training data moves right and bypasses the parallel file system in this running example; checkpoints return left through it. Solid arrows mark copies the training loop waits on; dashed arrows mark copies that run once per job or in the background. The dashed outline is one GPU node: every copy the training loop waits on stays inside it.



Every copy that leaves the node also needs a network, and the choice of network decides whom a storage burst can disturb. Many training nodes carry a small number of storage-facing network adapters on a separate front-end network, in addition to one compute-fabric adapter per accelerator. Routing staging reads and checkpoint copies over that front-end network isolates them from gradient collectives, but it caps each node’s storage bandwidth at a few front-end ports. Routing storage over the compute fabric offers far more bandwidth, and remote GDS reads use exactly that RDMA path, but then a checkpoint burst shares switch buffers and spine links with the job’s collectives and must be separated by traffic classes. For the running example, each node’s fair share of a 1 TB/s file system shared by 256 nodes is roughly 4 GB/s, and copying its roughly 10 GB checkpoint shard within the 10-minute interval needs far less, so a front-end network can carry it; image workloads that stream hundreds of GB/s across the cluster push designs toward the compute fabric. Through the C\(^3\) lens, storage traffic becomes communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)) load the moment it leaves the node, and the network chosen to carry it decides which collectives a storage burst can delay.
The volume of data moved during a 30-day training run reveals a counterintuitive reality. A single staging copy of the 6 TB serialized dataset from object storage to local NVMe accounts for a modest transfer. The checkpointing process, however, generates a vastly larger data stream. With a roughly 2,450 GB checkpoint created every 10 minutes across 256 nodes for 30 days, the system produces approximately 4,320 checkpoints, totaling roughly 10.6 PB of state that must traverse the storage hierarchy. Checkpoint data movement dwarfs training data movement for large models. The 6 TB training dataset is read once in this single-epoch run (and only a handful of times in a multi-epoch one), while the 10.6 PB of checkpoint data is generated anew, making checkpoint I/O the dominant storage workload. This insight explains why checkpoint staging strategy (write locally, replicate asynchronously) can have a larger impact on overall storage design than training data pipeline optimization for large-model runs. Because checkpoints dominate the bytes this run moves, they are the storage workload to design next, and the design must take a multi-terabyte save off the training critical path without ever exposing a checkpoint that cannot be restored.

Self-Check: Question

Which statement precisely describes the architectural data-path modification introduced by GPUDirect Storage (GDS)?

GDS caches the entire training corpus in GPU HBM to eliminate all storage I/O operations during training epochs.
GDS compresses training tensors directly inside the NVMe flash controller using hardware acceleration.
GDS routes network packets through host DRAM bounce buffers to perform real-time data integrity checksumming.
GDS establishes a direct DMA transfer path between NVMe storage (local or NVMe-oF) and GPU memory, eliminating the CPU-mediated bounce buffer in host DRAM while retaining CPU control-plane coordination.

A computer vision training pipeline uses complex CPU-based JPEG decompression and multi-step data augmentations (color jitter, affine warping). Explain why adopting GPUDirect Storage (GDS) without moving decompression to the GPU yields minimal end-to-end throughput improvement.
True or False: Enabling GPUDirect Storage (GDS) eliminates the physical round-trip network latency and P99 tail-latency spikes associated with fetching shards directly from remote cloud object storage endpoints.
In a high-throughput vision training node with 8 GPUs processing a combined 64,000 images per second, traditional CPU-mediated I/O requires \(120\ \mu\text{s}\) of CPU time per image (consuming \(\approx 7.68\) CPU seconds per wall-clock second, or \(\approx 8\) dedicated CPU cores). GDS reduces CPU overhead to \(30\ \mu\text{s}\) per image (\(1.92\) CPU seconds per second, or \(\approx 2\) cores). What is the primary systems benefit of this ‘CPU bypass dividend’?

It enables the cluster to eliminate all local NVMe SSDs in favor of remote tape archives.
It frees approximately 6 CPU cores per node that can be reallocated to computationally intensive data augmentation and pipeline orchestration without adding hardware.
It reduces GPU power consumption by \(75\%\) during tensor matrix multiplication.
It doubles the physical PCIe bus bandwidth between the CPU socket and the GPU accelerators.

Order the sequence of operations that occurs in the traditional (non-GDS) storage I/O path when an accelerator requests a batch from local NVMe: (1) The data loader process issues a POSIX read() system call traversing the VFS and filesystem drivers, (2) The NVMe controller initiates a DMA transfer of raw blocks into an OS kernel buffer in host DRAM, (3) The host CPU executes a memcpy to copy payload bytes from kernel space to user-space pinned memory, (4) The CPU initiates a cudaMemcpyAsync to trigger a PCIe DMA transfer from host DRAM to GPU HBM, (5) The accelerator launches compute kernels on the newly arrived tensor resident in HBM.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
After the 2,048 accelerators of the running cluster have been training for six hours, a power supply failure turns checkpoint storage into the difference between resuming quickly and repeating hours of work. The decisive storage questions are how quickly the most recent checkpoint was saved, where it resides, and whether it can be read back. Checkpoints are the most demanding write workload in the storage hierarchy. They are also among the most consequential: a lost checkpoint after a hardware failure means repeating hours or days of training. The storage architecture must therefore minimize \(\CheckpointWriteTime\), the time the training pipeline pauses to save a checkpoint, while stating when that checkpoint becomes durable and visible for restore. The save interval is an input to this storage analysis; selecting it from failure rates and recovery costs is a separate reliability decision derived in The Young-Daly checkpoint interval.
A 175B parameter model with mixed-precision Adam generates a resumable checkpoint of approximately 2,450 GB. The byte contract comprises 350 GB of FP16 model weights, 700 GB of FP32 master weights, and 1,400 GB for the two FP32 Adam moments. Learning-rate-scheduler state, random-number-generator state, and the data-loader cursor add little capacity but remain required for deterministic continuation. Gradients are omitted because the restored job recomputes them. Each participating worker process, called a rank, saves its assigned shard simultaneously, creating a checkpoint storm that the storage system must absorb without disrupting ongoing training reads. How large each rank’s shard is depends on the rule that a coordinated save writes each unique byte once, whatever the parallel layout. In the running layout of table 3, the Adam moments and master weights already exist as distinct per-node slices, while the FP16 weights repeat once per node, so the save writes one copy of the weights and each optimizer slice once. Spreading those unique bytes evenly gives each of the 256 nodes about 1/256 of the checkpoint. The third ZeRO stage (ZeRO-3), which partitions the weights as well, makes that even split the natural one, because every rank already owns a distinct slice. Breaking that rule is a real risk even in the running layout, where a save in which every node writes the FP16 weight copy it holds would multiply the weight bytes by the node count. Its cost is clearest in a deliberately extreme thought experiment, a smaller model whose complete resumable state is written once per GPU of the book’s reference cluster.



Writing one copy per replica takes 1,024 times longer than writing each unique byte once.

Definition 4.5: Checkpoint storm
Checkpoint storm is a burst of synchronized network and storage traffic that occurs when all nodes in an ML training fleet save model state simultaneously.

Significance: When each replica writes its own full copy, the naive storm takes \(\CheckpointWriteTime = \DataParallelDegree \times \text{per-replica state} / \StorageIngestBandwidth\), where \(\DataParallelDegree\) is the number of replicas writing at once and \(\StorageIngestBandwidth\) is the aggregate rate at which the target storage tier absorbs writes; a coordinated save that writes each unique byte once takes \(\text{unique state} / \StorageIngestBandwidth\). Under the chapter’s checkpoint contract, a 70B-parameter model, smaller than the 175B running example, stores 140 GB of FP16 weights, 280 GB of FP32 master weights, and 560 GB of Adam moments. With vanilla data parallelism across 1,024 replicas (one per GPU of the book’s reference cluster, rather than the chapter’s 256-node fleet), naively writing that complete state from every replica generates 1003.5 TB of simultaneous traffic. No 80 GB device can hold a 0.98 TB replica, so the case is a bound on write volume rather than a deployable layout. At 100 GB/s of aggregate storage ingest bandwidth, the write takes roughly 10,035.2 seconds, or over 167.3 minutes of training stall. A coordinated checkpoint protocol writes one logical copy. Replicated data parallelism can select one writer; ZeRO-3 instead distributes that copy across state-owning ranks. In the sharded example the total is roughly 0.98 TB, bringing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) down to roughly 9.8 seconds. Gradients do not appear in either total because recovery recomputes them.
Distinction: Unlike general I/O contention (which is stochastic and unpredictable), a checkpoint storm is synchronous and periodic: every node writes at the same moment because the training orchestrator triggers checkpoint after a fixed step count. Its predictability makes it both more damaging (all nodes compete simultaneously) and more tractable (it can be prevented by design through staggered scheduling or asynchronous serialization).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that checkpointing every 100 steps is “low overhead” whatever the save protocol. Under the naive protocol at 70B scale, if each training step takes 10 seconds and a checkpoint storm takes 10,035.2 seconds, checkpointing every 100 steps means spending most of the run on checkpoint I/O rather than useful training.



The severity of a checkpoint storm depends on two factors: the per-node shard size, determined by the model size and the sharding strategy, and the throughput of the first write tier, typically local NVMe. A concrete 175B example shows why the local-write phase, rather than the durable copy to the parallel file system, governs the exposed training pause.

Napkin Math 4.7: Tiered checkpoint stagingProblem: Assume sustained bandwidth, no snapshot-copy, serialization, or coordination overhead, and no interference from background copies. The resulting times are bandwidth lower bounds. A 256-node cluster saves a 175B-parameter checkpoint every 10 minutes. Each checkpoint totals 2,450 GB. Writing each unique byte once and spreading the bytes evenly across nodes, each node saves roughly 9.6 GB.

Per-node write to local NVMe (4 drives at 7 GB/s each = 28 GB/s): 9.6 GB \(\div\) 28 GB/s \(\approx\) 0.34 seconds.
Async copy to PFS: 256 \(\times\) 9.6 GB \(\approx\) 2.4 TB total. If the PFS provides 1 TB/s aggregate, the storm completes in roughly 2.4 seconds.
Per-node PFS bandwidth: If all 256 write simultaneously, each gets 1000 GB/s \(\div\) 256 = 3.9 GB/s.
Training pause: At least 0.34 seconds for the local NVMe write under this model. The PFS copy overlaps with the next training iteration.
Overhead lower bound: 0.34 seconds pause every 600 seconds \(\approx\) 0.06 percent training time lost to checkpointing.

Systems insight: Under these 1 TB/s aggregate-PFS assumptions, tiered staging reduces checkpoint overhead from about a 2.4 seconds PFS-direct write to a sub-second local write. The training pause can end at the local snapshot boundary before durable publication, but actual pause includes snapshot creation, serialization, and coordination in addition to this byte-transfer lower bound.


A PFS-direct save of a few seconds every 10 minutes costs well under 1 percent of the run, which can make tiered staging look unnecessary for the running example. The checkpoint-dominance argument of section 4.5.1 concerns bytes moved, not this pause, and the notebook’s figure holds only while its assumptions do. The job has the whole 1 TB/s file system to itself; shared among the ten concurrent jobs of section 4.3.6, it receives a tenth of the bandwidth, the same save takes ten times as long, and its burst slows the other jobs’ reads. Realized ingest also falls below the rated aggregate once serialization, metadata operations, and stragglers enter. The save interval shrinks as the fleet grows, because a larger fleet fails more often and the reliability analysis of The Young-Daly checkpoint interval then calls for more frequent saves, and a larger model scales every save with it. Tiered staging removes the shared-tier write from the exposed pause when the background copy keeps pace, although local snapshot creation, serialization, writing, and coordination still determine that pause.
The tiered staging strategy minimizes \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) by writing in two phases. In the first phase, each node writes its checkpoint shard to local NVMe at full bandwidth. With 4 NVMe drives providing 28 GB/s aggregate, a per-node shard of roughly 9.6 GB (an even 256-node split of the 2,450 GB total checkpoint) completes in roughly 0.34 seconds. In this staging model, the training pipeline can resume after every required local shard has completed and the snapshot is no longer being modified. The local-write calculation excludes snapshot-copy, serialization, and coordination overhead, so it is a bandwidth lower bound on the pause.
In the second phase, a background process asynchronously copies the local checkpoint to the parallel file system for durability. The copy can overlap training, but it still competes for memory, network, and storage service and must drain before repeated saves create an unbounded backlog. The two phases therefore land differently in the Fleet Law (equation 1.3). The local write is a pause that every rank takes at the same step boundary, and training resumes only when the slowest writer has finished its shard. That is the shape of a barrier rather than of a transfer between workers, a coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) cost, so the pause adds to the synchronization term \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) of each saving step, the term that already carries barrier and straggler waiting. The background copy belongs to no step’s critical path. While it stays hidden and drains before the next save, it adds nothing to the step time; it reappears only as interference, in \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) when it shares links with collectives or in exposed input wait when it slows shared-storage reads. If a node fails before its copy completes, the new generation may lose a required shard. Replication to peer nodes’ NVMe drives can protect against a single-node loss, provided replicas occupy independent failure domains. Waiting for that replication extends the pause beyond the local-only calculation. A design that resumes earlier must retain the previous committed generation until the new one reaches its declared durability boundary.
Durability alone does not make a distributed checkpoint visible safely. Each rank first writes its shard under an immutable generation identifier, computes a checksum over the completed bytes, and acknowledges the shard only after the target tier has persisted it. A coordinator then writes a manifest containing the training step, checkpoint schema, expected shard set, sizes, and checksums. The manifest or commit marker is published last using the target backend’s atomic publication primitive: an atomic create or rename on a file system, or an immutable manifest plus conditional creation or a versioned pointer under the object store’s consistency guarantees. PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint exposes the ordering directly: storage writers write rank data before the coordinator’s finish() operation writes metadata and marks the checkpoint successful, while the storage backend supplies the publication semantics (PyTorch Contributors 2026). Restore logic lists only committed generations, verifies every shard against the manifest, and rejects temporary, partial, or mixed-step state. This ordering separates writing bytes from publishing a restorable checkpoint: a crash can leave garbage to collect, but it cannot make an incomplete generation appear valid.

PyTorch Contributors. 2026. Distributed Checkpoint: Torch.distributed.checkpoint.
The exposed pause and the durability boundary therefore fall at different moments. Figure 7 aligns these decoupled milestones across four concurrent execution lanes: training pauses only during the local NVMe shard write (\(\TimeInstant_0\) to \(\TimeInstant_1\)), resuming on live state while the parallel file system absorbs the asynchronous copy (\(\TimeInstant_1\) to \(\TimeInstant_2\)) and the coordinator validates checksums before publishing the manifest last (\(\TimeInstant_3\)).






Figure 7: Two-phase checkpoint staging: Read the lanes left to right. Training pauses only for the local NVMe write (\(\TimeInstant_0\) to \(\TimeInstant_1\)); the copy to the parallel file system overlaps later training steps, and the coordinator publishes the manifest last (\(\TimeInstant_3\)). Between \(\TimeInstant_1\) and \(\TimeInstant_3\) the new generation exists only as staged shards, so the previous committed generation remains the restore point.



The total storage consumed by checkpoints over the life of a training run is substantial. A 175B parameter model checkpointed every 10 minutes over a 30-day training run generates roughly 4,320 checkpoints, each 2,450 GB, for a total of approximately 10.6 PB of checkpoint data. Retaining all of them is neither necessary nor economical. The retention policy this run adopts keeps the three most recent checkpoints on the parallel file system for fast recovery, copies every 100th checkpoint and the final checkpoint to object storage for long-term auditability, and deletes the rest. This policy reduces the parallel file system checkpoint footprint from 10.6 PB to roughly 7.35 TB (three live full checkpoints) while preserving 43 periodic historical snapshots in object storage, plus the final checkpoint when it does not coincide with that schedule, for posttraining analysis.
Incremental checkpointing offers a further optimization for reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\). Rather than saving the entire training state every time, an incremental checkpoint records changed state relative to a declared base or preceding generation. The delta must include changed optimizer and continuation state as well as parameters. For models where a large fraction of parameters are frozen (such as fine-tuning scenarios where only the last few layers are updated), incremental checkpoints can be orders of magnitude smaller than full checkpoints. Restoring a generation requires its base and every intervening delta, so smaller saves add recovery work and dependencies. Periodic full checkpoints bound that chain. The retention policy must preserve each dependency until no retained generation requires it.
Checkpoint storage interacts directly with the system’s failure model. From the storage perspective, the design goal is to minimize \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) (the time the training pipeline pauses) while defining which failures each saved generation survives. Failures can occur during background replication, so a locally staged generation and a durably committed generation must remain distinct. Reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) through tiered staging makes more frequent checkpoints affordable. Minimizing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\), however, only matters if the checkpoint can actually be read back; the costlier failure is a checkpoint that was written but never verified as restorable.

War Story 4.1: The backup that had not been restored (2017)Context: On January 31, 2017, a GitLab.com site reliability engineer working a database replication incident accidentally wiped the primary PostgreSQL data directory (GitLab 2017).
Mechanism: All five layered backup paths failed simultaneously: S3 dumps were silently empty due to a version mismatch, Azure disk snapshots were disabled, replication was broken, LVM snapshots were six hours stale, and WAL archiving was unimplemented.
Impact: Six hours of production database writes, user comments, and repository metadata were permanently lost, requiring an 18-hour emergency restoration from a staging snapshot.
Fix: GitLab instituted automated daily backup restoration testing, unified PostgreSQL versioning across environments, and implemented automated WAL archiving to S3.
Systems lesson: Storage reliability is a restore property, not a backup property. A checkpoint, replica, or dump only counts if the team regularly proves that it can be located, validated, and restored under incident conditions. ML systems encounter this exact vulnerability: a model checkpoint written to object storage or a feature store snapshot is useless if silent version mismatches or missing restore tests prevent resuming a multi-day training run after node preemption.



GitLab. 2017. Postmortem of Database Outage of January 31. GitLab postmortem.
That incident turns checkpoint storage from a capacity question into a restore-design question.

Checkpoint 4.4: Checkpoint storage design
A training cluster of 256 nodes saves a 175B-parameter model checkpoint every 10 minutes. Each checkpoint is 2,450 GB total, distributed across all nodes.

Per-node state: calculate the per-node checkpoint size.
Local write: calculate \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) for the local write when each node writes to local NVMe at 28 GB/s.
Async copy: calculate the per-node write bandwidth and async-copy time when the parallel file system provides 1 TB/s aggregate and all 256 nodes write simultaneously.
Tiered staging: explain why tiered staging (local NVMe first, then async PFS copy) is faster than writing directly to PFS.





In a sharded training setup with 256 nodes, no single node necessarily holds the complete training state. One node may hold a shard of the optimizer state, while other model-partitioning strategies split the weights themselves across devices. A complete checkpoint therefore requires every node to save its shard, and the checkpoint is publishable only after all expected shards have been durably written and verified against one manifest. This creates a coordination problem: the system must confirm that all 256 nodes have finished writing before it exposes the generation for restore.
The simplest approach coordinates a snapshot at one completed training step: all nodes pause, write their shards to local NVMe, then run a cluster-wide acknowledgement operation to confirm completion. Only when every node has acknowledged its write does training resume. Capturing the same step prevents mixing shards from step \(\SnapshotStepIndex\) with shards from step \(\SnapshotStepIndex+1\); a barrier after writing cannot repair a snapshot captured inconsistently. The slowest node determines when the completion barrier releases.
Asynchronous checkpointing reduces the training pause by writing in the background. Nodes first coordinate the training step to capture. Each node copies its accelerator-resident shard to a dedicated pinned host-memory buffer, then resumes training and writes the buffer to NVMe in a background thread. The snapshot buffer must remain immutable until the background write finishes; separate live-state buffers allow training to advance without changing the captured generation. If a node fails during the asynchronous write, its local shard may be incomplete. The job must wait for the required writes or peer replication before declaring this generation durable, even if training has already resumed.
The choice between synchronous and asynchronous checkpointing depends on the pause budget and save frequency. A 1-second pause at 200 ms per iteration costs five iterations; whether that overhead is acceptable depends on how much useful training occurs between saves. Asynchronous checkpointing reduces exposed write time when snapshot buffers and background bandwidth are available, but its buffer capacity, contention, and durability delay also enter the decision.
Beyond the choice of synchronous or asynchronous methods, checkpoint format optimization reduces the per-node I/O volume. In the simplest data-parallel setup, every node holds an identical copy of the model weights, so a naive checkpoint would redundantly save the same data from every node. Sharded checkpoint protocols avoid that redundancy by saving shards instead of full replicas. DeepSpeed’s zero-redundancy checkpointing applies the write-once rule through its ZeRO optimizer-state partitioning: each of the \(\ClusterNodeCount\) nodes saves only its \(1/\ClusterNodeCount\) shard of the optimizer state, and the system saves one consolidated copy of the weights. PyTorch’s Distributed Checkpoint protocol follows the same storage principle by writing each rank’s sharded data to a distinct file.
For the 175B model split evenly across 256 nodes, each node writes only its roughly 9.6 GB shard of the total 2,450 GB state. Had one node saved the full 2,450 GB itself, its 28 GB/s local stripe would need more than a minute; the shard takes around a second on one NVMe drive and well below a second on the stripe. For coordination, the local NVMe write bounds one component of the exposed pause, while the durable copy to the parallel file system can overlap subsequent training. Snapshot copying, coordination, and any replication required before resumption also contribute to the actual pause.
With the checkpoint accounting now derived in full, the running example’s storage demands can be consolidated against the same hierarchy, so the training dataset, checkpoints, and archive lineage are visible side by side.

Systems Perspective 4.2: The 175B model's storage footprintTable 5 assembles the complete storage picture for the running example, a 30-day training run of a 175B-parameter model on 256 nodes.



Table 5: 175B-Parameter Training Storage Footprint: Volume and primary storage tier for each data category in a 30-day, 256-node training run.

The total data moved through the hierarchy is approximately 10.6 PB of checkpoint data plus 6 TB per 1 epoch of training data reads. For a single-epoch language model training run, checkpoint I/O dominates data loading I/O by a factor of over 1,764.


Checkpoint accounting completes the training side of the storage picture. Inputs are read once per epoch and state is written thousands of times, each on its own path through the tiers, and every one of those placements carries a price set by the tier that holds the bytes and by how often they cross a billing boundary.

Self-Check: Question

A 256-node cluster saves a 175B-parameter resumable checkpoint (\(2.45\text{ TB}\) total: \(350\text{ GB}\) FP16 weights, \(700\text{ GB}\) FP32 master weights, and \(1.4\text{ TB}\) of Adam moments) every 10 minutes. Under tiered staging, each node writes its \(9.57\text{ GB}\) ZeRO-3 shard to local NVMe (\(28\text{ GB/s}\) local array) in \(\approx 0.34\text{ s}\), followed by an asynchronous background copy to a \(1\text{ TB/s}\) parallel file system taking \(\approx 2.45\text{ s}\). What is the exposed training pause time (\(T_{\text{write}}\)) per checkpoint?

Roughly \(2.8\text{ s}\), because training must remain paused until both the local write and the durable PFS copy complete.
Roughly \(0.34\text{ s}\), because the training barrier releases immediately after the fast local NVMe write completes, while the PFS replication proceeds asynchronously in the background.
Zero seconds, because modern storage drivers execute zero-copy writes without interrupting GPU tensor execution.
Roughly \(2.45\text{ s}\), because parallel file system latency determines the minimum barrier synchronization time across nodes.

True or False: In distributed ML infrastructure, storage reliability is defined primarily as a write-completion property: once all nodes successfully execute and acknowledge their checkpoint write calls, the checkpoint can be guaranteed reliable for cluster recovery.
A cluster of 1,024 accelerators trains a 70B-parameter model whose resumable checkpoint contains \(140\text{ GB}\) of FP16 weights, \(280\text{ GB}\) of FP32 master weights, and \(560\text{ GB}\) of Adam moments, or \(980\text{ GB}\) per full replica. Contrast naive full-replica checkpointing with ZeRO-3 sharded checkpointing across a \(100\text{ GB/s}\) shared storage fabric.
A 30-day training run of a 175B model generates 4,320 resumable checkpoints totaling roughly \(10.6\text{ PB}\) of state data. Which retention policy balances rapid failure recovery, long-term auditability, and storage cost without exhausting the parallel file system budget?

Retain all 4,320 checkpoints on the parallel file system to provide granular step-by-step rollback capabilities throughout the entire 30-day run.
Delete all intermediate checkpoints immediately after each step and rely exclusively on live memory replication across peer nodes for fault tolerance.
Retain the 3 most recent checkpoints on the parallel file system for fast local recovery, copy every 100th checkpoint to cloud object storage for long-term lineage, and purge older intermediate snapshots.
Compress all checkpoints with gzip and write them directly to cold tape archive without maintaining any copies on NVMe or parallel file systems.

Order the sequence of steps executed during a tiered asynchronous checkpointing operation: (1) Background daemons asynchronously transfer the local checkpoint shards from NVMe to the shared parallel file system, (2) The training orchestrator initiates a synchronized step barrier across all worker ranks, (3) Each rank snapshots its model weights and optimizer state shard into a local pinned DRAM buffer, (4) The training barrier releases and accelerators immediately resume forward-backward computation for the next step, (5) Each node flushes its pinned memory snapshot to local NVMe at full drive bandwidth.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
A 100 TB training dataset can reside on any tier of the hierarchy, but the cost differs by orders of magnitude depending on which tier is chosen and how the data is accessed. ML storage economics is not simply about choosing the cheapest tier; it is about minimizing total cost of data delivery, which includes storage costs, transfer costs, and the opportunity cost of idle accelerators.
The per-gigabyte rates quoted for each tier become concrete when applied to one 100 TB training dataset. The recurring annual storage costs diverge by orders of magnitude: object storage (S3 Standard) costs $24,000 per year, provisioned local NVMe costs $120,000 per year, and archival storage (such as Glacier) drops to $4,800 per year. By contrast, hypothetically provisioning the same capacity as GPU memory at $15/GB would require $1,500,000 in upfront acquisition cost alone, before factoring in amortization, power, or server housing.
The 5× cost difference between local NVMe and object storage motivates placing data on the least expensive tier that meets its delivery and recovery requirements. Device technology contributes to the gradient: HBM uses 3D-stacked silicon with through-silicon vias, and accelerator-adjacent capacity is constrained by packaging and node design. Shared storage pools capacity across clients but introduces network and service dependencies. The cost comparison must include those dependencies rather than infer the cheapest usable path from capacity price alone.



Repeated cross-boundary egress, not storage, dominates cloud cost.
Storage cost, however, is only part of the equation. Data transfer costs can dominate, especially in cloud environments. When compute runs in a different region or cloud from the bucket, as assumed here, reading the 100 TB dataset from object storage to compute instances incurs a transfer charge of $9,000. For multi-epoch training that reads the dataset 10 times, the egress cost alone reaches $90,000, more than the annual storage cost. This inversion, where reading data costs more than storing it, drives the architecture decision to cache data on local NVMe rather than streaming from object storage each epoch.
The economic analysis changes further when accounting for the opportunity cost of accelerator idle time. The book’s reference cluster of 1,024 GPUs, half the chapter’s running cluster, at $2/GPU-hour costs $49,152 per day. If input stalls reduce its compute-active fraction from 90 percent to 70 percent, the lost compute time is valued at $9,830 per day. Over a 30 days training run, this amounts to $294,912. That value sets a budget for evaluating a storage upgrade, but the recoverable benefit depends on how much exposed wait the upgrade removes. Capacity that does not relieve the limiting stage yields no corresponding compute-time saving.

Systems Perspective 4.3: The storage cost icebergThe visible cost of storage ($/GB/month) is the tip of the iceberg. Below the surface lie costs that often exceed the storage cost itself:

Egress fees: A representative cross-boundary egress charge of $0.09/GB makes a 100 TB dataset read once per epoch across 10 epochs cost $90,000 in egress alone.
IOPS charges: Object storage charges per-request fees. S3 Standard GET requests cost about $0.0004 per 1,000 requests, so a dataset of 100M individual files, read once, costs about $40 in GET request fees before data transfer or retrieval charges, even though the storage cost is $2,000/month.
Idle accelerator cost: If storage stalls reduce GPU utilization from 90 percent to 70 percent on a cluster of 1,024 GPUs at $2/GPU-hour, the lost compute costs $9,830/day (20 percent of $49,152 daily spend), dwarfing any storage savings.
Retrieval fees: Archive storage charges retrieval fees ($0.02/GB for Glacier) in addition to egress. Restoring a 100 TB dataset from Glacier costs $2,000 in retrieval fees plus $9,000 in egress.

The economically rational strategy often invests more in storage (local NVMe caching, parallel file system capacity) to reduce transfer costs and prevent accelerator stalls.


The cost iceberg reveals that raw storage capacity can account for less than half of the total expenditure; replication, metadata operations, API calls, and cross-region transfers can collectively dominate the bill at scale. Among those hidden line items, egress is the one that often flips the architecture decision. Unlike capacity charges, which scale with the volume of data stored, egress charges scale with the volume of data read, and ML training reads the full dataset on every epoch.

Napkin Math 4.8: The egress taxProblem: A team trains a vision model on a 50 TB image dataset stored in S3. Training runs for 20 epochs. The decision is whether to stream from S3 each epoch or stage to local NVMe.
Option A: Stream from S3

Storage: 50 TB \(\times\) $0.02/GB/month \(\times\) 12 months = $12,000/year
Egress: 50 TB \(\times\) 20 epochs \(\times\) $0.09/GB = $90,000 per training run
Total for 4 training runs/year: $12,000 + $360,000 = $372,000/year

Option B: Stage to local NVMe

Storage (S3 source of truth): $12,000/year
NVMe capacity (50 TB across cluster): 50 TB \(\times\) $0.10/GB/month \(\times\) 12 = $60,000/year
Egress (stage once per training run): 50 TB \(\times\) 4 runs \(\times\) $0.09/GB = $18,000/year
Total: $12,000 + $60,000 + $18,000 = $90,000/year

Systems insight: Local NVMe caching saves $282,000/year at 20 epochs per run, enough to fund 9 additional H100 GPUs at list price. Including the $60,000/year provisioned NVMe cost and the once-per-run staging egress, the break-even point is just over 4 epochs per run; by the fifth epoch, local caching is cheaper than streaming from S3 every epoch.


The notebook turns the iceberg into a decision rule: the cheapest storage tier is not always the cheapest delivery path. Object storage can remain the source of truth, but repeated reads make egress, request overhead, and idle-accelerator cost part of the storage design. Multi-epoch vision training may justify staging on local NVMe by the fifth epoch, while single-epoch language-model pretraining may leave the corpus in object storage and optimize the streaming path instead. The running example stages anyway, although it reads its corpus only once, because egress is not what decides it. Each node’s share of the shards fits easily on local NVMe, the staging copy happens once before the clock starts, and local reads keep object-store latency tails out of every training step. When compute and bucket share a region, transfer fees largely disappear and the same comparison turns on request charges, latency, and idle accelerators instead. The architecture is therefore chosen from access pattern, read count, and latency sensitivity rather than from $/GB/month alone.
The cost analysis extends to the parallel file system tier, which occupies a middle ground between NVMe and object storage in both performance and price. A parallel file system capable of delivering 1 TB/s aggregate bandwidth requires roughly 100 OSS nodes, each with multiple NVMe drives and high-bandwidth network connections. Because the throughput target, not the stored capacity, sets that server count, a bandwidth-sized system costs far more than its stored bytes alone would suggest. This expense is justified only if the alternative, streaming from object storage and paying egress fees, is even more expensive, or if the latency requirements of checkpoint writes cannot be met by object storage alone. The break-even analysis depends on the organization’s workload mix: a team running a single long training job may find that staging data on local NVMe and bypassing the parallel file system entirely is the cheapest option, while a team running many concurrent short jobs benefits from the shared namespace that a parallel file system provides.
The decision to build vs. buy storage infrastructure hinges on the trade-off between the high capital expenditure of an on-premises parallel file system and the recurring operational expenditure of cloud object storage. A 1-petabyte Lustre deployment, sized for capacity rather than for the 1 TB/s target above, costs roughly $3–5 million in hardware, plus an additional $500,000 per year in operational overhead for power, cooling, and engineering support. Storing 1 PB in a cloud object store at $0.02/GB/month costs $240,000 per year for storage alone. However, egress fees for accessing the data dominate the total cost: reading that petabyte at 10 reads/year adds $900,000 in data transfer fees. Under these assumptions, annual cloud delivery costs $1,140,000; after subtracting $500,000 of on-premises operations, the net savings are $640,000 per year. The resulting hardware break-even is roughly 4.7–7.8 years, and a payback within two years would require a hotter workload with many more full-dataset reads per year, lower capital expense, or non-egress drivers such as checkpoint latency and shared-namespace requirements. For the running example, the 6 TB serialized corpus is much smaller than 1 PB, so the local-storage case is driven more by latency, repeated experiments, and checkpoint staging than by one-year egress savings alone.
Hardware degradation introduces the need for a storage refresh cycle. NVMe drives are rated for a specific write endurance, measured in DWPD over a typical five-year warranty period. Many large-scale ML training workloads are predominantly read-heavy once the initial dataset is ingested, so drives in a training cluster can last beyond their rated write lifespan. The primary driver for a refresh cycle may therefore be density rather than wear: newer drives often provide more capacity at a similar price point. Refreshing a cluster from 7.68 TB to 15.36 TB NVMe drives doubles the local cache capacity, enabling larger datasets to be staged directly on compute nodes and reducing dependence on the parallel file system for steady-state reads.


The cost structure laid out above turns tiering into a placement policy: keep data only as close to the accelerator as its access frequency and latency requirement justify. A tiering strategy encodes that policy across the hierarchy. Its hot, warm, cold, and archive labels name placement roles for a dataset rather than devices, and they follow the scope brackets of figure 1. The node-local pair is the hot tier, and the three shared services become the warm, cold, and archive tiers. The tier sections called local NVMe a warm cache because it sat in front of shared storage; in this placement vocabulary the same drives belong to the hot tier, because they hold the data the running job consumes.
The fastest and most expensive layer is the hot tier (local NVMe + host DRAM), which holds data being actively consumed by the running training job. Datasets are staged from shared storage to local NVMe at job start. This tier is provisioned per-node and is not shared across the cluster, so data that multiple jobs or teams need simultaneously cannot live here alone.
That shared-access requirement is what justifies the warm tier (parallel file system), which holds datasets accessed by multiple jobs or teams, shared checkpoints for fault recovery, and model artifacts under active development. The parallel file system provides the shared namespace necessary for multi-tenant access with strong consistency.
Below the warm tier sits the cold tier (object storage), which serves as the canonical repository for all organizational training data. Datasets are authored and versioned in object storage, then promoted to warmer tiers when needed for training. Object storage also serves as the durable backup for checkpoints after they are staged from local NVMe through the parallel file system.
Data that must be retained for compliance or reproducibility but is not expected to be accessed during normal operations drops to the archive tier (Glacier or equivalent). Lifecycle policies automatically transition data from cold to archive after a configurable period, typically 90 to 365 days since last access.
The movement of data between tiers should be automated through lifecycle policies. A well-designed tiering system automatically promotes data from cold to warm when a training job requests it, and demotes data from warm to cold when no job has accessed it for a configurable period. Manual tiering introduces operational burden and inevitably leads to either over-provisioning (data left on expensive tiers) or under-provisioning (data unavailable when needed).
Return to the running example to see tiering in action. The 3 TB source corpus and 6 TB serialized training shards live permanently in object storage (cold tier). When a training job is scheduled, the orchestration system triggers a “data staging” phase that copies each node’s assigned tokenized shards from object storage (cold tier) to its local NVMe (hot tier) before the first iteration, as in section 4.5.1. The run’s single epoch then reads entirely from local NVMe, incurring no network traffic for training inputs. When the job completes, a cleanup process deletes the local NVMe copies; the parallel file system holds only the job’s recent checkpoints, which the retention policy of section 4.6 governs. The entire lifecycle, from staging through training to cleanup, is managed by policy rather than by the training engineer.
The economic benefit of automated tiering compounds over time. An organization retaining 50 training datasets of 10 TB each would need 500 TB of parallel file system capacity if all data were left in place. If ten datasets are active concurrently and the other forty can be demoted after their jobs finish, automated tiering reduces the dataset capacity required on the parallel file system to 100 TB, saving $144,000 per year at the parallel file system’s per-TB rate. These savings are invisible in any single experiment but substantial when accumulated across the fleet.


The staging decision determines where the job pays for data movement: before training starts, during the first epoch, or on every epoch. Three common patterns balance the trade-off between startup latency and steady-state throughput.
Prestaging copies the entire dataset from object storage to local NVMe before the first training iteration begins. This approach delivers the highest steady-state performance because all subsequent reads are served locally, but it imposes the longest job startup delay. Staging a 10 TB dataset across 256 nodes at 500 MB/s per node takes roughly 80 seconds per node under ideal conditions, and contention on shared parallel file system bandwidth can extend that stall to several minutes.
On-demand staging instead defers copying until the data loader first accesses each shard. This removes the upfront startup delay, but the first epoch must pay the full network-read cost. Such amortized overhead works best for multi-epoch training where local reads across later epochs repay the initial transfer latency.
Streaming keeps data off local storage entirely, reading records from the parallel file system or remote object store on every epoch. Streaming incurs zero startup delay and requires no local NVMe capacity, but every epoch repeatedly absorbs the network-read cost. This trade-off makes streaming best suited for single-epoch pretraining runs or for massive datasets that exceed the aggregate local NVMe capacity of the cluster.
Tiering and staging settle where training data and checkpoints live and what each placement costs. Serving reuses the same hierarchy for a different objective, the time to bring a model into HBM and the latency of serving-time state, rather than epoch throughput.

Self-Check: Question

A team trains a vision model on a \(50\text{ TB}\) dataset stored in cloud object storage (\(\$0.02/\text{GB-month}\)) for 20 epochs across 4 training runs per year. Reading from object storage across a network boundary incurs a \(\$0.09/\text{GB}\) data egress fee. Staging the dataset onto local NVMe caches costs \(\$0.10/\text{GB-month}\). The team should migrate the dataset to cold tape archive to eliminate both egress fees and provisioned storage costs.

In a 1,000-GPU cluster where compute time is billed at \(\$2.00\) per GPU-hour, an undersized storage system introduces an additional 20 percentage points of input stalls (reducing the active compute fraction from \(90\%\) to \(70\%\)). Calculate the daily cost of this lost compute capacity and explain why investing in high-performance storage is economically rational.
An enterprise evaluates building an on-premises 1 PB parallel file system (\(\$3\text{M to } \$5\text{M}\) capex plus \(\$500\text{k/year}\) opex) versus storing the 1 PB corpus in cloud object storage (\(\$240\text{k/year}\) storage) and paying \(\$0.09/\text{GB}\) egress fees for 10 full-dataset reads per year (\(\$900\text{k/year}\) egress). What is the realistic financial payback horizon for building the on-premises system under these parameters?

Between 4.7 and 7.8 years, because net annual cloud delivery savings (\(\$640\text{k/year}\)) require multiple years to amortize the multi-million dollar initial hardware expenditure.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
The fifth workload inversion of section 4.2 set serving apart from training. Full-corpus training streams datasets and writes checkpoints in bursts, while in the weight-resident serving baseline, inference reads model weights once at startup and then serves requests from HBM. The primary storage challenge shifts from sustained dataset throughput to model-loading latency, although retrieval indexes and KV-cache offload add serving-time I/O when those mechanisms are enabled.
The most critical metric for inference storage is model loading latency, often called cold-start time: the duration required to load a model from storage into the accelerator’s HBM. For the 175B parameter language model, the weights alone occupy 350 GB in FP16 format. Loading this sequentially from a single high-performance NVMe drive at 14 GB/s takes 25 seconds, an unacceptable delay for a user-facing application. Loading from a shared PFS at a per-node rate of 4 GB/s takes 87.5 seconds. From object storage at 1 GB/s, the delay reaches 5.8 minutes.
To reduce cold-start time, the model is sharded and loaded in parallel. If the 350 GB model is striped across 8 NVMe drives, each loading a 43.75 GB shard at 7 GB/s, the total load time drops to roughly 6.2 seconds. When using tensor parallelism across 8 GPUs, each GPU loads only its 43.75 GB shard. If the weights already sit in host DRAM, each GPU’s own PCIe link could move its shard in about 0.7 seconds, but the 8 transfers share the node’s 200 GB/s of host-memory bandwidth, so the full load takes about 1.8 seconds. For the most latency-sensitive applications, organizations maintain warm replicas: one or more copies of the model weights kept preloaded in host DRAM, ready for that host-memory-bound transfer. This trades DRAM capacity for a load of about 1.8 seconds instead of the 6.2 seconds striped NVMe read.
These load times describe one replica. The model rollout previewed in section 4.2 asks all 100 replicas to load a new version at once, 35 TB of weights in one burst. If every replica reads from object storage at the 1 GB/s single-client rate, the fleet asks the store for 100 GB/s. A store whose aggregate service matches that figure, the 100 GB/s of table 2, finishes the rollout in about 5.8 minutes, no slower than one replica’s cold start; any smaller aggregate share stretches the rollout in proportion. Reading from the 1 TB/s parallel file system instead would take about 35 seconds, but only by claiming the whole file system and starving every training job that shares it, the read-side mirror of a checkpoint storm. Serving fleets therefore stage the new version on local NVMe before switching traffic, roll the update across groups of replicas so that the old version keeps serving, or let replicas that have finished loading supply the rest.
During autoregressive generation, the server keeps a per-request record of the attention keys and values produced by earlier tokens so it can generate the next token without recomputing the entire prefix. This record, called the key-value cache (KV cache), grows with sequence length and can consume significant HBM. For long sequences (128K tokens or more), KV cache offloading to host DRAM or NVMe extends the effective context window at the cost of increased latency per generated token, because cache blocks must be moved back into HBM before attention can use them. The storage lesson is that inference maintains an active working set rather than presenting solely a model-loading demand. When serving must also retrieve external context to ground that generation, the storage pipeline faces an entirely different access pattern: low-latency random queries into high-dimensional vector indexes.

Self-Check: Question

The node’s \(4\text{ GB/s}\) share of the parallel file system, for about 87.5 seconds.
A single object-storage client at \(1\text{ GB/s}\), for about 5.8 minutes.

A warm replica keeps the \(350\text{ GB}\) of weights in host DRAM. Each GPU’s own host link could move its \(43.75\text{ GB}\) shard in about 0.7 seconds, yet the full load takes about 1.8 seconds. Explain why.
A serving fleet of 100 replicas of a 175B-parameter model deploys a new version, so all replicas must read \(35\text{ TB}\) of FP16 weights at once. Which statement correctly evaluates the shared sources?

A \(100\text{ GB/s}\) object store finishes in about 5.8 minutes, while the \(1\text{ TB/s}\) parallel file system would take about 35 seconds but only by claiming the whole file system from co-tenant training jobs.
The parallel file system is always the right source because 35 seconds is shorter, and serving reads cannot interfere with training jobs.
The object store finishes in about 35 seconds because each replica reads only its own share of the weights.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
An inference request that needs supporting documents cannot wait for a sequential scan of the training corpus. A retrieval system first converts documents into vectors that represent semantic meaning, then finds nearby vectors and returns their source documents as context. The same storage analysis still applies, but the unit of demand becomes a query and its index accesses, and the deadline becomes the serving latency budget. With a graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index, the storage system traverses a high-dimensional vector graph instead of streaming sequential blobs via formats such as TFRecord or Parquet. Graph indexes are one family among several, and the others impose different bandwidth, capacity, and recall trade-offs. Exact flat search compares the query against every stored vector. Inverted-file (IVF) partitioning clusters the vectors and searches only the few clusters nearest the query. Product quantization (PQ) compresses each vector into short codes so that more of the index fits in memory, at some cost in accuracy.

Systems Perspective 4.4: The IOPS bottleneck in high-dimensional searchFor graph-based ANN, this architectural pattern shifts the primary storage bottleneck from sequential read bandwidth to random-access IOPS. The search traverses a high-dimensional graph to find approximate nearest neighbors across billions of embeddings. Its performance is governed by the trade-off among recall, latency, and capacity, where recall is the fraction of the true nearest neighbors that the approximate search returns. Raising recall requires traversing a larger portion of the index, driving up IOPS and latency. The arithmetic of a disk-resident traversal shows why IOPS, not bytes, binds. Each hop that misses DRAM costs one dependent SSD read of roughly 100 μs (table 2), and the next hop cannot start until that read returns, so ten such hops already spend a millisecond of the serving budget in storage alone. Throughput is bounded separately. A drive whose 4 KB random reads run near 0.5 GB/s (section 4.2) completes on the order of \(10^5\) such reads per second, and every concurrent query draws on that same budget, while each read moves only a few kilobytes. A 1,536-dimension embedding in FP32 (4 bytes per value) consumes approximately 6.1 KB, so a billion-document corpus requires roughly 6.1 TB before graph adjacency lists. If those lists add 50 to 100 bytes per node, they add 50 GB to 100 GB, making raw vectors plus minimal graph metadata about 6.2 TB at the high end. Production indexes can be larger once identifiers, graph levels, allocator overhead, deleted-entry slack, and replication are included. In-memory hierarchical navigable small world graph indexes make graph navigation fast when the index fits in DRAM (Malkov and Yashunin 2020). Disk-backed graph indexes such as DiskANN trade DRAM footprint against SSD traversal while targeting high recall and low query latency (Subramanya et al. 2019).



Subramanya, Suhas Jayaram, Fnu Devvrit, Harsha Vardhan Simhadri, Ravishankar Krishnawamy, and Rohan Kadekodi. 2019. “DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-Point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 32.

Malkov, Yury A., and Dmitry A. Yashunin. 2020. “Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs.” IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 42 (4): 824–36. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.2018.2889473.
Graph-based retrieval therefore spends storage budget on index levels that keep random traversal inside the serving latency service-level objective. A disk-backed graph is economical only if the extra SSD accesses do not erase the quality gain from searching a larger corpus. Flat, IVF, and PQ designs move that budget toward scan bandwidth, partition probes, or decompression and approximation error. The same hierarchy now supports bulk model loading, request-scoped KV state, and retrieval, each with a distinct service-rate contract. Each of those serving workloads reads artifacts that training produced. The last storage workload reverses that direction. When the fleet generates its own training data, storage must hold both the new samples and a record of how every one was made.

Self-Check: Question

How does the storage performance bottleneck for a graph-based vector retrieval index at billion-vector scale contrast with the primary bottleneck of an ML training data loader?

Vector retrieval is bottlenecked by sequential streaming bandwidth (GB/s), whereas training data loaders are bottlenecked by random \(4\text{ KB}\) read IOPS.
Vector retrieval requires continuous multi-terabyte burst writes, whereas training data loaders perform purely read-only operations.
Vector retrieval is strictly compute-bound on matrix multiplication units and generates zero storage device interaction.
Vector retrieval traverses high-dimensional graph structures requiring high random-access IOPS and low point-lookup latency, whereas training data loaders require sustained high-bandwidth sequential streaming.

True or False: In graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search such as HNSW or DiskANN, increasing target recall from \(90\%\) to \(99\%\) generally requires exploring more graph nodes, increasing random storage accesses and query latency.
A billion-entry vector index of 1536-dimensional FP32 embeddings consumes roughly \(6.1\text{ TB}\) of raw vector data plus graph adjacency overhead. Explain why systems migrate from pure in-memory indexes (HNSW) to disk-backed graph indexes (DiskANN), and identify the primary hardware trade-off involved.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
The versioned-artifact contract of section 4.4.4 applies to generated training samples as well as collected ones. When a fleet generates candidate samples, filters them, and verifies the survivors, each stage adds storage traffic and records that must remain linked to the accepted payload. The pressure to generate comes from the volume’s scaling thesis. The scaling laws of AI Scaling Laws make loss fall as a power law in training data as well as in parameters within their fitted regime, so each step up in model scale calls for more tokens, and the compute-optimal allocation grows the token budget with the parameter count. As high-quality human-generated text becomes harder to expand, the fleet encounters the data wall: the point where additional training samples must increasingly come from synthesis, simulation, curation, or expensive human collection (Villalobos et al. 2024). This shift from simple collection to managed data generation sends more than payload bytes through the hierarchy. A “synthetic fuel line” must also store the provenance chain of every sample: which model generated it, which filters accepted or rejected it, which judge or verifier models scored it, and which downstream run consumed it. That lineage makes repeated reuse of generated material traceable. It supports investigation of model collapse, where recursive training on generated data can degrade the learned distribution (Shumailov et al. 2024); retaining provenance alone does not prevent the degradation. The storage design must separately budget retained artifacts and the repeated scans used to assess them.

Villalobos, Pablo, Anson Ho, Jaime Sevilla, Tamay Besiroglu, Lennart Heim, and Marius Hobbhahn. 2024. “Will We Run Out of Data? Limits of LLM Scaling Based on Human-Generated Data.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2211.04325.

Shumailov, Ilia, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson, and Yarin Gal. 2024. “AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data.” Nature 631 (8022): 755–59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07566-y.

Napkin Math 4.9: The synthetic taxProblem: A 1 TB synthetic dataset retains provenance metadata and undergoes three independent verification scans. How much persistent capacity and pipeline traffic does it require if judge outputs are not retained as full dataset copies?

Raw Payload: 1 TB.
Provenance Overhead: 40 percent extra for lineage hashes, generation logs, and reward-model scores.
Verification Traffic: 3 judge passes each read the payload, producing 3 TB of read traffic. Their scores reside in the provenance metadata rather than in three retained payload copies.
Capacity Result: Persistent capacity is 1 TB \(\times\) 1.4 = 1.4 TB, a 1.4× capacity factor.
Traffic Result: Writing the payload and metadata once and reading the payload three times moves 4.4 TB, a 4.4× traffic factor before generation and judge-model compute are counted.

Systems insight: Verification primarily taxes service rate and compute, while retained provenance taxes capacity. The two costs coincide only when the pipeline materializes each judge output as another full dataset. Synthetic storage must therefore budget bytes at rest separately from bytes moved and record which generator, filters, judges, and downstream runs produced each accepted sample.


The synthetic fuel line completes the chapter’s survey of storage workloads by making lineage part of the payload. Large-scale training, checkpointing, retrieval, and synthetic-data generation stress different tiers. Their common design requirement is to account for service rate and correctness alongside capacity. A store can have room for every artifact yet fail to deliver it on time, restore a complete generation, or identify the data that shaped a model. Every design in the chapter so far also assumes today’s six tiers, and the boundaries between those tiers are themselves moving.

Self-Check: Question

A team generates a \(1\text{ TB}\) synthetic text dataset. Retained provenance adds \(40\%\) metadata overhead, and 3 verifier models each read the payload once without materializing another full copy. What persistent capacity and total pipeline traffic are required?

\(1.4\text{ TB}\) of persistent capacity and \(4.4\text{ TB}\) of traffic: \(1\text{ TB}\) payload write, \(0.4\text{ TB}\) metadata write, and \(3\text{ TB}\) of verifier reads.
Exactly \(1.0\text{ TB}\), because verifier models run entirely in GPU registers without generating persistent storage artifacts.
Roughly \(0.4\text{ TB}\), because synthetic data compresses more efficiently than natural language text.
Roughly \(14\text{ TB}\), because every verifier model stores a full \(350\text{ GB}\) copy of its internal neural activations for every sample.

Explain why synthetic training data pipelines must treat storage as an active ‘provenance engine’ by recording the generating model, filters, and verifier scores for each accepted sample, rather than storing plain text files.
