title: 4 Data Storage
text:
While the six-tier hierarchy represents a common production baseline, memory and storage technologies can fill the bandwidth gaps between existing tiers, reshaping effective storage architecture for large-scale ML. The widest unfilled gap in the hierarchy sits between host DRAM and local NVMe, and Compute Express Link (CXL), the coherent capacity tier of Compute express link (CXL), targets exactly this gap. Seen from storage, CXL-attached memory is a “Tier 1.5,” slower than host DRAM but byte-addressable, with access latencies of roughly 200 to 500 ns against the roughly 100 μs of an NVMe read. It offers a capacity pool for the structures that the Tier 1 discussion showed competing for host DRAM. For the running example, CXL-attached memory could expand the effective host memory tier from 512 GB to over 4 TB per node. That pool could hold deeper prefetch queues, embedding-table spillover, or a local shard cache as large as the 3 TB compressed source corpus without paying NVMe access latency on every read, though it still falls short of the full 6 TB tokenized training copy on one node.
A different bottleneck appears when CPU-side decoding, not storage bandwidth, throttles the pipeline. The computational storage drive closes that gap by embedding processing elements (field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) or simple CPU cores) directly on the SSD controller, enabling decompression, filtering, or format conversion to happen at the storage device rather than consuming host CPU cycles. For ML pipelines where CPU-side decoding is the bottleneck, computational storage could eliminate the CPU from the data path entirely, complementing GDS by offloading work that direct DMA cannot address.
Checkpoint writes impose the pause \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) while a consistent snapshot reaches the first storage tier, and shrinking it makes frequent saves less costly. Persistent memory, despite market shifts such as the discontinuation of Intel Optane, remains the architectural idea that attacks that term directly. Byte-addressable non-volatile memory could lower the destination-device latency, but the checkpoint pause still includes snapshot creation, byte transfer, and coordination. A lower device-access latency reduces \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) only to the extent that this device lies on the pause’s critical path.
These technologies are not yet broadly deployed at the scale of the largest ML clusters, but they illustrate the direction of the storage hierarchy’s evolution. The fundamental principle remains unchanged, with faster, more expensive storage closer to the accelerator and slower, cheaper storage at the periphery. What changes is the granularity of the tiers and the size of the gaps between them.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Storage design errors are among the most expensive mistakes in ML infrastructure because they are discovered late, when training begins, and remediation requires either expensive hardware upgrades or time-consuming data reformatting. The following fallacies and pitfalls capture the most common errors that experienced storage engineers make when first encountering ML workloads.

Fallacy: NVMe is fast enough to feed GPUs directly without pipelining.
A single NVMe drive delivers 7 GB/s, while an H100 consumes 3.35 TB/s from HBM. The gap is roughly 479×. Even four drives in RAID-0 only close this gap to about 120× before overhead. Without pipelining and prefetching to hide the latency of loading from NVMe to host DRAM to HBM, every batch transfer introduces a stall equal to the transfer time. The HBM ratio measures tier disparity rather than the required input rate, because model state is reused many times for each batch loaded from storage. The relevant test compares measured input delivery with batch bytes divided by compute time, then checks whether buffering hides transfer latency and jitter. A device can have enough sustained bandwidth and still expose stalls when transfers are serialized with computation.


Pitfall: Relying on prefetching to hide object storage latency.
Prefetching hides latency only within the time covered by ready batches; it cannot hide an arbitrarily long interruption. With \(\PrefetchBufferCount\) batches ready and constant compute time, a complete interruption of supply exhausts the queue after \(\PrefetchBufferCount \times \IronLawComputeTime\) milliseconds. A slow request need not stall computation if other completed work remains available, but correlated delays can deplete many workers’ queues together. Provision buffer depth from measured delivery tails, test correlated interruptions, and verify that the sustained refill rate meets consumption. Local staging can reduce remote exposure when the required shards fit and remain valid.


Fallacy: Millions of small training files are harmless at scale.
Storing each training sample as an individual file (one JPEG per image, one JSON per text sample) creates repeated per-file work through operations such as open(), stat(), and close(). Metadata becomes the bottleneck when the resulting request rate exceeds the service’s capacity, even if byte bandwidth remains available. Aggregating samples into sequential shards amortizes that work (section 4.3.5). Packaging 10,000 to 100,000 samples per shard can reduce file-level operations by a corresponding 10,000 to 100,000\(\times\) when readers consume whole shards. The loader must still implement the intended sampling policy and avoid repeated enumeration.


Pitfall: Ignoring egress costs when designing the storage architecture.
Cloud egress costs are invisible during development but can dominate at scale. Under a representative $0.09/GB cross-boundary egress fee, a training job that reads a 100 TB dataset from object storage 10 times incurs $90,000 in egress fees, far exceeding the annual storage cost of $24,000 under the object-storage price assumption in section 4.3.7. These fees apply when reads cross a region, provider, or internet boundary; same-region reads may be free or discounted, which is exactly why the cost stays hidden until a cross-region or multi-cloud topology makes it unavoidable. Teams that prototype with small datasets on object storage and then scale up discover that their storage architecture is economically unsustainable. The fix is to budget egress costs explicitly and to design the data pipeline to minimize cross-tier transfers, typically by staging data on local NVMe at job start rather than streaming from object storage each epoch.


Fallacy: Average write bandwidth is enough for checkpoint design.
Checkpoints are written by all nodes simultaneously, creating bursts that can exceed steady-state bandwidth by 10\(\times\) or more. When the PFS write lies on the training critical path, sizing it only for average write load extends \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) during bursts and reduces effective training throughput. A synchronous PFS-direct design must provision enough burst bandwidth to meet its pause budget. With local staging, the first tier absorbs the burst and the PFS drains it in the background; the shared tier must then meet the durability deadline and keep up with repeated saves without an unbounded backlog.


Pitfall: Assuming faster accelerators automatically improve training throughput.
When an organization upgrades from A100 to H100 GPUs, they expect training time to decrease proportionally to the compute improvement. If the storage pipeline was already marginal on A100s, delivering data just fast enough to avoid stalls, the faster H100 compute simply hits the I/O wall sooner. The accelerator upgrade reduces \(\IronLawComputeTime\) without reducing \(\StepIoTime\), which means the data stall ratio increases. Every accelerator upgrade must be accompanied by a storage pipeline audit to ensure that the faster compute does not simply expose a previously hidden storage bottleneck.


Fallacy: RAID configurations optimized for databases are suitable for ML training.
RAID selection follows the tier’s failure contract. A disposable local cache can use RAID 0 to aggregate drives without parity, provided a durable source remains available and the fleet can tolerate restaging after a drive failure. Redundant layouts can still reduce disruption when restaging is slow or the cache supports an availability objective. A local checkpoint awaiting durable replication is not yet disposable merely because it lives on the same NVMe drives. Treating all ML storage as replaceable input data confuses capacity placement with recovery policy.


Pitfall: Creating full copies for each dataset snapshot.
Copying an entire dataset for every version duplicates unchanged content. For a 10 TB dataset with 5 percent of its bytes changed, a full copy retains 9.5 TB of redundant data. Content-addressable storage or delta encoding can reuse unchanged objects or blocks. If the storage granularity isolates the changed bytes, the new payload is roughly 500 GB, a 20\(\times\) reduction before metadata and redundancy overhead. Rewriting large compressed shards can reduce that saving because a small sample change may replace a much larger stored object. Versioning must therefore preserve lineage while choosing a reuse granularity compatible with the dataset format.


Fallacy: Compression always helps because it reduces the amount of data to read.
Compression reduces stored and transferred bytes but adds decoding work. If decoding further saturates an already limiting host processor, it makes that bottleneck worse, not better. If transfer is limiting and decoding has headroom, compression can improve delivery until another stage becomes the limit. Compare candidate representations using output-equivalent stage rates, including CPU or GPU decoding, rather than select the strongest codec from an I/O-bound label alone. The same choice can reduce capacity cost without improving training throughput. These fallacies all return to the same accounting exercise: where each byte lives, how often it moves, and which tier pays the cost.


Self-Check: Question

A team selects RAID 5 for a disposable local training-data cache whose immutable source is durably stored elsewhere. The fleet can tolerate restaging after drive failure. Why might RAID 0 be a better throughput-and-capacity trade-off under this failure contract?

RAID 5 cannot be formatted with modern Linux filesystems such as ext4 or XFS.
RAID 5 disables hardware DMA transfers, preventing the GPU from accessing host DRAM.
The cache can be reconstructed from its durable source, so RAID 0 can aggregate drives without parity overhead when restaging disruption is acceptable.
RAID 5 increases drive endurance wear by \(10\times\) compared to single-drive configurations.

A training team upgrades its cluster from A100 to H100 GPUs, expecting a \(3\times\) end-to-end training speedup. However, wall-clock epoch time barely improves, and GPU utilization drops from \(85\%\) to \(35\%\). Traces show shorter uninterrupted compute time, unchanged measured input-delivery rate, and increased time waiting for ready input batches, while communication and checkpoint pauses remain unchanged. Diagnose the measured bottleneck and explain why faster compute exposed it.
A team replaces a lighter codec with a denser codec on local-NVMe training shards. On this corpus, illustrative measurements give the lighter codec a 3:1 ratio and 1.5 GB/s decoded output per core, versus 4:1 and 0.5 GB/s for the denser codec. Before the change, worker profiles show decoding and augmentation saturating the host CPU and the ready-batch queue repeatedly draining. Afterward, decompression consumes more CPU time, the queue drains more often, and training step time increases although stored bytes decrease. What caused this measured regression?

Compressed shards cannot be read by NVMe controllers because flash drives require raw uncompressed binary blocks.
The pipeline was already CPU-bound on data decoding and augmentation, so adding heavy decompression work saturated the host CPU, starving the GPU of assembled batches.
The denser codec introduces non-deterministic bit flips that cause stochastic gradient descent to diverge.
The parallel file system rejects compressed shards larger than 1 GB due to POSIX file locking constraints.

True or False: Sizing a data loader’s prefetch buffer depth based on average storage read latency ensures that training runs will not experience data stalls during multi-week training jobs on shared object storage.
A team creates full \(10\text{ TB}\) copies of a pretraining dataset for every snapshot version, creating 20 versions over six months (\(200\text{ TB}\) total storage). Explain how content-addressable storage or delta encoding optimizes this workflow when successive versions differ by only \(5\%\).

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Storage in ML systems is an active, multi-tiered pipeline that supplies accelerator inputs, preserves restorable state, and records the lineage of training and serving artifacts. The hierarchy exists because workloads need different combinations of bandwidth, capacity, latency, durability, and cost, and the demand on it grows with the scaling laws that drive the fleet. Larger models call for more training tokens and carry larger checkpoints, so storage pressure rises at every step up the model-size curve. The data pipeline throughput equation, \(\RequiredInputBandwidth = \InputConsumerAcceleratorCount \times \TargetComputeTimeFraction\times \BatchDataVolume / \IronLawComputeTime\), sizes delivery for a chosen training rate when applied to the representation and distinct input consumers at each tier. Measured against the Fleet Law, storage succeeds when it contributes no exposed time. Prefetching preserves the Fleet Law’s assumption that the next batch is already resident. Tiered checkpoint staging shrinks the save pause that surfaces in \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) to the local write and takes the slow shared-storage copy off the step entirely, so that copy costs step time only when it contends with collectives or input reads. Both spend communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)) and coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) capacity to protect compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)).
Treating the hierarchy as a cache makes that sizing workload-specific. The hit rate and the service times of the hot and cold paths determine mean effective throughput, while the tail and correlation of misses determine whether a finite prefetch buffer drains. At the durable tiers, reliability also separates into three contracts: data survival, service response, and the version a reader may observe. These are durability, availability, and consistency, respectively; improving one does not automatically establish the others.
The diagnostic task is to identify which service contract fails before changing the storage tier. Low accelerator utilization can arise from metadata-intensive loading, a depleted prefetch queue, an exposed checkpoint write, or host-memory traffic crossing a contended NUMA link. Measure input wait separately from communication and synchronization before attributing it to storage. Full-corpus scans favor aggregated shards, while graph retrieval and live features require random access and explicit consistency. A depleted input queue can reflect slow storage, metadata contention, or insufficient decoding capacity; GDS helps when host payload copying is the limiting stage while retaining CPU control. Compare remedies by total delivery cost, including transfers and idle accelerators. For checkpoint writes, evaluate the shorter training pause together with the time until a complete generation becomes durable and publishable.

Key Takeaways: Feed the accelerators or waste them

Workload demand sizes the delivery path: Use \(\RequiredInputBandwidth = \InputConsumerAcceleratorCount \times \TargetComputeTimeFraction\times \BatchDataVolume / \IronLawComputeTime\) for the chosen training rate, then check each tier’s service rate and buffering (principle \(\ref{pri-storage-hierarchy}\)).
Workload determines the storage contract: Full-corpus scans favor sequential throughput and aggregated shards, and metadata operations can bind before byte bandwidth does (principle \(\ref{pri-io-wall}\)). Disk-backed graph retrieval must fit its random I/O within a serving deadline, and synthetic-data pipelines must budget verification traffic separately from retained capacity while preserving provenance for accepted samples.
Tail latency sets the cache budget: A high hot-tier hit rate is insufficient when cold misses are orders of magnitude slower. Use equation 1 as a mean baseline, then size prefetch buffers from p99 I/O latency and test correlated miss bursts against the compute window.
Pipeline correctness lives at commit boundaries: Replay preserves processing completeness only when stable identifiers and idempotent or transactional writes prevent duplicate effects. Event-time watermarks then make the separate freshness-completeness trade-off explicit.
Direct storage removes host payload copies: GDS retains CPU submission and coordination while bypassing host bounce buffers. The illustrative example assumes 4× less active CPU time per request; the benefit depends on whether payload copying limits the workload.
Checkpoint recovery is a storage protocol: Local NVMe staging can shorten pause time, but a restorable checkpoint also needs durable publication, a committed manifest, and verified shards; durability, availability, and consistency remain distinct contracts.
Economics drive tiering: The 5× local-NVMe/object-storage price ratio illustrates the incentive to keep data on cheaper tiers under the stated pricing assumptions (principle \(\ref{pri-storage-hierarchy}\)). Compare total delivery cost, including transfer charges and idle accelerators, before deciding where to stage it.



Checkpoint staging shows the C\(^3\) trade-off in one design decision. Writing first to local NVMe shortens the compute pause, but asynchronous replication adds communication traffic and requires coordination to publish only complete generations. Once the shared-file-system write leaves the critical path, the bottleneck can move to local flash endurance, peer-replication bandwidth, or manifest commit latency. Measuring only the shorter training pause would miss the new recovery boundary.

What’s Next: From storage to splittingCompute silicon, network fabrics, and storage hierarchies establish the physical resources of the machine learning fleet. Coordinating those resources into one training computation remains a separate problem. This chapter’s 175B running model already exceeds, in its FP16 weights alone, the 80 GB device of the HBM placement example, so its state and work must span devices. The partition determines which intermediate results and gradients must cross the fabric and when workers must synchronize. Part II moves from physical infrastructure to distributed execution: partitioning neural networks across data, tensor, pipeline, and sequence dimensions, orchestrating collective communication, and surviving hardware failures at fleet scale.





↪ Parallelism strategies (data, tensor, pipeline, and sequence) are developed in Distributed Training.
 

Self-Check: Question

A 2,048-GPU training cluster reports \(40\%\) GPU hardware utilization. Telemetry reveals: (1) GPUs spend \(45\%\) of iteration time waiting for data tensors, (2) Storage data disks on the parallel file system report less than \(5\%\) bandwidth utilization, (3) Data loader host CPU cores report \(100\%\) utilization, and (4) The dataset is stored as 50 million individual JPEG files. A worker CPU profile attributes most active CPU time to JPEG decoding, the MDS shows a sustained queue at its operation-rate limit, and the completed-batch queue repeatedly drains. Which remediation targets the two measured limiting stages?

The parallel file system network fabric is saturated; upgrade InfiniBand links between compute nodes and storage servers.
GPU HBM capacity is exhausted; apply aggressive 4-bit activation quantization to free GPU memory.
NVMe drive endurance limits have triggered write throttling; replace compute node local SSDs.
The workload is suffering from both metadata server saturation (individual small files) and CPU-bound decoding; repackage the dataset into large WebDataset tar shards and evaluate GPU JPEG decoding against its compute and HBM budget.

Synthesize how the ML storage hierarchy (spanning HBM, DRAM, NVMe, PFS, Object Storage, and Archive) co-designs bandwidth physics with capacity economics to prevent accelerator starvation.
Generation g is durably committed and retained. Training resumes after locally staging all shards of g+1, but a node fails before durable publication of g+1 and its required shard is lost. Which generation may restore, and what evidence is required before g+1 could become a restore candidate?

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Self-Check: Answer

An H100 accelerator consumes data from its HBM at roughly \(3.35\text{ TB/s}\), while a single local NVMe drive delivers sequential reads at roughly \(7\text{ GB/s}\). A team is designing the storage infrastructure for a 1,000-accelerator training fleet. Which conclusion follows directly from this bandwidth ratio?

The gap is easily bridged by standard NVMe RAID arrays because sequential read throughput scales without bound across drives.
The roughly \(480\times\) device-bandwidth gap motivates tiered staging, but required input bandwidth must be calculated from batch bytes and compute time rather than equated with HBM traffic.
The bandwidth gap is negligible because large-scale training is entirely compute-bound and rarely exercises HBM bandwidth.
The bandwidth gap disappears when high-speed InfiniBand fabrics deliver data directly into HBM from remote storage endpoints without local staging.

Answer: The correct answer is B. HBM and NVMe serve different traffic: model state and intermediate tensors can be reused many times for each input batch. The roughly \(479\times\) ratio illustrates tier disparity, not a storage-rate requirement. Batch bytes, compute time, concurrency, and buffering determine whether inputs arrive in time; neither RAID aggregation nor a faster network alone establishes that condition.
Learning Objective: Distinguish storage input demand from internal HBM traffic when interpreting the bandwidth gap
A 175B-parameter model trains for 30 days on 256 nodes, writing resumable mixed-precision Adam checkpoints of roughly \(2.45\text{ TB}\) (\(350\text{ GB}\) FP16 weights, \(700\text{ GB}\) FP32 master weights, and \(1.4\text{ TB}\) of Adam moments) every 10 minutes. Explain why ML storage design is fundamentally a joint physics-and-economics optimization problem.
Answer: HBM supplies high local bandwidth for active tensors but cannot economically retain the corpus and checkpoint history. Shared durable storage pools capacity at lower cost, while interfaces, contention, and client allocation determine the rate and latency a consumer receives. Tier placement must satisfy input-delivery and checkpoint-recovery budgets at the lowest total delivery cost. Remote input reads can suffice when their sustained rate and buffered latency meet demand; local staging is useful when they do not. Compare capacity cost, transfers, and exposed accelerator wait rather than infer a stall from remote placement alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze why ML storage architecture requires tiered placement that simultaneously satisfies bandwidth physics and capacity economics
True or False: A cluster benchmark demonstrating that compute hardware achieves advertised peak TFLOP/s and network fabric achieves advertised bisection bandwidth is sufficient evidence that end-to-end training throughput will scale linearly with accelerator count.
Answer: False. Isolated compute and fabric benchmarks evaluate floating-point throughput and inter-node communication in synthetic conditions without exercising the end-to-end data pipeline. Real training throughput requires continuously streaming input batches, loading model weights, and absorbing periodic checkpoint write storms; if the storage hierarchy cannot deliver input samples within the iteration window (\(T_{\text{iteration}}\)), accelerators sit idle regardless of peak compute capability.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why compute and network benchmarks in isolation fail to guarantee scalable end-to-end training throughput without storage pipeline validation
An accelerator upgrade reduces compute time per batch while the input representation and storage delivery time remain fixed. What is the primary systems consequence for training cluster design?

Training pipelines automatically increase data compression ratios to prevent accelerator starvation without requiring architectural adjustments.
Storage hierarchies can eliminate intermediate DRAM and NVMe caching tiers because modern network fabrics directly absorb the difference.
Checkpoint intervals must be decreased proportionally to the compute growth to keep local NVMe buffers from overflowing.
The compute window available to deliver each batch shrinks, so input I/O can become the bottleneck unless the measured delivery path keeps pace.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Faster computation leaves less time to fetch the next batch. Overlap and prefetching hide latency within their buffering window, but cannot fix a sustained service-rate deficit. Automatic compression is not guaranteed, removing staging does not improve a slow source, and checkpoint frequency does not set input delivery throughput.
Learning Objective: Explain the systems consequences of compute throughput scaling significantly faster than persistent storage bandwidth
In large-scale distributed training, when hundreds of nodes simultaneously pause computation to write gigabytes of model weights and optimizer states to persistent storage, the resulting synchronized burst of write traffic is called a ____.
Answer: The correct term is checkpoint storm. A checkpoint storm occurs when all data-parallel or model-parallel workers simultaneously flush their memory shards to local or remote storage, creating extreme write contention that must be absorbed via tiered staging (such as writing to local NVMe before asynchronously copying to a parallel file system).
Learning Objective: Explain the technical term for synchronized cluster-wide write bursts generated during distributed training state saves

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A storage procurement team is sizing storage hardware for a cluster dedicated to pretraining foundation models on a \(200\text{ TB}\) immutable text corpus. Which purchasing decision represents the most severe misallocation of budget based on ML workload characteristics?

Paying a premium for enterprise SSDs optimized for high \(4\text{ KB}\) random-read IOPS while under-provisioning sustained sequential read bandwidth (GB/s).
Aggregating raw text samples into \(256\text{ MB}\) to \(4\text{ GB}\) contiguous binary shards prior to training to amortize file-system metadata operations.
Provisioning local NVMe drives on compute nodes to serve as a warm read cache for multi-epoch training passes.
Sizing the parallel file system write tier to absorb synchronized multi-terabyte checkpoint write bursts from hundreds of nodes.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Paying a premium for enterprise SSDs optimized for high \(4\text{ KB}\) random-read IOPS while under-provisioning sustained sequential read bandwidth (GB/s). ML pretraining streams large contiguous batches sequentially, where a drive delivers \(7\text{-}14\text{ GB/s}\), whereas \(4\text{ KB}\) random reads drop throughput to \(\approx 0.5\text{ GB/s}\); optimizing for random IOPS buys capabilities the workload never utilizes while starving the pipeline of raw gigabytes-per-second throughput. Shard aggregation is the standard mitigation against metadata serialization, local NVMe caching prevents repeated network egress, and sizing for checkpoint bursts directly addresses the bursty write inversion.
Learning Objective: Evaluate storage procurement decisions against the sequential-streaming and bursty-write inversions of ML workloads
True or False: An in-memory LRU cache sized to \(300\text{ GB}\) placed in front of a \(3\text{ TB}\) uniformly shuffled pretraining dataset will achieve roughly a \(90\%\) hit rate after the first epoch warms the cache because all samples are reused across epochs.
Answer: False. A cache holding one-tenth of a uniformly shuffled corpus does not gain a 90 percent hit rate merely because samples recur in later epochs. Most cached samples are evicted before reuse. A fixed cyclic scan larger than the cache can approach zero hits; independently reshuffled epochs allow low but nonzero cross-epoch hits that depend on cache fraction and sample order.
Learning Objective: Analyze why temporal-locality caching strategies such as LRU fail on uniformly streamed ML pretraining datasets
Explain why ML data loaders implement shard-level shuffling combined with within-shard buffer mixing rather than true global per-sample random shuffling across petabyte-scale training corpora.
Answer: Shard-level shuffling and within-shard buffer mixing preserve sequential I/O while introducing sample-order variation. Adequate mixing depends on shard composition and buffer size: homogeneous shards may require finer shards or larger mixing buffers. Validate the layout against the loss curve of a fully shuffled baseline on a subset before committing the run.
Learning Objective: Justify shard-level shuffling under explicit mixing and convergence checks
When an inference platform deploys a new version of a 175B-parameter model (\(350\text{ GB}\) FP16 weights) across 100 serving replicas, how does the storage access profile contrast with a training checkpoint save?

It generates continuous small random writes to update parameter journals on each replica node.
It streams an incremental delta of only modified parameters over hours to minimize bandwidth utilization.
It creates a synchronized fan-out read burst of roughly \(35\text{ TB}\) (\(100 \times 350\text{ GB}\)) that must complete within the deployment latency budget while serving traffic continues.
It requires sustained multi-gigabyte-per-second sequential write bandwidth to central durable object storage.

Answer: The correct answer is C. It creates a synchronized fan-out read burst of roughly \(35\text{ TB}\) (\(100 \times 350\text{ GB}\)) that must complete within the deployment latency budget while serving traffic continues. A model rollout is the architectural mirror image of a checkpoint storm: instead of many nodes simultaneously writing state to storage (fan-in burst), many replica nodes simultaneously read the same large model weights from storage (fan-out burst). The small-random-writes option describes OLTP database journaling. The delta-streaming option assumes parameter-level differential rollouts that production serving frameworks avoid in favor of immutable weight images. The central-write option confuses read distribution to serving nodes with training checkpoint writes.
Learning Objective: Classify model rollout storage traffic as a synchronized fan-out read burst and quantify its cluster-wide volume
Order the sequence of performance degradation steps that occurs when a training cluster attempts to load a dataset stored as 200 million individual small JPEG files from a parallel file system: (1) Storage data disks and network links sit largely idle despite abundant rated bandwidth, (2) Thousands of concurrent workers execute open(), stat(), and close() system calls for every 10 KB sample, (3) The training loop stalls and GPU utilization collapses while waiting for batch collation, (4) Dedicated metadata servers (MDS) become saturated by hundreds of thousands of lock acquisitions and attribute lookups per second, (5) Data loader worker threads block on serialized file descriptor operations.
Answer: The correct order is: (2) Thousands of concurrent workers execute open(), stat(), and close() system calls for every 10 KB sample, (4) Dedicated metadata servers (MDS) become saturated by hundreds of thousands of lock acquisitions and attribute lookups per second, (5) Data loader worker threads block on serialized file descriptor operations, (1) Storage data disks and network links sit largely idle despite abundant rated bandwidth, (3) The training loop stalls and GPU utilization collapses while waiting for batch collation. The pathology begins when workers flood the namespace with per-file POSIX calls (2), overwhelming the metadata servers (4), which causes data loader worker threads to block waiting for metadata responses (5); because threads are blocked on metadata, payload requests never reach data disks (1), leaving GPUs starved for training batches (3).
Learning Objective: Analyze the causal failure cascade of the small-file metadata bottleneck in parallel file systems

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Order the six tiers from Tier 0 through Tier 5 in the chapter’s placement hierarchy, moving outward from accelerator-resident memory through node-local resources to shared storage and archive: (1) Local NVMe SSD, (2) Object Storage, (3) Host DRAM, (4) GPU HBM, (5) Parallel File System, (6) Archive / Cold Storage.
Answer: The correct order is: (4) GPU HBM, (3) Host DRAM, (1) Local NVMe SSD, (5) Parallel File System, (2) Object Storage, (6) Archive / Cold Storage. HBM is accelerator-resident; host DRAM and local NVMe serve the node; the parallel file system provides shared access; object storage retains durable organizational data; and archive preserves rarely accessed history. This is the chapter’s placement order, not a universal bandwidth ranking. HBM rates are per accelerator, DRAM and local NVMe rates are per node, and shared-service rates must be allocated among clients and checked against the actual delivery path.
Learning Objective: Order the six storage tiers by placement and distinguish that order from a bandwidth comparison
Host DRAM (Tier 1) executes a four-stage data loader pipeline: Read, Decode, Augment, and Collate. Why place the final collated batch in page-locked (‘pinned’) host memory for direct asynchronous DMA to GPU HBM without an intermediate staging copy?

Pinned memory automatically compresses tensors using host CPU vector units before PCIe transmission.
Pinned memory locks physical pages in host RAM so the PCIe DMA controller can copy data directly to GPU memory without an intermediate pinned staging copy.
Pinned memory replicates the batch across all NUMA nodes to ensure uniform memory access for parallel data loader threads.
Pinned memory guarantees transactional ACID durability on host storage in case the worker process crashes during transfer.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Pinned memory locks physical pages in host RAM so the PCIe DMA controller can copy data directly to GPU memory without an intermediate pinned staging copy. Standard virtual memory pages can be paged out or relocated by the operating system, forcing the GPU driver to copy data into an intermediate pinned staging buffer before initiating DMA; allocating pinned memory directly (pin_memory=True in PyTorch) eliminates this extra CPU memory copy and allows direct DMA across PCIe. The compression option is incorrect as pinned memory is an OS page-locking mechanism, not a compression algorithm. The NUMA replication claim is false because pinning prevents paging rather than replicating data or choosing NUMA placement. The ACID durability option confuses volatile host DRAM staging with persistent transaction logging.
Learning Objective: Explain the architectural function of pinned host memory in accelerating CPU-to-GPU DMA data transfers
A vision training cluster migrating to a high-performance parallel file system (PFS) with \(500\text{ GB/s}\) rated aggregate bandwidth reports that throughput during ImageNet training is capped at under \(5\text{ GB/s}\), with storage data disks showing negligible I/O activity. The dataset consists of millions of individual JPEG files. A worker trace shows repeated waits for file opens, and the MDS reports a sustained operation queue with rising lookup latency while its service rate is saturated. What bottleneck do these additional measurements establish, and which fix addresses it?

The network fabric is dropping packets due to congestion; enable flow control on top-of-rack switches.
The parallel file system is bottlenecked on drive endurance wear-leveling; replace SSDs with high-DWPD enterprise drives.
The dataset is stored as millions of individual image files, saturating the Metadata Server (MDS) with per-file POSIX lookups; repackage images into large sequential shards (such as WebDataset tar archives).
The GPUs are compute-bound and cannot consume data faster; decrease the batch size to increase I/O request frequency.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The saturated MDS service rate, rising lookup latency, and worker file-open waits establish a metadata bottleneck in this case. Repackaging images into sequential shards amortizes per-file operations across many samples. Idle data disks and low throughput alone would not establish this cause; the supplied metadata measurements distinguish it from a slow decoder or another blocked pipeline stage.
Learning Objective: Analyze parallel file system metadata saturation from telemetry signatures and prescribe shard-aggregation remediation
A training node uses four local NVMe drives configured in RAID-0 as a warm cache for \(25\text{ TB}\) of pre-shuffled training shards. Explain why RAID-0 is an appropriate engineering trade-off for this specific tier, and identify what workload change would make RAID-0 catastrophic.
Answer: RAID-0 aggregates drive bandwidth without parity capacity overhead, making it appropriate for a disposable warm cache when a durable source remains available and the fleet can tolerate restaging after a drive failure. It does not protect availability: losing one drive can invalidate the array. If the array holds the only copy of an unrecoverable artifact or a checkpoint not yet durably replicated, a drive failure can permanently lose that state; the cache placement policy cannot substitute for a recovery contract.
Learning Objective: Justify RAID-0 storage configurations for warm cache tiers and identify failure boundaries where lack of redundancy causes unrecoverable data loss
A multi-modal training job combines \(3\text{ TB}\) of text, \(50\text{ TB}\) of images, and \(200\text{ TB}\) of video. The infrastructure team provisions storage bandwidth based exclusively on the video modality because video represents over \(75\%\) of total dataset capacity. What can be concluded about this sizing decision from the supplied information?

Adequacy cannot be established from corpus capacity alone; sizing must include the combined sampled-batch byte rate and decoding, augmentation, and buffering demand of all active modalities.
The video stream will starve the parallel file system because image and text files use incompatible POSIX stripe sizes.
The model will fail to converge because object storage cannot maintain ACID consistency when serving multiple modalities simultaneously.
The training job will exhaust GPU HBM because video tensors automatically overwrite text embeddings during collation.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Retained corpus capacity does not determine per-step delivery demand. Sampling frequency, batch representation, and compute time set how many bytes each modality contributes to the feed, while transformations determine its decoding and augmentation work. Sum those demands across active streams and compare them with measured stage rates and buffer capacity. Video-only sizing omits that accounting, but the supplied corpus sizes do not prove a particular storage, host-DRAM, or decoding bottleneck.
Learning Objective: Distinguish retained corpus capacity from combined sampled-batch and transformation demand when sizing multimodal delivery
In a parallel file system architecture like Lustre, namespace management (file creation, directory paths, locks) is handled by a dedicated ____, while raw data blocks are striped across multiple Object Storage Servers (OSS).
Answer: The correct term is Metadata Server (or MDS). The separation of the Metadata Server (MDS) from Object Storage Servers (OSS) allows data bandwidth to scale linearly with the number of OSS nodes, though the MDS can become a bottleneck if datasets contain millions of small individual files.
Learning Objective: Explain the architectural role of the Metadata Server (MDS) in parallel file systems

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

The data pipeline throughput equation is \(\text{BW}_{\text{required}} = N_{\text{GPU}} \times \eta_{\text{target}} \times \frac{D_{\text{vol,batch}}}{T_{\text{iteration}}}\). If a cluster doubles its number of GPUs consuming distinct local batches from 1,024 to 2,048 while keeping per-GPU batch size, uninterrupted compute time per batch, and target active-time fraction constant, how does the required aggregate storage bandwidth scale?

It remains constant because data-parallel workers divide the fixed total dataset into smaller partitions.

A team generates a \(1\text{ TB}\) synthetic text dataset. Retained provenance adds \(40\%\) metadata overhead, and 3 verifier models each read the payload once without materializing another full copy. What persistent capacity and total pipeline traffic are required?

\(1.4\text{ TB}\) of persistent capacity and \(4.4\text{ TB}\) of traffic: \(1\text{ TB}\) payload write, \(0.4\text{ TB}\) metadata write, and \(3\text{ TB}\) of verifier reads.
Exactly \(1.0\text{ TB}\), because verifier models run entirely in GPU registers without generating persistent storage artifacts.
Roughly \(0.4\text{ TB}\), because synthetic data compresses more efficiently than natural language text.
Roughly \(14\text{ TB}\), because every verifier model stores a full \(350\text{ GB}\) copy of its internal neural activations for every sample.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Persistent capacity is \(1.4\text{ TB}\): the \(1\text{ TB}\) payload plus \(0.4\text{ TB}\) of provenance. Pipeline traffic is \(4.4\text{ TB}\): those \(1.4\text{ TB}\) of writes plus three \(1\text{ TB}\) verifier reads. Verification passes do not multiply capacity unless their outputs are materialized as additional full datasets.
Learning Objective: Distinguish persistent storage amplification from read and write traffic in a verified synthetic-data pipeline
Explain why synthetic training data pipelines must treat storage as an active ‘provenance engine’ by recording the generating model, filters, and verifier scores for each accepted sample, rather than storing plain text files.
Answer: If synthetic data is stored as unverified plain text without lineage, future models risk recursively training on uncurated, erroneous synthetic outputs produced by prior generations, triggering ‘model collapse’ where model diversity and output quality progressively degrade. Storing an immutable provenance chain (generating model ID, prompt template, rejection filters, and verifier reward scores) supports auditing so data can be filtered, re-weighted, or purged when a generator or judge model is found to possess systematic errors or biases.
Learning Objective: Justify retaining synthetic-sample provenance to support audits and filtering when recursive training degrades model quality
The degenerative failure mode where a machine learning model progressively degrades in quality and loses distributional diversity by recursively training on unverified synthetic data produced by earlier models is called model ____.
Answer: The correct term is collapse (or model collapse). Recursive training on generated data can degrade distributional diversity and output quality. Provenance supports audits, filtering, and removal of problematic samples; recording lineage alone does not prevent the degradation.
Learning Objective: Explain the mechanism of model collapse caused by recursive training on uncurated synthetic data

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team selects RAID 5 for a disposable local training-data cache whose immutable source is durably stored elsewhere. The fleet can tolerate restaging after drive failure. Why might RAID 0 be a better throughput-and-capacity trade-off under this failure contract?

RAID 5 cannot be formatted with modern Linux filesystems such as ext4 or XFS.
RAID 5 disables hardware DMA transfers, preventing the GPU from accessing host DRAM.
The cache can be reconstructed from its durable source, so RAID 0 can aggregate drives without parity overhead when restaging disruption is acceptable.
RAID 5 increases drive endurance wear by \(10\times\) compared to single-drive configurations.

Answer: The correct answer is C. A disposable cache need not own durability when its source remains available. RAID 0 removes parity overhead but increases exposure to cache loss and restaging. RAID 5 can still be justified by availability requirements; checkpoints awaiting durable replication are not disposable. Filesystem support and DMA are not disabled by RAID 5, and the stated endurance multiplier is unsupported.
Learning Objective: Evaluate RAID parity and striping trade-offs for disposable ML caches under explicit durability and availability requirements
A training team upgrades its cluster from A100 to H100 GPUs, expecting a \(3\times\) end-to-end training speedup. However, wall-clock epoch time barely improves, and GPU utilization drops from \(85\%\) to \(35\%\). Traces show shorter uninterrupted compute time, unchanged measured input-delivery rate, and increased time waiting for ready input batches, while communication and checkpoint pauses remain unchanged. Diagnose the measured bottleneck and explain why faster compute exposed it.
Answer: The traces establish an input-delivery limit: compute finishes sooner, but the unchanged pipeline does not supply ready batches at the new consumption rate. More of the iteration is therefore exposed input wait. Prefetching can hide delays within its queue window but cannot overcome a sustained delivery-rate deficit. The utilization and epoch-time figures alone would not identify this cause; the supplied timing measurements distinguish it from communication or checkpoint pauses. Profile individual read, decode, and transfer stages before selecting a remedy.
Learning Objective: Analyze training throughput regressions following accelerator compute upgrades using the I/O wall framework
A team replaces a lighter codec with a denser codec on local-NVMe training shards. On this corpus, illustrative measurements give the lighter codec a 3:1 ratio and 1.5 GB/s decoded output per core, versus 4:1 and 0.5 GB/s for the denser codec. Before the change, worker profiles show decoding and augmentation saturating the host CPU and the ready-batch queue repeatedly draining. Afterward, decompression consumes more CPU time, the queue drains more often, and training step time increases although stored bytes decrease. What caused this measured regression?

Compressed shards cannot be read by NVMe controllers because flash drives require raw uncompressed binary blocks.
The pipeline was already CPU-bound on data decoding and augmentation, so adding heavy decompression work saturated the host CPU, starving the GPU of assembled batches.
The denser codec introduces non-deterministic bit flips that cause stochastic gradient descent to diverge.
The parallel file system rejects compressed shards larger than 1 GB due to POSIX file locking constraints.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The supplied worker profiles and ready-batch queues establish a host-processing limit before the change; additional decompression work further reduces completed-batch delivery. The denser codec saves stored bytes but requires more CPU work for the same decoded output under these corpus-specific measurements. These illustrative rates are not fixed properties of named compression levels. Compare output-equivalent stage rates and input wait when choosing a representation.
Learning Objective: Analyze the CPU-versus-I/O trade-offs of data compression and identify when decompression overhead degrades pipeline throughput
True or False: Sizing a data loader’s prefetch buffer depth based on average storage read latency ensures that training runs will not experience data stalls during multi-week training jobs on shared object storage.
Answer: False. Average latency does not bound tail stalls. A starting buffer budget is \(Q_{\text{prefetch}} = \lceil T_{\text{I/O,p99}} / T_{\text{compute}} \rceil\) plus margin, but longer or correlated delays can still drain it; sustained delivery bandwidth must also keep pace with consumption.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why prefetch queues sized to average latency fail to prevent accelerator stalls under tail-latency variance
A team creates full \(10\text{ TB}\) copies of a pretraining dataset for every snapshot version, creating 20 versions over six months (\(200\text{ TB}\) total storage). Explain how content-addressable storage or delta encoding optimizes this workflow when successive versions differ by only \(5\%\).
Answer: The first version requires \(10\text{ TB}\). Nineteen subsequent versions with \(5\%\) new content each add \(0.5\text{ TB}\), for \(19.5\text{ TB}\) total before metadata and replication, saving \(180.5\text{ TB}\) against 20 full copies. Content-addressable storage references unchanged blocks rather than copying them; the reduction assumes changes remain localized at the stored block or shard granularity.
Learning Objective: Compare naive full-copy dataset versioning against delta-encoded content-addressable snapshotting in terms of storage efficiency

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A 2,048-GPU training cluster reports \(40\%\) GPU hardware utilization. Telemetry reveals: (1) GPUs spend \(45\%\) of iteration time waiting for data tensors, (2) Storage data disks on the parallel file system report less than \(5\%\) bandwidth utilization, (3) Data loader host CPU cores report \(100\%\) utilization, and (4) The dataset is stored as 50 million individual JPEG files. A worker CPU profile attributes most active CPU time to JPEG decoding, the MDS shows a sustained queue at its operation-rate limit, and the completed-batch queue repeatedly drains. Which remediation targets the two measured limiting stages?

The parallel file system network fabric is saturated; upgrade InfiniBand links between compute nodes and storage servers.
GPU HBM capacity is exhausted; apply aggressive 4-bit activation quantization to free GPU memory.
NVMe drive endurance limits have triggered write throttling; replace compute node local SSDs.
The workload is suffering from both metadata server saturation (individual small files) and CPU-bound decoding; repackage the dataset into large WebDataset tar shards and evaluate GPU JPEG decoding against its compute and HBM budget.

Answer: The correct answer is D. The MDS queue at its operation-rate limit confirms metadata contention, and the worker profile confirms decoding consumes the host CPU budget; the drained completed-batch queue connects these limits to input starvation. Sequential shards reduce per-file metadata demand, and GPU decoding is a candidate when the supported decoder, available compute, and HBM budget permit it. Compare completed-batch throughput and input wait after each change. High host CPU activity and idle data disks alone would not prove both causes.
Learning Objective: Evaluate composite storage and host-CPU data loading bottlenecks from multi-tier cluster telemetry and prescribe architectural remediations
Synthesize how the ML storage hierarchy (spanning HBM, DRAM, NVMe, PFS, Object Storage, and Archive) co-designs bandwidth physics with capacity economics to prevent accelerator starvation.
Answer: The hierarchy places small, frequently accessed working sets near compute and larger datasets and checkpoint histories on cheaper tiers. HBM serves internal tensor traffic; DRAM supports preprocessing and buffers, NVMe stages inputs and snapshots, and shared durable tiers retain authoritative artifacts. Workload input bytes and compute time size delivery, while measured service rates, tail latency, and cache misses determine buffering. Prefetching hides bounded delays but cannot overcome a sustained rate deficit, and durability claims depend on the chosen service contract.
Learning Objective: Explain how the ML storage hierarchy balances bandwidth physics and capacity economics to sustain high accelerator utilization
Generation g is durably committed and retained. Training resumes after locally staging all shards of g+1, but a node fails before durable publication of g+1 and its required shard is lost. Which generation may restore, and what evidence is required before g+1 could become a restore candidate?
Answer: Restore the retained committed generation g after verifying its manifest and shards. Resuming training after local staging does not publish g+1; the lost required shard prevents that generation from satisfying the restore contract. Before g+1 becomes a candidate, every expected same-step shard must be durably persisted and verified against the generation manifest, which is published last using the backend’s atomic publication primitive.
Learning Objective: Apply the distinction between local staging and durable checkpoint publication to a failure trace

← Back to Questions

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can adding accelerators make training slower?
Splitting a training job across machines creates more compute capacity, but it also requires those machines to exchange state and agree on updates. Each accelerator may finish its local work sooner while spending more of the step waiting for other workers. Once communication and waiting consume the time saved by parallel execution, adding accelerators raises the bill without shortening the run. Single-node optimization remains necessary, yet faster local arithmetic cannot remove a dependency on data that another machine has not delivered. Memory pressure complicates the decision, because a model may require distribution simply to fit, even when the resulting exchanges are expensive. Dividing its state across more devices can relieve that limit while exposing another in network bandwidth or scheduling. Conversely, replicating a model can process more examples at once without reducing the memory needed for each copy. Neither improvement alone establishes that training will finish sooner. Changing how examples are grouped or when updates become available can change the work required to reach the target quality. Engineers must therefore compare complete training configurations, accounting for memory, communication, update behavior, and elapsed time together. The practical question is where additional hardware buys useful progress and where it merely creates more coordination. That judgment determines which models and experiments fit the available schedule and budget. In C³ terms, each partitioning strategy trades parallelized compute against network-bound communication and coordination across workers.

Learning Objectives

Apply the Fleet Law to diagnose compute-, memory-, communication-, or coordination-bound distributed training regimes
Calculate scaling efficiency, estimate useful batch size, and budget synchronization overhead for data-parallel training
Design memory-sharding plans that trade accelerator capacity for additional communication
Map tensor, pipeline, expert, and data parallelism onto hardware bandwidth tiers and model structure
Analyze microbatch pipeline schedules for bubble overhead, activation residency, and synchronous update ordering
Evaluate synchronization and low-precision policies under staleness, straggler, and numerical-stability constraints
Synthesize hybrid parallelism configurations for frontier, recommendation, and alignment training constraints






The accelerator hierarchy, network fabric, and storage pipeline form the physical foundation of the fleet. The remaining challenge is algorithmic. A partition of the training job decides which intermediate results and gradients must cross that fabric and when workers must synchronize, and it must make those decisions while preserving the optimization process a single device would have followed. The universal scaling law (principle \(\ref{pri-universal-scaling}\)) explains why this pressure keeps rising. Frontier quality improvements demand disproportionately more compute, data, and parameters, so the training problem eventually outgrows any single machine in capacity, in calendar time, or in both. Data Storage closed on one instance of that growth, a 175B reference model whose FP16 weights alone exceed the memory of the device that must hold them.


↩︎ The power-law relationship between quality and compute, data, and parameters, and the compute-optimal allocation it implies, are established in AI Scaling Laws.
A hypothetical accelerator with 100 terabytes of memory and an exaflop of compute would make distributed training unnecessary for that model. Real accelerators instead have finite high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, compute throughput, and input bandwidth, and more capable designs move the distribution threshold without removing it. The reference workload must be evaluated against those limits before selecting a partition. In the Fleet Stack diagrammed in The Fleet Stack, distributed training occupies the Distributed Execution row of the Distribution band, the logic that partitions the mathematical workload across the physical fleet. Data, tensor, pipeline, and hybrid parallelism create different traffic patterns for the interconnect to carry.

Self-Check: Question

A research team is training a 3B-parameter transformer that fits comfortably in one H100 GPU’s 80 GB of memory, but projected single-GPU training would take 18 months to reach target loss. The dataset is 3 TB and fits on local NVMe storage. Which signal makes distributed training necessary in this scenario?

Dataset exceeding GPU HBM capacity, which automatically mandates tensor parallelism regardless of execution time
The presence of NVLink inside the node, which makes multi-machine scaling mandatory by default
Unacceptable wall-clock training duration, even though single-device memory capacity and local storage are sufficient
Fault tolerance limitations, because single-GPU training cannot survive hardware restarts

A team doubles a data-parallel cluster from 64 to 128 GPUs and observes that total step time drops by only 12 percent even though per-worker compute time halves. Using the distributed step-time equation \(T_{\text{step}}(N) = T_{\text{compute}}/N + T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}}\), explain what the observation establishes and what measurement would distinguish possible causes.
True or False: If a neural network’s parameters exceed a single GPU’s memory capacity, tensor parallelism can be scaled across standard commodity Ethernet switches between server racks, provided the global batch size is made large enough.
Framing distributed parallelism strategies as compiler loop transformations across the training loop’s iterators (batches, layers, and operations), which distributed strategy corresponds to vectorization (SIMD) of inner matrix multiplications?

Tensor parallelism, which partitions inner matrix-multiplication operations across devices and exchanges partial results over the interconnect
Data parallelism, which unrolls the outer batch loop across devices so each rank processes independent data indices
Pipeline parallelism, which stages sequential layer operations across devices analogous to CPU instruction pipelining
Model replication, which duplicates the entire forward and backward execution redundantly across machines

In the 3D Parallelism Cube (\(N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t\)), how do the three orthogonal scaling axes interact to allocate cluster accelerators for large models?

The three axes are mutually exclusive; choosing data parallelism precludes using tensor or pipeline parallelism in the same cluster
Tensor and pipeline parallelism can combine within a node, but data parallelism can only be used if model parallelism is disabled
The total accelerator count is the sum of the dimensions (\(N_{\text{total}} = d + p + t\)), with each parallelism type requiring a disjoint node pool
The axes compose multiplicatively (\(N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t\)), allowing systems to simultaneously shard layers (TP), pipeline stages (PP), and replicate the pipeline across data shards (DP)

The dimensionless ratio \(\rho = T_{\text{comm}}(N) / (T_{\text{compute}}/N)\), which screens communication demand relative to per-worker compute time, is defined as the ____.

See Answers →





Before optimizing algorithms, the physical constraints of the machine learning fleet must be understood. The performance of any distributed training job is governed by the Fleet Law (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)), which decomposes the per-step time:
\[ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \]


↩︎ The Fleet Law and its compute, communication, and coordination terms are established in The Fleet Law.
The communication-computation ratio, \(\CommunicationComputeRatio= \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)/(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\), compares communication time with ideally partitioned compute time for fixed global work. This \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\) is a ratio of two times, not the queue utilization of the incast model. It is the time consequence of communication intensity \(\CommunicationIntensity\) (equation 1.2), the bytes moved per operation of the workload. When transfers run at link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), the sustained-bandwidth parameter of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) message model, and each device computes at sustained rate \(\PeakRate\EfficiencyHw\), \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\approx \CommunicationIntensity \times \PeakRate\EfficiencyHw/\LinkBandwidth\), so the same workload becomes more communication-bound on faster accelerators or slower links. This ratio identifies the pressure to overlap communication; the complete step time also depends on how much exchange is hidden and how much coordination remains exposed.


↩︎ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) message model, with startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and sustained bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), is established in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model.

↪ The communication-computation ratio, evaluated for representative data-parallel and point-to-point transfers and related to communication intensity, is developed in The communication-computation ratio.

Two regimes follow from this ratio. When \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\gg \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), the cluster is compute-bound, and communication is small relative to useful computation, provided coordination and input delivery do not introduce another limit. Large-batch training of a dense convolutional model such as ResNet commonly sits here. When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\gtrsim 1\), \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) matches or exceeds \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\), the cluster is communication-bound, and insufficient overlap leaves substantial time waiting for gradients or activations. Large language models (LLMs) with billions of parameters to synchronize, and Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM)-style workloads whose embedding exchanges saturate the network, frequently land in this regime. These are typical operating points rather than fixed labels: batch size, partitioning, and placement can move the same workload across the boundary, so the ratio must be measured for the configuration at hand.


↪ The optimizations that help, and the ones that are wasted, for a compute-bound, communication-bound, or coordination-bound fleet are operationalized in The bottleneck diagnostic table.



Three signals motivate evaluating distributed execution. The first is memory exhaustion: model parameters, optimizer states, and activation storage exceed single-device capacity. For full mixed-precision training with Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam), the convention of 16 bytes per parameter can exceed an 80 GB accelerator at roughly 5 billion parameters before activations. Larger 10–20B models therefore need sharding, offload, or another memory-saving approach (Rajbhandari et al. 2020). The failed allocation establishes a capacity problem; it does not by itself choose the remedy.

↪ Accelerator HBM capacity, the ceiling these per-parameter budgets are measured against, is developed in Accelerator Memory Hierarchy.

The second signal is unacceptable training duration. Even when a model fits, single-device training may require weeks or months to converge, making wall-clock time itself a systems constraint. GPT-3’s 175B-parameter training run used a cluster of V100 GPUs (Brown et al. 2020), illustrating why the calendar, rather than HBM capacity alone, forces distribution at this scale.
The third signal is input demand at dataset scale. Dataset bytes determine storage capacity, while the training schedule determines the delivery rate. As The Data Pipeline Equation showed, either can motivate distributed data services, but a large dataset alone does not require distributing model computation. Together, capacity, calendar, and input delivery define the constraints a training configuration must satisfy.
The first signal, memory exhaustion, has a long history, traced in figure 1. Over the plotted span, single-accelerator memory grew about 38× from the K20 to the B200, while the memory needed to train a state-of-the-art model grew by roughly 4 orders of magnitude. Among the plotted models, the curves cross in 2020 at GPT-3, whose training state exceeded the largest accelerator then available by about 35×. The real crossing came earlier than the plot shows. By the 16-bytes-per-parameter convention above, any model beyond roughly 5 billion parameters already overflows one 80 GB device, and models between the plotted points, such as the 2019 Megatron-LM model developed with tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al. 2019), were partitioned for that reason. GPT-3 marks where the gap passed an order of magnitude, and every later plotted frontier model also sits far above the capacity curve. For those models, spreading state beyond one device’s memory is a precondition for training at all rather than a way to train faster.














Figure 1: The memory wall: Accelerator memory capacity plotted against the memory a state-of-the-art model needs to train. Capacity climbs steadily while demand climbs faster, and the widening gap is why weights, gradients, and optimizer state must be split across devices rather than merely compressed.



Whichever signal motivates distribution, the system must state which optimization update it implements. In the synchronous baseline developed first, the 1,024 GPUs of the volume’s Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) reference cluster, whose running instance in this chapter is a GPT-3-class 175B-parameter dense transformer, combine their contributions before advancing to the next parameter version. Matching the global batch, loss normalization, and optimizer state preserves the corresponding single-device update mathematically. Later synchronization models deliberately relax that update ordering and must be evaluated under their own convergence assumptions.


↩︎ The three systems archetypes and their binding constraints are established in Three systems archetypes.

Definition 5.1: Distributed training
Distributed training partitions the optimization loop across multiple compute nodes, distributing data or model computation and coordinating contributions according to a specified update protocol.

Significance: Partitioning training state across devices can meet a memory budget that exceeds one accelerator. GPT-3 (175B parameters) requires approximately 350 GB in BF16 (FP16 also stores 2 bytes per value, so the chapter’s byte counts hold for either format), more than 4× the 80 GB capacity of a single H100. If weights remain entirely in HBM, their aggregate capacity lower bound is 5 H100s. Adding BF16 gradients plus FP32 Adam master weights and moments gives about 2.8 TB, or at least 35 H100s before activations. These lower bounds do not establish a runnable placement; offload changes the capacity calculation, and the time budget can require more accelerators than memory alone.
Distinction: CPU threads can share a coherent address space, while accelerators generally hold separate training-state allocations even within one node. Distributed training extends coordination across those devices and node boundaries through collectives or point-to-point transfers governed by the chosen update protocol.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that distributed training scales linearly with node count. In practice, communication overhead grows with cluster size and the serial fraction of each step (Amdahl’s Law): a fixed serial fraction of the single-device baseline bounds strong-scaling speedup.






Distribution expands three costs that determine whether a partition is viable. Communication overhead includes gradient aggregation through AllReduce, which returns the same reduced tensor to each participant, or rank. For \(\Parameters\) parameters across \(\DeviceCount\) devices, a ring all-reduce, in which each worker passes gradient chunks only to its neighbor in a logical ring, sends approximately \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\times \GradientPayload\) bytes per worker per step, where the gradient payload \(\GradientPayload\) is the \(\Parameters\) gradient values times their storage width; this is not total fleet traffic.


↪ The ring schedule and the derivation of its \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) volume are developed in Collective Communication.
Fault tolerance becomes more demanding as the number of failure sources grows. Under independent constant-rate GPU failures, fleet-wide failure-free survival decays exponentially. If each of the 1,024 GPUs has mean time between failures (MTBF) of 50,000 hours, the modeled probability of at least one GPU failure in an hour is 2.0 percent, with mean interval 49 hours between such events. Whether each event interrupts training depends on recovery and redundancy. The MTBF cascade develops the assumptions.
Algorithmic stability adds a separate constraint when the partition changes global batch size or update ordering. Learning-rate scaling and warmup are candidate responses to large-batch behavior (Goyal et al. 2017), not requirements unique to multiple machines. A viable design must satisfy all three budgets.



The single-machine optimization methodology summarized in The D·A·M Taxonomy extends to distributed environments with important adaptations. Profiling must capture inter-device communication patterns and synchronization overhead in addition to computation and memory metrics. The solution space expands to data parallelism, model parallelism in its tensor and pipeline forms, and hybrid approaches. Data parallelism assigns different examples to model replicas; tensor parallelism splits the operations inside a layer; pipeline parallelism assigns successive layer groups to different devices.
A useful mental model treats these strategies as loop transformations, the same toolkit a compiler uses to restructure sequential code, now applied by a cluster-level compiler. The logical training loop nests iterators over the examples in a batch, the layers of the model, and the matrix operations inside each layer, and each parallelism strategy distributes one of them across devices.
Data parallelism resembles a parallel for-loop, assigning different batch indices to devices running the same model. Tensor parallelism resembles vectorization, or single instruction, multiple data (SIMD), by partitioning the work inside matrix operations. The analogy describes the work split, not a shared instruction stream or register file; the devices exchange tensor shards over an interconnect. Pipeline parallelism resembles instruction pipelining, assigning successive layer groups to stages. Overlapping microbatches can keep those stages active, subject to dependency delays and load balance.
Whichever loop a strategy unrolls, distributed training1 spreads the workload across machines that must coordinate to train a single model. Coordination here means keeping every model shard or replica on a compatible training step. Basic barriers can keep a small research run ordered, but long-running training jobs also need timeout, checkpoint, and recovery mechanisms so one failed worker does not waste days of compute.
1 Distributed training: Google’s DistBelief (2012) was an early framework for training neural networks across thousands of machines, but its parameter server architecture created bandwidth bottlenecks at central nodes. This limitation drove the shift to decentralized AllReduce patterns in successors like Horovod and PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP), where each data-parallel worker sends and receives about \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) times the gradient size per step rather than concentrating traffic at a single server (Dean et al. 2012; Sergeev and Balso 2018; Li et al. 2020; Patarasuk and Yuan 2009).
Dean, Jeffrey, Greg Corrado, Rajat Monga, Kai Chen, Matthieu Devin, Quoc V. Le, Mark Z. Mao, et al. 2012. “Large Scale Distributed Deep Networks.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), edited by Peter L. Bartlett, Fernando C. N. Pereira, Christopher J. C. Burges, Léon Bottou, and Kilian Q. Weinberger, vol. 25. Curran Associates.

Sergeev, Alexander, and Mike Del Balso. 2018. “Horovod: Fast and Easy Distributed Deep Learning in TensorFlow.” CoRR abs/1802.05799.

Li, Shen, Yanli Zhao, Rohan Varma, Omkar Salpekar, Pieter Noordhuis, Teng Li, Adam Paszke, et al. 2020. “PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 13 (12): 3005–18. https://doi.org/10.14778/3415478.3415530.

Patarasuk, Pitch, and Xin Yuan. 2009. “Bandwidth Optimal All-Reduce Algorithms for Clusters of Workstations.” Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 69 (2): 117–24. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2008.09.002.

↪ Checkpointing and recovery for long-running training jobs are developed in Fault Tolerance.
2 NVLink: NVIDIA’s point-to-point GPU interconnect delivers 300 GB/s–450 GB/s per-direction bandwidth, roughly 12×–18× InfiniBand HDR per port. This bandwidth gap is why tensor parallelism, which requires AllReduce on every layer, favors the fast NVLink domain, while pipeline and data parallelism can tolerate slower links when their traffic budgets fit. NVLink Switch systems can extend that fast domain beyond one server.3 NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library): NCCL provides topology-aware inter-GPU collective communication primitives, including AllReduce, across PCIe, NVLink, InfiniBand, and IP networks. Current NCCL deployments expose ring, tree, and related algorithm families through runtime selection and tuning controls, so training frameworks can avoid naive mappings that route all traffic through the slowest inter-node path (Jeaugey 2017; NVIDIA 2026).
Jeaugey, Sylvain. 2017. NCCL 2.0. GPU Technology Conference presentation.

NVIDIA. 2026. NCCL User Guide.

Each rung of the scaling path inherits earlier challenges. A single GPU already needs input delivery, memory management, scheduling, and recovery from interrupted work. Multiple GPUs add coordination across separate device memories, even within one node. Interconnects such as NVLink or PCIe carry these exchanges,2 with collective libraries such as NCCL selecting communication schedules.3
The leap to multi-node training adds network communication overhead, fault tolerance requirements, and cluster orchestration. Because each stage compounds the previous one’s bottlenecks, single-GPU performance must be optimized before scaling out, so inefficiency does not multiply across the fleet. Although frameworks abstract away much of this through sharded data parallelism and communication libraries, implementing distributed training efficiently still demands careful network configuration (InfiniBand tuning, topology-aware routing), infrastructure management through cluster schedulers, and debugging of nonlocal issues such as synchronization hangs and communication bottlenecks. Figure 2 maps this design space onto a 3D decomposition grid (\(\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\)), partitioning cluster execution across tensor parallelism (\(\TensorParallelDegree\), intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism (\(\PipelineParallelDegree\), sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism (\(\DataParallelDegree\), batch replication), where each individual cell represents a single accelerator coordinate.







Figure 2: The 3D parallelism cube: The configuration space decomposes cluster training across three orthogonal axes: tensor parallelism (\(\TensorParallelDegree\), intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism (\(\PipelineParallelDegree\), sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism (\(\DataParallelDegree\), batch replication). Each cell is one accelerator, identified by its \((\DataParallelDegree, \PipelineParallelDegree, \TensorParallelDegree)\) coordinate, so the cube holds \(\DeviceCount = \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\) devices. A feasible point must jointly satisfy model divisibility, per-device memory limits, and the network hierarchy that carries each axis’s traffic.



Under the three-dimensional partitioning of figure 2, called 3D parallelism, the total accelerator allocation scales as the product \(\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\). The axes represent distinct mathematical partitions, but they are not independent configuration knobs. Tensor and pipeline degrees must divide the model structure, the data-parallel degree and microbatch schedule must produce a viable global batch, every partition must fit memory, and each communication group must map onto an adequate topology and acceptable failure domain. Training systems therefore select a jointly feasible coordinate rather than tuning \(\DataParallelDegree\), \(\PipelineParallelDegree\), and \(\TensorParallelDegree\) in isolation.



Choosing the right parallelism strategy is not a matter of preference; it is a constraint satisfaction problem governed by parameter count \((\Parameters)\), batch size \((\BatchSize)\), and interconnect bandwidth. In this first feasibility screen, \(\LayerCount\) denotes layer count, \(\SequenceLength\) sequence length, and \(\HiddenDimension\) hidden width. The bandwidth requirements impose a hard constraint on hardware placement: each parallelism strategy must be matched to the interconnect available between the GPUs that need to communicate, or the design fails before it leaves the whiteboard.
