Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) extends the placement problem beyond one training model. The proximal policy optimization (PPO) example developed here generates responses, scores them with a preference-trained reward model, constrains policy drift against a reference, and uses value estimates to guide updates. These roles have different memory and compute requirements and need not run simultaneously. Direct preference optimization (DPO) provides a useful comparison because its standard offline form removes online generation and separate reward and value models. The engineering question is how the chosen learning procedure determines which state and work must coexist on the fleet.


The single-model pretraining baseline becomes a multi-role loop in PPO (Schulman et al. 2017), as used in InstructGPT-style systems (Ouyang et al. 2022). Table 7 separates policy, reference, reward, and value roles by execution mode and memory burden. In figure 16, the policy \(\Policy\) generates responses for scoring by the frozen reference and reward models and evaluation by the value model \(\CriticModel\). The penalized reward (\(\ResponseReward- \KlPenaltyCoefficient\,\text{KL}\)) subtracts a Kullback–Leibler divergence penalty, weighted by a coefficient \(\KlPenaltyCoefficient\) unrelated to link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), to discourage drift from the reference. Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) combines rewards and value estimates to judge how much better a response was than expected. Those estimates guide policy updates; the value model learns to predict returns, the cumulative discounted reward that follows each generated token. Reference and reward models remain forward-only in this loop, and shared-backbone implementations can combine roles without changing their distinct responsibilities.

The aggregate memory demand of the four-model PPO system dwarfs standard pretraining. A naive co-location of a 70B policy, 70B reference, 13B reward, and 13B value model requires approximately 1,494 GB of accelerator memory, before accounting for the KV caches and intermediate activations generated during sequence generation. A key-value (KV) cache stores attention keys and values for previously processed tokens so the policy can generate the next token without recomputing that state. It grows with the number and length of active sequences, creating a temporary memory budget distinct from weights and optimizer state. On H100 GPUs with 80 GB of HBM each, this system requires a minimum of 19 GPUs as an aggregate static-state capacity lower bound, including optimizer state and gradients. This division does not establish a feasible placement: each phase must also fit its KV or activation peak, workspaces, and uneven shards. Replicated policy groups increase the total state further.



The defining infrastructure challenge of RLHF is not the total memory footprint but the asymmetry between the models’ compute profiles. The policy and value models require full backward passes with gradient computation, activation checkpointing, and optimizer updates, compute-intensive operations that benefit from tensor parallelism and high arithmetic intensity. The reference and reward models, by contrast, perform only forward passes over generated sequences. Their scoring passes do not require optimizer state, and they need not decode token by token. The policy’s rollout phase creates the autoregressive generation workload and its KV-cache budget. Separating scoring from generation matters because forward-only execution does not imply a single memory or compute profile.
The asymmetry creates a placement dilemma. Co-location permits devices to serve different phases, but inactive model state can occupy memory needed for the active phase. Dedicated pools allow each role to use a suitable execution configuration, but pools may idle while waiting for another role’s output. Separation also adds transfers of generated sequences, scores, and updated policy weights. The design must compare phase utilization and data movement rather than assume that either placement eliminates waste.
The PPO rollout phase introduces autoregressive dependencies absent from the teacher-forced pretraining baseline. The policy generates responses before sequence-level rewards guide its updates. At small active batches, decoding is often memory bandwidth bound because each new token requires another model pass. For a Llama-2-70B-style grouped-query attention policy, KV storage grows by approximately \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \LayerCount \KvHeadCount \AttentionHeadDimension \ElementStorageSize\) per cached token per sequence. With 80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128-dimensional heads, 1,024 generated tokens, and 256 active sequences, the generated-token portion occupies 85.9 GB, or \(2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1024 \times 256 \times 2\) bytes. Dense multi-head attention using the full 8,192 hidden width for K and V would require 687.2 GB for that portion. Even with grouped-query attention, that portion alone already exceeds the 80 GB of HBM on one H100, and prompt tokens add KV state as well. This temporary cache must fit alongside the state live during rollout; its lifetime differs from training activations and optimizer state.
RLHF systems address this asymmetry through temporal multiplexing. During the generation phase, the cluster behaves like an inference system: the policy model generates sequences while the reference model computes log-probabilities, and the dominant resource is HBM reserved for token-by-token attention state. During the training phase, the same fleet switches back to training mode: gradients are computed through the policy and value models using the 3D parallelism configuration developed in section 5.10. During generation, batching active sequences and placing their KV state determine how much useful work shares each weight read. During the update phase, activation residency and gradient synchronization again govern the schedule. RLHF is not one steady training loop, but an alternation between inference-shaped work and training-shaped work, and standard training frameworks rarely manage that transition by themselves.



Standard offline DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) removes the separate reward and value models from the update loop by reformulating alignment as a loss over preference pairs. The policy learns from preferred and dispreferred responses using their log-probabilities relative to a frozen reference. Because those responses are already in the training data, the update requires neither online generation nor advantage estimation.
A DPO implementation that retains a resident reference has two model roles: the trainable policy and the frozen reference. For the 70B policy with 13B reward and value models used in section 5.11.4, static state falls from about 1,494 GB to 1,260 GB, a 16 percent reduction. Against a policy-sized PPO value model, it falls from 2,406 GB to 1,260 GB, or roughly 48 percent. These are configuration-specific state budgets. For fixed preference pairs and a fixed reference, reference log-probabilities can instead be precomputed, removing that model from the repeated update loop. Offline DPO needs no autoregressive rollout during those updates. Variable lengths still require padding, packing, or length-aware batching, and policy training can use the same partitioning, accumulation, and overlap mechanisms as pretraining.
The trade-off is how training obtains new feedback. Standard offline DPO learns from a fixed preference dataset, so the policy cannot try new responses and receive feedback on them during training. PPO-style training generates responses from the evolving policy and scores them, so the policy can improve on its own outputs and expose behavior the original dataset lacks, provided the reward signal is reliable. When the preference data already covers the target distribution, DPO’s fixed-data loop usually wins on infrastructure. When training must discover behavior beyond the dataset, as in training models on novel reasoning tasks, PPO’s online loop can justify the reward and value models, the generation phase, and the memory they occupy. The decision is settled by achieved quality per unit of total resource cost, not by either property alone.



To make the infrastructure trade-off concrete, consider aligning a 70B policy model using a policy/reference pool of 256 H100 GPUs (80 GB HBM each). PPO’s separate reward and value pools sit outside that allocation. The policy is a 70B-class model rather than the 175B reference, a size at which each role’s memory budget stays readable while the four PPO roles together still need at least 19 GPUs, more than one node.

PPO and DPO make variable sequence length a prominent scheduling concern. Pretraining often packs documents into fixed-length blocks, such as 2,048 or 4,096 tokens, although variable-length workloads also occur. Alignment batches combine prompts and responses whose lengths can differ substantially; an illustrative batch can span a 10–50\(\times\) length range. Those lengths determine activation residency, padding, and work assigned to each worker.
Length variance creates two interacting problems. Padding every sequence to the longest in a batch can leave most token positions unused. A batch of one 2,048-token sequence and fifteen 128-token sequences, padded to 2,048 tokens, fills only 3,968 of its 32,768 positions, so kernels that execute padded positions spend about 88 percent of their work on padding; kernels that skip them recover most of that waste. Dynamic batching groups similar lengths to reduce padding, but assignments across workers still need balancing. A worker processing longer sequences can have a larger activation peak and finish later, leaving other workers waiting for the required gradient contributions.
Sequence packing combines short sequences within a fixed-length input, with attention masking that keeps their contexts separate. Adaptive microbatching varies the number of sequences according to token count or a predicted memory budget. Both techniques also appear in pretraining; alignment adds the need to preserve response boundaries and the chosen preference or policy objective. Workers need not process equal token counts for a correct reduction. A token-mean PPO loss weights local means by valid-token counts, whereas standard DPO averages over preference pairs and uses pair counts (Rafailov et al. 2023). Packing changes layout, not that denominator. Unequal lengths can still create load imbalance, so balancing work remains a performance goal even when weighted reduction preserves the estimator.

RLHF is therefore not a detour from parallelism strategy; it is the case that shows why no strategy is sufficient by itself. The policy model may need tensor and pipeline parallelism, the reference and reward models behave like inference services, the value model may require training state, and the rollout data pipeline changes shape from step to step. With that stress test in view, the final comparison can return to the general engineering question: identify the binding constraint first, then choose the parallelism pattern that moves the least data while fitting the required state.

A parallelism strategy is useful only if it moves the binding constraint without creating a larger one. Assembling data, tensor, pipeline, and hybrid partitioning into a coherent decision procedure requires evaluating where each strategy relocates the execution tax across the cluster’s memory and interconnect hierarchy. For a new model, the decisive questions are which memory state fits, how often communication occurs, where the pipeline bubble appears, and which abstraction cost the engineering team can tolerate.
The canonical 3D core does not exhaust the partitioning space. Sequence parallelism accompanies tensor parallelism by partitioning along the sequence dimension the activations for operations such as layer normalization and dropout that tensor parallelism would otherwise replicate (Korthikanti et al. 2023). Context parallelism instead partitions a long attention context and exchanges key/value blocks or partial attention state across ranks (Liu et al. 2023). Expert parallelism partitions sparse feed-forward capacity and routes token activations to the selected experts. Table 9 places these extensions beside the 3D core without pretending they are independent of its batch, memory, and topology constraints.

The GPT-2 notebooks showed the trap in miniature. Moving the same model from one NVLink node to four Ethernet-connected nodes quadrupled the GPU count but cut parallel efficiency from 99.4 percent to 27.9 percent. The following misconceptions generalize that error, each treating one term of the step-time accounting as if it were the whole budget.

Fallacy: Linear speedup is achievable with sufficient engineering effort.
Amdahl’s Law limits speedup when a fixed serial component remains exposed. Synchronous gradient aggregation creates an update dependency, but some of its work can overlap backward computation. As section 5.8 shows, \(\ScalingEfficiency = 1/(1 + \DeviceCount(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime)/\IronLawComputeTime)\) depends on the exposed overhead relative to useful compute as \(\DeviceCount\) changes. A 1,000-GPU allocation therefore does not by itself justify a 1,000\(\times\) speedup forecast. Local kernel efficiency, memory feasibility, communication, and convergence must be evaluated against the specified baseline. Linear scaling is a result to demonstrate for an operating range, not a return guaranteed by device count.


Pitfall: Optimizing MFU without considering scaling efficiency.
A single-node MFU measurement does not predict fleet throughput by itself. For a fixed workload and hardware peak convention, scaling efficiency compares measured distributed throughput with ideal replication of that single-node baseline. Multiplying the baseline MFU by this scaling efficiency gives distributed MFU; multiplying an already measured distributed MFU by the same scaling efficiency counts communication and synchronization losses twice. The chapter’s own numbers make the difference concrete. A single node running at 50 percent MFU, scaled with the 83 percent scaling efficiency of the overlapped TP-8 layout in section 5.10, delivers about 41 percent MFU across the fleet. A planner who measures that 41 percent on the full cluster and then applies the 83 percent again would budget for about 34 percent and buy capacity the job does not need. Capacity planning must state the device count and measurement window for each metric. Checkpointing, recovery, and replay require additional accounting only when those losses fall outside that window, and useful goodput must count retained model progress rather than repeated work.


Fallacy: Hyperparameters tuned on small clusters transfer directly to large-scale training.
Engineers tune hyperparameters on 8-GPU workstations then deploy to 256-GPU clusters expecting identical behavior. At scale, convergence patterns change fundamentally. The most critical hyperparameter is learning rate: as section 5.7 explains, global batch increases with GPU count when local batch and accumulation depth remain fixed, so the learning-rate schedule must be revalidated. The linear scaling rule of section 5.8.5, which the one-hour ImageNet run established, suggests \(\ScaledLearningRate = \BaseLearningRate\times (\ScaledBatchSize/\BaseBatchSize)\), but this relationship holds only within bounds. As models scale, they eventually encounter the critical batch size of section 5.8.6, where adding more data per step yields diminishing returns in convergence.
Beyond the critical batch size, this relationship breaks down in a model-, data-, and optimizer-dependent way. A team that takes a small-cluster learning rate, multiplies it mechanically with GPU count, and jumps directly to a much larger global batch may see lower final quality or slower sample efficiency even though hardware throughput improved. Warmup schedules, weight decay adjustment, layer-wise optimizers such as LARS/LAMB, and careful momentum tuning can recover accuracy in some regimes, but require systematic experimentation at target scale. Organizations that skip these scaling studies waste thousands of GPU-hours on suboptimal runs.


Pitfall: Adding GPUs to data-parallel jobs without modeling communication.
More GPUs improve time to target only if the gain in processing rate outweighs communication overhead and any additional sample use. With fixed local batch size, adding data-parallel workers increases the global batch; fixing the global batch instead reduces local work and can expose more communication. The critical-batch analysis in section 5.8.6 supplies a workload-dependent statistical guide, not universal GPU-count or model-size thresholds. Compare complete learning curves and cost at the same target quality before committing to a larger allocation.


Fallacy: Memory capacity alone determines the parallelism strategy.
A model that exceeds device capacity needs a feasible partition, but memory fit does not select the fastest one. Tensor parallelism exchanges partial results within layers, while pipeline parallelism transfers stage-boundary activations and introduces scheduling bubbles. Their relative cost depends on layer shapes, microbatch count, placement, and overlap. Compare complete training-state and activation budgets together with measured time to target; an unsupported throughput percentage or a weights-only fit cannot settle the choice.


Pitfall: Applying FSDP or ZeRO without measuring efficiency trade-offs.
Engineers adopt FSDP universally after reading that it “reduces memory and enables larger models.” Sharding trades memory capacity for communication overhead: full-shard FSDP gathers parameters before layer execution and reduces gradient shards during backward, with another parameter gather when the forward pass resharded them. The relevant comparison begins with the complete training-state budget. Under the mixed-precision Adam convention established here, the 7B worked example exceeds single-device capacity before activations, so standard DDP cannot fit that state on an A100-80 GB. A weights-only fit does not establish a feasible training baseline. When the complete state, activations, and workspaces fit without sharding, DDP can avoid the repeated gathers; when they exceed the 80 GB capacity, the comparison must include a feasible alternative such as sharding or offload. FSDP provides value when it enables training at all or when the larger local batch it permits offsets its communication cost. ZeRO-Offload extends capacity through CPU memory but adds transfers of its own. The decision therefore requires measuring peak memory and exposed communication for the same workload and optimizer contract.


Fallacy: Parallelism overhead is roughly constant regardless of model size.
Engineers benchmark parallelism strategies on convenient small models then apply those conclusions to large-scale training. For dense transformers at fixed tokens per update, computation and gradient bytes both grow roughly proportionally with parameter count, as the earlier scaling analysis established. Larger parameter count alone therefore does not imply a better computation-to-communication ratio. Architecture, sequence length, local batch size, partition degree, and kernel efficiency determine how much useful work each rank performs; gradient representation and process-group membership determine how much it communicates. A larger model can also require a different partition that introduces new layer collectives or pipeline bubbles. Reliable strategy selection holds the workload and target quality explicit, then recomputes memory fit, local compute time, communication volume, and the available overlap window at the target scale. A small-model benchmark becomes transferable evidence only when those governing terms remain comparable.


Pitfall: Treating scaling efficiency as a property of the hardware alone.
A vendor benchmark might report 85 percent scaling efficiency at 1,024 GPUs, and procurement teams then plan capacity as if that number were a cluster constant. Scaling efficiency is a joint property of four things: the workload’s communication-to-computation ratio, the parallelism strategy (data, pipeline, tensor, hybrid), the network topology (fat-tree vs. torus vs. dragonfly), and the software stack (NCCL version, kernel fusion, overlap quality). Reference numbers from dense large-language-model benchmarks transfer poorly to other workloads and fabrics. They may overstate scaling for graph neural networks with irregular communication and for embedding-heavy recommendation models, whose AllToAll embedding exchanges and many small random lookups load the fabric differently from dense gradient AllReduce (section 5.7.4), and they say nothing about a commodity-Ethernet placement like the GPT-2 scale-out, which lost most of its parallel efficiency on leaving the node. Capacity planning should use measured scaling on the target workload, not a vendor hero benchmark.


Fallacy: Gradient accumulation is free.
Gradient accumulation can reduce synchronization from every microstep to once per window of \(\AccumulationStepCount\) microsteps, eliminating \((\AccumulationStepCount-1)/\AccumulationStepCount\) of those synchronization events when the implementation defers reduction. The saving has costs. A resident gradient buffer remains live throughout the accumulation window; for the 7B model, the FP16 buffer occupies 14 GB. Retaining graphs across microsteps or increasing the local batch size can add activation pressure. Accumulating eight microsteps makes updates 8\(\times\) less frequent per processed microstep, but wall-clock spacing also depends on the communication saved. Larger effective batches can change convergence, and narrow accumulation formats can lose small contributions or overflow. The dtype, loss normalization, and reduction schedule must therefore be validated at the intended batch size. Accumulation trades communication frequency against update spacing, memory residency, and numerical stability.

Scaling laws keep pushing frontier training budgets past what one machine can hold or finish in time, and distributed training is how the fleet absorbs that growth. It confronts the scaling wall, the workload-dependent operating point beyond which communication and coordination can consume the compute time saved by adding accelerators. A feasible design must preserve the intended optimization update while satisfying model-state, activation, batch-size, and interconnect constraints. Hardware throughput alone is insufficient; the comparison must also account for time to the target model quality.
Each partition relocates cost along the C³ axes. Data parallelism divides compute across replicas and pays in communication, the gradient aggregation whose exposed share set the scaling efficiency of the 175B communication example. Tensor parallelism divides work inside a layer and pays in communication on the critical path, which confines it to a fast domain. Pipeline parallelism divides layer depth and pays mostly in coordination, the fill and drain bubble that only more microbatches, better balance, or a smarter schedule can shrink. The 3D parallelism cube in figure 2 unites these trade-offs in one coordinate space (\(\DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\)). A feasible point must satisfy peak memory and global-batch constraints as well as communication and coordination budgets.
Sharding and model partitioning make different parts of the training state fit, while synchronization and precision policies determine whether the resulting updates remain useful. Hybrid layouts compose these choices within the bandwidth hierarchy. The alignment workload extends the same reasoning to multiple models and alternating generation and update phases, where peak memory depends on which state is live together.
The chapter’s strategies are complementary dimensions of one design space rather than alternatives. Systems such as Megatron-LM map tensor, pipeline, data, and expert exchanges to the communication domains that can carry them, and that matching is what delays the communication-bound regime as the fleet grows. The workload archetypes weight those dimensions differently. Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) combines dense-model partitioning with state sharding and, at long contexts, sequence or context partitioning; Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) shards sparse embedding state and pays in lookup traffic rather than layer collectives; Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) moves the coordination problem onto unreliable edge devices. In each case the binding constraint, not the archetype label, selects the configuration.

Key Takeaways: Parallelism relocates the tax

Splitting work moves the bottleneck: Distributed training does not make the underlying computation smaller; it converts memory pressure into communication volume, synchronization delay, or idle pipeline time (principle \(\ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}\)). The winning strategy is the split that sends overhead to the least binding part of the fleet.
Throughput must serve convergence: Larger global batches can improve hardware efficiency while yielding diminishing progress per sample. Compare time to the same target quality, and treat the critical-batch estimate as a workload-dependent guide for selecting batch size and update schedules.
Sharding buys memory with messages: ZeRO and FSDP partition optimizer state, gradients, and parameters (principle \(\ref{pri-memory-capacity-gap}\)), reducing replicated storage. Peak memory must still include activations, temporary gathers, and workspaces; exposed ReduceScatter and AllGather costs determine whether the capacity gain also improves throughput.
Tensor parallelism needs a fast domain: Splitting operations inside layers creates frequent communication on the dependency path. Place those groups on links with sufficient bandwidth and low latency; the relevant boundary is the communication domain, which may span nodes, rather than the server enclosure.
Pipeline parallelism trades bytes for bubbles: Layer staging reduces communication frequency, but fill and drain slots leave accelerators idle (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)). Microbatching with \(\MicrobatchCount\gg \PipelineParallelDegree\) is the mechanism that turns model depth into throughput rather than pipeline slack.
Hybrid layouts are joint decisions: Combine only the partitioning and sharding strategies needed to satisfy the workload’s constraints (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)). Model divisibility, batch size, peak memory, communication groups, and failure domains must form one feasible configuration; improving one axis can expose a limit on another.



The displacement of overhead (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)) makes a feasible partition the beginning of the design problem. A memory-saving split is useful only if its communication and schedule still meet the run’s time-to-quality budget. Every mechanism in this chapter shrinks the per-device compute term \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) or the per-device training state, and pays for it in \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), in \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) through barriers, stragglers, and pipeline bubbles, or in lost overlap. In C³ terms, no partition removes the execution tax of scale; it only relocates that tax among compute, communication, and coordination. The engineering judgment is therefore to compare complete configurations, including their exposed dependencies, rather than optimize each parallelism axis independently.

What’s Next: From logic to trafficSplitting the mathematics defines the logical exchanges the update protocol needs. Replicas AllReduce gradients, sharded layers ReduceScatter and AllGather their state, expert and embedding partitions route tokens through AllToAll, and pipeline stages pass activations point to point. Each exchange specifies a result that participants must receive, not how its bytes cross the physical fabric. The next chapter separates those result contracts from the ring, tree, and hierarchical schedules that carry them out and prices each schedule’s latency, bandwidth, and topology costs, so that the communication budgets charged to \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) here can be evaluated rather than assumed.

In Megatron-LM style tensor parallelism for a transformer layer, how are the linear projections in the multi-head attention block arranged to minimize cross-device collective communication?

Both QKV and Output projections are column-parallel, requiring an AllGather after each projection
Both QKV and Output projections are row-parallel, requiring an AllReduce before each projection
The QKV projection is column-parallel and the Output projection is row-parallel, requiring only a single AllReduce at the end of the attention block
The QKV projection is partitioned across pipeline stages while the Output projection is replicated across data-parallel ranks

In Megatron-LM, the first linear layer (QKV projection) is column-parallel (\(W = [W_1 | W_2]\)), producing partitioned intermediate activations without communication. The second linear layer (Output projection) is row-parallel (\(W = [W_1 ; W_2]\)), taking those partitioned activations directly as inputs and generating partial sums. Only a single AllReduce at the end of the row-parallel projection is required to sum the partial outputs. Using column-parallel for both layers would require an intermediate AllGather. Using row-parallel for both layers would require an AllReduce before the second layer. Splitting QKV and Output across pipeline stages confuses intra-layer tensor parallelism with inter-layer pipelining.

**Order the four sequential phases of token routing and execution in Expert Parallelism (Mixture of Experts) across distributed workers:

The expert GPU dynamically allocates host CPU memory over PCIe, halting computation on other ranks

In distributed training framework runtimes (such as PyTorch DDP), what mechanism combines multiple small layer gradient tensors into contiguous memory buffers before launching collective communication?

Activation checkpointing
ZeRO Stage 3 parameter gathering
Temporal multiplexing
Gradient bucketing

Answer: The correct answer is D. Gradient bucketing groups individual layer gradient tensors into larger contiguous memory buffers (typically 25–50 MB buckets) during the backward pass. Launching an AllReduce on a single aggregated bucket amortizes collective invocation latency and saturates network link bandwidth far more effectively than issuing hundreds of tiny per-tensor transfers. Activation checkpointing recomputes activations to save memory. ZeRO-3 parameter gathering reconstructs sharded weights on demand. Temporal multiplexing alternates execution modes in multi-model RLHF.
Learning Objective: Explain the role of gradient bucketing in amortizing collective communication latency
Contrast the collective communication primitive invocation frequency of standard DDP against full-shard FSDP with resharding for a model with \(N_L\) layers during a single training step.
Answer: DDP launches one AllReduce per ready gradient bucket, often overlapping those calls with backward computation. Full-shard FSDP with layer-level wrapping and resharding after forward typically adds an AllGather before forward, another before backward, and a ReduceScatter after backward: approximately \(3N_L\) calls. Actual counts depend on wrapping, bucketing, prefetch, and resharding policy.
Learning Objective: Compare collective communication primitive invocations between standard DDP and full-shard FSDP
Explain why framework optimizations such as CUDA graphs and asynchronous communication streams cannot eliminate the physical scaling penalty of distributed training as the cluster size \(N\) becomes very large.
Answer: Framework optimizations can reduce launch overhead and change readiness, overlap, and effective communication service time. They cannot make a required payload cross a finite-bandwidth link instantaneously. At fixed global work, adding ranks reduces local compute while required transfers and coordination can remain exposed. A scaling prediction therefore needs the actual workload, collective schedule, and critical path; a fixed-residual Amdahl ceiling applies only under that model’s assumptions.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the physical limits of framework-level communication optimizations

Self-Check: Answer

A team achieves 50 percent Model Flops Utilization (MFU) on a single node, scales to 1,024 GPUs, and measures a scaling efficiency \((\eta_{\text{scaling}})\) of 50 percent on their communication-heavy workload. What is the cluster’s realized model-FLOP rate during distributed execution as a fraction of peak hardware compute?

25 percent of peak compute (delivering 256 GPU-equivalents of model computation)
50 percent of peak compute (delivering 512 GPU-equivalents of useful work)
100 percent of peak compute (delivering 1,024 GPU-equivalents of useful work)
12.5 percent of peak compute (delivering 128 GPU-equivalents of useful work)

Answer: The correct answer is A. Starting from the single-node MFU baseline, the distributed model-FLOP rate is \(0.50\times0.50=0.25\) of fleet peak, or 256 peak-GPU equivalents. The scaling factor accounts for losses relative to that baseline. A measured distributed MFU would already include those losses and must not be multiplied by scaling efficiency again. Retained-progress goodput additionally requires accounting for replay and recovery outside this measurement.
Learning Objective: Calculate distributed model-FLOP rate from a local MFU baseline and scaling efficiency without double-counting losses
A procurement team plans capacity for a graph neural network workload using a vendor benchmark that reports 85 percent scaling efficiency at 1,024 GPUs for large-language-model training. Explain why this figure cannot be treated as a property of the cluster and what the team should measure instead.
Answer: Scaling efficiency is a joint property of the workload’s communication-to-computation ratio, the parallelism strategy, the network topology, and the software stack (collective library version, kernel fusion, overlap quality). The benchmark fixes all four for a language model; a graph neural network with irregular communication changes the first and likely the second, so the same hardware can deliver much lower efficiency. The team should measure scaling on the target workload, at the intended device count and parallelism layout, and plan capacity from that measured curve rather than from a hero benchmark.
Learning Objective: Explain why scaling efficiency must be measured on the target workload rather than inherited from vendor benchmarks.
Why is gradient accumulation NOT a cost-free substitute for true physical scale-out even though it reduces gradient AllReduce communication frequency by a factor of \(k\)?

It is mathematically incompatible with the Adam optimizer
It keeps a live gradient buffer resident, spaces optimizer updates by \(k\) microsteps, and requires appropriate accumulation precision and normalization
It requires dedicated InfiniBand links between CPU and GPU for each microstep
It forces batch normalization layers to synchronize across all nodes on every forward pass

Answer: The correct answer is B. One optimizer update follows \(k\) forward/backward microsteps, but this does not imply \(k\) times the wall-clock update latency: saved synchronization and the comparison schedule affect elapsed time. A live gradient buffer remains resident during the window. Unscaled FP16 accumulation can overflow; accumulation precision and loss normalization must preserve the intended update. Changes in effective batch size must be evaluated at matched target quality. Accumulation is compatible with Adam and requires neither special CPU-GPU links nor mandatory cross-node batch normalization.
Learning Objective: Analyze the memory, latency, and numerical stability trade-offs of gradient accumulation
The largest global batch size beyond which adding more samples per step yields diminishing reductions in the number of steps needed to reach target quality is called the ____.
Answer: critical batch size. Beyond this workload-dependent point, larger global batches can raise hardware throughput without proportionally reducing the steps to target quality, so hardware scaling and statistical scaling must be evaluated separately.
Learning Objective: Identify the critical batch size as the statistical limit on useful data-parallel scale-out.
True or False: If a 7B-parameter model fits comfortably in single-GPU memory with high compute utilization under standard DDP, universally enabling ZeRO-3 / FSDP full sharding will always increase training throughput by reducing per-GPU memory consumption.
Answer: False. FSDP trades memory capacity for parameter-gather and gradient-reduction traffic. If its memory savings do not enable a more efficient batch or layout, the exposed communication can lower throughput. The outcome depends on wrapping, resharding, overlap, and network capacity, so neither a universal gain nor a fixed percentage penalty follows from sharding.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the performance pitfall of applying FSDP when memory capacity is not binding

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

What fundamental architectural principle summarizes the trade-offs of all distributed training strategies in this chapter?

Amdahl’s law can be eliminated entirely by combining tensor and pipeline parallelism
Data parallelism scales indefinitely as long as Ring AllReduce is selected
Model parameters can be replicated infinitely without consuming network bandwidth
The displacement of overhead: distributed parallelism never eliminates total work, but only relocates the execution tax among memory footprint, communication volume, synchronization latency, and pipeline idle time

Answer: The correct answer is D. No parallelism strategy reduces the total mathematical work of training; each strategy only relocates overhead to different dimensions of the system (converting memory capacity limits into network communication volume, synchronization delays, or pipeline bubbles). The winning strategy is the one that shifts overhead to the least binding resource tier in the cluster. Amdahl’s law remains a hard mathematical bound. Data parallelism is bounded by critical batch size and network bisection bandwidth. Parameter replication requires gradient synchronization across workers.
Learning Objective: Synthesize the principle of displacement of overhead across distributed training strategies
Contrast the primary partitioning strategy and binding hardware bottleneck for Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) versus Archetype B (DLRM at Scale).
Answer: Dense language-model training can combine tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism with state sharding to meet memory, compute, and communication budgets. DLRM partitions large embedding tables across parameter servers or accelerator shards and exchanges rows selected by each batch. Capacity, random-access service, and skewed lookup traffic can bind; dense layer reductions are a different demand. The binding resource must be measured for the actual configuration.
Learning Objective: Compare distributed training archetypes by their primary partitioning strategy and binding hardware bottleneck
Explain why data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism are treated as orthogonal scaling dimensions rather than mutually exclusive strategies in the 3D Parallelism Cube, and provide an example configuration that combines them.
Answer: Data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism partition different dimensions of the workload (batch dimension, model depth across layers, and intra-layer tensor operations, respectively). Their coordinate counts compose multiplicatively, while their degrees remain coupled through memory, communication, scheduling, and useful global batch size (\(N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t\)). For example, a frontier training run may use \(\text{TP}=8\) within NVLink nodes, \(\text{PP}=16\) across nodes over InfiniBand, and \(\text{DP}=128\) across the cluster to balance memory, latency, and global batch throughput.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the orthogonal composability of the 3D parallelism cube axes

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can adding accelerators make training slower?
Splitting a training job across machines creates more compute capacity, but it also requires those machines to exchange state and agree on updates. Each accelerator may finish its local work sooner while spending more of the step waiting for other workers. Once communication and waiting consume the time saved by parallel execution, adding accelerators raises the bill without shortening the run. Single-node optimization remains necessary, yet faster local arithmetic cannot remove a dependency on data that another machine has not delivered. Memory pressure complicates the decision, because a model may require distribution simply to fit, even when the resulting exchanges are expensive. Dividing its state across more devices can relieve that limit while exposing another in network bandwidth or scheduling. Conversely, replicating a model can process more examples at once without reducing the memory needed for each copy. Neither improvement alone establishes that training will finish sooner. Changing how examples are grouped or when updates become available can change the work required to reach the target quality. Engineers must therefore compare complete training configurations, accounting for memory, communication, update behavior, and elapsed time together. The practical question is where additional hardware buys useful progress and where it merely creates more coordination. That judgment determines which models and experiments fit the available schedule and budget. In C³ terms, each partitioning strategy trades parallelized compute against network-bound communication and coordination across workers.

Learning Objectives

Apply the Fleet Law to diagnose compute-, memory-, communication-, or coordination-bound distributed training regimes
Calculate scaling efficiency, estimate useful batch size, and budget synchronization overhead for data-parallel training
Design memory-sharding plans that trade accelerator capacity for additional communication
Map tensor, pipeline, expert, and data parallelism onto hardware bandwidth tiers and model structure
Analyze microbatch pipeline schedules for bubble overhead, activation residency, and synchronous update ordering
Evaluate synchronization and low-precision policies under staleness, straggler, and numerical-stability constraints
Synthesize hybrid parallelism configurations for frontier, recommendation, and alignment training constraints

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
The accelerator hierarchy, network fabric, and storage pipeline form the physical foundation of the fleet. The remaining challenge is algorithmic. A partition of the training job decides which intermediate results and gradients must cross that fabric and when workers must synchronize, and it must make those decisions while preserving the optimization process a single device would have followed. The universal scaling law (principle \(\ref{pri-universal-scaling}\)) explains why this pressure keeps rising. Frontier quality improvements demand disproportionately more compute, data, and parameters, so the training problem eventually outgrows any single machine in capacity, in calendar time, or in both. Data Storage closed on one instance of that growth, a 175B reference model whose FP16 weights alone exceed the memory of the device that must hold them.


↩︎ The power-law relationship between quality and compute, data, and parameters, and the compute-optimal allocation it implies, are established in AI Scaling Laws.
A hypothetical accelerator with 100 terabytes of memory and an exaflop of compute would make distributed training unnecessary for that model. Real accelerators instead have finite high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, compute throughput, and input bandwidth, and more capable designs move the distribution threshold without removing it. The reference workload must be evaluated against those limits before selecting a partition. In the Fleet Stack diagrammed in The Fleet Stack, distributed training occupies the Distributed Execution row of the Distribution band, the logic that partitions the mathematical workload across the physical fleet. Data, tensor, pipeline, and hybrid parallelism create different traffic patterns for the interconnect to carry.

Self-Check: Question

A research team is training a 3B-parameter transformer that fits comfortably in one H100 GPU’s 80 GB of memory, but projected single-GPU training would take 18 months to reach target loss. The dataset is 3 TB and fits on local NVMe storage. Which signal makes distributed training necessary in this scenario?

Dataset exceeding GPU HBM capacity, which automatically mandates tensor parallelism regardless of execution time
The presence of NVLink inside the node, which makes multi-machine scaling mandatory by default
Unacceptable wall-clock training duration, even though single-device memory capacity and local storage are sufficient

A team doubles a data-parallel cluster from 64 to 128 GPUs and observes that total step time drops by only 12 percent even though per-worker compute time halves. Using the distributed step-time equation \(T_{\text{step}}(N) = T_{\text{compute}}/N + T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}}\), explain what the observation establishes and what measurement would distinguish possible causes.
True or False: If a neural network’s parameters exceed a single GPU’s memory capacity, tensor parallelism can be scaled across standard commodity Ethernet switches between server racks, provided the global batch size is made large enough.
Framing distributed parallelism strategies as compiler loop transformations across the training loop’s iterators (batches, layers, and operations), which distributed strategy corresponds to vectorization (SIMD) of inner matrix multiplications?

Tensor parallelism, which partitions inner matrix-multiplication operations across devices and exchanges partial results over the interconnect
Data parallelism, which unrolls the outer batch loop across devices so each rank processes independent data indices
Pipeline parallelism, which stages sequential layer operations across devices analogous to CPU instruction pipelining

In the 3D Parallelism Cube (\(N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t\)), how do the three orthogonal scaling axes interact to allocate cluster accelerators for large models?

The three axes are mutually exclusive; choosing data parallelism precludes using tensor or pipeline parallelism in the same cluster
Tensor and pipeline parallelism can combine within a node, but data parallelism can only be used if model parallelism is disabled
The total accelerator count is the sum of the dimensions (\(N_{\text{total}} = d + p + t\)), with each parallelism type requiring a disjoint node pool
The axes compose multiplicatively (\(N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t\)), allowing systems to simultaneously shard layers (TP), pipeline stages (PP), and replicate the pipeline across data shards (DP)

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Before optimizing algorithms, the physical constraints of the machine learning fleet must be understood. The performance of any distributed training job is governed by the Fleet Law (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)), which decomposes the per-step time:
\[ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \]


↩︎ The Fleet Law and its compute, communication, and coordination terms are established in The Fleet Law.
The communication-computation ratio, \(\CommunicationComputeRatio= \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)/(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\), compares communication time with ideally partitioned compute time for fixed global work. This \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\) is a ratio of two times, not the queue utilization of the incast model. It is the time consequence of communication intensity \(\CommunicationIntensity\) (equation 1.2), the bytes moved per operation of the workload. When transfers run at link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), the sustained-bandwidth parameter of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) message model, and each device computes at sustained rate \(\PeakRate\EfficiencyHw\), \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\approx \CommunicationIntensity \times \PeakRate\EfficiencyHw/\LinkBandwidth\), so the same workload becomes more communication-bound on faster accelerators or slower links. This ratio identifies the pressure to overlap communication; the complete step time also depends on how much exchange is hidden and how much coordination remains exposed.


↩︎ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) message model, with startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and sustained bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), is established in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model.

↪ The communication-computation ratio, evaluated for representative data-parallel and point-to-point transfers and related to communication intensity, is developed in The communication-computation ratio.

Two regimes follow from this ratio. When \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\gg \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), the cluster is compute-bound, and communication is small relative to useful computation, provided coordination and input delivery do not introduce another limit. Large-batch training of a dense convolutional model such as ResNet commonly sits here. When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\gtrsim 1\), \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) matches or exceeds \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\), the cluster is communication-bound, and insufficient overlap leaves substantial time waiting for gradients or activations. Large language models (LLMs) with billions of parameters to synchronize, and Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM)-style workloads whose embedding exchanges saturate the network, frequently land in this regime. These are typical operating points rather than fixed labels: batch size, partitioning, and placement can move the same workload across the boundary, so the ratio must be measured for the configuration at hand.


↪ The optimizations that help, and the ones that are wasted, for a compute-bound, communication-bound, or coordination-bound fleet are operationalized in The bottleneck diagnostic table.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Three signals motivate evaluating distributed execution. The first is memory exhaustion: model parameters, optimizer states, and activation storage exceed single-device capacity. For full mixed-precision training with Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam), the convention of 16 bytes per parameter can exceed an 80 GB accelerator at roughly 5 billion parameters before activations. Larger 10–20B models therefore need sharding, offload, or another memory-saving approach (Rajbhandari et al. 2020). The failed allocation establishes a capacity problem; it does not by itself choose the remedy.

↪ Accelerator HBM capacity, the ceiling these per-parameter budgets are measured against, is developed in Accelerator Memory Hierarchy.

The second signal is unacceptable training duration. Even when a model fits, single-device training may require weeks or months to converge, making wall-clock time itself a systems constraint. GPT-3’s 175B-parameter training run used a cluster of V100 GPUs (Brown et al. 2020), illustrating why the calendar, rather than HBM capacity alone, forces distribution at this scale.
The third signal is input demand at dataset scale. Dataset bytes determine storage capacity, while the training schedule determines the delivery rate. As The Data Pipeline Equation showed, either can motivate distributed data services, but a large dataset alone does not require distributing model computation. Together, capacity, calendar, and input delivery define the constraints a training configuration must satisfy.
The first signal, memory exhaustion, has a long history, traced in figure 1. Over the plotted span, single-accelerator memory grew about 38× from the K20 to the B200, while the memory needed to train a state-of-the-art model grew by roughly 4 orders of magnitude. Among the plotted models, the curves cross in 2020 at GPT-3, whose training state exceeded the largest accelerator then available by about 35×. The real crossing came earlier than the plot shows. By the 16-bytes-per-parameter convention above, any model beyond roughly 5 billion parameters already overflows one 80 GB device, and models between the plotted points, such as the 2019 Megatron-LM model developed with tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al. 2019), were partitioned for that reason. GPT-3 marks where the gap passed an order of magnitude, and every later plotted frontier model also sits far above the capacity curve. For those models, spreading state beyond one device’s memory is a precondition for training at all rather than a way to train faster.














Figure 1: The memory wall: Accelerator memory capacity plotted against the memory a state-of-the-art model needs to train. Capacity climbs steadily while demand climbs faster, and the widening gap is why weights, gradients, and optimizer state must be split across devices rather than merely compressed.



Whichever signal motivates distribution, the system must state which optimization update it implements. In the synchronous baseline developed first, the 1,024 GPUs of the volume’s Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) reference cluster, whose running instance in this chapter is a GPT-3-class 175B-parameter dense transformer, combine their contributions before advancing to the next parameter version. Matching the global batch, loss normalization, and optimizer state preserves the corresponding single-device update mathematically. Later synchronization models deliberately relax that update ordering and must be evaluated under their own convergence assumptions.


↩︎ The three systems archetypes and their binding constraints are established in Three systems archetypes.

Definition 5.1: Distributed training
Distributed training partitions the optimization loop across multiple compute nodes, distributing data or model computation and coordinating contributions according to a specified update protocol.

Significance: Partitioning training state across devices can meet a memory budget that exceeds one accelerator. GPT-3 (175B parameters) requires approximately 350 GB in BF16 (FP16 also stores 2 bytes per value, so the chapter’s byte counts hold for either format), more than 4× the 80 GB capacity of a single H100. If weights remain entirely in HBM, their aggregate capacity lower bound is 5 H100s. Adding BF16 gradients plus FP32 Adam master weights and moments gives about 2.8 TB, or at least 35 H100s before activations. These lower bounds do not establish a runnable placement; offload changes the capacity calculation, and the time budget can require more accelerators than memory alone.
Distinction: CPU threads can share a coherent address space, while accelerators generally hold separate training-state allocations even within one node. Distributed training extends coordination across those devices and node boundaries through collectives or point-to-point transfers governed by the chosen update protocol.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that distributed training scales linearly with node count. In practice, communication overhead grows with cluster size and the serial fraction of each step (Amdahl’s Law): a fixed serial fraction of the single-device baseline bounds strong-scaling speedup.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Distribution expands three costs that determine whether a partition is viable. Communication overhead includes gradient aggregation through AllReduce, which returns the same reduced tensor to each participant, or rank. For \(\Parameters\) parameters across \(\DeviceCount\) devices, a ring all-reduce, in which each worker passes gradient chunks only to its neighbor in a logical ring, sends approximately \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\times \GradientPayload\) bytes per worker per step, where the gradient payload \(\GradientPayload\) is the \(\Parameters\) gradient values times their storage width; this is not total fleet traffic.


↪ The ring schedule and the derivation of its \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) volume are developed in Collective Communication.
Fault tolerance becomes more demanding as the number of failure sources grows. Under independent constant-rate GPU failures, fleet-wide failure-free survival decays exponentially. If each of the 1,024 GPUs has mean time between failures (MTBF) of 50,000 hours, the modeled probability of at least one GPU failure in an hour is 2.0 percent, with mean interval 49 hours between such events. Whether each event interrupts training depends on recovery and redundancy. The MTBF cascade develops the assumptions.
Algorithmic stability adds a separate constraint when the partition changes global batch size or update ordering. Learning-rate scaling and warmup are candidate responses to large-batch behavior (Goyal et al. 2017), not requirements unique to multiple machines. A viable design must satisfy all three budgets.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
The single-machine optimization methodology summarized in The D·A·M Taxonomy extends to distributed environments with important adaptations. Profiling must capture inter-device communication patterns and synchronization overhead in addition to computation and memory metrics. The solution space expands to data parallelism, model parallelism in its tensor and pipeline forms, and hybrid approaches. Data parallelism assigns different examples to model replicas; tensor parallelism splits the operations inside a layer; pipeline parallelism assigns successive layer groups to different devices.
A useful mental model treats these strategies as loop transformations, the same toolkit a compiler uses to restructure sequential code, now applied by a cluster-level compiler. The logical training loop nests iterators over the examples in a batch, the layers of the model, and the matrix operations inside each layer, and each parallelism strategy distributes one of them across devices.
Data parallelism resembles a parallel for-loop, assigning different batch indices to devices running the same model. Tensor parallelism resembles vectorization, or single instruction, multiple data (SIMD), by partitioning the work inside matrix operations. The analogy describes the work split, not a shared instruction stream or register file; the devices exchange tensor shards over an interconnect. Pipeline parallelism resembles instruction pipelining, assigning successive layer groups to stages. Overlapping microbatches can keep those stages active, subject to dependency delays and load balance.
Whichever loop a strategy unrolls, distributed training1 spreads the workload across machines that must coordinate to train a single model. Coordination here means keeping every model shard or replica on a compatible training step. Basic barriers can keep a small research run ordered, but long-running training jobs also need timeout, checkpoint, and recovery mechanisms so one failed worker does not waste days of compute.
1 Distributed training: Google’s DistBelief (2012) was an early framework for training neural networks across thousands of machines, but its parameter server architecture created bandwidth bottlenecks at central nodes. This limitation drove the shift to decentralized AllReduce patterns in successors like Horovod and PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP), where each data-parallel worker sends and receives about \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) times the gradient size per step rather than concentrating traffic at a single server (Dean et al. 2012; Sergeev and Balso 2018; Li et al. 2020; Patarasuk and Yuan 2009).
Dean, Jeffrey, Greg Corrado, Rajat Monga, Kai Chen, Matthieu Devin, Quoc V. Le, Mark Z. Mao, et al. 2012. “Large Scale Distributed Deep Networks.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), edited by Peter L. Bartlett, Fernando C. N. Pereira, Christopher J. C. Burges, Léon Bottou, and Kilian Q. Weinberger, vol. 25. Curran Associates.

Sergeev, Alexander, and Mike Del Balso. 2018. “Horovod: Fast and Easy Distributed Deep Learning in TensorFlow.” CoRR abs/1802.05799.

Li, Shen, Yanli Zhao, Rohan Varma, Omkar Salpekar, Pieter Noordhuis, Teng Li, Adam Paszke, et al. 2020. “PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 13 (12): 3005–18. https://doi.org/10.14778/3415478.3415530.

Patarasuk, Pitch, and Xin Yuan. 2009. “Bandwidth Optimal All-Reduce Algorithms for Clusters of Workstations.” Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 69 (2): 117–24. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2008.09.002.

↪ Checkpointing and recovery for long-running training jobs are developed in Fault Tolerance.
2 NVLink: NVIDIA’s point-to-point GPU interconnect delivers 300 GB/s–450 GB/s per-direction bandwidth, roughly 12×–18× InfiniBand HDR per port. This bandwidth gap is why tensor parallelism, which requires AllReduce on every layer, favors the fast NVLink domain, while pipeline and data parallelism can tolerate slower links when their traffic budgets fit. NVLink Switch systems can extend that fast domain beyond one server.3 NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library): NCCL provides topology-aware inter-GPU collective communication primitives, including AllReduce, across PCIe, NVLink, InfiniBand, and IP networks. Current NCCL deployments expose ring, tree, and related algorithm families through runtime selection and tuning controls, so training frameworks can avoid naive mappings that route all traffic through the slowest inter-node path (Jeaugey 2017; NVIDIA 2026).
Jeaugey, Sylvain. 2017. NCCL 2.0. GPU Technology Conference presentation.

NVIDIA. 2026. NCCL User Guide.

Each rung of the scaling path inherits earlier challenges. A single GPU already needs input delivery, memory management, scheduling, and recovery from interrupted work. Multiple GPUs add coordination across separate device memories, even within one node. Interconnects such as NVLink or PCIe carry these exchanges,2 with collective libraries such as NCCL selecting communication schedules.3
The leap to multi-node training adds network communication overhead, fault tolerance requirements, and cluster orchestration. Because each stage compounds the previous one’s bottlenecks, single-GPU performance must be optimized before scaling out, so inefficiency does not multiply across the fleet. Although frameworks abstract away much of this through sharded data parallelism and communication libraries, implementing distributed training efficiently still demands careful network configuration (InfiniBand tuning, topology-aware routing), infrastructure management through cluster schedulers, and debugging of nonlocal issues such as synchronization hangs and communication bottlenecks. Figure 2 maps this design space onto a 3D decomposition grid (\(\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\)), partitioning cluster execution across tensor parallelism (\(\TensorParallelDegree\), intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism (\(\PipelineParallelDegree\), sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism (\(\DataParallelDegree\), batch replication), where each individual cell represents a single accelerator coordinate.







Figure 2: The 3D parallelism cube: The configuration space decomposes cluster training across three orthogonal axes: tensor parallelism (\(\TensorParallelDegree\), intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism (\(\PipelineParallelDegree\), sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism (\(\DataParallelDegree\), batch replication). Each cell is one accelerator, identified by its \((\DataParallelDegree, \PipelineParallelDegree, \TensorParallelDegree)\) coordinate, so the cube holds \(\DeviceCount = \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\) devices. A feasible point must jointly satisfy model divisibility, per-device memory limits, and the network hierarchy that carries each axis’s traffic.



Under the three-dimensional partitioning of figure 2, called 3D parallelism, the total accelerator allocation scales as the product \(\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\). The axes represent distinct mathematical partitions, but they are not independent configuration knobs. Tensor and pipeline degrees must divide the model structure, the data-parallel degree and microbatch schedule must produce a viable global batch, every partition must fit memory, and each communication group must map onto an adequate topology and acceptable failure domain. Training systems therefore select a jointly feasible coordinate rather than tuning \(\DataParallelDegree\), \(\PipelineParallelDegree\), and \(\TensorParallelDegree\) in isolation.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Choosing the right parallelism strategy is not a matter of preference; it is a constraint satisfaction problem governed by parameter count \((\Parameters)\), batch size \((\BatchSize)\), and interconnect bandwidth. In this first feasibility screen, \(\LayerCount\) denotes layer count, \(\SequenceLength\) sequence length, and \(\HiddenDimension\) hidden width. The table identifies traffic sources rather than complete byte budgets; datatype width, partition degree, and communication frequency enter the worked mechanisms below. Table 1 quantifies the parallelism communication costs for each strategy, revealing which approaches are physically feasible for a given hardware topology.



Table 1: Parallelism Communication Costs: Tensor parallelism exchanges partial layer results frequently and favors a fast communication domain, which can span servers. Pipeline parallelism transfers boundary activations; its bandwidth need depends on tensor shape and microbatch schedule. Data parallelism synchronizes gradient bytes, whose exposed cost depends on overlap and topology. Memory sharding addresses capacity but does not automatically reduce communication.
