The bandwidth requirements impose a hard constraint on hardware placement: each parallelism strategy must be matched to the interconnect available between the GPUs that need to communicate, or the design fails before it leaves the whiteboard. A quick back-of-envelope bandwidth feasibility check catches that mismatch before any code is written.


↩︎ The communication domains and bandwidth hierarchy used to evaluate placement are established in Bandwidth hierarchy.

Systems Perspective 5.1: Bandwidth feasibility checkFrequent tensor-parallel collectives must fit the layer-time budget. The test compares the time one layer’s local share of computation takes with the time its collectives take on each candidate link. For the forward pass of one GPT-3 layer split 8 ways, processing one 2,048-token sequence at half of an H100’s dense FP16 peak:

Local compute per layer: about 1.9 ms
Tensor-parallel transfer per layer over NVLink: about 0.4 ms
The same transfer over one NDR InfiniBand port: about 3.5 ms

On NVLink the exchange is a fraction of the layer’s compute; across InfiniBand it would take longer than the compute it serves. The amount hidden depends on independent work available in the execution schedule. NVLink is one suitable fast domain, but the test uses message bytes, exposed latency, and sustained link rate rather than an interconnect brand or chassis boundary. Cross-rack placement may favor pipeline or data parallelism when the available fabric cannot meet the tensor-parallel budget; their activation and gradient traffic must also be checked.


The communication costs in table 1 already narrow the choice before any mechanism has been developed, because a strategy is viable only when its traffic fits the tier that must carry it. What each formula implies in practice depends on the mechanics of data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism developed over the rest of the chapter, and section 5.12 turns the same constraints into a decision procedure once those mechanics are in place.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
When a model fits on one accelerator but training takes weeks, replicating its computation lets several workers process examples concurrently. The initial data-parallel baseline gives each worker the same model state and a local portion of one global minibatch. Combining those local contributions before the optimizer update preserves the intended global-batch estimator; the sampling and weighting conditions below explain when that equivalence holds.

Definition 5.2: Data parallelism
Data parallelism distributes training examples across workers that execute the model and combine their contributions to its optimization updates.

Significance: With \(\DeviceCount\) workers each processing a local batch of \(\LocalBatchSize\) examples once per update, the global batch size is \(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\). At fixed local work, 1,024 workers offer an ideal 1,024\(\times\) throughput increase before exposed overhead. A 1B-parameter model with BF16 gradients contributes a 2 GB gradient payload; ring AllReduce moves \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) times that payload per worker. Realized speedup depends on local compute, collective service, overlap, and load balance.
Distinction: The replicated synchronous baseline keeps a full model copy on each worker and aggregates gradients before each optimizer update. Model parallelism instead partitions the model’s computation. Sharded data parallelism, developed below, retains data-parallel computation while distributing training-state storage.
Common pitfall: Data parallelism does not scale indefinitely with worker count. Holding the local batch \(\LocalBatchSize\) fixed while adding workers grows the global batch. Beyond the workload-dependent critical batch size, additional examples yield diminishing reductions in the steps needed to reach target quality (Shallue et al. 2019). The crossover developed in section 5.8.6 therefore limits the statistical benefit even when gradient variance continues to decrease.




He, Kaiming, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. 2016. “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition.” 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 770–78. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2016.90.
Data parallelism applies when examples can be processed independently, as in training a ResNet model (He et al. 2016) on ImageNet. Each replica computes its local loss gradient, and the workers combine those contributions to reproduce the intended global-batch gradient. The averaging rule makes the sampling and weighting assumptions explicit.
Consider a model with parameters \(\ModelParameters\) training on a dataset \(\TrainingDataset\). The loss function for a single data point \(\ModelInput_i\) is \(\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)\). In standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with batch size \(\BatchSize\), the gradient update for a minibatch is: \[
\MinibatchGradient= \frac{1}{\BatchSize} \sum_{i=1}^\BatchSize\nabla_{\ModelParameters} \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)
\]
In data parallelism with \(\DeviceCount\) devices, each device \(\WorkerIndex\) computes gradients on its own minibatch \(\MiniBatchSet_k\): \[
\MinibatchGradient_k = \frac{1}{|\MiniBatchSet_k|} \sum_{\ModelInput_i \in \MiniBatchSet_k} \nabla_{\ModelParameters} \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)
\]
When all workers use the same local batch size, the global update averages these local gradients: \[
\GlobalBatchGradient= \frac{1}{\DeviceCount} \sum_{k=1}^\DeviceCount\MinibatchGradient_k
\]
Under that equal-batch assumption, the averaging is mathematically equivalent to computing the gradient on the combined batch \(\CombinedBatch= \bigcup_{k=1}^\DeviceCount \MiniBatchSet_k\): \[
\GlobalBatchGradient= \frac{1}{|\CombinedBatch|} \sum_{\ModelInput_i \in \CombinedBatch} \nabla_{\ModelParameters} \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)
\]
For unequal local batch sizes, the combined-batch gradient is the weighted average \(\GlobalBatchGradient= (1/|\CombinedBatch|)\sum_k |\MiniBatchSet_k|\MinibatchGradient_k\). The equivalence shows why data parallelism maintains the statistical properties of SGD training: sampling the intended global batch across devices, computing local gradient sums independently, and normalizing by the aggregate denominator reproduces its estimator. The reduction step uses an AllReduce over local gradient sums and valid-item counts.
Three batch quantities recur from here on, and the chapter keeps them apart. A worker’s local batch \(\LocalBatchSize\) is the set of examples it processes for one update, playing the role of \(\MiniBatchSet_k\) above. The global batch \(\GlobalBatchSize= \DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) is the set the update averages over. Pipeline parallelism later splits a batch into \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches of size \(\MicrobatchSize\) that flow through stages one after another; the word microbatch is reserved for those pipeline slices.


↪ The ring and tree AllReduce cost models that set the price of this synchronization are developed in AllReduce.

Checkpoint 5.1: Data parallelism mechanics
Verify your understanding of how data parallelism distributes work:

State placement: determine whether data parallelism shards or replicates the model state (weights) across GPUs.
Global batch size: calculate the effective global batch size for 8 GPUs with a per-GPU batch size of 32.
Single-device equivalence: explain why data parallelism is mathematically equivalent to single-device training with a larger batch size.
Binding constraint: identify the primary hardware resource that constrains data parallelism as more nodes are added: GPU TFLOP/s or network bandwidth.



The method parallels gradient accumulation, where a device accumulates contributions from multiple forward and backward passes before one optimizer update. Both techniques use gradient addition and the intended loss denominator to process a larger effective batch. Distribution adds communication, partial failures, and coordination to that arithmetic. The implementation must preserve the update while accounting for those costs.


The implementation details matter because the SGD equivalence only holds when each phase preserves the intended aggregate sampling and weighting, complete local gradient contributions, and a single synchronized update. The concrete workflow follows the dataflow from assigning local batches to synchronizing the computed gradients. Figure 3 diagrams this five-stage execution pipeline across four GPU swimlanes, tracking how identical model replicas ingest disjoint batch shards, compute local gradients (\(\MinibatchGradient_0\)–\(\MinibatchGradient_3\)), and synchronize through a ring AllReduce collective before applying uniform parameter updates.







Figure 3: Data parallelism implementation pipeline: The five-stage workflow for data-parallel training: (1) partition the global batch, (2) assign sharded mini-batches to individual GPUs, (3) compute independent forward and backward passes to produce local gradients \(\MinibatchGradient_i\), (4) execute an AllReduce collective across the cluster to obtain the average gradient \(\GlobalBatchGradient\), and (5) update parameters identically across all devices. This strategy preserves the mathematical semantics of single-device SGD while distributing the compute burden.



The gradient synchronization stage of figure 3 (stage 4) establishes a dependency: each rank must receive the completed reduction before applying its optimizer update. The exposed wait can reflect bandwidth, collective startup, or a late contribution. Measuring that wait determines whether synchronization limits scaling; the dependency alone does not identify the binding resource.


Data splitting is the first place where the SGD equivalence can fail, but uniqueness and equal-sized shards are sufficient conditions rather than the invariant itself. The aggregate examples or tokens, their sampling probabilities, and their gradient weights must reproduce the intended global-batch estimator. Uniform sampling without replacement can assign disjoint shards; sampling with replacement can legitimately repeat examples; and variable-length batches can assign unequal token counts if the reduction weights each worker by its valid-example or valid-token denominator. An unweighted mean of unequal local means instead overweights workers with smaller denominators.
The sampler is therefore an integral component of the distributed training system rather than merely an input-loader convenience. A distributed sampler coordinates workers by rank and can deterministically partition or draw indices from a seeded sampling stream. For a 1.2 million-example dataset distributed evenly across 32 GPUs, each GPU processes approximately 37,500 examples per epoch. If the sampler pads the final batch by repeating examples, the loss normalization or sample weights must account for those repeats when exact epoch-level weighting matters. A recorded seed and deterministic index stream make sample assignment repeatable; bitwise run reproducibility additionally depends on kernel determinism, collective reduction order, numerical precision, and checkpointed random-number-generator state.



For a replicated model whose local forward and backward operations require no cross-worker state, the computation phase is embarrassingly parallel. Each GPU executes the model on its local batch; synchronized normalization or additional model partitioning can introduce communication within that phase. To isolate the activation term, consider an unpartitioned 175B reference model at a local batch of 4 sequences and sequence length 2048. This is a hypothetical memory budget, not a feasible one-GPU training configuration: weights and optimizer state must fit as well. Without optimization, storing these activations for backpropagation would consume roughly 1.1 TB of HBM, an order of magnitude beyond the capacity of even an H100 GPU. Activation checkpointing recomputes selected activations during the backward pass rather than retaining them, reducing this example’s footprint to ~19.3 GB at the cost of extra computation.
The capacity test must include activations rather than stopping at bytes per parameter. Numeric Precision and Training Memory tabulates the 16-byte-per-parameter training state from which this test starts. At the point of peak residency, \[
\TotalMemoryFootprint = \WeightMemory + \GradientMemory + \OptimizerStateMemory + \ActivationMemory,
\] with communication buffers and temporary workspaces consuming additional headroom. Sharding reduces the first three terms according to its stage, whereas sequence length, local batch size, and pipeline scheduling govern \(\ActivationMemory\). Activation checkpointing reduces that last term by retaining only selected boundaries and recomputing the omitted forward operators during backpropagation (Narayanan et al. 2021). The memory saved is therefore purchased with additional FLOPs and a longer critical path; a feasible parallelism plan must budget both effects.

Narayanan, Deepak, Mohammad Shoeybi, Jared Casper, Patrick LeGresley, Mostofa Patwary, Vijay Korthikanti, Dmitri Vainbrand, et al. 2021. “Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM.” Proceedings of the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 1–15. https://doi.org/10.1145/3458817.3476209.
As the backward pass traverses the computation graph in reverse, it produces gradients for the parameters held by each replica or shard. Under pure data parallelism, a full 175B FP16 replica would imply a 350 GB gradient tensor per worker, which exceeds single-accelerator memory budgets; large runs therefore combine data parallelism with sharding, tensor parallelism, or pipeline parallelism. Each local gradient contributes to the intended global-batch estimator. Aggregation can begin as gradient tensors become ready, overlapping later backward computation, but the optimizer must wait for the completed contributions it consumes. This readiness schedule connects local computation to collective communication.



Gradient synchronization combines local contributions into the synchronous update. Each replica must receive the aggregate before applying that update. In a centralized parameter-server design with fixed per-worker payload and update frequency, the server receives \(\mathcal{O}(\DeviceCount)\) incoming traffic. That concentration becomes a bottleneck when demand exceeds the server tier’s service capacity; sharding the server state or changing the communication pattern can relieve it.
The replicated synchronous baseline distributes aggregation through collective communication. AllReduce lets each worker contribute its local gradient tensor and receive the same reduced result, which the training loop normalizes to obtain the global average. In sharded variants such as ZeRO and FSDP, ReduceScatter and AllGather change which result each worker retains. ReduceScatter combines corresponding tensor elements, then leaves a different reduced shard on each worker. AllGather collects distinct shards and returns their concatenation to every worker without summing them. These contracts support gradient sharding and on-demand parameter reconstruction. Small messages emphasize startup latency; large messages emphasize sustained bandwidth. Centralized aggregation remains another design choice, particularly for the sparse workloads developed later.
At the Distributed Execution row of the fleet stack, the loop specifies an AllReduce contract while its implementation determines the cost. For a large worker group, ring AllReduce transfers approximately \(2\GradientPayload\) bytes per worker for an \(\GradientPayload\)-byte gradient payload. Collective Communication derives this approximate \(2\GradientPayload\) volume and compares algorithms whose startup costs, topology, and contention differ. It also examines how libraries such as NCCL schedule exchanges within and across communication domains.
When a measured collective deviates from these estimates, the diagnosis compares the trace against what each candidate algorithm would predict on the same hardware. The worked example below concerns a trace that the modeled flat-ring schedule cannot explain. The leading candidate is a hierarchical AllReduce, which first ReduceScatters the tensor over NVLink across the eight ranks in each node. Each rank retains one eighth of the reduced tensor. Eight inter-node groups then AllReduce corresponding shards concurrently, after which a local AllGather reconstructs the full result on every rank. The example assumes an independent InfiniBand port for each local rank, so each port carries one shard; the node’s aggregate payload has not fallen by a factor of eight. The flat-ring comparison assumes that each rank’s full-tensor ring traffic crosses its inter-node port at the stated link rate.


↪ Hierarchical AllReduce and its cost relative to a flat ring are developed in Hierarchical AllReduce.

Example 5.1: Debugging slow gradient synchronizationScenario: In this hypothetical diagnostic trace on an A100 cluster with HDR InfiniBand, one generation older than the reference H100 cluster and chosen because its narrower inter-node links make the flat-ring penalty easy to see, an AllReduce of a 3 GB gradient tensor across 128 nodes (1,024 GPUs) takes 100 ms.
Diagnosis: Three times bracket the trace. The idealized hierarchical estimate is 48.5 ms, the observed collective takes 100 ms, and the flat-ring estimate is 239.8 ms. Under the modeled routing and port assumptions, the observation falls well below the flat-ring estimate, so that flat-ring schedule cannot explain it, and a hierarchical algorithm becomes the leading hypothesis, which runtime traces must confirm by identifying the actual algorithm, channels, and routes. Because the observation still exceeds the hierarchical ideal, lower achieved transfer rates, startup, or waiting must account for the residual. Suppose switch counters also show inter-node InfiniBand links at 60 percent utilization. That aggregate utilization does not exclude a saturated port or uplink during the exposed collective interval. Per-port and per-channel traces over that interval must distinguish transfer-capacity limits from channel imbalance or a late participant before raw bandwidth can be ruled out.
Systems lesson: Debugging collective communication requires evaluating physical link utilization against algorithmic bounds. The gap between the 48.5 ms idealized hierarchical estimate and the 100 ms trace motivates checking congestion, channel placement, startup, and stragglers. Change topology only after identifying the exposed bottleneck.


Stepping back from that specific cluster to the architectural design space, figure 4 diagrams three synchronization topologies: the bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce that circulates chunks along neighbor links (\(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) volume), the centralized parameter server constrained by network interface card (NIC) saturation at the server node, and the dense mesh of logical All-to-All peer traffic (\(\DeviceCount(\DeviceCount-1)\) messages). In dense synchronous data-parallel settings, ring AllReduce avoids a single reducer bottleneck by distributing traffic evenly across participating links, as Baidu’s implementation illustrates (Gibiansky 2017).

Gibiansky, A. 2017. Bringing HPC Techniques to Deep Learning. Baidu Research Technical Blog.






Figure 4: Communication patterns and their costs: Ring AllReduce and a parameter server illustrate two ways to aggregate updates. All-to-All instead routes distinct data to each peer; the complete graph shows logical destinations, not a requirement for dedicated physical links. A switched fabric can carry this traffic, with cost determined by message size, routes, and contention.



The panels separate an aggregation algorithm, a centralized architecture, and a collective traffic pattern. They do not provide interchangeable implementations of the same operation. Only the first two aggregate gradients; the All-to-All panel previews the exchange that sparse embedding tables and mixture-of-experts layers need, in which every worker sends different data to every other worker (section 5.9.3). Libraries choose algorithms and routes for the requested collective on the available fabric; a logical complete graph does not guarantee one-round physical delivery.



Distributed training systems use synchronization models to specify when workers observe and apply updates. The baseline is bulk synchronous parallel (BSP), the superstep-and-barrier model. In the replicated training loop, workers compute from one parameter version, combine their gradient contributions, and complete the update before computing from the next version. This is a dependency order, not a requirement that every device update at the same wall-clock instant. Relaxing it changes the optimization process as well as the waiting time.


↩︎ Bulk synchronous parallel execution and its barrier cost are established in How ML Networking Inverts Data-Center Assumptions.
BSP provides synchronous update semantics: every worker computes from the same parameter version and reaches the next update boundary together. With the same global batch and reduction, this matches the corresponding synchronous single-device update mathematically. It does not by itself guarantee bitwise reproducibility. Floating-point reduction order, nondeterministic kernels, data-order state, and failure recovery can still change the result. The synchronization cost is that the slowest worker determines iteration time. A worker that keeps producing correct results but runs markedly slower than its peers is a straggler, and under BSP every straggler delays the entire step.
Stale synchronous parallel (SSP) relaxes this constraint by allowing workers to proceed up to \(\StalenessBound\) iterations ahead of the slowest worker before blocking. This bounds staleness while reducing synchronization delays. SSP requires careful learning rate tuning since workers compute gradients on slightly different parameter versions. The bounded staleness guarantee provides a middle ground between BSP’s strong consistency and fully asynchronous approaches (Ho et al. 2013).
Asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier, allowing a worker’s contribution to be applied while others continue computing; asynchronous SGD is the optimizer run under that protocol. Less barrier waiting can improve update throughput, but communication and shared-state contention remain. Gradients computed from older parameter versions introduce staleness that can affect convergence. Section 5.8.4 develops the objective and delay assumptions needed to evaluate that trade-off.
The key trade-offs across synchronization models are summarized in table 2.



Table 2: Synchronization Model Trade-offs: BSP, SSP, and ASP trade consistency for throughput along a spectrum. BSP preserves synchronous update boundaries but pays for the slowest worker; SSP permits bounded progress ahead of slower workers; ASP removes the global update barrier without a finite protocol-wide staleness bound. Throughput and time to target quality depend on the workload and implementation. Reproducibility requires a separate deterministic-execution contract.

Figure 5 sequences execution traces for four workers across BSP, SSP, and ASP, isolating how global barriers force faster workers into idle wait blocks while straggler W3 completes, how bounded slack (\(\StalenessBound=1\)) throttles drift with brief pauses, and how asynchronous updates remove the global barrier without imposing a finite staleness bound. Communication and resource contention can still leave workers waiting.







Figure 5: Distributed synchronization models: The timelines compare three synchronization strategies. Top: bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) forces all workers to wait at a global barrier every step. Middle: stale synchronous parallel (SSP) allows workers to proceed up to \(\StalenessBound\) steps ahead of the slowest worker. Bottom: asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier while allowing gradient staleness; communication and resource contention can still delay progress.



The choice of synchronization model directly affects both system throughput and model convergence. Training teams often use BSP for controlled final runs because synchronous steps simplify comparison and replay, while exploring SSP or async approaches during hyperparameter search where throughput can outweigh exact update equivalence. Reproducible replay still requires deterministic sampling, kernels, collective ordering, and restored random state.



An optimizer update that consumes an AllReduce result must wait for every required contribution. Workers can execute independent computation while a collective is in flight, but they must issue compatible collectives in the same group order and wait for completion before consuming the result. This coupling creates failure modes absent from single-device training.
A worker failure can leave peers waiting for a contribution that will never arrive. The runtime may report a communication error, or the operation may remain blocked until a timeout detects the failure. Watchdogs bound that wait so the job can enter recovery rather than retain an unusable allocation indefinitely.



One missing worker stalls the entire AllReduce barrier.
Collective mismatches occur when workers issue incompatible operations, tensor shapes, or ordering within a communication group. Conditional computation can create such a mismatch if some workers omit an expected reduction. Variable sequence lengths or different expert routes do not inherently violate the protocol; the runtime must construct a compatible communication schedule for those varying local computations.
Stragglers extend an iteration when their late work lies on its critical path. Thermal throttling, network congestion, or OS jitter can delay a required contribution even when other workers are ready. At 1,000 GPUs with a 1 percent straggler probability per GPU per step, the expected count is 10 stragglers per step, but the number that matters under BSP is the chance of a step with none at all. That chance is the per-GPU on-time probability raised to the GPU count, about 0.004 percent. Almost every step therefore waits for at least one slow worker, which is why the slowest worker, not the typical one, sets step time. The resulting exposed wait depends on how late that contribution arrives and what independent work remains.
Deployed systems address these issues through timeouts, heartbeat monitoring, and elastic training mechanisms.


↪ Heartbeat and collective-timeout failure detection, and the trade-off between restarting healthy workers and leaving peers blocked, are developed in Failure detection mechanisms.



Parameter updating closes the replicated synchronous contract. Workers apply the aggregated gradient using matching parameters, optimizer state, and update settings. Each worker can then update its local model independently with SGD, momentum, or Adam. Identical gradients alone are insufficient if optimizer moments, learning rates, or step counts differ across replicas.
In a system with 8 GPUs training a ResNet model, each GPU computes local gradients based on its data subset. After gradient averaging via ring all-reduce (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009), every GPU has the same global gradient values. Each device then independently applies these gradients using the optimizer’s update rule. With SGD and learning rate 0.1, the update becomes weights = weights - 0.1 * gradients. The example shows why the update can remain decentralized without sacrificing mathematical equivalence to single-device training.
The cycle of splitting data, computing gradients, synchronizing results, and updating parameters repeats for each batch. Frameworks automate this cycle, but they cannot remove the ordering constraint that makes the replicas coherent: every worker must update only after the synchronized gradient is complete.




Data parallelism is a common starting strategy because it preserves each replica’s model computation while distributing examples. Near-linear throughput scaling requires local compute efficiency, balanced input delivery, and small exposed synchronization costs. Once those costs become material relative to useful work, the benefit of another worker diminishes (Ben-Nun and Hoefler 2019). Whether the global batch stays fixed or grows determines how both computation and statistical efficiency change. Holding the global batch fixed while adding workers is strong scaling: each worker’s local batch shrinks, so communication must hide behind less computation. Holding the local batch fixed so that the global batch grows with \(\DeviceCount\) is weak scaling: per-worker computation stays constant, but each update averages more examples, which eventually stops reducing the number of updates needed. The rest of the chapter refers to the two regimes by these names.

Ben-Nun, Tal, and Torsten Hoefler. 2019. “Demystifying Parallel and Distributed Deep Learning: An in-Depth Concurrency Analysis.” ACM Computing Surveys 52 (4): 1–43. https://doi.org/10.1145/3320060.
Weak scaling pays off when the larger global batch still reaches the target accuracy. Goyal et al. (2017) trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet in about one hour on 256 GPUs at a global batch of 8,192 images; the learning-rate rules that let that batch reach the target accuracy are developed in section 5.8.5. Replicated data parallelism retains the model’s local operators, and frameworks can trigger gradient reductions as backward computation produces them. Each replica executes a complete forward and backward pass, avoiding the layer-stage fill and drain bubbles of pipeline parallelism. Input stalls, imbalance, and exposed reductions can still leave devices idle.
Three constraints limit these advantages. The memory wall arises because a replicated worker holds parameters, gradients, and optimizer state; the 175B-parameter example requires more than 1 TB per replica before activations. Communication limits useful scaling when its exposed cost grows relative to local work. As \(\DeviceCount\) grows, the ideal ring bandwidth term \(\frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount} \frac{\GradientPayload}{\LinkBandwidth}\) approaches a constant for a fixed gradient payload \(\GradientPayload\) and link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), while startup, topology, and shrinking local computation can worsen the balance. Statistics binds under weak scaling, where \(\GlobalBatchSize= \DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) grows and added samples eventually yield diminishing reductions in update count. Strong scaling avoids that limit but reduces local work, exposing the communication trade-off.

Napkin Math 5.1: GPT-2 data parallel scaling: Single nodeA GPT-2 scaling scenario makes the efficiency loss concrete by holding the model fixed and changing only the communication domain. GPT-2 stands in for the 175B reference here because it fits on one GPU, so pure replicated data parallelism applies and communication is the only variable. The first case keeps all eight GPUs inside a single NVLink node.
Single-GPU baseline

Batch size: 16 (with gradient checkpointing, fits in 32 GB)
Time per step: 1.8 s
Baseline time for 50K single-GPU steps: 25 hours

The following durations hold the total sample budget fixed, so larger global batches require fewer optimizer updates. They assume those samples attain the same quality; the calculation establishes throughput scaling, not convergence equivalence.
8 GPUs: single node with NVLink

Per-GPU batch: 16, global batch: 128
Gradient synchronization: 5.2 GB @ 450 GB/s (NVLink, per direction) \(\approx\) 11.7 ms

Performance results:

Compute: 1800 ms per step
Communication: 11.7 ms per step
Total: 1811.7 ms per step
Speedup (throughput): 8×
Parallel efficiency: 99.4 percent

Training time: 25 hours ÷ 8 = 3.1 hours


Inside the node, NVLink keeps gradient exchange small relative to compute, so efficiency stays near 99.4 percent. The picture inverts once the same model must synchronize across nodes over a commodity network.

Napkin Math 5.2: GPT-2 data parallel scaling: Commodity scale-out
The second case scales the same GPT-2 run across multiple nodes, replacing the intra-node NVLink hop with inter-node Ethernet for the bulk of the AllReduce. The 10 Gb Ethernet link models a commodity cloud tier without a dedicated training fabric, far slower than the InfiniBand of the reference cluster, which makes the cost of leaving the node easy to see.
Commodity network configuration: 32 GPUs across 4 nodes

Per-GPU batch: 16, global batch: 512
Intra-node communication: 11.7 ms (NVLink)
Inter-node communication: 5.8 GB @ 1.25 GB/s (10GbE) \(\approx\) 4650 ms

Performance results:

Compute: 1800 ms (27.9 percent of time)
Communication: 4661.7 ms (72.1 percent of time), so communication dominates and becomes the bottleneck.
Total: 6461.7 ms per step
Speedup (throughput): 8.9× faster → 2.8 hours
Parallel efficiency: 27.9 percent



The scale-out run bought its larger global batch with four nodes on a slow network. A single node can reach the same global batch another way, by running several local microsteps and accumulating their gradients before one AllReduce. The comparison below is therefore between two placements, one node with accumulation against four nodes without it; accumulation’s job is to keep the global batch equal, while the saving comes from never leaving the NVLink domain.

Napkin Math 5.3: Gradient accumulation speedupProblem: A GPT-2 run on a commodity 10G network is communication-bound at 32 GPUs across 4 nodes, costing $359 for a fixed number of samples. Can a single 8-GPU node that uses gradient accumulation to match that global batch process the same samples for less?
Math:

Effective batch size: 8 GPUs \(\times\) batch 16 \(\times\) 4 accumulation steps = 512.
Communication overhead: With 4-step accumulation, the job AllReduces once every 4 steps (overhead = 11.7 ms / (4 \(\times\) 1800 ms) \(\approx\) \(0.162\%\)).
Training duration: Total time is 3.1 hours.
Scale-out baseline cost: 4 nodes \(\times\) 2.8 hours \(\times\) $32/hr = $359.
Accumulation cost: 3.1 hours \(\times\) $32/hr = $100.

Systems insight: The one-node plan saves $259 (72.1 percent). Almost all of that saving comes from placement, because the four-node run spent most of each step on the slow inter-node link and the single node never uses it. Gradient accumulation is what makes the single node a fair substitute, because it reproduces the four-node global batch, and its own contribution to speed is small, since the same node already ran at 99.4 percent parallel efficiency without accumulation. Accumulation on a multi-node job still requires inter-node synchronization once per window.


In this GPT-2 scenario, changing the communication domain drops efficiency from 99.4 percent to 27.9 percent. Accumulation can preserve the effective batch while avoiding the slow scale-out link, at the cost of additional local computation between updates. It leaves each worker’s replicated model state unchanged, however; reducing that memory burden requires sharding.



The memory constraints of replicated data parallelism motivate techniques that shard training state while retaining each worker’s full forward and backward computation. The Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO) (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) and PyTorch’s Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) (Zhao et al. 2023) implement this approach.4 They can make a model feasible without partitioning its layer computations across devices.

Rajbhandari, Samyam, Jeff Rasley, Olatunji Ruwase, and Yuxiong He. 2020. “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models.” SC20: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1109/sc41405.2020.00024.

Zhao, Yanli, Andrew Gu, Rohan Varma, Liang Luo, Chien-Chin Huang, Min Xu, Less Wright, et al. 2023. “PyTorch FSDP: Experiences on Scaling Fully Sharded Data Parallel.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 16 (12): 3848–60. https://doi.org/10.14778/3611540.3611569.
4 ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer): Introduced by Microsoft researchers in 2019 and released in the DeepSpeed library (Rasley et al. 2020), ZeRO’s stages progressively partition optimizer states, gradients, and parameters. FSDP draws on the fully sharded approach associated with ZeRO’s deepest stage; the shared partitioning principle does not imply identical implementations or communication schedules.
Rasley, Jeff, Samyam Rajbhandari, Olatunji Ruwase, and Yuxiong He. 2020. “DeepSpeed: System Optimizations Enable Training Deep Learning Models with over 100 Billion Parameters.” Proceedings of the 26th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery & Data Mining, 3505–6. https://doi.org/10.1145/3394486.3406703.

Definition 5.3: Sharded data parallelism
Sharded data parallelism partitions optimizer state, gradients, and at the deepest stage the parameters themselves across data-parallel workers. Each worker processes its own minibatch shard and uses collectives to obtain the parameters and reduced gradients it needs. Full sharding reduces each worker’s persistent state toward \(1/\DeviceCount\) of the replicated training state; activations and temporary buffers still contribute to peak memory.

Significance: Under the mixed-precision Adam convention used here, 16 bytes of state per parameter gives a 7B-parameter model 112 GB of training state, exceeding a 80 GB accelerator before activations. ZeRO Stage 3 across 64 workers reduces persistent state per device to 1.75 GB (0.25 bytes per parameter). The resulting AllGather and ReduceScatter traffic trades memory capacity for communication whose exposed cost depends on the interconnect and available overlap.
Distinction: Unlike vanilla data parallelism, which replicates training state, sharded data parallelism partitions its storage. Unlike model parallelism, it retains each worker’s full forward and backward computation. Fully sharded execution gathers parameters for the current computation; the resharding schedule determines when it releases them.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that sharding is free memory. The on-demand AllGathers place parameter traffic on the critical path of every layer in every step; on slower interconnects or at small per-worker batch sizes, the exposed communication erodes throughput faster than the memory savings help. Capacity is purchased with bandwidth.



The scale of the savings is clearest on a model whose replicated training state only modestly overflows one accelerator, so that the effect of each sharding stage stays visible; the 175B reference returns when the question becomes whether sharding alone is enough.

Napkin Math 5.4: ZeRO memory savingsProblem: Training a 7B parameter Llama-2 model in mixed precision requires 16 bytes per parameter for weights, gradients, and optimizer state. Does the full training state fit on a single A100-80 GB, and how does ZeRO Stage 3 with 64 GPUs change the per-device memory requirement?
Baseline: Standard DDP (replicated state) Per-Parameter Memory Cost:

Weights (FP16): 2 bytes
Gradients (FP16): 2 bytes
Optimizer state (FP32): 12 bytes (4 master weight + 4 momentum + 4 variance)
Total: 16 bytes/parameter

Total Memory for 7B Model:
\[C_{\text{state,total}} = 7 \times 10^9 \times 16 \text{ bytes} \approx 112 \text{ GB}\]
Baseline outcome: Out-of-memory (OOM) on A100-80 GB.
Optimization: ZeRO-3 (fully sharded) With \(\DeviceCount=\) 64 GPUs, state is partitioned:

Weights: 2\(/\DeviceCount\) bytes
Gradients: 2\(/\DeviceCount\) bytes
Optimizer: 12\(/\DeviceCount\) bytes
Total: 16\(/\DeviceCount=\) 0.25 bytes/parameter effective storage!

Per-GPU Memory:
\[C_{\text{state,ZeRO3}} = \frac{112 \text{ GB}}{64} \approx 1.75 \text{ GB}\]
Result: The persistent state fits, leaving ~78 GB for activations, gathered parameters, temporary buffers, and runtime allocations. Their simultaneous peak determines whether the chosen batch size fits.


ZeRO reaches that result in stages, and the intermediate stages matter because each one buys memory with a different communication pattern. Optimizer sharding alone (ZeRO-1) already brings the replicated footprint of the same model under the accelerator ceiling, because optimizer state is three-quarters of it; gradient sharding (ZeRO-2) and parameter sharding (ZeRO-3/FSDP) continue toward the fully sharded figure (figure 6). Table 3 pairs each stage with the collectives it uses.














Figure 6: ZeRO memory reduction: Standard data parallelism (DDP) replicates all model states across every GPU. ZeRO progressively partitions these states: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states, ZeRO-2 adds gradient sharding, and ZeRO-3 shards the parameters themselves; each dashed outline marks the replicated stack a stage no longer holds. ZeRO-3 achieves linear memory scaling, enabling models with 100B+ parameters to fit on accelerators that could not hold the replicated state.






Table 3: ZeRO Sharding Stages: Each stage shards a different layer of training state and trades a different communication primitive. ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 both replace the gradient AllReduce with a reduction to each shard’s owner and a parameter AllGather, matching DDP volume, and differ only in whether each worker keeps a full-size gradient buffer; ZeRO-3 (FSDP) adds per-layer AllGathers during forward and backward passes, unlocking near-linear memory scaling at \(1.5\times\) communication.











Stage

ZeRO-1

Reduce to owner + AllGather (\(1\times\) DDP volume)

ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states across GPUs. Each GPU stores only \(1/\DeviceCount\) of the Adam optimizer-related state. Gradients need only be reduced to the worker responsible for each parameter shard; after updating that shard, workers AllGather the updated parameters to restore the full replicas. This schedule supports the table’s baseline communication volume; a full gradient AllReduce followed by a parameter AllGather would add traffic. Under the 12-byte convention that counts FP32 master weights, momentum, and variance, memory savings reduce optimizer state from \(12\DeviceCount\) bytes/param to \(12\) bytes/param total across the cluster.
ZeRO-2 additionally shards gradients. ReduceScatter leaves each GPU with its \(1/\DeviceCount\) shard of reduced gradients. Each worker updates its \(1/\DeviceCount\) parameter partition using the corresponding optimizer state, then AllGather restores the updated parameter replicas. In the ideal ring accounting, each phase transfers \(\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) elements per worker, for \(2\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) across both phases. This matches DDP’s byte volume (\(1\times\)) when gradient and parameter communication widths match. Replicated parameters avoid forward parameter gathers, although model operations may still communicate. Under the FP16-gradient convention, gradient storage falls from \(2\DeviceCount\) bytes per parameter across \(\DeviceCount\) workers to \(2\) bytes per parameter in total, or \(2/\DeviceCount\) per GPU, apart from transient buffers.
ZeRO-3 and FSDP also partition parameters, leaving each GPU with a \(1/\DeviceCount\) persistent slice. The full-shard schedule considered here gathers each unit before forward computation, releases its unsharded parameters, and gathers them again for backward. ReduceScatter distributes the completed gradients for local shard updates. Figure 7 contrasts the stored state across four ranks. Under matching communication widths, ZeRO-1 (\(\OptimizerStateMemory/4\)) and ZeRO-2 (\(\OptimizerStateMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4\)) retain baseline \(1\times\) communication volume; ZeRO-3 (\(\WeightMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4, \OptimizerStateMemory/4\)) adds the second parameter gather, yielding \(1.5\times\) the baseline volume in this accounting.







Figure 7: ZeRO state partitioning across GPU ranks: Which copy of each training state every GPU holds, for 4 workers. A filled full-width tile is a replicated copy; a quarter-width segment inside a dashed outline is that GPU’s shard, stepping one quarter per rank. ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state (\(\OptimizerStateMemory/4\)), ZeRO-2 adds gradients (\(\GradientMemory/4\)), and ZeRO-3 shards parameters too (\(\WeightMemory/4\)). The footers give per-worker communication volume relative to DDP: only ZeRO-3 pays more, for the parameter AllGathers.



Full sharding adds parameter-readiness dependencies that replicated DDP avoids. With one sharding unit per layer, the forward pass needs an AllGather to reconstruct parameters (\(\LayerParameterPayload\) bytes); resharding after forward requires another gather before backward (\(\LayerParameterPayload\) bytes), followed by a ReduceScatter for gradients (\(\LayerParameterPayload\) bytes under equal communication precision). For a model with \(\LayerCount\) layers, this schedule performs about \(3\LayerCount\) collective operations per step; DDP instead AllReduces gradient buckets as they become ready. At large worker counts, the ideal per-worker transfer volumes approach \(3\ParameterPayload\) bytes versus \(2\ParameterPayload\) for DDP, where \(\ParameterPayload\) is the model’s parameter bytes at the communication precision, not full training state, and equals \(\GradientPayload\) when parameters and gradients travel at the same width. These volumes do not determine elapsed time alone. While layer \(\LayerIndex\) computes, layer \(\LayerIndex+1\) can prefetch parameters, subject to memory headroom and fabric contention.
The choice between FSDP and DDP begins with peak memory. If replicated state, activations, and working buffers fit, DDP avoids repeated parameter gathers. When optimizer and gradient storage are the obstacle, ZeRO-2 offers savings while leaving parameters replicated. If parameters themselves do not fit, ZeRO-3/FSDP, offload, or partitioned computation must address that remaining constraint. For a 70B+ model on 80 GB devices, the need for tensor parallelism depends on the gathered layer size, activation budget, and throughput target; parameter count alone does not decide it.
Memory-efficient data parallelism requires careful tuning of sharding strategy (by layer, by transformer block, or flat) and mixed precision settings. The sharding granularity determines the trade-off: finer sharding reduces per-GPU memory but increases communication frequency as more AllGather and ReduceScatter operations must execute per training step.



ZeRO and FSDP shard dense state that every step touches in full. Recommendation models pose the opposite problem, and for them the parameter server (PS) architecture, formalized by Li et al. (2014), remains common. A parameter server architecture separates workers, which compute gradients, from servers, which store parameters and apply updates.
For dense models such as ResNet or BERT, that separation concentrates traffic, as section 5.7.1.3 noted. With \(\DeviceCount\) workers, a server’s inbound links must absorb \(\DeviceCount\) gradient streams at once. This incast problem is why dense training moved to ring AllReduce, in which every worker sends and receives at its own link rate and the aggregate load spreads across all nodes.
Recommendation systems reverse the balance. Their parameters are dominated by embedding tables (often 10 TB+) that no single GPU can hold, and their updates are sparse, because a batch of users interacts with only a tiny fraction of the items.
In a sparse parameter-server design, embedding tables are sharded across servers, and workers request only rows indexed by their local minibatches. A sparse pull returns those embedding vectors; a sparse push sends updates for the touched rows. This pattern avoids exchanging the complete table, but hot rows, lookup rates, and network contention can still limit throughput. Embedding-sharding frameworks such as TorchRec also support accelerator-based layouts, so sparse partitioning should not be equated with a CPU-only server architecture. This is the volume’s Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) regime, and it differs from the dense running example in which resource binds first.

Lighthouse 5.1: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): DLRM vs. LLM scalingEach workload scales through a distinct mechanism and is bound by a different resource. Dense LLMs scale through data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism, constrained by compute throughput and by the bandwidth that dense gradient and activation collectives need over fabrics such as NVLink and InfiniBand. Sparse recommendation models such as DLRM scale by sharding embedding tables of 10 TB or more across parameter servers or accelerator memory, where aggregate memory capacity, lookup rate, and the latency of many small random accesses dominate. The distinction shapes cluster design: accelerator pods built around high-bandwidth dense fabrics for LLMs, and memory-capacity-rich layouts for recommendation systems, whether the embedding shards live in CPU-hosted servers, in accelerator HBM, or in a tiered hybrid that keeps hot rows on accelerators and cold rows in host memory.


Dense or sparse, the resulting design must turn added resources into faster progress toward target quality. The next section measures that progress.

Self-Check: Question

A 7B-parameter transformer in mixed precision requires 112 GB of static memory for standard replicated DDP (14 GB for FP16 weights, 14 GB for FP16 gradients, and 84 GB for FP32 Adam master weights, momentum, and variance). Under ZeRO Stage 3 (or FSDP Full Shard) across 64 GPUs, what is the resulting static training memory per GPU?

\(112\text{ GB}\), because ZeRO-3 only reduces dynamic activation memory rather than model state
\(28\text{ GB}\), because only optimizer states are sharded while parameters and gradients remain fully replicated
\(1.75\text{ GB}\), because weights, gradients, and optimizer states are each partitioned equally across all 64 workers
\(0.25\text{ GB}\), because INT4 quantization eliminates floating-point representation entirely

An 8-GPU node can use four-step gradient accumulation to match the effective batch of 32 GPUs connected by 10 Gb/s Ethernet. Explain why the smaller allocation can cost less even when the larger allocation completes the fixed-sample workload sooner.
Order the memory sharding stages of data parallelism from least sharded (highest memory footprint) to deepest sharded (lowest memory footprint):


ZeRO-2 (shards optimizer states and gradients using ReduceScatter)
Standard DDP (full replication of parameters, gradients, and optimizer states)
ZeRO-3 / FSDP (shards optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters with layer-wise AllGather/ReduceScatter)
ZeRO-1 (shards optimizer states only, keeping parameters and gradients replicated)


If a model’s parameters, gradients, optimizer state, activations, and working buffers already fit comfortably within single-GPU memory with high compute utilization under standard DDP, what is the expected throughput impact of enabling ZeRO-3 / FSDP Full Sharding?

Throughput will increase linearly by \(N\times\) because sharding reduces per-GPU gradient memory
Throughput can decrease because FSDP introduces additional AllGather collectives before forward and backward passes and ReduceScatter on the critical path
Throughput will remain exactly identical because NCCL automatically hides all collective communication overhead
Throughput will double because parameter sharding eliminates the backward pass entirely

Why did modern distributed training frameworks replace centralized parameter servers with decentralized AllReduce collective topologies for dense synchronous training?

Parameter servers are restricted to CPU hosts and cannot interface with GPU accelerators
AllReduce eliminates all network traffic by updating weights locally without exchanging data

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
When doubling the number of GPUs yields only 1.5\(\times\) speedup for the same work, scaling efficiency is 75 percent. The ratio quantifies the shortfall but does not identify its cause; communication, synchronization, input delivery, and changed local kernel efficiency require separate examination. Understanding why scaling efficiency degrades and how convergence changes with parallelism also requires distinguishing hardware throughput from time to a target loss. The scaling metrics apply to every strategy; the convergence analysis that follows concerns data-parallel batch growth and stale updates. It supplies a batch-size constraint that tensor and pipeline configurations must also respect when they are combined with data parallelism.


Whether scaling from one device to many is worthwhile is measured by scaling efficiency, a fleet-level ratio. If a model trains in time \(\SingleDeviceRunTime\) on one device, ideal (linear) scaling would train it in time \(\SingleDeviceRunTime/\DeviceCount\) on \(\DeviceCount\) devices; communication overhead, pipeline bubbles, and load imbalance reduce the speedup. Equation 1 restates the ratio:
\[\ScalingEfficiency = \frac{\SingleDeviceRunTime}{\DeviceCount\times \MultiDeviceRunTime} \tag{1}\]
where \(\MultiDeviceRunTime\) is the training time on \(\DeviceCount\) devices. Measured per step of the same work, \(\SingleDeviceRunTime\) is the quantity the Fleet Law writes as \(\IronLawComputeTime\), the single-device compute time that its compute term divides by \(\DeviceCount\). An efficiency of 1.0 means perfect linear scaling; an efficiency of 0.5 means the run achieves only half the ideal speedup.

Definition 5.4: Scaling efficiency
Scaling efficiency \((\ScalingEfficiency)\) is the ratio of actual training throughput to ideal linear throughput when increasing the number of ML compute devices (\(\DeviceCount\)).

Significance: The ratio in equation 1 measures added devices against the specified baseline. At 0.50 efficiency, a 10,000-GPU run delivers the throughput that 5,000 perfectly scaled devices would, so half of the accelerator-hours buy no progress relative to ideal scaling. The equivalence is to an idealized baseline; a real 5,000-GPU run would have its own, typically higher, efficiency, and the loss is spread across every device as waiting rather than concentrated in idle ones.
Distinction: Unlike single-node efficiency, which captures local bottlenecks like \(\Bandwidth\), scaling efficiency measures how performance changes with device count. Communication time \((\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount))\) and synchronization contribute, but changing local kernel shapes or input delivery can also affect the ratio.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that scaling efficiency is constant. In reality, it depends on both device count and problem size. For a fixed model, the communication-to-compute ratio typically worsens as \(\DeviceCount\) increases (Amdahl’s Law). At a fixed \(\DeviceCount\), a smaller model or local batch leaves less computation per device to hide startup latency and coordination, so its efficiency falls sooner.



For data-parallel training of the 175B reference model, the per-step communication cost is dominated by the AllReduce of 350 GB of gradients, and how much of that exchange hides behind computation decides the efficiency.
The scaling efficiency depends critically on computation per communicated byte. At fixed tokens per update, increasing parameter count raises both transformer computation and gradient bytes roughly proportionally, so model size alone does not guarantee better scaling. Larger batches raise computation per optimizer step without changing gradient size; the catch is that large batches can harm convergence and so require learning-rate tuning and warmup schedules. Network bandwidth enters directly because doubling InfiniBand bandwidth halves the bandwidth term, but efficiency changes according to the full step-time denominator rather than in direct proportion. The network fabric is therefore a first-order determinant of cluster productivity, not a secondary concern. Every point of scaling efficiency it recovers is returned across the much larger accelerator investment, which is why fabric spending is judged by the efficiency it buys rather than by its own price.
These factors interact, so efficiency cannot be inferred from model size or GPU count alone. The following worked model fixes the parameter count, tokens per update, accelerator count, effective bandwidth, local compute efficiency before communication, and overlap before calculating one efficiency point. Changing any of those inputs requires recomputing the full step-time model.

Napkin Math 5.5: Scaling efficiency for a 175B modelSetup: A communication-only model for training a 175B model on a DGX H100 cluster with 400 Gb/s InfiniBand per GPU. Pure replicated data parallelism is a counterfactual baseline here: the calculation isolates gradient exchange but does not establish that the full training state fits on each device.

Compute per step (assuming batch size 2M tokens, 6 FLOPs per parameter per token): \(\TrainingStepOperations = 6 \times 175 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^6 \approx 2.1 \times 10^{18}\) FLOPs
Per-GPU compute time on 1,024 GPUs, each at 1,979 TFLOP/s peak in the 8-bit floating-point (FP8) format developed in section 5.8.9 (50 percent local compute efficiency before communication). The general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) run in FP8 while the gradients below still cross the wire in FP16, because the collective’s data type is chosen independently of the arithmetic’s: \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount \approx 2.1\) seconds
AllReduce time (for 350 GB of gradients using ring-AllReduce with overlap): \(\ExposedCommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) \approx 11.9\) seconds (raw ring transfer takes \(2 \times (N-1)/N \times 350 / 50\), about 14 seconds; the schedule could hide 75 percent of that transfer, but the available compute window caps hidden communication at 15 percent of raw transfer time)
Scaling efficiency: \(\ScalingEfficiency = \PerDeviceComputeTime/(\PerDeviceComputeTime+ \ExposedCommunicationTime)\), which is equation 1 with the per-device compute window \(\PerDeviceComputeTime= \IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) and the exposed term standing for \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime\). Here the numerator is 2.1 s and the complete denominator is 14 s, giving 15 percent. The exposed communication term already subtracts the hidden portion from the raw transfer time and includes collective synchronization; subtracting overlap again would double-count the same saving.

Systems insight: The low efficiency (15 percent) shows why naive data parallelism at this scale is insufficient. It is one operating point, fixed by 2M per update, 1,024 GPUs, and 15 percent overlap, not a universal threshold; another cluster size requires recomputing per-device compute time, collective cost, overlap, and topology. Hierarchy-aware systems recover much of the lost efficiency by combining data parallelism with tensor parallelism, which communicates over NVLink, and pipeline parallelism, which overlaps computation with communication.




The scaling efficiency analysis shows that the effective parallelism strategy is not determined by the model architecture alone but by the interaction between the model’s communication requirements and the infrastructure’s bandwidth hierarchy. Each combination of parallelism strategy and infrastructure topology produces a different scaling efficiency curve, and selecting the wrong combination can waste a significant fraction of the cluster’s capacity. The preceding napkin math showed pure data parallelism stalling near 15 percent efficiency at this scale; recovering that lost capacity means mapping each parallelism dimension onto the bandwidth tier that can carry its traffic. Section 5.10 works that combination through three concrete configurations and formalizes it as hierarchy-aware parallelism, once tensor and pipeline parallelism have been developed.
Selecting a parallelism mapping determines which devices exchange each tensor and when that tensor becomes ready. The resulting collective cost depends on payload size, group size, topology, and contention. Its exposed share also depends on the remaining compute window. Those dependencies explain why neither a fixed AllReduce overhead percentage nor a mandatory combination of parallelism axes predicts performance across workloads.
AllReduce complexity depends on latency \((\MessageStartupLatency)\) and bandwidth \((\LinkBandwidth)\). In the ring volume formula, \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) describes the fraction of the buffer transferred per worker in each phase, not achieved link utilization. Tree-based approaches reduce communication depth to \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) steps, making them attractive for small messages dominated by startup latency. Large gradient buffers emphasize sustained bandwidth instead. Message size, topology, and contention therefore determine which algorithm is faster; the next chapter develops those cost models.


↪ The message size at which ring AllReduce overtakes tree AllReduce, derived from the latency and bandwidth terms of each algorithm, is developed in The algorithm crossover point.
Interconnect selection determines whether large-scale deployments remain compute-bound or collapse into communication-bound regimes, and the bandwidth requirements for efficient distributed training are substantial, particularly for transformer models. BERT-Base (110M parameters) requires approximately 440 MB of gradient synchronization per iteration in FP32, while BERT-Large (340M parameters) requires approximately 1.4 GB. A ring AllReduce across 64 GPUs moves nearly twice the gradient bytes through each GPU’s link, so finishing BERT-Large synchronization within 50 ms requires roughly 54 GB/s of sustained per-GPU bandwidth, and BERT-Base about a third of that. For 175B-parameter language models, exact bandwidth requirements depend on the 3D-parallel configuration, gradient accumulation, overlap, and interconnect topology rather than a single universal number.
Synchronization frequency presents a trade-off between communication efficiency and convergence behavior. Accumulating gradients for 4 microsteps reduces synchronization frequency by 75 percent, but the realized step-time reduction depends on the compute/communication mix and how much communication can overlap with backpropagation. In standard implementations, gradient accumulation reuses one resident gradient buffer and accumulates in place; memory pressure comes from keeping that buffer resident and from any larger local batch or activation choices, not from storing 4 independent gradient tensors. Asynchronous methods remove the global update barrier while retaining communication costs, and introduce staleness that can degrade convergence for large learning rates.




An Amdahl-style model separates work that scales with device count from a fixed residual cost. Step time on \(\DeviceCount\) devices then exceeds \(\SingleDeviceRunTime / \DeviceCount\) because the residual does not shrink with the compute share. Amdahl's Law at fleet scale develops this model at fleet scale. Its speedup ceiling assumes that the residual remains a fixed fraction \(\SerialFraction\) of the single-device baseline.
That baseline fraction is not the synchronization share a profiler reports for a distributed step, because the compute share has been divided by \(\DeviceCount\) while the residual has not. A residual of 1 percent of the single-device step occupies about 84 percent of each step on 512 GPUs. Reading the observed share as \(\SerialFraction\) would therefore overstate the residual many times over and predict a far lower speedup ceiling than the model implies.
Figure 8 illustrates this scaling tax up to 512 GPUs on log-log axes, complementing the scaling efficiency bound (principle \(\ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}\)). In this illustrative fixed-residual model, a small baseline fraction (\(\SerialFraction= 0.1\%\)) stays closer to ideal scaling than a larger fraction (\(\SerialFraction= 1\%\)). A residual equal to a tenth of baseline time (\(\SerialFraction= 0.10\)) limits asymptotic speedup to \(1/\SerialFraction= 10\times\). Actual collective and coordination costs can change with worker count, so predicting a training run requires the more explicit Fleet Law below.














Figure 8: The scaling tax: Effective speedup \(\DeviceCount/(1+(\DeviceCount-1)\SerialFraction)\) against GPU count on log-log axes, for illustrative fixed residual fractions \(\SerialFraction\) of baseline step time. Ideal scaling (dashed) is linear. Each curve bends away from it and flattens near \(1/\SerialFraction\): at 512 GPUs, \(\SerialFraction\) = 0.1 percent still delivers about two-thirds of ideal speedup, 1 percent about one-sixth, and 10 percent under 10\(\times\) in total. Darker curves carry larger \(\SerialFraction\).



Predicting a run requires returning to the Fleet Law (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)) from section 5.2. As the fleet-scale counterpart of the single-machine iron law, it separates compute, communication, and coordination into additive terms, labeled here with their C³ names:
\[ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \underbrace{\frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount}}_{\text{Compute Term}} + \underbrace{\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)}_{\text{Communication Term}} + \underbrace{\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)}_{\text{Coordination Term}} - \OverlappedTime \]
In this decomposition, the compute term \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) captures the batch’s compute time after ideal partitioning across \(\DeviceCount\) devices. The communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) represents fabric transfer time, analogous to the iron law’s data-movement ratio \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\). For a large-message Ring AllReduce, its bandwidth contribution is \(\frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount} \frac{\DataVolume}{\LinkBandwidth}\), where \(\DataVolume\) is the payload being reduced (the gradient bytes \(\GradientPayload\) under data parallelism, or a shard of model state under sharding) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is sustained per-link bandwidth; this expression omits per-message startup latency. The coordination term \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) accounts for exposed ordering and straggler delays not already included in communication time. Finally, \(\OverlappedTime\) subtracts communication hidden behind computation. Each wait must enter the accounting once.


↪ The single-machine iron law and its data-movement term are developed in Iron Law Mapping.
The Fleet Law leads to the scaling efficiency metric for fixed global work. Substituting its step time for \(\MultiDeviceRunTime\) in equation 1, with \(\IronLawComputeTime\) standing for \(\SingleDeviceRunTime\) per step as noted there, gives:
\[ \ScalingEfficiency = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount\times \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)} = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{\DeviceCount(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime)}{\IronLawComputeTime}} \]
This is the scaling efficiency bound (principle \(\ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}\)): perfect linear scaling \((\ScalingEfficiency = 1.0)\) is a theoretical limit, not a practical target. Real systems fall short of it by an amount that depends on the configuration and grows with \(\DeviceCount\). The 175B data-parallel example above reached only 15 percent, and the hybrid layouts later in the chapter recover much of that loss without reaching 1.0. The gap between \(\ScalingEfficiency = 1.0\) and the achieved efficiency is the scaling tax, paid in communication and coordination as the price of distributed execution.
The equation reveals the scaling wall: as \(\DeviceCount\) increases, the compute term \((\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\) shrinks, but the communication and synchronization terms can remain constant or grow. Eventually, the denominator is dominated by overhead, driving efficiency toward zero. Beyond wall-clock time, this communication overhead imposes an energy tax that scales with physical distance between devices.



Communication energy climbs from HBM out to the network.

Systems Perspective 5.2: The energy tax of scaleDistributed training is a race against energy as much as against time. Within one GPU, moving a bit from HBM to the cores costs a few picojoules, roughly 2–5 pJ/bit; Energy cost of data movement expresses the same cost per access, about 64 pJ for one 16-bit operand. Moving that same bit across an NVLink interconnect costs 5–10 pJ/bit. Moving it across an InfiniBand network through switches costs 20–50 pJ/bit.
At the scale of 10,000 GPUs, the multiplication by aggregate bandwidth is what changes the engineering problem. A full H100 NVLink envelope is roughly 9 PB/s across the cluster; at 7.5 pJ/bit, that movement represents about 540 kW before cooling and switch overhead. The aggregate NDR InfiniBand envelope is smaller (500 TB/s), but at 35 pJ/bit it still represents about 140 kW. Communication-computation overlap is therefore necessary for wall-clock efficiency, but avoiding unnecessary movement is the direct way to reduce the power term itself.


As the device count grows for a fixed workload, the balance can move from a linear scaling regime toward a communication-bound regime. The transition has no universal GPU count: it depends on compute per device, message sizes, topology, and overlap. Coordination overhead becomes consequential when its exposed time is no longer small relative to useful computation. Measurements at the intended workload and placement must establish the efficiency curve.



More GPUs shrink each step’s compute, not its communication.
Hardware selection critically impacts these scaling characteristics. NVIDIA DGX A100 systems, one generation older than the reference H100 nodes, provide 300 GB/s of NVLink bandwidth per GPU in each direction, with aggregate NVSwitch bandwidth at the system level, enabling high parallel efficiency inside an 8-GPU node. Multi-node scaling requires a network fabric with enough bisection bandwidth; EDR-class 100 Gb/s links, the InfiniBand generation before HDR, can support smaller multi-node jobs, while HDR-class 200 Gb/s links can support larger clusters when topology, placement, and overlap are well matched.
The efficiency metrics directly influence the choice of parallelism strategy. Data parallelism works well in the linear scaling regime but becomes communication bound at scale. The model-parallel strategies developed after this section replace part of that gradient traffic with other costs, and the same efficiency equation will price each of them once its mechanism is in place.
Hardware efficiency metrics govern throughput, but convergence theory determines whether distributed training reaches the same solution quality as single-device training. Parallelism affects optimization convergence in three ways: convergence rate changes with batch size, adding workers yields diminishing returns beyond the critical batch size, and learning-rate schedules must be revalidated when the global batch changes.



The fundamental convergence result for distributed SGD explains what synchronous averaging preserves. Informally, when the gradient cannot change abruptly as parameters move and averaging over more workers reduces the noise in each gradient estimate, synchronous SGD makes steady progress toward parameters where the gradient is small. Formally, let \(\LossFunction\) be lower bounded by \(\LossLowerBound\) and have \(\SmoothnessConstant\)-Lipschitz gradients, so the smoothness constant limits how sharply the gradient can change as parameters move. Each worker computes gradients from \(\LocalBatchSize\) independent samples. At update \(\OptimizerStepIndex\), the aggregated estimator \(\MinibatchGradient_t\), the average of the \(\DeviceCount\) workers’ local gradients, is unbiased, and its conditional variance satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\|\MinibatchGradient_t-\nabla\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_t)\|^2\mid\ModelParameters_t]\leq\SampleGradientStandardDeviation^2/(\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize)\). These assumptions bound progress toward a small gradient norm, not convergence to a global minimizer or a particular validation accuracy.

Theorem 5.1: Convergence rate for distributed SGDFor the update \(\ModelParameters_{t+1}=\ModelParameters_t-\LearningRate\MinibatchGradient_t\) with constant step size \(0<\LearningRate\leq 1/\SmoothnessConstant\), after \(\OptimizerUpdateCount\) synchronized updates,
\[
\frac{1}{\OptimizerUpdateCount}\sum_{t=0}^{\OptimizerUpdateCount-1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_t)\|^2\right]
\leq
\underbrace{\frac{2\bigl(\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_0)-\LossLowerBound\bigr)}{\LearningRate \OptimizerUpdateCount}}_{\text{optimization term}}
+
\underbrace{\frac{\LearningRate \SmoothnessConstant\SampleGradientStandardDeviation^2}{\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize}}_{\text{stochastic-variance term}}.
\]
Choosing \(\LearningRate=\min\!\left\{1/\SmoothnessConstant,\sqrt{2(\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_0)-\LossLowerBound)\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize/(\SmoothnessConstant\SampleGradientStandardDeviation^2\OptimizerUpdateCount)}\right\}\) balances the two terms. Before the smoothness cap becomes active, the stochastic contribution scales as \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize \OptimizerUpdateCount})\).


The theorem isolates the benefit that follows from the assumptions. With equal local batch size \(\LocalBatchSize\), synchronous data-parallel SGD computes the same minibatch estimator as one worker using batch size \(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) for that update, and the estimator variance decreases as \(1/(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize)\). It does not say that every increase in batch size proportionally reduces time to a target loss; learning-rate limits and critical-batch-size effects still apply. This distinction is the statistical efficiency of distributed training, separate from hardware efficiency.
The theorem assumes perfect synchronization (BSP). When workers proceed at different rates or use stale gradients, convergence guarantees degrade as staleness increases.



The operational guarantees of BSP, SSP, and ASP established in section 5.7.1.4 have convergence consequences, but there is no universal additive staleness penalty independent of the objective, step-size schedule, worker count, and delay model. The staleness parameter \(\GradientStaleness\) quantifies how many updates occur between computing and applying a gradient, tying throughput to solution quality (Ho et al. 2013; Dutta et al. 2018).

Definition 5.5: Gradient staleness
Gradient staleness (\(\GradientStaleness\)) is the number of parameter updates that occur between the time a gradient is computed and the time it is applied to the global model state.

Significance: It represents the synchronization error in distributed optimization. Increasing \(\GradientStaleness\) can improve throughput by reducing barrier waits \((\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount))\), but it typically degrades the rate of convergence, requiring more optimizer steps, and therefore more FLOPs, to reach the same accuracy.
Distinction: Unlike network latency, which is a physical delay, staleness is an algorithmic offset that arises from the choice of synchronization protocol (e.g., ASP, SSP).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that staleness is “always bad.” In reality, it is a throughput-convergence trade-off: for some large-scale workloads, allowing bounded staleness is one practical way to keep thousands of GPUs in use.



The convergence behavior differs across these models in ways that directly affect training cost and solution quality. In BSP (\(\GradientStaleness=0\)), all workers compute on the same parameter version and aggregate before updating. Under the assumptions of theorem 5.1, the synchronized estimator inherits the \(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) minibatch guarantee.
SSP (\(\GradientStaleness\leq \StalenessBound\)) allows workers to proceed up to \(\StalenessBound\) iterations ahead of the slowest worker. Ho et al. (2013) bound the average regret of their SSP update sequence, the per-update gap between the loss its iterates incur and the loss of the best fixed parameters chosen in hindsight, at \(\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{(\StalenessBound+1)\DeviceCount/\OptimizerUpdateCount})\) for \(\DeviceCount\) workers and \(\OptimizerUpdateCount\) updates. The bound assumes convex Lipschitz component functions, a bounded domain, and a decreasing step size. It makes the staleness dependence explicit, since the bound grows with \(\StalenessBound\), but it measures a different quantity from the gradient-norm bound of theorem 5.1, which covers nonconvex objectives, so the two rates cannot be compared directly.

Asynchronous SGD imposes no protocol-wide finite delay bound. Removing the barrier can improve update throughput, but a convergence rate requires additional assumptions about realized delays, the objective, and the step-size schedule. Dutta et al. (2018) analyze this as an error-runtime trade-off in which worker speed and gradient staleness jointly determine whether accepting a delayed update helps. Therefore neither a fixed square-of-average-delay penalty nor the complete loss of \(\DeviceCount\)-worker variance reduction follows from asynchronous execution alone.
