title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
The 175B running example has now exhausted each family on its own. Data parallelism with ZeRO-3 makes the state fit, but it regathers every layer’s parameters across the data-parallel fabric on every step. On the reference cluster that regather is the 1.1 TB per worker per step priced in section 5.9, roughly 21 seconds on one NDR InfiniBand port against a compute window of about 2.1 seconds, so communication would take about 10× as long as the computation it serves. Tensor parallelism confined to one 8-GPU node, meanwhile, still leaves several hundred gigabytes of training state per device. The preceding strategies address different constraints and need not be used in isolation. Section 5.7 established how replication and state sharding distribute examples and storage; section 5.9 showed how partitioned operations and pipeline stages distribute computation. Hybrid design chooses the dimensions needed to satisfy memory, communication, and global-batch constraints together.
Hybrid parallelism applies both families orthogonally: model parallelism splits the architecture to fit available memory, while data parallelism scales throughput across multiple model replicas. Training a 175B parameter language model on a dataset of 300 billion tokens demonstrates this approach in practice. The neural network layers distribute across multiple GPUs through model parallelism, while data parallelism enables different GPU groups to process separate batches. This dual strategy addresses both memory constraints from model size and computational demands from dataset scale simultaneously, and it is precisely this combination that defines Archetype A training at large-model scale.

Lighthouse 5.2: Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Physics of 3D parallelismArchetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) illustrates the motivation for hybrid parallelism. Parameter count \((\Parameters)\) must first be converted to a complete memory budget before comparison with device capacity \((\DeviceMemoryCapacity)\), while dataset size \((\DatasetSize)\) and the deadline determine the throughput target. Tensor parallelism partitions layer computations within a suitable communication domain; pipeline parallelism assigns consecutive layers to stages; and data parallelism distributes examples from \(\DatasetSize\) across replicas. A design combines the dimensions that address its constraints; efficient execution does not require all three in every case.


To see why the combination matters, consider three parallelism configurations for training the 175B model on a 1,024-GPU cluster organized as 128 nodes of 8 GPUs each. The progression from pure data parallelism through tensor and pipeline parallelism makes the efficiency gain concrete.
Configuration A: Pure Data Parallelism (DP-1024) is a communication counterfactual rather than a feasible placement for this model. The FP16 weights alone occupy 350 GB, so an A100 or H100 cannot replicate them; sharding only optimizer states does not change that fact. If replication were possible, all 1,024 ranks would form one data-parallel group, and each rank would participate in an AllReduce of the 350 GB gradient tensor across the InfiniBand fabric. The 15 percent calculation in section 5.8 isolates that communication cost.
Configuration B: TP-8, DP-128. Within each of 128 model replicas, 8 GPUs use tensor parallelism over NVLink. The corresponding tensor shard from every replica forms one 128-rank data-parallel group, so the layout contains 8 such groups. Each rank AllReduces its 1/8 gradient shard, 43.75 GB rather than 350 GB, and TP communication remains within the fast NVLink domain. This is a communication comparison only. At 16 bytes per parameter each GPU would still hold about 350 GB of training state, so the layout also needs optimizer and gradient sharding across its data-parallel group before it fits. The inter-node AllReduce time drops from 14 seconds to approximately 1.75 seconds. If the compute time is still 2.1 seconds, the unoverlapped efficiency improves to about 54.5 percent. The smaller transfer also fits inside the compute window, so the same optimistic schedule assumed for the data-parallel baseline can now hide its full 75 percent of the transfer behind backward computation, which lifts efficiency to about 83 percent.
Configuration C: TP-8, PP-4, DP-32. Each of 32 model replicas uses 8-way tensor parallelism within a stage and 4 pipeline stages across nodes. For each of the 8 \(\times\) 4 tensor-and-pipeline shard positions, the corresponding ranks from all replicas form one 32-rank data-parallel group. Each rank therefore AllReduces a \(350/(8\times4)\approx10.94\) GB gradient shard. Pipeline communication forwards activations between stages and has lower volume than a full-model AllReduce. The trade-off is the pipeline bubble: at the beginning and end of each training step, some pipeline stages are idle while waiting for activations from earlier stages or gradients from later stages. The bubble fraction is approximately \((\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\MicrobatchCount+\PipelineParallelDegree-1)\), so with 4 pipeline stages and 32 microbatches per training step, the bubble wastes roughly 9 percent of compute (\(3/35 \approx 8.6\%\)). The smaller shard takes about 0.44 seconds to AllReduce, and under the same overlap model as configuration B most of it hides behind backward computation. Charging the bubble against the compute window and adding the remaining exposed transfer gives a predicted efficiency of about 87 percent, a few points above configuration B’s 83 percent. The pipeline cuts the data-parallel traffic by another factor of 4, and that saving slightly outweighs the bubble it introduces. Configuration C does not fit memory by itself either. Its training state is about 87.5 GB per GPU, above the 80 GB of an H100. Adding ZeRO-1 across its 32-rank data-parallel group closes that gap. Each GPU then keeps its tensor-and-pipeline slice of weights and gradients but only a 1/32 share of that slice’s optimizer state, about 24 GB in all, which leaves most of the HBM for activations and buffers. ZeRO-1 matches plain DDP’s ideal data-parallel byte volume at matching communication widths (table 3), but equal bytes do not preserve the overlap schedule. Gradient reduction to owners must precede their optimizer updates, and the updated-parameter AllGather follows those updates. The predicted efficiency remains conditional on that schedule achieving the modeled exposed communication time. TP-8, PP-4, DP-32 with ZeRO-1 passes this simplified persistent-state memory budget; its reduction, update, and parameter-gather readiness must still be priced before accepting the throughput prediction.
Within this comparison’s communication model, the configuration that places frequent tensor-parallel exchanges in the fast NVLink domain, pipelines across nodes, and leaves only small data-parallel gradient shards for InfiniBand has the best predicted efficiency. Peak memory, kernel shape, and scheduling still need verification before that prediction becomes a runnable design. The infrastructure hierarchy dictates the parallelism hierarchy. Here, hierarchy-aware parallelism means matching exchange requirements to measured communication domains rather than choosing each degree independently.

Definition 5.12: Hierarchy-aware parallelism
Hierarchy-aware parallelism is the strategy of mapping different parallel execution modes to the physical bandwidth tiers of the cluster.

Significance: It places high-frequency synchronization (for example, tensor parallelism) on fast links such as NVLink, while assigning lower-frequency exchanges (for example, data parallelism) to slower tiers when their transfers fit the schedule. This alignment can improve scaling efficiency \((\ScalingEfficiency)\) by reducing exposed communication time \((\CommunicationTime)\) and latency \((\Latency)\); the gain depends on readiness, contention, and available overlap.
Distinction: Unlike uniform parallelism, which treats all node-to-node links as equal, hierarchy-aware strategies respect the bandwidth cliffs between die, node, and rack boundaries.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that any model can be sharded across any number of nodes. In reality, if the hierarchy mapping is wrong (for example, sharding a large tensor across a slow inter-rack link), the communication time will dwarf the compute time, making the scale-out useless.



The dependence runs both ways: a parallelism configuration also determines which traffic the fabric must carry. In the TP-8, PP-4, DP-32 layout, tensor reductions stay within each fast local domain, pipeline traffic crosses neighboring stages, and data-parallel groups synchronize corresponding shards across replicas. Rail-optimized and hierarchical fabrics can exploit that structure, but a workload mix that adds expert All-to-All traffic changes the global bandwidth requirement. Infrastructure planning must therefore evaluate the anticipated communication groups together rather than optimizing the fabric for a single layout.


↩︎ Rail-optimized fabrics, which cable each GPU slot position to its own rail switch, are established in Rail-optimized topology.


The following layout trains a 175B-parameter model using 3D parallelism, the coordinated composition of data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism introduced with figure 2, across thousands of devices. This approach composes the strategies geometrically to match the physical topology of the hardware. The example traces their interactions; parameter count alone does not require all three dimensions.
Consider a training fleet configured with tensor parallelism (TP) of 8 GPUs, pipeline parallelism (PP) of 16, and data parallelism (DP) of 128. This configuration uses 16,384 GPUs (8 GPUs \(\times\) 16 \(\times\) 128) organized into a hierarchy of bandwidth domains, sixteen times the 1,024-GPU reference cluster so that every level of the hierarchy is exercised.
The training step begins at the data-parallel level. Each of the 128 model replicas receives a distinct slice of the global batch. Within each replica, the model is split across 16 pipeline stages (nodes), with microbatches flowing sequentially from the embedding layer on Node 0 to the loss calculation on Node 15. At the finest granularity, within each node, the 8 GPUs fuse into a single “super-accelerator” via TP. The transformer matrix multiplications are split across these devices; column- and row-parallel pairs retain local intermediate shards and exchange partial results at the reduction points already derived. For a 175B-scale hidden dimension, the activation payload is roughly 201.3 MB; the resulting tensor-parallel traffic is about 4.2 GB per pipeline stage per microbatch in the forward pass, or 8.5 GB including the backward pass. Across the full 96-layer replica, the forward tensor-parallel traffic is about 67.6 GB. This traffic is the highest-intensity in the system, but its exposed latency can remain small relative to compute because the chips communicate over 300 GB/s–450 GB/s of local bandwidth per direction.
The backward pass exposes dependencies between parallelism dimensions. Nodes exchange activation gradients point-to-point, roughly 201.3 MB per microbatch per stage boundary in this example. A smaller payload still stalls a stage if it arrives after the stage needs it. Data-parallel synchronization creates another dependency: although full-model gradients occupy about 350 GB, each data-parallel group exchanges only the corresponding tensor- and pipeline-parallel parameter shard. Gradient bucketing groups ready gradients as backward computation proceeds. Which exchange limits the step depends on its readiness, service time, and overlap; data parallelism is not necessarily the final bottleneck.
The architectural imperative is bandwidth matching: each exchange’s startup and transfer time must fit its available compute or overlap interval. In this mapping, frequent TP exchanges use the NVLink domain (300 GB/s per direction or higher), while PP transfers cross nodes and DP reductions overlap backward computation. Accumulation can enlarge the compute interval between DP synchronizations, subject to the global-batch constraint. An infeasible mapping leaves part or all of the 16,384 GPUs fleet waiting. Comparing service time with the schedule completes the feasibility check introduced in section 5.6.



Applying this bandwidth-matching principle to physical infrastructure transforms cluster design into a placement problem: each parallelism dimension must sit on the network tier that can tolerate its traffic. Tensor parallelism is the most latency-sensitive because it launches frequent AllReduce operations inside transformer blocks, so it favors the fast NVLink domain, intra-node in this example, at 300 GB/s–450 GB/s per direction. Pipeline parallelism moves activation tensors only at stage boundaries, so it can span nearby nodes over InfiniBand (50 GB/s–100 GB/s). Data parallelism produces the largest payload, the gradient synchronization, but it occurs once per step and can be overlapped with backward computation. Memory capacity per device (80 GB–80 GB) sets the hard limit for every placement.
For the 3D training loop’s layout on 16,384 GPUs, built from 8-GPU NVLink nodes, this reasoning leads to a concrete placement. Fix tensor parallelism at \(\TensorParallelDegree=8\) so the bandwidth-heavy matrix-multiplication collectives stay within one 8-GPU node. Map pipeline parallelism across nodes in the same high-bandwidth rack or island, here \(\PipelineParallelDegree=16\), with \(\PipelineParallelDegree=8\) as the alternative when the per-device memory budget allows. Use data parallelism for the remaining scale-out dimension across pods. The result is not a generic rule but a consequence of matching each traffic pattern to the cheapest fabric tier that can carry it.
With the placement fixed, the next question is whether the static model state fits inside each accelerator’s HBM budget.
The memory budget for a 175B model must include every persistent training component. Under the mixed-precision Adam convention used here, each parameter has FP16 weights and gradients, an FP32 master weight, and two FP32 optimizer moments, totaling 16 bytes before activations and workspaces. With tensor parallelism degree 8 alone, these components occupy 350 GB per device, exceeding H100-class capacity. Adding 16 pipeline stages spreads that state across the product of the two degrees, yielding 21.9 GB per device under even partitioning. A budget that counts only weights and optimizer moments, about 13.7 GB per device here, understates this total. Activation peaks, layer imbalance, and communication workspaces must fit in the remaining memory before this configuration is feasible.
Once the configuration fits in memory, the same layout has to satisfy the communication hierarchy that motivated it. Each parallelism dimension imposes a distinct traffic profile on the network. Tensor parallelism is the most chatty, requiring two AllReduce operations for every transformer block (one for the attention projection, one for the MLP) in both the forward and backward passes. These repeated messages expose both collective startup latency and payload-transfer time; their placement requires the fast communication domain used by the tensor-parallel group. Pipeline parallelism, in contrast, involves point-to-point transfers of activation tensors (size \(\MicrobatchSize \times \SequenceLength\times \HiddenDimension\)) only at the boundaries of the pipeline stages. While these messages are moderate in size, they occur less frequently, making them manageable over standard InfiniBand links. Data parallelism synchronizes matching tensor-and-pipeline shards across replicas. The full gradient buffer is 350 GB, but each data-parallel group reduces only its corresponding shard; no rank in this hybrid layout AllReduces the full buffer. Each shard is synchronized once per global batch update. Gradient bucketing can overlap this transmission with independent backward computation once each bucket is ready. The exposed cost depends on both available fabric bandwidth and the remaining computation window before the optimizer needs the reduced shard.
The last cost is not bandwidth but scheduling: a pipelined model is only efficient when enough microbatches are in flight to keep all stages busy. This remaining cost is the pipeline bubble developed in section 5.9.2.2. Applying its bubble fraction \(\frac{\PipelineParallelDegree-1}{\MicrobatchCount+ \PipelineParallelDegree - 1}\) to this hybrid layout, \(\PipelineParallelDegree=16\) stages with \(\MicrobatchCount=32\) microbatches waste \(\frac{15}{47} \approx 31.9\%\) of theoretical compute capacity, nearly one-third, against roughly 9 percent for configuration C’s 4 stages at the same microbatch count. The deeper pipeline is chosen at this scale for two reasons. Sixteen stages spread the full training state to about 21.9 GB per device without optimizer sharding. Filling 16,384 GPUs with configuration C’s 32-GPU replicas would instead need four times as many data-parallel replicas, which multiplies the global batch \(\DataParallelDegree \times \MicrobatchCount\times \MicrobatchSize\) by four at the same per-replica schedule. The shallow pipeline spends global batch; the deep one spends bubble. The 1F1B scheduling that reclaims activation memory, and the larger microbatch counts it makes practical, drive the bubble fraction down asymptotically, but every added microbatch also enlarges the global batch, so the bubble target must be reconciled with the critical-batch constraint from section 5.8.6.



The Blackwell reference illustrates how a wider fast communication domain changes 3D parallelism choices. NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s of bidirectional bandwidth per GPU, twice the Hopper reference’s capacity. Higher bandwidth reduces the transfer term for a fixed payload; it does not by itself reduce message startup latency. Larger tensor-parallel (\(\TensorParallelDegree\)) groups, such as \(\TensorParallelDegree=\) 16 or \(\TensorParallelDegree=\) 32 across nodes, remain subject to topology and local-kernel efficiency. Blackwell’s FP4 support adds a separate numerical choice whose training use depends on the validated recipe and software stack.
Because a wider fast domain matters most for a model larger than the 175B reference, consider a 1 trillion-parameter model. One candidate uses \(\TensorParallelDegree=\) 16 across two 8-GPU nodes joined by NVLink Switch and \(\PipelineParallelDegree=\) 8. Relative to the Hopper reference’s \(\TensorParallelDegree=8\) and \(\PipelineParallelDegree=16\), this preserves the model-partition product while halving stage count. The bubble must be recomputed from the new stage and microbatch counts rather than assumed to halve. The 10 TB/s internal link joins Blackwell’s two dies behind one logical GPU; those dies are not separate software tensor-parallel ranks. The general lesson is that improving local bandwidth shifts pressure outward. Once intra-node exchanges bind less, the inter-node fabric that carries pipeline and data-parallel traffic, rail-optimized topology, and expert All-to-All service become the terms to evaluate, so the full placement still needs checking against the next tier.
The same placement constraints can be made operational through design-space search.

Example 5.2: Automated design space searchScenario: An engineering team schedules a 175B-parameter model across 8,192 H100 GPUs (80 GB HBM each), eight times the 1,024-GPU reference cluster so that the pipeline and data-parallel degrees both have room to vary, navigating the multi-dimensional 3D-parallelism search space (TP \(\times\) PP \(\times\) DP).
Diagnosis: Candidate configurations must fit within 80 GB HBM and satisfy the modeled communication budget. The search evaluates TP \(\times\) PP \(\times\) DP factorizations and selects TP=8 GPUs, PP=8, and DP=128 as the best predicted MFU among configurations feasible under its assumptions. That result is a candidate for measurement, not proof of the best attainable runtime.
Systems lesson: This search favors TP=8 GPUs within the reference topology’s fast domain and PP=8, with 36.4 percent projected MFU. The result balances memory, local computation, transfers, and pipeline idle time within the model. A different topology, microbatch schedule, or kernel efficiency can change the preferred factorization.


Adjusting any one dimension shifts the pressure onto the other two, making the factorization TP \(\times\) PP \(\times\) DP a tightly coupled system rather than three independent knobs.

Checkpoint 5.4: Hybrid 3D parallelism
Verify your understanding of how parallelism strategies combine:

Dimension roles: identify which dimension in a TP=8, PP=16, DP=128 configuration partitions operations within each layer inside one node.
Bubble vs. depth: determine how moving from PP=16 to PP=8 changes the pipeline bubble fraction.
DP vs. PP: explain the trade-off, with the budget fixed at that layout’s 16,384 GPUs, between increasing DP (data parallelism) and increasing PP (pipeline parallelism).
Latency sensitivity: identify which dimension, TP, PP, or DP, is most sensitive to inter-node latency.



A projected MFU needs comparison with measured execution. Figure 15 places reported MFU from 2020–2024 systems against an illustrative 50 percent reference line. GPT-3’s 21 percent and PaLM’s 46 percent describe different hardware and workload configurations; their difference does not isolate the effect of parallelism or overlap. Llama 3’s reported result at 16,384 H100 GPUs (41 percent) is lower than at 8,192 GPUs (43 percent). Interpreting that change requires the batch, configuration, precision convention, and measurement window alongside device count.














Figure 15: The MFU progression: Model FLOPs Utilization across published training systems, ordered chronologically. Reported MFU rises from 21 percent (GPT-3, 2020) to 46 percent (PaLM, 2022), with later illustrated runs near 40–45 percent. These systems differ in hardware and workload, so the comparison does not isolate the effect of parallelism or overlap. The Llama 3 data points show lower reported MFU at the larger scale: MFU drops from 43 percent at 8,192 GPUs to 41 percent at 16,384 GPUs. Interpreting the difference requires the batch, execution configuration, and measurement convention. Data sources: Chowdhery et al. (2022), Dubey et al. (2024).


Chowdhery, Aakanksha, Sharan Narang, Jacob Devlin, Maarten Bosma, Gaurav Mishra, Adam Roberts, Paul Barham, et al. 2022. “PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2204.02311.

Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.


The three configurations and the worked layout tell one story. Pure data parallelism moves the full 350 GB gradient over the slowest tier and reaches only 15 percent scaling efficiency. Keeping tensor parallelism inside the NVLink domain cuts each rank’s share of that traffic by the tensor-parallel degree, and pipeline stages cut it again at the price of a bubble. Communication alone does not make a layout feasible, however. Each layout must also hold the full training state, which is why configurations B and C still need optimizer sharding and why the worked layout adds pipeline depth until the persistent state falls to about 21.9 GB per device. Hybrid parallelism is therefore the joint solution of a memory constraint, a bandwidth hierarchy, and a batch-size limit, and every axis added to satisfy one of them tightens another. Alignment training tests that joint solution hardest, because it asks one fleet to host several models with different memory and compute profiles at the same time.

Self-Check: Question

In a 3D parallelism layout (\(N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t\)), what hardware-matching principle dictates mapping tensor parallelism intra-node while pipeline parallelism spans inter-node links?

Pipeline parallelism requires more memory bandwidth than NVLink can provide, forcing it onto InfiniBand
Tensor parallelism requires only point-to-point transfers, making it insensitive to link latency
Hierarchy-aware parallelism maps frequent TP exchanges to the fastest local fabric and PP boundary transfers to slower inter-node links.
Data parallelism cannot execute across nodes that use tensor parallelism internally

A 175B-parameter model uses mixed-precision Adam with 2-byte weights, 2-byte gradients, a 4-byte master copy, and two 4-byte moments per parameter. With tensor degree \(t=8\) and pipeline degree \(p=16\), calculate the ideally balanced static memory per GPU before data-parallel state sharding, and explain why tensor parallelism alone cannot fit this state on 80 GB GPUs.
For one rank in a balanced 3D layout with eight transformer layers per pipeline stage, 32 microbatches per update, two tensor-parallel reductions per layer in each pass, and one unbucketed data-parallel reduction after accumulation, order these communication patterns by invocation count per update, highest to lowest:


Data-parallel gradient reduction
Tensor-parallel reductions
Pipeline stage-boundary transfers


In a 16,384-GPU cluster configured with \(\text{TP}=8\), \(\text{PP}=16\), and \(\text{DP}=128\), how many GPUs participate in each individual data-parallel AllReduce communicator group?

\(16{,}384\text{ GPUs}\), because all accelerators in the cluster must synchronize in a single global collective
\(128\text{ GPUs}\), because each rank communicates only with its corresponding tensor-and-pipeline shard position across the 128 model replicas
\(8\text{ GPUs}\), matching the tensor-parallel degree within each local node
\(16\text{ GPUs}\), matching the pipeline stage depth across the cluster spine

True or False: A uniform fat-tree network topology providing equal bisection bandwidth between all node pairs is always more cost-effective than a rail-optimized topology when training large language models with hierarchy-aware 3D parallelism.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) extends the placement problem beyond one training model. The proximal policy optimization (PPO) example developed here generates responses, scores them with a preference-trained reward model, constrains policy drift against a reference, and uses value estimates to guide updates. These roles have different memory and compute requirements and need not run simultaneously. Direct preference optimization (DPO) provides a useful comparison because its standard offline form removes online generation and separate reward and value models. The engineering question is how the chosen learning procedure determines which state and work must coexist on the fleet.


The single-model pretraining baseline becomes a multi-role loop in PPO (Schulman et al. 2017), as used in InstructGPT-style systems (Ouyang et al. 2022). Table 7 separates policy, reference, reward, and value roles by execution mode and memory burden. In figure 16, the policy \(\Policy\) generates responses for scoring by the frozen reference and reward models and evaluation by the value model \(\CriticModel\). The penalized reward (\(\ResponseReward- \KlPenaltyCoefficient\,\text{KL}\)) subtracts a Kullback–Leibler divergence penalty, weighted by a coefficient \(\KlPenaltyCoefficient\) unrelated to link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), to discourage drift from the reference. Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) combines rewards and value estimates to judge how much better a response was than expected. Those estimates guide policy updates; the value model learns to predict returns, the cumulative discounted reward that follows each generated token. Reference and reward models remain forward-only in this loop, and shared-backbone implementations can combine roles without changing their distinct responsibilities.

Schulman, John, Filip Wolski, Prafulla Dhariwal, Alec Radford, and Oleg Klimov. 2017. “Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1707.06347, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1707.06347.

Ouyang, L., J. Wu, X. Jiang, D. Almeida, C. L. Wainwright, P. Mishkin, C. Zhang, et al. 2022. “Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 27730–44. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2011.






Figure 16: One PPO-style RLHF step: The policy generates responses to a batch of prompts. The frozen reference model supplies log-probabilities for the KL penalty, the frozen reward model supplies a scalar score, and the trained value model supplies value estimates. The penalized reward and value estimates form advantages, which update the policy and value models. Blue cards carry gradients and optimizer state; slate cards run forward passes only and hold weights alone, as each card’s weight, gradient, and optimizer-state strip shows; strip widths follow the 2, 2, and 12 bytes per parameter of mixed-precision Adam, unlike the equal-width columns of figure 7. That asymmetry drives placement.






Table 7: RLHF Model Coordination Roles: PPO-style RLHF coordinates models with different execution modes and memory footprints, so placement decisions must separate trainable policy and value state from inference-only reference and reward state.











Model
Role in PPO-style RLHF
Execution mode
Memory burden




Policy Model
The model being aligned and optimized.
Training mode with gradients, optimizer moments, and activations.
For a 70B-parameter model in mixed precision with Adam, memory is approximately 70B \(\times\) (2 \(+\) 2 \(+\) 12) = 1,120 GB, the same budget as standard pretraining.


Reference Model
A frozen copy of the pretrained policy that supplies the KL-divergence penalty.
Inference mode only.
FP16/BF16 parameters without gradients or optimizer state; a 70B model needs about 70B \(\times\) 2 = 140 GB, roughly 8× less than the training configuration.


Reward Model
A preference-trained scorer that produces scalar rewards for generated sequences.
Inference mode only.
Often smaller than the policy; a 13B reward model requires approximately 26 GB in FP16, but it must process every generated sequence.


Value Model
The PPO critic that estimates expected future reward.
Training mode, either separate or sharing a policy backbone.
A full-size separate critic can add another 1,120 GB; smaller models or shared-backbone designs reduce this to 200–400 GB.






The aggregate memory demand of the four-model PPO system dwarfs standard pretraining. A naive co-location of a 70B policy, 70B reference, 13B reward, and 13B value model requires approximately 1,494 GB of accelerator memory, before accounting for the KV caches and intermediate activations generated during sequence generation. A key-value (KV) cache stores attention keys and values for previously processed tokens so the policy can generate the next token without recomputing that state. It grows with the number and length of active sequences, creating a temporary memory budget distinct from weights and optimizer state. On H100 GPUs with 80 GB of HBM each, this system requires a minimum of 19 GPUs as an aggregate static-state capacity lower bound, including optimizer state and gradients. This division does not establish a feasible placement: each phase must also fit its KV or activation peak, workspaces, and uneven shards. Replicated policy groups increase the total state further.



The defining infrastructure challenge of RLHF is not the total memory footprint but the asymmetry between the models’ compute profiles. The policy and value models require full backward passes with gradient computation, activation checkpointing, and optimizer updates, compute-intensive operations that benefit from tensor parallelism and high arithmetic intensity. The reference and reward models, by contrast, perform only forward passes over generated sequences. Their scoring passes do not require optimizer state, and they need not decode token by token. The policy’s rollout phase creates the autoregressive generation workload and its KV-cache budget. Separating scoring from generation matters because forward-only execution does not imply a single memory or compute profile.
The asymmetry creates a placement dilemma. Co-location permits devices to serve different phases, but inactive model state can occupy memory needed for the active phase. Dedicated pools allow each role to use a suitable execution configuration, but pools may idle while waiting for another role’s output. Separation also adds transfers of generated sequences, scores, and updated policy weights. The design must compare phase utilization and data movement rather than assume that either placement eliminates waste.
The PPO rollout phase introduces autoregressive dependencies absent from the teacher-forced pretraining baseline. The policy generates responses before sequence-level rewards guide its updates. At small active batches, decoding is often memory bandwidth bound because each new token requires another model pass. For a Llama-2-70B-style grouped-query attention policy, KV storage grows by approximately \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \LayerCount \KvHeadCount \AttentionHeadDimension \ElementStorageSize\) per cached token per sequence. With 80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128-dimensional heads, 1,024 generated tokens, and 256 active sequences, the generated-token portion occupies 85.9 GB, or \(2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1024 \times 256 \times 2\) bytes. Dense multi-head attention using the full 8,192 hidden width for K and V would require 687.2 GB for that portion. Even with grouped-query attention, that portion alone already exceeds the 80 GB of HBM on one H100, and prompt tokens add KV state as well. This temporary cache must fit alongside the state live during rollout; its lifetime differs from training activations and optimizer state.
RLHF systems address this asymmetry through temporal multiplexing. During the generation phase, the cluster behaves like an inference system: the policy model generates sequences while the reference model computes log-probabilities, and the dominant resource is HBM reserved for token-by-token attention state. During the training phase, the same fleet switches back to training mode: gradients are computed through the policy and value models using the 3D parallelism configuration developed in section 5.10. During generation, batching active sequences and placing their KV state determine how much useful work shares each weight read. During the update phase, activation residency and gradient synchronization again govern the schedule. RLHF is not one steady training loop, but an alternation between inference-shaped work and training-shaped work, and standard training frameworks rarely manage that transition by themselves.



Standard offline DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023) removes the separate reward and value models from the update loop by reformulating alignment as a loss over preference pairs. The policy learns from preferred and dispreferred responses using their log-probabilities relative to a frozen reference. Because those responses are already in the training data, the update requires neither online generation nor advantage estimation.
A DPO implementation that retains a resident reference has two model roles: the trainable policy and the frozen reference. For the 70B policy with 13B reward and value models used in section 5.11.4, static state falls from about 1,494 GB to 1,260 GB, a 16 percent reduction. Against a policy-sized PPO value model, it falls from 2,406 GB to 1,260 GB, or roughly 48 percent. These are configuration-specific state budgets. For fixed preference pairs and a fixed reference, reference log-probabilities can instead be precomputed, removing that model from the repeated update loop. Offline DPO needs no autoregressive rollout during those updates. Variable lengths still require padding, packing, or length-aware batching, and policy training can use the same partitioning, accumulation, and overlap mechanisms as pretraining.
The trade-off is how training obtains new feedback. Standard offline DPO learns from a fixed preference dataset, so the policy cannot try new responses and receive feedback on them during training. PPO-style training generates responses from the evolving policy and scores them, so the policy can improve on its own outputs and expose behavior the original dataset lacks, provided the reward signal is reliable. When the preference data already covers the target distribution, DPO’s fixed-data loop usually wins on infrastructure. When training must discover behavior beyond the dataset, as in training models on novel reasoning tasks, PPO’s online loop can justify the reward and value models, the generation phase, and the memory they occupy. The decision is settled by achieved quality per unit of total resource cost, not by either property alone.



To make the infrastructure trade-off concrete, consider aligning a 70B policy model using a policy/reference pool of 256 H100 GPUs (80 GB HBM each). PPO’s separate reward and value pools sit outside that allocation. The policy is a 70B-class model rather than the 175B reference, a size at which each role’s memory budget stays readable while the four PPO roles together still need at least 19 GPUs, more than one node.

Napkin Math 5.9: RLHF infrastructure budget: PPO vs. DPOProblem: This alignment setup co-locates a 70B policy model with a 70B reference model and, for PPO, uses pools outside the 256-GPU policy/reference allocation for a 13B reward model and a 13B value model. Under 3D parallelism (TP=8 GPUs, PP=4, DP=8), how much memory resides on each policy GPU, and which separate model pools and generation-phase memory requirements does DPO remove?
PPO memory budget (per-GPU, with TP=8 GPUs, PP=4, DP=8 for policy)
The policy model under 3D parallelism with TP=8 GPUs and PP=4 distributes one replica’s 1,120 GB training state across 32 GPUs, yielding 35 GB per GPU. The reference model, requiring only 140 GB for inference, can instead be sharded across an additional 8 GPUs pool outside the policy allocation at 17.5 GB each, or co-located with the policy GPUs at an additional 4.4 GB per GPU (140 GB / 32 GPUs). The 13B reward model adds 26 GB shared across its pool. The 13B value model in training mode adds approximately 208 GB (13B \(\times\) 16 bytes/param) across its pool.
Total static memory (one co-located policy + reference replica on 32 GPUs): 35 GB + 4.4 GB \(\approx\) 39.4 GB per GPU, leaving \(\sim\) 46.5 GB for activations and KV cache. With generation-phase KV caches for a rollout batch containing 256 sequences and 1,024 tokens inside one \(\Glyph{T} \Glyph{P}{\times}\Glyph{P} \Glyph{P}\) policy replica, each policy GPU must reserve an additional 85.9 GB/32 GPUs \(\approx\) 2.7 GB for its KV cache shard. The remaining \(\sim\) 43.8 GB is generation-phase headroom. Once rollout KV state is released, the update phase recovers the 46.5 GB headroom before allocating training activations and other runtime buffers. The phase peaks must be evaluated separately.
DPO memory budget (same parallelism configuration)
The policy model uses the same 35 GB per GPU. The reference model adds 4.4 GB per GPU (co-located). No reward model, no value model, no KV cache for generation.
On the policy GPUs, total static memory is 35 GB + 4.4 GB = 39.4 GB per GPU, identical to PPO’s co-located policy/reference footprint. Both have 46.5 GB available before update-phase activations and runtime buffers when PPO releases its rollout KV cache. DPO removes the separate generation peak and the reward/value model pools; the absence of rollout KV state alone does not establish larger update microbatches.
Throughput comparison
PPO alternates generation and parameter updates. If generation consumes 60 percent of an iteration in this illustrative schedule, updates occupy the remaining 40 percent; this time fraction is not MFU. Update-phase MFU must be multiplied by that fraction to report update computation over the whole iteration, using the same allocated hardware denominator. DPO eliminates online generation, but its measured throughput still depends on sequence lengths, reference scoring, parallelism, and memory use. Table 8 separates the static-state comparison from these schedule-dependent effects.



Table 8: PPO vs. DPO state and execution phases: Static-state totals sum one copy of each model across its device pool, including trainable optimizer state and gradients. Data-parallel replication and phase-specific runtime allocations add to these totals; the table does not determine a minimum device count or measured MFU.

Systems insight: In this 13B reward/value-model scenario, DPO reduces the one-copy static-state budget by 15.7 percent by eliminating the reward and value models. It also removes online generation, but the throughput benefit requires a measured schedule. The choice between PPO and DPO is governed by infrastructure constraints as much as modeling preferences: organizations with limited GPU budgets may prefer DPO because it restores the workload to a fixed-data training loop. If the PPO value model is policy-sized rather than 13B, the memory reduction approaches the larger 2,406 GB to 1,260 GB comparison discussed in section 5.11.3.





PPO and DPO make variable sequence length a prominent scheduling concern. Pretraining often packs documents into fixed-length blocks, such as 2,048 or 4,096 tokens, although variable-length workloads also occur. Alignment batches combine prompts and responses whose lengths can differ substantially; an illustrative batch can span a 10–50\(\times\) length range. Those lengths determine activation residency, padding, and work assigned to each worker.
Length variance creates two interacting problems. Padding every sequence to the longest in a batch can leave most token positions unused. A batch of one 2,048-token sequence and fifteen 128-token sequences, padded to 2,048 tokens, fills only 3,968 of its 32,768 positions, so kernels that execute padded positions spend about 88 percent of their work on padding; kernels that skip them recover most of that waste. Dynamic batching groups similar lengths to reduce padding, but assignments across workers still need balancing. A worker processing longer sequences can have a larger activation peak and finish later, leaving other workers waiting for the required gradient contributions.
Sequence packing combines short sequences within a fixed-length input, with attention masking that keeps their contexts separate. Adaptive microbatching varies the number of sequences according to token count or a predicted memory budget. Both techniques also appear in pretraining; alignment adds the need to preserve response boundaries and the chosen preference or policy objective. Workers need not process equal token counts for a correct reduction. A token-mean PPO loss weights local means by valid-token counts, whereas standard DPO averages over preference pairs and uses pair counts (Rafailov et al. 2023). Packing changes layout, not that denominator. Unequal lengths can still create load imbalance, so balancing work remains a performance goal even when weighted reduction preserves the estimator.

Rafailov, Rafael, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, and Chelsea Finn. 2023. “Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36: 53728–41. https://doi.org/10.52202/075280-2338.
RLHF is therefore not a detour from parallelism strategy; it is the case that shows why no strategy is sufficient by itself. The policy model may need tensor and pipeline parallelism, the reference and reward models behave like inference services, the value model may require training state, and the rollout data pipeline changes shape from step to step. With that stress test in view, the final comparison can return to the general engineering question: identify the binding constraint first, then choose the parallelism pattern that moves the least data while fitting the required state.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
A parallelism strategy is useful only if it moves the binding constraint without creating a larger one. Assembling data, tensor, pipeline, and hybrid partitioning into a coherent decision procedure requires evaluating where each strategy relocates the execution tax across the cluster’s memory and interconnect hierarchy. For a new model, the decisive questions are which memory state fits, how often communication occurs, where the pipeline bubble appears, and which abstraction cost the engineering team can tolerate.
The canonical 3D core does not exhaust the partitioning space. Sequence parallelism accompanies tensor parallelism by partitioning along the sequence dimension the activations for operations such as layer normalization and dropout that tensor parallelism would otherwise replicate (Korthikanti et al. 2023). Context parallelism instead partitions a long attention context and exchanges key/value blocks or partial attention state across ranks (Liu et al. 2023). Expert parallelism partitions sparse feed-forward capacity and routes token activations to the selected experts. Table 9 places these extensions beside the 3D core without pretending they are independent of its batch, memory, and topology constraints.

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
A TP-8, PP-16, DP-128 layout that passes every feasibility check on paper can still hang at its first collective if two ranks disagree on group membership, or run slowly if gradient buckets become ready in an order the collective runtime cannot overlap. Choosing DDP, FSDP/ZeRO-style sharding, tensor parallelism, or pipeline parallelism is therefore also a decision about which constraints the runtime owns and which constraints the engineer must manage directly. Sparse workloads add a fourth contract, the parameter-server push/pull interface (Li et al. 2014) developed for Archetype B in section 5.7.4.

Li, M., D. G. Andersen, J. W. Park, A. J. Smola, A. Ahmed, V. Josifovski, J. Long, E. J. Shekita, and B.-Y. Su. 2014. “Scaling Distributed Machine Learning with the Parameter Server.” Proceedings of the 2014 International Conference on Big Data Science and Computing, 583–98. https://doi.org/10.1145/2640087.2644155.
The training framework defines process groups, gradient buckets, and the point in backpropagation when each reduction becomes ready; the collective runtime maps those reductions onto ring, tree, or hierarchical algorithms. The engineer must choose compatible group membership and bucket order and verify which communication remains exposed on the step’s critical path.
Layer-wise model parallelism requires explicit stage placement and load balancing, while pipeline parallelism adds microbatch scheduling logic to overlap forward and backward work. Tensor splitting instead changes the operators inside each layer, using the column-parallel and row-parallel pairing developed in section 5.9.2.3. FSDP adds parameter-gather and gradient-reduction boundaries around layer execution. Composing these abstractions requires preserving both the intended optimizer update and the memory and dependency budgets that each mechanism introduces.
Production frameworks expose these same strategies under different names, which makes a translation aid useful when reading their documentation or configuration files. title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
The GPT-2 notebooks showed the trap in miniature. Moving the same model from one NVLink node to four Ethernet-connected nodes quadrupled the GPU count but cut parallel efficiency from 99.4 percent to 27.9 percent. The following misconceptions generalize that error, each treating one term of the step-time accounting as if it were the whole budget.

Fallacy: Linear speedup is achievable with sufficient engineering effort.
Amdahl’s Law limits speedup when a fixed serial component remains exposed. Synchronous gradient aggregation creates an update dependency, but some of its work can overlap backward computation. As section 5.8 shows, \(\ScalingEfficiency = 1/(1 + \DeviceCount(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime)/\IronLawComputeTime)\) depends on the exposed overhead relative to useful compute as \(\DeviceCount\) changes. A 1,000-GPU allocation therefore does not by itself justify a 1,000\(\times\) speedup forecast. Local kernel efficiency, memory feasibility, communication, and convergence must be evaluated against the specified baseline. Linear scaling is a result to demonstrate for an operating range, not a return guaranteed by device count.


Pitfall: Optimizing MFU without considering scaling efficiency.
A single-node MFU measurement does not predict fleet throughput by itself. For a fixed workload and hardware peak convention, scaling efficiency compares measured distributed throughput with ideal replication of that single-node baseline. Multiplying the baseline MFU by this scaling efficiency gives distributed MFU; multiplying an already measured distributed MFU by the same scaling efficiency counts communication and synchronization losses twice. The chapter’s own numbers make the difference concrete. A single node running at 50 percent MFU, scaled with the 83 percent scaling efficiency of the overlapped TP-8 layout in section 5.10, delivers about 41 percent MFU across the fleet. A planner who measures that 41 percent on the full cluster and then applies the 83 percent again would budget for about 34 percent and buy capacity the job does not need. Capacity planning must state the device count and measurement window for each metric. Checkpointing, recovery, and replay require additional accounting only when those losses fall outside that window, and useful goodput must count retained model progress rather than repeated work.


Fallacy: Hyperparameters tuned on small clusters transfer directly to large-scale training.
Engineers tune hyperparameters on 8-GPU workstations then deploy to 256-GPU clusters expecting identical behavior. At scale, convergence patterns change fundamentally. The most critical hyperparameter is learning rate: as section 5.7 explains, global batch increases with GPU count when local batch and accumulation depth remain fixed, so the learning-rate schedule must be revalidated. The linear scaling rule of section 5.8.5, which the one-hour ImageNet run established, suggests \(\ScaledLearningRate = \BaseLearningRate\times (\ScaledBatchSize/\BaseBatchSize)\), but this relationship holds only within bounds. As models scale, they eventually encounter the critical batch size of section 5.8.6, where adding more data per step yields diminishing returns in convergence.
Beyond the critical batch size, this relationship breaks down in a model-, data-, and optimizer-dependent way. A team that takes a small-cluster learning rate, multiplies it mechanically with GPU count, and jumps directly to a much larger global batch may see lower final quality or slower sample efficiency even though hardware throughput improved. Warmup schedules, weight decay adjustment, layer-wise optimizers such as LARS/LAMB, and careful momentum tuning can recover accuracy in some regimes, but require systematic experimentation at target scale. Organizations that skip these scaling studies waste thousands of GPU-hours on suboptimal runs.


Pitfall: Adding GPUs to data-parallel jobs without modeling communication.
More GPUs improve time to target only if the gain in processing rate outweighs communication overhead and any additional sample use. With fixed local batch size, adding data-parallel workers increases the global batch; fixing the global batch instead reduces local work and can expose more communication. The critical-batch analysis in section 5.8.6 supplies a workload-dependent statistical guide, not universal GPU-count or model-size thresholds. Compare complete learning curves and cost at the same target quality before committing to a larger allocation.


Fallacy: Memory capacity alone determines the parallelism strategy.
A model that exceeds device capacity needs a feasible partition, but memory fit does not select the fastest one. Tensor parallelism exchanges partial results within layers, while pipeline parallelism transfers stage-boundary activations and introduces scheduling bubbles. Their relative cost depends on layer shapes, microbatch count, placement, and overlap. Compare complete training-state and activation budgets together with measured time to target; an unsupported throughput percentage or a weights-only fit cannot settle the choice.


Pitfall: Applying FSDP or ZeRO without measuring efficiency trade-offs.
Engineers adopt FSDP universally after reading that it “reduces memory and enables larger models.” Sharding trades memory capacity for communication overhead: full-shard FSDP gathers parameters before layer execution and reduces gradient shards during backward, with another parameter gather when the forward pass resharded them. The relevant comparison begins with the complete training-state budget. Under the mixed-precision Adam convention established here, the 7B worked example exceeds single-device capacity before activations, so standard DDP cannot fit that state on an A100-80 GB. A weights-only fit does not establish a feasible training baseline. When the complete state, activations, and workspaces fit without sharding, DDP can avoid the repeated gathers; when they exceed the 80 GB capacity, the comparison must include a feasible alternative such as sharding or offload. FSDP provides value when it enables training at all or when the larger local batch it permits offsets its communication cost. ZeRO-Offload extends capacity through CPU memory but adds transfers of its own. The decision therefore requires measuring peak memory and exposed communication for the same workload and optimizer contract.


Fallacy: Parallelism overhead is roughly constant regardless of model size.
Engineers benchmark parallelism strategies on convenient small models then apply those conclusions to large-scale training. For dense transformers at fixed tokens per update, computation and gradient bytes both grow roughly proportionally with parameter count, as the earlier scaling analysis established. Larger parameter count alone therefore does not imply a better computation-to-communication ratio. Architecture, sequence length, local batch size, partition degree, and kernel efficiency determine how much useful work each rank performs; gradient representation and process-group membership determine how much it communicates. A larger model can also require a different partition that introduces new layer collectives or pipeline bubbles. Reliable strategy selection holds the workload and target quality explicit, then recomputes memory fit, local compute time, communication volume, and the available overlap window at the target scale. A small-model benchmark becomes transferable evidence only when those governing terms remain comparable.


Pitfall: Treating scaling efficiency as a property of the hardware alone.
A vendor benchmark might report 85 percent scaling efficiency at 1,024 GPUs, and procurement teams then plan capacity as if that number were a cluster constant. Scaling efficiency is a joint property of four things: the workload’s communication-to-computation ratio, the parallelism strategy (data, pipeline, tensor, hybrid), the network topology (fat-tree vs. torus vs. dragonfly), and the software stack (NCCL version, kernel fusion, overlap quality). Reference numbers from dense large-language-model benchmarks transfer poorly to other workloads and fabrics. They may overstate scaling for graph neural networks with irregular communication and for embedding-heavy recommendation models, whose AllToAll embedding exchanges and many small random lookups load the fabric differently from dense gradient AllReduce (section 5.7.4), and they say nothing about a commodity-Ethernet placement like the GPT-2 scale-out, which lost most of its parallel efficiency on leaving the node. Capacity planning should use measured scaling on the target workload, not a vendor hero benchmark.


Fallacy: Gradient accumulation is free.
Gradient accumulation can reduce synchronization from every microstep to once per window of \(\AccumulationStepCount\) microsteps, eliminating \((\AccumulationStepCount-1)/\AccumulationStepCount\) of those synchronization events when the implementation defers reduction. The saving has costs. A resident gradient buffer remains live throughout the accumulation window; for the 7B model, the FP16 buffer occupies 14 GB. Retaining graphs across microsteps or increasing the local batch size can add activation pressure. Accumulating eight microsteps makes updates 8\(\times\) less frequent per processed microstep, but wall-clock spacing also depends on the communication saved. Larger effective batches can change convergence, and narrow accumulation formats can lose small contributions or overflow. The dtype, loss normalization, and reduction schedule must therefore be validated at the intended batch size. Accumulation trades communication frequency against update spacing, memory residency, and numerical stability.

50 percent of peak compute (delivering 512 GPU-equivalents of useful work)
100 percent of peak compute (delivering 1,024 GPU-equivalents of useful work)
12.5 percent of peak compute (delivering 128 GPU-equivalents of useful work)

It is mathematically incompatible with the Adam optimizer
It keeps a live gradient buffer resident, spaces optimizer updates by \(k\) microsteps, and requires appropriate accumulation precision and normalization

title: 5 Distributed Training
text:
Scaling laws keep pushing frontier training budgets past what one machine can hold or finish in time, and distributed training is how the fleet absorbs that growth. It confronts the scaling wall, the workload-dependent operating point beyond which communication and coordination can consume the compute time saved by adding accelerators. A feasible design must preserve the intended optimization update while satisfying model-state, activation, batch-size, and interconnect constraints. Hardware throughput alone is insufficient; the comparison must also account for time to the target model quality.
Each partition relocates cost along the C³ axes. Data parallelism divides compute across replicas and pays in communication, the gradient aggregation whose exposed share set the scaling efficiency of the 175B communication example. Tensor parallelism divides work inside a layer and pays in communication on the critical path, which confines it to a fast domain. Pipeline parallelism divides layer depth and pays mostly in coordination, the fill and drain bubble that only more microbatches, better balance, or a smarter schedule can shrink. The 3D parallelism cube in figure 2 unites these trade-offs in one coordinate space (\(\DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\)). A feasible point must satisfy peak memory and global-batch constraints as well as communication and coordination budgets.
Sharding and model partitioning make different parts of the training state fit, while synchronization and precision policies determine whether the resulting updates remain useful. Hybrid layouts compose these choices within the bandwidth hierarchy. The alignment workload extends the same reasoning to multiple models and alternating generation and update phases, where peak memory depends on which state is live together.
The chapter’s strategies are complementary dimensions of one design space rather than alternatives. Systems such as Megatron-LM map tensor, pipeline, data, and expert exchanges to the communication domains that can carry them, and that matching is what delays the communication-bound regime as the fleet grows. The workload archetypes weight those dimensions differently. Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) combines dense-model partitioning with state sharding and, at long contexts, sequence or context partitioning; Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) shards sparse embedding state and pays in lookup traffic rather than layer collectives; Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) moves the coordination problem onto unreliable edge devices. In each case the binding constraint, not the archetype label, selects the configuration.

Key Takeaways: Parallelism relocates the tax

Splitting work moves the bottleneck: Distributed training does not make the underlying computation smaller; it converts memory pressure into communication volume, synchronization delay, or idle pipeline time (principle \(\ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}\)). The winning strategy is the split that sends overhead to the least binding part of the fleet.
Throughput must serve convergence: Larger global batches can improve hardware efficiency while yielding diminishing progress per sample. Compare time to the same target quality, and treat the critical-batch estimate as a workload-dependent guide for selecting batch size and update schedules.
Sharding buys memory with messages: ZeRO and FSDP partition optimizer state, gradients, and parameters (principle \(\ref{pri-memory-capacity-gap}\)), reducing replicated storage. Peak memory must still include activations, temporary gathers, and workspaces; exposed ReduceScatter and AllGather costs determine whether the capacity gain also improves throughput.
Tensor parallelism needs a fast domain: Splitting operations inside layers creates frequent communication on the dependency path. Place those groups on links with sufficient bandwidth and low latency; the relevant boundary is the communication domain, which may span nodes, rather than the server enclosure.
Pipeline parallelism trades bytes for bubbles: Layer staging reduces communication frequency, but fill and drain slots leave accelerators idle (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)). Microbatching with \(\MicrobatchCount\gg \PipelineParallelDegree\) is the mechanism that turns model depth into throughput rather than pipeline slack.
Hybrid layouts are joint decisions: Combine only the partitioning and sharding strategies needed to satisfy the workload’s constraints (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)). Model divisibility, batch size, peak memory, communication groups, and failure domains must form one feasible configuration; improving one axis can expose a limit on another.



The displacement of overhead (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)) makes a feasible partition the beginning of the design problem. A memory-saving split is useful only if its communication and schedule still meet the run’s time-to-quality budget. Every mechanism in this chapter shrinks the per-device compute term \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) or the per-device training state, and pays for it in \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), in \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) through barriers, stragglers, and pipeline bubbles, or in lost overlap. In C³ terms, no partition removes the execution tax of scale; it only relocates that tax among compute, communication, and coordination. The engineering judgment is therefore to compare complete configurations, including their exposed dependencies, rather than optimize each parallelism axis independently.

What’s Next: From logic to trafficSplitting the mathematics defines the logical exchanges the update protocol needs. Replicas AllReduce gradients, sharded layers ReduceScatter and AllGather their state, expert and embedding partitions route tokens through AllToAll, and pipeline stages pass activations point to point. Each exchange specifies a result that participants must receive, not how its bytes cross the physical fabric. The next chapter separates those result contracts from the ring, tree, and hierarchical schedules that carry them out and prices each schedule’s latency, bandwidth, and topology costs, so that the communication budgets charged to \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) here can be evaluated rather than assumed.

text:
Self-Check: Answer

A research team is training a 3B-parameter transformer that fits comfortably in one H100 GPU’s 80 GB of memory, but projected single-GPU training would take 18 months to reach target loss. The dataset is 3 TB and fits on local NVMe storage. Which signal makes distributed training necessary in this scenario?

Dataset exceeding GPU HBM capacity, which automatically mandates tensor parallelism regardless of execution time
The presence of NVLink inside the node, which makes multi-machine scaling mandatory by default
Unacceptable wall-clock training duration, even though single-device memory capacity and local storage are sufficient
Fault tolerance limitations, because single-GPU training cannot survive hardware restarts

Answer: The correct answer is C. The deadline is the binding constraint even though the complete model fits and local storage is sufficient. Memory exhaustion can motivate sharding, offload, or other capacity remedies; dataset capacity and delivery rate can motivate distributed data services without forcing model computation across devices. NVLink enables exchanges when needed but does not mandate distribution. Single-device jobs can checkpoint and recover from interruption.
Learning Objective: Analyze which physical trigger necessitates distributed training when model memory and dataset storage are not binding constraints
A team doubles a data-parallel cluster from 64 to 128 GPUs and observes that total step time drops by only 12 percent even though per-worker compute time halves. Using the distributed step-time equation \(T_{\text{step}}(N) = T_{\text{compute}}/N + T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}}\), explain what the observation establishes and what measurement would distinguish possible causes.
Answer: The observation establishes that halving per-worker compute did not halve the complete step. Exposed communication, synchronization, reduced overlap, or another critical-path delay can explain the residual; the step-time ratio alone does not identify which one binds. Compare aligned rank timelines for gradient readiness, collective transfer, barrier waiting, input delivery, and kernel execution. Collective waiting may reflect a late participant rather than limited fabric capacity, so link utilization during the critical interval is needed to support a network diagnosis.
Learning Objective: Analyze how the communication-computation ratio limits scaling when per-worker compute shrinks faster than communication cost
True or False: If a neural network’s parameters exceed a single GPU’s memory capacity, tensor parallelism can be scaled across standard commodity Ethernet switches between server racks, provided the global batch size is made large enough.
Answer: False. Increasing global batch size does not guarantee that frequent tensor-parallel exchanges fit within the compute window. Slow inter-rack links can dominate every layer. Tensor parallelism should use the fastest available domain; pipeline or data parallelism usually better matches slower links, subject to measured workload and topology constraints.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the physical feasibility of tensor parallelism across commodity network fabrics
Framing distributed parallelism strategies as compiler loop transformations across the training loop’s iterators (batches, layers, and operations), which distributed strategy corresponds to vectorization (SIMD) of inner matrix multiplications?

Tensor parallelism, which partitions inner matrix-multiplication operations across devices and exchanges partial results over the interconnect
Data parallelism, which unrolls the outer batch loop across devices so each rank processes independent data indices
