The injection level determines which propagation paths the experiment includes. A register-level bit flip in a simulator such as gem5 (Binkert et al. 2011) can expose effects that a mutation of a PyTorch weight tensor omits. Conversely, hardware may mask an injected fault before software observes it. Location and propagation therefore matter when comparing results across fault models (Sangchoolie et al. 2017; Papadimitriou and Gizopoulos 2021).
This divergence comes from the multi-tier filtering formalized as error masking (Mohanram and Touba 2003). A physical soft error becomes an observable failure only if it passes two screens in turn (figure 11). The corrupted data must first be read, and the value read must then produce incorrect output or a crash. A hardware disturbance that hits an unused functional unit, is overwritten prior to use, or lands in dynamically dead instructions is silently absorbed within the microarchitecture or runtime (Ko 2021). Because tensor-level mutations inject perturbations downstream of these architectural filters, their empirical error rates must be evaluated at that higher abstraction level.

Figure 11: Error masking: Follow a soft error from the top. It becomes a failure only if the corrupted data is read and then also produces incorrect output; at each No branch it is masked, first by microarchitectural effects (unused components, overwritten values, squashed speculative instructions) and then by software effects (dead instructions, logical and compare operations, uninfluential branches). Because software-level fault injection sees only the second filter, it can misestimate a system’s true resilience to transient errors.



These masking effects determine which abstraction level an experiment should target.



Fault injection methods trade realism against experimental scale. Hardware-based injection, through field-programmable gate array (FPGA) emulation or accelerated particle-beam exposure of a running accelerator (Velazco et al. 2010), supplies the calibration point because its faults pass through the same circuit-level masking as production faults. Software-based injection is the scalable counterpart. Tools such as PyTorchFI (Mahmoud et al. 2020) perturb weights, activations, and gradients directly, covering many model states quickly without special hardware, and have shown that single bit-level faults can produce severe misclassifications, including “phantom” objects in detection models. The cost is an abstraction gap. A software tool that mutates a tensor skips the hardware masking that would have absorbed many of the same disturbances. Frameworks such as Fidelity (He et al. 2020) narrow that gap by mapping how faults in registers, memory hierarchies, and numerical units become software-visible errors, so that injected faults resemble what physical hardware would produce.

Example 7.1: Software fault injection limitsScenario: An engineering team validates a distributed training pipeline using software fault injection, concluding that tensor bit-flips always corrupt model gradient updates.
Diagnosis: Hardware-calibrated experiments reveal that software injection bypasses low-level hardware masking effects (such as ECC memory correction and gate-level masking) that prevent many register-level bit-flips from ever mutating software variables.
Systems lesson: In this experiment, bypassing hardware masking overstates the effect of the modeled physical faults. Tensor mutation still tests the software response to corrupted values; estimating production vulnerability additionally requires a calibrated model of which physical faults reach those values. The result must be interpreted at the injection level actually tested.


For fleet recovery, the most valuable experiments inject faults at the level where recovery decisions are made. Killing a rank in the middle of a collective, partitioning a node from the rendezvous service, delaying a heartbeat past its timeout, and corrupting one checkpoint shard each exercise one row of table 5. Running these experiments continuously in staging, and in controlled form in production, keeps rarely executed recovery code from decaying between real incidents (Basiri et al. 2016). A detection mechanism can identify corrupted or missing state, but only a recovery mechanism can replace it. Fault persistence determines whether to retry, quarantine, or replace a component, and checkpointing supplies the known-good training state from which any of those paths can resume.

When a top-of-rack switch dies two weeks into the training run of a 175-billion-parameter model, the cluster loses 64 GPUs instantly. The system cannot simply restart from scratch; the sunk cost of weeks of compute is too high. The failure analysis in section 7.1 established that large-scale training systems will experience such failures frequently, requiring robust mechanisms to preserve and resume progress.
Training fault tolerance has three obligations: preserve state, detect and classify failures, and resume or resize the job. Checkpointing supplies the first obligation. The sections that follow then build the rest of the recovery model: detection supplies evidence for a recovery decision, recovery procedures restore a consistent process group, and elastic recovery determines whether the job can continue with a changed worker set. Every one of those paths falls back on the saved copy that checkpointing produces, so the first question is what that copy must contain.

Definition 7.1: Checkpointing
Checkpointing is the periodic serialization of the complete training state (parameters, optimizer state, data loader position, and random state) to persistent storage at a recorded training step.

Significance: It minimizes lost work after a system failure by trading checkpoint I/O against rework. Writing too often wastes accelerator time on storage traffic; writing too rarely risks replaying many completed steps after a failure. The Young-Daly interval developed in this section chooses the cadence that balances write cost against expected lost work.
Distinction: A resumable checkpoint captures a consistent execution state, including optimizer state, random-number generator state, data position, and learning rate schedules. It can use full or incremental storage; bitwise replay additionally requires compatible deterministic execution.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that checkpointing is “just writing to disk.” For large models it is a storage-system stress test, because the simultaneous write from thousands of GPUs can trigger a checkpoint storm (definition \(\ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}\)) that saturates the shared network and storage bandwidth \((\Bandwidth)\).



A checkpoint is useful only if it resumes the recorded step consistently. In distributed training, every shard must belong to the same recoverable state; a collection of files from different steps does not preserve progress. For the interval model, assume that writing a checkpoint completes durably before it becomes available for recovery and that a failure discards the work performed since the last completed checkpoint.
Two recovery objectives turn those obligations into a contract. The recovery point objective (RPO) bounds acceptable lost progress, so checkpoint age and replication lag must fit within it. The recovery time objective (RTO) bounds the delay until useful work resumes, which covers detection, resource replacement, restore, and warmup. A 20-minute checkpoint interval cannot promise an RPO below 20 minutes without a more frequent durable log or replica, and asynchronous flushing can leave the last durable generation older still. A five-minute RTO is impossible if checkpoint reload alone takes eight minutes. These objectives apply to a stated fault model. Corruption discovered after several saves can require rollback beyond the newest durable checkpoint. The Young-Daly interval derived next minimizes expected waste; RPO and RTO impose service constraints that the expected-value optimum must still satisfy (Beyer et al. 2016).


When failures are expected during a job, the key engineering decision is how often to write that state, because every save costs I/O time and every unsaved step is work a failure can erase. The Young-Daly formula13 (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\), applied in section 7.13.2) gives a first-order estimate of that balance through a square-root rule:
13 Young-Daly formula: Young (1974) derived the first-order optimal checkpoint interval, and Daly (2006) independently refined it with tighter second-order bounds.
Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.
\[ \OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{7}\]
\(\CheckpointWriteTime\) in distributed ML training is not the time to flush a small process state; it includes transferring model weights and optimizer state to durable storage. The reference format here stores BF16 weights, separate FP32 master weights, and two FP32 moment tensors per parameter for Adam. A single resumable checkpoint for a 70B-parameter model therefore approaches a terabyte at 14 bytes per parameter; for the later 175B-parameter running example, it exceeds two terabytes. Reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) requires a smaller payload or higher sustained write bandwidth, and \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) itself is the central constraint that determines how tightly the checkpoint interval can be set before I/O overhead displaces productive training compute.
Of those 14 bytes per parameter, the optimizer state14 dominates the payload, exactly as in the storage sizing of the same resumable checkpoint in Checkpoint Storage, so the optimizer state rather than the model weights sets most of \(\CheckpointWriteTime\).
14 Adam optimizer state: Adam’s per-parameter first-moment (\(\AdamFirstMoment\)) and second-moment (\(\AdamSecondMoment\)) estimates are two FP32 values, 8 of the 14 bytes per parameter in the resumable checkpoint; with the FP32 master weights, optimizer-side state accounts for all but the 2 bytes of BF16 weights. For a 175B parameter model, the two moments alone reach 1.4 TB, which typically dominates checkpoint size and recovery time, making optimizer state the primary bottleneck in checkpoint I/O design.

Optimizer state, not weights, dominates checkpoint size.

To see the balance, consider an interval between saves. Doubling that interval approximately halves the checkpoint writes per unit of training, but a failure then loses twice as much work on average. Under the constant-rate, rare-failure approximation, failure occurs approximately uniformly within an interval, so the average lost work is half the interval. When write time is small relative to the interval, the wasted fraction from saving and replaying work is approximately the sum below. Detection, allocation, and restoration time require a separate recovery budget.
\[ \CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointInterval}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{8}\]
Setting the first derivative to zero (\(\frac{d\CheckpointWasteFraction}{d\CheckpointInterval} = -\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf} = 0\)) directly yields the square-root minimum of equation 7. The first term falls hyperbolically as the interval lengthens while the second climbs linearly, so total waste traces a U-shaped convex curve with a shallow floor. Its scaling consequence is the one to carry forward. As clusters grow, system MTBF drops, so the optimal interval shrinks, demanding higher-bandwidth storage to keep \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) small before the “checkpoint tax” consumes the cluster’s compute capacity. Because the relationship is a square root, halving MTBF tightens the interval by only \(\sqrt{2}\approx 1.4\times\), so doubling cluster size does not demand doubling checkpoint I/O bandwidth when checkpoint size and the other assumptions stay fixed. The next subsection applies the formula to the chapter’s own cluster, whose full-system MTBF the cluster cascade already derived.

The Young-Daly interval of equation 7 needs two inputs. The failure analysis in section 7.1 supplies the system MTBF term, and the checkpoint payload together with sustained write bandwidth supplies \(\CheckpointWriteTime\). With both in hand, the formula gives a candidate schedule for the chapter’s own cluster, subject to its recovery objectives.
The worked cascade’s 10,000-GPU cluster, roughly ten times the Archetype A reference cluster, supplies both inputs as computed values. That cascade (section 7.4) put full-system MTBF, including PCIe and network failures (the redundant power supplies add no term), at 3.87 hours. For the write time, the 175B running example’s 2.45 TB resumable checkpoint drains to shared storage at the sustained aggregate write bandwidth this chapter assumes for the cluster, 100 GB/s, which takes 24.5 s. Substituting these into the Young-Daly formula gives the canonical interval for this cluster.

Napkin Math 7.3: The Young-Daly optimal intervalProblem: A 10,000-GPU cluster has an MTBF of 3.87 hours. A full model checkpoint takes 24.5 s to write. What is the optimal checkpoint frequency?
Math: Apply the Young-Daly interval of equation 7 (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\)).

Convert to common units: \(\SystemMtbf =\) 3.87 hours \(\times\) 3600 s/hour = 13932 s.
Substitute and solve: With \(\CheckpointWriteTime =\) 24.5 s and \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures =\) 13932 s, the formula gives \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx\) 826.2 s, or about 13.8 min.

Systems insight: At this interval, the “checkpoint tax” (time spent saving + time spent re-computing) is minimized to approximately 5.9 percent. Checkpointing every hour instead would lengthen the expected rework after each failure, wasting about 13.6 percent of the cluster’s capacity. As clusters scale, the optimal interval must shrink to keep up with the falling MTBF.


The result connects measured or estimated interruption rates to checkpoint policy. At this interval, saving and expected replay together consume approximately 5.9 percent of training time in the first-order model, half from writes and half from replay, because at the square-root optimum the two terms of equation 8 are equal. Plotting those two terms for this cluster shows how forgiving the optimum is (figure 12). Write overhead falls hyperbolically and expected rework climbs linearly, so their sum has a shallow floor around 14 min. An interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while one several times too short or too long costs far more, which is why a rough MTBF estimate still yields a usable schedule.

How far the estimate itself can be trusted depends on the assumptions behind it.

Systems Perspective 7.3: Young-Daly formula assumptionsThe first-order Young-Daly formula provides valuable intuition but rests on assumptions that may not hold when write times are non-negligible relative to MTBF; the renewal model derived in Checkpoint Intervals Beyond the First-Order Approximation shows how finite checkpoint time changes the optimum. The assumptions are:

Exponentially distributed failures: Assumes a constant failure rate. Real systems exhibit “bathtub curve” behavior with higher rates during burn-in and wear-out phases.
Deterministic checkpoint time: Assumes \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is constant. In practice, checkpoint time varies 2–3\(\times\) due to storage contention, network congestion, and memory pressure.
Recovery cost is independent of the chosen interval: A fixed per-failure recovery cost does not change the first-order minimizing interval. Recovery can take longer than checkpoint writing because it also includes job scheduling delays, topology reconstruction, and warmup; it still belongs in the total-waste budget.
Aggregate interruption process: Independent constant-rate failure sources can contribute to one job-interruption rate. Shared power, cooling, or switch failures require a model of incident frequency and recovery cost; adding per-device rates alone misses those common causes.
Infinite timeline: Optimizes for long training runs. Short runs, where total time is comparable to MTBF, require different analysis.

When assumptions are violated, the optimal interval may shift significantly, but restart overhead should not be treated as if it were paid at every checkpoint. In the first-order lost-time model, restart time adds a per-failure recovery term to total expected waste; it does not replace \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) inside equation 7 unless a recovery-aware Daly-style model is explicitly derived and calibrated.


Along an execution timeline, a training run alternates productive compute intervals (\(\CheckpointInterval\)) with synchronous save barriers (\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)), and a failure charges two distinct penalties (figure 13). Uncheckpointed progress is discarded as lost rework, and the restart latency (\(\FailureRecoveryTime\)) to reload state and warm up execution pipelines follows before useful work resumes.






Figure 13: Checkpoint-recovery timeline: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint.



Recovery latency therefore matters as much as write duration, because every failure pays both the discarded compute since the last save and the restart delay. That delay includes job scheduling, checkpoint loading, and pipeline warmup. Production systems where recovery exceeds checkpoint write time by 3–5\(\times\) should include it in their total-waste and service-level objective (SLO) budgets, and should use a cited recovery-aware checkpoint model rather than folding recovery time into the per-checkpoint write term.



The interval calculation chooses when the system preserves state; the write path decides what each save costs while training waits. Equation 9 generalizes the save-side term of equation 8 to include any pause beyond the write itself:
\[ \CheckpointOverheadFraction= \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointExtraPauseTime}{\CheckpointInterval}  \tag{9}\]
Here, \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) is the dimensionless fraction of time lost to checkpointing, \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is checkpoint write time, \(\CheckpointInterval\) is the checkpoint interval, and \(\CheckpointExtraPauseTime\) is any training pause beyond the checkpoint write itself. This includes memory allocation, coordination, and serialization. Total first-order waste is then \(\CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \CheckpointOverheadFraction+ \CheckpointInterval/(2 \cdot \SystemMtbf)\), so checkpoint overhead in this section means the save side alone, with expected rework counted separately. How large \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) becomes depends first on whether training waits for durable storage.


The synchronous and asynchronous checkpointing approaches differ in when training waits for durable storage. Synchronous checkpointing coordinates workers at a consistent state boundary, writes their portions, and resumes training only after all writes complete. Blocking alone does not establish consistency; the protocol must ensure that every shard belongs to the same recoverable training state.
Asynchronous checkpointing separates that consistent capture from the durable flush. Workers snapshot their state to CPU memory or staging storage and protect the captured values from later updates, then continue training while a background process writes the snapshot to persistent storage.15 Recovery can use the new generation only after all required shards reach the storage tier that survives the modeled failure and the coordinator publishes completion.
15 Asynchronous checkpointing: Pipelines durable writes behind training by first capturing a consistent snapshot in staging memory or storage. Training must not mutate values still being captured. After capture, background flushing can overlap independent computation, subject to staging capacity and sustained drain bandwidth. Exposed capture time and resource contention remain overhead even when the durable write finishes off the training critical path.Memory footprint introduces a second contrast. Beyond write time, checkpointing consumes memory for serialization, transfer buffers, and any copied snapshot. A synchronous writer can read stable training state while updates are paused, so it does not necessarily need a complete second copy, but the pause can leave accelerators idle even with fast storage. Independent input prefetching may continue; forward or backward work that changes the captured state must wait unless the snapshot mechanism explicitly permits overlap. Asynchronous capture instead requires retained values that later updates cannot change, so its buffering policy can increase peak memory demand.



The financial impact of synchronous checkpointing at scale is severe when the storage path is slow. Suppose the same 175B checkpoint on the same cluster goes to a slower shared tier than the one assumed in the interval notebook, delivering about 20 GB/s instead, under a common hourly policy and with no staging to hide the write. A 10,000-GPU cluster then pauses for 2 minutes per save and burns \(10{,}000 \times \frac{2}{60} \approx 333\) idle GPU-hours, which at roughly $3 per GPU-hour costs about $1,000 in wasted compute for a single checkpoint. Hourly, that idle time compounds to $24,000 per day spent waiting for storage I/O. This is the cost that asynchronous capture removes from the critical path, which is why production systems stage checkpoints rather than block on the shared tier. Write time also varies widely across model types, because larger models require longer writes but also earn longer optimal intervals (table 6).

While the theoretical overhead of checkpointing appears manageable for individual models, writing these massive state files introduces a new bottleneck. When thousands of GPUs simultaneously attempt to write gigabytes of data to a shared file system, the resulting I/O congestion threatens to bring the entire cluster to a halt. The scale of that I/O burst is easiest to see by expanding the example from one model to thousands of simultaneous writers.

Example 7.2: The checkpoint stormScenario: A 10,000 GPUs distributed training cluster runs an embedding-heavy job whose per-worker model and embedding shard (10 GB) is several times the 2.4 GB per-GPU shard of the 175B running example. Every worker flushes its shard to shared storage at the same step instant.
Diagnosis: Simultaneous uncoordinated writes offer 100 TB to shared network and storage paths in one burst, the checkpoint storm of definition \(\ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}\). When that arrival rate exceeds sustained service capacity, queues grow and writers stall; finite buffering can also lead to drops or timeouts. The total byte count alone does not establish which resource fails first.
Systems lesson: A consistent capture need not become an uncontrolled storage burst. Staggered flushes, rate limits, and bounded host-memory or local-storage staging can keep background writes within the drain capacity. The system must still publish a generation only after it reaches the required durability tier.


Theoretical models project modest overhead percentages under uncontended conditions, yet real deployments often encounter checkpoint times far exceeding these estimates. Diagnosing such discrepancies requires examining the full system stack.

Example 7.3: Debugging checkpoint overheadScenario: In a hypothetical trace, a cluster with 64 nodes training a 70B model pauses for 15 minutes per checkpoint after each 45 minutes of useful computation. This is a 25 percent share of wall time, exceeding a 2 minutes pause target.
Diagnosis: An update-boundary snapshot stores BF16 weights, separate FP32 master weights, and both FP32 Adam moments: 980 GB before metadata. A single shared 10 Gbps NFS path (1.25 GB/s) needs at least 13.1 min to transfer those bytes. The longer observed pause is consistent with this bandwidth floor but does not identify every source of overhead.
Systems lesson: Local NVMe staging can move the remote transfer out of the training pause, provided snapshot copies and local writes fit their own budgets. It cannot accelerate the shared path’s sustained drain rate. Here the ideal drain time is shorter than the interval between snapshots; production must verify the effective rate, staging capacity, and contention. A snapshot on local staging alone does not survive loss of that node unless the recovery contract provides another copy.


That last caveat moves the question from what a save costs to what it survives. Staging hides the write from training, but where each copy lives decides which failures the saved state outlasts and how quickly it returns.




Tiered checkpoint storage architectures, with local NVMe for speed, distributed filesystems for durability, and object storage for long-term retention, provide the storage foundation on which recovery mechanisms operate. The fault-tolerance question is how recovery mechanisms use that infrastructure rather than how the storage hierarchy is designed.


↩︎ Tiered checkpoint storage designs and asynchronous write pipelines are established in Checkpoint Storage.
For fault tolerance, checkpoint placement determines which failures the saved state survives, while the restore path determines how quickly that surviving state becomes useful. On the 128-node Archetype A reference cluster, each node holds about 19.1 GB of the 2.45 TB checkpoint for the 175B running example. Reading that share from local NVMe at 5 GB/s takes about 3.8 s, with every node reading in parallel, while pulling the full checkpoint back through shared storage at 100 GB/s aggregate takes about 24.5 s. The local path is faster because it multiplies drive bandwidth by node count, but a sole copy on a lost node cannot restore that node’s shard. The replacement node must read its share from a copy outside the failed domain, such as a distributed filesystem or object store, whose recovery time is set by sustained aggregate reads, network capacity, and deserialization. A sound placement therefore keeps a fast local copy for the survivors and a durable remote copy for whatever the failure took away, and these rates must still be measured under the job’s own load.



Recovery from distributed checkpoints for sharded models requires understanding the coordination protocols that ensure checkpoint consistency. Checkpoint coordination involves two orthogonal dimensions: whether workers synchronize to capture a consistent state (coordinated versus uncoordinated checkpointing), and how that state flows to persistent storage (centralized versus distributed checkpointing).
In uncoordinated checkpointing, each worker records its local state independently without synchronizing with peers. While this avoids coordination barriers during healthy execution, recovery must search across independent shards for a mutually consistent cut. Because distributed ML workers exchange gradients and activations at every step, an uncoordinated rollback can cause dependencies to cascade backward through the entire training run—the classic domino effect (Elnozahy et al. 2002). Distributed ML systems therefore rely on coordinated checkpointing, in which workers synchronize (either at step boundaries or through explicit two-phase commit protocols) to ensure that saved shards together define a globally consistent recovery line.

Elnozahy, Elmootazbellah N., Lorenzo Alvisi, Yi-Min Wang, and David B. Johnson. 2002. “A Survey of Rollback-Recovery Protocols in Message-Passing Systems.” ACM Computing Surveys 34 (3): 375–408. https://doi.org/10.1145/568522.568525.
Once coordination guarantees consistency, the architectural decision is how those shards reach persistent storage: whether workers funnel their state through a single coordinator or write their partitions directly in parallel.


In centralized checkpointing, workers send their state to a coordinator process that assembles and writes the complete checkpoint. This approach simplifies checkpoint management and can produce self-contained checkpoint files, but all state crosses the coordinator’s network links, and coordinator failure interrupts the save. A streaming writer can avoid buffering the entire checkpoint, although it cannot remove the ingress bottleneck. That bottleneck is structural. The coordinator receives through one node’s network links, so its write time grows with total state volume, whereas independent writers each move only their own share of the state through their own links. The gap between the two patterns therefore widens in proportion to the number of writers. For the 175B running example, the 128 nodes of the reference cluster would funnel 2.45 TB through one node’s links instead of 19.1 GB through each. The pattern is viable while that one path meets the checkpoint budget; state volume and sustained bandwidth determine the limit more directly than a fixed worker count.
The decision boundary is the size of the state and the number of writers. Centralized checkpointing is attractive when operational simplicity matters more than aggregate bandwidth, but distributed and sharded approaches become necessary once the checkpoint itself is a fleet-scale object.



Distributed checkpointing eliminates this coordinator funnel by having each worker persist its own shard directly. Figure 14 contrasts the dataflow topologies: the centralized pattern concentrates traffic at the coordinator’s ingress, while the distributed pattern writes in parallel to local NVMe and drains the shards to remote object storage in the background. With fixed per-worker shard sizes and sufficient independent staging bandwidth, adding workers need not lengthen the local write pause. Shared drain capacity and completion coordination can still limit scaling. A coordinator signals when to checkpoint and confirms completion, but state flows directly from workers to storage without aggregation.






Figure 14: Distributed checkpoint architecture: Centralized vs. sharded checkpoint writes. In the centralized pattern (left), every worker funnels its shard through one coordinator, whose ingress bandwidth and buffering constrain the write path and whose failure halts the save. In the distributed pattern (right), each worker writes its own shard to local NVMe in parallel and a background process drains the shards to remote object storage, so the local blocking write time can remain roughly constant with fixed shard sizes and sufficient staging bandwidth; shared drain capacity still limits completion.



A synchronous version of the coordination protocol proceeds in six steps:

Coordinator broadcasts checkpoint request with checkpoint ID
Each worker reaches a consistent state (barrier synchronization)
Each worker writes an immutable shard to a generation-specific staging prefix and records its byte length and cryptographic digest
Each worker confirms durable write completion to the coordinator
The coordinator writes an immutable manifest after all confirmations; the manifest names the training step, topology, model and optimizer formats, data-loader position, random state, and the length and digest of every shard, then publishes a commit marker or atomic pointer to that manifest
Coordinator broadcasts checkpoint complete, training resumes

The idealized protocol assumes step 2 completes quickly. The barrier, however, waits for the slowest of thousands of arrivals, so a single slow worker can make it dominate the checkpoint pause even when the storage path has ample bandwidth. Measuring arrival skew separately from copying and writing reveals whether coordination or data movement limits the save.
The manifest, not the presence of a directory or a plausible set of shard names, defines a committed checkpoint generation. Restore accepts only a published manifest whose shards all match their recorded lengths and digests; staged shards without that final publication remain unreachable and can be garbage collected. This rule prevents a partially overwritten latest directory from masquerading as recoverable state and makes generation rollback explicit. The set of per-worker states a manifest names is a cut, and the cut is consistent when all of those states could have existed together at one moment of a valid execution, so that no shard reflects an update another shard has not yet seen. That consistency cut determines whether the system can claim strict, bounded-asynchronous, or eventual consistency.

Systems Perspective 7.4: Checkpoint consistency modelsStrict synchronous: All workers checkpoint at exactly the same training step. Provides strongest consistency but highest overhead from barrier synchronization.
Bounded asynchronous: Workers may progress at different rates while the checkpoint manager tracks which snapshots can form a consistent recovery cut. Bounding step skew alone is insufficient: the system must retain compatible shard versions or enough replay information to reconstruct that cut. Asynchronous flushing can also preserve a single synchronized snapshot while its writes complete in the background, avoiding training stalls without relaxing recovery consistency.
Eventual consistency: Workers save independently and recovery attempts to reconcile their versions. A usable design must retain enough compatible versions or replay information to reconstruct a valid state; arbitrary recent shards do not necessarily form a recoverable generation. Reduced coordination at save time therefore transfers work and storage requirements to recovery.


Steps 3 through 5 are two-phase commit,16 the classic distributed-systems protocol for making one decision atomic across many participants (Gray 1978), applied to a checkpoint. Steps 3 and 4 form its prepare phase, in which each worker stages its shard and reports success, and step 5 is its commit phase, in which the coordinator durably records the decision by publishing the manifest. The manifest publication rule inherits the protocol’s guarantee and its known weakness. If the coordinator crashes after workers prepare but before it records a decision, the system must not expose those shards as a valid checkpoint, and the prepared participants remain blocked until the original or a replacement coordinator recovers the durable decision. Uncommitted staged shards can be garbage collected only after recovery establishes that no commit decision exists.
16 Two-phase commit (2PC): Formalized by Gray (1978), 2PC ensures all participants either commit or abort atomically. The protocol’s known weakness is blocking, because a coordinator failure after participants prepare but before they learn the decision leaves the prepared participants waiting until the durable decision is recovered. A timeout can trigger coordinator recovery, but it cannot by itself authorize unilateral rollback.
Gray, J. N. 1978. “Notes on Data Base Operating Systems.” In Operating Systems: An Advanced Course. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-08755-9_9.
Atomic publication does not by itself make the published shards consistent. Synchronous gradient updates naturally create step boundaries where all workers have applied the same updates, but asynchronous training and pipeline parallelism require more careful coordination to define a consistent cut.



Modern distributed training frameworks partition model state across workers using techniques like ZeRO and FSDP, which shard parameters, gradients, and optimizer state instead of replicating them on every data-parallel worker. In these configurations, no single worker holds complete model state. Each worker holds only its assigned parameter shard plus corresponding optimizer state.


↩︎ How ZeRO and FSDP partition training state across data-parallel workers is established in Memory-efficient data parallelism with ZeRO and FSDP.
17 Sharded checkpointing: Each worker saves only its local partition rather than gathering state to a single writer. For ZeRO-3 or FSDP with 1,024 workers training a 175B model, each worker writes approximately 2.4 GB instead of one writer handling 2.45 TB, parallelizing I/O across all nodes. The trade-off is that recovery requires every shard to be available and consistent, making the checkpoint protocol more complex. Losing one storage device invalidates the generation only if a required shard cannot be recovered from another copy or sufficient storage redundancy.Sharded checkpointing17 (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) uses this distribution: each worker writes only its shard, dramatically reducing per-worker write volume. Recovery loads shards and redistributes state to workers based on the recovery configuration.
This approach enables efficient checkpointing even for massive models. A 175B parameter model with a 2.45 TB checkpoint distributed across 1,024 workers requires each worker to write only 2.4 GB, achievable in seconds with local NVMe storage.
When recovering with a different number of workers than the checkpoint, shard redistribution must remap state to the new worker configuration. This occurs due to elastic scaling or hardware changes. Framework support for flexible resharding enables recovery even when the worker count changes. However, possessing a valid checkpoint is not sufficient on its own. Sharding distributes the write work, while staging and drain control govern the shared I/O burst. The system must still identify the failure, trigger restoration, and coordinate the distributed shards before training can resume. The speed of detection and recovery determines the true cost of the interruption.

A GPU silently hangs, dropping its utilization to zero while its peer GPUs wait indefinitely at an AllReduce barrier. Every minute the system takes to notice this hung rank and reboot the node costs thousands of dollars in idle cluster time. Checkpoints preserve state, but the recovery process itself determines how much compute a failure wastes. In the accounting of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3), that waiting belongs to the synchronization term \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\). Every surviving rank idles at the barrier until the group is whole again, so detection, restart, and reload add directly to step time averaged over the run.
Equation 10 decomposes recovery time into four primary components:
\[ \FailureRecoveryTime= \FailureDetectionTime+ \JobRestartTime+ \CheckpointLoadTime+ \RecoveryWarmupTime \tag{10}\]
where \(\FailureDetectionTime\) is the time between the physical hardware fault and system classification as a failure, \(\JobRestartTime\) is the latency required for the job scheduler to allocate resources and launch replacement processes, \(\CheckpointLoadTime\) is the I/O duration to read checkpoint state from distributed storage into GPU memory, and \(\RecoveryWarmupTime\) is the interval needed to refill data pipelines, compile just-in-time (JIT) kernels, and stabilize training throughput. Each component presents distinct optimization opportunities, and the dominant term varies by cluster configuration. Understanding this decomposition enables targeted investment in the bottleneck rather than uniform improvement across all components.





Detection latency climbs from seconds (crash) to hours (silent corruption).
Heartbeat monitoring is the first detection layer and usually sets the floor on \(\FailureDetectionTime\). Each GPU rank periodically signals liveness to a coordinator, and if no heartbeat arrives within the timeout period \(\HandoverTimeout\), the coordinator declares failure. Setting \(\HandoverTimeout\) requires balancing false positive rate against detection latency. False positives declare healthy workers failed due to transient delays, while slow detection wastes compute during the detection window, a cost that scales linearly with the number of GPUs blocked in the collective.
For a heartbeat interval of \(\HeartbeatInterval\) seconds and network-delay standard deviation \(\NetworkDelayStandardDeviation\) in seconds, equation 11 defines the timeout heuristic:
\[ \HandoverTimeout = \HeartbeatInterval+ \TimeoutSafetyMultiplier\NetworkDelayStandardDeviation \tag{11}\]
Here, \(\TimeoutSafetyMultiplier\) is a dimensionless safety multiplier; values from three to five illustrate a tuning range rather than a guaranteed false positive rate. The heuristic treats the normal heartbeat delivery delay as small relative to the heartbeat interval. A deployment with substantial baseline delay or a heavy delay tail must account for those measurements as well as \(\NetworkDelayStandardDeviation\). The practical difficulty is distinguishing a genuinely dead rank from one that is temporarily slow, for example, a GPU lagging because it is writing a large checkpoint to attached storage while the collective is already waiting. Tuning \(\HandoverTimeout\) too tightly causes checkpoint writes to trigger false failure declarations; tuning it too loosely extends the window during which other ranks wait for the missing contribution.
Collective communication timeouts provide a second detection layer. During synchronous training, a collective required by the next step remains an incomplete critical-path dependency if a required rank disappears. AllReduce needs every rank’s contribution before it can produce the reduced result; the progress and failure behavior of other collectives depends on the operation and runtime. Transport and process-group timeouts bound how long the job waits before declaring the operation failed and entering recovery. NCCL18 provides configurable transport and reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) timeout parameters for this purpose, while higher-level frameworks may impose process-group operation timeouts. These settings are often set conservatively to avoid crashing jobs during legitimate periods of slow communication, which unfortunately extends \(\FailureDetectionTime\).
18 NCCL timeout: NVIDIA’s collective communication library exposes transport and RAS timeout controls such as NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT and NCCL_RAS_TIMEOUT_FACTOR (NVIDIA 2026). Higher-level launch and distributed-training frameworks can add their own restart and operation-timeout behavior (PyTorch Contributors 2026b). Aggressive timeout settings accelerate failure detection but risk false positives during legitimate long collective operations on large models, forcing a trade-off between detection latency and training stability that has no universal optimum.

Container orchestration health checks provide a third layer. Kubernetes, the container orchestration system, offers liveness probes (verifying that a process still responds and makes progress) and readiness probes (verifying that a process is ready to handle requests). Slurm, the batch scheduler common on HPC-style training clusters, instead runs a periodic node health-check program that can drain a node whose GPUs, links, or file systems fail their tests. Both operate independently of the training framework, catching failures that application-level heartbeats might miss; a liveness probe that tests forward progress rather than mere process existence can catch a process that is alive but deadlocked.
Loss spike detection exposes an anomaly, not its cause. Silent hardware corruption can produce an abrupt loss or gradient-norm spike, but so can a bad batch, an optimizer instability, a data-ordering defect, or a distributed-state mismatch. Robust systems therefore pause before the suspect update commits, preserve the input and worker evidence, and replay the step on known-good hardware. The system drains hardware only after that evidence implicates the device; otherwise, it repairs the data, optimizer, or synchronization path that produced the same symptom.
The operational question is therefore how long detection really takes once these layers interact.

Once a failure is classified, a cold-restart recovery path executes a coordinated sequence to restore consistency. The warm-restart alternative developed next preserves surviving processes when their state can be trusted.

Job termination: A SIGTERM is broadcast to all surviving workers. This cold-restart path tears down the affected training group so that no survivor continues using the old membership or partially completed collective state.
Resource reclamation: The scheduler marks the failed node as “draining” to prevent immediate rescheduling and requests a replacement from the spare pool.
Job restart: New containers are launched (from cache if available), and the training binary is re-initialized on all nodes.
Checkpoint loading: Each worker reads the state assigned to it from the distributed filesystem. When membership or parallelism changes, recovery remaps the saved shards to the new partitions.
State synchronization: Ranks handshake to establish a new communicator (for example, ncclCommInitRank), and workers verify they are all at the same training step.
Training resumption: The data loader restores its recorded position and sampling state, and the training loop resumes from the checkpoint step. A batch index alone suffices only when it reconstructs the same logical input stream.

Automatic recovery systems perform these steps without human intervention. Modern training frameworks integrate with cluster managers to automate parts of the sequence. DeepSpeed documents save/load routines for model and ZeRO optimizer checkpoints, which provide the durable state needed after failure (DeepSpeed Developers 2026a). PyTorch’s torchrun elastic launch documents failure and membership-change behavior through its rendezvous mechanism,19 the coordinator-backed protocol by which surviving workers agree on membership and ranks after a restart (PyTorch Contributors 2026b, 2026a).
19 Rendezvous: From French “rendez-vous” (present yourselves), this coordination protocol lets restarted workers discover one another and establish a new group before training resumes. Recovery waits for the membership policy to be satisfied, so slow startup, delayed communication, and missing workers can extend this phase. Heterogeneity affects those delays but does not by itself imply a proportional latency law.Recovery validation tests whether the restored job behaves consistently with its recorded state. Parameter shapes, dtypes, and shard identities must match the manifest. A short replay or validation workload then checks loss and gradient statistics under the expected numerical tolerance; different batches need not reproduce the last prefailure loss. Immediate divergence is evidence to investigate the checkpoint, data state, and execution configuration, not proof that the snapshot is corrupt. Falling back to an earlier validated generation is appropriate when the newest state cannot be trusted.
Recovery must also prevent the failed ownership epoch from returning. A coordinator grants each worker-group incarnation a monotonically increasing epoch (a membership counter, unrelated to a training epoch over the dataset) and associates membership with a renewable lease. Every state-changing write carries that epoch as a fencing token. Before replacement writes proceed, the recovery protocol advances the enforced epoch at each protected resource, which rejects writes carrying an older token. The old worker then cannot publish a checkpoint or update job progress, even if it resumes after a long pause; rendezvous likewise admits only the current membership. A lease alone is insufficient because expiration changes the coordinator’s ownership decision, not the old worker’s ability to reach storage. Fencing enforces that decision at the resource boundary (Kleppmann 2016).

Retries complete the recovery contract. An operation may be retried automatically only when it is idempotent or carries a stable operation identifier that lets the receiver deduplicate repeated effects. Each attempt inherits the caller’s absolute deadline rather than receiving a fresh timeout, and the system caps attempts with a retry budget shared across the request or recovery tree. Exponential backoff and jitter spread attempts in time, but they do not prevent overload if every layer retries independently. The budget therefore belongs at one retry-owning layer; exhausted budget returns a failure or invokes degradation instead of amplifying the original incident (Beyer et al. 2016; Nygard 2007).

On that basis, a 1,024-GPU cluster has MTBF of 49 hours and experiences about 0.49 failures/day, losing about 3 minutes daily, a modest 0.2 percent overhead. However, a 10,000-GPU cluster has GPU-only MTBF of 5 hours and experiences about 4.8 failures/day, losing about 31 minutes daily (2.1 percent overhead), equivalent to wasting roughly 5,127 GPU-hours every day (the daily lost minutes multiplied across all 10,000 GPUs).





The recovery procedure described in section 7.14.2 is a cold restart: every process in the affected job group exits, and the group reloads state from a valid checkpoint. This simplifies recovery by avoiding dependence on surviving in-memory state, but it can discard useful state. After one GPU fails in the 1,024-GPU reference job, every surviving worker may retain reusable values; an interrupted update or silent corruption, however, can make some of those values unsafe to keep.
A warm restart preserves the state of surviving workers. When a rank fails, surviving ranks detect the failure but do not exit. They enter a waiting state, preserving loaded model weights and optimizer states in GPU memory. The scheduler replaces only the failed node. The new node joins, loads its partition of the state from disk (or receives it via broadcast from a peer), and the communicator is rebuilt. The replacement and survivors must agree on the same committed training step before resuming. A shard restored from an older checkpoint cannot be combined with survivor shards that have advanced beyond it; the runtime must reconstruct the missing current state or roll the group back to a common recovery point. Training resumes only after that consistency check.
When the missing state can be reconstructed at the survivors’ current step, warm restart avoids a full-cluster reload and repeated warmup. For the 1,024 GPUs example, that fast path avoids rereading the full 2.45 TB checkpoint through shared storage, whose cold-path \(\CheckpointLoadTime\) is 24.5 s. The replacement still needs state transfer and initialization, and all ranks wait until it is ready. If consistency instead requires a rollback, the recovery budget must include the corresponding survivor-state restoration and lost work.
The trade-off is software complexity. Survivor-preserving warm restarts require specialized application and runtime support for dynamic membership changes without leaking CUDA memory, corrupting shared state, or deadlocking during communicator reconstruction. PyTorch’s elastic framework (TorchElastic) does not preserve worker processes across membership changes: it stops the surviving workers and starts a new worker group. DeepSpeed’s documented recovery path is checkpoint-centered rather than a survivor-preserving warm restart. A deployment that implements a warm-restart fast path still needs cold restart as a safety net. The cold-restart range in table 8 brackets the 6.4 min budget computed above. The warm-restart range is a planning range for the fast path, which avoids the full-cluster reload and warmup; its actual duration depends on how quickly the replacement receives its state and the communicator is rebuilt.

At the scale of 10,000+ GPUs, failures occur multiple times per day, so human operators cannot intervene manually on each incident. Recovery must be an autonomous control loop managed by the cluster control plane. Published reports from large training fleets describe multi-stage automation that classifies failures and selects the minimum viable remediation (Dubey et al. 2024; Kokolis et al. 2025; Zu et al. 2024).
The pipeline operates in four ordered stages:

Health monitoring daemon: Continuously scrapes GPU telemetry (ECC error counters, temperature, fan speed, NVLink status) alongside application metrics like training loss and step throughput, often from a sidecar container.
Failure classifier: Determines whether a signal indicates a fatal error (for example, NVIDIA Xid error 48: double-bit ECC error), a transient stall (for example, temporary network congestion), or a performance degradation (for example, thermal throttling).
Action selector: Chooses the cheapest response consistent with the affected state and communication group. A process hang on one rank usually requires restarting the whole communication group rather than one container, because every surviving rank still holds a communicator that includes the hung rank. A confirmed hardware fault requires draining the node and drawing a replacement from the spare pool, which is slower and consumes standby capacity. A network partition can justify a bounded wait that preserves in-memory state, but if the wait expires, replacement must fence the old ownership before accepting new writes.
Validation stage: Runs a recorded “canary batch” or validation workload under the expected numerical tolerance. Unexpected loss or gradient behavior triggers investigation of restored state and execution configuration, with fallback to an earlier validated snapshot when the new state cannot be trusted.

This automation shortens mean time to recovery from the tens of minutes that a page-diagnose-repair cycle takes when a human is in the loop to minutes for the common failure types. The Llama 3 team reports that automated tooling handled nearly all of the 419 interruptions in its 54-day snapshot (Dubey et al. 2024). The classification stage is critical. Treating every failure as a cold restart wastes compute on transient issues, while treating a hardware failure as transient allows corrupted computation to continue.




Definition 7.2: Straggler
Straggler is a worker in a distributed training job that processes tasks significantly slower than its peers, creating a synchronization bottleneck.

Significance: In a bulk synchronous parallel system, cluster throughput is bounded by the speed of the slowest rank. A single 10 percent performance drop on one node can reduce the effective compute capacity of thousands of nodes by 10 percent.
Distinction: The synchronization models of Synchronization models treat a straggler as a throughput problem; fault tolerance must also separate slow progress from a stopped participant. A straggler can produce correct results while delaying its peers. Slowness alone establishes neither incorrect values nor a failed process.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that stragglers are caused only by “bad hardware.” In reality, they are often caused by system jitter from background OS processes, network congestion, or thermal throttling that varies across the data center floor.



In synchronous training, a straggler sets the pace of the entire cluster, because AllReduce cannot complete until every rank has submitted its gradients.
For the simplified no-overlap straggler model, the step time becomes: \[ \StragglerStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \max(\FirstRankComputeTime, \SecondRankComputeTime, \dots, \LastRankComputeTime) + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) \]
Many stragglers are gray failures, the silent degradations of the chapter opening, seen from inside a synchronous job, and none of their common causes raises an explicit error. Thermal throttling reduces clock speed, degrading interconnect cables increase communication latency, OS background processes (memory scrubbing, log rotation) consume CPU cycles, and data loading from a congested network filesystem introduces variable I/O delays. A slow worker can continue meeting a liveness timeout while reducing training throughput, or become slow enough to trigger the same timeout as a failed worker. Progress measurements are therefore needed alongside liveness checks.
The challenge is distinguishing stragglers from failures. Stragglers should trigger mitigation (redistribute work, replace the slow node). Failures should trigger recovery (checkpoint-restart). Aggressive timeouts treat stragglers as failures, causing unnecessary job restarts that waste more compute than the straggler itself. Conservative timeouts waste compute waiting for stragglers that will never speed up.
Straggler mitigation strategies change either the work assignment or the execution resources. Dynamic load balancing moves work away from slow workers while preserving the intended update, whereas bounded staleness allows delayed gradients under an algorithm that tolerates them; its convergence cost depends on the workload and delay bound. Backup workers replicate selected tasks and accept one result per logical contribution, trading extra GPU cycles for a shorter wait without double-counting gradients. At the infrastructure boundary, proactive replacement uses hardware telemetry, such as rising operating temperatures or growing correctable-ECC error counts, to identify suspect components and replace them when the expected benefit exceeds migration and recovery costs.
A simple cost calculation shows why a severe straggler may be cheaper to replace than tolerate.



One straggler stalls every healthy peer at the barrier.

Napkin Math 7.5: The straggler taxConsider a 1,024-GPU cluster where a normal training iteration takes 1 second. A single GPU enters a thermally throttled state, clocking down to 50 percent speed, and now takes 2 seconds to complete its computation.
Because AllReduce cannot complete until every rank has submitted its gradients, the other 1,023 healthy GPUs sit idle waiting for the straggler.
Impact:

Normal step time: 1 second
Straggler step time: 2 seconds
Effective cluster speed: 1 step/2s = 0.5 steps/sec

A single failing device (0.1 percent of the hardware) has reduced the throughput of the entire cluster by 50 percent. At $3/GPU-hour, this straggler wastes $1,536/hour in idle compute.
Systems insight: Replacement is worthwhile only when the expected time saved exceeds recovery and replay costs. If the slowdown is expected to persist for the next \(\SlowdownPersistenceUpdateCount\) useful updates, whose step times are \(\DegradedStepTime\) on the degraded allocation and \(\HealthyStepTime\) after replacement, the simplified break-even condition is \(\SlowdownPersistenceUpdateCount(\DegradedStepTime-\HealthyStepTime) > \JobRestartTime+ \LostWorkReplayTime\). The right side includes waiting for capacity and restoring state. A short-lived slowdown may clear before replacement pays off; false-positive detection and uncertain persistence also affect the decision. MTBF describes failure recurrence, not how long this slowdown will last.


Replacing a slow node while maintaining the original GPU count requires available capacity. An \(\DeviceCount+1\) redundancy model reserves a hot spare for the isolation and promotion stages of figure 10, reducing allocation delay. Promotion still requires compatible resources, valid state, and communication-group reconstruction; an idle device alone does not guarantee recovery within seconds. A cold spare adds startup work, while a job without a reserved spare depends on the scheduler finding capacity or on repair. The hot spare buys shorter waiting time with devices that sit idle while the fleet is healthy. Fixed-size checkpoint-restart recovery restores the original resource count. Elastic recovery relaxes that requirement by allowing the job to continue with fewer workers when the remaining allocation can support it.

Suppose a 1,024-GPU training job loses an 8-GPU node to a hardware fault, but the cluster has no spare nodes available. A fixed-size recovery policy leaves the remaining 1,016 GPUs waiting until replacement capacity becomes available or the allocation is released. Elastic recovery allows the job to resize and continue with less compute, provided its state and parallel decomposition fit the smaller allocation.

Definition 7.3: Elastic training
Elastic training is the capability of a distributed training job to adjust its worker count across membership changes, potentially through a coordinated worker-group restart.

Significance: It converts a permanent capacity loss into a temporary interruption followed by reduced throughput. A pure data-parallel 1,024-GPU job that loses 8 GPUs retains 99.2 percent of its device count and may resume if the remaining devices can hold the state. Tensor- and pipeline-parallel jobs additionally need a feasible partition and compatible group sizes; retained device count does not guarantee the same fraction of throughput. The recovery policy must either preserve the effective batch size through additional accumulation or validate the optimization changes caused by a smaller batch.
Distinction: Unlike fixed-size checkpoint-restart recovery, which waits for replacement hardware to restore the original allocation, elastic recovery can restart or resume with a different worker count. The optimization loop may pause while membership, ranks, and state are re-established.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that elasticity is “automatic.” In reality, recovery requires coordinated adaptation: the training framework, the data loader, and the orchestrator must all synchronize their state to ensure that no data samples are lost or double-counted during the resize.



A small example shows the lifecycle in three phases (figure 15). Execution begins with a balanced four-node AllReduce ring at full throughput. When Node 3 drops out, the survivors pause at a rendezvous barrier and reload the last consistent checkpoint. The group then contracts into a three-node ring in which each worker takes a one-third larger data shard, resuming productive training at 75 percent throughput if the per-worker rate remains unchanged.







Figure 15: Elastic training recovery: Read the three phases top to bottom. Rather than restoring the original worker count before resuming, elastic training pauses when a node fails, reloads the last consistent checkpoint, re-forms the ring over the \(\DeviceCount-1\) survivors, and redistributes the failed node’s data shards among them. The job resumes at reduced throughput (75 percent here, assuming an unchanged per-worker rate), turning a hard failure into a temporary slowdown.





Shedding a lost node narrows the active ring instead of idling the whole allocation until replacement hardware arrives, so elastic recovery converts a job termination into a bounded capacity adjustment. The worker group may restart while the framework re-establishes membership, ranks, and state under the smaller resource allocation. When a failure reduces the worker count, the recovery path must adapt several training components before productive work resumes. Each adaptation addresses a specific consistency requirement that, if violated, would corrupt the model or waste computation.
Batch size adjustment is the first concern: with fewer workers, each worker must process more samples to maintain the global batch size, or the global batch size must be reduced. Reducing global batch size during recovery may require learning rate adjustment to preserve convergence properties.
Changing the global batch size changes the optimization regime as well as the amount of work per step. The linear scaling rule of Learning rate scaling rules multiplies the learning rate by the same factor as the batch size (Goyal et al. 2017), but its validation with warmup for growing batches does not establish a universal recovery rule. The same section’s square-root rule offers another candidate policy, and equation 12 restates it for a resized job, with learning rate \(\LearningRate\) and the batch ratio written as a worker-count ratio:

Goyal, Priya, Piotr Dollár, Ross Girshick, Pieter Noordhuis, Lukasz Wesolowski, Aapo Kyrola, Andrew Tulloch, Yangqing Jia, and Kaiming He. 2017. “Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1706.02677 abs/1706.02677.
\[ \ScaledLearningRate= \BaseLearningRate\times \sqrt{\frac{\ResizedWorkerCount}{\BaseWorkerCount}}  \tag{12}\]
where \(\ResizedWorkerCount\) and \(\BaseWorkerCount\) represent the resized and base counts of data-parallel workers, with per-worker microbatch size and accumulation count held fixed so global batch size scales directly with worker count. For a shrink, the square-root rule reduces the learning rate less than linear scaling does; that arithmetic does not establish which policy is more stable. Either policy requires validation for the optimizer, schedule, and workload. Preserving the global batch instead can avoid introducing this change in optimization regime.
Gradient accumulation offers that alternative: each surviving worker processes additional micro-batches before synchronization to maintain the original effective batch size. If worker count drops by half, doubling the accumulation steps preserves the number of examples per update and can retain the existing learning-rate schedule. Each worker then performs twice as much micro-batch computation per update, although communication and overlap determine the wall-time increase. Equal batch size does not imply bitwise-identical updates or identical behavior from operations that depend on micro-batch statistics.
Data loader redistribution must agree with the recovered training step and new membership. When workers are lost, the loader reassigns the remaining logical input stream so that the resize itself neither omits samples nor counts them twice in an update. Replaying work discarded by checkpoint rollback is expected; duplicating contributions within the resumed stream is a different error. The saved data position and sampling state distinguish those cases.
State resharding adds further complexity when using sharded model parallelism (ZeRO/FSDP), because the loss of a worker can remove the only live copy of its state shard. A surviving replica can supply that shard; otherwise recovery must reconstruct it from sufficient retained information or reload a complete checkpoint generation. Only then can the system redistribute valid state across the surviving workers. Changing shard ownership alone cannot recover missing values.


Hardware faults are not the only event that removes workers from a running job. Cloud providers often price preemptible (“spot”) instances below on-demand capacity, with the caveat that they can be reclaimed with little warning. Once workers vanish, recovery faces the same missing-state and membership problems as a hardware failure. An advance notice, when available, can allow a coordinated save or drain before departure and therefore changes the recovery opportunity.
Both fixed-size and elastic jobs can recover from preemption using checkpoints, but a fixed-size job must regain its required allocation before restarting. An elastic job can instead resume at reduced scale if enough capacity remains and the training invariants survive the resize. Recovery still pays for detection, state restoration, and group reconstruction; repeated reclamations can erase the apparent price advantage. In a scenario where spot capacity costs $0.60/hour instead of $3.00/hour, the savings can outweigh the lost work and resizing delays; Spot instances and preemptible VMs develops the full spot-versus-on-demand cost model.
Spot capacity makes worker departure frequent; federated training makes it the default.

Lighthouse 7.2: Archetype C (Federated MobileNet): Dropout as the normal caseArchetype C (Federated MobileNet) makes worker departure an expected part of training. Its phone-class clients train while charging, idle, and connected, so a client that disappears mid-round is an ordinary event rather than a fault to repair. The coordinator therefore selects more clients than a round needs and closes the round at a deadline. The round tolerates departures as long as enough compatible updates arrive; otherwise the coordinator abandons it (McMahan et al. 2017; Bonawitz et al. 2019). Model-version checks prevent updates computed against a replaced model from entering the current aggregate, the federated counterpart of fencing a stale epoch, while aggregation weights account for the examples contributed under the chosen learning algorithm. Version checks and weighting do not remove participation bias. Recovery must preserve the coordinator state needed to continue that algorithm, including the model, round position, and any persistent optimizer or sampling state, rather than assuming weights alone suffice. Client scheduling develops the round design, including deadlines, participation requirements, and the bias that arises when some kinds of devices report less often than others.

McMahan, Brendan, Eider Moore, Daniel Ramage, Seth Hampson, and Blaise Agüera y Arcas. 2017. “Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data.” International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 54: 1273–82.



The framework question is which resize invariants it can enforce automatically: group membership, shard ownership, data coverage, and batch math. The recovery adaptation mechanisms (batch size adjustment, learning rate recalibration, data loader redistribution, state resharding) must be implemented by the training framework, and frameworks differ in how much of this recovery logic they automate after a failure.
PyTorch Elastic (TorchElastic) uses agents to monitor workers and a rendezvous mechanism to establish group membership (PyTorch Contributors 2026b, 2026a). On a failure or membership change, TorchElastic stops all surviving workers, forms a new worker group, and starts its workers with new RANK and WORLD_SIZE assignments. It handles rank reassignment and communication-group reconstruction after restart, but leaves batch size, learning rate, and checkpoint semantics to user code.

PyTorch Contributors. 2026a. Torch Distributed Elastic Rendezvous. PyTorch documentation.
DeepSpeed (Rasley et al. 2020) provides ZeRO-based distributed training and checkpointing building blocks for large models (DeepSpeed Developers 2026a). Its recovery model is checkpoint-based: after a failure, the job reloads from the last durable checkpoint, and Universal Checkpointing addresses portability across some changes in parallelism and topology (DeepSpeed Developers 2026b). The elastic behavior still depends on the surrounding launcher and resource manager rather than being made transparent by the framework alone.
Ray Train, built on Ray’s actor model, provides a checkpoint-oriented recovery path for worker failure and node preemption. Ray can restart a worker group after a failure and resume from the latest available checkpoint, while the training function remains responsible for saving and loading sufficient state (Ray Project 2026).

When the worker group changes, Horovod can reset ranks and reconstruct communication, while the training script remains responsible for convergence-sensitive choices such as learning-rate or batch-size policy.

While these frameworks automate the mechanics of recovery, deciding exactly which model state must be preserved and resharded remains a workload-specific engineering choice.




The checkpoint and recovery strategies developed in section 7.13 and section 7.14 require adaptation because workloads lose different kinds of state when they fail. Section 7.7 priced those differences as failure costs; here they become checkpoint contents. The design question is therefore not simply how often to checkpoint, but which state variable would make a restart mathematically or economically wrong. For recommendation workloads, incremental checkpointing, tiered checkpointing, and embedding versioning can reduce the cost of preserving fresh state. Incremental storage can still reconstruct an exact generation from a base and its required deltas; accepting stale or approximate state is a separate choice. The common pattern is that recovery correctness is broader than weight restoration. LLMs can reload weights but resume with the wrong curriculum position; recommendation models can reload dense parameters but serve stale embeddings; vision models can reload weights but alter augmentation or normalization state; and scientific models can reload a neural network while losing the simulator state that made the data meaningful.
Elasticity and checkpointing provide the necessary resilience for long-running batch training jobs, but the operational calculus changes completely once the model is deployed to users. The challenge shifts from protecting weeks of batch computation to protecting milliseconds of real-time latency.

When users ask a voice assistant to turn off the lights, they will not tolerate a five-minute pause while the inference server reloads from a checkpoint. Serving models presents a fundamentally different challenge, because users expect millisecond-level responsiveness even when backend GPUs crash. The C³ budget for fault tolerance shifts accordingly. Training pays for coordination in synchronization time so that a failure does not erase completed compute, while serving pays in standing redundant compute and in routing coordination so that a failure does not break a latency contract.
A serving replica is a runnable copy of the model that can accept requests; the routing layer chooses a replica, and a readiness check determines whether that replica can serve successfully. Replicas may share external state stores or keep request state in accelerator memory, so replacing compute does not necessarily replace the state a request needs. Serving fault tolerance asks how those mechanisms behave when replicas, GPUs, or state stores fail under live latency budgets. The focus here is narrower than a complete serving architecture: each mechanism is treated as a reliability boundary for real-time inference.


The first serving decision is where request state lives, because that choice determines whether failover is a retry or a state-reconstruction problem. A stateless model worker retains no required per-session state between requests. It obtains the necessary context from the request or an external state store, so another ready worker can process the same request. A stateful application can therefore use stateless model workers, although its external store remains a reliability dependency.
The stateless pattern appears when the input itself carries all context: an image classifier processes one image, an object detector processes one frame, a single-turn text classifier processes one snippet, and an embedding service maps one input to one vector. Fault tolerance can then focus on replica health and request routing. Redundant replicas serve requests in parallel, load balancing sends traffic only to healthy replicas, health checks remove failed replicas from rotation, and automatic replacement starts a new replica when capacity falls. When a replica fails, in-flight requests to that replica can be retried elsewhere, because no quality-bearing session state has been lost.
Stateless serving offers the simpler architecture when the application permits it. However, many ML applications inherently require state across requests. Consider a chatbot: a single-turn question-answering system can operate statelessly, processing each question independently. A conversational assistant must preserve its history somewhere, but the model worker can still be stateless if each request carries the complete history or reads it from a durable external store. Worker-local state creates a stronger dependency when later requests rely on information available only at the selected replica.
Stateful serving appears when later work depends on retained session state. For a transformer, the key-value (KV) cache stores attention keys and values computed for earlier tokens so the worker can reuse them while generating subsequent tokens. This cache is derived state: if the authoritative token history and compatible model version remain available, a replacement can recompute it by processing that history again. Losing the history itself is a different failure because cache reconstruction no longer has its required input. Streaming speech recognition similarly maintains context from previous audio, recommendation sessions accumulate user context, and interactive editing maintains document state across edits. The fault-tolerance consequence is that failure loses quality-bearing state rather than serving capacity alone. KV cache loss requires reprocessing previous turns, session context loss forces users to repeat previous interactions, and accumulated user state loss degrades quality when context is unavailable. The mitigation choice follows the size, update rate, and quality value of that state: session affinity routes a session to the same replica, state checkpointing periodically saves session state, state replication maintains a standby copy, and graceful degradation keeps the service available at reduced quality if state cannot be recovered.
