Why does Google’s TPUv4 recovery design combine OCS-based replacement of unhealthy cubes with fault-tolerant routing for supported link-outage patterns?

Because TPU chips have zero local memory and cannot execute software routing algorithms.
Because optical circuit switches are cheaper than standard copper Ethernet cables for intra-rack links.
A machine outage can remove a required job participant, requiring a healthy replacement cube; a link outage can instead require a supported alternate communication path. The response must preserve the job’s communication topology.
Because OCS switches completely eliminate the need for checkpointing during multi-month training jobs.

Answer: The correct answer is C. OCS allows the recovery system to assemble job-sized slices from healthy spare cubes after machine outages. Fault-tolerant routing handles supported OCS outage patterns when alternate paths remain available. Replacing a participant and repairing a communication path are distinct responses; neither follows from the failed-device count alone. The other choices misrepresent memory architecture or economics, or incorrectly eliminate checkpointing.
Learning Objective: Analyze how optical circuit switching enables topology-preserving fault tolerance in tightly coupled accelerator pods.
During the training of Meta’s OPT-175B model on 992 A100 GPUs, describe how the team addressed both physical hardware failures and mathematical loss spikes.
Answer: For physical hardware failures (at least 35 manual and an estimated 70+ automatic restarts over two months from ECC memory errors, network issues, and lost GPUs), the team relied on restart from the latest checkpoint, with train-log freshness monitoring (a 15-minute threshold, later relaxed to one hour) contributing to detection delay; polling and response could extend the idle window. For mathematical loss spikes (numerical divergence and gradient overflow), the team rolled back to an earlier clean checkpoint and resumed with a reduced learning rate (ultimately roughly two-thirds of GPT-3’s rate). The two remedies differ, which is why the run had to retain checkpoint history rather than only its newest snapshot.
Learning Objective: Compare physical hardware fault recovery and algorithmic numerical divergence recovery in large-scale LLM training.
What fundamental principle of ML serving resilience is demonstrated by Netflix’s chaos engineering practice?

Resilience is an active practice of continuous verification: intentionally injecting latency, terminating feature caches, and simulating dependency outages under controlled conditions to empirically verify that fallback hierarchies function before real outages occur.
Fault tolerance code should only be executed during unplanned production disasters to minimize server load.
Machine learning models should never rely on external feature stores or databases.
Chaos testing is only applicable to CPU-based web servers and cannot be used in GPU inference clusters.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Netflix’s chaos engineering principles establish that fault tolerance mechanisms (such as model fallbacks, circuit breakers, and feature defaults) rot if left unexercised. Regularly injecting synthetic faults in production and staging verifies that fallback paths actually satisfy latency and availability SLOs when real dependencies fail. The other options contradict chaos engineering principles or assert false restrictions on ML systems.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the role of chaos engineering and active failure injection in validating ML serving fallback paths.
Explain how Microsoft DeepSpeed coordinates ZeRO sharded optimizer states with persistent checkpointing to achieve fault tolerance during distributed training on massive models.
Answer: ZeRO partitions optimizer state, gradients and parameters at different stages; ZeRO-3 partitions all three. A lost worker can remove a required live shard, so recovery needs another valid copy or a durable checkpoint. Distributed checkpointing writes the required state shards, while the launcher restores a valid worker group. Universal Checkpointing supports selected changes in parallelism and topology; training code still owns sufficient state capture, input coverage and batch policy.
Learning Objective: Evaluate state persistence and recovery mechanisms in ZeRO-sharded distributed training frameworks.

Self-Check: Answer

An engineering team operates a 1,000-GPU training cluster with a system MTBF of 50 hours (\(3{,}000\text{ minutes}\)) and a checkpoint write time of 5 minutes. The team intuitively chooses to checkpoint ‘every 15 minutes to stay safe.’ According to the Young-Daly formula, what is the mathematically optimal interval, and what is the consequence of the team’s intuitive choice?

Optimal interval is 15 minutes; the intuitive choice is mathematically perfect.
The first-order optimum is approximately 173 minutes (~2.9 hours); writing every 15 minutes adds more checkpoint overhead than it saves in expected rework under this model.
Optimal interval is 50 hours; checkpointing every 15 minutes causes disk sectors to wear out in days.
Optimal interval is 1 minute; checkpointing every 15 minutes risks losing 100% of the training dataset.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Applying the Young-Daly formula: \(\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot T_{\text{write}} \cdot \text{MTBF}_{\text{system}}} = \sqrt{2 \times 5 \times 3000} = \sqrt{30{,}000} \approx 173.2\text{ minutes}\) (approx. 2.9 hours). Setting an interval of 15 minutes deviates by more than an order of magnitude, spending massive cluster time on unnecessary storage writes. The 15-minute, 50-hour, and 1-minute options misapply the square-root law or make exaggerated failure claims. A stricter recovery point objective can justify a shorter interval even when it increases expected waste.
Learning Objective: Calculate Young-Daly optimal intervals to demonstrate why intuition-based checkpoint scheduling causes excessive I/O overhead.
Explain what a GPU-only independent-failure estimate, \(\mathrm{MTBF}_{\mathrm{system}}=\mathrm{MTBF}_{\mathrm{component}}/N\), omits about shared failure domains and their recovery consequences.
Answer: The independent-component formula omits separate shared failure modes such as power or switch outages, and it says nothing about their blast radius. Add those fault domains and their recovery consequences explicitly. Correlation alone does not necessarily increase the count of distinct incidents for fixed marginal component rates; a shared outage can group many component failures into one large event.
Learning Objective: Justify why independent component reliability models fail to capture the risk and blast radius of correlated infrastructure failures.
Why does adding more GPUs (\(N\)) to a distributed training job eventually encounter a ‘reliability ceiling’ where total wall-clock training time increases rather than decreases?

Because GPUs consume more electrical power than data center transformers can supply.
Because floating-point numbers lose precision when divided across more than 1,000 workers.
Because the Python interpreter cannot spawn more than 512 concurrent threads.
Because aggregate cluster failure rate scales linearly (\(N\lambda\)), shrinking system MTBF until the cumulative time lost to failure detection, job restarts, checkpoint loading, and rework exceeds the marginal compute speedup of additional parallelism.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Under independent failures, adding workers increases the aggregate failure rate. Recovery and replay can eventually cost more than the marginal compute speedup. Starting from single-node MFU, scaling efficiency accounts for distributed execution losses; a separate retained-progress factor covers excluded recovery losses. Measured distributed MFU already includes scaling losses and must not be multiplied by scaling efficiency again.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the reliability ceiling where aggregate cluster failure overhead outpaces parallel compute scaling.
Because modern accelerator hardware incorporates hardware ECC on High Bandwidth Memory and CRC on interconnects, application-level gradient checksums and loss validation checks are redundant and unnecessary in 10,000-GPU clusters.
Answer: False. ECC and CRC protect the error patterns covered by their implementations within storage and transport boundaries. They do not validate arbitrary arithmetic or software transformations. Checksums test byte integrity or agreement, while replay, independent computation, invariants and statistical checks provide different evidence about computed results. Coverage must match the declared fault model; no single check establishes end-to-end correctness.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the limitations of hardware ECC and justify the necessity of end-to-end software verification against silent data corruption.

Self-Check: Answer

What is the fundamental architectural distinction between distributed training fault tolerance and real-time model serving fault tolerance?

Training fault tolerance only operates on CPUs, whereas serving fault tolerance only operates on GPUs.
Training fault tolerance requires \(100\%\) uptime with zero dropped packets, whereas serving fault tolerance tolerates hours of total outage.
Training preserves accumulated progress through valid checkpoints and a recovery budget; interactive serving needs ready alternate capacity and required request context within its latency budget, or a validated fallback.
Training fault tolerance relies exclusively on active-active replication, whereas serving fault tolerance relies exclusively on cold disk restarts.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Training recovery preserves valid model, optimizer and input-stream state while budgeting lost work and recovery delay. Interactive serving has a much shorter request deadline, so it needs ready capacity and a policy to reconstruct, replicate or abandon derived state. Stateless requests need no session migration; stateful requests may require context recovery. Validated degradation applies when full service cannot meet the budget. The other choices misstate hardware or recovery requirements.
Learning Objective: Compare fundamental architectural requirements and latency budgets between training and serving fault tolerance.
Evaluate how the three core mechanisms of ML systems resilience—checkpointing, elastic recovery, and redundancy—complement one another to bound the financial and computational cost of hardware failures.
Answer: Checkpointing preserves recoverable training state and limits rework according to the age of the latest valid checkpoint. Elastic recovery permits progress with fewer workers when the algorithm and available memory support resizing. Independent serving replicas provide alternate capacity after a failure. These mechanisms complement one another, but their checkpoint validity, resize cost, state recovery, and failover latency must all satisfy the recovery contract.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the complementary roles of checkpointing, elastic recovery, and redundancy in large-scale ML infrastructure.
Once automated checkpointing and failover mechanisms are implemented and passed initial unit testing, fault tolerance code paths can be assumed to operate reliably in production without ongoing fault injection or recovery drills.
Answer: False. Fault tolerance mechanisms are rarely executed during normal operations and easily rot as software frameworks, CUDA versions, cluster topologies, and model architectures evolve. Production resilience requires continuous validation through automated chaos engineering and regular recovery drills to ensure fallback and restart paths function during real emergencies.
Learning Objective: Justify the principle that fault tolerance must be continuously exercised and validated in production systems.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why does scale transform hardware failure from rare exception to routine condition that systems must absorb continuously?
A single accelerator can run for years between hardware failures. A thousand accelerators turn that same component risk into failures every couple of days, and ten thousand see failures every few hours, while shared power and network faults can interrupt many workers at once. Individual devices need not become less reliable for the fleet to experience failures routinely. A program on one machine can often stop and restart when a component fails; a distributed training job must also recover agreement among surviving workers about which progress remains valid. Restarting quickly is of little value if the restored state silently changes the computation. Preserving more state reduces the work at risk, but consumes storage bandwidth and memory while the job is healthy. Waiting longer between saves reduces that overhead while increasing the progress a failure can erase. Serving imposes a different consequence: users may abandon a request before recovery completes, and replacing a worker may leave the request’s context unavailable. A response that arrives on time can still be unacceptable if recovery has discarded information needed to produce it. Engineers must therefore bound lost work and recovery delay while preserving the validity of training and the usefulness of service. The goal is continued useful execution despite repeated failures, with the costs and limits of recovery made explicit. In C³ terms, fault tolerance spends compute and communication on coordination so that component failures do not routinely become failures of the entire workload.

Learning Objectives

Calculate mean time between fleet failures from component rates and estimate interruption frequency for large training clusters
Classify hardware, software, and silent-data-corruption failures by detectability, blast radius, and recovery path
Select checkpoint intervals that balance write overhead against acceptable lost work and recovery delay
Design distributed checkpointing and elastic recovery plans for multi-terabyte model state across GPU fleets
Design serving redundancy, failover, and state-recovery policies under latency budgets and partial failures
Select graceful degradation strategies that preserve useful service when models, features, regions, or capacity fail
Evaluate fault injection and observability evidence to validate detection, isolation, and recovery behavior

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Imagine a 10,000-GPU cluster midway through a three-month training run for a new foundation model. The communication layer has done its job, and thousands of devices exchange gradients through AllReduce, AllGather, and AllToAll as if they were one machine. Then the arithmetic of scale catches up. A GPU fails every few hours, and if the system cannot absorb that ordinary physical event, synchronized training halts and millions of dollars of compute sit idle. Fault tolerance is the system property that lets distributed execution continue making useful progress when components fail, degrade, or disappear. In the Fleet Stack of The Fleet Stack, fault tolerance occupies the Reliability & Control row of the Distribution band, where it protects the progress that parallelism and communication produce.
That fragility is the direct consequence of successful synchronization. Every collective in Collective Communication assumed that all ranks in its process group arrive, and each dependent consumer waits for every contribution. One stalled device can therefore stop progress in its synchronous training group, even while unrelated jobs continue elsewhere in the fleet. Fault-tolerant ML systems preserve progress by detecting failure, checkpointing recoverable state, restarting or elastically reshaping jobs, and treating hardware churn as normal execution rather than an exceptional path. That reliability envelope covers both halves of the fleet’s work. Training needs recovery that preserves weeks of accumulated progress, while serving needs redundancy, failover, and graceful degradation that preserve a latency contract, and both draw their spare capacity from a shared fleet pool.


↪ How the scheduler holds spare capacity for failed jobs and prepositions replacement nodes while a missed heartbeat is confirmed is developed in Failure Rates at Scale.
The failures to be absorbed differ first in how long they persist, from a transient bit flip that clears on its own, through an intermittent error that returns under the load that exposed it, to a permanent component failure that repeats on every retry. That persistence decides whether the fleet retries, quarantines, or replaces a component (section 7.9.1). Failures also differ in how visibly they announce themselves. A gray failure is a component that stays alive but runs slowly or erratically, so it keeps answering the liveness checks that would flag a crash while every peer that waits on it slows down. Silent data corruption (SDC) goes further, producing wrong values with no error at all. Both pair low detection rates with a high blast radius, because the system keeps running on state it should no longer trust.
The recovery target here is trustworthy execution: preserving valid training progress and restoring a service after its infrastructure or software fails. A restored model can still make poor predictions on changed inputs even when every component executes correctly. Evaluating that behavioral robustness requires a separate contract for model quality under distribution shifts and adversarial inputs, developed in Robust AI. The distinction lets us use model-quality signals to diagnose a fault without treating every quality regression as evidence of failed hardware.
Because failures cannot be eliminated at this scale, fault-tolerant systems verify completion rather than assume it, treat failure as a normal code path, exercise recovery continuously, and account for partial failures that naive error handling may not anticipate. These techniques draw on decades of distributed systems research, but ML workloads change the economics. Training checkpoints are large but can be sized from the model and optimizer state, while some optimization algorithms tolerate bounded numerical perturbations without requiring bitwise replay. That tolerance must be established for the training method; stochasticity does not make arbitrary corruption or inconsistent recovery safe. A recovery design can exploit approximate execution only while preserving its declared convergence and quality requirements.
The transition from small-scale experimentation to large-scale production changes the relationship between systems and failures. A researcher training a model on a single GPU can go years without a hardware failure. That same workload on a 1,000-GPU cluster sees GPU-only failures every couple of days, and a production cluster fails more often once PCIe, power, storage, and network domains enter the failure budget. This shift from rare exception to routine occurrence demands different engineering approaches. The mathematical analysis that follows makes this transition precise and quantitative.



Fleet mean time between failures (MTBF) collapses from 50,000 h to 5 h as GPUs multiply.

Self-Check: Question

A production cluster operates 10,000 GPUs, where each individual GPU exhibits an independent MTTF of 50,000 hours and an availability of 99.99%. What is the resulting GPU-only cluster MTBF, and what is the probability that all 10,000 GPUs are simultaneously operational at any random instant?

Cluster MTBF is 50 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 90.5%.
Cluster MTBF is 500 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 99.0%.
Cluster MTBF is 5.0 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 36.8%.
Cluster MTBF is 0.5 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 1.0%.

Using an illustrative unprotected-memory soft-error rate of 250 FIT/Mbit and 80 GiB of HBM per device, explain why a 1,024-GPU training cluster needs ECC protection.
Because electronic components exhibit a constant failure rate during their useful life phase under the exponential reliability model, cluster operators should assign newly delivered accelerator nodes directly to multi-week foundation model pretraining runs without prior burn-in testing.
Sequence the following failure domains in ascending order of their physical containment hierarchy and typical blast radius (from smallest number of affected GPUs to largest):


Top-of-rack (ToR) switch failure isolating 32–64 GPUs
Single GPU hardware lockup affecting 1 GPU
Multi-rack Power Distribution Unit (PDU) failure affecting 100–500 GPUs
Node-level power loss (a fault that exhausts a node’s redundant PSUs) affecting 8 GPUs
Regional power grid disruption affecting all GPUs in a data center


During a distributed AllReduce operation, a single GPU rank experiences a silent bit flip in an exponent calculation. The rank does not crash, passes network timeouts, and contributes an anomalously large gradient to the collective average. How is this failure categorized, and what is its primary danger to the training run?

Byzantine failure; it silently poisons model weights and gradients while bypassing standard process-liveness and timeout detection.
Fail-stop failure; it immediately halts the AllReduce collective and triggers an automated container restart.
Transient network failure; it is automatically corrected by underlying InfiniBand packet retransmission protocols.
Benign gray failure; it is absorbed by stochastic gradient descent with zero impact on final convergence.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
System reliability engineering provides the foundational framework for understanding failure at scale (Birolini 2017). Individual components exhibit failure rates characterized by the failure rate parameter \(\ComponentFailureRate\),1 measured in failures per unit time. For a single component with constant failure rate \(\ComponentFailureRate\), the probability of surviving without failure until time \(\TimeInstant\) follows an exponential distribution,2 as in equation 1:
1 Failure rate (\(\ComponentFailureRate\)): Expressed in FITs (Failures In Time), where 1 FIT equals one failure per billion device-hours. A data center GPU with a 50,000-hour mean time to failure has \(\text{FIT} = 20{,}000\), corresponding to \(\HourlyComponentFailureRate = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\) failures/hour. That seems negligible for one device but becomes dominant at fleet scale: a cluster with 10,000 GPUs accumulates 200,000,000 FITs from GPUs alone, translating to an expected GPU failure every 5 hours.2 Poisson process: A statistical model for events occurring independently at a constant average rate. In this model, event counts follow a Poisson distribution and waiting times follow an exponential distribution, giving the survival function \(\ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\). With independent identical component hazards, the probability of at least one failure in a 10,000-component cluster is \(1 - e^{-\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\). The aggregate hazard \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\) scales linearly with component count; the failure probability is nonlinear in both \(\RequiredComponentCount\) and \(\TimeInstant\), approaching \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant\) only when that product is small.\[ \ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}  \tag{1}\]


↪ The independence, exponential-lifetime, and Poisson results this failure arithmetic rests on are developed in Probability tools for failure analysis.
3 GPU MTTF variation: This chapter uses 50,000 hours as a planning constant for current data center GPUs (A100 and H100 class), not as a guarantee for every deployed GPU. Published fleet studies from Google TPUv4 pods and Meta GPU clusters report that field reliability depends on topology, cooling, workload, and operational practice (Zu et al. 2024; Kokolis et al. 2025; Dubey et al. 2024). The planning constant therefore anchors the arithmetic, while operators should substitute measured fleet rates when they have them.
Zu, Y., A. Ghaffarkhah, H.-V. Dang, B. Towles, S. Hand, S. Huda, A. Bello, et al. 2024. “Resiliency at Scale: Managing Google’s TPUv4 Machine Learning Supercomputer.” 21st USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 24), 761–74.

Kokolis, Apostolos, Michael Kuchnik, John Hoffman, Adithya Kumar, Parth Malani, Faye Ma, Zach DeVito, Shubho Sengupta, Kalyan Saladi, and Carole-Jean Wu. 2025. “Revisiting Reliability in Large-Scale Machine Learning Research Clusters.” 2025 IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 1259–74. https://doi.org/10.1109/hpca61900.2025.00096.

Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.
The expected time to failure of this component equals \(1/\ComponentFailureRate\). In this book’s convention, mean time to failure (MTTF) names a single component’s expected time to its first failure while MTBF names the repairable system’s expected operating time between successive failures, excluding recovery downtime. Under the constant-rate exponential model used here the two coincide numerically, and the fault-tolerance model uses MTTF for per-component constants and MTBF for composed system rates. Data center GPUs often use planning MTTF values in the tens of thousands of hours, with field behavior depending on operating conditions, cooling effectiveness, manufacturing variation, and workload stress.3 Component failure rates catalogs the reference per-component FIT and MTTF values (GPU, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), network interface card (NIC), power supply, PCIe switch, optical cable, ToR switch) that anchor these \(\ComponentFailureRate\) and FIT figures, so a reader can substitute the constant for any device and reproduce the rates used throughout the fault-tolerance analysis.
When multiple independent components operate in a system where any single failure causes system failure, equation 2 formalizes how system reliability becomes the product of individual component reliabilities:
\[ \SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = \prod_{i=1}^{\RequiredComponentCount} {\ComponentReliability}_i(\TimeInstant) = \prod_{i=1}^{\RequiredComponentCount} e^{-\ComponentFailureRate_i \TimeInstant}  \tag{2}\]
For \(\RequiredComponentCount\) identical components with individual failure rate \(\ComponentFailureRate\), equation 3 gives the identical-component simplification:
\[ \SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}  \tag{3}\]
The system failure rate becomes \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\), and equation 4 expresses how the system MTBF scales inversely with component count. This inverse scaling explains why per-device reliability that looks excellent in isolation erodes at cluster scale:
\[ \SystemMtbf = \frac{1}{\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate} = \frac{\ComponentMttf}{\RequiredComponentCount}  \tag{4}\]
The consequence is a gap between failure cadence and job length. At 10,000 GPUs, the GPU-only calculation gives an expected interval of 5 hours, so a training run measured in weeks accumulates dozens of expected failures and one measured in months accumulates hundreds. These are planning averages, not a schedule of incidents; a shorter job can finish without failure even when its expected failure count exceeds one. Once the expected time between failures falls below the length of the job, fault tolerance becomes part of the execution budget for long-running fleet work.
Scale and reliability diverge sharply across training generations. By pairing accelerator counts (left axis, log scale) with modeled system MTBF (opposing right axis), figure 1 tracks how training fleets expanded by four orders of magnitude from 2012 (AlexNet on two GPUs) to 2024 (Llama 3 on over 16,000 GPUs), driven by the compute budgets that scaling laws reward (AI Scaling Laws). Applying the same per-device planning rate across those sizes compresses system MTBF from tens of thousands of hours to under ten hours. The opposing axis illustrates the scaling model rather than a history of measured failure rates, showing why recovery becomes an active scheduling constraint.














Figure 1: The rise of fleet-scale training: Accelerator count for state-of-the-art training runs from 2012 to 2024, with system mean time between failures on the opposing axis. Cluster size rises about four orders of magnitude and system MTBF falls correspondingly, which is what turns fault tolerance from a reliability feature into a scheduling constraint.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
The GPU-only calculation of equation 4 supplies the scale intuition; a real training system then composes GPUs, HBM, links, power supplies, storage paths, and redundancy into one failure budget. Component rates are usually quoted in the FIT units introduced with the failure rate, so the 50,000-hour GPU contributes 20,000 FIT to whatever system contains it. The new question is how different component rates compose, and the composition rule depends on the redundancy structure and the independence assumptions. For series systems (for example, a node where all 8 GPUs must work), failure of any component fails the whole. With independent constant-rate failures, the reliabilities multiply as in equation 2, so the rates add even when the components differ: \[\SystemMtbf = \frac{1}{\sum \ComponentFailureRate_i}\] which is why the system failure rate grows linearly with component count while system MTBF falls in inverse proportion.
The same product governs instantaneous availability, a different quantity from the survival function \(\ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant)\). Availability \(\SteadyStateAvailability\) is the probability that a component is up at a randomly chosen instant, counting repairs, whereas \(\ComponentReliability(\TimeInstant)\) is the probability that it has not yet failed by time \(\TimeInstant\). If each GPU is independently up with probability \(\GpuAvailability\), all \(\RequiredComponentCount\) are up together with probability \((\GpuAvailability)^\RequiredComponentCount\), which is the reliability gap of equation 1.1 evaluated here for the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster. That power erodes even very reliable hardware once \(\RequiredComponentCount\) reaches fleet scale.

Napkin Math 7.1: The 9s of availabilityProblem: A cluster of 10,000 GPUs runs with each GPU at 99.99 percent availability (only 52.6 minutes of downtime per year). Assuming independent up/down states, what is the probability that the entire cluster is up at the same instant?
Math:

Single GPU availability probability \((\GpuAvailability)\): A GPU with 99.99 percent availability has an all-up probability \(\GpuAvailability=\) 0.9999 at a randomly chosen instant.
Cluster availability probability \((\ClusterAvailability)\): \(\ClusterAvailability= (\GpuAvailability)^{\RequiredComponentCount}\).
Result: \((\GpuAvailability)^{\RequiredComponentCount} \approx\) 0.37.

Systems insight: Even when each GPU is available 99.99 percent of the time, a 10,000-GPU cluster has only a 37 percent chance that every GPU is simultaneously available. Hardware reliability alone is insufficient; software must handle failures automatically.



Systems Perspective 7.1: Scale transforms failureA cluster of 10,000 GPUs turns a per-GPU MTTF of 50,000 hours into a system MTBF of 5 hours. For a repairable system, steady-state availability is \(\SteadyStateAvailability= \MeanTimeBetweenFailures/(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures+\MeanTimeToRepair)\), where mean time to recovery (MTTR) is the recovery interval. Cutting MTTR from 30 minutes to 5 minutes raises availability from 90.91 percent to 98.36 percent. This stationary two-state model assumes unconstrained repair capacity and complete outage; correlated incidents, repair contention, and degraded operation require direct measurement (Birolini 2017). Systems must engineer recovery, not merely improve components.


Engineering faster recovery is one response to that arithmetic; redundancy is the other. For parallel systems providing redundancy, suppose that any surviving component can satisfy the required service. With independent failures and no repair during the observation interval, the system survives until every component has failed: \[\SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{\RedundantComponentCount} (1 - {\ComponentReliability}_i(\TimeInstant))\]
Series composition is the training job’s problem, because a synchronous step needs every participant. Parallel composition is the serving fleet’s lever, and it returns when interchangeable replicas protect a latency contract. Both rules, however, describe whatever the model calls a component, and the fault rate assigned to that component depends on which protections sit inside it.

Lighthouse 7.1: Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Memory soft-error scaleComposition makes the distinction between raw faults and job interruptions essential. Memory soft-error rates are quoted per megabit of storage rather than per device, so the exposure grows with memory capacity. As an illustrative raw-bit-error budget, assume 250 FIT per megabit across 1,024 GPUs with 80 GB each, the size of the Archetype A reference cluster. The resulting interval between raw memory errors is roughly 20 seconds. This is not a measured job-failure interval. Error-correcting code (ECC) protection can correct covered error patterns before they affect computation, while detected uncorrectable errors and escaped corruption require different recovery paths. At that raw rate, unprotected memory in the reference cluster would corrupt training state many times per hour, so ECC is a precondition for large-scale training rather than an option. A fleet reliability budget therefore needs the residual job-interrupting and silent-corruption rates under its actual protection scheme; raw bit-error rates alone cannot establish whether memory, logic, or interconnect dominates.


These raw bit-error rates justify ECC, but they are not the interruption rates that set checkpoint cadence; the worked cascade that follows uses device MTTF values that already include the effect of that protection. The cascade also treats its GPU, PCIe, power, and network contributions as separate categories, so a measured whole-node rate that already includes those paths cannot be added to them again.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Consider a training cluster designed for large language model development, roughly ten times the 1,024-GPU Archetype A reference cluster, with the following specifications:

10,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs
Individual GPU MTTF: 50,000 hours
Each GPU connected to host via PCIe (MTTF: 200,000 hours)
Each node contains 8 GPUs fed by 6 power supply units (MTTF: 100,000 hours each) in 4+2 redundancy, so the node keeps full performance with any 2 of them failed
Network infrastructure per node (NIC, cables): MTTF 150,000 hours

Together, these components define the failure domain used in the rate calculations in this worked example.


Each GPU operates within a failure domain that includes the GPU itself, its PCIe connection, and a proportional share of the node’s network infrastructure. Power enters the sum only through supplies whose single failure stops the node, counted as \(\SeriesPsuCount\) in the power equation. With the node’s supplies in redundant sets, no single unit qualifies, so the power term below is zero in this first-order calculation. The approximation omits the residual risk that additional independent failures exhaust redundancy before repair. A fault upstream of the chassis, such as the loss of the circuits feeding it, can also take down the whole node; that risk belongs to the correlated failures treated later in this chapter.
\[ \lambda_{\text{GPU}} = \frac{1}{50{,}000} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ failures/hour} \]
\[ \lambda_{\text{PCIe}} = \frac{1}{200{,}000} = 0.5 \times 10^{-5} \text{ failures/hour} \]
\[ \lambda_{\text{power/GPU}} = \frac{n_{\text{psu,series}}}{8} \times \frac{1}{100{,}000} = \frac{0}{8} \times \frac{1}{100{,}000} = 0 \text{ failures/hour} \]
\[ \lambda_{\text{network/GPU}} = \frac{1}{8} \times \frac{1}{150{,}000} = 0.083 \times 10^{-5} \text{ failures/hour} \]



\[ \lambda_{\text{total/GPU}} = (2.0 + 0.5 + 0.083) \times 10^{-5} = 2.583 \times 10^{-5} \text{ failures/hour} \]



\[ \lambda_{\text{system}} = 10{,}000 \times 2.583 \times 10^{-5} = 0.2583 \text{ failures/hour} \]
\[ \text{MTBF}_{\text{system}} = \frac{1}{0.2583} = 3.87 \text{ hours} \]
Under the model, the cluster experiences a failure every 3.9 hours on average. The expected failure cadence is 6.2 failures/day; a training run lasting one week has an expected count of 43 failures. Actual incident times vary, but the expected loss is large enough that recovery must be part of normal execution planning.


↪ The step-by-step composition of per-component failure rates into a fleet-wide system MTBF, reusable for any node design or cluster size, is developed in The MTBF cascade.
The cluster MTBF scaling in table 1 isolates the GPU-only baseline across cluster sizes. The full-system calculation is lower once PCIe and network failure domains are included. The same 10,000-GPU cluster therefore carries three MTBF values in this chapter, and each later calculation names the one it uses: the GPU-only 5 hours of this table, the full-system 3.9 hours of the cascade above, and the two-to-three-hour cadence that somewhat larger production runs report below. Two running scenarios carry the rest of the chapter. The 1,024-GPU Archetype A reference cluster sizes per-node state, restore paths, and the elastic and straggler examples, while the 10,000-GPU cluster of the cascade sets failure cadence and checkpoint intervals. The full-system MTBF is the default input; a calculation that uses the GPU-only value says so, usually because it compares cluster sizes on the common basis of table 1, and its failure count is then a lower bound.

Production measurements confirm the \(1/\AcceleratorCount\) trend of table 1 and show that the GPU-only line is optimistic. Plotted on log-log axes, measured MTTF values and fitted projections from Meta’s clusters follow the slope of the \(50{,}000\,\text{h}/\AcceleratorCount\) line across more than three orders of magnitude in job size but sit below it, because a job can be interrupted by far more than its GPUs (figure 2). The Kokolis et al. (2025) study of Meta’s Research SuperCluster reported measured MTTF values for observed RSC job sizes and projected a 1.8-hour MTTF for 16,384-GPU jobs. That projection lands next to the Llama 3 run of war story \(\ref{ws-vol2-introduction-llama3-failure-cadence}\), whose 419 unexpected interruptions across a 54-day snapshot on 16,384 H100 GPUs give an observed MTTF of about 3.1 hours. Together, the measured Llama run and Kokolis projection put 16,384-GPU training on a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours, bracketed by the 1.8-hour projection and the 3.1-hour measurement. This evidence turns the idealized \(1/\AcceleratorCount\) relation into an engineering constraint that determines checkpoint frequency, recovery architecture, and infrastructure investment.

At 16,384 GPUs, the Kokolis projection and the Llama 3 empirical measurement bracket a failure cadence of roughly two to three hours (the 1.8-hour projection and the 3.1-hour measurement), confirming that fault tolerance is a mathematical necessity, not an edge case. title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
The MTBF calculations in the reliability analysis quantify how often failures occur, which is critical for setting checkpoint intervals and sizing recovery infrastructure. Designing effective fault tolerance also requires understanding what kind of failures occur, which depends on precise vocabulary. A fault is the underlying defect or event, an error is the corrupted state it produces, and a failure is the externally visible behavior the training system must handle (Avizienis et al. 2004). A network partition that resolves in seconds demands different handling than a permanent GPU failure. A silent memory corruption that produces incorrect gradients requires different detection mechanisms than a node crash that stops responding entirely.

Avizienis, Algirdas, Jean-Claude Laprie, Brian Randell, and Carl Landwehr. 2004. “Basic Concepts and Taxonomy of Dependable and Secure Computing.” IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing 1 (1): 11–33. https://doi.org/10.1109/TDSC.2004.2.
No single label captures all of these differences. Reliability decisions require three orthogonal axes: persistence (transient, intermittent, or permanent), manifestation (fail-stop, degraded, or value-corrupting), and failure scope (one device, one node, a rack or power domain, or the whole job). A transient fault can therefore manifest as either a detected crash or silent corruption, while a permanent switch failure can remain confined to one rack or partition an entire job. The four subsections that follow are therefore not four parallel classes or mutually exclusive buckets (Constantinescu 2008; Lamport et al. 1982). Each takes the value of one axis that most changes recovery. Transient failures come from the persistence axis, because they show why a fault that clears can still leave state to repair. Fail-stop and Byzantine (value-corrupting) failures come from the manifestation axis, and correlated failures come from the scope axis. Two parts of the space are developed where they drive decisions. The intermittent and permanent persistence classes return with hardware faults (section 7.9.1), where persistence selects retry, quarantine, or replacement. The degraded manifestation, a gray failure that slows a worker without stopping it, returns with stragglers (section 7.14.5).


A transient fault clears without physical repair, but the state it corrupts can persist after the disturbance ends. Recovery must therefore retry or validate affected work before relying on that state. Large-scale training systems encounter several forms of temporary disruption. Network packet loss momentarily drops data while transport retransmission succeeds. Memory bit flips can result from cosmic-ray-induced single-event upsets.4 Under temperature spikes, thermal throttling temporarily reduces compute throughput without halting execution, while software timeouts emerge when transient contention delays communication beyond its allotted time.
4 Single-event upset (SEU): From particle physics, where “upset” denotes a nondestructive state change. Cosmic rays and alpha particles from chip packaging can flip bits in memory and logic; the observed rate depends on altitude, process technology, packaging materials, shielding, and workload (Ziegler et al. 1996; Baumann 2005). ECC memory corrects single-bit errors but cannot handle every multi-bit upset in the same word, leaving a residual silent-corruption risk that compounds across the terabytes of state in large-scale ML training.
Ziegler, J. F., H. W. Curtis, H. P. Muhlfeld, C. J. Montrose, B. Chin, M. Nicewicz, C. A. Russell, et al. 1996. “IBM Experiments in Soft Fails in Computer Electronics (1978–1994).” IBM Journal of Research and Development 40 (1): 3–18. https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.401.0003.

Baumann, R. 2005. “Soft Errors in Advanced Computer Systems.” IEEE Design and Test of Computers 22 (3): 258–66. https://doi.org/10.1109/mdt.2005.69.
Transient faults are particularly difficult to diagnose in ML training when they leave no explicit error signal. A memory bit flip during gradient computation can propagate into later updates if hardware protection and the computation itself do not mask it. Training can then continue with corrupted state. Large-scale SDC studies show escaped corruption, while DRAM field studies show memory errors are common enough that fleet-level monitoring matters (Dixit et al. 2021; Sridharan et al. 2015; Schroeder et al. 2009). In ML training, that same undetected-corruption pattern can surface as degraded gradients, anomalous loss curves, or rollback-worthy checkpoints rather than an explicit crash.
The appropriate response to transient failures depends on detection capability. Errors that trigger explicit exceptions can be handled through bounded retry logic. Silent corruption requires end-to-end validation. Checksums detect changed bytes in storage or transport, cross-rank digests reveal disagreement about a supposedly identical reduced buffer, and statistical or replay checks test whether the computation itself remains plausible. A rank that computes the wrong local gradient and then correctly checksums those wrong bytes passes an ordinary checksum; only independent recomputation, invariants, or model-level evidence can expose that error.



Fail-stop failures cause components to cease operation entirely and detectably. The failed component stops responding to requests and is suspected through timeout mechanisms, though a timeout alone cannot distinguish an outright crash from an isolated or delayed host. A GPU hardware failure renders an individual accelerator unresponsive, while a broader node crash abruptly terminates all training processes on the host. Similarly, a network partition severs communication between a healthy node and the remaining cluster, and a storage failure prevents workers from writing or reading checkpoint shards.
In synchronous distributed training, a failed participant can stall the job’s next update. A conventional AllReduce requires every participating rank to supply its input before the reduction can complete. A single GPU that goes silent, whether from a hardware fault, a process crash, or a network partition, can therefore block the ranks waiting on that result until recovery begins. If all 10,000 GPUs belong to a job whose progress depends on the failed group, the other 9,999 accelerators can be left waiting for the missing contribution. Smaller communication groups limit the immediate dependency, although later training stages can propagate the stall across the job.
A stopped component usually gives a clearer symptom than a component returning plausible but incorrect values. The missing response still leaves uncertainty about whether the component crashed or communication merely slowed. Once recovery starts, the system replaces or restarts the failed participant and restores the most recent valid checkpoint. Minimizing detection and recovery latency must therefore be balanced against false suspicions and the validity of the saved state.
A stopped rank announces itself only through silence, so detection rests on timeouts, and every timeout must separate a dead rank from one that is merely slow, such as a GPU still writing a large checkpoint while the collective waits. Section 7.14.1 sets that threshold once the full recovery-time budget is in view.



Where a fail-stop component ceases to participate, a value-corrupting component can keep running while returning incorrect results, as when a GPU returns wrong gradients without raising an error, a link delivers a corrupted packet whose error pattern the CRC happens not to cover, or a worker computes different results for identical inputs and state. Byzantine failures allow arbitrary behavior, including inconsistent messages to different participants (Lamport et al. 1982). ML systems can encounter this broader failure model through silent data corruption or adversarial corruption. Numerical instability and determinism violations also require validation when they break the execution contract, but ordinary rounding differences or intentionally stochastic outputs are not themselves evidence of a faulty worker. The recovery concern is a participant whose accepted contribution can corrupt shared state without a visible crash.

Lamport, Leslie, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease. 1982. “The Byzantine Generals Problem.” ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 4 (3): 382–401. https://doi.org/10.1145/357172.357176.
The two models leave different evidence (figure 3). A fail-stop worker such as W2 falls silent, and its missing heartbeats make it suspect. A Byzantine worker such as W6 keeps sending messages on schedule, so it passes every liveness check while the values it sends are wrong.






Figure 3: Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures: In the fail-stop model (left), a failed worker simply ceases to send messages, which a timeout flags as suspect without distinguishing a crash from delay or isolation. In the Byzantine model (right), a failed worker continues to participate but sends incorrect data (for example, corrupted gradients reported as valid), which can poison the global model state if not detected by redundant validation.



In an ML fleet the most common source of value corruption is not an adversary but hardware that changes a value without raising an error, the silent data corruption already met among transient failures. Its physical causes, the training signals that expose it, and the verification and hot-spare defenses that contain it are developed together in section 7.10, after the hardware faults that produce it.
Whatever its source, a Byzantine contribution violates a contract that liveness checks never test. Ordinary data-parallel workers process different batches and need not produce identical local gradients; the required contract is that each contribution correctly represents its assigned computation. A single Byzantine worker can violate that contract and corrupt the averaged gradient, potentially causing training to diverge or converge to a poor solution.
Redundant computation supplies one form of evidence against Byzantine failures. Workers repeating a computation from matching inputs, state, and random-number streams can compare results under a stated numerical tolerance. Statistical outlier detection and invariants provide additional evidence without fully repeating the computation. Each method has a coverage limit. Agreement can miss shared faults, while a statistical anomaly can arise from legitimate data variation. Detection overhead must therefore be evaluated together with the faults the method can expose.
Byzantine-resilient distributed training algorithms exist but impose significant overhead. Krum (Blanchard et al. 2017) keeps the single worker gradient whose nearest neighbors lie closest to it and discards the rest, while coordinate-wise trimmed mean (Yin et al. 2018) drops the largest and smallest values in each coordinate before averaging what remains. Both compute aggregates that stay robust to a bounded number of Byzantine workers, but they require more communication and computation than simple averaging. Without such protection, corrupted gradients can push the optimizer toward an unreliable model state while the training job appears healthy. Reliability must therefore protect semantic correctness rather than process liveness alone.5

Yin, Dong, Yudong Chen, Kannan Ramchandran, and Peter Bartlett. 2018. “Byzantine-Robust Distributed Learning: Towards Optimal Statistical Rates.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 5650–59.
5 Byzantine-resilient ML: Named after Lamport’s 1982 “Byzantine Generals Problem,” these algorithms (Krum, trimmed mean, and signSGD, which aggregates only the signs of gradient coordinates by majority vote) tolerate a bounded fraction of corrupted workers, with the exact bound depending on the algorithm and assumptions. For \(\AcceleratorCount\) workers, Krum requires pairwise distance computations over worker gradients, so overhead grows quadratically with worker count and directly competes with the throughput gains of data parallelism (Blanchard et al. 2017).
Blanchard, Peva, El Mahdi El Mhamdi, Rachid Guerraoui, and Julien Stainer. 2017. “Machine Learning with Adversaries: Byzantine Tolerant Gradient Descent.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 119–29.



The reliability calculations in section 7.2 assume independent failures. Real systems depart sharply from this assumption by exhibiting correlated failures, where common physical or operational dependencies take down multiple components simultaneously. At the node level, a power fault that exhausts the chassis’s redundant supplies, such as the loss of the circuits feeding it, takes down every GPU in the chassis. At the cluster level, a top-of-rack network switch failure isolates all attached nodes, while a cooling system failure can trigger thermal shutdowns across a row of racks. Beyond physical infrastructure, shared software dependencies create broad blast radii. A software bug in an updated CUDA driver can crash processes across nodes when they exercise the affected path, and operator error during cluster reconfiguration can render an entire fleet unreachable.
Correlated failures violate the independence assumption underlying equation 3. A model that counts only independent device failures omits shared hazards and their potentially larger blast radius; incident frequency and the number of affected devices must be modeled separately. Correlated failures can also defeat redundancy strategies. Three replicas of a model provide no protection against a shared power failure if all three run on the same power domain.
Defending against correlated failures requires understanding failure domains and ensuring redundancy spans independent failure domains. Table 2 catalogs common failure domains in ML infrastructure, from single GPUs to entire data center regions, each requiring distinct mitigation strategies. Figure 4 diagrams these nested containment boundaries, framing how physical disruptions scale upward from individual eight-GPU nodes to multi-rack power and network envelopes.



Table 2: Failure Domains in ML Infrastructure: Understanding failure domain boundaries enables placement of redundant components across independent domains, preventing correlated failures from defeating redundancy strategies.

The nesting of failure domains in table 2 has direct consequences for redundancy placement: placing replicas within the same domain provides zero protection against that domain’s failure mode.






Figure 4: Hierarchy of failure domains: Failure domains are often nested or overlapping. A GPU failure affects one device. A node failure affects 8 GPUs. A rack switch failure affects 32–64 GPUs (each rack is drawn with only two of its four to eight nodes). A power distribution unit (PDU) failure may affect multiple racks. The red rack shows one such correlated failure: a single top-of-rack switch fault removes every GPU it contains, while the neighboring rack is untouched, which is why replicas must span independent domains (for example, different racks or rows).



This containment hierarchy explains why replica placement must match the fault being tolerated. The highlighted rack in figure 4 contains nodes that share a top-of-rack (ToR) switch, so that switch’s loss can disconnect every attached node from the job. A neighboring rack with a separate switch can remain reachable during that event even if both racks share a power domain. The same placement does not protect against loss of their shared power source. Redundancy must therefore cross the relevant failure boundary, not merely occupy different devices.


↩︎ Top-of-rack aggregation and the physical rack failure domain are established in Top-of-rack (ToR) and the failure domain.

Checkpoint 7.1: Mapping failure domains
Verify your understanding of how failure domains nest and their operational impact:

Blast radius: calculate how many 8-GPU nodes a rack switch failure typically affects in a standard data center configuration.

Staged rollouts: identify the failure domain addressed by staged rollouts rather than hardware redundancy.
Nested domains: explain hierarchical containment and decide whether the rack failure domain still matters once the power domain containing that rack fails.




War Story 7.1: The supercomputer that swapped in spare cubes (2024)Context: Google’s Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) v4 machine-learning supercomputer used 4,096 TPU chips connected by a custom 3D torus inter-chip interconnect (ICI) fabric, and Google engineers published their operating experience with automatic fault resiliency and hardware recovery (Zu et al. 2024).
Mechanism: At 4,096-chip scale, machine and link failures could remove participants or paths required by a job’s configured communication topology.
Impact: Losing a required participant can interrupt the synchronous job across the slice. Losing a link instead raises a routing question: whether the remaining fabric can still provide the required communication paths.
Fix: Google used optical circuit switches (OCS) to assemble replacement slices from spare healthy TPU cubes, the pod’s building blocks of chips wired as a \(4{\times}4{\times}4\) mesh, for machine outages, together with fault-tolerant routing for supported OCS outage patterns. The response depended on which resource failed.
Systems lesson: Fault tolerance is a topology-management problem. In tightly coupled accelerator fleets, recovery must preserve the communication graph, not merely replace an individual component; otherwise one local hardware fault can become a cluster-wide training interruption.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
The failure taxonomy classifies failure types and domains, answering what kind of failures occur. Equally critical for fault tolerance design is determining when over an accelerator’s operating lifespan those failures strike. Figure 5 plots the hazard function \(\ComponentHazardRate(\TimeInstant)\) across component lifecycles, partitioning operational longevity into three distinct reliability regimes.
The first phase, infant mortality, exhibits elevated failure rates from manufacturing defects, improper installation, and early-life failure of marginal components. This phase typically lasts days to weeks for electronic components. Burn-in testing6 operates components under stress conditions before deployment to precipitate infant mortality failures before production use.
6 Burn-in testing: A controlled screening procedure stresses components before deployment to expose early-life defects. Temperature, voltage, duration, and acceptance criteria depend on the component and its qualified test procedure; a generic semiconductor screening recipe is not an operating specification for an assembled accelerator. Screening reduces the defective population entering service but does not certify every later workload or fault mode.
Birolini, A. 2017. Reliability Engineering: Theory and Practice. 8th ed. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-54209-5.

Klutke, G., P. C. Kiessler, and M. A. Wortman. 2003. “A Critical Look at the Bathtub Curve.” IEEE Transactions on Reliability 52 (1): 125–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/tr.2002.804492.
After surviving infant mortality, components enter the useful-life phase, where they exhibit relatively constant failure rates under the standard reliability-engineering model (Birolini 2017; Klutke et al. 2003). This phase represents the longest portion of component lifetime and is the period where the exponential reliability model in equation 1 applies most accurately. For data center GPUs, the useful-life window is an operational planning concept shaped by refresh cycles, cooling, utilization, and observed fleet health rather than a fixed physical duration.
As components age, they enter the wear-out phase, where failure rates increase due to accumulated wear. For GPUs, wear mechanisms include electromigration7 in circuits, thermal cycling stress on solder joints, and degradation of thermal interface materials. The onset of wear-out depends heavily on operating conditions; components operated at high temperatures or with frequent thermal cycling enter wear-out earlier.
7 Electromigration: Gradual displacement of metal atoms in conductors by electron momentum transfer, first characterized in early electromigration studies and later modeled in Black’s reliability equation (Black 1969). Mean time to failure decreases with higher current density and higher temperature, so sustained high-power accelerator workloads make thermal management a direct determinant of fleet lifespan.
Black, James R. 1969. “Electromigration–a Brief Survey and Some Recent Results.” IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices 16 (4): 338–47. https://doi.org/10.1109/T-ED.1969.16754.
The practical implication for ML systems is that fleet-wide failure rates can depend on age distribution. Under the bathtub model, a new cohort passes through elevated early-life risk, a relatively stable period, and eventual wear-out. Screening, operating conditions, and replacement policy determine how much of that pattern appears in field data. Mixed-age fleets combine cohorts at different stages, so their aggregate hazard need not follow the curve of a single cohort.














Figure 5: The bathtub curve: Hardware failure rates \(\ComponentHazardRate(\TimeInstant)\) vary over time. (1) Infant mortality: high failure rate initially due to manufacturing defects. (2) Useful life: constant, low failure rate where random failures dominate. (3) Wear-out: increasing failure rate as components age. Burn-in testing aims to filter out infant mortality failures before deployment.



These three hazard regimes in figure 5 translate directly into admission control and maintenance policies. Before assigning new or repaired nodes to a long training run, operators use matrix-multiply, memory, and communication stress tests to expose marginal components. During service, temperature trends, error counts, and performance degradation help identify devices for scheduled replacement. Screening moves failures out of expensive production runs. An infant-mortality failure caught during a few hours of stress testing costs only idle time, while the same failure weeks into a pretraining run forces a checkpoint rollback, which is why operators often route fresh or repaired nodes to short jobs first. Monitoring then checks whether the constant-rate model remains appropriate as the fleet ages.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
While the mathematics of failure rates apply universally, the failure impact by model type differs dramatically. The impact of losing an hour of training depends on what that training costs, how much state must be recovered, and how long recovery takes. Table 3 quantifies these factors across model architectures, revealing orders-of-magnitude variation from large language models (LLMs), where a lost day of progress costs hundreds of thousands of dollars in compute, to vision models losing modest amounts of progress.



Table 3: Failure Impact by Model Type: The cost of training failures varies dramatically by model type, driven by training duration, checkpoint overhead, and the value of accumulated training state. The Archetype A cost is one lost day on the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster; the vision, speech, and scientific rows give illustrative ranges rather than measured values. These differences demand model-specific fault tolerance strategies.
