Large language model training illustrates how a costly allocation magnifies each hour of lost progress. The chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster at approximately $3/GPU-hour incurs $0.7M in compute costs per day. A job checkpointed only once a day can lose up to a full day of progress to one failure, which costs $0.7M in wasted compute plus schedule delay. At the checkpoint interval derived in section 7.13.1, the same failure costs minutes of rework instead of a day. The checkpoint overhead is correspondingly large. At the 14-byte-per-parameter resumable format that the checkpointing analysis uses (BF16 weights, FP32 master weights, and two FP32 Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) moments), the 175B-parameter running example writes 2.45 TB at every save.
Recommendation systems such as Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) present a different challenge when training updates models continuously rather than episodically. For a workload whose useful signals change rapidly, delayed embedding updates can reduce recommendation quality even if serving remains available. A failure that loses recent updates therefore has a freshness cost as well as a replay cost. The recovery budget must reflect the workload’s measured sensitivity to stale state.8
8 RecSys freshness: Freshness makes recovery delay part of the model-quality budget. Its importance depends on how quickly useful user and item signals change and how strongly predictions depend on them. Comparing quality at different state ages establishes the permitted staleness; that measured limit determines how much checkpoint and replication overhead is justified.Vision models illustrate how a smaller state budget can permit more frequent saves on the same storage path. The vision transformer (ViT)-Large example has a checkpoint of about 1.2 GB, smaller than the large language and embedding-heavy examples here; actual overhead still depends on sustained write bandwidth and training step time. Recovery must preserve optimizer and schedule state as well as weights. Reproducible data processing also requires the augmentation configuration, random-number generator state, and data position, rather than only the initial shuffling seed.
Scientific workflows can require state beyond the model and optimizer. An iterative molecular-search pipeline, for example, must retain which configurations have been evaluated if those results determine its next candidates. A training pipeline that samples scientific datasets must preserve the sampling state needed by its own recovery contract. The governing question is which prior decisions affect future work; the checkpoint boundary must include that state wherever it resides.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Fault tolerance mechanisms consume resources: storage for checkpoints, bandwidth for checkpoint writes, compute cycles for redundant calculations, and engineering time for implementation and maintenance. Rational investment in fault tolerance requires quantifying both the cost of failures and the cost of prevention.
Failure costs include wasted compute, schedule delay, opportunity cost, and engineering time. Wasted compute measures GPU-hours expended on training steps that must be repeated. Schedule delay captures how extended time to a trained model impacts business timelines. Opportunity cost recognizes that compute consumed by recovery cannot be used for other training. Engineering cost accounts for time spent debugging failures and manually recovering.
Prevention costs include storage, throughput overhead, recovery infrastructure, and complexity. Storage cost scales with model size and checkpoint frequency. Checkpoint writes consume memory bandwidth and may stall training. Recovery infrastructure requires spare capacity and automated recovery systems. Fault tolerant systems are harder to develop and debug.
Optimal investment in fault tolerance balances these costs. For small-scale training on a few GPUs where failures are rare, minimal fault tolerance may be cost-optimal. Infrequent checkpoints and manual recovery suffice. For large-scale training on thousands of GPUs where failures occur multiple times daily, extensive fault tolerance provides positive return on investment. Frequent checkpoints, automatic recovery, and elastic training become essential. The checkpoint interval derived in section 7.13.1 is the same balance applied to one decision variable, chosen where the marginal cost of one more save equals the marginal rework it prevents.
Equation 5 presents a simplified economic model for expected cost per training run:
\[ \TotalTrainingRunCost= \BaseTrainingComputeCost+ \mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount] \times \FailureEventCost+ \FaultToleranceCost \tag{5}\]
where \(\BaseTrainingComputeCost\) is the base compute cost, \(\mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount]\) is the expected number of failures during training, \(\FailureEventCost\) is the cost per failure, and \(\FaultToleranceCost\) is the cost of fault tolerance mechanisms. The cost per failure includes wasted compute plus overhead.
Equation 6 formalizes when fault tolerance investment is justified:
\[ \frac{\partial \FaultToleranceCost}{\partial \FaultToleranceInvestment} < -\frac{\partial (\mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount] \times \FailureEventCost)}{\partial \FaultToleranceInvestment}  \tag{6}\]
where \(\FaultToleranceInvestment\) represents investment in fault tolerance mechanisms and the base compute cost is held fixed. The negative derivative on the right is the marginal reduction in expected failure cost. Additional protection reduces total expected cost while this reduction exceeds its marginal cost; an interior optimum equates the two when the cost functions have a suitable minimum.
One investment worked through the criterion shows what it decides. Let \(\FaultToleranceInvestment\) be a hot-spare node held idle beside the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster, so that a failed node’s replacement no longer waits for the scheduler to find capacity. Its marginal cost is 8 GPUs idling all day, about $576 per day. Its marginal benefit is the recovery time it removes from each failure while every other GPU waits. At the cascade’s 6.2 failures/day, each minute removed from every recovery is worth about $3,100 per day, so the spare pays for itself once it shortens each recovery by about 11 seconds, provided it is refilled before the next failure arrives some 3.9 hours later. The same node beside an eight-GPU job, whose GPU-only MTBF in table 1 is 6250 hours (260 days), would sit idle far longer than it could ever save. Scale reverses the verdict on the same hardware.
Three foundational principles guide every design decision in this domain.

Systems Perspective 7.2: Three rules of failure at scale

At scale, failures are continuous, not exceptional. A 10,000-GPU cluster experiences failures every few hours. Systems must be designed expecting failure as normal operation.
Checkpoint intervals have an optimum. The Young-Daly interval (developed in section 7.13.1) sets checkpoint frequency from write time and system MTBF under its stated assumptions, and it shrinks only with the square root of a falling MTBF.
Training and serving have fundamentally different fault tolerance requirements. A long training job can budget minutes for recovery while preserving accumulated progress; an interactive serving request may have only milliseconds left before its deadline. Those budgets motivate checkpoint recovery for training and ready alternate capacity for serving.



The rest of the chapter follows from these rules. Before any recovery mechanism can act, the fleet must recognize what failed, so the next sections examine where faults come from (hardware, silent corruption, and software) and how fault injection tests the detectors. Training recovery (checkpointing, detection and restart, elastic resizing) then puts rules 1 and 2 to work, and serving fault tolerance and graceful degradation answer rule 3. The first question is how the physical faults behind these failures look once they reach a fleet.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
A cosmic ray that flips one bit in a GPU’s high-bandwidth memory and a solder joint that cracks under thermal cycling are physical events, but the recovery system never observes them directly. It observes symptoms: a gradient spike with no process crash, a rank that disappears from the collective, or a node that fails only after it heats under sustained load. The failure taxonomy of section 7.5 already classifies such events by persistence, manifestation, and scope. For hardware, persistence carries most of the operational weight because it decides whether the fleet should retry, quarantine, or replace a component, while manifestation decides whether the fleet notices the fault at all.
ML workloads raise the stakes of each fault. A training step performs trillions of arithmetic operations on state that persists into later steps, so a wrong value can survive beyond the computation that produced it. The damage depends on the affected value and its later use. Under the IEEE 754 format,9 a sign-bit flip inverts a weight, while an exponent-bit flip can move a small gradient by many orders of magnitude. Fault-injection studies show that network resilience varies with model, layer, and bit position, so a few faults in vulnerable locations can cost disproportionate accuracy (Reagen et al. 2018). A valid-looking corrupted value can enter learned state without triggering the process failure that would otherwise initiate recovery.
9 IEEE 754: The IEEE 754 floating-point standard defines the binary32 format with 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits (IEEE Standards Association 2019). The bit layout creates an asymmetric vulnerability for ML: a sign-bit flip inverts a weight entirely (\(0.5 \to -0.5\)), while an exponent-bit flip can shift magnitude by orders of magnitude, so resilience mechanisms often prioritize the most sensitive bit positions rather than treating all bits as equally important.
IEEE Standards Association. 2019. IEEE 754-2019: Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic. https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229.

Reagen, B., U. Gupta, L. Pentecost, P. Whatmough, S. K. Lee, N. Mulholland, D. Brooks, and G.-Y. Wei. 2018. “Ares: A Framework for Quantifying the Resilience of Deep Neural Networks.” 2018 55th ACM/ESDA/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1109/dac.2018.8465834.

↪ How an FP16 exponent-bit flip rescales a value by \(2^{16}\) and can saturate an attention softmax is developed in Silent Data Corruption in Attention.

Fleet scale turns these rare device events into routine operating conditions. Smaller geometries and lower operating voltages can reduce the charge needed to disturb a stored value (Baumann 2005), and fleet studies at Google and Meta found that a small but persistent population of processors, on the order of a few per several thousand machines, computes wrong results without raising any error (Hochschild et al. 2021; Dixit et al. 2021). Studies of accelerator training fleets reach the same conclusion: rare hardware faults appear often enough that software-level detection and recovery become part of the training system design (He et al. 2023). ML system architects must therefore treat hardware as an unreliable substrate and budget for end-to-end integrity checks, replayed computation on high-value paths, and periodic consistency checks as system requirements rather than high-performance computing specialties.


Each persistence class from the taxonomy maps to a different fleet action, from retry for a fault that leaves nothing to repair, through quarantine for one that returns under load, to replacement for one that repeats on every attempt (figure 6). A transient fault, as section 7.5.1 established, leaves no lasting defect from that event, so the fleet’s question is only whether its effect escaped. A single-event upset, a voltage droop on an unstable power path (Reddi and Gupta 2013), a timing violation, or a soft error in combinational logic (Mukherjee et al. 2005) can corrupt a tensor, packet, or instruction. Detection and correction can prevent propagation; affected state may otherwise require rollback. During training, an undetected error in weights or gradients can compromise convergence and contaminate subsequent checkpoints (He et al. 2023). During stateless inference, an activation error can remain confined to one request (Mahmoud et al. 2020). If that activation enters retained state such as a KV cache, later outputs can also depend on it.

Reddi, Vijay Janapa, and Meeta Sharma Gupta. 2013. Resilient Architecture Design for Voltage Variation. Synthesis Lectures on Computer Architecture. Springer International Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-01739-1.

Mukherjee, S. S., J. Emer, and S. K. Reinhardt. 2005. “The Soft Error Problem: An Architectural Perspective.” 11th International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture, 243–47. https://doi.org/10.1109/hpca.2005.37.






Figure 6: The ML failure spectrum: Hardware faults ordered by how long they persist. A transient fault leaves nothing to repair, an intermittent fault returns under the load that exposed it, and a permanent fault repeats on every retry. Persistence decides the fleet response, from retry through quarantine to replacement, and fault tolerance engineering must handle all three to keep a fleet making progress.



A permanent fault announces itself through repeatability. The same accelerator, memory cell, or link fails again after retry, often at the same address or in the same workload phase. Manufacturing defects and wear-out mechanisms such as electromigration and oxide breakdown produce this signature, and the stuck-at fault, in which a signal remains fixed at 0 or 1 regardless of input, is its standard abstract model (Seong et al. 2010). Repeatability helps locate the defect but does not make the result trustworthy. A permanent datapath fault keeps producing wrong gradients until the device is drained from the cluster (He et al. 2023), and rerunning the computation on the same device reproduces the error instead of exposing it. The fleet must stop trusting the component, quarantine it, and restore from a checkpoint that predates its first bad write.

Seong, N. H., D. H. Woo, V. Srinivasan, J. A. Rivers, and H.-H. S. Lee. 2010. “SAFER: Stuck-at-Fault Error Recovery for Memories.” 2010 43rd Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture, 115–24. https://doi.org/10.1109/micro.2010.46.

He, Yi, Mike Hutton, Steven Chan, Robert De Gruijl, Rama Govindaraju, Nishant Patil, and Yanjing Li. 2023. “Understanding and Mitigating Hardware Failures in Deep Learning Training Systems.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589105.

Rashid, Layali, Karthik Pattabiraman, and Sathish Gopalakrishnan. 2015. “Characterizing the Impact of Intermittent Hardware Faults on Programs.” IEEE Transactions on Reliability 64 (1): 297–310. https://doi.org/10.1109/tr.2014.2363152.

Zhang, Jeff, Kartheek Rangineni, Zahra Ghodsi, and Siddharth Garg. 2018. “ThUnderVolt: Enabling Aggressive Voltage Underscaling and Timing Error Resilience for Energy Efficient Deep Learning Accelerators.” 2018 55th ACM/ESDA/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1109/dac.2018.8465918.
Intermittent faults create the most operational ambiguity because they produce evidence and then disappear. A node may pass a reboot test, rejoin the fleet, and fail again only when the next job drives the package into the same thermal, voltage, or communication regime. Cracked solder joints, aging packages, and contamination between contacts create these load-dependent conditions (Constantinescu 2008; Rashid et al. 2015), and reduced voltage margins cause timing errors that are hard to reproduce (Zhang et al. 2018). Sporadic errors of this kind can accumulate across iterations and degrade convergence without any explicit failure (Rashid et al. 2015). An intermittent node should therefore remain suspect until evidence clears it. The fleet drains it from long jobs, correlates its error logs, and readmits it only after it passes stress tests under the load that exposed the fault; otherwise one marginal component can make validation and recovery untrustworthy for every job that lands on it. Table 4 summarizes the three responses.



Table 4: Hardware Fault Persistence and Fleet Response: The persistence class of a hardware fault determines the evidence that exposes it and the action the fleet takes. Manifestation is a separate axis: any of the three classes can surface as a crash or as silent corruption (Constantinescu 2008).


Constantinescu, C. 2008. “Intermittent Faults and Effects on Reliability of Integrated Circuits.” 2008 Annual Reliability and Maintainability Symposium, 370–74. https://doi.org/10.1109/rams.2008.4925824.

Fault rates drive fleet decisions through compounding. The analysis in section 7.2 shows how per-device failure rates become fleet interruption rates, and memory errors compound in the same way. Field studies of DRAM in large data centers found errors frequent enough that error-correcting memory, background scrubbing, and error-rate monitoring are standard fleet practice rather than optional hardening (Schroeder et al. 2009; Sridharan et al. 2015). Protection consumes some capacity and bandwidth for check bits and scrubbing, but that cost is small compared with a corrupted multi-week run.

Schroeder, Bianca, Eduardo Pinheiro, and Wolf-Dietrich Weber. 2009. “DRAM Errors in the Wild: A Large-Scale Field Study.” ACM SIGMETRICS Performance Evaluation Review 37 (1): 193–204. https://doi.org/10.1145/2492101.1555372.
10 Hamming codes (1950): Richard Hamming developed error-correcting codes at Bell Labs after relay computers repeatedly detected errors in his unattended weekend jobs and abandoned them rather than repairing them. A Hamming code uses parity checks to locate a single-bit error with \(\mathcal{O}(\log \HammingDataBitCount)\) check-bit overhead; adding an overall parity bit yields the extended single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting form. Memory ECC implementations vary in code and coverage, so the system must account for both corrected errors and residual faults outside that coverage.
Hamming, R. W. 1950. “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes.” Bell System Technical Journal 29 (2): 147–60. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x.
11 CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check): Polynomial checksum family introduced by Peterson and Brown (1961). CRC coverage depends on the polynomial, frame length, and error model; it is best understood as a low-cost detection layer rather than a universal guarantee. In distributed ML training, checksums or hashes can validate gradient payloads exchanged during collectives; without a verification layer, a corrupted gradient packet can silently poison the parameter update for every worker in the collective.
Peterson, W. W., and D. T. Brown. 1961. “Cyclic Codes for Error Detection.” Proceedings of the IRE 49 (1): 228–35. https://doi.org/10.1109/jrproc.1961.287814.

Bushnell, Michael L, and Vishwani D Agrawal. 2002. “Built-in Self-Test.” Essentials of Electronic Testing for Digital, Memory and Mixed-Signal VLSI Circuits 1: 489–548. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-306-47040-3_15.

Hochschild, Peter H., Paul Turner, Jeffrey C. Mogul, Rama Govindaraju, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, David E. Culler, and Amin Vahdat. 2021. “Cores That Don’t Count.” Proceedings of the Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems, 9–16. https://doi.org/10.1145/3458336.3465297.
Detection works in layers with different coverage and cost. At the hardware layer, error-correcting codes10 (Hamming 1950) correct and detect the memory-error patterns covered by the implemented code, and link-level CRCs11 check corruption in transit. These protections operate within their enabled storage and transport boundaries; they do not validate an incorrect arithmetic result merely because its bytes arrive intact. Before deployment, built-in self-test and burn-in screening expose manufacturing defects and permanent faults (Bushnell and Agrawal 2002). During service, operators periodically pull nodes from production and run known-answer stress tests on arithmetic, memory, and interconnect, because defective processors often fail only on particular instruction mixes, data patterns, or operating points (Hochschild et al. 2021; Dixit et al. 2021).
The software layer draws its cheapest evidence from metrics the training loop already emits. Statistical checks on loss, gradient norms, and activations flag silent drift (Chandola et al. 2009), missed heartbeats identify suspected failures (Kawazoe Aguilera et al. 1997), and watchdog timers catch tasks that stall without crashing (Pont and Ong 2002). A node that stays alive but runs slowly or erratically, the gray failure of the chapter opening, can degrade progress while still meeting a liveness timeout, so section 7.14.5 treats it through straggler detection. Redundant computation adds stronger evidence on selected paths, either periodically or in response to an anomaly, by replaying a step on another device or comparing independently computed results. Its frequency depends on the residual corruption risk, the value of the protected state, and the cost of detecting an error late.

Chandola, Varun, Arindam Banerjee, and Vipin Kumar. 2009. “Anomaly Detection: A Survey.” ACM Computing Surveys 41 (3): 1–58. https://doi.org/10.1145/1541880.1541882.

Kawazoe Aguilera, Marcos, Wei Chen, and Sam Toueg. 1997. “Heartbeat: A Timeout-Free Failure Detector for Quiescent Reliable Communication.” In Lect. Notes Comput. Sci. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/bfb0030680.

Pont, Michael J, and Royan HL Ong. 2002. “Using Watchdog Timers to Improve the Reliability of Single-Processor Embedded Systems: Seven New Patterns and a Case Study.” Proceedings of the First Nordic Conference on Pattern Languages of Programs, 159–200.

Checkpoint 7.2: Classifying a hardware fault
Verify your understanding of the transient, permanent, and intermittent fault categories and the fault, error, failure progression:

Transient fault: classify a GPU that produces a wrong result once after a cosmic-ray strike and then computes correctly for the rest of the run, and justify why detection and rollback to a known-good checkpoint, not node replacement, match that fault.
Intermittent vs. permanent: distinguish an intermittent fault from a permanent one when both can produce a stuck-at value, including the diagnostic signal that separates them.
Fault-error-failure chain: trace a single bit flip through the fault, error, failure chain, identifying where error correction codes and checkpoint-restart each intervene.
Silent corruption: explain why silent corruption sits apart from the other fault manifestations even when its underlying fault is an ordinary transient bit flip.




Self-Check: Question

What type of fault does this represent, and what is the appropriate operational response?

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Of the hardware faults just classified, the costliest are the ones whose manifestation is silent. A corrupted value that raises no error passes every liveness check the fleet runs, and training keeps building on it. Defending against silent data corruption therefore requires checks that establish a correct result, not merely a live process, and choosing those checks starts with where the corruption comes from and how it surfaces in training.


Digital hardware implements deterministic operations, but physical fault occurrence requires a probabilistic reliability model. Two mechanisms illustrate the distinction. Single-event upsets (SEUs), the particle strikes introduced with transient failures, create fleet exposure that grows with device count and operating time even when the per-device rate is low. Manufacturing variances can leave “marginal” chips that pass initial QA but fail under particular inputs or operating conditions. Voltage and temperature margins matter, including supply disturbances during rapid current changes (\(d\AcceleratorSupplyCurrent/d\TimeInstant\)). These defects can produce repeatable errors, so a probabilistic fleet model does not imply that every individual fault is random.
Facebook documented a pervasive SDC issue where a hardware fault caused a valid file to be reported as “size zero” during decompression (Dixit et al. 2021); the system “worked” without crashing, but data was silently deleted. In ML, the same failure manifests as valid-looking but numerically corrupted gradients. The pipeline trace in figure 7 follows a single ALU or memory bit flip as it corrupts an individual tensor entry, taints gradient reduction during the backward pass, commits into weights, and finally surfaces as degraded quality at evaluation. The comparative timelines beneath contrast this silent latency with a standard detected error: while a hardware trap halts within milliseconds to restart cleanly from the last checkpoint, silent corruption commits contaminated state into checkpoints over hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a costly rollback.






Figure 7: Silent data corruption propagation: A hardware bit flip moves left to right from one wrong tensor value through the backward pass and the weight update, surfacing only at the final stage as degraded model quality. The two timelines below contrast a detected error, which traps within milliseconds and restarts from the last checkpoint, with silent corruption, which is saved into checkpoints for hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a rollback; the gap between the two is the cost of silence.



Telemetry from production training fleets shows this corruption is routine rather than anomalous. At modern training scales, hardware bit flips occur regularly, and erroneous computations from a single malfunctioning accelerator can propagate into the global model state, as Jeff Dean documented in his MLSys 2024 keynote on silent data corruption (Dean 2024) (figure 8).






Figure 8: Silent data corruption at scale: Jeff Dean presents on silent data corruption (SDC) at MLSys 2024, arguing that at the scale of large ML training jobs hardware errors occur routinely, and that incorrect computations from one buggy chip can propagate and infect an entire training run. Source: Jeff Dean, MLSys 2024 keynote (Google).



In the Google training telemetry presented by Dean (2024), figure 9 identifies an abrupt gradient-norm anomaly as an SDC event. The plot shows the symptom without identifying the damaged bit or circuit. Corrupting a floating-point exponent is one mechanism that can greatly change a tensor value and subsequent updates. Gradient clipping can limit update magnitude, but it does not reconstruct the correct gradient; an anomaly detector must trigger validation or recovery before suspect state is accepted.






Figure 9: Gradient norm deviation: Transient hardware faults, such as silent data corruption (SDC), can disrupt optimization by causing abrupt changes in gradient norms. Google’s production examples show SDC anomalies surfacing as visible gradient-norm spikes. Source: (Dean 2024).









Cumulative SDC probability nears certainty over a long run.
Even a small per-GPU SDC rate accumulates across repeated collective operations, and the accumulation grows with fleet size. Any single collective is unlikely to contain an SDC event. Under the illustrative rate used in the analysis that follows, the per-step probability remains small while the cumulative probability grows over a long training run, reaching \(1 - e^{-1} \approx 63\) percent once the expected number of events reaches one. On the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster, that rate gives one expected event roughly every 100 hours, or about 22 over the three-month run of the chapter opening. The notebook below scales the same estimate to a fleet ten times larger to show where the trend leads, since the expected interval shrinks in proportion to fleet size. Standard AllReduce reduces the supplied contributions; it does not establish that an alive worker computed a correct gradient. The fleet therefore needs validation appropriate to its fault model in addition to liveness checks.
Check-and-verify methods test data-path invariants, subject to the boundary drawn for transient failures in section 7.5.1. Digests test byte integrity and agreement within their error-detection limits; they cannot establish that the original computation was correct. Independent computation, an algorithmic invariant, or replay tests that additional claim under a declared fault model. A quick estimate shows how much exposure those checks must cover.

Napkin Math 7.2: SDC risk accumulationProblem: Under an illustrative generic SDC-rate assumption, calculate the probability that at least one GPU in a 100,000-GPU fleet experiences an SDC event during a single 2 s training step.

Fleet size: 100,000 accelerators.
Individual risk: \(10^{-6}\) per GPU-hour (an illustrative generic SDC-rate assumption).
The exposure: In a 2-second window, the fleet has \(100{,}000 \times (2/3600) \approx 56\) “GPU-hours” of exposure.
The probability: \(\Pr(\text{at least one SDC}) \approx\) 0.0056 percent.

Systems insight: Under this illustrative constant-rate assumption, a 100k-GPU fleet expects one SDC event every 18,000 steps (roughly every 10 hours), even though the per-step probability is only 0.0056 percent. A CRC or hash can protect each shard or reduced buffer against corruption in transit or storage, while a redundant reduction can test the arithmetic path independently. Robustness moves from being a restart problem to a verification problem only when the verification covers the failure mechanism being claimed.


Full replication protects a broader computation path at a correspondingly high resource cost. Dual modular redundancy runs every computation twice and compares the results, and triple modular redundancy runs it three times and takes a majority vote, paying 100 and 200 percent hardware overhead to detect or mask a fault within a single control deadline (Sheaffer et al. 2007; Arifeen et al. 2020). These guarantees depend on the replicas avoiding a shared fault. The price is justified in safety-critical embedded control, such as a vehicle’s onboard computers, where one wrong output can endanger people and the replicated hardware is a small computer. For fleet training, duplicating every step of a run on 10,000 GPUs doubles the compute devoted to those steps, before comparison and coordination costs. When corruption is rare and rollback can recover valid state, selective redundancy can protect useful progress at lower cost. Screening removes suspect devices, statistical checks run continuously, standby pools absorb drained nodes, and periodic or triggered recomputation checks selected execution paths.

Sheaffer, J. W., D. P. Luebke, and K. Skadron. 2007. “A Hardware Redundancy and Recovery Mechanism for Reliable Scientific Computation on Graphics Processors.” Graphics Hardware 2007: 55–64. https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh07/055-064.

Arifeen, Tooba, Abdus Sami Hassan, and Jeong-A Lee. 2020. “Approximate Triple Modular Redundancy: A Survey.” IEEE Access 8: 139851–67. https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2020.3012673.
Google’s reactive hot-spare protocol shows how those pieces combine in three stages (figure 10). When runtime monitors flag an anomalous gradient and replay implicates a suspect accelerator (G2), the scheduler isolates that device, promotes a standby hot spare (S) into the active ring, and provisions a replacement spare (S’) while the suspect unit undergoes hardware diagnostics (Dean 2024). The fleet pays in advance for one idle device per pool rather than for a duplicate of every computation, and the protocol shifts the burden of correctness from unverified hardware to system-level auditing.






Figure 10: Hot-spare failover: An \(\DeviceCount+1\) pool of four active GPUs and one standby spare. When loss or gradient sanity checks flag a suspect GPU and replay implicates it, the job drains that device and resumes on the spare from the last known-good state; the device goes to repair and a healthy unit refills the spare slot. Google’s data-center examples use this reactive pattern to keep training moving despite hardware faults, in contrast to running every computation on two or three redundant units and comparing results (Dean 2024). The standing cost is the idle spare.


Dean, Jeff. 2024. Exciting Directions in Systems for Machine Learning. MLSys 2024 invited talk.



Checkpoint 7.3: Detecting silent corruption
Verify your understanding of Byzantine failures and SDC:

SDC danger: explain why silent data corruption is more dangerous for ML training than a simple node crash.
Hot spare vs. restart: compare a hot spare redundancy strategy with traditional checkpoint-restart in terms of recovery latency.
Sanity checker: identify the metric used as a “sanity checker” to identify potential hardware faults: GPU temperature or gradient norm.
Byzantine scope: assess the True or False claim that Byzantine failures only occur when a malicious actor intentionally sabotages the training cluster.



These checks reduce the risk of an unreliable substrate, but they do not protect against faults that the software stack introduces itself, bugs that look like valid computation while corrupting the ML pipeline.

Self-Check: Question

In a 100,000-GPU training cluster where each device has an illustrative SDC probability of \(10^{-6}\) per GPU-hour, what is the expected SDC exposure and failure cadence during continuous AllReduce training with 2-second step times?

The cluster experiences roughly 55.6 GPU-hours of exposure per 2-second step, resulting in an expected SDC event approximately every 18,000 steps (every ~10 hours).
The cluster experiences an SDC event on every single step because 100,000 GPUs exceed the reliability threshold.
The cluster experiences an SDC event once every 1,000 days because \(10^{-6}\) is negligible for 2-second steps.
The cluster experiences an SDC event exactly every 50,000 hours regardless of cluster size.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
A team spends three months testing an LLM against complex prompt-level failure cases, only to realize that its preprocessing script kept only the last 512 tokens of each input, silently discarding the system prompt on long requests. The example exposes an ordinary source of ML failure that algorithmic testing can miss. A logic error in a data loader or prompt assembler can preserve valid tensor shapes while changing the computation’s meaning, allowing the pipeline to continue without a crash.
Software faults require a different recovery lens from hardware failures. Hardware faults enter from silicon, electrons, and physical wear; software faults enter through design choices, dependency versions, and pipeline glue. The fault-tolerance problem shifts from replacing a failed component to identifying which valid-looking transformation corrupted data, gradients, or predictions, and every boundary between framework, library, runtime, and distributed system is a place where such a transformation can hide.


Software faults in ML frameworks range from logic errors to resource leaks, concurrency bugs, and integration failures, and they propagate across system boundaries. A tensor leaked on every iteration lets a correctly sized job drift toward the device memory limit over hundreds of steps and then fail with an out-of-memory error, which makes root-cause attribution difficult without per-layer memory profiling. Race conditions in asynchronous updates can lose or overwrite parameter updates, and deadlocks12 leave workers waiting on messages that never arrive. Some of these faults appear only under high load, on particular hardware, or with a specific pairing of a high-level library and a low-level numerical library such as cuDNN, so root-cause analysis must treat the model code, the runtime, and its dependencies as one versioned artifact.
12 Pipeline deadlock: In pipelined training, a deadlock can form when stage 1 waits for a free buffer to send activations to stage 2 while stage 2 waits for stage 1 to accept its backward gradients. Neither stage can proceed, and because every other stage depends on them, the whole job stalls with no error raised, which a collective timeout eventually converts into a detectable failure.


Because many software faults leave the pipeline running while corrupting gradients, reliability evidence must establish which invariant failed and which recovery action is now safe. Several tests verify recovery guarantees that later sections build in full, and each needs only the invariant it protects. A restore drill checks a manifest, the record that names every checkpoint shard and the training step they share. A membership test kills or partitions a worker and checks that, once it has been replaced, it can no longer write state the job will trust. Every such test is judged against two bounds that a recovery must meet, how much completed work it may lose and how long it may take before useful work resumes. Checkpointing turns those bounds into the formal recovery objectives of section 7.13. Later sections of this chapter build the guarantees themselves, the manifest protocol in section 7.13.5.2 and the epochs, leases, and write fencing that stop a replaced worker in section 7.14.2.
The prompt-truncation bug from the opening example should never survive until runtime. A unit test should catch the tokenizer boundary, an integration replay should catch the batch shape and metadata path, and a fault-injection test should verify that the resulting alert blocks publication or rolls back to a known-good state for the injected case. Table 5 organizes these gates by the recovery claim each one supports.



Table 5: Reliability Evidence and Recovery Decisions: Tests earn operational value when each one establishes an invariant and authorizes a specific rejection, rollback, isolation, or restore decision.










Reliability evidence
Invariant exercised
Decision enabled




Boundary unit test
Tokenizer limits, tensor shapes, masks, and step metadata remain valid
Reject the change before distributed execution


Deterministic replay
A recorded batch produces equivalent state on known-good hardware
Separate input or software defects from suspect hardware


Checkpoint restore drill
A committed manifest restores every shard and resumes at its named step
Accept the generation as satisfying the recovery contract


Membership fault injection
A killed or partitioned worker loses ownership and cannot write after replacement
Validate ownership handoff and communicator rebuild


Corruption injection
A changed shard, reduced buffer, or checkpoint fails the intended verifier
Block the optimizer step or roll back before propagation


Dependency rollback test
A versioned runtime and artifact set can return to the last known-good combination
Authorize automated rollback instead of manual repair






These safeguards matter only when each gate targets a concrete corruption path. A test that checks only whether the tokenizer runs is too weak; it must assert that system prompts, labels, masks, and sequence-length metadata survive preprocessing with the intended semantics. Integration replay then follows one recorded batch through loading, sharding, collation, and model input construction. Fault injection tests whether the detector fires before the protected commit and whether recovery stays within the named bounds on lost work and recovery time for the injected fault. A passing case supports that tested contract, not complete coverage of every possible corruption. Restore drills, stale-writer rejection, and corrupted-shard rejection therefore provide evidence that generic build success cannot supply.
Several rows of table 5 claim more than a passing test. They claim that a detector fires and a recovery path holds when something breaks, and a claim of that kind can be checked only by breaking something on purpose.

Self-Check: Question

Why are GPU memory leaks in 70B+ parameter distributed training pipelines particularly destructive and difficult to diagnose compared to standard CPU memory leaks?

GPU memory is dynamically swapped to NVMe disk automatically, causing unpredictable I/O thrashing rather than out-of-memory errors.
GPU allocators immediately throw segmentation faults upon the first unreleased tensor, preventing any batch execution.
Accelerator memory is scarce (40–80 GB per device) and shared across weights, optimizer state, and activations; a small leak per batch gradually builds over hundreds of steps until triggering an un-checkpointed OOM crash mid-run.
GPU memory leaks only occur when using mixed-precision BF16 formats and disappear entirely when switching to FP32 weights.

Contrast a pipeline deadlock with a data race condition in distributed parallel training in terms of their system symptoms and impact on model convergence.
Justify why a silent data preprocessing defect (such as unintended prompt truncation or incorrect token masking) presents a much higher compute and financial risk than a syntax error that crashes on the first batch.
A preprocessing change silently truncates prompts and discards the system prompt. Sequence the reliability gates in the order that should catch the defect, from earliest and cheapest to the final proof that recovery works:


A fault-injection test showing that the resulting alert blocks publication or rolls back to a known-good state
A boundary unit test asserting that tokenizer limits, system prompts, and masks survive preprocessing
An integration replay that follows one recorded batch through loading, sharding, collation, and model input construction

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
An injected failure is useful evidence only when it resembles the production failure the system must survive. A multi-node training cluster that claims to tolerate network partitions should have that connection severed in a staging environment so engineers can observe what the orchestration layer does. Fault injection is the engineering discipline of deliberately perturbing a system to empirically verify that robustness mechanisms work before production traffic discovers the gap. Fault-injection tools for tensors and accelerators cover bit flips, corrupted tensor values, and accelerator-oriented failures (Chen et al. 2020; Tsai et al. 2021; Gräfe et al. 2023), while network partitions, latency injection, dependency termination, and API-response faults belong to chaos and distributed-systems testing practice (Basiri et al. 2016).

Chen, Zitao, Niranjhana Narayanan, Bo Fang, Guanpeng Li, Karthik Pattabiraman, and Nathan DeBardeleben. 2020. “TensorFI: A Flexible Fault Injection Framework for TensorFlow Applications.” 2020 IEEE 31st International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE), 426–35. https://doi.org/10.1109/issre5003.2020.00047.

Tsai, Timothy, Siva Kumar Sastry Hari, Michael Sullivan, Oreste Villa, and Stephen W. Keckler. 2021. “NVBitFI: Dynamic Fault Injection for GPUs.” 2021 51st Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks (DSN), 284–91. https://doi.org/10.1109/dsn48987.2021.00041.

Gräfe, Ralf, Qutub Syed Sha, Florian Geissler, and Michael Paulitsch. 2023. “Large-Scale Application of Fault Injection into PyTorch Models -an Extension to PyTorchFI for Validation Efficiency.” 2023 53rd Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks - Supplemental Volume (DSN-s), 56–62. https://doi.org/10.1109/dsn-s58398.2023.00025.


A fault-injection experiment must specify duration, location, granularity, and propagation path. Its fault model describes the originating disturbance, such as a transient single-bit upset or a permanent multi-bit defect. Its error model describes the resulting corrupted state or computation. Results for transient single-bit faults do not establish resilience to permanent multi-bit defects (Sangchoolie et al. 2017).

Sangchoolie, Behrooz, Karthik Pattabiraman, and Johan Karlsson. 2017. “One Bit Is (Not) Enough: An Empirical Study of the Impact of Single and Multiple Bit-Flip Errors.” 2017 47th Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks (DSN), 97–108. https://doi.org/10.1109/dsn.2017.30.

Binkert, Nathan, Bradford Beckmann, Gabriel Black, Steven K. Reinhardt, Ali Saidi, Arkaprava Basu, Joel Hestness, et al. 2011. “The Gem5 Simulator.” ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 39 (2): 1–7. https://doi.org/10.1145/2024716.2024718.

Papadimitriou, George, and Dimitris Gizopoulos. 2021. “Demystifying the System Vulnerability Stack: Transient Fault Effects Across the Layers.” 2021 ACM/IEEE 48th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 902–15. https://doi.org/10.1109/isca52012.2021.00075.
The injection level determines which propagation paths the experiment includes. A register-level bit flip in a simulator such as gem5 (Binkert et al. 2011) can expose effects that a mutation of a PyTorch weight tensor omits. Conversely, hardware may mask an injected fault before software observes it. Location and propagation therefore matter when comparing results across fault models (Sangchoolie et al. 2017; Papadimitriou and Gizopoulos 2021).
This divergence comes from the multi-tier filtering formalized as error masking (Mohanram and Touba 2003). A physical soft error becomes an observable failure only if it passes two screens in turn (figure 11). The corrupted data must first be read, and the value read must then produce incorrect output or a crash. A hardware disturbance that hits an unused functional unit, is overwritten prior to use, or lands in dynamically dead instructions is silently absorbed within the microarchitecture or runtime (Ko 2021). Because tensor-level mutations inject perturbations downstream of these architectural filters, their empirical error rates must be evaluated at that higher abstraction level.

Mohanram, K., and N. A. Touba. 2003. “Partial Error Masking to Reduce Soft Error Failure Rate in Logic Circuits.” Proceedings. 18th IEEE International Symposium on Defect and Fault Tolerance in VLSI Systems, 433–40. https://doi.org/10.1109/dftvs.2003.1250141.

Ko, Y. 2021. “Characterizing System-Level Masking Effects Against Soft Errors.” Electronics 10 (18): 2286. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics10182286.






Figure 11: Error masking: Follow a soft error from the top. It becomes a failure only if the corrupted data is read and then also produces incorrect output; at each No branch it is masked, first by microarchitectural effects (unused components, overwritten values, squashed speculative instructions) and then by software effects (dead instructions, logical and compare operations, uninfluential branches). Because software-level fault injection sees only the second filter, it can misestimate a system’s true resilience to transient errors.



These masking effects determine which abstraction level an experiment should target.



Fault injection methods trade realism against experimental scale. Hardware-based injection, through field-programmable gate array (FPGA) emulation or accelerated particle-beam exposure of a running accelerator (Velazco et al. 2010), supplies the calibration point because its faults pass through the same circuit-level masking as production faults. Software-based injection is the scalable counterpart. Tools such as PyTorchFI (Mahmoud et al. 2020) perturb weights, activations, and gradients directly, covering many model states quickly without special hardware, and have shown that single bit-level faults can produce severe misclassifications, including “phantom” objects in detection models. The cost is an abstraction gap. A software tool that mutates a tensor skips the hardware masking that would have absorbed many of the same disturbances. Frameworks such as Fidelity (He et al. 2020) narrow that gap by mapping how faults in registers, memory hierarchies, and numerical units become software-visible errors, so that injected faults resemble what physical hardware would produce.

Velazco, Raoul, Gilles Foucard, and Paul Peronnard. 2010. “Combining Results of Accelerated Radiation Tests and Fault Injections to Predict the Error Rate of an Application Implemented in SRAM-Based FPGAs.” IEEE Transactions on Nuclear Science 57 (6): 3500–3505. https://doi.org/10.1109/tns.2010.2087355.

Mahmoud, A., N. Aggarwal, A. Nobbe, J. R. S. Vicarte, S. V. Adve, C. W. Fletcher, I. Frosio, and S. K. S. Hari. 2020. “PyTorchFI: A Runtime Perturbation Tool for DNNs.” 2020 50th Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks Workshops (DSN-w), 25–31. https://doi.org/10.1109/dsn-w50199.2020.00014.

He, Yi, Prasanna Balaprakash, and Yanjing Li. 2020. “FIdelity: Efficient Resilience Analysis Framework for Deep Learning Accelerators.” 2020 53rd Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO), 270–81. https://doi.org/10.1109/micro50266.2020.00033.

Example 7.1: Software fault injection limitsScenario: An engineering team validates a distributed training pipeline using software fault injection, concluding that tensor bit-flips always corrupt model gradient updates.
Diagnosis: Hardware-calibrated experiments reveal that software injection bypasses low-level hardware masking effects (such as ECC memory correction and gate-level masking) that prevent many register-level bit-flips from ever mutating software variables.
Systems lesson: In this experiment, bypassing hardware masking overstates the effect of the modeled physical faults. Tensor mutation still tests the software response to corrupted values; estimating production vulnerability additionally requires a calibrated model of which physical faults reach those values. The result must be interpreted at the injection level actually tested.


For fleet recovery, the most valuable experiments inject faults at the level where recovery decisions are made. Killing a rank in the middle of a collective, partitioning a node from the rendezvous service, delaying a heartbeat past its timeout, and corrupting one checkpoint shard each exercise one row of table 5. Running these experiments continuously in staging, and in controlled form in production, keeps rarely executed recovery code from decaying between real incidents (Basiri et al. 2016). A detection mechanism can identify corrupted or missing state, but only a recovery mechanism can replace it. Fault persistence determines whether to retry, quarantine, or replace a component, and checkpointing supplies the known-good training state from which any of those paths can resume.

Self-Check: Question

Why might a software-based fault injection framework (such as PyTorchFI) overestimate a neural network’s vulnerability to radiation-induced soft errors when compared against physical beam testing on real silicon?

Software-based tools only inject faults into 8-bit integer quantized models, whereas physical radiation only affects 64-bit floating point registers.
Physical radiation only damages power delivery networks and never alters logic gate states in operational GPUs.
Software injection tools can only simulate permanent stuck-at faults and cannot model transient bit flips.
Software injection mutates high-level tensor variables directly, completely bypassing microarchitectural and circuit-level masking (such as ECC correction, speculative instruction discarding, and dead registers) that absorb soft errors in hardware.

Explain how error masking at both the microarchitectural level and the software level can prevent a physical soft error from causing a system failure.
Software-based fault injection frameworks are universally preferred over FPGA-based injection for production resilience certification because software tools capture register-level gate timing violations and physical alpha-particle strikes with higher fidelity.
Explain how fault-injection frameworks such as Fidelity bridge the abstraction gap between low-level hardware faults and high-level software models.

See Answers →

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
When a top-of-rack switch dies two weeks into the training run of a 175-billion-parameter model, the cluster loses 64 GPUs instantly. The system cannot simply restart from scratch; the sunk cost of weeks of compute is too high. The failure analysis in section 7.1 established that large-scale training systems will experience such failures frequently, requiring robust mechanisms to preserve and resume progress.
Training fault tolerance has three obligations: preserve state, detect and classify failures, and resume or resize the job. Checkpointing supplies the first obligation. The sections that follow then build the rest of the recovery model: detection supplies evidence for a recovery decision, recovery procedures restore a consistent process group, and elastic recovery determines whether the job can continue with a changed worker set. Every one of those paths falls back on the saved copy that checkpointing produces, so the first question is what that copy must contain.

Definition 7.1: Checkpointing
Checkpointing is the periodic serialization of the complete training state (parameters, optimizer state, data loader position, and random state) to persistent storage at a recorded training step.

Significance: It minimizes lost work after a system failure by trading checkpoint I/O against rework. Writing too often wastes accelerator time on storage traffic; writing too rarely risks replaying many completed steps after a failure. The Young-Daly interval developed in this section chooses the cadence that balances write cost against expected lost work.
Distinction: A resumable checkpoint captures a consistent execution state, including optimizer state, random-number generator state, data position, and learning rate schedules. It can use full or incremental storage; bitwise replay additionally requires compatible deterministic execution.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that checkpointing is “just writing to disk.” For large models it is a storage-system stress test, because the simultaneous write from thousands of GPUs can trigger a checkpoint storm (definition \(\ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}\)) that saturates the shared network and storage bandwidth \((\Bandwidth)\).



A checkpoint is useful only if it resumes the recorded step consistently. In distributed training, every shard must belong to the same recoverable state; a collection of files from different steps does not preserve progress. For the interval model, assume that writing a checkpoint completes durably before it becomes available for recovery and that a failure discards the work performed since the last completed checkpoint.
Two recovery objectives turn those obligations into a contract. The recovery point objective (RPO) bounds acceptable lost progress, so checkpoint age and replication lag must fit within it. The recovery time objective (RTO) bounds the delay until useful work resumes, which covers detection, resource replacement, restore, and warmup. A 20-minute checkpoint interval cannot promise an RPO below 20 minutes without a more frequent durable log or replica, and asynchronous flushing can leave the last durable generation older still. A five-minute RTO is impossible if checkpoint reload alone takes eight minutes. These objectives apply to a stated fault model. Corruption discovered after several saves can require rollback beyond the newest durable checkpoint. The Young-Daly interval derived next minimizes expected waste; RPO and RTO impose service constraints that the expected-value optimum must still satisfy (Beyer et al. 2016).


When failures are expected during a job, the key engineering decision is how often to write that state, because every save costs I/O time and every unsaved step is work a failure can erase. The Young-Daly formula13 (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\), applied in section 7.13.2) gives a first-order estimate of that balance through a square-root rule:
13 Young-Daly formula: Young (1974) derived the first-order optimal checkpoint interval, and Daly (2006) independently refined it with tighter second-order bounds.
Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.
\[ \OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{7}\]
\(\CheckpointWriteTime\) in distributed ML training is not the time to flush a small process state; it includes transferring model weights and optimizer state to durable storage. The reference format here stores BF16 weights, separate FP32 master weights, and two FP32 moment tensors per parameter for Adam. A single resumable checkpoint for a 70B-parameter model therefore approaches a terabyte at 14 bytes per parameter; for the later 175B-parameter running example, it exceeds two terabytes. Reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) requires a smaller payload or higher sustained write bandwidth, and \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) itself is the central constraint that determines how tightly the checkpoint interval can be set before I/O overhead displaces productive training compute.
Of those 14 bytes per parameter, the optimizer state14 dominates the payload, exactly as in the storage sizing of the same resumable checkpoint in Checkpoint Storage, so the optimizer state rather than the model weights sets most of \(\CheckpointWriteTime\).
14 Adam optimizer state: Adam’s per-parameter first-moment (\(\AdamFirstMoment\)) and second-moment (\(\AdamSecondMoment\)) estimates are two FP32 values, 8 of the 14 bytes per parameter in the resumable checkpoint; with the FP32 master weights, optimizer-side state accounts for all but the 2 bytes of BF16 weights. For a 175B parameter model, the two moments alone reach 1.4 TB, which typically dominates checkpoint size and recovery time, making optimizer state the primary bottleneck in checkpoint I/O design.

Optimizer state, not weights, dominates checkpoint size.

To see the balance, consider an interval between saves. Doubling that interval approximately halves the checkpoint writes per unit of training, but a failure then loses twice as much work on average. Under the constant-rate, rare-failure approximation, failure occurs approximately uniformly within an interval, so the average lost work is half the interval. When write time is small relative to the interval, the wasted fraction from saving and replaying work is approximately the sum below. Detection, allocation, and restoration time require a separate recovery budget.
\[ \CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointInterval}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{8}\]
Setting the first derivative to zero (\(\frac{d\CheckpointWasteFraction}{d\CheckpointInterval} = -\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf} = 0\)) directly yields the square-root minimum of equation 7. The first term falls hyperbolically as the interval lengthens while the second climbs linearly, so total waste traces a U-shaped convex curve with a shallow floor. Its scaling consequence is the one to carry forward. As clusters grow, system MTBF drops, so the optimal interval shrinks, demanding higher-bandwidth storage to keep \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) small before the “checkpoint tax” consumes the cluster’s compute capacity. Because the relationship is a square root, halving MTBF tightens the interval by only \(\sqrt{2}\approx 1.4\times\), so doubling cluster size does not demand doubling checkpoint I/O bandwidth when checkpoint size and the other assumptions stay fixed. The next subsection applies the formula to the chapter’s own cluster, whose full-system MTBF the cluster cascade already derived.


↩︎ The per-tier storage bandwidths that bound how quickly a checkpoint can be written are established in The ML Storage Hierarchy.



The Young-Daly interval of equation 7 needs two inputs. The failure analysis in section 7.1 supplies the system MTBF term, and the checkpoint payload together with sustained write bandwidth supplies \(\CheckpointWriteTime\). With both in hand, the formula gives a candidate schedule for the chapter’s own cluster, subject to its recovery objectives.
The worked cascade’s 10,000-GPU cluster, roughly ten times the Archetype A reference cluster, supplies both inputs as computed values. That cascade (section 7.4) put full-system MTBF, including PCIe and network failures (the redundant power supplies add no term), at 3.87 hours. For the write time, the 175B running example’s 2.45 TB resumable checkpoint drains to shared storage at the sustained aggregate write bandwidth this chapter assumes for the cluster, 100 GB/s, which takes 24.5 s. Substituting these into the Young-Daly formula gives the canonical interval for this cluster.

Napkin Math 7.3: The Young-Daly optimal intervalProblem: A 10,000-GPU cluster has an MTBF of 3.87 hours. A full model checkpoint takes 24.5 s to write. What is the optimal checkpoint frequency?
Math: Apply the Young-Daly interval of equation 7 (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\)).

Convert to common units: \(\SystemMtbf =\) 3.87 hours \(\times\) 3600 s/hour = 13932 s.
Substitute and solve: With \(\CheckpointWriteTime =\) 24.5 s and \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures =\) 13932 s, the formula gives \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx\) 826.2 s, or about 13.8 min.

Systems insight: At this interval, the “checkpoint tax” (time spent saving + time spent re-computing) is minimized to approximately 5.9 percent. Checkpointing every hour instead would lengthen the expected rework after each failure, wasting about 13.6 percent of the cluster’s capacity. As clusters scale, the optimal interval must shrink to keep up with the falling MTBF.


The result connects measured or estimated interruption rates to checkpoint policy. At this interval, saving and expected replay together consume approximately 5.9 percent of training time in the first-order model, half from writes and half from replay, because at the square-root optimum the two terms of equation 8 are equal. Plotting those two terms for this cluster shows how forgiving the optimum is (figure 12). Write overhead falls hyperbolically and expected rework climbs linearly, so their sum has a shallow floor around 14 min. An interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while one several times too short or too long costs far more, which is why a rough MTBF estimate still yields a usable schedule.














Figure 12: The checkpoint trade-off: Checkpoint save overhead (dashed blue) falls as the interval lengthens, while expected rework after a failure (dashed red) rises; their sum (solid) is minimized at the Young-Daly interval. The curves use this chapter’s 175B running example on its 10,000-GPU cluster, with a 24.5 s checkpoint write and a 3.9 h full-system MTBF, which put the optimum near 14 min. The minimum is shallow, so an interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while a far shorter or far longer one costs a great deal.



How far the estimate itself can be trusted depends on the assumptions behind it.

Systems Perspective 7.3: Young-Daly formula assumptionsThe first-order Young-Daly formula provides valuable intuition but rests on assumptions that may not hold when write times are non-negligible relative to MTBF; the renewal model derived in Checkpoint Intervals Beyond the First-Order Approximation shows how finite checkpoint time changes the optimum. The assumptions are:

Exponentially distributed failures: Assumes a constant failure rate. Real systems exhibit “bathtub curve” behavior with higher rates during burn-in and wear-out phases.
Deterministic checkpoint time: Assumes \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is constant. In practice, checkpoint time varies 2–3\(\times\) due to storage contention, network congestion, and memory pressure.
Recovery cost is independent of the chosen interval: A fixed per-failure recovery cost does not change the first-order minimizing interval. Recovery can take longer than checkpoint writing because it also includes job scheduling delays, topology reconstruction, and warmup; it still belongs in the total-waste budget.
Aggregate interruption process: Independent constant-rate failure sources can contribute to one job-interruption rate. Shared power, cooling, or switch failures require a model of incident frequency and recovery cost; adding per-device rates alone misses those common causes.
Infinite timeline: Optimizes for long training runs. Short runs, where total time is comparable to MTBF, require different analysis.

When assumptions are violated, the optimal interval may shift significantly, but restart overhead should not be treated as if it were paid at every checkpoint. In the first-order lost-time model, restart time adds a per-failure recovery term to total expected waste; it does not replace \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) inside equation 7 unless a recovery-aware Daly-style model is explicitly derived and calibrated.


Along an execution timeline, a training run alternates productive compute intervals (\(\CheckpointInterval\)) with synchronous save barriers (\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)), and a failure charges two distinct penalties (figure 13). Uncheckpointed progress is discarded as lost rework, and the restart latency (\(\FailureRecoveryTime\)) to reload state and warm up execution pipelines follows before useful work resumes.






Figure 13: Checkpoint-recovery timeline: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint.



Recovery latency therefore matters as much as write duration, because every failure pays both the discarded compute since the last save and the restart delay. That delay includes job scheduling, checkpoint loading, and pipeline warmup. Production systems where recovery exceeds checkpoint write time by 3–5\(\times\) should include it in their total-waste and service-level objective (SLO) budgets, and should use a cited recovery-aware checkpoint model rather than folding recovery time into the per-checkpoint write term.



The interval calculation chooses when the system preserves state; the write path decides what each save costs while training waits. Equation 9 generalizes the save-side term of equation 8 to include any pause beyond the write itself:
\[ \CheckpointOverheadFraction= \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointExtraPauseTime}{\CheckpointInterval}  \tag{9}\]
Here, \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) is the dimensionless fraction of time lost to checkpointing, \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is checkpoint write time, \(\CheckpointInterval\) is the checkpoint interval, and \(\CheckpointExtraPauseTime\) is any training pause beyond the checkpoint write itself. This includes memory allocation, coordination, and serialization. Total first-order waste is then \(\CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \CheckpointOverheadFraction+ \CheckpointInterval/(2 \cdot \SystemMtbf)\), so checkpoint overhead in this section means the save side alone, with expected rework counted separately. How large \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) becomes depends first on whether training waits for durable storage.


The synchronous and asynchronous checkpointing approaches differ in when training waits for durable storage. Synchronous checkpointing coordinates workers at a consistent state boundary, writes their portions, and resumes training only after all writes complete. Blocking alone does not establish consistency; the protocol must ensure that every shard belongs to the same recoverable training state.
Asynchronous checkpointing separates that consistent capture from the durable flush. Workers snapshot their state to CPU memory or staging storage and protect the captured values from later updates, then continue training while a background process writes the snapshot to persistent storage.15 Recovery can use the new generation only after all required shards reach the storage tier that survives the modeled failure and the coordinator publishes completion.
15 Asynchronous checkpointing: Pipelines durable writes behind training by first capturing a consistent snapshot in staging memory or storage. Training must not mutate values still being captured. After capture, background flushing can overlap independent computation, subject to staging capacity and sustained drain bandwidth. Exposed capture time and resource contention remain overhead even when the durable write finishes off the training critical path.Memory footprint introduces a second contrast. Beyond write time, checkpointing consumes memory for serialization, transfer buffers, and any copied snapshot. A synchronous writer can read stable training state while updates are paused, so it does not necessarily need a complete second copy, but the pause can leave accelerators idle even with fast storage. Independent input prefetching may continue; forward or backward work that changes the captured state must wait unless the snapshot mechanism explicitly permits overlap. Asynchronous capture instead requires retained values that later updates cannot change, so its buffering policy can increase peak memory demand.



The financial impact of synchronous checkpointing at scale is severe when the storage path is slow. Suppose the same 175B checkpoint on the same cluster goes to a slower shared tier than the one assumed in the interval notebook, delivering about 20 GB/s instead, under a common hourly policy and with no staging to hide the write. A 10,000-GPU cluster then pauses for 2 minutes per save and burns \(10{,}000 \times \frac{2}{60} \approx 333\) idle GPU-hours, which at roughly $3 per GPU-hour costs about $1,000 in wasted compute for a single checkpoint. Hourly, that idle time compounds to $24,000 per day spent waiting for storage I/O. This is the cost that asynchronous capture removes from the critical path, which is why production systems stage checkpoints rather than block on the shared tier. Write time also varies widely across model types, because larger models require longer writes but also earn longer optimal intervals (table 6).
The Archetype A row in table 6 uses the same 14-byte-per-parameter resumable checkpoint (2.45 TB) as the rest of the chapter. Its interval calculation uses the GPU-only cluster MTBF rather than the shorter full-system MTBF of the worked cascade, so the square-root rule gives a longer interval than the Young-Daly notebook. The table keeps the GPU-only basis because its purpose is comparison across model types. Switching every row to the full-system MTBF would shorten each interval, and raise each overhead, by the same square-root factor, leaving the ranking across rows unchanged. The ResNet-50 and BERT-Large rows count only FP32 weights, so their write times and resulting intervals are lower bounds for a resumable checkpoint. Their intervals of seconds describe the balance for that smaller payload; selecting a recovery cadence requires including optimizer, schedule, and input-stream state. Small-state jobs rarely run on a cluster this large, and their actual storage bandwidth and complete recovery state determine whether saves every few minutes or every epoch have negligible overhead. The large-state rows show why interval selection becomes consequential when each save moves hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes.



Table 6: Checkpoint Overhead by Model Type: The Archetype A row is the 175B running example at 14 bytes per parameter (weights, FP32 master weights, and Adam moments); the 20B, recommender, and vision transformer rows are representative scenario sizes, and the 4 TB embedding-heavy recommender is a smaller scenario than the 10 TB+ embedding tables of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) in table 3; the BERT-Large and ResNet-50 rows count FP32 weights only and omit optimizer state, so their write times understate a full resumable checkpoint. Larger models require longer save times but also benefit from longer optimal checkpoint intervals. The percentage column reports the save-side overhead \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) of equation 9 with no extra pause, not total Young-Daly waste; at the optimum, expected rework adds a comparable term.
