When a GPU inference server slows down, routing more requests to it can turn a local problem into a fleet-wide failure. Consider an illustrative rise in service time from 50 ms to 500 ms. Queues accumulate, client timeouts generate retries, and rerouted work consumes neighboring replicas’ headroom. The cause might be a stalled dependency, device degradation, or resource contention. The load balancer needs a policy for withdrawing an unhealthy replica while controlling the displaced load.
The circuit breaker pattern (Nygard 2007) limits repeated work sent to an unhealthy destination. In the closed state, the server receives normal traffic. When the configured error, timeout, or latency threshold is exceeded, the breaker opens and requests fail fast or become candidates for rerouting. After a recovery interval, a half-open state admits limited probes, closing on recovery or reopening on failure. Figure 17 shows these transitions. Opening a breaker does not create replacement capacity: rerouting must respect admission limits and retry budgets or it can overload the surviving replicas.






Figure 17: Circuit breaker states: The circuit breaker protects the system from cascading failure. Closed: normal operation. Open: error threshold exceeded; all requests fail fast to prevent resource exhaustion. Half-open: after a timeout, a limited number of requests are allowed through to probe the dependency’s health. Success resets to closed; failure returns to open.



Backpressure propagation complements the breaker by making overload visible upstream. When queue depth crosses a threshold, the server returns a signal such as 503 Service Unavailable; the load balancer marks the replica as degraded and routes fewer requests to it. If all replicas become degraded, the system shifts from routing control to admission control, rejecting some requests at the edge rather than accepting work it cannot serve within the latency SLO; load-shedding policies decide which requests to reject first. Circuit breakers isolate unhealthy replicas; backpressure tells the rest of the system to slow down before retries amplify the failure.


↩︎ Load shedding, model fallback, and the other strategies that trade quality for availability are established in Graceful degradation strategies.
Backpressure works only when the request contract propagates through the whole serving graph. The gateway converts the client timeout into an absolute deadline and every downstream stage subtracts elapsed time before admitting more work. If the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancellation must reach queued CPU work, accelerator batches, retrieval calls, and streamed output. A canceled request that remains in a continuous batch is zombie work: it consumes KV pages and decode bandwidth while producing no useful response. Some kernels cannot be interrupted mid-launch, so cancellation commonly takes effect at the next batch or token boundary; the scheduler must measure that cancellation lag rather than promise instantaneous preemption.
The same request identifier must connect routing, queueing, prefill, decode, cache allocation, and response streaming. A useful serving trace records admitted and rejected requests, queue delay, TTFT, TPOT, input and output tokens, cache pages, batch membership, preemptions, cancellations, and fallback decisions. Aggregate accelerator utilization cannot distinguish useful work from late or canceled work. SLO goodput and the wasted-token rate close that gap. SLO goodput reports how much completed work met its contract. The wasted-token rate is the fraction of generated tokens spent on requests that were canceled, timed out, or delivered after their deadline, the execution the system performed after the result had lost value.
A saturated LLM fleet operating under severe KV cache pressure has three workload-specific relief options. Engines can apply context eviction through an explicitly supported sliding-window or approximate policy with a quality check, or truncate retained history and recompute its state. Silently dropping old KV entries is not equivalent to recomputing a shorter conversation, because later cached states already depend on the earlier context. Disabling speculative execution reduces draft work, but reclaiming its memory also requires unloading draft weights and releasing the associated cache state. Finally, fallback routing can send eligible requests to a smaller model with available capacity, provided that model meets the application’s fallback quality contract.
These options change latency, resource use, or model behavior in different ways. The application must specify which changes are acceptable at each pressure tier. Context truncation can remove information essential to an answer, and a smaller model can fail the task’s quality requirement. In those cases, an explicit rejection can be preferable to an apparently successful but unacceptable response.
Routing relies on estimates of replica capacity, but shared hardware can make that capacity change when another workload becomes active. Critical production models may share a cluster or device with experimental models and developer endpoints. Protecting the serving contract under that interference requires multi-tenant isolation in addition to routing.

Consider a critical customer-support chatbot running on the same GPU server as an experimental computer vision script. If the experimental workload monopolizes the PCIe bus or memory bandwidth, the chatbot can miss its latency target. Sharing saves capacity only when the resulting interference remains within each service’s contract. Fleet quotas, fair-share hierarchies, and priority preemption decide how much of the cluster a serving system receives; the problem here is controlling contention among the tenants who share that allocation, request by request.


↩︎ Fleet quotas, hierarchical fair-share, and the priority classes that govern preemption are established in Multi-Tenancy and Quotas.


Sharing a serving pool can raise utilization and reduce separately provisioned capacity when tenant demand peaks occur at different times. This statistical-multiplexing gain weakens when bursts are correlated, and shared resources introduce interference even when aggregate demand fits. Pooling therefore needs both a demand model and enforceable isolation.



One tenant’s burst can degrade every workload sharing the pool.
A burst from one tenant can delay others through shared KV-cache capacity, network bandwidth, and accelerator time. The pool must preserve each tenant’s data boundary and service contract; different SLOs can require different admission limits, reservations, or placements. Noisy-neighbor effects come first because they directly connect shared-resource contention to those latency contracts.



The noisy neighbor problem occurs when one tenant’s workload degrades performance for others sharing the same infrastructure. The interference manifests across three resource dimensions simultaneously.
GPU memory contention can limit admission before compute capacity is exhausted. Consider three tenants sharing a 60 GB KV pool with nominal 20 GB shares. Without enforced limits, one tenant’s long-context requests can raise its allocation to 45 GB. In the scenario, the others lose capacity from 200 concurrent sequences each to 75, a 62.5 percent reduction. That is a concurrency loss, not a proportional throughput prediction; the effect depends on their execution regime and preemption costs. Egress bandwidth and accelerator time are additional shared resources whose contention must be measured alongside memory occupancy.


↩︎ The device-level interference channels of shared accelerators (memory bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device interconnect, and thermal dissipation) are established in Resource isolation.

Example 10.12: Quantifying noisy neighbor impactScenario: An inference platform serves 10 tenants on shared H100 GPUs at 100 QPS each under a 50 ms p99 SLO. Tenant 3 bursts to 500 QPS, 5× its baseline.
Diagnosis: Without quotas, contention raises pool-wide p99 into the 22 ms to 45 ms range in this scenario, eroding every tenant’s headroom while remaining within the stated target. With quotas, Tenant 3 is limited to 120 QPS and the other tenants retain 15 ms p99. Throttling turns Tenant 3’s excess into rejected or delayed requests, which are judged against Tenant 3’s own contract rather than spread across the pool.
Systems lesson: Shared capacity raises utilization only when it is coupled with isolation. Quotas turn pool-wide erosion of latency headroom into an admission decision confined to the tenant that caused it; without them, a larger burst or a tighter SLO turns the same erosion into violations across the pool.





Resource quotas limit what each tenant can consume, preventing any single tenant from monopolizing shared resources. Hard quotas turn shared serving into admission control. Request rate and concurrency bound arrival pressure, while input tokens, output tokens, KV-cache pages, accelerator time, and egress bytes bound the work performed after admission. A single scalar quota cannot protect all of these resources because two requests can have the same count but differ by orders of magnitude in prompt length or generated output. Listing 1 shows representative gates so a tenant can be throttled at the scarce resource boundary instead of degrading the whole batch.



Listing 1: Multidimensional Resource Quotas: A snapshot check compares prospective resource use with tenant limits. Atomic reservation and scheduler enforcement are separate requirements.


class TenantQuota:
    max_concurrent_requests: int  # e.g., 100
    max_kv_cache_mb: int  # e.g., 20,000
    max_qps: int  # e.g., 1,000
    max_input_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_output_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_batch_tokens: int  # e.g., 50,000


def check_quota_snapshot(tenant_id, request):
    quota = get_quota(tenant_id)
    usage = get_usage(tenant_id)

    if usage.concurrent + 1 > quota.max_concurrent_requests:
        return RateLimitError("concurrent request limit")
    if usage.kv_cache_mb + request.reserved_kv_mb > quota.max_kv_cache_mb:
        return RateLimitError("memory limit")
    if usage.requests_last_second + 1 > quota.max_qps:
        return RateLimitError("rate limit")
    if usage.input_tokens + request.input_tokens > quota.max_input_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("input-token limit")
    if usage.output_tokens + request.max_output_tokens > quota.max_output_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("output-token limit")

    if request.prefill_chunk_tokens > quota.max_batch_tokens:
        return RateLimitError("prefill chunk exceeds batch-token limit")

    return None  # Snapshot is eligible; no resources have been reserved.



This listing assumes that reserved_kv_mb includes the requested prompt and output-token budget, and that usage counters include outstanding reservations in their stated time windows. A passing snapshot is not an admission guarantee: simultaneous callers can observe the same free capacity. Production admission must check and reserve resources atomically, roll back failed admissions, and release reservations on completion or cancellation. The batch scheduler separately enforces the aggregate batch-token limit. Quotas protect the resources they account for; shared compute, networking, and control-plane contention still require isolation and measurement.
Soft quotas permit borrowing unused capacity while preserving an enforceable share when demand rises. The unit of account matters: equal request counts can hide large differences in prefill work, output length, and retained state. Input and output tokens therefore need separate accounting, with memory and concurrency limits alongside them. The progressive-filling approach in Dominant-resource fairness allocation reduces to max-min fairness when only one divisible resource constrains the allocation. For three tenants demanding 30,000, 20,000, and 80,000 output tokens/sec from an idealized 100,000-token/sec pool with equal token costs, the allocation is 30,000, 20,000, and 50,000. Coupled prefill, decode, and memory constraints require joint feasibility checks; independent fair allocations do not automatically compose into a feasible service.

Those reservations must be provisioned and enforced separately: priority alone cannot create capacity, interrupt every running kernel, or guarantee a deadline under unbounded critical traffic.

The scheduler sorts incoming requests by priority class, then by arrival time within each class. When a new critical request arrives, it jumps ahead of all standard and best-effort requests in the queue, so revenue-generating traffic does not queue behind background batch jobs, although work already running on the accelerator can still delay it.
Preemption extends this principle to requests already in flight, but priority does not make state movement free. The retain, swap, recompute, or reject choice of section 10.8.3 still decides how a displaced request’s KV state is handled; priority adds an input to that choice rather than replacing it. A priority class determines who may be displaced, while remaining service time, state size, and deadline slack determine which victim is cheapest. Ignoring those costs lets aggressive preemption consume more capacity than it releases.



The bulkhead pattern11 (Nygard 2007) partitions resources so exhaustion or failure in one allocation has a limited effect on others. The boundary may be a logical concurrency pool, a separate process, or dedicated hardware; each contains different failure modes. The pattern is named after ship compartments intended to contain flooding.
11 Bulkhead limits: A divider isolates failure only if it closes the relevant boundary. The Titanic’s incomplete bulkheads allowed water to cascade between compartments; similarly, a soft quota cannot isolate shared memory or bandwidth that remains globally exhaustible.
Nygard, Michael T. 2007. Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software. Pragmatic Bookshelf.
Dedicated replicas separate more resources than request limits inside one process. Figure 18 assigns distinct compute and memory pools to tenant groups, so an engine crash or exhausted local allocation in the standard tier need not stop the gold-tier engines. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane services can still carry interference across that boundary.






Figure 18: Bulkhead isolation patterns: To prevent cascading failures in multi-tenant systems, bulkheads isolate resources. Deployment-level bulkheads (shown) assign dedicated physical replicas to high-priority tenants, separating their compute and memory pools. Request-level bulkheads enforce strict concurrency limits within shared processes. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane dependencies remain possible paths for interference.



Deployment-level bulkheads isolate the named compute and memory resources for premium tenants. They do not remove shared network, storage, power, or control-plane failure domains. The trade-off is lower pooling efficiency and additional operational overhead from dedicated infrastructure.
Request-level bulkheads limit work admitted within a shared process. Example caps of 8,000 input tokens, 2,000 output tokens, and 30 seconds of execution constrain request size and duration when the scheduler enforces them. They still need concurrency limits, resource reservations, and cancellation handling; a token cap alone does not bound interference or isolate a process crash.
Crash containment follows the process or hardware boundary, not the request quota. A malformed request that crashes a shared worker can interrupt every tenant using that worker. Service tiers requiring stronger fault isolation therefore need placement boundaries that match that requirement.

Example 10.13: Bulkhead configuration for API tiersScenario: An LLM API platform serves Enterprise, Professional, and Free service tiers across shared and dedicated hardware.
Diagnosis: Unpartitioned pools allow Free-tier bursts or shared-worker failures to affect Enterprise requests. The example assigns Enterprise to dedicated GPU pools with a 99.9 percent availability target, allocates 70 percent of the remaining shared capacity to Professional, and caps Free at 30 percent best-effort capacity. Meeting that target still requires reliability evidence for the dedicated pools themselves.
Systems lesson: Bulkheads concentrate isolation overhead where business requirements dictate. Hardware partitioning reduces cross-tenant compute and memory contention. SLO compliance still depends on sufficient capacity, admission policy, shared dependencies, and failure handling.


Multi-tenant isolation limits the blast radius of excess demand, but it does not create capacity. Once protected queues approach their latency budgets, the service needs a control loop that can add replicas before admission begins to fail.

A serving autoscaler that reacts only to average accelerator utilization can scale in the wrong direction. Decode can saturate memory bandwidth while arithmetic units appear idle, long prompts can consume prefill capacity before request count rises, and queued work can violate an SLO while fleet-wide utilization remains moderate. The control signal must represent outstanding work relative to phase-specific service capacity. Every replica the controller adds is also a claim on accelerators that training jobs may hold, so fleet-level arbitration with training bounds how quickly and how far serving can grow.


↩︎ The arbitration between serving replicas and training jobs for shared accelerators, including the minutes-long cost of switching a device between them, is established in The training-serving resource boundary.
For a conventional fixed-cost model, queueing delay and request rate per ready replica can guide scaling. Autoregressive serving also needs prompt-token and output-token rates, KV occupancy, and measured phase service rates. A colocated replica must satisfy all phase requirements; disaggregated prefill and decode pools need separate counts and a feasible transfer budget. SLO goodput measures useful supply, but rejected work and backlog must remain visible as unmet demand. A latency threshold can detect deterioration after a model change, yet controller timing and headroom still need validation. Adding replicas also depends on their startup delay. Changing an existing accelerator allocation may require a restart or state migration, depending on the runtime and execution plan.
Scale-up and scale-down require asymmetric evidence. Scale-up acts on sustained queue growth, forecast demand, or declining deadline slack because cold-start delay makes late reactions expensive. Scale-down requires low demand over a longer window, enough spare capacity to survive one replica failure, and a drain plan for in-flight requests and any optional session cache. This hysteresis prevents oscillation in which replicas repeatedly load large weights, accept work, and terminate before amortizing startup cost.
The controller also needs observability that distinguishes demand from impaired supply. Request rate, input and output tokens, queue age, TTFT, TPOT, deadline misses, admission rejections, ready replicas, model-load failures, and per-phase service rate form the minimum feedback set. Without replica readiness and service-rate measurements, an autoscaler can respond to a sick replica by adding cold replicas indefinitely while the original failure remains hidden.

Example 10.14: Cold start timeline for Llama-70BScenario: An autoscaling engine provisions a Llama-70B replica during a traffic surge, using an H100-based allocation large enough for its FP16 weights, cache, and runtime state.
Diagnosis: The scenario’s sequential startup estimate is 6.7 minutes (\(\ReplicaColdStartTime= \ReplicaProvisioningTime+ \ReplicaModelLoadTime+ \ReplicaWarmupTime\)): 1 minute for provisioning, 4.7 minutes to fetch 140 GB of artifacts at the assumed 0.5 GB/s, and 1 minute for device loading and warmup. Cached artifacts or overlapping phases can shorten this path; scarce capacity and shared storage can lengthen it. If existing headroom cannot absorb the surge, newly requested replicas arrive too late to protect short deadlines.

Example 10.15: Predictive scaling for trafficScenario: A commercial chatbot service faces predictable diurnal traffic patterns, ramping from 500 QPS at night to 3,000 QPS at peak.
Diagnosis: A controller that waits for the morning ramps at 06:00 and 09:00 UTC before requesting capacity must cover the assumed 7-minute startup interval with existing headroom or admission limits. Without enough ready capacity, queues grow while replicas start. Forecasting can shift that wait ahead of the expected demand.

Discounted interruptible capacity12 enters serving through the same purchasing tiers that fleet capacity planning uses (Cloud Capacity Reservation Tiers): reserved capacity for the steady baseline, on-demand capacity for bursts, and spot capacity for work that tolerates revocation. None of these tiers makes a replica immune to failure, so the serving question is whether a revoked replica can drain, reroute, or recompute its requests without violating their SLO. The provider’s warning window is the binding constraint.

Listing 2: Spot Termination Handling: Graceful shutdown sequence that stops admission, deregisters from the load balancer, drains in-flight requests, and persists recoverable state.


async def handle_spot_termination():
    # Received 2-minute warning
    # 1. Stop admission and remove the replica from routing
    stop_accepting_requests()
    deregister_from_loadbalancer()

    # 2. Complete in-flight requests (if possible)
    await complete_inflight(timeout=90)

    # 3. Save state for resumption elsewhere
    save_kv_cache_to_storage()

    # 4. Terminate gracefully
    shutdown()

Routing still depends on readiness and available headroom. An eviction notice triggers draining when time permits; requests that cannot finish need a permitted retry, reconstruction, or rejection path.







Figure 20: Spot-aware traffic distribution: The gateway classifies requests by SLO and routes 70 percent of traffic, the SLO-critical share, to on-demand replicas that face no spot reclamation, and 30 percent, the best-effort share, to discounted spot replicas that can be preempted. When a spot worker receives an eviction notice, the gateway stops routing to it while it drains, and best-effort requests tolerate occasional retries. The traffic split is illustrative; cost savings depend on provisioned capacity, discounts, retries, and idle headroom.



Savings under this split depend on provisioned GPU-hours, discounts, retries, and reserve capacity rather than on the traffic share, and spot capacity changes none of the fault-tolerance requirements of the SLO-critical path.

Cross-region model sharding places communication on the request’s execution path. Pipeline stages can reside in separate regions, but every dependent stage crossing then pays the inter-region transfer cost. In an illustrative comparison of 75–150 ms network delays with 1–5 ms stage computation, a 10–100\(\times\) slowdown is possible; it is not a model-independent ratio. Such placement needs a reason strong enough to justify that cost, such as unavailable colocated capacity, and must be evaluated against the actual stage layout and deadline.
Because cross-region sharding is so costly on the steady-state path, most production designs keep inference co-located and use other regions for resilience. The cross-region question therefore shifts from splitting one request across regions to deciding how quickly traffic can move when a region fails.



When a region becomes unavailable, failover must choose a healthy destination permitted to process the request and able to absorb its work. Listing 3 illustrates a simplified timeout fallback. A production policy must also preserve the request’s remaining deadline, version requirements, and data-placement constraints when selecting the secondary region.



Listing 3: Active-Active Failover: A bounded retry policy selects eligible regions and limits each attempt to the remaining request deadline.


# Eligibility includes placement, version, readiness, and capacity.
def route_request(user_region, request):
    attempted = set()
    for attempt_budget in (2.0, 5.0):
        remaining = request.deadline - monotonic_time()
        regions = eligible_regions(request, excluding=attempted)
        if remaining <= 0 or not regions:
            break
        region = nearest_region(user_region, regions)
        attempted.add(region)
        try:
            # The endpoint atomically admits work and enforces the deadline.
            return call_region(region, request,
                               timeout=min(attempt_budget, remaining))
        except (Timeout, RegionUnavailable, AdmissionRejected):
            # Cancel abandoned work; retries require replay-safe semantics.
            cancel_attempt(region, request)
    return unavailable_or_deadline_exceeded(request)



Rerouting is only part of regional failover. The destination needs accessible, authoritative conversation history to reconstruct lost KV state and enough headroom for both reconstruction and continuing traffic. If the required history is unavailable or cannot be processed there under the placement policy, a healthy replica alone cannot restore the session.

The search-ranking scenario binds on cascade cost: each query coordinates many smaller models under one end-to-end latency budget rather than serving one large model. The ensemble combines specialized models for query understanding, document relevance, and result ranking.
The operational scale motivates a cascade architecture: the system must process billions of searches per day under a strict end-to-end latency target of less than \(200\text{ ms}\), evaluating thousands of candidate documents per query across dozens of specialized models. Screening candidates with cheaper models reserves the expensive ranking budget for a smaller set.
To meet this latency budget while evaluating thousands of documents, the ranking cascade diagrammed in figure 24 screens candidate pools across four progressively expressive tiers: early lexical and approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) embedding retrievers discard 99 percent of candidates within a 10 ms budget, reserving compute-intensive cross-attention transformers for the final top 100 items. This saving creates a recall constraint. A relevant document discarded upstream cannot be recovered by a more accurate downstream ranker, so each stage’s candidate budget must be evaluated for retained relevant items as well as latency.

A DevOps team applies their standard web-server load balancing rules to a new fleet of GPU inference nodes, only to watch tail latency explode because they ignored the extreme variance of autoregressive token generation. Web services also face variable work and queueing, but an inference fleet adds model residency, accelerator scheduling, and per-sequence state to those familiar concerns. The fallacies below arise when a serving design ignores these constraints or treats one optimization as a complete solution.

Fallacy: Inference at scale is synonymous with LLM serving.
The misconception, reinforced by LLM-centric discourse, leads to over-focus on LLM-specific techniques while ignoring the broader inference landscape. Published characterizations of large consumer platforms show recommendation and ranking models consuming most AI inference cycles, while vision, fraud detection, and classification models account for much of the rest (Gupta et al. 2020; Hazelwood et al. 2018). A practitioner who only understands continuous batching and KV cache management is unprepared for the feature-parallel batching and embedding sharding that dominate high-volume recommendation inference. Technique selection must match the actual workload.

Hazelwood, Kim, Sarah Bird, David Brooks, Soumith Chintala, Utku Diril, Dmytro Dzhulgakov, Mohamed Fawzy, et al. 2018. “Applied Machine Learning at Facebook: A Datacenter Infrastructure Perspective.” 2018 IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 620–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/hpca.2018.00059.


Pitfall: Using training infrastructure for production serving.
Training and serving have different requirements. Training balances aggregate throughput with convergence and time to solution; interactive serving must also satisfy per-request latency targets under external arrivals. Its batch size therefore depends on the workload and waiting budget. Interactive streaming may admit little batching, while bandwidth-bound LLM decode can benefit from many concurrent sequences. Training can resume from checkpoints after an interruption; serving needs a recovery policy that accounts for in-flight requests, retries, and the availability target. Hardware can be shared or repurposed, but a training configuration does not establish serving readiness. Batching, routing, and capacity management must be evaluated against the serving contract.


Fallacy: Continuous batching solves the whole LLM serving problem.
Continuous batching reuses slots released by completed requests, but it addresses only one dimension of the problem. Prefill can remain a bottleneck for long contexts because scheduling subsequent decode iterations does not remove the quadratic attention work of full-attention prefill. Section 10.10 demonstrates that KV cache memory, not compute, often limits batch size. Network bandwidth between sharded model components can dominate latency for large models. The value of continuous batching depends on the workload; slot reuse alone does not resolve these other constraints.


Pitfall: Sizing the fleet by average throughput.
Average throughput alone does not establish capacity for bursts. With unchanged work per request and service capacity, a 25 percent traffic increase from 80 percent utilization reaches 100 percent utilization, leaving no spare capacity to absorb variance. Whether the resulting queue violates an SLO depends on burst duration, the waiting budget, and admission policy. Cluster-level cold starts can delay relief for multiple minutes. Capacity planning must therefore account for peak load, burst duration, ready headroom, and the work the service can defer or reject.


Fallacy: Load balancing does not matter much for inference.
Simple load balancing strategies like round-robin can distribute request counts while leaving work uneven. The static placement analysis in section 10.13 motivates two probes, but its occupancy bounds do not predict production queue lengths. Serving comparisons must preserve arrivals, request lengths, cache affinity, and replica capacity. Work-aware routing earns its place when it improves measured tail latency without excessive coordination cost.


Pitfall: Ignoring the serving tax.
Distributed inference adds network round-trips and shard coordination to the serialization, routing, and queueing costs that can already surround a single-machine model. This serving tax depends on deployment topology and load. In the illustrative budget of section 10.4, 70 ms of model execution leaves only 30 ms for every other stage of a 100 ms request target, and queueing alone can consume that remainder as load rises. A kernel benchmark measures only the first term of equation 1; the serving latency is the measured sum along the complete request path.


Fallacy: More GPU memory always means larger batch size and higher throughput.
Larger GPU memory raises throughput only when the extra capacity supports useful work within the latency budget. Even when memory bandwidth is saturated, a larger decode batch can increase tokens per second by sharing weight reads across more sequences. That gain stops when compute, per-sequence KV-cache traffic, or the SLO becomes binding. The bottleneck hierarchy distinguishes these limits.
For an H100 with 80 GB memory and 3.35 TB/s HBM3 bandwidth, capacity and transfer rate are separate limits. More capacity may admit additional sequences, but the resulting batch must still meet compute, bandwidth, and latency budgets. Once extra sequences no longer improve useful throughput within those budgets, adding memory alone cannot help. Capacity planning therefore measures the bottleneck at the intended batch size and context length rather than assigning one permanent bottleneck to the model.


Pitfall: Neglecting multi-tenancy isolation until production.
In development and staging, single-tenant deployments work well. In production, noisy neighbors cause sudden, unpredictable performance degradation that is difficult to diagnose and resolve. A tenant bursting to 5\(\times\) normal traffic can degrade latency for all other tenants on shared infrastructure. As emphasized in section 10.14, resource quotas, priority scheduling, and bulkhead isolation must be designed into the system from the start, not retrofitted after production incidents.
These pitfalls identify what a serving evaluation must test: traffic variance, cost per completed request within the SLO, and interference across tenants. Correct technique selection must be followed by measurement under the intended load and failure conditions.

Inference at scale turns trained models and distributed hardware into a service under continuously arriving work. Training optimizes aggregate progress over a run; serving must also meet user-visible latency targets while paying recurring operating costs. The useful capacity of the fleet is the work it completes within its service contract, not the work its accelerators execute in isolation. Test-time compute sharpens the point. When quality is bought by spending more compute per query, the scaling curve that drove the fleet’s growth moves into the request path, and every increment of quality is paid again on every request.
Serving performance depends on the balance between compute and memory bandwidth. In the terms of the single-machine iron law recalled in The Fleet Law, long-prompt prefill can be compute-bound (\(\Operations/\PeakRate\)), while small-batch decode is often bandwidth-bound (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)). Each decode iteration reads active weights and the sequences’ KV state; batching shares weight reads across more tokens, whereas longer contexts increase KV traffic. Single-replica efficiency (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) therefore depends on phase, batch size, and context length. Variable output lengths make fixed batch membership waste capacity after shorter requests finish.
To maximize throughput under memory-bandwidth constraints, modern serving architectures co-design the memory hierarchy and the iteration scheduler. Continuous batching recovers idle slots by inserting new requests at token boundaries; PagedAttention reduces physical memory fragmentation through fixed-block allocation while retaining partial-page waste; and prefill/decode disaggregation assigns prompt processing and token generation to separate hardware pools sized around their measured compute, memory, and communication costs.
When model state exceeds device memory, sharding spreads a replica across accelerators; when demand exceeds a replica’s service capacity, additional replicas supply aggregate throughput. In Fleet Law terms, sharding divides the compute term \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) of equation 10 but adds communication and synchronization \((\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount), \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount))\) governed by interconnect latency floors (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) and transfer bandwidth (\(\LinkBandwidth\)). Replication, routing, isolation, and autoscaling add coordination costs through probes, admission decisions, and capacity changes, and multi-region placement adds wide-area round trips and cross-region failover to the same budget; transferring model or session state also consumes communication bandwidth. Their aggregate capacity and tail control require headroom and sometimes idle replicas. Across the serving hierarchy, the engineering objective is to increase useful completed work while preserving the latency and reliability contract under load.

Key Takeaways: Serving capacity is constrained by its contract

Serving cost recurs throughout deployment: Training is paid per model version, while inference expense accrues with traffic (principle \(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)). In the chapter’s high-volume recommendation scenario, lifetime serving cost reaches 525.6× the training cost, making efficiency a recurring economic lever.
Tail latency governs architecture: Batching, sharding, caching, and autoscaling must improve useful capacity within workload-specific service targets. Aggregate throughput is insufficient when queueing, first-token delay, or slow token delivery makes completed work miss its contract.
Decode turns memory into capacity: Long-prompt prefill often binds on compute, while small-batch decode rereads active weights and expands private KV state token by token (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)). Continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix reuse, and KV compression matter because they convert scarce HBM bandwidth and memory into admitted requests.
Model class sets the primitive: Vision models benefit from predictable static or dynamic batches, recommenders from feature-parallel embedding sharding, and LLMs from iteration-level scheduling. A fleet scheduler must match the workload shape instead of applying one universal batch-size rule.
Distribution always sends a bill: Sharding, routing, isolation, and failover buy capacity or resilience while consuming communication and coordination budgets. Power-of-two choices (principle \(\ref{pri-power-two-choices}\)) illustrates the value of limiting coordination: routing can use a small number of probes rather than polling every replica.



The serving cost dominance principle (\(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)) makes local efficiency valuable only when the service can turn it into useful capacity. Memory released by quantization may admit more sequences, but those sequences still compete for execution time and can push the endpoint beyond its latency budget. The economic comparison therefore holds the request mix, quality requirement, and service targets fixed before asking whether a change lowers the cost of completed work.

What’s Next: From data center to edgeThe serving designs developed here coordinate accelerator replicas under data-center memory, network, and availability assumptions; even the global stack’s edge points of presence only answer from cache and leave model execution in the clusters. Many applications also run models on smartphones and other personal devices, where sustained power is a few watts, memory is shared with foreground work, and connectivity is intermittent. When those devices must also adapt to local data, the fleet has to decide where learning happens, which device updates it accepts, and how a population improves a shared model without collecting raw examples.

Approximately \(1.3\times\)

Approximately \(630.7\times\)

Answer: The serving tax comprises exposed network, serialization, coordination, and queueing delays beyond model execution. In the four-level Serving Hierarchy (Request, Replica, Service, Platform), which level and primary optimization lever are correctly matched to their target bottleneck?

Request level: Ensuring fair-share GPU quotas and tenant isolation across organizations
Service level: Managing aggregate capacity across multiple replicas via load balancing and autoscaling
Replica level: Reducing client-side network RTT via edge caching and CDN routing

Answer: The correct answer is C. The Service level coordinates multiple replicas of the same model to deliver aggregate capacity through load balancing, request routing, and autoscaling. The proposal linking the Platform level to kernel fusion confuses fleet-wide multi-tenancy with intra-device execution; the proposal placing fair-share tenant quotas at the Request level incorrectly attributes platform governance to per-request transformations; and the proposal placing edge CDN caching at the Replica level confuses single-device execution with edge routing infrastructure.

**Order the four levels of the Serving Hierarchy from the most granular execution tier to the highest fleet-wide governance tier:


Service level (fleet routing, load balancing, autoscaling)

Platform level (multi-tenancy, cross-workload scheduling, placement)

Why can maximum-length KV cache preallocation waste memory when actual requests are shorter, and which allocation waste does paged memory management reduce?
Answer: Maximum-length preallocation reserves unused slots when a request is shorter than the limit; the wasted fraction depends on the length distribution. Paged allocation assigns fixed-size KV blocks on demand and reuses free blocks across sequences. It removes external fragmentation within the fixed-block pool, but the final partially filled page still wastes some capacity. Reclaimed memory helps only if the scheduler can use it within latency and quality limits.
Learning Objective: Explain the root causes of KV cache memory fragmentation under preallocation and how paged allocation mitigates them.
True or False: An autoregressive LLM must retain state during active decoding, but a serving API can still be stateless across completed requests if each new request supplies the required conversation history.
Answer: True. The active decode loop uses per-request KV state. Retaining that state across turns is a serving choice that can save prefill work and favor routing affinity; a full-history request can instead rebuild it on another replica.

Why is pure First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling problematic for multi-tenant LLM serving, and what mechanism does preemptive scheduling use to resolve it?

FCFS requires excessive GPU memory for block tables; preemptive scheduling replaces block tables with static pointers.
FCFS causes extreme AllReduce communication overhead; preemptive scheduling converts tensor parallelism to pipeline parallelism.
FCFS forces all requests to run at INT4 precision; preemptive scheduling dynamically promotes high-priority requests to FP16.
FCFS can let long requests occupy scarce slots while short requests wait; preemption pauses selected requests and manages their KV state to admit other work

Answer: The correct answer is D. Preemption can run at token boundaries, but the victim state must remain in HBM, move to host memory, or be rebuilt on resumption. These alternatives consume capacity, transfer bandwidth, or prefill compute. The policy must compare those costs with deadlines; preemption does not change model precision or replace tensor-parallel collectives.

At what approximate batch size \(B\) does each workload reach the ‘knee’ of its batching efficiency curve (\(B \approx T_{\text{fixed}} / T_{\text{var}}\))?

Vision knee at \(B \approx 10\); LLM decode knee at \(B \approx 20\)
Vision knee at \(B \approx 80\); LLM decode knee at \(B \approx 2\)
Vision knee at \(B \approx 4\); LLM decode knee at \(B \approx 40\)
Vision knee at \(B \approx 2\); LLM decode knee at \(B \approx 80\)

Answer: The correct answer is D. The knee of the batching efficiency curve occurs where the variable compute cost (\(B \times T_{\text{var}}\)) begins to exceed fixed overhead (\(T_{\text{fixed}}\)). For the vision model, \(B_{\text{knee}} \approx 2\text{ ms} / 1\text{ ms} = 2\). For LLM decode, \(B_{\text{knee}} \approx 40\text{ ms} / 0.5\text{ ms} = 80\). The larger LLM knee illustrates a stronger incentive to amortize weight reads across concurrent requests. For a static LLM batch that retains all slots and pads completed sequences until the longest sequence finishes, define the waste ratio \(W=1-\bar{S}/S_{\max}\). How can continuous batching reduce this waste?
Answer: The stated implementation allocates \(B S_{\max}\) token-step slots but performs only \(B\bar{S}\) useful token steps, leaving a waste fraction \(1-\bar{S}/S_{\max}\). Continuous batching can replace completed sequences with waiting requests at each iteration. This reduces padded-slot waste when enough admissible work is queued; it does not guarantee a full batch under light arrivals or memory pressure. Holding responses until the batch finishes is a separate response-barrier policy, not an inherent consequence of fixed membership.
Learning Objective: Analyze the mathematical formulation of batching waste in static LLM execution and the mechanism of continuous batching.
For a recommendation pipeline that first retrieves sparse features and then processes dense features before combining them, order: (1) Feature Interaction, (2) Dense Feature Processing, (3) Sparse Feature Lookup, (4) Ranking Head.
Answer: The correct sequence is (3) Sparse Feature Lookup -> (2) Dense Feature Processing -> (1) Feature Interaction -> (4) Ranking Head for the stated pipeline. Interaction consumes both sparse and dense representations; ranking consumes their combined features. Sparse lookup and dense processing can run concurrently in other implementations when neither depends on the other, so their serial order is an explicit scenario assumption.
Learning Objective: Structure the sequential execution stages of a feature-parallel recommendation model pipeline.
A stable inference service completes 1,000 requests/sec with an assumed mean end-to-end latency of 100 ms. Each replica executes full batches of eight in 80 ms, giving 100 requests/sec of service capacity. With a separate target of at most 80% mean service utilization, what mean in-flight work and candidate fleet size follow, without claiming a P99 guarantee?

Mean in-flight work is 100 requests; sizing service capacity at the 80% utilization target gives 13 replicas
Required concurrency \(Q_{\text{req}} = 1{,}000\); minimum SLO-sized fleet \(= 125\) replicas
Required concurrency \(Q_{\text{req}} = 80\); minimum SLO-sized fleet \(= 10\) replicas
Required concurrency \(Q_{\text{req}} = 100\); minimum SLO-sized fleet \(= 10\) replicas

Answer: The correct answer is A. Little’s Law gives 1,000 × 0.1 = 100 requests in flight on average, including waiting work. Under the idealized assumption that all other latency is waiting or batch formation, the fixed 80 ms service time gives 80 requests executing on average and leaves 20 waiting or accumulating. Ten replicas are the throughput-only saturation boundary. The assumed mean and tail SLO both require validation; dividing in-flight work by batch slots does not establish the fleet size.

Additional generated tokens, candidate evaluations, or search steps increase work per request and can extend KV-cache residency without changing the bottleneck of each decode step. Dynamic compute allocation budgets that work using measured quality gains, request deadlines, and fleet load. Parallel candidate evaluations consume capacity without necessarily adding the same serial latency.

The policy must be evaluated against arrival patterns, measured service rates, tail latency, and overload handling; neither a longer nor a shorter window is universally optimal.
Learning Objective: Evaluate adaptive batching control policies under varying traffic arrival intensities.

How does PagedAttention reduce memory waste in LLM KV cache management, and what system-level benefit can follow?

It compresses KV cache tensors using lossless entropy coding to reduce arithmetic intensity in attention kernels.
It replaces standard multi-head attention with grouped query attention by dynamically merging key-value heads.
It maps logical tokens to non-contiguous fixed-size physical blocks, reclaiming unused reservations so that more requests may fit
It offloads 100% of KV cache data to host CPU DRAM, eliminating GPU HBM usage entirely for active sequences.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Any free block can extend a sequence, removing external fragmentation within the fixed-block pool. Only the final partly filled block retains internal waste. Reclaimed capacity can support larger batches, but the gain depends on request lengths, available memory, and the latency contract. Paging changes allocation; it neither compresses tensor values nor changes the number of KV heads.

What is the ‘speculation tax’ in speculative decoding, and how does it influence whether speculative decoding should be enabled for a specific serving endpoint?

The latency penalty paid when draft models fail to generate valid UTF-8 token encodings.
The GPU memory allocated to draft model weights and draft KV cache, which reduces available HBM for batch concurrency.
The serialization tax incurred when transmitting draft tokens across InfiniBand interconnects.
The loss in model generation accuracy caused by greedy sampling during draft token verification.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Draft weights and draft KV cache consume memory that could otherwise support target-model concurrency. Speculation is useful when lower latency or more accepted output per target pass outweighs that capacity cost and draft execution. The result depends on load, acceptance, and both models; a latency-oriented endpoint does not automatically benefit, nor is every throughput-oriented endpoint harmed.

A chatbot has 1,000 concurrent users sharing a 2,000-token prefix and retaining 500 private response tokens each. For a hypothetical MHA model with 80 layers, 64 KV heads, head width 128, and FP16 cache, explain the reduction from about 6.6 TB to 1.3 TB with prefix sharing.
Answer: Each cached token uses 2 × 80 × 64 × 128 × 2 = 2,621,440 bytes. Without sharing, 2,500,000 token positions consume 6.5536 TB; storing the shared prefix once leaves 2,000 + 1,000 × 500 = 502,000 positions, or 1.316 TB. The reduction is 79.92%. This is an MHA scenario, not the smaller eight-KV-head GQA cache of Llama-2-70B; saved memory alone does not prove a fivefold throughput gain.

How can an un-chunked long prompt prefill delay active decode streams on the same worker, and what trade-off does chunked prefill introduce?
Answer: A policy that schedules a full long-prompt prefill before returning to decode can create a conspicuous gap in active streams’ time between tokens (TBT). An isolated stall can be diluted in a long response’s average time per output token (TPOT). Chunked prefill interleaves bounded prompt-token chunks with decode work, controlling how much prefill work enters each iteration. Smaller chunks can reduce interference while adding overhead and extending the incoming prompt’s TTFT. A token budget alone does not guarantee a time bound; both TTFT and TBT tails require measurement.
Learning Objective: Explain the operational mechanism of chunked prefill in preventing decode stalls and mitigating tail latency.
Switching from standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA) with 64 key-value heads to Grouped Query Attention (GQA) with 8 key-value heads reduces the KV cache memory footprint by a factor of ____\(\times\).

Learning Objective: Calculate the architectural compression factor of Grouped Query Attention on KV cache capacity.
**Order the steps executed during a single verification round of Speculative Decoding:


Target model runs a single batched parallel forward pass across all \(K\) candidate positions
Rejection sampling evaluates candidate tokens sequentially against target probability distributions
Draft model autoregressively generates \(K\) candidate tokens
KV cache block tables are updated to append accepted tokens and one target correction token, discarding rejected branches**

Answer: The correct sequence is (3) -> (1) -> (2) -> (4). - (3) The fast draft model autoregressively produces \(K\) speculative tokens in lightweight forward passes. - (1) The target model evaluates the proposed positions in one forward pass. How does SmoothQuant enable efficient 8-bit weight and 8-bit activation (W8A8) inference, and why is its speedup significantly higher during prefill than during decode?

It prunes 50% of model weights using structured sparsity, accelerating decode but having no effect on prefill.
It divides activations by a per-channel scale \(s\) and multiplies weights by \(s\), moving quantization difficulty toward weights; compute-bound prefill can benefit from native INT8 arithmetic while decode remains sensitive to memory traffic
It rotates the coordinate basis using randomized Walsh-Hadamard matrices, eliminating memory bandwidth bottlenecks during decode.
It converts floating-point weights into binary spikes, enabling single-cycle bitwise operations during token generation.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The equivalent transform is \(XW=(X\operatorname{diag}(s)^{-1})(\operatorname{diag}(s)W)\). It smooths activation outliers while increasing weight range, enabling an INT8 path when calibration preserves quality. Compute-bound prefill can benefit from higher arithmetic throughput; memory-bound decode depends on bytes moved and conversion costs. Speedup is workload-dependent, not guaranteed by the transform alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze the mathematical mechanism of SmoothQuant W8A8 quantization and contrast its performance gains during prefill versus decode phases.
What is the core algorithmic distinction between Generalized Post-Training Quantization (GPTQ) and Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (AWQ)?

GPTQ quantizes activations while leaving weights in FP16; AWQ quantizes weights while leaving activations in FP32.
GPTQ requires full model retraining for 100 epochs; AWQ is an online dynamic quantization method with no calibration.
GPTQ compensates residual quantization error across remaining unquantized columns using inverse Hessian information (\(H^{-1}\)); AWQ protects salient weight channels based on activation magnitudes without error feedback.
GPTQ applies only to convolutional vision models; AWQ applies exclusively to sparse recommendation embedding tables.

Answer: The correct answer is C. GPTQ performs layer-by-layer second-order error compensation: as each weight column is rounded to discrete grid points, the residual error is propagated to unquantized columns using the inverse Hessian matrix (\(H = X^T X\)). In contrast, AWQ observes activation magnitudes on a calibration set, identifies the top ~1% most salient channels, and scales those specific weight channels up prior to quantization to preserve precision without requiring iterative error compensation.
Learning Objective: Compare the algorithmic formulations and error-mitigation strategies of GPTQ versus AWQ.
Explain how QuaRot uses a data-free orthogonal rotation to reduce activation outliers, why its full quantization pipeline can still require calibration, and what runtime cost the rotation introduces.
Answer: An orthogonal rotation preserves \(XW=(XH)(H^TW)\) while spreading large activation coordinates across dimensions. The rotation can be chosen without calibration data, but a QuaRot pipeline using GPTQ still uses calibration activations to quantize weights. Inline Hadamard transforms add runtime work; their cost and W4A4 quality must be evaluated on the deployed model and workload.
Learning Objective: Explain the theoretical foundation of rotation-based quantization (QuaRot) and its operational trade-offs.
True or False: Modern NVIDIA Hopper (H100) GPUs provide native Tensor Core instruction acceleration for FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) delivering a \(2\times\) compute throughput multiplier over FP16, whereas Ampere (A100) Tensor Cores do not natively support FP8 execution.
Answer: True. H100 Tensor Cores support native FP8 and advertise twice the dense arithmetic throughput of their FP16 path, while A100 lacks native FP8 Tensor Core instructions. This is a hardware ceiling, not an automatic twofold application speedup or a guarantee of preserved model quality.
Learning Objective: Identify native Tensor Core precision support across NVIDIA Ampere and Hopper accelerator architectures.
**Order the sequential steps in the GPTQ column-wise layer quantization pipeline:


Compute the Hessian matrix \(H = 2 X^T X\) from calibration activations
Perform Cholesky decomposition on the inverse Hessian matrix \(H^{-1}\)
Round the current column weights to the nearest discrete quantized grid
Calculate the residual quantization error vector for the column
Propagate compensation updates to all remaining unquantized columns using the Cholesky inverse weights**

Answer: The correct sequence is (1) -> (2) -> (3) -> (4) -> (5). - (1) Pass calibration data through the model to compute activation cross-products and form the Hessian matrix \(H\). - (2) Compute the inverse Hessian and factor it via Cholesky decomposition to enable stable triangular error updates. - (3) Round the target column’s continuous weights to the nearest low-bit quantized values. - (4) Compute the quantization error difference between original and rounded column weights. - (5) Propagate the scaled error vector to remaining unquantized columns to adjust their values before subsequent quantization steps.
Learning Objective: Structure the computational workflow of GPTQ layer-by-layer second-order quantization.

Hot (1%) embeddings are replicated within selected shard groups; warm (10%) are column-sharded; cold (89%) are row-sharded by entity hash, with transport chosen for the runtime.

Hot embeddings are sharded row-wise across CPUs; cold embeddings are broadcast via AllReduce to all GPU Tensor Cores.

AllToAll dispatch transmits token activation vectors to the specific GPUs hosting the selected experts
Gating network evaluates input representations and computes top-\(k\) routing probabilities

Assign weight 1.0 to H100 and 1.0 to A100 so all servers receive equal traffic shares.

Route 100% of traffic to A100 servers first and overflow remaining traffic to H100 servers.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Total cluster capacity is \((10 \times 1{,}000) + (20 \times 600) = 10{,}000 + 12{,}000 = 22{,}000\text{ QPS}\). Capacity-proportional routing assigns each H100 server a weight of \(1{,}000 / 22{,}000 \approx 4.55\%\) (\(681.8\text{ QPS}\) load, \(68.2\%\) utilization) and each A100 server a weight of \(600 / 22{,}000 \approx 2.73\%\) (\(409.1\text{ QPS}\) load, \(68.2\%\) utilization). Equal routing leaves less latency headroom on the A100s (\(83.3\%\) utilization) than on H100s (\(50\%\) utilization). Both remain below their stated service capacities; these utilization values alone establish neither overload nor a tail-SLO violation.
Learning Objective: Calculate capacity-proportional routing weights to balance resource utilization across heterogeneous accelerator fleets.
The three-state resilience pattern that fails fast and stops routing traffic to a degraded or thermally throttled GPU replica before retries cascade across the fleet is called a ____.
Answer: circuit breaker (or Circuit Breaker / circuit breaker pattern). A circuit breaker transitions from closed to open when error rates or latencies exceed a threshold, isolating the degraded replica and protecting the rest of the fleet.
Learning Objective: Identify the circuit breaker pattern as the primary mechanism for preventing cascading failures in inference clusters.

Self-Check: Answer

Which statement best distinguishes deployment-level bulkheads from request-level bulkheads in a multi-tenant inference platform?

Deployment-level bulkheads enforce rate limits using software counters; request-level bulkheads isolate GPU power supplies.
Deployment-level bulkheads apply only to batch inference; request-level bulkheads apply only to interactive chat.
Deployment-level bulkheads dynamically quantize weights to INT4; request-level bulkheads dynamically compile CUDA graphs.
Deployment-level bulkheads physically isolate tenant tiers onto dedicated GPU replicas, while request-level bulkheads cap input/output token lengths and execution time within shared processes.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Dedicated replicas reduce direct contention between tenant tiers, while request-level caps bound individual work within shared processes. Dedicated replicas do not guarantee complete failure isolation: power, networks, storage, and control planes can still be shared. Rate limits and deadlines complement placement, rather than replacing hardware capacity planning.
Learning Objective: Compare the architectural mechanisms and isolation guarantees of deployment-level versus request-level bulkheads.
When multiple tenants with unequal demand compete for a shared GPU pool, the fair-allocation algorithm that maximizes the minimum allocation by bounding per-tenant consumption using token generation rate (tokens/sec) is called ____ fairness.
Answer: max-min (or Max-Min / max-min fairness). Max-min fairness allocates equal capacity up to each tenant’s demand, redistributing unused headroom from low-demand tenants to high-demand tenants.
Learning Objective: Identify the max-min fairness principle applied to multi-tenant inference resource allocation.

In an illustrative fresh-replica startup, fetching 140 GB of model artifacts takes five minutes while detection and controller decisions take seconds. Why are pre-warmed pools or predictive scaling useful?

Artifact loading dominates this scenario, so pre-warmed pools or advance provisioning can make capacity ready before the surge
\(T_{\text{decide}}\) dominates (10–15 minutes evaluating autoscaling PID loops); mitigated by switching to manual scaling.
\(T_{\text{detect}}\) dominates (30 minutes gathering Prometheus metrics); mitigated by removing metric telemetry entirely.
\(T_{\text{warmup}}\) dominates (1–2 hours running CUDA kernel JIT compilation); mitigated by disabling Tensor Cores.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Reactive decisions cannot supply ready capacity faster than provisioning, artifact loading, and warmup complete. A pre-warmed pool avoids much of that delay; forecasting starts the work before expected demand. Five minutes is a scenario assumption governed by effective storage bandwidth and cache state, not a universal cold-start duration or a reason to disable telemetry.
Learning Objective: Analyze the components of autoscaling response latency and evaluate strategies for mitigating cold-start delays.
When a cloud provider issues a 2-minute termination warning for a spot/preemptible GPU inference instance, describe a four-step shutdown sequence that reduces disruption within the remaining time budget.
Answer: First stop admission and deregister the replica. Then drain admitted requests within the remaining deadline. Preserve recoverable session history or transferable state where the service supports it; otherwise plan bounded retries or reconstruction on healthy replicas. Finally terminate workers before reclamation. This sequence reduces disruption but cannot guarantee every long request finishes or that all KV state can be copied within two minutes.
Learning Objective: Structure the graceful termination and state-preservation workflow for preemptible/spot inference instances.

Compare actual transfer times, message sizes, and the request deadline rather than treating RTT as the cost of every stage. Independent regional replicas avoid these per-request cross-region stage transfers when the model fits within each eligible region; placement must also satisfy policy and available-capacity constraints.

In an illustrative search-ranking cascade (L0: 1M to 10k in 10 ms; L1: 10k to 1k in 20 ms; L2: 1k to 100 in 50 ms; L3: 100 to 10 in 100 ms), what follows under a simplified additive candidate-work model?

It runs L3 on all 1,000,000 candidates using asynchronous DMA transfers without CPU involvement.
It replaces neural networks entirely with BM25 keyword matching across all stages.
It dynamically recompiles transformer weights at each stage using TensorRT-LLM.
It cuts final expensive L3 evaluations by \(10{,}000\times\) (from 1,000,000 to 100), reducing total candidate-scoring compute by \(\approx 5{,}600\times\) within a 180 ms budget.

If its 100 ms budget represents one ms of additive work per candidate, applying it to every candidate costs 1,000 seconds versus the assumed 0.18-second cascade budget, about 5,556-fold more. Compare the binding bottlenecks and serving topologies of the illustrative embedding-heavy recommendation scenario and autoregressive LLM API scenario.
Answer: The recommendation scenario prioritizes sparse embedding locality and memory capacity, placing large tables on memory-rich CPU/SSD servers and dense ranking on GPUs. The LLM scenario prioritizes growing KV state, variable request lengths, and decode bandwidth, using sharded replicas and iteration scheduling. These are workload design cases, not verified inventories of a named company’s private infrastructure; the topology follows the measured limiting resource.

True or False: In the illustrative two-tower video recommendation scenario, both the user tower and the content tower must execute synchronously for every swipe.
Answer: False. The scenario computes changing user representations online but precomputes slower-changing content embeddings and caches them. Online work then combines the user representation with stored candidates. Refresh cadence must satisfy the application’s freshness contract rather than a universal hourly schedule.

Which cross-cutting principle is demonstrated by the four illustrative serving scenarios: embedding-heavy recommendation, LLM generation, search ranking, and video recommendation?

Production inference rejects one-size-fits-all stacks: systems specialize hardware and batching to match their binding bottleneck (embeddings, variable decode, cascade cost, or asynchronous freshness).
All modern inference workloads are compute-bound and converge onto identical 8-way tensor-parallel GPU clusters.
Traditional static batching with First-Come-First-Served scheduling remains optimal for all production workloads when scaled to 1,000 GPUs.
Quantization to 1-bit binary representations is universally deployed across all production recommendation and search systems.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Embedding locality, variable decode work, cascade cost, and content freshness impose different constraints. Hardware placement, batching, and caching should match that limiting resource. The scenarios do not establish that every production deployment uses the same sharding configuration or precision; a common stack cannot be assumed optimal across these workload shapes.
Learning Objective: Synthesize the cross-cutting architectural principles governing production inference systems at scale.

Self-Check: Answer

A team upgrades a cluster serving a 13B LLM from 80 GB GPUs to 140 GB GPUs with identical HBM3 memory bandwidth (3.35 TB/s). At an unchanged small batch and context length, with resident weights and weight-read-dominated decode, why does extra capacity alone not raise the bandwidth-limited throughput ceiling?

Autoregressive decode is strictly compute-bound; increasing memory without adding Tensor Cores leaves execution time unchanged.
Autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound (\(D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW}\)); once model weights fit resident in memory, token generation speed is constrained by memory bandwidth, not total memory capacity.
140 GB GPUs automatically disable CUDA graph compilation, adding driver launch latency to every iteration.
The larger memory capacity forces PagedAttention block sizes to shrink from 16 tokens to 2 tokens.

Answer: The correct answer is B. At the same small batch and context length, when weight reads dominate decode and the resident model already fits, extra memory capacity does not increase the bandwidth ceiling. A larger admitted batch can nevertheless raise aggregate token throughput by sharing weight reads across more sequences while execution remains bandwidth-bound. The gain stops when KV traffic, compute, or the latency budget binds; crossing into a compute-bound regime is not required for batching to help.
Learning Objective: Analyze why memory bandwidth, rather than memory capacity, bounds autoregressive decode throughput.
A capacity planner provisions an inference serving fleet for 80% average utilization based on mean daily traffic. Why can traffic spikes exhaust headroom before reactive scaling helps, and what determines whether the P99 SLO is missed?
Answer: Waiting grows sharply as utilization approaches one. At an 80% baseline, a 25% traffic increase reaches exactly 100% utilization, leaving no spare capacity to absorb arrival or service-time variation; a larger sustained increase exceeds capacity. Cold starts can take minutes, so reactive scaling may arrive after latency failures begin. Whether a spike misses the P99 SLO depends on its duration, the arrival and service-time distributions, the waiting budget, and admission policy. Capacity planning therefore needs measured peak behavior and ready headroom alongside average traffic.
Learning Objective: Explain the queuing theory and autoscaling risks of provisioning inference fleets based on average rather than peak-plus-headroom demand.
True or False: Deploying continuous batching alone completely solves all throughput and latency bottlenecks in LLM serving.
Answer: False. Continuous batching reuses slots at iteration boundaries. It does not remove the quadratic attention work of long full-attention prefills, shrink the KV tensors needed by admitted requests, or eliminate communication within sharded replicas. Additional mechanisms are selected for the binding constraint: chunking can limit prefill interference, paging can recover allocation waste, compatible prefix reuse can avoid repeated work, and sharding or replication can supply needed capacity. No fixed combination establishes the service contract without workload measurements.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the scope and limitations of continuous batching within the end-to-end LLM serving pipeline.

Which statement best captures the central physical and economic synthesis of inference at scale presented in the chapter?

Inference costs are a fixed one-time expense, while training costs scale continuously with user traffic.
All inference workloads should be served using static batching on single-GPU instances to eliminate network communication.
Serving cost recurs with traffic throughout deployment; small-batch decode can bind on weight and KV traffic, so scheduling, memory allocation, and topology must be evaluated against the workload and service contract.
Multi-tenancy isolation can be safely omitted if GPUs are upgraded to Blackwell architectures.

Answer: The correct answer is C. For the high-traffic, small-batch LLM setting, serving cost accumulates with completed work over the deployment lifetime, and weight/KV traffic often limits decode. Efficient operation coordinates scheduling, cache allocation, sharding, and routing under latency and quality constraints. Cost dominance and bandwidth limitation depend on traffic, model, and serving regime; neither is universal across all inference workloads.
Learning Objective: Synthesize the core physical and economic principles governing large-scale inference systems.
Why must interactive inference evaluate tail latency alongside aggregate throughput, and how does its service contract differ from a training run?
Answer: Training evaluates aggregate progress, convergence, and time to solution over a run. Interactive inference receives external arrivals and must complete useful work within request-level latency, quality, and availability targets while paying recurring cost. High aggregate throughput does not establish timely responses when queues grow or token delivery stalls. Tail latency and SLO-compliant goodput therefore belong in the same evaluation; a latency-tolerant batch inference service can use a different contract.
Learning Objective: Explain why interactive serving evaluates tail latency and useful throughput under a request-level service contract.
The economic principle stating that recurring lifetime serving expense can exceed one-time training expense by orders of magnitude is known as the ____ principle.
Answer: Serving cost dominance. The serving cost dominance principle highlights that inference efficiency improvements provide continuous financial return over a model’s entire deployment lifetime.
Learning Objective: Identify the serving cost dominance principle governing the lifetime economics of machine learning systems.
