title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can lifetime inference cost dwarf training cost?
Training is paid for each model version; serving continues throughout that version’s operational lifetime. A model trained for millions of dollars may serve billions of requests, each consuming compute, memory, network, and energy. At high traffic, recurring inference expense can exceed the original training cost by orders of magnitude. Milliseconds of latency and small differences in accelerator utilization then compound across the service’s lifetime. A fast prediction measured on an otherwise idle machine does not reveal how the same model behaves when requests arrive together, vary in length, and compete for memory. Work can spend longer waiting than executing, while an apparently busy fleet produces responses that arrive too late to be useful. Keeping extra machines ready protects response time but incurs cost during quiet periods; admitting more work improves utilization only while the service can still meet its promises. Failures sharpen this tension because displaced requests consume the spare capacity intended to absorb demand changes. Continuing to accept work during overload can worsen the shortage when delayed requests trigger retries that compete for capacity. The engineering decision is therefore how much useful work the fleet can sustain at an acceptable cost while preserving response quality and timeliness. The answer depends on the request mix and service requirements, so a gain for one workload may become a loss for another. In C³ terms, compute reuse must pay for communication and coordination without exhausting the user’s latency budget.

Learning Objectives

Estimate lifetime serving cost from traffic volume, deployment duration, and measured per-request cost
Select batching, scheduling, and per-request compute-budget policies for vision, LLM, recommender, and streaming workloads
Analyze attention-cache capacity, fragmentation, and decode-time policies under workload-dependent serving constraints
Compare sharding, disaggregation, and quantized serving designs using communication, memory, and quality constraints
Evaluate routing, load balancing, and isolation controls against tail latency and noisy-neighbor risks
Design autoscaling and multi-region routing policies that balance cold starts, cost, and SLO compliance
Synthesize serving architectures that manage C³ trade-offs across request, replica, service, and platform layers

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Imagine a language model that costs $5 million to train over two months. Once deployed to a global user base serving thousands of queries per second, that same model can consume $5 million in inference compute every week. Inference is no longer a temporary batch job. It is a continuous, latency-sensitive service.
Performance engineering ends with a measured execution envelope, the cost and deliverable capacity of one replica once operator fusion, precision engineering, and graph compilation have done their work. Serving policy determines how that execution capacity is shared under externally arriving work. A faster forward pass supplies a better service rate, but it does not determine how long requests wait to join a batch, which replica receives them, which requests receive scarce cache space, or when the fleet needs another replica. These decisions connect the local execution toolkit to user-visible performance under load.


↩︎ The replica’s measured execution envelope, and the fusion, precision, compilation, and speculation levers that shape it, are established in Performance Engineering.
The service contract makes that distinction measurable. Offered load is the work arriving at the endpoint, including requests the service may reject; admitted load is the work it accepts. A service-level objective (SLO) specifies the required outcome over a measurement window, such as a latency percentile or successful-request fraction. For language models, request rate alone is insufficient because prompt and output lengths determine different amounts of work. Capacity comparisons must therefore hold the request mix and SLO fixed while measuring how much offered work completes successfully within the targets.
An admitted request passes through routing, preprocessing, queueing, batch formation, model execution, and response delivery. Figure 1 traces this traversal across the host CPU and accelerator boundaries: the host manages admission, tokenization, and detokenization, while the GPU executes the prompt prefill pass and iterative KV-cache decode loop, mapping noncompute serving overhead against the time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT, the average gap between streamed tokens) latency budgets. For an autoregressive model, prefill processes the prompt and builds cached attention keys and values; decode extends that KV cache as it generates subsequent tokens. Waiting before prefill delays the first token, while competition during decode delays the stream. The scheduler must budget both delays alongside execution time. Batching and cache management govern work within a replica, sharding changes the replica’s capacity, and routing and autoscaling distribute demand across replicas.


↩︎ The prefill-decode decomposition, with prefill’s high arithmetic intensity and decode’s weight-streaming regime, is established in The prefill-decode decomposition.







Figure 1: End-to-end inference pipeline: One language-model request crosses between CPU and GPU twice. The load balancer routes and admits it and the CPU tokenizes it; prefill then processes the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values to the KV cache, and decode reads and appends that cache one token per step before the CPU detokenizes the stream. The strip orders one request’s latency, with illustrative segment widths. Everything up to the end of prefill counts against time to first token, and the routing and CPU segments are serving-tax work that spends latency budget outside GPU compute.



Distribution adds placement and coordination decisions to the local serving problem. Load balancing1 must distribute requests across replicas with different amounts of unfinished work and available memory. Request routing must also account for model-specific characteristics: recommendation systems with large sharded embedding tables require different placement strategies than language models that generate responses token by token. When demand changes faster than new replicas can become ready, routing alone cannot restore capacity. Autoscaling, spare capacity, and admission limits must work together to protect the service’s latency targets.
1 Load balancing for inference: Request service times can span milliseconds to tens of seconds as models, prompt lengths, and generated outputs vary. Queue-aware routing exposes that remaining work more directly than assignment counts alone.Training and serving place costs on different timelines. A model version’s training expense can be amortized over its deployment, while serving capacity must follow recurring demand. An e-commerce recommendation service, for example, must accommodate peak shopping traffic without paying for an unnecessarily large idle fleet during quiet periods. Both training efficiency and serving efficiency matter, but the serving decision must also account for when requests arrive and how long they can wait. Building such a service requires three linked decisions: when distribution becomes necessary, how the architecture meets latency targets under varying load, and how resource utilization stays high enough that serving cost does not erode the value the model creates. The worked scenarios that follow size these decisions with stated inputs: registry values for real hardware and models, and labeled scenario assumptions for traffic, prices, and latency budgets. They show how a mechanism scales, not what any named deployment measured.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Memory, throughput, and latency limits motivate different forms of distribution. Exceeding one device’s capacity may require several devices within one machine; crossing the machine boundary adds network costs. Table 1 categorizes these constraints and candidate strategies, whose necessity depends on the permitted precision, placement, and service contract.
The first signal is memory exhaustion, which occurs when model parameters, key-value caches, or embedding tables exceed single-device capacity. A single NVIDIA H100 GPU provides 80 GB of HBM32 memory; Assumption Provenance records the provenance of this capacity figure and the other canonical hardware constants used throughout the analysis that follows. For an illustrative mixture-of-experts model with ~1.8T parameters, FP16 weights alone require ~3.5 TB. Keeping all those weights resident on accelerators requires multiple devices regardless of request volume; quantization and offloading change that placement constraint. Recommendation systems with trillion-parameter embedding tables face similar constraints: Meta’s DLRM architecture3 stores embedding tables that require multiple terabytes of memory.
2 HBM3 capacity and bandwidth: The H100 combines 80 GB of 3D-stacked DRAM with 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth, compared with 2.04 TB/s for HBM2e on the A100. Capacity determines whether model and cache state fit; bandwidth bounds memory-bound decode throughput.3 DLRM (Deep Learning Recommendation Model): Meta’s 2019 reference architecture combines dense features processed by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) with sparse features represented by embedding lookups (Naumov et al. 2019). This separation permits different placement strategies; it does not require embeddings on CPUs and MLPs on GPUs. Production recommendation characterizations show why this structure matters for serving: embedding-heavy recommendation models create memory-access and capacity constraints that differ from dense convolutional neural network (CNN), recurrent neural network (RNN), or large language model (LLM) inference (Gupta et al. 2020).
Naumov, Maxim, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Hao-Jun Michael Shi, Jianyu Huang, Narayanan Sundaraman, Jongsoo Park, Xiaodong Wang, et al. 2019. “Deep Learning Recommendation Model for Personalization and Recommendation Systems.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1906.00091.

Gupta, Udit, Carole-Jean Wu, Xiaodong Wang, Maxim Naumov, Brandon Reagen, David Brooks, Bradford Cottel, et al. 2020. “The Architectural Implications of Facebook’s DNN-Based Personalized Recommendation.” 2020 IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 488–501. https://doi.org/10.1109/HPCA47549.2020.00047.
Beyond memory constraints, throughput limitations emerge when request volume exceeds single-machine capacity even with optimal batching. Consider a recommendation system serving 100,000 queries per second with a 10 ms latency budget. If single-machine throughput peaks at 10,000 QPS, no amount of optimization on that machine can satisfy demand. Horizontal scaling across multiple replicas becomes mandatory.
Finally, latency requirements can motivate distribution even when memory is sufficient. A 70-billion parameter model requires approximately 140 GB of weight memory in FP16, exceeding a single 80 GB H100-class GPU before KV cache is considered. Quantization or larger-memory hardware can make a single-device configuration feasible, yet its execution time may still exceed the request budget. Sharding the model across multiple GPUs can divide computation and weight traffic, but it adds communication and synchronization. Because sharding shortens compute-bound prefill and bandwidth-bound decode by different amounts, the latency benefit must be measured for each phase against its own target.



Table 1: Triggers for distributed inference: Each constraint type indicates different distribution strategies. Memory constraints require model sharding; throughput constraints require replication; latency constraints may require either depending on whether the bottleneck is compute or memory bandwidth.

Memory, throughput, and latency triggers all become user-visible once an interactive endpoint starts streaming. Time to first token (TTFT) determines when the user sees a response begin, while time per output token (TPOT) determines whether the rest of the response arrives at a readable pace. TPOT is the average of the time between tokens (TBT), the gap between successive streamed tokens, which is the per-gap quantity Performance Engineering called inter-token latency (ITL). A stream can meet its TPOT target while a single long TBT gap still stalls the reader, so this chapter states average cadence as TPOT and per-gap tail targets as TBT. Protecting both first-token delay and stream cadence is why inference reverses many of the optimization priorities from training.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
The contrast between training and inference centers on the unit of useful progress. Training evaluates throughput together with convergence over a run; interactive serving evaluates completed requests against quality and latency targets. Offline inference can also prioritize throughput, while training still loses progress to stragglers and stalls. The distinction is therefore which delays violate the workload’s contract, not whether one activity cares about time and the other does not. Table 2 summarizes the priorities of long-running training and interactive serving across six system aspects.



Table 2: Training vs. inference system requirements: The fundamental inversion from throughput to latency optimization ripples through system design, state management, batch formation, and failure recovery.










Aspect

A training iteration that takes 2 seconds instead of the usual 1 second delays progress; repeated slow iterations can materially extend the run. An interactive request that takes 2 seconds against a 100-millisecond target misses its contract immediately, even if later requests finish quickly. Aggregate training progress and per-request serving deadlines expose different consequences of the same delay. The serving architecture must therefore control individual waiting times as well as total completed work.
State management differs fundamentally. Training maintains model state (parameters, optimizer states) that evolves gradually and can be captured in periodic checkpoints. Inference may maintain session state across requests, but authoritative conversation history and user context differ from derived key-value caches. The history must survive according to the service contract; a lost KV cache can be rebuilt from that history at the cost of repeated prefill. Retaining the cache across turns is a performance choice, developed in the architecture dimensions that follow.
Failure handling follows those different contracts. Training can restore a checkpoint and repeat lost work, with recovery time charged against the run’s completion target. Interactive serving has less time to recover an individual request. Redirecting work to a healthy replica requires spare capacity and recoverable request state; substituting a smaller model requires an acceptable quality fallback. SLOs define which failures and delays the service may tolerate. Recovery mechanisms reduce user-visible disruption only when their added work fits within that contract.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Distributing inference adds transfers and coordination to a request that already spends time in host processing and queues. This “serving tax” is the exposed work outside model execution that consumes the request’s latency budget. Its size depends on which components the request crosses and which costs can overlap.
Network communication contributes setup and transfer time at each cross-machine dependency. Synchronization between GPUs can expose that cost when the next operation needs a remote result. For an illustrative path with four sequential exchanges taking 50–500 microseconds each, the exposed contribution is 200 microseconds to 2 milliseconds. Actual collective time also depends on payload, topology, contention, and the number of communication rounds; a generic network round-trip time cannot be charged once per collective without checking its implementation.


↩︎ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model, which splits each transfer into a fixed startup latency plus a bandwidth-dependent term, is established in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model.
4 Zero-copy serialization: Formats such as FlatBuffers and Cap’n Proto can access wire-format data in place, avoiding a separate parse-allocate-copy cycle. The benefit depends on payload size, language runtime, and whether downstream operators can consume the same buffer representation.Serialization can add host work when a service converts structured data into a wire representation and reconstructs it at the receiver. Protocol Buffers, JSON, and Python’s pickle provide different representations and implementation paths, so their cost must be measured for the actual payload and runtime. Tensor transfers within a sharded model need not pass through the same object-serialization path as a service request. Formats such as FlatBuffers and Cap’n Proto4 permit access to wire-format data in place, avoiding a separate unpacking step when the consumer supports that representation. They do not eliminate network transfer or every downstream copy.
Load balancing adds a routing decision and sometimes another forwarding hop. Examining request metadata, consulting replica state, and forwarding to the selected backend consume time before execution begins. The measurement must separate decision time from waiting and transport so that a slow routing path is not mistaken for a slow model.
Coordination overhead emerges when a request fans out to several services and joins their results. Independent feature or model calls can run concurrently, but a dependent ranking stage must wait for the inputs it needs. The critical path therefore includes exposed coordination and the slowest required branch rather than the sum of every branch’s runtime. Queuing delay (\(\QueueingLatency\)) adds another cost whenever work arrives while the required resources are busy, even when average arrival rate remains below average service capacity.
The serving tax must be measured on the same request boundary as model execution. Equation 1 decomposes that latency, with each term counting an exposed contribution so concurrent work is not counted twice:
\[\EndToEndRequestLatency= \InferenceLatency+ \NetworkLatency+ \SerializationLatency+ \CoordinationLatency+ \QueueingLatency \tag{1}\]
An illustrative budget shows why the decomposition matters. If an interactive request has a 100 ms target and model execution takes 70 ms on an idle replica, routing, transfers, serialization, coordination, and queueing must all fit in the remaining 30 ms; the four sequential exchanges above can already claim up to 2 ms of it before any request waits for a busy replica. The measured contribution determines the intervention. Co-location can remove a network hop, fewer dependent exchanges can reduce startup costs, and a faster link can shorten large transfers. Queueing instead requires controlling admitted work or increasing usable capacity. Each choice spends resources to recover latency budget, connecting the request-level diagnosis to lifetime serving cost.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
At this traffic, one year of serving costs about nine times the training run.
The serving tax quantified in equation 1 consumes a fraction of the latency budget per request. The true economic impact of inference emerges when evaluating cost over a model’s entire operational lifetime. The serving cost dominance principle (\(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)) states that serving cost can dominate training cost by orders of magnitude because a model version incurs training expense before deployment while serving expense recurs with traffic. Both activities can consume purchased or rented infrastructure; the distinction here is expense timing, not financial capitalization. A quick cost calculation makes the multiplier concrete.

Napkin Math 10.1: The serving cost multiplierProblem: A team has spent $2,000,000 training a 70B parameter model and now serves it to 1,000,000 daily active users, each making 50 requests/day. Is training or serving the dominant cost over 1 year?
Math:

Training Cost: $2,000,000 (One-time).
Metric: Annual inference volume is \(10^{6}\,\text{users} \times 50\,\text{reqs} \times 365\,\text{days} \approx\) 18.25B requests/year.
Cost per Request: Assume a 70B model on H100 costs \(\approx\) $0.001/request (input + output).
Annual Serving Cost: 18.25B requests \(\times\) $0.001/request = $18,250,000.

Systems insight: Serving costs 9.1× more than training in the first year alone. A 10 percent reduction in cost per request, at unchanged request volume and service quality, saves about $1.8M in the first year, nearly paying for the original training run.


For one model version at a fixed query rate and average cost per served query, equation 2 combines training expense with recurring serving expense:
\[\ModelLifetimeCost= \TrainingCost + \ServingCostPerQuery\times \DeploymentDuration\times \ArrivalRate \tag{2}\]
where \(\TrainingCost\) is the one-time cost to train the model, \(\ServingCostPerQuery\) is the cost per query served, \(\DeploymentDuration\) is the deployment duration in appropriate time units, and \(\ArrivalRate\) is the query rate. The rate must count the same served queries used to estimate unit cost. That cost must include the chosen serving boundary, including idle or reserved capacity when it is billed. Changing traffic mix, fleet size, or price requires evaluating separate intervals rather than treating one unit cost as constant throughout deployment.
The same leverage can hold across application categories with different cost structures. In the chapter’s illustrative recommendation scenario, a DLRM trained for $12,000 ($3000 hardware for 1,000 GPU-hours at $3/GPU-hour, plus 3× additional engineering cost for data and experimentation) and served at 10,000 QPS for 730 days accumulates \(6.31 \times 10^{11}\) lifetime queries. At the assumed $10/million queries, those queries cost $6,307,200 to serve, producing a 525.6× ratio in this scenario. The cost structure motivates serving optimization: a reduction in cost per completed request yields recurring savings if workload volume and service quality remain fixed. Lower latency alone does not ensure that billed capacity or other costs fall. Figure 2 uses constructed cost curves to illustrate how unit cost can change with daily request volume. Against its assumed price of $0.05 per 1,000 tokens, the optimized curve crosses near \(2 \times 10^5\) requests per day, while the unbatched single-GPU curve crosses beyond \(3 \times 10^7\) requests. These crossings follow from the assumed curves, not measured profitability or guaranteed effects of INT4 and continuous batching. A deployment needs its own token mix, occupied capacity, and complete cost boundary to establish a break-even point.

The cost ranges in table 3 give a static comparison; figure 3 instead accumulates assumed monthly serving expense over a 36-month deployment. Its crossover occurs when the serving portion equals the initial training expense, not when total deployment cost first exceeds training cost. In the plotted recommendation scenario, that happens within days; in the 70B LLM scenario, it takes roughly six weeks. These timings follow from the specified expenses, not from model size or user count alone. A larger training expense, lower traffic, or shorter deployment can change which activity dominates. The comparison motivates evaluating serving efficiency early while keeping workload and quality fixed. For generative LLM services, serving-specific designs can improve throughput, cost, and power use (Patel et al. 2024).

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Large language models present distinctive serving challenges, but they are only one part of production inference. In large consumer platforms, recommendation and ranking workloads can dominate AI inference cycles and capacity (Gupta et al. 2020; Hazelwood et al. 2018). Vision and image processing, NLP and LLM workloads, fraud detection, ads, and other classification tasks create additional serving demands. Table 4 compares representative pressures: sparse lookup for recommendation, batch efficiency for fixed-shape vision, weight and cache traffic for LLM decode, and incremental deadlines for speech. These are starting points for diagnosis; the active bottleneck still depends on the model, input shape, and deployment.
Recommendation traffic illustrates why request volume must be derived from application behavior. A page load, scroll, or click can trigger ranking or retrieval, so one browsing session can produce many inference requests. A language-model application may likewise issue several model calls for one user action or run background tasks without an explicit query. Capacity planning therefore counts the model work triggered by each interaction rather than treating user count as request rate.
Workload structure also determines which techniques can help. Embedding sharding addresses the memory demands of large recommendation models, while their sparse access patterns make lookup locality a central design concern (Naumov et al. 2019; Gupta et al. 2020). Feature store architectures add a related requirement: the serving path must retrieve the inputs the model expects within its latency budget. Continuous batching and KV cache management instead address variable-length autoregressive work. Text-to-image systems such as DALL-E provide one multimodal model example (Ramesh et al. 2021), but multimodal serving volume and latency targets remain product-specific.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
The optimization techniques organize into a serving hierarchy ordered by scope, from one request up to a shared multi-tenant platform. Each level owns a different bottleneck and measurement boundary, so an optimization that helps one level can leave another unchanged. The request level follows one request through preprocessing, batch-formation waiting, response caching, and model execution, where the target is the latency a user sees. The replica level looks inside one model instance, where GPU utilization, KV-cache memory management, kernel efficiency, and model optimization determine how much useful throughput that replica can deliver before it saturates. The service level then works across many replicas of the same model, using load balancing, request routing, and autoscaling to turn individual replicas into aggregate capacity. The platform level works across services and tenants, where resource allocation, multi-tenancy, scheduling, and placement decide whether a shared serving fleet remains efficient without allowing one workload to degrade another.
Each level supplies a different measurement boundary. Table 5 associates request latency, replica throughput, aggregate service capacity, and cross-tenant efficiency with the controls most directly responsible for them. Their effects still cross boundaries: batching can increase replica throughput while adding request delay, and replica placement can change both communication cost and service capacity. The hierarchy helps locate the decision without treating its metric in isolation. In C³ terms, batching and cache management improve compute reuse, sharding introduces communication, and routing, isolation, and autoscaling coordinate the resources that make those gains usable.

Checkpoint 10.2: The serving hierarchy
Verify your understanding of where specific optimizations sit within the serving hierarchy:

Replica level: identify the hierarchy level at which KV-cache paging reduces GPU memory waste, and explain why that raises concurrent request capacity rather than single-request latency.
Caching level: distinguish response caching, which shortens one request’s path, from KV-cache paging, which raises a replica’s capacity, and place each in the hierarchy.
Load balancing: identify why load balancing belongs at the service level and explain how its choice of replica can affect both aggregate goodput and a request’s queueing delay.
Isolation level: evaluate the claim that multi-tenancy and resource isolation are primarily request-level concerns.



The chapter climbs the hierarchy in that order, while allowing a few techniques to cross levels. A survey of the architectural dimensions along which serving systems differ comes first. Batching then sets how long each request waits to share execution, the request-level decision that also feeds replica throughput. KV-cache layout, decode-time optimizations, and the disaggregation of prefill and decode into separate pools decide how many requests a replica can hold, and adapter state, weight quantization, and model sharding change the replica’s memory and compute budget. Load balancing turns replicas into a service, multi-tenancy and isolation govern the shared platform, autoscaling changes how much capacity the platform holds, and global placement extends the same decisions across regions. Precision is an input to every capacity calculation that follows: reducing weight precision frees resident memory, whereas reducing KV precision lowers the memory required per active sequence. These are separate budgets. Section 10.11 compares the serving trade-offs of these representation choices before sharding divides a replica across devices.


↩︎ Reduced-precision representations for weights, activations, and the KV cache, and the quantization methods that produce them, are established in Precision Engineering.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
A recommendation system that processes 100,000 embedding lookups per second across a sharded feature store requires a different serving architecture from a 70-billion-parameter language model generating tokens one at a time. Framework choice alone does not explain the difference. The workloads impose distinct constraints on batching, memory management, scheduling, and deployment topology. This section lays those dimensions out as a map, naming each decision and its alternatives briefly and using specific frameworks as examples rather than as the subject of study. The sections that follow develop the mechanisms behind each entry (continuous batching, paged KV memory, chunked prefill, disaggregation, session caches) together with their costs, and return to this map when they choose among them.


Batch formation sets the throughput-latency operating point. Static batching groups a fixed number of requests and suits predictable, fixed-shape inputs. For autoregressive language models, iteration-level admission lets new requests replace completed sequences instead of waiting for the longest sequence in a batch; Orca introduced this scheduling approach (Yu et al. 2022), and vLLM combines it with paged KV-cache management (Kwon et al. 2023). Recommendation systems with sharded embeddings can use feature-parallel batching to group sparse lookups by destination while also batching whole requests for dense computation. The common decision is which unit of work to group: whole requests, decode iterations, or feature lookups. Section 10.9 develops the mechanisms and their capacity trade-offs.



Serving systems differ fundamentally in how they manage accelerator memory, and this difference determines the maximum concurrent request capacity.

Definition 10.1: KV cache
KV cache is a per-request LLM inference memory buffer that stores key and value attention tensors for processed prompt and generated tokens. It avoids recomputing those tensors for the prefix; each new query still performs attention against the cached state.

Significance: Compared with recomputing full-prefix attention for each new token, caching changes the attention work from \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) in sequence length for full attention with fixed model dimensions. Retaining that state costs memory proportional to context length and the number of active sequences, potentially exceeding the weight footprint. KV cache fundamentals derives the fundamental sizing math.
Distinction: Model weights are shared across requests using the same model, while each sequence has its own logical KV state. Physical storage can still be shared for compatible common prefixes. The scheduler must budget for distinct retained state and its growth, rather than assume every request needs a wholly separate copy or that sharing removes the capacity limit.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that reducing model size proportionally reduces serving memory. In practice, the KV cache dominates HBM at long contexts, so a quantized 70B model can still be capacity-bound at batch sizes the weights alone would easily admit.



Preallocated memory management can reserve a fixed cache budget at admission for the prompt plus the permitted output. With a 4,096-token output allowance, a maximum-size reservation sets aside room for those additional tokens even if generation stops after 50. Prompt state consumes capacity as well. This policy makes future growth predictable, but the unused reservation cannot serve another request until it is released. Its waste depends on the gap between reserved and realized total sequence lengths.
Paged memory management, inspired by operating system virtual memory, allocates memory in fixed-size blocks (pages) and maps logical sequence positions to physical memory locations through a block table. As a request generates tokens, new physical blocks are allocated on demand. When generation completes, blocks no longer referenced by another request or retained for later reuse can return to the free pool. PagedAttention is the canonical design, and section 10.10.3 develops what removing contiguous per-sequence reservations does to fragmentation.
The memory management strategy changes admissible batch capacity by reclaiming space that contiguous preallocation leaves unused. Lower cost per request follows only when the recovered capacity produces more completed requests within the same latency and quality contract.



The scheduling policy determines which requests receive GPU time and in what order. This decision matters when some requests require 50 output tokens and others require 4,000. First-come-first-served (FCFS) scheduling orders admission by arrival time, but that order does not require executing each request to completion before starting another. In a serial or full-batch-barrier implementation, long requests can cause head-of-line blocking. An iteration-level scheduler can admit requests in FCFS order while advancing several sequences together. Tail latency then depends on available slots, cache capacity, and the amount of work admitted ahead of a request.
Preemptive scheduling allows the system to stop allocating decode iterations to one request so that another can run. Preemption is practical at token boundaries, but it is not free. The scheduler must retain the request’s KV pages in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), swap them to host memory, or discard them and repeat prefill when the request resumes. A useful victim policy compares those three costs with the waiting request’s remaining deadline rather than preempting at a fixed generation length. Retaining state consumes scarce capacity, swapping consumes interconnect bandwidth, and recomputation consumes prefill compute; under heavy load, rejecting low-priority work can cost less than repeatedly moving or rebuilding its state.
Priority-aware scheduling gives eligible high-priority requests precedence at scheduling boundaries. A production API might classify revenue-generating customer requests as critical, internal batch processing as standard, and free-tier traffic as best-effort. Already-running kernels and shared resources can still delay critical work; admission limits and reserved capacity must complement priority ordering.



The deployment topology maps model computation and state to physical hardware. A single-GPU deployment keeps execution local and avoids inter-device communication, provided weights, cache, and runtime state fit together. A 13B model’s FP16 weights (26 GB) leave most of an 80 GB H100 for KV state, whereas a 70B model’s 140 GB cannot be resident on one device at FP16. That makes a single device a useful baseline for models of the first kind, but not necessarily the lowest-latency design. Multiple devices can shorten execution enough to repay communication, while a model that fits at a short context may exceed one device’s capacity at higher concurrency. Topology selection therefore needs both a memory budget and measured execution times for the intended workload.
Multi-GPU tensor parallelism shards each layer’s weight matrices across multiple GPUs connected by high-bandwidth interconnect (NVLink at 900 GB/s bidirectional [450 GB/s per direction] on H100). Each GPU computes a partial result for every layer, and an AllReduce operation synchronizes the partial results before the next layer. This topology distributes an accelerator-resident model that exceeds one device’s memory. Ideal compute time falls with parallelism degree, but communication, imbalance, and kernel efficiency limit realized latency reduction. The model sharding section (section 10.12) analyzes the communication overhead quantitatively.
A third topology separates the two phases of a request. Prefill and decode can run on different pools of accelerators, each sized for its own token rate, with the prompt’s KV cache transferred from the prefill pool to the decode pool (Zhong et al. 2024). Whether that separation pays depends on how many bytes the transfer moves, so section 10.10.7 develops it once KV-cache sizing is in hand. Chunked prefill (section 10.9.6) is the colocated alternative, interleaving slices of a long prompt with ongoing decode steps on the same worker (Agrawal et al. 2024).
Every topology is judged by the same capacity metric. SLO goodput is the rate of completed requests that meet the stated TTFT and TPOT targets. It is the serving counterpart of the useful-progress goodput that coordination protects in training (Orchestration coordination layer (\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3)). A request that misses its contract counts for nothing, however busy the accelerators were while serving it, so increasing arrivals without completing more requests within those targets does not increase useful capacity.



A serving system’s statefulness determines what must be preserved when requests move between replicas. Vision inference and individual embedding lookups can expose stateless interfaces because they need no session history from an earlier request. A ready replica with the required model and data can then accept a rerouted request. Adding replicas still requires loading that state, distributing traffic, and checking downstream capacity; failure recovery also requires spare capacity and a policy for retrying interrupted work. Statelessness removes session-state migration from these operations, but does not remove their resource costs.


↩︎ Stateless and stateful failure recovery mechanics are established in Stateless vs. stateful serving.
An autoregressive request is stateful while it is generating because its KV cache belongs to that in-flight sequence. Cross-request statefulness is optional. An API may send the full conversation history with every turn and rebuild KV state during prefill, making any replica eligible for the next request. A serving platform may instead retain a completed turn’s KV state as a session cache, reducing repeated prefill at the cost of replica affinity, cache lifetime management, and recovery complexity. Sticky routing is an optimization for that retained cache, not a correctness requirement of autoregressive models.
The scaling divide is therefore an interface and cache-policy decision. Every live generation needs request-scoped state, but the service decides whether state survives the request boundary. Stateless cross-turn service can rebuild state from the supplied history, paying repeated prefill rather than requiring the previous replica’s cache. Session-cached service saves prefill work but must drain, migrate, or rebuild cached state during scaling and failure. Neither interface makes an interrupted generation free to recover. The architecture should choose affinity only when measured cache-reuse value exceeds the resulting imbalance and recovery costs.



Table 6 summarizes how the batching, memory, scheduling, topology, and state dimensions interact across the major workload types. Its entries are candidate combinations for the illustrated constraint regimes. A model class alone does not prescribe a scheduler or topology; the choice also depends on model size, request mix, available hardware, and service targets.

The architectural dimensions determine which serving system to select for a given workload. Rather than comparing frameworks feature by feature, an engineer identifies the workload’s position along each dimension (batching pattern, memory profile, scheduling requirements, deployment topology, and statefulness) and selects the system that matches. The optimization techniques in this chapter operate within this architectural framework, each addressing a specific dimension.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
A stream of hundreds of disparate chat requests arrives at an inference server every second. Processing them one by one leaves much of the GPU idle, starved for work between small decode steps. Waiting to gather a large static batch forces the first request in line to endure unacceptable latency. Batching at scale therefore needs policies that group requests as they arrive without violating tail-latency deadlines.
Processing multiple requests together shares weight reads and kernel launch overhead across more useful work. The resulting service-rate gain can reduce queueing, but waiting to form a batch adds delay; the net effect on request latency depends on load. Single-machine serving applies this insight through dynamic batching, which collects requests within a time window before processing them together.
At scale, batching must also account for workload structure. A policy suited to uniform vision inputs can leave slots unused during variable-length generation, while grouping sparse embedding lookups solves a different problem from batching dense execution. The unit of reusable work determines which policy is worth evaluating.
Although recommendation workloads often dominate consumer inference volume (section 10.6), batching strategies are presented in order of conceptual complexity: vision (straightforward batching), LLMs (continuous batching with KV cache), and recommendation (feature-parallel batching with distributed embedding). This ordering builds understanding progressively, even though production systems frequently encounter recommendation workloads first. The taxonomy that follows matches batching strategies to model characteristics, providing quantitative analysis of when each approach applies and what performance to expect.


Batching efficiency depends on how computation scales with batch size relative to memory and communication constraints. The execution timeline in figure 4 separates waiting to form a batch from waiting for the accelerator to become available. Unbatched serving adds no batch-formation delay, but later requests can still queue behind earlier forward passes. Static batching consolidates all four illustrated requests into one pass, adding formation delay and padding to accommodate different input lengths. Dynamic batching closes formation windows at fixed time intervals (\(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\)), producing two passes with two requests each in this example. The window limits intentional formation delay; it does not bound total queueing when ready batches arrive faster than the server can execute them.







Figure 4: Batching strategies compared: Four requests of different lengths arrive one time unit apart under three policies; the timings are illustrative. (a) Without batching, each request receives its own forward pass, so later arrivals queue behind earlier ones and the GPU runs four passes. (b) Static batching holds every request until the batch of four is full, then runs one pass padded to the longest request; early arrivals pay the longest wait. (c) Dynamic batching dispatches whatever has arrived when a short window closes, limiting intentional formation delay in this timeline while sharing each pass between two requests. Waiting for an occupied worker remains a separate source of delay.



For vision models, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs) processing fixed-size images, arithmetic work grows approximately in proportion to batch size. Requests share model weights, but activations and other per-request state still grow with the batch. Increasing batch size can therefore improve weight reuse and GPU utilization until compute capacity, memory capacity, or the latency budget becomes limiting. Static or dynamic batching exploits this reuse; the largest feasible batch is not necessarily the best operating point for an interactive service.
For LLMs in the decode phase, small batches perform little computation relative to the bytes required to load active model weights. In this regime, memory bandwidth binds. Larger batches reuse each weight load across more tokens, increasing arithmetic intensity until compute, KV-cache traffic, or the latency budget limits further throughput gains. For the same reason, small-batch decode does not inherit a new accelerator generation’s headline compute improvement. Across the generations from Volta to Blackwell, peak compute climbs 18\(\times\) while memory bandwidth expands by only 8.9\(\times\); figure 5 shows what that hardware divergence means for serving, where generation throughput tracks the slower curve whenever weight streaming dominates at small batch sizes.


↩︎ The accelerator trajectory behind this divergence, with compute outpacing memory bandwidth from one generation to the next, is established in Evolution of GPU architectures.
For recommendation systems, embedding lookup can limit throughput before dense computation does. Grouping sparse accesses can improve locality and distribute lookup work across shards, while batching the dense stages can improve matrix multiplication throughput. The serving policy must account for both stages and the communication between them rather than infer the bottleneck from the model category alone.














Figure 5: Decode inherits the bandwidth deficit: Peak compute and memory bandwidth for four accelerator generations, normalized to the V100. Compute rises 18\(\times\) against bandwidth’s 8.9\(\times\). In weight-bandwidth-bound decode, each iteration loads the active weights and reuses them across its output tokens; at fixed batch size, bandwidth growth constrains the gain. These hardware ratios are not measured workload speedups. Specifications come from the MLSysIM hardware registry.






Batch size is the single-replica control knob that moves a workload along the roofline, raising arithmetic intensity by reusing each weight read across more requests. At fleet scale the same knob also sets how long arriving work waits. Batching trades the reuse of weights and execution overhead against longer service times and additional request state. A model relating batch size \((\BatchSize)\), batch service time \((\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize))\), and batched service rate \((\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize))\) exposes that trade-off. Selecting an operating point also requires the arrival pattern, memory budget, and latency target.


↩︎ Batch size as the control knob that moves decode toward the ridge point on one replica is established in Batch size as the universal control knob.
The first model isolates batch execution. Here \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) is the service time once a batch begins execution; it excludes queueing and batch formation. Keeping the measurement boundary explicit prevents an execution-time improvement from being mistaken for an end-to-end SLO guarantee.
The service-time equation decomposes batch execution time into fixed overheads (kernel launch, memory loading) and variable costs (compute per sample):
\[\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = \BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime\]
In this formulation, \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) captures costs paid once per batch, such as loading weights from HBM and kernel launch latency, while \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) denotes the marginal cost of adding one request, such as the compute time for that sample. Treating these terms as constants is a local approximation for a fixed workload and execution regime. Kernel changes, cache traffic, and resource saturation can alter the measured curve as batch size grows.
The throughput equation describes the system’s capacity:
\[\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)} = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime}\]
The resulting batching efficiency curve shows diminishing returns from amortizing overhead. For small batch sizes (\(\BatchSize\)), \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) dominates service time, so increasing \(\BatchSize\) shares that cost and raises throughput substantially. As \(\BatchSize\) grows, the relative contribution of \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) shrinks and the model approaches its asymptotic rate \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\). This limit alone does not identify whether compute or bandwidth binds on the actual device. The knee of the curve, where fixed and variable costs become comparable, is a useful candidate operating point. It is not an optimum independent of the service contract; a tight latency budget may require a smaller batch, while a throughput-oriented workload may benefit from a larger one.



Throughput saturates toward \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\); past the knee, each larger batch buys less.
The execution-only feasibility condition is \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) \le \text{SLO}\). In a live service, execution receives only the budget remaining after routing, queueing, batch formation, and response delivery. The batch-size decision must therefore use that remaining budget rather than consume the full SLO. The following example contrasts a vision workload with a relatively high \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) and an LLM decode workload with a high \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) from weight loading, showing how those measured costs change the tuning decision.

The batch a service actually runs also depends on context length, cache capacity, kernel efficiency, and the latency target; continuous batching and paged allocation are the mechanisms that let a replica reach it.

Translating these batch-level equations into system-wide capacity planning requires a classical result from queuing theory: Little’s Law,5 which relates concurrency, throughput, and latency in any stable system.
5 Little’s Law: The identity holds for any stable system regardless of the arrival or service distribution, which is why it survives the bursty, variable-length traffic of inference. Because it relates averages, it bounds neither maximum service capacity nor tail latency.
Theorem 10.1: Little's Law for inferenceConcept: In any stable queuing system, the average number of requests in the system \((\RequestConcurrency)\) equals the arrival rate \((\ArrivalRate)\) multiplied by the average time a request spends in the system \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\).
\[ \RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \]
Application: Concurrency planning. This idealized service counts only batch formation, queueing, and execution in its end-to-end latency; routing and response delivery add no delay. Assume the mean latency given below and full execution batches of the stated size. A percentile SLO cannot generally be substituted for the mean in Little’s Law.

Target Throughput \((\ArrivalRate)\): 1,000 requests/sec
Assumed mean latency \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\): 100 ms (0.1 s)

Mean in-flight work \((\RequestConcurrency)\): \(1000 \times 0.1 =\) 100 concurrent requests
Capacity Planning: If a single GPU replica executes batches of 8 in 80 ms, and the fleet targets at most 80 percent mean service utilization:

Replica Throughput \(=\) \(8/0.08 =\) 100 req/s
Throughput-only lower bound \(=\) \(\lceil 1000/100\rceil =\) 10 replicas
Illustrative headroom-sized replica count \(=\) \(\lceil 1000/(0.8 \times 100)\rceil =\) 13 replicas

Verification: Maximum executing positions \(=\) \(13\text{ replicas} \times 8\text{ batch positions} =\) 104. These positions do not include requests waiting for execution or batch formation. Under the assumed fixed batch service time, Little’s Law on the execution boundary gives 80 requests executing on average; the remaining 20 of the assumed mean in-flight population are waiting or accumulating. The throughput-only lower bound would run at the stability boundary; the utilization-sized candidate runs at about 76.9 percent service utilization. The assumed mean latency still needs validation, and this arithmetic does not prove a percentile latency SLO; that requires an arrival/service model or a measured load test.


This stability boundary can be measured faithfully only when the load generator preserves the workload claim. The contract in Measurement at Scale distinguishes a fixed external arrival process from fixed-concurrency testing because response-paced generation can reduce arrivals during a stall and make the system appear to have more headroom than it does. The distinction between throughput capacity and latency capacity is exactly what queuing theory formalizes.


↪ The mean queuing delay under a batched M/G/1 surrogate, and how utilization headroom and batch size trade against latency, is developed in Queuing theory for batched inference.



Vision models represent the simplest batching case because inputs have uniform size (after preprocessing) and computation follows a predictable pattern. Single-machine batching principles apply directly, with scale introducing considerations of batch formation across multiple replicas.
Static batching collects exactly \(\BatchSize\) requests before processing. A full batch can improve weight reuse and kernel efficiency, but fullness alone does not establish maximum GPU utilization. Without a timeout or partial-batch dispatch policy, the first request can wait indefinitely if too few additional requests arrive.
Dynamic batching collects requests for a maximum time window \(\BatchingWindow\) or until reaching maximum batch size \(\MaxBatchSize\), whichever occurs first. For Poisson arrivals with rate \(\ArrivalRate\), equation 3 organizes expected request latency into queueing, formation, and execution contributions:
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestTimeInSystem] = \mathbb{E}[\QueueingLatency] + \BatchFormationDelay + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) \tag{3}\]
where \(\mathbb{E}[\QueueingLatency]\) is the expected queuing delay, \(\BatchFormationDelay\) represents mean batch formation delay (up to \(\BatchingWindow\)), and \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) represents mean inference time over the realized batch sizes \(\BatchSize\). Queueing here excludes time already counted as batch formation. The two waiting terms respond differently to load. Under Poisson arrivals the mean inter-arrival gap is \(1/\ArrivalRate\), so a higher arrival rate fills a batch faster and reduces formation delay. Queueing for a busy replica can nevertheless grow as arrival rate approaches service capacity; the batching timeout does not cap that queueing delay. The worked example that follows evaluates the capacity gained by spending part of the latency budget on batch formation.

Example 10.1: Dynamic batching for ResNet-50Scenario: A vision classification service receives requests at 5,000 QPS with a 50 ms p99 latency SLO across 10 replicas, so each replica sees 500 QPS. One image served alone takes 5 ms. The scenario assumes that a batch of about 5 images executes in 8 ms and a batch of about 10 in 12 ms, because a batch shares weight reads and kernel launches across its images.
Diagnosis: Each utilization below is the per-replica arrival rate multiplied by the service time one request consumes. Option A serves every image alone, which overloads the replica (\(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate \times \BatchServiceTime = 500 \times 0.005 = 2.5\) utilization). Option B holds a 10 ms batching window, which collects about 5 requests (arrival rate \(\times\) window). Their batch runs in 8 ms, so each request consumes 1.6 ms of execution, and utilization falls to \(\ServingUtilization = 500 \times 0.0016 = 0.8\). The wider 20 ms window of Option C collects about 10 requests whose batch runs in 12 ms, or 1.2 ms each, reaching \(\ServingUtilization = 500 \times 0.0012 = 0.6\) and a further 33 percent of per-replica capacity. Both options leave service headroom. Whether they also meet the p99 SLO depends on the window plus the queueing delay each utilization implies under the service’s real arrival pattern, which utilization alone does not determine.
Systems lesson: Dynamic batching is effective when the latency budget has unused slack. The serving policy converts latency headroom into throughput, but requires careful tuning to prevent SLO violations.




↪ A procedure for this tuning, from fitting the service-time model to checking the p99 target, is developed in Batch size selection framework given an SLA.
At scale with multiple replicas, batch formation can occur either at individual replicas or at a centralized batching layer. Replica-local batching has each replica independently form batches from its assigned traffic. This avoids a shared batching stage, but splitting a light arrival stream among many replicas can leave each waiting to fill its batch. Centralized batching pools arrivals before dispatching formed batches, potentially shortening formation waits, at the cost of an additional network hop and a shared scheduling bottleneck. Load balancing helps local batching, but equal request counts do not guarantee equal work or reproduce the formation benefit of pooling arrivals. The choice depends on arrival density, request compatibility, and replica service times.



The autoregressive bottleneck (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)) governs this regime: at small batch sizes, decode is typically bandwidth-bound because each iteration streams active model weights while generating only one token per sequence. Batching shares those weight reads across multiple requests. As the batch grows, compute or KV-cache traffic can become the binding constraint, so bandwidth-bound decode is an operating regime rather than a property of every serving configuration.

Definition 10.2: Continuous batching
Continuous batching is a serving strategy that updates batch membership at iteration boundaries, allowing new requests to enter without waiting for every request in the original batch to finish.

Significance: It reduces padding waste by refilling completed slots at iteration boundaries. Throughput gains require waiting requests, available KV-cache capacity, and scheduling overhead small enough to preserve the benefit.
Distinction: Unlike static or dynamic batching (which group requests at the request level), continuous batching operates at the Iteration Level, reshaping the active batch between decode iterations.
Common pitfall: Continuous admission must coordinate scheduling with KV-state ownership and lifetime. A Dynamic Memory Manager such as PagedAttention improves space utilization, but paging is not required: an implementation can recycle fixed-capacity request slots, at the cost of unused reserved space.



Autoregressive language models expose the limitation of fixed-membership batching. If new sequences cannot join until the entire batch finishes, completed requests leave capacity unavailable to waiting work. The Orca system (Yu et al. 2022) removed that barrier. Updating membership at iteration boundaries enables slot reuse. Once a request completes, another can enter if its prompt has been processed and sufficient cache capacity is available. The scheduler must account for that preparation rather than treat every replacement as a decode-only operation.

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.
Consider a fixed-width batch of 8 sequences. If one sequence completes after 10 tokens while others require 100 tokens, its slot contributes no useful output for 90 iterations. If the kernel continues executing padded work for that slot, the fraction of wasted compute attributable to it is:
\[\text{Wasted compute} = \frac{(100 - 10) \times 1}{100 \times 8} = 11.25\%\]
The waste grows with the spread of output lengths, a dependence that section 10.9.5 turns into a formula. A kernel that skips completed sequences avoids their padded arithmetic, but a fixed-membership policy still prevents waiting requests from using the vacated capacity. Algorithm 1 states the continuous-batching scheduler as a decode loop with a prefilled waiting queue. Completed requests release their pages in this simplified policy, eligible waiting requests enter freed slots, and the next kernel runs over the updated active set. For Archetype A workloads (GPT-4/Llama-3), refilling slots lets more useful tokens share each weight read. The gain comes from reusing transferred weights, not merely from saturating bandwidth, which a smaller batch may already do.


↩︎ Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), the autoregressive transformer whose serving must stream billions of weights for every generated token, is established in Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3).

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Continuous batching decode scheduler}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require prefilled waiting queue $Q$; active set $A$; KV-cache page allocator; active-token capacity $C_{\text{tok}}$; batched decode kernel
\Ensure generated tokens for completed requests; a continually refreshed active batch
\While{the service is running}
    \State admit requests from $Q$ while capacity and free KV-cache pages remain; allocate state, append to $A$
    \State reserve pages for the next decode step; preempt requests that do not fit
    \State run one batched decode kernel over the remaining sequences in $A$
    \State append each sampled token; extend its KV-cache pages
    \State remove completed or length-limited sequences from $A$; return their pages to the allocator
    \If{HBM pressure exceeds the policy threshold}
        \State move low-priority sequences from $A$ to the paused set; page their KV-cache to CPU DRAM
    \EndIf
    \State fill freed capacity from $Q$, or resume paused sequences whose pages now fit
\EndWhile
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(Q\)

Admitting, completing, and refilling slots on every iteration lets waiting work use capacity released before the longest sequence finishes. The illustrated preemption path adds HBM-to-CPU-DRAM transfers under memory pressure, so recovered capacity must repay both scheduling and state-movement costs. Figure 6 depicts the opportunity in slot-iterations: fixed membership leaves only 20 of 32 productive, while continuous admission fills all 32 under the illustrated arrival and capacity assumptions. Prefill and decode cells do not necessarily take equal time. Slot occupancy therefore measures the opportunity; the realized throughput gain depends on how much longer the inserted prefill cells take than the decode steps they share an iteration with.







Figure 6: Static vs. continuous batching: In static batching (a), completed slots cannot be reused until the longest request finishes, although completed responses may already be released. Continuous batching (b) admits waiting requests into freed slots at iteration boundaries, starting each with a prefill step. Over the eight iterations shown, 20 of 32 slot-iterations do useful work under static batching and all 32 under continuous batching; the hatched idle slots are the capacity recovered when arrivals and cache capacity permit.






The execution schedules contrasted in figure 6 raise a quantitative question: how much capacity can slot reuse recover? Static batching leaves slots idle until the longest sequence in a batch finishes, while continuous batching can refill those slots at iteration boundaries. Counting useful and unused sequence-iterations in a fixed batch bounds that opportunity; arrivals, KV-cache admission, prefill scheduling, and scheduler overhead determine how much of it a continuous batch actually recovers.


The 11.25 percent example of one early-finishing sequence generalizes to any mix of output lengths. For this waste model, traditional batching (also called static batching) retains a fixed batch width through all decode iterations until the longest sequence completes. Assume equal compute cost per sequence-iteration, including padded work for completed requests. For batch size \(\BatchSize\) with output lengths \(\{\RequestOutputLength_1, \RequestOutputLength_2, ..., \RequestOutputLength_{\BatchSize}\}\), the total compute performed under those assumptions is:
\[\StaticBatchingOperations= \BatchSize\times \BatchMaxOutputLength\times \SequenceIterationOperations\]
where \(\BatchMaxOutputLength= \max_i(\RequestOutputLength_i)\) and \(\SequenceIterationOperations\) is the compute cost per decode iteration per sequence. However, the useful compute is only:
\[\UsefulModelFlops = \sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \RequestOutputLength_i \times \SequenceIterationOperations\]
Equation 4 defines the waste ratio that quantifies the inefficiency:
\[\PaddingWasteFraction= 1 - \frac{\UsefulModelFlops}{\StaticBatchingOperations} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \RequestOutputLength_i}{\BatchSize\times \BatchMaxOutputLength} = 1 - \frac{\BatchMeanOutputLength}{\BatchMaxOutputLength} \tag{4}\]
where \(\BatchMeanOutputLength\) is the mean output sequence length. This reveals that waste depends entirely on the ratio of mean to maximum output length within the batch. For uniform output lengths \((\BatchMeanOutputLength= \BatchMaxOutputLength)\), waste is zero. For highly variable lengths, waste can exceed 50 percent.

The continuous-batching analysis relates recoverable slot capacity to the gap between a batch’s longest and average output lengths. Let \(\text{CV} = \OutputLengthStandardDeviation/ \WorkloadMeanOutputLength\) be the coefficient of variation of output lengths. For the idealized fixed-width schedule, suppose the longest request in a batch is roughly \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) standard deviations above the mean. The factor \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) is an assumption about the batch rather than a property of the workload, because a larger batch draws more samples and pushes its maximum further into the tail. With immediate refill and unchanged iteration time, the corresponding capacity ratio is:
\[\text{Improvement} \approx \frac{\BatchMaxOutputLength}{\BatchMeanOutputLength} = \frac{\WorkloadMeanOutputLength+ \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\OutputLengthStandardDeviation}{\WorkloadMeanOutputLength} = 1 + \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\cdot \text{CV}\]
where \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) specifies how far the batch maximum lies above the mean. The expression is therefore a scenario ceiling, set jointly by the workload’s CV and the assumed \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\), on the opportunity from filling otherwise unused slots. Scheduler overhead, KV-cache pressure, and refill gaps reduce the recovered fraction; changes in kernel efficiency or memory policy require a broader comparison. Neither column is a measurement or an independent result. Together they show how much of the ceiling a scheduler would have to recover to reach a given gain, which is the quantity a load test should measure.

The systems pattern is straightforward: continuous batching is most valuable when output lengths are unpredictable, mixed workload types share the same cluster, request volume is high enough to refill vacated slots, and latency SLOs make early completion valuable. It provides minimal benefit when output lengths are uniform, as in classification or embedding generation, when batch sizes are too small for slot reuse to matter, or when request volume is too low to refill vacated slots.
The ceiling depends on \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\), which the coefficient of variation alone does not set. The full length distribution and batch size determine how far a batch’s maximum lies above its mean, while arrivals, KV-cache admission, prefill scheduling, and scheduler overhead determine how much vacated capacity can be recovered. Serving teams must therefore compare policies under the same arrival trace, latency objective, and memory budget. Example 10.2 connects slot reuse to the memory-management choices of a published system.

Example 10.2: Continuous batching in vLLMScenario: An LLM serving engine (vLLM) manages autoregressive generation for incoming requests with highly variable output sequence lengths (Kwon et al. 2023).
Diagnosis: Fixed batch membership leaves completed slots unavailable to waiting requests. Continuous admission reuses that capacity, while paged allocation reduces unused cache reservations. The published vLLM design uses arrival order to prioritize requests, preempting later arrivals first under memory pressure. It considers both swapping cache state to CPU memory and recomputing that state when a request resumes.
Systems lesson: Continuous batching decouples batch membership from request-level boundaries. The paper reports 2–4\(\times\) higher throughput at comparable latency than FasterTransformer and Orca in its evaluated workloads. This is a system comparison, not an isolated measurement of slot reuse. Paged cache management contributes by reducing memory waste and permitting larger active batches.





The same variability that makes continuous batching valuable also makes it harder to operate. Its performance benefits come with implementation complexity that systems engineers must weigh.
Memory management must support overlapping request lifetimes. A simple fixed-membership implementation can reserve cache regions when a batch forms and release them together. Continuous admission must instead track which request owns each region and when that space becomes reusable. Fixed-capacity slots can support this policy, but they retain unused reservations; paging allocates space more incrementally at the cost of block tables and allocation bookkeeping. Completed state may also remain cached for reuse, so request completion and physical deallocation need not coincide.
Scheduler decisions also become more frequent. A simple fixed-membership policy checks whether a batch is full or its timeout has expired; continuous admission additionally tracks completions, available cache capacity, and eligible waiting requests at iteration boundaries. A constant-time readiness check is \(\mathcal{O}(1)\), while scanning all active sequences is \(\mathcal{O}(\BatchSize)\) per iteration. These describe particular operations, not the total complexity of either scheduler. Both policies must manage request metadata, and the cost of priority selection or preemption depends on the data structures and policy used. Because continuous admission repeats this work at every decode iteration, it must stay small relative to a decode step or it erodes the throughput that slot reuse recovers. Engines therefore keep the per-iteration path short and can prepare the next iteration’s batch on the host while the accelerator executes the current one.
Kernel design must also adapt. Batched GPU kernels traditionally assume fixed batch composition. Continuous batching requires kernels that handle variable-length sequences efficiently, often through techniques like packing multiple short sequences into shared attention masks or using specialized memory layouts that support dynamic batch membership.
