Example 10.3: Debugging high p99 latencyScenario: An LLM serving system exhibits high tail latency: p50 = 100 ms and p95 = 180 ms maintain SLO, but p99 spikes to \(\TailRequestLatency =\) 500 ms against a 200 ms target despite a monitored GPU utilization of 85 percent.
Diagnosis: The system runs across 4 A100 GPUs linked via PCIe Gen4 (32 GB/s per GPU) rather than NVLink. For a 100 MB payload, the bandwidth-only transfer estimate is \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) \approx\) 3.1 ms over PCIe versus 0.17 ms over NVLink. Collective startup, topology, and contention can add time. The service still runs an older request-level batching server rather than an iteration-level engine, with max batch size 32 and timeout 50 ms, so a batch holds its members until its longest generation finishes. The scenario assumes that 5 percent of batches experience head-of-line queuing delay \(\QueueingLatency\) as short requests wait behind long generations.
Systems lesson: The latency distribution motivates tracing both candidates. A transfer paid by every request contributes to every latency percentile, but its service-time cost can also amplify tail queueing near saturation. In this scenario, traces showing stable transfer times too small to explain the additional delay, together with short requests waiting behind long generations, identify the fixed-membership barrier as the immediate cause. Continuous admission removes that barrier; prefill scheduling, cache capacity, and other waits still require measurement. Until the server can be replaced, the following policy reduces output-length variation within request-level batches:

Request classification: Classify requests by expected output length (short: under 50 tokens, medium: 50 to 200 tokens, long: over 200 tokens)
Differentiated batching: Limit short batches to 8, medium to 16, long to 32

Grouping requests by expected length shrinks the spread of output lengths inside each batch, which is the quantity equation 4 says drives both waste and waiting. The scenario assumes a post-mitigation p99 latency of \(\TailRequestLatency =\) 185 ms; a real service confirms it by replaying the same arrival workload and measuring the tail.






Continuous batching admits work at iteration boundaries, but in production workloads, requests arrive with widely disparate prompt lengths. The prefill-decode decomposition already placed the two phases on opposite sides of the ridge point. Once continuous batching admits new prompts onto a worker that is decoding other streams, that difference stops being a property of each phase and becomes a scheduling conflict between them. Recalling the weight-traffic approximation makes the size of the conflict explicit.


↩︎ The ridge point that separates compute-bound from bandwidth-bound execution is established in Roofline model.
During the prefill phase, the engine computes key-value representations across all prompt tokens (\(\PromptLength\)) concurrently. Because all prompt tokens are processed in parallel, the linear projection general matrix multiply (GEMM) operations operate on large sequence dimensions (\(\GemmRowDimension= \PromptLength\)). For a projection layer with hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\), arithmetic intensity scales with prompt length: \[\PrefillArithmeticIntensity\approx \frac{2 \cdot \PromptLength\cdot \HiddenDimension^2}{2 \cdot \HiddenDimension^2} = \PromptLength\quad \left[\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{byte of weights loaded}}\right]\] Under this weight-traffic-only approximation, increasing \(\PromptLength\) beyond the accelerator’s ridge point moves the projection’s roofline ceiling to the compute limit. Reaching that ceiling still depends on kernel efficiency; attention, other memory traffic, and communication can limit the complete prefill phase.
In contrast, the subsequent decode phase generates a single token per sequence sequentially. At the decode batch sizes this chapter considers, from tens of sequences up to the knee near 80 in notebook 10.2, the arithmetic intensity \(\DecodeArithmeticIntensity\approx \DecodeBatchSize\) stays below the ridge point, placing the weight projections in a memory-bandwidth-bound regime under this approximation. Each decode iteration streams the active weights from HBM and reuses them across the batch. Larger batches and growing KV-cache traffic change that balance.



Long-prompt prefill reaches the compute ceiling; decode stays on the bandwidth slope.

Definition 10.3: Chunked prefill
Chunked prefill is an LLM serving mechanism that divides long prompt evaluations into discrete token chunks of size at most \(\PrefillChunkSize\), interleaving prefill computation with ongoing decode iterations within a shared token budget.

Significance: It limits the prompt-decode interference problem where monolithic prefills stall active decode streams for hundreds of milliseconds, giving the scheduler control over how much prefill work can lengthen the TBT of active streams. Meeting interactive streaming service-level objectives (SLOs) still requires measuring the resulting tail latency.
Distinction: Unlike continuous batching with monolithic prefill (which prefills each prompt in one uninterrupted pass before the worker returns to decoding), chunked prefill treats prefill as a multi-step iterative process co-scheduled alongside memory-bound decode tokens.
Common pitfall: Sizing the chunk budget \(\PrefillChunkSize\) too small incurs kernel launch and attention mask overheads, degrading overall prefill throughput. Sizing it too large allows prefill compute to monopolize execution time, causing TBT tail spikes.



With an unchunked prefill policy, the scheduler processes an incoming prompt through the model before returning to decode work. A full prefill comprises many layer kernels; the interference arises from scheduling that whole operation without interleaving other requests’ decode steps, not from assuming one indivisible kernel spans the entire prompt evaluation.
This delay lands in the TBT of requests already decoding on the same worker. A long response can dilute an isolated stall in its average TPOT, even though the user experiences a conspicuous gap. Repeated prefills or short responses can make the average deteriorate as well. Prioritizing the incoming prompt’s time to first token can therefore consume the streaming-latency budget of requests already decoding. The measured prefill duration and the endpoint’s TBT target determine whether interleaving is necessary.


To limit this interference, chunked prefill (definition 10.3, used by Sarathi-Serve (Agrawal et al. 2024)) partitions prompts into chunks of at most \(\PrefillChunkSize\) tokens. A candidate range such as \(256\text{--}512\) tokens must be tested against the model, hardware, and streaming deadline rather than treated as a universal setting. A prompt of length \(\PromptLength\) requires at least \(\lceil \PromptLength/ \PrefillChunkSize\rceil\) scheduling iterations; a smaller residual token budget can require more.
In each iteration, the scheduler constructs a hybrid batch combining active decode requests with prefill chunks under a global iteration token budget \(\IterationTokenBudget\), a count of tokens rather than a time, as formulated in equation 5:
\[\DecodeBatchSize+ \sum_{\PrefillRequestIndex \in \ActivePrefillRequestSet} \PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex} \le \IterationTokenBudget \tag{5}\]
where \(\DecodeBatchSize\) is the number of active decode tokens and \(\PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex}\) is the number of prompt tokens allocated to waiting prefill request \(\PrefillRequestIndex\), so every term counts tokens. The simplified loop assumes admission control reserves sufficient KV-cache capacity and a future decode slot for each admitted request, keeping the decode count within the iteration budget even after prefills are promoted. Each waiting request contributes at most one chunk per iteration, with its committed prompt offset unchanged until execution completes. Algorithm 2 formalizes this iteration-level hybrid scheduling loop.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Chunked prefill and hybrid batch scheduler}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require waiting prefill queue $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}$; active decode set $\mathcal{D}$; iteration token budget $N_{\text{budget}}$; maximum chunk size $C_{\text{chunk}}$
\Ensure generated tokens for decode requests; incremental KV-cache construction for prefills
\While{serving engine is active}
    \State $B_{\text{dec}} \gets |\mathcal{D}|$
    \State $N_{\text{rem}} \gets N_{\text{budget}} - B_{\text{dec}}$
    \State $\mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}} \gets \emptyset$
    \For{each $R_i$ in a snapshot of $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}$, in queue order}
        \If{$N_{\text{rem}} > 0$}
            \State $o_i \gets R_i.\text{offset}$
            \State $C_i \gets \min(C_{\text{chunk}}, N_{\text{rem}}, R_i.\text{prompt\_length} - o_i)$
            \State $\mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}} \gets \mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}} \cup \{(R_i, o_i, C_i)\}$
            \State $N_{\text{rem}} \gets N_{\text{rem}} - C_i$
        \EndIf
    \EndFor
    \State run hybrid forward pass using each prefill slice $R_i[o_i:o_i+C_i]$ and the decode set $\mathcal{D}$
    \State append newly generated tokens for all $R \in \mathcal{D}$
    \State remove completed decode requests from $\mathcal{D}$ and release their KV blocks
    \For{$(R_i, o_i, C_i) \in \mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}}$}
        \State update prompt offset: $R_i.\text{offset} \gets o_i + C_i$
        \If{$R_i.\text{offset} = R_i.\text{prompt\_length}$}
            \State promote $R_i$ from $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}$ to $\mathcal{D}$
        \EndIf
    \EndFor
\EndWhile
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}\)




Executing prefill and decode tokens together in shared projection operations amortizes weight loading across both phases, an effect termed decode piggybacking. Alternating separate prefill and decode operations limits scheduling interference but does not by itself establish this weight reuse.
In a small-batch isolated decode step, streaming the model parameters (\(\WeightMemory\) bytes) from HBM to registers achieves low arithmetic intensity because only \(\DecodeBatchSize\) tokens share the weight reads. Memory bandwidth then limits how much work the compute units can sustain, leaving arithmetic capacity available for a larger shared projection.
In a hybrid iteration, the model weights loaded from HBM into on-chip cache and registers are simultaneously reused for both the compute-dense prefill chunks (\(\sum_{\PrefillRequestIndex} \PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex}\) tokens in total) and the memory-bound decode tokens (\(\DecodeBatchSize\) tokens). Ignoring attention-state traffic, communication, and scheduling overhead gives the projection-only lower-bound estimate in equation 6:
\[\HybridIterationTime\gtrsim \max\left(\frac{\WeightMemory}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}, \frac{2 \cdot (\DecodeBatchSize+ \sum_{\PrefillRequestIndex} \PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex}) \cdot \ActiveParameterCount}{\PeakRate}\right) \tag{6}\]
where \(\ActiveParameterCount\) is the active parameter count, \(\SustainedMemoryBandwidth\) is HBM memory bandwidth, and \(\PeakRate\) is peak accelerator compute throughput. These quantities must describe the same device or shard. Balancing the total prefill token allocation against weight streaming can amortize weight-loading cost across both phases, but this lower bound cannot guarantee \(\HybridIterationTime\le \text{SLO}_{\text{TBT}}\). Chunk sizing must leave room for the omitted costs and be validated against measured tail latency under the intended workload.

Example 10.4: Sarathi: Chunked prefill implementationScenario: An LLM inference server receives a mix of long input prompts (\(10{,}000+\) tokens) and interactive short decode requests (Agrawal et al. 2024).
Diagnosis: When the worker schedules a full long-prompt prefill before returning to decode, that prefill can occupy execution for hundreds of milliseconds and create a TBT spike for active streams.
Systems lesson: Chunking moves the cost of a long prompt rather than removing it. At \(512\) tokens per chunk, a \(10{,}000\)-token prompt needs at least \(\lceil 10{,}000/512 \rceil = 20\) iterations to finish its prefill. With this prompt as the only prefill request, active streams share each decode iteration with at most one of its chunks, while the prompt’s own time to first token stretches across those 20 iterations. Multiple waiting prompts can contribute additional chunks within the total iteration budget. The chunk budget sets that exchange between other streams’ TBT and the long prompt’s TTFT, so it must be tuned against both measured tails.



Agrawal, Amey, Nitin Kedia, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, Alexey Tumanov, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2024. “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), 117–34.
The batching strategies examined so far expose different sources of reusable capacity. Fixed-shape vision inputs make request grouping straightforward, although execution capacity and deadlines still limit batch size. Autoregressive generation adds variable request lifetimes and growing KV state, requiring the scheduler to coordinate iteration membership with memory admission. The binding resource can change within either workload. What changes the batching policy is the combination of work shape, state lifetime, and service contract.
Recommendation systems add the placement of sparse state to this decision. Sparse embedding lookups can dominate memory access and communication in an embedding-heavy workload even when dense matrix multiplications account for much of the arithmetic. A single request may issue thousands of lookups across shards of tables holding billions of entries before the ranking head combines the results. Grouping those accesses by feature type and destination can improve locality, complementing request batching in the dense stages.




Recommendation batching starts by grouping work around embedding locality rather than request shape. Figure 7 traces this feature-parallel pipeline: an incoming request splits across user, item, and context feature types to query sharded embedding tables concurrently, after which a gather barrier concatenates the retrieved representations for the dense MLP ranking head.







Figure 7: Feature-parallel batching pipeline: Requests are batched by feature type (Users, Items, Context) and dispatched to specialized embedding servers in parallel. The retrieved embeddings are then concatenated and processed by the dense ranking head. This architecture enables scaling to trillions of parameters by decoupling embedding storage from dense compute.



Recommendation systems expose the same scheduling principle through sparse and dense computation paths. Sparse feature lookup retrieves embeddings for user, item, and context features, while dense feature processing transforms continuous inputs. These paths can execute concurrently before feature interaction combines their representations, often through attention or factorization. A ranking head then produces final scores. The interaction stage must wait for its required inputs, making a slow embedding shard part of the request’s critical path.
When sparse embedding access dominates latency, feature-parallel batching groups lookups by feature type and destination across requests. This organization exposes parallel work at the embedding shards while preserving the association needed to reconstruct each request for ranking:
Request 1: [user_id_1, item_ids_1, context_1]
Request 2: [user_id_2, item_ids_2, context_2]
Request 3: [user_id_3, item_ids_3, context_3]

Feature-parallel view:
User embeddings:  [lookup(user_1), lookup(user_2), lookup(user_3)]  → parallel
Item embeddings:  [lookup(items_1), lookup(items_2), lookup(items_3)]  → parallel
Context features: [process(ctx_1), process(ctx_2), process(ctx_3)]  → parallel

Then: Combine features per request for ranking
Feature-parallel batching is natural when embeddings are sharded across servers: each embedding server handles lookups for its shard across all requests in the batch. At hyperscale request volumes, this turns feature sharding into a serving strategy rather than a storage detail.

Example 10.5: RecSys batching at hyperscaleScenario: A hyperscale recommendation service handles 10 million QPS, querying 5,000 embedding lookups per request across 1,000 shards.
Diagnosis: The assumed distribution of requests requires 50 million lookups/sec per shard. That rate is the capacity target each shard’s lookup service must sustain. Accumulating requests over a 1 ms window forms batches of 50K lookups per shard, creating an opportunity to deduplicate, reorder, or coalesce lookups. Batching alone does not make random addresses sequential.
Systems lesson: Shard-level batching exploits sparse feature locality, but its benefit depends on cache hits, access distribution, and the amount of work each shard receives. The formation window spends part of the 5.2 ms end-to-end latency budget; measured lookup and communication times must fit in what remains alongside the dense stages.





Streaming workloads constrain how long batching may delay new input. Speech recognition, video analysis, and robotics process an ongoing sequence of observations, so each result must arrive in time for its application. Batching across ready streams can still improve efficiency if it respects those deadlines.
Streaming inference processes inputs incrementally rather than waiting for the complete recording or interaction. Illustrative input cadences include 10–20 ms audio chunks for speech recognition, 30–60 FPS video, and 100–1000 Hz sensor or control updates in robotics. These rates specify how often work arrives, not a universal inference deadline. Buffering, frame selection, and batching must follow the application’s latency and freshness requirements.
A streaming service must sustain the arrival rate while meeting the latency budget for each accepted input. The end-to-end processing path includes:
\[\StreamingEndToEndLatency= \InputCaptureTime+ \TransferTimeForPayload+ \InferenceLatency + \ResultActionTime\]
where the sum must fit the end-to-end latency budget. A pipelined implementation must also sustain the input arrival rate; its slowest stage must process frames at least as quickly as they arrive. The end-to-end budget may span several frame intervals, as the speech example illustrates.

Example 10.6: Streaming speech recognition pipelineScenario: A real-time streaming speech-to-text pipeline processes 20 ms audio frames under a strict 100 ms end-to-end latency budget (5 frames max delay).
Diagnosis: Waiting for a large batch from one stream can consume its latency budget before inference begins. The pipeline processes frames incrementally (\(\StreamingEndToEndLatency= \InputCaptureTime+ \TransferTimeForPayload+ \InferenceLatency + \ResultActionTime\)), overlapping audio capture with acoustic model evaluation. Ready frames from independent streams can share execution if the additional waiting and service time still fit the budget.
Systems lesson: Streaming inference requires both timely results and enough throughput to prevent accumulating backlog. Incremental pipelining supports these goals; whether batching helps depends on the available deadline slack and the number of ready streams.





Once batching is workload-specific, fixed parameters become fragile. Production systems therefore adapt batching behavior to current conditions.
Traffic-adaptive batching adjusts the batch window based on arrival rate:
\[\BatchingWindow= \min\left(\MaxBatchingWindow, \frac{\TargetBatchSize}{\ArrivalRate}\right)\]
When traffic is high, the window shrinks because the target batch size fills quickly. When traffic is low, the window extends but is capped to bound batch-formation delay. This cap does not bound the separate wait for a busy replica.
SLO-adaptive batching takes a complementary approach, monitoring latency percentiles and adjusting parameters aggressively:
if P99_latency > 0.9 * SLO:
    reduce B_max by 20%
    reduce T_window by 20%
elif P99_latency < 0.5 * SLO:
    increase B_max by 10%
    increase T_window by 10%
The feedback loop is a tuning heuristic, not a guarantee of latency headroom. Reducing batch size can shorten execution while also reducing service capacity and increasing queueing under heavy load. Feedback delay and noisy percentile estimates can cause oscillation, so the controller must be evaluated with the intended arrival trace and overload policy. Request-aware batching adds another dimension by considering request characteristics. For LLMs, prompt length can guide padding and prefill budgets, while estimated output length can guide grouping. Prediction errors and priority choices must be included when evaluating tail latency.
Production runtimes expose controls for this trade-off. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server uses max_batch_size to cap batches, max_queue_delay_microseconds to bound additional waiting for batch formation, and optional preferred_batch_size values for particularly efficient execution profiles. Preferred sizes do not create a separate queue for each batch size. The runtime forms a supported batch from queued requests when an instance is available; priority queues and overload policy are separate controls.
Table 11 gives an illustrative load-test pattern. Larger batches can absorb rising traffic until offered load approaches execution capacity; after that, longer queues need an admission or scaling response.

The batching strategies to this point focus on scheduling work under a chosen request budget. Output length remains uncertain, but the service can already cap generation. Reasoning-heavy inference makes that budget an explicit quality-cost decision: the service may allocate additional tokens or candidate evaluations when the expected benefit justifies their latency and capacity costs. This extends the scheduling question from when requests run to how much work they may consume.






Reasoning through 128 serial tokens turns a 100 ms answer into 12.8 s.

Wei, Jason, Yi Tay, Rishi Bommasani, Colin Raffel, Barret Zoph, Sebastian Borgeaud, Dani Yogatama, et al. 2022. “Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models.” Transactions on Machine Learning Research 4. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2206.07682.

Schaeffer, Rylan, Brando Miranda, and Sanmi Koyejo. 2023. “Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 55565–81. https://doi.org/10.52202/075280-2425.
Test-time scaling turns reasoning into a serving resource. The scaling laws that motivate the fleet were first measured for pretraining, where quality improves as a power law in parameters, data, and training compute. The same pattern has a third regime in which quality rises with the compute spent on each query at inference time. For a serving fleet that regime moves the scaling curve out of the training cluster and into the request path. Every increment of quality bought this way is paid on every request for the lifetime of the deployment, the recurring cost that the serving cost dominance law (principle \(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)) already prices. A request may issue more generated tokens, internal chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, or search steps before producing the answer. Whether that extra work buys quality is an empirical question. Capability studies describe abilities that appear abruptly with scale (Wei et al. 2022), while later analysis cautions that some apparent jumps are artifacts of the metric chosen (Schaeffer et al. 2023), so a serving budget should rest on measured quality gains for the workload rather than on the expectation of a jump.
From a serving-systems perspective, the relevant shift is the work issued per request. Additional reasoning consumes accelerator time and can extend both latency and KV-cache residency. Increasing test-time work does not necessarily change the bottleneck of each decode step. It instead requires a policy for the number of generated tokens, candidate solutions, or search steps a request may consume. The logic wall is the point at which serial reasoning tokens exhaust a request’s latency budget, or its share of fleet capacity, before additional reasoning stops improving the answer. A harder task may justify more work, but additional work does not guarantee a correct answer. Adaptive batching decides when requests run together; test-time compute allocation decides how much work each request is allowed to issue.


↩︎ Test-time scaling, the lifecycle regime that spends compute per request rather than per training run, is established alongside the empirical scaling laws in Resource-constrained scaling regimes.

Napkin Math 10.4: Scaling reasoning depthProblem: Calculate the latency impact of a model that uses 128 “Thinking Tokens” to solve a complex math proof vs. a standard answer.

Standard response: 1 token answer = 100 ms.
Reasoning response: 128 of internal search/CoT before the answer.
The latency: 128 \(\times\) 100 ms = 12.8 seconds.

Systems insight: The per-token time is a round figure chosen for easy arithmetic, more than ten times the batch-one decode step of the reference 70B replica in Batch size as the universal control knob. What the calculation teaches does not depend on it. Serial reasoning tokens multiply latency by the ratio of reasoning tokens to answer tokens, whatever each token costs, so a faster replica shortens both responses in proportion and leaves the 128-fold expansion intact. Against a direct answer of many tokens rather than one, the ratio shrinks accordingly; against a one-token answer it is largest. A search step that evaluates several candidates in parallel adds compute and KV residency without adding the same serial latency, which is why reasoning budgets must be stated in both time and capacity. At fleet scale, compute allocation weighs the measured quality gain against both the request deadline and the capacity the additional work consumes.


Variable work per request closes the batching story: continuous and adaptive batching handle variation the system observes, while test-time compute is variation the system chooses. Dynamic compute allocation assigns per-request compute budgets based on task difficulty, latency tolerance, and fleet load rather than applying a fixed decode budget to every prompt. With both the batching mechanism and the per-request compute budget now on the table, the remaining task is to decide which combination a given workload should run.



The selection problem is to match the batching mechanism to model shape, traffic variance, and latency budget. That match depends on where in the request path the latency budget is spent.

Checkpoint 10.4: Batching strategy trade-offs
Verify your understanding of different batching mechanics:

Static vs. continuous: for a vision service with highly uniform input sizes and predictable traffic, select static batching or continuous batching.
Waste ratio: explain when refilling completed slots can eliminate the static-batch padding waste (\(1 - \BatchMeanOutputLength/\BatchMaxOutputLength\)), and why low arrivals or KV-cache pressure prevent perfect slot reuse.
Adaptive batching: explain when shrinking the formation window reduces waiting without sacrificing throughput, and why it cannot resolve overload when arrivals exceed service capacity.
RecSys bottleneck: in feature-parallel batching for RecSys, identify whether the primary fleet-stack bottleneck is the GPU’s Tensor Cores or the distributed Embedding Store’s memory bandwidth.
Batching limit: explain why free HBM, not Tensor Core compute, often caps the achievable batch size for long-context LLM serving.



The end-to-end traversal diagrammed in figure 1 provides the final operational check on batching selection: noncompute stages such as host serialization, queuing, and network routing consume a substantial fraction of the latency budget, so batch formation and execution must be budgeted across the full pipeline rather than against accelerator runtime alone. The following questions identify candidate policies; memory admission, arrivals, and the remaining latency budget determine their usable settings:
Is it autoregressive text generation?
|- Yes → Continuous batching with chunked prefill
`- No → Is it real-time streaming speech/video/robotics?
        |- Yes → Streaming pipeline with minimal or no batching
        `- No → Do embedding lookups dominate latency?
                |- Yes → Feature-parallel batching (RecSys)
                `- No → Dynamic batching with adaptive parameters
The strategies in table 12 expose different tuning decisions: batch size for static execution, waiting time for dynamic batching, admission and iteration work for continuous batching, lookup grouping for sharded embeddings, and deadline-compatible grouping for streaming. Continuous batching responds to variable completion times; it does not make output lengths uniform. Each policy must be evaluated against both useful throughput and its latency budget.

Batching policy and memory admission are coupled. In a full-attention deployment that retains active KV state on the GPU, every admitted sequence consumes cache capacity as its context grows. A schedule with room for more decode work can therefore run out of memory before it reaches its execution limit. Managing that state is the next step in determining useful concurrency.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
As a full-attention LLM generates a 2,000-word essay, each new token attends to representations of earlier tokens. The KV cache retains the keys and values needed for that attention, with a per-request footprint that grows as generation proceeds. Large contiguous reservations can leave HBM reserved but unused or create gaps too small for another reservation. Admission can then fail even though the stored attention state occupies less than the available capacity.
Two classes of techniques meet at this boundary. KV-state capacity techniques, such as PagedAttention and prefix caching, decide where attention state lives and how much fragmentation the memory manager tolerates. Decode-time latency techniques, such as speculative decoding, change how much target-model work is needed per emitted token. Speculative decoding is not KV-cache compression; it trades extra draft-model state, target-model verification, and scheduler complexity for lower TPOT under the same memory budget. Prefill-decode disaggregation treats the attention state as a payload, because separating the two phases means moving each request’s cache between pools. Capacity accounting and adapter locality then determine how retained KV state and task-specific weights share the remaining memory budget.
Wherever they can, the calculations that follow share one reference replica, the 70B model on one eight-GPU H100 node that performance engineering established, with FP16 weights split eight ways. A few leave it on purpose to make a single point, and each says so where it does. The attention layout matters even more, because it sets the bytes cached per token. Grouped-query attention (GQA) with eight KV heads, the layout of the Llama-family 70B models, caches one eighth the state of a 64-head multi-head attention baseline, so each calculation names its hardware and attention layout, and numbers from different calculations compare only after conversion to the same configuration.


↩︎ The reference serving replica, a 70B model on one eight-GPU H100 node, is established in The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis.


Increasing batch size in LLM serving can encounter the KV cache wall before execution resources are fully used. The capacity model in figure 8 leaves the reference replica to show the wall on a single device. It combines an idealized 35 GB weight payload for a quantized 70B model with its full-attention, eight-KV-head GQA state on one H100, using a conservative decimal budget matching its nameplate label. This illustrative budget differs from the registered byte capacity used in the node estimator below. With the illustrated cache dimensions and precision, a batch of 8 reaches the memory boundary at roughly 17K tokens per sequence. Quantization metadata, runtime buffers, and other allocations reduce the capacity available in an actual deployment, so the plotted boundary is an optimistic sizing limit.














Figure 8: The KV cache wall: Total GPU memory usage for a 4-bit quantized 70B model (35 GB weights) on an 80 GB H100. While the model fits easily at small context lengths, the KV cache (sloped lines) eventually consumes all remaining HBM. At 128K context, a batch size of 2 is physically impossible on a single GPU (35 GB + 84 GB exceeds 80 GB), forcing the system to either reduce batch size, change the state representation, or distribute the state across devices.



The visualization explains why weight fit alone does not establish serving capacity. A long-context request can consume nearly all remaining memory in the illustrated configuration, leaving little space for other active sequences. Sharding can add headroom, but its communication cost must be weighed against alternatives such as lower concurrency or a smaller cache representation. The effect of a 128K context depends on the model’s cache dimensions and precision, not on context length alone.
The capacity model behind the figure, weight bytes plus per-token KV bytes multiplied by every token held, turns into an explicit batch-size limit for a production node.



A dozen 128K-token requests exhaust the whole KV budget.

Problem: A deployment serves an illustrative 70B-class GQA model with 128K context support (FP16 weights \(\approx\) 141.2 GB) on an 8\(\times\) H100 node (640 GB total HBM). The goal is to determine the maximum batch size for a context length of 128K tokens.
Formula: \[ \KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \times \LayerCount \times \KvHeadCount \times \AttentionHeadDimension \times \ElementStorageSize \] \[ \TotalMemoryFootprint = \WeightMemory + \KvCacheMemory, \qquad \KvCacheMemory = \BatchSize\times \SequenceLength\times \KvCacheBytesPerToken \]

\(\ElementStorageSize = 2\) bytes (FP16).

Step 1: Calculate memory per token. \[ m_{\text{token}} = 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327,680 \text{ bytes} \approx 0.33 \text{ MB/token} \]
Step 2: Calculate cache per request. \[ 131,072 \text{ tokens} \times 0.33 \text{ MB/token} \approx 42.9 \text{ GB/request} \]
Step 3: Determine max batch size. Available Memory for KV = 687.2 GB (Total) - 141.2 GB (Weights) - 20 GB (System) = 526.0 GB. \[ \text{Max Batch} = \left\lfloor \frac{526.0}{42.9} \right\rfloor = 12 \]
Systems insight: Even with grouped query attention (GQA), whose shared key-value heads the 8-head count in this calculation already reflects, each 128K-context request consumes tens of gigabytes of KV state. This configuration therefore admits only a limited number of concurrent long-context requests. PagedAttention can recover allocation waste, but cannot shrink the attention tensors counted here. Increasing concurrency beyond that limit requires changing the memory budget, cache representation, or placement of state.





Traditional memory allocation for KV cache preallocates contiguous memory for each sequence based on maximum expected length. This creates two forms of waste.
Internal fragmentation wastes memory within each allocation. Sequences shorter than the reserved capacity leave the unused portion idle. If the output reservation holds 4,096 tokens but the average output uses 100 tokens, 97.6 percent of that output reservation goes unused. Prompt state consumes additional space; this calculation does not give the unused fraction of the combined prompt-and-output allocation.
External fragmentation compounds this problem across allocations. As sequences complete and new ones start, memory becomes fragmented into noncontiguous free blocks. Even with sufficient total free memory, no single block may be large enough for a new maximum-length allocation.
Consider a simplified example with 8 memory slots and maximum sequence length of 4. Fixed-size reservations first create internal fragmentation:
Time 0: Allocate Seq A (slots 0-3), Seq B (slots 4-7)
        [A][A][a][a][B][B][B][b]
        lowercase = reserved but unused
External fragmentation can arise when the allocator also permits smaller contiguous reservations. In a later state, two sequences occupy two slots each, leaving separated gaps:
Time 1: Active Seq C and Seq D leave two 2-slot gaps
        [ ][ ][C][C][ ][ ][D][D]

Time 2: Try to allocate Seq E (needs 4 contiguous slots)
        [ ][ ][C][C][ ][ ][D][D]  <- Total free slots = 4, largest block = 2

Result: enough total free capacity exists, but no contiguous block is large enough.
Under variable sequence lengths, the two effects compound. The vLLM authors measured roughly 60 to 80 percent of reserved KV-cache memory going unused in the prior serving systems they studied, capacity that could otherwise have admitted more sequences (Kwon et al. 2023).



The fragmentation example exposes the allocator failure: enough KV-cache capacity can exist in aggregate while no contiguous block is available for the next sequence. PagedAttention fixes that serving problem by treating KV-cache storage like virtual memory rather than a single preallocated slab.
The shift changes the allocation problem, because capacity no longer has to be reserved as one contiguous block before the request starts, and that change alone can multiply the number of requests that fit before any byte of state is compressed.

Systems Perspective 10.1: Analogy: The inefficient hotelImagine a hotel storage room with 100 lockers. Each guest may bring up to 10 suitcases, but currently every guest has only one suitcase.
Under maximum-size reservation, the manager reserves 10 lockers for each guest. Ten guests exhaust the 100-locker budget while occupying only 10 lockers; the other 90 remain reserved but unused.
With on-demand allocation, each suitcase receives any free locker, and a directory records which lockers belong to each guest. At the current one-suitcase occupancy, the room can accommodate 100 guests. Additional suitcases still consume real capacity; allocation does not remove the storage limit.



Definition 10.4: PagedAttention
PagedAttention is an LLM serving memory management technique that applies virtual memory principles to KV cache allocation, storing attention states in noncontiguous, fixed-size physical blocks.

Significance: It eliminates external fragmentation within the fixed-block pool and bounds internal waste to the unused portion of each sequence’s final block. Recovering capacity from contiguous preallocation permits larger concurrent batches; the throughput gain depends on sequence lengths, demand, and the serving bottleneck.
Distinction: A contiguous allocation must find a sufficiently large free region; supporting later growth may require reserving extra space or relocating the allocation. PagedAttention uses a block table to map logical sequence indices to physical memory pages, allocating blocks as the sequence grows without requiring adjacent free space.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that PagedAttention speeds up individual token math. In reality, it is a capacity optimization: it improves system-level efficiency by allowing larger batch sizes, though it adds a small indirection overhead for the block-table lookups.



PagedAttention (Kwon et al. 2023), introduced in vLLM, applies virtual memory concepts to KV cache management. Instead of contiguous allocation, the KV cache is divided into fixed-size pages, using 16-token blocks in the original paper’s default configuration, and sequences are allocated pages on demand. Figure 9 contrasts this physical fragmentation against virtualized memory management: whereas contiguous reservation strands non-adjacent free slots when earlier sequences finish, PagedAttention uses a per-sequence block table to map logical token pages to scattered physical HBM slots on demand. The block size fixes how many tokens each page holds, so a sequence’s pages need not form one contiguous allocation run.

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.







Figure 9: KV cache fragmentation and the PagedAttention solution: The panels replay the eight-slot example from the text. (a) Contiguous reservation holds the maximum length of four slots per sequence, so the slots Seq A and Seq B never fill sit idle (internal fragmentation). (b) After sequences finish, four slots are free but the largest contiguous gap is two, so Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, cannot be admitted (external fragmentation). (c) PagedAttention maps Seq E’s logical pages through a block table onto any free physical blocks, so the same memory now holds it; only the unfilled tail of its final block remains unused.



Beyond the fragmentation bounds in the definition, paging gives two further capacity advantages. Sequences grow page by page without worst-case preallocation, and common prefixes across requests can share physical pages directly in memory. Together, these properties turn KV cache capacity into a schedulable resource rather than a fixed per-request reservation. The price is indirection, because custom attention kernels must gather keys and values from noncontiguous blocks through each sequence’s block table. Recovered capacity also raises throughput only when demand fills it. Allocator occupancy is not a throughput measurement, since throughput still depends on decode work, prefill interference, and the latency budget.



Many LLM workloads share common prefixes across requests. System prompts like “You are a helpful assistant…” are prepended to every request. Few-shot examples use the same examples for many queries. Document context involves multiple questions about the same document. Recomputing these shared prefixes wastes both compute (prefill) and memory (duplicate KV cache entries).
Prefix caching shares KV cache entries across requests with compatible common prefixes. Reuse requires the same token prefix and the same model computation, including any task-specific weight adapter and other inputs that affect the cached state. The cache key must distinguish those conditions, and the service must restrict sharing to the permitted users or tenants. Matching visible text alone is insufficient. Figure 10 diagrams valid block-level sharing: logical tables for independent requests map common prefix tokens to physical blocks B0–B5, skipping their repeated prefill work while storing request-specific suffix state separately.






Figure 10: Prefix caching via block sharing: PagedAttention enables efficient prefix caching by allowing multiple sequences’ block tables to point to the same physical blocks for shared content. In this example, the System Prompt is stored in blocks 0-5. Request A and Request B map their first 6 logical pages to these same physical blocks, storing only their unique suffixes in new blocks. This dramatically reduces memory usage and prefill computation for workloads with shared context.



With PagedAttention, prefix caching uses copy-on-write semantics, in which shared blocks stay shared until a request must write into one, and that request then receives a private copy. Three requests that share a system prompt map their first six logical pages to the same physical blocks:
System prompt → Physical blocks [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Request A page table: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 11]  <- shares prefix blocks
Request B page table: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 13, 14]  <- shares prefix blocks
Request C page table: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 15]  <- shares prefix blocks
All three requests reference the same physical blocks for the system prompt. In this block-aligned example, their distinct suffixes occupy new blocks. If a shared prefix ends partway through a block, appending a different suffix writes into a shared block, which is exactly the copy-on-write case, so that request receives a private copy or another representation that preserves the shared contents. The savings can be substantial when many concurrent requests share a compatible system prompt; notebook 10.6 quantifies them for a typical chatbot deployment.

Paged allocation in section 10.10.3 reduces unused reservations, while prefix sharing in section 10.10.4 avoids duplicate state. The next techniques reduce the bytes needed to represent that state. The calculation here uses a 64-KV-head multi-head attention (MHA) baseline so the grouped query attention subsection can isolate the head-count reduction as a separate architectural lever. For a 70B parameter model with 80 layers, 64 heads, head dimension 128, and sequence length 4096 in FP16, the KV cache requires:
\[\text{KV cache} = 2 \times 80 \times 64 \times 128 \times 4096 \times 2 \approx 10.7\text{ GB (FP16)}\]
A single request’s KV cache alone consumes a substantial fraction of the H100’s 80 GB of HBM. For a batch of 8 concurrent requests, the KV cache would require 85.9 GB, leaving no room for model weights or runtime state. Quantization reduces bytes per cached element, while architectural optimization can reduce the number of cached elements. These complementary levers change different factors in the capacity calculation.


Reducing the size of cached values through lower precision provides direct memory savings. Weight-only quantization reduces weight precision while keeping activations in high precision. While effective for storage, this does not reduce the KV cache. KV cache quantization explicitly targets the activations, storing cached keys and values in INT8, FP8, or even INT4.
Storing the cache payload in INT4 reduces it to approximately 2.7 GB per request, a 4× reduction before quantization metadata and any higher-precision residual state. Recovered memory can admit more sequences, but throughput depends on kernel support, conversion costs, and the latency target. Quality must also be evaluated for the intended contexts. Cached keys and values also have different distributions from the model weights and from each other. Keys tend to carry channel-wise outliers, which favors quantizing them per channel, while values lack that channel pattern and can be quantized per token.



Grouped query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023) changes the number of key-value heads cached per layer, while quantization changes bytes per cached element. GQA is a model architecture choice established through training or checkpoint adaptation, not a serving switch that discards heads from an unchanged model. Holding the other cache dimensions fixed, the representative comparison of 64 KV heads under MHA with 8 under GQA gives an 8\(\times\) reduction:

Ainslie, Joshua, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebron, and Sumit Sanghai. 2023. “GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 4895–901. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.298.
\[\text{KV cache (GQA)} = 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 4096 \times 2 \approx 1.3\text{ GB (FP16)}\]
At 1.3 GB, the GQA cache occupies less memory than the 10.7 GB required by MHA in this comparison. Combining GQA with INT8 KV cache quantization reduces the payload further, but per-request size still grows with context length. The architectural and numerical changes each require quality evaluation; recovered capacity permits additional sequences only while their execution remains within the service budget.

Repeating it with the 64-head MHA baseline, whose requests carry eight times more KV state, separates what the attention layout changes from what precision changes.
This comparison uses a conservative decimal HBM budget of 80 GB per GPU, matching the nameplate label rather than the registered byte capacity used by the node estimator.
Problem: A team serves a 70B model on 8\(\times\) H100 GPUs. Weights in FP16 consume 140 GB (17.5 GB/GPU). KV cache at FP16 consumes 10.7 GB per request. How does quantizing weights to INT4 and KV cache to INT8 change the maximum batch size?
Before optimization (all FP16):

Weights: 17.5 GB/GPU
Available for KV cache: 80 GB \(-\) 17.5 GB = 62.5 GB/GPU
KV cache per request: 10.7 GB \(\div\) 8 \(\approx\) 1.34 GB/GPU
Maximum batch size: \(\lfloor\) 62.5 GB divided by 1.34 GB \(\rfloor\) \(\approx\) 46 requests

After optimization (INT4 weights, INT8 KV cache):

Weights: 17.5 GB \(\times (4/16) =\) 4.38 GB/GPU (INT4)
Available for KV cache: 80 GB \(-\) 4.38 GB = 75.62 GB/GPU
KV cache per request (INT8): 5.4 GB \(\div\) 8 \(\approx\) 0.67 GB/GPU
Maximum batch size: \(\lfloor\) 75.62 GB divided by 0.67 GB \(\rfloor\) \(\approx\) 112 requests

Systems insight: The two layouts yield the same multiplicative dividend, because each maximum batch is free memory divided by per-request cache, and precision changes both quantities by the same factors whatever the head count. The layout sets the absolute count, and at either precision the MHA replica admits roughly an eighth as many requests. In both layouts, compressing the cache does more for admission than compressing the weights, since halving per-request state doubles the count while INT4 weights free only the weight share of each GPU. At serving scale the recovered headroom is an admission budget, not yet throughput. The scheduler converts it into completed requests only while the larger batch still meets TPOT, and the counts here omit runtime allocations and headroom, so they are optimistic upper bounds on what admission control should allow.






Speculative decoding pairs a small draft model proposing \(\SpeculativeDraftLength\) tokens with a target model verifying them in one parallel forward pass. With the exact acceptance-and-correction sampling procedure, the emitted sequence preserves the target distribution. Approximate verification rules do not inherit that guarantee. The draft acceptance rate \(\DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability\) determines how much proposed work survives, while drafting and verification costs determine whether it saves time. At fleet scale, the scheduler must also decide when to enable speculation, how its memory cost interacts with admission, and whether it improves the endpoint’s SLO-compliant capacity.


↩︎ The draft-and-verify mechanics of speculative decoding are established in Speculative decoding.
The latency benefit depends on accepted progress relative to drafting and verification time. When the draft model proposes \(\SpeculativeDraftLength\) tokens, high acceptance rates allow the target model to verify and emit multiple tokens in a single forward pass. When acceptance drops, rejected tokens are discarded while drafting and verification still cost time; generation can become slower than ordinary decoding. With the simplified constant, independent acceptance probability at each draft position used in that analysis, the expected number of tokens emitted per round, including the correction token, is \(\frac{1 - \DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability^{\SpeculativeDraftLength+1}}{1 - \DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability}\), which collapses toward 1 as acceptance falls. The following calculation assumes \(\SpeculativeDraftLength= 5\) draft tokens, a draft step 20\(\times\) faster than a target decode step, and a verification pass costing the same as one target decode step. Holding those costs fixed isolates sensitivity to acceptance:
Evaluating this model across representative acceptance regimes illustrates how sharply returns depend on draft accuracy: high acceptance (\(\DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability= 0.9\)) yields an expected 4.69 tokens per verification round for a 3.7× speedup, medium acceptance (\(\DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability= 0.7\)) delivers 2.94 tokens per round for a 2.4× speedup, and low acceptance (\(\DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability= 0.5\)) drops progress to 1.97 tokens per round, yielding a modest speedup of 1.6×.



Speedup shrinks quickly as draft acceptance falls.
Acceptance depends on the draft-target pair, sampling policy, and request distribution. The preceding calculations are sensitivity cases, not fixed acceptance rates for chat, reasoning, or code generation. A serving fleet must measure acceptance and useful token throughput for its actual traffic before selecting a speculation policy, and that policy must answer three serving concerns: memory, the SLO, and change over time.
The first concern is memory. The draft model is not free state. It requires memory for weights, and each in-flight request that uses it reserves additional draft KV state. Pairing a 7B draft model with a 70B target adds roughly 14 GB of FP16 weights per replica plus per-request draft cache. When colocated with the target, this speculation tax competes directly with the KV-cache admission budget developed in section 10.10.1: every gigabyte reserved for the draft is unavailable to target requests. Under a binding memory limit, that reservation lowers maximum concurrency. Placing the draft on separate devices preserves target memory at the cost of additional hardware and communication. The admission controller and the speculation policy therefore require a joint capacity and latency evaluation.
The second concern is which service-level objective the endpoint must meet. At sufficient acceptance, speculation can reduce TPOT; draft execution and cache residency can also reduce admission capacity. Neither latency nor aggregate-throughput benefit follows from the endpoint label alone. The scheduler should compare SLO-compliant goodput with and without speculation under the intended load. TTFT needs separate measurement because draft setup and prefill can add work before the first response token.
The third concern is that acceptance and load change over time. A scheduler can enable speculation when measured TPOT or goodput improves, then disable it when verification cost outweighs accepted-token progress. Disabling draft execution alone does not free resident draft weights; recovering that capacity requires unloading them, and releasing draft KV pages requires ending or migrating the associated speculative state. Alternative draft mechanisms change this budget: self-speculative decoding reuses the target model, Medusa (Cai et al. 2024) adds prediction heads, and lookahead decoding avoids a separate draft model. Each requires its own quality, acceptance, and resource evaluation.

Cai, Tianle, Yuhong Li, Zhengyang Geng, Hongwu Peng, Jason D. Lee, Deming Chen, and Tri Dao. 2024. “Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML).



Chunked prefill keeps prefill and decode on one worker and bounds how much prompt work lands between decode steps. Disaggregation takes the other route and gives each phase its own hardware. The KV-cache sizing of section 10.10.1 now supplies what that choice costs, because the cache a prefill builds is exactly the payload the decode pool must receive.
Figure 11 partitions the serving pipeline into specialized physical tiers. In the illustrated long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime, prefill is compute bound while decode is memory-bandwidth bound. Separate pools can therefore emphasize compute throughput for prefill and memory bandwidth for decode, with a remote direct memory access (RDMA) KV-cache transfer connecting the phases (Zhong et al. 2024). Separation prevents the two phases from competing on the same accelerator and permits independent parallelism and capacity plans. The transfer and queueing at each pool still contribute to request latency, and different batch or context sizes can change which resources bind.

Zhong, Yinmin, Shengyu Liu, Junda Chen, Jianbo Hu, Yibo Zhu, Xuanzhe Liu, Xin Jin, and Hao Zhang. 2024. “DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-Optimized Large Language Model Serving.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), July, 193–210.







Figure 11: Disaggregated Serving Architecture: A long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime separates compute-bound prefill instances from memory-bandwidth-bound decode instances, mediated by RDMA KV-cache transfer. Because prefill sets time to first token and decode sets time per output token, each pool is sized for its own token rate. Other batch and context sizes can change the binding resources.



The disaggregation decision therefore depends on a quantitative contract, not on the phase labels alone. If prefill produces \(\KvCacheMemory\) bytes of attention state and the usable inter-pool bandwidth is \(\LinkBandwidth\), then the handoff consumes at least
\[\KvCacheHandoffTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\KvCacheMemory}{\LinkBandwidth}, \tag{7}\]
where \(\MessageStartupLatency\) includes transfer setup and queueing for the operating point being evaluated; it is not a fixed network latency once load changes. The payload term sets the scale. A 128K-token request on the GQA model of notebook 10.5 carries tens of gigabytes of KV state, so moving it over a single 450 GB/s NVLink direction takes on the order of a hundred milliseconds, and an inter-node link takes longer still. Spreading the transfer across a tensor-parallel group divides that time only when each device has its own path to its counterpart in the decode pool. Because \(\KvCacheMemory\) grows linearly with prompt length, the long prompts that make disaggregation attractive are also the prompts whose handoff costs most, and that cost lands on TTFT.
Equation 7 therefore makes placement part of the service contract. The prefill pool must sustain the admitted prompt-token rate, the decode pool must sustain the admitted output-token rate, and both pools need headroom for the request-length distribution. Disaggregation earns its transfer tax only when eliminating phase interference and balancing the two pools raises SLO goodput. Otherwise, colocated chunked prefill avoids the additional handoff and pool coordination.



Effective KV-cache management begins with capacity accounting rather than an eviction policy. The serving process first reserves memory for weights, activations, runtime overhead, and safety headroom, then treats the remaining HBM as a managed pool for active sequences:
Available GPU memory = Total - Weights - Activations - Overhead
KV pool size = 0.9 * Available  # Leave 10% headroom

Max concurrent sequences = KV pool size / (avg_seq_length * per_token_cache)
That budget estimates how many sequences can coexist, but an average length does not reserve space for future growth. Admission must account for the admitted requests’ remaining budgets. LRU eviction can reclaim retained prefix blocks that no active request references. Reclaiming an active sequence’s state instead requires a preemption decision, made with the victim policy of section 10.8.3. What capacity accounting adds is the observation that freeing the most bytes is not necessarily the cheapest recovery, because the largest sequence is also the most expensive to swap or rebuild.

Example 10.7: KV cache memory hierarchyScenario: A multi-tenant LLM serving system experiences KV-cache HBM exhaustion (80 GB limit) during peak concurrency.
Diagnosis: Pure HBM allocation limits node concurrency to 50 active sequences in this scenario. Implementing a 3-tier memory hierarchy (HBM \(\to\) CPU DRAM \(\to\) Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) SSD) allows swapping inactive sequence pages to CPU DRAM or NVMe. The illustrative swap budgets of 1–5 ms and 10–50 ms, respectively, require validation for the bytes transferred, effective bandwidth, and contention; they are not fixed properties of the storage tiers.
Systems lesson: In this scenario, multi-tier paging raises retained sequence capacity from 50 to 500, while the active HBM-resident set remains limited to 50. Suspended sequences must be restored before execution resumes under this policy. The extra retention does not establish a throughput gain; restoration costs must fit the affected requests’ deadlines. Streaming active state from another tier would be a different execution policy with transfer costs on the decode path.





KV-cache management accounts for the attention state of concurrent sequences; adapter serving adds another claim on the same memory budget. A low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapter is a user- or task-specific weight delta that must be available when its request executes. LoRA modifies a shared base model without copying all of its weights. For 10,000 users with distinct adapters to the same 140 GB base model, sharing the base avoids storing a complete model per user. The serving process can keep the base resident while loading the adapters needed by active requests. Whether adapter storage or transfer becomes limiting depends on the active adapter mix, ranks, and reuse.

Systems Perspective 10.2: The context switch of machine learningAdapter locality becomes a performance constraint when a scheduled request needs weights that are not resident. Loading those weights from host memory resembles part of an operating-system context switch: execution must wait for the required state unless transfer overlaps other useful work. An adapter already in HBM need not be transferred from the host on every generation step. Coordinating admission with adapter placement can reduce these stalls, while grouping requests by adapter can improve reuse at the cost of waiting for compatible work. The policy must balance locality against the latency and fairness of less frequent adapters.




In multi-tenant environments, thousands of fine-tuned adapters share a single base foundation model. For a linear projection layer with base weights \(\WeightMatrix_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerOutputWidth \times \LayerInputWidth}\), an adapter \(\AdapterIndex\) parameterizes the forward transformation using low-rank decomposition matrices \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix_k \in \mathbb{R}^{\AdapterRank_k \times \LayerInputWidth}\) and \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix_k \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerOutputWidth \times \AdapterRank_k}\) with rank \(\AdapterRank_k \ll \min(\LayerInputWidth, \LayerOutputWidth)\) (typically \(\AdapterRank\in \{8, 16, 64\}\)), as formulated in equation 8:
\[\LayerOutputVector= \LayerInputVector\WeightMatrix_0^T + \frac{\AdapterScalingFactor_k}{\AdapterRank_k} \LayerInputVector\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix_k^T \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix_k^T \tag{8}\]
where \(\LayerInputVector\in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times \LayerInputWidth}\) is a row vector, \(\LayerOutputVector\in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times \LayerOutputWidth}\), and \(\AdapterScalingFactor_k\) is a fixed scaling factor, the hyperparameter usually written \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) in LoRA papers and renamed here because \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) already denotes startup latency and draft acceptance in this chapter. Each adapted projection adds \(\AdapterRank_k(\LayerInputWidth + \LayerOutputWidth)\) parameters instead of a full \(\LayerInputWidth\LayerOutputWidth\) weight matrix. The resident adapter budget therefore depends on which layers are adapted, their dimensions and ranks, precision, and the number of simultaneously loaded tenants.
However, serving requests with heterogeneous adapters in a single continuous batch introduces a critical execution dilemma between batch efficiency and kernel dispatch overhead.
Grouping requests by adapter reduces the distinct adapter state needed for a batch. For low-traffic adapters, however, waiting for a large compatible group increases formation delay, while dispatching immediately can leave a small batch. An adapter receiving dense traffic may benefit from grouping. The difficulty is retaining that locality without preventing requests for different adapters from sharing base-model execution.
Packing requests with different adapters into one batch allows the base projection \(\LayerInputMatrix\WeightMatrix_0^T\) to execute as a shared dense GEMM. A naive implementation then dispatches separate small kernels for each request’s adapter \((\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix, \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix)\). Hundreds of such launches per layer can make host dispatch and launch latency significant; an illustrative per-kernel cost (\(\sim 3\text{--}5\ \MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) per kernel) accumulates even when each adapter performs little arithmetic. Small kernels can also leave GPU streaming multiprocessors (SMs) underused. The following batched operation removes the need for one launch per request.

Definition 10.5: Batched gather-matrix-vector multiplication (BGMV)
Batched gather-matrix-vector multiplication (BGMV) is a GPU kernel operation that batches matrix-vector products across heterogeneous adapters, dynamically gathering adapter weights from a memory pool according to a per-token adapter index vector.

Significance: It reduces per-request kernel launch overhead in multi-adapter serving, allowing heterogeneous adapters to share kernel launches. The remaining overhead depends on adapter ranks, batch composition, and memory locality.
Distinction: A single dense GEMM applies one weight matrix across its input rows. BGMV gathers the adapter-specific weight slice for each element, combining heterogeneous matrix-vector products in one kernel operation.
Common pitfall: Batched execution does not itself solve allocation waste. Loading and unloading differently sized adapters can fragment a contiguous allocator. Paged adapter storage addresses that separate problem, provided the execution kernels support its layout.



Systems such as Punica (Chen et al. 2024) and S-LoRA (Sheng et al. 2024) resolve the execution dilemma through two architectural mechanisms (definition 10.5):


Instead of launching separate kernels for every request, batched or segmented gather-matrix-vector operations group heterogeneous adapters within each projection. Down-projection and up-projection can use separate kernels; Punica distinguishes shrink and expand operators (Chen et al. 2024).

Chen, Liyuan, Zihao Ye, Yonghao Wu, Danyang Zhuo, Luis Ceze, and Arvind Krishnamurthy. 2024. “Punica: Multi-Tenant LoRA Serving.” Proceedings of the 7th Conference on Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys).
For input activations \(\LayerInputMatrix= [\LayerInputVector_1; \LayerInputVector_2; \dots; \LayerInputVector_{\BatchSize}] \in \mathbb{R}^{\BatchSize\times \LayerInputWidth}\), the scheduler constructs an integer mapping vector \(\AdapterAssignmentVector\in \mathbb{Z}^\BatchSize\) where \(\AdapterAssignmentVector[\ExampleIndex] = \AdapterIndex(\ExampleIndex)\) denotes the adapter ID assigned to request \(\ExampleIndex\). The mathematical dataflow for each token is:

Gather: Select token activation \(\LayerInputVector_i\) and the adapter pointer from \(\AdapterAssignmentVector[\ExampleIndex]\).
Down-projection: Compute the vector-matrix product \(\FactoredIntermediateActivation_i = \LayerInputVector_i \AdapterDownProjectionMatrix^T \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times \AdapterRank}\). Because \(\AdapterRank\ll \LayerInputWidth\), this intermediate is smaller than the input activation; its physical placement depends on the kernel.
Up-projection: Multiply \(\FactoredIntermediateActivation_i\) by \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix^T \in \mathbb{R}^{\AdapterRank \times \LayerOutputWidth}\), yielding the adapter delta \(\FiniteChange\LayerOutputVector_i = \frac{\AdapterScalingFactor}{\AdapterRank} \FactoredIntermediateActivation_i \AdapterUpProjectionMatrix^T\).
Accumulation: Add \(\FiniteChange\LayerOutputVector_i\) to the output of the base model projection \(\LayerOutputVector_i = \LayerInputVector_i \WeightMatrix_0^T + \FiniteChange\LayerOutputVector_i\).

By gathering adapter weights within batched kernels, BGMV avoids dispatching a separate kernel for each request’s adapter. The gain must be measured against the actual adapter mix; irregular access and small ranks can still limit achieved bandwidth.



S-LoRA (Sheng et al. 2024) jointly manages adapter weights and KV state in a unified GPU memory pool. Its page holds a vector along the shared hidden dimension, rather than a fixed operating-system-sized byte allocation. Adapter matrices \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix_k\) and \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix_k\) occupy noncontiguous pages, allowing adapters of varying ranks (\(\AdapterRank\in \{8, 16, 32, 64\}\)) to share capacity with growing KV caches. Paging reduces fragmentation; both kinds of state still consume the same finite pool.
The published design keeps adapters in host memory and uses the waiting queue to predict which weights the next batch will need. Prefetching overlaps adapter transfers with current execution when sufficient time and free GPU memory are available. A cache miss whose transfer cannot be hidden still delays the affected request.
When scaling across multiple devices, S-LoRA aligns adapter inputs and outputs with the base layer while communicating low-rank intermediates (Sheng et al. 2024). With the weight orientation in equation 8, Megatron’s column-parallel and row-parallel conventions describe \(\WeightMatrix_0^T\). Two meanings of “rank” meet here, so device below means a tensor-parallel GPU, and the LoRA rank stays \(\AdapterRank_k\).

Sheng, Ying, Shiyi Cao, Dacheng Li, Coleman Hooper, Shuo Chen, Daxin Jiang, Christopher Rodriguez, et al. 2024. “S-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters.” Proceedings of the 7th Conference on Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys).
In a column-parallel layer, \(\WeightMatrix_0\) and \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix_k\) are split across devices along their output rows, and \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix_k\) along its \(\AdapterRank_k\) rows. Each device computes its slice of the \(\AdapterRank_k\)-dimensional intermediate \(\LayerInputVector\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix_k^T\), an AllGather assembles the full intermediate on every device, and each device multiplies it by its local slice of \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix_k^T\) to produce its share of the output.
In a row-parallel layer, \(\WeightMatrix_0\) and \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix_k\) are split along their input columns, and \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix_k\) along its output rows. Each device computes a partial \(\AdapterRank_k\)-dimensional intermediate from its input slice, and an AllReduce sums those partials. Each device then computes its slice of the adapter output, adds it into the matching positions of its base-layer partial output, and joins the base layer’s final AllReduce.
This layout reduces adapter replication but does not eliminate communication. Its additional collectives operate on rank-dimensional intermediates; the final output assembly shares the base layer’s collective. The trade-off is lower adapter memory per rank against added synchronization.
KV pages and adapter deltas share HBM with the base weights. Even when long contexts make the cache larger than the weights, reducing the weight footprint can release capacity for those other allocations. Weight quantization addresses this part of the budget, with numerical quality and execution cost determining how much of the storage saving becomes useful serving capacity.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
INT4 turns a two-GPU model into a one-GPU candidate.
Weight quantization for serving is a bottleneck-selection decision. Reducing precision can turn a 140 GB FP16 weight payload into a 35 GB INT4 payload, potentially making a model that previously needed multiple GPUs resident on one. The ideal payload reduction is 4\(\times\); metadata, runtime buffers, and KV state still enter the deployment’s memory budget. Quality loss is not fixed by bit width, and reduced storage does not guarantee proportional speedup. Both must be measured for the deployed representation and workload.

Systems Perspective 10.3: Quantization as a serving constraintIn serving systems, quantization is not merely a model-compression technique; it changes the binding resource. Post-training quantization can shrink a deployed model without retraining, while quantization-aware training spends training effort to preserve accuracy at lower precision. The systems question is which constraint the lower-precision representation relaxes: GPU memory capacity, HBM bandwidth during decode, accelerator instruction support, or cost per served token.




↩︎ The trade-off between post-training quantization and quantization-aware training is established in Post-training vs. quantization-aware training.
Quantization reduces numerical precision of model weights and activations, decreasing their memory footprint by 2–4\(\times\). Reducing weight traffic can improve bandwidth-bound decode, provided kernel support and dequantization overhead preserve the saving. The serving decision is which quantity should shrink: resident weights for fit, bytes moved per decode step for bandwidth, activations for prefill throughput, or the precision path supported by target hardware. Serving at scale also introduces distinct challenges: a deployment team may need post-training quantization without the original training corpus, quality must be preserved across diverse inputs, and hardware deployment targets vary from data center GPUs to edge accelerators. Lack of the original corpus does not imply data-free calibration; the methods that follow may still require representative deployment inputs. Production inference therefore starts from a decision model rather than from the methods. Table 14 ties each method family to the serving constraint it relaxes, and the subsections that follow take the methods in that order, recording for each only what changes when it is deployed: calibration cost, kernel path, and the evaluation a serving team must run.



Table 14: Serving quantization decision model: Quantization methods are useful only when they relax the resource that binds the serving system. The method family follows from the bottleneck: fit, bandwidth, prefill compute, or outlier robustness.











Binding serving constraint
Representation change
Method family
Risk to test before rollout




Model does not fit in memory
Quantize weights only
GPTQ, AWQ
Calibration mismatch and quality regression


Decode is bandwidth-bound
Reduce bytes read per token
W4A16 weight-only paths
Kernel support and KV-cache headroom


Prefill is compute-bound
Quantize weights and activations
SmoothQuant W8A8
Activation outliers and INT8 hardware path

Change the coordinate basis before quantization
Rotation-based methods
Transform overhead and limited runtime path








Large language models can exhibit activation ranges that make low-precision deployment difficult. The outlier activation problem arises when a few hidden-dimension channels carry magnitudes far larger than typical values (Xiao et al. 2023). A coarse scale loses resolution for smaller values, while a narrow range clips large ones. This trade-off is not unique to language models, but its channel structure motivates the methods below. Outliers and block-wise quantization develops the outlier mechanism and the algorithms that answer it (LLM.int8(), GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant); the subsections that follow keep only what each method changes for a serving deployment.
For a serving deployment the consequence is that no single INT8 scale suits both the outlier channels and the typical values, which is why the methods that follow differ, each protecting a different part of the serving contract.



GPTQ (Frantar et al. 2023), which uses second-order error compensation, is the weight-only choice when deployment needs 4-bit compression after training and can afford calibration data. Its serving value is that the model gets smaller without a full retraining run.

Frantar, Elias, Saleh Ashkboos, Torsten Hoefler, and Dan Alistarh. 2023. “GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-Trained Transformers.” In CoRR, abs/2210.17323. https://doi.org/10.48550/ARXIV.2210.17323.
GPTQ rounds weight columns while compensating the remaining columns using statistics collected from calibration inputs. Calibration and error compensation are offline costs paid when producing the quantized artifact, rather than on each serving request. Their duration depends on model size, calibration workload, hardware, and implementation; a fixed sample count is not a general deployment requirement. The resulting artifact still requires suitable inference kernels, and its quality must be tested when production inputs differ from the calibration distribution.
Table 15 identifies the measurements needed to evaluate a GPTQ deployment:



Table 15: GPTQ evaluation contract: Nominal bit width alone does not determine quality, compression, or speed. Report the deployed representation and measured workload rather than extrapolating fixed values across model sizes.









Measurement
Comparison contract




Quality change
Same model, task, and evaluation data before and after quantization


Memory reduction
Include scales, zero points, packing, and runtime buffers


Quantization time
State calibration data, hardware, and implementation


Serving performance
Compare SLO-compliant throughput at the same workload






GPTQ provides weight compression without a full retraining run, using a layer-local reconstruction objective to control error. That objective does not guarantee task quality after errors propagate through the complete model. Calibration coverage, quantization settings, and the deployed kernel path therefore belong in the evaluation alongside artifact size.



Activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) (Lin et al. 2024) approaches weight-only compression through activation statistics. It scales selected weight channels before quantization, applying the inverse scale to their inputs, often through a preceding operation. This protects salient channels without GPTQ’s sequential error-compensation procedure. Calibration cost and quality still depend on the model and data. If the scale cannot be fused into the deployed graph, an additional runtime operation spends some of the latency saving; it does not by itself erase the smaller weight footprint.

Lin, Ji, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Wei-Ming Chen, Wei-Chen Wang, Guangxuan Xiao, Xingyu Dang, Chuang Gan, and Song Han. 2024. “AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization for on-Device LLM Compression and Acceleration.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 6: 87–100.
Table 16 compares the methods’ error-control mechanisms and calibration roles, then the deployment check each requires; both need the same quality evaluation on the target model and task.



Table 16: AWQ vs. GPTQ: The methods use different calibration mechanisms. Quality, calibration time, and serving speed require comparison on the same model, data, precision, and runtime; neither column implies a universal ranking.










Aspect
GPTQ
AWQ

Calibration role

Deployment check
