Supported packing, fused scales, and kernels






The engineering choice follows the measured quality budget and deployed kernel path, not a fixed quality or calibration-speed ordering.



SmoothQuant (Xiao et al. 2023) targets W8A8 deployments where activation quantization matters, especially compute-bound prefill. Its per-channel rescaling transfers part of the activation range into the weights while preserving the full-precision layer calculation. Subsequent rounding to INT8 still introduces error. Folding scales into existing operations can avoid separate scaling kernels, but realized overhead depends on the deployed graph and kernels. Calibration must test the resulting ranges because production activation extremes can differ from those used to choose the scales.

Xiao, Guangxuan, Ji Lin, Mickaël Seznec, Hao Wu, Julien Demouth, and Song Han. 2023. “SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 38087–99.
In the W8A8 deployment regime, SmoothQuant enables INT8 quantization for both weights and activations. Table 17 bounds what each 8-bit path can buy relative to the FP16 baseline:



Table 17: W8A8 SmoothQuant vs. weight-only quantization: Ceilings derived from bytes per weight and the H100’s INT8-to-FP16 peak ratio, not measured speedups. Both schemes halve weight bytes, so both can at most halve weight traffic in bandwidth-bound decode. Only W8A8 moves prefill onto INT8 Tensor Cores. Realized gains and quality loss depend on kernels, calibration, and the request mix.

The critical distinction is which ceiling binds. Among these configurations, W8A8 enables INT8 matrix multiplication, with the illustrated 2× peak ratio providing a compute ceiling rather than a measured prefill speedup. Both quantized schemes halve the weight payload. If weight reads dominate decode, activation quantization does not further reduce that traffic, although it can change other memory and compute costs. Quantization and dequantization also add work. The end-to-end benefit therefore depends on the prompt/output mix, batch sizes, and measured execution path.



Traditional quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant) address quantization error through compensation or rescaling. Rotation-based quantization (Ashkboos et al. 2024) changes the coordinate basis so large values are less concentrated in a few channels. This can make lower precision viable without retaining designated outlier channels in higher precision.
The magnitude of an individual coordinate depends on the chosen basis. An appropriate rotation can redistribute a large coordinate across many components while preserving the full-precision computation through corresponding weight transformations. This redistribution does not guarantee uniform values or negligible rounding error for every input; the resulting quantized model still requires quality evaluation.


QuaRot uses orthogonal Hadamard transforms to redistribute large coordinates before low-bit quantization.6 The transform can be chosen without calibration data, but the full weight-quantization pipeline may use calibrated GPTQ. Orthogonal transformations preserve the full-precision calculation when corresponding weight and activation transforms are applied consistently; quantization still introduces approximation. Runtime rotations add work, so the serving decision compares measured quality and goodput on the target kernel path.
6 Hadamard Rotation in QuaRot (Quantized Rotation): QuaRot transforms activations as \(\RotatedActivationMatrix = \LayerInputMatrix \cdot \HadamardRotationMatrix\) and weights as \(\RotatedWeightMatrix= \HadamardRotationMatrix^T \cdot \WeightMatrix\), where \(\HadamardRotationMatrix\) is an orthogonal Hadamard matrix, computed structurally without being stored. Orthogonality preserves \(\LayerInputMatrix\WeightMatrix= \RotatedActivationMatrix\RotatedWeightMatrix\), so the layer output is unchanged. The outlier-spreading effect is concrete: a vector \([1000, 1, 1, 1]\) with one extreme value becomes roughly \([502, 500, 500, 500]\) after the transform, so no single coordinate dominates the quantization range.Table 18 contrasts two outlier-management mechanisms. The listed precision targets are evaluated operating points, not universal limits or guarantees.



Table 18: QuaRot vs. SmoothQuant: Calibration requirements belong to the complete quantization pipeline. Quality and speed must be measured for the selected model, bit widths, and implementation.

The QuaRot authors report that rotation keeps W4A4 quality close to FP16 on the models they evaluate, which is what makes 4-bit activation quantization a serving candidate at all (Ashkboos et al. 2024). Its 4-bit weights and 4-bit activations cut memory for the quantized tensors by roughly 4\(\times\) relative to FP16, but its quality relative to GPTQ’s 4-bit weight-only path must still be measured on the deployment’s own model and task. Learned-rotation variants optimize the rotation matrices themselves to reduce quantization error, adding offline optimization cost; the learned rotations are not a guarantee of globally optimal quality. Rotation methods extend low-precision choices, but the useful trade-off depends on measured quality, transform overhead, and the deployed kernel path.

Ashkboos, Saleh, Amirkeivan Mohtashami, Maximilian L. Croci, Bo Li, Pashmina Cameron, Martin Jaggi, Dan Alistarh, Torsten Hoefler, and James Hensman. 2024. “QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 100213–40. https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-3180.




Hardware and software support determine which quantization savings reach the serving workload. Native low-precision arithmetic can raise compute throughput, but a weight-only kernel can also save HBM capacity and traffic by reading packed weights and converting them on chip. The arithmetic format and the resident storage format need not be identical.
Table 20 summarizes NVIDIA Tensor Core precision support across Ampere and Hopper:

The 2\(\times\) ratio at INT8 and FP8 compares peak arithmetic throughput on those native paths, not measured serving speed. A100 provides native INT4 Tensor Core operations, although realized LLM speedup still depends on framework and kernel support; H100 INT4 deployment remains software/framework-dependent, and native FP4 first appears in Blackwell.

For batch-one decode dominated by weight reads, the following proportionality estimates throughput using the active model weights as the byte count. It omits KV-cache traffic and execution overhead and does not describe aggregate throughput at arbitrary batch size:
\[\text{Decode throughput} \propto \frac{\text{Memory bandwidth}}{\text{Model size in bytes}}\]
In the ideal memory-bound case, reducing FP16 weights to 4-bit values cuts weight traffic by 4\(\times\), but realized decode throughput depends on kernel support, dequantization overhead, KV-cache precision, batch shape, and whether HBM bandwidth is truly the bottleneck. The value of 4-bit serving is therefore strongest when it increases model residency or batch capacity, and throughput gains should be validated on the target serving workload.
The mapping in table 21 gives candidate configurations based on runtime support and the resource being constrained. W4A16 can reduce resident weight memory, W8A8 can exploit INT8 arithmetic, and FP8 can use a supported native path. Hardware capability narrows the choices but does not select the winner; the quality target and measured workload determine which representation is useful.



Table 21: Quantization deployment configurations: Mapping from quantization scheme to deployment target and supporting frameworks. W4A16 is common for consumer and memory-constrained deployments; W8A8 unlocks INT8 Tensor Core throughput; FP8 is the native low-precision path on H100/H200-class deployments; W4A4 is an aggressive compression target with more limited framework support.

Production serving frameworks determine whether a quantized artifact retains its intended memory and execution advantages. Expanding the entire model into resident FP16 weights can forfeit capacity savings, while converting packed weights inside a kernel can preserve reduced HBM storage and traffic. The serving stack must therefore report the resident representation and kernel path, budget KV state around actual allocations, and expose quality and latency regressions. Table 22 summarizes these responsibilities; the distinction between full-model expansion and on-chip conversion is essential when interpreting its dequantization warning.



Table 22: Quantized serving runtime contract: Framework-specific APIs differ, but every production path has to preserve representation, choose supported kernels, plan memory, and validate quality under the deployed traffic mix.









Runtime responsibility
Why it matters




Preserve the quantized artifact
Full-model expansion into resident FP16 forfeits the reduced weight storage and traffic.


Select compatible low-precision kernels
Unsupported operators fall back to slower or higher-precision execution.


Plan memory around weights and KV cache
The capacity gain matters only if the freed memory becomes useful batch headroom.


Validate quality and latency together
A lower-bit path that meets latency but fails task quality is not a serving win.






Weight quantization reduces the weight allocation, while PagedAttention reduces waste in allocating KV state. Ignoring other allocations gives the following optimistic concurrency estimate. A usable integer limit must round down after reserving runtime buffers, quantization metadata, and safety headroom; sharded deployments must satisfy the budget on every device:
\[\text{Max batch} = \frac{\text{GPU Memory} - \text{Quantized Weights}}{\text{KV Cache per Sequence}}\]
This comparison uses a conservative decimal HBM budget matching the A100 nameplate label, rather than the registered byte capacity used by the node estimator. A 70B model with 4-bit weights requires approximately 35 GB, leaving 45 GB on an 80 GB A100 for KV cache. With FP16 KV cache at about 2.6 GB per 1K-token sequence for the MHA baseline, this supports about 17 concurrent 1K-token sequences before other runtime overheads. With FP16 weights, the same 70B model would not fit on one A100 at all, so weight-only quantization changes both feasibility and batch capacity.



The final selection must satisfy memory, quality, and latency requirements together. Native support makes a precision path a candidate; it does not establish the model’s quality at that precision. Nor is there a universal quality ordering between 4-bit weight-only and 8-bit weight-and-activation quantization. Evaluate both against the same task baseline, retaining the reference representation when alternatives fail the quality budget. For compute-bound prefill, W8A8 offers the illustrated 2× INT8 compute ceiling. For decode dominated by weight reads, W4A16 can cut the weight payload by up to 4\(\times\), provided conversion and other costs leave a useful saving. Latency-sensitive and throughput-oriented services can benefit from either path under suitable workloads.
These precision choices affect cost per million useful tokens. The residency calculation above is what makes fewer GPUs possible at all, because INT4 weights shrink the resident payload enough for a 70B replica to fit on fewer devices. Table 23 isolates the effect of GPU count by assuming equal per-GPU prices and the same completed token rate across three configurations. Under that contract, reducing the number of billed GPUs reduces cost proportionally. The calculation does not establish that the smaller replicas sustain the same rate or meet the same quality and latency targets:



Table 23: Quantization impact on serving cost: Estimated cost per million tokens at three configurations. At equal unit prices and unchanged useful token throughput, halving the GPU count halves the cost; halving it again brings the per-million-token cost to one quarter of the FP16 baseline. The cost savings come almost entirely from fewer GPUs rather than from per-GPU throughput gains.









Configuration

The illustrated 2–4\(\times\) cost reduction follows from the assumed device-count reduction at unchanged useful throughput. If the smaller replica completes fewer qualifying tokens per second, cost per token falls by less and can increase. A deployment comparison must therefore combine billed replica cost with measured SLO-compliant output under the same quality contract.
Precision moves the capacity wall without removing it. A 175-billion-parameter model still needs about 87.5 GB for its 4-bit weight payload alone, more than one 80 GB H100 holds before KV state and runtime allocations. Keeping that representation accelerator-resident requires distributing it across devices. Offloading to host memory is another placement choice, but introduces transfers that must fit the latency budget. Sharding addresses the capacity problem while adding communication and coordination to each replica.

Self-Check: Question

How does SmoothQuant enable efficient 8-bit weight and 8-bit activation (W8A8) inference, and why is its speedup significantly higher during prefill than during decode?

It prunes 50% of model weights using structured sparsity, accelerating decode but having no effect on prefill.
It divides activations by a per-channel scale \(s\) and multiplies weights by \(s\), moving quantization difficulty toward weights; compute-bound prefill can benefit from native INT8 arithmetic while decode remains sensitive to memory traffic
It rotates the coordinate basis using randomized Walsh-Hadamard matrices, eliminating memory bandwidth bottlenecks during decode.
It converts floating-point weights into binary spikes, enabling single-cycle bitwise operations during token generation.

What is the core algorithmic distinction between Generalized Post-Training Quantization (GPTQ) and Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (AWQ)?

GPTQ quantizes activations while leaving weights in FP16; AWQ quantizes weights while leaving activations in FP32.
GPTQ requires full model retraining for 100 epochs; AWQ is an online dynamic quantization method with no calibration.
GPTQ compensates residual quantization error across remaining unquantized columns using inverse Hessian information (\(H^{-1}\)); AWQ protects salient weight channels based on activation magnitudes without error feedback.
GPTQ applies only to convolutional vision models; AWQ applies exclusively to sparse recommendation embedding tables.

Explain how QuaRot uses a data-free orthogonal rotation to reduce activation outliers, why its full quantization pipeline can still require calibration, and what runtime cost the rotation introduces.
True or False: Modern NVIDIA Hopper (H100) GPUs provide native Tensor Core instruction acceleration for FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) delivering a \(2\times\) compute throughput multiplier over FP16, whereas Ampere (A100) Tensor Cores do not natively support FP8 execution.
Order the sequential steps in the GPTQ column-wise layer quantization pipeline:


Compute the Hessian matrix \(H = 2 X^T X\) from calibration activations
Perform Cholesky decomposition on the inverse Hessian matrix \(H^{-1}\)
Round the current column weights to the nearest discrete quantized grid
Calculate the residual quantization error vector for the column
Propagate compensation updates to all remaining unquantized columns using the Cholesky inverse weights

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Quantization shrinks the representation; sharding keeps it and divides it instead. When a deployment must retain the 70B model’s FP16 weights in accelerator memory, or when even the quantized state exceeds one device, multiple GPUs hold partitions and execute together as one logical replica. The resulting design adapts tensor and pipeline parallelism from training, but must evaluate their communication and scheduling costs against inference deadlines.


Model sharding for inference addresses memory capacity and execution latency through different mechanisms. Table 24 identifies the constraints that motivate each candidate strategy; the timing analysis determines whether parallel execution repays its communication cost.
The first driver is memory capacity. If the selected representation must remain in accelerator memory but does not fit on one device, the replica needs multiple devices. For a model with \(\Parameters\) parameters at precision \(\NumericBitWidth\) bits, equation 9 gives the weight payload before metadata and runtime state:
\[\WeightMemory = \Parameters\times \frac{\NumericBitWidth}{8} \text{ bytes} \tag{9}\]
Applied to the 70B model in FP16 (16 bits), equation 9 recovers the payload quoted since section 10.2:
\[M_{\text{weights}} = 7 \times 10^{10} \times \frac{16}{8} = 140 \text{ GB}\]
The result exceeds the 80 GB capacity of an H100 GPU, establishing a weight-only lower bound of 2 shards for an accelerator-resident replica. KV state, buffers, replication within the chosen partition, and uneven placement can require a larger degree.
The second driver is latency. Even when a model fits in memory, sharding can reduce latency by parallelizing computation. Equation 10 is the Fleet Law (equation 1.3) applied to a single inference request, separating the compute term that sharding divides from the communication and synchronization terms it adds:
\[\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \tag{10}\]
where \(\DeviceCount\) is the number of devices in the sharding group, \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) is the communication overhead, \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) is synchronization overhead, and \(\OverlappedTime\) is communication hidden behind useful compute. In the common no-overlap simplification with negligible extra synchronization, this reduces to \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount+ \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\). Sharding provides latency benefit only when the nonoverlapped overhead is smaller than the time saved through parallelization.

Tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al. 2019) distributes individual layers across multiple devices, enabling parallel computation within each layer. The column-row partitioning scheme introduced for training applies here: splitting the first feed-forward linear layer by columns and the second by rows requires one AllReduce for that feed-forward sublayer. The attention output requires another, giving two AllReduce operations per transformer block in the scheme analyzed here. For transformer models, the primary target is the attention mechanism and feed-forward layers, which contain the majority of computation.

Shoeybi, Mohammad, Mostofa Patwary, Raul Puri, Patrick LeGresley, Jared Casper, and Bryan Catanzaro. 2019. “Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1909.08053.

↩︎ Column-row tensor partitioning and its two AllReduce operations per transformer block are established in Tensor parallelism.

The multi-head attention computation naturally partitions across attention heads. For a model with \(\AttentionHeadCount\) attention heads and tensor-parallel degree \(\TensorParallelDegree\), an even partition assigns \(\AttentionHeadCount/\TensorParallelDegree\) heads per device when the head count is divisible by that degree. With GQA, the smaller number of KV heads can require a different partition or replicated KV state. The local attention calculation for the evenly partitioned case is:
\[\text{Attention}_i = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\AttentionQueryMatrix_i \AttentionKeyMatrix_i^T}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}}\right) \AttentionValuesMatrix_i \text{ for heads } \AttentionHeadIndex\in \{1, \dots, \AttentionHeadCount/\TensorParallelDegree\}\]
Each device applies its shard of the attention output projection to its local heads. An AllReduce operation then sums those projected partial outputs across devices. The reduction combines contributions to the same output coordinates, rather than summing unrelated head outputs directly. Its latency includes collective startup and coordination as well as payload transfer over the interconnect.
The feed-forward layer (typically two linear transformations with activation) partitions along the hidden dimension, with the first linear layer split by columns and the second by rows, so the activation between them never leaves its device.
The communication pattern for tensor-parallel inference follows a two-phase synchronization per layer. Figure 12 diagrams this execution flow across two GPU ranks, isolating how column-row GEMM decompositions confine cross-device synchronization to two AllReduce barriers over NVLink, one after the multi-head attention projection and one after the feed-forward layer.






Figure 12: Tensor parallelism for inference: Computation is distributed across devices by splitting tensor operations. Attention heads are partitioned across GPUs, requiring an AllReduce operation to synchronize results. Feed-forward networks use a column-row splitting strategy that requires only one AllReduce synchronization per block. This partition can reduce latency when saved compute exceeds communication cost. The illustrated two-collective layer uses a fast local interconnect; its NVLink label is aggregate bidirectional bandwidth, not the per-direction transfer rate.



The inference time with tensor parallelism follows equation 11:
\[\TensorParallelLayerTime= \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\TensorParallelDegree} + 2 \times \AllReduceCompletionTime(\CollectivePayloadSize) \tag{11}\]
Equation 11 is the per-layer instance of equation 10. Here \(\IronLawComputeTime\) is the sequential compute time of one layer rather than of the whole request, \(\TensorParallelDegree\) is the tensor-parallel degree, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) is the full activation payload contributed by each rank to each AllReduce (the message size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) of the ring AllReduce cost model derived in Ring AllReduce and recalled with the other collective costs in section 10.12.7). Compute is ideally divided across ranks; the partial activation output still has the full reduced shape, (tokens in the step) \(\times\) (hidden width) \(\times\) (bytes per element). The factor of 2 accounts for the two AllReduce operations per transformer layer (attention and feed-forward).

Example 10.8: Tensor parallelism for Llama-70BScenario: An engineering team deploys Llama-70B (70B parameters, FP16 footprint 140 GB) across an 8-GPU H100 node with NVLink (Touvron et al. 2023).
Diagnosis: The calculation assumes 30 ms of serial layer compute as a reference, independent of the devices required to hold the weights: 12 ms for attention and 18 ms for the feed-forward block. That reference describes a long-prompt prefill, in which every prompt token passes through the layer in one step, so it is far larger than one layer’s share of a decode step on the reference replica. Ideal eight-way division gives 1.5 ms and 2.25 ms, and the two AllReduce operations of equation 11 add an assumed 0.3 ms each, for 4.35 ms per layer.
Systems lesson: The illustrative eight-way model gives a 6.9× reduction relative to its serial-compute reference (prefill time reduced from 2,400 ms to 348 ms). The entire shortfall from the ideal 8\(\times\) is the two collectives, a fixed cost per layer that dividing compute cannot shrink. Their share of the layer therefore grows as per-device compute falls, which is why a decode step, with far less compute per layer than this prefill reference, feels the collective cost most.

Pipeline parallelism distributes layers across devices sequentially, with each device handling a subset of layers. Unlike tensor parallelism, there is no synchronization within a layer, only between pipeline stages.
For inference, pipeline parallelism creates bubbles differently than in training. Figure 13 contrasts single-request latency against pipelined throughput: executing an isolated request serially across four GPU stages leaves three accelerators idle at every step, whereas maintaining multiple in-flight requests fills the pipeline and amortizes the initial bubble across steady-state token delivery.







Figure 13: Pipeline parallelism bubbles: (a) An 80-layer model split into four stages passes one request’s activations from stage to stage, so splitting the layers alone does not shorten its sequential computation; it must still traverse all four stages. (b) With many requests in flight, later stages idle during the fill bubble, and from slot t4 onward every stage is busy and one request leaves the pipeline per slot. Pipeline parallelism therefore suits throughput-oriented serving better than latency-critical interactive serving.



For a single request, pipeline staging does not parallelize the dependent layers. If stage execution times are unchanged, the request still pays their sum plus transfers, so staging alone provides no execution-latency reduction. A comparison against a memory-constrained implementation that offloads weights can differ because keeping stages resident changes those execution costs.
Pipeline parallelism instead scales throughput by sustaining multiple concurrent requests across execution stages, as tracked in the steady-state schedule of figure 13(b). Once the pipeline reaches saturation, throughput is limited by the slowest stage. For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) balanced stages with negligible transfer overhead, this is \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) times the throughput of executing the whole model sequentially on one device, not \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) times a single stage’s throughput. An individual request still traverses every stage, so its execution latency remains approximately the sum of the stage times.
Pipeline parallelism is particularly appropriate for inference when memory constraints require sharding across devices but latency targets are relaxed, when aggregate throughput matters more than individual request latency, or when inter-device network bandwidth is limited to point-to-point communication rather than high-speed AllReduce fabrics.

The decision starts with capacity feasibility, then compares latency and throughput on the available topology. Tensor parallelism can shorten layer execution when that saving exceeds its collective cost. Pipeline parallelism distributes resident layers with transfers between stages, but needs concurrent work and balanced stage times for high throughput. Neither a fast interconnect nor a relaxed deadline alone establishes the best choice; the request mix and measured execution costs determine the useful partition.



Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, such as DeepSeek-V3 or Mixtral, introduce unique serving challenges beyond those of dense models. In an MoE transformer layer, the feed-forward network is replaced by multiple parallel “expert” sub-networks and a lightweight router that selects a subset of experts for each token.
With fixed expert dimensions and a fixed number selected per token, adding experts grows total parameter capacity without proportionally increasing expert arithmetic per token. Routing, shared layers, and communication still contribute work. Expert parallelism places different experts on different GPUs to distribute their storage and execution. It is a placement choice when the model and workload require multiple devices, rather than an intrinsic requirement of every MoE model.


MoE serving separates two capacity measures. The total parameter count sets the weight-storage requirement at the chosen precision, while the active parameter count estimates the weight-related arithmetic and traffic for each token. Neither count includes all runtime costs. An accelerator-resident deployment must accommodate inactive experts as well as active ones, even though each token uses only a subset.
The following comparison isolates weight-related costs at batch size 1. Streaming all weights of a dense 400B FP16 model moves 800 GB per step. Counting only DeepSeek-V3’s 37B active parameters gives approximately 74 GB in FP16, a 10.8× reduction in weight bytes per token. The proportional estimate of weight-related arithmetic is 10.8× lower. These are payload and arithmetic comparisons, not equivalent-quality model comparisons or measured speedups; cache traffic, expert placement, routing, and communication affect realized latency.



MoE keeps every expert resident but activates few per token.
The trade-off is resident capacity: keeping all experts on accelerators avoids fetching inactive experts when routing changes. Offloading can reduce that resident footprint but adds transfer and scheduling costs. DeepSeek-V3’s full model in FP16 requires approximately 1342 GB, requiring many devices if the entire FP16 weight set remains accelerator-resident.

Napkin Math 10.8: MoE capacity planningThis comparison uses a conservative decimal budget of 80 GB per GPU, matching the H100 nameplate label rather than the registered byte capacity used by the node estimator.
Problem: A team deploys DeepSeek-V3 (671B total parameters, 37B active per token) for a chatbot application. The model uses FP8 weights (1 byte per parameter). The cluster has 8-GPU nodes, each with 8\(\times\) H100 GPUs (80 GB HBM per GPU, 640 GB per node). How many nodes are needed, and what is the per-token decode latency?
Math:

Memory: Total weight memory = 671 GB. A single node (640 GB) is insufficient. 2 provide 1,280 GB in aggregate. The remaining capacity must still accommodate KV state, metadata, buffers, and any replicated weights on each device.
Latency: Count 37B active parameters (37 GB) per decode step. If their reads were evenly distributed across 16 GPUs, each would read about 2.3 GB. At the stated 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, \(\PerDeviceWeightReadTime\approx\) 0.69 ms. The scenario adds 0.3 ms for routing. Expert placement and token routing do not guarantee this balance, especially at batch size 1.
Floor: The simplified sum is \(\approx\) 1.0 ms/token, corresponding to 1,000 tokens/s at batch size 1 under these assumptions. It is an optimistic estimate, not a measured rate or a rigorous latency bound; compute, KV traffic, synchronization, and imbalance remain unmodeled.

Systems insight: Sparse activation separates resident parameter capacity from the work selected for one token. Planning an accelerator-resident 671B model therefore requires both a per-device memory budget and a timing model for the actual expert placement. Dividing total active bytes by device count does not establish that every device can contribute bandwidth equally.





Distributing MoE models across GPUs introduces expert parallelism: each GPU holds a subset of experts, and tokens are routed to the GPU holding their assigned expert. In an MoE layer, a gating network selects \(\RoutedExpertCount\) experts (out of \(\ExpertCount\) total) for each token:
\[\text{Output} = \sum_{i \in \text{top-}k} {\RouterGateProbability}_i \cdot \text{Expert}_i(\text{input})\]


↩︎ Top-\(\RoutedExpertCount\) gating, and why sparse activation separates parameter count from per-token work, are established in Mixture of experts.
An even expert placement assigns each device \(\ExpertCount/\DeviceCount\) experts, where \(\DeviceCount\) is the number of expert-parallel devices. Figure 14 traces the path for a token: a top-2 softmax gating router selects expert destinations, an AllToAll dispatch sends the token representations to those ranks, and an AllToAll gather returns outputs for weighted recombination. An expert not selected by this token may process another token in the batch, so the illustration does not imply that every unselected device is idle.






Figure 14: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing: Expert parallelism distributes “experts” across different devices. For each token, a gating mechanism selects the top-\(\RoutedExpertCount\) experts. An AllToAll communication step dispatches tokens to the devices hosting their selected experts, the selected experts process the tokens in parallel while experts unselected by this token may serve other tokens, and a second AllToAll step gathers the results for the weighted sum. Distributed expert capacity adds all-to-all communication overhead.



The communication pattern differs from tensor parallelism. AllReduce delivers a combined reduction result (same data to all devices) and maps onto ring or tree schedules whose per-link traffic is fixed by the message size. Expert parallelism instead uses AllToAll to deliver routed token representations (different data to different devices based on routing), so the bytes each link and receiver carries depend on which experts the router selects; the host of a popular expert can become an incast point for many senders. If some experts receive more work, their hosts can determine completion time while less-loaded hosts wait. Balancing the number of stored experts does not guarantee balanced token traffic.
Training and serving offer different controls over this imbalance. An auxiliary loss can encourage more balanced expert use during training without guaranteeing balance on future traffic. An expert capacity factor limits accepted tokens relative to an even allocation; 1.25\(\times\) is an illustrative setting, not a universal requirement. Dropping excess work or rerouting it to another expert changes the model computation and requires quality validation. Expert buffering instead retains excess work for later execution, spending latency and queue capacity. These controls trade quality, waiting, and utilization rather than guaranteeing that routing remains balanced.



Router behavior affects both system performance and model quality. Expert collapse concentrates training traffic on a small subset of experts, leaving other experts undertrained despite their storage cost. Unstable assignments can also hinder specialization. At serving time, a changed input distribution can alter expert popularity and create hotspots without any change to the stored model. Token dropping skips selected expert work when a capacity limit is exceeded; in implementations that retain only the residual path for dropped assignments, the resulting computation differs from the uncapped model. Its quality impact must be evaluated along with any throughput improvement.
These failure modes follow from the basic MoE serving trade-off:7 computation is dynamically routed to different experts based on input, so the routing pattern becomes a systems workload rather than only a model-internal choice. Popular models like Mixtral (Jiang et al. 2024) use MoE to achieve high capacity with lower inference cost.
7 MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) Serving Trade-Off: Only a subset of experts activates per token (2 of 8 in Mixtral, 8 of 256 routed experts in DeepSeek-V3). Keeping all weights accelerator-resident gives a total-to-active weight ratio of roughly 3.6× (Mixtral) to 18× (DeepSeek-V3). Expert parallelism distributes that storage while adding token-routing communication; offloading is an alternative that trades resident capacity for weight transfers.
Jiang, A. Q., A. Sablayrolles, A. Roux, A. Mensch, B. Savary, C. Bamford, D. S. Chaplot, et al. 2024. “Mixtral of Experts.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2401.04088.

Example 10.9: Expert parallelism for Mixtral-8x7BScenario: Mixtral-8x7B (46.7B total parameters, ~12.9B active per token) is served across a 4-GPU group using top-2 routing.
Diagnosis: Replicating all 8 experts on every GPU requires the full 93.4 GB FP16 weight set per device, more than one 80 GB H100 holds. Placing 2 experts on each GPU (4-way expert parallelism) cuts each device’s share to about 25.8 GB, the shared attention layers plus its local experts, but every MoE layer now needs an AllToAll dispatch and gather to move tokens to the devices that hold their selected experts.
Systems lesson: Expert parallelism trades AllToAll communication for per-GPU parameter memory. The trade pays only when the collective, repeated at every MoE layer, fits inside the decode budget that the smaller resident footprint makes possible.


Expert parallelism couples state placement to input-dependent access. Embedding-heavy recommendation models face a related problem: entity popularity determines which stored vectors receive traffic. Their sharding strategy must therefore balance storage and lookup load, just as expert placement must account for both resident weights and routed tokens.




Recommendation systems typically contain embedding tables that dwarf dense model weights in size. Meta’s DLRM reference architecture uses model parallelism over embedding tables to mitigate memory constraints while scaling dense layers separately (Naumov et al. 2019). At production scale, this embedding-heavy structure requires sharding strategies distinct from tensor or pipeline parallelism.
Row-wise sharding partitions embedding tables by row (entity ID):
\[\text{Shard}_{\ShardIndex} = \{\EntityEmbedding_j : \text{hash}(\EntityIndex) \bmod \EmbeddingShardCount= \ShardIndex\}\]
Each shard contains approximately \(\EntityCount/\EmbeddingShardCount\) embeddings, where \(\EntityCount\) is the total number of entities and \(\EmbeddingShardCount\) is the shard count.
Column-wise sharding partitions each embedding vector across devices:
\[\EntityEmbedding_j = [\EntityEmbedding_j^{(0)}, \EntityEmbedding_j^{(1)}, ..., \EntityEmbedding_j^{(\EmbeddingShardCount-1)}]\]
Each device stores a slice of every embedding. Hybrid sharding combines both approaches: the hottest embeddings are replicated or column-sharded to spread their heavy access, while the long tail uses row sharding. The choice of embedding sharding strategy depends on lookup patterns and communication overhead. Table 26 compares row-wise, column-wise, and hybrid approaches:

Hybrid sharding composes memory capacity, latency, and communication requirements: one axis may keep weights resident, another may reduce per-token latency, and a third may route sparse components without forcing dense layers onto the wrong device. Hybrid sharding buys fit or latency by adding new communication patterns at every boundary between shards. The next question is whether the communication tax stays inside the latency and throughput budget.



The practical speedup from sharding depends critically on communication efficiency. Each sharding strategy has characteristic communication patterns with different bandwidth and latency requirements.
Equation 12 quantifies AllReduce communication time for tensor parallelism, where data is combined from all devices with the result available on all devices.
\[\AllReduceCompletionTime\approx 2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount} \times \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \tag{12}\]
where \(\DeviceCount\) is the number of devices, \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) is the collective payload size, \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is startup latency, and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the interconnect bandwidth. The factor of 2 accounts for the ReduceScatter and AllGather phases. Ring AllReduce derives this ring-AllReduce cost from its two-phase schedule and shows its bandwidth-optimal \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) scaling, showing that the per-rank bandwidth volume approaches a constant multiple of the payload while the ring startup term still grows with device count.
Equation 13 expresses the simpler point-to-point communication for pipeline parallelism, where data flows from one device to the next.
\[\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \tag{13}\]
where \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) is the point-to-point payload size, \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the network latency, and \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) is the transfer time. Equation 14 captures the more complex AllToAll communication for expert parallelism, where each device exchanges distinct data with every other device.
\[\AllToAllCompletionTime= (\DeviceCount-1) \times \left(\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount}{\LinkBandwidth}\right) \tag{14}\]


↩︎ AllToAll schedules, and why skewed destination traffic makes them harder to bound than AllReduce, are established in AllToAll Exchanges at Scale.
The AllToAll expression assumes equal-size peer exchanges scheduled in pairwise rounds. Skewed expert traffic, network contention, or a different collective algorithm can change its timing. Across all three models, usable bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\) and startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) provide an initial communication budget, not a complete prediction of request latency. The chosen topology and collective implementation must sustain that budget under the intended concurrent load.

In that regime the fixed per-collective latency in table 28, not bandwidth, sets the overhead share, and that decode regime is why tensor-parallel groups are normally kept inside one NVLink domain.
Each NVLink generation8 has raised this intra-node ceiling.
8 NVLink and tensor-parallel overhead: A faster NVLink generation raises the local communication ceiling, but the realized tensor-parallel overhead still depends on message size, collective implementation, topology, and how much computation can overlap the transfer.


The choice of sharding strategy depends on model architecture and deployment priorities. Table 30 evaluates each approach across four critical factors:



Table 30: Sharding strategy selection guide: Evaluation of tensor, pipeline, expert, and embedding sharding across latency targets, throughput priorities, interconnect constraints, and implementation complexity.

Strategy selection starts from the deployment bottleneck. Tensor parallelism is a candidate when reduced layer execution can repay frequent collectives; pipeline parallelism distributes layers and can sustain throughput when enough concurrent work fills the stages. Expert and embedding sharding distribute sparse state while adding routed communication. These choices can be combined, but each must fit the per-device memory budget and the measured latency contract.
Once a replica’s memory footprint and execution capacity are established, demand determines how many replicas the service needs. The next decision is where to send each arriving request. Routing must account for work already in progress and reusable state, so that replica capacity becomes useful fleet capacity.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Suppose ten model replicas are serving traffic when a request for a 5,000-word document summary arrives. Assigning it to an overloaded replica adds waiting and can increase interference for work already admitted there. The effect depends on admission, batching, and priority policies. Round-robin assignment does not inspect those differences in remaining work. A state-aware router uses memory and queue information to choose a feasible destination, while limiting the cost and staleness of its observations.

Lighthouse 10.2: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): The tail at scaleArchetype B (DLRM at Scale) uses \(\text{p99} \le 100\text{ ms}\) as its illustrative latency target. At \(10^{7}\) QPS, an event probability of \(10^{-4}\) implies an expected 1,000 such events per second. This count motivates examining the tail, but does not identify its cause. Two-choice routing can reduce imbalanced queuing delay \(\QueueingLatency\); traces must establish whether queueing, inference time \(\InferenceLatency\), or another component drives the misses.




Load balancing serves two primary goals that sometimes conflict: latency minimization and utilization maximization. Latency minimization routes requests to the replicas that can serve them fastest, considering current queue depth and processing time; utilization maximization spreads load evenly to avoid both idle replicas and overloaded replicas. The tension arises because latency-optimal routing may concentrate load on fast replicas, reducing their performance and leaving other replicas underutilized.
Evaluation therefore requires complementary signals for latency and fleet balance. Queue lengths reveal accumulated requests, but service times and scheduling order determine how long those requests wait. Estimated work per replica and its variance are more informative when request costs differ. Utilization spread reveals idle and saturated replicas, while decision overhead measures the cost of computing the routing choice. These signals must be evaluated alongside completed-request tail latency and admission outcomes; balanced counts alone do not establish a healthy service.



The simplest load-balancing strategies assign requests without considering server state. Round-robin sends request 1 to server 1, request 2 to server 2, and so on, which gives perfect distribution only when servers are homogeneous and request processing times are identical. Random assignment selects a server uniformly at random for each request; with many requests it converges to an even mean distribution, but its variance is higher than round-robin. Both strategies are reasonable baselines for identical servers, yet production serving rarely satisfies that assumption. Heterogeneous GPU generations, different memory configurations, variable request sizes, warmup behavior, and replicas nearing memory limits all make the state of the server fleet matter.
A static placement model isolates the imbalance caused by random choice: place \(\ReplicaCount\) equal-size jobs sequentially into \(\ReplicaCount\) initially empty bins, without departures. With uniform independent choices, the expected maximum bin occupancy follows the classical balls-into-bins result (Mitzenmacher 2001) in equation 15:


Two-choice routing flattens the tail imbalance of random placement.

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{max bin occupancy}] =\AsymptoticTightBound\left(\frac{\log \ReplicaCount}{\log \log \ReplicaCount}\right) \tag{15}\]
Here \(\ReplicaCount\) counts both jobs and bins. The asymptotic expression does not predict a finite serving queue at a given fleet size: arrivals, departures, job sizes, and service rates are absent from this model. The power of two choices (principle \(\ref{pri-power-two-choices}\)) changes the occupancy tail using one additional probe.



A foundational result in load balancing theory (Mitzenmacher 2001) shows that querying just two random servers before making a routing decision provides exponentially better load distribution than random assignment.9

Mitzenmacher, M. 2001. “The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing.” IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems 12 (10): 1094–104. https://doi.org/10.1109/71.963420.
9 Balls into bins (power of two choices): The quoted bounds concern \(\ReplicaCount\) equal jobs placed in \(\ReplicaCount\) empty bins without departures. Dynamic serving requires a queueing model or workload measurements.The procedure is deliberately small, but the load signal must match the serving workload. The destination must atomically admit or reject the request because probe results can become stale; a rejection requires bounded retry or overload handling. For a homogeneous vision fleet, current queue length may be enough. For an LLM fleet, active tokens, estimated remaining decode work, and KV-cache pressure better approximate the work a replica has already accepted. Algorithm 3 states a representative routing loop: probe two replicas, compare normalized work, and route without polling the whole fleet.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Power-of-two choices request routing}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require eligible replica set $\mathcal{S}$; request $r$; positive capacity weights $w_s$; per-replica work signal $W_s$ (queue length, active tokens, predicted work, or KV-cache occupancy); finite attempt budget
\Ensure an admitting replica for $r$, or an overload rejection
\For{each allowed attempt}
    \If{$\mathcal{S}$ is empty}
        \State \Return overload rejection
    \EndIf
    \State sample two candidate replicas $s_a, s_b$ from $\mathcal{S}$ with replacement \Comment{capacity-weighted}
    \State query $W_{s_a}, W_{s_b}$; estimate incremental work $\hat{c}(r)$ (expected output tokens or KV pages)
    \State $u_s \gets (W_s + \hat{c}(r)) / w_s$ for $s \in \{s_a, s_b\}$ \Comment{post-admission load}
    \State $s^\star \gets$ candidate with smaller $u_s$ \Comment{ties: cache affinity}
    \If{$s^\star$ atomically admits $r$ and reserves its local capacity}
        \State \Return $s^\star$
    \EndIf
\EndFor
\State \Return overload rejection
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(\mathcal{S}\)

Two probes avoid an all-replica scan. The practical algorithm uses predicted work and capacity weights; it is a serving heuristic, not the uniform static placement process. For the latter process, choosing the less occupied of two independently sampled bins gives equation 16:
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{max bin occupancy}]_{\text{two choices}} = \AsymptoticTightBound(\log \log \ReplicaCount) \tag{16}\]
This asymptotic contrast motivates limited probing. It supplies neither an exact queue length for a finite fleet nor a latency guarantee for variable-length inference requests.

Theorem 10.2: Power-of-two choices load-balancing boundFor \(\ReplicaCount\) equal-size jobs placed sequentially into \(\ReplicaCount\) initially empty bins, without departures, uniform random placement has maximum occupancy \(\mathcal{O}(\log \ReplicaCount/ \log \log \ReplicaCount)\) with high probability. Choosing the less occupied of two independent uniform candidates reduces this to \(\mathcal{O}(\log \log \ReplicaCount)\).
The bound shows that limited probing substantially improves maximum occupancy in this static model. Two probes avoid the \(\ReplicaCount\)-probe cost of examining every bin. Applying the idea to serving requires a load signal that reflects remaining work and available capacity; the theorem does not establish near-optimal latency for changing queues, heterogeneous replicas, or stale measurements.


The mechanism is the suppression of repeated unlucky placement. If \(\HighOccupancyBinCount\) of \(\ReplicaCount\) bins have occupancy at least \(\OccupancyThreshold\), one uniform probe hits that set with probability \(\HighOccupancyBinCount/\ReplicaCount\), whereas two independent probes both hit it with probability \((\HighOccupancyBinCount/\ReplicaCount)^2\). This observation explains the static tail improvement; it does not remove the need to account for service times and stale load signals in a live fleet.



When replicas have different service capacities, equal request rates produce different utilization. In a mixed A100 and T4 fleet, the lower-capacity replicas reach saturation first as demand increases; equal routing does not imply overload at every arrival rate. Weighted assignment accounts for measured capacity by allocating the following long-run request share to each server:
\[\Pr(\text{route to server } \ServerIndex) = \frac{\ServerRoutingWeight_i}{\sum_j \ServerRoutingWeight_j}\]
where \(\ServerRoutingWeight_i\) is the weight, or capacity, of server \(\ServerIndex\). Weighted two-choices applies the same idea to tail control: sample two servers with probability proportional to their weights, compare current load relative to capacity, and route to the lower relative load. The weighted-routing example makes this policy concrete for mixed GPU hardware.

Example 10.10: Heterogeneous GPU clusterScenario: A serving cluster mixes 10 H100 GPUs (1000 QPS each) and 20 A100 GPUs (600 QPS each), processing 15,000 QPS target traffic.
Diagnosis: Unweighted round-robin routes equal request counts (500 QPS) to all nodes, leaving H100s underutilized (50 percent) while leaving less latency headroom on A100s (83.3 percent). Weighted routing assigns H100s a weight of 4.5 percent and A100s a weight of 2.7 percent, balancing utilization across tiers (68.2 percent vs. 68.2 percent).
Systems lesson: Heterogeneous inference clusters require capacity-weighted routing. Equal request volumes produce unbalanced load when hardware tiers have different service rates.


Static weights handle known capacity differences, but production replicas also change over time. Adaptive load balancing adjusts weights dynamically based on observed performance:
For each server i:
    latency[i] = exponential_moving_average(observed_latency)
    weight[i] = 1 / latency[i]  # Inverse latency weighting
Inverse latency weighting reduces traffic to replicas whose observed latency rises. That observation mixes server condition with request cost: a replica receiving longer generations can appear slow even when its hardware is healthy. Delayed measurements can also make weights oscillate as traffic shifts. The heuristic therefore needs evaluation against comparable request classes, measurement lag, and overload behavior before its weights can be treated as capacity estimates.



An alternative to random selection is routing to the server with the fewest active connections or requests. Least-connections uses an active-request count in the model considered here, incrementing on dispatch and decrementing on completion. This accounts for unfinished requests that round-robin does not inspect, but a connection carrying multiple requests needs different bookkeeping. The policy improves routing only to the extent that the count represents the work and capacity competing at each replica.
The challenge is maintaining accurate connection counts in a distributed system. A centralized counter gives a single source of truth but can become a bottleneck. Distributed counters with gossip scale better but may route using stale information. Sampled least-connections combines the idea with two choices by probing only a subset of servers and choosing the minimum. Connection counts are themselves a proxy. Two in-flight LLM requests can differ fiftyfold in remaining decode work, from a 10-token reply to a 500-token essay, so active tokens or estimated remaining work track load more faithfully than the count of open requests.
No routing policy wins on every axis. Random and round-robin assignment have low decision overhead but ignore work in progress. Two-choice routing samples load state, while least-connections tracks outstanding requests at the cost of maintaining current counts. Neither counts nor limited probes fully describe remaining work when request costs vary widely. Which policy meets a tail target is an empirical question, evaluated with the same arrival trace, request-length mix, and replica capacities.



Many inference workloads maintain state that benefits from routing affinity. An LLM service may retain completed-turn KV state as a session cache, recommendation sessions may carry user context and recent interactions, and streaming inference may depend on model state from previous frames. For these workloads, routing the same user or session to the same server can avoid cache misses and state reconstruction. A stateless LLM API that receives the full conversation on every request does not require this affinity; it may still use prefix-aware routing when a reusable prefix happens to be cached.
Consistent hashing10 (Karger et al. 1997) maps requests to servers based on a hash of the routing key (user ID, session ID):
10 Consistent hashing: The ring-based algorithm was introduced for distributed caching (Karger et al. 1997) and later used in large-scale content delivery. Its limited-remapping property later made it useful wherever membership changes should preserve cache locality.
Karger, D., E. Lehman, T. Leighton, R. Panigrahy, M. Levine, and D. Lewin. 1997. “Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web.” Proceedings of the Twenty-Ninth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing - STOC ’97, 654–63. https://doi.org/10.1145/258533.258660.
\[\text{server}(\text{request}) = \operatorname{arg\,min}_{\HashRingServer\in \HashRingServerSet} \text{distance}(\text{hash}(\text{key}), \text{hash}(\HashRingServer))\]
where \(\HashRingServerSet\) is the set of servers mapped onto the ring, and each request routes to the nearest server clockwise.
For fixed ring membership, consistent hashing sends the same key to the same server. Membership changes affect only part of the ring. With balanced equal-capacity assignments and uniformly distributed keys, adding a server moves an expected \(1/(\HashRingServerCount+1)\) fraction of keys, while removing one affects its expected \(1/\HashRingServerCount\) share. Virtual nodes help smooth uneven ranges, but popular keys can still concentrate traffic even when key counts are balanced. For session-cached LLM serving, affinity increases the chance of reaching reusable state. That benefit must outweigh additional waiting; overload routing, failure, eviction, and remapping can still require repeated prefill.

Example 10.11: Consistent hashing for KV cache affinityScenario: A multi-turn LLM chat service routes user queries across a cluster of inference replicas without session affinity.
Diagnosis: A subsequent turn sent to a replica without compatible cached history must repeat prefill for the uncached prefix. Routing without affinity increases that risk but does not force a miss on every turn. With fixed membership, consistent hashing maps a user ID to the same replica and preserves unaffected mappings when membership changes. Retaining valid cached state on that replica is a separate requirement.
Systems lesson: Consistent hashing improves KV-cache locality across multi-turn sessions without requiring a full key remap during scaling. It reduces redundant prefill when the preferred replica remains healthy and timely, but overload routing, eviction, failure, and the remapped fraction still require cache transfer or reconstruction.


The same stateful routing machinery becomes a correctness boundary when cached state is user-specific.

War Story 10.1: When cache state crossed users (2023)Context: ChatGPT used Redis Cluster through the redis-py client to cache user information and conversation titles in a high-volume serving system (OpenAI 2023).
Mechanism: Under an Asyncio connection-pooling race condition, canceled requests left unread responses in recycled connection buffers, causing subsequent requests to receive cache data belonging to previous users.
Impact: On March 20, 2023, OpenAI took ChatGPT offline after a bug allowed some users to see another active user’s conversation titles. Further investigation found possible exposure of payment-related information for a subset of active Plus subscribers during a nine-hour window; full credit card numbers were not exposed.
Fix: OpenAI sent the Redis maintainers a patch for the redis-py cancellation path and added redundant checks that the data returned from the cache belongs to the requesting user.
Systems lesson: Stateful inference infrastructure needs isolation guarantees around caches, connection pools, and routing keys. A cache is part of the serving correctness boundary, not merely an optimization.



OpenAI. 2023. March 20 ChatGPT Outage: Here’s What Happened. OpenAI incident report.



A sharded replica is one routing destination even though several devices execute the request. The external router selects the shard group; the group’s execution plan determines the internal communication established in section 10.12. A tensor-parallel group runs every layer on all of its devices and joins their partial results with AllReduce (figure 12), presenting one destination whose latency already includes those collectives. Pipeline groups instead admit requests at the first stage and forward activations along the fixed stage sequence diagrammed in figure 13; the router must account for the group’s service capacity rather than treat each stage as an independent replica. In expert-parallel architectures, the gating network in figure 14 routes tokens dynamically across internal expert destinations after the external router has selected the replica, so expert imbalance and replica imbalance require different controls.
Figure 16 diagrams this two-tier scaling topology: an external load balancer distributes incoming queries across independent multi-GPU shard groups using round-robin, two-choice, or session-affinity policies, while intra-node NVLink AllReduce synchronization remains strictly encapsulated within each replica node.







Figure 16: Horizontal scaling with shard groups: The load balancer treats each shard group as a single logical inference server and chooses among groups by round-robin, two-choice, or session-affinity routing. Within a group, eight GPUs hold the tensor-parallel weight shards and join partial results with an NVLink AllReduce inside every layer, which the router never sees. Adding ready groups raises aggregate capacity; the group’s internal parallelism affects per-request latency.






Routing a request to a shard group, or moving a conversation to a different group, decides where its KV state lives. The sharding strategies of section 10.12 fix that placement inside a group. Pipeline parallelism keeps each layer’s cache on the stage that owns that layer, so tensor parallelism is the case that reshapes cache management, and migration is the case that moves it between groups.
Under tensor parallelism, the KV cache is sharded across devices along with attention heads. Each device stores cache for its subset of heads. A multi-head attention layout spreads many KV heads across the group, while grouped-query attention with eight KV heads leaves one per device in an eight-way group.
8-way tensor parallelism, 64 KV heads (MHA):
Device 0: KV cache for heads 0-7
Device 1: KV cache for heads 8-15
...
Device 7: KV cache for heads 56-63
Cross-device reuse requires compatible cache content and placement. Matching tensor-parallel configurations can align the head partitions, but the receiver must also use the same model state, prefix inputs, cache representation, and logical token positions. A different partition requires redistribution rather than direct shard reuse. Equal parallelism degree alone does not establish cache validity.
KV cache migration presents a further challenge. When the router moves a conversation to a different replica because of failure or rebalancing (routing keyed on a hash of the session ID, the consistent-hashing scheme developed in section 10.13.6), the service must either transfer available KV state or rebuild it. Transfer requires a reachable source or a saved copy; after an unrecoverable replica failure, the service rebuilds from authoritative conversation history:
Migration options:
1. Rebuild: Re-run prefill on new replica (cost grows with context length)
2. Transfer: Send KV cache over network (cache bytes / link bandwidth)
3. Hybrid: Transfer if small, rebuild if large

Decision threshold:
if cache_size_bytes/network_bandwidth < prefill_time:
    transfer()
else:
    rebuild()
For Llama 3 70B with GQA and a 4,096-token context, KV cache is about 1.3 GB total per sequence, or about 168 MB per device under 8-way tensor parallelism. At 100 Gb/s (12.5 GB/s), the bandwidth-only estimate for one shard is roughly 13 ms, while sending the full cache over one such link takes about 107 ms. The prefill approximation counts \(5.8 \times 10^{14}\) FLOPs (\(2 \times 7.1 \times 10^{10}\) parameters \(\times\) 4,096 tokens), giving roughly 180 ms on the tensor-parallel group at the assumed 40 percent utilization. Transfer is faster in this comparison, but achieving the per-shard time for the whole group requires concurrent links with sufficient aggregate bandwidth. Shared network bottlenecks, source availability, cache conversion, and destination queueing can change the decision. Long-context attention adds rebuild work omitted from this approximation, so measured transfer and prefill times should determine the policy.
The shard group boundary also defines readiness. A group can accept work only when the devices, model state, and cache capacity required for its execution plan are available, so the load balancer needs a health signal for the serving replica as a whole.



Load balancers can route around failure only if the health signal matches the failure mode. Health checks separate liveness, readiness, and inference correctness. On an accelerator replica, each tier must test a different part of the serving state, because a process that is alive may still be unusable when its weights are not loaded, its memory pool is exhausted, or its first request will trigger a long warmup. The probes therefore escalate from cheapest to most realistic:
GET  /health/live       -> 200 (process alive) or timeout (process dead)
GET  /health/ready      -> 200 (weights loaded, device initialized) or 503
POST /health/inference  -> 200 with valid output for a fixed test prompt, or error
Readiness checks can detect unloaded weights, incomplete warmup, or insufficient admission capacity even while the process remains alive. An inference probe additionally exercises the execution path and can compare a fixed prompt’s output or logits against expected bounds. Passing that probe does not establish correctness or capacity for every request shape, so production errors and latency remain necessary health signals. Failover then depends on the detected failure, available replacement capacity, and whether affected KV state can be transferred or must be reconstructed.


↩︎ Liveness, readiness, and inference-correctness probes, the failover time their settings bound, and stateful failover are established in Failover mechanisms.



When a GPU inference server slows down, routing more requests to it can turn a local problem into a fleet-wide failure. Consider an illustrative rise in service time from 50 ms to 500 ms. Queues accumulate, client timeouts generate retries, and rerouted work consumes neighboring replicas’ headroom. The cause might be a stalled dependency, device degradation, or resource contention. The load balancer needs a policy for withdrawing an unhealthy replica while controlling the displaced load.
The circuit breaker pattern (Nygard 2007) limits repeated work sent to an unhealthy destination. In the closed state, the server receives normal traffic. When the configured error, timeout, or latency threshold is exceeded, the breaker opens and requests fail fast or become candidates for rerouting. After a recovery interval, a half-open state admits limited probes, closing on recovery or reopening on failure. Figure 17 shows these transitions. Opening a breaker does not create replacement capacity: rerouting must respect admission limits and retry budgets or it can overload the surviving replicas.






Figure 17: Circuit breaker states: The circuit breaker protects the system from cascading failure. Closed: normal operation. Open: error threshold exceeded; all requests fail fast to prevent resource exhaustion. Half-open: after a timeout, a limited number of requests are allowed through to probe the dependency’s health. Success resets to closed; failure returns to open.



Backpressure propagation complements the breaker by making overload visible upstream. When queue depth crosses a threshold, the server returns a signal such as 503 Service Unavailable; the load balancer marks the replica as degraded and routes fewer requests to it. If all replicas become degraded, the system shifts from routing control to admission control, rejecting some requests at the edge rather than accepting work it cannot serve within the latency SLO; load-shedding policies decide which requests to reject first. Circuit breakers isolate unhealthy replicas; backpressure tells the rest of the system to slow down before retries amplify the failure.


↩︎ Load shedding, model fallback, and the other strategies that trade quality for availability are established in Graceful degradation strategies.
Backpressure works only when the request contract propagates through the whole serving graph. The gateway converts the client timeout into an absolute deadline and every downstream stage subtracts elapsed time before admitting more work. If the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancellation must reach queued CPU work, accelerator batches, retrieval calls, and streamed output. A canceled request that remains in a continuous batch is zombie work: it consumes KV pages and decode bandwidth while producing no useful response. Some kernels cannot be interrupted mid-launch, so cancellation commonly takes effect at the next batch or token boundary; the scheduler must measure that cancellation lag rather than promise instantaneous preemption.
The same request identifier must connect routing, queueing, prefill, decode, cache allocation, and response streaming. A useful serving trace records admitted and rejected requests, queue delay, TTFT, TPOT, input and output tokens, cache pages, batch membership, preemptions, cancellations, and fallback decisions. Aggregate accelerator utilization cannot distinguish useful work from late or canceled work. SLO goodput and the wasted-token rate close that gap. SLO goodput reports how much completed work met its contract. The wasted-token rate is the fraction of generated tokens spent on requests that were canceled, timed out, or delivered after their deadline, the execution the system performed after the result had lost value.
A saturated LLM fleet operating under severe KV cache pressure has three workload-specific relief options. Engines can apply context eviction through an explicitly supported sliding-window or approximate policy with a quality check, or truncate retained history and recompute its state. Silently dropping old KV entries is not equivalent to recomputing a shorter conversation, because later cached states already depend on the earlier context. Disabling speculative execution reduces draft work, but reclaiming its memory also requires unloading draft weights and releasing the associated cache state. Finally, fallback routing can send eligible requests to a smaller model with available capacity, provided that model meets the application’s fallback quality contract.
These options change latency, resource use, or model behavior in different ways. The application must specify which changes are acceptable at each pressure tier. Context truncation can remove information essential to an answer, and a smaller model can fail the task’s quality requirement. In those cases, an explicit rejection can be preferable to an apparently successful but unacceptable response.
Routing relies on estimates of replica capacity, but shared hardware can make that capacity change when another workload becomes active. Critical production models may share a cluster or device with experimental models and developer endpoints. Protecting the serving contract under that interference requires multi-tenant isolation in addition to routing.

Self-Check: Question

Why does the power-of-two-choices result motivate probing two replicas, and what limitation applies when using the classical balls-into-bins bounds to predict a 1,000-server serving fleet?

It eliminates all network packet headers by broadcasting requests to all 1,000 servers simultaneously.
Two probes improve static occupancy scaling from \(\Theta(\log R/\log\log R)\) to \(\Theta(\log\log R)\), but do not determine production queue depths or P99 latency
It guarantees zero queuing delay by dynamically compiling new CUDA kernels on the fly for each request.
It forces all requests to execute on CPU fallback nodes whenever GPU utilization exceeds 50%.

Explain why Consistent Hashing is critical for routing multi-turn LLM conversations, and describe what happens to KV cache state when an autoscaling event adds a new replica.
True or False: Standard HTTP 200 process liveness checks are sufficient to detect GPU inference degradation caused by thermal throttling or silent HBM memory pool exhaustion.
A heterogeneous inference cluster contains 10 H100 servers (delivering 1,000 QPS capacity each) and 20 A100 servers (delivering 600 QPS capacity each), serving a total target load of 15,000 QPS. What weighted routing ratio should be applied to achieve equal utilization across all hardware tiers?

Route 500 QPS equally to every server regardless of type, producing 50% utilization on H100 and 83.3% on A100.
Assign weight 1.0 to H100 and 1.0 to A100 so all servers receive equal traffic shares.
Assign capacity-proportional weights (H100 weight \(= 1000/22000 \approx 4.55\%\) per server; A100 weight \(= 600/22000 \approx 2.73\%\) per server), achieving uniform 68.2% utilization across all nodes.
Route 100% of traffic to A100 servers first and overflow remaining traffic to H100 servers.

The three-state resilience pattern that fails fast and stops routing traffic to a degraded or thermally throttled GPU replica before retries cascade across the fleet is called a ____.
