title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Consider a critical customer-support chatbot running on the same GPU server as an experimental computer vision script. If the experimental workload monopolizes the PCIe bus or memory bandwidth, the chatbot can miss its latency target. Sharing saves capacity only when the resulting interference remains within each service’s contract. Fleet quotas, fair-share hierarchies, and priority preemption decide how much of the cluster a serving system receives; the problem here is controlling contention among the tenants who share that allocation, request by request.


↩︎ Fleet quotas, hierarchical fair-share, and the priority classes that govern preemption are established in Multi-Tenancy and Quotas.


Sharing a serving pool can raise utilization and reduce separately provisioned capacity when tenant demand peaks occur at different times. This statistical-multiplexing gain weakens when bursts are correlated, and shared resources introduce interference even when aggregate demand fits. Pooling therefore needs both a demand model and enforceable isolation.



One tenant’s burst can degrade every workload sharing the pool.
A burst from one tenant can delay others through shared KV-cache capacity, network bandwidth, and accelerator time. The pool must preserve each tenant’s data boundary and service contract; different SLOs can require different admission limits, reservations, or placements. Noisy-neighbor effects come first because they directly connect shared-resource contention to those latency contracts.



The noisy neighbor problem occurs when one tenant’s workload degrades performance for others sharing the same infrastructure. The interference manifests across three resource dimensions simultaneously.
GPU memory contention can limit admission before compute capacity is exhausted. Consider three tenants sharing a 60 GB KV pool with nominal 20 GB shares. Without enforced limits, one tenant’s long-context requests can raise its allocation to 45 GB. In the scenario, the others lose capacity from 200 concurrent sequences each to 75, a 62.5 percent reduction. That is a concurrency loss, not a proportional throughput prediction; the effect depends on their execution regime and preemption costs. Egress bandwidth and accelerator time are additional shared resources whose contention must be measured alongside memory occupancy.


↩︎ The device-level interference channels of shared accelerators (memory bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device interconnect, and thermal dissipation) are established in Resource isolation.

Example 10.12: Quantifying noisy neighbor impactScenario: An inference platform serves 10 tenants on shared H100 GPUs at 100 QPS each under a 50 ms p99 SLO. Tenant 3 bursts to 500 QPS, 5× its baseline.
Diagnosis: Without quotas, contention raises pool-wide p99 into the 22 ms to 45 ms range in this scenario, eroding every tenant’s headroom while remaining within the stated target. With quotas, Tenant 3 is limited to 120 QPS and the other tenants retain 15 ms p99. Throttling turns Tenant 3’s excess into rejected or delayed requests, which are judged against Tenant 3’s own contract rather than spread across the pool.
Systems lesson: Shared capacity raises utilization only when it is coupled with isolation. Quotas turn pool-wide erosion of latency headroom into an admission decision confined to the tenant that caused it; without them, a larger burst or a tighter SLO turns the same erosion into violations across the pool.





Resource quotas limit what each tenant can consume, preventing any single tenant from monopolizing shared resources. Hard quotas turn shared serving into admission control. Request rate and concurrency bound arrival pressure, while input tokens, output tokens, KV-cache pages, accelerator time, and egress bytes bound the work performed after admission. A single scalar quota cannot protect all of these resources because two requests can have the same count but differ by orders of magnitude in prompt length or generated output. Listing 1 shows representative gates so a tenant can be throttled at the scarce resource boundary instead of degrading the whole batch.



Listing 1: Multidimensional Resource Quotas: A snapshot check compares prospective resource use with tenant limits. Atomic reservation and scheduler enforcement are separate requirements.


class TenantQuota:
    max_concurrent_requests: int  # e.g., 100
    max_kv_cache_mb: int  # e.g., 20,000
    max_qps: int  # e.g., 1,000
    max_input_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_output_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_batch_tokens: int  # e.g., 50,000


def check_quota_snapshot(tenant_id, request):
    quota = get_quota(tenant_id)
    usage = get_usage(tenant_id)

    if usage.concurrent + 1 > quota.max_concurrent_requests:
        return RateLimitError("concurrent request limit")
    if usage.kv_cache_mb + request.reserved_kv_mb > quota.max_kv_cache_mb:
        return RateLimitError("memory limit")
    if usage.requests_last_second + 1 > quota.max_qps:
        return RateLimitError("rate limit")
    if usage.input_tokens + request.input_tokens > quota.max_input_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("input-token limit")
    if usage.output_tokens + request.max_output_tokens > quota.max_output_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("output-token limit")

    if request.prefill_chunk_tokens > quota.max_batch_tokens:
        return RateLimitError("prefill chunk exceeds batch-token limit")

    return None  # Snapshot is eligible; no resources have been reserved.



This listing assumes that reserved_kv_mb includes the requested prompt and output-token budget, and that usage counters include outstanding reservations in their stated time windows. A passing snapshot is not an admission guarantee: simultaneous callers can observe the same free capacity. Production admission must check and reserve resources atomically, roll back failed admissions, and release reservations on completion or cancellation. The batch scheduler separately enforces the aggregate batch-token limit. Quotas protect the resources they account for; shared compute, networking, and control-plane contention still require isolation and measurement.
Soft quotas permit borrowing unused capacity while preserving an enforceable share when demand rises. The unit of account matters: equal request counts can hide large differences in prefill work, output length, and retained state. Input and output tokens therefore need separate accounting, with memory and concurrency limits alongside them. The progressive-filling approach in Dominant-resource fairness allocation reduces to max-min fairness when only one divisible resource constrains the allocation. For three tenants demanding 30,000, 20,000, and 80,000 output tokens/sec from an idealized 100,000-token/sec pool with equal token costs, the allocation is 30,000, 20,000, and 50,000. Coupled prefill, decode, and memory constraints require joint feasibility checks; independent fair allocations do not automatically compose into a feasible service.



The priority-aware scheduling listed among the serving dimensions (section 10.8.3) becomes an isolation tool once its classes map to tenants and service tiers. Fleet priority classes govern preemption across allocations; request priority applies inside a serving allocation. Table 31 illustrates a policy that combines precedence with reservations. Those reservations must be provisioned and enforced separately: priority alone cannot create capacity, interrupt every running kernel, or guarantee a deadline under unbounded critical traffic.



Table 31: Priority scheduling classes: Three-tier priority hierarchy for multi-tenant inference. Critical traffic gets 100 percent reserved capacity and can preempt any lower class; standard traffic shares capacity proportionally and can preempt best-effort; best-effort runs on leftover capacity with no guarantees.











Class
Use Case
Preemption
Resource Guarantee




Critical
Revenue-generating
Can preempt lower
100% reserved


Standard
General traffic
Can preempt best-effort
Weighted share


Best-effort
Background, batch
Cannot preempt
No guarantee






The scheduler sorts incoming requests by priority class, then by arrival time within each class. When a new critical request arrives, it jumps ahead of all standard and best-effort requests in the queue, so revenue-generating traffic does not queue behind background batch jobs, although work already running on the accelerator can still delay it.
Preemption extends this principle to requests already in flight, but priority does not make state movement free. The retain, swap, recompute, or reject choice of section 10.8.3 still decides how a displaced request’s KV state is handled; priority adds an input to that choice rather than replacing it. A priority class determines who may be displaced, while remaining service time, state size, and deadline slack determine which victim is cheapest. Ignoring those costs lets aggressive preemption consume more capacity than it releases.



The bulkhead pattern11 (Nygard 2007) partitions resources so exhaustion or failure in one allocation has a limited effect on others. The boundary may be a logical concurrency pool, a separate process, or dedicated hardware; each contains different failure modes. The pattern is named after ship compartments intended to contain flooding.
11 Bulkhead limits: A divider isolates failure only if it closes the relevant boundary. The Titanic’s incomplete bulkheads allowed water to cascade between compartments; similarly, a soft quota cannot isolate shared memory or bandwidth that remains globally exhaustible.
Nygard, Michael T. 2007. Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software. Pragmatic Bookshelf.
Dedicated replicas separate more resources than request limits inside one process. Figure 18 assigns distinct compute and memory pools to tenant groups, so an engine crash or exhausted local allocation in the standard tier need not stop the gold-tier engines. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane services can still carry interference across that boundary.






Figure 18: Bulkhead isolation patterns: To prevent cascading failures in multi-tenant systems, bulkheads isolate resources. Deployment-level bulkheads (shown) assign dedicated physical replicas to high-priority tenants, separating their compute and memory pools. Request-level bulkheads enforce strict concurrency limits within shared processes. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane dependencies remain possible paths for interference.



Deployment-level bulkheads isolate the named compute and memory resources for premium tenants. They do not remove shared network, storage, power, or control-plane failure domains. The trade-off is lower pooling efficiency and additional operational overhead from dedicated infrastructure.
Request-level bulkheads limit work admitted within a shared process. Example caps of 8,000 input tokens, 2,000 output tokens, and 30 seconds of execution constrain request size and duration when the scheduler enforces them. They still need concurrency limits, resource reservations, and cancellation handling; a token cap alone does not bound interference or isolate a process crash.
Crash containment follows the process or hardware boundary, not the request quota. A malformed request that crashes a shared worker can interrupt every tenant using that worker. Service tiers requiring stronger fault isolation therefore need placement boundaries that match that requirement.

Example 10.13: Bulkhead configuration for API tiersScenario: An LLM API platform serves Enterprise, Professional, and Free service tiers across shared and dedicated hardware.
Diagnosis: Unpartitioned pools allow Free-tier bursts or shared-worker failures to affect Enterprise requests. The example assigns Enterprise to dedicated GPU pools with a 99.9 percent availability target, allocates 70 percent of the remaining shared capacity to Professional, and caps Free at 30 percent best-effort capacity. Meeting that target still requires reliability evidence for the dedicated pools themselves.
Systems lesson: Bulkheads concentrate isolation overhead where business requirements dictate. Hardware partitioning reduces cross-tenant compute and memory contention. SLO compliance still depends on sufficient capacity, admission policy, shared dependencies, and failure handling.


Multi-tenant isolation limits the blast radius of excess demand, but it does not create capacity. Once protected queues approach their latency budgets, the service needs a control loop that can add replicas before admission begins to fail.

Self-Check: Question

Which statement best distinguishes deployment-level bulkheads from request-level bulkheads in a multi-tenant inference platform?

Deployment-level bulkheads enforce rate limits using software counters; request-level bulkheads isolate GPU power supplies.
Deployment-level bulkheads apply only to batch inference; request-level bulkheads apply only to interactive chat.
Deployment-level bulkheads dynamically quantize weights to INT4; request-level bulkheads dynamically compile CUDA graphs.
Deployment-level bulkheads physically isolate tenant tiers onto dedicated GPU replicas, while request-level bulkheads cap input/output token lengths and execution time within shared processes.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
A serving autoscaler that reacts only to average accelerator utilization can scale in the wrong direction. Decode can saturate memory bandwidth while arithmetic units appear idle, long prompts can consume prefill capacity before request count rises, and queued work can violate an SLO while fleet-wide utilization remains moderate. The control signal must represent outstanding work relative to phase-specific service capacity. Every replica the controller adds is also a claim on accelerators that training jobs may hold, so fleet-level arbitration with training bounds how quickly and how far serving can grow.


↩︎ The arbitration between serving replicas and training jobs for shared accelerators, including the minutes-long cost of switching a device between them, is established in The training-serving resource boundary.
For a conventional fixed-cost model, queueing delay and request rate per ready replica can guide scaling. Autoregressive serving also needs prompt-token and output-token rates, KV occupancy, and measured phase service rates. A colocated replica must satisfy all phase requirements; disaggregated prefill and decode pools need separate counts and a feasible transfer budget. SLO goodput measures useful supply, but rejected work and backlog must remain visible as unmet demand. A latency threshold can detect deterioration after a model change, yet controller timing and headroom still need validation. Adding replicas also depends on their startup delay. Changing an existing accelerator allocation may require a restart or state migration, depending on the runtime and execution plan.
Scale-up and scale-down require asymmetric evidence. Scale-up acts on sustained queue growth, forecast demand, or declining deadline slack because cold-start delay makes late reactions expensive. Scale-down requires low demand over a longer window, enough spare capacity to survive one replica failure, and a drain plan for in-flight requests and any optional session cache. This hysteresis prevents oscillation in which replicas repeatedly load large weights, accept work, and terminate before amortizing startup cost.
The controller also needs observability that distinguishes demand from impaired supply. Request rate, input and output tokens, queue age, TTFT, TPOT, deadline misses, admission rejections, ready replicas, model-load failures, and per-phase service rate form the minimum feedback set. Without replica readiness and service-rate measurements, an autoscaler can respond to a sick replica by adding cold replicas indefinitely while the original failure remains hidden.

Example 10.14: Cold start timeline for Llama-70BScenario: An autoscaling engine provisions a Llama-70B replica during a traffic surge, using an H100-based allocation large enough for its FP16 weights, cache, and runtime state.
Diagnosis: The scenario’s sequential startup estimate is 6.7 minutes (\(\ReplicaColdStartTime= \ReplicaProvisioningTime+ \ReplicaModelLoadTime+ \ReplicaWarmupTime\)): 1 minute for provisioning, 4.7 minutes to fetch 140 GB of artifacts at the assumed 0.5 GB/s, and 1 minute for device loading and warmup. Cached artifacts or overlapping phases can shorten this path; scarce capacity and shared storage can lengthen it. If existing headroom cannot absorb the surge, newly requested replicas arrive too late to protect short deadlines.
Systems lesson: Cold-start latency depends on artifact size, effective storage bandwidth, provisioning delay, compilation, and warmup. The controller must measure this distribution and begin provisioning far enough ahead that its high percentile fits inside the forecast horizon.



Example 10.15: Predictive scaling for trafficScenario: A commercial chatbot service faces predictable diurnal traffic patterns, ramping from 500 QPS at night to 3,000 QPS at peak.
Diagnosis: A controller that waits for the morning ramps at 06:00 and 09:00 UTC before requesting capacity must cover the assumed 7-minute startup interval with existing headroom or admission limits. Without enough ready capacity, queues grow while replicas start. Forecasting can shift that wait ahead of the expected demand.
Systems lesson: Predictive autoscaling converts demand forecasts into planned pre-warming windows (table 32). Starting 30 minutes ahead of the expected ramps exceeds the modeled startup time. Readiness still depends on actual provisioning and warmup, and forecast errors can leave the fleet short or idle. Reactive correction and an overload policy remain necessary.

Systems insight: Against an assumed reactive peak of 45 replicas, the forecast-based peak of 30 is a 33 percent reduction in peak replica count at equal unit cost. The reactive controller over-provisions because it reacts to a queue that has already formed and must add capacity for the backlog as well as the demand. Peak count is only part of the bill. Total spending counts replica-hours, including the pre-warming window, so the forecast pays only when the replica-hours spent warming ahead of demand are fewer than those the reactive overshoot would consume.


Example 10.15 illustrates the opportunity to prepare capacity before demand arrives. Figure 19 depicts a forecast that anticipates the surge, while the reactive curve starts later and temporarily lacks capacity. Whether that deficit produces queueing, rejection, or missed deadlines depends on admission and existing headroom. The predictive curve illustrates a successful forecast, not a guarantee that future demand or startup time will match it.














Figure 19: Predictive vs. reactive scaling: Reactive scaling (gray line) responds to traffic spikes after they occur, leaving a capacity deficit (red region) during cold start in this scenario. Predictive scaling (green line) anticipates traffic and begins provisioning before the spike peaks, shrinking that deficit to a brief, small shortfall at onset in the illustrated forecast. Its early ramp does not eliminate every interval when demand exceeds capacity.





Maintaining prewarmed replicas buys readiness before demand arrives. Warm pool sizing begins with the total capacity needed during the provisioning delay, then subtracts capacity already ready to serve. If peak demand doubles and the chosen headroom factor is 1.5, the target is three times baseline capacity, assuming unchanged per-replica throughput. Partly prepared replicas count only if they can become ready before that capacity is needed. The expression \(\text{Pool size} \times \text{GPU cost/hour} \times \text{Idle fraction}\) estimates the hourly cost attributed to idle GPU capacity; it excludes busy capacity and non-GPU resources. Table 33 distinguishes readiness levels and their activation costs:



Table 33: Tiered warm pool readiness levels: Readiness trades activation delay against idle resource cost. Actual delay and billing depend on the deployment. Cold capacity is subject to quotas and physical availability.

Warm

Cold

Acquire capacity, load, and warm up
Artifact storage; no allocated GPU






When a traffic spike hits, the controller routes work to ready replicas, activates prepared capacity, and requests additional instances if needed. Pool sizing must cover the measured provisioning delay and include an overload policy for capacity that cannot be acquired in time.



The scaling response budget is the sum of the control loop’s detection, decision, provisioning, and warmup delays. Equation 17 makes those phases explicit:
\[\AutoscalingResponseTime= \AutoscalingDetectionTime+ \AutoscalingDecisionTime+ \ReplicaProvisioningTime+ \ReplicaWarmupTime \tag{17}\]
Table 34 decomposes each term and identifies its primary optimization path:

Provisioning can dominate the illustrated budget, making already allocated capacity valuable. The earlier large-model example also shows that artifact loading can dominate startup; the relevant term is the one measured on the deployment’s critical path. Finer-grained metrics can reduce detection delay but increase noise, while prepared scaling decisions and precompiled engines reduce other costs. A warm pool removes only the phases already completed at its stated readiness level.



Discounted interruptible capacity12 enters serving through the same purchasing tiers that fleet capacity planning uses (Cloud Capacity Reservation Tiers): reserved capacity for the steady baseline, on-demand capacity for bursts, and spot capacity for work that tolerates revocation. None of these tiers makes a replica immune to failure, so the serving question is whether a revoked replica can drain, reroute, or recompute its requests without violating their SLO. The provider’s warning window is the binding constraint.
12 Spot-instance economics: equation 8.3 derives the effective cost of preemptible capacity from its productive fraction. For inference, revocation can also destroy in-flight requests and KV-cache state, so the productive fraction must be charged for draining, rerouting, and restoring capacity.Spot termination handling is a race against the provider’s warning window. Listing 2 orders the shutdown path so new work stops first, in-flight work drains while time remains, recoverable state is persisted, and the load balancer stops sending traffic before the instance disappears.



Listing 2: Spot Termination Handling: Graceful shutdown sequence that stops admission, deregisters from the load balancer, drains in-flight requests, and persists recoverable state.


async def handle_spot_termination():
    # Received 2-minute warning
    # 1. Stop admission and remove the replica from routing
    stop_accepting_requests()
    deregister_from_loadbalancer()

    # 2. Complete in-flight requests (if possible)
    await complete_inflight(timeout=90)

    # 3. Save state for resumption elsewhere
    save_kv_cache_to_storage()

    # 4. Terminate gracefully
    shutdown()



The gateway in figure 20 separates traffic by its tolerance for capacity revocation. SLO-critical work uses the non-spot pool, while eligible best-effort work can use interruptible capacity. Routing still depends on readiness and available headroom. An eviction notice triggers draining when time permits; requests that cannot finish need a permitted retry, reconstruction, or rejection path.







Figure 20: Spot-aware traffic distribution: The gateway classifies requests by SLO and routes 70 percent of traffic, the SLO-critical share, to on-demand replicas that face no spot reclamation, and 30 percent, the best-effort share, to discounted spot replicas that can be preempted. When a spot worker receives an eviction notice, the gateway stops routing to it while it drains, and best-effort requests tolerate occasional retries. The traffic split is illustrative; cost savings depend on provisioned capacity, discounts, retries, and idle headroom.



Savings under this split depend on provisioned GPU-hours, discounts, retries, and reserve capacity rather than on the traffic share, and spot capacity changes none of the fault-tolerance requirements of the SLO-critical path.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
A fleet confined to one region can batch, shard, route, isolate, and autoscale well, yet a user in Sydney still pays roughly a 200 ms round trip to a US-East deployment before any of that machinery acts, and a regional outage removes every replica at once. Extending resource isolation and failure boundaries beyond one data center introduces placement decisions at geographic scale. Distance, regional failures, and data-placement requirements can motivate regional replicas, caches, or a centralized service with an explicit network budget. Figure 21 illustrates three tiers: edge points of presence for reusable responses, regional gateways for authentication and routing, and GPU clusters for model execution. Its 10 ms, 50 ms, and 2 s budgets are scenario targets, not measured performance or universal deadlines. The application must define whether its execution budget governs first response, individual tokens, or completion of the entire request.







Figure 21: Serving deployment stack: A cache miss crosses three tiers before reaching a model replica. Tier 1 edge points of presence (PoPs) enforce authorization and reuse eligibility before answering repeated requests from cache; a miss passes to Tier 2, where the gateway applies rate limits and authentication and the router picks a destination; Tier 3 GPU workers run prefill and decode while an autoscaler sizes the fleet from queue depth and KV cache use. Tokens stream back up through the tiers to the client. The per-tier latency budgets on the right, drawn on a log scale, are illustrative.





Single-region deployment couples every user to the same geographic site and regional failure domain. Network round-trip time (RTT) adds a latency floor for distant users. Table 35 gives illustrative regional timings; actual paths, access networks, and congestion require measurement:



Table 35: Network RTT by user location: A single US-East deployment imposes a 75 to 200 ms RTT on European, Asian, and Australian users, an order of magnitude above the local-region floor. Sequential calls that cross this boundary can add repeated wide-area delay. Regional replicas can reduce that exposed delay when placement policy, workload volume, and available capacity justify them.

Network delays compound when a request makes sequential calls across the distant boundary; multiple model calls inside one backend region do not each pay another client-to-region RTT. Regional replication can shorten that path and separate failure domains. Data-placement policies also constrain eligible destinations. The General Data Protection Regulation permits international transfers under specified conditions rather than requiring blanket EU-only processing; applicable law and contractual commitments must be translated into explicit placement rules. Regional replicas, edge caches, and cross-region sharding then trade capacity, communication, and coordination within those rules.



In figure 22, a global load balancer selects among regions that satisfy placement policy, readiness, and capacity requirements. Measured network latency helps choose among those eligible destinations; geographic proximity alone does not determine completion time. A shared registry supplies versioned artifacts to the independent regional replicas.







Figure 22: Global load balancing across inference regions: A global load balancer routes each user to an eligible region with suitable latency and ready capacity (table 35 gives the round-trip times this avoids). Each region (US-East, EU-West, Asia-Pacific) runs independent replicas of the same model, and EU requests can stay in the EU to meet data-residency rules. A shared model registry supplies versioned weights to every region. If a region fails, the load balancer reroutes its users only to destinations that still satisfy placement, readiness, and capacity requirements.



The illustrative RTT comparison shows why nearby replicas can reduce network delay, but actual savings depend on the measured user-to-region paths. Replication also creates a version-management obligation. Push-based synchronization sends artifacts to each region, while pull-based synchronization lets regions fetch them after notification or polling. Neither mechanism alone guarantees consistent serving versions. Artifact verification, readiness gates, and coordinated activation determine when a region may serve the new version; hybrid synchronization combines push notification with pull verification.
During a rollout, regions may serve different versions. The application must decide whether that is acceptable and whether a request or session needs version pinning. A region-by-region canary deployment limits initial exposure to a small traffic share, such as 1 percent. Its observation window follows the required sample count, traffic diversity, and release criteria, not a fixed number of hours. At a 1 percent share, a region must route enough requests through the canary to detect the regressions its gates test for. Each expansion needs its own error-rate, latency, and quality gate, with compatible prior artifacts retained for rollback.


↪ The canary stage-duration calculation, which sizes the observation window from the required sample count and the canary’s traffic share, is developed in Canary deployment (equation 12.6).



Caching responses at the edge can avoid repeated central inference when a stored response remains valid for the incoming request. Before returning a hit, the edge must enforce authorization and match the relevant model version, conversation or retrieval context, generation policy, and freshness requirements. Identical visible queries do not necessarily permit the same answer, and fresh-sample semantics may prohibit reuse. Figure 23 shows the hit and miss paths with an illustrative 10 ms hit budget. A miss reaches the central cluster; only responses eligible for reuse should enter the edge store.







Figure 23: Cache hit and cache miss paths at the edge: A query first reaches the nearest edge point of presence (PoP). After enforcing authorization and reuse eligibility, the edge targets a cache-hit response in under 10 ms without touching a GPU. On a miss, the request passes through the regional gateway to the central GPU cluster, which runs prefill and decode. Generated tokens stream back to the user, and a response eligible for reuse can be stored at the edge for later queries. The saving depends on the rate of requests eligible for reuse; open-ended generation may offer few such requests.



The two paths in figure 23 highlight the latency difference: cache hits avoid the backend round-trip, while misses incur it. Effectiveness depends on request repeatability across workloads such as autocomplete, FAQ chatbots, open-ended chat, and code generation. Table 36 supplies illustrative hit-rate envelopes for sensitivity analysis; an actual design must derive hit rate and correctness from production traces.



Table 36: Illustrative edge-cache hit-rate envelopes: Assumed cache-hit ranges for four workload shapes. These values are scenario inputs, not universal workload statistics. Trace-derived repeatability, response validity, and latency saved determine whether caching is worthwhile.

Semantic caching13 (caching based on embedding similarity rather than exact match) can improve hit rates for open-ended workloads.
13 Semantic caching: A similarity lookup can reuse responses beyond exact string matches, but it adds retrieval work and can return an invalid answer when superficially similar queries require different responses. The similarity threshold therefore trades cache coverage against correctness.


Cross-region model sharding places communication on the request’s execution path. Pipeline stages can reside in separate regions, but every dependent stage crossing then pays the inter-region transfer cost. In an illustrative comparison of 75–150 ms network delays with 1–5 ms stage computation, a 10–100\(\times\) slowdown is possible; it is not a model-independent ratio. Such placement needs a reason strong enough to justify that cost, such as unavailable colocated capacity, and must be evaluated against the actual stage layout and deadline.
Because cross-region sharding is so costly on the steady-state path, most production designs keep inference co-located and use other regions for resilience. The cross-region question therefore shifts from splitting one request across regions to deciding how quickly traffic can move when a region fails.



When a region becomes unavailable, failover must choose a healthy destination permitted to process the request and able to absorb its work. Listing 3 illustrates a simplified timeout fallback. A production policy must also preserve the request’s remaining deadline, version requirements, and data-placement constraints when selecting the secondary region.



Listing 3: Active-Active Failover: A bounded retry policy selects eligible regions and limits each attempt to the remaining request deadline.


# Eligibility includes placement, version, readiness, and capacity.
def route_request(user_region, request):
    attempted = set()
    for attempt_budget in (2.0, 5.0):
        remaining = request.deadline - monotonic_time()
        regions = eligible_regions(request, excluding=attempted)
        if remaining <= 0 or not regions:
            break
        region = nearest_region(user_region, regions)
        attempted.add(region)
        try:
            # The endpoint atomically admits work and enforces the deadline.
            return call_region(region, request,
                               timeout=min(attempt_budget, remaining))
        except (Timeout, RegionUnavailable, AdmissionRejected):
            # Cancel abandoned work; retries require replay-safe semantics.
            cancel_attempt(region, request)
    return unavailable_or_deadline_exceeded(request)



Rerouting is only part of regional failover. The destination needs accessible, authoritative conversation history to reconstruct lost KV state and enough headroom for both reconstruction and continuing traffic. If the required history is unavailable or cannot be processed there under the placement policy, a healthy replica alone cannot restore the session.


↩︎ Regional headroom, session rebuilding, and the gradual return of traffic to a recovered region are established in Replication strategies.



GPU pricing varies by provider, contract, region, and time. Table 37 uses a hypothetical price snapshot to show how placement can balance cost against latency requirements; it must not be used for procurement:

$4.20/hr
75–100 ms






Cost-aware routing compares eligible regions for latency-tolerant work (listing 4). GPU price alone is insufficient: transfer charges, startup and idle capacity, retries, and achieved useful throughput determine the cost of completing the workload. Deadline and data-placement constraints must filter destinations before that comparison.



Listing 4: Cost-Aware Routing: The router filters eligible destinations before comparing completion cost for low-priority work or proximity for interactive work.


def route_batch_request(request):
    # Filter by placement, version, readiness, capacity, and deadline.
    regions = eligible_regions(request)
    if not regions:
        return no_feasible_destination(request)
    if request.priority == "low":
        return lowest_completion_cost_region(request, regions)
    return nearest_region(request.user_location, regions)



Time-of-day routing can reduce batch cost when regional price differences exceed data-transfer and coordination costs. Savings require a workload-specific calculation, and interactive traffic must retain its own latency budget.
Regional placement completes the serving hierarchy, from one request’s batch slot to a fleet that spans continents. The design cases that follow show how these techniques combine when a service must meet specific cost and latency targets.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
These four design cases are illustrative composites rather than descriptions of named companies’ internal deployments, and their request rates, latency budgets, hardware allocations, and update cadences follow the chapter’s scenario convention. Each case binds on a different constraint: embedding scale, variable-length generation, cascade cost, or multimodal freshness. Orca and vLLM supply the previously cited scheduling and memory-management mechanisms; the scenarios combine those ideas with routing, sharding, and admission control.


An embedding-heavy recommendation service binds on sparse lookup rather than dense forward-pass compute. This scenario models feeds, advertising, and content ranking with a large distributed embedding store.
The operational scale explains why embedding locality dominates the architecture: the service processes billions of requests per day under a p99 budget below \(10\text{ ms}\) for the ranking service, nested inside the roughly 100 ms end-to-end tail target of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale), spanning hundreds of distinct model variants over an entity catalog comprising trillions of unique sparse features.
The serving stack separates sparse lookup from dense ranking:
User request → Feature collection → Embedding lookup → Model inference → Response

                    |                     |                  |
                    v                     v                  v
             Feature Store        Embedding Servers      GPU Inference
             (CPU, DRAM)         (CPU + SSD, 1000s)     (GPU, 100s)
The hybrid sharding strategy in lighthouse 10.1 supplies the sparse path: replication protects hot entries, column sharding spreads warm-entry access, and row sharding places the cold tail. Feature-level batching then combines lookups across requests. The remaining design decision is where each stage runs. In the GPU-CPU hybrid architecture, memory-rich CPU servers serve sparse embeddings while GPUs execute dense ranking. Table 38 connects that placement to the end-to-end latency budget.



Table 38: Illustrative hybrid CPU/GPU architecture: Illustrative hardware-workload mapping for the recommendation scenario. CPU + SSD handles the bandwidth-bound sparse path; CPU handles low-arithmetic-intensity feature processing; GPU handles the compute-dense ranking forward pass. The component budgets exclude queueing and response delivery; their sum alone does not establish the p99 target.

The serving lesson is that recommendation latency is often dominated by embedding lookup rather than dense model inference. Feature-parallel batching and a hybrid CPU-GPU architecture match the hardware to the sparse and dense halves of the workload, which sets up a contrast with GPT-style API serving where request variance and autoregressive state dominate.



A multi-model generation API binds on request variance: short prompts, long-context requests, and different model sizes share capacity while users expect predictable TTFT. The infrastructure serves GPT-class models to large developer and application workloads while maintaining quality of service across diverse workloads.
The operating scale explains why continuous batching and admission control dominate the infrastructure: the platform serves millions of requests per hour under a time-to-first-token target below \(2\text{ s}\), hosting models that range from billions to hundreds of billions of parameters with context lengths reaching up to 128K tokens.
The serving stack separates routing, scheduling, cache management, and shard groups:
API Gateway → Rate Limiting → Request Router → Model Cluster → Response Streaming

                              | +---------+ |

The main design decision is to prevent long prompts from blocking decode service for everyone else.
An Orca-style design uses continuous batching to refill completed slots. Chunked prefill limits interference from long prompts by interleaving prompt chunks with ongoing generation. The TTFT target must be validated across prompt lengths; admitting a 128K-token prompt does not imply that it meets the short-request latency target. Table 39 contrasts the three approaches:



Table 39: Batching strategy comparison: Slot reuse and prefill interference are separate concerns. Continuous batching addresses the first; chunking gives control over the second. Neither mechanism alone establishes utilization or latency numbers.

Monolithic prefill can delay decode


Continuous batching

Monolithic prefill can still delay decode


Continuous + chunked

Limits prefill work per iteration; tail latency still needs measurement






The tensor-parallel degree must satisfy weight and KV-cache capacity while leaving enough latency budget for communication. This scenario allocates eight H100 GPUs per large-model shard group connected via high-speed NVLink for intra-node communication, with consistent hashing at the gateway to maintain session affinity and enable compatible cross-turn KV cache reuse. The eight-device allocation is a design choice to validate against the model, precision, and admitted context lengths, not a requirement of GPT-class models in general.
To prevent noisy neighbors from exhausting capacity, the illustrative API applies hierarchical rate limiting across multiple granularities: per-API-key request arrival limits, per-API-key token-per-minute consumption limits, organization-level capacity quotas, and global model capacity ceilings.
A possible capacity policy shifts resources between models based on queue depth, subject to model-loading delay and each service’s minimum allocation:
if large_model_queue_depth > threshold:
    # Migrate some smaller-model capacity to the larger model
    reallocate_cluster_capacity(from="smaller-model", to="large-model", fraction=0.2)
LLM APIs are governed by variance control. Continuous batching reuses execution slots, prefix caching avoids compatible repeated work, and multi-tier rate limiting bounds admitted demand. Their combined effect on latency still depends on prompt scheduling and available capacity. Search ranking faces a different shape of the same problem. Many cheaper models must cooperate under one strict deadline.



The search-ranking scenario binds on cascade cost: each query coordinates many smaller models under one end-to-end latency budget rather than serving one large model. The ensemble combines specialized models for query understanding, document relevance, and result ranking.
The operational scale motivates a cascade architecture: the system must process billions of searches per day under a strict end-to-end latency target of less than \(200\text{ ms}\), evaluating thousands of candidate documents per query across dozens of specialized models. Screening candidates with cheaper models reserves the expensive ranking budget for a smaller set.
To meet this latency budget while evaluating thousands of documents, the ranking cascade diagrammed in figure 24 screens candidate pools across four progressively expressive tiers: early lexical and approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) embedding retrievers discard 99 percent of candidates within a 10 ms budget, reserving compute-intensive cross-attention transformers for the final top 100 items. This saving creates a recall constraint. A relevant document discarded upstream cannot be recovered by a more accurate downstream ranker, so each stage’s candidate budget must be evaluated for retained relevant items as well as latency.






Figure 24: Ranking cascade architecture: To optimize latency and cost, search and recommendation systems use a cascade of increasingly complex models. Early stages (Retrieval) filter millions of candidates down to thousands using fast, cheap heuristics. Later stages use expensive, high-precision models only on the most promising candidates.



The central design decision is progressive refinement: rather than running one expensive model on all candidates, this scenario uses a ranking cascade. Table 40 shows the trade the cascade makes: each stage spends a larger latency budget on a smaller candidate set, so the expensive L3 ensemble is affordable only because L0 through L2 have already cut the candidates by four orders of magnitude.



Table 40: Illustrative ranking cascade: Each stage evaluates fewer candidates with a more expensive model. The final stage has the largest latency allocation in this scenario; candidate reduction makes that expense affordable.

The cascade reduces final L3 evaluations by 10,000× compared to running L3 on all candidates. If the stage budgets are treated as additive model work and L3 cost scales linearly with candidate count, the L3 allocation implies 1 ms per candidate. Applying L3 to the full million-candidate set would then consume about 1000 s of model work, while the cascade budget sums to 180 ms. The resulting reduction is roughly 5,600× under these assumptions. This accounting estimate is not a measured latency speedup; batching and parallel execution can change elapsed time without changing the candidate count.
A deadline-constrained ranking ensemble can use speculative execution when it has a validated fallback-quality policy. Here, speculation means launching candidate ranking work in parallel under a deadline, not draft-token verification for LLM decoding:
# Instead of sequential:
#   q1 = model1(query)
#   q2 = model2(query)
#   q3 = model3(query, q1, q2)

# Speculative parallel:
async_q1 = async model1(query)
async_q2 = async model2(query)
async_q3 = async model3(query, predicted_q1, predicted_q2)

# Use actual results if they arrive in time, otherwise use speculative
Search ranking deployments can run ranking models on Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).14 Their matrix execution, memory bandwidth, and supported numerical formats must match the ranking workload. Pod interconnect topology varies by generation and configuration; a distributed ranker must account for its actual collective communication costs rather than assume one topology or a guaranteed serving benefit.
14 TPUs for inference: Systolic-array execution can provide a regular timing profile for fixed-shape ranking workloads. Tail latency still depends on batching, input preparation, communication, and queueing around the accelerator.Each sub-request carries a deadline, and workers prioritize by deadline proximity:
Worker queue: [Doc1: 50 ms left] [Doc2: 30 ms left] [Doc3: 80 ms left]
                                      ↑ Process first

If deadline will be missed:
  Return cached/default result rather than timing out
The serving lesson is that ranking cascades reduce cost by spending expensive models only on a shrinking candidate set, at the risk of losing relevant items upstream. Deadline propagation and priority scheduling expose the remaining time budget; meeting it also requires sufficient capacity and a validated fallback when work cannot finish. Custom hardware can improve predictability when the workload matches the accelerator, but the next case adds a freshness constraint that hardware alone cannot solve.



The multimodal recommendation scenario binds on freshness under a tight ranking SLO: video understanding is expensive, new content arrives continuously, and user modeling remains online. It combines video understanding (vision) with user modeling (recommendation) for personalized content ranking, creating a multimodal inference challenge where different model types must coordinate.
The operating scale explains why clear online/offline separation matters: the system handles millions of video rankings per second under a tight p99 latency target below \(50\text{ ms}\), ingesting millions of new videos daily across video, audio, text, and user interaction signals.
The serving stack separates content and user paths:
User request → User embedding → Candidate videos → Video understanding → Ranking

                    |                  |                    |
                    v                  v                    v
             User Tower          Video Cache          Vision Models
           (Transformer)        (Pre-computed)        (On-demand)
The scenario separates user understanding (online) from content understanding (offline) through a two-tower architecture with caching.15 Table 41 contrasts the online and offline tower update cadences:
15 Two-Tower Architecture: Encodes user features and item features through separate neural networks (“towers”) into embeddings, then scores via dot product. The serving advantage: item embeddings can be precomputed offline and cached, reducing online candidate generation to the user tower forward pass and vector similarity search. Search latency depends on index size, placement, and the required recall. The trade-off is reduced model expressiveness from late interaction, since the towers cannot attend to each other’s features during encoding.


Table 41: Illustrative two-tower update cadence: User and video towers run on different cadences: user features change second-to-second and must run inference online; video features change much more slowly and are precomputed in hourly batches. This asymmetric scheduling is the design that takes vision inference out of the critical path for almost every request.

A newly uploaded video without a cached embedding needs an explicit policy: process it before admitting it to recommendations, serve a validated fallback, or run vision inference on demand if the request budget permits. The hourly refresh cadence alone does not meet the shorter ingestion targets below; those targets require a separate path for new content.
The online path below separates candidate generation from a later dense reranker. Its user-tower budget is distinct from the reranker budget:

The priority scheme allocates scarce ingestion capacity to time-sensitive content first. Meeting the stated targets still requires capacity for the corresponding arrival rates; priority changes who waits when demand exceeds capacity, rather than eliminating the wait.
The scenario combines multiple understanding modalities through late fusion, which combines independently computed modality embeddings or scores near the end of ranking rather than running one joint model over all raw modalities:
Video embedding (512d) -+
Audio embedding (256d) -+- Concat → Fusion MLP → Final embedding (256d)
Text embedding (256d)  -+
Late fusion separates the modality computations, but their outputs remain inputs to the fusion model. Updating one modality’s model can change the meaning or distribution of its embeddings even when their dimensions stay fixed. Each update therefore needs compatibility validation and, when that contract changes, regeneration of cached embeddings or adaptation of the fusion model.
The serving lesson is that freshness requires separating online and offline work. Two-tower architectures make aggressive caching possible because item embeddings can be refreshed asynchronously, while priority-based processing spends the freshest compute where it has the largest user impact.



Across these cases, the common pattern is specialization instead of a universal serving stack. Systems separate embedding and retrieval from ranking and generation, use hybrid CPU-GPU architectures to match hardware to workload characteristics, cache at multiple levels while accepting staleness, progressively refine candidate sets to avoid expensive work on unlikely items, and propagate deadlines so quality/latency trade-offs stay explicit under pressure. Table 43 identifies the primary technique and key innovation from each system. The four differ precisely because each is specialized to its own workload; that specialization is the shared pattern, not a contradiction of it.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
A DevOps team applies their standard web-server load balancing rules to a new fleet of GPU inference nodes, only to watch tail latency explode because they ignored the extreme variance of autoregressive token generation. Web services also face variable work and queueing, but an inference fleet adds model residency, accelerator scheduling, and per-sequence state to those familiar concerns. The fallacies below arise when a serving design ignores these constraints or treats one optimization as a complete solution.

Fallacy: Inference at scale is synonymous with LLM serving.
The misconception, reinforced by LLM-centric discourse, leads to over-focus on LLM-specific techniques while ignoring the broader inference landscape. Published characterizations of large consumer platforms show recommendation and ranking models consuming most AI inference cycles, while vision, fraud detection, and classification models account for much of the rest (Gupta et al. 2020; Hazelwood et al. 2018). A practitioner who only understands continuous batching and KV cache management is unprepared for the feature-parallel batching and embedding sharding that dominate high-volume recommendation inference. Technique selection must match the actual workload.

Hazelwood, Kim, Sarah Bird, David Brooks, Soumith Chintala, Utku Diril, Dmytro Dzhulgakov, Mohamed Fawzy, et al. 2018. “Applied Machine Learning at Facebook: A Datacenter Infrastructure Perspective.” 2018 IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 620–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/hpca.2018.00059.


Pitfall: Using training infrastructure for production serving.
Training and serving have different requirements. Training balances aggregate throughput with convergence and time to solution; interactive serving must also satisfy per-request latency targets under external arrivals. Its batch size therefore depends on the workload and waiting budget. Interactive streaming may admit little batching, while bandwidth-bound LLM decode can benefit from many concurrent sequences. Training can resume from checkpoints after an interruption; serving needs a recovery policy that accounts for in-flight requests, retries, and the availability target. Hardware can be shared or repurposed, but a training configuration does not establish serving readiness. Batching, routing, and capacity management must be evaluated against the serving contract.


Fallacy: Continuous batching solves the whole LLM serving problem.
Continuous batching reuses slots released by completed requests, but it addresses only one dimension of the problem. Prefill can remain a bottleneck for long contexts because scheduling subsequent decode iterations does not remove the quadratic attention work of full-attention prefill. Section 10.10 demonstrates that KV cache memory, not compute, often limits batch size. Network bandwidth between sharded model components can dominate latency for large models. The value of continuous batching depends on the workload; slot reuse alone does not resolve these other constraints.


Pitfall: Sizing the fleet by average throughput.
Average throughput alone does not establish capacity for bursts. With unchanged work per request and service capacity, a 25 percent traffic increase from 80 percent utilization reaches 100 percent utilization, leaving no spare capacity to absorb variance. Whether the resulting queue violates an SLO depends on burst duration, the waiting budget, and admission policy. Cluster-level cold starts can delay relief for multiple minutes. Capacity planning must therefore account for peak load, burst duration, ready headroom, and the work the service can defer or reject.


Fallacy: Load balancing does not matter much for inference.
Simple load balancing strategies like round-robin can distribute request counts while leaving work uneven. The static placement analysis in section 10.13 motivates two probes, but its occupancy bounds do not predict production queue lengths. Serving comparisons must preserve arrivals, request lengths, cache affinity, and replica capacity. Work-aware routing earns its place when it improves measured tail latency without excessive coordination cost.


Pitfall: Ignoring the serving tax.
Distributed inference adds network round-trips and shard coordination to the serialization, routing, and queueing costs that can already surround a single-machine model. This serving tax depends on deployment topology and load. In the illustrative budget of section 10.4, 70 ms of model execution leaves only 30 ms for every other stage of a 100 ms request target, and queueing alone can consume that remainder as load rises. A kernel benchmark measures only the first term of equation 1; the serving latency is the measured sum along the complete request path.


Fallacy: More GPU memory always means larger batch size and higher throughput.
Larger GPU memory raises throughput only when the extra capacity supports useful work within the latency budget. Even when memory bandwidth is saturated, a larger decode batch can increase tokens per second by sharing weight reads across more sequences. That gain stops when compute, per-sequence KV-cache traffic, or the SLO becomes binding. The bottleneck hierarchy distinguishes these limits.
For an H100 with 80 GB memory and 3.35 TB/s HBM3 bandwidth, capacity and transfer rate are separate limits. More capacity may admit additional sequences, but the resulting batch must still meet compute, bandwidth, and latency budgets. Once extra sequences no longer improve useful throughput within those budgets, adding memory alone cannot help. Capacity planning therefore measures the bottleneck at the intended batch size and context length rather than assigning one permanent bottleneck to the model.


Pitfall: Neglecting multi-tenancy isolation until production.
In development and staging, single-tenant deployments work well. In production, noisy neighbors cause sudden, unpredictable performance degradation that is difficult to diagnose and resolve. A tenant bursting to 5\(\times\) normal traffic can degrade latency for all other tenants on shared infrastructure. As emphasized in section 10.14, resource quotas, priority scheduling, and bulkhead isolation must be designed into the system from the start, not retrofitted after production incidents.
These pitfalls identify what a serving evaluation must test: traffic variance, cost per completed request within the SLO, and interference across tenants. Correct technique selection must be followed by measurement under the intended load and failure conditions.


Self-Check: Question

A team upgrades a cluster serving a 13B LLM from 80 GB GPUs to 140 GB GPUs with identical HBM3 memory bandwidth (3.35 TB/s). Autoregressive decode is strictly compute-bound; increasing memory without adding Tensor Cores leaves execution time unchanged.
Autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound (\(D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW}\)); once model weights fit resident in memory, token generation speed is constrained by memory bandwidth, not total memory capacity.
140 GB GPUs automatically disable CUDA graph compilation, adding driver launch latency to every iteration.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Inference at scale turns trained models and distributed hardware into a service under continuously arriving work. Training optimizes aggregate progress over a run; serving must also meet user-visible latency targets while paying recurring operating costs. The useful capacity of the fleet is the work it completes within its service contract, not the work its accelerators execute in isolation. Test-time compute sharpens the point. When quality is bought by spending more compute per query, the scaling curve that drove the fleet’s growth moves into the request path, and every increment of quality is paid again on every request.
Serving performance depends on the balance between compute and memory bandwidth. In the terms of the single-machine iron law recalled in The Fleet Law, long-prompt prefill can be compute-bound (\(\Operations/\PeakRate\)), while small-batch decode is often bandwidth-bound (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)). Each decode iteration reads active weights and the sequences’ KV state; batching shares weight reads across more tokens, whereas longer contexts increase KV traffic. Single-replica efficiency (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) therefore depends on phase, batch size, and context length. Variable output lengths make fixed batch membership waste capacity after shorter requests finish.
To maximize throughput under memory-bandwidth constraints, modern serving architectures co-design the memory hierarchy and the iteration scheduler. Continuous batching recovers idle slots by inserting new requests at token boundaries; PagedAttention reduces physical memory fragmentation through fixed-block allocation while retaining partial-page waste; and prefill/decode disaggregation assigns prompt processing and token generation to separate hardware pools sized around their measured compute, memory, and communication costs.
When model state exceeds device memory, sharding spreads a replica across accelerators; when demand exceeds a replica’s service capacity, additional replicas supply aggregate throughput. In Fleet Law terms, sharding divides the compute term \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) of equation 10 but adds communication and synchronization \((\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount), \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount))\) governed by interconnect latency floors (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) and transfer bandwidth (\(\LinkBandwidth\)). Replication, routing, isolation, and autoscaling add coordination costs through probes, admission decisions, and capacity changes, and multi-region placement adds wide-area round trips and cross-region failover to the same budget; transferring model or session state also consumes communication bandwidth. Their aggregate capacity and tail control require headroom and sometimes idle replicas. Across the serving hierarchy, the engineering objective is to increase useful completed work while preserving the latency and reliability contract under load.

Key Takeaways: Serving capacity is constrained by its contract

Serving cost recurs throughout deployment: Training is paid per model version, while inference expense accrues with traffic (principle \(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)). In the chapter’s high-volume recommendation scenario, lifetime serving cost reaches 525.6× the training cost, making efficiency a recurring economic lever.
Tail latency governs architecture: Batching, sharding, caching, and autoscaling must improve useful capacity within workload-specific service targets. Aggregate throughput is insufficient when queueing, first-token delay, or slow token delivery makes completed work miss its contract.
Decode turns memory into capacity: Long-prompt prefill often binds on compute, while small-batch decode rereads active weights and expands private KV state token by token (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)). Continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix reuse, and KV compression matter because they convert scarce HBM bandwidth and memory into admitted requests.
Model class sets the primitive: Vision models benefit from predictable static or dynamic batches, recommenders from feature-parallel embedding sharding, and LLMs from iteration-level scheduling. A fleet scheduler must match the workload shape instead of applying one universal batch-size rule.
Distribution always sends a bill: Sharding, routing, isolation, and failover buy capacity or resilience while consuming communication and coordination budgets. Power-of-two choices (principle \(\ref{pri-power-two-choices}\)) illustrates the value of limiting coordination: routing can use a small number of probes rather than polling every replica.



The serving cost dominance principle (\(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)) makes local efficiency valuable only when the service can turn it into useful capacity. Memory released by quantization may admit more sequences, but those sequences still compete for execution time and can push the endpoint beyond its latency budget. The economic comparison therefore holds the request mix, quality requirement, and service targets fixed before asking whether a change lowers the cost of completed work.

What’s Next: From data center to edgeThe serving designs developed here coordinate accelerator replicas under data-center memory, network, and availability assumptions; even the global stack’s edge points of presence only answer from cache and leave model execution in the clusters. Many applications also run models on smartphones and other personal devices, where sustained power is a few watts, memory is shared with foreground work, and connectivity is intermittent. When those devices must also adapt to local data, the fleet has to decide where learning happens, which device updates it accepts, and how a population improves a shared model without collecting raw examples.





↪ On-device adaptation under device resource budgets and federated learning across device populations are developed in Edge Intelligence.

title: 10 Inference at Scale
text:
Self-Check: Answer

A production recommendation model costs $50,000 to train (a one-time expense) and serves 10,000 QPS continuously for 2 years (730 days) at an operational cost of $10 per million queries. According to the serving cost dominance principle, what is the ratio of lifetime serving cost to training cost?

Approximately \(1.3\times\)
Approximately \(126.1\times\)
Approximately \(12.6\times\)
Approximately \(630.7\times\)

Answer: The correct answer is B. The model serves \(10{,}000 \times 86{,}400 \times 730 = 6.3072 \times 10^{11}\) queries. At \(10^{-5}\) dollars per query, serving costs 6,307,200 dollars, or approximately 126.1 times the 50,000-dollar training cost. The other ratios miscount accumulated queries or unit cost. This result depends on the specified sustained traffic, lifetime, and price rather than a universal cost ratio.
Learning Objective: Calculate the lifetime economic leverage of recurring inference expense relative to one-time training expense.
Explain the composition of the distributed ‘serving tax’ (\(T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{network}} + T_{\text{serialization}} + T_{\text{coordination}} + T_{\text{queuing}}\)) and describe how zero-copy serialization formats mitigate serialization overhead.
Answer: The serving tax comprises exposed network, serialization, coordination, and queueing delays beyond model execution. Zero-copy formats can expose compatible wire-format data without a separate parse-and-copy pass.
