title: 12 ML Operations at Scale
text:
Organizations where every data science team independently provisions GPU clusters, configures model registries, and wires up alerting dashboards duplicate infrastructure work. Platform engineering addresses this by treating the ML infrastructure itself as a product, providing supported paths that reduce repeated implementation and maintenance. Product teams still own model behavior and workload-specific decisions; the platform makes shared operational responsibilities explicit.
Platform engineering for machine learning creates shared infrastructure that absorbs recurring operational complexity while exposing the controls model teams need. Effective platforms balance self-service capabilities that accelerate development against governance requirements that enforce common release and reliability policies.


The abstraction-level decision is how much operational judgment the platform should centralize on behalf of model teams. Too little abstraction leaves every team paying the same infrastructure tax; too much hides the controls that unusual workloads need. The four levels in table 30 sit on that flexibility-vs.-convenience curve, distinguished by which concerns the platform owns and which it leaves to the model team.



Table 30: Platform abstraction levels: Platform engineering centralizes different parts of the ML lifecycle at each abstraction level. The right level depends on whether an organization values workload-specific control or shared operational invariants more.











Level
Platform owns
Model team still owns
Best fit and risk




Level 1
GPU capacity, storage volumes, network connectivity, and basic orchestration such as Kubernetes namespaces
Training code, serving stack, monitoring, and deployment path
Fits unusual workloads with strong infrastructure teams; becomes costly when many teams repeat the same operational work


Level 2
Standardized containers, ML-aware Kubernetes integration, persistent volumes, and basic service-mesh support
Experiment structure, training jobs, serving releases, and monitoring workflows
Reduces packaging duplication; operational correctness still depends heavily on each team


Level 3
ML-specific control loops such as topology-aware scheduling, hyperparameter tuning, distributed training, serving
Modeling judgment and workload-specific trade-offs
Absorbs failure modes that recur across teams; systems such as Kubeflow and Ray often sit near this level


Level 4
Full lifecycle product: IDEs, feature stores, experiment tracking, registries, CI/CD, monitoring, cost, governance
Higher-level product and modeling intent, with less direct low-level control
Maximizes speed and consistency; the platform team accepts responsibility for policy, reliability, and economic visibility






Managed services such as Vertex AI and SageMaker, and lifecycle tooling such as TensorFlow Extended (TFX)15 at Google (Baylor et al. 2017) and MLflow (Zaharia et al. 2018), support different parts of this spectrum. A product name does not establish the organization’s abstraction level. The decisive boundary is which lifecycle responsibilities the assembled platform actually owns, which controls model teams retain, and who supplies policy, reliability, and economic visibility for the gaps.
15 TensorFlow Extended (TFX): Google’s production ML pipeline framework includes TensorFlow Data Validation (TFDV), which checks data against schema expectations and configured drift and skew comparisons. Connecting those checks to a release policy allows a pipeline to stop before spending training resources on detected data defects. The checks cover declared expectations; a passing result does not establish that every value is correct or that a distribution change is harmless.
Baylor, Denis, Eric Breck, Heng-Tze Cheng, Noah Fiedel, Chuan Yu Foo, Zakaria Haque, Salem Haykal, et al. 2017. “TFX: A TensorFlow-Based Production-Scale Machine Learning Platform.” Proceedings of the 23rd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 1387–95. https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3098021.

Zaharia, Matei, Andrew Chen, Aaron Davidson, Ali Ghodsi, Sue Ann Hong, Andy Konwinski, Siddharth Murching, et al. 2018. “Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow.” IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin 41 (4): 39–45.



An internal ML platform is a versioned product, not a one-time infrastructure project. Its interfaces, supported workflows, reliability targets, and ownership boundaries must evolve without forcing every model team into synchronized migration. Each platform release therefore needs compatibility guarantees, a migration path, telemetry that distinguishes old and new paths, and a retirement date for deprecated behavior. The platform team also needs its own service-level objectives because a registry, feature service, or deployment controller outage can block every product team at once.
Adoption measures whether the platform removes work rather than merely centralizing it. Useful indicators include the share of production models on supported paths, time from validated artifact to bounded production traffic, exception rate, migration completion, support load, and repeated toil outside the paved road. A high signup count with persistent custom pipelines signals nominal adoption but weak product fit. Conversely, mandatory migration can raise the adoption percentage while increasing lead time and operational risk. The platform roadmap should therefore combine fleet outcomes with user evidence: incident reduction and cost attribution matter alongside time-to-first-deployment and the fraction of teams that can complete routine changes without platform intervention.
Lifecycle decisions must preserve an escape hatch for workloads whose constraints do not fit the shared path. Exceptions should be explicit, time-bounded contracts with named owners and integration obligations, not permanent forks. When exception volume grows around the same missing capability, the pattern becomes product evidence for the next platform version. When a capability no longer earns its maintenance and migration cost, the platform should deprecate it through measured dual-running, compatibility testing, and a final removal gate. This product discipline keeps the shared control plane from becoming the next source of technical debt.



Self-service deployment works only when the platform can let model teams move quickly while keeping risky choices inside governed boundaries. The design question is therefore which deployment decisions should remain team-owned and which invariants the platform must enforce before a model receives production traffic.


A well-designed deployment API abstracts operational complexity by making the model team’s intent declarative. The platform lesson is not the shape of a particular YAML file; it is which invariants the platform must capture before it turns a model version into fleet traffic. The invariants in table 31 are the platform contract behind that declarative interface. Prometheus16 is one common operational sink for the telemetry side of that contract.
16 Prometheus: An open-source monitoring system that scrapes and stores labeled time series. A fleet can export operational metrics and computed drift scores through the same metrics interface while retaining detailed prediction records elsewhere for analysis. The distinction is between compact alerting signals and the evidence needed to investigate them; it does not require every platform to adopt the same two-tier implementation.


Table 31: Self-service deployment invariants: A deployment API should encode the controls that keep local team autonomy from creating fleet-wide risk. The concrete syntax can vary, but the invariants must survive across platforms.









Declared intent
Platform invariant




Model artifact and version
The serving system loads exactly the validated model from the registry.


Resource envelope
GPU, memory, and replica requests stay inside quota and scheduling constraints.


Traffic policy
Canary, shadow, and rollback controls bound blast radius before full promotion.


Quality gates
Error, latency, drift, and task-quality thresholds block unsafe promotion.


Telemetry sink
Operational metrics flow into operational monitoring, while model-quality signals flow into drift and slice monitors.


Approval boundary
Sensitive data access, budget overruns, and high-risk release windows require review.






TensorFlow Serving provides model-serving lifecycle capabilities for loading, versioning, canarying, and rolling back models (Olston et al. 2017). A self-service platform adds the policy layer around those capabilities: model teams specify intent, and the platform translates it into scheduling, traffic routing, telemetry, and approval controls.

Olston, Christopher, Noah Fiedel, Kiril Gorovoy, Jeremiah Harmsen, Li Lao, Fangwei Li, Vinu Rajashekhar, Sukriti Ramesh, and Jordan Soyke. 2017. “TensorFlow-Serving: Flexible, High-Performance ML Serving.” CoRR abs/1712.06139. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1712.06139.




Efficient resource utilization is essential for platform economics, but training and serving place different demands on shared capacity. Training jobs can trade completion time for utilization within their deadlines; serving needs headroom to protect tail latency as requests arrive. A scheduler can manage both, provided its policy represents those distinct constraints rather than maximizing utilization alone.


Training resource policy must expose which jobs may wait or be preempted,17 which deadlines are binding, and who accepts the recovery cost. Scheduler mechanisms enforce those choices. The platform records checkpoint readiness, budget, priority, and accountable owner with each job so a utilization improvement does not silently transfer deadline or lost-work risk to a model team.
17 Job Preemption: The ability to terminate lower-priority workloads to free resources for urgent work. Preemptible capacity is also how cloud providers sell deep discounts, which section 12.9.5 prices. Without a usable checkpoint, a preempted 72-hour run may need to restart from scratch, potentially erasing the discount. Checkpoint frequency trades I/O overhead against wasted-compute risk; the right policy depends on job duration, interruption frequency, and recovery cost.
↩︎ Scheduler mechanisms for queueing, priority preemption, and elastic resizing of training jobs are established in Fleet Orchestration.




Serving workloads bind on latency rather than batch flexibility. Demand fluctuates with time of day, events, and seasonality, but a live request cannot be preempted without user impact. The serving control loop therefore starts from the latency SLO and asks how much capacity must be online before requests arrive.
Serving autoscalers translate request load and queue pressure into capacity decisions. Operations owns their policy envelope: the latency SLO, warm rollback capacity, tenant limits, budget, and authority to override normal scaling during an incident. Those commitments must remain visible in the release record so a cheaper allocation cannot silently remove the headroom on which validation relied.


↩︎ Autoscaling controllers that convert queue growth and token arrival rates into replica counts are established in Autoscaling and Capacity Control.



Once training and serving controls are separated, the shared platform still needs an aggregate measure of whether capacity is being converted into useful work. Equation 14 defines platform efficiency as the capacity-weighted average utilization across all resources:
\[\PlatformUtilization= \frac{\sum_{i} \ResourceUtilization_i \times \text{Cap}_i}{\sum_{i} \text{Cap}_i} \tag{14}\]
where \(\ResourceUtilization_i\) is the utilization of resource \(\PlatformResourceIndex\) and \(\text{Cap}_i\) is its capacity in a common unit over the same interval. Heterogeneous accelerators require a declared workload normalization; CPU cores, device counts, and bytes cannot be added directly. Weighting by capacity keeps the metric honest about where stranded work lives: an idle single GPU and an idle eight-GPU node are not equally wasteful, so a small underused resource should not drag the platform average down as hard as a large idle pool.
However, raw utilization is incomplete. The scheduler already separates allocated, compute, and productive utilization for a single cluster; the platform metric needs the same distinction. Effective utilization must also consider utilization quality to determine whether GPUs are doing productive work or waiting on data, utilization fairness to assess whether utilization is distributed appropriately across teams, and utilization cost to evaluate efficiency in terms of cost per unit of ML output.


↩︎ The allocated, compute, and productive utilization tiers are established in Resource accounting and observability.



A platform operates a 100-GPU training cluster with average GPU utilization of 65 percent, memory utilization of 80 percent, four-hour average queue waits, and an internal chargeback rate of $2.50/GPU-hour. Memory occupancy and compute utilization alone do not identify the bottleneck: profiling must separate input stalls, communication, kernel inefficiency, and scheduling gaps. Queue waits may also reflect burst arrivals or placement constraints rather than insufficient aggregate capacity. Suppose profiling identifies input stalls and confirms that recovering them increases useful throughput at the same quality target. Daily cluster spend is fixed by provisioned capacity at \(100 \times 24 \times \$2.50 = \$6,000/\text{day}\). Useful work, valued at the same chargeback rate, is the utilization times that spend, \(100 \times 24 \times 0.65 \times \$2.50 = \$3,900/\text{day}\); the remainder pays for idle or stalled accelerators. If data-loading optimization raises compute utilization to 80 percent, useful work rises to \(100 \times 24 \times 0.80 \times \$2.50 = \$4,800/\text{day}\) before adding any capacity. The recovered capacity has an annualized value of $328,500 at the stated rate, but the fixed cluster bill remains unchanged. Cash savings require reducing provisioned capacity or avoiding a future purchase; serving queued work creates value through additional output instead. After the validated bottleneck repair, scheduling and capacity planning address the remaining queue pressure.

Checkpoint 12.4: The annual cost of GPU cluster underutilization
Use daily cluster spend ($6,000/day) and useful-work value, utilization times spend ($3,900/day at 65 percent utilization), to extend the analysis to annual scale and compare against the platform ROI argument.

Underutilization cost: calculate the annual cost of underutilization for the 100-GPU cluster at 65 percent utilization, the cost after optimization to 80 percent, and the annual value of recovered capacity. State when that value would become cash savings.
Queue dynamics: Little’s Law (theorem \(\ref{thrm-inference-littles-law-inference}\)) holds for any stable queue, rather than serving requests alone. Applied to the training-job queue, the average number of jobs waiting equals the job arrival rate times the average queue wait. Calculate the job arrival rate for a 4-hour average wait with 100 jobs in queue and explain what additional job-size, service-time, and arrival-pattern measurements are needed to choose expansion or utilization optimization.
Savings vs. platform: compare the annual recovered-capacity value from cluster optimization to the $2M/year platform investment scenario. Holding the utilization gain and chargeback rate fixed, determine the GPU count where annual recovered-capacity value equals that investment, and state what must happen for the capacity value to become cash savings.







While utilization metrics capture resource busyness, they often fail to reflect true engineering value. A GPU spinning at 100 percent utilization on a hyperparameter tuning job that eventually fails due to a configuration error is “efficient” in terms of hardware but “wasteful” in terms of productivity. ML productivity goodput (MPG) turns that distinction into a fleet metric (Wongpanich et al. 2025).

Wongpanich, A., T. Oguntebi, J. Baiocchi Paredes, Y. E. Wang, P. M. Phothilimthana, R. Mitra, Z. Zhou, N. Kumar, and V. J. Reddi. 2025. Machine Learning Fleet Efficiency: Analyzing and Optimizing Large-Scale Google TPU Systems with ML Productivity Goodput.

↩︎ The Fleet Law and the ML productivity goodput metric introduced beside it are established in The Fleet Law.

The Fleet Law accounts for time within one distributed step; MPG complements it by locating lost productivity across a whole portfolio of jobs. Its three multiplicative factors share a common workload and time boundary, and they cut across C³ rather than mapping onto one axis:
\[\text{MPG} = \SchedulingGoodput \times \RuntimeGoodput \times \ProgramGoodput\]
In this decomposition, scheduling goodput (\(\SchedulingGoodput\)) measures the fraction of fleet capacity-time for which a job has all resources needed for synchronous progress. Partial allocations do not count as fully available work capacity. Runtime goodput (\(\RuntimeGoodput\)) measures productive, checkpoint-preserved progress relative to that allocated time, excluding initialization, input delays, and work lost after the last checkpoint. Program goodput (\(\ProgramGoodput\)) compares an ideal execution-time baseline with actual program execution time, exposing code, compiler, and communication inefficiencies. These boundaries prevent a single delay from being charged indiscriminately to several factors. Their product measures efficiency rather than an absolute throughput rate; the decomposition helps locate which layer limits useful fleet output.



Enterprise platforms earn their sharing dividend only if multiple teams can share infrastructure without sharing failures. The scheduler’s quotas and fair-share policies and the serving system’s isolation mechanisms, established in Multi-Tenancy and Isolation, already bound interference within one cluster or one inference service. What the platform adds is one namespace hierarchy across training and serving, plus cost isolation that follows each tenant’s spend, and neither the scheduler nor the serving system owns those alone. Multi-tenancy is therefore an isolation problem before it is an efficiency problem, and the platform must bound performance interference, data exposure, and cost spillover at the same time.


↩︎ Quotas, hierarchical fair-share, and burst borrowing are established in Multi-Tenancy and Quotas.


Tenants need isolation at every boundary where one team’s workload, data, or cost can affect another. Performance isolation uses resource quotas, fair-share scheduling, and network quality-of-service rules to bound interference from training spikes or serving bursts. Security isolation enforces access controls, network segmentation, and encryption across tenant data paths. Cost isolation combines granular metering with declared allocation rules for shared services and reserved capacity; not every shared cost can be assigned directly to an individual request. Together, these boundaries establish the conditions under which product teams can share infrastructure without negotiating every allocation manually.



A typical multi-tenant architecture uses hierarchical namespaces:
Platform
|-- Team A
|   |-- Development
|   |-- Staging
|   `-- Production
|-- Team B
|   |-- Development
|   |-- Staging
|   `-- Production
`-- Shared
    |-- Feature Store
    |-- Model Registry
    `-- Monitoring
Each team receives dedicated namespaces with resource quotas, while shared services operate in common namespaces with appropriate access controls. Without controls, one team’s demanding workload can degrade performance for others, the noisy neighbor problem, which at platform scale crosses the boundary between training and serving.18 Prevention requires controls at request, rate, priority, and budget boundaries.
18 Noisy Neighbor Problem: On a shared ML platform the interference often crosses workload classes, because training jobs allocate GPU memory greedily; a single job requesting all available HBM on a shared node can starve co-located inference services, causing latency spikes that violate SLOs. Sharing therefore requires an explicit fit, eviction, offload, time-sharing, or partitioning policy, and even physical partitioning leaves shared-fabric contention in place.To prevent any single tenant from overwhelming shared platform services, four complementary controls govern the request path. Request limits place hard caps on the compute and memory an individual invocation may consume, while rate limiting bounds aggregate query velocity across tenant boundaries. Under heavy cluster contention, priority classes ensure that mission-critical production traffic receives scheduling preference over ad-hoc or batch queries. Finally, burst budgets permit brief, temporary resource overages to accommodate legitimate spikes while preserving long-term fairness across the fleet. Together, these controls make fairness enforceable directly in the data plane rather than relying on after-the-fact operational negotiation.
Isolation makes sharing safe, but it does not make sharing pay. Cost isolation meters each tenant’s consumption; whether the shared fleet is worth its capital, how its spend reaches the teams that caused it, and when a workload’s cost justifies optimization are economic questions that the platform must answer with the same rigor it applies to releases.

Self-Check: Question

ML Productivity Goodput (MPG) decomposes fleet productivity into the product of which three efficiency factors?

Hardware CapEx \(\times\) Power Usage Effectiveness \(\times\) Depreciation Rate
Network Bandwidth \(\times\) GPU Clock Frequency \(\times\) High Bandwidth Memory Capacity
Model Parameter Count \(\times\) Batch Size \(\times\) Floating-Point Operations per Second
Scheduling Efficiency \(\times\) Runtime Efficiency \(\times\) Program Efficiency

Which shared-resource path can allow a training tenant to violate the latency SLO of a co-located inference tenant?

Competition for finite GPU High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) or shared RDMA fabric bandwidth can stall the inference tenant even when host CPU resources are isolated.
Linux kernel cgroups and container namespaces cannot be instantiated on systems containing GPU accelerators.
CPUs cannot run multi-tenant virtualization or container runtimes.
Multi-tenant GPU clusters require all tenant models to share the exact same weights in memory.

A platform reports utilization as the simple average across its resources. Why does the chapter weight each resource’s utilization by its capacity instead, and what must be true of the capacity units before the weighted average is meaningful?
In a 100-GPU training cluster operating at \(65\%\) average compute utilization and \(80\%\) memory utilization with 4-hour queue waits and a cost of \(\$2.50\)/GPU-hour, evaluate whether buying more GPUs or optimizing data-loading pipelines is the superior operational intervention.
Batch training workloads and live online serving workloads share the same operational constraints and should be managed under an identical cluster scheduling and preemption policy.

Full Lifecycle Product (Managed IDEs, feature stores, experiment tracking, registries, automated governance, Vertex/SageMaker)
Standardized Containers (ML-aware Kubernetes integrations, standardized images, persistent volume claims)
Infrastructure as a Service (Raw GPU capacity, bare namespaces, raw block storage, manual script execution)

title: 12 ML Operations at Scale
text:
A provisioned GPU incurs capacity costs whether it serves predictions, waits between training bursts, or remains reserved for rollback. Those idle periods have different meanings: a scheduling bottleneck strands capacity, while a justified reserve buys recovery capability. The operational machinery developed so far decides how models change safely; it does not decide whether the capacity underneath them is worth what it costs. Fleet economics therefore distinguishes productive use, deliberate headroom, and avoidable waste before treating higher utilization as an improvement.
Three economic levels prevent that ledger from collapsing unlike decisions into one cost number. Platform economics (section 12.2.3) asks whether common control-plane capabilities repay their fixed development and maintenance cost across the portfolio. Fleet economics asks whether shared hardware, facilities, and capacity commitments produce useful work at acceptable utilization and risk. Workload economics asks whether one training run, serving endpoint, or experiment earns its marginal compute, data, and engineering cost. A gain at one level does not establish value at the others. Faster jobs do not remove an existing capacity commitment, and high fleet utilization does not establish that a platform repays its adoption and maintenance costs. The placement and scheduling mechanisms in Fleet Orchestration operate within this capacity envelope. Operations owns the commitments around them: capital planning, portfolio return, lifecycle total cost of ownership (TCO), and cost attribution across teams.

Definition 12.1: ML systems TCO
Total cost of ownership (TCO) for ML systems is the complete economic accounting of developing, deploying, and operating machine learning capabilities across their full lifecycle.

Significance: It captures the cost inversion of scale: training incurs a cost per run, while inference accumulates with served work. The lifecycle example in section 12.9.2.2 shows a high-traffic service exceeding its initial training bill within two years under fixed traffic and unit cost.
Distinction: This lifecycle view includes serving efficiency alongside hardware, data, development, and recurring training costs. The energy and compute cost of each prediction depends on achieved hardware efficiency \(\EfficiencyHw\) as well as batching and model size.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that the initial training bill is the primary financial risk. In reality, the data debt and maintenance overhead are the “silent interest rates” that can make an accurate model economically unsustainable in production.



Platform economics was priced earlier in the chapter, so the analysis here follows the remaining levels downward. It prices the fleet first, then the workload, and closes with financial operations (FinOps), the controls that attribute that single ledger to teams and assign the authority to act on it.
Engineering constraints shape the feasible economic choices. Infrastructure must first meet quality, latency, reliability, and capacity requirements; useful computation per dollar then helps compare feasible designs over the system’s lifetime. At an assumed $350,000 per 8-GPU DGX H100 node, a 10,000-GPU cluster represents about $437.5M in node hardware capital expenditure before networking, facility, staffing, and maintenance costs. The purchase price, however, is only the beginning. Over the three-year planning horizon used here, those operating and supporting costs determine the full commitment. TCO19 connects that commitment to useful output and provides the basis for the broader ML-lifecycle accounting developed in section 12.9.8.
19 TCO Boundary: A fleet comparison must declare what its total cost of ownership counts. The boundary must include the supporting power, cooling, networking, facility, and staffing commitments. Moving from 20 percent to 80 percent useful utilization spreads fixed costs over more output, but whether that changes the ownership decision depends on the rental alternative, workload fit, and costs included in each option.Depreciation, power, and utilization also matter in traditional IT, but an accelerator fleet concentrates a large commitment in resources that can remain idle when data, communication, or scheduling falls behind. With hardware and facility commitments fixed, lower useful utilization spreads those costs over less completed work. The platform must therefore keep expensive capacity productive while preserving the headroom required for failures, rollbacks, and traffic spikes. The economic target is useful output within those operating constraints, not maximum device busyness.
Two reference prices anchor the arithmetic that follows. The internal fleet rate of $2/GPU-hour approximates what an owned H100 fleet operated at high utilization costs its own teams, and the on-demand cloud rate of $4/GPU-hour is the rental reference for build-vs.-buy comparisons. Other rates in the chapter, such as the internal chargeback price in the GPU cluster efficiency example, the FinOps spending scenario, or the non-energy accelerator-hour rate in the training cost example, are scenario choices and are labeled as such where they occur. Cluster sizes follow the same rule. The running fleet is the Archetype A reference cluster of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), the H100 cluster that trains the GPT-3-class reference instance; every later analysis prices it unless it names a separate scenario.


The total cost of an ML cluster decomposes into two broad categories. Capital expenditure (CapEx) covers the one-time costs of building the infrastructure: accelerators, servers, networking equipment, facility construction, and installation. Operational expenditure (OpEx) covers the recurring costs of running it: electricity, cooling, network bandwidth, staffing, maintenance, and software licenses.
For a large on-premises cluster, table 32 separates the cost stack into capital and operating centers, each with different utilization implications.



Table 32: Frontier training cost stack: Capital costs are dominated by accelerators, networking, and facilities, while operating costs are dominated by electricity and specialized staffing. The shares are broad planning ranges; in the running 1,024-GPU example, node hardware is about 75 percent of CapEx and electricity about 44 percent of OpEx.











Cost center
Cost class
Typical share
Included components and implications




Accelerators and servers
CapEx
50–60% of CapEx
GPUs or TPUs, host servers, baseboard management controllers, and local storage; this category dominates upfront purchase and depreciation.


Networking
CapEx

InfiniBand switches, HCAs, cables, and optical transceivers; the running example budgets about $5 million for a two-tier fat-tree serving 1,024 GPUs.

The running cost example is Archetype A’s reference instance, the 175B-parameter GPT-3-class model, trained on the reference cluster of 1,024 H100 GPUs spread across 128 nodes. For the illustrative training plan developed below, assume a 2–4-week run. Parameter count alone does not determine this duration; the later planning example states its token and throughput budget. Evaluating the TCO over a three-year lifecycle reveals a stark utilization dependency. The hardware CapEx dominates at $44.80M ($350,000 per node), supported by a $5 million investment in a two-tier InfiniBand fat-tree network and a proportional $10 million facility allocation. Operational costs add approximately $1.5 million annually for electricity (at $0.07/kWh with a PUE of 1.1) and specialized staffing, bringing the three-year total to roughly $64 million. If this dedicated cluster only trains six large models per year, the effective cost per run is $3.6 million. Renting the same 1,024-GPU allocation in the public cloud at $4/GPU-hour costs about $1.4M–2.8M per run (1,024 GPUs \(\times\) 336–672 hours \(\times\) $4), or $25M–50M over three years for six runs per year. Cloud rental is cheaper for this bursty scenario when idle allocations can be released. At the opposite extreme, continuous utilization spreads the owned cluster’s stated costs over every available hour, reducing the cost to approximately $2.39/GPU-hour, below the cloud reference rate. Ownership need not require continuous use; the actual break-even lies where useful demand repays the fixed commitment under matched cost boundaries.

The most consequential economic question is whether the fleet can sustain enough useful load to amortize fixed capacity. Build-vs.-buy is one expression of that question, but the same invariant appears inside a deployed platform: reserved capacity, fallback pools, regional replicas, and canary headroom all become economical only when their reliability value justifies their idle cost. Ownership pays a large CapEx step up front and then climbs a shallow operating slope, while cloud rental starts at zero and rises steadily; under sustained high utilization the rental line overtakes the owned cluster within a 30-month horizon (figure 11).

The same calculation explains why cloud pricing cannot be read as a simple price list. The scenario’s reserved discount of 40–60 percent converts optionality into commitment. Its spot or preemptible discount of 60–90 percent introduces interruption risk. The relevant comparison is cost per completed workload under the deadline or service contract. Checkpoint recovery, replacement capacity, and traffic fallback offer different ways to manage that risk; no single combination is required for every workload.
Owned capacity moves a different set of risks into the platform. Facility construction, networking, staffing, maintenance, and hardware obsolescence continue to accrue even when the GPUs are idle; their cost depends on site, power delivery, cooling design, and accounting boundary. A three-year-old GPU may be economically stranded if the next generation delivers 3\(\times\) more performance per watt. The engineering question is therefore not whether one purchasing channel is universally cheaper; it is whether the workload mix can keep fixed capacity useful enough to compensate for its lifecycle and operating risks.
Hybrid designs follow from the same invariant. Owned infrastructure can carry predictable baseline work, while cloud allocations absorb peak demand, early hardware access, or bursty training campaigns. The hybrid split is not a compromise between two vendor categories; it is a scheduling policy over capital risk, utilization, and deadline risk.
For the 175B model, workload cadence changes the ownership decision. Consider a dedicated training fleet used only 15–20 percent of the time because its annual training campaign leaves long gaps. A portfolio of experiments, hyperparameter sweeps, fine-tuning jobs, and model variants could instead sustain 70–80 percent utilization on the same hardware, provided those jobs fit its capacity and scheduling constraints. Serving can also fill gaps when the hardware and isolation policy support it. These illustrative utilization levels describe workload mixes, not consequences of training a particular model. A hybrid design can keep predictable baseline work on owned capacity and rent the temporary expansion, such as the 5–10\(\times\) baseline allocation assumed here for large training runs.


The TCO ledger must include the operational work that sustains the fleet. Hardware maintenance must diagnose failed GPUs, links, network adapters, and cooling components before a local fault becomes a fleet-wide slowdown. The five-hour fleet failure interval in the scenario of section 12.6.1 informs staffing, but does not determine headcount by itself. Staffing also depends on diagnosis and repair time, automation, concurrent incidents, and coverage requirements while the rest of the fleet keeps working.
The software side creates the same coupling. CUDA, GPU drivers, InfiniBand drivers, container runtimes, schedulers, monitoring systems, and training frameworks all participate in the achieved utilization number. A driver/toolkit incompatibility can silently degrade performance, while a scheduler or monitoring gap can strand accelerators behind failed jobs. Staffing depends on automation, service commitments, and operating scope because performance optimization is continuous: as models, frameworks, and hardware configurations change, communication patterns, memory pressure, and parallelism strategies change with them. Case 1 on the underutilized compute fleet works an underutilized fleet through the C³ diagnosis, ruling out communication before isolating the compute axis, which shows the performance engineer how to locate where the lost utilization goes rather than tuning blindly.

Cloud providers charge a margin above raw hardware and electricity partly because they absorb this operating burden. The point is not that cloud is simpler in every technical sense; it exposes a different interface. The platform either pays for internal expertise in GPU kernel behavior, InfiniBand operations, distributed-systems debugging, liquid cooling, and power infrastructure, or it pays a provider to hide some of that machinery behind a service contract. In both cases, the economics are still governed by useful work per dollar.



A more complete framework than TCO is total value of ownership, which includes the value generated by infrastructure rather than only its cost. Two clusters with identical TCO may create different outcomes if one reaches a result two weeks earlier, sustains higher scaling efficiency, starts jobs faster, checkpoints more cheaply, or serves the resulting model at lower cost per token. The value terms are hard to price exactly, but they are not optional in systems reasoning: time-to-result affects product deadlines, scaling efficiency affects final model quality under a fixed training window, experimentation velocity affects the number of hypotheses the team can test, and inference efficiency can dominate training cost over a multi-year deployment.
This value-oriented perspective changes the infrastructure decision from cost minimization to constraint management. A cheaper cluster that slows the research cycle or produces a model with higher serving cost may be more expensive over the model lifecycle. Conversely, a more expensive training platform can pay for itself if it enables a smaller or more efficient deployed model.
The inference dimension of total value of ownership (TVO) connects a training investment to the service it supports. Consider one training run of the 175B model costing $5M, followed by a three-year deployment without additional training in this comparison. The service handles 10 million queries per day, each generating an average of 500 tokens, for 5 billion tokens daily. At the assumed cost of $2 per million tokens, the daily bill is $10,000, or approximately $3.6M per year. With traffic and unit cost held constant, cumulative serving cost overtakes the $5M run after about 16 months and reaches roughly twice its cost over three years. This example illustrates the serving cost dominance law (principle \(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)); a lifecycle forecast must add retraining and changing demand when they occur. If an additional $2M investment produces a validated 20 percent reduction in serving cost at matched quality and traffic, the three-year gross savings are $2.2M, enough to recover that investment before any additional maintenance costs.
The lifecycle value of a model still depends on what the platform pays for the capacity that trains and serves it. Comparing owned and rented capacity at a larger fleet scale tests that commitment, provided each estimate states which costs it includes.

Systems Perspective 12.5: The infrastructure moatThe 10,000-GPU scenario illustrates how sustained demand can support ownership. A portfolio that keeps compatible capacity usefully occupied at 70–90 percent utilization spreads fixed costs over more work than one operating at 20–30 percent. These are illustrative demand regimes, not utilization guarantees based on organizational size. Continuous training pipelines, model refreshes, and compatible inference workloads can support the higher regime; sporadic campaigns favor the option to release rented capacity. This dynamic can create an infrastructure moat when a broad workload portfolio lowers unit cost enough to fund further investment. The advantage depends on useful demand and operating discipline, not fleet size alone.






ML accelerators depreciate as newer devices change the cost of useful work. A physically functioning accelerator can become uneconomic for a particular training workload while remaining useful for another. The peak arithmetic efficiencies in table 34 provide one screening measure, but depreciation and refresh decisions require sustained throughput at matched quality, memory capacity, energy consumption, and the cost of replacing otherwise usable equipment.
Resale value depends on supply, demand, memory capacity, software support, and the workload a buyer intends to run. A refresh budget should therefore test a range of resale assumptions rather than extrapolating a fixed historical depreciation rate across generations.
Refresh policy connects lifecycle planning to scheduling. The three-year horizon used in these examples is a planning assumption, not a universal accounting life or a required replacement date. Replacing the entire fleet at once creates a large CapEx spike, while staggered refresh spreads expenditure but leaves the scheduler with mixed-generation hardware. Placement must then account for different compute capabilities, memory capacities, and communication bandwidths. Keeping generations in separate job pools is one option; jobs that span generations need explicit support for their performance differences.
The same lifecycle logic determines where older accelerators remain useful. A GPU that is inefficient for the largest training runs may still serve smaller models, fine-tuning jobs, or memory-bound inference economically if its capacity, bandwidth, and energy cost meet those workloads’ requirements. A newer device’s peak arithmetic advantage alone does not settle that comparison. Resale, repurposing, and capacity-sharing arrangements preserve value only when the platform can route useful work to the appropriate generation without hiding performance cliffs from users.
Depreciation is most punitive for bursty workloads. If a team trains one large model per year, the GPUs lose value during the idle months even though they perform no useful computation. Cloud capacity amortizes the same depreciation across many customers, while owned capacity must amortize it across the owner’s own workload mix. That is why the utilization invariant appears again: the hardware must either stay busy or be cheap enough to strand.
Isolating hardware cost shows how much depreciation alone charges each run of the 175B model. Under the $350,000-per-8-GPU-node assumption, the 1,024-GPU (128-node) fleet costs $44.8M before network and facility costs. Assume a resale value of $7M–10M after three years in a market where newer accelerators offer 3–4\(\times\) the performance per watt. That performance assumption does not determine resale value by itself. The assumed residual value yields net hardware depreciation of $34.8M–37.8M. Allocated to only two large training runs, it contributes $17.4M–18.9M per run before electricity, staffing, or facility costs. At 80 percent useful utilization over three years, it instead contributes approximately $1.62–1.76 per used GPU-hour. This is the hardware component of owned cost, not a complete rate directly comparable with cloud rental. Utilization spreads that commitment across output; the full ledger determines economic viability.

Hardware refresh cycles are ultimately about useful work per lifecycle dollar (table 34). A higher arithmetic ceiling can lower energy per completed run only when the workload realizes enough of that ceiling to compensate for power and replacement costs. Memory-bound serving and communication-bound training can therefore justify different refresh choices for the same fleet.
A refresh comparison can hold either the arithmetic ceiling or the accelerator power budget fixed, and the two framings answer different questions. Consider replacing a V100 fleet of the reference cluster’s size, 1,024 devices with a combined accelerator TDP of 307.2 kW. On the dense FP16 basis of table 34, 130 H100s match that fleet’s arithmetic ceiling at about 91 kW of combined TDP. Held at the same 307.2 kW, the budget instead accommodates 438 H100s with 3.4× the original ceiling. The first comparison screens for a lower power envelope at matched peak arithmetic; the second screens for more arithmetic capacity within a fixed power envelope. Neither establishes achieved throughput or measured power.
The fleet matched by arithmetic ceiling is not automatically usable. The original fleet has 7.9× as many devices, so, with the same port count per device, the replacement offers proportionally fewer network ports, and its aggregate HBM falls from 35.2 TB to 11.2 TB. A replacement plan must pass memory-fit, topology, and latency checks before the arithmetic equivalence counts as capacity, and both framings compare peak ceilings rather than energy per completed run at matched quality.
Financial depreciation, resale value, and economic replacement are separate decisions. An accounting schedule does not establish when a device stops being useful, so the procurement analysis states its lifetime and residual-value assumptions and tests them against the workloads the older devices would still serve, such as memory-bound inference or fine-tuning.
The hybrid split described in section 12.9.2 also hedges refresh timing, because cloud bursts provide access to newer hardware before a large purchase commits the fleet to it.
The screening numbers bound the refresh decision for the 175B model without settling it. The H100’s 700 W TDP is more than twice the V100’s 300 W, yet run energy can still fall, because energy integrates measured power over elapsed time and the faster device finishes sooner. The dollar saving and payback period therefore come from a matched training configuration: measured or validated runtime, accelerator and host power, fabric and storage consumption, and the facility overhead applied to that IT total.



For organizations that choose the cloud path, the provider absorbs hardware ownership but exposes capacity, topology, and interruption risk as operating constraints. The specific instance types and pricing change frequently, so the durable distinction is not vendor branding; it is how the cloud allocation affects communication, scheduling, and fault tolerance.
First, the interconnect fabric determines whether distributed jobs and multi-node inference paths retain the scaling assumptions used in design. InfiniBand-like fabrics and Ethernet-based fabrics have different fixed-latency and per-byte costs; The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth Communication Model separates those terms so the platform can decide whether the topology penalty matters for a given workload.
Second, provisioning granularity determines how much topology the platform controls. Individual instances maximize flexibility but force the team to assemble placement, networking, and scheduling policy. Pod-level allocations provide a preconnected unit but reduce composition freedom.
Third, custom accelerator options apply the same generality-efficiency trade-off introduced at the silicon level. Specialized hardware can reduce the cost of supported operations, but end-to-end savings depend on workload mapping, software support, and migration effort. The choice mirrors the on-premises accelerator decision, except that changing platforms requires a cloud migration rather than replacing owned hardware.
The pricing models expose different commitments. On-demand instances preserve the option to release capacity; reserved instances exchange a commitment for a discounted rate under the contract; spot or preemptible instances offer discounted capacity subject to interruption. The comparison must use equivalent hardware, placement, and service terms rather than assume that these labels establish a universal price ordering. The purchasing choice is also a fault-tolerance decision, as the spot-instance economics below make concrete.
Spot instances and preemptible VMs develops spot economics from the scheduler’s side, where equation 8.3 inflates the spot price by the ratio of total to productive time. The operations view applies that relation to a capacity budget. At a 70 percent discount, a scenario choice within the 60–90 percent range that section cites, spot H100 instances cost approximately $1.20/GPU-hour instead of $4. For the 175B model, the 1,024-GPU, 2–4 week workload consumes approximately 344,000–688,000 allocated GPU-hours. The on-demand cost is therefore about $1.4M–2.8M, while spot pricing would reduce the bill to roughly $0.4M–0.8M before interruptions. Losing workers can stop a synchronous job’s progress until the runtime detects the loss and recovers. Recovery may restore the original allocation from a checkpoint or use a supported elastic configuration; resizing is not the only path. The checkpoint tax also consumes time. A blocking 30-second checkpoint after every 10 minutes of useful computation adds approximately 5 percent to that compute duration, before lost work and restart delays. Those overheads can erase the hourly discount or make the job miss its deadline, so both completion cost and elapsed time belong in the comparison.
Three practices can improve that comparison. Tuning checkpoint frequency balances write overhead against lost work. With an hourly durable checkpoint, an interruption loses at most one hour on every GPU the synchronous job holds, so for the run above the worst-case loss is 1,024 GPU-hours priced at $1.20/GPU-hour, before restart and replacement delays. Instance diversification broadens replacement options, but a synchronous job still needs compatible devices and adequate connectivity; spreading its ranks across zones can add communication cost without preserving progress after a rank loss. Automated fallback uses on-demand capacity when available under the required placement and deadline constraints. Serving can use interruptible capacity only when remaining replicas, routing, and replacement readiness preserve its service contract.
A critical consideration for cloud-based ML infrastructure is networking between instances. Unlike on-premises clusters where the network topology is custom-designed, cloud instances share the provider’s network fabric with other tenants. Cloud providers may offer placement groups or dedicated networking fabrics that reserve InfiniBand-like or equivalent bandwidth between instances within the same group.
Cross-group or cross-zone communication may traverse infrastructure with lower bandwidth and higher latency. Training frameworks must account for that heterogeneous topology, just as they must account for oversubscribed links or different network tiers in an owned cluster. A placement group is useful when its contract provides the connectivity the job needs; crossing its boundary requires measuring the effect on representative collectives and scaling efficiency.
Renting capacity for the 175B model therefore requires an allocation whose placement contract matches the parallelism plan. Availability and placement limits depend on provider, region, service, and reservation terms. A synchronous collective completes only as fast as its slowest link, so a job whose ranks straddle a placement-group boundary pays that boundary’s latency and bandwidth on every step. The working rule is to keep tensor- and pipeline-parallel groups, which exchange data within every layer or micro-batch, inside one placement group, and let only the less frequent data-parallel gradient traffic cross the boundary. Benchmark representative collectives on the actual allocation before treating nominal GPU availability as usable training capacity.

Infrastructure planning begins when a workload requirement becomes a facility requirement. Model architecture, precision, optimizer state, and batch configuration establish memory needs; the training algorithm and token budget establish work; the deadline establishes required sustained throughput. Parallelization then determines the communication that the fabric must support. Accelerator TDP contributes to the node power envelope, which also includes hosts, memory, and networking, and that envelope constrains rack density and cooling. Planning follows this causal chain from useful work to physical capacity and total cost of ownership.
The first step is workload characterization. Parameter count is only the starting point for memory sizing; activations, optimizer state, temporary buffers, and the chosen sharding or offload policy determine what must fit on each accelerator. The training objective and data budget establish total FLOPs, while acceptable training time determines the sustained FLOP/s requirement. For a frontier model, that budget is itself a scaling-law decision. The compute-optimal allocation of AI Scaling Laws (principle \(\ref{pri-universal-scaling}\)) chooses the parameter and token counts whose product the fleet must deliver. A capacity forecast therefore inherits both the fitted curve and the regime in which it was measured, and a plan that extrapolates past the breakdown conditions of Scaling law breakdown conditions commits capacity to a quality gain the curve no longer promises. Communication depends on the parallelization plan: data-parallel gradient synchronization uses AllReduce, mixture-of-experts routing can stress AllToAll, and pipeline parallelism introduces point-to-point transfers. Inference requirements add another constraint because the hardware that trains a model efficiently may not serve it economically.
With those constraints explicit, bottom-up sizing works from the accelerator outward. Roofline analysis, which compares a phase’s arithmetic intensity with the accelerator’s ridge point, identifies whether a workload phase binds on computation or memory bandwidth; training and serving each contain phases with different limits. Sustained TFLOP/s per dollar helps compare compute-bound phases, while bandwidth per dollar helps compare memory-bound phases. The fleet estimate must also account for communication, synchronization, and the latency or completion-time target.


↩︎ The roofline model and its ridge point are established in Roofline model.
Node sizing decides how many accelerators share a host and which memory tier carries optimizer state, activations, and data staging. For the 175B model, eight GPUs per node with tensor parallelism is a candidate configuration. Roughly 2 TB of host DRAM is an illustrative offload provision, not a requirement implied by parameter count; the state allocation and transfer bandwidth must justify it. Cluster sizing divides the compute budget by the deadline and sustained per-node throughput after model FLOPs utilization (MFU) losses. A maintenance pool and spares add capacity beyond that working allocation; the 5–10 percent allowance used here is a planning assumption to validate against the recovery policy.
Network design follows the primary collective and validates expected scaling against The mathematics of scaling efficiency. The fat-tree switch count and switch-cost estimate in Fat-tree (Clos) networks provide a capacity basis; procurement must price the actual topology and redundancy. A remote direct memory access over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) fabric requires correctly configured congestion control and fabric behavior under synchronized traffic. Packet loss and retransmissions can extend the slowest rank’s completion time, but their effect depends on the transport, load, and collective schedule. Compare measured end-to-end performance and operational cost rather than assuming either fabric is universally cheaper or faster.


↩︎ End-to-end congestion control for lossless RoCE fabrics under synchronized traffic is established in End-to-end congestion control with DCQCN and HPCC.
Power and cooling translate IT load through PUE, then sanity-check rack density locally: a four-node DGX H100 rack is roughly a 33.5 kW design point once GPUs, host systems, networking, power conversion, and cooling overhead are included. Higher density alters the cooling architecture in addition to increasing power consumption. TCO and schedule remain design variables because the cluster must arrive in time to matter, and GPU supply or electrical work often dominates lead time.
The same chain becomes concrete for the 175B training plan. A mixed-precision adaptive moment estimation (Adam) state policy with BF16 parameters and gradients, FP32 master parameters, and two FP32 optimizer moments uses 16 bytes per parameter before activations and temporary buffers. Tensor, pipeline, and optimizer-state sharding can distribute that state. Offload is an additional option when the resulting device budget still does not fit; model size alone does not force every technique simultaneously.
Cluster size then follows from the compute budget. At 6 FLOPs per parameter-token over 175 billion parameters and 300 billion tokens, the run requires 3.15 × 10²³ FLOPs. Using a BF16/FP16 planning basis rather than the FP8 headline peak, each H100 has 989 TFLOP/s peak and an assumed 445.1 TFLOP/s sustained at 45 percent MFU. With 1,024 GPUs, the cluster reaches roughly 455.7 PFLOP/s sustained under that assumption, yielding about 8 days. That token budget is the GPT-3 operating point, which is undertrained relative to compute-optimal allocation (Practical applications in system design). A plan that followed the compute-optimal ratio of tokens to parameters at the same model size would multiply the token count, and with it the cluster-days, so the scaling-law choice moves the capacity plan before any hardware question arises. The 2–4-week calendar allowance is a separate planning range for delays outside the MFU measurement window; communication or stalls already reflected in MFU must not be added again. The TP-8, PP-4, DP-32 configuration also creates tensor, pipeline, and data-parallel traffic whose placement must be validated on the proposed rail-optimized fabric.
The 128 nodes draw 33.5 kW per 4-node rack across 32 racks at approximately 1.1 MW under the stated rack accounting boundary. Cooling feasibility depends on airflow, heat rejection, and rack geometry; this power alone does not require liquid cooling. The 3-year TCO comes to approximately $64 million on-premises; renting the six-runs-per-year workload in the cloud is roughly $25M–50M depending on whether each run lasts 2 or 4 weeks, while continuous cloud use is more expensive. The break-even depends on sustained utilization beyond the initial training run. Procurement and facility schedules must be confirmed against available capacity. A three-month initial deployment is feasible only if its hardware and facility resources are already available within that window; it cannot be inferred from a longer procurement lead time.

The economics of ML infrastructure are not purely about hardware specifications and electricity rates. Capacity lead time is itself an operational risk: a platform that cannot acquire, reserve, or free capacity quickly enough may miss model launches, delay rollback-safe migrations, or run without the headroom needed for incident response.
The GPU supply chain introduces dependencies beyond the accelerator vendor. A deployment requires compatible processors, memory, packaging, and network equipment to arrive together. Supplier concentration matters when apparently independent purchase options depend on the same upstream capacity. A disruption to that shared dependency can delay several orders at once. Capacity planning must therefore examine supplier dependencies as well as quoted delivery dates; placing orders with multiple vendors does not by itself establish independent supply.
Capacity commitments can take much longer to change than model traffic. For planning, consider a large deployment (1,000+ GPUs) with a 6–12-month interval from purchase decision to usable capacity; the actual interval requires supplier and facility confirmation. That delay changes operations. The platform must forecast model growth, reserve refresh capacity, and maintain fallbacks before demand arrives rather than after dashboards turn red.
Facility readiness can lag silicon delivery. Consider a planning scenario with an 18–30-month facility schedule, an 18–24-month electrical substation schedule, a 12–18-month building-shell schedule, and 6–12-month GPU deliveries running concurrently. The longest prerequisite determines the critical path; additional spending cannot be assumed to remove permitting or equipment constraints. Designing headroom can preserve future expansion options, but the benefit requires a site-specific cost comparison. An assumed 30–50 percent electrical reserve at a 10–20 percent facility CapEx premium, for example, must be compared with expected growth and later expansion costs. The physical design of power delivery and cooling belongs to Power and thermal envelopes; the operational point is that its schedule becomes the fleet’s schedule.
The site fixes several of these constraints before any accelerator is purchased. Available power can determine whether the planned fleet fits at all. A 10,000-GPU pod has an estimated facility demand of 10–15 MW under the assumed load and PUE; actual energy cost also depends on operating hours and electricity rates. Legal constraints can also rule out an otherwise economical site, for example when data-residency or cross-border transfer rules govern where the intended data may be processed. Power alleys offer combinations of electricity supply, connectivity, and cooling opportunities, including free cooling, but existing regional capacity does not guarantee a timely connection for a new facility. Reusing a site with electrical infrastructure may shorten one part of the schedule while leaving network and cooling work on the critical path.
Mismatched schedules are expensive in both directions. Hardware delivered before the facility is ready ties up capital without producing useful work, as does a completed facility waiting for accelerators. Phased deployment can reduce the mismatch by commissioning usable capacity in waves while construction continues. An early phase lets the software team validate the distributed-training stack and tune collective kernels on the deployed topology while operators test power distribution and cooling; success at that scale does not establish readiness at full load. The time value of compute is the economic value of making useful capacity available earlier. It can justify premiums for modular halls or temporary colocation when the expected benefit exceeds their additional cost. Projected monthly model value is an input to that comparison, not a guaranteed loss for every month of delay: the estimate must account for launch readiness, demand, operating costs, and whether delayed value can be recovered later.
Hardware access becomes part of the deployment schedule for the 175B model as well. An illustrative 1,024-H100 allocation represents approximately $45 million in node hardware under the $350,000-per-8-GPU-node assumption established in section 12.9.2, but the operational risk extends beyond the purchase price alone. If the allocation arrives a quarter late, the platform may lack capacity for fine-tuning, shadow traffic, canary expansion, or rollback-safe serving during the model launch window. Capacity planning is therefore a reliability control rather than a procurement function alone.



The fleet ledger prices capacity, but it does not say which workloads deserve to consume it. That decision requires a TCO framework covering the ML lifecycle, alongside an assessment of the value each workload creates. The fleet analysis above established the CapEx and OpEx of the physical fleet. The lifecycle definition of TCO that opened the fleet analysis (definition 12.1) now applies workload by workload, widening the hardware lens to training and inference costs, with data and iteration completing a four-component model. Their relative weights depend on workload, traffic, retraining cadence, and operating requirements rather than a fixed distinction between ML and traditional software.


Equation 15 expresses the total cost of ownership as the sum of four distinct cost components, each with different scaling characteristics and optimization levers:
\[\text{TCO}_{\text{ML}} = \TrainingCost + \InferenceCost + \TotalDataCost + \IterationCost \tag{15}\]
Here, \(\TrainingCost\) is the initial training and evaluation cost, \(\InferenceCost\) is recurring serving cost, \(\TotalDataCost\) covers data acquisition, storage, cleaning, and governance, and \(\IterationCost\) captures subsequent experimentation and maintenance. The categories require a common accounting horizon and an explicit allocation rule. If retraining compute is charged to \(\TrainingCost\), it must be excluded from \(\IterationCost\); shared hardware depreciation and energy likewise enter these workload costs once rather than being added again as a separate fleet bill.
Budget projections that count GPU compute and storage can omit substantial operational work. In the illustrative budget of figure 12, engineering labor (20 percent), pipeline maintenance (10 percent), continuous retraining, monitoring, incident response, and governance together equal the visible infrastructure spend. The example shows what an incomplete ledger can miss; its proportions are not universal cost shares. Each organization must measure these obligations within the same accounting horizon as its infrastructure costs.














Figure 12: The TCO iceberg: The analysis separates visible infrastructure costs from operational costs that are easier to omit. In this illustrative budget, the hidden operational costs (engineering labor, pipeline maintenance, retraining, monitoring, incident response, and compliance) together constitute half of total cost.



The decomposition shows why optimization must follow the measured cost structure. An effort centered on experimentation may spend most on \(\IterationCost\), a training campaign on \(\TrainingCost\), and a high-traffic deployment on \(\InferenceCost\). These are workload regimes, not mandatory stages of organizational maturity. The ledger identifies which component merits attention under the current workload mix.



Training cost begins with the price of the GPU-hour. A 30-day run on a 256-node H100 cluster (2,048 GPUs) at the internal fleet rate of $2/GPU-hour is a direct investment of roughly $2.95M. At this scale the cost per training run \((\TrainingCost)\) becomes a design lever that sizes the fleet. Faster time-to-market pushes the planner toward more GPUs, but larger jobs also suffer diminishing parallel efficiency and a higher probability of hardware interruption. Total cost is therefore not merely a function of compute time; it must account for data staging, checkpointing, and the cost of recovery from interruptions.
Organizations must decide when to buy additional permanent capacity and when to recover useful throughput through better orchestration or model optimization. The decision also has an energy dimension. Less electricity consumption reduces the energy bill at a fixed tariff, but emissions depend on the energy source and time of use; a lower price alone does not establish lower carbon impact. The cost model below accounts for purchased energy, while an emissions comparison requires the corresponding carbon intensity.
Equation 16 formalizes training cost as a function of GPU count, training duration, non-energy accelerator-hour rates, data center energy overhead, and failure overhead:
\[\TrainingCost = \AcceleratorCount \times \BaselineTrainingDuration\times \left(\AcceleratorHourlyPrice+ \DevicePower \times \ElectricityPrice\times \text{PUE}\right) \times (1 + \FailureOverheadFraction) \tag{16}\]
where:

\(\AcceleratorCount\) is the number of GPUs allocated
\(\BaselineTrainingDuration\) is the baseline training duration in hours before the additional failure overhead
\(\AcceleratorHourlyPrice\) is the non-energy accelerator-hour cost
\(\DevicePower\) is per-GPU power draw in kW
\(\ElectricityPrice\) is the electricity price
\(\text{PUE}\) is the power usage effectiveness multiplier applied to the energy term
\(\FailureOverheadFraction\) is additional time from failures and recovery as a fraction of the baseline duration

The PUE factor captures facility energy overhead: a PUE of 1.1 means 10 percent additional energy relative to IT energy. It applies to energy consumption, not to the whole accelerator-hour rate. This equation uses GPU power as a simplified IT boundary; a full facility estimate must also include host, network, and storage power. The failure overhead \(\FailureOverheadFraction\) adds recovery time beyond the baseline. Checkpointing or restart time already included in measured baseline duration must not be charged again through this factor.


↩︎ Cluster mean time between failures and the checkpoint interval it implies are established in Failure Analysis at Scale.



Consider training a large language model:

Configuration: 256 H100 GPUs for 14 days
Base non-energy accelerator-hour rate (scenario choice): $3.50/GPU-hour
Energy adder: 700 W at $0.07/kWh and PUE 1.1 adds $0.05/GPU-hour
Effective rate: $3.55/GPU-hour
Failure overhead: 10 percent (scenario assumption relative to baseline duration)

\(\TrainingCost = 256 \times (14 \times 24) \times (\$3.50 + \$0.05) \times 1.1 \approx \$335,892\)
If this model requires quarterly retraining, annual training cost reaches approximately $1.3M. However, training cost often represents a small fraction of total TCO for production systems serving millions of users.






Serving can outgrow the training bill.
Inference costs can dominate when cumulative serving demand outweighs training and iteration costs. Equation 17 estimates continuously provisioned capacity from average daily demand and sustained per-GPU throughput measured under representative batching, the target latency SLO, and operating headroom. Daily volume alone does not size traffic peaks; the estimate requires a separate check against the arrival pattern, workload mix, and scaling response:
\[\AcceleratorCount = \left\lceil \frac{\DailyQueryVolume}{86{,}400 \times \AcceleratorTargetQueryRate} \right\rceil, \qquad \InferenceCost = \AcceleratorCount \times 24 \times 365 \times \AcceleratorHourlyPrice \tag{17}\]
where:

\(\DailyQueryVolume\) is the daily query volume
\(\AcceleratorTargetQueryRate\) is sustained queries per second per GPU at the target latency SLO, including batching and operating headroom
\(\AcceleratorCount\) is the integer number of continuously provisioned GPUs
\(\AcceleratorHourlyPrice\) is the hourly GPU cost

The key insight is that inference cost grows with query volume in discrete capacity steps. Utilization and batching reduce cost only when they improve measured throughput at the target latency SLO; they should not be applied again as independent divisors.



For capacity planning, express inference cost in terms of required GPU-seconds per query:
\[\InferenceCost = \AnnualQueryVolume\times \AcceleratorSecondsPerQuery\times \frac{\AcceleratorHourlyPrice}{3600}\]
where \(\AcceleratorSecondsPerQuery\) is allocated GPU-seconds divided by completed queries over the same accounting period. Allocated time includes idle headroom and provisioned capacity, so this definition reproduces the continuous-provisioning bill above. Measuring only busy kernel time instead estimates service demand and excludes those costs; it is not an equivalent billing formula without an allocation policy.



Data costs can grow faster than the user base when per-user history, transfer volume, and feature processing all rise together, even though each term below is linear in its own volume. Equation 18 decomposes data cost into three components that scale differently: storage cost \(\DataStorageCost\), egress cost \(\DataEgressCost\) for moving data out over the network, and processing cost \(\DataPipelineProcessingCost\):
\[\TotalDataCost = \DataStorageCost + \DataEgressCost+ \DataPipelineProcessingCost \tag{18}\]
Storage costs grow with data retention requirements: \[\DataStorageCost = \StoredDataVolume \times \StoragePrice \times \StorageRetentionTime\]
where \(\StoredDataVolume\) is a fixed data volume in GB, \(\StoragePrice\) is the monthly storage rate, and \(\StorageRetentionTime\) is its retention period in months. This product prices one volume retained at a constant rate; a growing dataset requires accounting for each period’s stored volume rather than multiplying the final volume by the entire history.
Egress costs scale with data transfer volume: \[\DataEgressCost= \TransferredDataVolume\times \EgressPrice\]
At the scenario egress rate of $0.09/GB, repeated transfers can become a significant cost driver for multi-region deployments and training data distribution. The applicable rate depends on the source, destination, and service contract; the estimate must distinguish billable transfers from included traffic.
Processing costs scale with compute requirements for extract, transform, load, feature engineering, and data validation: \[\DataPipelineProcessingCost= \ProcessedDataVolume\times \ProcessingPrice\]
Data processing costs often surprise organizations: a feature engineering pipeline processing 10 TB daily at $0.02/GB costs $73,000 annually.



Development costs capture the engineering investment in experimentation and model improvement. Equation 19 formalizes this as the experiment count multiplied by the combined per-experiment engineering and compute costs:
\[\IterationCost= \ExperimentCount\times (\PerExperimentEngineeringCost+ \PerExperimentComputeCost) \tag{19}\]
where:

\(\ExperimentCount\) is the number of experiments conducted
\(\PerExperimentEngineeringCost\) is the engineering cost per experiment
\(\PerExperimentComputeCost\) is the compute cost per experiment

Experiments that do not improve production metrics still incur costs. If 90 percent produce no improvement and every experiment has the same cost, expenditure per improving experiment is 10\(\times\) the per-experiment cost. A negative result can nevertheless rule out an unproductive direction or expose a risk. Experiment infrastructure should reduce avoidable engineering and compute work while preserving that learning value, rather than optimize the fraction of positive results alone.

This simple payback assumes savings remain constant over the interval; recovered capacity counts as cash savings only when it reduces expenditure or avoids a planned purchase.
The breakeven equation helps compare specific investments once their implementation costs and recurring savings are estimated.
