The subsections in this section follow those decisions rather than treating hardware security as a catalog of attacks. Hardware bugs test processor isolation. Physical attacks, fault injection, and leaky interfaces test whether direct access can change the system after software controls pass. Side-channel attacks test whether computation leaks through observable signals. Supply chain risks, from a single counterfeit part to a compromised part number, test whether the deployed component is the one the architecture assumes.


Hardware bugs answer the first deployment decision: whether processor isolation can be trusted after software access control appears to pass. ML teams must treat that isolation as an empirical claim, not a default guarantee. Attackers can exploit design flaws to access, manipulate, or extract sensitive data, breaching the confidentiality and integrity that users and services depend on. One of the most notable examples came with the discovery of Meltdown and Spectre,11 two vulnerabilities in modern processors that allow malicious programs to bypass memory isolation and read the data of other applications and the operating system (Lipp et al. 2018; Kocher et al. 2019).
11 Meltdown/Spectre: These attacks exposed isolation failures in affected processor families through transient execution and microarchitectural state. Mitigation costs depend on the processor, operating system, and workload, so an ML fleet must remeasure its data-loading and serving paths after applying protections.
Lipp, M., M. Schwarz, D. Gruss, T. Prescher, W. Haas, J. Horn, S. Mangard, et al. 2018. “Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space.” Proceedings of the 27th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security), 973–90.

Kocher, Paul, Jann Horn, Anders Fogh, Daniel Genkin, Daniel Gruss, Werner Haas, Mike Hamburg, et al. 2019. “Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution.” 2019 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 1–19. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2019.00002.
Spectre exploits speculative execution, a performance optimization in which a CPU executes instructions along a predicted path before it knows whether that path is correct. An attacker influences the prediction so that a victim transiently accesses sensitive data. Meltdown instead exploits affected processors that transiently make data available before enforcing the access restriction. In both cases, discarding the unauthorized or mispredicted computation can leave observable traces in microarchitectural state, such as CPU caches. Software-visible execution can therefore respect a boundary while the traces of transient execution leak across it.
Further research identified related transient-execution attacks, including Foreshadow, ZombieLoad, and RIDL, against different microarchitectural structures in affected processors. Their existence motivates examining each component’s isolation assumptions without assuming that every processor shares the same vulnerability. ML systems pair CPUs with GPUs, Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), or custom accelerators. A compromise can propagate across this heterogeneous stack when components share sensitive data, keys, or privileged access; the threat model must trace those relationships.
For a fleet, the consequence can be cross-tenant exposure. Host processors stage data for accelerators, run tokenizers and preprocessing, and hold decrypted keys. When tenants share a vulnerable host and the required attack conditions hold, a transient-execution flaw can expose sensitive state before any accelerator is involved. Mitigations depend on the vulnerability and deployment: restricting simultaneous multithreading or clearing affected microarchitectural state at isolation boundaries can reduce throughput on the data-loading and serving paths that keep accelerators fed. The fleet must remeasure those paths after applying the relevant protections rather than assume a fixed tax.
Such vulnerabilities pose concern in privacy-sensitive domains like healthcare, where ML systems routinely handle patient data. A breach could violate privacy regulations such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), leading to significant legal and ethical consequences. Similar regulatory risks apply globally. For personal data within its territorial and material scope, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) authorizes fines up to 2 percent of total worldwide annual turnover when an organization fails to implement appropriate security measures, and up to 4 percent for violations of its core processing principles or data-subject rights (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016).
Hardware security therefore extends beyond physical tamper prevention to architectural isolation: preventing processors, accelerators, and memory systems from leaking across boundaries the software assumes are sealed. Mitigations often carry performance costs, especially for data-bound ML workloads, so confidential computing (section 13.8.4) and trusted execution environments (TEEs) must be evaluated as capacity and latency decisions as well as security decisions.



Physical attacks answer the second deployment decision: what an adversary can observe or modify by touching the device, sensor, memory, firmware, or debug interface. Physical access introduces paths that a network access policy does not govern. An exposed debug port may permit memory reads, a replacement sensor may supply false inputs, and a writable firmware interface may change execution. Encryption and authentication remain useful when their keys and enforcement mechanisms stay protected; the threat model must identify which physical paths bypass those protections.
The failure mode depends on what the attacker can touch. Replacing a drone’s navigation module, swapping the sensor of a biometric access system, or misaligning a vehicle’s cameras changes system behavior without changing a single model weight. In edge fleets such as the phone-class devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet), the coordinator does not control clients’ physical environments. Device ownership does not automatically defeat protected storage or execution, but the coordinator cannot infer the integrity of a client’s data or updates from ownership or enrollment alone.
Internal components create the same risk at a lower layer. A hardware trojan inserted during chip fabrication can remain dormant until a specific input or state triggers it, then leak outputs, corrupt computation, or degrade performance in ways that are difficult to diagnose after deployment. Memory chips and accelerator buses can expose model parameters or training data when an attacker has physical access. Data centers are not exempt: an implant installed by someone with sufficient facility access can monitor administrative credentials or data streams and provide a persistent path into training and inference pipelines.
The defensive implication is that physical-access analysis belongs in the system architecture rather than solely in device packaging. Disabling production debug interfaces closes one access path; signed firmware and secure boot constrain which code can execute. Tamper detection can signal interference, while attestation and supply chain checks provide evidence about measured state and component provenance. These controls address different parts of the trust boundary, so none alone establishes that sensor inputs or runtime computations remain correct after deployment.



Fault injection is the active version of the physical-access decision: the attacker does not replace the model artifact but changes the computation while it runs. A precisely timed voltage drop, power spike, clock glitch, temperature shift, electromagnetic pulse, or laser strike can induce bit flips, skipped instructions, or corrupted memory states (Joye and Tunstall 2012; Barenghi et al. 2010; Hutter et al. 2009; Amiel et al. 2006; Skorobogatov 2009; Skorobogatov and Anderson 2003). For ML systems, those faults can force incorrect outputs, bypass security checks, degrade reliability, or expose internal state for later reverse engineering.

The ML-specific risk is that a small computation fault can become a semantic failure. An embedded classifier running on a microcontroller may misclassify a safety-important input, while a fault in memory or control logic may expose proprietary weights or architecture details. Unlike ordinary random faults, adversarially timed faults are chosen to land on computations the model or security protocol depends on.
The experiments of Breier et al. (2018) targeted activation-function implementations on a microcontroller with timed laser faults. Figure 11 identifies the vulnerable instruction in the observed ReLU implementation. For a positive accumulator, the copy instructions assign the activation to the output, and the following jmp end normally skips the zeroing block. A laser pulse timed to suppress that jump makes execution fall through into the clear instructions, overwriting the positive output with zero and forcing the neuron inactive. The conditional brge instruction is not the skipped instruction in this example, and the fault changes executed control flow rather than any stored model weight.

Fault injection attacks can also be combined with side-channel analysis, where attackers first observe power or timing characteristics to infer model structure or data flow. This reconnaissance helps them time faults against specific layers or operations, such as activation functions or final decision layers. The resulting effect still depends on the implementation, the induced fault, and any checks that detect or contain it.
Embedded and edge ML systems can be vulnerable when exposed hardware combines with resource constraints that limit runtime defenses. Access to system buses, memory, or power supplies can give attackers opportunities to induce faults, even when software access controls remain intact. The relevant protection comes from the device and execution stack: a lightweight model does not itself establish whether memory has error correction, computations have redundant checks, or packaging resists probing.
The defense must combine physical hardening with runtime evidence. Tamper-resistant packaging restricts access, while design obfuscation makes targets harder to locate without itself preventing interference. Error-correcting memory and redundant checks can detect or correct some induced errors; secure firmware constrains code changes but does not prevent a fault during execution. Model-output and sensor-consistency monitors can catch some fault-induced behavior that escapes lower layers; MAVFI demonstrates this pattern for micro-aerial-vehicle workloads with anomaly detection and recovery (Hsiao et al. 2023). These protections are hardest in cost- and power-constrained edge systems, where extra cryptographic hardware or redundancy may be unaffordable, so resilience has to be designed across the electrical, firmware, software, and system layers.

With an attacker, shared electrical resources can provide a path for interference. Co-tenants on a shared FPGA have induced timing faults remotely by drawing enough current to drop the supply voltage (Gnad et al. 2017). The check-and-verify defenses of Check-and-Verify Defenses Against Silent Data Corruption can therefore serve security as well as reliability. Their security coverage requires separate evaluation, however, because an attacker may target both the computation and its check rather than induce the independent errors a reliability analysis assumes.

Side-channel attacks answer the third deployment decision: whether computation is observable even when interfaces are locked down. They break the assumption that only explicit interfaces reveal information. Instead of targeting software or network vulnerabilities directly, these attacks use hardware characteristics such as power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, timing behavior, or acoustic signals to extract sensitive information.
The core premise of a side-channel attack is that a device’s operation can leak information through observable physical signals. Such leaks may originate from the electrical power the device consumes (Kocher et al. 1999), the electromagnetic fields it emits (Gandolfi et al. 2001), the time required to complete computations, or even the acoustic noise it produces. Carefully measuring and analyzing these signals allows attackers to infer internal system states or recover secret data.

ML accelerators executing inference are exposed to physical leakage as other computing devices are. A matrix multiplication on an edge accelerator can draw current in a pattern correlated with the weight values and input activations being processed. An attacker who can measure that signal may infer properties of the computation, but recovery depends on measurement quality, implementation details, and knowledge or control of inputs. Additional samples help only if the observable signal carries the relevant information. The side-channel surface for a deployed model therefore encompasses both the cryptographic operations protecting its keys and the inference computation itself.
One of the most widely studied examples involves Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) implementations, and its lessons inform the analysis of ML workloads. An implementation can leak information about a key without an attacker breaking the cipher’s mathematical construction. The same distinction between an algorithm and its implementation applies to the ReLU activations, softmax normalizations, and weight-load sequences that constitute a forward pass.
A useful example of this attack technique is a power analysis of a password authentication process (Kocher et al. 2011). Consider a device that verifies a 5-byte password (0x61, 0x52, 0x77, 0x6A, 0x73) received one byte at a time over a serial interface. With the correct password, the power profile stays stable across all five bytes. Figure 12 shows what happens when only the first three bytes are correct. The power pattern tracks the correct-password profile through the third byte (0x61, 0x52, 0x77), then jumps when the device rejects the fourth byte (0x42) and halts authentication. An entirely wrong password (0x30 repeated) produces the same jump immediately after the first byte.

For this early-exit comparison, the position of the jump tells the attacker how many leading bytes are correct. If repeated guesses are permitted and the signal is distinguishable, this collapses a search over all \(256^5\) five-byte strings into five successive searches of 256 values each. ML inference can expose analogous data-dependent behavior, although it does not generally reveal a password-like sequence of correct guesses. A microcontroller that branches on a ReLU input’s sign or hardware that skips zero values can produce signals correlated with activation sparsity. Recovering layer topology or parameters requires an additional inference step supported by the implementation and available measurements; a measurable power signal is where that analysis starts, not where it ends.
The underlying lesson is physical: computation emits signals, whether as the sound of a cipher machine (Wright and Greengrass 1987) or of a laptop running a cipher (Genkin et al. 2017), the clicks of a keyboard (Asonov and Agrawal 2004), or the current drawn by a processor. For a fleet, the important variant needs no probe at all. On shared hardware, the shared resource itself becomes the measurement instrument. Researchers built a power monitor from logic in their own region of an FPGA shared among users and used it to recover a cryptographic key computed in another user’s region (Zhao and Suh 2018). The sharing that makes multi-tenancy economical turns caches, memory bandwidth, and power delivery into channels between tenants.

Machine learning systems inherit this risk when accelerators or edge devices process sensitive data near an observable signal. A local speech-recognition device may leak timing or power patterns correlated with commands. An accelerator may reveal layer structure, parameter access patterns, or batch shape through timing, power, or electromagnetic traces. Side-channel defense therefore asks which signals are observable in the deployment environment and whether shielding, constant-time execution, noise, monitoring, or physical access controls can reduce the signal enough to preserve the trust boundary.



Leaky interfaces sit between physical access and lifecycle trust: every diagnostic, update, or communication interface is also a security boundary. Side-channel attacks leak through physical signals; leaky interfaces expose information or accept unverified inputs through channels the system already provides. These access points often go unnoticed during system design, yet they give attackers direct entry points to extract data, manipulate functionality, or introduce malicious code.
A leaky interface is any access point that reveals more information than intended or accepts commands from the wrong actor. The common causes are weak authentication, missing encryption, inadequate isolation, and development interfaces left exposed in production. Consumer, medical, and industrial systems have repeatedly shown the pattern: Wi-Fi-enabled baby monitors have exposed unsecured remote access ports,12 and pacemaker vulnerabilities13 have shown how wireless interfaces can become safety-critical control channels.
12 IoT Device Vulnerabilities: Default credentials, unencrypted communications, and outdated firmware create access paths into connected devices. A compromised smart camera can supply manipulated inputs or participate in distributed attacks; if it also contributes training data or federated updates, that path can carry poisoning attempts. The consequences depend on the device’s role and permissions.13 Medical Device Security: Connected medical devices require secure maintenance over long operating lifetimes. In a device that uses ML, compromised inputs, weights, or preprocessing can alter clinical behavior without stopping the device. Traditional device software can also fail silently, so the additional ML requirement is to evaluate learned behavior alongside firmware integrity and physical safety controls.14 Debug Port Vulnerabilities: JTAG and Serial Wire Debug can expose memory and execution control when debug access remains enabled and authorized checks are absent or bypassed. An attacker may then recover weights accessible in plaintext, but an exposed connector alone does not defeat correctly enforced debug locks or encryption whose keys remain unavailable.Debug ports14 left enabled on production devices are the canonical case. A consumer smart lightbulb, for example, exposed unencrypted Wi-Fi credentials through such a port, giving attackers a path into the home network without defeating any network defense.
The data center has its own privileged maintenance interfaces. A server’s baseboard management controller commonly supports power control, console access, and firmware management over an out-of-band network, independently of the host operating system. Compromising its credentials or firmware can therefore expose control paths that host access policies do not govern. The resulting reach depends on network segmentation, controller privileges, and firmware-update protections. The attestation checks of section 13.8.4 help only when trusted measurements cover the affected components and the attacker cannot forge the evidence or alter the verifier’s approved state. The same reasoning applies at the edge, where a maintenance interface that lacks authentication can expose user data, alter model weights, or disable security features.
Securing interfaces is therefore inventory work as much as cryptography. Strong authentication, encrypted communication, anomaly detection, access-control policy, periodic audit, and zero-trust defaults all serve the same principle: every interface must justify what it exposes and who can use it.



Supply chain risks extend the provenance decision from a single interface to every component and every stage of its life. The smallest unit is the counterfeit part. A counterfeit processor, memory module, sensor, or network device may look and function like a genuine one while degrading faster, failing under load, or containing hidden circuitry, so procurement becomes part of the security boundary. Organizations that unknowingly deploy such parts may also violate safety, privacy, or cybersecurity obligations, which makes component provenance evidence that the deployed system matches the certified one.
Figure 13 maps the full lifecycle through design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, and deployment. Each stage presents opportunities for tampering or substitution: recycled electronic waste can be relabeled as new, distributors can mix cloned parts into legitimate shipments, and insiders at manufacturing facilities can embed hardware trojans that routine functional tests may miss. Micrography, X-ray screening, and functional testing provide different evidence, with coverage and cost determined by the suspected modification. Procurement therefore needs risk-based provenance controls as well as inspection; passing a functional test does not establish a component’s origin or exclude dormant malicious behavior.
Fleet procurement changes the shape of this risk. A training cluster is bought in bulk from a small number of part numbers, so each of the 128 nodes of the reference cluster carries the same accelerators, network adapters, management controller, and firmware images as every other. A compromised shared design, firmware release, or production batch can therefore affect many nodes at once. Replication does not remove a vulnerability shared by the replicas, although one compromised unit is evidence about its part number, not proof that every unit carrying it is affected. The provenance bound on trust (principle \(\ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}\)) applies to silicon and firmware as much as to data. Supplier, batch, and firmware records help identify the affected population; supplier concentration increases common dependencies even when those records are complete.







Figure 13: Hardware supply chain attack surface: Each lifecycle stage admits its own compromise (red arrows) and needs its own assurance evidence (green gates); no single check covers the chain, and dashed lines carry each missed compromise forward to deployment. Unlike software, which can be patched remotely, a compromise that survives to deployment often requires physical replacement.



Figure 13 also shows the economic asymmetry. Software vulnerabilities can often be patched remotely, but a hardware compromise may require physical replacement. That possibility adds replacement cost, service interruption, and revalidation to the expected loss and strengthens the case for preventive checks before deployment.
A disputed 2018 case illustrates the importance of separating allegations from verified compromise. Bloomberg Businessweek reported that state-sponsored actors had implanted surveillance chips on server motherboards manufactured by Supermicro (Robertson and Riley 2018). Apple, Amazon, and Supermicro publicly denied the claims, and industry experts questioned the lack of verifiable technical evidence. The dispute does not establish that the named organizations deployed compromised hardware or lacked adequate provenance controls. It instead motivates a general engineering requirement: claims about deployed components need evidence from the relevant fabrication, assembly, distribution, and integration stages. Industrial policy, including the CHIPS and Science Act (United States Congress 2022), addresses a different level of the supply chain from component assurance. Component validation, runtime monitoring, attestation, and hardware roots of trust provide deployment checks whose coverage must be assessed against the suspected compromise.

The engineering takeaway is that hardware trust must be evidenced continuously across design, fabrication, procurement, deployment, and retirement. A trusted execution environment (TEE) isolates selected code and data from parts of the surrounding host. Attestation supplies cryptographic evidence about that protected environment before another component entrusts it with secrets. Neither mechanism establishes that a model is behaviorally correct, and both depend on an explicit set of trusted hardware and software components.

A reusable attack model can amortize its training effort across repeated attempts or multiple targets. Its effectiveness still depends on the observations, access, and resources available to the attacker. The defender must therefore evaluate automated probing against the same latency and capacity limits that constrain ordinary service.
Examining these offensive capabilities serves a defensive purpose. Security professionals have long recognized that effective defense requires understanding attack methodologies. This principle underlies penetration testing,15 red team exercises, and threat modeling throughout the cybersecurity industry.
15 Penetration Testing: Authorized simulated attacks evaluate weaknesses within an agreed scope. Infrastructure-focused tests may omit adversarial inputs, extraction through legitimate API queries, or training-data poisoning. An ML assessment must explicitly include these paths and the attacker’s permitted access; calling an assessment a penetration test says nothing about which of these paths it covered.The side-channel case makes this change concrete: the secret remains in hardware, but a learned classifier extracts information from the signals that hardware exposes.


To illustrate these offensive capabilities concretely, consider a specific case where machine learning transforms traditional attack methodologies. One of the most well-known and reproducible demonstrations of deep-learning-assisted side-channel analysis is the SCAAML framework (Side-Channel Attacks Assisted with Machine Learning) (Bursztein et al. 2024; Bursztein and Picod 2019). Developed by researchers at Google, SCAAML provides a practical implementation of this learned side-channel pipeline.
Figure 14 illustrates data-dependent power consumption during an AES S-box substitution. The left panel places a possible leakage interval within a longer trace; the right panel magnifies a schematic difference between processed values. Hamming weight counts the ones in a binary value: 1111 has weight 4, 0101 has weight 2, and 0000 has weight 0. The drawing orders amplitudes by that weight to illustrate a leakage model, not a measured law of CMOS switching. Actual leakage depends on circuit structure, state transitions, noise, and countermeasures. A classifier must learn a reproducible relationship in measured traces before these differences can support key recovery.














Figure 14: Power traces: Cryptographic computations reveal subtle, data-dependent variations in power consumption that reflect internal states during specific operations. The traces are schematic: amplitudes are illustrative and follow the Hamming-weight ordering rather than a measured capture.



Statistical side-channel methods use an explicit leakage model or profiles learned from measurements. A neural network instead learns features from labeled power traces and their corresponding intermediate values, such as the output of an S-box operation. Predicting an intermediate value is only one step in key recovery. The attacker combines those predictions with known input data and the algorithm’s relationships to score candidate key bytes across traces. Success requires the learned relationship to generalize to traces not used in training; a flexible classifier does not by itself guarantee that transfer.
In a SCAAML guide, Bursztein and Picod (2019) used convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to recover AES keys from power traces collected on an STM32F415 microcontroller running the open-source TinyAES implementation. The models predicted intermediate values of the AES algorithm, such as the output of the S-box16 in the first round, from power traces. The demonstration recovered a full 128-bit key by combining byte-level predictions. Its target was an unprotected implementation, so the number of traces it needed sets no expectation for devices with masking, shuffling, or other countermeasures.

Subsequent work expanded on this approach by introducing long-range models capable of exploiting broader temporal dependencies in the traces, improving performance even under noise and desynchronization (Bursztein et al. 2024). These developments highlight the potential for machine learning models to serve as offensive cryptanalysis tools, especially in the analysis of secure hardware.

Learned side-channel models can reduce the analysis effort or trace count of an attack when suitable training data and measurable leakage are available. In a fleet built from a few part numbers, reusable attack models create correlated risk. Transfer still requires evaluation across devices, firmware, measurement conditions, and countermeasures; matching part numbers alone do not guarantee it. The defensive response must address both the attacker’s access to measurements and the leakage of the computation. This combination leads to layered defenses around data, models, and execution infrastructure.

An adversary who bypasses an API rate limit may still face authorization checks, restricted outputs, or an isolated execution environment. These controls protect different assets and constrain different actions. Secure ML systems use defense in depth to limit what follows from a failed mechanism. The benefit depends on whether the remaining controls retain their enforcement power; several checks that share the same compromised credential or runtime do not provide independent barriers.
Figure 16 groups countermeasures across four architectural tiers. Hardware mechanisms include trusted execution environments, secure boot, HSM key custody, and physical unclonable function (PUF) device identities. Platform controls include container isolation, network segmentation, access control, and runtime telemetry. The model layer includes adversarial training,17 input validation, output monitoring, and rate limiting, while data-layer controls include differential privacy, encryption at rest, provenance tracking, and secure aggregation. These tiers partition defenses by the layer they protect, which differs from the data, model, interface, and infrastructure layers of section 13.6.1.1 that partition where an adversary enters. The two maps line up except at the interface. Interface controls such as rate limiting, input validation, and output monitoring guard the model’s query boundary, so the stack files them with the model tier, but the serving platform beneath enforces them, which is why the runtime-monitoring discussion below treats them as platform mechanisms. Infrastructure threats fall to the hardware and platform tiers. The dependency arrow highlights the runtime support that many controls require. A compromised host can expose raw records or alter a privacy mechanism before release, but it does not retroactively invalidate the differential privacy guarantee of an artifact already produced by a correctly implemented mechanism. The dependency analysis must identify the protected asset and release, not assume that every control fails together.

The result means that a robustness intervention must be reevaluated against privacy invariants rather than assumed to improve every security property at once.

Layered defense (also known as defense in depth) makes these dependencies explicit. Differential privacy bounds what a specified release reveals about an individual’s contribution; it does not protect a separate copy of raw training records from theft. Federated learning changes where training data reside but does not, by itself, bound what updates reveal. Hardware isolation can protect execution within its threat model without establishing that an application follows the intended data policy. Combining these mechanisms requires stating each guarantee and checking which assumptions the other layers preserve.







Figure 16: Layered defense stack: Controls are grouped by the layer they protect, from the silicon root of trust through platform isolation and model safeguards to data privacy. A compromised component can undermine controls that rely on its execution or stored state. These runtime dependencies must be checked against each control’s threat model; a correctly released differentially private artifact retains its release-level guarantee.



The stack also orders the analysis. A rate limit enforced by the serving platform is only as reliable as that platform, and the platform is only as reliable as the firmware and processor it runs on. The walk through the defenses therefore follows the stack rather than the model lifecycle. It starts at the bottom tier, where trust is anchored in silicon, then covers the platform controls that govern how a model is deployed and monitored, the model-tier choices that shape the learned function itself, and finally the data layer, where the remaining question is what a correctly computed release reveals.


Software defenses depend on the components that enforce them. If an attacker compromises the operating system through a privilege escalation exploit, checks enforced solely by that operating system can be disabled or falsified. An unlocked debug interface can similarly expose execution state that software policy was intended to protect. Controls enforced in a separate trust domain may remain effective, which motivates identifying exactly where each security decision is made and who can alter it.
This limitation motivates hardware security mechanisms: protections that operate below the software layer and remain useful even when the operating system, runtime, or application code is compromised. Hardware-based security creates a root of trust anchored in silicon, which gives higher-layer defenses something to rely on. Machine learning systems deployed in edge devices, embedded systems, and untrusted cloud infrastructure often depend on that anchor because the attacker may have physical access, co-tenant access, or administrative access to parts of the stack.
The trust boundary becomes especially important when systems must satisfy regulatory requirements. Healthcare ML systems handling protected health information under HIPAA must implement technical safeguards such as access control, audit controls, integrity protection, and transmission security. Systems processing personal data within GDPR’s territorial and material scope must also demonstrate appropriate technical and organizational measures, including data-protection-by-design principles. Hardware security does not satisfy these requirements alone, but it provides the boot, runtime, key-management, and device-identity guarantees that software controls often assume.
Each hardware security primitive answers one trust question. Secure boot asks whether the system started from authentic code. Trusted execution environments (TEEs) ask whether sensitive computation can run despite an untrusted host. Hardware security modules (HSMs) ask where cryptographic keys can be generated and used without exposing them to ordinary memory. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) ask whether a device can demonstrate a hardware-bound identity that is harder to copy than a software credential. These hardware security mechanisms separate startup integrity, runtime isolation, key custody, and device identity, and table 8 compares them after each has been examined. They work best when composed across hardware, firmware, and software boundaries rather than selected as standalone products.


A TEE is first a trust-boundary decision: which parts of the model, key material, input data, or attestation path must remain protected even if the surrounding host is compromised. A trusted execution environment (TEE) is the hardware-isolated processor region that implements that boundary. TEEs enforce confidentiality, integrity, and runtime isolation within a stated threat model. Their guarantee depends on the trusted hardware, firmware, and code inside the protected boundary; isolating a vulnerable application does not make that application correct.
In the context of machine learning, TEEs are important for preserving the confidentiality of models, securing sensitive user data during inference, and protecting execution from host-level tampering. Correct execution of an approved model says nothing about whether its predictions are accurate or safe. For example, a TEE can protect model parameters from being extracted by malicious software running on the same device, or ensure that computations involving biometric inputs, including facial data or fingerprint data, are performed securely. This capability is required in applications where model integrity, user privacy, or regulatory compliance are nonnegotiable.
Isolation of this kind appears at two scales. On consumer devices, a dedicated security coprocessor such as Apple’s Secure Enclave keeps credentials and biometric features protected even if the application processor kernel is compromised (Apple 2024b). In the data center, the relevant form is the confidential virtual machine, which protects an entire guest, including its model weights and user inputs, from the hypervisor and host operators, and which the fleet admits into a job only after remote attestation (section 13.8.4).
Remote attestation supports the distributed trust decision: before components exchange sensitive data or model updates, a verifier checks fresh evidence about measured code and its hardware-protected boundary against an admission policy. Binding a communication key to that evidence connects the accepted identity to the ensuing channel. Attestation alone does not establish the correctness of every runtime operation. For ML, protection follows the computation: inputs, weights, and activations remain covered only while their processing and storage stay within the chosen boundary. Memory is one deployment cost. The protected working set competes for platform-specific memory capacity. Some implementations support protected paging beyond resident capacity, so overflow can impose substantial movement costs rather than an absolute model-size limit. Compression or partitioning changes those costs and may also change which values remain protected.
TEE implementations combine execution isolation, protected memory, integrity mechanisms, and protected key storage in different ways. The isolation boundary may surround an application region, a secure processor mode, or an entire virtual machine. Access controls restrict which agents can read protected state, while memory encryption and authentication can extend protection beyond the processor boundary where the architecture supports them. Persistent storage needs its own protection when data leave protected memory. Within the execution boundary, computation uses plaintext directly. The deployment analysis must therefore trace where plaintext exists, which components can access it, and which integrity and freshness checks the platform actually supplies.
Platforms differ mainly in the size of the protected boundary. ARM TrustZone18 splits a mobile or embedded processor into secure and normal worlds. Intel SGX isolates individual enclaves inside an application’s address space on servers, and confidential virtual machines such as those built on AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX move the boundary out to a whole guest operating system, which lets unmodified ML serving stacks run inside it at the cost of a larger trusted code base.
18 ARM TrustZone: Introduced in 2004, TrustZone partitions an ARM processor into secure and normal “worlds” with hardware-enforced isolation. Its presence on a device does not by itself protect an ML deployment: the model, keys, and data path must actually be placed inside the secure world, which depends on whether the device vendor exposes secure-world applications beyond key storage.Figure 17 diagrams the isolation boundaries and bus interfaces of Apple’s system-on-chip (SoC) Secure Enclave. Its dedicated processor, true random number generator (TRNG), public key accelerator (PKA), and cryptographic engines operate separately from the application processor, which communicates through a mailbox interface. A memory protection engine encrypts and authenticates the enclave’s external memory, while protected key paths support storage encryption (Apple 2024b). This example demonstrates isolation of designated security operations and state. It does not imply that arbitrary application model weights or activations reside inside the Secure Enclave; their protection depends on the execution and data paths the platform supports.

The application processor reaches it only through a mailbox, enclave memory in DRAM passes through a memory protection engine, and storage keys go directly to the inline AES engine, so a compromised application processor never holds them. This architecture underpins the secure deployment of machine learning applications on consumer devices. For example, Apple’s Face ID system uses a Secure Enclave-protected biometric pipeline: TrueDepth camera data is transformed by a protected portion of the Neural Engine into a mathematical representation, then compared with enrolled facial data protected by the Secure Enclave. Face images captured during normal operation are discarded after the representation is computed, and Face ID data remains encrypted and device-local rather than being sent to Apple or included in backups (Apple 2024a). The ML systems lesson is that biometric models, templates, and comparison logic must be bound to hardware isolation and secure update paths, rather than treated as ordinary application data.

Apple. 2024a. Facial Matching Security. Apple Platform Security.
Trusted execution environments carry costs in every C³ dimension. Protected memory, memory encryption, and transitions between trusted and untrusted modes can add compute and latency, and battery-powered devices also pay in energy for secure memory accesses and cryptographic work. Development cost rises because code inside the boundary must follow isolation, attestation, and update protocols, and some deployments must also pass formal certification such as Common Criteria. Distributed training and federated inference add coordination work when their admission policy requires attestation and protected key exchange. A central verifier can perform admission checks; direct mutual attestation between every pair is not inherently required. TEEs therefore fit deployments whose threat model, whether adversarial users, cloud co-tenants, or malicious insiders, justifies that investment.



Hardware security features are budgeted like any other resource. Each primitive spends time at its boundary crossings and capacity in its protected memory, and both costs must be sized before a design commits to a primitive. Hardware security overhead must be measured for the chosen implementation. A secure-world transition has a cost per transition, not automatically a cost per inference: the result depends on how often the inference path crosses the boundary and what data it copies. Encryption, cache effects, and paging add separate costs. Energy overhead requires power and elapsed-time measurements; it cannot be inferred from a transition-latency figure alone.
Security features scale differently than computational resources. Protected memory capacity, not host memory, sets how much of a model can remain resident inside a TEE without paging. On an older Intel SGX configuration with a 128 MB enclave page cache (the protected resident memory), ResNet-50’s FP32 weights alone would fill about 76.3 percent of it. A ResNet-18 model is about 46.8 MB with FP32 weights or 11.7 MB with INT8 weights, while ResNet-50 is about 102.4 MB with FP32 weights or 25.6 MB with INT8 weights before activations and runtime buffers. The fleet’s reference model sits far beyond that scale. The FP16 weights of the Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) model occupy as many bytes as the 350 GB gradient it reduces each step, orders of magnitude more than an enclave page cache, which is why fleet-scale confidential computing draws its boundary around a whole confidential virtual machine, an entire guest protected from the host, rather than an application enclave. These constraints create architectural decisions that must be made early in system design.



FP32 ResNet-50 weights alone nearly fill an older enclave page cache.
Different threat models and protection levels require quantitative trade-off analysis. Encryption and authentication are distinct operations: AES encryption alone does not verify integrity. An authenticated mode or a separate authentication mechanism is needed when tampering is in scope, and the latency must be measured for the actual data volume and hardware.
TEE assurance depends on its protected initialization and attestation path, not merely on when the host boots. Some enclave designs explicitly tolerate an untrusted host operating system, while other trusted environments depend on a verified platform startup chain. Secure boot complements these boundaries by authenticating the components included in that chain; the threat model must identify which firmware and initialization code remain trusted.



Secure boot is a mechanism that ensures a device only boots software components that are cryptographically verified under the platform’s configured trust policy. At startup, each stage of the boot process, comprising the bootloader, kernel, and base operating system, is checked against a known-good digital signature. If any signature fails verification, the boot sequence is halted, blocking components that fail authentication. The chain rests on a trusted initial stage; signed but vulnerable software remains a risk.
In ML systems, especially those deployed on embedded or edge hardware, secure boot plays an important role. A compromised boot process may result in malicious software loading before the ML runtime begins, enabling attackers to intercept model weights, tamper with training data, or reroute inference results. Such breaches can lead to incorrect or manipulated predictions, unauthorized data access, or device repurposing for botnets or crypto-mining.
For machine learning systems, secure boot authenticates the components included in its verification chain. Model artifacts receive this protection only when a verified loader checks their signatures or a signed manifest before loading them; boot verification alone does not authenticate weights read later from storage. Secure update flows must extend the same verification policy to replacement firmware, runtimes, and model artifacts.
Secure boot frequently operates in tandem with hardware-based TEEs to establish an unbroken chain of trust prior to code execution. Figure 18 sequences this stepped verification handshake, pairing each trusted execution stage with an explicit cryptographic authentication gate (Regenscheid 2018). Execution proceeds from an immutable boot root through a verified bootloader and operating system, halting and rejecting the component if any signature check fails. For machine learning pipelines, Stage 3 explicitly extends this chain beyond conventional system software: the verified OS or loader authenticates the model manifest and artifact digest before launching the authorized ML workload. The terminal stage emphasizes that while boot-time authentication blocks unauthorized or tampered binaries, dynamic runtime controls remain necessary to guard against post-boot attacks and data-dependent exploits.

Startup trust is what makes the runtime isolation described earlier meaningful. Before the Face ID pipeline can use the Secure Enclave, signed boot chains verify the application processor software and the Secure Enclave firmware, so unauthorized modification causes verification to fail before any biometric data is processed (Apple 2021a, 2024b).

The trust chain also constrains updates. Apple devices use hardware-rooted authorization to install only system software and firmware versions that Apple is still signing, helping prevent tampered or downgraded components from entering the trusted stack (Apple 2021b). A secure initial boot therefore needs a controlled update path to preserve its assumptions over the device lifecycle.
Secure boot also creates key-management and lifecycle obligations. Enterprises must protect signing keys, distribute trusted verification material, and support revocation or recovery when an authorized key is compromised. The affected trust chain depends on that key’s authority and the platform’s recovery design. Verification adds startup work, and every component covered by the policy must remain authenticated through updates, whether by an individual signature or a digest bound into an authenticated manifest. The deployment must identify which components the chain actually covers.
At fleet scale, device identity and evidence of startup state support distinct admission decisions. The Device Identifier Composition Engine (Trusted Computing Group 2018) combines a device secret with software measurements to derive identities tied to the measured state. IEEE 802.1AR (IEEE 802.1 Working Group 2018) defines cryptographically bound device identities and their provisioning; a device identity alone does not establish which software is running. Fleet attestation (section 13.8.4) connects authenticated identity with acceptable state evidence before a node receives keys or joins a job.

Secure boot, when extended through the model loader and complemented by controlled updates, can establish that the configured authority approved the loaded components. Correct model behavior and freedom from vulnerabilities in the authenticated software remain separate claims. Runtime isolation and monitoring address different parts of that assurance argument.



While TEEs and secure boot provide runtime isolation and integrity verification, hardware security modules (HSMs) specialize in the cryptographic operations that underpin these protections. An HSM is a tamper-resistant physical device designed to perform cryptographic operations and securely manage digital keys. HSMs are widely used across security-important industries such as finance, defense, and cloud infrastructure, and they are relevant for securing the machine learning pipeline, particularly in deployments where key confidentiality, model integrity, and regulatory compliance are important.
HSMs provide an isolated, hardened environment for performing sensitive operations such as key generation, digital signing, encryption, and decryption. Unlike general-purpose processors, they are engineered to withstand physical tampering and side-channel attacks, and they typically include protected storage, cryptographic accelerators, and internal audit logging. HSMs may be implemented as standalone appliances, plug-in modules, or integrated chips embedded within broader systems.
In machine learning systems, HSMs can protect signing keys and the keys used to wrap data-encryption keys. The distinction matters: a root key may remain inside the HSM while a workload uses a released data key inside its authorized execution boundary. Two distributed workflows illustrate this role. An HSM can protect the certificate authority’s signing key used to certify enrolled devices; each device then proves possession of its own private key. Secure aggregation does not inherently require an HSM, and an authenticated but compromised client can still submit poisoned gradients. An HSM can also wrap a model-decryption key for a TEE’s attestation-bound public key after the verifier accepts the evidence. Keeping weights out of plaintext host memory then depends on the TEE’s key handling, loader, and execution path, not on the wrapping operation alone.
HSMs also play a role in maintaining the integrity of machine learning models. In many production pipelines, models must be signed before deployment to ensure that only verified versions are accepted into runtime environments. The signing keys used to authenticate models can be stored and managed within the HSM, providing cryptographic assurance that the deployed artifact is authentic and untampered. Similarly, secure firmware updates and configuration changes, regardless of whether they pertain to models, hyperparameters, or supporting infrastructure, can be validated using signatures produced by the HSM.
In addition to protecting inference workloads, HSMs can be used to secure model training. During training, data may originate from distributed and potentially untrusted sources. HSM-backed protocols can help ensure that training pipelines perform encryption, integrity checks, and access control enforcement securely and in compliance with organizational or legal requirements. In regulated industries such as healthcare and finance, such protections are often necessary to satisfy required safeguards. For instance, the HIPAA Security Rule requires technical safeguards such as access control, audit controls, integrity protections, and transmission security, while treating encryption and some integrity controls as addressable implementation specifications. GDPR lists pseudonymization and encryption as examples of appropriate technical and organizational measures where they fit the risk.
HSM deployment introduces a capacity and integration budget. Signing throughput, key-unwrapping latency, and network access to a remote HSM must be measured for the operations actually used, because the HSM sits on the signing and key-release path and its throughput, not the accelerator’s, bounds how fast keys reach the fleet. The protected key boundary can also require changes to application interfaces and fleet provisioning. Certification and procurement requirements, including applicable cryptographic-module standards, constrain which devices and configurations can be used.
Despite these operational complexities, HSMs remain a valuable option for machine learning systems that require high assurance of cryptographic integrity and access control. When paired with TEEs, secure boot, and software-based defenses, HSMs contribute to a multilayered security model that spans hardware, system software, and ML runtime.
HSMs combine key custody with protected cryptographic operations. Resource-constrained embedded systems may need a smaller mechanism for a narrower task: deriving a device-specific secret without storing a persistent copy of that secret. Physical unclonable functions use a chip’s physical properties for this purpose. They can support key derivation and identity, but do not replace the HSM’s full cryptographic processing and policy-enforcement role.



PUFs19 provide a hardware-intrinsic mechanism for cryptographic key generation and device authentication by exploiting physical randomness in semiconductor fabrication (Gassend et al. 2002). Unlike traditional keys stored in memory, a PUF generates secret values based on microscopic variations in a chip’s physical properties. These variations are inherent to manufacturing processes and difficult to clone or predict, even by the manufacturer.
19 PUF (Physical Unclonable Function): Manufacturing variation can support device-specific key derivation without storing a persistent copy of the key. Separate device keys limit the reach of a storage-key compromise, but they do not prevent extraction of plaintext model weights during execution or attacks that predict a vulnerable PUF’s responses.
Gassend, Blaise, Dwaine Clarke, Marten van Dijk, and Srinivas Devadas. 2002. “Silicon Physical Random Functions.” Proceedings of the 9th ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, 148–60. https://doi.org/10.1145/586110.586132.
These variations arise from uncontrollable physical factors such as doping concentration, line edge roughness, and dielectric thickness. As a result, even chips fabricated with the same design masks exhibit small but measurable differences in timing, power consumption, or voltage behavior. PUF circuits amplify these variations to produce a device-unique digital output. When a specific input challenge is applied to a PUF, it generates a corresponding response based on the chip’s physical fingerprint. These physical differences make responses device-dependent, although an attacker may still predict responses from a vulnerable design without physically cloning the chip.
This challenge-response mechanism allows PUFs to serve several cryptographic purposes. They can be used to derive device-specific keys that never need to be stored externally, reducing the attack surface for key exfiltration. The same mechanism also supports secure authentication and attestation, where devices must prove their identity to trusted servers or hardware gateways. These properties make PUFs a natural fit for machine learning systems deployed in embedded and distributed environments.
For ML fleets, a PUF can reduce the need to inject and persistently store a unique secret in each device. The phone-class devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) and the cameras and drones of edge deployments still need enrollment: the verifier must associate a device with trusted authentication evidence and manage its admission and revocation. A PUF-derived key can encrypt the on-device model at rest, so copying the stored file does not yield the device-bound key that decrypts it. Authentication can use enrolled challenge-response information or a credential backed by a derived key, depending on the design. Both protections have limits. Plaintext weights extracted during execution expose the shared model regardless of how the storage key was generated, and successful authentication establishes which device is speaking, not that its runtime software is uncompromised.

PUFs also present engineering challenges. Their responses drift with temperature, voltage, and aging, so production designs add error correction or helper data and calibrate devices during fabrication, at some cost in layout area and test time. Managing large sets of challenge-response pairs raises questions of storage, consistency, and revocation, and the statistical structure of some PUF designs makes their responses predictable to machine learning-based modeling attacks if enough pairs are observed.
Within those limits, PUFs reduce the key-management burden for large device fleets and supply a hardware-bound identity that complements secure boot, TEEs, and HSMs.



The design choice is not whether hardware-backed protection is better than software-backed protection, but which primitive owns which trust boundary. While software-based defenses offer flexibility, they ultimately rely on the security of the hardware platform. As machine learning workloads operate on edge devices, embedded platforms, and untrusted infrastructure, hardware-backed protections become important for maintaining system integrity, confidentiality, and trust.
TEEs provide runtime isolation for model inference and sensitive data handling. Secure boot verifies the authorized startup components included in its chain of trust. HSMs offer tamper-resistant storage and cryptographic processing for secure key management, model signing, and firmware validation. PUFs bind secrets and authentication to the physical characteristics of a specific device, supporting hardware-bound identities subject to the PUF design’s resistance to modeling and physical attacks.
These mechanisms address different layers of the system stack, ranging from initialization and attestation to runtime protection and identity binding, and complement one another when deployed together. Table 8 compares their roles, use cases, and trade-offs for machine learning system design.

Together, these hardware primitives support a defense-in-depth strategy for securing ML systems in adversarial environments. Their integration needs an explicit assurance argument: which components remain trusted, which evidence supports that trust, and which attacks fall outside the protection. Safety-sensitive devices and distributed learning systems need this argument as much as they need the mechanisms themselves.
Hardware primitives supply evidence and enforcement for selected platform properties. Deployment controls use those capabilities to decide which model artifacts may load and which callers may use them. The transition from platform assurance to application policy is therefore a composition problem: the loader and serving endpoint must enforce the intended permissions within the protected boundary.




A trusted platform establishes where a model runs; deployment controls decide who can load it, who can call it, and whether its behavior survives contact with users, operators, and attackers. A model’s vulnerability is not solely determined by its training procedure or architecture; it also depends on how the artifact is serialized, packaged, deployed, and accessed during inference. As models move into edge devices, public APIs, and multi-tenant platforms, deployment security must preserve the integrity, confidentiality, and availability of model behavior.
Deployment-stage controls protect the packaged artifact and the inference interface, while the design-stage controls of section 13.11.4 shape the model’s behavior itself. Deployment controls also have to survive ordinary optimization work such as quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation, where performance improvements must not compromise artifact integrity, ownership evidence, or access-control boundaries.
Once training is complete, the model must be securely packaged for deployment. Authenticated encryption protects stored artifacts when its keys remain inside the intended trust boundary; a signed manifest authenticates the expected artifact digest before loading. Obfuscation may raise reverse-engineering effort but does not provide the confidentiality contract of encryption. Runtime key custody and the loader’s verification policy determine whether packaging protection survives execution.
Deployment environments must enforce access policies at inference endpoints. OAuth supplies delegated authorization; mutual TLS authenticates certificate-bearing peers; API keys identify credentials that the service maps to permissions and quotas. Role-based access control (RBAC) can restrict those permissions by operational role. These mechanisms support the query controls in section 13.7.1.4, but a credential is not proof of a unique human or organization. An attacker who can obtain many accounts can still distribute queries across identities, so account issuance, cumulative budgets, and abuse detection remain part of the boundary.
An API key demonstrates possession of a credential and allows the backend to enforce its associated policies. Keeping keys out of source code reduces accidental exposure in version control, but environment variables alone do not prevent leaks through logs, process inspection, or a compromised runtime. Secret retrieval, scoped permissions, rotation, and redacted logging must be designed together. Model verification against an authenticated manifest, input limits, rate controls, and security-event logging complement credential management.
The secure deployment patterns established here integrate naturally with development workflows, ensuring security becomes part of standard engineering practice rather than an afterthought. Runtime monitoring (section 13.11.3) extends these protections to operational environments.



Secure deployment controls who can load the model and call the endpoint, but runtime monitoring asks whether the live system is still behaving like the approved system. Attackers may craft inputs that pass static checks, exploit learned behavior, or target system-level infrastructure after deployment. Production ML systems span cloud services, edge devices, and embedded systems, so defensive strategies must connect real-time observation to threat detection and incident response across each environment.
Runtime monitoring must decide whether an input should reach the model, whether the output is behaving normally, and whether the serving system is still the one originally deployed. The corresponding mechanisms are input validation, output monitoring, and system integrity checks.


Input validation checks incoming data before it reaches a machine learning model. Format and range checks enforce explicit input contracts, while statistical and semantic checks estimate whether an input fits expected conditions. These checks can reject malformed inputs that disrupt preprocessing or inference and some adversarial inputs crafted to trigger incorrect predictions. Passing validation establishes only that the implemented checks accepted the input, not that the model will handle it correctly.
Small, carefully chosen changes to input data can cause models to make high-confidence but incorrect predictions (Goodfellow et al. 2015). Such inputs may satisfy ordinary type and range checks. Input validation therefore complements model robustness evaluation; it cannot replace testing how the learned function behaves on valid but adversarial inputs.

Goodfellow, I. J., J. Shlens, and C. Szegedy. 2015. “Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Validation techniques range from low-level checks (for example, input size, type, and value ranges) to semantic filters that estimate whether an image contains a recognizable object or a recording includes speech. For example, a facial recognition system might validate that an uploaded image is within a specified resolution range (for example, \(224{\times}224\) to \(1024{\times}1024\) pixels), contains RGB channels, and passes a lightweight face detection filter. These checks reject inputs that violate the format or face-detection contract; an adversarial image that satisfies that contract can still reach the model. Similarly, a voice assistant might require audio files between 1 and 5 seconds long, a valid sampling rate (for example, 16 kHz), and a positive result from a speech activity detector (SAD). The detector can reject some music or noise while also missing quiet speech or accepting nonspeech, so its error rates belong in the validation assessment.
In generative systems, input validation can include prompt filtering against an application’s content policy. A medical education application, for example, might reject requests to generate fabricated treatment claims. Filters may use keyword lists, regular expressions, or lightweight classifiers that estimate prompt intent. Their effectiveness depends on the policy, detector, and inputs tested, including paraphrases and adversarial prompts. They cannot establish that an accepted prompt will produce an acceptable output, which is why output monitoring remains necessary.
In some applications, distributional checks are also used. These assess whether the incoming data statistically resembles what the model saw during training. For instance, a computer vision pipeline might compare the color histogram of the input image to a baseline distribution, flagging outliers for manual review or rejection.
These validations can be lightweight (heuristics or threshold rules) or learned (small models trained to detect distribution shift or adversarial artifacts). Their value depends on which invalid or hostile inputs they reject and how often they reject legitimate inputs. Since an accepted input can still induce an incorrect result, the next boundary is the model’s output.



Even when inputs pass validation, adversarial or unexpected behavior may still emerge at the model’s output. Output monitoring observes confidence, prediction entropy, class distribution, or response patterns to flag deviations from expected behavior. A monitor can contain a detected failure when its fallback acts before the output causes harm. Missed detections, delayed alerts, and incorrect fallbacks limit that protection, so detection quality and response timing belong in the same evaluation.
The signal a monitor watches depends on the model’s modality. For a discriminative classifier, unexpected changes in confidence, class frequencies, or output entropy can trigger investigation, but do not identify their cause. A legitimate workload change, model defect, or attack can produce similar deviations. Content-moderation monitors can compare predicted “safe” labels with auxiliary reference signals; fraud-detection monitors can flag sudden score changes during high-volume periods. In each case, the system compares the live stream with an expected distribution and applies a chosen response, such as human review or a conservative baseline, while investigation distinguishes the possible causes.
Generative models, such as text-to-image systems, introduce unique output monitoring challenges. These models can produce high-fidelity imagery that may inadvertently violate content safety policies, platform guidelines, or user expectations. To mitigate these risks, postgeneration classifiers are commonly employed to assess generated content for objectionable characteristics such as violence, nudity, or brand misuse. These classifiers operate downstream of the generative model and can suppress, blur, or reject outputs based on predefined thresholds. Some systems also inspect internal representations (for example, attention maps or latent embeddings) to anticipate potential misuse before content is rendered.
However, prompt filtering alone is insufficient for safety. Research has shown that text-to-image systems can be manipulated through implicitly adversarial prompts, which are queries that appear benign but lead to policy-violating outputs. The Adversarial Nibbler project introduces an open red teaming methodology that identifies such prompts and demonstrates how models like Stable Diffusion can produce unintended content despite the absence of explicit trigger phrases (Quaye et al. 2024; Parrish et al. 2023). These failure cases often bypass prompt filters because their risk arises from model behavior during generation, not from syntactic or lexical cues.

In the domain of language generation, output monitoring plays a different but equally important role. Here, the goal is often to detect toxicity, hallucinated claims, or off-distribution responses. For example, a customer support chatbot may be monitored for keyword presence, tonal alignment, or semantic coherence. If a response contains profanity, unsupported assertions, or syntactically malformed text, the system may trigger a rephrasing, initiate a fallback to scripted templates, or halt the response altogether.
Output monitoring can combine rule-based heuristics with learned detectors trained on historical outputs. These detectors feed alerts into incident response pipelines or block outputs before release. Adversarial training aims to improve the model’s behavior, while monitoring adds a separate opportunity to detect and contain failures during operation. Any claimed damage bound must account for missed detections, response latency, and the consequences of the selected fallback.
These principles appear in output filtering frameworks. For example, Llama Guard is an LLM-based input-output safeguard that classifies human-AI conversations against policy categories (Inan et al. 2023). Similarly, ShieldGemma, developed as part of Google’s open Gemma model release, applies configurable scoring functions to detect and filter undesired outputs during inference (Google 2024). Both systems exemplify how safety classifiers and output monitors can be integrated into the runtime stack to support scalable, policy-aligned deployment of generative language models.

While input and output monitoring focus on model behavior, system integrity checks compare model files, execution environments, and serving infrastructure with approved state. Their coverage depends on what is measured, when it is measured, and whether the measurement path remains trusted. Verifying a file before loading detects covered artifact changes at that point; it does not establish that all subsequent execution remains untampered.
One of the most common integrity mechanisms is cryptographic model verification. Before a model is loaded into memory, the system can compute a cryptographic hash (for example, SHA-256) of the model file and compare it against the expected digest in an authenticated, signed release manifest.
Access control and audit logging complement cryptographic checks. ML systems should restrict access to model files using role-based permissions and monitor file access patterns. For instance, repeated attempts to read model checkpoints from a nonstandard path, or inference requests from unauthorized IP ranges, may indicate tampering, privilege escalation, or insider threats. In cloud environments, container- or VM-based isolation20 helps enforce process and memory boundaries, but these protections can erode over time because of misconfiguration or supply chain vulnerabilities.
20 Container vs. VM Isolation: Containers share the host kernel, which keeps overhead low and model scale-out fast but leaves a kernel attack surface shared with co-tenants. VMs separate guest kernels and memory at additional resource cost, yet hypervisor flaws and shared-hardware side channels can still enable cross-tenant attacks on a multi-tenant serving fleet.21 HIPAA ML Requirements: For electronic protected health information, the HIPAA Security Rule treats encryption at rest and in transit as addressable specifications, which an organization implements when reasonable and appropriate or replaces with a documented equivalent (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2005). Its audit-control standard requires mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems holding that information, scoped by risk analysis rather than a mandate to log every read. Cloud services handling it generally require Business Associate Agreements. In an ML pipeline, these duties become risk-based audit coverage, protected checkpoints, controlled access, and evidence that the safeguards are operating.

For example, a regulated healthcare ML deployment can organize integrity evidence around three gates. The loader compares the model artifact’s cryptographic hash with an authenticated, signed release manifest. Dependency validation checks approved package versions and authenticated artifact digests; a pinned version number names a package without proving that its contents are the approved ones. Platform attestation checks measured state against an approved configuration, with coverage determined by the attestation mechanism rather than an assumption of continuous execution verification. These gates supply evidence relevant to HIPAA21 and other applicable obligations, but the organization must assess the complete system and its operational use to establish compliance.
Some systems also implement runtime memory verification, such as scanning for unexpected model parameter changes or checking that memory-mapped model weights remain unaltered during execution. While more common in high-assurance systems, such checks are becoming more feasible with the adoption of secure enclaves and trusted runtimes.
System integrity checks and input/output monitoring provide complementary evidence. Integrity checks can identify changes to measured artifacts even when predictions appear normal; behavioral monitors can flag failures even when every artifact matches its approved version. Their combined evidence guides investigation and containment without equating artifact authenticity with correct model behavior.
Integrity checks become ML supply-chain controls only when they connect every deployable artifact. A signed model file is insufficient if the training dataset, dependency lockfile, preprocessing code, registry promotion event, container image, and deployment attestation cannot be tied to the same release record. That release record makes the provenance bound on trust (principle \(\ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}\)) operational, and it gives rollback and forensic analysis a concrete object. Operators can ask which data snapshot produced the checkpoint, which dependencies built the serving image, which registry principal promoted it, and which production endpoints loaded it.



A detected breach, anomaly, or performance degradation must lead to a defined response. The immediate task is containment; recovery then restores a trustworthy service and addresses the cause. ML systems add model checkpoints, training-data lineage, and learned behavior to the software versions, credentials, and runtime state that incident responders already need to examine.
Detection thresholds and automated rollback triggers work here as they do for any production model; security changes the signal set and the order of operations. Escalation can come from input validation (a rise in invalid inputs), output monitoring (a drop in prediction confidence), or integrity checks (a failed model signature verification). A security trigger must also preserve evidence before the automated response changes the system’s state, because a rollback that overwrites the suspect artifact destroys the record an investigation needs.
