title: 13 Security & Privacy
text:
A training job on the reference cluster of 1,024 GPUs (128 nodes with 8 GPUs each) depends on contributions from many participants. Each optimizer step of the Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) reference model reduces 350 GB of FP16 gradients across the job, and each checkpoint interval produces a 2.45 TB artifact containing valuable learned state. Public inference controls do not govern these internal exchanges. Four boundaries determine how a node compromise can propagate: the gradient each worker contributes, the fabric that carries it, the accelerators and caches tenants share, and the evidence used to admit nodes into the job.


Data-parallel training averages the workers’ gradients, but an unconstrained mean cannot bound the effect of one arbitrarily large contribution. Weighting each of the \(\DataParallelDegree\) contributions by \(1/\DataParallelDegree\) does not solve that problem when the contribution’s magnitude is unbounded. In robust-statistics terms, the mean has a breakdown point of zero, because a single corrupted input can move it arbitrarily far. Byzantine failures introduces aggregation rules such as Krum and coordinate-wise trimmed mean, whose guarantees require assumptions about the number of faulty workers and the honest updates (Blanchard et al. 2017; Yin et al. 2018). An intentional adversary can adapt its update to the deployed norm or distance checks and repeat the attempt across steps. Evaluation must therefore test attacks against the active control rather than rely only on evidence from random faults.

Blanchard, Peva, El Mahdi El Mhamdi, Rachid Guerraoui, and Julien Stainer. 2017. “Machine Learning with Adversaries: Byzantine Tolerant Gradient Descent.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 119–29.

Yin, Dong, Yudong Chen, Kannan Ramchandran, and Peter Bartlett. 2018. “Byzantine-Robust Distributed Learning: Towards Optimal Statistical Rates.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 5650–59.
Robust aggregation also changes the collective’s information requirements. Ring AllReduce computes a sum with about \(2(\DataParallelDegree-1)/\DataParallelDegree\) times the gradient size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) in per-worker communication as \(\DataParallelDegree\) grows; its result does not provide a separate gradient for every worker. A direct implementation of a median, trimmed mean, or distance-based rule can instead gather all individual gradients. Gathering them at every worker receives \((\DataParallelDegree-1)\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes per worker, a factor of \(\DataParallelDegree/2\) relative to the ring traffic expression. Unlike the device count \(\DeviceCount\) of the Fleet Law, the \(\DataParallelDegree\) here is the data-parallel degree, which counts model replicas rather than accelerators. The comparison assumes a data-parallel degree of 64 on the reference cluster, which leaves each replica two full nodes of 8 GPUs (for example, tensor parallelism inside each node). At that degree \(\DataParallelDegree/2\) gives 32× the ring traffic. Because the gradient synchronization is bandwidth-dominated, its share of \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) grows by roughly that factor unless the extra traffic can be overlapped with backward computation. That ratio is the cost of the gather-based implementation, not a lower bound for every robust protocol. Worker admission through attestation (section 13.8.4) restricts which environments join the job, but does not prove their gradients are benign; update checks or redundant computation address different evidence. Federated deployments face heterogeneous attestation support and independently controlled clients. Federated privacy examines the additional conflict between inspecting individual updates and hiding them through secure aggregation.


↩︎ Ring AllReduce and its \(2(\DataParallelDegree-1)/\DataParallelDegree\) per-worker traffic bound are established in Ring AllReduce.



Gradients can reveal information about the examples that produced them. Gradient inversion, examined for federated clients in section 13.11.6.2, demonstrates reconstruction under particular observation and training conditions. The exposure of a gradient shard, aggregate, or activation therefore needs its own analysis of what the observer can recover. Remote direct memory access (RDMA) can move payloads directly between accelerator memories without staging them through host memory, but this data path does not itself establish confidentiality. If the fabric carries plaintext, protection depends on who can access its links, switches, endpoints, and management plane. A dedicated facility can restrict that access without eliminating the boundary.


↩︎ RDMA and GPUDirect transports, which move payloads directly between accelerator memories, are established in RDMA and GPUDirect.
Encrypting collective traffic can add to the communication term of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3). The size of that addition follows from the ring traffic just derived. For the large gradient buckets that dominate a step, the bandwidth term of the AllReduce, about \(2(\DataParallelDegree-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/(\DataParallelDegree\LinkBandwidth)\) for link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), outweighs the per-message latency, so a cipher that sustains only half the link rate halves the effective \(\LinkBandwidth\) and roughly doubles that part of \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\). A cipher that keeps pace with the link adds latency but little transfer time, while a host-based path that stages accelerator data adds copies that GPUDirect RDMA avoids. Adapter or link-layer encryption can protect traffic without that staging path, subject to the endpoints and keys included in its trust boundary. The added latency and any lost overlap must be measured on the actual collective schedule, because repeated increases in \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) affect the capacity required for the run.



Multi-tenancy places customers’ state on shared silicon, but the isolation depends on the sharing mechanism. Volta-era and later Multi-Process Service implementations provide separate client GPU address spaces; that property alone does not establish a boundary between mutually distrustful users. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions memory, cache, and compute resources in hardware (NVIDIA 2026). Sequential reuse introduces a separate requirement to clear accessible residual memory before reassignment. Serving can also leak through shared prefix caches: if a hit changes response timing, one tenant may infer that another requested a matching prefix. Tenant-scoped caches remove cross-tenant reuse from that path at a potential hit-rate cost, while leaving other timing channels and within-tenant access boundaries to be assessed.

NVIDIA. 2026. NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU User Guide.

↩︎ The accelerator sharing options and the isolation strength each provides are established in Security and namespace isolation.

Each of these controls spends capacity, through reserved partitions, fragmentation, scrubbing time, or lost cache reuse. Measuring that capacity effect requires a matched workload and resource budget; a smaller partition cannot be compared with a whole accelerator and labeled pure security overhead.

Systems Perspective 13.2: The tax of secure multi-tenancyConsider a hypothetical comparison of two serving configurations with the same allocated accelerator capacity, models, request mix, and latency target. Assume the baseline sustains 1,000 tokens per second and the configuration with additional security controls sustains 850 tokens per second. These are scenario inputs for a capacity calculation, not measured overheads for MIG or another isolation mechanism.
For this matched comparison, the throughput loss is 1,000 tokens - 850 tokens = 150 tokens per second, or (150 tokens/1,000 tokens) = 15 percent. Spatial partitioning does not inherently require tenant context switches. Its capacity cost may instead arise from fragmentation or idle reserved resources, which should be recorded separately from execution overhead.
Systems insight: The assumed controls reduce useful throughput by 15 percent under the stated comparison. In a measured deployment that loss would split among the mechanisms of this section. Hardware partitions strand capacity whenever a tenant’s load falls below its slice, memory scrubbing between tenants takes time out of every reassignment, and tenant-scoped prefix caches give up the hits that cross-tenant reuse would have supplied. Each source has a different remedy. Right-sizing partitions recovers stranded capacity, while cache scoping is the price of closing a timing channel and cannot be tuned away without reopening it. Fleet planning must therefore record each source separately; none can be inferred from comparing a whole accelerator with a smaller partition.





Worker admission needs evidence about the environment receiving data and keys. Across 128 nodes with independent restarts and updates, that evidence must be evaluated consistently. Remote attestation lets a verifier appraise authenticated claims about a node against an admission policy. The central claim is a set of measurements, cryptographic hashes of the firmware and software the node loaded, recorded and signed by the node’s hardware so that compromised software cannot rewrite them. Before releasing the key for the 2.45 TB checkpoint, the service can require fresh evidence covering the relevant firmware and workload measurements. Coverage depends on the platform; a valid measurement does not prove that approved code is free of vulnerabilities or that every runtime update is correct. The provenance bound on trust (principle \(\ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}\)) links this evidence to the release path. Confidential computing adds runtime protection for code and data placed inside a hardware-enforced boundary, under the platform’s stated adversary model. Section 13.11.1 develops those mechanisms and their limits.
Attestation and key management add coordination work when admission or recovery requires renewed evidence and key delivery. The policy must specify when evidence expires and which changes require another check. Key rotation also needs a transition plan, while revocation after a suspected compromise may require interrupting work that no longer has valid authority. Hardware security modules can protect the keys used to authorize or wrap secrets, with node-level custody governed separately. When these operations delay participants or restart, their cost enters \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) and the recovery path. A node that restarts after a failure must present fresh evidence and receive the checkpoint key again before it rejoins, so every failure costs that re-admission delay on top of the restart time and lost work that the checkpoint-interval calculation already charges.


↩︎ The Young-Daly checkpoint interval, which balances checkpoint write cost against expected lost work, is established in The Young-Daly checkpoint interval.
The four boundaries draw on all three C³ axes. Redundant computation and memory scrubbing add compute work, while tenant-scoped caches can reduce reuse. Robust aggregation and encrypted collectives can add communication cost; attestation and key rotation add coordination. These controls also depend on components beneath the job. A driver with access to plaintext state, a compromised memory path, or an observable power signal can undermine a protection enforced higher in the stack. The hardware threat model must identify which of those components remain trusted and which observations the attacker can obtain.

Self-Check: Question

A 64-worker data-parallel job replaces ring AllReduce with a gather-based coordinate-wise median implementation: every worker gathers every individual gradient before computing the median. Approximately how does per-worker gradient traffic change under this schedule?

It rises by about 32 times, because this implementation gathers the 63 peer gradients instead of moving about twice the gradient size in the ring.
It is unchanged, because this median implementation uses only the sum returned by ring AllReduce.
It roughly doubles, because gathering all individual gradients costs one extra ring pass.
It falls, because the implementation discards outlier gradients before receiving them.

Two hypothetical serving configurations use the same allocated accelerator capacity, models, request mix, and latency target. The baseline sustains 1,000 tokens/s and the configuration with additional security controls sustains 850 tokens/s. Explain what this 15% capacity loss establishes and why comparing a whole GPU against a smaller MIG partition would not isolate security overhead.
True or False: RDMA movement between accelerator memories establishes gradient confidentiality even when the fabric payloads are plaintext.
A multi-tenant LLM service shares one prefix cache across all tenants, and cache hits are distinguishable in time-to-first-token measurements. What can a probing tenant infer, and which control removes this cross-tenant cache-reuse path?

Evidence that a probed prefix was recently processed outside the probing tenant; per-tenant cache scoping removes this shared-reuse path at the cost of a lower hit rate.
The model weights of the serving replica; encrypting the weights at rest closes the channel.
Another tenant’s API key; mutual TLS between client and gateway closes the channel.
The exact output tokens of other tenants; rounding output probabilities closes the channel.

When a 128-node training job waits for fresh remote attestation and key delivery before admission or recovery, explain why that delay enters the coordination term and recovery path of the Fleet Law. Distinguish it from steady-state protected-execution costs.

See Answers →

title: 13 Security & Privacy
text:
When a serving team moves model weights into production, it often treats encryption, access control, and API policy as the security boundary. Hardware attacks break that assumption. A processor can leak across isolation domains, a field device can be opened, a bus or power rail can expose signals, and a counterfeit component can enter the system before deployment begins. The result is not a separate hardware appendix to the threat model; it is the substrate that can invalidate software controls after those controls appear to pass.
The practical deployment question is which substrate layer can still violate trust. A cloud LLM endpoint is mostly an isolation problem: one tenant’s process, memory, and accelerator context must not reveal another tenant’s prompts or weights. An embedded vision sensor is mostly a physical-access problem: the attacker may probe power, attach to a debug port, or replace a module. A regulated procurement pipeline is mostly a provenance problem: the organization must know which components were built, handled, patched, and retired. These cases use different defenses, but they share the same reasoning pattern.
Hardware security planning therefore begins with four fundamental checks. Processor isolation must separate tenants, cryptographic keys, model weights, and intermediate activations from untrusted code and co-tenants. Physical-access controls must protect devices, sensors, memory, and debug interfaces when attackers can physically touch the hardware. Side-channel evaluation tests whether observable power, timing, electromagnetic, bus, or thermal signals expose sensitive computation despite those boundaries. Finally, supply-chain validation checks evidence that the deployed component matches the component the system was designed and certified to use. Each check needs an explicit attacker model; passing it does not establish protection against access or measurements outside that model.
Table 6 keeps the hardware threat landscape visible, but the table should be read as a set of deployment decisions rather than a taxonomy to memorize. The defensive strategies in section 13.11 return to the same decisions from the perspective of trusted execution, attestation, and hardware roots of trust.



Table 6: Hardware threat landscape: Hardware security decisions group diverse vulnerability families into isolation, physical-access, side-channel, and provenance questions that determine whether software protections remain meaningful in deployment.










Deployment Decision
Trust Failure to Analyze
Threat Families It Organizes




Processor isolation
Cross-tenant or cross-process leakage after software access control appears to pass.
Hardware bugs, speculative execution flaws.


Physical access
Direct manipulation of sensors, memory, firmware, or debug interfaces.
Physical attacks, fault injection, leaky ports.


Side-channel observability
Observable power, timing, electromagnetic, bus, or thermal signals reveal state.
Side-channel attacks, leaky interconnects.


Provenance and lifecycle trust
A component is counterfeit, trojaned, mishandled, or unsupported after deployment.
Counterfeit hardware, supply chain risks.






The subsections in this section follow those decisions rather than treating hardware security as a catalog of attacks. Hardware bugs test processor isolation. Physical attacks, fault injection, and leaky interfaces test whether direct access can change the system after software controls pass. Side-channel attacks test whether computation leaks through observable signals. Supply chain risks, from a single counterfeit part to a compromised part number, test whether the deployed component is the one the architecture assumes.


Hardware bugs answer the first deployment decision: whether processor isolation can be trusted after software access control appears to pass. ML teams must treat that isolation as an empirical claim, not a default guarantee. Attackers can exploit design flaws to access, manipulate, or extract sensitive data, breaching the confidentiality and integrity that users and services depend on. One of the most notable examples came with the discovery of Meltdown and Spectre,11 two vulnerabilities in modern processors that allow malicious programs to bypass memory isolation and read the data of other applications and the operating system (Lipp et al. 2018; Kocher et al. 2019).
11 Meltdown/Spectre: These attacks exposed isolation failures in affected processor families through transient execution and microarchitectural state. Mitigation costs depend on the processor, operating system, and workload, so an ML fleet must remeasure its data-loading and serving paths after applying protections.
Lipp, M., M. Schwarz, D. Gruss, T. Prescher, W. Haas, J. Horn, S. Mangard, et al. 2018. “Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space.” Proceedings of the 27th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security), 973–90.

Kocher, Paul, Jann Horn, Anders Fogh, Daniel Genkin, Daniel Gruss, Werner Haas, Mike Hamburg, et al. 2019. “Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution.” 2019 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 1–19. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2019.00002.
Spectre exploits speculative execution, a performance optimization in which a CPU executes instructions along a predicted path before it knows whether that path is correct. An attacker influences the prediction so that a victim transiently accesses sensitive data. Meltdown instead exploits affected processors that transiently make data available before enforcing the access restriction. In both cases, discarding the unauthorized or mispredicted computation can leave observable traces in microarchitectural state, such as CPU caches. Software-visible execution can therefore respect a boundary while the traces of transient execution leak across it.
Further research identified related transient-execution attacks, including Foreshadow, ZombieLoad, and RIDL, against different microarchitectural structures in affected processors. Their existence motivates examining each component’s isolation assumptions without assuming that every processor shares the same vulnerability. ML systems pair CPUs with GPUs, Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), or custom accelerators. A compromise can propagate across this heterogeneous stack when components share sensitive data, keys, or privileged access; the threat model must trace those relationships.
For a fleet, the consequence can be cross-tenant exposure. Host processors stage data for accelerators, run tokenizers and preprocessing, and hold decrypted keys. When tenants share a vulnerable host and the required attack conditions hold, a transient-execution flaw can expose sensitive state before any accelerator is involved. Mitigations depend on the vulnerability and deployment: restricting simultaneous multithreading or clearing affected microarchitectural state at isolation boundaries can reduce throughput on the data-loading and serving paths that keep accelerators fed. The fleet must remeasure those paths after applying the relevant protections rather than assume a fixed tax.
Such vulnerabilities pose concern in privacy-sensitive domains like healthcare, where ML systems routinely handle patient data. A breach could violate privacy regulations such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), leading to significant legal and ethical consequences. Similar regulatory risks apply globally. For personal data within its territorial and material scope, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) authorizes fines up to 2 percent of total worldwide annual turnover when an organization fails to implement appropriate security measures, and up to 4 percent for violations of its core processing principles or data-subject rights (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016).
Hardware security therefore extends beyond physical tamper prevention to architectural isolation: preventing processors, accelerators, and memory systems from leaking across boundaries the software assumes are sealed. Mitigations often carry performance costs, especially for data-bound ML workloads, so confidential computing (section 13.8.4) and trusted execution environments (TEEs) must be evaluated as capacity and latency decisions as well as security decisions.



Physical attacks answer the second deployment decision: what an adversary can observe or modify by touching the device, sensor, memory, firmware, or debug interface. Physical access introduces paths that a network access policy does not govern. An exposed debug port may permit memory reads, a replacement sensor may supply false inputs, and a writable firmware interface may change execution. Encryption and authentication remain useful when their keys and enforcement mechanisms stay protected; the threat model must identify which physical paths bypass those protections.
The failure mode depends on what the attacker can touch. Replacing a drone’s navigation module, swapping the sensor of a biometric access system, or misaligning a vehicle’s cameras changes system behavior without changing a single model weight. In edge fleets such as the phone-class devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet), the coordinator does not control clients’ physical environments. Device ownership does not automatically defeat protected storage or execution, but the coordinator cannot infer the integrity of a client’s data or updates from ownership or enrollment alone.
Internal components create the same risk at a lower layer. A hardware trojan inserted during chip fabrication can remain dormant until a specific input or state triggers it, then leak outputs, corrupt computation, or degrade performance in ways that are difficult to diagnose after deployment. Memory chips and accelerator buses can expose model parameters or training data when an attacker has physical access. Data centers are not exempt: an implant installed by someone with sufficient facility access can monitor administrative credentials or data streams and provide a persistent path into training and inference pipelines.
The defensive implication is that physical-access analysis belongs in the system architecture rather than solely in device packaging. Disabling production debug interfaces closes one access path; signed firmware and secure boot constrain which code can execute. Tamper detection can signal interference, while attestation and supply chain checks provide evidence about measured state and component provenance. These controls address different parts of the trust boundary, so none alone establishes that sensor inputs or runtime computations remain correct after deployment.



Fault injection is the active version of the physical-access decision: the attacker does not replace the model artifact but changes the computation while it runs. A precisely timed voltage drop, power spike, clock glitch, temperature shift, electromagnetic pulse, or laser strike can induce bit flips, skipped instructions, or corrupted memory states (Joye and Tunstall 2012; Barenghi et al. 2010; Hutter et al. 2009; Amiel et al. 2006; Skorobogatov 2009; Skorobogatov and Anderson 2003). For ML systems, those faults can force incorrect outputs, bypass security checks, degrade reliability, or expose internal state for later reverse engineering.

Joye, Marc, and Michael Tunstall. 2012. Fault Analysis in Cryptography. Inf. Secur. Cryptography. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-29656-7.

Barenghi, A., G. M. Bertoni, L. Breveglieri, M. Pellicioli, and G. Pelosi. 2010. “Low Voltage Fault Attacks to AES.” 2010 IEEE International Symposium on Hardware-Oriented Security and Trust (HOST), 7–12. https://doi.org/10.1109/hst.2010.5513121.

Hutter, Michael, Jorn-Marc Schmidt, and Thomas Plos. 2009. “Contact-Based Fault Injections and Power Analysis on RFID Tags.” 2009 European Conference on Circuit Theory and Design, 409–12. https://doi.org/10.1109/ecctd.2009.5275012.

Amiel, Frederic, Christophe Clavier, and Michael Tunstall. 2006. “Fault Analysis of DPA-Resistant Algorithms.” In Fault Diagnosis and Tolerance in Cryptography. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/11889700_20.

Skorobogatov, S. 2009. “Local Heating Attacks on Flash Memory Devices.” 2009 IEEE International Workshop on Hardware-Oriented Security and Trust, 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1109/hst.2009.5225028.

Skorobogatov, S. P., and R. J. Anderson. 2003. “Optical Fault Induction Attacks.” In Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems - CHES 2002. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-36400-5_2.
The ML-specific risk is that a small computation fault can become a semantic failure. An embedded classifier running on a microcontroller may misclassify a safety-important input, while a fault in memory or control logic may expose proprietary weights or architecture details. Unlike ordinary random faults, adversarially timed faults are chosen to land on computations the model or security protocol depends on.
The experiments of Breier et al. (2018) targeted activation-function implementations on a microcontroller with timed laser faults. Figure 11 identifies the vulnerable instruction in the observed ReLU implementation. For a positive accumulator, the copy instructions assign the activation to the output, and the following jmp end normally skips the zeroing block. A laser pulse timed to suppress that jump makes execution fall through into the clear instructions, overwriting the positive output with zero and forcing the neuron inactive. The conditional brge instruction is not the skipped instruction in this example, and the fault changes executed control flow rather than any stored model weight.

Breier, Jakub, Xiaolu Hou, Dirmanto Jap, Lei Ma, Shivam Bhasin, and Yang Liu. 2018. “Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks.” Proceedings of the 2018 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security abs/1806.05859: 2204–6. https://doi.org/10.1145/3243734.3278519.






Figure 11: Fault injection attack: A timed laser pulse that skips the unconditional jump at line 6 forces a positive ReLU activation through the zeroing block at lines 7–10. The fault changes executed control flow without changing the stored model parameters.



Fault injection attacks can also be combined with side-channel analysis, where attackers first observe power or timing characteristics to infer model structure or data flow. This reconnaissance helps them time faults against specific layers or operations, such as activation functions or final decision layers. The resulting effect still depends on the implementation, the induced fault, and any checks that detect or contain it.
Embedded and edge ML systems can be vulnerable when exposed hardware combines with resource constraints that limit runtime defenses. Access to system buses, memory, or power supplies can give attackers opportunities to induce faults, even when software access controls remain intact. The relevant protection comes from the device and execution stack: a lightweight model does not itself establish whether memory has error correction, computations have redundant checks, or packaging resists probing.
The defense must combine physical hardening with runtime evidence. Tamper-resistant packaging restricts access, while design obfuscation makes targets harder to locate without itself preventing interference. Error-correcting memory and redundant checks can detect or correct some induced errors; secure firmware constrains code changes but does not prevent a fault during execution. Model-output and sensor-consistency monitors can catch some fault-induced behavior that escapes lower layers; MAVFI demonstrates this pattern for micro-aerial-vehicle workloads with anomaly detection and recovery (Hsiao et al. 2023). These protections are hardest in cost- and power-constrained edge systems, where extra cryptographic hardware or redundancy may be unaffordable, so resilience has to be designed across the electrical, firmware, software, and system layers.

Hsiao, Yu-Shun, Zishen Wan, Tianyu Jia, Radhika Ghosal, Abdulrahman Mahmoud, Arijit Raychowdhury, David Brooks, Gu-Yeon Wei, and Vijay Janapa Reddi. 2023. “MAVFI: An End-to-End Fault Analysis Framework with Anomaly Detection and Recovery for Micro Aerial Vehicles.” 2023 Design, Automation & Test in Europe Conference & Exhibition (DATE), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.23919/date56975.2023.10137246.

Gnad, D. R. E., F. Oboril, and M. B. Tahoori. 2017. “Voltage Drop-Based Fault Attacks on FPGAs Using Valid Bitstreams.” 2017 27th International Conference on Field Programmable Logic and Applications (FPL), 1–7. https://doi.org/10.23919/fpl.2017.8056840.
A data center fleet rarely faces a laser, but it faces the same class of failure in two other forms. Without any attacker, marginal processors corrupt computation silently at fleet scale. With an attacker, shared electrical resources can provide a path for interference. Co-tenants on a shared FPGA have induced timing faults remotely by drawing enough current to drop the supply voltage (Gnad et al. 2017). The check-and-verify defenses of Check-and-Verify Defenses Against Silent Data Corruption can therefore serve security as well as reliability. Their security coverage requires separate evaluation, however, because an attacker may target both the computation and its check rather than induce the independent errors a reliability analysis assumes.


↩︎ Silent data corruption from probabilistic hardware faults at fleet scale is established in The physics of silent corruption.



Side-channel attacks answer the third deployment decision: whether computation is observable even when interfaces are locked down. They break the assumption that only explicit interfaces reveal information. Instead of targeting software or network vulnerabilities directly, these attacks use hardware characteristics such as power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, timing behavior, or acoustic signals to extract sensitive information.
The core premise of a side-channel attack is that a device’s operation can leak information through observable physical signals. Such leaks may originate from the electrical power the device consumes (Kocher et al. 1999), the electromagnetic fields it emits (Gandolfi et al. 2001), the time required to complete computations, or even the acoustic noise it produces. Carefully measuring and analyzing these signals allows attackers to infer internal system states or recover secret data.

Kocher, Paul, Joshua Jaffe, and Benjamin Jun. 1999. “Differential Power Analysis.” In Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO’ 99. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48405-1_25.

Gandolfi, Karine, Christophe Mourtel, and Francis Olivier. 2001. “Electromagnetic Analysis: Concrete Results.” In Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems — CHES 2001. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-44709-1_21.
ML accelerators executing inference are exposed to physical leakage as other computing devices are. A matrix multiplication on an edge accelerator can draw current in a pattern correlated with the weight values and input activations being processed. An attacker who can measure that signal may infer properties of the computation, but recovery depends on measurement quality, implementation details, and knowledge or control of inputs. Additional samples help only if the observable signal carries the relevant information. The side-channel surface for a deployed model therefore encompasses both the cryptographic operations protecting its keys and the inference computation itself.
One of the most widely studied examples involves Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) implementations, and its lessons inform the analysis of ML workloads. An implementation can leak information about a key without an attacker breaking the cipher’s mathematical construction. The same distinction between an algorithm and its implementation applies to the ReLU activations, softmax normalizations, and weight-load sequences that constitute a forward pass.
A useful example of this attack technique is a power analysis of a password authentication process (Kocher et al. 2011). Consider a device that verifies a 5-byte password (0x61, 0x52, 0x77, 0x6A, 0x73) received one byte at a time over a serial interface. With the correct password, the power profile stays stable across all five bytes. Figure 12 shows what happens when only the first three bytes are correct. The power pattern tracks the correct-password profile through the third byte (0x61, 0x52, 0x77), then jumps when the device rejects the fourth byte (0x42) and halts authentication. An entirely wrong password (0x30 repeated) produces the same jump immediately after the first byte.

Kocher, Paul, Joshua Jaffe, Benjamin Jun, and Pankaj Rohatgi. 2011. “Introduction to Differential Power Analysis.” Journal of Cryptographic Engineering 1 (1): 5–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13389-011-0006-y.






Figure 12: Side-channel attack vulnerability: Power consumption patterns reveal information about a password comparison; consistent power usage indicates correct password bytes, while abrupt changes signal incorrect input and halted processing. Even without knowing the password, an attacker can infer it by analyzing the device’s power usage during authentication attempts. Source: Colin O’Flynn.



For this early-exit comparison, the position of the jump tells the attacker how many leading bytes are correct. If repeated guesses are permitted and the signal is distinguishable, this collapses a search over all \(256^5\) five-byte strings into five successive searches of 256 values each. ML inference can expose analogous data-dependent behavior, although it does not generally reveal a password-like sequence of correct guesses. A microcontroller that branches on a ReLU input’s sign or hardware that skips zero values can produce signals correlated with activation sparsity. Recovering layer topology or parameters requires an additional inference step supported by the implementation and available measurements; a measurable power signal is where that analysis starts, not where it ends.
The underlying lesson is physical: computation emits signals, whether as the sound of a cipher machine (Wright and Greengrass 1987) or of a laptop running a cipher (Genkin et al. 2017), the clicks of a keyboard (Asonov and Agrawal 2004), or the current drawn by a processor. For a fleet, the important variant needs no probe at all. On shared hardware, the shared resource itself becomes the measurement instrument. Researchers built a power monitor from logic in their own region of an FPGA shared among users and used it to recover a cryptographic key computed in another user’s region (Zhao and Suh 2018). The sharing that makes multi-tenancy economical turns caches, memory bandwidth, and power delivery into channels between tenants.

Wright, Peter, and Paul Greengrass. 1987. Spycatcher: The Candid Autobiography of a Senior Intelligence Officer. Viking Penguin.

Genkin, Daniel, Adi Shamir, and Eran Tromer. 2017. “Acoustic Cryptanalysis.” Journal of Cryptology 30: 392–443. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-015-9224-2.

Asonov, Dmitri, and Rakesh Agrawal. 2004. “Keyboard Acoustic Emanations.” IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2004. Proceedings. 2004, 3–11. https://doi.org/10.1109/secpri.2004.1301311.

Zhao, M., and G. E. Suh. 2018. “FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks.” 2018 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), 229–44. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2018.00049.
Machine learning systems inherit this risk when accelerators or edge devices process sensitive data near an observable signal. A local speech-recognition device may leak timing or power patterns correlated with commands. An accelerator may reveal layer structure, parameter access patterns, or batch shape through timing, power, or electromagnetic traces. Side-channel defense therefore asks which signals are observable in the deployment environment and whether shielding, constant-time execution, noise, monitoring, or physical access controls can reduce the signal enough to preserve the trust boundary.



Leaky interfaces sit between physical access and lifecycle trust: every diagnostic, update, or communication interface is also a security boundary. Side-channel attacks leak through physical signals; leaky interfaces expose information or accept unverified inputs through channels the system already provides. These access points often go unnoticed during system design, yet they give attackers direct entry points to extract data, manipulate functionality, or introduce malicious code.
A leaky interface is any access point that reveals more information than intended or accepts commands from the wrong actor. The common causes are weak authentication, missing encryption, inadequate isolation, and development interfaces left exposed in production. Consumer, medical, and industrial systems have repeatedly shown the pattern: Wi-Fi-enabled baby monitors have exposed unsecured remote access ports,12 and pacemaker vulnerabilities13 have shown how wireless interfaces can become safety-critical control channels.
12 IoT Device Vulnerabilities: Default credentials, unencrypted communications, and outdated firmware create access paths into connected devices. A compromised smart camera can supply manipulated inputs or participate in distributed attacks; if it also contributes training data or federated updates, that path can carry poisoning attempts. The consequences depend on the device’s role and permissions.13 Medical Device Security: Connected medical devices require secure maintenance over long operating lifetimes. In a device that uses ML, compromised inputs, weights, or preprocessing can alter clinical behavior without stopping the device. Traditional device software can also fail silently, so the additional ML requirement is to evaluate learned behavior alongside firmware integrity and physical safety controls.14 Debug Port Vulnerabilities: JTAG and Serial Wire Debug can expose memory and execution control when debug access remains enabled and authorized checks are absent or bypassed. An attacker may then recover weights accessible in plaintext, but an exposed connector alone does not defeat correctly enforced debug locks or encryption whose keys remain unavailable.Debug ports14 left enabled on production devices are the canonical case. A consumer smart lightbulb, for example, exposed unencrypted Wi-Fi credentials through such a port, giving attackers a path into the home network without defeating any network defense.
The data center has its own privileged maintenance interfaces. A server’s baseboard management controller commonly supports power control, console access, and firmware management over an out-of-band network, independently of the host operating system. Compromising its credentials or firmware can therefore expose control paths that host access policies do not govern. The resulting reach depends on network segmentation, controller privileges, and firmware-update protections. The attestation checks of section 13.8.4 help only when trusted measurements cover the affected components and the attacker cannot forge the evidence or alter the verifier’s approved state. The same reasoning applies at the edge, where a maintenance interface that lacks authentication can expose user data, alter model weights, or disable security features.
Securing interfaces is therefore inventory work as much as cryptography. Strong authentication, encrypted communication, anomaly detection, access-control policy, periodic audit, and zero-trust defaults all serve the same principle: every interface must justify what it exposes and who can use it.



Supply chain risks extend the provenance decision from a single interface to every component and every stage of its life. The smallest unit is the counterfeit part. A counterfeit processor, memory module, sensor, or network device may look and function like a genuine one while degrading faster, failing under load, or containing hidden circuitry, so procurement becomes part of the security boundary. Organizations that unknowingly deploy such parts may also violate safety, privacy, or cybersecurity obligations, which makes component provenance evidence that the deployed system matches the certified one.
Figure 13 maps the full lifecycle through design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, and deployment. Each stage presents opportunities for tampering or substitution: recycled electronic waste can be relabeled as new, distributors can mix cloned parts into legitimate shipments, and insiders at manufacturing facilities can embed hardware trojans that routine functional tests may miss. Micrography, X-ray screening, and functional testing provide different evidence, with coverage and cost determined by the suspected modification. Procurement therefore needs risk-based provenance controls as well as inspection; passing a functional test does not establish a component’s origin or exclude dormant malicious behavior.
Fleet procurement changes the shape of this risk. A training cluster is bought in bulk from a small number of part numbers, so each of the 128 nodes of the reference cluster carries the same accelerators, network adapters, management controller, and firmware images as every other. A compromised shared design, firmware release, or production batch can therefore affect many nodes at once. Replication does not remove a vulnerability shared by the replicas, although one compromised unit is evidence about its part number, not proof that every unit carrying it is affected. The provenance bound on trust (principle \(\ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}\)) applies to silicon and firmware as much as to data. Supplier, batch, and firmware records help identify the affected population; supplier concentration increases common dependencies even when those records are complete.







Figure 13: Hardware supply chain attack surface: Each lifecycle stage admits its own compromise (red arrows) and needs its own assurance evidence (green gates); no single check covers the chain, and dashed lines carry each missed compromise forward to deployment. Unlike software, which can be patched remotely, a compromise that survives to deployment often requires physical replacement.



Figure 13 also shows the economic asymmetry. Software vulnerabilities can often be patched remotely, but a hardware compromise may require physical replacement. That possibility adds replacement cost, service interruption, and revalidation to the expected loss and strengthens the case for preventive checks before deployment.
A disputed 2018 case illustrates the importance of separating allegations from verified compromise. Bloomberg Businessweek reported that state-sponsored actors had implanted surveillance chips on server motherboards manufactured by Supermicro (Robertson and Riley 2018). Apple, Amazon, and Supermicro publicly denied the claims, and industry experts questioned the lack of verifiable technical evidence. The dispute does not establish that the named organizations deployed compromised hardware or lacked adequate provenance controls. It instead motivates a general engineering requirement: claims about deployed components need evidence from the relevant fabrication, assembly, distribution, and integration stages. Industrial policy, including the CHIPS and Science Act (United States Congress 2022), addresses a different level of the supply chain from component assurance. Component validation, runtime monitoring, attestation, and hardware roots of trust provide deployment checks whose coverage must be assessed against the suspected compromise.

Robertson, J., and M. Riley. 2018. The Big Hack: How China Used a Tiny Chip to Infiltrate U.S. Companies - Bloomberg.

United States Congress. 2022. CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 (Public Law 117-167). Public Law 117-167, 136 Stat. 1366.
The engineering takeaway is that hardware trust must be evidenced continuously across design, fabrication, procurement, deployment, and retirement. A trusted execution environment (TEE) isolates selected code and data from parts of the surrounding host. Attestation supplies cryptographic evidence about that protected environment before another component entrusts it with secrets. Neither mechanism establishes that a model is behaviorally correct, and both depend on an explicit set of trusted hardware and software components.

Checkpoint 13.3: Knowledge check: Hardware security
Before moving from hardware trust to ML-enabled attacks, check that each vulnerability family is attached to the deployment decision it tests.

Processor isolation: explain how a transient-execution flaw can expose a co-tenant’s prompts or keys even after software access control passes.
Physical access: distinguish what fault injection changes in a running computation from what a side-channel attack observes about it.
Interfaces: identify a maintenance or debug interface in a training node or edge device that host access policies do not govern.
Correlated risk: explain why a compromised part number threatens a fleet differently from a compromised individual device.



These hardware threats endanger the model, its data, and the execution environment that protects them. Machine learning can also change roles: the same pattern-recognition capability that makes models valuable can help an adversary analyze leakage and attack that environment.

Self-Check: Question

Vulnerabilities like Meltdown and Spectre exploit transient execution in modern processors. What microarchitectural mechanism can let an attacker infer protected data across an intended isolation boundary?

Transient instructions can encode protected data in cache state that remains measurable after the processor discards their architectural effects.
Speculative execution permanently overwrites physical DRAM cells with ciphertext keys without notifying the OS kernel.
The CPU floating-point unit truncates FP32 tensor activations to INT8 during branch prediction.
Speculative branch predictors disable hardware-level AES encryption engines on PCIe accelerator interconnects.

In laser fault injection experiments on embedded neural network microcontrollers (e.g., Breier et al., 2018), researchers targeted the assembly instructions implementing the ReLU activation function. Explain the assembly-level mechanism of this attack and its effect on the model’s output.
An attacker places an oscilloscope probe near the power rail of an edge ML microcontroller running a proprietary convolutional network. How can the attacker infer model architecture or recover layer weights without accessing the device’s firmware or API?

By sending malformed TCP packets that trigger core dumps over the microcontroller’s UART interface.
By measuring instruction-dependent power consumption waveforms where current draw varies with weight values, multiplication operand hamming weights, and ReLU pre-activation signs.
By overwriting the microcontroller’s secure boot ROM keys using over-the-air firmware updates.
By inducing thermal shutdown to force the microcontroller to reboot into an unauthenticated recovery bootloader.

True or False: A production edge device exposes an unauthenticated JTAG/SWD interface that permits reads of plaintext model weights in flash. Physical access to that interface can bypass host software permissions for those reads.
Place the five stages of the hardware supply chain in sequential order from initial creation to operational deployment:


Fabrication: Silicon wafer processing and packaging where hardware trojans can be inserted into ASIC masks
Distribution: Shipping, warehousing, and logistics where physical tampering or component substitution can occur
Design: Architecture specification and RTL creation where design flaws or backdoors can be introduced
Deployment: Integration into production servers and edge fleets where counterfeit parts manifest operational failures
Assembly: PCB assembly and soldering where inferior or cloned components can be substituted
