\(\ArithmeticIntensity = 96/6 = 16\) FLOP/byte
\(2 \times 96^3 \times 10 \text{ pJ} = 17.69\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{J} = 0.0177\text{ mJ}\)
\(3 \times 96^2 \times 4 \times 160 \text{ pJ} = 17.69\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{J} = 0.0177\text{ mJ}\)
Balanced at the crossover


Large matrix (\(\SquareGemmDimension = 1000\))
\(\ArithmeticIntensity = 1000/6 = 167\) FLOP/byte
\(2 \times 10^9 \times 10 \text{ pJ} = 20\text{ mJ}\)
\(3 \times 10^6 \times 4 \times 160 \text{ pJ} = 1.92\text{ mJ}\)
Improve compute efficiency


Vector addition (\(\VectorElementCount= 1000\))
\(\ArithmeticIntensity = 1000/12000 = 0.083\) FLOP/byte
\(1000 \times 10 \text{ pJ} = 0.00001\text{ mJ}\)
\(12000 \times 160 \text{ pJ} = 0.00192\text{ mJ}\)
Reduce data movement through fusion






Systems insight: Energy optimization follows the same bottleneck logic as latency optimization. Dense matrix multiply rewards efficient arithmetic; element-wise work rewards reducing memory movement.


The energy roofline model reveals why different optimization strategies suit different workloads. When arithmetic dominates the energy account, large dense matrix operations benefit from lower energy per executed operation. When data movement dominates, element-wise kernels benefit from data layout optimization, kernel fusion to reduce memory round-trips, and on-chip memory utilization. Faster execution alone does not establish either saving; average power and execution time must be measured together. This framework guides architectural and algorithmic choices for sustainable AI system design.




Quantifying AI system energy consumption requires measurement at multiple levels of the hardware stack, from chip-level instrumentation to facility-wide monitoring. The method choice is itself an engineering trade-off: hardware counters provide fine attribution, mobile profilers expose platform-specific subsystems, edge instruments capture duty-cycle behavior, and system-level tools connect component measurements to the facility overhead that component counters miss.


Modern processors expose manufacturer-provided power telemetry that software can query through device interfaces. These counters provide workload-correlated estimates within the rails and sampling windows the device reports; they are not universal ground truth for wall-plug energy, and their update rate, calibration, and component coverage vary by platform. External instruments remain necessary when a comparison requires traceable total energy or finer temporal resolution.
Intel’s running average power limit (RAPL) interface exposes cumulative energy counters for supported power domains, with coverage depending on the processor. A controlled measurement samples the relevant counter before and after the workload and divides the energy delta by elapsed time to recover average power. This makes RAPL useful for host-side work, provided the account identifies the domains actually reported and handles counter rollover. Package and subdomain counters must not be added when their coverage overlaps. RAPL does not measure discrete GPU energy, and access can require elevated permissions.
NVIDIA GPUs expose power information through the NVIDIA Management Library, accessible via the nvidia-smi command-line tool or programmatic bindings. GPU power monitoring must distinguish an instantaneous reading from a sensor-averaged value; the reported behavior depends on the device and query. Integrating samples requires a cadence and workload interval appropriate to that averaging window. Sampling an averaged signal more frequently does not recover short power spikes. Supported accumulated-energy counters can simplify interval accounting, but their scope and resolution still need checking, and neither method supplies full facility energy by itself.
Edge devices and microcontrollers often lack built-in power counters and require external instrumentation. Select current range, voltage measurement, sampling rate, and analog bandwidth to capture the workload’s active and sleep intervals. Board-level monitors can integrate inference energy; resolving shorter events requires adequate instrument bandwidth and careful treatment of filtering and aliasing. A fast sample rate alone cannot attribute energy to individual operations.



On mobile platforms, measurement depends on how much subsystem attribution the host operating system exposes. Some platforms report per-rail or per-component power for the CPU, GPU, neural processing unit, and radio, which lets a developer see which subsystem dominates total draw. Others expose only relative energy-impact scores or thermal states, which are useful for spotting regressions during development but cannot support an absolute energy claim. Vendor profilers that correlate power traces with kernel execution sit between these extremes. The design question is therefore not which tool to use but whether the reported quantity covers the electrical boundary the comparison needs; a relative score cannot be converted into joules per inference. When it cannot, external instrumentation is required. Table 5 summarizes edge power measurement instruments by measurement role and the checks each role requires.



Table 5: Edge Power Measurement Instruments: Choose instrumentation by the event duration, dynamic range, and electrical boundary being measured. Verify configured specifications rather than assuming one device is universally sufficient.










Instrument class
Measurement role
Required checks




Board current monitor
Integrate energy on selected rails
Voltage, sample interval, shunt losses, and event duration


Multi-rail monitor
Attribute energy among components
Channel synchronization and coverage


Wide-range external analyzer
Capture sleep and active intervals
Bandwidth, range transitions, and calibration


Automated power analyzer
Repeat duty-cycle and battery tests
Triggering, integration window, and supply behavior









Edge energy measurements are useful only when they reflect the deployed duty cycle rather than an idealized active-only inference burst. Reproducible evaluation requires controls matched to that workload. Simultaneous current and voltage logging must span the active and quiescent states being measured, capturing rail voltage fluctuations rather than inferring power from current alone. A sustained-load comparison requires thermal and frequency stabilization; cold starts and periodic bursts instead need measurements of their actual state transitions. Realistic duty-cycle accounting records both peak inference draw and time-averaged power across typical idle intervals. Component attribution may isolate or subtract peripheral loads to expose accelerator consumption, but a deployment estimate must include the radios, sensors, and other subsystems needed to deliver the service. For duty cycle accounting, equation 8 expresses this relationship between active and idle power:
\[\AveragePower= \ActiveInferencePower\times \InferenceDutyCycle + \StandbyPower\times (1 - \InferenceDutyCycle) \tag{8}\]
where \(\InferenceDutyCycle\) is the duty cycle (fraction of time performing inference).



Comprehensive energy accounting requires combining chip-level measurements with infrastructure overhead. The component terms must be disjoint: GPU-board telemetry that already includes device memory must not be added to another measurement of that same memory. They must also cover the IT boundary, with storage and server support loads included in the relevant measured terms. Equation 9 formalizes total energy as the sum of those component contributions scaled by facility overhead:
\[\FacilityEnergy= (\CpuEnergy+ \GpuEnergy+ \MemorySubsystemEnergy+ \NetworkEnergy) \times \text{PUE} \tag{9}\]
No single counter spans the full energy path, so system-level profilers like Intel VTune, NVIDIA Nsight Systems, and open-source tools such as PowerJoular aggregate measurements across components. On-chip counters estimate device power and may differ in sampling rate, coverage, and calibration; a rack power distribution unit (PDU) provides an independent measurement of the downstream IT load. A rack PDU does not measure central chillers, pumps, lighting, or upstream conversion losses. Facility energy must instead come from facility meters or from an explicitly time-matched PUE applied to the measured IT load.
Equation 10 expresses the relationship between measured component power and total facility power:
\[\FacilityPower= \InformationTechnologyPower\times \text{PUE} = (\AggregateServerPower+ \NetworkEquipmentPower+ \StorageEquipmentPower) \times \text{PUE} \tag{10}\]
Facility energy is still not a footprint. Converting it to emissions requires a grid factor, and the hardware that drew it carries manufacturing emissions that no power meter records.

Self-Check: Question

An attention kernel has an arithmetic intensity of 3 FLOP/byte. An illustrative chip-and-memory energy model assigns 10 pJ per FLOP and 100 pJ per byte moved from DRAM, excluding static and facility energy. Which intervention directly targets the larger modeled energy contribution?

Increasing arithmetic precision from FP16 to FP32 to execute more FLOPs per memory transaction.

A 2 MW IT load cluster improves its Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) from 1.58 to 1.10 without altering any model weights or server SKUs. In the CMOS dynamic power equation \(P_{\text{dynamic}}=\alpha_{\text{sw}}CV^2f\), the parameter \(\alpha_{\text{sw}}\) is the ____, summarizing capacitance-weighted switching per clock cycle under the chosen counting convention.
An engineer needs to profile the energy consumption of a sub-watt microcontroller executing an on-device wake-word detection model that spends 98 percent of its time in deep sleep drawing 30 \(\mu\text{W}\). The microcontroller lacks on-chip energy counters. Which measurement approach is appropriate?

Sampling the Linux RAPL interface at 100 Hz to capture CPU package power states.

title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
Consider a data center supplied by a hydro-heavy grid. Its operational carbon intensity can be far below a fossil-heavy grid, but hydroelectric generation is not lifecycle-zero, and the AI system is not carbon-free. Reservoir construction and operation have impacts, while mining the silicon, manufacturing the GPUs, and pouring the concrete for the data center emitted carbon before the servers were turned on. A complete footprint calculation must account for operational electricity, embodied carbon, and the ecological effects excluded from a carbon-only metric.
The accounting model builds that footprint term by term. It first fixes whose inventory each emission belongs to, then gives operational carbon, embodied carbon, and their lifecycle sum each an equation that generalizes across workloads, grids, and amortization assumptions, and it closes by applying all three to one large training run.


The training, inference, and manufacturing account groups emissions by the activity that produces them. The three emission scopes defined by the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol (World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable Development 2023), an accounting standard for organizational emissions inventories, instead classify them relative to a reporting organization. These are different views of the same footprint, not additional totals to add together. Connecting the workload account to the organizational inventory requires naming who owns the equipment, purchases the electricity, and buys the service.
Within an owned data-center facility boundary, Scope 1 emissions include direct combustion in owned generators and refrigerant leakage from cooling equipment. Purchased electricity used to run cooling belongs in Scope 2, not Scope 1.
Scope 2 emissions represent indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat, and cooling consumed by the reporting organization. Purchased electricity is often the dominant category for an operator’s owned facility, and it varies dramatically by geographic location and grid energy mix. Electricity used by a cloud provider is Scope 2 for that provider, but a customer’s purchased cloud service is generally accounted for in the customer’s Scope 3 value chain. The physical electrons do not change; the reporting boundary does. The placement example in section 15.2 uses a declared pair of illustrative factors; actual accounting requires factors matched to the location, time, and method.
Scope 3 emissions constitute the most complex category, encompassing hardware manufacturing, cloud supply chains, transportation, disposal, and downstream use. Semiconductor manufacturing is carbon-intensive.15 The manufacturer reports the same fabrication emissions inside its own organizational boundary, so the two inventories describe one physical emission from two sides. How long operation takes to match that embodied term depends on how hard and on which grid the hardware runs. At rated power on the US-average grid, an H100’s operational emissions equal its allocated manufacturing footprint in roughly three to four weeks, the break-even worked with the lifecycle phases (section 15.8.1.1); at low utilization or on a clean grid, the same equality takes months or years. Under company-wide or value-chain AI accounting, Scope 3 can dominate even when Scope 2 dominates a single owned facility’s operational footprint.
15 Lithography and Embodied Energy: Advanced semiconductor fabrication can use energy-intensive lithography, including extreme ultraviolet (EUV) processes. Emissions per usable chip depend on the process sequence, facility energy mix, yield, die area, and allocation method. Neither transistor count nor a nominal process-node label alone determines the number of exposure steps or manufacturing footprint.16 Edge AI Energy Trade-off: Edge inference can reduce network transfers and response latency, while distributing computation across devices with different duty cycles and power states. It does not eliminate network or cloud work. Compare local compute, idle power, sensors, communications, and any remaining server work over the same service period; distributed consumption is harder to attribute, but remains part of the accounting boundary.Downstream use can also enter Scope 3, including end-user smartphones, IoT devices, and edge computing.16 Companywide totals do not by themselves identify the footprint of a particular AI service; that attribution still requires workload-level accounting.
The operational emissions of a final training run and its deployed service omit the development that produced them, including failed experiments, hyperparameter searches, and the build and test infrastructure. Repeated experiments can exceed the cost of the final run. A search that trains \(\SweepCandidateCount\) candidates at a fraction \(\SweepCandidateCostFraction\) of the final run’s cost adds \(\SweepCandidateCount \SweepCandidateCostFraction\) final-run equivalents before the chosen model starts, so a sweep of 50 candidates at 10 percent of full scale costs 5× the run that gets reported. Continuous integration, compilation, and evaluation add further work whose contribution depends on run frequency and scale. The development boundary must record these activities before assigning their emissions to the reporting organization’s inventory; the phase of model development does not itself determine the emissions scope.
The GHG Protocol17 arranges these scopes as concentric reporting boundaries that widen outward from the operator’s direct control (figure 7). On-site diesel generators sit in Scope 1, purchased grid electricity for compute and cooling in Scope 2, and upstream semiconductor fabrication and end-of-life recycling in Scope 3.
17 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol: The framework distinguishes direct emissions, purchased energy, and other value-chain emissions (World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable Development 2023). Their relative shares depend on the reporting organization and workload boundary. Explicit classification prevents purchased cloud services or manufacturing from disappearing from an account limited to an operator’s own electricity.
World Resources Institute, and World Business Council for Sustainable Development. 2023. Greenhouse Gas Protocol: Corporate Standard.






Figure 7: GHG Emission Scopes: Concentric rings place the reporting organization’s data center at the center, with Scope 1 (direct emissions) innermost, Scope 2 (purchased energy) around it, and Scope 3 (value chain) outermost. Representative sources sit inside each ring. The rings show reporting distance from the operator’s direct control, not relative size. Scope definitions follow the GHG Protocol (World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable Development 2023).



With the scopes and the development boundary defined, the activity phases of section 15.8.1.1, the lifecycle stages of section 15.12, and the scopes can be laid side by side (table 6). Each row is one set of emissions seen three ways, so a total built from one column must never be added to a total built from another.



Table 6: Three Views of One Footprint: The activity phases group emissions by the work that causes them, the lifecycle stages by when they occur, and the GHG scopes by which organization reports them. The same physical emissions appear once in each view; the scope assignment changes with the reporting organization, not with the hardware.











Activity phase
Lifecycle stage
Scope for an owner-operator
Scope for a cloud customer




Training (development runs and the final run)
Design and experimentation; use
Scope 2 for purchased electricity; Scope 1 for on-site generation
Scope 3 (purchased service)


Inference (serving)
Use
Scope 2 for purchased electricity; Scope 1 for on-site generation
Scope 3 (purchased service)


Manufacturing (embodied carbon)
Manufacture; disposal
Scope 3 (capital goods and end-of-life treatment)
Scope 3 (within the purchased service)






Categorizing these emissions into Scope 1, 2, and 3 frameworks provides a standardized vocabulary for corporate environmental reporting. Correctly applying this framework in practice requires classifying the various hidden emission sources across a typical ML platform’s operational lifecycle.

Checkpoint 15.2: Accounting for invisible carbon
Audit the carbon footprint of a machine learning platform by classifying the following emission sources into Scope 1 (Direct), Scope 2 (Indirect Energy), or Scope 3 (Value Chain). State the reporting organization before assigning each scope:

Backup generation: classify diesel burned by backup generators during a grid outage at an owned facility.
Leased cloud cluster: classify the electricity for both reporting entities, the cloud operator that purchases it and the customer that purchases the compute service.
Embodied manufacturing: classify the embodied carbon emitted during the manufacturing of the GPUs by TSMC.
End-user operation: classify emissions from the end-user’s smartphone battery while running a deployed mobile inference app.






Operational carbon emissions result from electricity consumption during training and inference, scaled by grid carbon intensity. Equation 11 quantifies this as the product of facility-level energy and grid carbon intensity:
\[\text{CO}_{2,\text{operational}} = \FacilityEnergy\times \text{CO}_{2,\text{grid}} \tag{11}\]
where \(\FacilityEnergy\) is the facility-level energy from equation 9 (component energy already scaled by \(\text{PUE}\)) and \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{grid}}\) is the carbon intensity of the electricity grid. The facility overhead enters once, through \(\FacilityEnergy\), so it does not appear again in the carbon equation. A concrete training emissions calculation illustrates this framework.

Napkin Math 15.5: Training emissions calculationProblem: Quantify the operational carbon footprint of training a 7B parameter model on 64 A100 GPUs for 14 days, assuming continuous accelerator draw at the rated power and the stated rack-support and facility overheads.
Math:

Compute energy: 64 GPUs \(\times\) 400 W \(\times\) 336 hours = 8,601.6 kWh.
Apply IT support and PUE: host processors, memory, and networking add to the accelerator load. This calculation borrows the ratio of IT power to accelerator power from the DGX H100 rack profile itemized later in table 7, a modeling proxy for an A100 server’s support load rather than a measurement of it, which scales accelerator energy by 1.38 to 11,827.2 kWh, so total facility energy = 11,827.2 kWh \(\times\) 1.12 = 13,246.5 kWh.
Calculate emissions: On US average grid (429 g/kWh \(\text{CO}_2\)), emissions = 5.7 t. On Quebec hydro grid (20 g/kWh), emissions = 264.9 kg.

Systems insight: The grid factor alone produces a 21.5× difference in training emissions for this pairing, the same placement lever quantified in notebook 15.2. The model architecture is unchanged.





The training-emissions notebook priced electricity only. At the same energy use, a lower grid emissions factor reduces operational carbon and increases the relative importance of chip fabrication and data center construction. For that same A100 run, the amortized manufacturing share derived at the end of this section is about 1.6 percent of total emissions on the US-average grid but about 25.8 percent on Quebec’s grid. Whether embodied carbon becomes the largest term depends on the manufacturing footprint, utilization, and service life, so those quantities must enter the comparison before an engineer can choose between reducing electricity use and extending hardware service.
Embodied carbon encompasses emissions from raw material extraction, semiconductor fabrication, assembly, transportation, and end-of-life disposal. For AI hardware, manufacturing emissions are dominated by the energy-intensive nature of advanced semiconductor processes.
Advanced-node AI accelerators carry substantial manufacturing footprints: an NVIDIA A100 GPU embodies approximately 150 kg CO2e per unit (Luccioni et al. 2023), and NVIDIA’s HGX H100 product carbon footprint implies roughly 164 kg CO2e per H100 when the baseboard footprint is allocated evenly across its eight GPUs (NVIDIA Corporation 2025), including wafer fabrication at advanced process nodes, high-bandwidth memory production, and packaging. Equation 12 amortizes this embodied carbon over the hardware lifetime to compute per-use emissions:
\[\text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied,daily}} = \frac{\text{CO}_{2,\text{manufacturing}}}{\HardwareServiceLife\times 365} \tag{12}\] with \(\HardwareServiceLife\) in years.
The manufacturing emissions have already occurred when the hardware enters service. Amortization allocates that burden over time; it does not describe additional manufacturing emissions accumulating each day. Utilization and service life determine how much useful work shares the initial burden.

Systems Perspective 15.1: Embodied carbon amortizationRenting a GPU for an hour uses hardware whose manufacturing emissions have already occurred. The workload account allocates a share of those emissions to the rental interval, regardless of whether the monetary fee explicitly prices carbon.
Expressing equation 12 per hour and multiplying by the job’s duration makes that allocation explicit: \[\text{CO}_{2,\text{total}} = \text{CO}_{2,\text{operational}} + \left( \frac{\text{CO}_{2,\text{manufacturing}}}{\HardwareServiceLife \times 365 \times 24} \times \JobDuration \right)\] with \(\HardwareServiceLife\) in years and \(\JobDuration\) in hours.
Scenario: Training a model for 10 hours on 8 NVIDIA H100s. This accelerator-only illustration uses thermal design power (TDP) as a constant-power assumption and excludes host, network, and facility energy. Its embodied share uses the allocated baseboard footprint; it is not a complete fleet lifecycle inventory.

Operational: 8 \(\times\) 0.7 kW \(\times\) 10 hours = 56 kWh. At 0.429 kg/kWh (US-average grid) = 24 kg.
Embodied: 8 \(\times\) 164 kg = 1312 kg.
Amortization: Lifetime = 3 years, the standard service life (26280 hours).

Hourly “Rent” = 1312 kg / 26280 hours \(\approx\) 0.050 kg/h.
Job Cost = 0.050 kg/h \(\times\) 10 hours = 0.5 kg.


Systems insight: For long-lived hardware in dirty grids, electricity dominates (24 kg vs. 0.5 kg). However, in clean grids (hydro, 0.020 kg/kWh), operational drops to 1.1 kg, making embodied carbon a significant fraction (~30.8 percent) of the total footprint.


The perspective’s H100 job, like the lifecycle notebook later in this chapter, amortizes over the 3-year standard service life. Returning to the earlier A100 training run, the recap that follows keeps that setup’s own assumption, a 4-year extended service life. The difference matters because a longer life spreads the same manufacturing carbon over more service, lowering the per-job share; the sensitivity analysis after the lifecycle notebook treats service life as one of the assumptions that can reverse a decision. For an accelerator with 150 kg embodied carbon (the A100 estimate cited earlier) and that 4-year data center lifetime, the first step is daily amortization: 150 kg / (4 years \(\times\) 365 d/year) \(\approx\) 0.103 kg/day.
The second step assigns that daily share to the job. A training run lasting 14 days on 64 accelerators carries 64 \(\times\) 14 days \(\times\) 0.103 kg \(\approx\) 92.1 kg CO2 of amortized embodied carbon.
Added to the 5,682.7 kg of operational emissions calculated earlier for the US average grid, the embodied contribution of 92.1 kg is approximately 1.6 percent of the run’s total emissions. If training occurred in Quebec’s low-carbon grid, where the same run produced 264.9 kg of operational emissions, the same embodied contribution would be about 25.8 percent of the total. The manufacturing term did not change; the cleaner grid shrank everything around it.



The workload account groups operational emissions into training and inference, then adds embodied emissions. Equation 13 aggregates these contributions; completeness depends on the inventory assigned to each term. Development experiments and supporting services must enter that inventory rather than disappear when the account starts with the final training run:
\[\text{CO}_{2,\text{lifecycle}} = \text{CO}_{2,\text{training}} + \text{CO}_{2,\text{inference}} + \text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied}} \tag{13}\]
Each term has its own physical drivers (figure 8). The embodied term \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied}}\) is fixed before the hardware runs, at roughly 150 kg to 164 kg CO2e per accelerator for the devices priced above. The training term \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{training}}\) is a one-time cost set by cluster scale, PUE, and checkpoint I/O, while the inference term \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{inference}}\) recurs for as long as request traffic and KV-cache residency keep serving replicas powered. Their relative proportions therefore shift over the deployment lifetime, as the worked account in notebook 15.6 and the serving crossover in section 15.11.2 show.






Figure 8: The Carbon Lifecycle of an ML System: Manufacturing contributes embodied carbon, while training and inference contribute operational carbon through energy, facility overhead, and grid intensity. Block widths show timing, not magnitude. The relative size of each term is workload-specific: serving volume, grid factor, and hardware lifetime determine which one dominates.



The equations become a decision tool once each factor is measured or declared. A worked account for a large training run shows how the operational and embodied terms combine, and which of them dominates.

Napkin Math 15.6: Partial lifecycle carbon estimationProblem: Estimate facility operational emissions plus allocated accelerator-baseboard manufacturing emissions for training a 70B parameter model.
Variables: 2,048 H100 GPUs, 30 days, 700 W TDP, rack-profile support power, PUE 1.12, grid intensity 429 g \(\text{CO}_2\)/kWh.
Math: Accelerator power = 2,048 \(\times\) 0.7 kW \(\approx\) 1,433.6 kW. Applying the DGX H100 rack profile for host, memory, networking, and conversion support raises the IT load to 1,971.2 kW; facility power = 1,971.2 kW \(\times\) 1.12 \(\approx\) 2,207.7 kW. Energy = 2,207.7 kW \(\times\) 24 h/day \(\times\) 30 days \(\approx\) 1,589,575.7 kWh. Emissions \(\approx\) 681.9 t \(\text{CO}_2\).
Embodied: Assume manufacturing footprint is \(\approx\) 164 kg \(\text{CO}_2\) per H100 GPU, allocating NVIDIA’s HGX H100 baseboard product carbon footprint evenly across its eight GPUs (NVIDIA Corporation 2025). This worked account uses time-based allocation: it assigns the job the fraction of manufacturing emissions corresponding to its 1-month occupancy of a 3-year service life. Under that declared rule, (2,048 \(\times\) 164 kg) \(\times\) (1 month / 36 months) \(\approx\) 9.3 t \(\text{CO}_2\).
Result: 681.9 t + 9.3 t \(\approx\) 691.3 t \(\text{CO}_2\).
Systems insight: The operational term dominates this partial lifecycle account. It includes facility electricity and allocated HGX baseboard manufacturing, but omits manufacturing of host systems, networking, storage, and facility infrastructure, as well as other unmodeled lifecycle stages. A complete footprint must extend the inventory to those boundaries.


Time is one defensible allocation basis, not a universal one. Shared fleets may instead allocate embodied emissions by accelerator-hours, reserved capacity, or a workload’s share of useful computation. The chosen denominator must be reported and applied consistently; otherwise a low-utilization job can appear artificially inexpensive merely because another tenant absorbs the idle capacity. These workload shares support engineering comparisons; they do not determine the reporting year or category in a corporate emissions inventory. Procurement decisions need the unallocated fleet total as well as the workload-attributed share, because amortization changes ownership of an emission in the ledger but does not remove it from the atmosphere.
Every lifecycle estimate should therefore carry an uncertainty interval rather than a single authoritative total. Average workload power, PUE, grid intensity, hardware lifetime, utilization, and manufacturing footprint are measured or modeled with different errors. A sensitivity analysis varies the assumptions that could reverse the decision, including clean-grid versus carbon-intensive operation, three- versus five-year service life, and low versus high serving volume. It then reports whether the preferred design remains preferred. Precision in arithmetic cannot compensate for an unstable system boundary.
The balance among these terms changes with serving volume and duration. A high-volume service can exceed its entire training footprint within months, or within days at higher traffic, a crossover that section 15.11.2 works through for a deployed model.
The account becomes an engineering tool when it runs on every job rather than once after the fact. Listing 1 implements a partial lifecycle carbon calculator that combines measured energy, the rack support multiplier, a declared facility PUE, an explicitly selected grid-intensity factor, and amortized embodied carbon. Its example reproduces the 64-A100 run, with each input drawn from the facility, grid, or hardware profile it describes; section 15.13.3.2 compares the sources of the grid factor.



Listing 1: Lifecycle Carbon Calculation: Computing total carbon footprint including operational and embodied emissions.


from mlsysim import Hardware, Infrastructure, ReferenceStats, Systems


def calculate_carbon_footprint(
    gpu_power_watts: float,
    num_gpus: int,
    training_hours: float,
    it_power_multiplier: float,
    pue: float,
    grid_intensity_gco2_kwh: float,
    gpu_embodied_kg: float,
    gpu_lifetime_years: float,
) -> dict:
    """Estimate operational emissions plus allocated GPU manufacturing emissions."""

    # Operational emissions (plain floats: watts, hours, kWh, grams)
    gpu_energy_kwh = gpu_power_watts * num_gpus * training_hours / 1000
    it_energy_kwh = gpu_energy_kwh * it_power_multiplier  # + host, net
    facility_energy_kwh = it_energy_kwh * pue  # overhead, applied once
    operational_kg = (
        facility_energy_kwh * grid_intensity_gco2_kwh / 1000
    )

    # Embodied emissions (amortized by time over the service life)
    daily_embodied = gpu_embodied_kg / (gpu_lifetime_years * 365)
    training_days = training_hours / 24
    embodied_kg = num_gpus * training_days * daily_embodied

    return {
        "energy_kwh": facility_energy_kwh,
        "operational_carbon_kg": operational_kg,
        "embodied_carbon_kg": embodied_kg,
        "total_carbon_kg": operational_kg + embodied_kg,
        "embodied_fraction": embodied_kg
        / (operational_kg + embodied_kg),
    }


# Example: 7B model training on a 64-GPU A100 cluster for 14 days.
# Each input names its source: PUE is a facility property, the
# grid factor a property of the electricity supply.
_rack = Systems.Racks.DGX_H100_4Node  # proxy support-load profile
_facility = Infrastructure.FacilityCooling.BestAir  # PUE 1.12
_grid = Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg  # annual-average factor
_run = ReferenceStats.MidScaleTrainingCarbonProfile
result = calculate_carbon_footprint(
    gpu_power_watts=Hardware.Cloud.A100.tdp.m_as("W"),  # 400 W
    num_gpus=Systems.Clusters.Lab_64_A100.total_accelerators,  # 64
    training_hours=_run.TrainingDays.m_as("h"),  # 336 h
    it_power_multiplier=(
        _rack.it_power / _rack.accelerator_power
    ).m_as(""),
    pue=_facility.pue,
    grid_intensity_gco2_kwh=_grid.carbon_intensity_g_kwh,
    gpu_embodied_kg=Hardware.Cloud.A100.embodied_carbon_kg,
    gpu_lifetime_years=(  # 4-year extended service life
        Infrastructure.Pricing.Capital
        .AcceleratorExtendedServiceLifeYears.rate
    ),
)
print(
    f"Total carbon footprint: {result['total_carbon_kg']:.0f} kg CO2"
)
print(f"Embodied fraction: {result['embodied_fraction']:.1%}")



Teams can integrate this partial carbon account directly into orchestration dashboards. Calculating operational and embodied emissions for individual training runs, however, captures only one dimension of fleet resource use. At campus scale, data centers introduce power-delivery and cooling constraints that individual run metrics leave invisible.

Self-Check: Question

When a hyperscaler relocates a training cluster from a fossil-heavy grid (800 \(\text{gCO}_2/\text{kWh}\)) to a clean hydro grid (20 \(\text{gCO}_2/\text{kWh}\)), its sustainability dashboard reveals that embodied carbon becomes the dominant component of total lifecycle emissions. Explain the mechanism behind this inversion and its implications for hardware procurement.

title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
A training cluster can fit its accelerator power budget yet exceed its facility budget once support systems and cooling enter the account. Whether a facility can host the cluster at all is a feasibility question; the sustainability question is whether a change in power delivery or cooling reduces lifecycle cost while preserving that feasible operating envelope. The relevant comparison includes annual energy, local water use, equipment lifetime, and the energy wasted when cooling failures interrupt useful work.
Facility sustainability therefore has to be read as a chain of constraints rather than as a single PUE number. Persistent megawatt demand sets the grid and emissions exposure, power delivery determines how much electricity becomes useful IT load, cooling determines whether dense racks can operate without throttling, and water use determines whether a technically efficient site is locally sustainable. The physical mechanisms below matter here because each assigns losses or resource use to a different accounting boundary.


At facility scale, the optimization target is no longer a single model but the overhead and grid context surrounding every watt of IT power. The PUE and geographic calculations already showed why the same IT workload can impose different facility and carbon costs; here the relevant change is aggregate demand. The same IEA Energy and AI analysis behind the 2030 electricity projection cited at the chapter’s opening also tracks emissions, a different quantity. It estimated emissions from data-center electricity use at about 180 Mt at the time of the analysis and projected roughly 300 Mt by 2035 in its Base Case, still below 1.5 percent of total energy-sector emissions.18 The energy burden grows with data-center capacity, training workloads, and inference demand (Patterson et al. 2021), so component efficiency must be evaluated against fleet expansion (Thompson et al. 2021; Dodge et al. 2022).
18 Data Center Emissions Scale: IEA’s 2025 Energy and AI analysis reports three distinct quantities. Data centers consumed roughly 1–2 percent of global electricity at the time of the analysis, a share projected to approach 3 percent by 2030, with AI contributing to demand growth. Emissions from data-center electricity use, about 180 Mt at that time, are projected at around 300 Mt by 2035 in the Base Case, below 1.5 percent of total energy-sector emissions. The largest hyperscale facilities can draw over 100 MW continuously, equivalent to powering tens of thousands of homes.
Thompson, N. C., K. Greenewald, K. Lee, and G. F. Manso. 2021. “Deep Learning’s Diminishing Returns: The Cost of Improvement Is Becoming Unsustainable.” IEEE Spectrum 58 (10): 50–55. https://doi.org/10.1109/mspec.2021.9563954.

Dodge, Jesse, Taylor Prewitt, Remi Tachet des Combes, Erika Odmark, Roy Schwartz, Emma Strubell, Alexandra Sasha Luccioni, Noah A. Smith, Nicole DeCario, and Will Buchanan. 2022. “Measuring the Carbon Intensity of AI in Cloud Instances.” 2022 ACM Conference on Fairness Accountability and Transparency, 1877–94. https://doi.org/10.1145/3531146.3533234.


The relevant facility quantity is persistent megawatt-class load, not the model name alone. Hyperscale campuses house large fleets of accelerator servers and hold loads of 100 MW or more for years at a time.19 A newer accelerator lowers a job’s energy only when that workload realizes the efficiency gain. Even then, lower energy per job need not reduce campus demand if the fleet uses the released capacity to perform more work.
19 Hyperscale Data Center Footprint: A hyperscale campus makes long-lived investments in substations and transmission connections. Algorithmic improvements can reduce demand but do not remove the costs already incurred for that capacity. Supply contracts and operating schedules remain adjustable, subject to their terms and the physical connection.
Masanet, Eric, Arman Shehabi, Nuoa Lei, Sarah Smith, and Jonathan Koomey. 2020. “Recalibrating Global Data Center Energy-Use Estimates.” Science 367 (6481): 984–86. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aba3758.
Whether that demand keeps growing depends on the race between workload growth and efficiency. Masanet et al. (2020) show that efficiency gains held global data-center energy nearly flat through the 2010s even as computing output grew several-fold; sustained AI demand growth can erode that offset, which is why the IEA projection cited earlier rises rather than remaining flat.
Beyond computational demands, cooling can account for 30–40 percent of facility energy in the conventional air-cooled data-center designs surveyed by Ebrahimi et al. (2014). This is a design-regime range, not a constant for modern hyperscale or liquid-cooled facilities; section 15.10.4 derives the site-specific overhead through PUE and the cooling architecture.

Ebrahimi, K., G. F. Jones, and A. S. Fleischer. 2014. “A Review of Data Center Cooling Technology, Operating Conditions and the Corresponding Low-Grade Waste Heat Recovery Opportunities.” Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 31: 622–38. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2013.12.007.
The United States alone illustrates how cloud and AI infrastructure can reshape national energy planning. US data center electricity consumption roughly tripled from 58 TWh in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023, reaching 4.4 percent of national supply, according to measurements and projections from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) (figure 9). For 2028, LBNL’s scenarios range from 325 to 580 TWh; the high end would consume roughly 12 percent of all US electrical generation. These scenarios describe possible demand, not a measured capacity ceiling. They motivate evaluating efficiency gains alongside the generation, transmission, and connection capacity needed to serve that demand.














Figure 9: The Energy Gap: US data center electricity consumption tripled from 58 TWh (2014) to 176 TWh (2023). LBNL projects consumption of 325 to 580 TWh by 2028, with AI workloads treated as an important driver of growth. At the high end, data centers would consume approximately 12 percent of US electricity, motivating evaluation of the generation, transmission, and connection capacity needed to serve that projected demand.







The environmental impact of AI workloads has become a measurable concern, even though the IEA estimate cited earlier puts emissions from data-center electricity use at about 180 Mt, below 1.5 percent of total energy-sector emissions. Strubell et al. (2019) made this concern concrete by estimating that development-scale training and architecture search for a large NLP model could emit as much carbon as several passenger vehicles over their lifetimes. Patterson et al. (2021) later showed that the most widely quoted architecture-search estimate depended strongly on proxy-task, hardware, data-center efficiency, and grid carbon-intensity assumptions. Carbon benchmarks are therefore only as good as the boundary behind them. Two estimates of the same search can differ by orders of magnitude when one assumes older hardware, an average facility, and a fossil-heavy grid while the other measures the deployed configuration.20
20 Neural Architecture Search (NAS) Carbon Cost: The ~284,000 kg CO2e figure from Strubell et al. (2019) represents an unoptimized Evolved Transformer search that drops sharply when accounting for TPU hardware, grid mix, and proxy tasks (Patterson et al. 2021). The systems lesson is boundary discipline: search, tuning, and failed trials belong inside the carbon accounting boundary, but reusable architecture search should be amortized across all downstream deployments. Efficient NAS techniques (weight sharing, hardware-aware search) reduce this search budget, making meta-optimization a primary sustainability lever (Elsken et al. 2019).
Strubell, Emma, Ananya Ganesh, and Andrew McCallum. 2019. “Energy and Policy Considerations for Deep Learning in NLP.” Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 3645–50. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/p19-1355.

Patterson, David, Joseph Gonzalez, Quoc Le, Chen Liang, Lluis-Miquel Munguia, Daniel Rothchild, David So, Maud Texier, and Jeff Dean. 2021. “Carbon Emissions and Large Neural Network Training.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2104.10350.

Elsken, Thomas, Jan Hendrik Metzen, and Frank Hutter. 2019. “Neural Architecture Search.” In The Springer Series on Challenges in Machine Learning, vol. 20. Springer International Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-05318-5_3.
The GPT-3 calculation in notebook 15.1 put one training run at hundreds of trans-Atlantic passenger round trips. Such run-level comparisons convey scale, but they do not by themselves describe the footprint of a deployed service.
The operational lesson is that carbon accounting must distinguish training from recurring inference over a declared observation period. In figure 10, the Meta recommendation workloads (RM-1 through RM-5) split operational emissions roughly evenly between training and inference, while inference dominates the language-model example. RM-1 totals approximately 0.85 million kg \(\text{CO}_2\text{e}\) in the plotted account. The public baselines, including GPT-3 and BERT-NAS, report training only; their bars do not establish a lifetime training-to-inference ratio. For high-traffic Archetype B deployments (Archetype B (DLRM at Scale)), both recurring serving and model updates belong in the account before deciding which phase offers the larger reduction.














Figure 10: Operational Carbon Footprint of Large-Scale ML Tasks: Stacked bars show operational CO2e over the reported accounting periods for Meta’s recommendation models (RM-1 through RM-5), a language model (LM), and several open-source large models (BERT-NAS, Evolved Transformer, T5, Meena, GShard-600B, Switch Transformer, GPT-3). The recommendation-model bars divide roughly evenly between training (light and mid orange) and inference (solid orange), while the public open-source baselines report training-only footprints (hatched gray outline), underscoring that inference serving at scale can rival or exceed training emissions for deployed systems. Source: (Wu et al. 2022).



Whichever phase dominates, every operational term in these accounts begins as electricity delivered to a rack and leaves as heat that must be removed from it. Delivering 120 kW to a single cabinet (the rated draw of one GB200 NVL72 rack) starts at the substation, and every conversion stage between the grid and the chip takes its share along the way.



Power and thermal envelopes traced the electrical path from the grid to the voltage regulator and introduced the PUE ratio (equation 2.2); this section asks where along that path energy and reliability margin are lost, and which of those losses a sustainability account must carry. Capacity planning fails when engineers budget only accelerator TDP. The first constraint sits outside the building. Large grid-supplied ML facilities need sufficient substation and utility-interconnection capacity. Internal distribution improvements cannot raise that import limit; on-site generation or storage adds a separate supply whose capacity, duration, and reliability must enter the design.



Substation lead time can run 4× longer than GPU procurement.

Systems Perspective 15.2: The interconnection queueDeploying 10,000 GPUs and deploying the electrical substation required to power their IT load (9.6 MW, after the 7 MW GPU subtotal is expanded for rack support power) operate on different timelines. In this planning comparison, GPU procurement takes 6 months, while permitting, engineering, procurement, construction, and grid connection for a new 10+ MW substation take 24 months. The infrastructure path is therefore 4× longer than the accelerator path. Actual schedules depend on the site, utility, equipment availability, and approvals, so the ratio illustrates a dependency rather than a universal lead time.
Systems insight: In this comparison, power delivery determines when the fleet can begin useful work even if the accelerators arrive on schedule. The US generation-and-storage interconnection queue is distinct from a data center’s load-connection request; neither queue total directly measures available capacity for a new ML facility. Procurement must therefore follow a site-specific power-delivery schedule. Otherwise, delivered silicon can remain “electrically stranded” while the facility waits for its connection or transformer.


Inside the facility, every conversion stage turns part of the delivered power into heat. Using typical stage efficiencies, utility-to-medium-voltage transformation loses 1–2 percent; an online double-conversion uninterruptible power supply (UPS) loses 3–5 percent, while an eco-mode design that bypasses double conversion during normal operation loses 1–2 percent; the power distribution unit (PDU) loses 2–3 percent; and voltage regulation on the baseboard loses another 5–8 percent. Compounding these stage losses, roughly 9–17 percent of the power drawn from the grid is dissipated as heat before it reaches a transistor, depending mainly on the UPS mode and the voltage regulators, and the server power supplies add their own conversion loss on top, bringing the end-to-end path close to the roughly 80 percent efficiency traced in Power and thermal envelopes. The accounting boundary decides where each loss appears. Losses upstream of the IT boundary, such as the transformer, UPS, and facility distribution, raise PUE; server power supplies and baseboard voltage regulators sit inside the measured IT load, and their heat must be removed by the same cooling system that serves the accelerators. Higher-voltage distribution is one of the few design changes that shrinks this overhead directly. Delivering the 5,600 W of one eight-GPU H100 baseboard requires approximately 467 A at 12 V but 117 A at 48 V DC; at equal conductor resistance the fourfold reduction in current cuts \(\ConductorCurrent^2\ElectricalResistance\) distribution losses sixteenfold, although the realized saving depends on conductor design and the added conversion stages.
At ML rack power densities, the difference between 95 percent and 98 percent distribution efficiency is meaningful. Using 33 kW as a reference rack load, a first-order estimate applies the difference between those efficiencies as 3 percent of that load, yielding approximately 0.99 kW per rack. Across 300 racks, the estimated reduction is 297 kW, equivalent to roughly 36 GPU nodes or 9 four-node racks under this power mix. Sustaining that reduction over a 3-year lifecycle at $0.07/kWh gives estimated electricity savings of ~$546,361. An exact fixed-load comparison divides delivered power by each efficiency before subtracting input powers. The released capacity can support more work or lower consumption; spending it on additional nodes does not preserve the same electricity saving.
To make this concrete, consider the power budget for a single rack containing four DGX H100 nodes:
Table 7 itemizes a rack-attributed power budget rather than only GPU TDP. In this scenario, host, fabric, and equipment-side conversion losses belong to the IT load and sum to the IT subtotal; the row below it is an illustrative non-IT allocation at the stated PUE. A facility calculation multiplies the IT subtotal by its own PUE rather than reusing that allocation, and facility-side conversion losses are covered by PUE and must not be added again.

The conversion row excludes facility-side losses, which belong in PUE. Applying a different facility PUE requires replacing the non-IT allocation, not multiplying the full table total.

Evaluating DGX H100 power allocation (table 7) reveals that 32 GPUs at 700 W each deliver 22.4 kW, but host, fabric, and conversion losses raise the IT subtotal to 30.8 kW, about 38 percent above the GPU subtotal. That IT subtotal is the load to multiply by a facility’s PUE; the table’s final row is one such allocation, which brings the rack-attributed total to about 50 percent above the GPU subtotal. Infrastructure planners who size their facility based on GPU TDP alone will underestimate the electrical load and may discover during commissioning that their power capacity is insufficient.
Synchronized training also changes the shape of the load. The correlated power swings introduced with grid dynamics (section 15.5) now appear inside the delivery chain, where coordinated computation and communication phases align across thousands of accelerators; Power delivery networks and transient dynamics analyzes how local decoupling, voltage regulators, and UPS controls filter these synchronous transients before they reach the utility connection.
For an illustrative device-side calculation, assume 1,024 GPUs change together from 400 W to 700 W each over 100 μs. The assumed aggregate step is 307 kW, giving a ramp rate of 3.07 GW/s. This is a load-side scenario, not a measured utility input. Its sustainability consequence appears at the interconnection. Rack- or facility-level energy buffering (section 15.5), sized to the measured energy deficit rather than to a fixed allowance per rack, lets the grid see a smoother load, and a well-characterized, controllable load is easier both to connect and to schedule against grid conditions.

Checkpoint 15.3: Power delivery physics
Verify the data center power path:

Load correlation: explain why synchronous ML training produces more correlated load changes at the facility connection than independent web traffic.
Loss accounting: identify which conversion losses in the delivery chain raise PUE and which remain inside the measured IT load.
Power budgeting: use table 7 to explain why a node with 8 GPUs at 700 W each must be budgeted well above its 5.6 kW GPU subtotal.
AC-DC conversion: identify the conversion-stage efficiencies, distribution losses, load profile, and reliability requirements needed to compare rack-level and server-level conversion at the same delivered IT load.



At the largest scales, the data center’s power draw represents a significant fraction of the local electrical grid’s capacity. A 100,000-GPU cluster, roughly a hundred times the book’s 1,024-GPU reference cluster, at 700 W per GPU has a 70 MW accelerator subtotal, but rack-profile support power raises the IT load to 96.2 MW before PUE. With PUE, the total facility draw approaches 107.8 MW, the load of a small city. Such installations require dedicated feeds from the electrical grid, often with purpose-built substations and transmission lines. The substation lead time of 24 months in the interconnection-queue perspective above makes power availability one of the longest-lead-time constraints in building ML infrastructure.
At large-cluster scale, the same delivery limit becomes a grid-procurement problem rather than an electricity bill. Later large systems often lack energy disclosures comparable to the chapter’s opening anchor, which is precisely why the measurement contract requires workload telemetry instead of relying on published model documentation alone.
This grid-procurement problem worsens when model and data growth multiply each other. Compute-optimal allocation (Compute-optimal resource allocation) scales parameters and tokens together, and at fixed training tokens per parameter, doubling the model parameters also doubles the token count, so training work grows by approximately 4\(\times\); energy does so only at unchanged realized efficiency. More generally, under the same dense-training cost model, computational work grows approximately with the product of parameter count and training-token count. A model with 10\(\times\) the parameters, trained on 10\(\times\) the data, therefore requires approximately 100\(\times\) the training work; energy grows by that factor only if realized FLOPs per joule remain unchanged.
The electricity consumed by a single large-model training campaign can become nonnegligible relative to the output of a power plant. A 100 MW training facility operating at full capacity for one year consumes 876 GWh, which a 100 MW wind farm cannot match (at 30 percent capacity factor, a wind farm produces about 262.8 GWh per year, so the training facility would require the equivalent of approximately 3.3 large wind farms).
Power availability and power source are connected infrastructure decisions, but annual energy matching does not establish continuous supply. Organizations training large models may locate near renewable sources or purchase renewable energy certificates (RECs) to claim the attributes of renewable generation. A certificate does not physically deliver electricity or remove the facility’s demand from the grid; the design must still provide power when and where the workload runs.
Procurement can also support additional low-carbon supply. Microsoft’s 2024 agreement with Constellation supported a planned nuclear-reactor restart, while Google’s geothermal partnership with Fervo began supplying the Nevada grid in 2023. These examples address the need for generation beyond variable wind and solar output. They do not make one generation technology mandatory; the engineering requirement is a supply portfolio that meets the facility’s demand across time, with transmission, storage, and workload flexibility accounted for.
Once power is available, its carbon intensity determines the emissions attributed to each megawatt-hour under the chosen accounting method. The placement comparison in notebook 15.2 already showed how far that factor can move one run’s emissions; at facility scale the same lever becomes a siting decision that persists for the life of the building. Low-carbon electricity can coincide with favorable prices, but neither follows from the other. A siting comparison must evaluate the delivered tariff and emissions factor separately, alongside power availability and the workload’s location constraints.



The Rack established the thermal envelope of dense racks; the sustainability question is how much energy and water removing that heat costs, and how the choice between air and liquid cooling changes both once rack densities push beyond what traditional air conditioning can extract. Nearly all electrical energy consumed by a GPU eventually becomes heat through switching, leakage, and resistive losses. During a transient, some energy raises the temperature of the chip and surrounding materials. In steady operation, that stored thermal energy stops increasing, so cooling must remove heat at approximately the rate of electrical consumption. The IT electrical load inside the rack, represented by 30.8 kW, therefore sets the steady heat-removal requirement. Allocated non-IT facility overhead produces additional heat outside this rack boundary. When heat removal falls behind generation, temperatures rise; the available thermal margin determines how long the system can tolerate the imbalance before throttling reduces clock speeds and throughput. Sustained overheating can damage the hardware.



When cooling falls behind, temperature climbs through the thermal margin until throttling caps it.
Air cooling, the dominant technology for decades, works by blowing room-temperature air across heat sinks attached to the chips. The air absorbs heat at a rate determined by its specific heat capacity, roughly 1.0 kJ/kg/K. The heated air is exhausted from the rear of the rack, typically 15–20 degrees Celsius warmer than the inlet, and directed to a computer room air conditioning (CRAC) unit that cools it before recirculating.
The fundamental problem is that air is a poor thermal conductor. Its thermal conductivity is only 0.026 W/m/K, compared to 0.6 W/m/K for water and 400 W/m/K for copper. Removing a large heat load with air requires substantial volumetric flow. Fan power depends on that flow, pressure drop, and fan efficiency; rack power alone does not specify a fixed cooling fraction.
The physics can be made precise with a simple calculation. The heat removal capacity of a fluid flow is:
\[\CoolantHeatLoad = \CoolantMassFlowRate\times \SpecificHeatCapacity\times \FiniteChange\CoolantTemperature\]
where \(\CoolantHeatLoad\) is the heat removed (watts), \(\CoolantMassFlowRate\) is the mass flow rate (kg/s), \(\SpecificHeatCapacity\) is the specific heat capacity (J/kg/K), and \(\FiniteChange\CoolantTemperature\) is the temperature difference between outlet and inlet. For air with \(\SpecificHeatCapacity\) of 1,005 J/kg/K and a typical \(\FiniteChange\CoolantTemperature\) of 15 K (inlet at 20 degrees C, outlet at 35 degrees C), removing 100 kW requires a mass flow rate of 100,000 \(\div\) (1,005 \(\times\) 15) \(\approx\) 6.6 kg/s. At sea-level air density of 1.2 kg/m³, this corresponds to a volumetric flow rate of 5.5 m³/s, or approximately 11,713 CFM (cubic feet per minute). Moving this much air through the confined space of a server rack requires powerful fans that themselves consume substantial power.
At higher power densities, the airflow and pressure required to cool a rack raise fan energy and can make air cooling impractical before the IT load itself reaches a power limit. The exact crossover depends on rack geometry, inlet temperature, pressure drop, and fan-control policy rather than on one universal rack-power threshold. PUE (equation 2) captures facility fans, chillers, and facility-side conversion losses as overhead on top of the IT load. Server fans lie within the IT load itself, so their energy remains in the denominator as well as the facility total. Cooling choices must therefore be compared using total facility energy for the same useful work, not PUE alone.
Water has a specific heat capacity of 4.18 kJ/kg/K, over four times that of air, and a thermal conductivity roughly 23× higher. Its much greater density also lets a small fluid volume carry substantial heat. To appreciate the magnitude of the difference, consider how much fluid must flow to remove 700 W from a single GPU. Air at a 15-degree temperature rise requires tens of liters per second of airflow (a small wind tunnel). Water at the same temperature rise requires only about 0.01 liters per second (a thin stream). This thousands-fold difference in volumetric flow permits compact liquid paths, but it does not determine pumping energy. Pressure drop through cold plates, pipes, and fittings, together with pump efficiency, determines the power needed to sustain that flow.
Direct-to-chip liquid cooling routes coolant through cold plates mounted on GPU packages. The cold plate contacts the heat spreader through thermal interface material; the resulting thermal resistance depends on the package, interface, plate design, and flow. The coolant carries heat through manifolds and pipes to a coolant distribution unit (CDU) at the rack or row level. The permissible supply temperature depends on the equipment, so liquid cooling need not require chilled water.
In a two-loop design, the CDU transfers heat from the chip-level coolant to the facility water loop, which carries it toward cooling towers or dry coolers. Isolation lets each loop maintain its required fluid chemistry and pressure. The chip-level coolant must satisfy the equipment’s compatibility and cleanliness requirements to control deposits, corrosion, and blockage; purity alone does not establish suitability.
Liquid cooling can reduce server airflow requirements, although memory modules (DIMMs), voltage regulator modules (VRMs), and other components without cold plates may still need fans. If facility cooling consumes 3–8 percent of IT power, that contribution alone adds 0.03–0.08 to PUE; facility-side electrical losses and other non-IT loads must also be included. Reducing server-fan power changes the IT load instead, so it does not translate directly into the same PUE reduction. Lower fan demand can also reduce noise, subject to the remaining fans, pumps, and heat-rejection equipment.
A more aggressive approach, immersion cooling, submerges entire server boards in a tank of nonconductive dielectric fluid. The fluid absorbs heat from wetted surfaces, replacing server airflow; high-heat-flux components may still need heat sinks or directed flow. Fluid contact shortens some heat-transfer paths, but flow, local heat flux, material compatibility, and heat-exchanger capacity still determine component temperatures.
Single-phase immersion cooling uses a fluid that remains liquid throughout the process, with heat carried away by convection currents in the tank. The heated fluid rises to the surface, is pumped through a heat exchanger to reject the heat to the building’s chilled water loop, and returns to the bottom of the tank.
Two-phase immersion cooling takes this further: fluid boils at heated surfaces, carries latent heat to a condenser, and returns as liquid. Heat removal depends on the fluid, pressure, condenser capacity, and operating conditions. The complete facility still consumes energy for heat rejection and electrical distribution; the cooling mechanism alone does not specify its PUE.
The trade-off is serviceability. Accessing a failed component requires handling fluid-wetted hardware, and the dielectric fluids themselves are expensive ($20–$50 per liter). A single immersion tank holding four server boards may contain 500–1,000 liters of fluid, representing $10,000–$50,000 in coolant cost alone. The operational procedures for immersion-cooled facilities differ sharply from air-cooled ones, requiring specialized training for technicians and different approaches to cable management, since all wetted materials must be compatible with prolonged fluid exposure. Depending on the fluid and its additives, metals can corrode, while polymer insulation and seals can swell or degrade. Qualifying compatible materials adds engineering work and can constrain component choices. Table 8 compares the air and liquid regimes in which these serviceability costs enter the design decision.



Table 8: Cooling Architecture Trade-Offs: Feasible rack density follows from the particular equipment and facility design. The example design points differ by 10× in rack power, yet there is no universal rack-power threshold or PUE that separates air and liquid cooling. Compare qualified operating envelopes and total facility energy.

The parallel heat-transfer conduits diagrammed in figure 11 trace why direct-to-chip liquid cooling supports higher heat flux than forced air: cold plates route chip heat directly into circulating fluid with high volumetric heat capacity before reaching facility heat rejection, whereas air systems rely on convective dissipation across finned heat sinks. Ambient wet-bulb temperature (the lowest temperature that evaporation can bring outdoor air to, which bounds evaporative heat rejection) and rack power density determine whether an air, liquid, or hybrid loop satisfies the chip junction temperature envelope.
Pairing these dissipation paths with the engineering trade-offs in table 8 separates thermodynamic feasibility from lifecycle economics. First establish that the proposed cooling medium maintains die temperatures and component serviceability under peak workload. Then compare installed capital expenditure, pumping and fan parasitics, water consumption, maintenance overhead, and equipment lifespan under the same computational load. A higher-density liquid-cooled installation may reduce operational energy, but its capital payback period cannot be inferred from rack power alone.

Napkin Math 15.7: The cooling taxConsider a 1,024-GPU cluster of H100s at 700 W each. To isolate the PUE multiplier, this simplified calculation treats accelerator power as the entire IT load and assigns all non-IT overhead to cooling. It therefore understates facility power by omitting host, memory, network, and storage support; a procurement estimate must restore those terms before applying PUE.

IT power: 1,024 \(\times\) 700 W = 716.8 kW
Air cooling (PUE 1.55): Total facility power = 716.8 kW \(\times\) 1.55 = 1,111.0 kW. Cooling overhead = 394.2 kW.
Liquid cooling (PUE 1.08): Total facility power = 716.8 kW \(\times\) 1.08 = 774.1 kW. Cooling overhead = 57.3 kW.

Savings: Liquid cooling saves 336.9 kW of continuous power. At $0.07/kWh, the annual savings are approximately $206,585. Over a 3-year hardware lifecycle, the cooling savings alone total $619,754, which is the figure to set against the installed capital cost of the liquid-cooling system when computing its payback period.








Figure 11: Air and Liquid Heat Paths: Air transfers chip heat through a heat sink and moving air; direct-to-chip liquid cooling transfers it through a cold plate and coolant. Both require heat rejection. Capacity, parasitic energy, and water use depend on the engineered system rather than the cooling medium alone.



The final link in the cooling chain is heat rejection: getting heat from the facility water loop to the outside environment. A cooling tower sprays warm water over a fill medium, packing that spreads the water into thin films to enlarge its contact with the air, and uses evaporation to carry heat into the atmosphere. Evaporating a kilogram of water removes its latent heat of vaporization, 2,260 kJ/kg. Sensible heating instead depends on both the specific heat capacity, 4.18 kJ/kg/K, and the permitted temperature rise. Evaporation can therefore carry substantial heat with a small mass flow, but the evaporated water must be replaced.
A 10 MW data center with evaporative cooling towers can consume well over 100 million liters of water per year, depending on climate and cooling design, which has become a significant concern in water-stressed regions. At the evaporative WUE of 1.8 L/kWh used earlier, continuous operation consumes about 158 million liters per year, roughly 350–415 household-years of water use under the earlier annual household baseline. As ML data centers grow to 100 MW and beyond, their water footprint becomes a meaningful factor in local resource planning.
Dry coolers use fans to blow air over a radiator without evaporating cooling water. They avoid that direct water consumption, although electricity generation can still carry an upstream water burden. Heat rejection depends on the temperature difference between coolant and ambient air, so hot weather can reduce capacity or require more fan power. Hybrid designs use dry cooling when conditions permit and evaporative assistance when needed, trading water consumption against electrical demand and thermal margin.
Waste heat reuse treats thermal output as a resource. It is the district-heating and industrial coupling introduced in section 15.5, evaluated now at the temperatures a liquid loop delivers. A liquid-cooling loop returning water at 50–65 degrees Celsius supplies low-grade heat that may serve nearby district heating, greenhouses, or other suitable sinks. Usability depends on the required supply temperature, seasonal demand, and transport losses; a heat pump may be needed. If an illustrative 10 MW thermal stream has an 80–90 percent recovery fraction, 8–9 MW is recovered before accounting for heat-pump electricity. Heat-pump output includes that electrical input and must be accounted for separately. Crediting useful heat does not reduce PUE below 1.0. Exported heat is instead reported through energy reuse effectiveness (ERE), which subtracts the reused energy from total facility energy before dividing by IT energy, or through a separate net-energy balance.
The viability of waste heat reuse depends on the proximity of heat consumers. Urban data centers, despite their higher land and electricity costs, are often better positioned for waste heat reuse than remote facilities because they are close to residential and commercial heating loads. The result is a counterintuitive economic optimization: a data center in a Nordic city may have higher electricity costs but lower net operating costs after waste heat revenues, compared to a remote facility with cheaper electricity but no heat consumers nearby.
For a dense training fleet, cooling is a configuration constraint. The aggregate accelerator TDP sets only part of the heat load; hosts, memory, networking, and conversion losses add to it. Rack layout and cooling capacity determine whether the intended configuration can sustain its workload or must reduce density or power. Liquid cooling is one way to expand that envelope, with its own serviceability and lifecycle costs.


Cooling failures threaten both hardware and useful fleet work. When coolant flow stops, a dense rack loses heat-removal capacity and must throttle or shut down before thermal runaway. N+1 redundancy in CDUs, temperature monitoring, and automatic load shedding limit the affected capacity. An emergency air path can support reduced-power operation where the facility design provides one.
Serviceability also changes the failure budget. Leaks can damage equipment and drain cooling capacity, while quick-disconnect fittings allow node replacement without draining the entire loop. Their seals and coolant compatibility therefore belong in the maintenance plan. The fleet-level consequence depends on how much synchronized work shares the failed cooling domain.
The economics of cooling reliability shift when moving from independent inference servers to tightly coupled training clusters. In a distributed training run using synchronous parallelism, a cooling-loop failure that idles a pod-scale slice can halt the entire job. Consider a cooling failure that triggers a thermal shutdown of a 256-GPU pod within a 10,000-GPU cluster, about ten times the 1,024-GPU reference cluster. The example counts lost compute capacity, excluding repair and replacement costs. If the repair time for a CDU pump is 4 hours, the immediate loss of 256 GPUs at $4 per GPU-hour is $4,096. Assuming the job cannot continue elastically and the remaining 9,744 GPUs remain unavailable for other work, the synchronous blast radius inflates the cost to $160,000 in lost compute time. Adding checkpoint retrieval and rollback of 30 to 60 minutes of lost computation brings the illustrative lost-compute total to $180,000–$200,000 before any additional recovery delay. Those capacity costs are dollars, not joules. The energy account starts from the work later discarded. Rerunning the 30 to 60 minutes since the last checkpoint on all 10,000 accelerators at rated power repeats about 3.5–7 MWh of accelerator energy, before host and facility overhead. Power drawn by idle accelerators during the outage and the restart work add to that total, and both must be read from the actual shutdown or idle states rather than assumed. Compare expected outage losses and recovery behavior against the cost of N+1 cooling redundancy rather than treating redundancy as an unconditional requirement.



One cooling failure can idle the whole training job.
Coolant condition is another reliability input. Deionized water and compatible inhibitors control galvanic corrosion, the damage caused by electrochemical differences between metals in the loop. Biofilm on heat-transfer surfaces impedes cooling and increases pumping demand. Maintenance must preserve coolant chemistry and heat-transfer performance; the sustainability account includes both that overhead and the useful work lost when cooling fails.

Self-Check: Question

A facility aisle is qualified to remove a sustained 25 kW of IT heat per rack with its existing air-cooling design under the specified inlet temperature and airflow. The proposed AI workload measures 60 kW per rack over its sustained operating interval. Which observation establishes the need to change the cooling design or reduce the rack load?

Web workloads have higher peak memory bandwidth requirements, causing localized thermal spikes.
AI training generates bursty, millisecond-scale CPU spikes followed by long idle periods, creating thermal cycling fatigue.
The measured 60 kW rack load exceeds this aisle’s qualified 25 kW air-cooling envelope; a qualified liquid, hybrid, or redesigned air system, or a lower rack load, must restore thermal feasibility.
AI models require lower ambient operating temperatures to maintain FP16 arithmetic precision.

A cloud provider can procure and install 10,000 GPUs within six months, but building the required electrical substation and securing utility interconnect approval takes 24 months. Explain why electrical power delivery represents the binding bottleneck for data center expansion, and state the systems consequence of this lead-time disparity.
In direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems, coolant is circulated from the server cold plates to a rack- or row-level ____, which exchanges heat with the facility secondary water loop without mixing the fluids.
An engineering team is auditing the greenhouse gas emissions of an AI platform. Which option correctly maps the five operational sources to their respective GHG Protocol scopes?


S1: Diesel fuel burned by backup generators during a power outage at an owned facility.
S2: Grid electricity purchased to power an owned GPU cluster.
S3: Grid electricity consumed by cooling chillers in the same owned facility.
S4: Embodied carbon from manufacturing the GPUs at an external foundry.
S5: Electrical energy consumed by end-user smartphones running the deployed mobile inference app.

S1: Scope 1; S2: Scope 2; S3: Scope 2; S4: Scope 3; S5: Scope 3.
S1: Scope 2; S2: Scope 1; S3: Scope 2; S4: Scope 3; S5: Scope 3.
S1: Scope 1; S2: Scope 2; S3: Scope 1; S4: Scope 2; S5: Scope 3.
S1: Scope 3; S2: Scope 2; S3: Scope 2; S4: Scope 1; S5: Scope 1.



A distributed training job expands from 1,024 to 2,048 accelerators. Explain which mechanisms can increase communication energy and what measurements establish its share of step energy for the actual run.
Order the thermal stages of heat removal in a direct-to-chip liquid-cooled data center, from the silicon die to the external environment: (1) heat transfers through a thin thermal interface material (TIM) into a copper cold plate, (2) the Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) heat exchanger transfers thermal energy from the closed rack loop to the facility secondary loop, (3) external cooling towers or dry coolers reject heat into the ambient outdoor atmosphere, (4) liquid coolant absorbs heat as it flows through microchannels directly above the accelerator package, (5) active switching in transistor junctions generates heat on the silicon die.
