title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
Cooling infrastructure manages the intense thermal load of the cluster, but the total magnitude of that load depends on whether the fleet is executing a concentrated training run or a globally distributed inference workload. Training a large language model is a concentrated, highly visible energy event that consumes thousands of megawatt-hours over weeks or months. Serving the same model to a billion daily queries is the opposite shape of load: energy spent continuously, query by query, year after year. Understanding where the majority of the energy budget goes dictates where optimization efforts must concentrate.
Training and inference share opportunities to reduce computation, data movement, and idle power, but their success criteria differ. Training must reach the target model quality within its completion budget; inference must serve the required demand at the agreed quality and latency. The lifecycle energy account identifies which phase contributes most, while those constraints determine which interventions can reduce its cost without sacrificing useful work.


Training large AI models can require computational infrastructure with hundreds of thousands of cores and specialized AI accelerators operating continuously for months. Microsoft’s 2020 disclosure of the OpenAI dedicated supercomputer, built specifically for large-scale AI training at the time, reported 285,000 CPU cores, 10,000 GPUs, and network bandwidth exceeding 400 gigabits per second per server (Langston 2020). This 2020 figure remains useful as a calibrated reference point rather than a claim about the largest infrastructure available in later generations.

Langston, Jennifer. 2020. Microsoft Announces New Supercomputer, Lays Out Vision for Future AI Work. Microsoft Source.
The intensive computational loads generate heat that cooling infrastructure must continuously remove, the overhead quantified for the cooling treatment in section 15.10.4. Reducing it requires co-optimization of hardware architecture, parallelism strategy, and algorithmic efficiency.
Three training accounts have appeared so far, at very different scales: the GPT-3 run at 1,287 MWh, the 7B model on 64 A100s at 13,246.5 kWh of facility energy (5.7 t on the US-average grid), and the 70B model of notebook 15.6 at 681.9 t of operational emissions. Each is a single final run. Development multiplies each one, because a sweep of \(\SweepCandidateCount\) candidates at a fraction \(\SweepCandidateCostFraction\) of full scale adds \(\SweepCandidateCount \SweepCandidateCostFraction\) final-run equivalents (5× for the sweep in section 15.9.1), and retraining during service repeats part of that cost. Training energy is therefore paid once per completed run but recurs across the model’s development and update cycle, and each run also affects facility sizing and checkpoint storage.


Distributing a training job across accelerators introduces coordination costs alongside the energy spent on computation. Distributed parallelism strategies exchange gradients, parameters, or activations while synchronization stalls leave idle accelerators drawing baseline power.21 The resulting energy share cannot be inferred from cluster size alone because topology, collective algorithm, message volume, overlap, and utilization determine the account. Some all-to-all patterns also increase traffic faster than aggregate useful work as the participating set grows.
21 Parallelism Energy Overhead: Data, model, and pipeline parallelism impose distinct communication and idle-power costs. Data parallelism reduces gradients, tensor parallelism exchanges partial activations, and pipeline parallelism introduces bubbles. A valid comparison reaches the same model-quality target under the same completion constraint, then measures each strategy’s runtime and system energy, including communication and waiting. Fixing time-to-train by assumption would hide one of the effects the comparison needs to expose.
↩︎ Parallelism strategy selection and the communication cost of each strategy are established in Parallelism Strategy Selection and Engineering Trade-offs.

The Fleet Law (equation 1.3) turns this overhead into an energy account. If the fleet draws average power \(\AveragePower\) while executing one step on \(\DeviceCount\) accelerators, the energy of that step is approximately
\[\TrainingStepEnergy\approx \AveragePower\times \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \AveragePower\left( \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \right) \tag{14}\]
The compute term accounts for local mathematical work; communication and synchronization make the distributed update possible. When these costs remain exposed, they extend the step while accelerators, hosts, and the fabric continue drawing power, adding powered time on the communication and coordination axes of C³. Their energy share depends on power during those intervals as well as on their duration. A quarter of the step spent in unhidden communication accounts for a quarter of its energy only if average fleet power during that interval equals the average over the whole step; accelerators stalled at a collective can draw less than at full arithmetic load, so the share must be read from a power trace. Overlap, smaller messages, and fewer stragglers shorten the step, and they save energy to the extent that the shorter powered interval is not offset by higher average power or by extra work to reach the same model quality. The parallelism choices of Distributed Training are therefore sustainability choices as well.
Beyond the communication term, coordinated resource management offers four levers with distinct effects on energy and emissions. Dynamic workload placement consolidates compatible jobs so genuinely unused hardware can enter lower-power sleep states, with true savings verified at the facility meter rather than inferred from idle node counts. Carbon-aware scheduling (section 15.8.1.2) can reduce emissions even when energy use is unchanged, subject to data-movement overhead, completion deadlines, and reliability bounds. Multi-tenant sharing raises accelerator compute and memory occupancy across concurrent tasks, but contention can lengthen execution and increase energy per completed job. Adaptive inference batching groups compatible requests to improve throughput within their latency limits; changing training batch size instead requires checking the work needed to reach the target model quality. Each lever must therefore be evaluated against completed useful work and its service constraints, rather than occupancy alone.
All of these training costs stop accruing when the run stops. For high-volume services, the larger term is often the deployment that follows, as the crossover calculation in section 15.11.2 shows.




Inference workloads execute every time an AI model responds to queries, classifies images, or makes predictions. Unlike training, inference scales dynamically and continuously across applications such as search engines, recommendation systems, and generative AI models. Although each inference request consumes far less energy than a training run, the cumulative energy of a high-volume deployed service can rival or exceed its training energy (Wu et al. 2022).


Cumulative inference emissions overtake the one-time training cost.

A worked example makes the crossover concrete. Consider a model serving 10 million queries per day at 0.001 kWh of attributed facility electricity per query, including its share of idle capacity and support systems. At this serving rate, daily energy consumption reaches 10,000 kWh (10 million queries \(\times\) 0.001 kWh), which accumulates to 3,650,000 kWh over a year of continuous service. Evaluated against the average US grid carbon intensity of 0.429 kg/kWh, this electricity demand produces 1,565.9 t (1,565,850 kg) of greenhouse gas emissions annually.
Compared with the earlier 7B/64-A100 training example (5.7 t), the smallest of the three training accounts and therefore the fastest to overtake, cumulative inference emissions exceed training emissions after approximately 1.3 days of deployment at this scale. The serving scenario and the training run describe different models, so the comparison does not trace one model’s lifecycle; it shows how quickly this serving volume would overtake a training run of that size. For larger training runs, the crossover can shift to weeks or months depending on query volume, per-query energy, and grid intensity. The lifecycle perspective therefore sets the priority: optimize inference efficiency for widely deployed models, and focus training efficiency efforts on models that undergo frequent retraining or experimental iteration.
Production measurements in figure 10 show why this crossover must remain workload-specific. Inference dominates the language-model account, while training and inference contribute roughly equally for the recommendation models. Training FLOPs alone omit serving costs, but the larger phase must be established from the service’s measured workload and observation period.
Inference workloads, like other software services, scale with demand. An always-available service consumes energy both while processing requests and while maintaining capacity for expected latency and availability. The sustainability account must include query volume, workload mix, and idle provisioned resources.

Checkpoint 15.4: The training-inference flip
Consider a vision model where training requires 2,000 GPU-hours at an average accelerator power draw of 300 W. Once deployed, the model serves 1 million requests per day for 730 days, with each request occupying an accelerator for 50 ms at an average draw of 100 W. Assume requests do not overlap on an accelerator. This active-only account excludes idle capacity, host systems, networking, and facility overhead.

Training energy: calculate the accelerator energy accounted for during training.
Inference energy: calculate the active-request accelerator energy subtotal over the stated product lifespan.
Optimization focus: compute the ratio of these inference and training subtotals and identify which phase merits investigation. Explain why choosing the largest achievable lifecycle reduction also requires the omitted energy terms and the savings available from candidate interventions.





Prefill and decode stress distinct memory and arithmetic pathways, so meaningful energy comparisons require a declared serving workload. Figure 12 diagrams these contrasting computational dataflows: prefill amortizes loaded weights across all prompt positions simultaneously, whereas each autoregressive decode iteration reuses weights only across active sequence batch slots to emit one token at a time. Batch size, context length, precision, and the latency target dictate whether memory bandwidth or arithmetic execution limits realized utilization.


↩︎ Why small-batch decode is bound by memory bandwidth, and how batching reuses each weight load, is established in Batching characteristics across model architectures.






Figure 12: Reuse in Prefill and Decode: Prefill reuses weights across prompt positions; a decode iteration can reuse weights across active sequences. At small batches, weight and KV-cache traffic can leave arithmetic units underused. These paths show mechanisms, not measured utilization or a universal energy-per-token ratio.



The structural dataflow split diagrammed in figure 12 governs per-token energy through data movement and arithmetic intensity. During prefill, parallel matrix operations reuse weights across prompt positions and can achieve high compute utilization when the workload exposes enough parallel work. During decode, each iteration produces one token per active sequence while accessing model parameters and an expanding KV cache. At small batches, this traffic can leave arithmetic units underused; batching improves weight reuse, subject to memory capacity and latency constraints.
The energy roofline of section 15.8.3.3 puts a number on that underuse. At batch size one, each decode step reads every FP16 weight (2 bytes) to perform two FLOPs with it, an arithmetic intensity of 1 FLOP/byte against an energy crossover of 16 FLOP/byte (equation 7). Under the chapter’s modeled coefficients, moving each parameter’s bytes from DRAM costs 320 pJ while the arithmetic on it costs 20 pJ, so movement is 16× the arithmetic and about 94 percent of the modeled dynamic energy per generated token, before any KV-cache traffic is counted. The coefficient is the table’s off-package DRAM value; the high-bandwidth memory that feeds an accelerator costs less per byte (Energy cost of data movement), which narrows the ratio without reversing it at batch one. Batching \(\BatchSize\) sequences reuses each weight load \(\BatchSize\) times and raises the intensity to \(\BatchSize\) FLOP/byte, so the two terms balance only near a batch of 16. Batching is therefore the first energy lever for decode, bounded by memory capacity for the KV cache and by the latency target.
Static power waste occurs when powered circuitry waits rather than producing useful outputs. Reducing that waiting can improve energy efficiency, but a comparison must meter the same hardware boundary and preserve output quality, context, latency, and serving load. Prompt processing and autoregressive generation perform different work; equal token counts alone do not establish a fair energy ratio.




Edge intelligence moves inference onto user devices or nearby computing nodes. Local execution can avoid transferring raw inputs to a data center, but it also adds or extends computation at the edge. The sustainability comparison must include both effects, together with any remaining cloud work and the hardware needed to serve the same task. Device power budgets constrain both local inference and learning, so the comparison must account for duty cycling, selective cloud escalation, and the repeated computation and model transfers required by federated training.


↩︎ The power, memory, and compute budgets of edge devices, and how on-device training amplifies them, are established in Design Constraints.

Sudhakar, Soumya, Vivienne Sze, and Sertac Karaman. 2023. “Data Centers on Wheels: Emissions from Computing Onboard Autonomous Vehicles.” IEEE Micro 43 (1): 29–39. https://doi.org/10.1109/mm.2022.3219803.
Running inference at the edge does not eliminate energy concerns. In autonomous vehicles, time-critical perception and control must operate within response deadlines despite variable network connectivity. Onboard computation therefore remains part of the operating budget. Sudhakar et al. (2023) model the potential emissions of a widely deployed autonomous-vehicle fleet, showing how device power and operating time can accumulate at global scale. Their comparison concerns fleet-level scenarios, not an assertion that each vehicle consumes as much energy as a data center.
The same accounting applies to smartphones, wearables, and sensors. Aggregate operational energy depends on the number of devices, their power states, and the time spent in each state. A small average draw per device can still produce a large fleet total; attributing that total to AI requires separating the additional workload from the device’s other functions.
Local processing and duty cycling can reduce energy when they avoid enough communication and remote work to offset the device’s added costs. The comparison must preserve task quality and service availability and include device manufacturing when deployment requires new hardware. These conditions lead directly to the power and energy budgets that constrain the edge design.


Edge devices operate within battery, thermal, and supply limits that differ from those of data center accelerators. These limits follow from the deployment rather than the processor’s instruction set. The engineering choice is to match each inference workload to a device that meets latency and accuracy requirements within its sustained power and energy budgets.
Power budgets reflect the physical constraints of battery capacity, thermal dissipation, and deployment environment. Table 9 groups edge AI power budget categories and shows how these constraints propagate. TinyML devices (microcontrollers that run small models in kilobytes of memory) must fit average demand to battery-life or harvesting targets while also supporting peak draw. Mobile devices must balance user experience with battery life, and automotive systems face thermal constraints within enclosed vehicle compartments despite having access to vehicle power.

Sustainable deployment requires matching workload requirements to appropriate power tiers.

TinyML devices are the smallest members of edge fleets, sitting below the 2–10 W phones of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) in both memory and power. Their energy efficiency is a sustainability concern because billions of edge inference calls add up to a measurable carbon footprint at fleet scale. TinyML efficiency depends heavily on duty cycling, where devices alternate between deep sleep and active inference. The duty-cycle model of equation 8 applies directly, with \(\InferenceDutyCycle = \InferenceActiveTime/\DutyCyclePeriod\) and the deep-sleep draw in place of idle power.
Consider a keyword-spotting model on a Cortex-M4 microcontroller, an extreme case that obeys the same battery arithmetic as the Archetype C phones. The device draws 15 mW of active inference power for 20 ms in each detection cycle, falls to a deep-sleep draw of 10 microamps at 3.3 V (33 µW) between evaluations, and repeats on a 1 s detection period during continuous listening. Substituting these values into equation 8 yields the average power draw:
\[P_{\text{avg}} = 15\text{ mW} \times 0.02 + 0.033\text{ mW} \times 0.98 = 0.30 + 0.032 \approx 0.33\text{ mW}\]
A 250 mAh coin cell at 3 V nominal stores 750 mWh, enough for approximately 2,260 hours, about 94 days, under this idealized budget. The estimate covers compute only. Continuous listening also requires powered sensing and input buffering while the microcontroller sleeps, and their energy, regulator losses, and battery derating must enter any deployment estimate.



On-device learning can require more work and memory than inference alone. When personalization uses gradient-based fine-tuning, backpropagation adds backward computation to the forward pass; other adaptation methods have different costs. A dense training step may require roughly 2–3\(\times\) the forward arithmetic, while activation, gradient, and optimizer-state memory must be budgeted separately.
The mobile power envelope constrains how long an on-device update can run. In the representative budget used here, sustained processing remains within 2–3 W, while bursts can reach 5–10 W for limited periods. Thermal headroom depends on the device and its operating conditions. An adaptive algorithm must fit this sustained envelope as well as the available battery energy, memory, and update deadline; processor TDP alone does not establish feasibility.

Napkin Math 15.8: The energy of learningProblem: Consider fine-tuning a small language model (1B parameters) on a user’s smartphone overnight. Is this feasible within a 5 percent battery budget?
Math:

Phone battery: Typical capacity is approximately 15 Wh, or about 54,000 J.
Budget: 5 percent of 54,000 J = 2,700 J.
Training cost, using illustrative per-parameter energy coefficients for a mobile accelerator (assumed for this scenario, not measured on a particular phone), with the backward pass at twice the forward cost because it computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights, so one training step costs about three forward passes:

Forward pass: \(\approx\) 2 nJ/param.
Backward pass: \(\approx\) 4 nJ/param.
Total per token: 6 nJ/param \(\times 10^9\) params = 6 J/token.

Capacity: 2,700 J / 6 J/token = 450 tokens.

Systems insight: The calculation establishes a token capacity, not whether the proposed adaptation fits. That decision also requires the token count needed to reach the quality target, the available memory, and sustained device power. If the required work exceeds the battery budget, parameter-efficient fine-tuning or sparse updates are candidates for reducing cost; their measured energy and achieved quality must establish whether they close the gap.


The local-processing decision compares the energy of the required computation with the communication and remote computation it avoids. Per-bit radio costs motivate the comparison, but the full job must also include repeated training rounds and model transfers.

Systems Perspective 15.3: The energy hierarchy

Trade-off: The architectural choice between processing data locally and sending it to the cloud is governed by an energy budget. The energy-to-communication ratio motivates comparing local work with transmission, but a decision requires the total energy of each alternative at the required quality and latency.
Energy cost per operation (approximate):

32-bit integer add: 0.1 pJ
32-bit float mult: 3.7 pJ
Wireless transmit (1 bit): 100,000–500,000 pJ (Bluetooth/Wi-Fi)

Systems insight: Under these illustrative component costs, a transmitted bit consumes far more energy than one arithmetic operation. The radio cost is quoted per bit; multiplied by eight it reaches roughly 0.8 to 4 million pJ per byte, about two orders of magnitude above the lower bound given for the wired network row of table 3. This motivates local processing but does not establish an offloading threshold: include memory, radio startup and protocol overhead, idle power, and remote computation in the full edge-cloud comparison. Local processing wins only when those complete terms favor it.




Radio transmission dwarfs local arithmetic in energy.



TinyML can operate from harvested ambient energy when the available supply supports the full device workload. Sustained operation requires both an adequate long-term energy budget and a way to handle intervals when harvesting falls below demand, through storage, duty cycling, or suspended execution.
Consider the energy harvesting power budgets in table 10. A keyword spotting model optimized to 0.5 mW average power matches the nominal output of approximately 5 cm² of indoor solar harvesting only near the top of the listed illumination range, before conversion losses and other device loads. This average-power comparison does not establish uninterrupted operation. The design must cover sensing, storage losses, and periods of dim or absent light, or permit the workload to pause. Ambient supply removes the need for purchased operating electricity only when it covers that complete budget; manufacturing, storage, maintenance, and disposal still enter the lifecycle account.



Table 10: Energy Harvesting Power Budgets: Ambient energy harvesting enables batteryless TinyML deployments when average power consumption remains within harvesting capacity. Solar harvesting provides the highest power density for most deployments.

Beyond individual device efficiency, architectural patterns determine total system energy consumption across edge-cloud boundaries. A cascade architecture deploys a task-appropriate small edge model to filter inputs before cloud inference. Equation 15 expresses total energy as the sum of local processing plus probabilistically-triggered cloud costs:
\[\CascadeInferenceEnergy= \LocalInferenceEnergy + \CascadeEscalationProbability\times (\CloudOffloadEnergy + \CloudInferenceEnergy) \tag{15}\]
where \(\CascadeEscalationProbability\) is the probability of requiring cloud inference (measured on the deployment input distribution).
Consider an illustrative visual inspection system where a lightweight edge model, such as MobileNetV3-Small, consumes 0.5 mJ per image classification, whereas a high-capacity cloud model, such as ResNet-152, requires 50 mJ per inference. Transmitting an image across a cellular uplink adds 10 mJ. If the edge model resolves routine cases locally and escalates only ambiguous inputs, for an escalation rate \(\CascadeEscalationProbability\) of 10 percent, substituting these parameters into equation 15 gives the average cascade energy:
\[E_{\text{cascade}} = 0.5 + 0.10 \times (10 + 50) = 0.5 + 6.0 = 6.5 \text{ mJ/image}\]
Compared to always-cloud inference at 60 mJ per image, this illustrative cascade reduces the modeled energy by 89 percent. Quality requires a separate test of local decisions, missed escalations, and the cloud model; the energy calculation says nothing about accuracy.



Always-on systems can use hierarchical wake detection to reduce average power across stages of increasing capability and draw. In this illustrative model, an analog front end consumes 10 µW while monitoring for voice activity. A detected event activates a compact neural network wake detector drawing 100 µW. A positive wake decision then triggers full-model inference at 10 mW for 50 ms. The energy calculation uses those assumed state powers and event rates; a deployed system must also account for false activations, missed wake words, and transition costs when evaluating its energy and service quality.
For an illustrative speech-active fraction of 5 percent and a wake-event rate of 0.001 per second (one event per 1,000 s), each full-model event lasts 0.05 s. The front end draws continuously, the wake detector draws only during speech, and the full model contributes its event rate times its event energy:
\[P_{\text{avg}} = 0.01 + 0.05 \times 0.1 + 0.001 \times 10 \times 0.05 = 0.0155\text{ mW}\]
The hierarchical approach achieves 15.5 µW average power compared to 10 mW for always-active full inference, a reduction of roughly 645× within this modeled boundary. Battery lifetime also requires battery capacity, conversion losses, sensors, and other device loads.



Training at the edge keeps raw data local but replaces its transfer with repeated model downloads and client-update uploads. This is the regime of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet), where phones train a shared model within a sustained power budget of a few watts. Equation 16 contrasts the energy trade-offs between federated and centralized approaches, where \(\FederatedRoundCount\) is the number of rounds, \(\ParticipatingClientCount\) is the number of participating clients per round, \(\ClientUpdateUploadEnergy\) is one client-update upload, \(\RawDataUploadEnergy\) is one client’s raw-data upload, and \(\CloudTrainingRunEnergy\) is the energy of one centralized cloud training run:
\[\FederatedTrainingEnergy= \FederatedRoundCount\left[\ParticipatingClientCount\left(\ClientLocalTrainingEnergy+ \ModelDownloadEnergy+ \ClientUpdateUploadEnergy\right) + \ServerAggregationEnergy\right]\] \[\CentralizedTrainingEnergy= \ParticipatingClientCount\times \RawDataUploadEnergy+ \CloudTrainingRunEnergy \tag{16}\]
Federated learning becomes more energy-efficient only when repeated model communication, local training, and aggregation consume less energy than raw-data transfer and centralized training at comparable model quality. The comparison must cover the same client population and account for repeated participation across rounds. Data being larger than one model update is insufficient by itself because downloads and uploads recur. Privacy and energy benefits require separate evidence: keeping raw data local does not by itself prevent updates from revealing private information, and any protection mechanism adds its own costs to the energy account.
Training, serving, and edge deployment all draw operational energy, and none of these accounts includes the hardware that performs the work. That physical supply chain, from fabrication through disposal, is the lifecycle term the next section examines.

Self-Check: Question

Which systems analogy and operational reality best explains why inference often dominates total lifecycle energy for widely deployed foundation models?

Inference requires higher instantaneous wattage per accelerator than training because real-time serving disables dynamic voltage scaling.
Training is like a one-time rocket launch that burns concentrated energy over several weeks, whereas inference is like operating a commercial airline fleet that burns energy continuously across billions of recurring user interactions over years.
Inference models must perform a full backward pass on every user query to maintain accuracy, doubling computational cost.
Inference cannot run on specialized accelerators, forcing cloud operators to use energy-inefficient legacy CPUs.

Profiling an autoregressive LLM serving pipeline shows that the prefill phase achieves 55 percent Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU), while the token-generation decode phase achieves only 6 percent MFU with high HBM bandwidth utilization. What is the physical mechanism causing decode energy inefficiency?

Decode executes in FP32 precision while prefill executes in INT4 precision.
Prefill bypasses high-bandwidth memory entirely by storing all weights in CPU host RAM.
Decode requires running backpropagation to generate key-value cache embeddings for each new token.
Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: each generated token requires reading all model weights from HBM with low arithmetic intensity, leaving tensor execution units idling while drawing static leakage and clock distribution power.

A mobile application team proposes running nightly on-device full backpropagation fine-tuning for a 1B-parameter model on user smartphones. Using the concept of the ‘battery wall’, explain how to assess a 5 percent overnight battery budget and identify alternatives if the measured workload exceeds it.
True or False: Shifting machine learning inference from centralized cloud data centers to hundreds of millions of edge devices automatically eliminates the application’s overall environmental impact because edge devices consume milliwatts rather than megawatts.
A TinyML sensor runs inference for 10 ms at 20 mW active power and sleeps for 990 ms at 20 \(\mu\text{W}\) deep-sleep power during a 1-second monitoring period. Calculate the average power draw, and explain how duty cycling enables multi-year battery operation.
Order the stages of a hierarchical wake-word cascade designed to minimize average energy consumption on a smart speaker from lowest power to highest power: (1) large language model or full automatic speech recognition running on host processor or cloud, (2) small convolutional or recurrent neural network wake-word classifier verifying the trigger phrase, (3) ultra-low-power Voice Activity Detection (VAD) circuit listening continuously at microwatt power.

title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
The environmental cost of an AI accelerator begins long before its first FLOP is calculated (Gupta et al. 2022; Luccioni et al. 2023; NVIDIA Corporation 2025). The per-H100 manufacturing footprint quantified in section 15.9.3 is incurred before the device is ever powered on.22 A training fleet of a few thousand such accelerators therefore carries a manufacturing debt of the same order as the operational emissions of a GPT-3-scale training run on the US-average grid (about 552,123 kg). A comprehensive life cycle assessment (LCA) quantifies the cumulative environmental impact across four key phases: design, manufacture, use, and disposal. LCA can reveal manufacturing as a major share of lifecycle impact, making it a critical sustainability lever that operational efficiency improvements alone cannot address.

Gupta, Udit, Young Geun Kim, Sylvia Lee, Jordan Tse, Hsien-Hsin S Lee, Gu-Yeon Wei, David Brooks, and Carole-Jean Wu. 2022. “Chasing Carbon: The Elusive Environmental Footprint of Computing.” IEEE Micro 42 (4): 37–47. https://doi.org/10.1109/MM.2022.3163226.
22 Life Cycle Assessment (LCA): Standardized by ISO 14040/14044, LCA traces environmental impact from raw material extraction through disposal (International Organization for Standardization 2006a, 2006b). For AI hardware, LCA separates embodied manufacturing emissions from operational energy use, making hardware refresh cycles and accelerator lifespan extension first-order sustainability levers that operational efficiency alone cannot substitute.
International Organization for Standardization. 2006a. ISO 14040:2006 Environmental Management – Life Cycle Assessment – Principles and Framework. ISO standard.

International Organization for Standardization. 2006b. ISO 14044:2006 Environmental Management – Life Cycle Assessment – Requirements and Guidelines. ISO standard.
These four phases organize the same emissions by time rather than by activity or reporting scope, as the second column of table 6 records, so a phase total must never be added to an activity or scope total.
Life Cycle Assessments can show that discarding functional hardware purely for modest efficiency gains causes more environmental harm through embodied carbon than it saves in operational power. The tipping point where new hardware becomes environmentally justified depends on utilization and grid intensity, a break-even worked in section 15.12.6.
Each of the four lifecycle stages adds its burden through a distinct physical mechanism (figure 13). System design fixes much of the lifetime load, manufacturing embeds carbon, water, and chemical burdens during fabrication, operation draws grid electricity for training and serving, and decommissioning produces electronic waste unless hardware is refurbished or its components recovered.






Figure 13: AI System Lifecycle: Four stages in sequence, each dropping the burden it adds, with a recovery loop from decommissioning back to manufacture. Design decisions fix much of the load the later stages carry; manufacturing adds embodied carbon, water, and chemicals; use adds operational energy at the grid’s carbon intensity; decommissioning adds e-waste unless hardware is refurbished or its components recovered.



The lifecycle sequence connects design choices to costs incurred at different times. Experimentation consumes resources before deployment; manufacturing adds embodied carbon; and use couples the workload to grid and cooling constraints. Retirement creates a choice among reuse, recovery, and disposal. Extending useful service spreads the hardware’s embodied burden over more work, but it does not reverse emissions already incurred. The environmental benefit depends on the replacement it avoids and the operating cost of keeping the existing equipment in service.


The design phase encompasses the research, development, and optimization of ML models before deployment. Public training-energy figures generally describe a final run rather than the trial-and-error that preceded it. Automated neural architecture search (NAS) can evaluate many configurations, and section 15.10.2 showed that two estimates of the same search can differ by orders of magnitude depending on whether the boundary includes proxy searches, full runs, data-center overhead, grid mix, and reuse across downstream models (Strubell et al. 2019; Patterson et al. 2021). Later efficient NAS methods use weight sharing, continuous relaxations, and hardware-aware search to reduce that search budget (Elsken et al. 2019). Excluding search does not make the remaining figures comparable either, because final runs also resist ranking by model size (table 11).



Table 11: Final-Run Training Footprints: Reported energy and operational emissions of five large training runs (Patterson et al. 2021). Each row is a final run under its authors’ boundary; search, failed runs, and evaluation are excluded, and the grid factor differs by data center. The reported final run for the 600-billion-parameter GShard model emitted under a tenth as much as the 11-billion-parameter T5 run. The table records both lower energy use and lower emissions per megawatt-hour for GShard; across the five runs, the latter quantity varies by a factor of about 3. These different workloads and operating conditions do not isolate the saving from sparse activation alone. Parameter count therefore cannot rank their emissions, and operation count would still need an execution-efficiency and grid account. Search and failed experiments require a separate development inventory before these final-run figures can support a lifecycle comparison.
Addressing the design phase’s sustainability challenges requires innovations in training efficiency: sparse training, low-precision arithmetic, weight-sharing, and energy-aware NAS approaches. Transfer learning and fine-tuning pretrained models reuse pretrained representations instead of requiring every task to be trained from scratch (Raffel et al. 2020).



Before an accelerator exists, its fabrication consumes physical resources that an energy account alone does not quantify: ultrapure water, process chemicals, and materials. Their burdens occur across extraction, refining, fabrication, and assembly sites, rather than solely where the finished hardware operates. Water demand must be evaluated against local availability and competing uses, while material supply depends on the component and manufacturing process (Jha 2014; Chen 2006). These resource accounts extend the lifecycle boundary beyond carbon without reducing unlike impacts to a single energy total.

Jha, A. R. 2014. Rare Earth Materials: Properties and Applications. CRC Press. https://doi.org/10.1201/b17045.

Chen, H.-W. 2006. “Gallium, Indium, and Arsenic Pollution of Groundwater from a Semiconductor Manufacturing Area of Taiwan.” Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology 77 (2): 289–96. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00128-006-1062-3.

Environmental Management—Water Footprint—Principles, Requirements and Guidelines, Pub. L. Nos. ISO 14046:2014 (2014).

The Green Grid. 2011. Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE): A Green Grid Data Center Sustainability Metric. White Paper 35. The Green Grid.
Water accounting requires more than a single WUE ratio. Water withdrawal measures water removed from a source, whereas water consumption measures the portion not returned to the same watershed in a usable form. The account must separate direct on-site cooling water, which equation 3 and the cooling-tower calculation in section 15.10.4 estimate, from indirect water used to generate electricity and manufacture hardware, then attach each flow to its watershed, season, and local scarcity (Environmental Management—Water Footprint—Principles, Requirements and Guidelines 2014; The Green Grid 2011). One liter consumed during a wet season in a low-stress basin is not equivalent to one liter consumed during a drought in a stressed basin, so decision-grade comparisons report both physical volume and a stress-weighted result. Reclaimed-water percentages also need a declared denominator because recirculating water inside a facility can reduce withdrawal without eliminating evaporative consumption.
Semiconductor fabrication uses ultrapure water for chemical-mechanical planarization, wet etching, and wafer rinsing (Cooper et al. 2011).23 Complete environmental accounting requires auditing gross process flow, freshwater withdrawal, recycled volume, and evaporative consumption as distinct quantities. Figure 14 distinguishes internal reuse from flows that leave the facility. Treatment returns reclaimed water to the intake stream and can reduce freshwater withdrawal, whereas evaporation remains a consumptive loss within the local water account. That classification does not mean the water permanently disappears from the hydrological cycle.

Cooper, Tom, Suzanne Fallender, Joyann Pafumi, Jon Dettling, Sebastien Humbert, and Lindsay Lessard. 2011. “A Semiconductor Company’s Examination of Its Water Footprint Approach.” Proceedings of the 2011 IEEE International Symposium on Sustainable Systems and Technology, 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1109/issst.2011.5936865.
23 Semiconductor Water Scale: A fab water inventory must separate intake, internal reuse, discharge, and consumption. Water per usable die depends on process flow, yield, allocation, and site conditions; a smaller process-node label does not establish a universal per-die multiplier.





Figure 14: Semiconductor Water Cycle: Intake supplies process water; treatment returns part of the flow for reuse. Recycling can reduce freshwater withdrawal, while evaporation and other unreturned flows determine consumption. State the denominator of any reuse fraction.



The separate flows in figure 14 show why a recycling fraction cannot determine absolute consumption. The same reuse percentage can accompany very different intake volumes and evaporative losses. Facility siting therefore requires the underlying water volumes and local watershed conditions, not a reuse percentage alone.
Fabrication also uses chemical products for etching, doping, and cleaning: strong acids such as hydrofluoric and sulfuric acid, organic solvents, and toxic dopant gases such as arsine and phosphine. Their hazard comes from toxicity, reactivity, and the treatment burden of the waste streams they produce, not from their energy content. Chemical inventories and safety data sheets identify hazardous ingredients, although undisclosed formulations can limit the assessment (Kim et al. 2018). The environmental account needs the substances and quantities used at the specific facility, together with their release and treatment pathways. An energy total alone cannot describe these chemical burdens.

Kim, Sunju, Chungsik Yoon, Seunghon Ham, Jihoon Park, Ohun Kwon, Donguk Park, Sangjun Choi, Seungwon Kim, Kwonchul Ha, and Won Kim. 2018. “Chemical Use in the Semiconductor Manufacturing Industry.” International Journal of Occupational and Environmental Health 24 (3-4): 109–18. https://doi.org/10.1080/10773525.2018.1519957.

Rhodes, Christopher J. 2019. “Endangered Elements, Critical Raw Materials and Conflict Minerals.” Science Progress 102 (4): 304–50. https://doi.org/10.1177/0036850419884873.
AI hardware and its manufacturing supply chain depend on critical materials whose supply disruption can constrain production. Criticality is not synonymous with geological rarity or membership in the rare earth group. Materials such as indium appear in critical-materials and endangered-elements analyses because supply can depend on byproduct extraction, substitution options, and recycling constraints (Rhodes 2019). The relevant dependency may lie in a processor, package, peripheral component, or fabrication process. Table 12 summarizes these different roles across the hardware system.



Table 12: Critical Materials for AI Hardware: Semiconductor manufacturing relies on specific materials, including silicon, gallium, germanium, indium, tantalum, cobalt, tungsten, copper, helium, and rare earth elements, that face increasing supply constraints and geopolitical risks, potentially impacting AI hardware production and innovation. The table details these materials, their applications in AI systems, and the associated supply vulnerabilities requiring proactive mitigation strategies.

The construction and operation of fabs and data centers also directly impacts natural ecosystems through habitat disruption, water stress, and pollution from chemical discharge. Semiconductor-industry effluents can contaminate nearby fluvial sediments with heavy metals and trace elements (Hsu et al. 2016). Waste generation from fabrication, including gaseous emissions, VOC-laden air, and metal-contaminated wastewater, requires advanced treatment systems, and end-of-life hardware adds the e-waste stream examined in section 15.12.5.

Hsu, Liang-Ching, Ching-Yi Huang, Yen-Hsun Chuang, Ho-Wen Chen, Ya-Ting Chan, Heng Yi Teah, Tsan-Yao Chen, Chiung-Fen Chang, Yu-Ting Liu, and Yu-Min Tzou. 2016. “Accumulation of Heavy Metals and Trace Elements in Fluvial Sediments Received Effluents from Traditional and Semiconductor Industries.” Scientific Reports 6 (1): 34250. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep34250.
These water, chemical, and material demands are what fabrication spends to produce each usable accelerator. The manufacturing phase that follows explains why an AI accelerator spends more of them than its wafer area suggests.



The manufacturing footprint combines the embodied carbon established in section 15.9.3 with the water, chemical, and material demands in section 15.12.2. Accelerator design changes how much of that resource investment produces a usable device.
Two structural properties of AI accelerators enlarge this footprint per usable device. First, high-performance accelerators are often fabricated at or near the reticle limit, the maximum die area a single lithography exposure can print. A larger die yields fewer candidates per wafer, and because the probability that a die escapes every random defect falls roughly exponentially with its area, a defect density that kills 5 percent of small dies may kill 20 percent or more of reticle-limit dies. The water, chemicals, and lithography energy spent on every defective die must then be allocated to the working ones. Second, the memory bandwidth that large-scale training and inference require pushes accelerators toward advanced 2.5D and 3D packaging, such as TSMC’s Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS), which places high bandwidth memory stacks beside the logic die on an interposer. The inventory must include those memory stacks, the interposer, and the added assembly stages rather than counting only the accelerator die. Each usable accelerator therefore embodies more process water, chemicals, and energy than its logic-die area alone suggests.
Longer useful service spreads that manufacturing investment across more work, while lower-toxicity materials, recycling, and cleaner manufacturing address the production burden itself (Cenci et al. 2021; Irimia-Vladu 2014).

Cenci, Marcelo Pilotto, Tatiana Scarazzato, Daniel Dotto Munchen, Paula Cristina Dartora, Hugo Marcelo Veit, Andrea Moura Bernardes, and Pablo R. Dias. 2021. “Eco-Friendly Electronics—a Comprehensive Review.” Advanced Materials Technologies 7 (2): 2001263. https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.202001263.

Irimia-Vladu, M. 2014. “‘Green’ Electronics: Biodegradable and Biocompatible Materials and Devices for Sustainable Future.” Chemical Society Reviews 43 (2): 588–610. https://doi.org/10.1039/c3cs60235d.



The operational energy consumed during training and inference is detailed in section 15.11. What merits attention here is the pattern of this consumption and its interaction with grid infrastructure. A GPT-3-scale run spreads 1,287 MWh over weeks of sustained power draw, but the character of that draw differs across workload types, and the difference shapes which scheduling interventions are practical.
A large distributed training run draws sustained aggregate power with the correlated phase transitions described in section 15.10.3, but its completion deadline may leave scheduling flexibility. Checkpoints created for fault recovery also provide restart points for deliberate pauses. A carbon-aware scheduler can use them to shift work toward lower-emissions intervals when the expected benefit exceeds checkpoint, restart, and idle-power costs. The decision requires a local emissions forecast and enough deadline slack; late-afternoon or overnight operation is not universally preferable. Fault tolerance thus supplies a mechanism for flexibility without proving that every pause saves emissions. Online inference has tighter delay budgets and may support bounded preemption, while offline inference can often be deferred more freely.


↩︎ Checkpoint-restart mechanics and the failure-driven choice of checkpoint interval are established in Checkpointing and Progress Preservation.
The duck curve describes the ramp in net load (demand minus variable solar and wind output) as solar generation falls in the evening. A constant data-center load raises the level of net demand but does not by itself increase the ramp rate. A flexible load can reduce the required ramp by curtailing during that interval. Schedule from local forecasts and marginal emissions signals; a universal daily pause window would ignore regional generation and transmission conditions.



Hardware upgrade cycles (Slade 2007) connect AI deployment to the broader electronic waste (e-waste) problem. In 2019, global e-waste reached roughly 54 million metric tons (Forti et al. 2020), of which 17.4 percent was documented as formally collected and recycled (Singh and Ogunseitan 2022). These totals cover electrical and electronic equipment generally, not AI hardware alone. Replacement schedules also differ from physical lifetimes; a server retired from one workload may still support another. When equipment is discarded, hazardous substances in its components require controlled recovery and treatment rather than uncontrolled dumping or processing (Grossman 2007).

Slade, G. 2007. Made to Break: Technology and Obsolescence in America. Harvard University Press. https://doi.org/10.4159/9780674043756.

Forti, V., C. P. Baldé, R. Kuehr, and G. Bel. 2020. The Global e-Waste Monitor 2020: Quantities, Flows and the Circular Economy Potential. United Nations University/United Nations Institute for Training and Research; International Telecommunication Union; International Solid Waste Association.

Singh, Narendra, and Oladele A. Ogunseitan. 2022. “Disentangling the Worldwide Web of e-Waste and Climate Change Co-Benefits.” Circular Economy 1 (2): 100011. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cec.2022.100011.

Grossman, E. 2007. High Tech Trash: Digital Devices, Hidden Toxics, and Human Health. Island press.
Memory capacity, bandwidth, and interconnect compatibility can motivate replacement before accelerators physically fail. In tightly integrated systems, a new accelerator generation may require baseboard, networking, or server changes; PCIe-based designs can offer different upgrade options. Evaluate the actual compatibility boundary and reuse path. Replacement does not automatically mean disposal, and a functioning retired node may remain useful for less demanding workloads.
The deployment of embedded AI integrates inference into edge appliances and consumer electronics. Figure 15 charts the broader connected-device fleet, with historical estimates rising from 8.6 billion in 2019 to 15.1 billion in 2023 and a projection of 29.4 billion by 2030 (Statista 2022). These counts indicate the scale of the device ecosystem, not the number of AI systems or the amount of e-waste. Waste generation also depends on service life, repair, and reuse. Adhesive enclosures, nonreplaceable batteries, and proprietary components can make repair difficult, increasing the risk that a limited failure leads to whole-device disposal (Baldé et al. 2017).

Baldé, Cornelis P, Vanessa Forti, Vanessa Gray, Ruediger Kuehr, and Paul Stegmann. 2017. “The Global e-Waste Monitor 2017: Quantities, Flows and Resources.” United Nations University, International Telecommunication Union, International Solid Waste Association.














Figure 15: IoT Device Growth: Connected devices worldwide, with historical counts through 2023 (unhatched) and projections from 2024 onward (hatched) (Statista 2022). The counts describe the connected-device ecosystem, not the number of AI systems or the amount of e-waste. Waste generation also depends on service lifetimes, repair, reuse, and disposal.


Statista. 2022. Number of Internet of Things (IoT) Connected Devices Worldwide from 2019 to 2030.


Limited software support, restricted repair, and difficult disassembly can push devices toward replacement instead of reuse. The lifecycle boundary must then follow the retired equipment to its next use or treatment destination. Moving hardware out of the operator’s inventory does not remove its environmental burden; the account must distinguish useful reuse, controlled recovery, and disposal that transfers costs to other communities.



Countering the linear “take-make-dispose” model requires a shift toward a circular economy (Stahel 2016) that prioritizes reuse, refurbishment, and recycling. Extending the functional lifespan of AI hardware spreads a fixed manufacturing footprint over more service. Extending server life from 3 years to 5 years reduces embodied carbon allocated per year of service by 40 percent. This allocation result motivates evaluating longer use, but a claim of avoided emissions requires comparing the replacement and operating costs of the alternatives.

Stahel, Walter R. 2016. “The Circular Economy.” Nature 531 (7595): 435–38. https://doi.org/10.1038/531435a.

Federal Trade Commission. 2021. Nixing the Fix: An FTC Report to Congress on Repair Restrictions. Federal Trade Commission.
Four lifecycle interventions support longer hardware service by making systems repairable, upgradeable, supported, and reusable. Right-to-repair initiatives seek to reduce service restrictions, including barriers to replacement parts, tools, and repair information (Federal Trade Commission 2021). Modular design supports upgradeability by separating replaceable subsystems so that an accelerator or network upgrade need not require discarding the entire chassis. Extended support cycles provide the driver updates and security patches needed to keep functioning equipment usable. Secondary-use programs match retired accelerators to workloads they can still serve, such as batch processing, development, or research. Each intervention must preserve the performance, compatibility, and security required for useful continued operation.
These interventions move sustainability from disposal management to lifecycle engineering. A replacement decision compares two ways of delivering the same future service, continued operation of the existing fleet and operation of a replacement fleet. The original manufacturing emissions have already occurred under either choice. Replacement adds a new manufacturing burden that pays back only through operational savings over the remaining service interval, so the tipping point is the time those savings take to equal it. Suppose a replacement accelerator carries the same allocated manufacturing footprint as an H100 (164 kg CO2e) and completes the same work with 50 percent less energy. Against an existing accelerator running continuously at the rated 700 W, the replacement repays its manufacturing emissions in about 6.5 weeks on the US-average grid, but only after about 2.7 years on Quebec’s grid, nearly the whole of a 3-year standard service life. Lower utilization stretches both intervals in proportion. The same upgrade can therefore repay itself within weeks on a fossil-heavy grid and become a net loss on a clean one if the replacement leaves service before it breaks even. This accelerator-only account omits host and facility overhead, and disposal and any useful second life for the retired hardware shift it further, so a lower annual amortized figure alone cannot settle the decision.

Self-Check: Question

For a fixed inventoried manufacturing footprint, what happens to annualized embodied carbon when useful hardware life extends from three years to five years, before considering changes in operational energy?

The fixed manufacturing footprint is amortized over five years rather than three, reducing its annualized allocation by 40 percent; total lifecycle savings still depend on operational energy and the inventory boundary.
Older accelerators automatically consume 40 percent less electrical power per FLOP as silicon pathways break in over time.
Extending accelerator lifespans from three to five years eliminates electronic waste entirely because hardware decomposes organically after five years.
Data center PUE automatically drops to 1.0 after servers have operated for more than four years.

A research paper reports that training a new vision-language model consumed 500 MWh for its final successful training run. Explain why reporting only the final run systematically underestimates the development phase’s total carbon footprint, and identify two mitigation practices.
True or False: If an AI training data center is powered 100 percent by dedicated geothermal and hydroelectric power, the use phase is completely unconstrained and engineers no longer need to consider grid dynamics or cooling efficiency.
Standardized under ISO 14040 and ISO 14044, a comprehensive ____ evaluates the cumulative environmental impact of AI hardware across raw material extraction, manufacturing, use, and end-of-life disposal.
A cloud provider considers retiring functional accelerators because a new generation offers a 12 percent improvement in performance per watt. Which option identifies a circular-economy candidate for evaluation, without claiming that this efficiency specification alone determines the lowest-emissions choice?

Immediately shred and dispose of all prior-generation accelerators to eliminate any hardware with lower peak energy efficiency.
Replace all servers instantly because any improvement in operational efficiency automatically offsets the embodied carbon of manufacturing a replacement fleet.
Evaluate redeployment to compatible secondary workloads, comparing continued useful service with replacement manufacturing and measured operating emissions over the same remaining service interval.
Overclock the older accelerators beyond thermal limits to match new hardware throughput regardless of cooling failure risk.
