title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
When a data center hits its absolute power ceiling, the operator cannot simply buy more GPUs. Supporting additional useful work requires reducing the power needed for that work, changing its schedule, or securing additional feasible capacity. Algorithmic optimization can reduce executed work and data movement; infrastructure changes can reduce overhead. Carbon-aware placement addresses a different constraint by changing the emissions associated with electricity use, even when energy demand stays fixed.
The measurement frameworks identify where environmental costs concentrate in a particular workload. Repeated experiments can make development dominant; sustained serving can make inference dominant; and clean electricity or limited use can increase the relative importance of manufacturing. The measured balance guides intervention. Algorithmic changes can reduce the number or cost of operations, infrastructure changes affect execution and facility overhead, and governance sets the budgets and incentives under which those choices operate.
Implementation must account for the rebound introduced with fleet growth in section 15.3, known as the Jevons paradox24 (principle \(\ref{pri-jevons-paradox}\)). The tenfold-efficiency, hundredfold-volume example there supplied the arithmetic; the mechanism is that cheaper computation enables applications that were previously economically infeasible, so usage can grow enough to erase or exceed the expected energy savings. This rebound effect makes absolute outcomes, including carbon budgets, necessary companions to rate efficiency (FLOP/s per watt). Renewable sourcing changes the emissions associated with electricity but does not cap consumption. Governance must track workload growth against the intended resource budget to determine whether efficiency gains reduce the fleet’s total impact.
24 Jevons Paradox: Jevons (1865) described how efficiency could stimulate demand enough to increase total coal use. Price reductions alone do not establish either energy factor; measure both unit energy and demand.
Jevons, William Stanley. 1865. The Coal Question: An Inquiry Concerning the Progress of the Nation, and the Probable Exhaustion of Our Coal Mines. Macmillan; Co.


The most counterintuitive obstacle to sustainable AI is not inefficiency but success, which is why mitigation must choose both which layer owns each reduction and which absolute budget prevents rebound. Energy-efficient model design, optimized hardware deployment, sustainable infrastructure operations, and carbon-aware scheduling each attack a different term in the lifecycle footprint. Framework selection matters only insofar as it changes computation, memory movement, utilization, or reporting. Lifecycle-aware design keeps the optimization from ending at deployment by checking whether savings survive training, inference, manufacturing, and use.
Figure 16 illustrates rebound on an elastic demand curve (\(\DemandPriceElasticity> 1\)). When unit cost falls from \(\ComputeUnitCost_0\) to \(\ComputeUnitCost_1\), the green shaded area represents the saving on baseline volume \(\ComputeDemandVolume_0\). Demand expands to \(\ComputeDemandVolume_1\), creating a red area (\(\ComputeUnitCost_1 (\ComputeDemandVolume_1 - \ComputeDemandVolume_0)\)) that exceeds the original saving in this schematic. With monetary unit cost on the vertical axis, the areas measure expenditure. They represent energy only under an additional assumption that unit cost changes in proportion to energy per operation; an emissions comparison also needs the applicable carbon intensity.














Figure 16: Jevons Paradox in AI Workloads: A schematic elastic demand curve. When unit cost falls from \(\ComputeUnitCost_0\) to \(\ComputeUnitCost_1\), demand grows from \(\ComputeDemandVolume_0\) to \(\ComputeDemandVolume_1\). The green rectangle is the expenditure saved on the original volume; the red rectangle is the expenditure on added volume at the lower unit cost. In this schematic, the red area exceeds the green. These areas represent energy only if unit cost changes proportionally to energy per operation; an emissions comparison also requires carbon intensity.



Total energy depends on measured energy per query and query volume. Demand elasticity describes how volume responds to price; translating that response into energy requires a separate account of how unit energy changes.

Checkpoint 15.5: The efficiency trap (Jevons paradox)
An engineering team optimizes a translation service, reducing measured energy per query by 50 percent (2\(\times\) efficiency gain) at fixed quality. Assume the service passes that saving through as a proportional price reduction and that grid intensity stays unchanged.

Inelastic demand: calculate the change in total energy consumption when demand is inelastic and price change does not affect usage.
Elastic demand: calculate the net change in total energy consumption when a 50 percent cost reduction leads to a 300 percent increase in query volume.
Rebound effect: define how this “rebound effect” challenges the assumption that “efficient models are automatically green models.”



The Jevons paradox does not invalidate efficiency as a strategy; it makes governance and capacity planning part of the result. At the level of individual systems, reducing energy per useful task remains a direct sustainability lever. A reduction in latency or monetary cost is a candidate improvement whose energy effect must still be measured.

Systems Perspective 15.4: Efficiency as sustainabilityModel optimizations become sustainability tools only when they reduce measured lifecycle cost at fixed quality. Pruning can remove computation and memory traffic when the hardware skips the resulting structure. Quantization reduces representation size and may accelerate supported kernels, while knowledge distillation trades additional training for a smaller serving model. Each technique can also fail to reduce wall energy when its overhead or deployment regime leaves the dominant term unchanged.
Performance engineering supplies candidate interventions, but the environmental result still needs measurement. A faster run reduces energy only if the shorter duration outweighs any increase in average power; lower memory use helps only if it removes powered work or capacity. Hardware-software co-design becomes a sustainability gain when these savings survive the lifecycle boundary and the deployed workload volume.
The fundamental insight is that sustainable AI engineering overlaps strongly with efficient AI engineering, but extends beyond it. The engineering principles that enable systems to scale, perform better, and cost less to operate can also reduce environmental impact, but sustainability adds lifecycle accounting, carbon-aware placement, absolute resource budgets, water and materials constraints, and governance against rebound effects. Sustainability is an integral part of good systems engineering, not a synonym for efficiency alone.





Lifecycle-aware development starts from the largest environmental term in the workload and then selects the intervention that changes that term. Algorithmic design, infrastructure optimization, operational practice, and governance reduce impact only when they are sequenced around the measured bottleneck rather than applied as a generic checklist (Uddin and Rahman 2012).

Uddin, Mueen, and Azizah Abdul Rahman. 2012. “Energy Efficiency and Low Carbon Enabler Green IT Framework for Data Centers Considering Green Metrics.” Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 16 (6): 4078–94. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2012.03.014.


Large deep learning models can require substantial computation during training and inference.25 The engineering question is how much of that work a particular task needs at its required quality. Parameter count alone does not identify redundant computation, and removing weights saves energy only if the resulting implementation avoids work or data movement. Sustainable algorithm design therefore evaluates the model and its execution together, measuring energy per useful task rather than treating a smaller representation as sufficient evidence of improvement.
25 FLOP/s vs. FLOPs: FLOP/s denotes a rate; FLOPs denotes an operation count. Neither alone determines energy. Integrating system power over execution time includes arithmetic, data movement, idle intervals, and supporting components. A faster implementation can reduce static energy by finishing sooner, but its total saving depends on the power required to achieve that rate.When the measured bottleneck is unused structure, bit width, or serving scale, the sustainable design lever changes. Table 13 maps the bottleneck to the intervention that changes the energy term.



Table 13: Algorithmic Energy Levers by Bottleneck: Pruning, quantization, and distillation reduce energy through different mechanisms, so the right choice depends on the measured bottleneck rather than on a generic compression goal.











Technique
Measured bottleneck
Energy mechanism
Representative evidence




Pruning
Unused model structure
Removes redundant weights, reducing model size, compute, and memory movement during inference
Structured pruning can remove complete channels or blocks; measure energy and quality for the resulting executable model


Quantization
Bit width
Lowers numerical precision so arithmetic units and memory transfers move fewer bits
Q8BERT demonstrates an 8-bit BERT representation with a smaller model footprint and task-dependent quality retention (Zafrir et al. 2019)


Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al. 2015)
Serving scale
Moves repeated inference cost into a one-time teacher-student training process
DistilBERT retains 97% of BERT accuracy with 40% fewer parameters and 60% faster inference (Sanh et al. 2019)




Zafrir, Ofir, Guy Boudoukh, Peter Izsak, and Moshe Wasserblat. 2019. “Q8BERT: Quantized 8Bit BERT.” 2019 Fifth Workshop on Energy Efficient Machine Learning and Cognitive Computing - NeurIPS Edition (EMC2-NIPS), 36–39. https://doi.org/10.1109/emc2-nips53020.2019.00016.

Sanh, Victor, Lysandre Debut, Julien Chaumond, and Thomas Wolf. 2019. “DistilBERT, a Distilled Version of BERT: Smaller, Faster, Cheaper and Lighter.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1910.01108, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1910.01108.



The table’s three levers have different deployment caveats: pruning26 depends on sparsity structure and hardware support, quantization27 can affect arithmetic and memory movement, and knowledge distillation28 amortizes its extra training cost across repeated serving.
26 Pruning Energy Impact: Pruning saves inference energy only when the implementation eliminates arithmetic or memory transfers at the required quality. Unstructured sparsity in large language models (LLMs) can reduce stored weights without delivering a proportional wall-energy saving. Sparse formats, supported kernels, indexing, load balance, and static power determine the realized result; a parameter sparsity percentage is not an energy-reduction factor.27 Quantization Energy Savings: Lower precision reduces representation size and can reduce arithmetic and memory energy, but neither term scales universally with the square or ratio of bit width. Hardware support, kernel fusion, conversion costs, batching, and whether execution is compute- or memory-bound determine the realized result (Gholami et al. 2022). Report model size separately from measured wall energy, and compare both at the required quality and latency.
Gholami, Amir, Sehoon Kim, Zhen Dong, Zhewei Yao, Michael W. Mahoney, and Kurt Keutzer. 2022. “A Survey of Quantization Methods for Efficient Neural Network Inference.” In Low-Power Computer Vision: Improve the Efficiency of Artificial Intelligence. Chapman; Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/9781003162810-13.
28 Knowledge Distillation: Introduced by Hinton et al. (2015), distillation trains a compact “student” model on soft probability targets from a larger “teacher,” capturing inter-class relationships that hard labels discard. The sustainability comparison must amortize teacher and student training across the actual serving volume and measure energy at the required output quality.
Hinton, Geoffrey, Oriol Vinyals, and Jeff Dean. 2015. “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network.” arXiv Preprint.
Pruning, quantization, and distillation form the core toolkit for sustainable AI development, but their sustainability value depends on the measured bottleneck. The design question is not how to implement each compression method from first principles; it is how to rank these levers against memory movement, serving volume, carbon intensity, and lifecycle cost.
While model compression, efficient architectures, and carbon-aware scheduling provide the technical mechanisms for efficiency, deploying them haphazardly yields diminishing returns. To achieve maximum impact, engineering teams must synthesize these isolated techniques into a coherent, prioritized strategy that attacks the largest sources of emissions first.

Checkpoint 15.6: Prioritizing decarbonization strategy
Deploying a 70B LLM for a latency-sensitive application:

Technique ranking: state the measurements needed to rank INT4 quantization, unstructured pruning, carbon-aware scheduling, and knowledge distillation for this service. Separate reduced energy demand from reduced carbon per unit of energy.
Systems justification: propose a conditional ranking for a memory-bound service at fixed quality and latency, including hardware support, expected serving volume, extra training cost, and whether requests can move across regions or time.






Repeated model updates add to the lifecycle footprint even when each deployed version is efficient. The relevant comparison is the work required to maintain the service’s quality over time, including development and retraining; a retraining cycle that repeats the development sweep of section 15.9.1 pays its 5× final-run multiple again on every update. Transfer learning and fine-tuning can reuse a pretrained model instead of repeating training from scratch (Raffel et al. 2020), but the comparison must include adaptation, evaluation, and any additional work needed to recover quality on the target task. Reuse is a candidate saving whose value depends on that complete update cycle.

Raffel, C., N. Shazeer, A. Roberts, K. Lee, S. Narang, M. Matena, Y. Zhou, W. Li, and P. J. Liu. 2020. “Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 21 (140): 1–67.

Xu, Dianlei, Tong Li, Yong Li, Xiang Su, Sasu Tarkoma, Tao Jiang, Jon Crowcroft, and Pan Hui. 2020. “Edge Intelligence: Architectures, Challenges, and Applications.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2003.12172.
The deployment boundary matters just as much as the training boundary. Edge deployment can reduce communication energy by running inference on specialized low-power hardware at the point of use (Xu et al. 2020), but the lifecycle account must include the embodied carbon of manufacturing and replacing those devices. Embedding LCA methodologies into AI workflows allows teams to see this trade-off early: a cloud model, an edge model, and a hybrid cascade may have different winners depending on query volume, device lifetime, grid carbon intensity, and retraining frequency (International Organization for Standardization 2006a, 2006b). Henderson et al. (2020) argue for systematic reporting of ML energy and carbon footprints precisely so these comparisons can be made consistently. As the Jevons paradox warns, the accounting must also include usage growth, because optimizing one stage may increase total impact if lower costs enable wider deployment.



Benchmarks matter when they make efficiency visible at procurement and design time. The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard (ML.ENERGY Initiative et al. 2023) reports inference energy measurements under declared model and serving configurations. MLPerf power submissions pair performance results with system-level power measurements under benchmark rules. These results support comparisons within the stated workload, quality, and measurement conditions; converting them into carbon footprints still requires electricity and lifecycle accounting beyond the benchmark.

ML.ENERGY Initiative, Jae-Won Chung, Jiachen Gu, Zhewei Yan, Tony Lo, Yejin Park, and Mosharaf Chowdhury. 2023. The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard. SymbioticLab, University of Michigan.
The right efficiency metric depends on the serving regime. Batch inference is naturally expressed as correct samples per joule, latency-sensitive serving as SLO-compliant queries per joule, and generative workloads as joules per accepted output token at a declared quality threshold. Raw throughput per joule rewards systems that lower accuracy, truncate outputs, or miss latency objectives. Standardization does not make one platform universally green; it fixes useful work, quality, the measurement window, and the energy denominator well enough for procurement and architecture decisions to be argued quantitatively.
For sub-watt TinyML deployments, the MLPerf Tiny benchmark suite applies this discipline to constrained devices (Banbury et al. 2021). Tasks include visual wake words, keyword spotting, anomaly detection, and image classification. The closed division constrains implementations to reference-equivalent models, while the open division permits broader model choices. Reading accuracy, latency, and energy together within the declared division prevents a change in task or model quality from masquerading as a hardware-efficiency gain.

Banbury, Colby, Vijay Janapa Reddi, Peter Torelli, Jeremy Holleman, Nat Jeffries, Csaba Kiraly, Pietro Montino, et al. 2021. “MLPerf Tiny Benchmark.” arXiv Preprint.
Energy and latency still have to be read together through the energy-delay product (EDP) (equation 17), which balances energy consumption against response time by penalizing solutions that save power only by taking too long:
\[\text{EDP} = \TotalEnergy \times \Time= \AveragePower\times \Time^2 \tag{17}\]
where \(\TotalEnergy\) is energy consumed, \(\Time\) is execution time, and \(\AveragePower\) is average power. The quadratic delay term penalizes solutions that achieve low energy through excessive delays. Lower EDP is preferable under this particular trade-off score, after quality and latency requirements have been satisfied. It does not authorize missing a service deadline or replace energy per completed task.
For TinyML deployments, EDP provides a score for comparing feasible operating points. Reducing clock frequency can lower power while extending execution; reducing voltage can lower switching energy as well, when the hardware permits it. Static power and the longer active interval can offset those gains. The preferred setting therefore comes from measured energy and delay across supported configurations, after excluding settings that miss the workload’s deadlines.
Sustainability metrics complement performance benchmarks by recording the resource cost of useful work. Regulation is beginning to require such records. The EU AI Act’s documentation obligations for covered general-purpose models, examined with the other regulatory mechanisms in section 15.14.1, include known or estimated energy consumption. Such requirements make the measurement boundary and provenance part of the reporting evidence rather than an optional annotation to a performance result.




Algorithmic optimizations can reduce operation counts, data movement, or the energy of execution. The operational environment determines the facility overhead and emissions associated with that work. Renewable energy integration, carbon-aware workload scheduling, and cooling optimization act on these surrounding terms, so each intervention must be evaluated at the boundary it changes.


A single hyperscale data center can consume over 100 MW of power, comparable to a small city.29 Renewable energy integration, advanced cooling, and AI-driven optimization offer complementary interventions. Their value depends on whether the measured problem lies in the electricity source, heat-removal overhead, or operating controls.
29 PUE Gap: The PUE model in section 15.8.2.3 shows that facility overhead scales with every watt of IT load. At 100 MW, even a small PUE change therefore represents megawatts of cooling and power-delivery capacity, but its carbon value still depends on the grid signal.30 24/7 Carbon-Free Energy (CFE): Hourly matching strengthens the time resolution of electricity procurement and accounting. Its physical impact depends on deliverability, additional clean supply, storage, and grid conditions. It does not eliminate manufacturing emissions or prove that every consumed electron came from a carbon-free generator.Major cloud providers have announced renewable-energy commitments, but variable generation leaves a supply-matching problem. Storage and flexible scheduling can help address it alongside transmission and other generation sources; the appropriate combination depends on the site and workload. Google’s published 2030 target for 24/7 carbon-free energy30 illustrates the harder version of this goal: matching electricity consumption with carbon-free generation, including nuclear as well as renewables, hour by hour rather than only on an annual basis.
Cooling overhead depends on rack density, climate, and the heat-removal design, as quantified in section 15.10.4.31 Liquid cooling can support dense accelerator configurations, but its energy benefit depends on the complete pumping and heat-rejection system. Control policy supplies another lever. The DeepMind case in section 15.8.2.4 shows how measured operating data can guide cooling adjustments within thermal constraints; its reported savings describe the evaluated site rather than a universal reduction for any facility.
31 Cooling Energy Density: AI accelerator racks can exceed 100 kW per cabinet, far above the design envelope of many conventional air-cooled facilities. Direct liquid cooling removes heat closer to the device and can reduce fan and chiller work, but the realized facility-energy reduction depends on coolant temperatures, pumps, heat rejection, climate, and the air-cooling baseline. For AI data centers, the cooling system is no longer passive infrastructure overhead but an active constraint on how many accelerators can be physically co-located.


Every carbon-aware decision inherits the quality of the grid signal behind it, and the right signal depends on the decision. Grid carbon intensity varies with generation mix, which changes hourly with demand, renewable availability, and plant dispatch. The US Energy Information Administration publishes historical grid emissions factors by region, updated annually; these averages give a coarse baseline for inventories or early planning, but they cannot resolve the hourly effect of moving a flexible workload. Electricity Maps provides time-resolved, flow-traced average and lifecycle intensity estimates across covered grids, while WattTime provides marginal operating-emissions signals that estimate the generator response to added or removed load.
The two kinds of signal answer the two questions that the measurement contract (section 15.8) separated. Time-matched average factors support the attributional inventory of a completed run. Marginal factors support the consequential question of how shifting or eliminating a run would change system emissions, which is the question a scheduler asks.



Carbon-aware scheduling, introduced with the geographic and temporal levers in section 15.8.1.2, now has the grid signals it needs. Its benefit depends on the signal it acts on and on the additional energy the move itself causes.


↩︎ Scheduling against an external price signal, trading waiting and preemption against deadlines, is established in Cost-aware scheduling policies.
Carbon-aware scheduling is fundamentally a load-shifting software problem. The scheduler queries one of the grid signals compared above and combines it with workload flexibility. A feasible shift must finish before the deadline, retain access to data and accelerator capacity, and preserve the job’s reliability constraints. Its net benefit must exceed checkpoint, transfer, restart, and idle-capacity emissions. Pausing useful work without reducing the cluster’s powered load can erase the expected saving.
Google’s carbon-intelligent computing platform32 illustrates this approach by using forecasts and virtual capacity limits to delay flexible work (Radovanovic et al. 2021). In the multi-tier accounting cascade of figure 4, temporal load shifting modulates the grid emissions factor applied to facility electricity rather than reducing raw compute FLOPs. That is a carbon intervention, not automatically an energy reduction; checkpointing, transfer, and a different runtime can also change electricity consumption.
32 Carbon-Aware Scheduling at Scale: Google’s system forecasts carbon intensity and flexible demand, then sets virtual capacity curves that shift work within operational constraints (Radovanovic et al. 2021). This demonstrates a scheduling mechanism; a deployment’s saving depends on its workload flexibility, grid signal, and power response.
Radovanovic, Ana, Ross Koningstein, Ian Schneider, Bokan Chen, Alexandre Duarte, Binz Roy, Diyue Xiao, et al. 2021. “Carbon-Aware Computing for Datacenters.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2106.11750, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2106.11750.
33 Marginal vs. Average Emissions: An average factor describes the electricity mix attributed to consumption; a marginal factor estimates the emissions change caused by changing demand. The pair applies the attributional-versus-consequential split of the measurement contract in section 15.8 to the grid signal. Neither factor is a universal multiplier for the other; use a documented methodology, forecast horizon, and region appropriate to the decision.Because a scheduler asks how moving a job changes emissions, it needs a marginal signal rather than the average factor an inventory uses, and the providers compared above expose signals with different methodologies and coverage.33 A feasible schedule must satisfy three constraints on one time axis at once, the grid carbon signal \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{grid}}(\TimeInstant)\), the job’s execution state, and cluster headroom \(\ClusterHeadroom(\TimeInstant)\) (figure 17). The job waits, checkpointed, through the high-carbon peak, runs for \(\JobDuration\) in a low-carbon trough where headroom exists, and still finishes with slack before its deadline. Waiting pays only when the avoided grid emissions exceed the checkpoint I/O, idle standby, and state migration that the wait itself causes.






Figure 17: A Feasible Carbon-Aware Schedule: Three constraints share one time axis. The job waits, checkpointed, through the high-carbon hours of the grid signal and runs in the low-carbon window only where cluster headroom exists, finishing with slack before the deadline. The equation below the timeline charges the shift for its checkpoint, idle-wait, and migration carbon, so waiting pays only when the avoided emissions exceed those terms. The curve is schematic, not a measured grid trace.



Renewable generation variability complicates batch training dispatch across power grids. Figure 18 charts hourly electricity generation across the European Union over a full week in November 2023, stacking resource generation bands beneath the total demand curve, which peaks between 310 and 365 GW on weekdays. Nuclear remains near 70 GW, solar contributes midday output, and wind ranges from 27 GW on Sunday to 111 GW on Thursday. The resulting generation mix varies across days as well as within each day. Wind contributes to that variation, but demand, other generation, storage, and electricity exchanges also affect fossil dispatch. Carbon-aware scheduling therefore needs regional grid forecasts rather than a fixed assumption about which hours are cleanest.














Figure 18: European Electricity Generation over One Week: Hourly public net generation by source for the European Union in week 47 of 2023 (20 to 26 November), stacked, with the load curve on top. Nuclear forms a nearly flat base, hydro follows the daily demand cycle, and solar adds only small midday bulges this late in the year. Wind swings across days rather than hours, from about 27 GW on Sunday to about 111 GW on Thursday, so the fossil gas and coal that fill the remaining gap move from day to day. Lower-carbon windows for deferrable training therefore come from the forecast for a specific week and region, not from a fixed daily pattern. Source: Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE) public power data, from ENTSO-E and national statistics.



Energy-aware AI frameworks complement scheduling when they optimize the workload rather than only shifting its location. Zeus improved training energy efficiency by 15.3–75.8 percent across its evaluated workloads by automatically finding energy-performance trade-offs (You et al. 2023), while Perseus reduced large-model training energy consumption by up to 30 percent by mitigating energy bloat (Chung et al. 2023). These tools, alongside CodeCarbon for emissions tracking (Schmidt et al. 2021), democratize energy optimization beyond hyperscale companies.

You, Jie, Jae-Won Chung, and Mosharaf Chowdhury. 2023. “Zeus: Understanding and Optimizing GPU Energy Consumption of DNN Training.” 20th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 23), 119–39.

Chung, Jae-Won, Yile Gu, Insu Jang, Luoxi Meng, Nikhil Bansal, and Mosharaf Chowdhury. 2023. “Reducing Energy Bloat in Large Model Training.” Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 30th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles abs/2312.06902: 144–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/3694715.3695970.
Scheduling changes where and when work runs; the cooling interventions established in section 15.10.4 change facility overhead. Liquid cooling and immersion cooling still require pumps, coolant distribution, and heat rejection in the energy boundary. The combined strategy must measure these interventions together rather than add their isolated savings.




The value of Google’s case study is that it groups mitigation into four levers that correspond to terms this chapter has tracked, namely the model’s work, the machine’s efficiency, the facility’s overhead, and the grid’s carbon factor. Table 14 summarizes the “4 Ms” that Google engineers identified for reducing the carbon footprint of rapidly expanding AI workloads (Patterson et al. 2022).



Table 14: Google’s 4 Ms Sustainability Framework: The framework combines model architecture, hardware specialization, infrastructure efficiency, and carbon-aware placement each acting on a different term of the footprint. Their combined effect requires a consistent end-to-end account: component factors can be multiplied only when they describe compatible workloads and measurement boundaries.











Lever
Intervention
Reported efficiency effect
Example mechanism




Model
Select efficient AI architectures such as sparse models or neural-architecture-search-derived designs
5–10\(\times\) lower computation requirements without compromising model quality
Evolved Transformer and Primer

Use AI-specific hardware rather than general-purpose systems
2–5\(\times\) performance-per-watt improvement; TPUs show 5–13\(\times\) greater carbon efficiency relative to nonoptimized GPUs
Tensor Processing Units

Real-time monitoring of renewable energy usage across infrastructure






Patterson et al. (2022) combine model, hardware, facility, and electricity-source improvements in a comparison of Transformer training configurations. Their example reports an energy reduction factor of 83 and a CO2 emissions reduction factor of 747 relative to its stated baseline. A combined factor can come from a consistent accounting model supported by measurements, but the component ratios must refer to compatible workloads and boundaries. Multiplying unrelated best-case factors does not establish the same result.
In the period studied by Patterson et al. (2022), AI workloads represented less than 15 percent of Google’s total energy consumption despite expanding deployment. That share is evidence about relative consumption; it does not by itself establish constant or declining absolute energy when the denominator also changes. Assess absolute growth from measured energy totals alongside the reported efficiency improvements.
Empirical case studies demonstrate how sustainable-AI engineering can improve both capability and environmental impact. For example, Patterson et al. (2022) compare GPT-3 with Google’s GLaM and report improved quality metrics alongside reduced training computation and lower-carbon energy sources, while the GLaM model paper explains the mixture-of-experts architecture behind that efficient scaling (Du et al. 2022).

Patterson, David, Joseph Gonzalez, Urs Holzle, Quoc Le, Chen Liang, Lluis-Miquel Munguia, Daniel Rothchild, David R. So, Maud Texier, and Jeff Dean. 2022. “The Carbon Footprint of Machine Learning Training Will Plateau, Then Shrink.” Computer 55 (7): 18–28. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2022.3148714.

Du, Nan, Yanping Huang, Andrew M. Dai, Simon Tong, Dmitry Lepikhin, Yuanzhong Xu, Maxim Krikun, et al. 2022. “GLaM: Efficient Scaling of Language Models with Mixture-of-Experts.” In International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), edited by Kamalika Chaudhuri, Stefanie Jegelka, Le Song, Csaba Szepesvari, Gang Niu, and Sivan Sabato, vol. 162. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research. PMLR.

↩︎ Mixture-of-experts execution and the All-to-All routing it requires are established in Expert parallelism (mixture of experts).

The strategy in the case study, which combines systematic measurement, carbon-aware development, transparency in reporting, and renewable energy transition, is useful as a framework for sustainable AI scaling. The analysis also argues that earlier extrapolations overstated ML energy requirements by large factors because they did not account for efficiency improvements and workload measurement boundaries, underscoring the importance of empirical measurement over theoretical projections.



Measurement, optimization, and scheduling frameworks provide the analytical foundation, but implementation requires prioritization organized around the dominant lifecycle term.
Measurement must precede optimization. The development-time trackers introduced with the geographic and temporal levers (section 15.8.1.2) supply the empirical baseline, which is what distinguishes a genuine reduction from energy merely displaced across a system boundary.
Geographic and temporal siting provides an immediate operational lever. Comparing candidate deployment sites requires pairing workload electricity with documented grid carbon-intensity factors for the target operating window, while accounting for facility overhead, inter-site data transfer penalties, runtime changes, and reliability constraints before claiming a net emissions reduction.
Algorithmic efficiency attacks computational volume directly. Rather than defaulting to the largest trainable parameter count, teams evaluate pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation against target latency and accuracy thresholds. Each lever saves energy only through the bottleneck it changes (table 13); for quantization, realized benefits depend on integer kernel support, memory bandwidth bottlenecks, data conversion overhead, and batching constraints. Transfer learning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning can avoid some work required by training from scratch, but their benefit depends on the adaptation task, achieved quality, and total update cost.
Platform selection and lifecycle governance complete the framework. An accelerator with better energy per task may draw more instantaneous power while finishing sooner; its value depends on the workload and complete hardware lifecycle. Longer service spreads manufacturing emissions over more useful work and may avoid replacement, but it also preserves the existing equipment’s operating costs. The balance between embodied and operational emissions therefore makes hardware longevity a context-dependent trade-off rather than an automatic win.
The cumulative impact of technical choices depends on the incentives under which organizations deploy them. Electricity prices reward some efficiency gains, but prices need not capture water stress, manufacturing emissions, or local environmental burdens. Policy and regulatory frameworks can bring those omitted costs into reporting, procurement, and investment decisions.

Self-Check: Question

An AI company deploys quantization and knowledge distillation, reducing the energy cost per user query by 50 percent. Over the following year, the company’s total data center electricity consumption increases by 75 percent as lower per-query costs enable new product features and attract 3.5\(\times\) more queries. Which phenomenon explains this outcome?

Amdahl’s law, which states that sequential execution limits parallel speedup.
Dennard scaling breakdown, where transistor power density increases with scaling.
Jevons paradox, where technological efficiency improvements lower the effective cost of a resource, stimulating increased demand that outweighs per-unit efficiency gains.
The memory wall, where DRAM bandwidth fails to keep pace with arithmetic throughput.

A model compression team evaluates unstructured weight pruning, INT8 quantization, and knowledge distillation for serving a transformer. Explain the hardware mechanisms that can turn each technique into measured energy savings, and why theoretical compression alone is insufficient.
A platform team has recurring batch training jobs that can move across regions or time while preserving quality. Which intervention is a candidate for lowering operational carbon without changing the model, provided capacity, data access, deadlines, and net emissions are checked?

Replacing all ReLU activation functions with GELU activations across training scripts.
Increasing the batch size to maximize GPU execution unit occupancy.
Switching from PyTorch to a C++ inference engine for training loops.
Implementing carbon-aware spatial and temporal scheduling to route training jobs to data center regions and time windows with surplus renewable energy and low carbon intensity.

A hardware startup develops an ultra-low-power neural accelerator for microcontroller-class edge devices, advertising 0.1 mJ per visual wake-word inference. Which MLCommons benchmark suite provides the standardized models, datasets, and strict external power measurement protocols required to verify these claims against competitors?

MLPerf Tiny, which standardizes embedded vision, keyword spotting, and anomaly detection workloads along with external energy measurement specifications for sub-watt systems.
MLPerf Training, which measures time-to-train for large-scale distributed foundation models.
SPEC CPU 2017, which benchmarks general-purpose computing performance on enterprise servers.
CodeCarbon, which tracks software-level Python energy consumption using system counters.

Explain the difference between average and marginal grid emissions, and identify the evidence a scheduler needs to estimate the emissions effect of a proposed workload shift.
Order the following stages of a carbon-aware scheduler’s decision: (1) compare complete projected emissions of feasible candidates, including checkpoint, transfer, restart, and idle costs, (2) obtain documented grid forecasts and workload requirements, (3) dispatch the selected feasible action, (4) monitor progress and re-evaluate against constraints, (5) filter candidates by deadline, capacity, data access, power, cooling, and reliability requirements.

title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
A training cluster can reduce its electricity bill by moving to a cheaper region while increasing its emissions. If the bill omits that environmental cost, a cost-minimizing placement decision may favor the higher-emissions site. Reporting requirements expose the trade-off; carbon pricing, procurement conditions, and other policy instruments can change the incentives. Their effect depends on which activities they cover and how organizations implement them.
For a systems reader, policy is the control plane that changes the objective function. Reporting rules make hidden energy and embodied-carbon costs measurable, carbon pricing turns location into a scheduling variable, and procurement standards make lifecycle accounting part of infrastructure design. The regulatory mechanisms in section 15.14.1 matter because they determine which optimizations become economically rational at fleet scale.


Reporting rules act at different organizational boundaries. The EU AI Act34 includes model-level technical-documentation obligations, while the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD)35 addresses sustainability reporting by covered companies. Model energy records can inform both, but neither establishes a universal requirement to meter every AI job. Engineers must identify the covered entity or model, applicable dates and exemptions, and the evidence the reporting method requires.
34 EU AI Act (2024): The Act presumes high-impact capabilities above \(10^{25}\) FLOPs of training compute and imposes additional obligations on general-purpose models with systemic risk. Annex XI includes computational resources and known or estimated energy consumption in required technical documentation; qualifying open-source models without systemic risk can be exempt from these documentation obligations. Article 101 permits fines for specified provider violations up to 3 percent of annual worldwide turnover or EUR 15 million, whichever is higher. Application dates, model scope, and exemptions must be checked before turning these provisions into an engineering reporting requirement.35 Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD): Directive (EU) 2026/470 narrows reporting thresholds to more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450 million in net annual turnover, assessed at group level where applicable. Member States must transpose its reporting amendments by March 19, 2027; entity scope, exemptions, and reporting-year rules still determine applicability. Covered reporting follows European Sustainability Reporting Standards rather than a separate inventory of AI jobs. The engineering contribution is traceable information on relevant electricity, procurement, and value-chain impacts.36 Emissions Trading for Compute: Applying cap-and-trade to AI emissions is a policy analogy here, not a description of an established compute-allowance market. Such a design would need a declared emissions boundary, measurement method, enforcement mechanism, and rules for trading allowances.Policy can also impose a priced resource constraint. A hypothetical emissions cap for AI operations would specify tonnes of CO2e and allow trading of unused emissions allowances, following the general logic of emissions trading systems (ETS).36 A power cap in MW or an energy budget in MWh would constrain different quantities and must not be called the same credit. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, by contrast, applies to embedded emissions in specified imported goods and electricity; it does not generally price an AI service by its compute location.
Incentives and procurement conditions can change which designs organizations choose. A grant can support efficiency research, while a procurement contract can require declared energy measurements or lifecycle evidence. These conditions need measurable criteria rather than an undefined “green” label. Scope 3 emissions also depend on whose inventory is being prepared: purchased hardware and outsourced cloud services enter the customer’s value-chain account, while the supplier classifies its own activities within its organizational boundary. The same physical emissions must not be added twice merely because two organizations report them.



Voluntary commitments and common standards supplement government requirements, but a commitment is not evidence of a measured reduction. Annual renewable-energy matching and 24/7 carbon-free energy (CFE) address different time resolutions. Hourly matching makes periods of unmatched demand visible, while the resulting physical emissions still depend on the generation and grid context (Monyei and Jenkins 2018). Evaluating a provider’s progress therefore requires the reported method and results, rather than merely its announced target.

Monyei, C. G., and Kirsten E. H. Jenkins. 2018. “Electrons Have No Identity: Setting Right Misrepresentations in Google and Apple’s Clean Energy Purchasing.” Energy Research & Social Science 46: 48–51. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2018.06.015.

Schmidt, Victor, Kamal Goyal, Aditya Joshi, Boris Feld, Liam Conell, Nikolas Laskaris, Doug Blank, Jonathan Wilson, Sorelle Friedler, and Sasha Luccioni. 2021. CodeCarbon: Estimate and Track Carbon Emissions from Machine Learning Computing. Zenodo software citation. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4658424.

Lacoste, Alexandre, Alexandra Luccioni, Victor Schmidt, and Thomas Dandres. 2019. “Quantifying the Carbon Emissions of Machine Learning.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1910.09700.
Internal carbon pricing gives emissions a weight in project decisions. A “shadow price” lets an organization compare alternatives using both financial cost and attributed emissions; its influence depends on the price, accounting boundary, and whether decision makers use it. Measurement tools supply inputs to that comparison. Projects like CodeCarbon and ML CO2 Impact let developers estimate model carbon footprints within their workflows (Schmidt et al. 2021; Lacoste et al. 2019), but the estimates still need declared power, location, and allocation assumptions.
Standardized benchmarks provide evidence for particular efficiency claims. MLCommons defines MLPerf power-measurement protocols that connect system energy with workload performance under declared conditions. The Green Software Foundation’s Software Carbon Intensity specification addresses a different boundary, combining operational and allocated embodied emissions per functional unit. A benchmark result or a calculation method is not itself an independent sustainability audit. Accountability requires checking the reported inputs, scope, and comparison against the claim being made.



Effective AI sustainability governance requires evidence that matches the claim. Misleading presentation of environmental performance, or greenwashing,37 can arise from selective boundaries or omitted trade-offs as well as unsupported offset claims. Accountability combines workload telemetry with facility measurements and supply-chain inventories. Runtime power counters alone cannot establish Scope 1–3 completeness or the environmental costs of manufacturing.
37 Greenwashing in AI: Typical forms are claiming “carbon neutrality” through offsets while expanding data center capacity, or highlighting per-query efficiency gains while total compute grows faster. Green-claims rules can require verifiable evidence for environmental claims. For ML engineers, the technical litmus test is whether sustainability reporting covers all three GHG Protocol scopes, or conveniently omits Scope 3 (hardware manufacturing, cloud supply chain) where much of AI’s carbon can reside.Pledge-style disclosure is useful only when it creates auditable data rather than reputational cover. The Montréal Carbon Pledge, originally a commitment by institutional investors to measure and disclose carbon footprints annually, is a useful model precisely because its value lies in the disclosed data, not the pledge itself; the same standard applies to an AI organization, whose sustainability claims are only as credible as the workload-level measurements behind them.



Transparency establishes the evidence base; environmental justice asks how the burdens and benefits revealed by that evidence are distributed. Site selection is where much of that distribution is decided, which makes it an environmental-justice decision rather than a facilities decision alone. Environmental sustainability extends ML systems responsibility from model behavior to ecological stewardship (Vinuesa et al. 2020). The computational resources required for AI development concentrate environmental costs on specific communities while distributing benefits unequally across global populations. Data centers impose both grid demand and cooling-water demand, and the local burden depends on the energy mix, watershed, and competing regional uses.

Vinuesa, Ricardo, Hossein Azizpour, Iolanda Leite, Madeline Balaam, Virginia Dignum, Sami Domisch, Anna Felländer, Simone Daniela Langhans, Max Tegmark, and Francesco Fuso Nerini. 2020. “The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.” Nature Communications 11 (1): 233. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-14108-y.
38 Environmental Justice in Data Center Siting: A site-cost model can omit burdens borne by nearby residents, such as competing water demand or changes to local infrastructure. A low financial cost therefore does not establish a low community burden. Site evaluation must identify who benefits, who bears the resource costs, and how affected communities participate in the decision alongside the analysis of grid intensity and water stress.That geographic concentration creates environmental-justice risks that align with broader responsible AI frameworks.38 The fairness claim here is narrow and systems-specific. An ML fleet allocates benefits, electricity demand, water use, land pressure, and e-waste across different communities. Communities hosting AI infrastructure can bear disproportionate environmental burdens while having limited access to AI’s economic benefits.
These distributional concerns fall into four groups (figure 19). Environmental justice concerns local water withdrawal and grid strain; intergenerational equity concerns atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\) persistence and long-lived infrastructure; resource competition concerns agricultural and municipal claims on land, water, and minerals; and the transparency gap concerns undisclosed per-model energy, carbon, and water ledgers. Engineering acts most directly on the last group, because auditable telemetry is what allows the other three to be assessed at all; the measurement contract of section 15.8 supplies that telemetry.






Figure 19: Ethical AI Concerns: The distributional concerns raised by AI infrastructure fall into four groups. Environmental justice, intergenerational equity, and resource competition stand on the transparency layer, because each can be assessed only with the per-model energy, carbon, and water ledgers that the transparency gap leaves undisclosed. That layer, drawn with the heavier outline, is the one engineering telemetry addresses most directly.



Impact assessments and community participation make these trade-offs visible before a site is committed. Any claim that such an assessment is legally required must identify the applicable jurisdiction, rule, and project scope.



The research agenda follows the same engineering logic as the mitigation framework: reduce data movement, close the measurement gap, and avoid redundant computation. Non-von Neumann computing architectures,39 including neuromorphic computing and in-memory computing, can reduce selected transfers, extending the event-driven and spiking designs of section 15.7 from avoided work to avoided movement. Evaluate the remaining arithmetic, conversion, control, and peripheral energy at the required quality; eliminating one cost does not eliminate the whole system account.
39 Von Neumann Bottleneck: Separating processing from memory requires data transfers whose energy depends on locality and arithmetic intensity. If movement contributes a fraction \(\DataMovementEnergyFraction\) of total energy, eliminating that term alone gives at most a \(1/(1-\DataMovementEnergyFraction)\) reduction factor when the remaining terms are unchanged. For an illustrative 60–80 percent share, that bound is 2.5–5\(\times\), before accounting for replacement circuitry.
Henderson, Peter, Jieru Hu, Joshua Romoff, Emma Brunskill, Dan Jurafsky, and Joelle Pineau. 2020. “Towards the Systematic Reporting of the Energy and Carbon Footprints of Machine Learning.” CoRR abs/2002.05651 (248): 1–43. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2002.05651.
A critical implementation barrier is the “measurement gap”: AI teams need standardized, workload-level reporting of energy use and carbon emissions rather than relying only on coarse proxy metrics (Henderson et al. 2020). Coarse methods often rely on proxies such as GPU-hours multiplied by average grid intensity, which fail to capture the real-world dynamics required by reporting regimes that care about time, location, and workload boundary. Developing and standardizing granular, real-time energy and carbon accounting tools is essential for both compliance and effective optimization.
A second research direction reduces redundant computation before it reaches the accelerator. Data selection, model design, and training procedure all affect the environmental cost of learning (Wu et al. 2022). Smarter data sampling, active learning, and data valuation can reduce work spent on low-value examples, but the resulting model quality and coverage must be measured rather than assumed. An integrated approach combining algorithmic efficiency, hardware innovation, renewable energy adoption, and transparent governance is necessary to align AI development with environmental constraints.

Wu, Carole-Jean, Ramya Raghavendra, Udit Gupta, Bilge Acun, Newsha Ardalani, Kiwan Maeng, Gloria Chang, et al. 2022. “Sustainable AI: Environmental Implications, Challenges and Opportunities.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 4: 795–813.
Reducing redundant computation can improve operational efficiency, but compliance and environmental benefit require their own evidence. A sustainable design must show that the saved work survives the complete lifecycle account and the resulting deployment scale. Incorrect boundaries or assumptions can otherwise turn a local improvement into a larger total footprint.

Self-Check: Question

An industry observer claims that policy interventions and carbon pricing are unnecessary because ‘free-market competition will naturally incentivize data center operators to minimize energy use and carbon emissions.’ Which counterargument best explains why market mechanisms alone fail to guarantee sustainable AI deployment?

Data center operators are legally restricted from purchasing power from renewable energy utilities.
Electricity prices can omit emissions and other environmental burdens, so minimizing the electricity bill need not minimize the complete environmental account; pricing, reporting, or procurement requirements can change the decision incentives.
AI models running on renewable electricity automatically suffer from higher inference latency than models on fossil power.
Hardware vendors have already achieved the physical thermodynamic limit of computing efficiency, leaving no room for further optimization.

How do modern regulatory frameworks such as the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the EU AI Act directly affect the systems engineering practices of organizations deploying large-scale AI?

They impose an absolute global cap banning the training of any machine learning model exceeding 100 billion parameters.
For organizations and systems within their applicable scope, they create documentation and disclosure duties that require traceable energy and sustainability evidence; the exact obligations depend on the framework and deployment.
They mandate that all AI inference must be executed exclusively on battery-powered mobile devices rather than cloud servers.
They require that all machine learning models be retrained weekly using uncompressed full-precision floating-point arithmetic.

Explain how an applicable emissions trading system or carbon tax changes a workload scheduler’s cost objective, and what conditions determine whether cleaner placement becomes economically preferable.
True or False: If a technology enterprise purchases enough annual Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) to match 100 percent of its data centers’ annual electricity consumption, its evening foundation-model inference workloads running on a fossil-fueled regional grid can be accurately characterized as zero-carbon operations.
Explain how future non-von-Neumann computing paradigms (such as neuromorphic computing and in-memory analog computing) address the fundamental physical bottleneck responsible for AI energy consumption.

title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
Sustainability involves counterintuitive physics where efficiency improvements can increase total consumption and geographic choices can outweigh component-level optimizations. These fallacies and pitfalls capture errors that waste compute budgets and planetary resources through misallocated optimization effort.

Fallacy: Cloud computing automatically makes AI systems more environmentally sustainable.
Engineers assume cloud providers operate efficiently and sustainably. Cloud infrastructure can improve utilization and facility efficiency, but it transfers neither the physical footprint nor the customer’s accounting responsibility out of existence. Training a 7B model on 64 A100s for 14 days produces 5.7 t CO2 on the US average grid (429 g/kWh) but only 264.9 kg CO2 on Quebec’s hydroelectric grid (20 g/kWh operational), a roughly 21.5× difference for this US-average-versus-Quebec pairing. The hydroelectric figure is an operational factor, not a lifecycle-zero one. As demonstrated in section 15.9, cloud comparisons must disclose region, energy boundary, utilization, embodied allocation, and whether the electricity is Scope 2 for the provider or Scope 3 for the customer.


Pitfall: Focusing only on operational energy consumption while ignoring embodied carbon and lifecycle impacts.
Teams optimize training efficiency while ignoring manufacturing emissions. In low-carbon grids, embodied carbon can dominate fleet-level footprint accounting. As quantified in section 15.9.3, an A100 accelerator embodies roughly 150 kg CO2 from manufacturing (Luccioni et al. 2023); for the earlier 14-day, 64-A100 training run, the unamortized upfront burden is roughly 9.6 t CO2. Amortized over a 4-year service life, the share attributable to this specific job is about 90 kg. The job comparison must use that allocated share; a fleet lifecycle comparison must instead compare the full manufacturing burden against operations over the same fleet lifetime. Comparing the entire manufacturing burden with one short job’s electricity would mix boundaries. Extending hardware lifetime from 3 years to 5 years reduces amortized embodied carbon by 40 percent, but procurement decisions must also evaluate the operational cost of retaining the hardware.

Luccioni, Alexandra Sasha, Sylvain Viguier, and Anne-Laure Ligozat. 2023. “Estimating the Carbon Footprint of BLOOM, a 176B Parameter Language Model.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 24 (253): 1–15.


Fallacy: TDP is actual power consumption.
Thermal design power is a hardware design specification, not the measured power of a particular workload. Actual draw depends on the device, configured power limit, utilization, memory traffic, clocks, and idle intervals. A TDP-based calculation is a stated capacity scenario; it does not establish serving energy or facility energy. Carbon and electricity-cost estimates that drive placement decisions (section 15.9) should use measured power over the workload interval and include the support systems within the chosen boundary.


Pitfall: Using PUE as a complete environmental metric.
Data-center operators report PUE in sustainability disclosures and engineers may treat it as a complete environmental score. PUE measures only facility energy relative to IT energy. A lower-PUE facility can still cause more electricity-related emissions if its grid factor is sufficiently higher, and neither factor accounts for hardware manufacturing or local water stress. Compare matched emissions factors and complete lifecycle boundaries rather than ranking sites by PUE alone.


Fallacy: Efficiency improvements automatically reduce total environmental impact.
Engineers assume that halving inference cost cuts environmental impact in half. The Jevons paradox warns that efficiency improvements can increase total consumption by enabling expanded usage. In a rebound scenario, suppose reducing token cost from $0.06 to $0.002 per 1,000 tokens accompanies a proportional 30× reduction in measured energy per query at fixed output length and quality. A 100× increase in query volume then raises total energy by 3.3× and, at unchanged grid intensity, emissions by the same factor. Any implementation change that lowers per-query energy can still raise total energy when usage grows by a larger factor. Teams must therefore evaluate deployment volume against the intended carbon or resource budget; per-query gains alone do not control the rebound illustrated in figure 16, where the red area of new consumption at the lower unit cost completely swallows the green area of initial efficiency savings.


Pitfall: Treating carbon offsets as a substitute for reducing actual emissions.
Organizations may purchase offsets without establishing that the credited reduction is additional, durable, independently verified, and free of double counting. An offset does not change the electricity consumed by the workload or its immediate emissions. Teams should report physical emissions reductions separately from compensation claims, with the offset boundary and uncertainty visible. Geographic placement can reduce electricity-related emissions when the complete workload comparison supports it; neither an offset purchase nor a renewable label substitutes for that calculation.


Fallacy: Component-level optimization guarantees lifecycle improvement.
Teams reduce training cost to improve sustainability without analyzing deployment scale. A training change that increases serving energy must be evaluated over expected query volume: the crossover occurs when accumulated additional serving emissions exceed the one-time training saving. Edge deployment adds device manufacturing and replacement to any avoided data-center and transmission emissions. Keeping hardware longer avoids new manufacturing but may consume more operating energy than replacement. Each comparison requires the same useful service, grid-factor boundary, and lifetime; there is no universal query count or upgrade age that settles it. Effective sustainability requires the complete account in section 15.9.4.


Pitfall: Evaluating sustainability at the component boundary instead of the lifecycle boundary.
A pruned model may contain fewer weights while its sparse representation adds indexing and execution overhead. If those costs outweigh the arithmetic and transfers avoided, the smaller model need not consume less energy. The same boundary error appears when hardware teams report accelerator efficiency without procurement carbon, platform teams report PUE without grid intensity, or model teams report training emissions without expected serving volume. The lifecycle boundary in section 15.9.4 requires evaluating training, serving, embodied carbon, regional grid mix, hardware lifetime, and demand growth together before calling a change sustainable.


Self-Check: Question

True or False: Migrating a machine learning training workload from an on-premises enterprise cluster in a low-carbon region (20 \(\text{gCO}_2/\text{kWh}\)) to a commercial cloud data center in a coal-heavy region (750 \(\text{gCO}_2/\text{kWh}\)) is guaranteed to reduce the workload’s carbon footprint because hyperscale cloud providers operate at lower PUE.
A systems team aggressively compresses a model using unstructured pruning to cut training FLOPs by 60 percent. In production, serving the sparse model requires specialized, custom-fabricated NPU accelerators and requires double the serving iterations to reach quality parity. Which pitfall does this scenario illustrate, and what is the proper engineering mitigation?

Local optimization of training compute without full-lifecycle assessment; the mitigation is conducting end-to-end Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) that accounts for hardware manufacturing, deployment scale, and serving energy before committing to architectural changes.
Failure to apply Amdahl’s law; the mitigation is increasing CPU clock frequency.
Violating the GHG Protocol; the mitigation is reclassifying Scope 3 emissions as Scope 1.
Ignoring PUE; the mitigation is installing liquid cooling on the development workstations.

Explain why an offset purchase does not replace evidence of physical emissions reductions, and what must be established before claiming a reduction from placement, efficiency, or hardware reuse.

title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
The lifecycle boundary connects training, serving, embodied carbon, grid mix, hardware lifetime, and demand growth. Sustainable AI asks whether the machine learning fleet can operate within available energy, water, and material resources even after its models and infrastructure have been optimized.
The measurement contract makes comparisons meaningful by fixing useful work, required quality, system boundaries, attribution, time, location, and uncertainty. Operational and embodied carbon accounting then identify which lifecycle term an intervention can change. Memory traffic, idle equipment, cooling, and power delivery can all consume energy beyond useful arithmetic; lower FLOP counts alone do not establish lower environmental impact.
The Fleet Law connects execution time to the fleet energy account. A step’s energy is approximately its average fleet power times \(\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)\) (equation 14), so exposed communication and synchronization extend the interval over which the system draws power. Recovery adds further work outside successful steps. The C³ terms therefore matter to both performance and sustainability, although the power trace determines their energy cost. PUE extends an IT-energy estimate to the facility boundary, the grid factor attributes operational emissions, and embodied carbon adds the hardware lifecycle burden rather than converting operating joules.
Mitigation follows that diagnosis. Algorithm and hardware changes must reduce measured resource use while preserving quality, latency, and reliability; scheduling must account for grid intensity and the cost of moving work; hardware replacement must weigh operational savings against new manufacturing emissions. Water availability and the distribution of environmental burdens also matter when choosing where and how a fleet can grow.

Key Takeaways: Efficiency alone is not enough

Power is a hard ceiling: A fleet cannot compute past the megawatts, cooling, water, and grid capacity its site can supply. Sustainability is therefore an existence constraint on model scale, not a public-relations layer around an otherwise finished architecture.
Demand can outrun efficiency: Lower energy per query does not ensure lower fleet energy use. At fixed work per query, total energy rises when query volume grows by a larger factor than per-query energy falls, so efficiency targets need an absolute resource budget.
Memory traffic can dominate serving energy: During bandwidth-bound autoregressive decode, accelerators can draw power while waiting for weights and state. Quantization, batching, or memory-optimized hardware help sustainability only when they reduce measured energy at the required quality, latency, and reliability.
Carbon starts before boot: Hardware manufacturing creates emissions before the first query runs, and its lifecycle share rises on clean grids and under low utilization. Keeping or replacing hardware therefore requires comparing new manufacturing emissions with operational savings over the same future service.
Location changes the footprint: Moving flexible work to a cleaner grid can reduce operational carbon only when the saving exceeds transfer, restart, and idle-capacity emissions. Placement must also preserve deadlines, data access, capacity, and reliability; regional intensity ratios alone do not establish the net benefit.



Sustainability changes the scale at which efficiency must be judged. A reduction per query is a local result; the fleet result depends on how many queries run, where they run, and what hardware their service requires over time. Two forces push demand past efficiency. The sustainability paradox introduced at the start of the chapter is the first, as scaling laws (principle \(\ref{pri-universal-scaling}\)) price each further quality gain in more compute per model. The Jevons paradox of AI (principle \(\ref{pri-jevons-paradox}\)) is the second, as cheaper work invites more of it. Both make the distinction consequential, because efficiency creates room within a resource budget while demand determines how much of that room is consumed. Deployment decisions therefore need both a useful-work efficiency target and an absolute resource budget.

What’s Next: From sustainability to responsibilityA fleet that is secure, robust, and within its power budget is not automatically fit to deploy. Security, robustness, and sustainability each answer a technical question about what a production system can support. The siting analysis in section 15.14.4 already showed that a feasible fleet can place its water, grid, and waste burdens on communities that see little of its benefit. The model’s decisions raise the same question about the people they act on. An accurate, fast model can still concentrate its errors among people with little power to challenge them. Responsible AI therefore asks who receives the system’s benefits, who bears its costs, and how an affected person can contest a decision. The carbon inventory and lifecycle account built here become one input to the assurance record that answers it. They supply evidence for that judgment; they do not settle whose interests the fleet should serve.





↪ Governance frameworks, algorithmic fairness, and ethical guardrails are developed in Responsible AI.

Which statement best captures the textbook’s overarching thesis regarding sustainable AI engineering?

Redesigning all neural networks to use binary 1-bit weights.

title: 15 Sustainable AI
text:
Self-Check: Answer

A hyperscaler plans a 500 MW campus for a new foundation model cluster, but the local utility interconnect approval is capped at 320 MW for the next three years. The organization’s capital reserves could cover the electricity cost multiple times over. Which framing best captures why sustainable AI treats energy as a first-class engineering constraint rather than a financial or reporting concern?

Carbon accounting frameworks mandate disclosing total planned capacity upfront, creating an administrative filing hurdle before training begins.
Electricity price fluctuations create budget volatility, so the primary engineering intervention is financial hedging.
Corporate sustainability reporting requires purchasing voluntary offsets for unapproved megawatts, adding financial cost without altering physical infrastructure.
Power delivery and grid interconnect capacity impose a hard physical ceiling that capital cannot bypass on deployment timescales, making power an operational constraint that model architectures and cluster sizing must fit within.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Power delivery and grid interconnect capacity impose a hard physical ceiling that capital cannot bypass on deployment timescales, making power an operational constraint that model architectures and cluster sizing must fit within. The chapter’s central thesis is that sustainability is a physical capacity ceiling, not a financial or reporting line item: a 500 MW cluster facing a 320 MW interconnect cannot operate at planned scale regardless of capital expenditure. An administrative-reporting framing mistakes accounting disclosures for physical bounds; a financial-hedging framing treats capacity as a price risk rather than a physical limit; and a voluntary-offset framing ignores physical grid interconnect constraints.
Learning Objective: Classify energy and power delivery as physical system constraints rather than financial or reporting concerns
A research team plans a 10,000 MWh training run, measured as facility electricity. Quebec and Poland both meet its capacity, data-access, quality, and deadline requirements, and transfer overhead is negligible. The stated grid factors are approximately 20 and 820 grams of CO2 per kWh, respectively, on a common boundary. An algorithmic change would reduce facility energy in Poland by 15 percent at unchanged quality. Calculate the emissions under these alternatives and justify which offers the larger reduction in this scenario.
Answer: At the supplied factors, Quebec emits 200 tonnes of CO2 and Poland emits 8,200 tonnes. The algorithmic change in Poland lowers that result to 6,970 tonnes, so Quebec offers the larger reduction among these alternatives. This conclusion depends on the stated equal-energy baseline and feasible placements; a regional intensity ratio alone does not rank unmeasured interventions or establish the effect of shifting actual grid demand.
Learning Objective: Calculate scenario emissions and compare feasible placement and algorithmic interventions under a declared accounting boundary
True or False: Because successive generations of specialized AI accelerators deliver substantial improvements in energy efficiency (FLOP/s per watt), organizations can rely on hardware innovation alone to keep total data center power consumption flat while scaling model parameters.
Answer: False. Hardware improvements alone do not guarantee flat fleet power. Total energy depends on workload volume and realized work per joule at a consistent boundary; power also depends on the execution schedule. A historical compute-growth curve does not determine either quantity without those measurements.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the claim that hardware efficiency scaling alone can offset exponential growth in AI compute demand
Thousands of GPUs alternate between dense computation and collective communication, producing correlated changes in device power. Explain how bidirectional energy storage can buffer the change at a protected electrical boundary, and what measurements determine its timing and capacity.
Answer: When load falls, storage can absorb surplus input; when load rises, it can discharge to cover the deficit while upstream supply responds. The controller must follow the measured load and supply response at the protected boundary, including losses, state of charge, and power limits. Device-side changes need not propagate unchanged to the grid, and buffering can act during a transition rather than only after it.
Learning Objective: Explain how energy storage buffers synchronized training load changes and identify the measurements needed to size it
A systems team aims to overcome the energy wall for future foundation model architectures. Which design direction most directly targets the physical root cause of energy waste identified in the chapter?

Increasing clock frequency and supply voltage to maximize compute throughput per unit silicon area.
Enforcing dense, synchronized execution across all model layers so accelerator execution units maintain 100 percent active duty cycles.
Adopting event-driven and sparse-activation architectures that execute compute only on salient tokens or state changes, minimizing dense data movement across memory hierarchies.
Replacing FP16 tensor cores with FP32 standard execution units to maximize numeric accuracy per memory access.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Event-driven and sparse-activation designs can avoid unnecessary computation and transfers when inputs or activations permit it. The saving depends on event rate, sensing and static power, sparse execution overhead, and achieved quality. Raising voltage increases dynamic power at fixed activity and frequency; keeping units active does not establish useful work per joule. Dense computation is not universally movement dominated.
Learning Objective: Design architectural strategies that address data-movement dominance to mitigate the AI energy wall

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

An attention kernel has an arithmetic intensity of 3 FLOP/byte. An illustrative chip-and-memory energy model assigns 10 pJ per FLOP and 100 pJ per byte moved from DRAM, excluding static and facility energy. Which intervention directly targets the larger modeled energy contribution?

Replacing the accelerator with one offering double the peak TFLOP/s while retaining the same memory bandwidth and memory technology.
Increasing arithmetic precision from FP16 to FP32 to execute more FLOPs per memory transaction.
Fusing normalization and attention operators and tiling intermediate activations to keep data in on-chip SRAM, reducing DRAM traffic.
Lowering facility PUE from 1.5 to 1.1 to eliminate memory stall cycles.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The crossover is 10 FLOP/byte, so at 3 FLOP/byte movement contributes more energy than arithmetic in this model. Fusion and tiling can reduce that traffic when implemented successfully. Peak throughput alone establishes neither an energy saving nor the execution bottleneck; PUE does not eliminate memory stalls. Measure the complete workload to confirm the saving.
Learning Objective: Apply the energy-roofline crossover to classify a kernel’s dominant energy component and select the corresponding optimization
A 2 MW IT load cluster improves its Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) from 1.58 to 1.10 without altering any model weights or server SKUs. Calculate the annual electricity savings in megawatt-hours (MWh) assuming 24/7 continuous operation, and explain why facility optimization is considered a first-order sustainability lever.
Answer: At \(\text{PUE} = 1.58\), total facility power is \(2\text{ MW} \times 1.58 = 3.16\text{ MW}\). At \(\text{PUE} = 1.10\), total power drops to \(2\text{ MW} \times 1.10 = 2.20\text{ MW}\), saving \(0.96\text{ MW}\) continuously. Over one year (\(8{,}760\text{ hours}\)), this saves \(0.96\text{ MW} \times 8{,}760\text{ h} \approx 8{,}410\text{ MWh}\). This demonstrates that facility infrastructure optimization delivers multi-gigawatt-hour savings equivalent to massive algorithmic optimizations without requiring changes to model code or accuracy.
Learning Objective: Calculate annual facility energy savings resulting from PUE improvements and justify infrastructure optimization as a high-leverage sustainability intervention
In the CMOS dynamic power equation \(P_{\text{dynamic}}=\alpha_{\text{sw}}CV^2f\), the parameter \(\alpha_{\text{sw}}\) is the ____, summarizing capacitance-weighted switching per clock cycle under the chosen counting convention.
Answer: switching activity factor. It scales dynamic power linearly at fixed capacitance, voltage, and frequency; more switching is not necessarily more useful computation or greater energy efficiency.
