Five single-machine models reappear throughout the distributed chapters, each extended by a fleet-scale term. The D·A·M Taxonomy states the single-machine forms; the list below records only what changes at scale.

Iron law (\(\Time\approx \DataVolume/\Bandwidth + \Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw) + \Latency\), Iron Law Mapping): At fleet scale, the data-movement term expands to include inter-node communication, and the Fleet Law replaces the single-machine sum.
Roofline model (The roofline bound): At fleet scale, a third ceiling appears. Network-bound workloads are limited by inter-node bandwidth, which the communication-computation ratio in section 1.3.3 measures.
Amdahl’s Law: Caps strong-scaling speedup at \(1/\SerialFraction\) for serial fraction \(\SerialFraction\) (Amdahl 1967). At fleet scale, the serial fraction includes synchronization barriers, exposed collective communication, and pipeline bubbles (section 1.3.2).
Training state rule (Numeric Precision and Training Memory): Mixed-precision training with the Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) optimizer holds about 16 bytes per parameter during training and about 14 bytes per parameter in a resumable checkpoint, before activations and framework metadata. At fleet scale, this footprint determines how model state is partitioned across devices (ZeRO, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism).
Little’s Law (\(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\)) (Little 1961): Relates in-flight requests to arrival rate and time in system. At fleet scale, it sizes the number of serving replicas behind a load balancer (Queuing theory for batched inference).


Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.
The transition from single-machine to fleet-scale reasoning requires extending these models with new dimensions: network topology, failure probability, and coordination overhead. The numbers in the next section provide the quantitative foundation for that extension.

title: Foundations recap
section: Numbers Every Fleet Engineer Should Know
text:
Numbers Every Fleet Engineer Should Know
Just as single-machine analysis depends on a set of core numbers, fleet-scale engineering is governed by a set of predictable ratios and scaling behaviors. The single-machine numbers still apply within each node, but a new set of numbers governs the spaces between nodes. Hardware ratios vary with generation and provisioning; failure-rate scaling also depends on the assumed failure model. These reference values provide sanity checks while the stated models explain how to substitute different assumptions.

Systems Perspective 1.1: Node-level numbers for fleet reasoningFleet reasoning depends on a few node-level numbers that directly affect fleet design: the training state rule of about 14 bytes per parameter for common Adam checkpoint state, with larger footprints when gradients, activations, metadata, or extra optimizer buffers are included; NVLink vs. high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth for intra-node parallelism placement; and peak FLOP/s and HBM capacity for model FLOPs utilization (MFU), effective FLOP/s, batch sizing, and model sharding. Table 2 and the communication numbers below give inter-node and current-generation values; the memory hierarchy and roofline ridge points within a node (Accelerator Memory Hierarchy) provide the necessary baseline. Those node-level baselines make the fleet-level ratios easier to interpret.



Systems Perspective 1.2: Three fleet numbers that matter most

Bandwidth gap: NVLink per-direction bandwidth within a node is ~9× faster than an InfiniBand NDR port between nodes. This ratio determines where parallelism boundaries belong, with model parallelism within a node and data parallelism across nodes.
MTBF scaling: A cluster’s mean time between failures is the single-component MTBF divided by the number of components (\(1/\RequiredComponentCount\) scaling). At 100,000 GPUs, expect a failure every 30 minutes.
Effective utilization: After MFU, scaling efficiency, and overhead losses compound, a cluster with 1,024 GPUs delivers roughly 34.0 percent of its peak FLOP/s as useful training work.



Table 2 condenses the fleet-scale numbers into one place. Use it for back-of-envelope checks; use the detailed tables in each subsection when designing or debugging.

Invariant scaling ratios
These relationships expose architectural trade-offs and model assumptions; their numerical ratios must be re-evaluated for the target system.

Network hierarchy ratio
The bandwidth gap between intra-node and inter-node communication is an important architectural comparison. Chip-to-chip links (NVLink, ICI) connect through short, wide, dedicated paths on a shared substrate. Inter-node links (InfiniBand, Ethernet) must traverse cables, switches, and protocol stacks. These design differences often favor intra-node bandwidth, but lane counts, multiple network ports, and topology determine the actual ratio.
Currently, NVLink 4.0 provides 9× more per-direction bandwidth than an InfiniBand NDR port. The ratio compares one accelerator’s aggregate intra-node connectivity with one network port; it is not a universal constant. Parallelism placement must compare the workload’s traffic with the sustained bandwidth actually provisioned at each boundary.


Failure scaling law
For \(\RequiredComponentCount\) independent components under a constant-failure-rate assumption, system MTBF (equation 1) scales inversely with component count:
\[ \SystemMtbf = \frac{\ComponentMttf}{\RequiredComponentCount}  \tag{1}\]
Under this model the relation is exact rather than approximate. Doubling the cluster size halves the time between failures. At 100,000 GPUs with a per-GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours, the cluster experiences a GPU failure every 30 minutes. No fault tolerance strategy can avoid this; the question is how quickly the system recovers.


AllReduce overhead scaling
The bandwidth-optimal Ring AllReduce algorithm transfers \(2(\AcceleratorCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\AcceleratorCount\) bytes per participant, where \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) is the collective payload size and \(\AcceleratorCount\) is the number of participating GPUs (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009). As \(\AcceleratorCount\) grows large, this approaches \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) per GPU, so the per-GPU bandwidth term is nearly independent of the number of GPUs; aggregate cluster traffic still grows with the number of participants. This is why Ring AllReduce scales well in the bandwidth term. The latency term, however, grows as \(2(\AcceleratorCount-1) \times \MessageStartupLatency\), making latency the bottleneck for small messages on large rings. This trade-off motivates hierarchical AllReduce strategies that use Ring AllReduce within nodes and Tree AllReduce across nodes.

Patarasuk, Pitch, and Xin Yuan. 2009. “Bandwidth Optimal All-Reduce Algorithms for Clusters of Workstations.” Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 69 (2): 117–24. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2008.09.002.

Communication defines the boundaries of parallelism. These latency differences favor low-latency fabrics for frequent synchronization. Cross-data-center training must amortize transfers, place pipeline boundaries carefully, or relax synchronization when its learning algorithm permits.


Compute numbers
Raw peak FLOP/s is a necessary but misleading metric for fleet capacity planning. Single-device execution losses and additional scaling losses reduce effective throughput. Multiplying the two is valid only when their measurement windows exclude overlapping costs. Understanding these losses transforms fleet sizing from guesswork into engineering.
MFU measures what fraction of peak FLOP/s a training workload actually achieves. Well-optimized large-model training on current hardware achieves 30–50 percent MFU. The gap comes from memory stalls, kernel launch overhead, pipeline bubbles, and suboptimal operator fusion. These are workload-dependent reference values. Fleet-step MFU already includes in-step communication and pipeline losses; a separate scaling factor applies only to a single-device baseline that excludes those losses.
Scaling efficiency (\(\ScalingEfficiency\)) measures how much useful computation survives as accelerators are added. Modeled scaling efficiency for the 175B reference job (table 5) shows how per-GPU throughput erodes as cluster size grows at a fixed global batch.

At fleet scale, coordination (failure recovery, checkpointing, and maintenance) consumes a measurable fraction of wall-clock time. These numbers quantify the costs of keeping a large cluster running.

title: Foundations recap
text:
Scaling Physics
The numbers in the previous section describe what the hardware can do. Scaling physics describes what happens when more of it is brought to bear. Reasoning starts from the ceiling on a single accelerator (the roofline) and then asks what survives as devices are added, governed by three models: Amdahl’s Law extended to fleet overhead, the communication-computation ratio, and weak scaling behavior.

From the accelerator roofline to the fleet
Fleet performance rests on per-accelerator performance. The roofline bound states the single-accelerator roofline, \(\AttainableComputeRate = \min(\PeakRate, \ArithmeticIntensity\times \Bandwidth)\), and its ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate/\Bandwidth\), which is about 295.2 FLOP/byte for an H100. A kernel below the ridge is memory bound, and a kernel above it is compute bound.
The roofline is a single-accelerator law, but its logic is what scales. At fleet level the binding bandwidth is no longer HBM but the interconnect, and the bytes moved are the gradients and activations crossing the network. The ratio of network time to local arithmetic time is the communication-computation ratio (section 1.3.3), the roofline of the fleet and the lens the rest of this section applies.
A training job provisioned with 4,096 GPUs achieves only 2.5× the throughput of a 1,024-GPU run. That observation implies about 51.9 percent scaling efficiency at the larger size, so scaling physics provides the diagnostic tools to determine whether the system is performing as physics allows or whether there is an engineering problem to fix.


Amdahl’s Law at fleet scale
Amdahl’s Law establishes that the maximum speedup of a parallel system is limited by its serial fraction \(\SerialFraction\). At fleet scale, the “serial fraction” includes more than sequential code. It covers every operation that forces all \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs to wait:

AllReduce synchronization: All GPUs must complete their gradient computation before any can proceed.
Pipeline bubbles: The warmup and cooldown phases of pipeline parallelism leave stages idle.
Checkpoint writes: Even asynchronous checkpoints contend for storage bandwidth.
Python-level overhead: Single-threaded operations in the training loop (data loading, metric logging).

To see the fleet-scale implications, consider a training workload where 10 percent of wall-clock time is spent in synchronization, communication, and other serial overhead. Amdahl’s Law gives the following speedups:

With 32 GPUs: 7.8× speedup (~24 percent scaling efficiency)
With 256 GPUs: 9.7× speedup (diminishing returns begin)
With 1,024 GPUs: 9.9× speedup (approaching the ceiling)
With 8,192 GPUs: 10× speedup (nearly at the Amdahl limit)
With \(\DeviceCount\to \infty\): capped at 10×

With just 10 percent serial overhead, no amount of hardware can deliver more than 10× speedup on this fixed workload. This is why fleet-scale training does not simply add more GPUs to the same problem; it scales the problem (weak scaling) to keep the serial fraction small relative to the total work.

Systems Perspective 1.3: The compound overhead trapThe 10 percent serial fraction above is optimistic. In practice, fleet-scale serial overhead accumulates from multiple sources: 5 percent pipeline bubbles + 3 percent checkpointing + 10 percent failure recovery + 5 percent maintenance. These are not all strictly serial in the Amdahl sense (some overlap with computation), but they illustrate how quickly small per-category overheads compound into significant throughput loss.




The communication-computation ratio
Any distributed training strategy must determine whether computation between synchronization points takes long enough to hide the communication. Equation 2 defines the communication-computation ratio (\(\CommunicationComputeRatio\)) that answers this directly:
\[ \CommunicationComputeRatio= \frac{\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)}{\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount}  \tag{2}\]
When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio< 1\), computation takes longer than communication; hiding that communication still requires independent work and sufficient resources. When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio> 1\), the system is Communication-Bound, and GPUs spend more time waiting for data than computing on it.
The ratio is the time-domain form of the communication intensity (CI) defined in Communication intensity (the CI ratio), the bytes a step moves across the network per FLOP it executes locally. If each device moves \(\NetworkTrafficVolume\) bytes across the network per step at effective network bandwidth \(\NetworkBandwidth\) and executes its \(\Operations\) local FLOPs at realized rate \(\RealizedDeviceComputeRate\), then in the bandwidth-dominated regime
\[ \CommunicationComputeRatio\approx \frac{\NetworkTrafficVolume/\NetworkBandwidth}{\Operations/\RealizedDeviceComputeRate} = \CommunicationIntensity \times \frac{\RealizedDeviceComputeRate}{\NetworkBandwidth}, \qquad \CommunicationIntensity = \frac{\NetworkTrafficVolume}{\Operations}  \tag{3}\]
Equation 3 shows that exposed communication begins when \(\CommunicationIntensity\) exceeds \(\NetworkBandwidth/\RealizedDeviceComputeRate\), the network counterpart of the roofline ridge point. Because a device executes far more FLOP/s than its network link moves bytes per second, that threshold is a small fraction of a byte per FLOP, and a faster accelerator lowers it further. An accelerator upgrade alone can therefore turn a compute-bound job into a communication-bound one.
Communication-to-computation ratios across representative scenarios (table 11) reveal why parallelism strategy must match the workload.

When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\gg 1\), the system is communication-bound and GPUs sit idle waiting for data. The NVLink row is a bandwidth-only point-to-point lower bound; a tensor-parallel collective also incurs topology, latency, and contention costs.

The 7B model on 256 GPUs achieves \(\CommunicationComputeRatio=\) 0.11, so communication takes about 11.2 percent as long as computation, which can be partially overlapped. The 340M model on the same cluster has \(\CommunicationComputeRatio=\) 3. Communication dominates, which makes this configuration communication-bound. The solution is either to use fewer GPUs (reduce \(\DeviceCount\) in the AllReduce) or to increase the computation per step (larger batch size, gradient accumulation).
For the single 16 MB point-to-point payload, the ideal bandwidth-only lower bound is \(\CommunicationComputeRatio=\) 0.036. This is not a tensor-parallel collective model and cannot by itself establish whether an implementation is compute-bound.


Weak scaling at fleet scale
Amdahl’s Law paints a pessimistic picture because it assumes a fixed problem size. In practice, fleet-scale training often follows Weak Scaling: the problem size (tokens, data, model parameters) grows proportionally with the number of GPUs. Gustafson’s Law captures this more optimistic view (Gustafson 1988).

Gustafson, John L. 1988. “Reevaluating Amdahl’s Law.” Communications of the ACM 31 (5): 532–33. https://doi.org/10.1145/42411.42415.
The key insight for fleet-scale ML is that weak scaling reflects how fleets are actually used, not merely a mathematical convenience. Engineers do not use 8,192 GPUs to train a 7B model faster; they use them to train a 70B or 700B model in reasonable time. As models and training batches grow, engineers often increase the compute performed between synchronization points. For dense Transformers, compute is commonly estimated as about 6\(\times\) parameters \(\times\) tokens, while gradient communication scales with parameter bytes, so the communication-computation ratio \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\) depends on batch size, sequence length, accumulation, and parallelism layout rather than on parameter count alone.

Systems Perspective 1.4: The compound loss of fleet utilizationA 1,024-GPU H100 cluster has a peak aggregate throughput of 1,012,736 TFLOP/s. This illustrative decomposition keeps the factors disjoint: MFU represents per-device kernel and memory efficiency, scaling efficiency represents distributed communication and pipeline losses, and operational goodput represents checkpointing, failure recovery, and maintenance. The effective throughput is:
\[\EffectiveFleetThroughput = \DeviceCount\PeakRate \times \ModelFlopsUtilization \times \ScalingEfficiency \times \GoodputRatio\]
\[= 1,012,736 TFLOP/s \times 0.50 \times 0.83 \times 0.82 \approx 344,634.1 \text{ TFLOP/s}\]
The cluster delivers 34.0 percent of its peak FLOP/s as useful training work. The remaining 66.0 percent is explained by retained factors of 50 percent MFU, 83 percent scaling efficiency, and 82 percent operational goodput.
These losses reflect the physics of fleet-scale computation rather than a failure of engineering. Additional GPUs can increase useful throughput while reducing efficiency, but the gain must be measured against smaller configurations. The goal is not to reach 100 percent utilization; the goal is to deliver trained models faster than any smaller configuration could.

title: Foundations recap
text:
Thermal and Power Physics
Compute performance ultimately converts to heat, and heat must be removed. At fleet scale, thermal and power constraints are primary concerns. They determine where construction is feasible, how densely accelerators can be packed, and what the operating costs will be. A cluster that is architecturally sound but thermally infeasible cannot be built.
A cluster design calling for 10,000 H100 GPUs at 700 W each (a 7 MW GPU-only power proxy) gives 10.8 MW after applying PUE 1.55. The complete facility budget must also include host, memory, storage, and network power inside the IT boundary before applying PUE. This is the electrical load of a small town. Before optimizing software, the physics of power delivery and heat removal must be feasible.

Power density wall
The shift from traditional data center workloads to AI training has created a Power Density Crisis. Table 12 quantifies the gap.



Table 12: Power Density: Traditional vs. AI Workloads: AI racks consume roughly 5.8× the power of traditional racks. The 5.8× increase in rack power density between traditional and AI workloads is a fundamental constraint on facility design, not merely an engineering challenge. Existing data centers built for 12 kW racks cannot simply be “retrofitted” with AI hardware. The electrical distribution, cooling infrastructure, and floor loading must all be redesigned. This is why new AI-focused data centers are being built from the ground up with liquid cooling as the baseline assumption.


The energy hierarchy at scale
PUE measures facility energy overhead: total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy (The Green Grid 2007; Uptime Institute 2022). A PUE of 1.0 would mean all facility energy is delivered to IT equipment; values above 1.0 represent overhead for cooling, power conversion, lighting, and other facility systems.

title: Foundations recap
text:
Summary
Fleet scale changes every constraint a single machine imposes. ML fleets combine the tight coupling of high-performance computing for training with the elastic fault tolerance of warehouse-scale computing for serving, and they cannot adopt either tradition wholesale. NVLink provides about 9× more per-direction bandwidth than an InfiniBand NDR port, which is why bandwidth-hungry parallelism stays inside the node. Cluster MTBF scales as \(1/\RequiredComponentCount\), so at 8,192 GPUs a GPU fails about every 366.2 minutes, with 98 percent probability of at least one failure in 24 hours. After disjoint factors for MFU (about 50 percent), scaling efficiency (about 83 percent), and operational goodput (about 82 percent), a 1,024-GPU cluster delivers about 34.0 percent of peak FLOP/s as useful work.
Three considerations govern the design response. The communication-computation ratio \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\) indicates the potential for overlap and the pressure from communication; dependencies and available resources determine how much communication can be hidden behind computation. Weak scaling, which grows the problem with the fleet, preserves useful work per device, while strong scaling remains the right choice when the goal is to finish fixed work sooner. Rack power density, about 5.8× the traditional reference for current AI racks, determines the cooling design, subject to the installed heat-removal capacity rather than a universal threshold.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Individual accelerators fail rarely, but scaling to thousands of nodes multiplies component failure rates until interruption becomes a continuous operating condition. At cluster scale, mean time between failures (MTBF) drops from years to hours, turning failure recovery into a core execution path. This appendix collects the quantitative reliability calculations behind the book’s fault-tolerance chapters, deriving failure probabilities, Young-Daly optimal checkpoint intervals, and availability stacking models. In C\(^3\) terms, it develops the coordination axis, where checkpointing, recovery, and availability determine how much of the fleet’s compute and communication becomes useful work.


This appendix is designed as a reference, intended for moving from intuition (“failures happen more often at scale”) to quantitative engineering decisions (“how often should one checkpoint?” or “how many spare nodes are needed?”).
The worked examples in this appendix use a 10,000-GPU training fleet, a larger variation on the 1,024-GPU Archetype A reference cluster, unless noted otherwise.

“How often will something fail?” Start with section 1.1 and the MTBF cascade in section 1.1.3.
“Where does the \(1/\RequiredComponentCount\) come from?” The probability tools in section 1.1.1 derive it from independent exponential lifetimes.
“How often to checkpoint?” Use the Young-Daly model in section 1.2.1 and the worked example in section 1.2.3.
“How much time is lost to recovery?” See the recovery anatomy in section 1.3.1 and the goodput analysis in section 1.3.2.
“When to use redundancy vs. checkpointing?” Compare strategies in section 1.4.1 and availability stacking in section 1.4.2.
“What if checkpoints are not cheap relative to MTBF?” Use the higher-order interval in section 1.5.
“How can one flipped bit derail training?” See the silent data corruption model in section 1.6.




Consider a training run on a 10,000-GPU cluster running for 30 days. The probability that at least one modeled node component fails during that time is effectively 100 percent, and that answer determines whether the system needs fault tolerance as a core design requirement or merely a nice-to-have.
Individual hardware components are remarkably reliable. A data center-grade GPU operates for tens of thousands of hours before failing. The physics of large-scale systems, however, works against reliability: every additional component is another opportunity for failure, and the aggregate failure rate scales linearly with component count. Component-level failure rates aggregate systematically into cluster-wide failure predictions.


Four results from elementary probability carry nearly all of the failure arithmetic in this book. Each assumes that components fail independently; correlated failures, such as a shared power feed or a common software bug, violate that assumption and must be modeled separately.
The first is the product rule for independent events. If a job needs all \(\RequiredComponentCount\) of its components and each is available with probability \(\ComponentAvailability\), the job’s components are all available with probability
\[ \JobAvailability= \ComponentAvailability^{\RequiredComponentCount} \approx e^{-\RequiredComponentCount(1-\ComponentAvailability)} \quad \text{for } \ComponentAvailability \text{ close to } 1  \tag{1}\]
Equation 1 is the reliability collapse behind the reliability gap in The reliability gap. A per-component availability that looks excellent in isolation decays exponentially in \(\RequiredComponentCount\).
The second is its complement, the probability that at least one of \(\RequiredComponentCount\) independent events occurs when each has probability \(\IndependentEventProbability\):
\[ \Pr(\text{at least one}) = 1-(1-\IndependentEventProbability)^{\RequiredComponentCount} \approx \RequiredComponentCount \IndependentEventProbability\quad \text{when } \RequiredComponentCount \IndependentEventProbability\ll 1  \tag{2}\]
The linear approximation in equation 2 holds only while \(\RequiredComponentCount \IndependentEventProbability\) is small; as \(\RequiredComponentCount\) grows, the probability approaches 1. This is the arithmetic of straggler amplification: a delay that strikes any one worker rarely strikes some worker of a large synchronous job on almost every step.
The third is the exponential lifetime model. A component with constant failure rate \(\ComponentFailureRate\) survives to time \(\TimeInstant\) with probability \(e^{-\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\) and has mean time to failure \(1/\ComponentFailureRate\). The model is memoryless. A component that has run for a year is no more likely to fail in the next hour than a new one, which is why it describes the useful-life phase and not burn-in or wear-out. The earliest of \(\RequiredComponentCount\) independent exponential failures is itself exponential with rate \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\), so the time to the first failure among \(\RequiredComponentCount\) identical components has mean \(1/(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate)\). That single fact is the origin of the \(1/\RequiredComponentCount\) scaling of system MTBF in equation 5.
The fourth is the Poisson count. Under the same model, the number of failures in an interval \(\FailureObservationInterval\) is Poisson distributed with mean \(\FailureObservationInterval/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\), so the probability of no failure is \(e^{-\FailureObservationInterval/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}\). Equation 6 below is the complement of that event, and the expected number of failures per day in table 2 is the Poisson mean.



Reliability engineers characterize components using two complementary metrics. The Failure in Time (FIT) rate counts failures per \(10^9\) device-hours of operation, a unit chosen because individual components fail so rarely that failures-per-hour would produce inconveniently small numbers. The reciprocal quantity, Mean Time To Failure (MTTF), calculates average lifetime in hours (equation 3):
\[ \MeanTimeToFailure = \frac{10^9}{\text{FIT}}  \tag{3}\]
Reference FIT rates and MTTF values (table 1) characterize component reliability in typical GPU training nodes, grounded in large-fleet and warehouse-scale experience (Kokolis et al. 2025; Zu et al. 2024; Barroso et al. 2019). These values assume the steady-state “useful life” phase of the bathtub curve, where the failure rate is approximately constant, dominated neither by infant mortality (early life) nor by wear-out (end of life) (Klutke et al. 2003).

Klutke, G., P. C. Kiessler, and M. A. Wortman. 2003. “A Critical Look at the Bathtub Curve.” IEEE Transactions on Reliability 52 (1): 125–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/tr.2002.804492.

Each component in isolation appears highly reliable; a GPU lasts 5.7 years on average. The difficulty begins with how a node behaves when many such components operate simultaneously.



The following model treats a compute node as a series system, in which any modeled component failure interrupts it. A component enters the sum only when its failure alone stops the node, so redundant power supplies, spare links, and recoverable device errors stay out of it. For independent components with constant failure rates, equation 4 sums the individual rates into the node-level failure rate:
\[ \frac{1}{\NodeMtbf} = \frac{\AcceleratorsPerNode}{\GpuMttf} + \frac{\NicsPerNode}{\NicMttf} + \frac{\SeriesPsuCount}{\PsuMttf} + \cdots  \tag{4}\]
Think of each component as a ticking clock counting down to failure. A DGX H100 node with 8 GPUs and 8 network interface cards (NICs) has 16 independent clocks, and the node fails when the first clock reaches zero. More clocks mean a shorter expected wait. The node’s 6 power supply units (PSUs) add no clocks. They run as a 4+2 redundant set, so the node keeps full performance with 2 of them failed, and a failed unit is normally replaced long before enough others fail to stop the node.
For a cluster of \(\ClusterNodeCount\) identical nodes, the same logic applies one level up, as equation 5 shows:
\[ \SystemMtbf = \frac{\NodeMtbf}{\ClusterNodeCount}  \tag{5}\]
This is the MTBF Cascade: reliability degrades linearly with component count at each level, and the levels compound. A node with 4,687.5 hours MTBF sounds reliable. A cluster of 1,250 such nodes has an MTBF of just 3.75 hours, so a failure every few hours is the expected steady state. Table 2 carries that arithmetic across fleet sizes, with aggregate MTBF falling in inverse proportion to GPU count.



Table 2: Cluster MTBF by Scale: As cluster size grows, the aggregate MTBF shrinks proportionally. At 10,000 GPUs, failures occur every few hours; at 100,000 GPUs, they occur continuously. The transition from hundreds of GPUs to tens of thousands is a qualitative regime shift. At 256 GPUs, about 6.1 days pass between failures. At 10,000 GPUs, the cluster expects multiple failures per shift. At 100,000 GPUs, failures are a continuous background condition, and the system is never fully healthy.



The MTBF determines the average time between failures, but training jobs have fixed durations. Practitioners ask for the probability that their job will be interrupted at least once.
Under the exponential failure model (constant failure rate), equation 6 gives the probability of at least one failure during a job of duration \(\JobDuration\):
\[ \Pr(\geq 1\ \text{failure}) = 1 - e^{-\JobDuration/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}  \tag{6}\]
When \(\JobDuration\gg \MeanTimeBetweenFailures\), this probability approaches 1 rapidly. Table 3 shows the concrete numbers for various cluster sizes and job durations.

For any cluster above a few thousand GPUs running jobs longer than a day, the probability of experiencing at least one failure is effectively 100 percent. This is why Fault Tolerance treats fault tolerance not as a defensive measure but as a fundamental architectural requirement.
The exponential failure model assumes a constant failure rate, which holds during the steady-state useful-life phase. During burn-in (first few hundred hours) and wear-out (approaching end-of-life), failure rates are higher. In practice, fleet operators observe that newly deployed nodes exhibit 2–3\(\times\) higher failure rates in their first week, making burn-in testing essential before admitting nodes to production clusters.
The inevitability of failure during long training jobs raises a practical question: given that failures will interrupt execution, how is the lost progress minimized?





Every checkpoint saves progress but costs time. Checkpoint too rarely and a failure destroys hours of training. Checkpoint too frequently and the overhead of writing checkpoints itself becomes the bottleneck. The Young-Daly formula gives the first-order optimal balance point, and it depends on just two measurable quantities: how long a checkpoint takes to write and how often failures occur (Young 1974; Daly 2006).

Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.


The optimal checkpoint interval balances two competing costs. Writing a checkpoint takes time \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) (the checkpoint cost), during which no useful training occurs. The longer the interval between checkpoints, however, the more work is lost when a failure strikes, on average half the interval. Equation 7 states the Young-Daly formula that minimizes the expected total overhead:
\[ \OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \times \CheckpointWriteTime \times \SystemMtbf}  \tag{7}\]
where \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is the checkpoint write time in seconds and \(\SystemMtbf\) is the cluster or job-level system MTBF in seconds.
The intuition behind equation 7 is geometric-mean-like. When checkpoints are cheap relative to the MTBF (\(\CheckpointWriteTime \ll \SystemMtbf\), the common case), the optimal interval sits between the two time scales. If checkpoints took zero time, the optimal cadence is every step. If the system never failed, no checkpoints would be required. The square root interpolates between these extremes.
The formula assumes that failures follow an exponential distribution (memoryless property) and that checkpoint cost \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is small compared to \(\SystemMtbf\). The examples below adopt these assumptions. Correlated outages, changing hazard rates, long writes, and asynchronous persistence can require a more detailed model.



Checkpoint size determines the write time \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) that feeds into the Young-Daly formula. For common mixed-precision training checkpoints with the adaptive moment estimation (Adam) optimizer, each parameter requires approximately 14 bytes of persistent state:

2 bytes for BF16 model weights
4 bytes for FP32 master weights
4 bytes for FP32 first moment (Adam \(\AdamFirstMoment\))
4 bytes for FP32 second moment (Adam \(\AdamSecondMoment\))

Equation 8 aggregates these per-parameter costs into the total checkpoint footprint:
\[ \text{Checkpoint Size} = \Parameters\times 14 \text{ bytes/parameter}  \tag{8}\]
Here, \(\Parameters\) is the number of trainable model parameters whose persistent optimizer and weight state must be serialized.

The checkpoint strategies in Fault Tolerance discuss techniques for reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) (asynchronous checkpointing, incremental deltas, and distributed storage), all of which improve the Young-Daly result by shrinking the \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) factor under the square root.



Combining the checkpoint write time with the 10,000-GPU MTBF gives a concrete checkpoint cadence.

Napkin Math 1.1: Young-Daly: 175B model on a 10,000-GPU clusterSetup: Consider training a 175B-parameter model on a 10,000-GPU cluster. The cluster MTBF is 3.75 hours (table 2). The checkpoint size is 2,450 GB, and the parallel storage system writes at 100 GB/s.
Step 1: Checkpoint write time (\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)). \[T_{\text{write}} = \frac{\text{Checkpoint Size}}{\text{Write Bandwidth}} = \frac{2,450 \text{ GB}}{100 \text{ GB/s}} = 24.5 \text{ s}\]
Step 2: Apply the Young-Daly formula (equation 7). \[T^\ast_{\text{ckpt}} = \sqrt{2 \times T_{\text{write}} \times \text{MTBF}_{\text{system}}} = \sqrt{2 \times 24.5 \text{ s} \times 3.75 \text{ h} \times 3{,}600 \text{ s/h}} = 13.6 \text{ min}\]
Interpretation: The optimal checkpoint interval is approximately 14 minutes. The overhead from checkpointing alone is \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx\) 3.0 percent of training time.
Systems insight: If the cluster were doubled to 20,000 GPUs, the MTBF would halve, and the optimal interval would shrink to 9.6 minutes, so the system checkpoints more frequently because failures happen more often. This illustrates the fundamental tension at scale: larger clusters are faster but demand more frequent interruption to protect progress.


The boundary conditions of the Young-Daly formula merit attention. When \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) approaches \(\SystemMtbf\) (checkpoint cost approaches MTBF), checkpoint and rework overheads become so large that checkpoint/restart alone may fail to maintain useful forward progress. In such cases, redundancy or elastic training becomes necessary, as discussed in section 1.4.1.





When a failure occurs, the system does not instantly resume training. Detection, rescheduling, reloading state, and replaying lost work each consume time. Understanding this recovery anatomy reveals which phase dominates and where to invest engineering effort.


Recovery is not a single event but a pipeline of phases, each with its own time budget. Equation 9 sums them into total recovery time:
\[ \TotalFailureRecoveryTime= \FailureDetectionTime+ \JobRestartTime + \CheckpointLoadTime + \LostWorkReplayTime \tag{9}\]
The terms are all durations: failure detection, replacement scheduling, checkpoint reload, and replay of lost training work since the last checkpoint. Their sum is the wall-clock time before the job returns to productive training.
Table 5 breaks recovery into the phases that determine how long the cluster remains below full productivity after a failure.

Decomposing this sequence shows that replay time \(\LostWorkReplayTime\) typically dominates, controlled directly by the checkpoint interval: on average, half the interval must be replayed. This creates a reinforcing loop with the Young-Daly formula. Shorter intervals mean less replay but more checkpoint overhead, and the formula finds the minimum of this sum.
The other phases offer engineering optimization targets. \(\FailureDetectionTime\) can be reduced with more aggressive heartbeat intervals (at the cost of false positives). \(\JobRestartTime\) depends on having hot spare nodes preallocated, a fleet orchestration decision covered in Fleet Orchestration. \(\CheckpointLoadTime\) scales with checkpoint size and storage bandwidth, motivating the checkpoint compression and sharding techniques discussed in Fault Tolerance.



Not all time spent on a training cluster produces useful progress. Rawput is the step rate the configured cluster could sustain without checkpoint or recovery interruptions. Goodput is the rate of committed training steps that contribute to the final model:
\[ \text{Goodput Ratio} = \frac{\text{Committed Useful-Step Rate}}{\text{Fault-Free Step Rate}} \approx \frac{\UsefulTrainingTime}{\AllocatedWallTime} \]
The modeled gap between rawput and goodput comes from two sources:

Checkpoint overhead (\(\sim\) 3.0 percent): Training pauses during each checkpoint write.
Recovery and rework overhead (\(\sim\) 3.9 percent): Time lost to detection, rescheduling, reloading, and replaying work discarded after each failure.

At 10,000-GPU scale, failures and checkpointing together can consume a substantial fraction of wall time. If they consume a fraction \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\), a fixed amount of useful work takes \(1/(1-\OperationalOverheadFraction)\) times its fault-free duration, not merely that duration plus \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\) of it. The fleet orchestration strategies in Fleet Orchestration and ML Operations at Scale focus on narrowing this gap, because every percentage point of overhead recovered translates directly to dollars saved and training time shortened.

Systems Perspective 1.1: The hidden cost of scaleA common misconception is that doubling cluster size halves training time. In practice, doubling from 5,000 to 10,000 GPUs halves the MTBF and increases failure-related overhead. The effective speedup is less than 2\(\times\), and at extreme scale, adding more GPUs can actually increase wall-clock time if the fault tolerance mechanisms cannot keep pace. This is the reliability analogue of Amdahl’s Law: the serial overhead of recovery bounds the benefit of parallelism.







Checkpoint/restart is not the only fault tolerance strategy. For serving workloads where downtime is measured in lost revenue, redundancy provides a fundamentally different trade-off. Elastic training can resume on a smaller allocation when valid state and a feasible parallel decomposition remain available. Choosing the right strategy depends on the workload’s tolerance for latency, cost, and complexity.


The three canonical strategies represent different points in the trade-off space between cost, complexity, and recovery speed.
Checkpoint/restart periodically saves full system state and rolls back to the last checkpoint after failure. It is the workhorse of large-scale training: conceptually simple, well-understood, and effective when MTBF is much larger than checkpoint cost. The weakness is that recovery requires stopping all workers and replaying lost computation.
Redundancy maintains alternate copies of state or computation. A surviving serving replica can take over only when routing, readiness, capacity, and the required request state meet the latency budget. Dedicated duplicate or triplicate execution costs 2–3\(\times\) the compute resources; active-active serving instead shares normal traffic across replicas while reserving failover headroom. The justified overhead depends on the workload and recovery contract.
Elastic training allows a job to resume with fewer workers when the smaller allocation can hold its state and support its parallel decomposition. Membership changes can still require a coordinated restart and checkpoint reload; TorchElastic restarts the worker group. Workers may be added back when capacity becomes available. The recovery path must restore missing shards, preserve data coverage, and either preserve the effective batch size or validate a changed optimization policy. Elasticity can reduce waiting for replacement capacity, but does not guarantee a shorter interruption. Table 6 summarizes the trade-offs.

For serving workloads, availability is typically expressed as a percentage: 99 percent (“two nines”), 99.9 percent (“three nines”), and so on. Redundancy improves availability by running \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) independent replicas. Under an idealized model with reliable routing and enough capacity on any surviving replica, the system is unavailable only when all replicas are simultaneously down, which equation 10 captures:
\[ \RedundantServiceAvailability= 1 - (1 - \ReplicaAvailability)^\RedundantReplicaCount  \tag{10}\]
where \(\ReplicaAvailability\) is the availability of a single replica and \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) is the number of replicas.
Evaluating availability stacking with independent replicas (table 7) quantifies the gain from adding serving capacity.

Stacking independent redundant replicas achieves dramatic availability gains: two 99-percent-available replicas yield 99.99 percent availability, reducing annual downtime from roughly 87 hours to under an hour. This is why inference serving systems almost universally deploy multiple replicas behind a load balancer. The cost of an extra replica is small compared to the business value of four-nines availability.
The independence assumption is critical, however. Correlated failures, such as power outages affecting an entire rack, software bugs triggered by a specific input, or network partitions isolating a failure domain, defeat availability stacking. This is why Fault Tolerance emphasizes failure domain isolation: replicas must be placed in different racks, different power zones, and ideally different data centers to reduce shared failure modes. Placement alone does not eliminate common software, control-plane, or regional dependencies.





Young’s approximation is most accurate when checkpoint time is small relative to the failure interval. Daly’s analysis develops higher-order checkpoint models (Daly 2006). The simplified renewal model below shows why finite checkpoint time changes the optimum without claiming to reproduce Daly’s full recovery model.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.


Let \(\CheckpointInterval\) be useful compute time between completed checkpoints. Assume Poisson failures with rate \(1/\SystemMtbf\), identical failure exposure during computation and writing, and zero detection, restart, or reload delay. A failed attempt loses its partial progress and repeats the interval. The expected elapsed time to complete one uninterrupted compute-plus-checkpoint attempt is:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] = \SystemMtbf \left( e^{\frac{\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime}{\SystemMtbf}} - 1 \right)  \tag{11}\]
Writing \(\CheckpointAttemptDuration= \CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime\) for the attempt duration, the renewal equation is \(\mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] = \mathbb{E}[\min(\NextFailureTime, \CheckpointAttemptDuration)] + \Pr(\NextFailureTime< \CheckpointAttemptDuration) \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime]\), where \(\NextFailureTime\) is an exponential failure time. Since \(\mathbb{E}[\min(\NextFailureTime, \CheckpointAttemptDuration)] = \SystemMtbf (1 - e^{-\CheckpointAttemptDuration/\SystemMtbf})\), solving the equation gives equation 11.
Expanding the exponential through its quadratic term gives the wasted time per completed interval:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] - \CheckpointInterval \approx \CheckpointWriteTime + \frac{(\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)^2}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{12}\]
When \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf\) is small, dividing equation 12 by \(\CheckpointInterval\) leaves the leading terms \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointInterval/(2 \cdot \SystemMtbf)\) of the wasted-time fraction. Minimizing those terms recovers Young’s interval \(\sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}\). For finite checkpoint costs, differentiate the unexpanded elapsed time per unit useful work, \(\mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime]/\CheckpointInterval\), instead. Its stationary point satisfies:
\[ e^{(\OptimalCheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)/\SystemMtbf}\left(1 - \frac{\OptimalCheckpointInterval}{\SystemMtbf}\right) = 1, \qquad 0 < \OptimalCheckpointInterval < \SystemMtbf  \tag{13}\]
For positive checkpoint cost, the equivalent derivative numerator \(e^{(\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)/\SystemMtbf}(\CheckpointInterval/\SystemMtbf - 1) + 1\) increases from a negative value at zero to a positive value at \(\SystemMtbf\). A one-dimensional root search on equation 13 therefore finds the unique optimum of this simplified model.


The first-order formula is a useful planning estimate when writes are short compared with MTBF. When that condition fails, use a model that includes the deployment’s checkpoint semantics, recovery delays, and failure exposure. The numerical condition above covers only the stated zero-restart-delay renewal model; asynchronous writes and correlated failures require different assumptions.






Not all hardware faults manifest as explicit system crashes, ECC double-bit errors, or kernel traps. Silent Data Corruption (SDC) occurs when single-bit errors or arithmetic logic unit (ALU) faults slip past parity checks, corrupting tensor values in SRAM, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), or register files without triggering an exception. In deep learning workloads, SDC is particularly dangerous because single corrupted floating-point values propagate through non-linear operations, destabilizing fleet-wide training (Dixit et al. 2021).

Dixit, H. D., S. Pendharkar, M. Beadon, C. Mason, T. Chakravarthy, B. Muthiah, and S. Sankar. 2021. Silent Data Corruptions at Scale. arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.11245.


Consider an IEEE 754 half-precision floating-point (FP16) tensor element representing a query entry \(\QueryComponent\), activation value, or weight matrix entry. FP16 allocates 16 total bits: 1 sign bit (\(\FloatSignBit\)), 5 exponent bits (\(\FloatExponentField\)), and 10 mantissa bits (\(\FloatMantissaField\)).
For a finite normal value, with exponent field \(1 \le \FloatExponentField\le 30\), the scalar \(\FloatEncodedNumber\) represented by the bitstring \((\FloatSignBit, \FloatExponentField, \FloatMantissaField)\) is given by:
\[ \FloatEncodedNumber= (-1)^\FloatSignBit\times 2^{\FloatExponentField- 15} \times \left(1 + \frac{\FloatMantissaField}{1024}\right) \]
Suppose a cosmic ray, voltage drop, or SRAM failure causes a single bit flip in the most significant exponent bit (bit 14). The exponent value changes from \(\FloatExponentField\) to \(\FlippedFloatExponentField = \FloatExponentField\pm 16\):
\[ \BitFlippedFloatNumber= (-1)^\FloatSignBit\times 2^{(\FloatExponentField\pm 16) - 15} \times \left(1 + \frac{\FloatMantissaField}{1024}\right) = \FloatEncodedNumber\times 2^{\pm 16} \]
If both the original and corrupted exponent fields encode finite normal values, the magnitude increases by a factor of \(2^{16}=65{,}536\) or decreases by its reciprocal. Exponent fields of zero or all ones instead invoke the subnormal, zero, infinity, or NaN encodings, so the displayed normal-value formula does not apply.



For one attention head, let \(\AttentionScoreMatrix = \AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension} \in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength}\) be the pre-softmax score matrix for sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\). Suppose an SDC event corrupts one element of token row \(\MatrixRowIndex\) of the query matrix \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), and write the resulting perturbation as \(\FiniteChange\AttentionQueryMatrix\), with only that element nonzero:
\[ \CorruptedAttentionScoreMatrix = \frac{(\AttentionQueryMatrix+ \FiniteChange\AttentionQueryMatrix) \AttentionKeyMatrix^T}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}} = \AttentionScoreMatrix + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreMatrix \]
where \(\FiniteChange\AttentionScoreMatrix\) is nonzero only in row \(\MatrixRowIndex\), with entries \(\FiniteChange \AttentionScoreEntry = \FiniteChange\QueryVector_i \cdot \KeyVector_j/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\) for the corrupted query row \(\FiniteChange\QueryVector_i\) and key row \(\KeyVector_j\).
The attention probability perturbation for token row \(\MatrixRowIndex\) is:
\[ \FiniteChange\AttentionWeightVector_i = \operatorname{softmax}\left( \AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow \right) - \operatorname{softmax}\left( \AttentionScoreRow \right) \]
A large corrupted query component can strongly change several attention logits, with the signs and magnitudes determined by the corresponding key components. If one resulting logit exceeds every other logit by an increasingly large margin, the attention distribution approaches a one-hot vector:
\[ \operatorname{softmax}(\AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow)_j \to 1, \qquad \operatorname{softmax}(\AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow)_{k \neq j} \to 0 \]
This is a conditional saturation limit, not an inevitable consequence of a bit flip. The selected key depends on the corrupted logits; a corrupted query element does not identify one corrupted key. The softmax derivative is \(\partial \SoftmaxOutputProbability_j/\partial \AttentionScoreSummand = \SoftmaxOutputProbability_j(\KroneckerIndicator_{jk}-\SoftmaxOutputProbability_k)\), which tends toward zero under saturation rather than diverging. Other paths through the computation can still produce large or nonfinite activations and gradients. If invalid state enters the optimizer or a collective, it can propagate across ranks; detection and recovery must therefore verify state before resuming from a clean checkpoint.





Failure is a physical constraint of scale. Under independent, constant component failure rates, a single GPU’s mean lifetime is 5.7 years, yet the modeled 10,000-GPU cluster fails on average every 3.75 hours, because node failure rates sum across components and cluster MTBF divides by node count. The probability that a job is interrupted grows with its duration relative to that interval, so long runs on large clusters must plan for recovery rather than hope to avoid it.
Recovery has four modeled phases (detection, rescheduling, reloading, and replay), and replay is controlled by the checkpoint interval. The Young-Daly formula \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \CheckpointWriteTime \, \SystemMtbf}\) (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\)) balances write overhead against expected rework when writes are short compared with the MTBF, and section 1.5 examines finite-cost effects under a simplified renewal model. Checkpoint/restart suits batch training, redundancy suits latency-sensitive serving, and elastic training sits between them. Independent replicas reduce unavailability multiplicatively, to \((1-\ReplicaAvailability)^\RedundantReplicaCount\) for \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) replicas, but only to the extent that failure-domain isolation keeps their failures independent.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
This appendix is designed as a reference, intended for moving from intuition (“failures happen more often at scale”) to quantitative engineering decisions (“how often should one checkpoint?” or “how many spare nodes are needed?”).
The worked examples in this appendix use a 10,000-GPU training fleet, a larger variation on the 1,024-GPU Archetype A reference cluster, unless noted otherwise.

“How often will something fail?” Start with section 1.1 and the MTBF cascade in section 1.1.3.
“Where does the \(1/\RequiredComponentCount\) come from?” The probability tools in section 1.1.1 derive it from independent exponential lifetimes.
“How often to checkpoint?” Use the Young-Daly model in section 1.2.1 and the worked example in section 1.2.3.
“How much time is lost to recovery?” See the recovery anatomy in section 1.3.1 and the goodput analysis in section 1.3.2.
“When to use redundancy vs. checkpointing?” Compare strategies in section 1.4.1 and availability stacking in section 1.4.2.
“What if checkpoints are not cheap relative to MTBF?” Use the higher-order interval in section 1.5.
“How can one flipped bit derail training?” See the silent data corruption model in section 1.6.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Consider a training run on a 10,000-GPU cluster running for 30 days. The probability that at least one modeled node component fails during that time is effectively 100 percent, and that answer determines whether the system needs fault tolerance as a core design requirement or merely a nice-to-have.
Individual hardware components are remarkably reliable. A data center-grade GPU operates for tens of thousands of hours before failing. The physics of large-scale systems, however, works against reliability: every additional component is another opportunity for failure, and the aggregate failure rate scales linearly with component count. Component-level failure rates aggregate systematically into cluster-wide failure predictions.


Four results from elementary probability carry nearly all of the failure arithmetic in this book. Each assumes that components fail independently; correlated failures, such as a shared power feed or a common software bug, violate that assumption and must be modeled separately.
The first is the product rule for independent events. If a job needs all \(\RequiredComponentCount\) of its components and each is available with probability \(\ComponentAvailability\), the job’s components are all available with probability
\[ \JobAvailability= \ComponentAvailability^{\RequiredComponentCount} \approx e^{-\RequiredComponentCount(1-\ComponentAvailability)} \quad \text{for } \ComponentAvailability \text{ close to } 1  \tag{1}\]
Equation 1 is the reliability collapse behind the reliability gap in The reliability gap. A per-component availability that looks excellent in isolation decays exponentially in \(\RequiredComponentCount\).
The second is its complement, the probability that at least one of \(\RequiredComponentCount\) independent events occurs when each has probability \(\IndependentEventProbability\):
\[ \Pr(\text{at least one}) = 1-(1-\IndependentEventProbability)^{\RequiredComponentCount} \approx \RequiredComponentCount \IndependentEventProbability\quad \text{when } \RequiredComponentCount \IndependentEventProbability\ll 1  \tag{2}\]
The linear approximation in equation 2 holds only while \(\RequiredComponentCount \IndependentEventProbability\) is small; as \(\RequiredComponentCount\) grows, the probability approaches 1. This is the arithmetic of straggler amplification: a delay that strikes any one worker rarely strikes some worker of a large synchronous job on almost every step.
The third is the exponential lifetime model. A component with constant failure rate \(\ComponentFailureRate\) survives to time \(\TimeInstant\) with probability \(e^{-\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\) and has mean time to failure \(1/\ComponentFailureRate\). The model is memoryless. A component that has run for a year is no more likely to fail in the next hour than a new one, which is why it describes the useful-life phase and not burn-in or wear-out. The earliest of \(\RequiredComponentCount\) independent exponential failures is itself exponential with rate \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\), so the time to the first failure among \(\RequiredComponentCount\) identical components has mean \(1/(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate)\). That single fact is the origin of the \(1/\RequiredComponentCount\) scaling of system MTBF in equation 5.
The fourth is the Poisson count. Under the same model, the number of failures in an interval \(\FailureObservationInterval\) is Poisson distributed with mean \(\FailureObservationInterval/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\), so the probability of no failure is \(e^{-\FailureObservationInterval/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}\). Equation 6 below is the complement of that event, and the expected number of failures per day in table 2 is the Poisson mean.



Reliability engineers characterize components using two complementary metrics. The Failure in Time (FIT) rate counts failures per \(10^9\) device-hours of operation, a unit chosen because individual components fail so rarely that failures-per-hour would produce inconveniently small numbers. The reciprocal quantity, Mean Time To Failure (MTTF), calculates average lifetime in hours (equation 3):
\[ \MeanTimeToFailure = \frac{10^9}{\text{FIT}}  \tag{3}\]
Reference FIT rates and MTTF values (table 1) characterize component reliability in typical GPU training nodes, grounded in large-fleet and warehouse-scale experience (Kokolis et al. 2025; Zu et al. 2024; Barroso et al. 2019). These values assume the steady-state “useful life” phase of the bathtub curve, where the failure rate is approximately constant, dominated neither by infant mortality (early life) nor by wear-out (end of life) (Klutke et al. 2003).

Klutke, G., P. C. Kiessler, and M. A. Wortman. 2003. “A Critical Look at the Bathtub Curve.” IEEE Transactions on Reliability 52 (1): 125–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/tr.2002.804492.

Each component in isolation appears highly reliable; a GPU lasts 5.7 years on average. The difficulty begins with how a node behaves when many such components operate simultaneously.



The following model treats a compute node as a series system, in which any modeled component failure interrupts it. A component enters the sum only when its failure alone stops the node, so redundant power supplies, spare links, and recoverable device errors stay out of it. For independent components with constant failure rates, equation 4 sums the individual rates into the node-level failure rate:
\[ \frac{1}{\NodeMtbf} = \frac{\AcceleratorsPerNode}{\GpuMttf} + \frac{\NicsPerNode}{\NicMttf} + \frac{\SeriesPsuCount}{\PsuMttf} + \cdots  \tag{4}\]
Think of each component as a ticking clock counting down to failure. A DGX H100 node with 8 GPUs and 8 network interface cards (NICs) has 16 independent clocks, and the node fails when the first clock reaches zero. More clocks mean a shorter expected wait. The node’s 6 power supply units (PSUs) add no clocks. They run as a 4+2 redundant set, so the node keeps full performance with 2 of them failed, and a failed unit is normally replaced long before enough others fail to stop the node.
For a cluster of \(\ClusterNodeCount\) identical nodes, the same logic applies one level up, as equation 5 shows:
\[ \SystemMtbf = \frac{\NodeMtbf}{\ClusterNodeCount}  \tag{5}\]
This is the MTBF Cascade: reliability degrades linearly with component count at each level, and the levels compound. A node with 4,687.5 hours MTBF sounds reliable. A cluster of 1,250 such nodes has an MTBF of just 3.75 hours, so a failure every few hours is the expected steady state. Table 2 carries that arithmetic across fleet sizes, with aggregate MTBF falling in inverse proportion to GPU count.



Table 2: Cluster MTBF by Scale: As cluster size grows, the aggregate MTBF shrinks proportionally. At 10,000 GPUs, failures occur every few hours; at 100,000 GPUs, they occur continuously. The transition from hundreds of GPUs to tens of thousands is a qualitative regime shift. At 256 GPUs, about 6.1 days pass between failures. At 10,000 GPUs, the cluster expects multiple failures per shift. At 100,000 GPUs, failures are a continuous background condition, and the system is never fully healthy.



The MTBF determines the average time between failures, but training jobs have fixed durations. Practitioners ask for the probability that their job will be interrupted at least once.
Under the exponential failure model (constant failure rate), equation 6 gives the probability of at least one failure during a job of duration \(\JobDuration\):
\[ \Pr(\geq 1\ \text{failure}) = 1 - e^{-\JobDuration/\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}  \tag{6}\]
When \(\JobDuration\gg \MeanTimeBetweenFailures\), this probability approaches 1 rapidly. Table 3 shows the concrete numbers for various cluster sizes and job durations.

For any cluster above a few thousand GPUs running jobs longer than a day, the probability of experiencing at least one failure is effectively 100 percent. This is why Fault Tolerance treats fault tolerance not as a defensive measure but as a fundamental architectural requirement.
The exponential failure model assumes a constant failure rate, which holds during the steady-state useful-life phase. During burn-in (first few hundred hours) and wear-out (approaching end-of-life), failure rates are higher. In practice, fleet operators observe that newly deployed nodes exhibit 2–3\(\times\) higher failure rates in their first week, making burn-in testing essential before admitting nodes to production clusters.
The inevitability of failure during long training jobs raises a practical question: given that failures will interrupt execution, how is the lost progress minimized?

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Every checkpoint saves progress but costs time. Checkpoint too rarely and a failure destroys hours of training. Checkpoint too frequently and the overhead of writing checkpoints itself becomes the bottleneck. The Young-Daly formula gives the first-order optimal balance point, and it depends on just two measurable quantities: how long a checkpoint takes to write and how often failures occur (Young 1974; Daly 2006).

Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.


The optimal checkpoint interval balances two competing costs. Writing a checkpoint takes time \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) (the checkpoint cost), during which no useful training occurs. The longer the interval between checkpoints, however, the more work is lost when a failure strikes, on average half the interval. Equation 7 states the Young-Daly formula that minimizes the expected total overhead:
\[ \OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \times \CheckpointWriteTime \times \SystemMtbf}  \tag{7}\]
where \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is the checkpoint write time in seconds and \(\SystemMtbf\) is the cluster or job-level system MTBF in seconds.
The intuition behind equation 7 is geometric-mean-like. When checkpoints are cheap relative to the MTBF (\(\CheckpointWriteTime \ll \SystemMtbf\), the common case), the optimal interval sits between the two time scales. If checkpoints took zero time, the optimal cadence is every step. If the system never failed, no checkpoints would be required. The square root interpolates between these extremes.
The formula assumes that failures follow an exponential distribution (memoryless property) and that checkpoint cost \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is small compared to \(\SystemMtbf\). The examples below adopt these assumptions. Correlated outages, changing hazard rates, long writes, and asynchronous persistence can require a more detailed model.



Checkpoint size determines the write time \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) that feeds into the Young-Daly formula. For common mixed-precision training checkpoints with the adaptive moment estimation (Adam) optimizer, each parameter requires approximately 14 bytes of persistent state:

2 bytes for BF16 model weights
4 bytes for FP32 master weights
4 bytes for FP32 first moment (Adam \(\AdamFirstMoment\))
4 bytes for FP32 second moment (Adam \(\AdamSecondMoment\))

Equation 8 aggregates these per-parameter costs into the total checkpoint footprint:
\[ \text{Checkpoint Size} = \Parameters\times 14 \text{ bytes/parameter}  \tag{8}\]
Here, \(\Parameters\) is the number of trainable model parameters whose persistent optimizer and weight state must be serialized.
Mixed-precision Adam checkpoint sizing (table 4) demonstrates how state scales from manageable gigabytes to frontier-scale terabytes:

At frontier scale (175B+ parameters), these sizes reach the terabyte range. This makes checkpoint write time a significant cost that directly affects the Young-Daly optimal interval. The checkpoint strategies in Fault Tolerance discuss techniques for reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) (asynchronous checkpointing, incremental deltas, and distributed storage), all of which improve the Young-Daly result by shrinking the \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) factor under the square root.



Combining the checkpoint write time with the 10,000-GPU MTBF gives a concrete checkpoint cadence.

Napkin Math 1.1: Young-Daly: 175B model on a 10,000-GPU clusterSetup: Consider training a 175B-parameter model on a 10,000-GPU cluster. The cluster MTBF is 3.75 hours (table 2). The checkpoint size is 2,450 GB, and the parallel storage system writes at 100 GB/s.
Step 1: Checkpoint write time (\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)). \[T_{\text{write}} = \frac{\text{Checkpoint Size}}{\text{Write Bandwidth}} = \frac{2,450 \text{ GB}}{100 \text{ GB/s}} = 24.5 \text{ s}\]
Step 2: Apply the Young-Daly formula (equation 7). \[T^\ast_{\text{ckpt}} = \sqrt{2 \times T_{\text{write}} \times \text{MTBF}_{\text{system}}} = \sqrt{2 \times 24.5 \text{ s} \times 3.75 \text{ h} \times 3{,}600 \text{ s/h}} = 13.6 \text{ min}\]
Interpretation: The optimal checkpoint interval is approximately 14 minutes. The overhead from checkpointing alone is \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx\) 3.0 percent of training time.
Systems insight: If the cluster were doubled to 20,000 GPUs, the MTBF would halve, and the optimal interval would shrink to 9.6 minutes, so the system checkpoints more frequently because failures happen more often. This illustrates the fundamental tension at scale: larger clusters are faster but demand more frequent interruption to protect progress.


The boundary conditions of the Young-Daly formula merit attention. When \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) approaches \(\SystemMtbf\) (checkpoint cost approaches MTBF), checkpoint and rework overheads become so large that checkpoint/restart alone may fail to maintain useful forward progress. In such cases, redundancy or elastic training becomes necessary, as discussed in section 1.4.1.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
When a failure occurs, the system does not instantly resume training. Detection, rescheduling, reloading state, and replaying lost work each consume time. Understanding this recovery anatomy reveals which phase dominates and where to invest engineering effort.


Recovery is not a single event but a pipeline of phases, each with its own time budget. Equation 9 sums them into total recovery time:
\[ \TotalFailureRecoveryTime= \FailureDetectionTime+ \JobRestartTime + \CheckpointLoadTime + \LostWorkReplayTime \tag{9}\]
The terms are all durations: failure detection, replacement scheduling, checkpoint reload, and replay of lost training work since the last checkpoint. Their sum is the wall-clock time before the job returns to productive training.
Table 5 breaks recovery into the phases that determine how long the cluster remains below full productivity after a failure.



Table 5: Recovery Time Breakdown: Each phase contributes to the total time between failure and full-speed resumption. For the 10,000-GPU, 175B-model scenario, replay dominates because it recomputes work lost since the last checkpoint.

Decomposing this sequence shows that replay time \(\LostWorkReplayTime\) typically dominates, controlled directly by the checkpoint interval: on average, half the interval must be replayed. This creates a reinforcing loop with the Young-Daly formula. Shorter intervals mean less replay but more checkpoint overhead, and the formula finds the minimum of this sum.
The other phases offer engineering optimization targets. \(\FailureDetectionTime\) can be reduced with more aggressive heartbeat intervals (at the cost of false positives). \(\JobRestartTime\) depends on having hot spare nodes preallocated, a fleet orchestration decision covered in Fleet Orchestration. \(\CheckpointLoadTime\) scales with checkpoint size and storage bandwidth, motivating the checkpoint compression and sharding techniques discussed in Fault Tolerance.



Not all time spent on a training cluster produces useful progress. Rawput is the step rate the configured cluster could sustain without checkpoint or recovery interruptions. Goodput is the rate of committed training steps that contribute to the final model:
\[ \text{Goodput Ratio} = \frac{\text{Committed Useful-Step Rate}}{\text{Fault-Free Step Rate}} \approx \frac{\UsefulTrainingTime}{\AllocatedWallTime} \]
The modeled gap between rawput and goodput comes from two sources:

Checkpoint overhead (\(\sim\) 3.0 percent): Training pauses during each checkpoint write.
Recovery and rework overhead (\(\sim\) 3.9 percent): Time lost to detection, rescheduling, reloading, and replaying work discarded after each failure.

At 10,000-GPU scale, failures and checkpointing together can consume a substantial fraction of wall time. If they consume a fraction \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\), a fixed amount of useful work takes \(1/(1-\OperationalOverheadFraction)\) times its fault-free duration, not merely that duration plus \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\) of it. The fleet orchestration strategies in Fleet Orchestration and ML Operations at Scale focus on narrowing this gap, because every percentage point of overhead recovered translates directly to dollars saved and training time shortened.

Systems Perspective 1.1: The hidden cost of scaleA common misconception is that doubling cluster size halves training time. In practice, doubling from 5,000 to 10,000 GPUs halves the MTBF and increases failure-related overhead. The effective speedup is less than 2\(\times\), and at extreme scale, adding more GPUs can actually increase wall-clock time if the fault tolerance mechanisms cannot keep pace. This is the reliability analogue of Amdahl’s Law: the serial overhead of recovery bounds the benefit of parallelism.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Checkpoint/restart is not the only fault tolerance strategy. For serving workloads where downtime is measured in lost revenue, redundancy provides a fundamentally different trade-off. Elastic training can resume on a smaller allocation when valid state and a feasible parallel decomposition remain available. Choosing the right strategy depends on the workload’s tolerance for latency, cost, and complexity.


The three canonical strategies represent different points in the trade-off space between cost, complexity, and recovery speed.
Checkpoint/restart periodically saves full system state and rolls back to the last checkpoint after failure. It is the workhorse of large-scale training: conceptually simple, well-understood, and effective when MTBF is much larger than checkpoint cost. The weakness is that recovery requires stopping all workers and replaying lost computation.
Redundancy maintains alternate copies of state or computation. A surviving serving replica can take over only when routing, readiness, capacity, and the required request state meet the latency budget. Dedicated duplicate or triplicate execution costs 2–3\(\times\) the compute resources; active-active serving instead shares normal traffic across replicas while reserving failover headroom. The justified overhead depends on the workload and recovery contract.
Elastic training allows a job to resume with fewer workers when the smaller allocation can hold its state and support its parallel decomposition. Membership changes can still require a coordinated restart and checkpoint reload; TorchElastic restarts the worker group. Workers may be added back when capacity becomes available. The recovery path must restore missing shards, preserve data coverage, and either preserve the effective batch size or validate a changed optimization policy. Elasticity can reduce waiting for replacement capacity, but does not guarantee a shorter interruption. Table 6 summarizes the trade-offs.



Table 6: Fault Tolerance Strategy Comparison: The latency and overhead ranges are illustrative, not guarantees; elasticity does not inherently require spare capacity. For serving workloads, availability is typically expressed as a percentage: 99 percent (“two nines”), 99.9 percent (“three nines”), and so on. Redundancy improves availability by running \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) independent replicas. Under an idealized model with reliable routing and enough capacity on any surviving replica, the system is unavailable only when all replicas are simultaneously down, which equation 10 captures:
\[ \RedundantServiceAvailability= 1 - (1 - \ReplicaAvailability)^\RedundantReplicaCount  \tag{10}\]
where \(\ReplicaAvailability\) is the availability of a single replica and \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) is the number of replicas.
Evaluating availability stacking with independent replicas (table 7) quantifies the gain from adding serving capacity.
