Stacking independent redundant replicas achieves dramatic availability gains: two 99-percent-available replicas yield 99.99 percent availability, reducing annual downtime from roughly 87 hours to under an hour. This is why inference serving systems almost universally deploy multiple replicas behind a load balancer. The cost of an extra replica is small compared to the business value of four-nines availability.
The independence assumption is critical, however. Correlated failures, such as power outages affecting an entire rack, software bugs triggered by a specific input, or network partitions isolating a failure domain, defeat availability stacking. This is why Fault Tolerance emphasizes failure domain isolation: replicas must be placed in different racks, different power zones, and ideally different data centers to reduce shared failure modes. Placement alone does not eliminate common software, control-plane, or regional dependencies.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Young’s approximation is most accurate when checkpoint time is small relative to the failure interval. Daly’s analysis develops higher-order checkpoint models (Daly 2006). The simplified renewal model below shows why finite checkpoint time changes the optimum without claiming to reproduce Daly’s full recovery model.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.


Let \(\CheckpointInterval\) be useful compute time between completed checkpoints. Assume Poisson failures with rate \(1/\SystemMtbf\), identical failure exposure during computation and writing, and zero detection, restart, or reload delay. A failed attempt loses its partial progress and repeats the interval. The expected elapsed time to complete one uninterrupted compute-plus-checkpoint attempt is:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] = \SystemMtbf \left( e^{\frac{\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime}{\SystemMtbf}} - 1 \right)  \tag{11}\]
Writing \(\CheckpointAttemptDuration= \CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime\) for the attempt duration, the renewal equation is \(\mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] = \mathbb{E}[\min(\NextFailureTime, \CheckpointAttemptDuration)] + \Pr(\NextFailureTime< \CheckpointAttemptDuration) \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime]\), where \(\NextFailureTime\) is an exponential failure time. Since \(\mathbb{E}[\min(\NextFailureTime, \CheckpointAttemptDuration)] = \SystemMtbf (1 - e^{-\CheckpointAttemptDuration/\SystemMtbf})\), solving the equation gives equation 11.
Expanding the exponential through its quadratic term gives the wasted time per completed interval:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] - \CheckpointInterval \approx \CheckpointWriteTime + \frac{(\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)^2}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{12}\]
When \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf\) is small, dividing equation 12 by \(\CheckpointInterval\) leaves the leading terms \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointInterval/(2 \cdot \SystemMtbf)\) of the wasted-time fraction. Minimizing those terms recovers Young’s interval \(\sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}\). For finite checkpoint costs, differentiate the unexpanded elapsed time per unit useful work, \(\mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime]/\CheckpointInterval\), instead. Its stationary point satisfies:
\[ e^{(\OptimalCheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)/\SystemMtbf}\left(1 - \frac{\OptimalCheckpointInterval}{\SystemMtbf}\right) = 1, \qquad 0 < \OptimalCheckpointInterval < \SystemMtbf  \tag{13}\]
For positive checkpoint cost, the equivalent derivative numerator \(e^{(\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)/\SystemMtbf}(\CheckpointInterval/\SystemMtbf - 1) + 1\) increases from a negative value at zero to a positive value at \(\SystemMtbf\). A one-dimensional root search on equation 13 therefore finds the unique optimum of this simplified model.


The first-order formula is a useful planning estimate when writes are short compared with MTBF. When that condition fails, use a model that includes the deployment’s checkpoint semantics, recovery delays, and failure exposure. The numerical condition above covers only the stated zero-restart-delay renewal model; asynchronous writes and correlated failures require different assumptions.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Not all hardware faults manifest as explicit system crashes, ECC double-bit errors, or kernel traps. Silent Data Corruption (SDC) occurs when single-bit errors or arithmetic logic unit (ALU) faults slip past parity checks, corrupting tensor values in SRAM, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), or register files without triggering an exception. In deep learning workloads, SDC is particularly dangerous because single corrupted floating-point values propagate through non-linear operations, destabilizing fleet-wide training (Dixit et al. 2021).

Dixit, H. D., S. Pendharkar, M. Beadon, C. Mason, T. Chakravarthy, B. Muthiah, and S. Sankar. 2021. Silent Data Corruptions at Scale. arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.11245.


Consider an IEEE 754 half-precision floating-point (FP16) tensor element representing a query entry \(\QueryComponent\), activation value, or weight matrix entry. FP16 allocates 16 total bits: 1 sign bit (\(\FloatSignBit\)), 5 exponent bits (\(\FloatExponentField\)), and 10 mantissa bits (\(\FloatMantissaField\)).
For a finite normal value, with exponent field \(1 \le \FloatExponentField\le 30\), the scalar \(\FloatEncodedNumber\) represented by the bitstring \((\FloatSignBit, \FloatExponentField, \FloatMantissaField)\) is given by:
\[ \FloatEncodedNumber= (-1)^\FloatSignBit\times 2^{\FloatExponentField- 15} \times \left(1 + \frac{\FloatMantissaField}{1024}\right) \]
Suppose a cosmic ray, voltage drop, or SRAM failure causes a single bit flip in the most significant exponent bit (bit 14). The exponent value changes from \(\FloatExponentField\) to \(\FlippedFloatExponentField = \FloatExponentField\pm 16\):
\[ \BitFlippedFloatNumber= (-1)^\FloatSignBit\times 2^{(\FloatExponentField\pm 16) - 15} \times \left(1 + \frac{\FloatMantissaField}{1024}\right) = \FloatEncodedNumber\times 2^{\pm 16} \]
If both the original and corrupted exponent fields encode finite normal values, the magnitude increases by a factor of \(2^{16}=65{,}536\) or decreases by its reciprocal. Exponent fields of zero or all ones instead invoke the subnormal, zero, infinity, or NaN encodings, so the displayed normal-value formula does not apply.



For one attention head, let \(\AttentionScoreMatrix = \AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension} \in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength}\) be the pre-softmax score matrix for sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\). Suppose an SDC event corrupts one element of token row \(\MatrixRowIndex\) of the query matrix \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), and write the resulting perturbation as \(\FiniteChange\AttentionQueryMatrix\), with only that element nonzero:
\[ \CorruptedAttentionScoreMatrix = \frac{(\AttentionQueryMatrix+ \FiniteChange\AttentionQueryMatrix) \AttentionKeyMatrix^T}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}} = \AttentionScoreMatrix + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreMatrix \]
where \(\FiniteChange\AttentionScoreMatrix\) is nonzero only in row \(\MatrixRowIndex\), with entries \(\FiniteChange \AttentionScoreEntry = \FiniteChange\QueryVector_i \cdot \KeyVector_j/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\) for the corrupted query row \(\FiniteChange\QueryVector_i\) and key row \(\KeyVector_j\).
The attention probability perturbation for token row \(\MatrixRowIndex\) is:
\[ \FiniteChange\AttentionWeightVector_i = \operatorname{softmax}\left( \AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow \right) - \operatorname{softmax}\left( \AttentionScoreRow \right) \]
A large corrupted query component can strongly change several attention logits, with the signs and magnitudes determined by the corresponding key components. If one resulting logit exceeds every other logit by an increasingly large margin, the attention distribution approaches a one-hot vector:
\[ \operatorname{softmax}(\AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow)_j \to 1, \qquad \operatorname{softmax}(\AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow)_{k \neq j} \to 0 \]
This is a conditional saturation limit, not an inevitable consequence of a bit flip. The selected key depends on the corrupted logits; a corrupted query element does not identify one corrupted key. The softmax derivative is \(\partial \SoftmaxOutputProbability_j/\partial \AttentionScoreSummand = \SoftmaxOutputProbability_j(\KroneckerIndicator_{jk}-\SoftmaxOutputProbability_k)\), which tends toward zero under saturation rather than diverging. Other paths through the computation can still produce large or nonfinite activations and gradients. If invalid state enters the optimizer or a collective, it can propagate across ranks; detection and recovery must therefore verify state before resuming from a clean checkpoint.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Failure is a physical constraint of scale. Under independent, constant component failure rates, a single GPU’s mean lifetime is 5.7 years, yet the modeled 10,000-GPU cluster fails on average every 3.75 hours, because node failure rates sum across components and cluster MTBF divides by node count. The probability that a job is interrupted grows with its duration relative to that interval, so long runs on large clusters must plan for recovery rather than hope to avoid it.
Recovery has four modeled phases (detection, rescheduling, reloading, and replay), and replay is controlled by the checkpoint interval. The Young-Daly formula \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \CheckpointWriteTime \, \SystemMtbf}\) (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\)) balances write overhead against expected rework when writes are short compared with the MTBF, and section 1.5 examines finite-cost effects under a simplified renewal model. Checkpoint/restart suits batch training, redundancy suits latency-sensitive serving, and elastic training sits between them. Independent replicas reduce unavailability multiplicatively, to \((1-\ReplicaAvailability)^\RedundantReplicaCount\) for \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) replicas, but only to the extent that failure-domain isolation keeps their failures independent.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Every quantitative example in this book, from cluster failure rates to collective-communication costs to carbon footprint estimates, uses a specific set of assumed numbers: canonical cluster sizes, fabric bandwidths, accelerator reliability, power usage effectiveness, regional carbon intensity, and model utilization ranges. This appendix collects those fleet-scale assumptions in one place so the book’s arithmetic can be audited, checked against chapter napkin math, or substituted into worked examples.


Use this appendix to verify a fleet-scale estimate, swap in an alternative assumption (for example, NDR vs. HDR fabric, Quebec vs. Poland carbon intensity, or a different model FLOPs utilization (MFU)), or identify which numerical constants a chapter calculation depends on. Locate the relevant section, read the Value and Unit columns, and substitute those values into target arithmetic.
A short napkin-math callout at the start shows how several assumptions combine (failure rate, AllReduce time, carbon footprint). Hardware and link bandwidths are ceilings unless a chapter states an effective-bandwidth discount. Treat the tables as this edition’s shared assumption sheet, not immutable physical laws.

Napkin Math 1.1: Quick calculations with these assumptionsThese tables support quick distributed-systems napkin math. Three examples show how several assumptions combine.
Problem: Estimate how many GPU failures a cluster should expect per day.
Variables: Use a cluster of 8,192 GPUs and an individual GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours.
Math: The GPU failure rate is 8,192 GPUs/50,000 hours \(\approx\) 0.16 failures/hour, or roughly 3.9 failures/day.
Result: This estimate excludes network interface card (NIC), PSU, and cable failures. At 100,000 GPUs, the GPU-only rate is approximately 48 failures/day; adding NIC, PSU, and cable failures can roughly double the operational incident stream.
Systems insight: At fleet scale, failure becomes a continuous background process rather than an exceptional event.
Problem: Estimate how long an AllReduce takes for a 70B model.
Variables: Use BF16 parameters and InfiniBand NDR with a nominal byte rate of 50 GB/s per port.
Math: The gradient payload is 70 \(\times 10^9 \times\) 2 bytes = 140 GB. The ring AllReduce napkin estimate is 2 \(\times\) 140 GB/50 GB/s \(\approx\) 5.6 s.
Result: The collective can consume a significant fraction of a training step.
Systems insight: Pipeline and tensor parallelism exist partly to shrink the gradient volume each rank must communicate.
Problem: Estimate the carbon footprint of a 10,000-GPU training run.
Variables: Each H100 draws 700 W at thermal design power (TDP). Use power usage effectiveness (PUE) 1.12, Quebec grid intensity 20 g/kWh, and Poland grid intensity 820 g/kWh.
Math: A GPU-only facility-power proxy is 10,000 GPUs \(\times\) 700 W \(\times\) 1.12 = 7.84 MW. In Quebec, 7.84 MW \(\times\) 720 h/month \(\times\) 20 g/kWh = 112.9 t CO\(_2\) per month.
Result: The same run in Poland emits 4,628.7 t, a 41× difference.
Systems insight: Grid carbon intensity can dominate the emissions difference for the same hardware, model, and training duration. This proxy excludes host, memory, network, and storage power; total IT power must include those loads before applying PUE for a complete facility estimate.

Cross-region communication introduces latency floors set by the speed of light in optical fiber. For a 5,000 km link (roughly New York to London), the minimum one-way latency is 5,000 km/200,000 km/s = 25 ms, orders of magnitude higher than intra-data-center latency. This physical constraint is why geo-distributed training uses asynchronous methods or careful placement of pipeline stages, and why federated learning (Edge Intelligence) tolerates stale gradients.
Network specifications define how fast data moves, but they say nothing about how often the machines sending that data fail. The next section quantifies the reliability of individual components, the building blocks from which cluster-level failure rates are derived.




At fleet scale, component failures are not exceptional events but statistical certainties. Reliability Assumptions here fix MTTF for each major component class in a data-center GPU node and the time to detect and recover from failures. These values drive analysis in Fault Tolerance and scheduling in Fleet Orchestration; deeper failure modeling appears in Reliability Foundations.

Communication models quantify the overhead of coordination. The sustainability cost of that coordination (the power drawn, the water consumed, the carbon emitted) requires separate assumptions for the physical infrastructure surrounding the compute.

Economic constants set the price per unit of resource. Capacity planning instead asks what fraction of each resource unit does useful work. Capacity planning constants quantify the gap between peak capability and achievable throughput.



Capacity-Planning Assumptions quantify two related phenomena: (1) the fraction of peak hardware performance that real workloads achieve (model FLOPs utilization), and (2) how efficiently that performance scales as more machines are added (scaling efficiency). Together they determine the effective compute available for a given cluster size and budget, which is the number that matters for project planning.
The planning equation is multiplicative: \[ \EffectiveFleetThroughput = \DeviceCount\PeakRate \times \ModelFlopsUtilization \times \ScalingEfficiency \times (1 - \OperationalOverheadFraction) \]
Here \(\EffectiveFleetThroughput\) is effective fleet throughput, \(\DeviceCount\PeakRate\) is nominal cluster peak throughput, MFU is the single-device baseline measured over productive steps, \(\ScalingEfficiency\) captures the additional in-step losses from distribution, including communication and pipeline bubbles, and \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\) removes only out-of-step checkpoint, recovery, and maintenance time. These windows must be disjoint: measured fleet-step MFU already includes scaling losses, so it must not be multiplied by scaling efficiency again. The three subsections that follow fix those factors in order.


MFU measures useful model FLOP/s divided by hardware peak FLOP/s over a stated measurement window. Synchronization and idle time within that window lower MFU even though they contribute no model FLOPs. An MFU of 0.50 means the workload achieves half the peak FLOP/s. This appendix is the book’s shared fleet-scale assumption sheet. Every napkin-math estimate in the chapters should trace to a row in the tables above, and table 19 records whether that row comes from a datasheet, a fleet study, an MLSysIM model, an illustrative rate, or a book convention. Reliability rows set the failure clock, with failure a steady-state condition at 10,000 or more GPUs (Reliability Foundations models it in depth). Communication rows decide whether synchronous training is viable, and the 33× startup-latency gap between InfiniBand NDR and TCP explains why training clusters favor RDMA fabrics. Sustainability rows expose location as a lever, since grid carbon intensity differs by 82× between Norway and Poland. Capacity rows bridge peak hardware to useful throughput. At 8,192 GPUs, about 56 percent of ideal scaling is realized for the reference job at a fixed batch, and the listed overheads consume about 23 percent of wall time. When a deployment differs in fabric, region, MFU, or cluster size, substitute its values and re-evaluate the corresponding formulas.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Use this appendix to verify a fleet-scale estimate, swap in an alternative assumption (for example, NDR vs. HDR fabric, Quebec vs. Poland carbon intensity, or a different model FLOPs utilization (MFU)), or identify which numerical constants a chapter calculation depends on. Locate the relevant section, read the Value and Unit columns, and substitute those values into target arithmetic.
A short napkin-math callout at the start shows how several assumptions combine (failure rate, AllReduce time, carbon footprint). Hardware and link bandwidths are ceilings unless a chapter states an effective-bandwidth discount. Treat the tables as this edition’s shared assumption sheet, not immutable physical laws.

Napkin Math 1.1: Quick calculations with these assumptionsThese tables support quick distributed-systems napkin math. Three examples show how several assumptions combine.
Problem: Estimate how many GPU failures a cluster should expect per day.
Variables: Use a cluster of 8,192 GPUs and an individual GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours.
Math: The GPU failure rate is 8,192 GPUs/50,000 hours \(\approx\) 0.16 failures/hour, or roughly 3.9 failures/day.
Result: This estimate excludes network interface card (NIC), PSU, and cable failures. At 100,000 GPUs, the GPU-only rate is approximately 48 failures/day; adding NIC, PSU, and cable failures can roughly double the operational incident stream.
Systems insight: At fleet scale, failure becomes a continuous background process rather than an exceptional event.
Problem: Estimate how long an AllReduce takes for a 70B model.
Variables: Use BF16 parameters and InfiniBand NDR with a nominal byte rate of 50 GB/s per port.
Math: The gradient payload is 70 \(\times 10^9 \times\) 2 bytes = 140 GB. The ring AllReduce napkin estimate is 2 \(\times\) 140 GB/50 GB/s \(\approx\) 5.6 s.
Result: The collective can consume a significant fraction of a training step.
Systems insight: Pipeline and tensor parallelism exist partly to shrink the gradient volume each rank must communicate.
Problem: Estimate the carbon footprint of a 10,000-GPU training run.
Variables: Each H100 draws 700 W at thermal design power (TDP). Use power usage effectiveness (PUE) 1.12, Quebec grid intensity 20 g/kWh, and Poland grid intensity 820 g/kWh.
Math: A GPU-only facility-power proxy is 10,000 GPUs \(\times\) 700 W \(\times\) 1.12 = 7.84 MW. In Quebec, 7.84 MW \(\times\) 720 h/month \(\times\) 20 g/kWh = 112.9 t CO\(_2\) per month.
Result: The same run in Poland emits 4,628.7 t, a 41× difference.
Systems insight: Grid carbon intensity can dominate the emissions difference for the same hardware, model, and training duration. This proxy excludes host, memory, network, and storage power; total IT power must include those loads before applying PUE for a complete facility estimate.

The relationship between cluster size and system behavior is not linear. A 256-GPU cluster might go days between failures; a 100,000-GPU cluster experiences multiple failures per hour. This nonlinearity is why the chapters on fault tolerance (Fault Tolerance) and fleet orchestration (Fleet Orchestration) treat failure as a continuous background process rather than an exceptional event.
The network fabric determines whether gradient synchronization takes milliseconds or seconds, and whether pipeline parallelism is viable across node boundaries.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Distributed training and inference are bottlenecked by data movement between machines as often as by computation within them. Network Assumptions fix bandwidth and latency for every interconnect tier, from NVLink/PCIe within a node (NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2020; Choquette 2023), through InfiniBand, remote direct memory access (RDMA), and Ethernet fabrics (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000; Gangidi et al. 2024; NVIDIA 2026; Ethernet Alliance 2025), to the speed-of-light WAN floor (physics identity).


Within a single node, GPUs communicate over NVLink or PCIe. These bandwidths (table 4) determine whether tensor parallelism (which requires high-bandwidth, low-latency communication) is viable within the node boundary. These values are collected here for convenience and reused throughout the fleet-scale chapters.

Cross-region communication introduces latency floors set by the speed of light in optical fiber. For a 5,000 km link (roughly New York to London), the minimum one-way latency is 5,000 km/200,000 km/s = 25 ms, orders of magnitude higher than intra-data-center latency. This physical constraint is why geo-distributed training uses asynchronous methods or careful placement of pipeline stages, and why federated learning (Edge Intelligence) tolerates stale gradients.
Network specifications define how fast data moves, but they say nothing about how often the machines sending that data fail. The next section quantifies the reliability of individual components, the building blocks from which cluster-level failure rates are derived.

title: System Assumptions
text:
At fleet scale, component failures are not exceptional events but statistical certainties. Reliability Assumptions here fix MTTF for each major component class in a data-center GPU node and the time to detect and recover from failures. These values drive analysis in Fault Tolerance and scheduling in Fleet Orchestration; deeper failure modeling appears in Reliability Foundations.


Table 6 lists the MTTF for each component class. These are steady-state values that exclude the “infant mortality” period (first 30–90 days) and the “wear-out” period (beyond rated lifetime). Sources include large-GPU research-cluster analysis Kokolis et al. (2025), TPUv4 supercomputer resiliency and operations Zu et al. (2024), and warehouse-scale machine design Barroso et al. (2019).



Table 6: Component Mean Time To Failure: Steady-state MTTF anchors from (Kokolis et al. 2025; Zu et al. 2024; Barroso et al. 2019). Combined DGX H100 node MTBF \(\approx\) 4,687.5 h (195.3 d) for 8 GPUs and 8 NICs in series, the same node composition as the MTBF cascade in The MTBF cascade. The node’s 6 PSUs run 4+2 redundant, so no single PSU failure stops it and they add no term. The PCIe switch and HBM rows are node components that series model leaves out, and the top-of-rack switch and cable rows are network failures outside the node. Economic constants set the price per unit of resource. Capacity planning instead asks what fraction of each resource unit does useful work. Capacity planning constants quantify the gap between peak capability and achievable throughput.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Capacity-Planning Assumptions quantify two related phenomena: (1) the fraction of peak hardware performance that real workloads achieve (model FLOPs utilization), and (2) how efficiently that performance scales as more machines are added (scaling efficiency). Together they determine the effective compute available for a given cluster size and budget, which is the number that matters for project planning.
The planning equation is multiplicative: \[ \EffectiveFleetThroughput = \DeviceCount\PeakRate \times \ModelFlopsUtilization \times \ScalingEfficiency \times (1 - \OperationalOverheadFraction) \]
Here \(\EffectiveFleetThroughput\) is effective fleet throughput, \(\DeviceCount\PeakRate\) is nominal cluster peak throughput, MFU is the single-device baseline measured over productive steps, \(\ScalingEfficiency\) captures the additional in-step losses from distribution, including communication and pipeline bubbles, and \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\) removes only out-of-step checkpoint, recovery, and maintenance time. These windows must be disjoint: measured fleet-step MFU already includes scaling losses, so it must not be multiplied by scaling efficiency again. The three subsections that follow fix those factors in order.


MFU measures useful model FLOP/s divided by hardware peak FLOP/s over a stated measurement window. Synchronization and idle time within that window lower MFU even though they contribute no model FLOPs. An MFU of 0.50 means the workload achieves half the peak FLOP/s. Table 15 lists the reference MFU ranges used in training time and cost estimates throughout this book.

Scaling efficiency \(\ScalingEfficiency = \SingleDeviceRunTime/(\DeviceCount\times \MultiDeviceRunTime)\) measures how much of the added compute actually reduces training time. Production systems retain more at scale by training with a larger global batch and, where they pipeline, by interleaving stages. title: System Assumptions
text:
Table 18 fixes the unit conventions used in every quantitative example in this book. Each row gives the multiplier \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) in 1 alias \(=\) \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) base. Data prefixes use decimal SI (\(\text{KB} = 10^3\) bytes, not 1024). Throughput quantities (FLOP/s, GB/s) combine these aliases with time; adding incompatible dimensions (bytes to FLOP/s) is a category error in napkin math, not a unit conversion.
Hardware capacity labels are the one deliberate exception. Reference tables may retain vendor nameplate numbers and labels; the byte budgets used in calculations follow the device assumptions stored in the book’s hardware registry. For example, the book models an 80 GB accelerator with \(80 \times 2^{30}\) bytes, so a node of eight such devices holds \(640 \times 2^{30}\) bytes rather than \(640 \times 10^9\). These are modeled capacity assumptions, not universal guarantees inferred from the labels. Every other data quantity, including model footprints, KV-cache sizes, checkpoint volumes, and collective payloads, uses the decimal prefixes above. Where a worked example subtracts a computed footprint from a device capacity, the stored capacity byte budget is converted to decimal units alongside the footprint so that the arithmetic printed on the page is the arithmetic a reader can reproduce.

title: System Assumptions
text: This appendix is the book’s shared fleet-scale assumption sheet. Every napkin-math estimate in the chapters should trace to a row in the tables above, and table 19 records whether that row comes from a datasheet, a fleet study, an MLSysIM model, an illustrative rate, or a book convention. Reliability rows set the failure clock, with failure a steady-state condition at 10,000 or more GPUs (Reliability Foundations models it in depth). Communication rows decide whether synchronous training is viable, and the 33× startup-latency gap between InfiniBand NDR and TCP explains why training clusters favor RDMA fabrics. Sustainability rows expose location as a lever, since grid carbon intensity differs by 82× between Norway and Poland. Capacity rows bridge peak hardware to useful throughput. At 8,192 GPUs, about 56 percent of ideal scaling is realized for the reference job at a fixed batch, and the listed overheads consume about 23 percent of wall time. When a deployment differs in fabric, region, MFU, or cluster size, substitute its values and re-evaluate the corresponding formulas.
